items.title: From Linda Alvord
items.text:
Meeting Ken Iverson could cause mental transformations. Your mental shards of ideas might experience changes much as your laundry does in a washing machine. First all your notions about a topic slosh around in your head, back and forth in a washing cycle that confronts inconsistencies and redundancies. Then at some moment, a spin cycle rearranges everything. Conflicting concepts and incongruities confront each other in an endless swirl. A moment of absolute silence changes everything. Excess ideas are gone. And a rinse cycle reveals unifying concepts and unseen connections with amazing clarity. And thus, your ‘Tools of Thought’ are clean, refreshed, and ready for use.

Thankfully I had the opportunity to spend time with Ken and experience these kinds of changes. I also have his legacy of APL and J and a vast array of books, articles and labs to lead my thinking in new directions. Mostly, I treasure the memories of his presence.

items.title: Beaton’s Recipe for Least Squares
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 36

by J.I. Ansell and A.M. Sykes

items.title: Introduction
items.text: An exhaustive search through academic papers on the subject of least-squares algorithms would no doubt reveal enough titles to fill the space allotted for this article! So why another one? The aim here is to look at the least-squares algorithm that replaces ‘domino’ in the generalized linear regression models volume (called ASLGREG) in ASL. As such, it updates the article by Sykes and Ansell (published in Vector Volume 1 Number 4, - see [3]) entitled ‘When domino is not sufficient’. As this title suggests, it looks at a particular implementation of Beaton’s least-squares operator, which in turn involves the notion of sweeping on successive predictor variables. For the sake of completeness, some aspects covered in that paper are also mentioned here.

items.title: Beaton’s Method
items.text:
Householder’s least-squares operator (alias ‘domino’ to APLers) operates on the design matrix of a linear statistical model in which each column consists of the values of one predictor variable. In contrast, Beaton’s method manipulates a symmetric matrix of sums of squares and products formed from the predictor variables followed by the y variable, by performing successive sweeps (see [1]). The sweep on the ‘k’th variable is given by:

    ∇ S←K SWEEP S;T;TV
[1]   S←S-(TV∘.×TV←S[K;])÷T←S[K;K]
[2]   S[;K]←S[K;]←TV÷|T
[3]   S[K;K]←-÷T
    ∇

Where S denotes the sum of squares and products matrix. The values of S after the sweep on the kth variable all have appropriate statistical interpretations. In particular, having ‘swept’ variables 1,2,…k, the top-left k by k matrix is minus the covariance matrix of the regression coefficients; the first k elements in the last column (corresponding to the y variable) are the regression coefficients, and the bottom right-hand corner element is the residual sum of squares of the y variable after regression on variables 1 to k. Also note that repeating the same sweep twice is equivalent to not having swept on that variable at all, a feature useful for stepwise procedures.

As an example, consider the regression data used in our previous paper.

      ⎕←D←1,X1,X2,X3,[1.5]Y
1     2.5     1.05    0.625    2.6
1     2.375   1.96    3        1.3
1     3.125   1.7     1.75     2.5
1     1       0.87    1.375    1.5
1     1.875   1.3     1.75     3
1     1.5     1.73    3.125    2.2
1     0.875   1.68    3.5      2.2
1     0.125   1.04    2.5      2.4
1     3.5     1.47    0.875    1.7
1     1.625   1.57    2.625    2.2

Now form the sums of squares and products matrix:

      ⎕←S←(⍉D)+.×D
10      18.5    14.37  21.125 21.6
18.5    44.094  27.791 34.203 39.575
14.37   27.791  21.804 32.276 30.684
21.125  34.203  32.276 53.328 45.05
21.6    39.575  30.684 45.05  49.12

Now sweep on the first three columns, i.e. regress y on the constant vector, x1 and x2

      3 SWEEP 2 SWEEP 1 SWEEP S
¯1.9034     0.040355   1.203    ¯4.885E¯15  2.6029
 0.040355  ¯0.11619    0.1215   ¯0.8       ¯1.5763E¯3
 1.203      0.1215    ¯0.99359   2.5       ¯0.30615
¯4.885E¯15 ¯0.8        2.5       1.5099E¯14 5.9952E¯15
 2.6029    ¯1.5763E¯3 ¯0.30615   5.9952E¯15 2.3546

Hence the regression coefficients are given by 2.6029, ¯1.5763E¯3 and ¯0.30615, as verified by using ‘domino’:

      Y⌹D[;1 2 3]
2.6029 ¯1.5763E¯3 ¯0.30615

Also, the residual sum of squares of the y data after regression is 2.3546, which may also be verified by the raw APL code:

      +/T×T←Y-D[;1 2 3]+.×B←Y⌹D[;1 2 3]
2.3546

the kth diagonal element (the pivot) plays a crucial role in the sweep operation since it is used to divide other quantities. A pivot close to zero may lead to considerable numerical inaccuracies. however, the sweep makes no distinction between the y+variable and other variables not so far swept on. Hence the pivot represents the residual sum of squares for that variable when regressed on the variables swept so far. For example, the 4 4 element of the result of the sweeps above, equal to 1.5099E¯14 shows that the variable x3 can be represented as a linear combination of the previous variables: in fact the figures in column 4 show that X3=(¯.8×X1)+2.5×X2.

items.title: Collinearity
items.text:
When predictor variables are (near-) linearly dependent, as in the example above (a situation labelled collinearity), the use of domino either produces a DOMAIN ERROR or large regression coefficients which have huge variances and which are highly correlated. In simple terms, duplication of information confuses the algorithm, and results can sometimes owe more to the small details of the algorithm than the original problem.

A simple way out of this dilemma is to miss out the variable(s) which duplicate(s) information. This is where the pivot plays its role. Before pivoting on the kth variable, s[k;k] can be related to the correlation coefficient of the kth variable on those that have been pivoted. Hence it is possible to decide to not include the kth variable if 1 minus its r-squared value is, say, less than .001 - the criticality parameter.

Frane in his paper on checking the tolerance in regression calculations (see [2]) showed that prior to using the kth pivot, it is also easy to see whether, if the kth variable had been included previously, variables currently included would have failed the inclusion test. In either case, the kth variable is omitted.

Frane’s illustrative example uses the correlation matrix C of three predictor variables given below.

      C
1                  0.99498743710662   0.099498743710662
0.99498743710662   1                  0
0.099498743710662  0                  1

If the sweep operator is applied to variables 1 and 2, then the pivot for the third sweep is .01, which is above the criticality parameter .001.

      2 SWEEP 1 SWEEP C
¯100      99.499  9.9499
 99.499 ¯100     ¯9.9
  9.9499  ¯9.9    0.01

However, if variables 2 and 3 were swept first, then the pivot for sweeping on the variable 1 is then less than .001.

      3 SWEEP 2 SWEEP C
1E¯4      0.99499 0.099499
0.99499  ¯1       0
0.099499  0      ¯1

items.title: The Basic Design
items.text:
It is clear from the above discussion, that Beaton’s method can thus be applied to produce the covariance matrix of the estimates, the estimates, the residual sum of squares, and information on what variables are nearly linearly dependent on previously included variables. In addition, as the consecutive sweeps are performed, the residual sum of squares of the intermediate models can be ‘taken down and used in evidence’.

Hence the result of the weighted least squares routine ∆WLS takes the form of an n by [n+3] matrix m such that:

(a) M[⍳N;⍳N] is the covariance matrix of the estimates (b) M[;N+1] is a column of the regression coefficients (c) M[;N+2] is a column of the consecutive residual sum of squares (d) M[;N+3] is a boolean vector with a zero value indicating that the corresponding variable has been omitted, for one of two possible reasons.

The function BEATON (also supplied in ASLGREG) illustrates this form of output. It operates, using a right argument equal to the sum of squares and products matrix, and a two-element vector left argument specifying the criticality parameter and the number of variables to be swept.

      .001 3 BEATON S
¯1.9034     0.040355  1.203    ¯4.885E¯15  2.6029     1 2.464
 0.040355  ¯0.11619   0.1215   ¯0.8       ¯1.5763E¯3  1 2.449
 1.203      0.1215   ¯0.99359   2.5       ¯0.30615    1 2.3546
¯4.885E¯15 ¯0.8       2.5       1.5099E¯14 5.9952E¯15 0 0

      .001 4 BEATON S
¯1.9034     0.040355 1.203    ¯4.885E¯15  2.6029      1 2.464
 0.040355  ¯0.11619  0.1215   ¯0.8       ¯1.5763E¯3   1 2.449
 1.203      0.1215  ¯0.99359   2.5       ¯0.30615     1 2.3546
¯4.885E¯15 ¯0.8      2.5       1.5099E¯14  5.9952E¯15 0 2.3546

Because of the collinearity already noted, these two statements provide nearly identical results. Note the succession of residual sum of squares, namely 2.464 (after fitting the constant term) 2.449 after additionally fitting x1, and so on. Applying BEATON to Frane’s correlation matrix of predictor variables gives the following result.

      .001 3 BEATON C
¯100      99.499  9.9499 1 0.9901
 99.499 ¯100     ¯9.9    1 0.01
  9.9499  ¯9.9    0.01   0 0.01

Thus the function BEATON incorporates a check for both possible occurrences of collinearity. As such it follows the methodology suggested by Frane, and also, according to the paper by Clarke (see [1]), that employed in the Royal Statistical Society’s generalized linear modelling package GLIM.

items.title: The Constant Vector
items.text: Most (but not necessarily all) regression models include an intercept term (the constant vector). Sweeping on it essentially converts the sums of squares and products matrix S to the equivalent one where each variable is replaced by the same variable centred about its mean. However, this conversion is subject to potentially large rounding errors, and should be avoided. (This is the essential reason why, in our previous paper, Beaton’s method was out-performed by, for example Bjorck’s method.) Hence to apply Beaton’s method successfully this factor must be taken into account.

items.title: The Final Recipe - ∆WLS
items.text:
The result of applying ∆WLS has already been described above. But what are its parameters? First the left argument is a two-element numeric vector consisting of the criticality parameter and a boolean value, with 1 indicating that the constant vector is included, 0 that it is excluded. The effect of this flag, if set, is that the sums of squares and products matrix calculated is that centred around the mean. All regression results are then transformed back to standard form before delivery.

Secondly, the right argument is a segmented string indicating in order the names of the design matrix, the y-variable, (optionally) a prior-weight vector, and (optionally) a boolean vector indicating predictor variables not to be included. As an example illustrating its use consider the following quadratic regression problem.

      DES←(⍳10)∘.*0 1 2
      YV←(DES+.×1 ¯1 2)+¯50+?10⍴100
      YV
 21 16 60 64 49 27 108 113 175 233
      YV⌹DES
49.483 ¯17.46 3.4583

      .001 1 ∆WLS 'DES/YV/'
 1.3833    ¯0.525      0.041667   49.483   1   45874
¯0.525      0.24129   ¯0.020833  ¯17.46    1   10926
 0.041667  ¯0.020833   1.8939E¯3   3.4583  1    4611.6

Notice how the last column gives sufficient information to test that the quadratic term is necessary - this is exploited in ASLGREG by the provision of a TESTHYPOTHESIS function.

Now repeat the fit missing the last point out.

      PW←(⍳10)<10
      .001 1 ∆WLS 'DES/YV/PW/'
 1.619     ¯0.67857    0.059524   39.833   1 22060
¯0.67857    0.34134   ¯0.032468  ¯11.173   1  6507.4
 0.059524  ¯0.032468   3.2468E¯3   2.7273  1  4216.5

As a final example, consider the data used already, contained in the matrix D (with the y-variable in the last column).

      .001 1 ∆WLS 'D[;1 2 3 4]/D[;5]/'
 1.9034    ¯0.040355  ¯1.203    0  2.6029     1 2.464
¯0.040355   0.11619   ¯0.1215   0 ¯1.5763E¯3  1 2.449
¯1.203     ¯0.1215     0.99359  0 ¯0.30615    1 2.3546
 0          0          0        0  0          0 2.3546

The penultimate column shows that variable x3 has not been included, because it is linearly dependent on x1 and x2.

items.title: Accuracy Considerations
items.text:
How well does the proposed algorithm ∆WLS perform according to the benchmark introduced in our previous paper? The answer is: very well indeed. In that paper ([3]), Greenfield’s data (depending on two parameters n, and m) was analysed by different methods and the number of significant figures correct quoted. For n equal to 0 and m bigger than 4, domino gave domain error, and other methods gave varying numbers of significant figures.

The function GREENFIELD constructs x,y data, applies ∆WLS, and compares the answer with the true answer, outputting a 2 by 3 matrix such that each row consists of the estimate, true estimate and percentage relative error.

    ∇ R←GREENFIELD N_M
[1]   ⍝ Creates Greenfield's data given N_M as two non -ve intgrs
[2]   ⍝ Compares least-squares output from ∆WLS with true values
[3]   ⍝ Outputs both and the relative % error to the nearest intgr
[4]   ⍝ See Sykes and Ansell Vector Vol.1 No.4
[5]    Y←7+ 1 2 3 4 5 ×10*-N_M[1]
[6]    X←1,[1.5]8+ 1 3 2 4 5 ×10*-N_M[2]
[7]    R← 1E¯3 1 ∆WLS 'X/Y/'
[8]    R←R[;3],(7+(0.3×10*-N_M[1])-7.2×10*--/N_M),0.9×10*--/N_M
[9]    R←⍉ 3 2 ⍴R,100×|(R[1 2]-R[3 4])÷R[1 2]
    ∇

      GREENFIELD 0 5
¯719992.699978941  ¯719992.7       2.92493227896128E¯9
  89999.9999973676   90000          2.92490262339789E¯9

      GREENFIELD 0 13
¯72148849499738.5  ¯71999999999992.7  0.206308902744647
  9018606187468.23   9000000000000    0.206308902744626

As m increases, the size of error increases. By m equal to 13, the previous methods used gave no correct significant figures. As examples such as the ones above show, ∆WLS has a relative error of at most .2% for the range of m values from 0 to 13.

items.title: Speed
items.text:
How quick is ∆WLS, compared with domino? To make such a comparison is slightly unfair on ∆WLS as the latter gives so much more information than domino. It is annoying that Householder’s method has the potential to give all the information that ∆WLS does. It was such a consideration that prompted one of us to write a statistician’s form of domino - see [4]; nevertheless it is the obvious comparison to take.

The following table gives timings of domino and ∆WLS in milliseconds for a variety of design matrix sizes: the timings were made using Dyalog APL on an IBM Model 70.

+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                |               Number of Columns                 |
|                |       5               10               20       |
|----------------|-------------------------------------------------|
|                |    ⌹/∆WLS          ⌹/∆WLS           ⌹/∆WLS      |
|                |    ------          ------           ------      |
|            50  |    60/270          160/660          550/1760    |
| Number of 100  |   110/440          330/880         1150/2470    |
| Rows     1000  |  1210/2750        3410/6480       11200/17800   |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

As expected, the larger the problem, the more ∆WLS gains on domino, as the former only operates on columns to produce the sum of squares and products matrix; thereafter, the sweep operator is much faster than the equivalent Householder operation on a column. For small problems the ratio seems to be about 4:1, but for only medium sized problems (e.g. 100 by 20) this has dropped almost to 2:1.

items.title: Conclusion
items.text: Beaton’s recipe can be programmed efficiently in APL to provide a reliable, accurate, and flexible algorithm that is reasonably fast. It is superior to domino in coping with problems of collinearity. It is particularly gratifying to be able to analyse a particular model and to be able to extract residual sums of squares of intermediate models without further calculation.

items.title: References
items.text:
[1] Clarke M.R.B. The Gauss-Jordan Sweep Operator with Detection of Collinearity. AS178, Applied Statistics Volume 31 No. 2, 1982, pp166-168.

[2] Frane J.W. A Note on Checking Tolerance in Matrix Inversion and Regression. Technometrics Volume 19, No. 4, November 1977, pp 513-514.

[3] Sykes A.M. and Ansell J.I. When Domino Is Not Sufficient. Vector Volume 1, no. 4, pp 155-160.

[4] Sykes A.M. A Second Generation Domino for Statisticians. Proceedings of APL87, Dallas, pp 369-380.

items.title: ASL: The Basic Statistics Volume
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 45

by Jake Ansell (University of Edinburgh)

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
To give structure to the ASL library it is divided into shelves. Whilst most shelves have specific application the Bottom Shelf is a general shelf which will contain functions to be used throughout the library. Each shelf may be divided into a series of volumes.

The Bottom Shelf will eventually consist of the four volumes: basic statistics, numerical analysis, data management and utilities. ASL volumes are not packages but a set of well tested and established APL routines. Packages may, of course, be constructed from the routines. Those wishing to provide commercial packages based on ASL will be allowed to do so through a licensing agreement with the British APL Association.

In this article we will review the Basic Statistics volume including a brief outline of the material contained within the shelf. Since the design process for this volume differs from those previously described (the Graphics and Regression Shelves) I have added some comments on design and standards. (The Basic Statistics volume may possibly form the blueprint for the development of subsequent shelves.)

A list of the functions in the Basic Statistics volume was given in the first edition of Random Vector. For those who desire a more formal account Norman Thomson has produced a Basic Statistics specification document based on APL2 which discusses in more detail aspects of the volume.

items.title: Contents of the Volume
items.text:
At the first ASL Workshop, held at Gregynog, Wales, it was decided that the Basic Statistics should cover the material required to teach first year undergraduate or A Level students Statistics. This would then be enhanced as the library grew with the inclusion of functions common to more than one shelf.

The statistics currently within the volume can be divided into the following areas:

  • Descriptive and Summary Statistics
  • Distribution functions
  • Significance tests
  • ANOVA
  • Time Series
  • Regression and Random Number Generators

It was realised though there would be need for some mathematical and utility functions. The current version consists of about 120 functions, though some are variants with particular attributes.

The majority of functions unsurprisingly belong to the first set, Descriptive and Summary Statistics. This includes functions to calculate means, variances, standard deviations and similar quantities as well as simple line printer barcharts. Not included are functions which need better graphic output than simple line graphics such as box-whisker, pie charts etc. These are contained within the Graphics Shelf.

As far as distributions are concerned we have been conservative providing only functions relating to Binomial, Poisson, Hypergeometric, Chi Squared, Normal, F and t. Where appropriate the functions provided yield the density, quantile and tail probability value. More specialised functions will appear either in subsequent basic statistics volumes or in a separate Distribution shelf.

To be controversial we have included a number of test statistics based on traditional or frequentist approach to Statistics. Again it is hoped eventually to provide appropriate Bayesian approaches to inferential problems. The tests provided are both parametric and non-parametric, for example TSTAT yields the value of t-test statistic and MANNWHIT provides a Mann-Whitney test statistic value.

In more specialised areas we have restricted ourselves to very basic functions, for example the bivariate measures are limited to correlation. In Time Series, functions such as moving averages, seasonal adjustment and exponential weighted moving averages are given. Similarly restrictions are imposed on ANOVA with one-way and two-way functions provided. Again it is expected that other shelves will provide more adequate cover of these areas.

Whilst the Regression shelf provides a powerful suite of programs for regression, it was still felt appropriate to have basic regression functions in the Bottom Shelf. Hence the Bottom Shelf provides functions to obtain parameter estimates, predictions, residuals and ANOVA tables for linear (multiple), simple linear and polynomial regression.

Again random number generators have been provided for a basic set of distributions and should cover those generally used. It is expected that a wider range of alternative routines will be provided in a Random Number shelf.

items.title: Development Process
items.text:
Early in the evolution of ASL it was felt that the best way to proceed would be to establish working parties which would review material which had been produced or collated by a single author. When the working party was satisfied the material would be released to a larger group for testing and comment.

In the context of Bottom Shelf this approach has worked relatively well. Obviously there is a need to ensure that the working party does not continually till the same ground and that it attempts to maintain consistency over its decisions. A feature of software developed by voluntary labour is that timescales tend to be rather elastic. However even within the Basic Statistics volume the implementation time has not been unduly long and where delays have occurred it has been to ensure better software has been produced.

The ASL programmer, Tuks Gillespie, acted as collator and designer for the material in the Basic Statistics volume. The original source material on which she based her work was Norman Thomson’s Bottom Shelf: Basic Statistics [1] and University College of Swansea’s first year statistics course material based on APL. The working party which reviewed the software was Alan Hawkes, Norman Thomson, Alan Sykes, Alan Meyer, Mike Day, and Jake Ansell. The group meet regularly over about eighteen months. The group which tested the software is too large to name fully, however Maurice Jordan and Tony O’Hagan deserve special mention given the considerable effort they put in to testing and commenting on the material. Maurice Jordan adapted his APL testbed functions for basic statistics and subjected the volume to rigorous inspection.

items.title: Standards
items.text:
Within such a major undertaking it is clear that there is a need for standards. Considerable attention has been paid to developing standards which will last throughout the likely extended lifetime of the project. There have been two major inputs: comments taken from APL programmers (particularly Adrian Smith), and those standards which have emerged through development of the software.

A more detailed article might eventually be written about the standards ASL has evolved. At the present time I will concentrate on those that directly affect presentation of the function. A major step in writing an APL function is naming it. Two aspects initially have to be taken into account. Firstly the name must identify as clearly as possible the function’s use and secondly it must not clash with other names.

Even in the Basic Statistics volume the working party has devoted time ensuring appropriate names are used. Names will usually conform to the following pattern <root><inflection><serial no.>, where the root is the type of function, and the inflection modifies the root to identify a function performing a specific task. Where alternative algorithms are available to implement this task, the serial number identifies the particular algorithm used. (Users would select the algorithm they preferred.) CHIQUANT1 is an example of this convention.

To avoid the problem of name clashes a Names Guardian has been established which will record name usage and decide on the new name(s) if there are any clashes.

Within a function (where plausible) variable names are used which imply type or structure of variable. For example for binomial functions N_P is the variable name used for the parameters.

Every ASL function will be fully commented and where appropriate will be annotated. The comments statements start with a two letter code and a list of those used are given below:

FN Purpose/objective RE Result SS Shelf Source RA Right Argument LA Left argument AL Algorithm detail

This, of course, allows for automatic documentation, particularly helpful in ensuring consistency of production.

items.title: Reference
items.text: [1] Norman Thomson, [1990], ‘Bottom Shelf: Basic Statistics’.

items.title: Significance Tests
items.text:
Given the stock market collapse, we might be interested to know whether 1988’s figures are the same as 1986’s. If they are, has the market recovered?

If we are willing to assume that the data is normal and independent then we can use a parametric test. We first test the data to see if the variances are the same with a variance test. This is based on the ratio of the two variances:

    M[⍳12] VARRATIO M[23+⍳12]
0.5579

The value has to be compared to the F Distribution to see if it is significant. Given the value is less than one, we can take the reciprocal test is against F on 11,11 degrees of freedom.

    11 11 FTAIL1 ÷M[⍳12] VARRATIO M[23+⍳12]
0.1737

The probability is fortunately in the central region of the distribution and hence we can assume the data have similar variances. We can now carry out the two sample t test.

    M[⍳12] TWOSAMT M[23+⍳12]
¯5.092

The value obtained should be compared to the t distribution on 22 degrees of freedom.

    22 TTAIL M[⍳12] TWOSAMT M[23+⍳12]
0.9999789111

The result indicates that the populations are different, since the probability is in the tail of the distribution. It may be that one is doubtful about the normal assumption? Therefore a non-parametric test might be more sensible. The Mann-Whitney test is an appropriate choice.

    M[⍳12] MANNWHIT M[23+⍳12]
26

This value could be compared to the appropriate table but if the analyst is willing to take the normalised value, he could compare with the t distribution as an approximation. The sample is relatively large.

    M[⍳12] MANNWHITTS M[23+⍳12]
¯2.655811238

This produces the normalised value of the test statistic. The probability value would be

    22 TTAIL M[⍳12] MANNWHITTS M[23+⍳12]
0.9927809917

Fortunately a similar result as before. We might consider comparing the three years assuming the values are random observations from the years, although this is a little doubtful. The one way ANOVA test can be used to test whether the three years differ.

    J←(12 12 12/1 2 3) ONEWAY M
    J

33     20873.27475      632.5234773      0
35     35524.6251         0               0

We have assigned the result to J so that we can test the variance ratio against the F distribution.

    J[1 2;1] FTAIL1 J[1;4]
1.547062728E¯4

A low probability, implying difference, as might be expected.

items.title: Linear Regression
items.text:
In this data we might be interested to see if there is a relationship between Turnover and Household and the number of employees. Obviously as prospective franchise buyers we wish to predict Turnover.

Can we predict Turnover from Households? The model would be a linear regression:

T = b0 + b1 H

The model is fitted using a set of routines REGLINEST and REGLINRESID etc., but we can use REGLINREP to get a brief report. We store the results again, to test against the F distribution.

items.title: Reliability Data Analysis
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 37

by Jake Ansell and Mulhim Al-Doori

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
It has always been assumed that software would be added to ASL through the efforts of individuals or groups. However it would not be wise if no opportunity were given for others beyond the authors to comment at an early stage on the material and the functions developed.

In this article a brief description of the functions which are contained within the Reliability Data Analysis volume is given. A beta-test version of the software is to be produced in the near future. Before this though it would be helpful to have the views of others on the functions included and those they feel should be added.

The software discussed is part of a larger project which is the development of an Expert System for Reliability Data Analysis. The Expert System is being developed in APL. A subsequent article may describe the details of the Expert System.

APL is a natural language for this volume since most of the algebra is linear in form, either based on raw data or on the ordered statistics. Hence for the most part the routines follow the mathematics without the need for great sophistication. There is though the need for iterative procedures, especially Newton-Raphson-based approaches for estimation.

The data analysis volume is assumed to be part of a larger shelf where there would be routines for Reliability Analysis and Modelling. Fault tree programmes might be written based on APL routines for logic manipulations for analysing systems. Also a Stochastic Model could be added following work done at Swansea under the supervision of Alan Hawkes.

In the future it may be that the Data Analysis volume might share code with related shelves, such as a Survival Analysis Shelf or a more general Medical Statistics Shelf. This emphasises that the software described is only a first attempt, and not the definitive model for the volume. Contributions are welcomed and as authors we would be delighted to see the shelf grow. The names used for functions might equally transform with suggestions from others.

At present we see the possibility of six sections to the volume. These are:

  • Elementary Analysis
  • Graphical Analysis
  • Distributions
  • Covariate Analysis
  • Growth Models
  • Dependency Analysis

items.title: Elementary Analysis
items.text:
As with the bottom shelf this is seen as a collection of routines which have been found to be useful in the analysis of reliability data, especially in the initial stages of such an analysis. It augments the Bottom Shelf. For example the coefficient of variation (COEFVAR) and the index of dispersion (INDIS) are added since they indicate whether the data is under- or over-dispersed compared to the Poisson Process. This aids in model selection. Also included is a function to calculate the cumulative mean time to failure, since again many practitioners find it a useful measure.

For chronological data Ascher has frequently suggested the need to test for trend. Hence the volume contains two of the standard trend test measures, the Laplace Trend (TRENDLP) and the MIL-HNBK-189 (TRENDMIL) test.

items.title: Graphical Analysis
items.text:
Graphical analyses are often used in Reliability. Engineers find them comprehensible and informative. They can give rise to parameter estimates, but more appropriately can indicate the validity of the model. It is assumed that the volume will provide just the values to be plotted and not the plotting routines, which should exist within ASLGRAPH. Hence the volume will produce X-Y coordinates for plotting.

The routines cover the standard plots to assess lifetime distributions such as Weibull (WEIBPLOT), Hazard (HAZPLOT) and TTT (TTTPLOT) plots. These plots often shed light on the appropriateness of a distribution but may also indicate possible problems with the data. A function also exists to produce a Duane Growth Plot (DUANEPLOT). This plot is often used to assess whether time between failures is increasing (good) or decreasing (bad).

Beyond these there will be functions to produce plots for more sophisticated analysis, such as residual plots for covariate analysis (see Covariate section) and for examining dependency such as Walls’ method (WALLSPLOT).

items.title: Lifetime Distributions
items.text:
Obviously looking into the future there should be a separate shelf for distributions, covering the common distributions. Already, though, certain aspects of some distributions have been covered by the Bottom Shelf. In the interim it seems sensible to include some routines associated with lifetime distributions in this volume. (A lifetime distribution is generally taken to be a distribution which takes only positive values.) Hence included in this volume are routines for parameter estimation for a number of lifetime distributions.

Given the reliability context these functions allow for the possibility of censoring, currently right-hand censoring. The distributions considered are the Exponential, both one- and two-parameter forms (EXPEST, EXP2EST), the Weibull, two- and three-parameter forms (WEIBEST, WEIB3EST), the Gamma (GAMMAEST) and Log Gamma (LGAMMAEST).

Since it is also possible to obtain empirical estimates for distributions we have included Kaplan-Meier for reliability function (KMEST) and Nelson-Altschuler for cumulative hazard function (NAEST).

items.title: Covariate Analysis
items.text:
Cox’s Regression Model, referred to as the Proportional Hazard Model (PHM), has led to a resurgence of interest in modelling lifetimes through the use of covariates. There is a wide range of possible models. The current volume contains functions for two models: PHM and Weibull Regression. These functions include estimation of parameters with approximate standard deviations, (PHMBETA, WEIBREGBETA), likelihood values, (PHMLIKE, WEIBREGLIKE), and residuals, (PHMRESID[I], WEIBREGRESID). (The [I] indicates more than one residual available.)

Specific formulations of other models are covered by ASLREG either directly or by transformation, for example Gamma, Log Gamma and Log Normal Regression. Hence it seems inappropriate to repeat them in this shelf.

items.title: Growth Models
items.text:
It had been assumed that as technology develops, systems and components will improve especially in the context of hardware. The more pragmatic will realize this is not the case. In Reliability, however, there are a number of models for describing growth which assume positive growth for hardware: the Duane Growth Model, ARINC and others. Most of these models should contain a governmental health warning. For some of the models there is more than one estimator for the parameters of the models. For the Duane Growth model it is possible to use either graphical methods or Crow’s estimate for Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process, (CROWEST).

Beyond hardware models there are a stream of software models such as Jellinski-Moranda (JMEST) and Littlewood-Verrall (LVEST). These models equally have drawbacks, but the Littlewood-Verrall model has the advantage that improvement is only expected at every failure, not required.

items.title: Dependency Analysis
items.text: There is a wide range of possible approaches, for example Engineering yields the beta-Factor model and its extensions, whilst Statistics provides a rich medium for analysis of dependency. Currently there is not a single approach regularly used and hence at this stage we have decided not to include any specific methods except the graphical approach to analysis suggested by Walls (WALLSPLOT).

items.title: Conclusions and Comments
items.text: This article has briefly covered what is contained within the volume. It is hoped to release the volume for beta-test later in the year; it will be supplied with limited documentation. If you have comments on the material so far included, or wish to suggest further functions which might be added, please write to me at the address given in the editorial on page 30.
