items.title: ASWI Programming Standards
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 111

by FHD v.Batenburg, TRC Bonnema, L v.Geldrop, H v.Loon, B Smoor

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
This paper describes a set of standards proposed by the committee of the "APL-Share-Ware-Initiative", ASWI for short. These standards are an integration of the various standards applied by BSO/Management Support (Utrecht, Netherlands), Philips/PASS-PC’S (Eindhoven, Netherlands), and the Institute for Theoretical Biology (Leiden, Netherlands).

The objective of this standard is two-fold. The first objective is to define a set of rules according to which APL programming should be carried out, in order to improve program maintainability. It is recognized that in a professional APL programming environment, where different people work for different clients, a need exists for a concise and standardized use of APL.

The second objective is to smooth the introduction to new programs for potential users. To fulfil this objective a set of standard names is proposed which should be available in every workspace and which act and inform according to preconceived, generally accepted notions. This ensures that a novice will always know how to move around in the on-line documentation of a foreign workspace.

We ask all programmers participating in ASWI to adhere to these standards for the following reasons. First of all, standards are a boon for not-too-experienced programmers because - hopefully - standards reflect the accumulated wisdom of experts. Secondly, standards are useful because the writers can fall back to automatisms and can focus their thinking on the real hard nuts in the program. And finally, readers can access the information faster when they don’t need to puzzle things out but can rely on standards instead. This holds for good standards, but it holds for mediocre standards too.

So, even non-superb standards are often better than very clever incidentally used constructions. For this reason, we urge programmers to deviate from this standard in exceptional cases only and then to document these deviations carefully in order to ensure program maintainability.

The remaining text will cover the following topics:

  • naming conventions
  • branching conventions
  • documentation conventions
  • comments
  • messages
  • miscellaneous

items.title: Naming Conventions
items.text:
This paragraph outlines the various standards for naming of systems, workspaces, functions, variables and labels.

Systems. An APL system is a collection of one (or more) APL workspaces and files which conceptually form a whole. Together they perform the functions described in the functional specification of the system. The system is identified by a 3 character identifier (no more, no less). Each of the characters should be alphabetic capitals. Valid identifiers are in the range of ‘AAA’ to ‘ZZZ’. We will refer to the system identifier as "SID" hereafter.

Examples:

DLG - Dialogue system PLT - Plotting system RNA - RNA analysis SCR - Screen utilities TED - Text editing system WHL - Whaling population growth simulation

Workspaces. The workspace is identified by a name of 3 or more characters of which the first three are the SID. All characters should be capitals and digits may be used (not in the SID). It is advisable not to use names with more than eight characters.

Preferably a system is contained in 1 workspace. If this is not feasible (for example for reasons of memory requirements) the system should be divided into functionally cohesive subsystems distributed over different workspaces. The names of those workspaces all start with the same SID.

Example:

WHLDATA - file which contains all data of whale simulation. WHLSIM - workspace which performs population simulation. WHLANAL - workspace which statistically analyses results.

Functions. We distinguish between user functions, sub-functions and imported functions.

  1. USER FUNCTIONS

    By user functions we mean: - driver or main functions (the ones that start up the system). - functions to be activated by the end-user directly.

    User functions can be recognized by: - an easy-to-remember name. - error-proof and with error messages in the language of the end-user. - sometimes no parameters. - sometimes no explicit result.

    A user function has a name of at least 5 characters of which the first three are the SID and the next two are alphabetic capitals. The remaining characters may be alphanumeric capitals.

    Examples:

    1. PLTHISTGRAM, PLTPIE & PLTGRAPH
    2. WHLSETPARMS, WHLSIMULATE, WHLGRAPH

  2. SUB-FUNCTIONS

    Sub-functions are functions that are not used by the end-user directly. In general this type of function is called from other APL functions. A sub-function has a name of at least 6 characters of which the first three are the SID, followed by "_". The rest of the characters may be alphanumeric capitals.

    Try to recognize functionally related sub-functions, and characterize them with common characters in position 5 and 6 of their names. (For systems with many functions, you can apply this principle recursively for remaining characters.)

    Example:

    SIM_… all simulation programs of system with SID=SIM. SIM_DS… all discrete sub-functions. SIM_CN… all continuous sub-functions. SIM_CNAS… all continuous sub-functions for "assignment". SIM_CNTR… all continuous sub-functions for "transfer". SIM_CNSP… all continuous sub-functions for "splitting".

  3. IMPORTED SUB-FUNCTIONS

    Sub-functions which are copied from other workspaces are "imported sub-functions". They retain their original name. Because their names don’t start with the proper SID, their foreign origin remains obvious.

    If you introduce any change in the code of that function, the name should be changed in accordance to the new workspace in which it resides. (If necessary, you can explain the origin in the comment.)

Standard Names. The following niladic functions should always be present in the workspace whenever applicable.

  1. SIDLX in ⎕LX←'SIDLX' Niladic program SIDLX will either start the main program SIDBEGIN or present the most general information which is provided by ∆SIDABSTRACT (see paragraph DOCUMENTATION). For example in workspace WHLSIM:

    ⎕LX←'WHLLX'
⎕FX 'Z←WHLLX' 'Z←∆WHLABSTRACT'

    and in workspace DLGUTILS:

    ⎕LX←'DLGLX'
⎕FX 'DLGLX' 'DLGBEGIN'

  2. SIDBEGIN If a workspace has one user function only, then this function is invoked by function SIDBEGIN. In workspaces with more than one user function or with sub-functions (utilities) only, function SIDBEGIN only presents those alternative functions. For example in workspace WHLSIM:

    ⎕FX 'WHLBEGIN' 'WHLSIMULATE'

  3. SIDRECOVER Any system which might be corrupted by unexpected errors or crashes should provide a function SIDRECOVER to repair the damage as well as possible. If automatic recovery is awkward or impossible, SIDRECOVER should direct the user to the proper information, or describe the best procedure to do so. For example in workspace WHLSIM:

    ⎕FX 'WHLRECOVER' '...' '...' '...'

Variables. This paragraph will outline the conventions for shared variables, global, sub-global and local variables.

Global Variables. A global variable is a variable which is not local to a function, or a variable which is stored in an APL file. So a global variable is always available for reference by every APL function in the workspace.

The name of a global variable is at least 5 characters long. The first three characters are the SID. The next characters are lowercase alphanumerics.

The use of global variables must be restricted as much as possible! Examples:

  1. SCRappl, SCRfrs, SCRsubglbls, SCRmiss.
  2. RNAenergyrules, RNAsequence, RNAstructure, RNAparams.

Sub-global Variables. A sub-global variable is a variable, which is not a global variable but is accessed by more than one function. The name of a sub-global variable is at least 6 characters long. The first three are the SID, followed by "_". The remaining characters are all lowercase character. Examples:

  1. WHL_menu, WHL_params, WHL_select.
  2. RNA_options, RNA_choice.

The use of sub-global variables must be restricted as much as possible!

Local Variables. A local variable is a variable which is local to that function. The name of a local variable may be A-E or H-K or M-Q, S-Y. Or alternatively formulated, all capitals except F, G, L, R, or Z. For clarity longer, mnemonic names could be used up to 4 characters in order to improve the readability of the programs.

The name of the arguments and the explicit result of a function are L, Z and R or short mnemonic names which start with L, Z or R.

Z: the variable name Z is reserved for the explicit result. L: the variable name L is reserved for the left argument of a function. R: the variable name R is reserved for the right argument of a function. F: the function name F is reserved for the left argument of an operator. G: the function name G is reserved for the right argument of an operator. I,J,K: it is advisable to reserve I, J and K for counters and important indices. T: We suggest using T for temporary line-locals (a line-local is a variable which gets its value somewhere else in the same line).

The variables F, G, L and R should not be assigned a value in any function.

When mnemonic names are used for the arguments or for the explicit result, the following rules must be obeyed:

  1. the names may be up to 4 characters long (longer names might conflict with names of user functions).
  2. the names must be alphanumeric capitals.
  3. F, G, L, Z and R may never be used.
  4. the first character should be L, R, Z if that variable is the left argument, right argument, or explicit result.
  5. the standard names for labels should not be used for variables.
  6. comment lines explaining the meaning of the arguments and the explicit result, must still be in the function and conform to the current standard.

Shared Variables. The names of shared variables are still under discussion. We welcome any suggestions.

Labels. The only permissible label names are B#, E# (with # a number), BE, XX and EXIT. See next paragraph.

items.title: Branching
items.text:
There are numerous ways in APL to branch to function lines. But it is also true that this excessive number of possibilities has given APL a bad name. Imagine an APL function in which different ways of branching are used (for example: →L×⍳C, →(C)⍴L, →C↑L, →C↓L, →(C)/L). It is clear that in reading such a function, a substantial amount of time is needed to solve the flow in that function.

For reasons of structured programming one should not think in branches but in conceptual blocks of code which are executed once, multiple times or not at all. Each block is marked by a label B# at its first statement and by a label E# at its last statement, with # a unique number for each block.

So, we suggest new programs adopt the following 4 types of construction:

  1. Condition:

    B3:→(...)/1+E3
...
E3:...

  2. For-loop & Repeat while:

    B1:→(...I←I+1)/1+E1       B8:→(...)/1+E8
   ...                       ...
   ...                       ...
E1:→B1                    E8:→B8

  3. Repeat until:

    B3:...
   ...
   ...
E3:→(...)/B3

  4. If/else & Case:

    B4:→(...)/B4a,B4b,B4c,1+E4
B4a:...
   ...
   →1+E4
B4b:...
   ...
   →1+E4
B4c:...
   ...
E4:...

Remember that the numbers identify different blocks in one function (not different types of construction).

Short conditions or repetitions can be coded as:

BE:→(...)/1+1↑⎕LC ⋄ short conditional expression
BE:→(...)/1+1↑⎕LC ⋄ short repeating expression ⋄ →⎕LC
BE: short repeating expression ⋄ →(...)/1↑⎕LC
BE:→(...)/1↑⎕LC ⍙ short repeating expression

Here "⍙" stands for "lev" or for "⎕FX 'Z←L ⍙ R' 'Z←L'".

Never branch to results of a calculation or to absolute line numbers!

To exit a function prematurely, do not use "→0". Use label "EXIT" instead which is at the end of a function. So apply the following type of construction:

XX:→(...)/EXIT
   ...
   ...
XX:→(...)/EXIT
   ...
   ...
EXIT: last and empty(!) line of program

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
This paragraph outlines the proposed on-line documentation for programmers and for end-users. We suggest implementing the following documentation in functions which yield the text as their resulting vector, with each line separated by a return-character. Use uppercase and lowercase characters as in normal text (not uppercase only).

Our convention is simple and straightforward: document anything you like by using an APL function which yields a character vector, and give this function the same name as the item you are documenting, prefixed with "∆". For example, if you document the global variable "WHLxyz" the documentation is generated by function "∆WHLxyz".

Programmers’ Documentation. By on-line programmers’ documentation we mean a description of all components of an APL system in the workspace or on file so that it can be used rapidly at all times by a programmer. This documentation is intended for system maintenance and development.

The following items should be documented and on-line available:

  1. SYSTEM. If any general information exists which should be available for the programmer, then it is documented in variable ∆SIDSYSTEM. Example: if important information exists for system WHL, it is documented in ∆WHLSYSTEM.
  2. GLOBAL VARIABLES. Global variables must be described briefly (1 line per variable) by function ∆SIDGLOBALS. If more extensive information is useful, then that particular variable is also described separately. Example: global variables RNAenergyrules, RNAsequence could be described extensively in ∆RNAenergyrules and ∆RNAsequence.
  3. SHARED VARIABLES. Shared variables must be described briefly (1 line per variable) by ∆SIDSHARED. Similar to the global variables, more extensive information can be presented separately. Example: shared variable CTL can also be described in ∆CTL.
  4. VERSION-CONTROL. If you don’t have a proper version-control system we suggest you apply the variable ∆SIDHISTORY to document any changes. Example:
      ⎕←∆RNAHISTORY
Problem               |Date  |Author  |Change
----------------------+------+--------+-----------------
-File selector without|031089|V.Batenb|RNA_FIL[5 7.1 11]
 folders              |      |        |RNA_BOX new
                      |      |        |RNA_curfile new
-Absolete energyvalues|211189|JJ.Riet |RNArule new values

A component file is documented in its 0th component.

User Documentation. On-line user documentation is useful for experienced users who have forgotten some particular details and want to refresh their memory. This requires that the information is short and compact and can be found easily by following standard procedures.

On-line user documentation is also useful for the novice, but here it has two different purposes. First the user wants to learn if the workspace will attend to his needs (investigation process) and second how to use it or where to find more elaborate information (application process). The first purpose -investigation - also requires short compact information; only the second purpose needs more elaborate information.

Both types of user are properly served with standard names to find their information. For this the following names serves:

  1. ∆SIDABSTRACT ∆SIDABSTRACT returns 1 (or at most 2) lines which describe the system very briefly (compare this with the more extensive descriptions in ∆SIDDESCRIBE and ∆SIDHOW). If function SIDLX does not start function SIDBEGIN, then it activates ∆SIDABSTRACT. For example:

    ⎕FX 'Z←∆WHLABSTRACT' 'Z←''Simulate whale hunting for...'''
⎕FX 'Z←WHLLX' 'Z←∆WHLABSTRACT'

  2. ∆SID ∆SID generates 6 lines with the following basic information: 1. SID. 2. complete name of the workspace. 3. version number, release and/or last modification date; anything which uniquely distinguishes this workspace from earlier or newer versions. 4. copyright holder. 5. name, address or telephone number of person or company to be contacted for information. 6. manuals, books and other documentation of the system.

  3. ∆SIDDESCRIBE Program ∆SIDDESCRIBE describes what the Workspace will do: the purpose of the Workspace. Program ∆SIDDESCRIBE should inform the reader in a nutshell if the workspace is appropriate for his problem. It does not teach the reader how to work with the workspace (that is the function of ∆SIDHOW), but only tells what the workspace does. This extensive information is summarised in ∆SIDABSTRACT.

  4. ∆SIDHOW Program ∆SIDHOW describes how to work with the workspace. It describes the various options of the user-functions and the required syntax. If the Workspace contains several user functions which can be activated by the user independently, than ∆SIDHOW at least summarises each user function.

  5. ∆SID- If ∆SIDHOW is insufficiently brief, then for each function a describing "∆SID-" could be added which explains the particulars of that function. So the syntax of each user functions SIDxyz (which should at least briefly be described in "∆SIDHOW") can be described more elaborately in ∆SIDxyz.

    This documentation is the only elaborate one, because it is primarily intended for the novice to learn how to operate the various functions. Example: function WHLSIMULATE has its syntax described in ∆WHLSIMULATE, function RNAFOLD in ∆RNAFOLD.

      ⎕←∆CPXPOLARHOW
Purpose: convert polar to cartesian coordinates
Syntax: PL ← CPXPOLAR CRT

CPXPOLAR converts cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates.
Its inverse program is CPXCART.

The right argument CRT specifies the cartesian coordinates. It
can be a vector of pairs, or a 2-column table with X-Y values.

The result PL are the polar equivalents. The rank and size of
PL are identical to those of CRT. Each pair is the modulus and
the angle in radians.

Example   1   0      <--> CPXPOLAR   1    0
          1   0.78                   0.71 0.71
          1   1.57                   0    1

items.title: Comments
items.text:
Use comments to describe what is done and why, but not how it is done (that’s what APL is for). Any APL function should at least contain the following comments

[1] ⍝⍝ description what the function does
[2] ⍝ R: description of the right argument
[3] ⍝ L: description of the left argument
[4] ⍝ Z: description of the result
[5] ⍝ G: names of used globals and subglobals, if any
[6] ⍝ P: name of programmer, dates of changes

Example:

[0] Z ← L VBL_DOCMENT R;A;L∘IO
[1] ⍝⍝ Document system and print to various devices.
[2] ⍝ R[i;]: Character names of output devices i.
[3] ⍝ L[]: Title to be printed.
[4] ⍝ Z: '' if OK, else error message.
[5] ⍝ G: VBLprint; VBLerr; VBLglobal        <=== bad design, many
[6] ⍝ P: EvBatenburg; 6/83,3/84,8/84,2/85.       (sub-)globals

Furthermore we suggest 2 types: section comment and line comment.

  1. Section comments explain several lines of code. This type of comment uses a whole line in the function.
  2. Line comments illuminate the code of a line. This type of comment trails at the right of that particular line. Example:
⍝ This explaines the following lines
.....code.... ⍝ This explaines the code at the left

items.title: Messages
items.text:
Messages are still under discussion. We welcome anybody who has suggestions.

React immediately where the error is discovered. If a test discovers an error, this is the place where the first action should be taken. Avoid printing of error messages in sub-functions, but express the occurrence of an error in the explicit result. (For example: ’’(empty vector) instead of computed array, 0 (zero) instead of computed array, error message instead of computed array)

Also avoid letting a sub-function halt the system by "→". The reason for both suggestions is that a sub-function may very well be unhappy with an exceptional condition, but its caller might better be suited to react to such a condition.

items.title: Miscellaneous
items.text:
In this section a few remarks are made on APL programming practice. The size of an APL function should be within working conditions and preferably less. This means that if one is working with a screen that displays 20 lines of 80 characters each, the size of APL functions should preferably be less than, or equal to 20 lines of 80 characters.

Good APL functions…

  1. are readable.
  2. perform one conceptual task only.
  3. can be used as building blocks.
  4. are like APL primitive functions; so they will give a defined result for all parameter values.
  5. work for missing left argument (default) and don’t crash for empty arrays.
  6. receive data in the right argument and control in the left argument.

Good APL functions are not necessarily (CPU) efficient. What is (CPU) efficient today may very well be (CPU) inefficient tomorrow (and vice versa).

Re-think again about your design if an APL function…

  1. is bigger than your screen.
  2. uses branches.
  3. uses (sub-)global variables.

items.title: ASWI Programming Standards; some Whys.
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 101

From: F.H.D. van Batenburg, 15 June 1992

Vector 8.2 published our ASWI standards for programming and documentation. This publication listed our proposal as a number of prescriptions without elaborating upon the reasons behind the various ideas.

It is not always easy to determine what is obvious in a proposal and what is not. In the discussions we had in reaching the ASWI standard some points were discussed at length, while others were taken for granted immediately among the participants. But some reactions from Dutch users among whom we circulated a preliminary version showed still different attitudes. This shows — not surprisingly, of course — how different experiences make up for the initial acceptance or rejection of different points.

Recently, Ray Cannon reacted in Vector 8.4 against various parts of the ASWI proposal. I am pleased to see his comments as they help us to pinpoint the most "offensive" parts and hence enable us to select those points which need more explanation, or which need to be changed.

In this sequel I will explain some of the considerations regarding:

  • SID in user-functions
  • SID in sub-functions
  • SID in standard functions
  • lowercase characters
  • length of names of local variables
  • miscellaneous

items.title: SID in User-functions
items.text:
Let us start with the SID in the name of functions. ASWI proposes to start the names of all user-functions with a 3-letter code, the SID (System IDentification). First of all, this proposal did not descend from heaven as a purely hypothetical idea. On the contrary, it is the formalisation of a long-standing practice at Philips and a big bank in Holland during more than a decade. Subsequently that proposal did not generate any discussion in the ASWI committee (or, as yet, elsewhere), because those users were already very satisfied with this practice. This alone, however, doesn’t make the benefits obvious, and Ray’s objection indicates that some elaboration of the reasons is indeed required.

Yes, in extreme cases, it is harder to find a particular function if all the functions in the workspace start with the same SID. But in general, a WS is not only filled with functions with the same SID. In my simulation workspace for example, one finds DLG-functions to manage the user-dialogues (copied from workspace DLG), one finds MDF-functions (from workspace MDF with Machine-Dependent-Functions), one finds GRF-functions (from a graphics workspace), and so on. Now a )FNS or a ⎕NL 3 beautifully lists each of those groups together. So this is much more of a help than a hindrance.

Moreover, I see this recipe applied in real-world applications often enough (for example in the file-workspaces of APL.68000 where the Atari-functions are called STREAD, STTIE, STWRITE and the Macintosh functions are called MTIE, MREAD and MWRITE). Nor were there any objections in the past to the names of the functions TSTEXPONENTIAL, TSTNORMAL and TSTPOISSON in my workspace TSTDISTR (this workspace tested against various distributions). Nor with the functions RNDEXPONENTIAL, RNDNORMAL and RNDPOISSON in my workspace RNDVARTS (this workspace generated random numbers according to different distributions).

So, again, I would say that those facts indicate that application of a SID was considered useful long before our proposal.

Furthermore, I wouldn’t object if functions in the APL Statistical Library had for example the prefix DES for all descriptive statistical functions and had the prefix TST for all testing functions, or even TNR for a collection of functions with statistical tests which assume normal-distributed variates and TOT for other tests. I must admit that I can also imagine that one prefers MEAN instead of DESMEAN and SPEARMAN instead of TSTSPEARMAN because MEAN and SPEARMAN are so well established names that one doesn’t want to burden the user with those prefixes. So this example is an in-between, for which there is probably as much in favour of the prefix as there is against it.

Ray is quite right that sometimes a SID- prefix in the name is undesirable, but I don’t think that APL programmers are much disturbed by such a SID-prefix. However I can imagine that a SID prefix might be undesirable for the end-user sometimes …

  • not if the end-user doesn’t see the main-program because the workspace starts in ⎕LX there is no problem.
  • not if the end-user has to activate just a few functions like LITRETRIEVE and LITSEARCH in a literature system, although I must admit that here our recipe might be debatable.

  • but yes, I definitely agree that …

    LITRETRIEVE LITALL LITBOOKS LITOF 'BROWN'

    is ludicrous and should be…

    RETRIEVE ALL BOOKS OF 'BROWN'

So in general I would say that a SID prefix is often very useful and that such a proposal in ASWI is merely a formalisation of a long-standing practice. I must admit however, that our proposal was probably stated somewhat too categorically and that it should have left some room for exceptions.

items.title: SID in Sub-functions
items.text:
For imported subfunctions there is nothing wrong with using a SID-prefix either. Regarding Ray’s statement "a utility should be independent of its origin" I would like to comment that a utility should not be independent of its task; and its task determines its prefix. I found it very useful that the graphics of STSC started with ⎕G and the file functions with ⎕F and the window functions with ⎕W. Again, nothing purely theoretical, but a real-life implementation before our proposal came to life.

Now what about a prefix for IOTA? If I knew why Ray programmed a function IOTA, I wouldn’t have problem finding a proper SID. Was the intention to simulate standard APL functions among which was IOTA? Then why not APLIOTA, APLESTI, APLRHO, and APLTAKE? Then the SIM-workspace would either contain an APLIOTA or a SIM_IOTA. The name APLIOTA indicates that this is the original utility from the APL-workspace. And the name SIM_IOTA would indicate that the function is not any longer working as one might expect, because it is more or less subtly adapted for use in the SIM-workspace.

The advice from ASWI is to change the name of an imported subfunction as soon as one tampers with it to adapt it for the particular application in which it is imported. Ray comments to that "a true utility’s name should be independent of its origin, if the origin of a function is important, then comment it, don’t clutter up the space name". To this I would say: if you adapt a utility for a particular application it is not a "true utility" any more. It is exactly to warn against unsuspected deviant behaviour that this proposal will protect you. Comments alone are certainly not powerful enough (do you consult the comments every time you invoke a utility? For many I don’t).

items.title: SID in standard functions
items.text:
The only case in which I have some real misgivings about the ASWI standard is about the SID-proposal regarding the standard names like SID∆BEGIN, SID∆ABSTRACT, SID∆DESCRIBE, SID∆HOW etcetera. There was much debate in the ASWI committee about this.

  1. One group argued that they often merged several workspaces together. If no prefix was used, with each new workspace copy the previous BEGIN, ∆DESCRIBE and ∆HOW would be replaced. As they wanted to consult all the descriptions they preferred a prefix so one could still recognise all descriptions.
  2. The other group argued that most of those ∆FUNCTIONS are used by novices who don’t know the workspace. So they don’t know the SID either and they just want to load the workspace and type ∆ABSTRACT or ∆DESCRIBE to see what they have in their hands without bothering about any SID.

We finally opted for the first case, but our committee was not unanimous.

items.title: Lower-case Characters
items.text: For global variables ASWI requires that a name consists of lower-case characters preceded by the SID, and for sub-global variables a name of lower-case characters preceded by SID_. Ray is right that it is useful to mention the alternative of underscored characters for implementations without lower-case characters. We didn’t do this because basically our proposal was drawn for a project of shareware program development using APL2/PC and APL.68000. However, to take other APL implementations into account would give our proposal a broader impact. So I propose to mention in the ASWI committee the alternative of underscored characters in the next version.

items.title: Length of Names of Local Variables
items.text: ASWI requires that names of local variables do not exceed 4 characters. Although the particular number 4 is somewhat arbitrary of course (why not 5, or 3?) my experience is that APL functions tend to lose their surveyability rapidly with lengthy names. As most of the APL functions and operators occupy 1 character, a variable of, say, 4 characters already dominates a code-line much more than warranted. So my personal preference is to use 1 or 2 character names in small functions, and highly incidental 3 or 4 characters in bigger functions. It is my experience that "natural names" can be abbreviated to 2 or 3 characters and still be recognisable. The ASWI committee doesn’t share Ray’s fear that shortening a "natural name" will diminish readability. We believe the contrary.

items.title: Miscellaneous
items.text:
The ASWI standard ends with a Miscellaneous paragraph with "a few remarks…on APL programming practice". Here we suggest that "good" APL-functions…

5. work for missing left argument (default) and don’t crash for empty arrays.

6. receive data in the right argument and control in the left.

Both suggestions are gross over-simplifications. They were intended to steer APL programmers towards some preferred standard practice. These remarks were not intended to mean literally that either…

  • a function which desperately needs data in its left argument is a bad function.
  • a function which has a default for a missing left argument is always a good function.
  • a function which has control and data in the left and right arguments respectively is always a good function.
  • a function which has data in both the left and the right argument is always a bad function.

What we did want to accomplish was to force a programmer to reflect about his design and to wonder…

  • "is there a compelling reason why I want to deviate from this suggestion and have no default for the left argument?" (if so, fine). By the way, an empty vector ('') is a suitable substitute for a missing left argument in implementations without ambivalent functions. I will propose in the ASWI committee to mention the alternative of '' in the next version.
  • "if I have two types of information — one processed data and the other control information which steers the function — is there a compelling reason not to distinguish those types and not to present the controlling information in the left and the processed data in the right argument?" If there is a compelling reason to deviate, then fine again.

I hope to have clarified most of the points in the ASWI proposal to which Ray objects. We do indeed think that the ASWI proposals aid readability and maintainability. The recipes are not as ephemeral and hypothetical as Ray probably thought. Most of them were derived from our own everyday experience. As to Ray’s suggestion of applying them to see if they help or hinder, we can assure him that we will do so, and have done so.

Ray’s comments have been worthwhile contributions to improve our standards with regard to:

  • giving a little bit more leeway to omit a prefix SID in user-functions.
  • reconsidering the SID in standard functions.
  • mentioning underscored characters as the alternative to lower-case characters.
  • mentioning the ''-alternative to missing left arguments.

F.H.D. van Batenburg, Leyden University Institute for Theoretical Biology, Kaiserstraat 63, Leiden, Holland

items.title: Font for the Future
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 64

by F.H.D. van Batenburg

It was a pleasant surprise to read Bill Chang’s paper [1] and to learn that WWW uses 8 bits for file transfer which would enable us to transmit APL characters. If only we could agree over a proper APL character set and mapping.

His proposal to agree on a common positioning of the APL characters seems very important to me. I wish we could all agree quickly on this so we can exchange code electronically and read it easily. This might raise the discussion how "easy" an ASCII transliteration scheme is. I think that an agreed ASCII transliteration is very useful and will remain so as long as people work with hardware or software that cannot display any particular chosen font. And that will still be the case quite a few years from now. However for me the APL characters are the easiest to read and any ASCII transliteration is a second best choice that is forced upon me by the hardware or software. So when my hard- and software allow it, I prefer the APL symbols.

In his comments in Vector 12.2 [2], Adrian Smith stresses his need to cut and paste between his Web browser, word processor and APL program (Dyalog and Manugistics). Again a plea for a quick decision for a universally agreed mapping of APL characters.

However much I can agree over the importance of such a "universal agreed-upon mapping" of APL characters, I would like to bring up another requirement that might conflict with the above-mentioned cut/paste requirement. I want to enter APL in my word processor just as if I am using the APL 2741 keyboard. This means that by pressing key <3>, I would like to see "3" in my text, by pressing <Shift+3> I would like to see "<", pressing <Alt+3> should display "#", and pressing <Alt+shift+3> should display "⍒".

As far as I know, on the PC (Windows 3.1) the position of the characters in the fontfile determines their particular keys. There is no user-definable mapping table to associate a particular character in the fontfile to a specific Alt/Shift/key combination. So there is no way to tell Word that pressing key <A> or key-combination <Shift+A> should bring anything else forward but character 96 in fontfile APL, respectively character 66 (origin 1). Or is there?

The same holds true for the Macintosh; yes, I can switch to another generic mapping (for example "German-mapping" instead of "USA-mapping") but this will work for all subsequent fonts and is not specific to a particular APL font, or within a particular application. I know that Unix enables font-keyboard mappings, and that Dyalog APL does so, but I don’t know of any way to do that in Word for Windows or in Word on my Macintosh.

So based on the assumption that there is a 1:1 relationship between the character position in the font file and the position on the keyboard, I defined a TTF font mapping on the Macintosh, using Fontmonger with the font that Vector provided (thank you Adrian) that makes it possible for me to type in all APL text as if it was a real 2741 typewriter, using <Alt> and <Alt+Shift> combinations for "overstrikes".

Figure 1: Keyboard mapping of Macintosh TTF font APL_2741.

The figure shows that typing is mostly according to the "APL keyboard". Lowercase keys yield APL capital characters, uppercase yield APL non-overstrike functions (yes, I know that the word "overstrike" has lost its meaning since we do not overstrike any more, but I still use it to indicate the more complex characers), and <Alt+...> yields the normal APL overstrikes. All very regular, in accordance with the APL keyboard specification.

Only the <Alt+Shift+...> combinations are a bit irregular. As you can see there are several places that map to the same character. For example "i" is associated with <Alt+I> as well as with <Alt+Shift+I>, and the same <Alt+...> and <Alt+Shift+...> convergence holds for "e", "n" and "u". This is a particular quirk of the "USA-keyboard" font-mapping of the Mac-O.S., so I have to put up with it. For this reason I could not place the underscored epsilon "⍷" at <Alt+Shift+E>, underscored iota "⍸" at <Alt+Shift+I> nor "⍗" on the same key alongside the "↓", much as I would like to.

Furthermore <Alt+Shift+6>, <...+8>, <...+9> and <...+10> do not yield "^", "*", "(" and ")". The reason was that I did not want to put one character on two positions in the font. For example "*" is already defined by key <Shift+P> and the corresponding character is placed in position 81. Associating <Alt+Shift+8> also with an asterisk would result in another asterisk placed in font position 162. Searching in text for an asterisk would either bring forward the one in position 81 or the other one in position 162, but not both. This is of course not acceptable in text processing, unless the two asterisks have a very different appearance. Similarly for searching on caret "^" (yes, that one looks a bit different from APL’s and-function "∧", but not that different as you can see) and opening and closing parentheses.

The <Alt+Shift+...> also includes the framing characters and four arrowheads (at <Alt+Shift+G>, <...+H>, <...+V> and <...+B>) that connect to the lines made by the framing characters.

With this font, typing a manual or a paper (this one for example) is very easy. As mentioned before, on the Mac one can apply the 2741 key-mapping in any text processor: Word, ClarisWorks, BBEdit, SimpleText or whatever. I don’t need to run a parallel APL session from which to cut and paste into my text, so I can also give a manuscript to an "APL-phobic" secretary and ask her to type it in for me.

Although I have not yet ported this font to the PC, such an approach will work as well on the PC. The normal and shifted keys will yield APL caps and APL non-overstrike functions in all text processors. Unfortunately Word for Windows does not allow one to use <Alt+...> and <Alt+Shift+...> to access a particular character. However for this I used to apply utility COMPOSE (a utility that DEC put into the public domain) and typed <Specialkey>+∇+| in order to get "⍒" and <Specialkey>+○+\ to get "⍉". Here the overstrike concept came to life again.

What is the mapping that makes this work? See Figure 2 opposite.

This shows the character positions in font APL_2741 on the Macintosh. It is different from Bill Chang’s proposal, unfortunately, but also has much in common. Positions 1–33 are not used, and positions 128–169 are used sparingly. The first 128 positions are very much in line with most other proposals. Positions 170–256 are different, however. This is done to agree with the Macintosh key-mapping; as the PC has no <Alt+..> and <Alt+Shift+..> mapping in Word, I do not expect this mapping to disagree with any Word for Windows on the PC.

Figure 2: APL_2741 Light

Are all APL characters included?

  • Yes. All characters that are mentioned in the ISO extended standard are included.
  • No. Many APL characters that are entered in the UCS2 standard [5] and [6]) are not included. All non-overstrike APL characters are there, but many overstrikes such as quad-equal, quad-diamond, down-tack-underbar, quote-underbar, circle-underbar, leftshoe-stile, downshoe-stile and many others are missing. All of them are without meaning in the current APL systems that I know of (but my knowledge is limited in this respect).
  • Yes. All APL characters that Jim Brown proposed in [3] and Bill Chang in [1] and Adrian Smith in [4].
  • No. Not all the non-APL characters that Jim Brown, Bill Chang and Adrian Smith proposed. They included national characters like the pound and the yen character and many, many accented characters.

My proposition with respect to national characters and accented characters is: do not include those characters in the APL character set. If inclusion would be easy, like the relatively small load cf 11 framing characters, we could include them, but as it is a big problem we should exclude them. All accented characters are simply too much to expect to live together with a full APL character set in a file of 265 minus 64 reserved positions. This does not mean that those characters are unimportant, but only that they create a problem that can easily be circumvented by asking the user to use his ordinary text font if he/she wishes to use special accented or national characters. Those fonts are particularly suited for the national characters. These characters just don’t belong to the APL character set.

As long as the UCS2 character set (a proposal where each character is represented by 16 bits) is not implemented everywhere it would be useful to agree on one character set mapping with all the current APL characters. And even after general acceptance of the UCS2 such a characterset configuration could be useful as the APL characters in UCS2 are spread out over several tables [5] and I suspect that one derived table that contains just the APL characters will often be used internally.

Is this an answer to Bill Chang’s proposal? Unfortunately not. The alternative mapping and different reasoning presented here do not solve the problem of "what mapping" to choose, but rather enlarge the problem. My purpose was to put forward another criterion for font-mapping: typing in a text processor.

It seems that we now have several alternative suggestions that are not compatible, and even mutually exclusive. Let me finish with those questions and ask the APL users to think (and write) about an answer.

  1. What characters do we want in a set of 256 (minus 64)? Live APL characters? Also the "dead" ones? National characters? Accented characters? frame (single and double) characters? (My suggestion is to take the live APL characters and framing characters only as shown in Figures 1 and 2.)
  2. Do we choose a mapping such that we can cut/paste between Windows text processors (I assume this implies any Windows Web-browser) and Dyalog APL?
  3. Do we choose a mapping such that we can cut/paste between Windows text processors and Manugistics APL?
  4. Do we choose a mapping such that we can cut/paste between Macintosh text processors and 68000 APL?
  5. Do we choose a mapping such that we can type APL in our Macintosh text processors? (This would be my preference.)
  6. Do we choose a mapping such that we can type APL in our Windows text processors?

I have no answer to these questions that is satisfying for everybody. On the contrary, some alternatives seem mutually exclusive to me. We could ask ISO to choose a character mapping. This would hand over this Gordian knot to the ISO committee to unravel, but I do think that it is better if we could come to an agreement together. So I am anxious to know your opinion.

Dr F H D van Batenburg Section Theoretical Biology, E.E.W. of Leiden University Kaiserstraat 63 2311GP Leiden The Netherlands

items.title: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 125

by F.H.D. van Batenburg
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: 1. Introduction
items.text:
In the years after Edsgar Dijkstra wrote his complaint "GOTO considered Harmful" (Dijk68), an important discussion followed among software professionals regarding structured programming. APL did not join in this discussion. As a result of that discussion, program languages implemented concepts to enable programmers to program in a structured way. APL however remained in splendid isolation, cherishing its beloved jump "→".

This is very unfortunate because the tools you have influence the way you think. The essence of the discussion was not so much about better tools, but about thinking. Having jumps let you think in flow whereas structured concepts make you think in structure (blocks if you like) which is much better.

It was only in 1978 that Wiedman (Wie78), Reeves and Besemer (Ree78) started the discussion in APL. After their initiative, many authors followed with proposals to add control structures (see long list of references compiled by De Kerf (Ker86)) but APL vendors effectively ignored this. Finally, in 1994 Manugistics came with an implementation that copied the concepts as well as the keywords of conventional languages. A few years later in 1996, Dyalog APL followed suite and so did J; all of them copying the concepts and the keywords.

To my opinion, this is not good. Granted, these control structures have been essential improvements to hitherto unstructured languages and these concepts are worthwhile tools to structure a program. But why should APL slovenly copy these implementations lock, stock and barrel? After all, "COS(X)", "MIN(X,Y)" and "CEIL(X)" are nowadays also part of the standard repertoire of most languages (and rightfully so), but nevertheless APL programmers are much happier with "2○X", "X⌊Y" and "⌈X".

My point is that APL should copy the ideas of useful concepts (and possibly improve upon them), but not copy the way such concepts are implemented and certainly not a keyword implementation. Instead, APL should have chosen an APL-lish implementation using symbols instead of keywords and preferably one powerful symbol that does it all.
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: 2. A Better Structure Control
items.text:
APL2C has chosen such an APL-lish implementation for structure and structure control. APL2C is an APL implementation that is developed by T.Otto (Ott00). It is a fully functional APL2-type implementation. The name APL2C is chosen because one can produce C-source code from a workspace. This enables programmers to modify the C-code at will, add other modules if needed, and at the end compile the whole combination into an executable.

The implementation for structure control is based on a further development of my ideas as published in Bat82-Bat94. In APL2C the symbol that does all the structuring and its control is the del "∇" which for that reason will be called control. The choice of this symbol agrees well with its original purpose to indicate start and end of function definition. As Willhoft argued, for a long time the only block available in APL was a function, so "∇" seems a suitable symbol for blocks (Wil93). This does not clash with the function definition anymore because function definition is done by )EDIT or by double click (as is common in most Windowing implementations). Symbol control is used monadically to indicate the beginning of a block and it is used niladic to mark the end of a block.
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: Iteration
items.text:
An example will show how this works. We begin to show iteration. The following code:

∇4+5
 Z←'HALLO'
 Z←'WORLD'
∇

is a block that will be executed 9 times; first the expression at the right of the monadic control is executed and the resulting value 9 will instruct control to print out 9 times two lines with HALLO on the odd lines and WORLD on the even lines.
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: Condition
items.text:
The previous example showed iteration, but condition is quite similar. For loops, the expression at the right of control is an integer indicating how many times to execute the block, for conditions it suffices when the integer is either one or zero. For example to do something only if FLAG is non-zero you could program:

∇0≠FLAG
 :::some interesting computation:::
∇
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: While
items.text:
The examples above have shown how condition and iteration is implemented in APL2C. The while-construction is implemented in a similar way. After all, a while-construct is an iteration, but an iteration that is executed as long as the controlling expression is true. Therefore the implementation is identical to the fixed iteration, however, to tell APL to recheck the controlling expression a negative value is used.

For example to read input until the user enters an empty line:

∇-0≠⍴,IN←,⍞
 ::: some interesting computation:::
∇

Another example that codes an iteration until the result does not change any more is:

OLD←1+NEW←INITIALVALUES ⍝ initially different values
                          for NEW and OLD
∇-OLD≢NEW
 OLD←ANALYSE NEW←OLD
∇
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
What about alternatives like IF-ELSE and SELECT? To program alternatives APL2C needs a vector for the right argument of control. This vector prescribes what to do for each alternative. The alternatives in the block are marked by a label-less colon ":". If the number of alternatives do not match the length of the vector, APL2C returns a LENGTH ERROR. An example will illustrate this:

∇2 3∊⎕NC'XXX'
:Z←'VARIABLE'
:Z←'FUNCTION'
∇

This will print VARIABLE if the ∇-expression yields 1 0, it prints FUNCTION if the expression yields 0 1 and it will print nothing if the expression is 0 0. Just hypothetically, imagine that the ∇-expression yielded "¯2 7". In that case APL2C would have printed 2 times the word VARIABLE, 7 times the word FUNCTION and after that (because of the negative number ¯2) APL2C would execute the ∇-expression again.
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: Nesting
items.text:
It is no problem to create nestings in APL2C. Just to wrap the whole idea up in one complicated (not so realistic) example, imagine the following code:

∇CN←¯2 3×COND1 ⍝control1
:action1
 action2
:∇10             ⍝control2
  action3
  action4
 ∇
∇

If CN get the value ¯2 0 then action1 and action2 are done twice after which APL2C does the expression in control1 again.

If CN get the value 0 3 then action3 and action4 are done, and done another 9 times to satisfy the value 10 in control2, and this is done another 2 times to satisfy the 3 in control1. As there was no negative number in control1, this ends the total block.
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: Iteration counter
items.text:
In the previous examples, the iterations did not need a variable to keep track of the iterations. Sometimes you do not need one, but there are often occasions where it is convenient to know the iteration number. If so, you could of course explicitly program this, but it is more convenient if such a counter is available.

The iteration count can be found in Iteration Counter "+ZIC". This variable is a 2-row matrix with one row for the current iteration counter, and the second row for its terminal value. So within one single block, it is a one-column matrix. With nested blocks "ZIC[;1]" gives the current counter and the final value for the innermost block and the last column gives the counter and final value for the outer-most block.

For example:

∇5 3 ¯8 0
: ~~~~~  ⍝ here ⎕IC is 2 1⍴(1-5),5
:∇4      ⍝ here ⎕IC is still 2 1⍴(1-3),3
  ~~~~~  ⍝ but here ⎕IC is 2 2⍴(1-4),(1-3),4,3
 ∇
:~~~~~   ⍝ here ⎕IC is 2 1⍴(1-8),¯8
:~~~~~   ⍝ alternative 4 is never executed
∇
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: Single-line shortcut
items.text:
For small actions, a shorter alternative is available for iterations and conditions. This is the single-line alternative where control is used dyadically with controlling expression at the right and the action at the left. For example:

LEFT←3∇2≠⎕NC'LEFT' ⍝ Only assignment ifor missing LEFT
⎕←'Thank you...'∇1000 ⍝ Thousand times thanks
ANALYSE IN∇-0≠⍴IN←,⍞ ⍝ Analyse as long as input is given
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: Formatting
items.text: The examples that were presented not only showed the working of control, but also how APL2C formats the blocks. Each block is indented one space and the colon for alternatives is outdented so as to show to which control they belong.
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: 3. Conclusion
items.text:
You have seen how APL2C handles structure and its control. In this implementation all structured control concepts are blended together in one simple, but very powerful, construct control. This takes the essence of structured control, but implements it more in the spirit of APL. The result are programs where structure is better recognized than in current alternatives.

For a more complete example, the Vector website shows two programs that were structured to begin with. Both programs are shown in their original programming style as well as a remake using control. It shows how the programs get shorter and more comprehensible.

If you are interested in experiencing how this works you could download a demo version of APL2C. You can find more information as well as a full featured trial version with a time limit of half a year, at website: //www.apl2c.com.
path: A New Life For ∇: Structure Control

items.title: 4. Literature
items.text:
Bat82 Batenburg,F.H.D.van(1982): New control structures in APL. Quote Quad.13(2)15-20 Bat85 Batenburg,F.H.D.van Prins,R.(1985): QL/APL: A leap back - or forward? Vector 2(2)115-117 Bat88 Batenburg,F.H.D.van(1988): The Code-line: A "New" Structured Concept. Quote Quad.19(2)14-19 Bat91 Batenburg,F.H.D.van (1991): L-one-two-three (L1:...L2:...L3:...) considered harmful. Proc. APL91 p.330-337 Bat94 Batenburg,F.H.D.van (1994): Restriction riddance: more power to parentheses. Quote Quad 25(1)220-224. Dijk68 Dijkstra,E.W.(1968): GOTO statement considered harmful. ACM Comm. 11(3)147-148 Ker86 Kerf,J.L.F. De (1986): APL and structured programming: an annotated biography. APLCAM 8(2)340-363 Ott00 Otto,T.(2000): Oral presentation at APL conference 2000 Ree78 Reeves,A.P. Besemer,J.(1978): Special control structures in APL. Proc APL93 p.304-315
