items.title: Are 4GLs killing APL?
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 49

by Desmond Booth

Before answering this question, it is necessary to consider two related questions:

Who uses 4th generation languages?

What is a 4th generation language?

The first question is perhaps easier to answer. The concept of the Information Centre has grown over the last few years, and it is clearly in the Information Centre that 4th generation products will find their home. This gets us no closer to resolving our main topic, however, as we must still ask:

What is an Information Centre?

Why does it exist?

This discussion will first describe Information Centres, in order to understand the growth in demand for 4th generation languages. It will then use a 4th generation product, DATAPORT, to demonstrate 4th generation characteristics by example. Finally, it will show why the use of APL in 4th generation products is an advantage. It will come as no surprise, therefore, that the answer to “are 4th generation languages killing APL?” will be “NO.”

It has been suggested by sceptics (Ed: see Romilly Cocking’s article in Vol. 1. No. 1.) that Information Centres have arisen because IBM have seen the IC concept as a means of selling blue boxes. Whilst it is true that IBM have put enormous resources into promoting IC’s, it is now clear that, as usual, they have been backing a winner. During the last twenty years organisations have moved more and more of their corporate information to the data processing environment, and potential users have found it increasingly difficult to cope with the problems of accessing this information. Sometimes this has been because of the sheer volume of data available, at other times the technical difficulties of access have made the time scale of data interpretation too long. Hence the expression “application backlog” became an emotive term in many DP departments.

The Information Centre concept arose, therefore, in order to formalise methods by which non DP professionals (now often referred to as “End Users”) could access and interpret this wealth of computerised data. Professionals would be made available to advise and assist where necessary, but the users would use advanced computing tools to achieve results at terminals without the need for intervention by the DP department.

APL was introduced to the Information Centre not, as has been suggested, to fill machines, but because IBM had used two APL products — APL/DI and ADRS — internally to great effect themselves. In fact, considering IBM’s vast internal committment to APL it is surprising that APL is not pushed more into the limelight. Nevertheless, both APL/DI and ADRS found great following in emergent Information Centres, and still remain the most frequently used End User tools.

At the same time that Information Centres using mainframes as the computing vehicle started to emerge, the micro computer revolution occurred. Suddenly people found themselves confronted with computing tools which were easy to use! And productive! Visicalc changed the face of End User Computing, but this was only the beginning. Command driven systems, once considered to be at the forefront of technology, were replaced by sophisticated menu-driven systems, with on-line help facilities giving real power to the users’ fingertips, without the need for heavy committment to learning how to use the systems offered. Mainframe systems fought back, and the term “4th generation” was spawned.

“4th generation” is a term widely used, but rarely defined, since it embodies such a diversity of concepts. Rather than attempt a definition, I will use a new Information Centre product, DATAPORT, to achieve a definition by example.

DATAPORT is a 4th generation Information Centre tool providing full-screen data entry, display and analysis capabilities together with interfaces to other proprietary Information Centre products. DATAPORT uses APL as a “core technology”, draws heavily on spreadsheet experience to provide a fast, consistent environment for End User applications.

The 4th generation aspects of DATAPORT can be divided into three main areas:

user-friendliness;

functionality;

interface capabilities.

Looking first at that over-worked expression “user-friendly,” what does it mean? The experience of micro computer users is clear. It is possible to “throw” a micro and a good spreadsheet at a user and never hear from them again. Expect for a stream of converts asking for their own PC! Clearly this is a result of user-friendliness, but how is it achieved? Certainly aspects such as menu options and on-line help are part of the answer, but not by any means all. This is why older generation software does not necessarily respond to being tarted up with menus and help — a new, consistent approach is called for. This is achieved in DATAPORT by using the following:

combination of command and menu driven design;

two level help facility;

clear, consistent error messages;

full support for 3270 technology;

selection of options by cursor control;

all of which are incorporated into a truly elegant design. The result is a product which not only encourages beginners to learn without “painful” experiences, but also enables experts to work quickly and efficiently.

Friendliness is fine, but ultimately it is the results which matter. DATAPORT functionality extends the well developed concept of windowing to the multiple dimesions which are so important for modelling the real world. In combination with calculation facilities which enable formulae to be expressed in terms of rows, columns, or even pages at a time, the multi-dimensionality enables users to rapidly develop applications. It will come as no surprise to experienced APLers that the calculation facilities take full advantage of the APL product core to provide unparalleled power of expression.

It is in the interface capability, though, that DATAPORT is furthest ahead. Friendliness and functionality have developed gradually, but here is something new. The capability of “talking” to other software, whether mainframe or micro based, without the user knowing anything about the relevant data structures, is revolutionary. Current interfaces include links to database products including FOCUS and RAMIS; core Information Centre products APL/DI and ADRS; other mainframe based products including SAS and Tel-a-Graf; and simple interfacing to the popular micro spreadsheets including LOTUS and Visicalc.

Having now achieved some clarification of the implications of “4th generation” the advantages of APL in this environment are clear. Whilst the use of APL is of no direct benefit to the End User (in fact it is important that the user be unaware of APL, in terms of upper/lower case requirements, APL characters, or such “peculiarities” as right to left evaluation) the benefits for those supporting the software are tremendous. Even the simplicity of installation of APL, merely requiring the loading of a workspace, is a benefit in terms of the avoidance of the need for that all-to-scarce resource, the systems programmer. But it is in the ease of customisation that the main benefit lies. Frequently this can be achieved with minimal awareness of product internals. Even where the relevant system is not APL based, the use of APL to provide a front end, or interface to other products in the manner of DATAPOINT, is frequently because of the ease of transforming data structures in APL.

The above assumes that APL expertise is available. But the natural environment for 4th generation products is in the Information Centre, with its historical use of APL. It may well be that APL is the only language supported by an IC; in any case IC’s will be well equipped to work with APL products.

It is seen then, that rather than killing APL, the emergence of 4th generation languages, whether APL based or not, will stimulate the continuing growth of APL as the vehicle for the best of End User software.

items.title: APL and Graphics Standards
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 75

by Dick Bowman

Now that the bang of your head on the table (reaction to the word “standards”?,) has woken you up again, there are some things to be said about linking APL to the computer graphics world and doing it sensibly, so that we can take advantage of what other people are doing, and they have less of an opportunity to think of us as a bunch of iconoclastic weirdoes.

items.title: What’s APL Got To Do With Graphics?
items.text:
Quite a lot, I think; on two bases:

a) Graphics offers the same sort of productivity to users that APL offers to program developers. Taking the view that one major attraction of APL for the program writer is the ability to see what’s going on as it happens, there is a symmetry to also being able to provide visualisation to the end user at a similar level of immediacy. You just can’t tackle this by filing data away and logging on to another system every time you want to draw a picture; graphics have got to be immediately accessible from within the APL environment (I recognize that there are recent developments on some implementations which do, in principle, offer very flexible access to non-APL facilities). b) More seriously, taking graphics at a more abstract level than piecharts and histograms, what is being manipulated by a graphics program is objects. Now what are objects but collections of coordinates in n-dimensional space? At a simple level, in 2D space we could have a square defined as a set of four pairs of x—y values. We would then like to be able to move it, rotate it and magnify it. The obvious approach is to handle the square as a 2x4 or 4x2 array. One would think that a language which handles arrays implicitly would be at something of an advantage over scalar languages.

items.title: What Has The Computer Graphics World Been Up To?
items.text:
Once upon a time graphics were a hideously expensive business to get into (particularly interactive screen-based graphics) and you needed all the computational power you could get. Graphics programs were written to operate with specific hardware: inside your graphics program you would be specifically incrementing the pen of, say, a Calcomp pen plotter.

Gradually, an evolutionary process occurred in which falling entry costs and device diversity led to increasing recognition of the problems associated with customisation of application programs to specific items of hardware. For example:

i) Calcomp software — many other manufacturers supplied software to permit their hardware to emulate Calcomp pen plotters. ii) Manufacturer packages — stemming from the wider introduction of hardware with more extensive features (e.g. graphics input); a prime example being the Tektronix PLOT10 package. iii) Independent standards — the SIGGRAPH Core proposal, the ISO GKS, or “Graphical Kernel System” standard. There are two immediate points of comparison between Core and GKS; Core is intrinsically a 3D standard, while GKS is 2D. GKS nevertheless looks closer to becoming an accepted standard in the ISO-BSI meaning of the word.

There is good reason to suppose that graphics standards which emerge from a wider base than individual manufacturers or users will achieve some stability and widespread recognition. Already in the world of FORTRAN programming you acquire leper status if you persist in writing graphics applications without due regard for either Core or GKS. Equally, manufacturers are beginning to produce graphics terminals which are themselves bound to the standards (note this reversal of direction).

One other aspect of GKS which is worthy of note is that the standard introduces a concept of language binding; implementations of the standard which are invokable from a particular programming language must all use exactly the same calling protocol — even to the extent of using the same subroutine names.

Something else about GKS should strike a familiar note; the main line-drawing primitive is the “polyline” — it draws a line through a set of points. In other words, GKS treats single points as a special case of multiple points.

items.title: What’s The APL World Been Up To?
items.text:
So far as I can tell, the APL community has been its usual independent self; often invoking the cry “we don’t need to worry about that, we’re too busy being productive”. I don’t want to detract in any way from the excellence of some of the work that’s been done in APL with graphics as its end-point; the IPSA graphics which lie behind packages like SUPERPLOT spring immediately to mind, as does the achievement of IBM in making the 3279 display screen combine graphics with text dialogue. There have already been proposals for implementing the Core standard in APL (1,2).

Nevertheless, I get a distinct flavour of low-tech when I look at the general approach to graphics in the APL world; devices like Anderson-Jacobson paper terminals seem to be the norm, with few applications stretching beyond the business graph.

Equally, I am interested to note that the “leader” among APL graphics software is probably IBM’s GRAPHPAK (3), at least in terms of market penetration. If GRAPHPAK has a philosophical stance, it certainly isn’t one of alignment with either Core or GKS.

Looking to the future, I predict that we’ll be seeing a lot of the APL*PLUS/PC graphics functions (4); but you don’t design a graphics package by copying Microsoft Basic: anyone intending to work seriously with this system is going to do themselves a long-term favour by creating a set of appropriately-designed cover functions.

items.title: Can We Do Anything About It?
items.text:
The first step we have to take is to recognize that there is indeed a problem.

As a next step, we should begin to familiarize ourselves with what the rest of the world is doing. Both GKS and Core have complete (if dry) descriptive documents (5,6); there’s also a quite readable textbook about GKS (7). Further background reading on computer graphics is plentiful, (8) being a recommended example.

I would suggest also that anyone planning to work in the graphics area makes a conscious decision to implement functions at the level defined within either Core or GKS, building up in classic fashion to the levels needed within the application. Even if you initially intend only to produce the usual business graphs you’ll have laid a foundation for the more imaginative displays exemplified by (9).

One could do worse than adopt GKS as a standard for two reasons:

a) GKS looks like beating Core to the status of being an accredited standard as opposed to a draft proposal; b) 2D systems have limitations, but they should be easier to produce and have a pragmatic advantage that the most useful (if not the prettiest) business graphics are 2D. Most graphics terminals also are 2D.

Having homed in on GKS, we then note it as concerning itself with language bindings; if we want to be taken seriously we’d better get down to at least agreeing these among ourselves. Multiple contradictory APL implementations of GKS, all with differing function names, are not going to go down well with the rest of the graphics world.

items.title: Is Anyone Out There Working on an APL GKS Implementation?<sup>1</sup>
items.text:
APL has a lot to offer the graphics world. Non-APL graphics users are beginning to show some signs of recognising that they have needs for the sort of solutions that APL offers. It may be hard for you to accept, but the majority of them have never even heard of APL.

We can make ourselves known, but before we do this there has probably got to be some element of setting our own house in order. I suggest that we begin to dialogue with the GKS people to see whether a GKS language binding for APL is a viable proposition. The British APL Association could provide a platform on which we might base an approach, but there’s no point doing anything unless we can agree amongst ourselves what we want to do. Any such proposal would in no way remove incentives for individuals to produce packages as they see fit.

Valerie Lusmore: I findit quite ironic in a waythat | supposeif I wasstill working for my first employers in APL, I would probably besitting on the otherside of the house, because I workedfor many years for Sharp s in the stages when they were doing what I would call the original enhancements to APL. I camein at a base level where APL had what I would call the two basic and original enhancements, the formatter and thefile system, which we would perhapsnot consider enhancements but necessities. Without those I think APL would never have spread atall. Withoutthoseit would have beenso difficult to do anything that nothing would ever have happened. HaveI goneto the otherside? No. ... I left Sharps. I went out in the real world. And, like many of us in this room, I thought APL was so marvellous that we wouldn t really needtosell it. That s a classic mistake we haveall made. APL hasspread despite the fact that most of us do notsell very well because we feel that somethingso obvious yes, the customeris stupid! He mustrealise the advantagesof this wonderful tool, after all if I find it a marvelloustoolit s quite obvious the customer should discoverit s a marvellous tool. I m afraid the customer doesn t understandthat atall ~ he says Tough. I can buy this, that and the other, and I have a salesman dancing in attendance. I think what wouldhelpis if we got our act together with the marketing;if we took things out there into the market place. In the times that we havesat here,all of us talking to ourselves, and wearestill talking to ourselves, we haven t brought in very many people from the outside world to this conference. Afterall this is our private time away from the rest of the world. In thattime, if we had put as mucheffort into spreading the word outside as we haveputinto improving thingsinsidefor ourselves, we could probably have doubled whatis going on, and ensured actual continuity. But the marketplaceis outside andif we followed through(there's a very nicelittle phrase that I have heard in someoftheliteracy campaigns and I think we should adoptit for ourselves; and becauseit s APL we could each doit twice a year.) If we wentinto this and said Eachone, teach one we d betaking that out into the market place. We wouldn t be staying in here. items.title: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 45

reviewed by Dick Bowman

IBM Product 38F1753 (APL2 for the IBM PC Version 1.0). Price £348, available now from authorised IBM dealers.
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: Background
items.text:
Having used APL2 in a mainframe environment for several years I’ve tended to feel a little reluctant to do PC-based development in the recent past; I value the expressive power of APL2’s language enhancements and am frustrated when these things become unavailable to me. I think that one of the essences of APL is fast problem-solving, and the restrictions imposed by the implementations hitherto available in the PC environment can be very real ones. Depending on your particular application they can outweigh the benefits of improved user interface and so forth which are achievable on the smaller machines.

The product at hand is therefore exceptionally welcome; it offers the opportunity to use APL2 on your PC or PS/2 at a reasonable price (and I firmly believe that we have to see APL offered at prices comparable to those of other languages).
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: Hardware Requirements
items.text: In brief, any sensibly-configured PC or PS/2 should be satisfactory; this review was performed using a 640k AT equipped with EGA adapter, monitor and 80287 coprocessor. The product is supplied on both 5.25 and 3.5 inch disks. In fact you also receive two versions of the interpreter, one for 16-bit hardware, the other for 32-bit; regrettably I was unable to investigate the latter.
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: Does It Feel Comfortable?
items.text:
Subjective impressions are hard to quantify, but important; in many ways this is the main question I was looking to answer. What I wanted was a sense that unless I deliberately intended to use specific machine features I should be unconcerned about whether I was using APL2 on a PC or a mainframe system (my reference frame is APL2/370 Release 1.3, running under TSO on Amdahl hardware).

Installation was straightforward, to start APL2/PC there are two steps (easily automated)…

a) Load the APL2 character font; an option provides a 43-line display if you use the EGA adapter - I found it acceptable.

b) Decide which Auxiliary Processors are needed for your session and start APL2 with this set. In fact APs may be added and discarded at will - and there are workspace size benefits from using only the necessary subset. As you correctly surmise, APL2/PC follows the IBM party line about using APs to provide facilities outside the core language; which is alright by me, but it is definitely different from ⎕EVERYTHINGUNDERTHESUN.

Once started there’s a very strong impression of responsiveness which contrasts most favourably with TSOlag. Keyboard layout is ‘IBM normal’ and how you take to this depends on how conditioned you are to expect specific layouts on specific machines - if it’s a problem you can reconfigure the keyboard as necessary; with all of the ‘new’ APL2 symbols present the default layout is reasonable although I’d very much like to see an agreed keyboard once more (both the IPSA ‘union’ and STSC ‘unified’ have their merits, even though they differ from one another). Expected, present, and welcome is a type-ahead facility - something which is annoying by its absence on APL2/370.

You have a choice of interface style; either ‘PC-normal’ with a continuous scroll or a session manager format which is a close approximation to that of APL2/370. Given that the latter is preferable in my accustomed mainframe context I used it most - although given a fully free choice my ultimate wish-fulfillment would be continuous scroll in both environments. The main irritation I get from the discrete-page style of the session manager being that the most interesting bit is always at the bottom of the page; on the mainframe PF8 is an escape valve which allows you to force a page throw. This doesn’t work properly with APL2/PC.

Another (minor?) annoyance stems from my preference to use the non-default DISPLAY HOLD OFF option so that long output sequences come to their natural conclusion without my personal intervention. Although the session manager has a compatible look-and-feel to the mainframe version implementation is different and it’s not possible to save a personal profile; what you have to do is to set the options up as you begin your session (again, you can automate the process).

Having made contact with an unfamiliar APL system my first instinct is to type )LIB and see if there are any interesting toys to play with; APL2/PC provides a novel response in that the display resembles ‘DOS DIR’ format rather than the conventional APL style - there’s more information presented, but it does tend to overflow the page. A full set of workspaces come with the product in the accustomed IBM manner - for the sake of familiarisation I looked at two of them…

AP124 An emulation of the obsolete mainframe Auxiliary Processor 124 for alphanumeric panel use is accessible via this workspace. All the facilities you were accustomed to in the days of VSAPL are present, augmented by functions FSSCAN and FSINKEY providing the immediate response so necessary for PC applications (indeed, all applications) and analogous to STSC’s ⎕INKEY function. I didn’t have enough time with the product to explore the discrepancy between this workspace offering only a 25-line display and the clear evidence that 43-line support is achievable - possibly a documentation problem. GRAPHPAK Another old faithful rears its head; the demo worked fine except that the documented instructions were missing. A major disappointment was that graphics were restricted to CGA compatibility.

At this point I felt that I had established that an APL system existed, it had a fairly familiar feel and seemed subjectively quite fast; the logical next step was to quantify the performance.
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: A Small Application
items.text:
Undaunted, the next task was to look at a small application and assess any problems in its implementation; just to make a change from the routine this was an application which takes data from a digitising tablet and converts to Ordnance Survey grid references. An incarnation using APL*PLUS/PC has been in use for several months, so the requirement is well understood - the questions being how closely would the two versions resemble one another and how ‘usable’ is APL2/PC.

Function editing is the first thing to sort out - APL2/PC has an inbuilt editor which is fairly rudimentary, but a pair of alternative fullscreen editors are provided within one of the supplied workspaces. Most of my time was spent using one of these (EDIT2) - it provides an excellent set of edit capabilities. Nevertheless, it has an inherent problem deriving from its own nature as an APL function; if you edit a suspended function you resume execution with the function as it was before you edited. Which is not particularly good news if you’re trying to do some serious debugging; APL2/PC sorely needs a fullscreen editor like the mainframe )EDITOR 2 (which for all of its defects at least lets you change the suspended function and resume with the new version). Even though EDIT2 is reasonably fast time-lags are noticeable and one might expect an intrinsic editor to be faster.

The next ‘problem’ is language incompatibility with APL2/370; there are a number of problems here which I regret, in particular

a) Restrictions on the use of axis specification

b) Selective specification isn’t implemented at all

I find the latter most intrusive, because it tends to run naturally with the index function (which is implemented) and stylistically I would prefer to live without bracket indexing.

The application in question accessed a digitising tablet attached to the AT’s COM1 port, which led to quite different code detail. The APL*PLUS version takes its input using ⎕ARBIN statements; APL2/PC uses AP232 (in my case via the supplied cover functions). Once acclimatised to the different style everything’s fine and works well - but I can’t underemphasise that this is not just a funny version of the STSC product and that this has to have some influence on your detailed coding. I don’t think either product has a monopoly on ‘good’ - they’re just different and if you can’t personally live with that then too bad. There was originally a problem in getting started, documentation and workspace differing from one another about setting parity options; the resulting error messages are none too helpful. I ran into this generic problem rather more frequently than I would have liked to, I feel that someone ought to smooth out these differences.

Another minor problem encountered with the AP120 session manager was that sometimes overtyped entry wasn’t fully re-executed; most of the time it was alright, but occasionally it wasn’t.
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: Graphics
items.text:
Let’s not beat about the bush; unless you have the readies for extra hardware like the 8514 monitor, or extra software like the Graphics Development Toolkit, APL2/PC graphics capabilities are pretty grim. Grim as spelt C-G-A.

I have a personal bias toward graphic applications, so I felt that after several years of at the very minimum EGA systems, this was more than a little miserable.

What there was worked fine, and if you don’t need graphics it won’t be very upsetting to not pay for what you don’t want. But, if you do, then be ready to spend some more money. As the Enid Lumley of APL I was unable to explore the more exotic alternatives.
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: What Can/Should APL2/PC Be Used For?
items.text:
So far, this might all seem grim reading; but I feel positive about the product - I’m sure it fills at least a niche, and probably a quite large one.

So far I’ve not commented on what I think is the most important innovation APL2/PC brings us - grandly called the Application Package Maker and with a description furtively hidden on pages 347-348 of the manual. What it does is very simple; it takes your APL workspace and converts it into an executable DOS file. Which means that whenever anyone calls you and wants a one-off solution to a computing problem, if you can come up with an APL2 solution then you can package it and ship it out with no fuss or ado about them having to have an interpreter of their own, or a run-time version, or indeed anything that costs money. Economies of scale were always good for multi-copy run-time APL applications, what IBM have done (and, to be fair, MicroAPL before them) is to make APL realistic for the cottage industry.

Another area I see particularly attractive is multi-environment systems; now you can use essentially the same APL on both the mainframe and micro components of the system. I can live with the niggles, if it means I can use the same utility code everywhere.

An option I find surprisingly less attractive is use of the PC as a local responsive development environment; I think the differences from the mainframe product might be more of an obstacle here. I suspect that a great deal of mainframe APL also has to concern itself with interfaces to other systems and languages which by their nature are not present on the PC; also the relatively poor editing options of the present APL2/PC product for me outweigh any gains in responsiveness. Also take a look at those APL2/370 timing figures if you’re embarking on heavy computation.

Other aspects of APL2/PC which could be factors are AP488, which provides an interface to GPIB/IEE488 hardware, and what looks to be a quite detailed explanation of how to write your own auxiliary processors.
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: What Improvements Are Desirable?
items.text:
The most irritating aspect of APL2/PC ought maybe to be the easiest to achieve improvement with; there are too many places where the manual and the reality are inconsistent.

It seems to me that one of the most positive aspects of STSC’s APL*PLUS/PC product is that it has a support structure; this would appear to be a major factor for success and I’d like to feel that IBM could set up a scenario by which APL2/PC queries could be handled promptly and easily (to some extent this also has to come from the users themselves). In all fairness my own problems were always dealt with in an exemplary manner, but I’m a little worried on behalf of Tom and Harry.

Graphics and editing are glaring weaknesses; the former may not concern everybody - but I definitely feel that both need attention.

And for a final shot, I’d like the gap between APL2/370 and APL2/PC to become smaller.
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: Conclusions
items.text: This review may sound negative - perhaps that’s the nature of such things. But I wouldn’t like to leave you with the impression that I condemn the product out of hand. Far from it; I enjoyed using APL2/PC, I intend to switch the PC end of my applications onto it, I look forward to sending out run-only APL applications without an interpreter order form. And above all, I look forward to having some of those end-users decide to try APL themselves because they liked the flavour of what they got.
path: Review: IBM’s APL2 on the PC (16-bit)

items.title: Seize the Time
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 86

by Dick Bowman

People have accused me of being very quiet recently; or busy at other things. Well, maybe, but I’ve come to some sort of conclusion about APL, and it’s one that I feel bears the seeds of being potentially a very positive conclusion. Of course, we don’t have a foregone conclusion. Let’s think about revolutions, and the climate which causes revolution to happen…

Basically we have two ingredients in the revolution which might interest us most within our technical domain; an external situation where there is (or may soon be) a need for vastly increased productivity in building computer applications, and an internal situation where the tools at our disposal have improved significantly in the recent past. Of course, I’m writing here from a very narrow perspective, not one that sees APL as a notational advance for human thinking, just one that builds software to do useful, interesting, or paid-for things.

The first thing that made me realise we have to do something was seeing a flyer for a ‘Rapid Application Development’ conference, which conspicuously (to me) omitted any reference to APL. Now, don’t I remember ‘Rapid Application Development’ being one of the keystones of our existence? Are we being frozen out, or are we freezing ourselves out?

items.title: Productivity
items.text:
At APL92 one of the regular APLxx attendees made a rather surprising remark; I paraphrase him as saying that his company (an APL consulting house) was doing very well out of the recession. So he said it again. Why? Well, where he operates companies are very concerned about getting the most for their money, recognise the productiveness of APL, and as a consequence the demand for APL is at a premium over demand for less productive application building tools.

Here’s one avenue to exploit.

Equally, to stay with this newfound optimism, let’s believe that one day this recession will come to an end. It may happen sooner than we (and our employers, actual or potential customers) expect; the pace of recovery may be much faster once it begins. At this point there are going to be a lot of projects to plan, process models to update and so forth; all things where computing application development is a crucial precursor.

But where’s the mainstream computing world nowadays? Look around yourself and you’ll see the vast majority of ‘for sale’ development happening in C; which is fine for a final product to be sold by the truckful, or to be run over and over again. But have you costed out development in C against use of a high level language? Watch out though, the gap is narrowing.

items.title: APL Advance
items.text:
The new generation of APL interpreters is more interesting than many of us realise; what’s important is that in their various ways they recognise the true significance of both human and software interfaces. Dyalog and Manugistics bring us integration into Windows and other GUIs; APL2 comes as a family of more-or-less compatible products; Sharp APL for the PC provides a realistic APL at a realistic price (take a look at this one, it really is quite something); and MicroAPL gives us access to the Mac. What it’s up to us to do is to begin capitalising on the tools available to us.

Here’s a quote from the latest (November 1992) Byte magazine. ‘… what you mostly need to develop Windows applications at the moment is patience…’ (their italics, page 253). Well, I don’t have a lot of patience, but I do have some tools that let me build Windows applications using APL pretty well. They could be better, but so could everything. We have an advantage right now, we may not have it this time next year.

items.title: Choose Your Applications
items.text:
One of my never-ending problems with APL is affordability, and it’s a situation that probably can’t change overnight. Some of us find scenarios where a single run of an application can justify not only the high-price APL interpreters but also the Sun workstation to use it on; not all of us are so lucky. But generally speaking I think there are two major application scenarios for APL to capitalise on.

  • High value, non-repetitive modelling applications; the sort of place where a program never runs the same way unchanged. These are the people who can afford Dyalog as it’s priced now; they have an excellent starting point.
  • Personal programming, filling in the holes left by ready-made packages, where the programming team is y-o-u; Sharp APL/PC (I forget the precise name) looks good here.

Of course there are other application profiles, and you may very well find that APL is an excellent fit for your purposes in these; but I think that the two above are the most likely candidates for significant growth.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
This is really my point; I think we have to take it upon ourselves to do a lot better here than we have in the past. Look at what the ‘average’ professional C programmer draws on: in addition to the base compiler there are debuggers, profilers, forms designers, utility libraries and so on. It’s all very well for a prominent APL vendor to say that we get all of these inside their package, but my credibility is strained.

My impression of the typical APL programmer’s toolkit is that it takes one of three forms:

  • The stuff that came with the interpreter
  • A ramshackle collection accumulated over the years, or homegrown
  • Nothing at all

This has to change, and pretty dramatically. I think we have to begin a collective programme to build a more comprehensive and universally accepted toolkit. What I want to see develop is a situation where instead of APLers being able to agree on 20% of their known universe they can agree on 80%.

Here’s what I suggest as some significant categories for toolkits:

  • Meta-APL, which expands the common language core (all those APL2 emulations of ⎕VR and so forth)
  • Interfaces, both in the form of software and tutorial documents, so that hooking up APL to popular packages becomes a no-brainer activity
  • Code management systems, for the mega-applications

Of course, this is not going to be a trivial pursuit. It may be a lot less ‘fun’ than exploring J. But it just may be part of the route to earning a better living with APL. It’ll take time and it’ll take money. These tools will have to be paid for, and I’d hope that we move into a mode where APL software is both inexpensive and readily bought and sold. We have to build it for ourselves and sell it among ourselves (just like the antique shops) so that when newcomers arrive they’ll walk into a richer environment.

At the end of the day one of the prime indicators of health in an industry is the amount of third-party activity that surrounds the centre; at present I perceive APL as having very little. I think this will change. I think it has to change.

items.title: Hooking up to the Internet
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 113

by Dick Bowman

As we all know, the population density of APLers is not as high as we might wish; this makes us need to reach around the world to find the number of people we want to discuss APL topics with. Which is a problem, because long-distance phone calls cost money and the propagation delays of paper communications cost us immediacy.

But there is an answer, and I’d like to share with you what little I know so far.

I’ve addressed this to Vector, because the technology is only just becoming readily available to the individual in Britain now; the US has had better access for some time, and many companies already use similar facilities for their national and global communications.

The technology I’m talking about is Internet, and you can recognise someone who has access to it by their habit of sticking an email address with an ‘@’ sign on it to everything they write. I’d been frustrated for some time because I found that people expected me to be on the Internet, but those who were on were exceptionally vague about how it all worked. So I found out, and this is what I want to share with you. None of the services, publications, etc. that I mention here should be construed as being recommended, praised or condemned; they just happen to be sources that I’ve used to achieve successful connection. By the nature of my geographical location my specifics will be specific to a person based in London, but the sources will point you to possibilities everywhere in the world.

items.title: The Internet and Other Nets
items.text:
The Internet is the world’s largest computer network; but that said it’s both anarchic and amorphous. It does not run as a commercial enterprise, so the first avenue for entry (look under ‘I’ in the phone book) doesn’t work. The thousands of computers that comprise the net are mostly in educational and research establishments, and have hooked themselves together on a more-or-less voluntary basis. What you have to be able to do is to reach one of these machines.

Other networks such as CompuServe are not the Internet, although you can exchange email between these networks. Indeed I used CompuServe for this purpose for over a year. It’s not perfect, but it works (within the documented limitations).

items.title: Information Sources
items.text: Try asking around locally; you stand a good chance of success if you have connections into a local college or university. You might also write to RIPE NCC, Kruislaan 409, NL-1098 SJ Amsterdam, Netherlands (phone +31 20 592 5065); naturally they prefer email (ncc@ripe.net). There’s also a book packed with useful information (remember, this anarchy does not provide a user manual) called ‘The Whole Internet Users Guide and Catalog’, written by Ed Krol, published by O’Reilly and Associates Inc. (ISBN 1-56592-025-2).

items.title: Types of Connection
items.text:
From now onward I’m going to assume that you’ve decided to pursue this with the aim of getting your PC connected, because this is all I have personal experience of. The Internet is, to some degree, oriented towards UNIX but it truly is an agglomeration of all sorts of hardware and software. Suitable software for PCs, Amigas, Macs, UNIX and so forth is all quite readily available (and a lot easier to get once you’re connected — this is infuriating unless you feel well motivated at times).

There are two choices to make; either be a user at an established site, or become a site of your own. So if you call up your local college and they say OK you end up as mrapl@uhull.edu.uk (you choose the bit that goes before the @ in your email address). I did it the other way (which lets you choose some of the bit that comes after the @).

items.title: Who Pays for All of This?
items.text:
I just knew you’d ask sooner or later; the glib answer is ‘the US Government, of course’. Yes indeed, ole Mom and Pop in their Kansas grocery store are paying to let you and me exchange email with our pals in the Obninsk nuclear research facility. It’s not quite as ideal as that, but every site covers its own cost as an overhead — you don’t pay Internet Inc. (how could you, they don’t exist).

The corollary to this is that there is a policy of ‘acceptable use’; what you do on the Internet ought to be connected in some sense with education or research. The policy isn’t rigidly monitored, but it would be bad form to take advantage of Internet connections to operate a company email network between your London and New York offices.

What you’ll have to pay is the hardware and software cost of setup, whatever your service provider charges, and telephone costs (to reach the service provider, not the same thing as the services you use).

items.title: The Financial Good and Bad News
items.text:
I connect to a service provider called Demon Internet Services, who are based in London; their charges are £12.50 for initial enrolment and a monthly charge of £10. No usage charges. This is possibly a little more than I used to pay for CompuServe — but all I did there was to send and receive Internet mail.

The financial down side is that your service provider will probably encourage you to use at least a V32 modem (9600 bps); this is not unreasonable from their perspective because they’ve got a finite number of ports and if all of you folks with your ‘by appointment to Queen Mary’ mahogany-cased 300 baud acoustic couplers hog the lines all day then the service provider is going to have to buy some more lines and modems (and pass the cost on). You’ll probably find that it’s good news for you as well, because the modern-day email user has lost the knack for economical mail that always made the I P Sharp system such a pleasure to use.

The financial up side is that you will not need to splash out on a PC comms package, because you’ll get a special one from your service provider. This is because your machine is becoming a full-fledged (if leaf-only dialup) node on the Internet, and this runs on TCP/IP — you’re going to have a whole lot more going on than type a few keys, press Enter, wait for response.

items.title: The Software
items.text:
Once again the hardened Internet nutter is going to tell you to download the software. Great, you don’t have it yet and you’re not paying for that fast modem until you know the service is worth having. Never mind, they’ll probably sober up long enough to send it to you on diskette.

Now, about this software…

It’s awe-inspiring stuff.

Take a backup. Take two, they might come in handy.

What I have is three things called KA9Q, SNEWS and PCELM; they all conspire to work together in one directory — but there are a few loose ends lying around and we’ve ended up with a few new environment variables. Along the way I encountered a totally trashed hard drive, DOS software that insisted on directory names being separated by forward slashes, DOS commands that produced gibberish, a CMOS clock that totally lost track of time and a PC that decided Eastern Standard Time was the timezone to be in.

But it all (sort of) works now, and on a scale of 1 to 10 I rate this stuff as harder than APL, but simpler than Visual Basic. The user interface is rudimentary and I’m not convinced that the file structures are robust enough to survive any sort of software failure. Nevertheless I can do the three major things that I want Internet access for — and who knows, there may be better stuff for me to download (or I might write myself some tools to do some of the manipulations I need).

items.title: Email
items.text:
My principal motivation was to be able to send and receive email. Easy to do — just fire up PCELM and write the messages (handy tip — the PCELM configuration file has a parameter called ‘edit’ that lets you call up a simple text file editor, like DOS’s ‘edit’, a configuration line that says ‘edit edit’ is not the best idea you’ll have all year). Next time you start up KA9Q all your outgoing mail gets sent and you receive all that’s coming your way. This may include mail you sent earlier being bounced back because of bad addresses — although if this happens it often happens while you’re logged on to the network, surprising. Go back to PCELM to read and reply to the mail.

I’d better warn you of two types of characters you’ll encounter sooner or later. There’s the Email Vacuum Pump, who thinks that reading email is an adequate activity and never replies to anything. Then there’s The Phantom, who sends you mail that you can’t reply to because the address they gave you is bad according to the system. Both of these characters are more numerous on the Internet than they are on other systems.

items.title: News
items.text:
News is a sort of mutated mail, that gathers together messages on related topics and sends you the whole lot. You can elect to join news groups, receiving all the traffic and making some of your own if you like. For example, if you have an interest in zymurgy, then there’s a news group. If you have less common interests, then you can join a newsgroup called ‘comp.lang.apl’.

News also makes you realise why that fast modem is important; my first news download got me more than 600 messages — all from my local service providers newsgroups. By the time a mail message has been through the mill a few times with bits appended, and with the Internet routeing stuff glued to the front it can be quite hefty (none of the IPSA To:BOW From: BOW ‘No’ succinctness here).

You elect to join (and leave) mailgroups through all of the software you got as a starter set — mostly it’s SNEWS, but there’s other stuff scattered around as well. Incidentally, you may not get a backlog of news as soon as you join a newsgroup; it took a day or so before comp.lang.apl started to trickle in.

Once your machine has grabbed the news (happens automatically when you dial in) you have to run a local program called UNBATCH to distribute it in a sort of orderly way into the newsgroups you set yourself up with before reading it with SNEWS. As I write this most of mine goes into place called ‘junk’ because I’m being fed more than I’ve organised myself to deal with — but I can still read it there. I get around about 50 news items per day and anticipate this figure remaining fairly constant as I disconnect from the irrelevant and hook myself into the more personally interesting. Thus proving that fast modems do not save money on phone bills — they just let you grab more stuff. A program called EXPIRE lets you clear off the old stuff, but I haven’t found a way yet to build an archive of the interesting ones only, maybe I have to do that myself.

There are literally hundreds of news groups; I downloaded a 500k byte file giving details — it almost certainly is not all that are available.

items.title: FTP
items.text:
File transfer is a real gem; if someone on the Internet with a machine that allows logins wants to make a file available to other users then they can do it. You don’t even need an account on the machine you’re grabbing the file from. The facility is called ‘anonymous ftp’, so if you know what you’re looking for and the name of the machine all you have to do is start up ftp and log on as ‘anonymous’. Even if you don’t know precisely what you’re looking for but you know a place to look you can still log on and move around the directories.

Naturally, there are limits to all of this, and the information providers choose what to put in the accessible places. But if the file’s there, and you’re allowed to reach it, all you have to do is to get it and it’s on your own machine. Remember, this is education and research, no money changes hands; you’re dealing mostly with a country that has open access laws for things paid for out of the public purse.

items.title: Other Resources
items.text:
Krol’s book talks at length about Archie, Gopher, WAIS and the World-wide Web; all ways of helping you find information you need on computers connected to the Internet. Not all of these are available on all hosts, and I really haven’t had time to explore any of it. You may be interested to know that even though Internet really isn’t about APL at all one of the resources singled out by Krol is WAIS. Much of the development for WAIS was done at Thinking Machines — remember them?

Telnet may or may not prove useful; it lets you log on to other computers, wherever they may be, for your local phone call. Not everyone will let you have an account, but some will. Your activity may not be regarded as benign if you use a computer in Japan just for the hell of it. This may rebound on the other people who are benefitting from the appropriate use of a very significant resource.

items.title: Summary
items.text:
This is being written while most of this is very new to me; I would hope that by the time you read it I’ll know much more. I’ve used email as a way of keeping in contact with APLers around the world for several years; it works very well. I thought it was important to write this at an early stage in my direct connection to Internet because if I left it any longer I’d join the ranks of ‘oh sure, just sign up’.

Other networks exist, and their specific natures may suit your purposes very well. Nothing except money makes this an either-or situation. If you’re on another network (like CompuServe) we can still exchange email; we can share more if you’re on Internet directly (and to be fair, you can share things with other CompuServe accounts that you can’t let out to us).

Give it a try, you have only your hard disk to lose. The more of us there are reading comp.lang.apl the more of us there are going to be writing to comp.lang.apl, and the higher the chances of finding really useful stuff every day.

Can’t get the software going? Send me an email.

items.title: Error Trapping Tutorial in Dyalog APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 100

by Pauline Brand (Dyadic Systems Ltd)
path: Error Trapping Tutorial in Dyalog APL

items.title: Background
items.text:
We often give courses to people who taught themselves APL and now have several years’ programming experience to their credit, and we have found that a surprising number of them have not discovered some of the “non-language” features available in most APLs, in particular “error trapping” or “event handling”.

The purpose of this article is to show some of the ways in which the ideas of error trapping can be used to great effect to change the flow of control in a system.
path: Error Trapping Tutorial in Dyalog APL

items.title: Introduction to Error Trapping
items.text:
Most APLs have error trapping facilities in one form or another, but this article discusses the facilities available to a Dyalog APL programmer.

First, we must have an idea of what is meant by error trapping. We are all used to entering some duff APL code and seeing a (sometimes) rather obscure, esoteric error message echoed back:

      10÷0
DOMAIN ERROR
      10÷0
     ^

Now, these sorts of error messages are fine for us clever APL programmers, but meaningless to most of our users. We need to find a way to bypass the default action of APL, so that we can take an action of our own.

Every error message reported by Dyalog APL has a corresponding error number (see the Appendix). Many of these error numbers plus messages are common across all versions of APL. The code for DOMAIN ERROR is 11, whilst LENGTH ERROR has code 5.

Dyalog APL provides system functions and variables that allow you to find out this information without looking it up in the table:

      10÷0
DOMAIN ERROR
      10÷0
     ^

      ⎕EN                           ⍝ ERROR NO FOR LAST ERROR
11

      ⎕EM 11                        ⍝ ERROR MESSAGE FOR CODE 11
DOMAIN ERROR

      ⎕DM                           ⍝ DIAGNOSTIC MESSAGE
DOMAIN ERROR    10÷0   ^
                                    ⍝ 3-ELEMENT NESTED VECTOR OF
                                    ⍝ MESSAGE, NUMBER AND CARAT

      DISPLAY ⎕DM                   ⍝ DISPLAY TO SHOW STRUCTURE
.→------------------------------.
|.→-----------..→--------..→----.|
||DOMAIN ERROR||      10÷0||    ^||
|'------------''---------''-----'|
'∊-------------------------------'

      ↑⎕DM                          ⍝ MIX (↑) OF VECTOR GIVES A
DOMAIN ERROR                        ⍝ SIMPLE MATRIX, WHICH IS
      10÷0                          ⍝ THE SAME AS THE ERROR MSG
     ^                              ⍝ DISPLAYED BY APL

We also need a facility to tell APL “whenever error 11 occurs, instead of doing what you normally do, take this action instead”. In Dyalog APL, we use the system variable ⎕TRAP, which can be assigned a nested vector of trap specifications. Each trap specification is itself a nested vector, of length 3, with each element defined as:

  • list of error number(s): the error numbers we are interested in.
  • action code: Either ‘E’ (Execute) or ‘C’ (Cut Back). There are others, but they are seldom used.
  • action to be taken: APL expression, usually a branch statement or a call to an APL function.
path: Error Trapping Tutorial in Dyalog APL

items.title: Setting a Simple Trap
items.text:
So a single trap specification may be set up as:

      ⎕TRAP←5 'E' 'ACTION1'

and a multiple trap specification may be set up as:

      ⎕TRAP←(5 'E' 'ACTION1')((1 2 3 4) 'C' 'ACTION2')

The action code E tells APL that you want your action to be taken in the function in which the error occurred, whereas the code C indicates that you want your action to be taken in the function where the ⎕TRAP was set; if necessary, APL must first travel back up the SI stack (cut-back) until it reaches that function. These action codes are best illustrated by example.

Let’s try setting a ⎕TRAP on DOMAIN ERROR:

      ⎕TRAP←11 'E' ' ''PLEASE GIVE A NON-ZERO RIGHT ARGUMENT'' '

When we enter:

      10÷0

APL executes the expression, and notes that it causes an error number 11. Before issuing the standard error, it scans its ⎕TRAP table, to see if you were interested enough in that error to set a trap; you were, so APL executes the action specified by you:

      10÷0
 PLEASE GIVE A NON-ZERO RIGHT ARGUMENT

Let’s reset our ⎕TRAP:

      ⎕TRAP←0⍴⎕TRAP                 ⍝ NO TRAPS NOW SET

and write a function to take the place of the intrinsic ÷ …

      ∇ R←A DIV B
[1]     R←A÷B
[2]   ∇

Then run it:

      10 DIV 0
 DOMAIN ERROR
      DIV[1] R←A÷B
     ^

Let’s edit our function and include a localised ⎕TRAP:

      ∇ R←A DIV B;⎕TRAP
[1]   ⍝ SET THE TRAP
[2]    ⎕TRAP←11 'E' '→ERR1'
[3]   ⍝ DO THE WORK; IF IT RESULTS IN ERROR 11, EXECUTE THE TRAP
[4]    R←A÷B
[5]   ⍝ ALL OK IF WE GOT TO HERE, SO EXIT
[6]    →0
[7]   ⍝ WILL GET HERE ONLY IF ERROR 11 OCCURRED
[8]   ERR1:'PLEASE GIVE A NON-ZERO RIGHT ARGUMENT'
      ∇

Running the function with good and bad arguments has the desired effect:

      10 DIV 2
5
      10 DIV 0
PLEASE GIVE A NON-ZERO RIGHT ARGUMENT

⎕TRAP is a variable like any other, and since it is localised in DIV, it is only effective in DIV and any other functions that may be called by DIV. So ….

      10 DIV 0
DOMAIN ERROR
      10÷0
     ^

still gives an error, since there is no trap set in the global environment.

What happens to our function if we run it with other duff arguments:

      1 2 3 DIV 4 5
LENGTH ERROR
DIV[4] R←A÷B
         ^

Here is an error that we have taken no account of. Change DIV to take this new error into account:

      ∇ R←A DIV B;⎕TRAP
[1]   ⍝ SET THE TRAP
[2]    ⎕TRAP←(11 'E' '→ERR1')(5 'E' '→ERR2')
[3]   ⍝ DO THE WORK; IF IT RESULTS IN ERROR 11, EXECUTE THE TRAP
[4]    R←A÷B
[5]   ⍝ ALL OK IF WE GOT TO HERE, SO EXIT
[6]    →0
[7]   ⍝ WILL GET HERE ONLY IF ERROR 11 OCCURRED
[8]   ERR1:'PLEASE GIVE A NON-ZERO RIGHT ARGUMENT' ⋄ →0
[9]   ⍝ WILL GET TO HERE ONLY IF ERROR 5 OCCURRED
[10]  ERR2:'ARGUMENTS MUST BE SAME LENGTH'
      ∇

      )RESET

      1 2 3 DIV 4 5
ARGUMENTS MUST BE THE SAME LENGTH

But here’s another problem that we didn’t think of:

      (2 3⍴⍳6) DIV (2 3 4⍴⍳24)
RANK ERROR
DIV[4] R←A÷B
         ^

Often when we’re writing a system, we can’t think of everything that may go wrong ahead of time; so we need a way of catching “everything else that I may not have thought of”. The error number used for “everything else” is zero:

      )RESET

      ⎕TRAP ← 0 'E' ' ''INVALID ARGUMENTS'' '     ⍝ SET GLOBAL TRAP
      (2 3⍴⍳6) DIV (2 3 4⍴⍳24)             ⍝ AND RUN FUNCTION
INVALID ARGUMENTS

In this case, when APL executed line 4 of our function DIV, it encountered an error number 4 (RANK ERROR). It searched the local trap table, found nothing relating to error 4, so searched further up the stack to see if the error was mentioned anywhere else. It found an entry with an associated Execute code, so executed the appropriate action AT THE POINT THAT THE ERROR OCCURRED. Let’s see what’s in the stack:

      )SI
DIV[4]*

      ↑⎕DM
RANK ERROR
DIV[4] R←A÷B
       ^

So although our action has been taken, execution has stopped where it normally would after a RANK ERROR.
path: Error Trapping Tutorial in Dyalog APL

items.title: Beware of Global Traps!
items.text:
We must be careful when we set global traps; let’s call the non-existent function BUG whenever we get an unexpected error:

      )RESET
      ⎕TRAP ← 0 'E' 'BUG'
      (2 3⍴⍳6) DIV (2 3 4⍴⍳24)

Nothing happens, since APL traps a RANK ERROR on line 4 of DIV, so executes the trap statement, which causes a VALUE ERROR, which activates the trap action, which causes a VALUE ERROR, which …. etc., etc. If we had also chosen to trap on 1000 (ALL INTERRUPTS), then we’d be in trouble!

Let’s define a function BUG:

      ∇ BUG
[1]   ⍝ CALLED WHENEVER THERE IS AN UNEXPECTED ERROR
[2]    '*** UNEXPECTED ERROR OCCURRED IN FUNCTION',⊃1↓⎕SI
[3]    '*** PLEASE CALL YOUR SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION'
[4]    '*** WORKSPACE SAVED AS BUG.',⊃1↓⎕SI
[5]   ⍝ TIDY UP ... RESET ⎕LX, UNTIE FILES ... ETC
[6]    ⎕SAVE 'BUG.',⊃1↓⎕SI
[7]    '*** LOGGING YOU OFF THE SYSTEM'
[8]    ⎕OFF
      ∇

Now, whenever we run our system and an unexpected error occurs, our BUG function will be called.

      10 DIV 0
PLEASE GIVE NON-ZERO RIGHT ARGUMENT

      (2 3⍴⍳6) DIV (2 3 4⍴⍳12)

*** UNEXPECTED ERROR OCCURRED IN FUNCTION DIV
*** PLEASE CALL YOUR SYSTEM ADMINISTRATOR
*** WORKSPACE SAVED AS BUG.DIV
*** LOGGING YOU OFF THE SYSTEM

The system administrator can then load BUG.DIV, look at the SI stack, discover the problem, and fix it.

In many cases, you can of course achieve the same effect of a trap by using APL code to detect the problem before it happens. Consider the function TIE∆FILE, which checks to see if a file already exists before it tries to access it:

      ∇ R←TIE∆FILE FILE;FILES
[1]   ⍝ TIE FILE FILE WITH NEXT AVAILABLE TIE NUMBER
[2]    FILES←⎕FLIB 'MYDIR'                ⍝ ALL FILES IN MY DIRECTORY
[3]    FILES←DBR¨↓FILES                   ⍝ REMOVE TRAILING BLANKS
[4]    →ERR×⍳~(⊂FILE)∊FILES               ⍝ REQD FILE IN LIST?
[5]    FILE ⎕FTIE R←1+⌈/0,⎕FNUMS          ⍝ TIE FILE WITH NEXT NUMBER
[6]    →0                                 ⍝ ... AND EXIT
[7]   ERR:R←'FILE DOES NOT EXIST'         ⍝ ERROR MESSAGE
      ∇

This function executes the same code whether the file name is right or wrong, and it could take a while to get all the file names in your directory. It would be neater and more efficient to take action ONLY when the file name is wrong:

      ∇R←TIE∆FILE FILE;⎕TRAP
[1]   ⍝ TIE FILE FILE WITH NEXT AVAILABLE TIE NUMBER
[2]    ⎕TRAP←22 'E' '→ERR'                ⍝ SET TRAP
[3]    FILE ⎕FTIE R←1+⌈/0,FNUMS           ⍝ TIE FILE WITH NEXT NUMBER
[4]    →0                                 ⍝ ... AND EXIT IF OK
[5]   ERR:R←'FILE DOES NOT EXIST'         ⍝ ERROR MESSAGE
      ∇
path: Error Trapping Tutorial in Dyalog APL

items.title: Cutting Back the Stack
items.text:
Let us consider the effect of using Cut-Back instead of Execute. Consider the system illustrated below, in which the function REPORT gives the user the option of 4 reports to be generated:

                  REPORT

   REP1      REP2      REP3      REP4

                ...  DIV  ...

where REPORT looks something like this:

      ∇ REPORT;OPTIONS;OPTION;⎕TRAP
[1]   ⍝ DRIVER FUNCTIONS FOR REPORT SUB-SYSTEM. IF AN
[2]   ⍝ UNEXPECTED ERROR OCCURS, TAKE ACTION IN FUNCTION WHERE
[3]   ⍝ ERROR OCCURRED
[4]    ⎕TRAP←0 'E' 'BUG'                      ⍝ SET GLOBAL TRAP
[5]    OPTIONS←'REP1' 'REP2' 'REP3' 'REP4'    ⍝ AVAILABLE OPTIONS
[6]   LOOP:→END×⍳0=⍴OPTION←MENU OPTIONS       ⍝ ASK USER TO CHOOSE
[7]    ⍎OPTION                                ⍝ EXECUTE RELEVANT FUNCTION
[8]    →LOOP                                  ⍝ REPEAT UNTIL EXIT
[9]   END:                                    ⍝ NOW END
      ∇

Suppose the user chooses REP3, and an unexpected error occurs in DIV.

The good news is that the system administrator gets a snapshot copy of the workspace that he can play with:

      )LOAD BUG.DIV                       ⍝ LOAD WORKSPACE
SAVED ......

      )SI                                 ⍝ WHERE DID ERROR OCCUR?
DIV[4]*
REP3[6]
⍎
REPORT[7]

      ↑⎕DM                                ⍝ WHAT HAPPENED?
RANK ERROR
DIV[4] R←A÷B
       ^

      ∇                                   ⍝ EDIT FUNCTION ON TOP OF
STACK
[0] R←A DIV B
.........

The bad news is, our user is locked out of the whole system, even though it may only be REP3 that has a problem. We can get around this by making use of the CUT-BACK action code:

      ∇ REPORT;OPTIONS;OPTION;⎕TRAP
[1]   ⍝ DRIVER FUNCTIONS FOR REPORT SUB-SYSTEM. IF AN
[2]   ⍝ UNEXPECTED ERROR OCCURS, CUT THE STACK BACK TO THIS
[3]   ⍝ FUNCTION, THEN TAKE ACTION
[4]    ⎕TRAP←0 'C' '→ERR'                     ⍝ SET GLOBAL TRAP
[5]    OPTIONS←'REP1' 'REP2' 'REP3' 'REP4'    ⍝ AVAILABLE OPTIONS
[6]   LOOP:→END×⍳0=⍴OPTION←MENU OPTIONS       ⍝ ASK USER TO CHOOSE
[7]    ⍎OPTION                                ⍝ EXECUTE RELEVANT FUNCTION
[8]    →LOOP                                  ⍝ REPEAT UNTIL EXIT
[9]   ERR:MESSAGE'UNEXPECTED ERROR IN',OPTION ⍝ TELL USER
[10]   MESSAGE:'REMOVING FROM LIST'           ⍝ ... WHAT'S HAPPENING
[11]   OPTIONS← OPTIONS ~⊂OPTION              ⍝ REMOVE OPTION FROM LIST
[12]   →LOOP                                  ⍝ ... AND REPEAT
[13]  END:                                    ⍝ END
      ∇

Suppose the user runs this version of REPORT and chooses REP3. When the unexpected error occurs in DIV, APL will check its trap specifications, and see that the relevant trap was set in REPORT with a cut-back code. APL therefore cuts back the stack to the function in which the trap was set, THEN takes the specified action. Looking at the SI stack above, we can see that APL must jump out of DIV, then REP3, then ⍎, to return to line 7 of REPORT; THEN it takes the specified action.
path: Error Trapping Tutorial in Dyalog APL

items.title: User-defined Events
items.text:
It would be useful to be able to employ this idea of cutting back the stack and taking an alternative route through the code, when a condition other than an APL error occurs. To achieve this, we must be able to trap on events other than APL errors, and we must be able to define these events to APL. We do the former by using event codes in the range 500 to 999, and the latter by using ⎕SIGNAL.

Consider our system; ideally, when an unexpected error occurs, we want to save a snapshot copy of our workspace (execute BUG in place), then immediately jump back to REPORT (cutback on an event, not an APL error) and reduce our options. We can achieve this by changing our functions a little, and using ⎕SIGNAL:

      ∇ REPORT;OPTIONS;OPTION;⎕TRAP
[1]   ⍝ DRIVER FUNCTIONS FOR REPORT SUB-SYSTEM. IF AN
[2]   ⍝ UNEXPECTED ERROR OCCURS, MAKE A SNAPSHOT COPY OF THE
[3]   ⍝ WORKSPACE THEN CUTBACK THE STACK TO THIS FUNCTION
[4]    ⎕TRAP←(0 'E' 'BUG')(500 'C' '→ERR')    ⍝ SET GLOBAL TRAP
[5]    OPTIONS←'REP1' 'REP2' 'REP3' 'REP4'    ⍝ AVAILABLE OPTIONS
[6]   LOOP:→END×⍳0=⍴OPTION←MENU OPTIONS       ⍝ ASK USER TO CHOOSE
[7]    ⍎OPTION                                ⍝ EXECUTE RELEVANT FUNCTION
[8]    →LOOP                                  ⍝ REPEAT UNTIL EXIT
[9]   ERR:MESSAGE'UNEXPECTED ERROR IN',OPTION ⍝ TELL USER
[10]   MESSAGE:'REMOVING FROM LIST'           ⍝ ... WHAT'S HAPPENING
[11]   OPTIONS← OPTIONS ~⊂OPTION              ⍝ REMOVE OPTION FROM LIST
[12]   →LOOP                                  ⍝ AND REPEAT
[13]  END:                                    ⍝ END
      ∇

      ∇ BUG
[1]   ⍝ CALLED WHENEVER THERE IS AN UNEXPECTED ERROR
[2]    '*** UNEXPECTED ERROR OCCURRED IN FUNCTION',⊃1↓⎕SI
[3]    '*** PLEASE CALL YOUR SYSTEM ADMINISTRATOR'
[4]    '*** WORKSPACE SAVED AS BUG.',⊃1↓⎕SI
[5]   ⍝ TIDY UP .... RESET ⎕LX, UNTIE FILES ... ETC
[6]    ⎕SAVE 'BUG.',⊃1↓⎕SI
[7]    '*** RETURNING YOU TO DRIVER FUNCTION FOR RESELECTION'
[8]    ⎕SIGNAL 500
      ∇

Now when the unexpected error occurs, the first trap specification catches it, and the BUG function is executed in place. Instead of logging the user off as before, an event 500 is signalled to APL. APL checks its trap specifications, sees that 500 has been set in REPORT as a cut-back, so cuts back to REPORT before branching to ERR.

Event handling, which employs a combination of all the system functions and variables described, allows us dynamically to alter the flow of control through our system, as well as to handle errors gracefully. It is a very powerful facility, which is simple to use but is often neglected.
path: Error Trapping Tutorial in Dyalog APL
