items.title: Finnish Forests Conference Reports
items.text:
reported by Adrian Smith (adrian@causeway.co.uk)

“The official language of this conference is APL” Arto Juvonen opening the seminar.

items.title: Journey and Welcome
items.text:
It has become a tradition of the Finnish APL group to gather every spring for a technical seminar on APL-related topics. This year they were a little more adventurous than usual and held the meeting at a splendidly Art Deco hotel a mere 6km from the Russian border.

Arriving at the hotel

The weather was not quite as severe as one might have hoped – only just below freezing with very little new snow. However the venue was very comfortable, the food and sauna was just what you expect from a Finnish trip (excellent), and the APL was consistently interesting and well presented. Many speakers worked partially in English, and most of the other papers had sufficient visuals that there was benefit in simply watching the systems being demonstrated, or in reading the diagrams. Of course from a personal point of view, it was great to meet a bunch of keen, committed developers who are adding to APL’s installed application base with well-crafted professional systems.

items.title: The Hotel and Seminar Facilities
items.text:
The hotel was of the big, solid stone kind with immensely wide, shallow stairs and splendidly cavernous hallways. By contrast, the seminar facility was modern and well thought-out, with comfortable sitting-out areas.

Seminar facility viewed from the hotel

Video-projection was very good, and the 40 or so attendees were able to spread themselves around the tables where everyone could see and hear. There were lots of breaks for coffee and cakes – essential to the success of any technical meeting where people must have the chance to talk as well as sit and listen.

items.title: Actuarial Forecasting Methods Lasse Koskinen
items.text:
This was one of the few papers given entirely in Finnish, but it is so long since I worked with pension data that I probably would have missed most of the technical points anyway. The graphs were interesting though, and gave slightly more weight to my suspicion that a lot of pension funds are in deep trouble and are wondering how to start spinning the message to their subscribers.

The mortality curves which Lasse showed have moved a long way to the right since I last draw these charts (back in 1979), and the contribution curves have moved left, as everyone expects to retire at 60, or even 55. Interest rates are way down, so the compound effect of a shorter payment period, longer-living pensioners and low capital growth makes me wonder how long this system can keep going! And no, I never did ask Lasse what that bump in his graph was ... maybe it was the war?

items.title: Modernisation of the timeseries information systems at Tilastokeskus Jaakko Laasko and Veli-Matti Jantunen
items.text:
Statistics Finland is responsible for a massive database of economic trends data comprising some 50,000 series and around 60,000 lines of text. This is moving from an old mainframe database into a modern Windows-based information system. The system is being redeveloped in Dyalog APL and relies heavily on the tree-control to make sense of the vast hierarchy of data series which previously were accessible only after a long trawl through trees of mainframe menus.

It was also good to see some nice RainPro charts, well integrated into the system, and to find an eager volunteer to help me build proper phrase-table support into the RainPro viewer.

items.title: Vector Markup Language and APL Graphics Adrian Smith
items.text: Rather late in the day, the organisers found themselves with a free slot in the programme so they were subjected to a rerun of my VML talk from Orlando. The full paper is included immediately following these notes, but it is worth mentioning that JASC (the PaintshopPro people) are working on a design tool for SVG (the proposed successor to VML) which gives me rather more confidence that SVG will happen. If you read my VML notes, you will begin to see why I think that this would be a very good thing, and would make RainPro’s life much easier! See www.w3c.org for the latest news and www.jasc.com to download a trial version of their ‘Trajectory’ SVG design tool.

items.title: Modelling Blackjack with APL Ian Clark
items.text:
Once again, we have the full paper for you to read, following these notes. We also have a photo of Ian’s van, snapped by your intrepid Vector newshound at its most northerly location yet!

Yes, Ian drove to Imatra! Makes us wimps who took train, plane and bus feel pretty sheepish.

items.title: Improving APL Performance with J Anssi Seppälä
items.text:
For me, this was by far the most stimulating session given at the conference. I am reminded of Jim Sinclair’s comment at Orlando “If you are coding in the right sweet-spot for the language, you are incredibly productive”.

Anssi works with the electricity supply industry in Finland – we saw his load monitoring and forecasting (straight Dyalog/Causeway/RainPro) system at Lancaster in 1996.

His more recent work has been directed towards the statistical analysis of the quality of the electricity supply (e.g. of timeseries of noise in the networks) which is written in VB with both Dyalog APL and J acting as OLE servers. The Dyalog server is simply to allow him to drive NewLeaf as a reporting tool, but the J server is much more interesting.

The ‘quality’ of the supply is measured by a series of arcane equations which must all be faithfully replicated from the appropriate government documents. Rather than attempting to code these in VB (horrible thought!) Anssi has simply defined a collection of J verbs (like ‘sum’ and ‘mean’ and several much harder ones) which taken together form a ‘little language’ which is specifically designed for the expression of electricity supply quality. Then he can simply give his users a crib-sheet for the language and they can use Notepad to maintain the equations themselves!

With some minor irritations (“Divide – that crazy % thing”) this works really well. The J scripts are both the documentation of the algorithm and the working program; version control is easy and the J project management helps a lot, as the same script can be in several systems, but only gets changed in one place. Anssi commented “the more I can work with text files, the easier it is – I am no longer a fan of the APL workspace”.

items.title: Reporting and control in the Finnish Health Service Richard Eller and Wang Xiao Bei
items.text:
It would be good to have a comprehensive write-up of this system in English! Richard outlined a very complex APL+Win application which was used for invoice matching where the health service had subcontracted laboratory testing.

The gui design was highly complex, as it reflected all the problems inherent in allocation and distribution of invoices, and the subsequent attempts to match payments which might be spread across several invoices.

The system design was made much more ‘interesting’ by the earlier involvement of IBM who had used this as a major pilot project for Lotus Notes. This left the APL system fronting up a humungous Notes database, and the (unsaid) impression was that the database architecture was a classic of an imposed technical solution which was totally unfit for the problem it had been used to solve. As always, the APL systems on show were very reliable, it was Notes that collapsed in a very messy heap and required a full system reset so that the demo could continue!

items.title: Decision-making algorithms in a virtual world Tomas Gustafsson
items.text:
This was one of those talks which could just be appreciated visually rather than technically, although the underlying design is part of a serious system. The slide shows a small aeroplane with a tree growing out of one wing – the whole thing spinning contentedly around in real time.

Tomas’s real application is harbour simulation, and the serious APL interest is in modelling the decision-process of pilots and captains when faced with hazards. This can lead to much more genuine (simulated) reactions of the computer-controlled vessels when faced with threats such as on-coming tankers. However the fun part was APL driving a 3D OCX (unfortunately the company where Tomas found this has gone very quiet of late, so his ‘trial version’ may be the last?) which allowed you to build 3D models very simply and then rendered them for you extremely fast.

items.title: Managing timber movement with APL and MapX Juha Sundström
items.text:
This was a set of simple ideas put together in a very effective way to make a nice robust application. The basic idea is that you click on the map to fire off a database query, which can tell you lots of useful information about the timber located in that part of the forest.

Hopefully the screen-snap gives you some idea of the style of the system – for more background on the exact relationship between MapX, APL, Oracle and the Unix scripts which glue it together, we must wait for an English translation. Sorry!

items.title: Summary and Acknowledgements
items.text:
For me, it was on almost all counts a worthwhile trip. The harder question is whether to recommend others to take the plane/boat to Helsinki to join the Finnish group next year (always assuming they keep the tradition going).

In some ways, it is a little unfair on the Finns if too many visitors turn up, as several of the presenters felt obliged to offer simultaneous translation for the benefit of the handful of non-Finnish speakers in the audience. Clearly, this must reduce the value of the sessions to the locals, as it cuts the amount of material which can be covered in the time available.

On the other hand, we visitors were able to throw some interesting material into the pot, and also to answer a whole variety of APL-related problems, such as ‘why do I keep getting Dels and Deltas around my text vectors when I paste code into Word97?’ (Answer – turn off smart quotes!). I think it depends on the type of paper on offer – the more technical the material the less the language matters!

Finally, a personal ‘thank you’ to Kimmo and Anita Kekäläinen for giving Gill and me the run of their downstairs flat in Helsinki for Friday and Saturday nights. We spent a most enjoyable day in Helsinki on the Saturday, and even managed to persuade the nice girl on the Finnair check-in that it was OK to take a couple of Reindeer skins home in hand-luggage.

items.title: APL for Financial Calculations
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 76

by D.O. Forfar

In 1982, in a contribution to a colloquium on non-life insurance (XVI ASTIN Colloquium, Liege), the Swiss actuary J.A. Bardola concluded that APL was a very attractive programming language for non-life insurance problems.

In a paper to the International Congress of Actuaries (Sydney, 1984), the French Actuary L. Moreau described the use of APL in the French insurance company Assurances Generales de France (AGF) - one of the largest insurance companies in France. The uses to which APL was put were:

  1. the development of APL functions to calculate all actuarial functions - the ‘pocket actuary’;
  2. a system of forecasting financial accounts whereby the accounts for subsequent years were simulated on the basis of certain assumptions;
  3. a model simulating the ‘life’ of 10,000 insurance policies and calculating the profitability of the portfolio of policies;
  4. the checking of mortality tables;
  5. the analysis of the mortality and surrender experience of policies.

A book entitled "APL, the Language and its Actuarial Applications", by S. Stiers, M.J. Goovaerts and J.de Kerf (North Holland) was published in 1987. One of the authors, M.J. Goovaerts, is Professor of Actuarial Mathematics at the University of Leuven (Belgium) and at the University of Amsterdam. The book contains a wealth of examples of the application of APL to problems in finance, life and non-life insurance, credibility theory, statistics, numerical analysis etc.

Papers on the application of APL to insurance problems have also appeared in the journal of the German Actuarial Society. A paper will soon be appearing in the Journal of the Institute of Actuaries (by the author of this note).

There are now a substantial number of financial institutions (insurance companies, insurance brokers, banks, hire purchase companies etc.) in the UK using APL. As will be seen from the references referrred to above there is considerable use in Europe of APL for insurance calculations; indeed its use on the continent may well exceed that in the UK.

The syntax of APL lends itself very well to financial problems - in a sense APL may be described as a natural language for the solution of financial problems. The vector, matrix, multi-dimensional array structure of the language, the special symbols and the use of simple functions as building blocks to more complex functions can be exploited in powerful ways.

We may take a very simple example as an illustration.

We suppose that an insurance company undertakes to make annual payments of £1 on an annuity policy at the end of each of the next n years.

Years          1      2      3              n
         ______________________ .... _________
               |      |      |              |
Payments      £1     £1     £1             £1

For those readers who remember their compound interest the present value of these payments is:

   n
   Σ     1
  r=1 -------
      (1+i)^r

where i is the rate of interest, or in APL:

+/(÷1+I)*⍳N

If the payments, instead of being £1 at the end of each of the years, are (a1,a2,a3……an) then the value ot the payments is +/A×(÷1+I)*⍳N

If the rate of interest is not i, but varies from year to year, being i1,i2,……in during each of the next n years, then the same APL expression holds with I being the vector (i1,i2,……in).

The above is a very simple example of the great economy of expression, without loss of clarity that can be obtained for the solution of financial problems in APL.

My own insurance company (the Scottish Widows’ Fund) uses APL in the Actuarial Department and in the Pensions Department. The Actuarial Department makes extensive use of APL as follows:

  1. Calculation of actuarial functions (the ‘pocket actuary’).
  2. Calculation of premium rates on different actuarial bases - the actuarial assumptions underlying the rates may be changed interactively and the effect on the rates can be seen immediately.
  3. Profit testing of unit-linked products.
  4. Solution of miscellaneous actuarial problems, by developing appropriate APL functions. These can usually be developed very quickly.
  5. A system is available to our branch offices to enable them to request from their branch terminals premium and annuity rates. The system is menu driven and written (in APL) and maintained by the Actuarial Department - with no reference to IT Department apart from the general security/supervisory role. The rates are calculated, when requested, directly from the underlying actuarial bases. Printed books of tables of rates would be so voluminous as to be impracical.
  6. Modelling of the office as a whole. The assets and liabilities of the office are entered into the model which can be run forward either deterministically or stochastically on different future financial scenarios and different bonus strategies investigated and their effect on statutory solvency ratios determined etc.

It has been our experience that actuarial students have had little difficulty learning APL. They have enjoyed using it as they as they have recognised its power to solve financial problems. The use of APL in the Actuarial Department has enabled productivity in certain areas of the department to increase by a factor of between two and three.

items.title: Mr Babbage’s Secret
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 61

by Ole Immanuel Franksen

When Charles Babbage died in 1871, the ‘Times’ remarked in his obituary that he had lived to be almost 80 “in spite of organ-grinding persecutions”. A prolonged opponent of street musicians and other noise pollution was how society remembered him — the genius who declared, looking back upon his life: “The great object of all my inquiries has ever been to endeavour to ascertain those laws of thought by which man makes discoveries”.

Today, Babbage is recognized as the great pioneer of the digital computer. Modern electronics has made his dream come true. To appreciate the significance of this evolution, let me draw a historical analogy with the introduction of logarithms, one of the first practical means for facilitating more advanced computations.

In 1627, after years in the treadmill of arithmetic, Kepler finally published the ‘Rudolphine Tables’. Based on the life-long labour of Tycho Brahe, these tables also contained logarithms, for the first time put to astronomical uses. Kepler became acquainted with Napier’s logarithms some ten years earlier, and he wrote enthusiastically: “A Scottish baron has appeared on the scene (his name I have forgotten) who has done an excellent thing by transforming all multiplication and division into addition and subtraction…”. This enthusiasm did not please Maestlin, Kepler’s old professor, who rebuked him: “It is not fitting for a professor of mathematics to manifest childish joy just because reckoning is made easier.

Since Napier did not as first explain the underlying principle, Maestlin’s remark was not without merit. The potential of technological advances is in the novel principles they uncover. Babbage’s perhaps most successful book: ‘On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures’, support this thesis. Published in 1832, in the midst of the industrial revolution, it is hailed today as a scientific landmark in economics as well as in manufacturing engineering. In it, Babbage carried the concepts and abstract models of description from the world of natural phenomena into the realm of man-made systems. He said in its preface:

“Having been induced during the last ten years, to visit a considerable number of workshops and factories, both in England and on the Continent, for the purpose of endeavouring to make myself acquainted with the various resources of mechanical art, I was insensibly led to apply to them those principles of generalization to which my other pursuits had naturally given rise”.

We are also in the midst of an industrial revolution, brought about by the modern computer. Within a few decades, we have witnessed a rapid change from electromechanical relays to vacuum-tubes, transistors and complex chips. Yet Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws have not changed. Independent of the technological stage, they have ruled the electrical behaviour of the hardware. The means and the emphasis have changed, but the basic principles still hold.

What a contrast to the development on the software side! From the very beginning, we have identified the aim of our teaching with programming — the dull drilling of current technology. Over the years, the adherents of each individual programming language have fought, in the words of Oehlenschläger, the nineteenth century Danish poet, for each their own “little Hassan with the crooked legs”.1 Notwithstanding that education is simpler than re-education, it is re-education which has carried the day. For we have taken no heed of Babbage’s advice to apply “those principles of generalization to which my other pursuits had naturally given rise”.

These other pursuits suggest that we are facing a two-fold problem in our teaching for the future. We need to distinguish between:

(1) A theory, giving the principles or laws of data and data-operations. (2) An art, establishing the empirical guide-lines and preferred standards for systems design.

To recognize this dichotomy between laws of data and guidelines of systems design is of vital importance; for laws of data and data-operations are independent of the changing technology, whereas the art of systems design is not. Both problem areas present formidable challenges which must be met here and now, since each in its way demands adjustments, changes, or even reorientations in our curricula. Note, though, that I am not talking about the development or invention of entirely new ideas or principles. Because, as I see it, the inventions are made, tested and documented in the traditional sciences. What we need to do is to collect them, adapt them and bring them down from the level of the highly-trained specialists.

Piet Hein,2 my fellow countryman who pins down truth by humour in his “Grooks”, once said that humour cannot be defined: — for those who were likely to define it, had no sense of humour. Data is another familiar concept which escapes a rigoristic definition, at least in the scientific sense. The mathematician Gödel proved that in any logically consistent system, there had to be some undefined terms basic to the system. The notion of data is one such basic term common to the various sciences. However, since Galileo the important thing has been, not definition nor explanation, but measurement. For something to classify as a measurement, it must be verifiable, and hence repeatable. In other words, we must be able to identify certain invariant properties or relationships.

The notion of data is closely related to the scientific concept of measurement, since observation and the recording of observations are the only link between the real world and a corresponding theoretical model. Yet, the concept of measurement is strangely absent from our discussion of data and their handling by computers. The fact remains, though, that some of the most important properties of data derive from the invariant scale-form underlying the associated measurements. Common scale-forms are defined across the disciplines, from psychology and sociology at one end to physics and engineering at the other. It lies in the scale-form that it is meaningful to subtract calendar years, but not telephone numbers, and that it is meaningless to take the ratio of calendar years. In fact, scale-forms help us to classify data-operations.

But data are more than mere recordings of individual measurements. I am thinking here of the relationships between data, the so-called data-structures, which always depict certain invariant properties of the system under consideration. The computer is merely a tool whose justification lies in its application for solving problems. The data-structure “measures” the interconnections or interrelations in the applications. Lists, tables, boxes and nested arrays are geometrical representations of these systems properties. Geometry is the fundamental model of description in any scientific discipline, so it would be natural to expect that there should also exist a geometry of data. Indeed, there does; and APL illustrates part of it.

The geometry of data differs from the classical geometries on two accounts. Its spaces are finite, and its binding property is not distance but well-ordering. That is, every non-empty subset has a first element. Certain properties of these subsets, that I might perhaps call data-spaces appear strange at first, because common-sense notions of the conventional metric space break down, such as the usual conception of dimensionality. However, since the geometry of data satisfies Felix Klein’s definition of a geometry, put forward in 1872 in his famous Erlanger Program, this formulation paves the way for the enunciation of laws of data, as we use the APL notation to push this geometry into an associated algebra.

The laws of data are concerned with preservation of properties under various operations. They do not compare with, and they are essentially different from the well-known natural laws of Newton, Hooke, Ohm, Kirchhoff, and all the other classical physicists. Yet, analogies to the data laws, classified mathematically as algebraic invariants, are abundant in modern phsyics and chemistry. The power of adopting this approach is that we are now able to introduce laws in various areas of application: production engineering, management, administrative systems, and modern control theory, for which it has not been possible to formulate laws in the axiomatic sense of classical physics. To illustrate, the bill of materials, the cost aggregation of an assembly, the scheduling of processes, and the state-equations of a control system, may now be explained as similar, so-called isomorphic, data-structures.

Thus, as I have tried to indicate here, a new perspective has opened up towards a geometrical theory about laws of data and data-operations. This theory is in the mainstream of all the other sciences and their areas of application. It is teachable and testable in the conventional scientific sense, and it is essentially independent of the stage of current technology.

Let me now turn to the other problem area we have to face in our education, namely the art of systems design. The building-up of systems is encountered in many disciplines. Still, it has been cultivated in its purest form in engineering, for the essence of this topic area is design. Consequently, many of the basic ideas and approaches to be used in connection with the computer may be introduced by emulation of the time-honoured engineering approach.

However, for our universities and high-schools to adopt the spirit and attitude of design is perhaps the most difficult challenge in our time. The training of our teachers has been geared towards analysis of existing systems emphasizing problems with a unique solution. Now, the computer will force us to complement this type of education with the experimental or cut-and-try approach so characteristic of the design process. We have to emphasize the scaffolding, how to solve multiple-answer problems, and to establish criteria for evaluating the feasible solutions.

Of course, what is important here, is not the actual design, but rather the development of an attitude in the mind of the student: an intellectual courage and certain rather formal working habits. What makes this such a perplexing task, however, is the fact that the student does not command any discipline well enough to actually solve a meaningful design problem. Faced with a series of often trivial and usually uncorrelated problems, the attention is focused on all kinds of side issues, so that when the first excitement of using a computer is over, the desire to learn has become a desire to leave.

What is needed, therefore, is an area of application requiring no or very little prerequisite knowledge, yet complex enough to admit of meaningful or even exciting problems. Also, it should be possible gradually to introduce a rich and inspiring variety of mathematical solution techniques emphasizing the geometrical view on data and data-operations.

This problem as well as the other challenges I have mentioned in relation to the computer education in our universities and high-schools, have much occupied my colleagues in FinnAPL. The excellent ‘FinnAPL Idiom Library’ which they published in 1981, is a tangible result of their thoroughness in this endeavour. So, naturally, during a visit to Helsinki a few years ago, I found myself in the midst of a heated discussion on this vitally important educational issue. My Finnish colleagues were so enthusiastic that, in the spirit of the moment, I somewhat rashly accepted their challenge, later politely formulated as an invitation, to write a book showing how Babbage’s cryptographical hobby could be brought to bear on the teaching of computers. This is the book ‘Mr. Babbage’s Secret’ which, thanks to the gracious support of IBM in the Nordic countries, has been published on the occasion of this conference.

Newton said that if he had seen further than others, it was because he had stood on the shoulders of giants. He immersed himself in the past for the very same reason that the engineering constructor digs into the ground — to secure the future. The more powerful the tool, the greater its potential possibilities, the more we need to have perspective and inspiration. Consideration of the great scientists of the past provides this longer view. From their work on the kind of problems confronting us now, we can learn, to quote Alfred Whitehead, “to see what is general in what is particular and what is permanent in what is transitory”. It is this aspect that makes history fascinating. It is here we may ascertain, as Babbage expressed it, “those laws of thought by which man makes discoveries”.

This historical perspective brings us round a full circle to the starting point of Charles Babbage’s early work on computers. What he and his contemporaries wanted, and what the modern end-users want, is to use the computer as a problem-solving tool. Their interest and effort are in the application. They have no desire to become computer specialists in order to transform their problem formulation into a form acceptable to the computer. Instead, they want the communication with the computer to take place in a form which is natural relative to the problem at hand.

For two reasons in particular, APL represents a breakthrough in this direction. One feature is the reintroduction into computer programming of the fundamental fact that, basically, people perceive data as geometrical objects. The other feature is APL’s elegant and simple mode of interactive communication, offering the user the opportunity of gradually improving his design by experiments. It is noteworthy how well these two features meet the two basic educational needs — in the area of a geometrical theory of data, and in the art of systems design.

I do not intend here to go into the actual contents of my book, except to say that it is centered around the notion of laws of data and the use of the computer as a workbench. APL is applied as a mathematical notation as well as a programming tool to make the approach operational. In fact, some thirty user-defined APL functions are documented in the book and, with a little patience, everything I have done, can be done in a 64 K workspace. Half of the figures are in APL, so together with the terminal sessions APL occupies slightly more than one quarter of the total number of pages. Yet it is no textbook nor an introduction to APL. It is a tale based entirely on historical facts, many of which are published here for the first time.

When Hans Christian Andersen had written his first tales, he turned to the physicist Hans Christian Oersted for advice, whether or not he should publish. Oersted was enthusiastic, and thus became directly responsible for launching Andersen unto his life’s work. What a strange combination: that the discoverer of electromagnetism should counsel the poet on tales for children. Perhaps it was not so strange after all; for Andersen’s tales have that special quality, often lost in translation, that they are ambivalent. Submerged in each tale for children there is also one for adults. Undoubtedly, this was what fascinated Oersted.

Babbage’s preoccupation with secret writing exhibits a similar trait: an exciting hobby and a fascinating scientific work. This similarity made any other form than the tale inconceivable. In Babbage’s endeavours there would be something to inspire teacher and student alike. For he had fun.

In my introduction, I touched upon Babbage’s battle against street-musicians. Let me therefore conclude by recounting a true episode from one of the times Babbage had hauled an offender before a magistrate. The latter asked Babbage whether a man’s brain would be injured by listening to a hand organ, to which Babbage retorted: “Certainly not, for the obvious reason that no man having a brain ever listened to street-musicians”.

Are we listening, or are we just playing it by ear?

  1. Ed.- The cited work will be too well-known to our readers to merit formal reference. ↩

  2. Ed.— Here is an example of one of Piet Hein’s Grooks: “It is sad to lose a glove, but not nearly so sad as losing one glove, throwing away the other, then finding the first again” ↩

items.title: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 116

by Robert J. Frey
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
This paper is a preliminary investigation, motivated by a series of simple examples rather than theory, into how object-oriented (OO) extensions can be made to APL in a parsimonious manner, i.e. in a way which maintains compatibility with the existing language, which introduces few new language constructs and which, most importantly, does not change those characteristics which make APL unique.

The first section contains a brief introduction to OO programming concepts. This is followed by a two-stage description of our proposed extensions. The paper next gives a short critique and suggestions for future research. It concludes with several examples where OO capability yields simpler and more robust designs than are possible in APL. The work here is preliminary, but we have tried to be as complete as possible in the development of our ideas.
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Object-Oriented Programming and System Design
items.text:
Software modularity and reusability have proven to be elusive goals in computer programming. By modularity we mean software elements which: correspond to syntactic units in the language, have explicit interfaces and provide a high degree of information hiding. A modular language allows us to decompose complex problems into subproblems which can then be solved separately. Because such modules tend to be relatively simple and focus on the solution of a single functional requirement, modularity makes software more understandable and encourages the construction of new software elements by combining existing ones in new ways. Finally, modularity restricts the scope of both design changes and execution side-effects to one (or at least a few) modules [Meyer 88].

Reusability imposes certain requirements on modules. First, modules should have a measure of generality: e.g. if we implement a linked list module, then linked lists composed of different types of elements should not require different versions of the module. Second, similar types of module should behave in similar ways: e.g. ordered lists and unordered lists should have many common aspects of behaviour. Third, related functions and data must be grouped together. Fourth, users of a module must be able to use it without knowing how it is implemented. And fifth, related groups of modules should be able to share common parts of their implementations [Meyer 88].

Object-oriented programming languages seek to achieve modularity and reusability through four characteristics: abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Abstraction means that the user only needs to know what a module does, not how it does it. Encapsulation means that the details of both the interface and implementation are grouped together into a unit. In fact, objects are encapsulations of abstractions [Pinson 88]. Abstraction and encapsulation focus on achieving the goal of modularity.

Inheritance and polymorphism on the other hand provide mechanisms for managing objects in ways which enhance their reusability. Inheritance refers to the ability of one object (the child) to inherit some of its behaviour from another (the parent). If a child can inherit from more than one parent, then this is said to be multiple inheritance [Meyer 88].

Polymorphism is the ability to take on more than one form. This is manifested in two ways. First, the same name may mean different things depending upon the type of object being referenced. Thus, if we have a list of polygons, then asking a "square" what its area is calls a different routine than the same request of a "circle". Second, in strongly typed languages it represents a relaxation of type checking to the extent that if a routine calls for an instance of a particular type, then it is also valid to use a type which is a child of it [Meyer 88].

Although the details vary from language to language, objects are typically referenced by an <object><message><arguments> triple. The message generates a call to one of the methods located in object with the arguments given.

The form is often object.message(arguments) as it is in Eiffel, C++, Objective-C and Turbo Pascal. This notation is an extension of structure or record field referencing. For more information readers are encouraged to consult the many good introductions to OO programming such as [Cox 87], [Meyer 88], [Pinson 88] and [Stroustrup 86] in the bibliography.
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Extending a Non-OO Language
items.text:
While there exist languages which were envisioned from the start to be OO, e.g. Smalltalk and Eiffel, many OO languages have been developed by extending an existing language to directly support an object paradigm. Turbo Pascal, LISP, Objective-C and, the best known, C++ are all examples. In fact, the oldest and still one of the best is SIMULA which grew from ALGOL [Meyer 88].

Many of the features of OO design can be used in a non-OO language by establishing a disciplined approach to object definition using a metaphor native to the language at hand. For example, we can bind data and functions together in C by building structures which contain pointers to functions. In C++ this programming-discipline-plus-object metaphor has been replaced by extensions to the language itself. Nevertheless, the motivating metaphor remains: C++ objects look very much like structures. Structures are themselves just the simplest objects, ones containing only data [Stroustrup 86].

We want to extend APL to support an OO paradigm in a way which both preserves the character of the language and still provides abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Given those objectives, we must begin with some native metaphor which gives us most of the capabilities of OO programming in the language as it is now. There are many ways support of OO programming can be added to APL, but most of the obvious ones are precluded by these requirements. For example, adding some form of typing or fixed object definition would change the language in ways we would find unacceptable. Alternatively, binding of data and functions by permitting functions to exist as array elements (or gerunds in J) is extremely cumbersome: arrays do not permit us to reference their elements by name.

What structure exists in APL which can be exploited in this way? APL contains variables, functions and operators (in J, nouns, verbs, adverbs and conjunctions) bound together in a workspace. Elements in a workspace are defined through assignment augmented by a collection of structure functions, such as reshape and transpose. Thus, in APL the most natural mechanism for binding together disparate elements into groups within which they can be referenced by name is the workspace itself.

We propose that the creation of objects in APL be accomplished by binding together variables, functions and operators into a subspace — a local workspace in which all name references are strictly internal and in which communication with the "outside" is accomplished primarily by passing arguments to and receiving results from a set of public functions. Such a metaphor is parsimonious; yet, allows us to introduce a full complement of OO features into the language.

Subspaces will be described in two parts. The first will introduce a single new notational convention into APL. In this preliminary form subspaces provide a facility somewhat more powerful than, say, packages in APL2 or modules in Modula-2, but somewhat less than true classes in a full OO language such as Smalltalk. We have chosen the J dialect of APL [Iverson 91] as the basis for our exposition because it is relatively new and perhaps more amendable, because it appears to be extremely portable, and because its developers have generously released its source code.
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Extending J — The In-Object Paradigm
items.text:
By way of an example, we define an association list subspace. The list. subspace (the period is significant) uses a global noun .data, which is a two-column table of boxed elements. Each row (TAG; ITEM) of .data contains the association tag and data for the list. The noun .data is global only within the list. subspace, and as is true for all objects within a subspace it cannot be referenced directly outside the subspace.

Names can be referenced by identifying the subspace, using the form subspace.name. In the case of .data the "." prefix precludes this form of reference, forcing private usage of the pronoun. Note the conventions introduced so far:

subspace. subspace reference subspace.name reference to name within subspace .name strict internalization of name within subspace

Obviously, subspace names must contain at least two characters; otherwise, there would be conflicts with existing J primitives (such as i. or e.). We assume the session manager has been extended so that the subspace context can be set and that all definitions immediately below occur within the context of the list. subspace.

We will need the following proverbs. Unless otherwise noted they return the final value of .data; this is for purposes of exposition only and is represented schematically by LISTDATA. The non-J character "←" (left arrow) is used below to indicate the type of value returned. The first is a dyadic proverb which creates or re-initializes the list.

usage:        LISTDATA ← TAG  list.create  ITEM
definition:   create =. '' : ' .data=:1 2$x.;y.'

The next is a monadic proverb which tests for the presence of a tag in the list, returning a 1 if found and a 0 otherwise, represented schematically by BOOLEAN.

usage:        BOOLEAN ← list.contains TAG
definition:   contains =. '(<y.)e. 0{"1 .data' : ''

This monadic proverb returns the item from the list given its associated tag.

usage:        (TAG; ITEM) ← list.fetch TAG
definition:   fetch =. '>((0{"1 .data)i.<y.){1{"1 .data' : ''

The last is a slightly more complex example. The dyadic proverb list.insert will add a new item or update an existing one. It uses two private (i.e. private to list. not private to list.insert) proverbs, .add and .replace. Note that the reference is to contains and not list.contains because list.insert executes within the context of the list. subspace.

usage:         LISTDATA ← TAG list.insert ITEM
definitions:
     .add =. '' : ' .data=: .data, x.;y.'
     .replace =. '' : '.data=:(x.;y.)((0{"1 .data)i.<x.)} .data'
     insert =. '' : 'x. ((.add' .replace)@.contains x.) y.'

Here is a sample session using the list. subspace:

   'abc' list.create 10 20 30
┌───┬────────┐
│abc│10 20 30│
└───┴────────┘

   'def' list.insert 100 200
┌───┬────────┐
│abc│10 20 30│
├───┼────────┤
│def│100 200 │
└───┴────────┘

   list.contains 'abc'
1
   list.fetch 'abc'
10 20 30

   'abc' list.insert 50 1000 2 10 3 5
┌───┬────────────────┐
│abc│50 1000 2 10 3 5│
├───┼────────────────┤
│def│100 200         │
└───┴────────────────┘

   list.contains 'yz'
0

   'yz' list.insert 1 1 2 3 5 8
┌───┬────────────────┐
│abc│50 1000 2 10 3 5│
├───┼────────────────┤
│def│100 200         │
├───┼────────────────┤
│yz │1 1 2 3 5 8     │
└───┴────────────────┘

  list.contains 'yz'
1

Note that .data is not directly accessible outside the subspace, although later we will provide a general mechanism for by-passing the interface to reference private names. Users of list. do not need to concern themselves with implementation, only usage. If we wanted to give a user read only access to .data we could define a proverb:

getdata =. ' .data' : ''

We can assign one subspace to another; "inheritance" for subspaces is handled as inheritance for other elements in J, by "assignment" suitably augmented by "structure functions":

anotherlist. =. list.

This sentence would duplicate the elements of one subspace in the other. If we executed anotherlist.create, the create proverb would execute in the context of the subspace from within which it was called. Thus, the .data pronoun that was re-initialized would be the copy in anotherlist. while the copy in list. would remain unchanged.

As it does in J normally, a simple assignment of one subspace to another results in inheritance by reference for verbs. Invoking a proverb in anotherlist. causes the associated proverbs in the original list. subspace to be called, but that execution would occur in the context of the anotherlist. subspace. If we wished to accomplish inheritance by value, then we would apply the fix adverb f. as follows:

anotherlist. =. list. f.

This would result in an actual copy of verb values from one subspace to another.

The difference is important. In the first case changes in list. would be reflected in anotherlist. and in the second the two subspaces would have independent existences. The precise mechanisms of inheritance would be different for different dialects of APL, but we would certainly always want to be able to control which sort of inheritance, by reference or by value, we were applying. This allows us to set up subspace prototypes without introducing strict typing into the language. Multiple inheritance could be supported by having the "methods" of a particular subspace refer back to more than one prototype.

Subspaces in their current form give us a capability somewhat more than simple modules as in Modula-2, Ada and some Pascals because they function as more than simple libraries of procedures and functions with a well-defined interface. Each subspace is an independent context, and one would anticipate that multiple instantiations would be the rule. Also, real inheritance is provided for in this scheme.

As a matter of fact, subspaces alone add a number of capabilities to APL and J that are extremely useful. For example, we can have verbs with static nouns (nouns with values that persist between calls), record structures (subspaces consisting only of nouns), program modules and libraries and simple objects such as our list. subspace above. All this goes a long way towards satisfying our original goals of modularity and reusability even if it falls short of full OO capability.
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Extending J — The On-Object Paradigm
items.text:
To see where subspaces fail to give us full OO capability, we’ll return to our simple example. Assume we have two lists, alist. and blist., which we wish to merge and assign the result to the alist. list. A natural expectation would be to define a monadic proverb merge in the alist. subspace which is used:

alist. =. alist.merge blist.

This is a more general use of subspaces because it involves an operation on a subspace rather than in one. To accomplish this extension we introduce one new conjunction ::, which returns the entire subspace upon completion. There are also two prospaces, L. for the left subspace argument and R. for the right. And we must have a conjunction s. to force a reference in one subspace to execute in the context of a specified subspace. Then merge can be defined:

merge =. 'insert"1 R. s. .data' :: ''

Definitions made with the : conjunction use the "in" paradigm and definitions made with the :: conjunction use the "on" paradigm. It is through the s. conjunction that inheritance from prototypes is accomplished. Thus, in our original example if the anotherlist. subspace inherits from the prototype-parent subspace, then a verb method in the child becomes:

list. s. method

… in the child.

We must also be able to treat subspaces as we would any other first-class object. For example, if we have a subspace employee_record. containing only the pronouns name, id_number and address, then

employee_record.name list.insert employee_record.

… would insert that subspace as an element in the list. subspace. Note that what is stored is not a reference to employee_record. but its value. If we subsequently deleted the named subspace then the list would still contain those values. Thus, subspaces do not need to be named explicitly, any more than, say, the elements of a numeric array need to be individually named.

It is clear that unless we can use subspaces as software elements in their own right, and not simply as a way for grouping references, we do not have a true OO programming language.
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Review and Critique
items.text:
Have we achieved the four capabilities required for OO programming: abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism?

Subspaces are true abstract data types. Users need only concern themselves with the interface and not the implementation. We could change our list. subspace in some very fundamental ways, e.g. making it file-based rather than using an in-memory array, and, as long as we did not change its interface, not a single line of user code would need to be changed.

Encapsulation is achieved by clearly separating public and private names. The interface between a subspace and the outside world is clearly defined. A limited form of access to private references is granted via the new s. conjunction.

Inheritance for subspaces is handled as it is for any other object in APL or J: by assignment augmented by appropriate structural operators. We further assume the session manager is extended so that a user can "enter" and "leave" a subspace so that the construction of a subspace can also proceed in the same way a user creates a workspace now. Multiple inheritance is supported.

Finally polymorphism, it turns out, is easy. APL and J are naturally polymorphic. Because they are not statically typed, there is no need to employ special mechanisms which allow for type generalization.

One concern one may have is that subspaces encourage the use of side-effects. Clearly, if one’s ideal of programming is to use tacit programming in J to produce pure functions, this will be of some concern. However, properly constructed subspaces will encapsulate their state in private names and, hence, will not have side-effects.

Anyone who has worked on large APL-based systems has had the experience of seeing a clear and coherent design become obscured in implementation by the large number of global variables and low-level support functions that inevitably seem to clog up the workspace. It is little comfort that we have avoided side-effects in our functions when our workspaces are littered with them.

The ability to group variables and functions into packages, as is possible in some APLs, is a major advance, but falls short of providing all the capabilities we need to begin to build modular and reusable software in a disciplined manner. Packages do not go far enough and are too difficult to use. They are not really part of language.

Another issue is that of efficiency and complexity. As the depth and size of the inheritance tree grows, there is a real possibility that the overhead required to call functions, and the difficulty of understanding the system in toto, will become too great to be tolerated. Experience with Smalltalk, however, has shown this not to be the case. It should be possible to design an OO-extended APL or J interpreter which both performs well and is adequately supported by tracing and browsing tools. In fact, because many operations will occur using ordinary APL and J primitives (unlike Smalltalk where everything is an object including integers, characters, etc.) it should be possible to produce interpreters which have significantly better performance than found in Smalltalk.
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Some Applications
items.text:
Here are some possible applications. Consider static nouns in verbs: there are many instances where some notion of state must be encoded in one or more global variables. For example, in a pseudo-random number generator, the next number in the sequence is calculated by applying some function to the previous one.

Subspaces consisting only of nouns are record-like objects which nevertheless do not impose static typing on the language and maintain APL’s characteristic flexibility. A vector, each element of which is a boxed subspace of "employee records", is a much easier thing to work with than a matrix in which we must know the convention that column 1 is the name, column 2 the address, etc.

Standard libraries or software modules can be implemented with subspaces. For example, a time series "library" subspace can be designed so that it expects input in the form of some "record" subspaces which have "fields" describing the start and end dates, the frequency (daily, monthly, etc.) and the time series data themselves. It would be easy then to define a library function that could add together two time series, producing as a result a new time series containing the sums at their intersecting dates.

Another example where software modules would be useful would be as interfaces to external processes or devices. Graphics is a good example in which a module interface which hid global variables and low-level functions would be welcome. A database interface is another.

OO languages are inherently extensible. SIMULA, although it is often characterized as a simulation language, is actually an OO language which has been extended using its native facilities to support discrete event simulation [Meyer 88]. The same could be done for an OO-APL. Artificial intelligence is another area in which language extensibility could be exploited.
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Conclusion
items.text:
Subspaces are a simple and parsimonious way to introduce many useful extensions into APL; the most significant of which is to support a full object-oriented model. As experience with Smalltalk has shown, efficient and usable interpreters and environments can be implemented, and there is every reason to expect that an OO-extended APL or J could implemented even more efficiently.

APL is extremely powerful, but it is not particularly extensible and does not adequately support information hiding. These shortcomings can make it unnecessarily difficult to design, implement and manage medium to large systems. It is time we rectified these deficiencies.

Robert J. Frey, Ph.D Renaissance Technologies Corporation 100 North Country Road Setauket, NY 11733, U.S.A.
path: Object Oriented Extensions to APL and J

items.title: Matrikx Reloaded
items.text:
by Simon Garland (simon@kx.com)

Although the array language K is immediately accessible to programmers familiar with APL or J, comparatively few have spent any time looking into it. For anyone who wants to add a new language to their toolkit this short article describes how to download and install a trial version – and points to further information for those who would like to learn more.

items.title: Installation:
items.text:
Download and run a copy of kdbsetup.exe from the download page [2] of the Kx website [1], this 200K file will install the array language K and the database Kdb. It will install on any dialect of Windows, although NT or XP are more comfortable to use as the 95/98/ME command prompt is so clunky.

The trial version has restrictions on the amount of data it will work with, and the number of messages that can be sent between K sessions – but otherwise is a full version.

items.title: Try K:
items.text:
Open a command window, and type

k

and you’ll be in immediate execution mode in a K session, try a few familiar things:

C:\k>k
K 2.95t 2003-04-03 Copyright (C) 1993-2003 Kx Systems
Evaluation. Not for commercial use.
\ for help. \\ to exit.
  2+2
4
  2+2 3 4
4 5 6
  +/2 3 4
9

to get out just type \\ in immediate execution mode.

K includes a built in reference, access it by typing a single \ followed by a return in immediate execution, that will give you a list of pages available. Enter the particular one you want to see (\+ to list the verbs for example).

If you type something complicated and get suspended you can clear the execution stack with a single \ at the suspension prompt. Here a nonsense function foo is defined to add its argument to a string and cause an error:

  foo:{"string"+x}
  foo 17
type error
{"string"+x}
         ^
>  \

If you just want to disable suspensions while looking around enter the command \e 0 on a new line – the error will still be displayed but the stack will be cut back:

  \e 0
  foo 17
type error
Try Kdb:

Get out of your previous K session if you still have it open by entering \\ and then start a Kdb session by entering:

k db
this time you’ll be in a kdb session as shown by the ksql> prompt:
C:\k>k db
K 2.95t 2003-04-03 Copyright (C) 1993-2003 Kx Systems
Evaluation. Not for commercial use.
\ for help. \\ to exit.
KDB 2.5t 2003-06-25
ksql>

as Kdb is a database we’ll load in a sample database to make things more interesting, at the ksql> prompt type in:

ksql>load 'trade.t'
ksql>
Note the single quotes, strings are delimited by double quotes in K, single quotes in Kdb – that makes it easier to embed KSQL strings in K code.
Now try some simple KSQL:
ksql>tables
`stock `trade
ksql>vars stock
`stock `industry
ksql>count stock
6
ksql>select from stock where industry='auto'
.((`stock
   `xx `yyyy
   .,(`K;1;))
  (`industry
   `auto `auto
   ))
ksql>count trade
100000
ksql>vars trade
`stock `price `amount `date
ksql>select avg price by stock from trade
.((`stock
   `aaa `bbb `ccc `dd `xx `yyyy
   .((`T
      ,`stock
      )
     (`K;1;)))
  (`price
   74.93937 74.93437 74.89528 74.95792 74.73562 74.71044
   ))
ksql>

Notice that the table columns are just vectors: At last – a database that you can work with not against/despite! You can open a simple viewer on the database by typing in:

ksql>show ''

or you can view the results of a query by prefixing a show to the constraint:

ksql>show select avg price by stock from trade

you can escape from Kdb to K by entering a single \ at the ksql> prompt

ksql>\
  2+2 3 4
4 5 6

and you return from K to Kdb by entering .d.l`

ksql>\
  count stock
value error
count
^
parse error
  .d.l`
ksql>count stock
6
ksql>

exit from a Kdb session with \\ as you would from a K session.

Summaries of KSQL, and the Kdb SQL92 implementation can be found in the two files s.txt (SQL92) and t.txt (KSQL) in the directory c:\k\db created when you installed kdb earlier.

items.title: Documentation:
items.text:
If the 5-10 minutes it took to try this out has caught your interest the best way to learn the basics of K and Kdb is to read through the Kdb manual Getting started with Kdb available from the Documentation page [3] on the Kx website. Although its focus is on Kdb it takes you through the basics of K as well.

Apart from the other manuals on the Documentation page [3] there is a K reference card available from Mike Powell’s directory on the User Contributions page [4].

When learning a new language it’s often helpful to have other people’s code to read, there is a large library of K and Kdb code on the Kx site in Arthur Whitney’s directories [7].

More general articles about K and Kdb are indexed on Eberhard Lutz’s Kaylang page [8]
