items.title: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 49

by Neville Holmes
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Abstract
items.text: This paper briefly describes proposals for a standard general purpose arithmetic called composite arithmetic, gives special attention to the register form of that proposal, reviews some of the basic functions needed for that arithmetic, compares those functions to the practice followed by APL and J, and urges the APL/J community to support and contribute to the establishment of a standard for composite arithmetic.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
That a recently published proposal for a standard for general purpose arithmetic[1] should have an APLish flavour is not a coincidence. The proposal followed directly from dissatisfaction with the ideas expressed in an earlier paper published in Quote-Quad[2] which itself arose from a consideration of extensions made by J[3] to the system traditionally used by APL to represent numbers.

The proposal also embraces a viewpoint on automatic calculation which characterizes APL and other typeless programming notations, the viewpoint which holds that users of a notation should not have to make decisions about how numbers shall be represented that could be better made automatically.

The composite arithmetic proposal goes further than this in holding that calculations that can be done exactly should be done exactly, and if they can’t then the trustworthiness of their results should be made plain. In this, the proposals go beyond APL’s present compass.

Adherence to these principles means that the representation of numbers and the machinery that is needed to work on those representations are more complex than say the traditional so-called floating point representations and machinery[4]. But composite arithmetic can also be more reliable under the kind of extreme conditions that the users and designers of APL interpreters take pride in being able to deal gracefully with. And improved technology now makes such complexity practical.

The purpose of this paper is to outline the central area of the composite arithmetic proposal, and to disclose some of its difficulties, in the hope that APL people might bring their very particular experience in the area to improve the proposal and to promote work towards getting a general purpose arithmetic standard adopted.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Composite Arithmetic
items.text:
The proposal for composite arithmetic proposes three forms for the representation of numbers, where by forms is meant sets of closely related formats.

  1. Storage form is for the efficient storage of numbers in data and program files. Binary encoding is used.
  2. Register form is for the effective storage of numbers undergoing arithmetic. Binary encoding is used in a long accumulator format [5].
  3. Display form is for the clear and truthful display and input of numerical values. Character encoding of a variety of decimal representations is used.

Since all arithmetic is carried out notionally on register form values, all conversions between forms are as shown in the following diagram.

┌─────────┐         ┌──────────┐         ┌─────────┐
│ storage │--->-----│ register │---<-----│ display │
│  form   │---<-----│   form   │--->-----│  form   │
└─────────┘         └──────────┘         └─────────┘

The main concern of this paper is to consider the operation of some of what to APL people are primitive functions, otherwise to be known as arithmetic operations. The results that can be given by these functions are limited by the means available to represent those results in register form. Therefore the main explication of this paper must be preceded by a short description of register form.

The proposed composite arithmetic anticipates that results, though they are always produced in register form, will normally be stored in files in much shorter storage form[6], and presented to users, and keyed in by them, in the much more familiar display form[7]. Register form, being much longer, is not expected to be used normally for the long term storage of results.

Values are encoded binarily in register form, but, for the purposes of explanation here, a decimal encoding is needed for use in explanations. In what follows, it is therefore convenient to use the proposed composite arithmetic’s display form conventions in giving examples and values. The following summary merely gives a basis for understanding display form, in advance of explanation of different kinds of values as they are needed in describing register form. A summary of display form is given in a companion article in APL Quote-Quad [7] prepared before this one.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Display Form
items.text:
The approach suggested for the display form of composite arithmetic is to suppose a poor character set (such as ASCII or EBCDIC) and a rich character set (such as is easily supported by modern printers), and to define alternative usages for the two. Because this paper is being keyed in on an ASCII machine, only the poor alternative is used here.

The decimal digits are the basis for display form. However, composite arithmetic requires that credible digits be distinguished from dubious digits. In this paper the underline character signals the onset of dubiety. Thus 1234 represents an exact value. However, 12_34 represents an uncertain or inexact value, but guarantees that it is somewhere in the range 1184 to 1284 including both the extremes and all the integral and nonintegral intervening values.

Beyond the digits themselves, certain punctuation marks are used to compose number representations. These are shown in the following table alongside examples of their usage.

¯ negative sign ¯1 negative one . fraction point 0.1 one tenth r denominator point 1r2 one half k scaling up point 1k2 one million m scaling down point 1m2 one millionth
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Register Form
items.text:
Register form comprises four formats, all of the same length, namely 4096 binary digits. Which format is used depends on the kind of value loaded into it from one of the other forms, or from a calculation. The arithmetic chooses the format, not the programmer.

┌──────┬─────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ tags │         v a l u e       │      f i e l d ( s )     │
└──────┴─────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
4095   4091                     2047                         0

The first four bits of register form are used for tags. The first two tag bits specify the format in use, along the following lines. (The original proposal [1], for simplicity of presentation, described only three formats, subsuming the integer within the rational.)

00 exact integer 2s complement 01 exact rational signed 10 inexact fractional 2s complement & signed 11 inexact logarithmic 2s complement & signed

An integer of format 00 takes up all the bits that aren’t tag bits, all 4092 of them, but the other three formats have a separation point in the middle of the form, so that for format 01 the low order denominator is 2048 bits long and for the other formats the same low order 2048 bits are used for the fractional part of the representation. The numerator of format 01 is 2044 bits long, and the sign of the rational value is kept in the fourth tag bit.

Between them, formats 00 and 01 allow exact arithmetic to be applied to a great range of values, typically to produce exact results. Whether or not such results can be put into exact storage or display forms is another question, but the arithmetic is without error of calculation on such values. The provision of a rational form means that even divisions are carried out exactly for typical exact divisors and dividends.

Certain special values are standardly represented. Exact zero and two infinities, represented strictly as 0 1r0 and ¯1r0 in display form, are coded in the third and fourth tag bits of format 00. Indefinity, a value including arithmetic indeterminacy [8] and represented strictly as 0r0 in display form, is coded in the third tag bit, and the arithmetic sign is coded in the fourth tag bit, of format 01. Other special values are coded into inexact formats, but inexact formats are more complex, and need particular explanation.

The sheer size of register form means that the majority of inexact arithmetic, the arithmetic customarily carried out on so-called floating-point representations [4], is actually carried out on very long fixed point representations, and so has the potential to give very accurate results.

It is perhaps worthwhile to review here the difference between accuracy and precision, given that the terms are often confused [9]. Precision is about how exact the representation of a number is, whereas accuracy is about how well the representation expresses the value it represents. Thus, 3.24159 is precise to five decimal places, but as a value of π it is not even accurate to one decimal place.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Inexact Formats
items.text:
Two register formats are proposed to hold inexact values. These formats are more complex than the exact formats because they are designed to keep a record of accuracy. For this, both formats include a pointer to the last credible bit in the value, that is, to the rightmost bit of completely reliable value. The other bits are here called "dubious". Thus the arithmetic is required to keep track of reliability. Note that the dubious bits are not negligible because they mark the centre of the interval of unreliability. (The original proposal [1], again for simplicity, only mentioned reliability tracking in passing, but its importance warrants its inclusion in composite arithmetic from the beginning.)

┌──────┬───────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ tags │ doubt │  i n t e g e r   │      f r a c t i o n     │
└──────┴───────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
4095   4091    4079              2047                         0

Both the inexact register formats hold signed values with a fractional part, and in twos complement form.

The first inexact format (10) keeps its value directly, the second (11) keeps its value as its binary logarithm. The long accumulator design of the register [5] means that the vast majority of inexact arithmetic can be done in the first format, and the second format is called into use only when results from the first format overflow or threaten to lose accuracy.

Certain special inexact values need to be held in register form. The first such class of special values is that of the inexact zeroes, and the second class is that of the reciprocals of such values. These two kinds of values are effectively intervals which include zero or infinity. The third tag bit signifies which class, and the inexact infinities are represented by their reciprocal, which is apt because they are usually generated by an inexact zero divisor. An interval including both positive and negative values is called "double", the other kind "single".

These special inexact values arise, because inexactness is being acknowledged and kept track of, when all significant digits are dubious. The arithmetic intended for inexact values is a kind of interval arithmetic [10]. The proposed standard does not constrain the arithmetic to this particular kind of arithmetic, but does require any arithmetic operation to maintain at least as much accuracy as arithmetic carried out directly on register form would. An implementation could include better arithmetic, but the arithmetic implied by the register format as defined is a kind of hybrid of conventional range arithmetic [11] and significance arithmetic [12].

In inexact register formats, the full value normally gives the centre of the interval, and the doubt pointer indirectly gives the width of the interval. In the primary format the centre is the arithmetic mean of the ends of the interval, in the secondary format it is normally the geometric mean. Inexact infinities in either format, and all double intervals in secondary format, need exceptional representations which it is not relevant to review here.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: The Arithmetic
items.text:
The results of any arithmetic, that is, of the application of any arithmetic operations to register form values, is straightforward for straightforward values. But there are two broad classes of values that are not straightforward, the inexact and the special.

An examination of the arithmetic of certain operations, then, is largely an examination of the results when they are applied to inexact and to special values.

However, there are some general rules. Indefinity yields indefinity. Otherwise, inexactness yields inexactness. Otherwise, exactness yields exactness.

Of course, the application of such rules depends on the particular arithmetic operation. The arithmetic operations are what APL has traditionally called primitive functions. Since it is usual in discussions of computer arithmetic to talk of instructions operating on data, the APL tradition is inappropriate here, but it is useful to contrast monadic operations and dyadic operations.

Just what operations are provided in a standard is a matter that can only be decided after considerable discussion. Basic monadic operations like negation and magnitude and maybe reciprocal are necessary, and the dyadic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division are also necessary. And there are many other possibilities which would spring to the mind of an APLer.

There are other operations which might be considered necessary to deal with some of the aspects peculiar to composite arithmetic, in particular to inexact representations.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Operating on Instructions
items.text:
A primary requirement is to be able to test whether a value is exact or not. But this test should not be considered in isolation. Given that testing is needed, what tests are needed beyond exactness?

The traditional tests result from comparison of two values, and are basically tests of whether the first value is equal to, or is greater than, the second, or some combination of these two and their opposites. For exact values in composite arithmetic, these tests are straightforward, and could easily be specified and provided. But it is not so for inexact or special values. It is extremely unlikely that one instance of _1 (not negative, but entirely dubious, being in display form a particular value somewhere between ¯4 and 6) would equal another, or that _1 would equal _01, and it is at the very least debatable whether 1r0 even equals itself.

The way around this is to revert to the idea that comparison is fundamentally testing the nature of the result of a subtraction of the two values being compared. Under composite arithmetic there is a need to be able to test for different kinds of values, and comparison can then be subsumed under such testing as simply the special case of testing the result of a subtraction.

Values can be different in kind along three dimensions, namely

  • exact/inexact
  • positive/negative/signless
  • normal/indefinite/infinite/zero,

where "signless" is meant to include the ambiguity of a double interval of uncertainty in the case of an inexact zero or infinity. These three dimensions are not truly orthogonal since some combinations cannot occur, for example, an exact signed zero. It is maybe also necessary to be able to test whether a value is primary or secondary, but this is somewhat redundant.

In the case of comparison, now, the subtraction of two normal values would yield an exact zero if they were both exact and equal, and an inexact zero if either or both were inexact and the two were possibly equal.

It is of interest to note that there is not, in composite arithmetic as described here, any need for the comparison tolerance familiar to APL users. Comparison tolerance is fairly complex because it is a regularly implied doubt intermittently applied. In composite arithmetic, the comparison of two exact values is, appropriately, exact. If at least one of the values is inexact, then the actual tolerance is not absent but implicit in the result.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Monadic Arithmetic Operations
items.text: Only the relationship between one value and its result need be considered for monadic operations in composite arithmetic. In this sense they are simpler than dyadic operations. Of main interest is the behaviour of different kinds of values rather than of any specific value.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Negation and Magnitude
items.text:
Negation and magnitude operations are closely related. In both, negative values are converted to positive values of the same magnitude. Otherwise, for negation positive values are turned to negative ones of the same magnitude.

Indefinity and exact zero are unchanged by the operations. Exact values yield exact results, except only for the lowest possible integer value, whose positive equivalent cannot be represented exactly in register form. Interestingly enough, this maximum negative integer value would have to converted straight to secondary inexact format because it would be much too big for the primary format.

Inexact values yield inexact values with unchanged doubt, again except only for the lowest possible primary value, which would have to be converted to secondary, or maybe to the maximum positive value with an extra bit of doubt.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Floor and Ceiling
items.text:
Floor and ceiling monadic operations, familiar primitive functions for experienced APL people, have a lot of interest in composite arithmetic because they can change the very nature of a value, for example by converting an inexact value into an exact one. The two operations can be considered together, as the ceiling operation is only systematically different from the floor in a fairly obvious and consistent way.

Firstly, exact infinities and zero, indefinities, and integer values would all be unchanged. All rational values would be changed to integers. Some inexact values could be changed to integers, providing their interval did not have an integer value within it, and this could apply also to inexact zeroes with single intervals.

Inexact values whose doubt extends their interval across at least one integer, in particular all inexact zeroes with double intervals and all inexact infinities, would remain inexact, though their centre point might change. Indeed, just what the change of centre point in these cases should be could make an interesting study.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Centre and Tolerance
items.text:
Operations that provide a breakdown of inexact values are needed, and the two obvious ones would give the centre of the interval of uncertainty and its radius (or tolerance). From these two values the limits of the interval can be calculated simply by addition and subtraction for all but inexact infinities.

Applied to exact values, the centre operation leaves the value of its operand unchanged, and the tolerance operation yields an exact zero. This can fairly arbitrarily apply also to indefinity and exact infinity. Inexact values never yield a tolerance of exactly zero, so taking the tolerance of a value also provides a check on whether it is exact or inexact.

For inexact values the centre operation will give an entirely credible value, that is, an inexact value with all its value bits credible. For primary inexact values this will merely involve changing the doubt to zero, but for secondary inexact values this involves calculating the arithmetic mean of the limits of the interval so that the limits can still be calculated by adding the tolerance to, or subtracting it from, the centre.

The tolerance of inexact values is derived from their doubt, and is itself entirely credible. It will either be an inexact zero, or a positive non-zero. Of interest, though, is the question of the circumstances under which the tolerance of a secondary inexact value should be given in primary format, as at least the tolerance of the centre of a secondary inexact value must be, since an entirely credible inexact zero cannot be represented in secondary inexact format.

Inexact zeroes, being always primary, can be handled the same as ordinary primary inexact values. Inexact infinities, however, must be anomalous, since their centres aren’t any sort of mean of their limits. And what should the centre of a double infinity be ? Probably the best result would be an indefinity. And if the centre of a single infinity is taken as the appropriately signed infinity (exact?), as it must be, the tolerance is infinite, and, even if it wasn’t, the limits can’t be calculated in the usual way because, apart from any other trap, subtracting the infinity of a tolerance from the infinity of a centre gives an indefinity, which is no kind of limit at all.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Dyadic Arithmetic Operations
items.text: The consideration of dyadic operations requires consideration of the results arising from combinations of various kinds of operands. The consideration is richer both because of the much greater number of cases of operand kinds, but also because the nature of dyadic operations is typically more complex than the nature of monadic ones.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Higher and Lower
items.text:
The higher and lower operations are very similar, and simpler than most other dyadic operations, so they serve as a useful starting point. These are sometimes called "greater" and "lesser", which is misleading, because these words really, in the ordinary meanings of these words, apply to the magnitude of operand values — clearly ¯1000000 is greater than 0.0001 even though it is lower in the number line. Linguistic considerations aside, only the higher operation need be considered here, since the operation of the lower can easily be inferred from it.

The result of higher is indefinite when an operand is indefinite. Positive infinity is higher than any definite value, and any definite value is higher than negative infinity. The higher of any two other exact values is standardly determinable simply from their relative position on the number line.

The result of higher when one operand is inexact and the other ordinarily exact is slightly more complicated but can be fairly easily pictured by imagining the two operands depicted on the number line. The exact value occupies a point, the inexact covers an interval. If the exact value is outside the interval and lower than it, then the inexact value is the result. If the exact value is outside the interval and higher than it, then the exact value is the result. If the exact value is inside the interval, then the exact value is the lower limit of the result and the upper limit of the inexact value is also the upper limit of the result.

In this last case a very important principle may be involved. While the lower and upper limits of the interval of the result may be specifiable and calculable, the interval may not be exactly representable in a register format. In this case the result must be the representable interval of least tolerance that encompasses the interval that can’t be represented.

The combination of one exact and one inexact operand is closely analogous to the situation with two inexact operands where the tolerance of one of the operands is zero. The case of particular interest is where the two intervals overlap. Here the lower limit of the result is the higher of the lower limits of the two operands, and the higher limit of the result is the higher of the higher limits of the two operands. This is quite a general statement if exact value are considered to have two limits of the same value.

One remaining troublesome case remains, and that is where an operand is a double inexact infinity. The result is indefinite.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Addition and other Arithmetic
items.text:
The considerations for the addition operation are somewhat the same as those for higher and lower. For the general case, the lower limit of the result is the sum of the lower limits of the two operands, and the higher limit of the result is the sum of the higher limits of the two operands. As for the higher and lower operations, particular behaviour is involved for particular kinds of operands, with double inexact infinities giving indefinite results, as also do adding infinities exact or inexact of opposite sign.

As for the subtraction operation, it is tempting to define it in terms of the addition of the negated right operand. This would be a mistake because then the subtraction by the largest negative integer would almost always give a secondary inexact result, whereas an exact result will often be more appropriate. Similarly, division should not be defined as multiplication by the reciprocal.

One group of operations could prove particularly useful for the manipulation of inexact values. These are the remainder, the quotient, and what might be called the bulk operation because it yields the product of the quotient and the divisor or modulator. The quotient is always an integer, and when the modulator and the divisor are exact then the bulk is also. The result of the bulk operation might be thought of as the extraction of as much of the dividend as can be put together from units of the modulator. The bulk plus the remainder reconstructs the dividend. However, these operations become complex when the modulator is inexact.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Conclusion
items.text:
The paper outlining the proposal for using composite arithmetic as the starting point for a standard general purpose arithmetic also gives reasons why such a standard is needed to complement the highly successful binary floating-point arithmetic standard [1].

The floating-point standard is a relatively simple one, being mainly concerned with part of what is for composite arithmetic called storage form, and with the arithmetic to be carried out on values in that form [13,14].

Composite arithmetic needs three forms, and this paper has outlined the proposals for its register form, and for some of the arithmetic to be carried out on values in that form, a form on which the floating-point standard is silent [see also 15].

APL/J users and developers have long and most unusually relevant experience with the type-less style of calculation proposed for composite arithmetic. Should the APL community, particularly those members belonging to the IEEE Computer Society, agree that a standard like the one proposed would be of benefit in exposing and promoting the kind of computational approach that APL has for so long (and for so little popular result) promoted and embodied, then that community has an opportunity here to help build support for a standard for general-purpose computing, and to contribute significantly to making that standard as good as possible.
path: Some Basic Functions for Composite Arithmetic

items.title: Letter: Sudoku Madness
items.text:
from Neville Holmes (nholmes@leven.comp.utas.edu.au)

I just read your Sudoku message on the J Forum. By a strange coincidence, one of my students chose Sudoku for his J assignment.  He was having a lot of trouble, so I wrote the script below to give him a start. He didn’t get all that far with writing some player support but I’ll be working with him after I come back from overseas.

Because I’m leaving early Friday for a week of meetings in the US I haven’t got time to do much more than send you the code. For it is that I’ve commented it fairly fully for the student’s sake, but against it is that I left the assignments global to make it easy for him to test it.

Perhaps its interest is that I’ve generalised it way beyond the 3×3×3, which is, I think,  a bit of a straight jacket. Also, you should be able to jazz up the code because I’m not an expert by any means, and the code is just one evening’s work.

 NB.
 NB. General Sudoku Arrays
 NB.
 NB. Generate an array of numbers, for example, shape 2 3 4 5
 NB.   which is thought of as a 2x3 array of 4x5 rectangles,
 NB.   or a 2x4 by 3x5 array of numbers, where
 NB.   (a) no number is repeated within
 NB.       0. any 4x5 subarray,
 NB.       1. any 2x4 subarray, and
 NB.       2. any 3x5 subarray,
 NB.   (b) the numbers are whole
 NB.          from 1 to the maximum of 4x5, 2x4, and 3x5.
 NB.
 NB. Final Functions : Dsply Fnl  (try "Dsply Fnl 2 2 3 3" or "Dsply Fnl 3")

 NB. Some Utility Functions

 Dsply =: <"2       NB. Dsply y : boxes the 4x5 subarrays
 PnDy  =: ,"2@(0 1&|:)@:(,"2)@(0 2&|:)
                    NB. PnDy y : converts to 8x10 array
 InDy  =: Dsply@(]$({.~ -@(*/)))~ >@(1&{)
                    NB. x InDy y : constructs & displays intermediate array
 Vldt  =: 2&>.@(4&$)@,@:>.
                    NB. Forces 4 integers greater than 1
 Mxmm  =: >./@(*/)@:((2 3$2 0 1 3 2 3)&{)
                    NB. Calculates the maximum of 4x5, 2x4, and 3x5

 NB. Functions to set up running list of boxes

items.title: A Beginner’s Guide to Low Cost APLs
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 29

by Dick Holt

This article is a beginner’s guide to low-cost APL interpreters, compiled by the APLSIG of the Capital PC User Group (CPCUG). Comparisons emphasize work and business applications — because it’s the workplace that generates demand for technological innovation, and pays for it. I emphasize free or low cost APLs, because these are likely entry points for exactly the kind of people who are most badly needed by the APL community — namely newcomers.

It’s an "apples and oranges" comparison because the various APLs are themselves "apples and oranges". It may contain errors of fact, as well as opinions that are wrongly informed. Corrections are invited. [I will be pleased to receive, pass on and publish any comments/corrections — Ed.]

A central theme of this article is that APLs vary widely in size, speed, performance, and price. An advantage of this heterogeneity is that APL offers "something for everyone". A disadvantage is that there is little compatibility among versions. In any event, at least two free or low cost APLs — with big workspaces, good speed, and many useful features — should now be increasingly attractive to people who have never used APL before.

To begin, here are a few speed and size comparisons, referenced to the free demo of APL*PLUS v10.1, a widely used commercial APL:

Table 1: Size, and Relative Speed: For five simple benchmark tests (B1-B5).

Interpreter B1 B2 B3 B4 B5 ⎕WA * CLEAR WS APL*PLUS demo >1.00 >1.00 1.00 1.00 1.00 0 APLI386 1.13 2.11 >0.24 0.97 >0.03 1044k APLIPC 1.11 2.36 0.50 1.25 0.12 262k APLISW 1.39 2.36 0.50 1.25 0.12 312k TryAPL2 4.52 2.48 4.17 >0.36 >0.03 233k Sharp APL/PC 1.46 2.41 0.67 1.40 0.15 195k I-APL 20.78 30.95 26.50 10.22 79.40 31k

All benchmarks times are normalized to APL*PLUS demo = 1.00

Benchmark B1: Q*9; where Q is (2.5+⍳1800): 1800 exponentiations.
Benchmark B2: (⍳3000)÷44.3: 3000 floating point divisions.
Benchmark B3: +/⍳15000: 15000 integer additions.
Benchmark B4: 20!40, looped 1000 times (no, looping doesn't
              cost all that much time).
Benchmark B5: length 10,000 boolean vectors, and-ed and or-ed
              10 times (100,000 boolean operations).

* Defaults for my machine: ⎕WA for APLI386 is as large as RAM permits, and may be increased further by a user-transparent virtual (on-disk) workspace. ⎕WA for APL*PLUS demo is zero, since the )CLEAR WS is, by design, inaccessible. ⎕WA for others is configuration dependent, except for I-APL, which is limited to 31.6k on DOS machines (less if cover functions are used for graphics, files, help, etc.).

Benchmarks are designed to avoid WS FULL in I-APL, and to run in a few minutes or less on my machine. Times are normalized to APL*PLUS, and are independent of disk speed.
path: A Beginner’s Guide to Low Cost APLs

items.title: Observations
items.text:
Speed and size vary enormously. APLI386 has a ⎕WA 30 times larger than I-APL (on my machine), and does integer addition 17 times faster than TryAPL2. For exponentiation, TryAPL2 is 3-4 times slower than all except I-APL. All Iverson software is 2-4 times faster than APL*PLUS for +/⍳15000. APLI386 is more than 100 times faster than I-APL for +/⍳15000.

For dyadic shriek (!), TryAPL2 is 3 times faster than both APL*PLUS and APLI386, and 29 times faster than I-APL. Although not commonly used, dyadic ! is purposely chosen to highlight speed variations. Non-integer arguments for ! weren’t tested.

For boolean operations — a putative strong point of APL — APLI386 and TryAPL2 are 30 times faster than APL*PLUS, and more than 2500 times faster than I-APL. Both APLI386 and TryAPL do boolean operations so fast that I had to run them 10E7 times to find out which was faster. TryAPL2 seems to be about half of one percent faster than APLI386.

These speed tests aren’t directly comparable: Iverson APLI386 uses the 32-bit instruction set of the 386 chip — none of the others do. Benchmarks can be notoriously misleading, and your times may be different. Run your own tests.

Blitzing speed and big workspaces are important, but they’re not the only things to consider. Effective use of APL also depends on features like a full-screen editor, vendor support, useful application development tools, good documentation, and smooth upgrade paths.

Hardware is also a factor. Only APLI386 requires a 386 machine. All others work on a 386 and on lesser machines. Among free or low-cost interpreters, only TryAPL2 requires a colour monitor (EGA or better), but Iverson’s APL characters are inaccurate on a monochrome monitor.

Can I do "real work" in any of these low-cost APLs?

APL*PLUS demo No — User-defined functions/system commands inaccessible TryAPL2 Yes — But with del editor, no DOS or APL files APLI386 Yes — 386 required, also does Windows APLIPC Yes — 386 not required Sharp APL/PC Yes — Limited: poor documentation, not easily available APLISW ? — Limited: no DOS files, no APs I-APL ? — 31k WS, slow, no error trapping

To be fair, the APL*PLUS demo and I-APL aren’t designed to do real work. They’re designed to showcase product features or to teach APL. Within varying limits, real work is feasible with all other APLs.

Table 2 Upgrade Path and Prices ($US)

Interpreter Type Disk Price Documentation Price *** $ Full Product $ 386 Version APL*PLUS demo flat free* free/on screen $695 $1700 TryAPL2 nested free* free LJ print $500 Included APLI386 boxed $30 $30 2 books Is full product APLIPC boxed $30 $30 2 books APLI386 APLI386 APLISW boxed free some on screen APLIPC APLI386 Sharp APL/PC boxed free unavailable? APLIPC APLI386 I-APL flat free $25 Any of the above

* Free from original source (see "Sources" below), and downloadable free from the BBS\APL. Request to download may be needed. Some suppliers may charge a nominal fee.

** Disks, but not documentation, may be downloaded free from the BBS\APL, and may also be available elsewhere.

*** Documentation for Sharp APL/PC may be hard to get and is hard to use. Iverson documentation is an imperfect hybrid of Sharp APL/PC (orphaned v17) material, mainframe material, and new on-screen Iverson material.

Prices may be discounted: street price, volume, educational, dealers, etc. Ask. See "Sources" below.

IBM (TryAPL2 and APL2/PC), Iverson (and Sharp), and APL*PLUS II (386 version) all provide "nested" or "boxed" arrays — all in incompatible ways. Also, many "flat" features aren’t compatible among various APLs, and APL*PLUS isn’t fully compatible with APL*PLUS II.

Because of numerous and deep incompatibilities, switching from one APL to another can be an obstacle to upgrading.
path: A Beginner’s Guide to Low Cost APLs

items.title: Keyboard and Other Incompatibilities
items.text:
Keyboards for IBM and APL*PLUS are similar. They’re the traditional APL keyboards. Iverson keyboards are slightly different, but resemble the APL*PLUS "unified" keyboard as used in the APL*PLUS demo. Many Iverson APL keys are in the "traditional" place, differing mainly in the use of lower case, and in the use of <ALT> rather than <SHIFT> to get special APL characters. Most Sharp keys are in the same place as Iverson keys. Users of these APLs can probably switch from one to another without too much difficulty, at least as far as the keyboard is concerned. Non-keyboard incompatibilities — mainly in quad functions and shared variables — are also difficult. TryAPL2, APL*PLUS demo, Iverson Software, and CPCUG APL lessons all have on-screen keyboard diagrams and on-screen help.

Because I-APL attempts to adhere to ASCII, its keyboard is almost completely unrelated to any other APL keyboard. Does this mean that the I-APL keyboard is "bad"? No. It’s simply that switching from I-APL to any other more powerful APL is harder than switching among these other APLs. From a beginner’s perspective, all APL keyboards are "bad". In its 1991 APL classes, the CPCUG found the APL keyboard to be the greatest single obstacle to learning APL. Students who begin with I-APL must learn a new APL keyboard if they want to upgrade to a more powerful APL.
path: A Beginner’s Guide to Low Cost APLs

items.title: Editors
items.text:
A full-screen editor is essential for modern programming, in APL or in any other language. Among commercial products, APL*PLUS and APL*PLUS II have a superior built-in assembly language editor. Iverson products have a full-screen editor function that may be copied into your WS. IBM’s APL2/PC also has an editor function that may be copied into your WS, or you may also use something like IBM’s "Personal Editor" for APL2/PC. TryAPL2, Sharp APL/PC, APLISW, and I-APL have only the obsolete "del" editor. The del editor is a line editor like DOS’s EDLIN, lacking only most of its convenience.

Full-Screen Management

APL*PLUS v10 — Yes, excellent, versatile, strong APL*PLUS demo — No, screen management is user-inaccessible TryAPL2 — Yes, uses shared variables IBM APL2/PC — Yes, uses shared variables APLI386 — Yes, uses shared variables APLIPC — Yes, same as APLI386 above Sharp APL/PC — Yes, difficult I-APL — Yes, has FSCREEN.IWS with GET and PUT cover functions APLISW — No Files DOS Files APL Component files APL*PLUS demo No No, quad functions inaccessible APL*PLUS Yes Yes IBM APL2/PC Yes Yes APLI386 Yes Yes APLIPC Yes Yes Sharp APL/PC Yes Yes I-APL Yes (cover fns) No (cover fns available) TryAPL2 No No APLISW No No

Documentation

APL*PLUS demo — On-screen keyboard tutorial/description of features. TryAPL2 — On-screen doc. & lessons; LJ printable user manual. APLI386 — On-screen, plus two inexact books. APLIPC — Identical to APLI386 above. APLISW — Some, on-screen. I-APL — Good on paper, not much on-screen. Sharp APL/PC — None on-screen, paper not easily available, difficult.

On-screen Help Supplied

APL*PLUS demo — Excellent, also excellent for full products. TryAPL2 — Good, in WS TRYDOC.TRY. IBM APL2/PC — I don’t know. APLI386 — F1: Fairly complete, paper documentation essential. APLIPC — F1: Identical to APLI386 above. APLISW — F1: Identical to APLI386 above. Sharp APL/PC — No. I-APL — No.

Function Keys: settable on all except APLISW and I-APL. Varying degrees of pain on all others.

APL Lessons Availability: CPCUG APLSIG’s generic, interactive, on-screen lessons are available for all APLs discussed here, some also in French.

Non-English Language Keyboard/Character Support: This feature is important only if you care about being competitive in today’s global marketplace (not everybody does). Among APLs discussed here, only TryAPL2 includes instructions for the keyboard and National Code Pages. On-screen non-English characters and non-English keyboards can be made in other APLs, with varying degrees of pain.

Calls to Machine Language/C/Fortran etc.

APL*PLUS — Yes APL*PLUS demo — Yes, example provided of calls to C TryAPL2 — No, requires AP210, not included in demo IBM APL2 — Yes, FORTRAN WS included in product APLI386 — ⎕NA type improvements planned APLIPC — ⎕NA type improvements planned I-APL — Yes, machine language expertise needed APLISW — No Commercially Motivated Vendor Support Kaizen Strategy?* Market Responsive? APL*PLUS — Hot-line + bbs Yes, to a fault Highly so APL*PLUS demo — Ask salesperson Apparently Very Likely TryAPL2 — Hot-line, free Yes Apparently IBM APL2 — Hot-line, free Yes, not to a fault Unknown APLI386 — Hot-line, toll Yes Apparently APLIPC — Hot-line, toll Yes Apparently APLISW — No No No I-APL — No No No

* Kaizen is the Japanese term for a reliable corporate commitment to unceasing, market-driven, improvement and innovation.

Run-Time Systems: Programming APL for run-time systems, whether for commercial use or just for your work group, requires strong skills in error trapping. All APLs here, with the exception of I-APL, have error trapping features — and all are incompatibly different. TryAPL2’s error trapping is undocumented.

IBM APL2 includes a free run-time .EXE system. APL*PLUS and APL*PLUS II provide run-time systems at varying prices: APL*PLUS 5-pack is $250, unlimited is $995; APL*PLUS II 5-pack is $875, unlimited is $5000.

Pricing strategy for Iverson APLI386 and APLIPC make run-time systems inexpensive for distribution in small numbers. If you develop an application that will sell many copies, APL*PLUS may be cheaper. I-APL may be distributed free, but commercial use is prohibited.

Odds and Ends: Iverson Software products (and Sharp) have built-in complex numbers. However, complex number cover functions are not hard to write, and are available as shareware, or come with some other APLs. Only I-APL uses "direct definition" functions. Only APL*PLUS II and Iverson APLI386 do windows. Only I-APL is available on a very wide range of machines, such as ATARI, BBC, Archimedes, or Mac II.

Other Info Graphics Color Printer Support APL*PLUS Yes Yes V. good APL*PLUS demo Yes Yes not accessible IBM TryAPL2 Yes Yes V. good for LJ IBM APL2/PC Yes Yes V. good, via AP80 APLI386 Yes Yes V. good (LJ, PS, DM) APLIPC Yes Yes Identical to APLI386 I-APL Possible Possible Limited APLISW No No No

items.title: APL97 Conference Survey Results
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 92

analysed by Dick Holt

(This article has already appeared in several local APL newsletters)

This article summarizes the APL97 attender feedback survey. It compares results, where possible, with similar prior surveys. It describes attenders’ satisfaction with various features of APL97. The purpose of this article is to help the APL/J community to improve future conferences.

Briefly, attenders rated APL97 as a huge success. 10 of 14 Conference features rated higher than in two comparable prior surveys, most of them notably so. The 4 exceptions (below), may appear to be comparable to prior surveys, but for varying reasons, are not.

(1) "Proceedings" rated slightly lower at APL97 than in the 1994 survey (Proceedings were unavailable at APL96). Some APL97 attenders noted that Proceedings on a CD ROM and weren’t easily readable on-site (but only 30% looked at the CD ROM — see Q17). Even so, the CD ROM helped APL97 to reduce lead times and to keep costs low. The APL97 Proceedings rating reflects its format, not its content. As a result, it’s not comparable to prior survey data.

(2) In contrast, APL97 attenders rated the Software Library highly compared to prior surveys. Again, this reflects the CD ROM format rather than content.

(3 & 4) "Cost of conference" and "Other costs" aren’t comparable to prior surveys. We changed the APL97 questionnaire to distinguish, for the first time, between "Cost of conference" (e.g. registration and banquet), and "Other costs" (e.g. travel and lost earnings). "Cost of conference" at APL97 rated in 1st place, clearly showing APL97’s success in reducing those costs over which its organizers had control. Yet, "other Costs" rated low. In statistical jargon, APL97 data for "Cost" and "Other Costs" are confounded if compared with prior survey data.

items.title: Now to the Survey Questions and Answers
items.text:
Q1 asked attenders to rate APL97 features on a scale of 1 to 5 (most-to-least satisfied). Average ratings, listed in order of decreasing satisfaction, are shown below:

Table 1. Satisfaction with APL97 Conference Features

Feature Rating Feature Rating cost of conference 1.10 x social/vacation 1.77 * location 1.29 * papers 1.81 * website 1.32 n proceedings 1.84 x program handbook 1.36 n other costs 1.89 x archives, etc. 1.43 n dinner cruise 2.03 * tutorials 1.58 * business opportunities 2.06 * software library 1.59 x job information 2.19 * accommodation 1.68 * vendor hospitality 2.34 n workshops 1.72 * posters, displays 2.58 * vendor forums 1.74 * others? — only 1 response

* = ratings higher than 94/96 surveys n = not asked in 94/96 surveys x = not comparable to 94/96 surveys

Small differences in ratings (+/- 0.2) probably aren’t significant.

See References 1 and 2 for 94/96 survey data.

Q2: What was the most useful feature, and why? Multiple responses are combined below:

  • Arrangements: Very good arrangements; good programs; program was well thought out
  • Workshops: learned about very pertinent stuff; got to try things; best way to learn is to try; participants received real hands-on experience and training in advanced features.
  • Tutorials: practical how to do; excellent content; stream of J tutorials; subjects were mostly practicable; APL info.
  • Workshop and vendor forums
  • Convenient (for us in Toronto). Very knowledgeable crowd.
  • Vendor forums: clear understanding of current market; got the latest developments
  • Meeting people
  • CD rom proceedings — may make software accessible, pretty current

Q3: What was the least useful feature, and why?

  • Vendor forums too far from presentations (multiple comments)
  • Workshops — great idea but poor presentation. Overhead info too dead, too small and too dim to be read or used.
  • Workshops — topic selection poor for me
  • CD rom proceedings — can’t read papers at conference or on trolley; Missing proceedings (see Q17); hosp suites instead of open is best.

Q4 and Q5 concern Conference attendance. Overall, 79% of respondents had attended a prior SIGAPL conference, and 84% said that they would attend a future one (90% and 92% at APL96).

When asked why they might attend a future SIGAPL Conference, respondents said:

"I use APL and J professionally; Fun and fruitful; It’s my business; It has become a habit; Interested in APL employment and meeting other APLers; Greater APL involvement; Useful info; Worth attending; Business; Helps to keep abreast of developments; For APL related information, products, contacts; Meeting people; Stimulating to get new ideas."

Q6: Are you a member of SIGAPL? Y=70% (APL96: Y=90%)

Q7: Years of experience with APL? With J? A simple answer: an average of 13.6 years with APL, and 2.7 years with J. Prior surveys showed a trend of increasing years of APL experience (15.6 in 94, 16.9 in 96). That trend is lightly reversed at APL97.

A more interesting answer: about 28% of respondents are experienced in both APL and J. Their joint years of APL and J experience are shown in the 2x12 table below:

APL yrs:  6  20   8  15  14  21  25   8  13  20  20  25
  J yrs:  2   6   1   5   1   5   3   2   1   1   6   1

Similar cross-tabulations, mainly of interest to vendors, may be constructed using the APL97SRV.ZIP file mentioned below.

Q8: Your State/Province/Country? This question is key to the analytic validity of this article. These analyses are valid only if the questionnaire respondents are a statistically representative of the population of all APL97 attenders. A 10,000 draw bootstrap (Monte Carlo) shows that the survey sample is indeed representative of APL97 attenders.

# of APL97 Attenders from: # of Survey Responses from: Bootstrap mean Bootstrap 2 sigma Canada 96 11 16.5 5.8 USA 82 18 14.1 5.6 Europe 61 12 10.5 5.0 Other 11 2 1.9 2.4 Total 250 43

See Reference 2 for details of the bootstrap technique. The US is somewhat over-represented, and Canada is somewhat under-represented in the sample, however both are within 2 sigma limits of their bootstrap means. "Europe" and "Other" are easily on the mark. Attenders came from 4 Canadian Provinces (mostly Ontario), 20 US states, 10 European nations (including Russia), and from Japan, Saudi Arabia, and South Africa. The survey response rate was 17%, well below the 27% response rate for the APL96 survey. Why? Because APL97 survey forms were available only adventitiously, rather than being inserted in Conference Bags at registration.

Q9: "Your occupation?" showed a wide array of responses. Most were in the area of software development (32%) and education (16%), both very close to APL96, followed by actuary (7%) and scientist (7%). Others include student, engineer, financial analyst, webmaster, consultant, business, and others.

Q10: "In what applications have you used APL/J?" Applications mentioned most often were:

banking/finance .39 insurance/actuary .09 education .30 engineering .07 business/manufacturing .12

Many respondents named multiple applications including advertising, medicine, oil, law, elections, beverage, forestry, travel, biology, nutrition, and others.

Q11. Are you actively developing code in APL, J, or other Array languages?

APL only : 56% J only : 7% Both APL and J : 9% Other array also: 14%

Q12: Where did you first hear about APL97?, and Q13: What was your major source of ongoing information about APL97?

mailing email c.l.a. Vector QQ Nouvelles Other Q12: 14% 26% 19% 2% 5% 0% 23% Q13: 16% 53% 21% 7% 7% 5% 14%

APL97 publicity reached far and wide. Web sites were most often cited as "other." Electronic publicity was the most wide reaching.

Q14 and Q15 concerned Vendors. 56% of survey respondents visited vendor Hospitality Suites, and of those who visited, 86% felt that they provided a useful contribution to APL97.

Q16 asked for comments on Exhibitors/Vendors. Opinions were mixed, and physical location was apparently an issue:

On the plus side:

"Hospitality was one of the main reasons for attending, finding out about new products and watching them demonstrated; Suites harder to get to but receive more attention there; More emphasis on the seriously interested; Hospitality is better; Hospitality is better more focused."

On the minus side:

"I prefer … a single exhibitor area. This was too scattered; Exhibits were close, hospitality was remote; Prefer central open exhibit area, really *near* lecture rooms; Too far from meeting room; Hospitality suites too formal … a barrier to go there; Wish vendor sites near coffee between papers; Hospitality suites should have been in same building."

One respondent noted that the survey didn’t distinguish among vendors, and that some vendors had better hospitality suites than others. Almost all one-word responses to Q16 favoured the "open-concept" over the hospitality suite approach for Vendors’ exhibits.

Q17: CD ROM: Only 30% of respondents looked at the CD ROM, and 60% of those who did found it useful. But this isn’t the full story. Many noted that they couldn’t easily read the CD at the Conference.

Below is an example of suggestions for future CD ROMS. See also Q3 (least useful feature).

"(1) The CD was a good idea but it went too far: Please distribute attendance list ON PAPER at start of Conf (later a more updated version on www is fine too). (2) I do like to have the proceedings ON PAPER. If not, my boss will not consider any contribution I make to the Conf … as valuable and will not pay for my trip. (3) I do like to have the proceedings on paper to read on the first night of the conf. (4) I appreciate a low cost conf, but am willing to pay more for proceedings on paper."

You may order the APL97 CD ROM from www.torontoapl.org for $C20, postage paid world-wide, via cheque, money order, Visa, Master, or Amex. Toronto SIGAPL will make the CD ROM electronically available and updated at, or linked to, its web page (www.torontoapl.org).

Q18: Was the Program Handbook useful? Y = 74%

Program handbook comments:

"Add good map of the area … is needed; Pg 18-20: begin-end times, like in the flyer, easier to read than the begin time only; Set start times on print-out more carefully; Suggest adding start and end times; Keep schedule in center — easy to open and find; Put day, time, and location beside each description to change more bigger one size; Perhaps include a floor map of room locations; It was exactly up to its task."

Q19a: Want Annual APL/J conference in Toronto? Y=28% N=28% B=44% Q19b: Want a Bi-annual conference? Y=49% N=19% B=37% Note: some respondents may have interpreted the word "bi-annual" (twice/yr) in Q19b to mean "biennial" (every 2 years).

Q20a: Are you aware of the APL Skills Database? Y=62%

Q20b: Other services wanted? There were a lot of blanks in response to Q20b. Items mentioned were:

"Part-time employment; more web stuff; Résumé marketing service?; internet conference; (1) debugging tools, (2) Ecklers (Paul Davidson) coding protocols, (3) version control software; and workshop, — contest"

Q21: Topics for future conferences?: Verbatim responses were:

"Performance consideration in real-life software developed in APL/J; Application in scientific & mathematical problems; OLE controls (i.e. getting them to work in APL); General tips on programming style, efficiency, etc; Language and interface enhancements in APL; working products; How J/APL is useful; Making APL/J useful to end users (as opposed to developers); Success stories using APL/J as well as unsuccess stories; Vendors cooperation in research for improving APL."

Q22: Other comments or Suggestions? In the respondents’ own words:

"Keep up the good work; Thank you Committee! Ryerson’s facilities, especially classroom were much superior to what was available in past at U.T.; It would be great to have a participants list in the registration kit at the beginning conference. Always is it good service (many other Conferences use it and I enjoy it); Encourage presenters to have a script beforehand. Some of the projections via overhead was unreadable. Need to schedule beforehand. Great conference. Thank you; Allow a 1.25 — 1.5 hours for lunch. Lunch is too short (several comments); Ran out of coffee/refreshments during break; Great Conference, all the organizers deserve a lot of credit; More interesting content than any recent conf; Thank you for a great conference; Thanks for your effort in sponsoring APL97. It was certainly one of the best ever; Overhead projections not readable in 90% of the workshops, Sit at the back of the room to test for yourself; I compliment Toronto SIG on a very well done conference, including location and accommodations, and program pamphlet; Advanced applications are nice, but for the average programmer, the problem is: 1) ease of reading code, 2) debugging it, 3) with multiple programmers, how to keep their work organized; Some workshops were less useful as all we did was typing … creating images in J which left us some assignment. We were too busy typing to follow the message/contents of the workshop. Suggestion: reduce the number of terminals and operators; Good Conference; An excellent conference. The program committee should be commended for a job well done."

File APL97SRV.ZIP containing all analysis fns and APL97 survey data, is downloadable free from the BBS\APL [telephone number omitted], in File Area FREE. APL97SRV.ZIP has also been sent to Toronto SIGAPL and Waterloo for electronic distribution.
