items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 48

notes by Duncan Pearson
path: The First International J User Conference (Toronto, June 24th — 25th 1996)

items.title: Background
items.text:
The first J User Conference was held in Toronto on the 24th and 25th June. It was very well attended, with 123 people filling the Pharmacy Management Building of the University of Toronto, and also very well organised by Strand Software, the sole distributor of J. Everyone that I met at the conference was friendly and interested to know what I was doing, as well as willing to discuss his own work.

The barbecue on the Monday evening on Algonquin Island was particularly enjoyable in this respect, as with the food, wine and beer everyone relaxed and mingled freely. The university accommodation where we stayed was comfortable and modern, and only a short walk from the conference building; the whole university being very central in Toronto itself. The area round the university is a marvellous mix of coffee, book, food and computer shops with one thing I hadn’t seen before — something rather like a laundromat that instead of having washing machines had computers, I presume for the students’ theses. All in all it was a most enjoyable two days and I will certainly plan to return for the second conference at the same time next year.

The conference itself consisted of two plenary talks followed by parallel talks in two streams. The first plenary, which also served as an introduction to the conference, was by Eric Iverson and during it I was unfortunately busy compiling the final versions of the code for our demonstration in the second plenary, during which I was obviously again too busy to take notes. Of the remainder of the conference I attended mostly the talks about the use of J in conjunction with other software rather than those on the more esoteric aspects of the language, so this account of the conference may be a little one-sided. I have picked three talks that particularly interested me.
path: The First International J User Conference (Toronto, June 24th — 25th 1996)

items.title: Data Rummaging in J — Joey Tuttle
items.text:
Joey’s business is something that I didn’t know existed till the conference. He is a "junk fax" distributor. For clients that have a fax to send identically to a large mailing list his company will handle the distribution. This includes the resending of failures, the logging of unobtainable numbers, the removal of duplicate addresses and, very importantly to them, the correct billing of the client.

The general data analysis is done in J acting on flat ascii files produced by the various automated stages of the process. The disregard of J for the size of the data, its consistent handling of the empty case and its ease of development make it the ideal tool for the job. One thing that came across in the talk was the variety of different formats in which the data arrived and the way in which those formats changed, often with little notice, necessitating a change to the analysis software. The other was the sheer size of the data. Part of the analysis was of an itemised ’phone bill the paper version of which ran to 20,000 pages. However the most instructive thing was the choice of simple format ascii files for the data communication between processes as the most flexible and reliable method. This was reflected later on in Bjorn Helgason’s talk.
path: The First International J User Conference (Toronto, June 24th — 25th 1996)

items.title: Use of J to Manage Large Computer Networks — Bjorn Helgason
items.text:
This talk was interesting to me for two reasons. Firstly it reinforced Joey Tuttle’s message about the use of simple ascii files for communication between asynchronous processes and secondly it gave advice about the development of a complex system using J. Interestingly Bjorn’s presentation package was not Powerpoint, but a J program written with the Window driver, reminiscent of David Piper’s presentation at the BAA GUI development day.

The essence of his approach to network management was that everything that happens on the network should be logged in an ascii file in a specific place on the network — the design of the directory structure is obviously important here — and that J programs should analyse these files. The logs contain meaningful keywords, another thing central to Joey Tuttle’s approach, and the J programs’ analysis of the files is based on these keywords. The J programs are MAPI enabled and if necessary can send mail to alert administrators to non-standard situations. Again following the principle of simplicity in communication, the only protocols used are TCP/IP and FTP, the FTP scripts being generated and run automatically by J programs.

The J of the system is, in contrast to most published J, very simple. It needs to be maintained not only by Bjorn but also by others with only a rudimentary knowledge. Control structures and a consistent naming scheme are used for clarity with all global variables used in a script defined first in the same way as defined constants in a C source file. In general Windows NT is used, in preference to Windows 3.1 or Windows 95, for its greater reliability. A dedicated machine is used for each discrete task, in Bjorn’s words "cheap, stand-alone and left alone". Synchronisation of processes on different machines is done by access to a central control file (as with Clifford Reiter’s fractal and Roger Hui’s prime calculation).

In addition to the subject matter of the talk Bjorn also gave us the benefit of his practical experience in developing J, tips on how best to use the development environment and on the structure of large quantities of code in scripts. To me, a relative tyro, these were useful sidelights.
path: The First International J User Conference (Toronto, June 24th — 25th 1996)

items.title: Using J with ODBC and Delphi — John Baker
items.text:
The title of this talk was slightly misleading as it was nearly all about the OLE interface to J run from Delphi. The simplicity, high capacity and reliability of this was undoubtedly something with which John was clearly very pleased. As he said "What a concept — software that works". He demonstrated a simple use of it in the prime factorisation of the first 1000 integers (in J the verb q:) and the display of the results in a Delphi table control. In the resulting timings only 5% of the overall time was spent in communication, while 85% was spent by Delphi in populating the table.

The code showed the simplicity of the interface. In C the programmer is exposed to the complexity of the variant data structure that is used to communicate in OLE. In Delphi the interface to OLE hides the complexity to a greater extent. However John noted that in the process it loses any J error information. The process of starting a J server and of executing expressions in it was very simple and involved creating an OLE object in the Delphi module and executing its "Do" method with the expression to be executed as argument. The result was an array the dimensions of which could be queried and which could be indexed in the normal way. This is much easier than in C.

John then showed an application using J to calculate sunrise and sunset times. It was very polished and showed something of Delphi’s capabilities. Clearly for the J programmer who wishes to ship easily installed applications with fast user interfaces, and who has access to Delphi, this is a combination that deserves serious consideration.
path: The First International J User Conference (Toronto, June 24th — 25th 1996)

items.title: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!
items.text: by Kai Jäger
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
As APLers, using an application from “Microsoft’s Office Suite” like Excel or Word as an OLE object makes sense in some cases. For example, printing under Windows can be a real nightmare!

Because APL has a great strength in dealing with tables, one often wishes to print them. Since Excel offers great features and flexibility for doing this, why should we not use it for this task? One possible way to do this is to use the Excel OLE object from within APL.

If you can’t beat them, join them!

This article will look into how to: start Excel; load a specified spreadsheet; get some or all of the data into (or out of) your workspace; and use Excel as a printing machine from APL. Also, to try to make this useful for APLers with no or little experience of using OLE objects, I will show some typical techniques to get information about a specific OLE objects.

This article is not addressed to experienced programmers, and doesn’t assume you are familiar with MSDN and Visual Studio.

A typical example of what we want to do is to call a command (say via a context menu) that exports selected rows from a grid in an APL GUI application out to Excel.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Starting Excel
items.text:
The first thing to do is to start Excel as an OLEclient from APL:

'MyOleObj'⎕WC'OLEClient'
'Excel.Application'

If Excel was already running on your PC, that’s fine.  If Excel was not already running, nothing will seem to happen, but Excel will now be running in the background. This is because the Excel GUI is not displayed by default. We can expressly ask Excel to display:

MyOleObj.Visible←1

Now let’s set the Caption of the Excel main window:

MyOleObj.Caption←'APL
and Excel'

Next we need to create a brand new workbook, since without such a workbook, nothing could happen in Excel:

'MyOleObj.MyWorkbook'⎕WC
MyOleObj.Workbooks

“MyWorkbook” need not necessarily be a child of “MyOleObj”, since there is no hierarchical dependency — but why not?
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Workbooks and Templates
items.text:
Do you wish to use a specific template? You probably know templates from Word (the *.dot-files); in Excel a corresponding mechanism is also available. An Excel template is a document with the file extension “xlt”. If your template is not held in Excel’s default template directory, make sure you specify the full path name:

#.MySheets←MyOleObj.MyWorkbook.Open'Standard.xlt'

If you are not interested in using a template, use the method “Add” instead:

#.MySheets←MyOleObj.MyWorkbook.Add
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Worksheets
items.text:
We can deal now with the newly-created workbook, which by default contains 3 sheets. Let’s create a new object that represents one of the sheets in our workbook. Because we have just created this workbook, it is by definition the active one, so we can deal with the “ActiveSheet”:

#.MySheet←#.MySheets.ActiveSheet

OK, that’s fine so far.  For the next step we will insert some data and column titles into the sheet. First let’s create two variables, one holding the column titles, the other one is needed to represent our “table”:

ColTitles←'The Very First Lastname' 'Firstname' 'Street' 'Code'  'Town'
Values←0 5⍴''
Values⍪←'Jäger' 'Kai' 'Thisstreet 1' 9999 'Nuremberg'
Values⍪←'Taylor' 'Stephen' 'Thatstreet 2' 123456 'London'

The next step will be to insert the column titles into our sheet. We will need to specify starting and ending points. The starting point is (1,1), and the end point is (1,5) since we have 5 columns. (Excel works in origin 1).  What is a bit strange is that the two points defining the range are “Objects” of type “Range”.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Visual Basic and Why it is Helpful
items.text:
Let’s introduce now a good way to get information about OLE objects, methods and properties. Make Excel the topmost window and then press Alt+F11. This should open the Visual Basic for Applications IDE. If not, it is perhaps not installed as part of Office on your computer; but you can easily install this stuff.

Now you have access to the Visual Basic Help, a valuable source about the OLE object model of Excel! For example, enter the word “Range” into the “Search help” field. Then select “Range (List)” (or similar) from the list.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Syntax Problems: Default Methods…
items.text:
In the Help window you will find valuable information on how to deal with “Range”. If you look around the help information, you will find statements similar to:

      Worksheets(1).Cells(1, 1).Value = 24

The problem is that this won’t work in APL as it stands! This is because in Visual Basic, for example, some objects have a “default method”.  If a named object with a default method (for example “Worksheets”) is referenced without specifying a method, the default method is called. There is no such mechanism available in APL, so we need to call the “default method” explicitly. The “default method” for Worksheets is “Item”, so the statement translated into APL would be:

((MyOleObj.Worksheets.Item 1).Cells.Item 1 1).Value2 ←24

Note that here instead of “Value” the name “Value2” is used – we will come back to this later!
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Arranging a Range
items.text:
Let’s define two objects of type Range, useful as start and end points:

StartPoint←MySheet.Cells.Item(1 1)
EndPoint←MySheet.Cells.Item(1,⍴ColTitles)
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Accessing Data: Methods and Properties
items.text:
Now we can reference “Value”, but be careful: it is not a property, it is a method. This method does not use an argument (in documentation it is specified as “void”). From APL a void argument is supplied as an empty numeric vector:

      (MySheet.Range(StartPoint EndPoint)).Value ⍬
24  [Null]  [Null]  [Null]  [Null]

So we get back 24, together with some NULLs!

With the statement:

(MySheet.Range(StartPoint EndPoint)).Value2←ColTitles

we can assign the 5 cells in the first row in one single step.

You can check the cells by calling the appropriate method “Value”, but don’t forget the right argument; otherwise you get a pointer to the method instead of the contents of the cells:

(MySheet.Range StartPoint EndPoint).Value ⍬

As you may have noticed, here is another difference between Visual Basic and APL! In Visual Basic you use “Value” for both, referencing and specifying the contents of a certain cell. In APL, you need to call the method “Value” with a right argument to reference the cell contents, while you need to specify the “Value2” property to change the cell contents.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Specifying Columns and Data
items.text:
Let’s insert the real data into the Excel sheet now. Again we need a “start point” and an “end point”. The start point is (2,1), the end point is 1 0 + the number of rows and cells.

StartPoint←MySheet.Cells.Item(2,1)
EndPoint←MySheet.Cells.Item(1 0+⍴Values)

And now we can set the real data:

(MySheet.Range(StartPoint EndPoint)).Value2←Values
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Changing Column Width
items.text:
Currently all the columns are of the standard width. We should now tell Excel that we want the column width to fit the data. “Columns.AutoFit” is a method of the “Range” object, and it is therefore no surprise, that only the contents of the cells within that range are taken into consideration.  This means that executing the statement:

(MySheet.Range(StartPoint EndPoint)).Columns.AutoFit

ignores the width of the cells in the first row, since this row is not part of the “Range” object we are currently using. Furthermore, (with some versions of Excel) an annoying result is printed in the session manager. Fortunately, both problems could be solved relatively easily. Instead of our own “Range” object, we can use the built-in object “UsedRange”. This “Range” includes at least all the cells that contain a value. “At least” because maybe there are some empty rows or columns embedded within the data, but this is unimportant here,

To suppress any annoying result, we can simply use an empty dynamic function:

{}MySheet.UsedRange.Columns.AutoFit

That’s it! Easy, isn’t it?
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Suppressing Useless Warnings
items.text:
Sometimes, Excel displays some really annoying dialogue boxes. A typical example is the “This macro has an invalid signature…” message box. If you need to make sure that no such dialogue box interrupts you, simply set:

MyOleObj.DisplayAlerts←0

But when you have finished, don’t forget to set this back to 1!
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Excel as Printer Server
items.text:
We started wanting to use Excel as a “printing machine”, and in fact we are able to do so by automating really everything. For such a task, you would not of course want to set

MyOleObj.Visible←1
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: The “PageSetup” Object
items.text:
Before executing the print command, maybe you want to specify a number of parameters important for print tasks. For this we need a “PageSetup” object:

MyPageSetup←MySheet.PageSetup
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Specifying a Header
items.text:
Now we can specify a centred header:

MyPageSetup.CenterHeader←'APL and Excel'

...or a left header:

MyPageSetup.LeftHeader←'Stephen Taylor'

...or a right header:

MyPageSetup.RightHeader←'Kai Jäger'

...or a footer which should be centred:

MyPageSetup.CenterFooter←'Written for Vector'

...or a left footer:

MyPageSetup.LeftFooter←'Page 1'

...or a right footer:

MyPageSetup.RightFooter←'2004-12-26'
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Miscellaneous Print Properties
items.text:
Maybe you do not want to print the whole spreadsheet but only part of it. For this, we again need a “Range” object:

StartPoint←MySheet.Cells.Item(1 1)
EndPoint←MySheet.Cells.Item(1 0+⍴Values)
MyRange←MySheet.Range(StartPoint EndPoint)
MyPageSetup.PrintArea←MyRange.AddressLocal ⍬
MyPageSetup.CenterHorizontally←0
MyPageSetup.CenterVertically←1
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Display Print Results
items.text:
To display the result, we need to call the method “PrintPreview”. This method also does not use an argument:

MySheet.PrintPreview ⍬

Got a DOMAIN ERROR?! We come back to this shortly.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Printing…
items.text:
To print the sheet, merely call the method “PrintOut” (again with an empty vector as right argument).

MySheet.PrintOut ⍬
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Coming to an End
items.text:
If you want save the newly created spreadsheet, simply call the method “Save”As:

MySheet.SaveAs 'MyFilename.xml'

And finally we want quit Excel:

MyOleObj.Quit
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Reading a Spreadsheet from Disk
items.text:
Finally you may have a problem very close to what we discussed so far:

You (that is, your APL program) knows about an existing spreadsheet, or at least you expect there is such a spreadsheet, and now you want to read this data into your workspace. Of course you need the name and the folder where the spreadsheet can be found, but you prompt your user for that.

There are different ways to read the data from a spreadsheet into APL: you can use DDE (which is a wobbly thing); or you can use ODBC; or you can use Excel via OLE. Although the ODBC solution has some advantages (Excel is not needed, and it’s fast), we will only discuss the OLE solution here.

We already know how to load a specific file into Excel:

file←'C:\My Documents\My Spreadsheet.xls'
MyOleObj.MyWorkbook.Sheet←MyOleObj.MyWorkbook.Open file

As you can see, the Open method is able to load not only a template but also an ordinary spreadsheet.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Again: the “Range” Object
items.text:
Again the UsedRange object could be used to access all data in the current worksheet. This is fine since we don’t need to know anything about the data contained in that spreadsheet:

MyRange←MyOleObj.ActiveSheet.UsedRange
Data←MyRange.Value ⍬

That’s it!
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Valuable Sources of Information
items.text:
So far we can do some useful things, but for a more complex task we need a general overview over the Excel OLE object model, of course.

This information is available on the MDSN pages on the web by Microsoft. The link is quite easy to remember:

http://msdn.microsoft.com/library/default.asp?url=/library/en-us/dv_wrcore/html/wrconExcelObjectModelOverview.asp

However, maybe you are interested in an alternative way: enter http://msdn.Microsoft.com into the browser’s address field and then the words <excel object model> into the search field. Select http://msdn.microsoft.com/library/en-us/dv_wrcore/html/ wrconExcelObjectModelOverview.asp from the result list.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Hints and Tips
items.text:
Note that:

  • there may or may not be some empty rows and columns around the real data
  • some cells may contain a NULL
  • Dates are returned as numeric vectors of length 7 – like ⎕TS!

To find out which cells are empty, use ⎕NULL:

Data≡¨⎕NULL

If you need to read the data from the second sheet of a workbook instead of the first one:

(MyOleObj.Sheets.Item 2).UsedRange.Value ⍬

If there is no such sheet available, because that file consists of one sheet only, you will get a DOMAIN ERROR here.

However, this technique may be dangerous: another user may have moved the second worksheet to be the third one now. So it is maybe a better idea to use the name of the sheet you are interested in. For example, if you know that this worksheet is named “ABC”, you can do this:

(MyOleObj.Sheets.Item'ABC').UsedRange.Value ⍬

And of course you can use this syntax, too:

MySheet←MyOleObj.Sheets.Item'ABC'
MySheet.UsedRange.Value ⍬

A note on APL syntax:

MySheet.Range(StartPoint EndPoint).AddressLocal ⍬

gives a Length Error but

MySheet.Range(StartPoint EndPoint)).AddressLocal ⍬

works just fine.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: The F1 key in APL
items.text:
If Visual Basic for Applications is installed together with Office, entering the name of an OLE item (object, property, method or event) and then pressing F1, should display a proper help file. However, on some but not all machines that does not work. Instead a message box is displayed stating that the help file could not be found:

(The exact file name and location will vary depending on the versions of Office and Windows running on your PC.)

We found that a common reason for this is that the file VBAXL10.chm is not found in C:\Programme\Microsoft Office\Office11 but in C:\Programme\Microsoft Office\Office11\1031\VBAXL10.CHM instead.

This is really annoying! One possible solution is to simply copy the help file from C:\Programme\Microsoft Office\Office11\1031 to C:\Programme\Microsoft Office\Office11 (UK and US readers should look in Program Files).
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Visual Basic Macros
items.text: A final suggestion. Sometimes you might need to do something but are unable to find out how from the documentation. In such a case it may be helpful to use a Visual Basic Macro: start “Recording Macro” within Excel, perform the needed actions, stop recording and then take a look into the Visual Basic code. Although there are some differences between Visual Basic and APL, this may still be helpful.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Interruptions and Trapping
items.text:
If you need to use OLE automation within a real application, be aware that sometimes astonishing things may happen. Just because a certain operation works well 20 or 30 times does not mean that it will run at every time! Sometimes there are DOMAIN ERRORs or the like, that you are not able to reproduce or to explain, and of course this is really bad news. However, you will get a feeling for how to deal with the code over the time. Adding some explicit “:Trap” statements might be a good idea here, but you should avoid “:Trap 0”.

For example: the user decides to “print" a document with the “Microsoft Document Image Writer” Office 2003 comes with. Then the user gets a “Save File" dialog, because this printer driver does not print but create a file you may display with a viewer. If for any reason the user then presses the “Cancel”button in this “Save”Dialog box, you get a DOMAIN ERROR in APL!

Therefore you should not use

MySheet.PrintOut ⍬

but:

:Trap 11 ⋄ MySheet.PrintOut ⍬ ⋄ :EndTrap

Thanks to Ray Cannon for help in editing this article.
path: Master and Slave: Dyalog APL Directs Excel!

items.title: Dynamic Functions in Practice
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 50

by Veli-Matti Jantunen (seminar given at Forests in Finland VI)

[ed] These notes have been adapted from a PowerPoint original, with the addition of some commentary and consolidation of several of the bullet points.

Last summer at the Yale conference I tried to convince Bill Rutiser that they should implement Dynamic functions in APL+Win, too. Bill asked dryly: "Where do you need them?".

I don’t know how convincing I was (under the scorching Yale sun), but I vaguely remember giving estimates that up to 30 percent of all the code I write is dynamic, and my productivity has increased in proportion to that. Besides, dfns have given me back the delight, i.e. the same delight I had when I first met APL aeons ago.

Now I should change that percentage to, say, 45.

items.title: A Small APL Teaser
items.text:
• change the nested vector:
   ,A←'Arto' 'Conrad' 'Kimmo' 'Adrian' 'Jukka'
 Arto  Conrad  Kimmo  Adrian  Jukka

to …

 Arto  darnoC  Kimmo  nairdA  Jukka
  • fewer than nine APL characters, please
  • you are allowed to use dynamic functions ;)

items.title: APL Difficulties
items.text:
i.e. APL design flaws.

  • only one function type

We have to use the same function type with small utilities and huge applications

  • local variables in the header line

Nowadays this should be vice versa <sigh!>.

  • local functions are hard to handle
  • inefficient argument handling

You never know when the WS FULL appears..

  • functions’ loading time backlash
  • especially with small functions

When the function is opened for use, the code is parsed especially the header line and labels among others (e.g. possible control structures). This can be dramatic with e.g. DeleteTrailingBlanks ¨ HUGE_NESTED_VECTOR.

items.title: Direct Definition
items.text:
There have been some proposals how to circumvent some of the limitations.

  • as seen in the (Sharp) APL literature..

I can still remember reading the first APL Conference Proceedings, and testing those examples with VS APL … they didn’t work.

vec:   ,⍵
sum:   +/⍵
mvec:  (sum vec ⍵)÷⍴vec ⍵
mean:   ⍵ : 0∊⍴⍵ : mvec ⍵
  • implemented at least in I-APL
  • no practical use

items.title: Dyalog Peculiarities
items.text:
Dyalog APL has some interesting extensions to the APL language.

  • specific functions (∪⎕≢) and operators (∘⍨&)
  • function assignment
sum←+/
rank←⍴∘⍴
fn←very_long_function_name

This last one is quite handy: if you need, say, a utility function DoSomethingUseful from the namespace #.utils repeatedly in one function, you can make a local assignment dsu←#.utils.DoSomethingUseful, and use that (function pointer) instead of the original name monster.

  • namespaces
  • syntax differences (e.g. shy result)
  • control structures (:If, :For, :Trap, ..)
  • dynamic functions (first seen at Lancaster 1996)

items.title: Dynamic Function
items.text:
• delimited with braces {}

… where the braces contain legal APL expressions!

  • doesn’t need to return a result, and it can include another D: function
  • may call traditional APL functions and operators as well
  • uses D: language, which differs slightly from traditional APL
  • laconic syntax
  • D: behaves like functional languages (e.g. static variable scope)

items.title: Arguments
items.text:
• D: functions are ambivalent
  • the right argument symbol is ⍵
  • the (possible) left argument symbol is ⍺
  • arguments are pointers, thus one cannot modify the arguments

There’s one exception to this rule

  • it is not necessary to use the arguments

items.title: Efficiency
items.text:
• D: is pretty simple for the interpreter
  • delimited function structure

no branches, labels, control structures, headers..

  • no extra data copying behind the scene
  • effectively used with operators

=> usually 10-20% time saving

items.title: Some Examples
items.text:
{⍵×10} 1+2
30
   {1+2} 'hello world'
3
   'vege' {⍺,⍵} 'table'
vegetable
   {(⍵*0.5) +/⍵*2} 3 4
5
   root←{⍵*0.5}
   square←{⍵*2}
   root +/square 5 12
13

items.title: Basic Idioms
items.text:
{}        eat
{⍵}       dex
{⍺}       lev
{⍵ ⍵}     duplicate
{⍵/⍳⍴⍵}   indices of a binary vector
{⍵~' '}   blank removal
{⍺[⍵]}    controlled indexing

This is extremely useful with looping and sparse indexing!

{⍵[⍋⍵]}   upgrade vector
{⍵[⍋⊃⍵]}  upgrade nested vector

Did I mention that I’m an APL2 bigot?

{'.'⎕WS'Cursor'⍵}   GUI control

items.title: D: function may have line separators ⋄
items.text:
• result = the value of the first non-assigned expression
  • every assigned name is local

items.title: D: functions are edited with the APL editor
items.text:
• empty lines and comments are OK
  • one-liners can be edited in the session, too

items.title: Pretty Obvious
items.text:
• global variables are editable

.. but only if you create them beforehand

   a←b←⍳3 ⋄ {}{(a←⍵)(b[]←⍵)} 7 6 5
   a b
1 2 3  7 6 5
  • D: function can be assigned to a name

n.b. syntax and name class differences!

   mean←{(+/⍵)÷⍴⍵} 1 2 3
   mean←{(+/⍵)÷⍴⍵}
SYNTAX ERROR
    mean←{(+/⍵)÷⍴⍵}
      ∧

items.title: Variable Scope
items.text:
• D: functions have a static scope (traditional APL has a dynamic scope)
   type←{way←'static'
        FN1←{way←'dynamic' ⋄ FN2 ⍵}
        FN2←{way ⍵}
        FN1 ⍵}

   type 'scope'
static  scope

items.title: Guard
items.text:
• the only control structure of D:, symbol :
  • format: condition:expression
  • if condition = 1, the expression will be executed and the D: function is closed, otherwise the next line will be executed
   {2|⍵:'odd' ⋄ 'even' ⋄ 'never'} 313
odd
  • even the guard may contain a D: function
    { ..multiple lines producing
   a boolean result.. } ⍵: { .. }

items.title: Default Argument & Shy Result
items.text:
• the default value of the left argument can be assigned: ⍺←default
  • the assignment takes place only if the left argument doesn’t exist
   root←{⍺←2 ⋄ ⍵*÷⍺}
3 root 64
  4
root 64
  8
  • shy result can be attained with guard
1:dummy←result

items.title: Recursion
items.text:
Recursion and operators are much more used with dynamic functions than with traditional APL.

  • D: function may call itself
  • the function symbol is ∇
fact←{⍵=1:1 ⋄ ⍵×∇ ⍵-1}
  • pretty efficient with tail call
fact←{1{⍵=0:⍺ ⋄ (⍺×⍵)∇ ⍵-1}⍵}
fact←{⍺←1 ⋄ ⍵=0:⍺ ⋄ (⍺×⍵)∇ ⍵-1}
  • going through a nested structure
{1<≡⍵:∇¨⍵ ⋄ fn ⍵}

items.title: Dynamic Operators
items.text:
• "functions with four arguments"
  • operands ⍺⍺ and ⍵⍵, recursion uses ∇∇
  • the mere existence of ⍺⍺ makes D: an operator
   else←{⍺:⍺⍺ ⍵ ⋄ ⍵⍵ ⍵}
   1 + else - 22
  22
0 + else - 33
  ¯33

items.title: Multiline Idioms
items.text:
{1<≡⍵:,⍵ ⋄ ,⊂,⍵}    ensure vector of vecs
{2=⎕NC ⍵:⍎⍵ ⋄ def}  default value
⊃{rowfn ⍵}¨↓mat     process matrix lines
{⎕IO←0 ⋄ ⍺+⍳1+⍵-⍺}  integers ⍺..⍵

D:-functions can be used as capsules, thus avoiding the mess with wrong system variables etc.

{⎕ML←3 ⋄ ∊⍵}                    enlist
{⎕ML←0 ⋄ ∊⍵}                    type
{⎕ML←3 ⋄ (⍵≠⍺)⊂⍵}               APL2 partition
{⎕ML←2 ⋄ (1,1↓⍺)⊂⍵}             binary partition
{⎕RL←+/¯3↑⎕TS ⋄ ⍵[(⍴⍵)?⍴⍵]}     randomise vector

items.title: Conditional Structures
items.text:
you can make your own controls

:If
   {if_cond:expr_1 ⋄ expr_0}

:Select
      {case1_cond:expr_1
       case2_cond:expr_2
          ..
        expr_0}

items.title: Looping Structures
items.text:
:For (no connection between loops)

          {expression}¨⍳n

:For (variables updated between loops)

     ↑{expression}/n⍴x

 condition{(b z)←⍵ ⋄ ⍺:z

          ..algorithm..

        a ∇ b z} var init

:While and :Until ⍺ storage, ⍵ counter

   gcd←{⍵=0:⍺ ⋄ ⍵ ∇ ⍵|⍺}

items.title: Error Trapping
items.text:
• errors can be trapped with error codes (0=all errors), symbol ::
errcode(s)::err_expr
  • when an error occurs, the err_expr will be executed (unwind)
  • nested traps are possible
fopen←{0::0
       22::⍵ ⎕FCREATE 0
    24 25::⍵ ⎕FSTIE 0
           ⍵ ⎕FTIE 0
          }

items.title: Possible Uses
items.text:
• file handling
openc←{0::0 ⋄ 22::⍵ ⎕NCREATE 0 ⋄ ⍵ ⎕NTIE 0}
isfil←{0::0 ⋄ {1}⎕NUNTIE ⍵ ⎕NTIE 0 0}
isdir←{0::0 ⋄ {1}⎕NUNTIE(⍵,'\nul')⎕NTIE 0}

These aren’t by far the most useful routines for file handling purposes, but serve as good examples how you can use ad hoc error trapping.

  • non-resulting expression giving a result ;)
'fm' ⎕WC 'Form'
'fm' {0::⍵ ⋄ {⍵} ⍺ ⎕WS 'BCol' ⍵} 255 0 0
255 0 0

items.title: Unwinding
items.text:
• error trapping brings us back to the trapping line, and that environment comes back, too
beartrap←{0::'erroneous divider:' q
          q←⍵
          ⍺÷q}

   1 beartrap 2
0.5
   1 beartrap 0
VALUE ERROR
   beartrap[1] 0::'erroneous divider:' q
                                       ∧

items.title: Creating Globals
items.text:
• it is possible to make globals in D:
  • according to the guide:
      {⍎'GLOB←⍵'} 1 2
  • or with the compose operator:
      {GLOB∘←⍵} 3 4
  • or with the full path name:
   {#.GLOB←⍵} 5 6
   {(⍎'' ⎕NS '').GLOB←⍵} 7 8

items.title: Tricks
items.text:
Most of these are copied from dfns@dyadic.com mail group.

  • does ⍺ exist?
⍺←1 1 1⍴⎕AV ⋄ ⍺≡1 1 1⍴⎕AV:..  so-so algorithm
0=⎕NC '⍺':..               version 9
⍺←{⍵} ⋄ 1≡⍺ 1:..           works everywhere
  • an array of constants, the structure of which is copied from another array
{const}¨array
  • "modify" the argument
{q←,⍵ ⋄ ((q='¯')/q)←'-' ⋄ (⍴⍵)⍴q}
  • initialise the left argument
1∘{⍵=0:⍺ ⋄ (⍺×⍵)∇ ⍵-1}
  • a quick alternative to sink←
{0}expr:              ⍝ sink ← expr
  • chaining (to avoid intermediate variables)
{ expr
}{expr
}{expr
 }data
  • passing D: function to its sub-D: function
fun←{{fun ⍵}⍵}   ⍝ hardcoded name
fun←{∇{⍺⍺ ⍵}⍵}   ⍝ via operand!

items.title: Where Is D: Appropriate?
items.text:
• idioms!

There’s no need any more to have unnecessary intermediate variables

  • ad hoc algorithm testing within session

This is one of the real strengths: you can test and retest your code without messing the workspace with temporary variables and functions.

  • coding of clean algorithms

logic "shines through"

  • local functions

on the fly.

Let’s assume that you have a traditional DeleteTrailingBlanks function (one-liner, perhaps). You can change it pretty easily to a dynamic function with the same name. But you can as well (if you need it only in one processing part) make it as a local function within that routine. Or, as I have done it with one application, make a DynInit function, which creates a toolbox of (semiglobal) D: functions, which only exist during the run time. I have found this approach quite useful for my needs.

  • speeding up your ol’ toolbox

The most part of the old workhorses can be very quickly changed to D: functions.

  • APL communication

Because D: code is straightforward, you can show APL code easier than before (e.g. working APL code can be fully shown in PowerPoint presentations).

  • having fun

This is the part I like most ;)

items.title: Where Is D: Inappropriate?
items.text:
• GUI callbacks :(

This may change in the future!

  • BIG applications

(strongly a personal opinion)

Maybe this is just an old-dog-new-tricks syndrome, but I think that the old function syntax with control structures et al. shines here.

  • BTW: ⎕CS is not supported

items.title: Packing: General
items.text: This part of my presentation was meant to be the "practical" part just as to fulfil the promises of the original header line. The idea came last autumn when there was a short but lively discussion about packing in the dfns mailgroup.

items.title: Huffman coding
items.text:
• the most common item is replaced with the shortest binary index
  • decoding is very s l o w in APL

items.title: Lempel-Ziv-Welch packing
items.text:
• a "running" algorithm: if the next part to be handled is already found in the dictionary, it can be replaced with the pointer only -> efficient
  • many variations have patents pending
  • inefficient to code in APL

I know that someone has tried this ;)

items.title: APL Packing
items.text:
Although these methods are not usually comparable with the professional ZIP/ARJ/RAR packers, they have their own uses within the workspaces.

  • traditional simple zero-packing
zapN←{(⍴⍵)(,⍵≠0)((,⍵≠0)/,⍵)}
unzN←{⎕IO←1 ⋄ (1⊃⍵)⍴(2⊃⍵)\3⊃⍵}

This is pretty quick, and especially useful when handling sparse multi-dimensional APL arrays.

  • running length packing (RLE) is slightly more complicated
zapR←{b←{0∊⍴⍵:⍵
         {¯2-/⍵/⍳⍴⍵}(1,2≠/⍵),1
        },⍵
      ⎕IO←1 ⋄ (⍴⍵)b((,⍵)[+\b])}
unzR←{⎕IO←1 ⋄ (1⊃⍵)⍴(2⊃⍵)/3⊃⍵}

Quite useful with bitmaps.

  • unique packing is quite handy
zapU←{⎕IO←0 ⋄ u←∪,⍵ ⋄ (⍴⍵)u(u⍳,⍵)}
unzU←{⎕IO←0 ⋄ (0⊃⍵)⍴(1⊃⍵)[2⊃⍵]}

This works nicely where there are only a small set of unique items in a big variable.

  • outer resource: free zlib.dll
  • Vector 18.1: Lanzavecchia/Smith

Pros: universal, free, efficient. Cons: you cannot bundle them within the workspace, you need to have extra code to ensure that those resources exist.

We need a couple of D: functions (because .dll handles only 8-bit integer vectors).

zapZ←{(⍴⍵)(32768 ZLIB.DeflateIV 83 ⎕DR,⍵)}
unzZ←{(1⊃⍵)⍴323 ⎕DR 32768 ZLIB.InflateIV 2⊃⍵}

items.title: Problem: Bitmaps
items.text: Nowadays GUI apps contain lots of bitmaps: company logos, backgrounds, icons, pictures. Toolbars contain toolbuttons with lots of icons, both standard (which are easily copied from system resources) and hand-crafted (which are buried within the workspace). If you put these parts outside the application, there's the controlling problem, if you enclose them inside your ws, it will grow exponentially, if you don't squeeze them tightly.

items.title: Let’s Test …
items.text:
This is my first test I made after writing a couple of pack-unpack routines.

   'bmp' ⎕WC 'Bitmap' 'D:\bmp\lion'
   cb←'bmp' ⎕WG 'CBits'
   (⍴cb)(⎕SIZE 'cb')
480 568  1090580

First we read a bitmap (in this case we could have read the Bits and CMap properties to save space, but that would have spoiled the results ;) ). We need a tool which tells us the time used with packing/unpacking, the size of the packed data and the percentage saved. Besides, it should test if the data is unpacked unchanged. A dynamic operator is quite suitable for this purpose:

   Tst←{
    ai←⎕AI ⋄ q←⍵⍵ ⍵
    ⍵≢⍺⍺ q:'wrong result'
    sz←∊{s←⍵ ⋄ ⎕SIZE's'}¨q ⍵
 (2⊃⎕AI-ai)(1⊃sz)('%',⍨0⍕100×÷/sz)
       }

items.title: Results
items.text:
unzN Tst zapN cb
   90 1124720   103%

Quick! But the compressing ratio is not nice...

   unzR Tst zapR cb
 240  822148    75%

Chops one quarter off the size, not bad!

   unzU Tst zapU cb
 180  272784    25%

… but this seems to be an approach worth using!

   ZLIB.Init
   unzZ Tst zapZ cb
1132  136692    13%

This works as expected: best compression this far.

   unzB Tst zapB cb
 731  116440    11%

… but this method seems to outperform (in this case) even the ZLIB!!

Let's have a closer look at the last function pair. Actually these are nothing but enhanced unique packing, which works surprisingly well in this case. I have tested with many bitmaps, and usually ZLIB seems to be the winner, but for my purposes these two functions have given a sufficient compression. And hey, you can easily write this algorithm with traditional APL, too!

zapB←{⍝ BMP packer, opened with unzB

   ⎕IO←0 ⋄ u←∪,⍵        ⍝ unique items
   i←u⍳,⍵               ⍝ indices
   w←⌈2⍟⍴u              ⍝ max. width
   b←1,2≠/i             ⍝ repeats
   j←0∨,(w⍴2)⊤b/i       ⍝ binarise
   ((⍴⍴⍵),(⍴⍵),u)b j    ⍝ package

     }

unzB←{⍝ Open a zapB'd package

   ⎕IO←0 ⋄ q←0⊃⍵ ⋄ s←0⊃q ⍝ get vars
   r←s⍴1↓q ⋄ u←(s+1)↓q    ⍝ ⍴, unique items
   w←⌈2⍟⍴u                ⍝ index width
   e←{¯2-/(⍵,1)/⍳1+⍴⍵}1⊃⍵  ⍝ expander
  ⍝ create indices from bit vector
   i←2⊥w{(⍺,⌊(⍴⍵)÷⍺)⍴⍵}2⊃⍵
   r⍴u[e/i]               ⍝ open
     }

These functions, among others (e.g. Shanno-Fano packing), are included in the newest dfns.dws workspace.

items.title: Data Compression with Dfns
items.text:
by Veli-Matti Jantunen, Statistics Finland (veli-matti.jantunen@stat.fi)

“There are zillions of programs already written in other programming languages which address data compression; some of them might even be better at the job than an APL programmer could knock up in half an hour… Build APL on top of common tools rather than write everything for ourselves all the time.” –Dick Bowman

“The ultimate compression: binary information only contains ones and zeros, and because zeros mean nothing, you can just count the ones… I’m sure that someday someone will invent the way to extract thus easily compressed data…” —Anonymous

items.title: Why bother?
items.text:
The years in the DOS world have left their scars: I still try to squeeze everything possible to smaller entities. I detest the idea of my workspace containing unnecessary white space or other compressible stuff, which unnecessarily doubles the download time or fills every diskette, not to mention the myriad of different version workspaces on my hard disk.

This article tells briefly how I developed a data compressor (actually plenty of them), but the reader should appreciate that I had the support of a dfns mailgroup behind me all the time. I could always just send my airy-fairy ideas and code fragments to the group and got useful feedback every time, either via the mailgroup or direct. Thanks to every one of you! APL development is fun, especially with professional help ;-).

items.title: Early Habits
items.text:
The simplest data packing algorithms have been in use for years. When these tools were converted to dfns, the ideas shone through nicely. Null packing simply rips off the zeroes and uses the Boolean vector to mark their places.

packN←{

     cmp←{mask←,⍵ 1↑0⍴⍵ ⋄ (⍴⍵)mask(mask/,⍵)}

     exp←{(shape mask items)←⍵ ⋄ shape⍴mask\items}

     ⍺←1 ⋄ ⍺:cmp ⍵ ⋄ exp ⍵

 }

Note that this clever programming style (shamelessly adapted from John Scholes) lets you write both the packer and the unpacker functions in the same body. Furthermore, you can write the testing operator which utilises this structure:

     PackTest←{⍵≡0 ⍺⍺ ⍺⍺ ⍵}
     packN PackTest 2 3 4⍴10 0 0 20 0 0 0
1

Unique packing is a nice and quickly implemented method (if you have cases with more than 127 but less than 256 unique elements, you may subtract 128 from the indices when compressing to abuse the internal representation; remember to add them when extracting).

packU←{⎕IO←0
     cmp←{u←∪,⍵ ⋄ (⍴⍵)u(u⍳,⍵)}
     exp←{(0⊃⍵)⍴(1⊃⍵)[2⊃⍵]}
     ⍺←1 ⋄ ⍺:cmp ⍵ ⋄ exp ⍵
 }

The third widely used tool is simple RLE packing, which can be found commented upon (!) in the dfns workspace (packR), just like the other packing functions mentioned here.

items.title: New Tricks to an Old Dog
items.text:
When Adrian and Stefano revealed in their Vector article how to use the GZIP engine to squeeze data inside the workspace, I felt that surely there must be better ways to pack data than I had been using. Although the idea to use external dll is a quick and effective one, I happen to be an old stick-in-the-mud: no external parts if possible. Back to the old drawing board - and discussion about compressing algorithms ignited instantly in the dfns mailgroup.

My aim was to develop a quick compressor with a decent packing ratio and as universal use as possible. I could always use GZIP as a measurement rod, and thus could separate interesting but useless ideas apart from those that seemed worth a closer look.

items.title: Borrowed Ideas
items.text:
Stefano explained an old algorithm that was used to pack certain text data, which contained long patterns of the same character. The idea was something like this: there is one character (“esc”) that is used to denote the packed parts, the following character tells how many times the third character is to be repeated. When I had finished the function it became clear that this was meant to be a packer for special purposes, not the all-round text packer, although it bears the name packT.

The next idea was to try to find an open algorithm (as opposed to LZW, which is patented, and anyhow seemed too complicated for me), and I came across the Shanno-Fano algorithm, which belongs to the Huffmann compression family.

The compressor (packS) was pretty straightforward to do (use variable length keys, use the shortest for the most frequent items), the uncompressor was a pain in the brain. Eventually I cooked up something that works, but every time I look at the packH code (John’s version of Huffmann compressor), I feel uneasy.

items.title: An APL Approach: Do It Yourself
items.text:
After furious coding I felt it a little bit awkward to try to mimic other people’s ideas instead of doing something original.

The idea came to me when I was finishing this GUI application with lots of bitmaps hanging around. Although the first compression can be made by diminishing the palette to 16 colours, they still use much of the ws estate. Sixteen colours means sixteen indices which means that they can be presented with just three bits! One night with motivation, and I had it: first find the unique items and store them separately, then calculate the smallest amount of bits that those indices need, and decode them as a Boolean vector. Afterwards, I added a quick RLE coder, and the bitmap packer packB was born. I was astonished to see how well it performed when compared with the really professional tools. Especially the extracting speed was a pleasant surprise.

But this wasn’t quite the general tool I was looking for.

After some months’ quiet life, I got this simple idea: instead of packing single items, I could concentrate on paired items. The pairings can be derived with the unique vector’s outer product with itself, and using Booleans and clever indexing I realised that the packing ratio was in some cases better than with the earlier functions.

The last idea thus far came the next day: what about packing the items according to frequencies so that the first 1 will start a new key, i.e. the shortest keys would be 0, 1 0, 1 1 0, and 1 0 0. Quickly, this idea was coded as:

packQ←{(⎕ML ⎕IO)←3 1
     key←⊃,/{⍵{↓⍺ ⍺↑⍵}¨⊂⍵∘.>⍵}⍳23
     cmp←{dt←,⍵ ⋄ u←∪dt
         f←{+/⍵=dt}¨u ⋄ u←u[←f]
         b←∊(1,¨(⍴u)↑key)[u⍳dt]
         u((⍴⍴⍵),⍴⍵)b}
     unc←{(u d b)←⍵ ⋄ r←(↑d)⍴1↓d
         p←b≤¯1↓0,b ⋄ r⍴u[key⍳p⊂b]}
     ⍺←1 ⋄ ⍺=1:cmp ⍵ ⋄ unc ⍵
 }

Which is by far the best I have been able to put together.

items.title: A Teaser: An Enchanting Universal Algorithm
items.text:
Just an idea: any simple array can be changed to the binary form and back without loss of information. Take two integers, the first is the random seed for roll, the next is the number of binaries to be created. Because there are patterns that can be really long, and thus easily created, this might be the Ultimate Packing Algorithm.

Why doesn’t it work? (I don’t confess I tried, though.)

Happiness is a warm compressor!

P.S. To subscribe to the dfns group, send email to dfns@dyalog.com with subject: subscribe
