items.title: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 125

by John R. Jensen and Kirk A. Beaty
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Abstract
items.text:
This document describes APL2/X, an interface between the X Window System and APL2, designed and built at the IBM Cambridge Scientific Center. APL2/X enables all of the X Window System Xlib calls and data-structures to be used from the APL2 environment. In so doing, it enables APL2 to use a true windowing environment. Several APL2 sample programs using the interface have been coded to illustrate and validate the interface.

The X Window System is a large application written in C. APL2/X has therefore been built upon, as well as heavily influenced, a general APL2-to-C interface that runs on APL2/6000 under AIX, on APL2/370 under VM/CMS and MVS/TSO, and on APL2/PC under PC/DOS. When running under AIX or DOS, a new auxiliary processor, AP144, is used. When running under VM or MVS, APL2 will communicate with C using APL2’s associated processor 11.

The APL2 AP144 X Window System interface has been announced as an integral part of the APL2/6000 product (5765-012). The APL2 X Window System interface for VM/CMS has been released as part of the TCP/IP Version 2 for VM product (5735-FAL). The other implementations remain experimental.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Overview of the X Window System
items.text:
Since the X Window System is probably not that well-known in the APL2 community, a brief introduction may be in order. It is similar to other windowing systems such as Microsoft Windows and Presentation Manager in that it gives you a multitude of calls to control a windows-oriented system, handling the manipulation of the windows on the screen, drawing of text and graphics, and managing the event queue. It is the de-facto standard in the UNIX world, but it can also be used from other operating system environments as well.

The output capabilities of the X Window System can be summarized as follows:

  • Managing a multitude of overlapping windows on one or more display screens.
  • Drawing of graphics primitives (lines, arcs, rectangles and polygons with or without fills).
  • Writing high-quality text.
  • Supporting colour.
  • Image support.

Inputs are received in the form of events. Events can be generated by:

  • The user using the workstation keyboard.
  • The user manipulating the mouse (moving it, using the mouse buttons).
  • Other events, such as when a window is cleared and needs to be redrawn.

Other important facts about the X Window System:

  • Network transparent - An application running on one machine can display on the same machine, or another.
  • Vendor independence - The underlying display hardware is hidden by the protocol from the application, enhancing portability.
  • Concurrency - Several applications active on the workstation at any one time.
  • Information sharing across applications.

The X Window System is separated into three major components:

Component Use Client The client services represent the interface to the application programs. It consists of all the calls that the application programs can use to invoke the various services of the X Window System. It communicates with the X Window System server through the defined X Window System network protocol. Server The server receives the network protocol requests, and acts upon them, drawing windows, graphics, text and images on the display. It also generates event messages whenever the user performs an action such as typing a letter, moving the mouse, etc., and returns these events to the user via the client services. Window Manager The window manager controls the appearance of the various windows on the display. Different window managers exist. A window manager now in common use is the OSF/Motif window manager that gives the X Window System the same "look and feel" as that of the OS/2 Presentation Manager.

These three components of the X Window System need not run on the same physical machine. As shown in Figure 1, the application may be running on, say, a VM host, communicating through the X Window System client services with an X Window System server running on a RT PC or a RISC System/6000. The information flow between these machines is handled by TCP/IP. The net effect of this is that the application’s results appear on the workstation’s display as though the application had been run locally.

Figure 1. The X Window System client-server relationship

It is also possible for a single client to display on many servers at once. Likewise, a server can also service many clients at the same time, displaying the output of many application programs at once. Figure 1 illustrates the relationship.

The X Window System defines a layered architecture. Figure 2 shows the layers of the hierarchy. An application can draw upon the calls of all of these layers.

+-----------------------+
| Application Program   |
|  +--------------------+
|  | OSF/Motif          |
|  +--------------------+
|  | X Widgets          |
|  +--------------------+
|  | X Intrinsics       |
|  +--------------------+
|  | Xlib               |
+-----------------------+
| X Network Protocol    |
+-----------------------+

Figure 2. The X Window System hierarchy

The X Window System network protocol is at the base of this hierarchy, ultimately defining the traffic flowing between the client and server components.

The next level up is the Xlib level. Most application programmers will never interface with the X Window System at a lower level than the Xlib level. It consists of about 400 separate calls written in C, and more than a 100 data structures.

The next two layers, the X Intrinsics and the X Widgets, form sets of routines that create higher-level abstractions. These are then used as a basis for a number of X-based toolkits. A number of standard toolkits are provided with the X Window System, supplied by various vendors. OSF/Motif can be viewed as one of the more elaborate toolkits in existence today. It provides calls to handle such commonly occurring functions as menus, scrollbars, pop-up windows and the like.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Using the X Window System from APL2
items.text:
APL2/6000 using the X Window System in native mode (Figure 3), and APL2/VM using the X Window System in compatibility mode (Figure 4):

Figures 3 and 4. Using the X Window System from APL2/6000 and from APL2/VM

APL2/6000 has several ways that it uses X Window System. The session manager (AP120) uses it, as does the fullscreen manager (AP124).

The simplest way to use the X Window System today from APL2 is to use it in compatibility mode. Thus, the existing interfaces remain unchanged, but the display will now take place on the X Window System workstation. Two possibilities exist to do this:

X3270 is a terminal emulator that enables you to run a 3270-type session on an X Window System workstation, given the proper network attachments. It supports different size fonts including APL2, GDDM-style graphics, 3277GA emulation and some mouse-support. X3270 is an announced IBM product.

GDDM/XD is an interface which permits the display of graphics output from GDDM on workstations supporting the X Window System It is available as part of the TCP/IP product for both VM and MVS. It displays both character and graphics output in a separate window on the X Window System workstation.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Exploiting the X Window System from APL2
items.text:
APL2/X takes a different approach to the X Window System. In order to exploit fully the X Window System from the APL2 environment it is essential that APL2 have direct access to the basic X Window System calls. How this is achieved will be the topic for the rest of this paper.

All the X Window System calls are defined in a table, along with parameter type codes that are used to validate argument inputs and generate call outputs. All calls to the X Window System from APL2 are done using the single APL2 function XWIN, rather that define APL2 functions for each separate X Window System call.

The XWIN function uses the associated processor 11 in the VM environment to communicate with C, and the new auxiliary processor AP144 in the AIX environment, but this usage is completely transparent to the user. To him or her there is a single, common interface to the X Window System from APL2.

(rc [results]) ← [c] XWIN command [parm] [parm]...
command The name of the X Window System call to be invoked, specified as an APL2 character vector. [parm] All but a few of the X Window System calls require additional input parameters to be specified. These are given after the name of the call itself, in the same order as listed in the X Window System documentation. [c]

An optional vector of up to two elements controlling the behaviour of the XWIN function. The two elements are orthogonal to each another:

The first element determines what is returned by the function:

c = 0 x The function never returns anything c = 1 x Return an integer return-code rc c = 2 x Return any result data produced by the call, if any. If no data is produced, nothing is returned in z. c = 3 x Return a one- or two-element vector. The first element always contains the return-code. The second element, if present, contains the result data produced by the call.

The second element determines what happens if the call results in an error:

c = x 0 Ignore any errors c = x 1 Generate a message to the console listing the cause of the error c = x 2 Halt execution on occurrence of an error c = x 3 Generate a message to the console listing the cause of the error, followed by halting the execution of the program.

If only the first element is given, the second is assumed equal to 0. c can be omitted entirely. The behaviour will then be equivalent to a setting of "2 3".

[rc] The operation return-code. [results] The output from the call (if any) is returned in the form of an explicit result. This result includes the X Window System explicit result (if any), as well as any implicit results passed back via output parameters given on the call. More on this topic below.

The different control options caters to many different possibilities. If called with a setting of "3 0", then XWIN will pass back an error code as part of the function return. It is then up to the calling program to check this code and take appropriate action on a non-zero return-code.

If, on the other hand, XWIN is called with a control setting of "2 3", then XWIN will in effect provide a default error handler to check the return-codes as they are returned from each call to APL2/X. If an error is encountered, then XWIN will suspend operation in the function to give the programmer a chance to correct the problem.

The call XOpenDisplay can serve to illustrate the close correspondence between the X Window System calls issued from C and from APL2. In C, a call to this might look like:

dp = XOpenDisplay("");

The same call can be issued from APL2 via APL2/X:

dp ← XWIN 'XOpenDisplay' ''

The X Window System call name becomes the first parameter specified on the call through APL2/X. Apart from this, everything else remains the same.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: HelloWorld
items.text:
It seems as though it is a rite of passage for a windows-based package to have a HelloWorld sample program; APL2/X follows this trend. We will use the APL2 function HelloWorld to introduce many of the concepts of APL2/X.

The goal of HelloWorld is to create a window on the workstation, display some text, and then wait for the user to initiate any further processing. The program is notified of the user’s actions. It responds to three different types of actions on the part of the user:

  • Pressing the left mouse button: When this button is pressed, the text "Hi!" will be written at the tip of the pointer.
  • Pressing any alphanumeric key: The key symbol is written in the window at the tip of the pointer, except in the case of a "q" being pressed. A "q" terminates the application, closing the window.
  • A window expose: This event is generated whenever the window is uncovered. It is a signal to the application to redraw the initial content of the window. Any text written to the window as a result of either of the two actions mentioned above are lost.

HelloWorld exhibits two fundamental concepts of windows-based systems: window manipulation and responding to user-generated events. As such, it serves as an excellent vehicle to introduce these concepts. The discussion here will focus on how to run the HelloWorld program from the APL2 environment, with each X Window System call being generated from APL2. The design of this program is described in:

Oliver Jones: Introduction to the X Window system Prentice Hall, 1989; ISBN 0-13-499997-4

See this text for a full description of each of the X Window System calls.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Initialization
items.text:
∇
[0]   HelloWorld;⎕IO;dp;w;gc;s;e;k;rw;bp;wp;m;hello;
       hi;done;None;hp;hints;rc;nl;x;ep
[1]   ⍝ Sample X program, based on helloworld.c from
[2]   ⍝ Oliver Jones:
[3]   ⍝ Introduction to the X Window system
[4]   ⍝ Prentice-Hall, 1989;  ISBN 0-13-499997-4
[5]    ⎕IO←0
[6]
[7]   ⍝ Define some constant text-strings
[8]    hello←'Hello, World.'
[9]   ⍝ The exclamation point makes hi ugly:
[10]   hi←'Hi',('A'=⎕AF 65)⊃⎕AF 90 33
[11]

The initial section of the functions merits few comments. All that happens in this section is the setting up of the text strings that will be shown in the window later on, and definition of some local identifiers. The only note-worthy item is the way the exclamation point has to be defined. This ensures portability of the code.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Connect to X Window System
items.text:
[12]  ⍝ Initialization
[13]   →(0=dp←XWIN 'XOpenDisplay' '')↓lopen
[14]   ⎕←'XOpenDisplay failed ... HelloWorld aborted'
[15]   →lexit
[16]  lopen:
[17]

The first call to X Window System is to open a connection to the display. The call results in a ‘handle’ or magic number that will be used to identify the connection in all subsequent X call requests. The handle is saved in the dp variable.

Notes:

  • All X Window System calls pass through the XWIN function.
  • The first parameter to this function is always the name of the X call.
  • If the X call requires parameters to be specified, then these are given following the name of the call. The XOpenDisplay call has one parameter: the name of the display to be used. This is given as an APL2 character string. (The default display will be used, as we have specified an empty string.)
  • Character strings are passed (and returned) by value. APL2/X will convert these parameters to the C char * pointers that X ultimately requires. APL2/X also handles NULL-termination of the character strings.
  • All output from invoking X Window System calls are returned as explicit results of XWIN.

The HelloWorld function as described performs minimal error checking. This should obviously be changed for programs and applications targeted for a production environment.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Get more information
items.text:
[18]  ⍝ Default pixel values
[19]   s←XWIN 'XDefaultScreen' dp
[20]   bp←XWIN 'XBlackPixel' dp s
[21]   wp←XWIN 'XWhitePixel' dp s
[22]

Once the connection to the display is established, X can provide the calling program with a lot of information. Here we retrieve the number designating the default screen and the pixel values for black and white.

Notes:

  • All input and output parameters on these three calls are integers. They are passed to (and returned from) X Window System by value.
  • APL2/X handles any required conversion between boolean and integer data types. Floating point numbers cannot be used.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Using X constants
items.text:
[23]  ⍝ Define an X constant[24]   None←0
[25]
[26]  ⍝ Prepare to set window position and size
[27]   (rc nl)←'H¯' axGetFF 'XSizeHints'
[28]   m←+/PPosition PSize
[29]

X Window System defines a large number of named constants in its C header files. These constants should also be available to APL2. However, there are too many constants defined to keep them all in the workspace. (Although technically feasible, it would define so many symbols in the workspace that it would obscure the "real" application variables.)

The simplest solution to this problem is to specify these constants by value rather than by name. However, by doing so we lose a lot of the information content associated with the constant, and we increase any future maintenance burden.

Another fairly simple solution is to define the needed constants as APL2 variables, and then to use these variables whenever the constant is called. The variables can either be defined as global variables, or as local variables within the applicable functions, as is done with None. This is not a recommended solution, though, as it relies on the constants staying forever unchanged. (None will be used further down in the function, in the call to XSetStandardProperties.)

A better way is to use the support for constants built into APL2/X. APL2/X groups the constants by categories. Each group can be brought into the workspace independently of other groups, ensuring that the latest values are used. The axGetFF function loads a named group of constants and establishes them as APL2 variables in the workspace. PPosition and PSize are examples of two such constants.

Notes:

  • axGetFF returns a list of names of constants established in the workspace. We will use the list later on to clear away the variables when they are no longer needed.
  • The name of the group of constants is specified as the right argument to axGetFF. This name is in fact the name of an X data structure. We will return to this topic below.

  • PPosition and PSize each contain 32 individual bits, although given to APL2 as four-byte integers. The simple adding works here because their bits are orthogonal. In the general case this cannot be assumed to be the case, so a combination of decode, logical operation and encode is the advisable course to take, e.g.:

    m←2⊥∨/(32⍴2)⊤PPosition PSize
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Creating a new structure instance
items.text:
[30]  ⍝ Build an XSizeHints structure instance
[31]   hp←XWIN 'New' 'XSizeHints'

APL2/X provides extensive support for X Window System data structures. A number of these commands exist to help you manipulate the X Window System data structures from APL2. The command is specified as the first parameter, and the structure name as the second parameter. Additional parameters will often be required; these follow the structure name on the call.

In this case, New allocates space for a new instance of the XSizeHints structure and returns the address of this instance to APL2. The structure instances are stored in C free storage space (i.e. via calls to the C malloc() routine).
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Importing a structure into APL2
items.text:
[32]   hints←XWIN 'Get' 'XSizeHints' hp

To be used from within the APL2 workspace the structure must be imported into the workspace. This is done by using the Get command. This commands copies the values of the structure into an APL2 vector. Each field in the structure is mapped to an element in the vector in the same order as in the X Window System structure definition. APL2/X handles the appropriate data conversions when copying the data.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Changing the values in a structure (within APL)
items.text:
[33]   hints[H¯flags H¯x H¯y]←m 200 300
[34]   hints[H¯width H¯height]←350 250

Once copied into the workspace the structure instances can be used like any regular APL2 array. Here five of the fields are updated.

The indices of the elements to be changed are given by constant variables prefixed by H¯. These constants were generated by the axGetFF function when the XSizeHints structure definition was loaded in line 27. To recall:

[27]   (rc nl)←'H¯' axGetFF 'XSizeHints'

The axGetFF function establishes a number of global variables in the workspace. These variables can be divided into two separate groups:

Field indices

These variables are used to indicate the location of a given field in a structure. They provide a rough equivalence between the C structure member operation hints.mask and the APL2 version hints[H¯mask].

Since structure field names all tend to be very common identifiers, eg. "x", "name", or "size", it is possible (and advisable) to specify a prefix that will be applied to each field name before it is established in APL2. This avoids name conflicts between the various structures’ field-name index variables. "H¯" is the prefix used in the example given here.

Constants We met these earlier on. They are combined with the structure definitions because they often are used in conjunction with these. It is common that the valid values for a given field in a structure are given by constants, but they can be put to whatever use is wanted. Names of constants are never changed; i.e. the prefix does not apply to constants.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Updating a structure instance (within C)
items.text:
[35]   XWIN 'Put' 'XSizeHints' hp hints
[36]

Changing the values of a structure variable only has effect within APL2. The Put command is necessary to make the updated structure values available to the X Window System calls.

The Put command expects exactly three parameters:

  1. the name of the structure (e.g. 'XSizeHints'),
  2. a pointer to an already defined storage location (e.g. hp), and
  3. the data values to be stored in the structure instance (e.g. hints).
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Creating a simple X Window System window
items.text:
[37]  ⍝ Window creation
[38]   rw←XWIN 'XDefaultRootWindow' dp
[39]   x←hints[1 2 3 4],5 bp wp
[40]   w←XWIN 'XCreateSimpleWindow' dp rw,x

We are now in a position to create our application window. This is accomplished with these two calls. From an APL2/X point of view these are both very ordinary calls.

Note: The hints values can be used like any other APL2 variable. Here four of them are used to specify the window start and extent.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Using the structure pointer
items.text:
[41]   x←hello hello None('A' 'test')2 hp
[42]   XWIN 'XSetStandardProperties' dp w,x

The XSizeHints structure created is now put to use. As the name of the call implies it defines defaults for a number of the window attributes.

Notes:

  • XSetStandardProperties uses an argv parameter. This type of parameter is specified from APL2 as a vector of character vectors. (argv and argc are well-known C variable types. X uses them in several of its calls).
  • The argv parameter is followed by an argc parameter. The information content of this parameter is in a sense redundant in APL2, since the information can be determined by examining the argv variable. One of our general design rules in building the APL2/X interface has been to maintain a fidelity to the standard X Window System call syntax, even though at times it means specifying more information in the call than is strictly necessary.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Freeing the structure after use
items.text:
[43]   XWIN 'SFree' 'XSizeHints' hp
[44]

Note: It is important that the structure is freed after it is no longer needed. If this is not done, it will continue to occupy space in storage, and may lead to storage fragmentation in the long run.

  • The name SFree is used in place of Free so as not to conflict with the free associated with the C malloc function.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Creating a Graphics Context
items.text:
[45]  ⍝ Graphics Context creation and initialization
[46]   gc←XWIN 'XCreateGC' dp w 0 0
[47]   XWIN 'XSetBackground' dp gc bp
[48]   XWIN 'XSetForeground' dp gc wp
[49]

A graphics context is the X Window System version of a magic paintbrush. It is used on any drawing calls to define colours, patterns, and like items. We define one here, so we can use it later on to write some text to the window.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Show the window outline
items.text:
[50]  ⍝ Window mapping
[51]   XWIN 'XMapRaised' dp w
[52]

We are now ready to show the window to the user. This call will do just that. But note that we have yet to write any text into it, nor are we quite ready to accept input from the user just yet.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Which events are we interested in
items.text:
[53]  ⍝ Input event selection
[54]   m←'ButtonPressMask' 'KeyPressMask'
[55]   m←m,⊂'ExposureMask'
[56]   (rc m)←m axGetFF1 'XEvent'
[57]   XWIN 'XSelectInput' dp w(+/m)
[58]   ep←XWIN 'XGetEventBuffer'
[59]

XSelectInput tells the X Window System which events we are interested in being notified about. It is a straight-forward call, except that the last parameter is a bit-mask. The various constants defining the individual bits are defined in the XEvent structure. We could now use the axGetFF function introduced earlier to load in all fields and constants, and then use the variables thus established. However, we chose to take slightly different route:

The axGetFF1 function is used in place of axGetFF. Instead of establishing variables based on the names of the fields and constants it returns the values of a set of named items. Since we are only interested in three specific constants, we use axGetFF1 to retrieve their values.

  • The values retrieved represent individual bits. It is therefore possible to just add them instead of performing a bit-wise "or".
  • Bit-flags are returned in "packed" form, i.e. as integers.

The XGetEventBuffer establishes a pointer to the buffer used to hold events. The same buffer is used for all events, hence we only need to make this call once per session. More on this below, in the discussion of the key events.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Get the event codes
items.text:
[60]  ⍝ Get some more constants
[61]   m←'KeyPress' 'ButtonPress'
[62]   m←m,'Expose' 'MappingNotify'
[63]   (rc m)←m axGetFF1 'XEvent'
[64]  ⍝ ... and some event structure layouts
[65]   nl←nl,1⊃'K_' axGetFF 'XKeyEvent'
[66]   nl←nl,1⊃'B_' axGetFF 'XButtonEvent'
[67]   nl←nl,1⊃'E_' axGetFF 'XExposeEvent'
[68]

X Window System notifies us of the user’s actions by returning events to us upon our requesting them. The type of events will be limited to ones enabled by the XSelectInput call just executed. One of the fields in the returned event will specify the type of event that is being returned. These event types are also defined in the XEvent structure. To be able to distinguish the returned events by type we set up a vector with the expected types with the axGetFF1 function.

We also load in the field definition variables describing the event structures we might receive. They will help us access the right fields in the structures.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: The event loop
items.text:
[69]  ⍝ Main event-reading loop
[70]   done←0
[71]  levent:→(done=0)↓lend
[72]

We now sit in an event loop, responding to the incoming events as they come in from the display, until done.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: XNextEvent
items.text:
[73]  ⍝ Read and process the next event
[74]   x←lKeyPress lButtonPress lExpose lMappingNotify
[75]   →(m=K_type⊃e←XWIN 'XNextEvent' dp)/x
[76]

XNextEvent returns the next event in the queue to us. Once the event has been returned the event type is compared with the mask defined earlier to set up the proper branch. Effectively this serves as a "Case-on-Event" statement. The event is returned as a vector of structure fields, much the same way that the structure Get call would return a structure instance.

This differs from the way that the XNextEvent call is handled in X Window System. In native X Window System, the XNextEvent call also specifies a second parameter, a pointer to an XAnyEvent structure. XNextEvent fills in the structure fields, thereby making the event values available the calling program. This is an example of how APL2/X differs from native X Window System by automatically handling the call’s output parameters.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Handling the Expose events
items.text:
[77]  lExpose: ⍝ Repaint window on expose events
[78]   →e[E_count]↑levent     ⍝ Count > 0 ?
[79]   x←e[E_display E_window],gc,50 50
[80]   XWIN(⊂'XDrawImageString'),x,hello(⍴hello)
[81]   →levent
[82]

Expose events are generated whenever a window is made visible on the screen. Multiple expose events may be generated, so it makes sense only to respond to the last one. X Window System caters for this approach by providing a count of future, already pending expose events as one of the fields in the expose event itself. We use this field to ignore all but the last expose event.

When we receive the final expose event we want to write the content of the hello variable to the screen. This we do using the XDrawImageString call.

  • All events provide the value of the originating display connection in the e[E_display] item in the event structure. This identifies the origins of an event, in case of multiple, concurrent display connections have been established. Here its value equals that of dp.
  • Most (but not all) events also specify the window that generated the event (some events do not come from windows). This equals the value of w here.
  • The last parameter ((⍴hello)) may seem superfluous. This is certainly the case in the APL2 environment, where the information could be had from the preceding parameters. Again, as stated earlier, APL2/X sticks as closely to the defined syntax of the X Window System calls as possible. In this case, the inconvenience of having to specify this size field did not outweigh the desire to maintain fidelity to the X Window System call syntax.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Handling the ButtonPress events
items.text:
[83]  lButtonPress: ⍝ Process mouse-button presses
[84]   x←e[B_display B_window],gc,e[B_x B_y]
[85]   XWIN(⊂'XDrawImageString'),x,hi(⍴hi)
[86]   →levent
[87]

The comments here mimic those made for Expose events. The only noteworthy change is the use of events[B_x B_y] to indicate the position where the writing is to start. This coordinate pair is returned as part of the ButtonPress event structure, and indicates the position of the tip of the mouse pointer when its button was pressed. The net effect of this code fragment is to write the text "Hi!" at the mouse pointer when the mouse button is pressed.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Handling the KeyPress events
items.text:
[88]  lKeyPress: ⍝ Process keyboard input
[89]   →(done←(↑k←∊1⊃XWIN 'XLookupString' ep)∊'qQ')↓levent
[90]   x←e[K_display K_window],gc,e[K_x K_y]
[91]   XWIN(⊂'XDrawImageString'),x,k(⍴k)
[92]   →levent
[93]

KeyPress events are generated when the user presses any of the keys on the keyboard. However, information about the key pressed is not part of the returned event structure, so we need to use the XLookupString call to acquire this information. This call has one input parameter, the event whose key we want to ascertain. This parameter can be specified either as the set of values returned on the XNextEvent call, or using the pointer to the event buffer that we set up earlier on. The latter method is faster, as it does not involve passing a lot of information through the interface, so we use it here.

The key pressed is returned as the second element of the XLookupString return. We test on this field to see if it matches a "q". If so, we terminate the program. If not, we print the key character at the current mouse pointer location.

All event structures are exactly as defined by X Window System, except for the XKeyEvent structure returned by the KeyPress (and KeyRelease) events. The XKeyEvent structure contains one additional field not found in the X Window System definition: the character representation of the key. This last field is named "key" and is appended to the end of the structure.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Mapping Notify
items.text:
[94]  lMappingNotify: ⍝ Reset keyboard
[95]   XWIN 'XRefreshKeyboardMapping' e
[96]   →levent
[97]

MappingNotify events are generated when the keyboard mapping needs to be re-established (i.e. when it has been changed elsewhere). See the referenced text for more information on this call.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Termination
items.text:
[98]  lend: ⍝ Termination
[99]   XWIN 'XFreeGC' dp gc
[100]  XWIN 'XDestroyWindow' dp w
[101]  XWIN 'XCloseDisplay' dp
[102]  nl←⎕EX¨nl
[103] lexit:
     ∇ 1991-4-16 18.43.0 (GMT-4)

Before terminating the HelloWorld sample program we free up the resources we have used. Some of these resources are controlled by X Window System, so the X Window System must free them.

We also clear the workspace of all the APL2/X-defined variables. These could conceivably be saved with the workspace, obviating the necessity of loading them every time the application is run. A production level application probably should take this latter approach, unless the underlying structures change very frequently.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Current Status
items.text:
At the time of this writing, all the X Window System Xlib calls have been implemented. The full interface is available as AP144 in the APL2/6000 product (5765-012), and as part of the TCP/IP Version 2 for VM product (5735-FAL).

Where do we go from here? A number of possibilities are possible as experimental work in the Cambridge Scientific Center. The following is a list of some of these:

  • Port APL2/X to MVS.
  • Implement selected higher-level calls from the Toolkit and OSF/Motif.
  • Build an APL2 workspace of functions to make better use of the X Window System calls. The present set of functionality is very rich, but very tedious to work with. It is like using GDDM directly (via AP126) to generate 3270 panels, without the use of any APL2 cover functions, except that the problem is further magnified.
  • Enable other packages written in C to be used from APL2. Since APL2/X is built upon a general APL2-to-C interface, these possibilities are made available. One such set of functions would be the TCP/IP communications protocol.
path: An Interface Between APL2 and the X Window System

items.title: Generic Local Objects
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 103

by Zdenek V Jizba

items.title: Abstract
items.text: A proposal is made to provide a facility to define classnames in the header of a user defined function. Rationale for this proposal is based on requirements for building Expert Systems with APL.

items.title: Structure of Expert Systems
items.text:
An Expert System Shell is a collection of specialized software to support the many different types of activities that such a system requires. For example, a shell allows for the maintenance of “rules”, supports one or more “Inference Engines”, and provides for communications with external data sets. Of course it also supports many other functionalities.

To build an Expert System, the Knowledge Engineer starts with the shell, and adds specialized information, also known as the “Knowledge Base”. This information usually consists of a collection of rules to define the behaviour of the system, special hierarchical dictionaries to relate various technical terms of the domain, and may also include specialized software.

Over the last decade I have been studying the possibility of using APL (and APL2) to build such Expert Systems. As I gained experience, a number of concepts have evolved that integrate the unique aspects of APL with the paradigms that are commonly used in the field of Artificial Intelligence. It appears that no matter what the computer language, the specialised needs of a new paradigm always bump against the limitations imposed by that language. The solution of these problems has often in the past been to design new languages. I believe that a much better solution would be to expand the scope of existing language. This is especially true of APL.

The STSC APL*PLUS for the PC supports a number of features that facilitate the development of Expert Systems. There are, however, a number of features that would enhance even more the power of APL in building applications in the field of Artificial Intelligence. This note describes one such feature. It deals with a way to define classes of local names in the header of a function. Although I give a specific proposal, the form is not particularly important. What is important is the underlying concept. In what follows, I attempt to explain my justification for the need.

items.title: Shell and Domains
items.text:
An Expert System deals with one or more domains of expertise. (These will hence be called just domains.) In its APL implementation, a domain may consist of a collection of APL functions, rules, variables, dictionaries, and other data structures. A cardinal rule of good Expert System design is a complete separation between the shell and the domain. This means that before the domain is invoked, the shell must not have ANY domain specific objects. When the domain dependent task is activated, the many domain objects are brought into the workspace, or are created. On completion, the results of the process are stored in appropriate objects, and the domain is wiped out from the workspace, returning to the clean initial state.

One might ask, why this need for separation? There are many reasons, but consider a complex problem that requires not one, but a series of domains to be applied sequentially. Then add the requirement for any one domain to call another domain as a kind of sub task. In such an environment any attempt to maintain global domain objects (functions and variables) would create chaos.

There is a simple way to separate domain objects from shell objects in APL. All one needs, is to define special domain specific functions called “drivers”. A driver function includes in its header the names of all domain specific functions and variables. Unfortunately, there is a limit on the length of defined function headers. This is a significant constraint in the design of some domains.

The need for restricting object names is not limited to domain drivers. An inference engine is a global object in the workspace, but it processes rule sets that are local to the domain. Such rule sets typically require communication of data between different rules. This can be handled by creation within rules of variables that must be global to all rules, but local within the function driving the rule set. Here again the natural APL solution is to define specific variables that are local to the APL inference engine driver. The more of these variables that can be defined in the header, the more flexibility one has in designing the rule set.

Individual rules also may be quite complex. In my approach, a rule contains at least three components. One is a (generally unique) tag that identifies the rule, another is the antecedent, and one is the consequent. Both the antecedent and the consequent are valid APL expressions. In the antecedent there may be any number of expressions, including assignments, separated by the APL*PLUS diamond. (Only the last expression must return a result. This result must be a boolean scalar.) The consequent may also contain multiple expressions separated by the diamond.

This structure and form of rules allows generation of variables that can be used in making decisions. These variables form a kind of scratch pad memory and should be local to the APL function that processes a single rule. This function, therefore, must also include local variable names that can be used only as long as that rule is being evaluated.

One way of thinking of rules is as a special type of defined function. A rule has a name, produces no result, and has no loops or branching other than a decision whether to evaluate the consequent. A rule also produces side effects that are global to the rule, but local to the rule set. Yet, a rule is not a separate object. It is a part of a larger object called a rule set. In my implementation, rule sets are defined as segmented strings (see APL*PLUS for definition of segmented strings). There is a segmented string for each component of a rule set. Rule sets are stored in component files when under development in the shell. For run time versions, rule sets can be brought into the workspace as segmented string variables.

I have named three types of APL defined functions that require localization of generic object names. These are the drivers for specific domains, inference engines to process rule sets, and individual rule processors. In some of these, the number of named objects may be so large that the current limit on the length of the header may be inadequate.

items.title: Implementation of Generic Variables
items.text:
Although I have been severely constrained by the limit of header length, so far I have found ways of getting around such limitations. In general, I give single letter names to generic variables, and three letter names to domain specific APL functions. Within the inference engine function, eight single letter variables in lower case are global to all rules within a rule set. Within the rule evaluation function, another eight upper case letters are used for scratch pad memory. (These two functions also require many other local object names that are specific to the function task, so the header is quite long.) The remaining upper and lower case single letters are available for domain specific variables.

When a new domain-specific APL function is defined, the domain driver must also be re-defined by adding the new function name to its header. The access to the workspace of the newly defined function must also be defined. Some of this extra effort could be eliminated and the headers could be streamlined if APL supported the naming of generic object names.

In future I foresee domains where the number of named objects will exceed the available space in function headers. Hence the following proposal.

items.title: Proposal
items.text:
One way to implement generic localization of names would be to apply the same techniques that are already in use elsewhere:

ONE* would localize all names beginning with ONE TWO? would localize all four letter names TWOx

In addition I would suggest the following convention:

$aa would localize all two letter names starting with two lower case letters $Aa would localize all two letter names starting with an upper case letter followed by a lower case letter $a* would localize all names of arbitrary length in lower case $Aa* would localize all names starting with an upper case letter followed by lower case letters.

I am not acquainted with the inner workings of APL interpreters. It is possible that some of my proposals may be impractical to implement. For example, the usage of the * cannot be implemented until specific named objects are created. This may be difficult to achieve, and even if possible may slow down the interpreter too much. The usage of the ? and of the $ on the other hand is more like a short hand notation, because the number of valid names defined by these symbols is limited.

If neither of my suggestions is feasible, there is still the possibility for expanding the maximum length of the header.

items.title: Problems for APL Buffs (I)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 109

by Zdenek V Jizba

items.title: Author’s Note
items.text:
Last night, it occurred to me that some of the problems I coped with during my professional career might be of interest to the APL community. This morning I put together a few notes on one of these subjects, and am sending them to you under the title "Problems for APL Buffs"

The concept of a random number is closely associated with a population frequency distribution. When a random sample is taken, a histogram of this sample should look like the frequency function of the population from which the sample was taken. The larger the sample, the closer should the histogram approach in shape that frequency curve.

In APL, a source of random numbers is available with the roll:

      ?10⍴3
1 2 3 3 1 3 2 2 1 3

In the above example (I am using 1 as the index origin) the digits 1 2 and 3 should appear with roughly equal frequency. Therefore the underlying frequency distribution is a discrete function, and is defined as one third at the points 1 2 and 3. With the roll, and with some simple transformations, it is possible to generate random samples from arbitrary frequency distributions. A frequency function where each value has an equal chance of occurrence is called a uniform distribution.

Consider now a two-dimensional frequency function:

      ?3 2⍴10
5  3
1 10
1  6

Each row is now a sample of two values. The associated frequency function is not a curve (or more accurately, points on a line for the discrete case), but a surface. There are two dimensions for the random variables, and one dimension for the probabilities. The extension to higher dimensions is straightforward.

items.title: Rotations
items.text:
Another type of random sample is one dealing with rotations. Consider points in the x/y plane:

      P←3 2⍴5 0 4 3 3 4

      P
5 0
4 3
3 4

If we desire to rotate these points ‘randomly’, what does that mean? (From here on, whenever I use the word random I will mean ‘random in a uniform sense’.) The analogue of a uniform distribution for a rotation is one where each angle from 0 to 360 is equally likely. But given the angle, one still has to come up with a transformation that would change X,Y values to a new set of rotated ones X′,Y′. We can readily define such a function:

      ∇ U←ROT W
[1]   ⍝ Two dimensional rotation
[2]      U←2 2 ⍴ 1 1 ¯1 1 × 2 1 1 2○○W÷180
      ∇

Suppose that we desire to rotate the rows in P in such a way that the first point (row-1 of P) moves to the place of the second point. (The angle is that for which the tangent is 3÷4 or 36.8698976…)

      Q←P+.×ROT M←36.86989764584402

      Q
4                3
1.4              4.8
4.4408921E¯16    5

To rotate these points back, there are two ways of doing it:

      Q+.×ROT -M
5   4.4408921E¯16
4   3
3   4

or …

      Q+.×⍉ROT M
5   4.4408921E¯16
4   3
3   4

The reason is that the two-by-two array is a special one, belonging to a class of matrices called unitary. Its transpose is equal to its inverse; the matrix multiplied by its transpose produces the unit matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

items.title: Moving on the Sphere
items.text:
The next question that one might ask is: what about three dimensions? Suppose we have points in space and we want to rotate these in a random way: how could we define random?

Things get a little more complicated here. To ‘simplify’ matters, consider a landmass on the globe (we will assume here that the Earth is a perfect sphere). If we desire to move England to, say Australia, we could do that in two steps. First we move the centre of gravity of England to the desired point. Then we rotate England around this centre of gravity as in the two dimensional case. Intuitively, a random motion on the unit sphere would be defined by picking any point on the sphere with equal likelihood, followed by a random rotation.

How would one define an APL function that randomly selects a point on a sphere? THAT might be a useful function. But is the motion that we have just defined truly random? Consider the following: it is well known that any motion on a sphere is equivalent to a simple rotation. The pole of that rotation has a special name: it is called the Euler pole. Given an Euler pole, and an angle of rotation, one can generate any motion of a two-dimensional object on the surface of a sphere.

This provides us with a second possible definition of random motion on a sphere: first select a random location on the sphere as before; then call this point an Euler pole, and select a random rotation in the plane. Are these two definitions of random motion equivalent? (I do not know the answer!)

So we have several interesting APL problems here. First consider writing an APL function that would generate a random unitary matrix for rotation in three dimensions. Next, given such a matrix, find the associated Euler pole and rotation. Another problem: given two points on the surface of a sphere (say London and Edinburgh) and a new location for the first point and a geographic direction for the second one (i.e. a desired rotation) find the appropriate unitary matrix. Finally: given an Euler pole, and a rotation, find the associated unitary matrix.

If these problems are too trivial, try this one. Define random rotation in more than three dimensions, and write an algorithm to generate the associated unitary matrix. Make sure that the matrix involves only rotations, and does not include inversions, which is a totally different subject.

If these problems are too abstract, here is one that is more practical: you have a map on the scale of 1:25000 from very high latitudes (the grid of parallels and meridians is not cartesian). You can digitize points on that map to about 4 significant digits of accuracy. Write an APL function to convert the digitized cartesian co-ordinates to latitudes and longitudes. If you use some of the functions discussed above, your function should be less than six lines of code.

items.title: Problems for APL Buffs (II)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 117

by Zdenek V Jizba

Chevron Oilfield Research Corporation (a subsidiary of CHEVRON) has a program called "Adopt-A-School". Under this program, employees volunteer to give short lectures on science to fifth and sixth grade schools in the La Habra area. On learning about this program, I volunteered as an annuitant to prepare talks under the title "computers as tools for thought".

The plan is to use I-APL. Using the direct definition mode, one can easily design a lecture that minimizes teaching hard-to-understand concepts, and maximizes the excitement of learning. For example, to avoid using special symbols, I define all primitive functions by their names:

      COUNT:⍳⍵

      ODDS:(2×COUNT ⍵)-1

      REDUCE:⍎⍺,'/',⍕⍵

      SCAN:⍎⍺,'\',⍕⍵

The first two functions are defined and discussed in the class, but the last two are merely illustrated with examples.

      '+' REDUCE COUNT 100
5050

This particular example is used as an occasion to relate the story of Gauss, who as an 11 year old solved such a problem to the amazement of his teacher.

As I was preparing these lectures, I uncovered some other dusty corners of 17th century mathamatics. This note takes off from here, and leads into the fascinating subject of integers.

One question asked of the class is "how can one find the square of a number without using multiplication?". After drawing squares on the black board, one can easily justify the following:

      '+' REDUCE ODDS 5
25

In fact the next expression shows this to be true for the first 10 integers:

      '+' SCAN ODDS 10
1 4 9 16 25 36 49 64 81 100

So we can generate a list of consecutive squares from a list of consecutive odd numbers. Since there are odd numbers that also are squares, we have a way to generate triplets such that the sum of the squares of the first two will equal the square of the third.

This can be best shown by defining function FERMAT:

      ∇ U←FERMAT W
[1]    ⍝Generate all quadratic triplets
[2]     U←1+2×W
[3]     U←U,(((U*2)-1)÷2)∘.+ 0 1
      ∇

(As an exercise, you might want to explain the formula)

      F←FERMAT 0,⍳10

We can look at this array:

      F
 1    0    1
 3    4    5
 5   12   13
 7   24   25
 9   40   41
11   60   61
13   84   85
15  112  113
17  144  145
19  180  181
21  220  221

and note that it includes the triplet {1 0 1} which certainly holds but does not seem to belong. We can verify that the sum of squares of the first two columns equals the square of the third column:

      ∧/(F[;3]*2)=+/F[;1 2]*2
1

The question that immediately comes to mind, is whether this function generates ALL such triplets (we will of course ignore all multiples such as 6 8 10). Might there not be other ways to build yet more distinct triplets? But before we tackle this question let me explain why I named the function FERMAT.

In the 17th century, there was a mathematician names Fermat, who specialized in what is now called "Diophantine analysis". In this branch of algebra, only integers are acceptable solutions to problems. Around 1637 Fermat was reading a book written by Diophantus of Alexandria with the title of "Arithmetica". On the margin of one of the pages, Fermat wrote the following:

"To divide a cube into two other cubes, a fourth power, or in general any power whatever into two powers of the same denomination above the second is impossible, and I have assuredly found an admirable proof of this, but the margin is too narrow to contain it." (see p.509 " The World of Mathematics" J R Newman, ed. Simon and Schuster 1956")

This theorem became famous, because all attempts to reproduce his proof since that time have failed. As we will see, one can go a long way towards an insight into the kind of thinking that drove Fermat to his conclusion.

Coming back to our problem, the question is whether there are integers \(\{a,b,c\}\) such that \(a<b<c\) other than those generated by function FERMAT. We will restrict the search only to those triplets for which the largest common divisor is 1. Clearly we must search sets where \(1<c-a\). It turns out that this question can be resolved not only for powers of two, but arbitrary powers as well.

In equation form we can write (It could be done using APL, but here algebraic notation seems better):

\[\begin{equation*} \text{(1)}\quad (b+k)^N - b^N = a^N \end{equation*}\]

When \(k=1\), and \(N=2\), we have the solution in FERMAT. Therefore we want to study the case when \(k>1\). First we rewrite (1):

\[\begin{equation*} \text{(2)}\quad (b+k)^2\, (b+k)^{N-2} - b^2b^{N-2} = a^N \end{equation*}\]

and note that for \(N=2\) the equation is reduced to (1). Expanding the square polynomial, and collecting terms we get:

\[\begin{equation*} \text{(3)}\quad b^2[(b+k)^{N-2} - b^{N-2}] + k(k+2b)(b+k)^{N-2} = a^N \end{equation*}\]

Now the expression in brackets is the difference of two powers, and it can be factored as the product of two polynomials:

\[\begin{equation*} \text{(4)}\quad \{[(b+k)-b] \times P[(b+k),b,(N-3)]\} \end{equation*}\]

Here the polynomial \(P[(b+k),b,N-3]\) is shorthand for:

\[\begin{equation*} \text{(5)}\quad P[x,y,M]=X^M + X^{M-1}Y+.....+XY^{M-1} + Y^M \end{equation*}\]

But since \((b+k)-b=k\), we find that \(k\) can be factored out from the left hand side of equation 3. Let us assume that \(k>1\). Then, since \(k<a\) (why?), we must have \(a=i{.}j\) where \(i\) an \(j\) are integers (why?). Assuming that \(ij\), we can now rewrite (1):

\[\begin{equation*} \text{(6)}\quad ((b+k)/i)^N - (b/i)^N = j^N \end{equation*}\]

Since \(\{a,b,c\}\) have 1 as the greatest common divisor, the ratios \((b\div i)\) and \((c\div i)\) are not whole numbers. Can the sum of the powers of fractional numbers add up to an integer power? Let us assume that the answer is yes and pursue the consequences. We can use (6) to write the function GFERMAT to calculate triplets for arbitrary \(k\).

      ∇ U←K GFERMAT W;B
[1]    ⍝Generate all quadratic triplets for given K
[2]     U←((W*2)-K*2)÷2×K
[3]     →(0=⍴U←(B←U=⌊U)/U)/0
[4]     W←B/W
[5]     U←W,U∘.+0,K
      ∇

When \(k=1\) we should get the same result as with FERMAT:

      1 GFERMAT ⍳20
 1    0    1
 3    4    5
 5   12   13
 7   24   25
 9   40   41
11   60   61
13   84   85
15  112  113
17  144  145
19  180  181

Now let us try this function with \(k=2\):

      2 GFERMAT ⍳20
 2    0    2
 4    3    5
 6    8   10
 8   15   17
10   24   26
12   35   37
14   48   50
16   63   65
18   80   82
20   99  101

There seem to be three kinds of triplets. First, there is the permutation {3 4 5}. Next we have multiples of triplets generated with \(k=1\) {6 8 10}. Finally there are some new sets {8 15 17}. We can try to remove the first two kinds by adding some more filters to GFERMAT:

      ∇ U←K PFERMAT W;B
[1]    ⍝ Generate all quadratic triplets for given K
[2]     U←((W*2)-K*2)÷2×K
[3]     →(0=⍴U←(B←U=⌊U)/U)/0
[4]     W←B/W
[5]     U←W,U∘.=0,K
[6]     B←(∧/0=K|U)∨∧/0=2|U
[7]     U←(~B∨>/U[; 1 2])⌿U
      ∇

Now we can try out this function:

      2 PFERMAT ⍳20
 8   15   17
12   35   37
16   63   65
20   99  101

      3 PFERMAT ⍳2000

      4 PFERMAT ⍳2000

Why do you suppose we get results with \(k=2\) only?

Finally, for \(k=1\) and \(N=2\) we have from (1):

      ∧/(F[;1]*2)=+/F[;2 3]
1

(Why?) When we can also show that "a" must be an odd number. Also note the following:

      (-/F[;3 1])÷2
0 1 4 9 16 25 36 49 64 81 100

Can you explain it? At this point I stop. You of course may pursue this and entertain yourself. You may develop additional insights, and remember, you have a powerful ally in APL.

items.title: Object Oriented Programming and APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 109

by Zdenek V Jizba

It has been frequently suggested that software development lags behind the fast advancing technology of hardware. The chief reason for such statements is the difficulty in development of new, ever more complex applications. Our software tools often fail to take the fullest advantage of state of the art in our hardware.

To be sure, a great deal of effort is being placed on development of our software tools. Improvements in programming languages, as well as new techniques in programming are constantly being introduced. These often receive much publicity. Examples of improvements in software efficiency, or breakthroughs in problem solving include the following: "Structural programming" "Prolog and Artificial Intelligence", "Neural nets" and more recently "Object Oriented Programming (OOP)".

Object Oriented Programming in particular, has been of considerable interest to the APL community. This is attested by a number of published papers and by proposed conference themes. Before we turn our attention to OOP, it is useful to refresh our memory about the evolution of computer programming languages.

Most programming languages are invented by an individual or a group of individuals, who have some concept of how one should communicate problem solving to a computer. The commonly used name for this concept is "Paradigm". The table below is an incomplete list of distinct paradigms for a variety of languages.

PARADIGM CHARACTERISTICS LANGUAGE VonNeuman architecture efficient translation to machine language Fortran, C Compact notation array processing APL Object Oriented Programming Class Hierarchy Smalltalk Tree structures List processing Lisp Predicate Logic Horn clause Prolog

When a programming language becomes established it seldom remains unchanged. As new demands demonstrate weaknesses, it begins to evolve. What originally may have been a simple concept, becomes more complex as more features are added to it. Compare, for example the first version of APL to the most recent releases of APL with nested arrays.

If there are those who feel that once a language has proven itself, it should become cast in concrete, they should realise that this is the path to oblivion. Programming languages have been invented to solve specific classes of problems. Today, many of these problems have been solved, as a visit to any PC software store will demonstrate. The problems that have not yet been solved, and these are many, pose a great deal of challenge. We need the sharpest possible tools for their solution. Perhaps the best way to improve our tools is to continue evolving the power and productivity of our programming languages.

Looking at the table of paradigms, one should note that each one tends to have its strength in one particular domain of problem solving. VonNeuman languages are good for efficient usage of existing hardware architectures. APL is good for compact expression of solutions to mathematical and business problems. Smalltalk excels in the handling of graphical displays. Lisp and Prolog are strong in problems dealing with logic.

A significant trend in recent times has been the merging of two or more paradigms into a single language. A good example of this is C++, which is a VonNeuman type language, that has been enhanced by the addition of Object Oriented Programming features. Even APL has not escaped this trend, as we could note by studying Nial.

If there is a weakness to APL, it would be its lack of expressiveness to display graphical images. This shortcoming as well as the need to extend features that ease development of AI applications has prompted me to explore the potential of Object Oriented Programming as a possible paradigm to augment current APL.

In this communication we will explore three questions. What is an Object Oriented language? Can APL be used in an Object Oriented programming style? What would it take to make APL an Object Oriented Programming language?

items.title: What is an Object Oriented Programming Language?
items.text:
The concept of Object Oriented programming was developed by the creators of Smalltalk. This paradigm is rooted on four fundamental ideas:*

  1. Abstraction
  2. Encapsulation (information hiding)
  3. Inheritance
  4. Polymorphism (operator overloading)

*FOOTNOTE: Object Oriented Programming has its own vocabulary of technical words. We will use underlined text to emphasise these. Smalltalk, in turn also uses special conventions to describe its components. Classes, for example are expressed as proper names with upper case first letter. As an example, object and Object are related but distinct concepts.

We will try to explain each of these concepts with simple examples. However, these turn out to be only properties of a more fundamental concept, namely that of an object. The abstract concept of an object cannot exist in a vacuum. Every object must belong. Indeed the name of the item to which an object belongs is called a class.

The definition is circular. A class is also an object, and as such it must belong too. This approach leads to what is known as a "Class hierarchy". At the highest level of this hierarchy is the class known as Object. (To complete the circularity of the definition the class Object in Smalltalk belongs to a metaclass, but this principle can be ignored in elementary expositions.)

How does one develop programs in Smalltalk? Every object, or a class (there is a distinction between these two concepts, which we will for the time being ignore), can receive messages, and act upon them. Indeed messages are the ONLY means of communication with objects. A message can be in the form of a request, or can be a command to do something.

At this point it might be useful to pause in the abstract explanations, and to give specific examples. In APL the following expression is simple and straight forward:

      5 + 2
7

We have a dyadic primitive function that takes a left and a right argument. The function then evaluates the expression producing the result (7). In Smalltalk, this same expression produces the same result, but the interpretation is completely different:

  5       +         2
object selector parameter
       [     message    ]

The object (integer 5) receives the message to add two to itself. The primitive function + is called a method (or selector in this special case), which the object called an integer understands, and knows how to process. Why is such a distinctive point of view so important? Because it leads to a totally alien (from the point of view of APL) way of problem solving. This is illustrated by the next two examples:

In APL the following expression is very similar to the first one:

      5.2 + 3.1
8.3

We have the same primitive function in a dyadic expression. In Smalltalk, we are dealing with a different object, namely (real 5.2). The method has the same symbol, but is evaluated in a different way. The property of assigning the same symbol (name) to a method in different contexts is called polymorphism. As a Smalltalk user would put it, we are overloading the plus operator. (Overloading is but one example of polymorphism). The next example is even more revealing:

      5 > 2
1

In APL we are dealing with another dyadic function, but in Smalltalk things are totally different. The object (integer) does not know how to evaluate >. The reason is that the symbol > is evaluated in exactly the same way for an integer as for a real number. So why should there be two copies of a function that does the same thing to objects in different classes (integer and real)?

The solution in Smalltalk is to recognise that both integer and real are subclasses of another class called Number. Therefore when the object 5 sees the method > and fails to recognise it, it seeks to find that method in its superclass namely Number. As it turns out, the class Number also fails to find this particular method. It seems that there are classes other than numbers (e.g. date) for which the > symbol has a meaning.

Not finding the method > in class Number, Smalltalk goes to the next superclass which is Magnitude, and discovers that this class knows how to proceed. This process of searching up the higher levels in the class hierarchy is called inheritance.

We should not leave this brief and admittedly sketchy description of Object Oriented paradigm without mentioning the other two attributes, namely Abstraction and Encapsulation.

In principle, at the most fundamental level, Smalltalk could be defined by only one class, namely that of an Object. But now if we want to solve arithmetic problems, we must define those methods (addition multiplication …) that are needed for this purpose. Since there are many types of problems where these primitive functions are not used, it does not make sense to define addition in the class Object. What Smalltalk allows is to define a new class, a subclass of Object.

This subclass is to contain all of the methods that may be needed to solve the problem. However, before doing that, it is important to evaluate the possibility of other similar problems that might not be of arithmetical nature, but which may need some of the same primitive methods. This is the rationale for defining Magnitude as a subclass of Object, Number as a subclass of Magnitude, and Integer as subclass of Number. This feature of segregating an classifying objects by common denominator methods (and sometimes even variables) is called abstraction.

The attribute called encapsulation is a natural consequence of abstraction and the usage of messages as the only means of communication. An object will respond only to a valid message. That message may request access to either a function (method) or data. Neither the method nor the data (there may be exceptions but this is not relevant for this elementary discussion) is available outside the object. This idea that functions as well as information is strictly local to each object is called encapsulation.

Earlier we treated objects (not to be confused with the class Object) and classes as the same. This is not quite true. When a new class is defined, it contains a special method, called the class method, that has the capability of generating specific instances of that class called objects (there are also class variables). Each instance is in some ways a copy of the class, in the sense that it can respond to messages, store data and produce results. Instances are like leaves on a tree. They exist, do a useful function, and fall off when no longer needed. Leaves, unlike branches (classes), however, cannot bud into new branches (subclasses).

items.title: Can APL Be Used in an Object Oriented Programming Style?
items.text:
The brief answer is: certainly. It is always possible to develop a workspace (or a collection of workspaces) together with suitable files to simulate any particular paradigm. However, some characteristics of Object Oriented Programming might be more difficult to produce than others. Consider encapsulation: we would have to be able to generate arrays that contain local functions and variables. Clearly APL does not have such facility.

On the other hand, by allowing functions and variables to be stored in files, and by providing suitable cover functions (also to be stored in files) we can simulate that kind of an effect. If this approach is inefficient, we could release the requirement of encapsulation, by allowing class functions and variables to be global. However, the price of that would be a restriction on other aspects of OOP such as polymorphism. Consider the following example:

We define an APL (APL2 would be better) function called PLUS. This function behaves in every way the same as the primitive +:

      5 PLUS 2
7
      PLUS/2 3
5
      'F' PLUS '1'
10

The last example shows that PLUS is overloaded in the sense that it also evaluates hexadecimal character strings. But now, because PLUS is a global function, and not local to the class hexadecimal, we are no longer able to use it to define addition of character strings in systems with base other than 16.

With true encapsulation, we could generate objects (number systems) to arbitrary base such that function PLUS would be evaluated correctly. Let us sketch briefly how true encapsulation might be implemented in APL. To illustrate the approach, let us continue with the example of function PLUS. Let us assume that we desire to also work with octal notation. We will do it by creating objects using only a current version of APL.

What would such numeric objects look like? Since objects must have characteristics of functions as well as data, we have to decide whether to use defined functions or arrays. For the numeric example, we will use defined functions, but later we will also show an example where a nested array can be used more efficiently. We start by defining the monadic function OCTAL:

OCTAL 8 10

We would like to use function PLUS to do addition in this number system:

(OCTAL 7) PLUS OCTAL 7 16

Since function PLUS is global, the result of OCTAL 7, the character ‘7’ would be interpreted as hexadecimal ‘7’ which is the same as decimal 7. The answer we would actually get is ‘E’ which is incorrect. In fact the symbol ‘E’ is not even defined in the octal system.

The APL OOP solution is to create class Octal, and to transfer the expression as a message to that class. (Note that function OCTAL is in caps, but class Octal is a proper name).

So far so good, but how does one go about insuring that the correct class method (APL function) will evaluate this expression? It is done under a special function called a "driver". A simple driver called GO is illustrated below:

    ∇ GO ;E
[1]  ⍝ Driver for OOP expressions
[2]   ⍞←'      '
[3]   E←⍞
[4]   EVAL E
[5]   →2
    ∇

This niladic function is an infinite loop that simulates an APL prompt. Whatever is entered at the keyboard, becomes the character string (E) which is evaluated by function EVAL. The objective of function EVAL is threefold:

  1. It has to determine the "domain of expertise" of expression E.
  2. It has to create the object capable of solving the problem.
  3. It turns over expression E to that object as a message.

Note that if EVAL merely executes E, function GO is "invisible" to valid APL expressions. This means that as far as APL expressions go, GO does absolutely nothing, except use up extra computer time. (It would cause an error halt for any System Commands though.)

Let us take a closer look at function EVAL:

    ∇ EVAL E;D;DRIVER
[1]  ⍝ Driver for evaluation of non-APL expressions
[2]   D←GETCLASS E
[3]   GETDRIVER D
[4]   DRIVER E
    ∇

To see how this function works, consider the following expression:

(OCTAL 7) PLUS OCTAL 8

Function GETCLASS extracts first the tokens from that expression. (Here we use the word "token" to mean any character strings not enclosed in quotes.) The token PLUS is recognised as a function, but the token OCTAL is not identified. With the help of a dictionary, EVAL determines that OCTAL is associated with class Octal. This label is returned by GETCLASS to local variable D.

Next, function GETDRIVER loads into the workspace function DRIVER, a class method in class Octal (a polymorphic function). This driver contains in its header the names of all methods as well as variables that are associated with that class. DRIVER is then given the string E for evaluation. The details of the algorithm in DRIVER vary from class to class. Here we show only a portion of the header that is pertinent to the current problem:

    ∇ DRIVER E;...;OCTAL;PLUS....
[1]   ⍝ Driver for messages in class Octal
[...]
    ....
    ∇

Function DRIVER first retrieves from component files whatever methods will be needed to solve the expression. At this point expression E becomes an executable APL expression. On completion of its task, DRIVER, which is local to EVAL disappears together with all associated methods and variables.

In practice, this example is much too simplistic. Our next expression may also belong to the same class. It would make sense than to write the code in such a way that a series of messages default to the same class (or instance of a class) until a new "domain of expertise" is called for. The simplest way would be to invoke function GO within DRIVER. This approach may be adequate for specific situations, but does not address the general problem.

Let us now look at another problem. In this next example, the OOP solution involves dealing with arrays. Consider the property of inheritance and the following nested arrays:

      JOHN
'NAME' 'John'
'CLASS' 'Relative'
 ...
'ISA' 'PERSON'
 ...

Person
 ...
'ISA' 'Human'
 ...

Human
 ...
'HANDS' 'two'
 ...

These arrays have been generated in a previous session when a particular family tree was stored under class Relatives. The arrays do not reside in the workspace, but will be loaded (from appropriate component files) in response to the message described below by function DRIVER which is specific to class Relatives.

To borrow terminology from the field of Artificial Intelligence, these arrays are called frames. The array called JOHN (an instance), has many rows and two columns (only those pertinent to this example are shown). The array Person (a class) shows only the row associated with class variable ISA, and the array Human (another class) shows the row associated with class variable HANDS. These arrays have been made available through functions EVAL and DRIVER as a result of examination of the following expression:

JOHN HANDS

FOOTNOTE: Since my work to date has been done under APL*PLUS, the above arrays would be stored in Component files as segmented strings.

The allocation of a proper domain of expertise may not be obvious in this case. Function EVAL may handle that with the following dialogue:

      JOHN HANDS
What are we talking about? Relatives
two

(Before solving the expression, the user is asked to specify the appropriate domain of expertise. Entering ‘Relatives’ should be adequate.)

If John is an instance of class Relatives, we may find that the variable HANDS is not defined in that class. However the label ISA points to possible inheritance in class Person. The search for a response to message HANDS eventually will lead to the contents of line ‘HANDS’ in class Human.

The practice of naming first the object, followed by the message is unwieldy and too restrictive. With the power of APL, some additional parsing functions should enable us to provide a more human-like communication:*

      How many hands does JOHN have?
two

*FOOTNOTE: The attendees of my APL87 tutorial on the subject of Expert Systems had the option to take home with them a workspace and associated component files that illustrated this expanded notion.

Clearly, the array Person is more complex. Since it defines a class, it should contain additional information:

      Person
'CMETHOD' '...'
'CVARIABLE' '.....'
'ISA' 'Human'
'FUNCTION' '...'
 ....

CMETHOD, for example may specify an APL function to be invoked whenever an instance of class Person is to be generated. (There may be more than one class method, since Person may require responding to more than one type of message.) CVARIABLE may specify one or more names (and possibly contents) of class variables. Some of the class components such as ISA may also be transferred to each instance. These would be called instance methods and instance variables. (Instance methods and variables may also be defined within an existing instance). ISA in instance JOHN is an example of a variable that points to a possible inheritance path. FUNCTION in Person could contain a list of local APL functions (methods) that will respond to messages sent to instances of class Person.

There is no implication that the approach illustrated in these two examples is the only or even the best way to handle Object Oriented programming with APL. It merely demonstrates the feasibility of using APL in that way.

Although the workspace approach to Object Oriented Programming may seem adequate, it is not. In a WINDOWS environment, such as that pioneered by Smalltalk, it is possible to re-enter a suppressed object by a mere click on the mouse. This would be roughly equivalent to being able to re-enter a defined function, and to reuse previously generated local variables. This is clearly not feasible with current versions of APL. The examples illustrated in this section could be made re-entrant, but only at prohibitive costs in execution speed.

items.title: What Would it Take to Make APL Object Oriented?
items.text:
Developing Object Oriented programming style in APL is feasible, but requires building a superstructure of defined functions in a workspace. It also may require the generation of special component files to implement true encapsulation. The natural next step is to ask, if it would be possible to enhance APL so that the Object Oriented approach is built into the language.

In this section, we will consider such a modification, but do it with the caveat that it is not a proposal. At this stage, it is not clear whether the evolution of APL should take such a radical direction. We shall call the new version of this language APLOOP.
