items.title: Internet Programming with the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 74

by Andrei Kondrashev
path: Internet Programming with the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor

items.title: Processes and Threads
items.text: Multitasking is the ability of an operating system to run multiple programs concurrently. Under the Windows NT operating system, concurrently running programs are called processes. Each process has a private virtual address space, its own copy of the executable code, GDI objects, etc. Very few Windows resources can be shared between different processes. Processes have limited possibilities to communicate with each other. All interprocess communication methods are strictly controlled by the operating system. Multithreading is the ability of a process to multitask within itself. Each process starts with a single thread. Additional threads can be created later on. All threads of a process run in the same virtual address space and share all resources of the process. A thread can execute any part of a process’ code, including a part executed by another thread. This allows many independent and concurrently running threads that are using the same code, to perform similar operations on different data. All threads can access global variables of the process, but they use their own stacks that make the thread’s local variables unique. Windows NT implements multitasking at the thread level.
path: Internet Programming with the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor

items.title: HTTP
items.text:
HTTP (stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol) is an application-level networking protocol. HTTP can be implemented on top of any reliable transport protocol (usually TCP). Well-known port number for HTTP is 80. HTTP is a multi-purpose data transfer protocol. It can be used to transfer any type of data. HTTP is a "sessionless" protocol. When a client needs to get data from the server, it connects to the server’s port 80 and sends an HTTP request. The server replies with the HTTP response and closes the connection. Thus, the term "sessionless" means that the session consists of only a single act of message exchange. A good example of a "session-oriented" application protocol is FTP. HTTP is very easy to implement, but relatively tricky to use in interactive network applications. Despite the fact that modern Web browsers and servers are able to re-use the TCP connection to increase performance, that does not change anything for the application programmer. From his point of view, each HTTP request initiates an absolutely new session with the server. No previous exchange history is directly available.

An HTTP request consists of three parts: the HTTP request line, HTTP request headers, and the HTTP request body. The structure of the request line is:

<METHOD><SP><URL>[<?><PARAMETERS>]<HTTP/1.0><CRLF>

Where:

Characters "<" and ">" are used to separate different elements of the line; <METHOD> can be "GET", "HEAD", or "POST"; <SP> means the blank space ASCII character; <URL> is a universal resource locator; <PARAMETERS> is an optional list of parameters; <CRLF> means two ASCII characters: carriage return and line feed.

The universal resource locator (URL) is a character string that identifies the resource (data file, or something that will produce the data file) on the Internet. Generally, it consists of the address of the Internet server and the path information. Both IP and DNS addresses can be used to address the server. The path information indicates the location of the resource on the server. The server will map this virtual path using its own internal rules to find the physical location of the resource requested.

Parameters (or query string) may specify additional information for the server’s data-producing process. Parameters are separated from the URL by the "?" character. For example:

www.lingo.com/isap/isap.dll?ws=counter

The method defines how the additional request information is being transferred to the server. If the method is "GET" or "HEAD", the request does not contain the request body. If the method is "POST", the request body contains additional information to be used by the server’s data-producing process.

The request headers follow immediately after the request line. Header fields (each must be terminated with CRLF) carry additional information about the request and the client itself. If the request body is present, there will be at least the Content-Type and the Content-Length headers. An empty line (contains CRLF only) indicates the end of request headers.

The request body can be anything. The type of the information is defined by the Content-Type header. If it is missing, plain ASCII text is assumed. This is an example of an HTTP request (note the empty line between the request’s headers and body:

POST www.lingo.com/isap/isap.dll?mydoc.htm HTTP/1.0
Accept:image/gif,image/jpeg,*/*
Content-Type:application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length:7
- empty line here -
ws=demo

The structure of the HTTP response is similar to the structure of the HTTP request. Only the request line is replaced with the response status line. This is an example of the HTTP response:

HTTP/1.0 201 OK
Content-Type:text/html
Content-Length:44
- empty line here -
<HTML><BODY>This is a response</BODY></HTML>

The response body can be any binary output: plain text, HTML, GIF or JPEG images, movie clips, etc. It also can contain client-side-specific data, such as a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, for example. There are two distinct ways the HTTP server can prepare the response:

  • server returns a static document defined by the URL;
  • server runs a data-producing program defined by the URL, and that program prepares the document that is returned by the server.

The client doesn’t distinguish between these cases, and doesn’t care how the HTTP response was produced.
path: Internet Programming with the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor

items.title: HTTP Servers and APL
items.text:
A program that understands HTTP requests, and is able to send back to the client HTTP responses, is called an HTTP (or Web) server. As we saw above, HTTP is a very simple protocol. All Web "magic" happens on the client side. A Web browser is a rather complex program that parses HTML, creates forms, decides what method and URL to use, optimizes communications with the server, etc. The server, in its turn, is relatively simple. One of the most important features that any HTTP server should support, is the ability to run external data-producing programs that generate HTTP responses dynamically. This feature drives all commercial use of the Internet. A data-producing program can be run as a separate process on the server’s computer or as a separate thread of the server’s process.

The simplicity of an HTTP server is very tempting. As soon as the socket programming became available under all major APL (and J) implementations, it was possible to develop HTTP servers purely in APL. If the socket interface has a callback feature, a pretty decent simple HTTP server can be implemented in about 30 lines of APL code. This server, of course, will be able to use APL programs to generate dynamic HTTP responses. Let’s discuss what’s wrong with this idea.

Poor performance. Up to 99% of the work that any Web server has to perform is simple file transfer. It means that the APL program will frequently ⎕NTIE, ⎕NREAD, and ⎕NUNTIE the files. APL is not very suitable for these operations. There will be multiple moves of data between various buffers before the data will be, finally, dumped to the TCP output buffer. Note that Windows NT is able to send files over the TCP connection very efficiently, in the background, taking almost no CPU time. Internet servers use this facility, so the performance of an APL-based server that has to send many static documents will be much worse in comparison with, let’s say, Microsoft Internet Information Server, that has been specifically designed to perform such operations very efficiently. Next, as of this writing, an APL-based server cannot take direct advantage of the fact that it is running under a multitasking operating system. Only non-preemptive multitasking can be implemented under all currently available APL systems, until real multithreading is available. As a result, the simple file transfer operations that IIS does in parallel on all active connections, would be executed sequentially by an APL server. Of course, the performance is something application-dependent. You may decide that the performance of an APL server is acceptable for you. My point here is that standard tools will perform better anyway.

All industry-standard Internet servers must support various security and encrypting features. In order to implement the necessary level of security, the server must be deeply integrated with the operating system. APL programs run under control of an APL interpreter that isolates them from the operating system. Of course, anything is achievable, but is the result worth the effort spent? Probably not, especially because full-scale security and encrypting cannot be implemented purely in the APL environment anyway.

The maintenance issue is rather important. Usually, in large organizations a special department performs everyday routine maintenance of all servers such as data backup, setting the permissions on the server’s resources, and so on. In most cases those people are not programmers at all. They are "certified" users (network administrators, etc.), who completed special training and who know exactly how to do certain things. Infrastructure departments don’t like to use non-standard critical software developed by a third-party vendor, because it might be difficult to find and/or to train the supporting personnel. This is why, for example, it is so easy to invent yet another programming language, but it is so difficult to make someone else use it. It’s the same story with Internet servers: clients prefer to use system software developed by Microsoft, IBM, or Netscape, but not by MyCompany, Inc.

An APL HTTP server won’t be able to run anything except APL. This is not good. There are many other Internet programming tools around. There will be more, for sure. Not all tools are equally suitable for all purposes. The freedom to choose the right tool and to use more than one of them simultaneously on the very same Internet server is important for many companies that use the Internet commercially.
path: Internet Programming with the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor

items.title: Résumé
items.text:
APL Web servers are possible, but their usage is limited to Intranets (because of lack of sufficient security). They can be acceptable for really heavy applications that are used by a very limited number of concurrent users, in cases when a data-producing program is so complex that other issues become less important in comparison with the advantages of direct use of APL. There are various tricks that allow deploying APL servers indirectly and under control of "standard" Web servers. As an example, you may look at http://www.1travel.com. The hotel booking part of this Web site is supported by a hidden APL server (implemented by Lingo Allegro USA, Inc. and Shepp & Associates LLC).

The access to this server is fully controlled by another Internet application written in a language other than APL.

However, APL is a very suitable language for Web-based applications. Much better, from my point of view, than anything else available on the market now, including Perl. The only (and usual for APL) problem is how to use it together with other existing software systems and only in the area where APL is unbeaten: the data processing. Let’s look at what is currently available.
path: Internet Programming with the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor

items.title: CGI vs. IISAPI
items.text:
One of the most popular and simple methods of creating dynamic HTTP responses is called Common Gateway Interface (CGI). The idea of CGI is very simple. When the server determines that the URL defines a data-producing program, it creates a new process using the code defined by the URL. The server sets the process’s environment variables in order to pass the parameters of the request: REQUEST_METHOD, CONTENT_TYPE, CONTENT_LENGTH, and others. The server also re-directs the process’s standard input and standard output devices to the TCP socket that supports the HTTP connection. Thus, a CGI program can simply use the standard input/output functions to read and write to the socket. The CGI process terminates when the program has sent all data to the socket. The main advantage of CGI is that virtually any programming language can be used, including APL. All that you need is the ability to access the environment variables, and to read and write to the standard output device. Because the processing of HTTP requests heavily involves string manipulation operations, special languages have been designed specifically to use with CGI.

What’s bad about CGI? First of all, each CGI request must be supported by its own process. For example, if there are ten CGI requests processed by the server, there will be ten concurrently running processes (probably, executing exactly the same code) on the server computer. Despite the fact that NT tries to re-use code and resources from the previous instances of the same program, by mapping portions of physical memory to the virtual memory of different processes, it is not always possible to avoid the replication of the same code. When APL runs, the workspace will be duplicated for sure. You can use the Task Manager to analyse how much it costs you to run more than one instance of your application.

Secondly, it takes some time to start a CGI process. For such a "heavy" system as APL, this time can be substantial (we will need to load a workspace too). Next, because a CGI process terminates when it’s done with the request, it cannot take direct advantage of previous runs of the same program. For example, if a CGI program must access a database server in order to create the response, it will have to log on to the server every time, when it starts. For many industry standard database servers, the logon is a very unpleasant and long procedure (may take dozens of seconds), which will add an additional overhead to the HTTP server response time. All these reasons make CGI practically unusable for sophisticated server-side processing. CGI programs can be used only for very simple operations and should be coded in compiled languages that produce small executables.

Different vendors of HTTP servers introduced various alternatives to CGI for developing data-producing programs. The rest of this article will discuss so-called server extensions for the Microsoft Internet Information Server (IIS).

IIS exposes a special application interface (IISAPI) that can be used by developers to create very effective data-producing programs. Server extensions are Windows dynamic link libraries (DLL) and they run as threads of the IIS process. When IIS receives a request that requires running an extension, it loads the corresponding DLL and uses the DLL’s code to start yet another thread. The DLL remains in the IIS virtual address space even after the request is completed. Because threads can share the same executable code, IIS needs to have only one copy of the extension DLL to run any number of concurrent independent threads, which require this DLL in order to generate HTTP responses. Many different extension DLLs can be used at the same time.

Thus, the first obvious advantage of IISAPI versus CGI is that IIS extensions require zero loading time. Secondly, they do not waste memory, if more than one concurrently executed request requires running the same data-producing program. Extensions are more effective than CGI, because they can take advantage of the fact that they are part of the server. The IIS exports functions that allow the program to perform data exchange operations more efficiently, rather than just reading and writing to the standard input/output device. IIS extensions can also use the fact that they are not removed from the memory. They can be permanently connected to a database server, for example. IISAPI provides the best possible performance in comparison with all other available server-side Internet programming tools.

The only disadvantage of IIS extensions is that they are relatively difficult to develop. Only the C language can be used for programming. An extension DLL must be thread-safe. It means that the DLL must work correctly, even if more than one thread, based on the same code, is run by the same process. Any additional DLLs that could be used by an extension, must be thread-safe too. If you are planning to use ODBC, be prepared that most ODBC drivers are not thread-safe. So, for us, as APL programmers, it would be very desirable to use APL as an IIS extension. Lingo Allegro USA, Inc. developed the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor (ISAP) that can be used with Dyalog APL to develop IIS extensions in APL.
path: Internet Programming with the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor

items.title: Internet Server Auxiliary Processor
items.text:
The idea of ISAP is to provide the interface between Microsoft Internet Information Server and Dyalog APL. From IIS’s point of view, it has to be just an extension DLL. From Dyalog APL’s point of view, it should be something that can accept commands and data from APL. ISAP needs to inform APL about incoming HTTP requests, and to be able to execute IIS functions on behalf of APL, such as getting information about requests, reading client data, and sending back HTTP responses. And it has to be able to handle multiple concurrent requests too.

Figure 1 shows the architecture of the IIS-ISAP-Dyalog APL interface.

Figure 1

When ISAP.DLL is loaded by IIS for the first time, there is only one main ISAP’s thread running. This thread handles communications with Dyalog APL using one shared variable. Immediately after loading, ISAP starts Dyalog APL with an application workspace. How to start APL and what workspace to use is specified in ISAP’s initialization file. When an HTTP request that refers to ISAP.DLL in its URL arrives at the server, the server starts a new thread of ISAP. This new thread is called a channel. The channel posts a notification message to APL and switches into a wait state, effectively allowing other threads to run. The notification message has only one parameter - the channel number. After the notification message is received, an APL application can execute commands on this channel. More than one channel can exist at the same time. The APL application can work with the channels in any order it wants. It can process more important requests before less important ones, for example. It can split time-consuming requests into steps and process short requests between the steps of long requests. All of this is decided by the APL programmer.

The SERVER function below is a generic IIS-based application.

     SERVER;_ISF
[1]  SETGLOBALS
[2]  →SHARE↓EXIT
[3]  '_ISF'⎕WC'FORM'('COORD' 'PIXEL')('EVENT'5'SERV_CB')('VISIBLE'0)
[4]  SAY'NOTIFY'('_ISF'⎕WG'HANDLE')
[5]  '.'⎕WS'EVENT' 131 'SERV_CB'
[6]  ⎕DQ'.'
[7] EXIT:CLEANUP
[8]  END

When Dyalog APL starts the application workspace, this function is executed as the result of the execution of the latent expression. First, the application performs its initialization by running the SETGLOBALS function. This is application-specific. Next, it executes the SHARE function, which is a part of ISAP. This function establishes the connection between ISAP and Dyalog APL by sharing a variable. After that, the application creates an invisible window, called _ISF, that will receive the notification messages from ISAP (of course, you can use any other name for the form object). _ISF’s callback function (SERV_CB) must process at least one message, message 5, which is ISAP’s notification message. Other events can be processed too, if the application is going to implement any kind of non-preemptive multitasking within itself. When the notification window is created, the program sends the NOTIFY command to ISAP, which informs it about which window should receive the notification messages. The callback function should also handle event 131 - Windows shutdown - in order to perform any necessary clean-up (such as disconnection from a database server, updating and closing files, and so on). Finally, the SERVER goes into the message waiting state. When ⎕DQ exits, which can happen on IIS shutdown, the application performs the necessary exit procedures by executing the CLEANUP function. The END function is a standard ISAP procedure that terminates ISAP.

The SAY function is a part of ISAP and is used to send commands to the auxiliary processor. The general syntax is:

R←SAY COMMAND ARGUMENTS

COMMAND is a simple character vector—the command’s mnemonic. ARGUMENTS is a general APL array that depends on the command used. The function returns the result of the command, as its explicit result, or generates error 667 that has to be trapped by the application. Most of ISAP’s commands should pass the channel number as one of their arguments. ISAP will execute such commands in the context of the appropriate thread of the IIS. Many commands are executed by ISAP asynchronously. It means that in cases where it is possible ISAP will return control to APL before IIS completes the execution of the command. This allows APL and IIS run simultaneously, increasing overall server performance.

All real work on processing HTTP requests takes place in the SERV_CB function. This function could be very straightforward and simple, if the application only needs to process a single HTTP request, or it can be rather sophisticated, if you want to run more than one APL application under IIS. It can process HTTP requests in the order it receives them, or it can implement a non-preemptive multitasking to process many requests simultaneously. These are choices that are left completely up to the APL programmer. ISAP doesn’t care which approach you use. Figure 2 shows the principal diagram of HTTP request processing under ISAP.

Figure 2

The processing always starts with the GETINFO command (unless you don’t care what request you are processing). This command returns a 19-item nested vector that carries the complete information about the IIS channel and the HTTP request. It also contains the posted data from the client, if the POST method was used in the HTTP request. All data, returned by this command, are translated to the Dyalog APL character set, including any characters that are transmitted as escape sequences.

The processing of any request must end with the CLOSE command. This command informs IIS that the processing of the request has been completed. IIS terminates the corresponding ISAP’s thread and closes the TCP connection with the client.

An APL programmer can use anything available in the APL language and other ISAP’s commands between GETINFO and CLOSE in order to send an HTTP response back to the client. Any type of response body can be used: HTML, image, or a custom binary file. It is also possible to redirect the request to another URL on the same server, or to a URL on some other server on the Internet. ISAP supports several commands that produce GIF and x-bitmap images that can be constructed using the standard graphical functions of Dyalog APL.

You can download the complete ISAP documentation from the Lingo Allegro USA, Inc. Web site at http://www.lingo.com.
path: Internet Programming with the Internet Server Auxiliary Processor

items.title: Sample Application: Page Reference Counter
items.text:
One of the most popular applications running on Web sites is a page reference counter. This application displays (usually in the form of a nice looking picture) the number of references to a page (usually, the site’s home page). Of course, if some Web page is generated dynamically, the page counter can be generated as text simultaneously with the page content. However, this is not convenient to use. Many pages are very complex and the most of their content is static. A better approach would be to take advantage of the fact that some HTML elements require an additional HTTP request to be sent by a browser. One such element is an embedded image. Images can be inserted in the HTML document using the <IMG> tag. The SRC parameter of the tag denotes the URL that the browser should use in the HTTP request in order to obtain the image file. Thus, if we use the URL to a picture-producing program, instead of a static picture file, it will do the job. This approach allows the use of the same counter-generating program to count any page on the Internet by simply inserting the appropriate <IMG> tag in the document we want to count references to.

The following is the example of an HTML file that can be found at http://209.19.63.4/docs/count.htm (the IP address is fictional):

<HTML><HEAD>
<TITLE>Internet Server Auxiliary Processor</TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY BGCOLOR="#FFFFFF" TEXT="#000000">
<CENTER>
<H1>The Counter Demo</H1>
<P>Number of hits to this page:
<P><IMG SRC="/ISAP/ISAP.DLL" BORDER=0 ALT="Counter">
</BODY></HTML>

We are assuming that the ISAP.DLL file can be found in the /ISAP virtual directory on the server. To make our example as simple as possible, we will create an application that is able to handle only one HTTP request. This is why the SRC parameter of the <IMG> tag refers to ISAP.DLL without any additional information, such as the application name, which would be needed, if we wanted to execute more than one APL application using ISAP on the same server.

First of all, we need to decide how we will keep the information about pages and their reference counters. In APL the simplest way to do this is to use a two-column nested matrix. The first column is a nested vector of simple character vectors that are URLs of pages that we are counting. The second column is a simple numeric vector, each element of which is the current number of references to the corresponding URL from the first column. We could store this matrix in an APL file. The application will read this file at initialization time, and will write the updated matrix back to the file when it terminates. The file will have the same name as the application workspace, and will be stored in the same directory. We need to create this file manually and to initialize its first component with an empty matrix.

There are many ways to construct the counter’s image. One possibility is to use bitmaps that represent elements of the counter. How the counter will look is a matter of taste. Let’s use a fixed length counter with, let’s say, seven decimal places. We will fill unused decimal places with a "blank" element. It means that we need eleven bitmaps of the same size that represent "blank" and ten digits. I have created such bitmaps that look like the elements of an LCD display. It is a good idea to read these bitmaps from the disk during the initialization to save time while processing requests. We should delete them, when the application ends. We will assume that all bitmaps are stored in the same directory where the application workspace resides, and that the file names are B0.BMP, …, B10.BMP, where B10.BMP represents the blank element. It will be possible to change the appearance of the counter by replacing the bitmaps.

Now we are ready to write the SETGLOBALS and CLEANUP functions for our server application (see the SERVER function above).

     SETGLOBALS;PATH
[1]  ⎕WSID ⎕FSTIE TN←1+⌈/0,⎕FNUMS
[2]  URL←⎕FREAD TN,1
[3]  COUNT←URL[;2] ⋄ URL←URL[;1]
[4]  PATH←(-(⌽⎕WSID)⍳'\')↓⎕WSID
[5]  PATH←(⊂PATH,'\B'),¨(⍕¨¯1+⍳11),¨⊂'.BMP'

The REFERER parameter of the HTTP request will be the URL of the parent Web page (the count.htm file). IIS will recognize that the extension program should be run and will call ISAP. ISAP sends the notification message to APL signaling that it is time to start the processing of the request.

The SERV_CB function that will be called by the interpreter, when the notification message arrives, first checks whether Windows or IIS is going to be shut down. If so, the application terminates. Otherwise, the fourth element of the message is ISAP’s channel number. The function sets the trap for error 667 that can be generated by ISAP commands. If everything is OK with the code, this error can be generated when, for example, a client presses the browser’s Stop button before our program sends the response. In this case, IIS will close the TCP connection with the client, and the attempt to send the response will fail. If this happens, we simply need to close the channel. It is converted into upper case and stored in the DATA variable. Lines 9-16 update the database and retrieve the current value of the counter for the URL. The value of the counter is represented as a nested vector of seven names of the bitmap objects that we created before. items.title: Multitasking
items.text:
The idea of using APL for server-side Internet programming assumes that we should be able to run more than one APL application from the same server. The simplest, but not the best, way of doing this is to run more than one copy of ISAP.DLL (must be placed in different virtual IIS directories) connected to its own copy of Dyalog APL. The only advantage of this approach is that Windows NT will run the applications in parallel without any effort spent from our side. Another approach would be to implement the multitasking using only a single copy of ISAP and Dyalog APL. This is much better, because it saves a lot of computer resources and in many cases can work even faster than straightforward replication.

Figure 4 shows the idea of an application manager that can run multiple APL applications using only one copy of Dyalog APL.

Figure 4

The application manager consists of the root namespace (the manager itself) and the library of applications (several namespaces). When an HTTP request invokes the application manager, it obtains the request’s channel number (in our case 2) and creates an empty namespace, called CLIENT2. So, the channel number serves as a thread identifier. After that, the manager reads the request parameters and stores them as a thread global variable. The request must include the application name. In our example, the value of the request’s WS parameter identifies the namespace to run. The manager copies all objects from the corresponding library namespace to the CLIENT2 namespace and starts the execution of the thread by executing the value of some global variable in the namespace (the namespace’s "latent expression"). When the execution of the "latent expression" is completed, the application manager closes the channel, deletes the namespace, and exits the callback function.

This idea of running many applications using a single copy of Dyalog APL is used on Lingo Allegro USA, Inc.’s Web site. You can download a sample workspace that will explain all the details of this approach. Other similar solutions are also possible.

This method, however, will not allow us to run more than one "application thread" at the same time. The reason for this is that the application manager cannot receive any new messages until the callback function exits. In order to implement non-preemptive multitasking, the program manager must interrupt the execution of a "thread" and exit from the callback function more or less often. Of course, the manager cannot really "interrupt" the execution of a program in a namespace, but a namespace itself can yield control to the program manger. A good opportunity for that, for example, could be a situation when a program places a request to a database server and waits for its answer. The program manager should be able to recognize such situations and to exit the callback function without expunging the namespace. The namespace will continue its execution, when the notification message arrives from the database access tool, and the program manager calls the namespace from the point where the namespace’s execution was interrupted. Of course, a database auxiliary processor has to have a callback mechanism, like Lingo Allegro’s AP747 does. Any external operation that is executed by Windows in a separate thread, and which causes an APL program to wait for its results, is a suitable moment for a namespace to yield control to the application manager. However, there must be a callback feature in place that is able to signal back to APL that the program can continue its execution.

Not all applications need to be interrupted. For example, the page counter program that we showed above needs just a fraction of a second to complete. Such applications can be run in a single step of execution. If a namespace just runs, performing long calculations, interrupts can be organized artificially. In this case, the namespace must post (not send) an appropriate message using the ⎕NQ function in order to resume its execution at a later time.

As soon as APL interpreters have real multithreading, server-side applications would become much simpler and would have much better performance.

Exploring ActiveX Data Objects from Dyalog APL by J. Korablev and G. Roche (Gunter.Roche@gmx.de)

Abstract This paper presents a short overview of the ActiveX Data Objects (ADO) model and the main steps for application development in Dyalog APL. ADO wascreated by Microsoft in order to provide an easy-to-use application level interface to currently known data sources. This interface is based on the underlying system service OLE DB andis used in tools for rapid application development. ADO is easily accessible for users, becauseit is included with popular Microsoft products such as Internet Explorer 4.0, Internet Information Server 4.0 etc. ADO is also available for download from the Microsoft Web site (the OLE DB SDK, the Microsoft Data Access Components 2.0, and the Data Access SDK). The implementation of ADO in Dyalog APL is based upon OLE Automation, a mechanism thatallows one application to control another, and which provides the ability to mix code written in different programming languages.

Introduction. OLE DB and ADOarethe low andhighlevels of interface that enable Universal Data Access. This is Microsoft strategy for providing access to all types of information from a variety of data sources (relational and non-relational data, mainframe ISAM/VSAM, hierarchical databases, emails and file system, text, graphical, and more). For each kind of the data source there is a specific service component, called a provider. An integral part of OLE DB is the OLE DB Provider for ODBC, which enables OLE DB to communicate with today s popular ODBC drivers and data sources.

There is a definite difference between ADO and OLE DB from the developers point of view, OLE DBenables universal access to any data. ADOfacilitates it for developers of programs. Since ADO is located on top of OLE DB,it has a low memory overhead, and a small disk footprint. ADO supports key features for building client/server and Web-basedapplications, includingthe following:

* Independently-created objects. This allows the programmer to create and work only with the objects that are required.

116

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

* Improved performance by updatingall data on the server in a single update (Batch Updating).

* Support for stored procedures.

¢ Different cursor types.

* Automatic or manual parameters managementfor better performance and morecontrol.

ADOis implemented as an OLE Automation Server andis accessed from Dyalog APL using the OLEClient object. Note that OLE is very dependent on the Visual Basic programming language and APL syntax is more restricted than Visual Basic. This discussion of the ADO object model aims to cover the main steps involvedin application development with Dyalog APL.

ADO Object Model ADOconsists of 7 objects as described in the followingfigure:

Connection a

Recordset

\ |

Figure 1. ADO object model andthe interaction between objects

The Connection (drives a connection under a definite provider), Command (executes a command, such as a command text, stored procedure, command prepare etc.), and Recordset(a set of records returned by commands) objects are top-level objects that can be created and destroyed independently. They are

117

VECTOR Vol:16 No.4

registered in the Windowsregistry as ADODB.Connection, ADODB.Command, and ADODB.Recordset, respectively.

In addition to these three top-level objects, there are four other subsidiary objects, that exist only within the context of their parent objects, and cannot be created separately, namely Parameter, Field, Error and Property.

The Parameter (ADODB.Parameter in the Windowsregistry) object can be created. independently of a Command object. In this case it must be included in a Parameters collection of a Commandbefore it is used in a command. Parameter objects can be created from the Parameters collection too, where they are placed automatically as a result of a statement syntax setting in a Command object. Calling its Execute method assigns corresponding Value properties to all Parameterobjects in the collection. It provides the facility to use bind variables in SQL expressions. The Field object provides structural information about a single column of data within a Recordset. The Error object supplies extended error information about an error condition generated by the provider. The Property object describes provider-defined characteristics of an ADO object.

Each of the Error, Property, Parameter and Field objects are accumulated in the corresponding collections: Errors, Properties, Parameters, and Fields. (A Collection is a special kind of object that contains a set of other objects; you can think ofit as a vectorof objects.)

There are two ways to access the properties and methods of ADO objects from Dyalog APL. If, when an instance of an ADO object is created as an OLEClient object, the AutoBrowse property is set to 1 (the default), the methods and the properties of this object appear as functions and variables in the OLEClient namespace. In principle, with a few exceptions, a method corresponds to an APL function and a property corresponds to an APLvariable. This is possible because ADO objects have a type-library file with type information, that includes the name of the methods and properties exported by the object, together with descriptions of the arguments to each method and descriptions of the data types of each property. An alternative, is to specify AutoBrowse as 0 when creating the OLEClient. This causes Dyalog APL to create an empty namespace whose methods are accessible using 3 UNQ and whose properties may be queried and set using OWG, OWS. This approach is faster, because APL does not have to read the object s type-library for the information it needs to establish functions and variables corresponding to the object s methods and properties. However, in practice it is much better/safer/more maintainable to leave AutoBrowseas 1.

118

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

Basic ADO Application Steps This section describes the general flow and the basic steps for developing ADO applications in Dyalog APL. Most such applications use some variation of the following steps:

* Connect to a data source by meansof a Connection object. Optionally, begin an explicit or implicit transaction.

* Optionally, create a Commandobject to represent an SQL command with or without parameters.

* Optionally, if a parameterized commandis involved, specify columns,tables, and values in the SQL commandasvariable parameters via the Parameter object.

« Execute the command.This can be carried out by the Command, Connection, or Recordset object. * After executing, a result is returned in a storage object Recordset.

* Optionally, view,sort, filter, and navigate the data in a Recordset.

* Edit, add, delete the data in a Recordset. Work directly with columns or rows via the Fields collection and Field objects. * Ifitis all right, update the data source with changesfrom the object Recordset.

* Ifa transaction was used, commit or rollback the changes made during the transaction. This is a function of the Connection object.

* Retrieve the providers information about each object via a Properties collection. Each collection contains a set of Property objects for a specific instanceof an object.

* Retrieve the information abouterrors during connection (Error objects via Errors collection).

The interaction between the ADO objects (methods, properties and objects collections for object creation) was shown in Figure 1.

Open a Connection The first step in any application is the connection to the data source. The data sourceis described in a connectionstring. The parameters, specified in a connection string, may differ for each provider and data source.

119

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

The main way for ADO to open a connection is to call the Connection.Open method with connection string, user id, password, and connection scheme (if undefined-1) as parameters:

4 Create object 'ADODB.Connection' eit#.OWC'OLEClient' 'ADODB.Connection' a Open connection #.C1.Open' Provider=SQLOLEDA ;UserID=sa;Password=;database=pubs' sat ''{-4)

Another way is to invoke the shortcut method, Recordset.Open, to both open a connection and instantiate a commandobject in one operation:

a Create object ADODB.Recordset' "Ri'#.OWC'OLEClient' 'ADODB.Recordset' 8 Open a connection Con+'Provider=SQLOLEDB;User ID=sa;Password=;database=pubs' #.R4.Open select « from authors' Con 2 3 1 a Create namespace for this connection from property "Ct' #.0WC #.R1,ActiveConnection a Create namespace for a command object from property 'Comi #.0WC #.R1,ActiveCommand

Number2 in Open means dynamic cursor withoutrestrictions, 3 means optimistic lock type, 1 interprets the text string in the first parameter as an SQL-command,

Alternatively, it is possible to use the Commandobject:

a Create object 'ADODB.Command' Comi'#.0WC 'OLEClient' 'ADODB.Command' a Open a connection #.Comi .ActiveConnect ion+' Provider=SQLOLEDB;User ID=sa;Password=;database=pubs' a Create namespace for this connection from property '#,.C1'#.0WC #,.Com1,ActiveConnection

Methods for OLE objects require a set of parameters of which some(or evenall) are optional. Typically, the values for missing parameters are supplied by defaults or are allocated instead from properties. For example, the Open method of the Recordset object takes up to five parameters that specify Source, ActiveConnection, CursorType, LockType and Options respectively. Each of these can bespecified by an equivalent property and then omitted from the methodcall itself. For example, from Visual Basic for Applications (VBA):

xstEmployees.CursorType = adOpenKeyset rstEmployees.LockType = adLockOptimistic rstEmployees.Open "employee", cnni, , , adCmdTable

120

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

APLdoes not have any syntax to allow you to omit an elementfrom the argument to a function. In Dyalog APL, this problem is circumvented by naming the appropriate parameters explicity. Only those parameters that follow missing ones need to be named.For example:

rstEmployees.Cursor?ype+ad0penkeyset rstEmployees.LockType+adLock0ptimistic rstEmployees.Open'employee' 'cnni'('OptionstadCmdTable)

Create a Command A query command,typically written in SQL, requires the data source to return a Recordset object, containing rows of requested information, or used to change data in the database. The following steps with the collections, methods, and properties of a Commandobject will doit: * Define the executable text of the command(for example, an SQL statement) in the CommandText property.

* Define parameterized queries or a stored procedure. In the command, ? placeholder substrings are replaced with parameters when a command is executed. This is possible only with the Commandobject.

* Specify the type of command in the CommandTypeproperty.

¢ Control whetheror not the provider saves a compiled version of the command in the Prepared property to optimize performance.

#.Comi .CommandText+'select * from authors where state=?' #.Com2 ,CommandType+1 #,Com1.Prepared+1

Depending on the functionality of the data provider, some Commandcollections, methods, or properties may generate an error when referenced.

Execute the Command There are three methods that return a Recordset: Connection.Execute, Command.Execute, and Recordset.Open. These methods are optimized to provide the benefits of each object:

* Both Execute methods return fast but read-only, forward-only Recordset objects.

121

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

"#,R1'#,.C1. Execute select +» from authors' 1 1 a Connection object a Command object without parameters #,Com\ .CommandText+'select « from authors where state=''CAt'! #.Ri'#,Comi.Fxecute 1 '' 4

The second parameterof the connection object method andthefirst parameter of the command object method is meaningless in Dyalog APL (any number). Both ofthe last parameters specify commandtextinterpretation.

* The Command.Execute methodallowsthe use of parameterized commands that can be invoked repeatedly.

a Command object with parameters #,Comit .CommandText+'select » from authors where state=?' '#.R1i'#.Coml.Execute ('CA') 1

* As mentioned abovein the example of creating a connection, the Open method allowsyouto define the strategy and object used to access the data in the CursorType parameter; and the degree of isolation from other users, and whether the cursor should support updates in immediate or batch modesin the LockType parameter.

Manipulate the Data In ADO almostall processing of data is performed using Recordset objects. All Recordset objects consist of records (rows) and fields (columns) and are used to manipulate data from a provider: 1, Use MoveFirst, MoveLast, MoveNext, and MovePrevious methods, as well as the Move method, and Filter properties to navigate the data. Forward-only Recordset objects support only the MoveNext method. 2. Examinethe position in the data set by meansof the BOF and EOF properties for a begin and endoffile during processing, the edit modevia the property EditMode,thestate of the object with State property.

3. Fetch the data using the GetRows method. 4. Edit the data directly in the fields of the currentrecord:insert using the AddNew method, update using the Update methods, delete via the Delete method.If a provider supports batch updating, more than one record can be transmitted in a singlecall to the database by means of the UpdateBatch method.

"Ri'#.OWC'OLECIient' 'ADODB.Recordset' a Connect to OLEDB Provider for ODBC and open the Recordset object C+' Provider=MSDASQL ;UserID=sa;Password=;Data Source=LocalServer;database=proba' #.R1.0pen select * from table' C231

122

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

a Fetch 5 records in the variable 'Table #.Pable«#.R1,GetRows 5 a Return to first record #,R1.MoveFirst #.R1L.Flds #.OWC #.R1.Fields Create fields collection #.R1.Plds.Fldi'#.R1.Flds.Item 0 Create 1. Field object

peepoaoe #,.RL.Plds.Fld2'#.R1.Flds.Item 1 Create 2. Field object '#.R1.Flds.Fld3'¢.Ri.Flds,Item 2 Create 3. Field object #,R1,AddNew © Switch on insert mode 4#.R1.Flds,Fid1,Valueeé Set value of 1.field #.R1.PFlids,Pld2.Value+'description' a Set value of 2.field a Insert large data by means of AppendChunk method of Field object #.Ri.PFlds.Fld3.AppendChunk First part of long data. ' #.R1.Pids.Pld3.AppendChunk Second part of long data.' #.R1.Update @ a Update database

Control the Transactions When a set of changes that were made to the data source must be saved or cancelled as a single unit, the following transaction methods of the Connection object are employed:

* BeginTrans begins a new transaction;

* CommitTrans saves any changes and endsthe currenttransaction;

* RollbackTrans cancels any changes made during the current transaction and ends the transaction.

In the above code #.C1.BeginTrans can be included, for example, after #.R1.MoveFirst and #.C1.Commitfrans or #.C1.RollbackTrans after #.Ri.Update @.

If a provider supportsit, the transaction can also be controlled using the Execute methodof the Connection object or Commandobject, with command text for the begin, commit and rollback transaction (for example, BEGIN TRAN', COMMIT TRAN!, ROLLBACK TRAN"of TransactSQL of MS SQL Server).

Not all providers support transactions. The sign that the provider supports transactions is the provider-defined property Transaction DDL , appearing in the Connection object s Properties collection. If the provider does not support transactions, calling one of these methods will return an error.

Retrieve the Information from Collections The main information about the Property, Parameter, and Field objects (from the corresponding collections Properties, Parameters, and Fields) can be retrieved

123

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

using the Name and Value properties. Nameprovides the name of an object as a string value, Value indicates the value assigned to a Property, Parameter, or Field object and has the Variant data type. Only Name and Value properties are uniform for these objects. Other properties are mainly different.

Any operation on the database involving ADO objects can generate one or more data provider warnings and errors. As each error or warning occurs, one or more Error objects are placed in the Errors collection of the Connection object.

An Error object s properties can be retrieved in order to obtain specific details about each error or warning, including the following:

* The Description property, which describes the situation in detail. * The Number property, which contains unique identification of an error or a warning.

* The Source property, which identifies the origin of a problem. * The SQLState is a five-character code for any problem encountered during the Processing of an SQL statement. * NativeError properties, which describe the provider-specific error or warning code.

The procedure with all these objects is similar:

c1'#.QWC'OLECIient' ADODB.Connection' a Open connection #.C1.Open' Prov ider=SQLOLEDB; UserID=sa;Password=;database=pubs' 'sat ''(-1) '#.Ci.Errs'#,QwWe #.C1,Errors a Create errors collection '#.Ci.Errs.Erri #,C1.Frrs.Item 0 a Create 1. Error object DISPLAY #.C1.Errs.Erri.Number a Show error number DISPLAY #.C1.Fres.Erri.Description 8 Show error description #.C1.Errs.Clear 8 Remove all of the objects from a collection

The property Item of the Errors collection (and of othercollections too) takes a parameter (an index) and returns an object, so it actually behaves more like a method.

Comparison between Different Approaches to Data Access Dyalog APL can choose from many of Microsoft's technologies for accessing data sources, These include:

* Open Database Connectivity (ODBC)forrelational data via the ODBC API code,

124

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

* Remote Data Objects (RDO) for ODBC data.

* Data Access Objects (DAC)for local data (Microsoft Jet database engine).

« DAOfor ODBC data (ODBCDirect).

* Microsoft ActiveX Data Objects (ADO)forall types of data.

All the above-mentioned object models (RDO, DAO, ODBCDirect, ADO) were invented to give developers the ability to avoid direct programming of the corresponding API. They are an artificial layer over this API, and provideall their functionality in an object modelof type easy-to-use , rather than in a collection of function calls ina DLL.

Today, there are features that are not available in ADO, but which are present in one of the alternative object technologies. However, the aim of ADO is to become a superset of DAO and RDO.

One of ADO s benefits here is the declaration of a simple and understandable languagefor accessing data. ADO nowplaysthe role of the standard data access language for Microsoft tools and program products. For example, the current versions of Internet Information Server, Internet Explorer, Visual Basic, Visual C++, and Visual J++ can use ADO as their primary data access and control language. The nextrelease of Microsoft Office promises to dothis too.

A list of the major features found in ADO, DAO, RDO or ODBC API applications, is presented in the following table.

125

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

ADO, DAO, RDO and ODBC API Feature Comparison

Feature ODBC ADO DAO RDO API 2.0 3.5 2.0

Type of data source ODBC Any Microsoft ODBC Jet, ISAM, ODBC

Level of programming Low High High High

Asynchronousconnection N Y N Y

The use of ADO from Dyalog APL compared with the base ODBC API DLL shows on the one handa little more general performance of the DLL-approach, because of the usual benefit of compiled DLLs vs. interpreted Dyalog APL. On the other hand, the performanceof the base function calls in the DLL compared to the speed of the methods in ADO for connecting, query preparing, executing, fetching and closing is practically equal. Finally, ADO is more universal than the DLLs in offering functions, data types, and data sources. Additionally, ADO providesfull controlofall steps for data access in Dyalog APL.

The small differences in performance can be mitigated by optimal organisation of the program structure .

126

VECTOR Vol.16 No.4

Conclusions ADO provides the capability to carry out query and manipulation (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE,and DELETEstatements) of all types of data. To access most popular telational data ADO can use OLE DBdirectly, or it can use the OLE DB Provider for ODBC. To access other types of data, there are other kinds of data providers.

Notall ADO features were discussed here, for example:

« Free threading, that allowsoneto build very powerful and scalable Web server applications.

* Asynchronous queries, that return controlto the application before the query is completed.

° Remote Recordsets, that allow one to retrieve and manipulate data remotely, then updatethe source.

* Events, that allow ADO 2.0 to exposea list of events that can be used to control all aspects of the connection, query, and table access process.

Since ADO is a COM-based component, called using the Automation interface, Dyalog APL can use ADO and combine high-performance access to any data source with its own capabilities of efficient array data processing.

items.title: APL - a Client-Server Language?
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 114

by Morten Kromberg (Insight Systems)

It is becoming increasingly difficult to sell a product if the magic words Client/Server are not clearly visible on the package. As a result, the term has become broadened by marketing departments to mean everything from dumb terminal emulation performed by a PC, through remote SQL queries, to applications using the most sophisticated peer-to-peer networked messaging systems or Object Request Brokers.

items.title: What’s New?
items.text:
Is there any reason why the pragmatic APL user, intent on solving real problems (sorry, I mean pursuing real opportunities), should take notice? After all, many APL programmers were writing Client/Server applications back in 1980. Page 97 of the original SHARP APL Reference Manual by Paul Berry (copyright I.P. Sharp Associates, 1979), contains a complete coding example (almost an entire page) of a multi-user server mechanism based on an "object-oriented" communications mechanism called Shared Variables (if I may allow myself the liberty of widening the term object-oriented a bit).

The data processing community has succeeded in reinventing Shared Variables in a number of guises, some of which are now supported by a critical mass of applications and development tools. The driving force behind most of the market interest in these mechanisms is that they make it practical to split an application into independent Client and Server modules. Even when both modules run on the same machine, this strategy can simplify the architecture of complex systems. When client and server can run on two different machines, it becomes possible to "downsize" applications and move the presentation layer, plus some computation to workstations, which have superior price/performance ratios when compared to mainframes. In the current economic climate, this is the immediately attractive aspect of client/server computing — but in the long term, the ability to "upsize" applications is also important. When the usage of an application increases, or data must be made available to other parts of an organisation, it is often necessary to upgrade from a local or LAN-based database to a more secure or robust multi-user server environment.

items.title: Client/Server is just what APL needs
items.text:
Modern workstation operating systems are perfect environments for APL. APL’s hunger for CPU and memory resources can easily be satisfied by modern workstations; APL’s performance is often better on a workstation than on a shared mainframe. By succumbing to Client/Server, you can finally make the manager of data processing happy and remove your APL code from his or her mainframe — and still maintain access to all that corporate data!

The evolution of tools for software development has resulted in a number of extremely useful tools and powerful paradigms for organisation (OO), distribution (SQL and Client/Server) and presentation (GUI). APL retains most of its competitive edge with respect to general-purpose manipulation and analysis, but this advantage is of little value if we cannot deal effectively with the other aspects of application development and delivery.

The APL vendors have come a long way in providing the mechanisms that we need to attach ourselves to standard tools available under workstation operating systems. Support for Dynamic Link Libraries (DLL), Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) and the Clipboard have made it possible for us to plug straight into thousands of tools and applications written by people who had never heard of APL.

We need to extend this capability across the network using Client/Server techniques. The immediate requirement is to enable APL as a client, so that we can make use of all the servers that are available to users and developers using other tools than APL. But we should not forget that the unique capabilities of APL also make APL interesting as a Server — especially if we can just make APL applications available in the same way as any other service such as a database, ticket sales, or mail server — without anyone having to know that we used APL to write it!

items.title: Client/Server Models
items.text:
We all know what Client/Server means, so rather than bore you with repetitions, let us take a look at how Client/Server products are marketed to the non-APL community (the so-called Information Technology Marketplace). The Client/Server product vendor will tell you that his or her product supports n distinct Client/Server models.

This means that the physical split between client and server can be inserted in n different locations in the simplified application model below:

End User User Interface Functionality Data Access Data

The split can be inserted between two layers or in the middle of a layer. Four of the most common models are described in a little more detail below:

items.title: Distributed Presentation
items.text: The X-Windows system has become relatively popular in the Unix environment. With X-Windows, the split is inside the user interface layer. Some presentation code is embedded in the application on the host (X-Windows terminology calls this end the Client, just to confuse you), and the rest is in the X-Windows Server which runs at the user’s end and provides presentation services to the application. Although this mechanism can be used to offload an important part of the presentation from the host CPU, a good deal remains, and the network load is rather heavy. The main advantage is that administration and coding is still as simple as it was on the mainframe, since the entire application is still running on a single machine.

items.title: Remote Database
items.text: With the current state of the art, Client/Server tends to mean the use of a remote SQL database. The split is between the functionality and data access layers. Despite the fact that this is the most common form of Client/Server computing, and that it is still rapidly growing, it is not the final solution. The problem is that SQL is an awful language for describing transactions. As the name implies, it was not designed for that. It is a query language. Performing all but the most trivial updates using SQL over the network is painful, inefficient and will always be a fragile mechanism.

items.title: Remote Transaction
items.text:
The split is inserted in the functionality layer. Client and Server communicate using transactions that correspond to logical events in the application. The conversation might consist of messages like "Debit the amount X from account Y", or "Give me the latest forecast for currency X". In the first example, the steps required to implement the transaction might be:

  1. Check whether account Y exist
  2. Check credit limit
  3. Register transaction
  4. Update balance

Using Remote Database, each step is likely to require at least one network transaction. With Remote Transaction, all the logic is embedded in a portion of the application running on the server, which is much closer to the database in terms of turnaround time, bandwidth, and reliability. This is potentially the most complex solution in terms of coding, but with good modular coding techniques (and that includes object orientation), it is the most flexible solution.

items.title: Distributed Database
items.text: Some database systems are able to distribute the data itself, so that different parts of it reside on different computers. The management of a relational database that is split in this manner is complex. No matter how sophisticated your mechanism for ensuring the data integrity (often referred to as Two Phase Commit mechanisms) is, you will have to deal with worst-case scenarios such as restoring a distributed database from backups of different machines. To be safe, you will have to write code that is tolerant of small failures of integrity.

items.title: Next Year’s Model
items.text:
The state of Client/Server is evolving in a direction where it is becoming easier to implement Remote Transaction systems. The first step in this direction is the implementation of added functionality in many commercially available SQL servers. You can now use stored procedures, or triggers, which means that the server has a simple procedural language which makes it possible to perform complex updates in a single call. Unfortunately there has been no standardisation of these new features, so applications that use them are not portable between different SQL databases.

The architecture of the future may be something like CORBA — the Common Object Request Broker Architecture, which enables dedicated servers to reside on an intelligent network, and allows applications to issue high-level calls on the network without knowing where in the network any particular service resides. A lot of work needs to be done to make this practical; for example, vendors must agree on a cross-network security system which makes it possible for you to log into the network once, and then use facilities under multiple host operating systems using the privileges assigned to you by a common security system — but there is little doubt that these systems will become commonplace during the next 5 to 10 years.

items.title: What is Available Now?
items.text: Let us assume that your goal is to develop applications that make use of the cheap memory and processing power available on workstations, to provide your users with a nice, easy-to-use graphical user interface, which can be integrated seamlessly with other applications on the desktop. You should buy a workstation running Macintosh System 7, Unix, OS/2, or Microsoft Windows, and one of the excellent new APL interpreters which provide access to all local services and applications available in the selected environment.

items.title: Access to Remote Databases
items.text:
The remote service you are most likely to need is an SQL database. This access will be available to you in at least four different ways:

  1. A Proprietary API Extender from database vendor
  2. An API Converter, such as the Q+E Library
  3. ODBC: Open Database Connectivity (or ODAPI)
  4. A Generic Middleware product such as SequeLink

Application Programme Interfaces for SQL databases tend to have almost identical functionality. Typical calls are:

LOGON You must LOGON to the service OPEN Open a database cursor PREPARE Prepare a particular SQL statement for execution DESCRIBE Return column names and data types of result set BIND Transfer values for variable parts of the statement EXECUTE Do it FETCH Fetch results COMMIT Make the effect of a sequence of executes permanent ROLLBACK Discard changes (opposite of COMMIT) CLOSE Free resources allocated to a cursor LOGOFF Disconnect from the server

How do the four delivery mechanisms differ?

  1. Proprietary API Extenders

    All databases make their API available in the host environment. AP127 for APL2 or SHARP APL, and the Oracle Interface for Dyalog APL under AIX are examples of products which hook APL interpreters up to database managers running on the same machine as APL itself.

    Almost all database vendors provide an extension of the database API, which is available to programmers on workstations. Examples are SQL/NET from Oracle, INFORMIX-NET from Informix, and the DOS/Windows Application Enabler for OS/2 Database Manager. These API extenders simply make the same API which is available to programmers on the host available on a remote system.

    The problem with these proprietary extenders is that they are all different, despite the fact that the functionality they provide is almost identical. Each API will use calls with slightly different parameters. If you use one of these tools, you must rewrite your application if you need to use another database.

    The database vendors often provide modules which make the API easily accessible from within selected development tools; either their own, or tools from vendors with whom they have strategic partnerships. As long as you stick to these, and your network provides the (often limited) list of protocols which the API Extender supports, you are OK.

  2. API Converters

    The "API confusion" caused by proprietary API extenders has been the driving force behind the development of products such as the Q+E Library. The Q+E product provides a single API, which bolts on to a large variety of proprietary API extenders. Q+E converts your calls and your data to the formats required by each proprietary API. The DB+ product from TMT-Team is an interface from APL to Q+E, which in turn provides access to all database servers supported by Q+E.

    Note that you still have to have a proprietary API Extender present in order to use these converters. Simultaneous access to multiple services may be complicated, since all required API extenders must be loaded simultaneously; they may have different requirements with respect to network protocols, etc.

  3. ODBC

    Instead of writing more API Converters, Microsoft provided a specification for a common API called Open Database Connectivity (ODBC), in the hope that database and middleware vendors would write compliant ODBC drivers, and that development tool vendors will deliver tools which can use these drivers. Microsoft has declared that it will provide ODBC drivers for its own database managers and that development tools such as Visual Basic and Microsoft Access will be able to use ODBC. The only piece of code provided directly by Microsoft is the ODBC Driver Manager, a switching station which loads ODBC drivers when applications request connections to them, and passes ODBC calls to the drivers after performing a small amount of validation.

    It is important to note that Microsoft and Borland primarily see tools like Access and Paradox (respectively) as development tools rather than database servers. Support for access to remote databases using ODBC or ODAPI — Borland and IBM’s alternative standard API (the best thing about standards is that there are so many of them!) was provided at an early stage, but there were no ODBC or ODAPI interfaces giving access to data stored in Access and Paradox until recently.

    The database vendors are scrambling to provide ODBC-compliant versions of their proprietary API extenders, and ODBC is rapidly reaching critical mass. This will eventually do away with the need for products like the Q+E Database Library, and Pioneer Software, the company behind this product, is moving on to the business of providing ODBC drivers on behalf of the database vendors. Providing a fully functional ODBC driver is no simple task, since the full ODBC specification is far richer than most database APIs. In fact, very few drivers support the full API, and one of the most irritating aspects of using ODBC is that you need to inquire about the level of functionality provided by a particular driver, and possibly adopt alternative strategies depending on the answer you get back. The result is that quite a bit of API Confusion remains, and one of the points made by recent Q+E advertising material is that they provide a "consistent set of ODBC drivers" (!?).

    Examples of additional features of ODBC not usually found in other APIs are calls to translate SQL statements between ODBC SQL and the native SQL supported by the server; scroll backwards; do cellwise or columnwise fetches; or even retrieve columns that were not specified in earlier fetches. Many of these ODBC calls make sense when dealing with a local database such as Access or dBase, but are very hard to implement efficiently for a remote database.

    The ODBC Support provided by tools such as Visual Basic or Excel tends to be at a much higher level than the ODBC API itself. For example, Visual Basic provides the concept of a Dynaset, which is created by naming a Table or View. The Visual Basic ODBC interface copies data into local storage, and you can make it easy for the user to browse or modify the data with a minimum of programming effort. However, it is often hard to control the resources used to implement this functionality, and solutions which run extremely fast when tested using a dBase driver with almost unlimited bandwidth may have totally unacceptable performance when used across the network. It is important to note that this behaviour is not a function of ODBC itself, but rather of the high-level access to it that is built into some development tools.

    Using proprietary ODBC drivers, or ODBC converters that bolt on to a traditional API Extender, you still have the same problems with respect to compatibility of the underlying (network) products. Drivers from different vendors will not always peacefully inhabit a Windows system side by side. To solve this problem, you need a generic middleware solution.

  4. Generic Middleware

    Generic middleware products solve the compatibility problem by providing their own transport layer. You do not buy any communications software from your database vendor — the middleware server component connects straight to the database API on your host, performs API conversion at the host end, and uses whatever network you have available to transfer data to the middleware client component running on a workstation. This means that you only have a single product running on your workstation, even if you are using several networks to connect to a number of database systems on a variety of host platforms.

    The middleware vendors are also capable of providing an ODBC driver under Windows. A single ODBC driver can thus provide access to multiple services without risk of conflicts. The fact that the middleware product is in control of both ends of the network conversation means that it can optimise the use of the network to provide better performance than a lot of proprietary ODBC drivers, which are often bolted on to API Extenders which were not designed with ODBC in mind. As an additional benefit, you get a completely consistent ODBC implementation across all supported databases.

    The networked versions of AP127 available from IBM and Soliton have a "generic" middleware architecture, but these vendors provide access to a small number of clients, network protocols, host operating systems, and database managers. A product like SequeLink supports just about all databases running under OS/2, Unix, VMS, AS/400, VM, and MVS, over NetBIOS, SPX/IPX, more than 20 "flavours" of TCP/IP, AppleTalk, SNA and DecNET, from Macintoshes, Windows, OS/2, Unix and VMS clients.

    The SQAPL Client product from Insight Systems is an interface to SequeLink. Because identical SequeLink APIs are available on so many platforms, SQAPL can provide access to all services accessible through SequeLink from APL*PLUS II under Windows and Unix, APL2 under OS/2 and Unix, and Dyalog APL under Windows, OS/2 and Unix — providing exactly the same API in all environments.

items.title: Access to Non-SQL Services
items.text:
At the moment, SQL and Client/Server are more or less synonymous — but I do not believe that this will continue to be true. SQL is a query language, and will continue to be used for that purpose — but SQL is not a particularly elegant or effective language for expressing updates or transactions. We need other mechanisms to initiate transactions, or to make Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs).

Vendors of Unix systems often provide RPC kits, which make it possible to compile an application consisting of a client and a server part. It is very hard to provide flexible systems in this manner, because the two parts are so closely interlinked. Changes require recompilation and testing of both ends of the application. If communication problems cause the partners to get "out of synch", it may be hard to return the system to a known state.

Vendors of Transaction Monitors such as IBM’s Customer Information Control System (CICS) are beginning to provide API extenders in the same way as the SQL database vendors. This makes it possible to code and test transactions on the host, and use the same transactions from host applications and Client/Server applications running on workstations.

Advanced communications protocols such as TCP/IP and IBM’s APPC (LU6.2) also provide mechanisms by which two consenting applications can exchange data over the network, but this approach still requires a bit too much network expertise for the comfort of the average APL programmer — and of course the solutions will be dependent on the particular network protocol being used.

items.title: CORBA
items.text: A working group with origins in the Object-Oriented community has defined CORBA — the Common Object Request Broker Architecture. This architecture will extend the development environments of the future (it is assumed that these will be Object-Oriented to some degree), so that they can send messages to objects, without worrying about whether the objects exist nearby, or somewhere on the network. CORBA needs to be built into the networks and integrated with security facilities of all networks and hosts involved, and the required technology is still under development in the laboratories. Once we have it, the network will more or less disappear from sight, and it will be as easy to extract data from a server on another planet as it is to open a spreadsheet. Let’s hope we all have fibre-optic telephone cabling by then!

items.title: While we wait for CORBA
items.text: For the time being, Generic Middleware is as close as we can get. Products such as SequeLink provide "open" servers, which you can use to encapsulate any existing host application. By customising an open server, you can call your favourite C program, CICS or OS/400 (RPG) transactions under MVS and OS/400 — or even APL! The SQAPL Server product from Insight Systems makes APL2/6000, APL*PLUS II/UNX and Dyalog APL/X available as SequeLink Servers under Unix. You can execute APL function calls from any SequeLink Client — not just the SQAPL Clients. You can make APL function calls from Excel under Windows, OS/2 or the Mac — from Omnis 7, WingZ, Visual Basic, Smalltalk, and so forth — using exactly the same API as you would to make SQL requests.

items.title: A Glimpse of The Future
items.text:
We are beginning to get a glimpse of a future in which the users’ workstation provides a single entry point to any number of local, departmental, corporate, national, or even global services — many of which will be running on dedicated server machines located somewhere on a widely branched network, but all seeming to be an integrated part of the users’ desktop.

This future is not far off — and as always, APL is a step ahead. With the SQAPL Server, APL became one of the first general-purpose languages to have a dynamic function call mechanism bolted on to a generic middleware product. So far, the only language available has been SQL, plus a few operating system command shells implemented for the VAX and Unix. The APL Server is available for three of the most popular APL interpreters available under Unix.

APL will be a First Class Citizen of the new world order. From APL, we can not only call local and remote services, but we can provide services to local applications via standard calling mechanisms, from the Clipboard through DDE to DLLs, and to remote applications via Middleware. When CORBA arrives, you can be sure that APL will be there to meet it!

items.title: OOF: Getting a better Grip on OLE Objects
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 121

by Morten Kromberg

This paper was first published in FinnAPL News.
path: OOF: Getting a better Grip on OLE Objects

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
During the last few years, I have made a few short experimental trips into Object Land, primarily from Dyalog APL, and each time I ended up feeling intensely frustrated. I seemed to have to go through endless steps in order to access functionality which, judging from code examples in magazines, seemed to be much more accessible to users of "inferior" tools like Visual Basic. All the code examples I found in magazines, on the web, or using the Excel Macro Recorder, required a real translation effort, and turned into somewhere between three and ten times as many lines of code as the original. This article describes the results of my attempts to improve this situation; a tool which is freely available to anyone who is interested (see under Acknowledgements below).

For several years, I successfully evaded the issue by assuming the guise of a manager (apologies to those of you who are not familiar with this term; try looking it up on the web). Finding myself unable to keep this up indefinitely, I have now accepted that it is inevitable that I must try to understand objects a bit better. Being an APL’er, the next step is obviously to build a tool which maps the world into my preferred co-ordinate system. I named the tool "OOF" because, in addition to being a TLA (Three Letter Acronym) for OLE Object Functions, "OOF" is "FOO" backwards, and symbolises the struggle of an ageing developer who wants to get rid of all those statements which simply manipulate objects, and get back to the function calls which he understands.
