items.title: Soviet APL: a Historical Outline
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 102

by Alexei I. Miroshnikov

This paper is a personal survey of the significant events in Soviet APL history. It is intended to give the audience a general view of the evolution and implementation of the Soviet APL interpreters, as well as outline the successive applied systems.

items.title: The Beginning
items.text:
Academician N.N.Moiseyev was the first Soviet scientist to get acquainted with APL in 1975. At the University of Toronto he was astonished to see how easily and speedily his Canadian colleagues could produce programs and obtain necessary results using APL. On his return Moiseyev initiated the creation of the first Soviet APL interpreter.

The APL/BESM realization(implementation) on a powerful Soviet BESM-6 computer was undertaken by S.P.Prokhorov, who was at that time working at the Computer Centre of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR [1]. When Prokhorov left the Centre in 1980, the APL/BESM system was on the whole completed. It underwent test running at several computing centres including the Leningrad Research Computing Centre of the Academy of Sciences. Although APL/BESM was not to become a finished programming product, its development was the starting point for the Soviet APL interpreters.

Moiseyev’s visit to Canada had one more effect, viz. the APL interpreter was incorporated into the CDC CYBER-172 software bought in 1978 for the former Leningrad Research Computer Centre, now the Leningrad Institute for Automation and Informatics of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR (LIIAS). The APL 2.0 version, developed under the direction of J.H.Burrill at MIT, had for a long time been the only legally imported APL interpreter in the Soviet Union [2]. Since 1979 intensive application of the APL 2.0 version has been undertaken by the North-West Branch of the Central Research Economic Institute at the State Planning Committee of the RSFSR, at the mathematical simulation department headed by V.V.Ponomaryov [3]. Research associate A.I.Miroshnikov of the same department developed an intelligent graphic APL terminal, emulated on the mini-computer Wang-2200 for the CYBER-172 incorporated into the Leningrad computer network of the Academy of Sciences.

The APL story is closely linked with IBM. The Soviet Union was no exception in that respect. It was along with the IBM/360 computer system that APL found itself in this country. One of the largest computer development centres, the Computer Research Institute in Minsk, together with the Institute for Computer Machinery (Sofia, Bulgaria) used APL as a tool for analysis and synthesis of digital systems [4]. Inclusion of APL into the standard software for the Soviet computer series ES (compatible with IBM/360 and IBM/370 systems) was being considered. Unfortunately this upsurge came to nought, mostly due to the lack of adequate terminal equipment in the USSR and conservative attitudes of the leading scientists. This was the period of general enthusiasm about structured programming in the USSR. Production of a series of APL-terminals for Bulgaria by the Minsk Computer Works was to become the chord finale at this stage of the APL history.

items.title: Independent Realisations of APL
items.text:
Frederico Fellini (the great film producer) once said that there is always somebody in the world who is shooting Anna Karenina. In the Soviet Union at different times several groups of developers quite independently attempted to realize APL.

In the Moscow Energetics Institute (MEI) under E.T.Semyonova, APL was realized in the late seventies. APL/MEI was based on the DOS ES batch mode and involved APL-program preparation on cards [5]. Later A.Sokolov developed an APL terminal with an APL character set on the basis of the Soviet 7920 terminal. APL/MEI was one more variation of APL/360 and, as distinct from the latter, had a great number of errors. It is for this reason perhaps that this version was not applied anywhere apart from the one organization which had invested money in its development. Later the developers team from MEI rewrote APL anew in … LISP. This APL was used only by the developers themselves.

About the same time at NIIMM in Yerevan (Armenia) an interactive system with APL as a command language was realized [6]. This system was to solve the problem of designing microprogram support for the central processor of the ES1046 computer that was then being developed. Again, for this APL version APL\360 was the prototype.

In the early eighties a group of specialists from the Siberian Department of the Academy of Sciences (Novosibirsk) was developing special software for image processing on the multiprocessor complex SM2/PS-2000 [7]. Having realized on parallel architecture a set of primitives for processing data arrays, the developers discovered all of a sudden that they had effectively realized a subset of APL. The report on this work was a great success at the first Soviet APL seminar in Obninsk in 1986. The developers were quite optimistic but further information on their work is lacking.

The town of Obninsk, not far from Moscow, had for a long time remained quite obscure. Intensive research in the field of nuclear energetics carried on in the town lent secrecy to any information about it. It is for this reason perhaps that nobody outside Obninsk knew about the APL application there. In the late seventies A.I.Kononov had adapted an APL\360 version to the ES series computers replacing APL characters by the Russian letters resembling the former in their outlines, similar to APL/BESM [8]. This version differed from the others in that it provided a multi-user mode of computer application. All the APL interpreters developed in the Soviet Union are single-user ones. Since the early eighties the APL SV system has been used in the teaching process (in the Central Institute for Skill Improvement) [9], which is an IBM VS APL version adapted to the Soviet computers [10].

In 1983 the "Radio and Communication" publishers issued a book by N.A.Magariu "The APL Programming Language" [11]. With no relation to the latter a team of researchers and students from the Kishinyov state University undertook development of an APL interpreter for SM-2 mini-computers, compatible with HP computers. This version differs from APL/360 principally in that it makes it possible for the user to determine in advance the set of APL primitives he will use during the session, similar to the auxiliary processors specification by the user in IBM APL.

items.title: Publicity for APL
items.text:
In 1984 the annual international conference on APL was held in Helsinki, Finland. After the conference ended K.Iverson, R.Bernecky and T.Seppala visited Moscow [13]. At that time Soviet APL users were isolated from each other and the visit of APL veterans remained unnoticed by most of them. Iverson was not to meet like-minded persons, but rather laymen of no great capabilities, which did not exactly make a favourable impression upon him.

After the journal "Vycheslitelnaya Tekhnika" had been published in 1990 "Computer Machinery" - the Russian "BYTE" with a circulation of 73 thousand copies) that was wholly devoted to APL [12], in the Soviet Union there made its appearance a team from the joint venture "Ural" that had developed its own APL-like language for IBM PC compatibles.

items.title: New Wave
items.text:
The new APL wave in the Soviet Union is again connected with IBM. As had happened before, APL got into the USSR together with the IBM hardware. But this time it was a "strange" programming product APL*PLUS/PC developed by the American STSC, which was unknown in the USSR altogether. The position of APL*PLUS/PC was further consolidated due to the incredible popularity of the statistical graphics system STATGRAPHICS, realized in APL*PLUS among the Soviet users.

The first APL presentation for IBM PC was arranged by Professor P.I.Medow (the University of Toronto, Canada) at the Computer Centre of the Academy of Sciences in Moscow, and also LIIAS in Leningrad in 1983. Moreover, Professor Medow presented his colleagues in Moscow and Leningrad with two APL computers MCM-70, which inspired lots of people to learn APL. Since 1983 the APL*PLUS/PC system, though illegally, has been applied at the North-West Branch of the Central Research Economic Institute [14].

The problem of intellectual property has a most dramatic influence upon computer science development in the USSR. The notion of intellectual property is not to be found in the Soviet legislation as yet, and thus in the USSR neither a Soviet citizen nor a foreign company have any actual rights to their own programming product. It goes without saying that the Soviet scientists and programmers are aware that by using illegal programming products they are breaking the law, but under the present conditions they are forced to violate the universal legal and moral standards as they are not able to acquire the necessary programs officially. In summer 1989 an international forum was held in Pereslavl-Zalessky near Moscow devoted to the intellectual property issues in computer software. The world’s leading firms, such as IBM, Microsoft, ICL, Xerox, Lotus, Ashton-Tate and others took part. At the organizers’ invitation A.I.Miroshnikov represented the Soviet APL community - and this was to be the first act of international recognition of APL in the Soviet Union.

When in 1985 S.P.Prokhorov had at his disposal two new IBM XT computers, he had no problem in choosing the programming system - it could be only APL*PLUS. Prokhorov and N.Zezjulinsky, working 16 hours a day during 3-4 weeks developed a system for effective control over the Stavropol region’s agriculture (the same region where Gorbachev, the current president of the USSR, had worked). This successful development was reported in the central newspapers and in an all Union TV broadcast. Nevertheless the system did not gain popularity - there were too few organizations owning IBM PCs at that time.

In 1985 at the Computer Centre of the Academy of Sciences in Moscow A.V.Kondrashev realized an APL-interpreter version for SM-4, the Soviet version of DEC PDP-11 [15]. This APL interpreter was the first Soviet APL version to gain popularity and to be commercially successful. Similar to APL/BESM (Kondrashev had begun as a student in Prokhorov’s team) APL/VTCAN makes use of the Russian spelling of system commands, functions and the names of variables. Seeking to make maximum use of the potentialities of a micro-computer with only 64K RAM M.Koganov and A.V.Kondrashev realized APL/VTCAN on a ROM-card inserted into the frame of the Soviet micro-computer DVK (the desktop version of the PDP-11) [16].

Having thus changed from swapping with a disk to using immediate ROM they managed to improve considerably the interpreter’s properties. APL/VTCAN supports a 32-36K workspace and a symbol table of 64 names including local variables and labels, and is more suited to teaching, or to functioning as an intelligent terminal. Nevertheless it was used to carry out a few software projects: a modelling system for the BN-600 nuclear reactor diagnosis (A.Scomorokhov, Obninsk), the DIASTAT statistics program package (V.Vladimirov, Obninsk), the interface to RBD-MICRO (V.Neradovsky, Leningrad), and at least three different accounting systems (Sverdlovsk and Leningrad).

items.title: Birth Of The Soviet APL Community
items.text:
In 1986 in Obninsk the first seminar-school was held, which has now become annual. A working team on APL, as yet informal, is being formed, that aims at popularizing APL and coordinating the development work dealing with it. The 1986 seminar was marked by great enthusiasm - many of the participants, working in the same town, actually didn’t know each other. In 1988 the first Soviet organization dealing with production and popularization of Soviet APL products came into being - the scientific technical co-operative "Dialog".

In 1989 Kondrashev transferred APL/VTCAN to a more modern Soviet micro-computer Electronika-85, compatible with DEC Professional 380. On the APL/85 version the workspace was enlarged four times (64K for functions and 64K for variables) and it became possible to use a 20M hard disk [17].

In 1989 a decision was taken in the Soviet Union governmental circles to reorganize four ministries dealing with computer development and production into one ministry with a unified policy in the field of computer machinery: following IBM. Consequently financing of projects based on computers compatible with HP and DEC products was limited, and the interest in any software except that for IBM-compatible machines fell dramatically. The only Soviet APL-interpreter found itself in a difficult situation.

Though there were a great number of attempts to realize the APL programming system, there were relatively few successful ones. At present there are practically only three teams in the USSR that are specifically engaged in developing applied programs in APL. The principal direction of the Obninsk team’s work is developing teaching programs for APL/VIDEO, statistical programs (in the Central Institute for Skill Improvement), prototyping of algorithms and modeling system development for nuclear reactor diagnosis (in the Institute for Physics and Power Engineering). The team of scientists from the Computer Centre of the Academy of Sciences (Moscow), which is using APL*PLUS/PC, specializes in developing programs for simulating economic processes, with wide application of graphics.

At the Central Research Economic Institute (Leningrad) and LIIAS (Leningrad), APL is used as a practical tool for developing DSS and algorithm models of economic systems and processes [18]. These models serve as a basis for the Institute’s work, providing the leadership of the GOSPLAN of Russia and the Planning Committee of Leningrad region with results of the analysis and forecasts of economic development. The Leningrad team of users has always had at its disposal powerful hardware and quite modern software: CDC APL 2.0 and STSC APL*PLUS.

It has developed drivers that make it possible to use Cyrillic in different APL versions, as well as realizing full adaptation for application in the USSR of the STATGRAPHICS statistical graphics system. The experience they have acquired enables the team, together with the system for preliminary planning, to prepare for object construction designed for commercial use on the Soviet Union territory [19].

Nowadays two APL systems are mainly used in the USSR: APL/VTCAN and APL*PLUS/PC. APL/VTCAN versions are used on SM-4 series minicomputers (about 40 copies of it have been installed) and on different versions of DVK-3 microcomputers (more than 100 copies have been distributed). Unlike the Soviet APL version, which is rather difficult to copy, the APL*PLUS/PC system is copied and used uncontrollably. At least 20 users of this popular APL version are known to the author, half of whom work in Leningrad. Besides these, two multiuser APL systems are being used on mainframes: APL/VIDEO in Obninsk on an IBM/370 compatible and APL 2.0 on CDC Cyber-172 in LIIAS in Leningrad. One more single-user APL/MEI system is being used in Moscow.

items.title: A Breakthrough
items.text:
The year 1990 will go down into the history of the Soviet APL community as the year of the breakthrough. That year two Soviet representatives read their papers at the annual international APL90 conference in Copenhagen for the first time and joined SigAPL.

"The Russian Advance", supported by Finnish and Dutch national APL associations, was received rather optimistically. The world APL community was faced all of sudden by a strange APL user community, who managed to retain the APL-pioneers’ enthusiasm while working in isolation and in rather strained conditions. It was this factor as well as the general interest towards the USSR that made ACM SigAPL support the idea of holding the APL92 conference in Leningrad, USSR.

In September the Union of the Soviet APL users was registered in Obninsk. ACM came forward with an initiative of establishing five free ACM Chapters (or Local SIGs) in the USSR, with the view to organizing the Soviet SigAPL as well.

On October 11-12 the first international meeting on APL in the USSR - the Finnish-Soviet seminar "APL and Application Software" - was held in Leningrad, which was a big success. 50 Soviet APLers and 26 participants from Finland and Sweden took part.

At the end of 1990 the first state company - InfoStroy - was established in Leningrad, whose aim is to develop and distribute APL-based application systems, and also to supply APL systems for different computer classes. At the same time the Leningrad APL Users Group was formed which is contributing to APL development in the USSR along with the Union of the Soviet APL-users.

Though APL can hardly be called a widespread programming language in the USSR, the great way it has grown in this country during the last year with the help of the international APL community gives us hope for success in the near future.

items.title: One Small Step for APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 75

by David S. Moffat

It was a warm sunny August mornng in 1982 when I entered Imperial House as the newest member of the Chief Accountant’s Department. My role, inter alia, was to look after the department’s newly acquired Spectrum computer, and to learn a new language – APL. I had done a little research before joining Imperial and discovered that it was a language programmers either loved or hated – and most people I spoke to hated it.

My previous experience had been gained with Micromodeller, running on an Apple, and the PPL general ledger package running on an IBM mainframe. Both are environments where the user develops his own system without programmer intervention. I had also played with ALGOL and BASIC, but a long time ago.

The Chief Accountant’s Department had little experience of micro-computers and due to redecoration of its offices was temporarily relocated. For at least one of the above reasons the Spectrum had been housed in a disused photographic darkroom. The environment, whilst not affecting the operation of the machine (provided the windows weren’t opened) did little to engender my enthusiasm for the new task. I was shown how to switch the machine on, most people knew how to type B to boot, but few knew how to use APL.

A week later and in one fell swoop I was introduced to the teach yourself system, provided by MicroAPL, Gilman and Rose’s “APL an Interactive Approach” and Adrian Smith’s book “Design Handbook for Commercial Systems”, and then I was left to my own devices. These aids to learning either had a soporific effect on railway journeys or left me confused, so I reverted to John Le Carre but he couldn’t help. I found, later, that the non-fiction books helped enhance existing knowledge but lacked the stimulation I needed to gain initial expertise. Therefore, I decided to embark on a series of one day courses on a child’s guide on how to write the ultimate “one liner”. The hieroglyphics gradually began to make sense, but I was not filled with a sense of wonder at the dawning of a new age, and I would have been quite happy if this American import could have been re-incarcerated with the Essense’s Dead Sea Scrolls, in the Qumran Hills.

My new found knowledge – if that’s what three days’ training in a classroom environment could be called – was soon to be put to the test by building a simple system. I had two basic problems:

  1. I had to replicate an outdated manual system.
  2. There was no detailed specification.

A task which would now take me a day to complete, took me two weeks. The system is still running but it is unsophisticated – and it has more than one line!

The whole experience left me wondering, yet again, why had we chosen a language, which took so long to learn and was so unfriendly. This was not a unique experience as other members of my department felt likewise and resorted to pencil and paper or flocked to the PC.

It was about six months later that I began to get involved in producing a full system specification to be implemented by a trained Analyst/Programmer, whom I watched build the system, and only then did I begin to see what all the fuss was about.

During the subsequent three years I have been closely involved in specifying and building complex accounting systems, and during that time I have acquired a reasonable knowledge of the language. However, I still would not class myself as an APL programmer because I primarily hold an accounting role, the demands of which prevented specialisation in “a programming language”.

I now realise what can be achieved with the language. It has the following obvious advantages:

  • It has a short development time for even the most complex systems.
  • Routines can be developed into small building blocks or functions which can be interrelated and are easy to debug.
  • Data is easily controlled within the workspace.

However, it does tend to have a few disadvantages:

  • It is so brief as to be curt.
  • The characters are not obvious and cannot be read by anyone but programmers and other dead races.
  • It requires a special keyboard and printer.

A well built APL system can give great benefits to the user. However, in the real world, systems are rarely static, the continuing changes in company structure, legal requirements and commercial demands necessitate frequent changes. APL systems are often not easy to change quickly, even for a skilled programmer, unless he is the author. APL allows each person his own style, which partially evolves from his level of competence but also from his approach to the problem.

I have also found that APLers adopt a self-documentation approach to their systems, with a line of text at the start of each function, thus avoiding tedious manuals but not satisfying auditors. Self-documentation benefits those familiar with the system but is probably inadequate for a newcomer, and hence usually results in only authors changing their systems. Because only the originator can make changes, Murphy’s Law says he is usually not at hand when needed to make amendments, as his expertise is in use elsewhere. This criticism is true, to some extent, of other languages but despite their failings these are easier to learn or are less hostile, because of their use of near English commands. Novices gain a fillip from success and users like to gain familiarity with their systems but APL does not encourage them. Harassed users do not always have the time to brief and control their systems analyst, particularly late at night with an early morning deadline, and inevitably there is a desire to control your operating tools.

If a company has made a heavy investment in a computer system it wants to gain the full benefit from not only its main workhorse applications, but also from ad hoc analytical tools for business decision making usually called the “what-if”. This need has led to the growth of the spreadsheet and PC market and a stampede for freedom from programmers, but it seems wasteful to have at least two computers, two terminals, two printers, two languages, etc, etc. The ideal solution to quote ICL would be to have “one per desk” – one machine, one language, at least within each culture. This is not a universal solution to chain everyone to only one supplier, but it can be both expensive and confusing for a non-expert to have to use two computers. Familiarity and dexterity helps speed up the decision-making, particularly with a universal tool – but that tool needs to be both flexible and easy to learn. There ought to be standardisation for the non-expert within a company or department. The guy at the sharp end probably doesn’t care whether he is using APL, Basic or whatever, what he wants is to get the job done in the most efficient way, with the minimum of fuss.

There is no doubt that APL has many advantages over other languages but I believe you experts are not developing it to its potential. There could be great satisfaction and one should not also forget financial reward, in developing the ultimate solution. Could you develop the quantum leap from Lotus 123 et al. I know you are developing many bespoke systems for major customers which form building blocks with other systems. I have also seen interfaces with spreadsheets and heard suggestions about using the PC as a dumb terminal, but is anyone developing for one or two generations out, and more importantly is it likely to expand outside the small world of VECTOR?

My dictionary defines vector as “any quantity requiring direction to be stated as well as magnitude in order to define it properly”. Most people in the business community have heard of Lotus, few will know of APL. Perhaps you in the APL community need more magnitude and more direction. If, as I believe, the product is a good one, you should be able to go out and sell it in the right way with easy to use systems which are well marketed. You are the prophets but have you been left in the wilderness?

If I show my ignorance of what is available, then I am probably representative of the vast majority of your potential customers, who have insufficient information about the power of APL. Don’t wait for the Big Blues of this world to lead the way, expand outside the comfort of the VECTOR clique and develop more user-friendly, generalised products which can help the novice build his own routines, which should enable “what-if” modelling and may eventually interface with other bespoke systems. The development of cheap hardware has created the most receptive audience you could ask for. The keyword system developed for the QL was a good attempt to meet this demand, but it did not go far enough to simplify access to the APL environment, but it did get reviewed outside the computer press.

In writing this I have attempted to be controversial and draw together the adverse comments of others. If you are stimulated to respond please remember you should address the silent majority.

items.title: ASLGREG: Predictions with Confidence Limits
items.text:
by Ellis Morgan

I present a possible approach to adding predictions to the ASLGREG Regression and Generalised Linear Models Workspace. I include ideas to increase robustness and a method that allows STEPWISE to return a linear predictor equation that can be passed to FIT and other ASLGREG functions.

Many of the good ideas behind this are due to Alan Sykes and I am grateful for his help and his tolerance as I change his code and workspace structure. I propose that my extensions should be added to ASLGREG and welcome comments and suggestions for improvement.

items.title: ASLGREG
items.text:
My descriptions of the following examples are sparse where they cover old ground, see: ASLGREG by Alan Sykes (Vector 7.4); the ASLGREG manual (available from BAA Administration); ASLGREG reviewed by Jon Sandles (Vector 9.2).

      85000 65000 55000 70000 82500 78500 49950 46950

The workspace is ASLGREG, HOUSEDATA sets up Alan Sykes data on 29 houses. Other variables are TYPE (1 terraced, 2 semi-detached, 3 detached, 4 bungalow), AGE, BEDS(number of bedrooms) and AREA.

      START
Regression Volume 1 Version 2
A.M.Sykes & E.P.Morgan, February 1993

      LPA←STEPWISE 3 3
      LPA

It can be dangerous to proceed from STEPWISE to PREDICT without thought but, provided diagnostics are displayed too, it is good to be able to do so. In the new workspace LP is ambivalent and the left argument, when present and equal to one, makes each item in the linear predictor an APL expression. items.text:

Row   AREA   BEDS   TYPE   Observed   Predicted   Upper   Lower   ---   ----   ----   ----   --------   ---------   -----   -----   1   1326   4   1   60.5   74.89   82.3   67.48   2   782   3   2   47.5   74.39   78.24   70.55   3   312   1   2   46   48.35   53.83   42.87   4   1460   3   3   110   112   120.3   103.6   5   1056   4   3   148   128.2   137.7   118.8

PREDICT is similar to DIAGNOSTICS in that the right argument specifies the columns to print. In this case I am calling for: S the explanatory variables before interactions, nesting and other equations; Y for the observed Y value; M for the predicted Mean value; U and L for the Upper and Lower confidence limits of the mean. The optional left argument of PREDICT is described below and specifies the confidence level (default is 80%) and the type of limit (default is independent for each prediction).

items.title: PREDICTING for a few extra observations
items.text:
The simplest way is to add a few extra observations to your data, giving the response variable a value of zero and then keep them out of the fitting process by giving them a weight of zero. All real cases will have a weight of one.

      PRICE←0 0,PRICE
      TYPE←3 4,TYPE
      BEDS←4 3,BEDS
      AREA←1200 800,AREA

Two new “cases” at the beginning.

      YVAR'PRICE÷1000'
Y variable is PRICE÷1000
Units set to 31

      W←0 0,29⍴1
      PRIORWEIGHT 'W'
Prior Weight Variable is W

      SINK←FIT LPA
      DISPLAY 'ESTP'

items.title: PREDICTING for a table of new observations
items.text:
Any number of sets of explanatory data can be used for predicting.

      A←800 800 1000 1000 1000 1200 1200
      B←2 3 3 4 5 4 5
      T←1 2 2 3 3 3 4
      SUBSTITUTE'BEDS,B:AREA,A:TYPE,T'

Here I have associated the variables A, B and T with the original explanatory variables using the function SUBSTITUTE.

      REFRESH 7
Prediction New offset Variable Reset to the Default

REFRESH stores the new data in a “predicting matrix”, a global variable called newmat which PREDICT will use in much the same way as DIAGNOSTICS uses the variable desmat set by FIT. The REFRESH right argument is the number of new cases, if any of your new data is the wrong length a message results. Of course in a function you would call it with something like REFRESH ⍴A. Here you see evidence that ASLGREG does generalised as well as ordinary linear regression, the message tells you that the default value is used for the offset associated with this set of explanatory variables (zero in this case as I have set no offset).

      PREDICT'SMUL'
Row   A   B   T   Predicted   Upper   Lower   ---   -   -   -   ---------   -----   -----   1   800   2   1   57.5   62.38   52.63   2   800   3   2   75.39   79.27   71.51   3   1000   3   2   86.47   91.23   81.72   4   1000   4   3   125.1   134.6   115.7   5   1000   5   3   86.47   91.23   81.72   6   1200   4   3   136.2   145.7   126.8   7   1200   5   4   97.56   103.7   91.38

Now PREDICT detects that newmat is present and uses it to calculate predictions and limits. Note that newmat is expunged by YVAR or by SUBSTITUTE ''. This suggests the following sequence of functions:

To predict with the original data

SUBSTITUTE '', PREDICT

To recalculate the equation and predict

FIT, PREDICT

To change one of the explanatory variables and predict again

A[2]←900 (say), REFRESH, PREDICT

To use a different set of explanatory variables

SUBSTITUTE, REFRESH, PREDICT

items.title: Implementation
items.text:
I have tried to make sure that user functions written for version 1 will work with version 2. This will be completely true if you use only those functions defined in the ASLGREG manual with a version of APL that allows ambivalent functions. The functions LP, FIT and TESTHYP are now ambivalent, providing a left argument of zero in you current functions is all you need to do. If you are using any subroutines (that is functions whose name begins with ¨) then you may find they have changed, in particular the link and error functions have changed and your own new link functions will need modifying.

items.title: Membership Questionnaire
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 36

notes by Jill Moss

For APLication last year we devised a survey for people to fill in. Although it was by no means constructed according to orthodox statistical procedures, we hoped that our little questionnaire would tell us something about the people attending the Conference, and thereby perhaps provide us with a snap-shot of a ‘typical’ APLer (if there is such a thing). We have finally got round to analysing the results and hope that readers of VECTOR will find them as fascinating as we did!

Our first question asked which types of APL people used. IBM will be pleased to learn that APL2 won in the popularity stakes (I can assure readers that this was not because we had a lot of people from IBM fill in the forms!). Most people, however, said they used more than one type of APL. After APL2, it was pretty close between VS APL and APL*Plus (mainframe and PC). (Sorry Dyadic and I P Sharp!)

Our second question asked how many people the respondent knew personally who write APL programs. Answers here varied from “NIL” (from Richard Webber up at Doncaster Metropolitan Institute of Higher Education) to “HUNDREDS” (Dick Bowman exaggerating, of course!). In fact, the highest ‘score’ goes again to IBM, where one respondent claimed to know 200 other APL programmers.

A totally statistically meaningless question (just to really get up the nose of all those statisticians) asked people to hazard a guess as to how many people they thought write APL programs in the UK, Europe and the World (we left out the Universe). Surprisingly, most people said about the same – between 500 and 2000 in the UK, between 5000 and 10,000 in Europe and 10,000 to 50,000 world-wide. (There were some silly answers of course, which I have conveniently omitted). Has anybody got any real figures here? It would be interesting to know.

We then had a really sexist question – ‘How many women do you know who write APL programs?’ We included this because we suspected that the majority of APLers are male and we wanted to check this out. However, although 18% said they didn’t know any, and 25% only knew one, surprisingly 21% said they knew more than 10 women who write APL programs, so perhaps there are more of them about than we suspected! Despite the fact that 90% of our respondents were male, over half of them said they worked with women who were writing APL programs, which I find very encouraging (so why weren’t more of them at the Conference then, or maybe they just don’t like filling in questionnaires?).

Our next question asked how many days per month the respondent spent writing APL programs. Of the replies, exactly half said that they spent more than 10 days per month, although almost 18% said that they spent no more than 2 days per month actually writing APL programs, and 3 people said they did no programming at all in APL (one of these is a Manager, one an Economist and I don’t know what the third does but I suspect he is also a Manager as he later put down that he had learnt APL over five years ago).

Although the vast majority of the people who completed our questionnaire were employed by very large companies, half said that, where they worked, there were no more than five other people writing APL programs. This confirms our suspicions that APL tends to be found in ‘small pockets’ within large organisations. These organisations included companies in the Banking, Insurance, Manufacturing and Energy Industries, with colleges of further education being quite well represented. Surprisingly, there were not many people from government or local authorities (perhaps because their budgets are too tight to allow employees to attend APL conferences?).

A telling question was ‘When did you first learn APL?’. This was designed to establish the ‘age’ of the APL population and to find out whether there is much new blood coming into the language. A staggering 71% learnt APL over five years ago, with only 10% having come into it within the past three years. (One person – the Economist – put that he had never learnt it. It would be interesting to discover if he found the conference useful and whether he was inspired to learn APL afterwards.)

Most people had been on a course to learn, and the vast majority of them (88%) said that they thought the course worthwhile (a pat on the back for the C & D trainers here, I suspect!).

Slightly more than a third write APL programs to produce results which are used by other people, a third produce systems which are used by non-programming staff, while just over a quarter produce systems and programs which are used by other APL programmers. Unfortunately, 79% said they did not have any budgetary authority (were we preaching to the converted at Canterbury and perhaps more emphasis should be placed on attracting Managers and others who hold the purse-strings if the use of APL is to increase?)

More than 50% said that they thought their company used contract programmers occasionally, but by far the most telling (and depressing) indicator of the extent to which APL usage is expanding came with the results of our last couple of questions, concerning the recruitment of permanent staff. We asked ‘How many people have been recruited by your company/department over the past year?’ and ‘Of these, how many were replacements for people who had left, and how many were new vacancies?’. Almost 60% said that no APLers had been recruited where they worked over the past 12 months, and a total of over 98% said that the number recruited was between NIL and 2. Of these, over half of all new recruits were to replace people who had left. Not very good news for those of us keen to see an expansion in the use of the language.

So what picture does this give us of our typical APLer? I would say, from these results, our typical APLer is probably male, works within a large organisation employing a handful of other people writing APL programs (some of whom might be female!), learnt APL more than five years ago and uses APL2, VS APL and maybe APL*Plus to write programs, the results of which are used by other people within the company. He probably found his job (via APL People, of course!) when the person who was there before left. In fact, what we knew all along! Apologies to all those who don’t fit this stereotype, which is probably most of you reading this article.

items.title: Polynomial Interpolation
items.text:
Interpolation means the process of using a table of values of an independent variable \(x\) with corresponding function values \(f(x)\), to determine a value of \(f(x)\) at a non-tabular value of \(x\). For many functions, a polynomial which passes through the tabulated points gives an adequate representation near the non-tabular value. Such a polynomial is then used to interpolate values of \(f(x)\) at other values of \(x\) without explicit calculation of its coefficient values.

There is a variety of techniques for doing this, among them Lagrangian polynomials and Neville’s algorithm. The technique used here is known as Newton’s Divided Differences, and consists of taking successive differences of f-values which are divided at each stage by the matching differences in the column of x-values. The values of the nth column of f-differences are divided by the differences of the corresponding x-values which are n apart, for example:

x      f       1st      2nd      3rd
               diff     diff     diff
0      4
               2
1      6                0.2
               3                 -0.15
5      18               -1
               -4
8      6

In the 1st diff column 18-6 is divided by 5-1, and 6-18 by 8-5. In the 2nd diff column, 3-2 is divided by 5-0 and -4-3 by 8-1, and so on.

The result of the verb divdifs is x laminated with the values at the head of the columns, viz.

0 1 5    8
4 2 0.2 _0.15

from which the original values of f could, if required, be reconstructed by reversing the arithmetic.

The J realisation which follows is in the style of a Pascal program, which is a natural way of expressing an iterative algorithm of this sort. Indeed this algorithm illustrates the ease with which transition is possible between J and more familiar programming languages.

NB. Obtain leading values in divided difference columns
divdifs =. 0 : 0
:
i =.0 [ f=. a=. y. [ n=.#x.                 NB. initialization
loop) $.=.>(n > i=.i+1) { end;$.            NB. for i = 1 to n-1 do
j =. i-1                                    NB. start of inner loop
loop1) $. =. >(n > j=.j+1) { end1;$.        NB. for j = i to n-1 do
t =. (j{f - (j-1){f)%(j{x. - (j-i){x.)      NB. a[j]:=
a =. t j } a                     NB. ((f[j]-f[j-1])/(x[j]-x[j-i])
$.=.loop1                                   NB. end of inner loop
end1) f =. a                                NB. update f
$.=.loop                                    NB. end of outer loop
end) x.,:a                       NB. result is x,:leading diff'nces.
)

Interpolation is performed by an algorithm which uses the leading divided differences. A merit of this technique is that as the algorithm progresses through its iterations the result vector grows by catenating interpolated values of successively higher polynomial degree as more points are brought into consideration from the right of the data.

NB. Program to perform polynomial interpolations of increasing order
interpol =. 0 : 0
''
:
f =. 1{x. [ x =. 0{x.          NB. f = function values, x = x-values
a =. 1{t =. x divdifs f        NB. a = leading divided differences
n =. #a [ i =. 0 [ p =. 0{a    NB. p =a[0], first estimate
sol =. a                       NB. sol is result vec (see last NB.)
loop) $. =. >(n>i =.i+1) { end;$.      NB. for i = 1 to n-1 do
j =. i [ t =. 1                        NB. start of inner loop
loop1) $. =. >(_1<j=.j-1) { end1;$.    NB. for j = i-1 downto 0 do
t =. t*(y. -j{x)                       NB. t := t*(y. -x[j])
$. =. loop1                            NB. end of inner loop

)

   x =.8 9 9.5 11
   f =. 2.079442 2.197225 2.251292 2.397895
   xf =. x,:f

2.079442 2.22078 2.21924 2.21921

It is not necessary that the x values be in ascending order. For example, using the first example given above the successive polynomial interpolations are

items.title: Choleski Decomposition ("Square Root") of a Matrix
items.text:
This is a method of factorisation of a symmetric matrix

\[\begin{equation*} A = LL' \end{equation*}\]

where L is a lower triangular matrix. If A is positive definite the elements of L will be real, otherwise some will be complex. The mathematical equations which govern the method are:

\[\begin{gather*} m_{11} = \sqrt{a_{11}} \\[1ex] m_{jj} = \sqrt{a_{jj} - \sum_{s=1}^{j-1} m_{js}^2} \qquad j = 2,\ldots\ldots,n \\[1ex] m_{j1} = \frac{a_{j1}}{m_{11}} \qquad j = 2,\ldots\ldots,n \\[1ex] m_{jk} = \frac{1}{m_{kk}} \left( a_{jk} - \sum_{s=1}^{k-1} m_{js} m_{ks} \right) \qquad k+1,\ldots\ldots,n;\, k \end{gather*}\]

These lead to the definition of some subsidiary verbs as follows:

ssqbut1=. +/@( (-:i.@#@]) # *:@] )     NB. 2 ssqbut1 4 2 7 3 5 yields the
                                       NB. sum of squares of 4 2 3 and 5

                                       NB. sqrt(2), 3/sqrt(2), 4/sqrt(2)

                                       NB. of a matrix

                                       NB. same size as y. filled with x.

k=. 0 [ n=.#M=. 1 fillM1 y.          NB. initialisation

t=. %: k{k{y.- (k ssqbut1 (k{M))     NB. t = sqrt(Akk - sum(Mks^2)
M=. t((n+1)*k) } M                   NB. Mkk:= t
j =. k                               NB. start of inner loop
loop2) $. =. >(n>j=.j+1) {end2;$.    NB. if j>= n go to end2
t=. (j{k{y.- (k{M) +/ .* j{M )% t    NB. t:=(Ajk - sum MjkMks)/Mkk
M=. t ((j * n) + k) } M              NB. Mjk:=t
$. =. loop2                          NB. end of inner loop
end2)                                NB. j=n
$. =. loop1                          NB. end of outer loop
end1)M
:

items.title: Networking APL micros
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 49

by Richard Nabavi

items.title: What is Networking?
items.text:
Of all the buzzwords in the computing industry, ‘Networking’ is the one which is the most misused, and yet the most indicative of underlying user needs for computing in the late ’80s. Just as in the early seventies, ‘Interactive’ and ‘Real Time’ were regarded as the adjectives to look for in assessing computer systems, today manufacturers all claim that their systems have a networking capability.

In reality, networking can mean different things. Looking through the computer magazines, there seem to be three main ways in which the word is used (or misused). These can be described as Point-to Point, File Serving, and True Networking.

items.title: Point-to Point Networks
items.text:
Many vendors of ‘networking’ products are in fact talking about something very simple. This is illustrated in Figure 1, and a typical example of such a system is Clearway, a product of Real Time Systems Ltd. Essentially, what this consists of is a coaxial cable (or, more generally, any means of transmitting messages, such as a fibre optic link) into which a number of devices can be linked. Typically, the devices which will be hooked on to the cable will be terminals, printers and computers. The idea is that, instead of wiring terminals and other peripherals to computers via ordinary ‘RS232’ cables, the network is used instead to provide a multitude of point-to-point links between the various devices. In other words, this sort of ‘network’ is really doing nothing except making neater the connections between devices, which otherwise would be connected via a mess of independent cables.

The advantages of a system such as Clearway are obvious. As new devices are added, you do not need to rewire your building. A single terminal can switch between different computers under software control, instead of having to replug RS232 cables every time you wish to log on to a different computer. This is a lot more efficient than conventional wiring, plugboard and switches, but these sorts of systems should not be confused with networking of computers, since they do not allow the sharing of data between different CPU’s connected to the network, They represent a very useful simplification of the problems of lots of data cables around a building, but they do not involve any radically new approaches to data processing or the way in which computers are used.

items.title: File Serving Networks
items.text:
Many of the claims which computer vendors make for networking capability refer to something which again should not be confused with true networking. This is what I call the File Server type of system. The philosophy behind this is again fairly simple, and can be very useful. The ‘network’ is built around a single central computer, usually with a hard disk and perhaps a printer and other peripherals connected to it, into which are connected (in a ‘star’ configuration) external satellite computers (see Figure 2). These satellite computers will usually be small microcomputers, with no disc facility at all (or perhaps with a small amount of floppy disc storage). The idea is that hard disc storage is relatively expensive, and that users in many applications will wish to share common data. Note that, in this type of system, the computers in the network fall into two distinct classes — File Servers (of which there will usually be only one), and Satellite Units.

A number of points should be apparent. The first is that only the File Servers need to have an advanced, multi-tasking operating system. This is because the Satellite Units are supporting only one terminal, and, when a request is made, for example, to read a record from a file, the Satellite Unit which made the request will wait until the record is returned as data by the File Server. The second point is that the expansion capability of the network is limited by the response time of the central File Server. Essentially, we have only one computer serving all the disc read/writes for everyone on the network, which is not much better than having only one multi-user computer in the first place. Thirdly, although there may be peripherals such as printers or graph plotters attached to some of the Satellite Units, these will not be accessible to other Satellite Units. In other words, we are re-creating the concept of a central computer — comprising disc files and peripherals — which is accessed by remote users, who may or may not have some local printing facilities. For many of us, it was to get away from the restrictions of centralized computing that we first turned towards microcomputers, and the re-creation of a central computer is like bringing back the bath water with the baby.

items.title: True Networking
items.text:
By now it should be becoming clear what I mean by a true networking computer system. The characteristics are:

  • The ability to connect together a number of computers, each logically equivalent as far as the network is concerned;
  • Each of the computers on the network to be single or multi-user as is most convenient;
  • Each of the computers to have the possibility of disc storage, although the amount and type of storage will vary between the different machines;
  • Each of the computers in the network to have the possibility of being connected to a number of peripherals;
  • Any user on any machine on the network to be able to access (transparently to the applications software) any file on any disc on any machine in the network (subject of course to normal security checks);.
  • Any user on any machine on the network to be able to access any peripheral on any machine on the network;
  • Full multi-user controls including file and record locking to apply across the whole network.

Further features which in practice we have found desirable are:

  • The ability for any user to initiate a task on a remote machine, either attached to his terminal or to run as a background task. A good example where this is useful is to start a print spool job on a remote machine;
  • The ability to connect simultaneously to several networks;

Figure 3 shows a typical small configuration, which is in fact MicroAPL’s in-house network system.

Fig.1 — Point to Point Networking

Fig.2 — File Server Networking

Fig.3 — MICROAPL In-House Network

items.title: Operating System Support of Networking
items.text:
Most discussions of networking concentrate on the characteristics of the physical connection between devices on the network. Unfortunately, most computers in use today are based on operating systems which were conceived before networking was developed. This means that networking has to be added on as an ‘extra’, and is not built-in to the design of the systems software. The consequence of this is that limitations have to be imposed on what you can do with the network. For example, some major manufacturers have announced Ethernet connections between their computers, but when you come to examine the capabilities in detail, you find that the only way in which data can be accessed on a remote machine is by copying the whole file from the remote machine to your home machine.

In order to illustrate the way in which networking can be built in to the system software of a modern computer, let us look at MIRAGE, one of the few operating systems which was designed right from the beginning to cater for network operation. MIRAGE is a multi-user, multi-tasking operating system which was written by a UK company, Swifte Computer Systems Ltd, for Motorola 68000 computers. It has been in use since 1981 on MicroAPL’s range of 68000-based micros, and it implements networking in a very simple way.

To understand the way in which MIRAGE handle network file accesses, let us first consider how the operating system refers to a file on a single machine. Files are organized in ‘directories’ on logical discs on the system. For example, suppose a user wanted to type out the contents of a text file called ‘SYSTEM.HELP’ which was sitting in the ‘DOC’ directory on logical disc 3 of his machine. Using the MIRAGE utility ‘TYPE’, he would enter at the keyboard:

TYPE DSC3:SYSTEM.HELP[DOC]

‘DSC3:’ refers to the name of the logical disc on which the file resides, the directory in which it resides is entered between square brackets, and the file name is divided into a main file name (‘SYSTEM’) and a file extension (‘HELP’). As a convenience, it is not always necessary to enter all of this information, since each user has a default disc and directory into which he is ‘logged’, and which he can change at any time. For example, by entering:

LOG DSC3:DOC

he can change his default directory to be DOC on DSC3:. If he then enters:

TYPE SYSTEM.HELP

the operating system will by default look for the file in the correct place.

The extension of this to a networked system is simple. As well as specifying the directory and disc on which a file is to be found, you specify a machine on the network. This is done by adding to the front of the file name a ‘Node’ name (‘Node’ means machine on the network). This is distinguished from the logical disc name by being terminated by two colons rather than one. The home machine is always ‘SYSO::’. Thus, in the example above, the user could if he wished have used the full file name:

TYPE SYSO::DSC3:SYSTEM.HELP[DOC]

This means: Type out the file SYSTEM.HELP, which is to be found in directory DOC on disc 3 on my home machine. To access a file on a remote machine, you simply change the Node name to that of another machine on the network. For example, a user on a remote machine who wanted to type out the same file might enter:

TYPE EXT4::DSC3:SYSTEM.HELP[DOC]

where EXT4:: is the name (as viewed from his computer) of the machine on which the file resides. Naturally, it might become rather tedious to have all the above information for every file reference, so you can log into a remote directory. For example:

LOG EXT4::DSC3:DOC

would cause the default node, disc and directory to be the ones we were interested in.

Another couple of examples should give an idea of the possibilities. To copy a whole file from a remote machine to your own:

COPY SYS0::DSC0:MYHELP.DOC[HELP] = EXT4::DSC3:SYSTEM.HELP[DOC]

This copies the file SYSTEM.HELP from the DOC directory of disc 3 on remote machine EXT4:: to the HELP directory of disc 0 of the user’s home machine, renaming the file to MYHELP.DOC in the process.

To copy a file from one remote machine to another remote machine:

COPY EXT6::DSC0:MYHELP.DOC[HELP] = EXT4::DSC3:SYSTEM.HELP[DOC]

This is the same as the previous example, except that the file is being copied from remote machine EXT4:: to remote machine EXT6::.

items.title: High Level Language Support of Networking
items.text:
Clearly, all the above facilities are of limited use if they cannot also be used by high-level languages such as BASIC, Pascal, APL, and so on. Equally, in a true networking environment, applications software such as word-processing software and spreadsheets should be able to access files anywhere on the network. This again shows how important it is for networking capabilities to lie right at the heart of the system software, so that high-level support for these facilities should ‘fall-out’ automatically without special arrangements. We can see how this works by considering how APL.68000 under MIRAGE can access files across the network.

Let us first consider how APL finds files on a single machine. The user might, for example, enter:

)LIB

which would print out his default library of APL workspaces. He can also access up to 9 other libraries, by (for example) asking for:

)LIB 5

What in fact happens here is that the APL interpreter maintains, for each user, a table (technically an APL system function Quad-MOUNT) of his current ten libraries. By default, these are logical discs 0 to 9 on his home machine, with his default MIRAGE directory. Thus, the default table looks like this:

SYSO::DSC0:JIM
SYSO::DSC1:JIM
SYSO::DSC2:JIM
.....
.....etc.

At any time, the user (or the applications program) can modify any or all of the rows of this table. For example, the first three rows of the table might be changed to:

SYSO::DSC0:JIM
SYSO::DSC4:MARY
SYSO::DSC5:LUKE

This would mean that library 0 would be directory JIM on disc 0, library 1 would be directory MARY on disc 4, and library 2 would be directory LUKE on disc 5.

The extension to a networked configuration is obvious and very simple. You simply specify the node for each logical library. For example:

EXT3::DSC0:APL
EXT6::DSC3:SUE
EXT9::DSC2:DAVE

In this example, libraries 0, 1 and 2 are all on different remote machines.

For those familiar with APL.68000, note that as well as workspace loading, saving, and copying, the Quad-MOUNT table also specifies the location for component file accesses using APL.68000’s file system. Up to ten different nodes/discs/directories may be specified using Quad-MOUNT. If this is not enough, you can change Quad-MOUNT dynamically under program control to give access to an unlimited number of file locations. In addition, print spool files may be directed to a remote machine, as may arbitrary input/output, so that, for example, a graphics package may produce graphs on a flat-bed plotter which happens to be connected to a different computer.

The important thing to appreciate here is that an application program, written in APL, need not be modified to run off a file on a remote machine. Suppose that, for example, we have written a management information system which was originally designed to run on a single machine, with files on DSC0: and DSC1: of that machine. Later on, we link the machine into a network, and we want users on any machine to be able to access the same files, without changing our applications software. All that is necessary is for the above table (the ‘Quad-MOUNT’ table) to be initialized to set up the first two rows for access to the machine on which the files exist, and then the user will be able to run the application without any changes. The initialization can of course be automated so that the user is unaware that it is happening, if desired.

Access to the network via other languages is similar; essentially, we merely change the node part of the file name to go to a remote machine. To run the word-processing software off a remote disc, you simply LOG into the remote directory before running it. With the single exception of one piece of software which maintains memory-resident disc buffers, all programs written under MIRAGE can run unchanged across a network.

items.title: File and Record Locking on a network
items.text:
Probably the most embarassing question you can ask a supplier who claims to support networking is whether file and record locking operate across the network. The importance of this question will be obvious to anyone who has experience in writing multi-user applications software, since by definition networked systems are multi-user. A quick example should show what we mean.

Suppose we have a stock control system, and the files can be updated both by the Goods Inwards department and by the Goods Outwards department — which seems reasonable. Consider the case where a consignment of 100 Size 10 Wonderflanges arrives, and at about the same time an order for 18 of the same item is being despatched. The stock level before all this happens is 134.

The Goods Inwards people go to their computer terminal and call up the stock record for the Size 10 Wonderflanges, and at the same time the Goods Outwards people also do the same. Goods Inwards type faster, and so they enter the arrival of 100 items, to make a stock level of 234, and the record is written back to the file. Meanwhile, Goods Outwards see that there were 134 items in stock, and they enter their Goods Out details to reduce the stock to 116, and this record is written back to the stock file, overwriting the record which Goods Inwards have just written. The final result is that the stock level will be erroneously recorded as 116 instead of 216.

This is an absolutely standard problem in multi-user systems, and careful consideration will show that there is no way to avoid the difficulty unless the operating system maintains some form of file or record locking feature. What happens then is that, before updating the file, the record is ‘locked’ and no other user can access it until the update sequence is complete. Depending on the sophistication of the operating system, this lock might be on the whole file, or on specified records, and it might be a lock against all accesses, or only against writing. Whatever arrangement is used, a commercial multi-user system must have some form of file locking if multiple on-line file updating is to be possible.

Exactly the same considerations apply to networked systems. If true networked processing is to be possible, any user must be able to lock any file on any disc on any machine on the network (again, subject to security considerations). MicroAPL’s systems can in fact provide file and record locking across the network, as well as providing two levels of lock (read only or read/write). Again, the fact that the lock is occurring over the network is transparent to the applications software.

items.title: Case Study No. 1: Imperial Group
items.text:
So far we have considered the facilities offered by MicroAPL’s networking software in theory. How does it work in practice?

One example of a network used by a MicroAPL client is a group of large MicroAPL Spectrum supermicros installed at the London headquarters of Imperial Group. These systems serve over thirty users, with a large number of different printers, graph plotters and other peripherals attached to the machines on the network. The multi-user machines are used for two main (related) applications:

  • Consolidation of the management accounts of the various companies in Imperial Group to provide an overall set of Group accounts.;
  • On-line display of thousands of graphs detailing performance of the different parts of the Group against budget, previous year’s performance, etc. This is done on Tektronix colour screens installed in the boardroom and in the offices of the senior executives of the Group. Hard copy of graphs is produced on Hewlett Packard flatbed plotters.

This installation is an example of the use of networking to create a large effective logical computer out of a number of smaller machines. Initially, two separate machines were purchased (one for each of the above applications) and data transfer between the machines was via magnetic tape cartridge. The initial two machines were gradually expanded with extra memory and extra I/O ports, and then linked together using an Ethernet link to facilitate exchange of data between machines. Subsequently, further processing power was added by linking in another machine with a larger disc capacity. At the time of writing, the installation has been built up to an overall system of 48 RS-232 I/O ports, approximately 8 Megabytes of RAM, and 144 Megabytes of disc capacity, with two tape drives for back-up and data exchange.

A number of benefits accrue from this approach. Extra capacity in terms of CPU power, RAM, disc capacity, I/O ports and peripherals can be added as and when it is needed, with no need to change software as the installation grows. The use of several independent computers on a network gives the advantage of some degree of fault tolerance whilst permitting the sharing of common data and peripherals. Data can be backed up on to a remote machine, reducing the need for expensive tape units and simplifying backup and recovery procedures. New releases of software can be tested on one of the machines on the network, with access to the real data, whilst maintaining the previous version on other machines on the network. System maintenance — both in hardware and in software terms — is easier than it would be on a single minicomputer of comparable overall performance.

items.title: Case Study No. 2 — BASF
items.text:
The Imperial Group system is an example of a tightly-coupled set of machines; the only practical alternative to their network of supermicros would be a minicomputer or small mainframe. A different type of installation — built out of similar building blocks — is to be found at the large BASF complex at Ludwigshafen in Germany.

BASF have purchased a number of MicroAPL Spectrum machines of different configurations. These include machines with 5″ and 8″ floppy discs, 5″ Winchesters, 36 Mb 8″ Winchesters and 72 Mb 8″ Winchesters. The systems are used for a variety of applications and are scattered about the very large site. Some are used in multi-user mode, others are single-user dedicated systems. Devices connected to the systems vary between ordinary terminals and printers to laboratory instruments. The systems are used for scientific and engineering work, as well as straight commercial work.

In this case, an Ethernet cable of 1.5 kilometres has been used to link together the various machines. The purpose here is to allow simple exchange of information (even though some of the systems are of different configurations so that they cannot, for example, swap floppy discs to exchange data), and to avoid the isolation of having separate computers in various locations. Whereas in Imperial Group the effect of installing networking has ben to create effectively one large logical computer, here the different computers are exchanging data less frequently and are not necessarily running related software. The installation of the network has meant improved communications, easier exchange of programs in a development environment, and access across the network to any peripheral, disc or tape on any machine.

The BASF network is thus an example of a network of powerful micros which could run independently, but which form a much more flexible set of systems when linked together. The alternative would have been to stick with a collection of non-networked microcomputers, with all the disadvantages of isolation which that solution can cause. The problems of non-linked machines would have been particularly bad in view of the size of the Ludwigshafen site; whereas in many cases it may be acceptable to walk from one machine to another with a floppy disc if you want to exchange data, when the other machine is a mile away you do not want to do this too often.

items.title: The real challenge — true multi-vendor networking
items.text:
The systems we have been talking about so far are very flexible, but are limited in one very crucial respect. This is that the computers connected to the network have to be running the same operating system. Thus, you cannot simply take an assortment of different computers from a variety of manufacturers and link them together.

True multi-vendor networking does not exist at this moment. Whilst a number of specialist suppliers have worked on bridging this gap, the solutions offered for multi-vendor networking have to be very restricted. This is not surprising, since the facilities offered by different operating systems — let alone how those facilities are implemented — vary enormously. Therefore the ideal of being able to access files on any machine on the netwok, irrespective of the make and model of the machine, is very far off.

Worse than this, even if you could load a program from a remote machine into a computer of a different type, this would still only be of limited usefulness. Try to run a program written for the 8088 chip in an IBM PC on the 68000 processor in an Apple Lisa and you will not get very far. Even pure data files will be of different formats for different machines, with the possible exception of text files which are fairly standard. Even Unix does not provide machine independent program and data files, because of the multiplicity of different Unix versions and the fact that many programs are compiled into the native code of the machine they run on. The establishment of accepted vendor-independent standards for connection of systems is still at a fairly early stage, although some progress has been made.

Having said this, at MicroAPL we have looked into the question of providing at least some machine-independent networking facilities, by effectively emulating the MIRAGE operating system network interface on different machines. This would at least provide access to data on various remote machines, although the applications program might have some conversion to make use of the data. This work is only at a very preliminary stage, but we have at least established the technical feasibility of the approach, and we hope to work with a couple of our existing customers over the next eighteen months to set up a working system providing access to various mini- and micro-computers.

items.title: Conclusion
items.text: Networking of small computers is still at an early stage of development, but customers today can already reap very real benefits from the work that has already been done. The main obstacles to development are the lack of general standards for data exchange at the file level, and the fact that most operating systems in use on small computers were not conceived with networking in mind. The term ‘networking’ is used in many different senses, and vendors’ claims should be examined carefully to establish exactly what facilities are offered, and what software support they require.

items.title: GKS – Opportunity for APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 78

by Richard Nabavi

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
Traditionally, APL has been out of the mainstream of computing. A lofty disregard for most of the things which DP professionals regard as important has characterised the world view of APLers, although in many cases this disregard has been justified by subsequent events. The result of this has been that APL has continued on its own course, with little recognition of the good things which the non-APL computing world has been doing. Even today, you come across APL ‘experts’ who seem oblivious to the power and simplicity of spreadsheets such as Visicalc and Lotus 1—2—3. It is illuminating to look through the proceedings of the annual APL conferences, where you find surprisingly few papers which look outside the confines of the APL workspace.

Probably the greatest step forward in overcoming the insularity of APL has been the introduction over the past few years of versions of APL for microcomputers. Many of the micro implementations of APL have included good ‘hooks’ to the outside world to allow easy integration of, for example, word processing with APL applications. APL users are becoming more aware of the advantages of this kind of synergy, and this is certainly progress. Another very significant move is the current work being done on the ISO standard for APL; most industry commentators now feel that the main concern of users is moving away from the performance of their computer systems, towards issues of portability, standardisation, and links between different software suites. The forthcoming ISO standard for APL seems to me to be strong evidence for the argument that the APL community is taking these trends seriously.

It is surprising, therefore, that there has been so little interest in the APL world in the GKS or “Graphical Kernel System” standard. This is even stranger when you consider that APL has for a long time been quite closely associated with graphical applications (admittedly usually of the business graph variety, rather then animated or CAD/CAM graphics). I feel that it is time that the APL community considered its response to GKS.

items.title: What is GKS?
items.text:
For many years, computer graphics has evolved in a very hardware-dependent way. Major manufacturers such as Tektronix and Calcomp have produced graphical devices with their own interface protocols and conventions, and of course with different capabilities. As usual, IBM has gone its own way, and has remained incompatible with any other supplier, whereas smaller manufacturers have often tended to emulate the protocols of the main vendors, by for example, selling equipment which is ‘Tektronix 4010 compatible’. On the software side, the routines to access graphics devices have also been highly diverse in the way they have handled graphic instructions. The net result of all this has of course been that applications software which makes use of graphics has tended to be much more machine-specific than software which uses only text input/output.

In keeping with the overall trend in the computing industry towards a greater emphasis on international standards, various influential groups and individuals have been working since 1975 on a graphics standard which would remove this ‘Tower of Babel’ style of graphics development, and substitute a clear, well defined and above all flexible standard protocol for interfacing computer software to graphics devices. The initial work was done by the German standards institute (DIN), and later taken up by experts from 16 countries, including a strong UK team. The final result of all this is an ISO standard, which is now complete, and which has international support from most major suppliers of graphics devices. In addition to its International status, GKS is expected to be adopted as a national U.S. standard by ANSI, although another rival graphics standard (‘Core’) has its supporters in the States.

items.title: What does GKS look like?
items.text:
Because of the need for the GKS standard to be comprehensive, as well as free of dependencies on particular hardware or programming languages, it is expressed as a rather abstract model, expressed in a number of levels. Some VECTOR readers may be familiar with one vendor’s low-level graphics system, namely IBM’s GDDM, and so I will illustrate the features of GKS by reference to GDDM.

GKS defines a number of a logical graphics functions such as ‘POLYLINE’ (draw a series of lines) and ‘FILL AREA’ (fill arbitrary polygons with specified colours and patterns). These are low-level commands, and correspond roughly with GDDM’s low-level concepts. The most basic GKS commands (which nonetheless are sufficient to implement very good graphics systems) are defined as Level 0a, and are intended to be suitable for business graphics, as well as providing the low-level support for higher level commands. Level 0a defines only graphics output, without any digitising or interactive graphics capability. An implementation of GKS might, therefore, restrict itself to being an implementation at Level 0a, and ignore the more sophisticated features.

Levels 0b and 0c are the same, except that they add input facilities for interactive graphics applications.

Moving up to Level 1 of GKS, further features are added, including support of multiple workstations, display of several pictures simultaneously, manipulation of parts of pictures, etc. Level 1 (again subdivided into 1a, 1b and 1c) would generally be used for simple Computer Aided Design or interactive simulation software.

Finally, Level 2 adds features such as copying whole graphs, or ‘segments’ of graphs, between workstations, use of pre-defined picture segments, etc. This level is aimed at sophisticated CAD and graphical editor applications.

Provision is made at each stage for the application to query whether or not a particular feature is supported by the software and/or the hardware in use.

items.title: Language Binding
items.text:
The GKS concepts described above are defined in an abstract fashion. For example, POLYLINE is defined as a GKS function for drawing a series of straight lines, and it takes a set of parameters consisting of the number of points (needed for crude languages which have not heard of the APL ‘shape’ primitive), and the XY coordinates of the points through which the series of straight lines should be drawn. The line is drawn using a preselected linetype, width and colour.

The jargon ‘language binding’ is used to describe a standard way of interfacing a given computer language to the abstract GKS functions. Associated with the ISO standard is a ‘language binding’ for Fortran. This specifies, for example, that the GKS function POLYLINE should be accessed by a Fortran subroutine called GPL, using the syntax:

CALL GPL (N,PX,PY)

where N is the number of points, and PX and PY are two arrays of the coordinates, expressed as real numbers.

As well as the Fortran binding, there is also a semi-standard Pascal binding, although this has not been incorporated in the GKS ISO document.

To understand this more closely, consider GDDM again. GDDM defines a set of graphics functions which can be accessed from a number of languages. In APL, the interface (‘binding’ in GKS jargon) is AP126, whereas other languages have their own IBM-defined methods of accessing GDDM.

items.title: An APL binding for GKS
items.text:
This is where we come to the crunch. Is it possible, or indeed even desirable, to propose a standard interface between APL and GKS?

My own view is that it is highly desirable that there should be a standard APL interface to GKS. The main reasons for this are:

(a) It will increasingly be the case that mainframes, minicomputers and even microcomputers will be supplied with GKS implementations. It is highly desirable that APL should be able to access these, and it would be a great pity if each vendor came up with its own syntax (again!) for doing what other languages wil be able to do in a standard way. (b) It will also be increasingly the case that manufacturers of graphics devices will design the interfaces to their hardware with GKS in mind. If APL is to get the best out of such hardware, access via GKS routines will be both simple and efficient. (c) It will add greatly to the international credibility of APL, and further the progress which the APL ISO standard has made, if the APL community is seen to be taking international standards like GKS seriously.

As to the question of whether it is possible to define an APL binding for GKS, my answer is yes.

items.title: How would an APL binding for GKS look?
items.text: It seems to me that there are three possible ways of defining a standard interface between APL and GKS.

items.title: Method 1
items.text:
The interface to GKS could be defined by a Shared Variable Processor. This would look roughly like IBM’s AP126 processor which links APL with GDDM. Most probably, there would be a Control variable (CTL) and a Data variable (DAT) which between them would govern the interface to GKS. CTL would be used to indicate the GKS function required, and DAT would be used to pass parameters (such as coordinates) to GKS and receive back data from enquiries to GKS. GKS functions would be indicated by (probably) numeric codes. For example, to draw a polyline, we might enter:

DAT <— LINEDATA
CTL <— 11

In this example, LINEDATA would be a 2 by N numeric matrix of the points through which the polyline would pass, and 11 would be the code which the binding standard had assigned to the GKS function POLYLINE. (This is the number defined by the so-called Metafile format for GKS, so there would be a correlation between the APL codes and the GKS main standard).

If it were felt advantageous to avoid numeric codes, we could use an alternative form:

DAT <— LINEDATA
CTL <— 'POLYLINE'

i.e. We could use text names or mnemonics to indicate the GKS call required (although this could reduce efficiency of execution).

The advantages of Method 1 are as follows:
