items.title: The Global Information Centre
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 45

by Fred Perkins

This talk also began with a rather cynical view of information centres and leading up to it was a short history of their beginnings. In the mid-to-late 70’s, at a time when users and DP departments were growing apart, backlogs were getting bigger and users were getting angrier. IBM came up with the concept of the Information Centre and marketed it extremely well. They gathered together a collection of applications software, which, in the hands of the users would put the emphasis back on them, with support being provided by DP. The outcome? — “Never have so many waited so expensively for so little” — according to Fred Perkins. He cited some of the problems associated with IC’s:-

a) user isolation

b) lack of tools to help make systems portable

c) Growth/migration problems

d) tools not part of the IC concept

e) incompatibilities between mainframe and PC’s

f) packages in different languages

g) inability to access data outside the company and across different systems.

The rest of the talk was devoted to the IP Sharp Global Information Centre. It claims to overcome all of these problems mainly due to the following:-

a) Single development language — Sharp APL, identical on the PC to that on the mainframe.

b) Worldwide communications network, with access to the world’s largest on-line library of numeric data bases.

c) Sophisticated applications software products.

d) Full support for a wide variety of hardware devices.

items.title: Information Centre as Strategy
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 90

by Fred J. Perkins

The challenge facing the DP Department today is that of meeting demands for flexible and efficient access to, and control of, the information resources at the heart of any successful company’s operation. The Information Centre potentially does meet the challenge. There are however many pitfalls, and as the issues are very much at the centre of an organisation’s total strategy for computing, communications, and office automation, it is important to understand the history of the development of Information Centre concepts. There are perhaps more accounts of failure than of success, but this should not deter an organisation from seeking to follow what is fundamentally a very sound strategy.

The Information Centre concept came about in the early 1970’s. Traditionally, DP departments had been predominantly batch or transaction processing in their orientation. Unhappily, interactive users were generally unwelcome on such systems, as their demands were spasmodic, unpredictable, and all too often liable to cause system crashes. Controllable, regular jobs run as card decks were much more acceptable to the DP manager with his scant resources.

The gulf that arose between the DP department and the end users is one familiar to most large organisations. It benefited only the external service companies, who were able to charge premium prices for access to systems which end users felt were much more responsive to their real needs.

However, as computer hardware costs came down, and minicomputers (and later, microcomputers) came almost within the budget capabilities of user depatments, serious problems of anarchy arose, as users set about solving their problems entirely outside the influence of the DP department. At the same time, the growth of such systems, isolated by their incompatibilities, began to cause real difficulties in the efficient control and integration of the information resources of the organisation.

items.title: The concept of the Information Centre
items.text:
The Information Centre was a concept, originally developed by IBM, which attempted to bring order to the impending chaos. Its fundamental aim was to shift the DP focus back on to the end user, but under the control and direction of the Data Processing department. This aim would be achieved by providing tools and basic support from the DP group, together with sufficient education to allow the user to solve his own problems, largely in a “Do It Yourself” mode.

The Information Centre was a management philosophy, implemented in software. It offered a small number of “strategic” software packages and building blocks aimed at end users, typically in the M.I.S. department. Basic database mechanisms were provided to allow the user access to corporate data.

Hence, the increasing levels of end user expertise in the use of computer systems was channelled into a relatively small number of basic application systems, and the DP department role moved from one of total responsibility for the development of systems to one of encouraging user self sufficiency within a controllable environment. Backlogs in system implementation timescales would largely disappear, and in any event they were now on the shoulders of the user himself.

The concept was excellent. It was welcomed from all sides of the debate, and quite a few organisations established Information Centres which even today still serve their companies well. A truce was established between the users and the DP department.

items.title: Defects in the original concept
items.text:
Computing however is probably one of the most rapidly changing environments of the last decade, and the flaws in the Information Centres soon became apparent.

It has been said of the Information Centre that “never in the field of human endeavour have so many waited so expensively, for so little.” This may indeed be true. It would be naive to believe that a major new concept propounded by a hardware manufacturer was done out of purely philanthropic motives. The underlying motive was undoubtedly to promote the sale of large computer systems, and associated software packages that would perhaps encourage rapid consumption of hardware resources.

Perhaps the single most obvious flaw in the original offerings was the lack of integration between the elements that made up the Information Centre. Indeed, the most cohesive product on offer was probably the marketing brochure itself!

Users were quick to discover the “missing links” of I.C. implementation. These fell into 3 main areas:

  • End user terminal hardware
  • Communications
  • Implementation software

items.title: Hardware:
items.text: Professional DP users were quite happy to utilise bulky complex terminals, generally from a single supplier, and heavily oriented towards use by computer programmers. End users however, were demanding flexibility and portability of user terminals, and wanted the ability to take advantage of all manner of user-friendly and application-specific devices, like flatbed plotters, viewdata terminals, and communicating word processors and micros. The Information Centre did little to promote the attachment of anything other than a small range of “standard” devices.

items.title: Communications:
items.text: The early Information Centre tended to assume that all users would be in relatively close proximity to the central mainframe. But organisations were becoming more international in their outlook. Information pertinent to the running of today’s companies is typically highly geographically distributed. Communications facilities available to the Information Centre implementors were woefully inadequate. The network was more often a barrier to communication than an interface between remote sites.

items.title: Implementation software:
items.text:
Although “integration” was a watchword, the basic offerings of the Information Centre gave little hope of achieving this. The applications packages, being a collection from different historic origins, were implemented in the whole range of computer languages, and to entirely different standards of design and user interface. So, while the user might be content if his requirements were met entirely by one package, attempts to interface between them, or extend and customise them, were liable to meet with frustration. The implementation backlogs, which had begun to decrease with the arrival of the Information Centre, increased again along with the growth of demands for the ability to properly exploit, or extend the range of, the basic facilities.

The “missing links” manifested themselves in several problem areas:

User Isolation: I.C. users were victims of the ultimate in “Personal Computing”, but unable to communicate with each other, or with each other’s data.

Lack of Portability: Software applications, often with significant development effort, were rarely made available to other parts of the organisation, and “reinventing the wheel” became the rule rather than the exception.

Growth and Migration Problems: Ideas and solutions were typically incapable of growing beyond quite tight constraints, dictated by the implementation mechanisms.

Integration Difficulties: With few standards or guidelines, the “Do It Yourself” approach made any attempts at integration extremely difficult.

Insufficient Tools/Data: The Personal Computing philosophy, by encouraging users to think small, denied them access to the main strategic systems which often contained the most valuable data.

Add to these problems the arrival of the cheap, but very powerful, micro, with highly “user friendly” software packages, and it can be seen that the DP department is once again under attack. These micros can be bought at prices often well within an individual’s unqualified signing approval, and yet they often provide power and sophistication above that achievable on the company’s largest computers.

items.title: Towards a better strategy
items.text:
We are very nearly at a stage where it will be possible, if we want, to place on every executive’s desk a user workstation which can provide virtually infinite computing power, together with essentially unlimited memory capacity. But what do we want to do with it? All too often, this fundamental question is left unanswered.

For the end user, the cost of the hardware technology will no longer be any obstacle to the accessibility of computer systems. As computerisation spreads within organisations, there will be increasing demands for provision of new data and information to help the user in making decisions. End user systems will spread and overlap with each other.

The micro itself is NOT the answer to these new problems and opportunities. In a short time, the anarchy which has typified the growth of standalone microcomputer systems will be replaced by a need to re-integrate scattered, and often incompatible, systems. Equally, users will come to realise that their Lotus 1-2-3 or Multiplan systems are not an end in themselves, but should be only front ends to larger corporate databases and systems, since their inputs and outputs belong in, and relate to, other parts of the organisation. The end user does not function in isolation.

items.title: The Global Information Centre
items.text:
The Global Information Centre (GIC) takes the basic framework of the Information Centre, addresses its problems, and adds the missing links in the earlier concept. There are several fundamental components which are critical in achieving true acceptability by both end users and DP managers — though each may regard the relative priorities as different.

The GIC assumes that in the typical situation, users may well be scattered around the world; that they will want to use a variety of terminal technology to access corporate systems, including intelligent terminals and micros; that there will be a requirement at a later stage to integrate applications systems, software, and data, even though the eventual needs may not be apparent at the outset; and that the DP department will want to offer a growth and development strategy with new products attractive to end users, while at the same time maintaining central coordinated control over corporate DP development.

The GIC strategy therefore does not prohibit end user acquisition of micros, though it insists that they must be capable of interfacing, at hardware and software levels, into the other elements of the GIC. Far from being seen as a restriction, many users will gain a feeling of comfort from the knowledge that their chosen micro system forms part of the long term strategy in their organisation.

Account should also be taken of Word Processing, automated PABX’s, Local Area Networks, and the full range of office automation technology. They all can, and should, be integrated into the GIC strategy. This does not imply a commitment to a single-vendor policy, but simply a requirement that all selected vendors comply with INTERFACING standards. Careful attention should be paid to a vendor’s commitment to Open System Interconnection (OSI).

The principal missing links which then, should be added to the original definition of the Information Centre are:

  • Worldwide Communications
  • Corporate AND external public data
  • Technology Independence
  • INTEGRATION
  • CO-ORDINATION

The best examples of Global Information Centre implementation are today probably in the service companies, whose historical development has been along Information Centre lines even before the phrase was coined.

items.title: Case Study: I P Sharp Associates
items.text:
I P Sharp has in effect been running a Global Information Centre for some 15 years. It has developed almost entirely driven by client demands, serving users in a variety of organisations and industries who looked outside their own organisations for solutions to their problems.

The key elements of the Sharp GIC are as follows:

WORLDWIDE COMMUNICATIONS NETWORK: A private packet-switched network, developed internally in the absence of suitable available technology. A principal design goal was that it should be invisible to the end user, yet flexible in terms of the technology supported. Also interfaced to public networks, it provides local call access from some 600 cities worldwide.

SINGLE IMPLEMENTATION LANGUAGE: Utilising only SHARP APL, a proprietary enhancement to APL, all applications are implemented in the same language. Hence maintenance, integration, and interfacing of packages becomes relatively straightforward. The APL language (James Martin has said it is the only serious contender for the title of Fifth Generation Language) provides an extremely powerful user-friendly environment, with great attractions for systems programmers and end users alike. Applications, simple or complex, can be written quickly and elegantly — and can be easily modified when required.

INTEGRATED APPLICATIONS PACKAGES: Although a vast suite of packages and building blocks is available, a kernel of applications are seen as essential for the GIC:

  • Financial Consolidation
  • Financial Modelling
  • Generalised Record Management
  • Time Series Database Maintenance and Analysis
  • Business Graphics
  • Electronic Mail

— and these applications all readily interface to each other.

DATABASES: While the basis of the corporate Information Centre is very much an organisation’s own private data, an increasingly common demand is arising for external data. The I P Sharp GIC offers some 50 million time series in areas like Finance, Economics, Energy, Aviation, Demography, and others. These databases can all be accessed using the same tools as are used for private data, and data from several sources, private and public, can be combined.

IBM PC INTEGRATION: An identical implementation of the Sharp APL environment on the IBM PC, together with software to interconnect mainframes to PC’s allows applications and data to migrate from one to the other, and also permits interfacing to other PC applications.

SUPPORT and EDUCATION: Undoubtedly, the key to any successful DP strategy lies in the level of support and education available to the end user. The GIC user is encouraged to utilise the services of some 60 local branch offices around the world, where he can be assured, by virtue of the GIC structure, that the staff are acquainted with the user’s applications (and can help him in his native language!).

The DP department too, requires support, but at a system level. This is provided 24 hours a day by staff specialising in, and using, precisely the same software environment as on the client machine.

items.title: A Strategy for the future
items.text:
Whether following the I P Sharp philosophy, or that of another vendor, the fundamental issues remain the same. End users are increasingly becoming unconcerned with the technical implementation issues, whilst their demands continue to increase. On the one hand, they will say they want more “simplicity” in systems they use, but at the same time they expect much more sophistication.

The need is therefore very clearly for an implementation infrastructure that meets the needs of both the DP department and of the end user, even though their goals often conflict.

The Information Centre concept recognised that the end user was becoming more important in the computing environment. There can be no doubt that this trend is continuing, and so it is evident that the major issue of the next decade will be that of software development, with the end user as the main driving force.

The Global Information Centre, and the principles which underly it, do, it is suggested, offer a viable strategy for the future.

items.title: IBM-based APL communications
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 62

by Tim Perry

The specific example Tim used was of an IBM factory with around 2000 employees, and 1300 terminals. A combination of APL and VM/CMS was expected to support a growth path like this:

                       1983      1984      1985
Mainframes       :       3         5         3
Versions of APL  :       3         4         1 (APL2)
Users            :     200       400       600
PCs              :       2        35        70
Cost/Unit        :     100        50        25
Units/hr         :     100       180       250

i.e. a four-fold reduction in the cost of a unit of computing, with a similar increase in the amount of useful computing achieved per logged-hour. The use of VM/CMS was seen as vital, in that it gave APL a consistent environment across the board from the PCs to the biggest mainframes, and thus facilitated communication between APL systems and also between APL users. If need be APL could use the power of CMS or CP to send messages worldwide, look up someone’s address in the global phone directory, or access a host of other useful software which Tim could only hint at (it being somewhat internal to IBM).

Tim dropped a number of interesting hints about the way you can put some go-faster stripes on your APL, for example by giving it a fixed chunk of memory to run in, which all users share. This has the beneficial side effect of making all 200 CMS commands available (not just the usual subset). He also emphasised the need to restrict the user base so that good response times were always guaranteed — programs like FRANGO need to be watched very carefully lest they slow everyone down.

Other simple things you can do include:

  • using the CMS stack to get at the output of CP commands (such as Query Time) for genuine information on resource usage.
  • making sure you use the best AP for the job in hand (generally AP110, but look for AP999 which is well hidden in the small print, and is 25 times faster than AP111).
  • using PGF or (even better if you can get it) Chart for your graphics. The new AP126 lets you call Chart (or the ICU to its friends) direct, and it also allows you to call back pictures off file and get a sensible result when the FSSHOW is terminated. This lets you build a very effective (and rather cheap) Prestel imitation complete with top-quality graphics.
  • going for big workspaces (1.5 to 15 Mbyte), but keeping the maximum object size below 64K.

All of which is helping to make APL increasingly useful as a communication tool for people. The use of online help and news means that any piece of useful software (be it good or awful) gets quickly spread around the system, while the availability of standard packages (ADRS/ADI) also helps users to swap data and ideas around.

In conclusion, if you are serious about the idea of management support via computers you need APL, VM/CMS (preferably plus classified bells and whistles), and someone to put quite a lot of effort into tweaking the system. Given these conditions, the resulting system can be very effective, and surprisingly efficient.

items.title: Assurance Quotation Services
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 88

by Harry Phillips

Three years ago, an assurance company wanted to design and launch a new product for employers leaving firms and taking their pension benefits with them in a “Section 32 Buy-Out”. In order to make the contract financially attractive and capable of matching a wide variety of existing pension schemes, it had to rely on complex actuarial logic. The resulting procedures and calculations could not be managed manually. Although a computerised quotation service was required before the launch in two months time, the marketing staff were free to modify the contract up to the last minute.

The cost and delay associated with a Head Office quotation service meant that a DIY facility in the hands of our local staff or even our clients would give us a competitive edge.

Initial decisions to be made:

  1. System to be constructed by computer or user department.
  2. Mainframe or Micro. system.
  3. Batch or Interactive Procedures.
  4. Software to be used.

If the system were to be built by the computer department it would have to be scheduled in with other work and a fixed specification provided. The time limit meant that work had to start immediately without an agreed specification. Thus it had to be a user department job. Batch processing procedures are, by their very nature, unsuited to a quotation service supporting salesmen in a competitive market. Interactive procedures giving immediate results were required if at all practical.

A system on line to the mainframe would restrict usage to those with the right equipment, only be available during normal office hours and offer variable response times. The computer department would want to know what volume of traffic to plan for and what response times would be required. With this information they would quote a price and ask for authority to buy the extra hardware. Since answers to these questions were not known and negotiating time was unavailable, a PC based system was examined. This would run on any IBM-PC compatible machine, any time anywhere and give known response times.

The choice of software was made by a process of elimination:

a) Since support for the volume and variety of existing software was a major drain on resources, any proposal which added to the problem would be questioned. APL was well established on the mainframe and its ever growing cost was prompting requests reconsider its use. Developing a quotes programme in APL for the IBM PC would be a step in the right direction and would not be resisted. This eliminated introducing ‘C’.

b) Since the quotes service had to run on up to 200 remote PC’s in our sales offices or the clients office, the cost of running the service per PC was important. Few new PC’s would be required as many were already in place and the volumes per machine would be small. APL-PLUS offered a run time version whereby we could obtain 200 copies at a reasonable price. Our marketing department were happy to foot the bill in advance so that the quotes service could be distributed without recipients having to buy software. We also had to agree to deliver in 2 months. This eliminated the IBM version of APL for PC’s and most integrated packages.

c) Speed of system development was critical and the complexity of actuarial logic was a major consideration. Experience had shown ‘BASIC’ to be too slow in development and ‘Dbase’ inadequate for complex calculations. The staff who were to develop the quotation service had substantial expertize in APL and had access to actuarial subroutines already written for mainframe systems. They were happy to use APL on the PC as long as we provided an XT with a maths co-processor as the development machine (that dates the project).

Having chosen to base the quotation service around the IBM PC using the run time version provided by APL-PLUS we had to solve the following:

1) The end product must fit on one floppy disk for distribution. This must include operating instructions and help screens, so that paper instruction could be restricted to a single sheet.

2) The service had to run on a variety of configurations, twin floppies and hard disk, colour and monochrome, most common printers, with and without a maths co-processor. Speed on the slowest configuration had to be reasonable.

3) Since the actuarial terms and conditions, including the calculation of all rates, were to be incorporated in the programme, security was essential. The ability to quickly change terms and conditions without recalling disks was also critical, particularly when interest rates are volatile. The actuaries had to be convinced that they still had complete control over the terms and conditions being quoted on behalf of the society.

These problems were all overcome and the new contract launched with its supporting quotation service operational from day one at Head Office. Distribution of floppy disks soon followed after the contract stopped being modified. The framework which we developed for this contract has been extended, and now offers a series of pensions contracts via a menu.

items.title: The *Take Care* System
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 63

additional notes from Peter Pichler

Take Care, an infrastructure application for patient-related information, written in APL, is the largest health-care system in operation in Sweden. In the summer of 2003 there are

  • 700,000 patient record files accessed from
  • 4,000 clients all over Stockholm at
  • 25 server calls per second from
  • 1,700 concurrent users on open socket connections;
  • 8,500 registered users have online access to the patient records stored in a central database all based on APL component files.

The server is a mirrored UNIX machine running 30 workspaces on 30 different ports, listening for incoming traffic, plus some extra workspaces for communication with other systems.

Let’s start from the beginning, ten years ago. By coincidence I met a nurse who introduced me to the world of hospitals. By that time, computers were common in primary care, but there were few in hospitals, for many reasons. The systems there were lab systems and cashiers’ financial records.

So we sat down and asked ourself "what would it take to make an administration journal system for the whole of Sweden (9 million people)?" We were allowed to visit the journal archive at a medium-sized hospital in mid-Sweden, and could study the paper files there. Some were small and some were huge.

As a result of that study, we found that APL component files were the perfect data storage. It felt almost as if component files were made for patient records. So one file per patient was a natural thing to select. In Sweden each person has a unique personal number that’s used all his life. A small formula translates that personal number into a file name and we had easy access to the files.

Having seen the lack of support systems for hospital care, this was a challenge and at the same time a real opportunity: to be able to build a system, starting with CLEAR WS.

All data was to be stored in the central database. The data recorded in the files would never be erased or changed. We studied the laws, and soon learned that no recorded information may be changed or updated. Any changes had to be traceable. So we simply stored any new version of the same document in what we call a new instance. That is a three-dimensional structure, where each version of the stored document carries information about who, where, when, etc.

items.title: Simplicity
items.text:
Not even capable of programming my video, I knew at that time the importance of simplicity. The user interface must be clear, easy to understand and intuitive. Doctors and nurses do not work with computers, so a fast access to patient information must be very intuitive. The need for training must be minimal.

Everything we did focused on finding the important parts of a specific problem, and then making that as simple as possible. The benefits of this approach showed later on: users liked the system. As a very important effect, we also got very fast response times, almost everything subsecond. And that is true even when there are 1,700 concurrent users on the system.

items.title: Terminology database
items.text:
Having a background in statistics, I also knew the need for "speaking the same language"; so one of the first things we did was to add a terminology database to the system. Definition of terminology used is available online.

We continued to design the server parts as well. The system was to become a central system, with access to all data from everywhere within the local network. In Stockholm there was already a large network in place. No medical information is stored on the clients.

After a year or so we were looking for the implementation guide for EDIFACT. And by coincidence, there was Svante Lewald at the other end of the telephone, wondering what we were doing. So we told him of this fantastic new system, how easy it would be to add new functionality and so on.

He was at the time responsible for the clinical chemistry laboratory at Huddinge Hospital.

"We are ready to receive electronic lab orders from journal systems, but so far no vendor can do that."

Our reaction was, "Great, let’s do that!"

So we started designing the form for ordering lab tests. There was a well-established paper based system in place, so we had to make Take Care better than that. No one was going to make doctors use Take Care instead of paper.

Our first test started at the lung clinic, and after a few weeks we found doctors ordering lab tests happily with Take Care. This inspired us to develop further.

So far we had no contracts whatsoever. All our work had been done just to prove that it was possible to develop. In 1996 we got our first contract with Huddinge Hospital.

The lab order to the clinical chemical lab was very successful: electronic orders went straight into the lab system, and blood tests could start earlier, because no more registration was needed: just read the barcodes of the already-registered order. Test results were recorded in Take Care and stored in the journal files. The doctors had easy access to the complete history of test results for a patient.

The next laboratory to join Take Care was clinical bacteriology. The order form was programmed to have some intelligent guidelines making the quality of the orders better.

items.title: Version handling
items.text:
We continued to add functionality, documenting journal texts, all based on the terminology database we had included at an early stage. The work defining terms really took off.

We also knew that we would have a lot of users running the system in the future, so the system updates had to be stable and automatic. Code tables and workspaces and namespaces are distributed automatically from the server to the Windows PCs as required. This means any new release is mostly a matter of replacing a handful files on the server. (So far we have had 408 releases since December 1996. Every one of the today’s approx 4,000 clients runs the same version of the system.)

items.title: Error control
items.text:
We also built in automatic error control. If and when an error occurs on the client PC, we can catch it with ⎕TRAP and send that on to the server. So we see every domain error, etc., that occurs in the system.

Shipping new releases frequently makes things easy for us this way too. Should we introduce errors with the new code, it will take a fraction of a second before we can see it in the error log. (And there will be a lot of them too.) This has happened a few times, and we could act long before users reported the error. If no new errors pop up in the first hour or so, we can happily go on holiday.

items.title: Y2000
items.text:
Then the year 2000 was approaching. Some of the older systems used for cashiers and finance were not going to work after 2000. In November 1998 we were asked if we could develop a new cashier, and economic and diagnosis reports. There was very little time, and we had no idea what we were going into, but we said Yes and had a seven months extreme period, calling in two more APLers to help us.

We had an intensive period with users around us all the time so we could construct what was needed as we went. In March 1999 we delivered the first parts, and the whole hospital managed to train their personnel and everything worked well as 2000 arrived.

items.title: Onsite customers
items.text:
After that we continued to add functions in close cooperation with the users: meeting them once a week, discussing solutions and implementing them once we understood what we were supposed to do.

Nobody knows, the customer at least of all. Mostly they have only an idea – a good start. The first screens are taken back to the users, and we continue from there, testing, and detecting missing and unnecessary things.

While we work, we always focus on simplicity, removing every button or field we possibly can. Then comes a point when we look at the newly developed functionality and wonder "why did we not find this solution from the start – is this all?" And when that happens, we know we have made it.

Here are some parts of the system:

  • Activity Organiser
  • Prescriptions
  • Intelligent Remittals
  • 10 Laboratories
  • Patient Registration (e.g. for operations)
  • Consultation Remittals (to and from the hospital)
  • Resource Planning
  • Scanning
  • Images import
  • Emergency Department, where they all use digital dictation: a Philips Speech mike integrated with Take Care

items.title: The Future
items.text:
Today more functionality is being added, and new customers are invited. Having joined Profdoc, Scandinavia’s largest vendor in the health-care arena, we find our future looks very exciting. Now we have access to well-defined data that just await analysis. An hypothesis test function is waiting to become reality and, who knows, we might be able to help the clever people out there make new medical discoveries.

The development continues…

items.title: GDDM and AP126
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 109

by David Piper

items.title: 1. Abstract.
items.text:
Full screen management is in many ways the natural way for APL to communicate with the user. The screen looks like a window onto an APL array, why not use it as such? In the IBM world, full screen management is limited to the use of auxiliary processors (APs), usually the Graphical Data Display Manager (GDDM) AP – AP126.

In order to implement efficient, easily used systems, screen dialogue must be managed as efficiently as possible in order to provide adequate response times. This article shows that functions provided by GDDM can be easily used to improve the efficiency of screen dialogues. A future article will discuss the use of functions provided by GDDM R4.0 and by AP126 itself.

items.title: 2. Introduction – Facilities Discussed.
items.text:
The facilities discussed fall into two basic categories:

  • Those integral to GDDM.
  • Additional facilities provided by AP126.

The facilities provided by GDDM are available to any program using GDDM (even those not written in APL), the power of APL makes these especially easy to use. The extra functions provided by AP126 are unique to the APL environment. This article discusses those functions provided by GDDM; it is hoped another article will describe the use of the facilities provided by AP126, and additional features of GDDM (R 3.0 and 4.0) which are of use in the development of complex dialogues.

items.title: 2.1 Facilities provided by GDDM.
items.text:
The following facilities provided by GDDM are not commonly used, and will be the subject of this discussion:

  • Use of logical pages (all GDDM releases)
  • Logical pages larger than the terminal (GDDM R3.0 and higher)

The discussion applies specifically to VS APL R4.0, running under MVS/SP and TSO/E, but should apply to other operating systems too, since no file handling is involved.

items.title: 2.2 Facilities provided by AP126
items.text:
The additional facilities available using AP126 are referred to in the VS APL Terminal Users Guide as ‘AP126 Service Requests’. There are 10 of these, given call values from -1 to -10, the majority of these are not of particular use in application development. The most useful services are mentioned here for the sake of completeness, but are not discussed in detail in this article.

Service -8 (Query subset of fields for modification), allows an application to read data from the screen as required by the application, rather than all at once. More importantly, it also allows only modified fields to be read rather than all fields on the screen.

Service -9 (Query current hardcopy destination), allows an application to check for a currently open printer. A printer may therefore be left ‘open’ between print requests, avoiding the large overhead of being ‘opened’ and ‘closed’ repeatedly.

Service -10 provides a useful method for implementing graphics in a system. This service request allows the Interactive Chart Utility (ICU) to be invoked from APL, using APL vectors or arrays of numbers as the data to be charted.

items.title: 3. Logical Pages.
items.text:
The usual way of organising a full screen dialogue can be summarised as follows:

DIALOGUE:

  • DISPLAY a panel
  • READ the panel
  • VALIDATE the data
  • PROCESS the data
  • REPEAT

This concept seems perfectly adequate for managing a screen dialogue, until the overheads involved in the DISPLAY process are considered. For the sake of clarity, the DISPLAY process can be broken down further:

DISPLAY:

  • VALIDATE the format array
  • FORMAT the screen buffer
  • WRITE fixed text (prompts etc)
  • WRITE dynamic text (date, time etc)
  • WRITE default input values
  • TRANSMIT panel to screen

If the panel format could be stored in some way, so that it only has to be re-sent to the terminal, the first three processes could be omitted from the DISPLAY process (after the first DISPLAY). The use of logical pages allows precisely this. Each screen format, with its fixed text, can be placed on a separate page, and restored to the terminal as required. The new DISPLAY process could be summarised as follows:

DISPLAY:

  • GET page
  • WRITE dynamic text
  • WRITE default input values
  • TRANSMIT panel to screen

The GET process either creates and formats a new page, or re-selects an existing page as required.

GET:

  • IF page EXISTS
    • SELECT page
  • ELSE
    • CREATE page
    • VALIDATE the format array
    • FORMAT the screen buffer
    • WRITE fixed text (prompts etc)

items.title: 3.1 Managing Logical Pages.
items.text:
The use of logical pages does introduce the problem of management of the pages. This problem can be broken into two parts:

  • Selection of pages for display of new panels.
  • Re-selection of existing pages to re-display panels.

The first problem is one of selecting a page not previously used, the second is one of selecting the correct page from a list of existing pages. The examples that follow assume that a share with AP126 has already been established, using the variables:

  • CTLs – the AP126 control variable.
  • DATs – the data variable associated with CTL126.

items.title: 3.2 Creating New Logical Pages.
items.text:
GDDM has a function which returns a page number not currently in use – FSQUPG (FS – Full Screen, Q – Query, UPG – Unique PaGe. AP126 Code 307). This function returns the highest possible unused page number. The first call returns page number (-1)+2*31, the highest 4 byte integer.

Note: In early versions of release 3.0 of GDDM, the FSQUPG function returns LOW page numbers first, there is a PTF to correct this error.

A major benefit of using the FSQUPG function, is that no matter many pairs of variables are shared with AP126, unique page numbers are always returned. Thus several applications (systems, utilities etc), all using different sets of shared variables, can run in the same workspace without risk of using pages already acquired by other facilities. This principle extends to using GDDM with the APL Session Manager, which uses page number 1001.

Once the unique page number has been found, the page must be created. This is performed using the FSPCRT function (P – Page, CRT – CReaTe. AP126 code 302). The arguments to the FSPCRT function are the page number, the depth and width of the page, and the page type. This last parameter is ignored by GDDM release 4.0, but is required for compatibility with earlier releases of GDDM. A function to query for and create a page with a new page number (CNPAGE) is listed in appendix A.

The act of creating a page causes the new page to become current, so the panel format/write activities can proceed normally. Once complete, the panel can be displayed and read in the normal manner, all screen I/O functions addressing the current GDDM page.

items.title: 3.3 Re-displaying Existing Pages.
items.text:
Once a page/panel couple has been formatted and displayed, the only activity that has to occur before re-display of the page is changing the current page number to the one containing the required panel. To do this effectively, a method of relating panel identities (names, numbers or some other ID) to GDDM page numbers must be used.

The IBM supplied workspace FSC126 allows panels to be designed, each panel having a name recognised by all the utility functions in the workspace. The names can easily be used to build a table relating panel names to page numbers. When a panel is displayed for the first time (ie its page is created), the panel name is appended to the bottom of the table, and the page number is appended to the vector of page numbers. The index of the name in the table can then be used to reference the page number vector. Once the page number has been looked up, the page can be reselected by using the FSPSEL function (P – Page, SEL – SELect. AP126 code 305). The FSPSEL function takes the page number to be selected as its only argument.

A function to perform these actions is shown in appendix A (CSPAGE), the function either selects an existing page, or creates a new page if required. This function could be combined with IBM’s DISPLAY function (from FSC126) if the new page was to be formatted. An example of this is shown in the HOWTO function in appendix A. Note, the code in the REDISP function is specific to the use of the utilities provided by the FSC126 workspace. This function would have to be changed if different screen management utilities were to be used.

It must be ensured that the panel name table and the page vector are nullified whenever GDDM is re-initialised. The easiest way to ensure this is to reshape the table and vector into nulls in the function run as the latent expression in the workspace.

items.title: 3.4 Integrating with Existing Systems.
items.text:
The above discussion shows that it is relatively easy to implement paging techniques within an existing screen management system such as that provided in the FSC126 workspace. The only change required is to ensure the correct page is selected before any screen I/O processing occurs.

In most cases, it will be possible to combine functions using logical paging with functions that do not in the same workspace. This is because, by default, page 0 is used. Functions using paging MUST ensure that the default page (page 0) is re-selected after their processing is complete.

items.title: 4. Large GDDM Logical Pages
items.text:
From release 3.0 onwards, GDDM allows the use of pages which are longer than the physical terminal. Pages wider than the physical terminal are not supported. Using long pages allows vertical scrolling to be performed very easily. GDDM only requires the line to be placed at the top of the terminal to be passed as an argument to the FSPWIN function (P – Page WIN – WINdow. AP126 code 309). If the bottom or top of the logical page would appear in the middle of the physical page, GDDM adjusts the position so that the logical top/bottom coincides with the physical top/bottom.

The use of long pages reduces the need to re-write text to the page every time a scroll operation is performed. The AP need only be invoked to perform the scrolling activity, not to perform I/O to the logical page. If some of the text has to be refreshed on the page then the correct GDDM functions must be invoked to perform this.

items.title: 4.1 Using Large Logical Pages
items.text:
Large pages will be of most use for browsing APL objects, rather than for activities requiring text to be refreshed as lines are inserted, deleted or changed by the user. Data being browsed does not need to be refreshed. Even so, if a very simple editor is being used, which does not allow lines to be deleted or inserted from the text, the use of a large page will make the editor more efficient by removing the need to refresh text on the page.

Using screen sized pages, a BROWSE function can be summarised as follows:

BROWSE:

  • GET browse panel
  • WRITE a panel full of text
  • READ the panel
  • SCROLL text

The SCROLL function is changed by the use of long pages:

SCROLL: (normal page size)

  • CALCULATE new top line
  • WRITE new panel of text

SCROLL: (long pages)

  • CALCULATE new top line
  • POSITION window

When using long pages, all the text is written to the panel during the initialisation stage, not just one panel full. This increase in panel I/O is offset by reductions during scrolling activity.

items.title: 4.2 Horizontal Scrolling
items.text:
Logical pages wider than the physical screen size are not supported by GDDM. The limitations imposed by this restriction can be obviated by allowing horizontal scrolling to occur only in units of one screen width. The BROWSE function must create sufficient pages to contain the width of the text being browsed. Scrolling horizontally then simply becomes a matter of selecting the the correct logical page. This is a more efficient process than continually performing I/O operations to the same logical page.

The ‘page mode’ scrolling can also be used for vertical scrolling in releases of GDDM not supporting large logical pages. An ideal application for this type of browse function is to preview a paginated report. Whether all pages should be formatted in advance is application dependent and will typically depend on the volume of text being browsed.

For a ‘page mode’ browse function allowing both vertical and horizontal scrolling, the SCROLL function becomes:

BROWSE:

  • CALCULATE new top line
  • CALCULATE new horizontal page
  • GET page
  • POSITION window

The GET function is described in section 3.

items.title: 5. Conclusions.
items.text:
The use of logical pages can make a considerable difference to the speed of dialogues in systems using GDDM for screen management. In addition, the use of logical pages is quite straightforward to implement within a set of existing dialogue management utilities.

By removing the need to re-format a panel every time it is to be displayed, response times can be improved by as much as 50%. Logical pages can also be of use elsewhere in full-screen dialogues, for example when implementing ‘browse’ or ‘edit’ utilities, enabling scrolling to be carried out extremely rapidly.

items.title: Using VSAPL under TSO
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 127

By David Piper

In VECTOR 2.2 Adrian Smith raised some points about the difficulty of running VS APL under TSO rather than under VSPC. Whilst I agree that TSO leaves rather a lot to be desired in terms of user friendliness when running from the “READY” prompt, a lot can be done to improve things. TSO is a very flexible environment, in which just about anything can be achieved. The disappointing thing with TSO, is that the user-friendliness is left to the installation to create, and doesn’t exist in the product itself. The following describes some directions which might be investigated in order to implement a better TSO environment.

items.title: ISPF for Dialogue Management
items.text: One of the great benefits of using TSO is the availability of ISPF, with its flexible, and simple to use Dialogue Management Services. These facilities can be used to create very friendly dialogues running under TSO to conduct the user from the Broadcast Messages (where the READY prompt is normally first seen) into any other part of TSO. The dialogues can use a combination of full screen menus, data entry panels and tutorial panels. ISPF also allows an “expert mode” to allow very rapid navigation through menus for experienced users. ISPF can thus provide an environment suitable for use by both naive and experienced users.

items.title: VS APL Session Manager
items.text:
A piece of advice that can be freely offered is: Don’t use the APL Session Manager. When this first became available, I was involved in performing some bench-marks on it. The initial figures derived were so appalling, that the bench-mark exercise was dropped, and the availability of SM withdrawn. The initial figures indicated that SM had the following impact:

  • A five-fold increase in CPU usage on screen bound activities
  • A doubling of CPU usage on CPU bound activities (no screen I/O involved except to invoke and terminate!)

Along with this impact on CPU, there was a considerable increase in Paging activity etc.

Since stopping the use of the SM, I have often wondered just how useful it is under TSO anyway, since any number of lines on the screen can be re-entered for execution simply by overtyping a single character. The lines entered in this way will be executed in the order they appear on the screen (this incidentally is a feature I miss under CMS, where it appears only INPUT lines can be retrieved for re-execution, and then only one at a time). The only benefit SM appears to offer is to “extend” the screen, so that data, already scrolled off the terminal can be recalled for execution. I think the overheads involved are hard to justify on this small benefit. If the APL SM is to be used, the colour of the output can be changed by using the HILIGHT operand of the VSAPL command. Since, by default, colour is linked to hilighting, specifying HILIGHT(OFF) when invoking APL will cause input from the user and output from the computer to be displayed in green.

items.title: Logging On
items.text:
Assuming a logon through VTAM, this can be rather daunting! However, if the implementation has a reasonable service level applied to TSO, one bash on the attention key (or PA1 if locally attached) is sufficient to return to the LOGON prompt. The logon process can then start again by typing:

LOGON userid

The full screen logon provided with TSO/E is another matter however, and seems to be full of Bugs (eg prompting for the correct password to be entered, but protecting the password field at the same time!). Most users seem to find the variety of options on the Full Screen logon overwhelming, so turn it off. The typical user should be able to logon in at most 3 steps:

  • VTAM logon to TSO – LOGON APPLID(xxxx)
  • TSO will then prompt for USERID
  • Once the USERID is validated, a PASSWORD will be prompted for.

If RACF is installed, a fourth stage will occur when the password expires – prompting for a new password. Other information may be prompted for if insufficient data has been added to SYS1.UADS. It should be possible to cater for users’ needs simply by defining a logon procedure with a default region size, so no other information need be entered during LOGON. This process can be shortened further if a VTAM menu package is available e.g. NETMON or NET/MASTER. If correctly installed, these will allow the logon to be achieved in a single step; in fact NET/MASTER allows automatic logon to TSO to occur.

items.title: Screen Erasure Problems.
items.text:
Messages such as:

SCREEN ERASURE CAUSED BY ERROR-RECOVERY PROCEDURE

will originate from incorrectly customised control units in 99% of cases, and can be solved quite happily with some effort at correcting this type of error. This sort of message normally results from GDDM, or other screen manager, thinking the terminal can do something when in fact it can’t.

items.title: Sharing Workspaces
items.text:
There is absolutely no need for the use of PROJECT libraries under TSO. If it is necessary to share a workspace (eg to fix a bug), this can be achieved quite happily by simply copying it (using the NONUM operand of the copy command). Alternatively, other users’ workspaces can be accessed by changing the PROFILE PREFIX, and using )LOAD as though the WS were your own. If a security package such as RACF or ACF2 is installed, access must be granted before the )COPY or )LOAD is attempted.

The RACF GROUP concept can also be used to share a whole set of workspaces between a large number of userids without recourse to the project library facility. The RACF Group allows a common PROFILE PREFIX to be shared amongst many user ids. Any workspace with this profile prefix will appear in the )LIB listing of all users with the same prefix. Generic access rules can be used to provide the same facility under ACF2. Whether a user is able to )LOAD or )SAVE a workspace depends on the access level given under RACF. This concept is more flexible than that of the project library, since a given user will be able to )SAVE some workspaces, only )LOAD others, and may have no access at all to the remainder.

items.title: Clearing the Screen
items.text: One of the TSO manuals (I think its “OS/VS2 TSO Guide to Writing a Terminal Monitor Program or a Command Processor”, GC28-0648) gives a listing of a very short assembler program which will clear the screen. By placing this in one of the TSO load libraries, it can be invoked as a TSO command by using )TSO or AP100.

items.title: VSAM Record Locking
items.text: I am reliably informed that VSAM record locking works perfectly under TSO, for multiple region use. If multiple CPU access is envisioned, the Global Resource Serialisation feature is required.

items.title: Printing
items.text:
Printing to local 328X type printers under TSO is something of a problem. This type of printing is supported by two installed user programs (IUP) – programs not actively supported by IBM:

  • DSPRINT – in use on many sites.
  • JES328X – less widely used but more reliable.

Neither of these products will support the use of APL characters without a considerable re-write. In addition, because these are IUPs, the command syntax may differ from site to site, although a common core syntax is normally implemented. GDDM also provides a print facility – ADMPRINT. This has been considerably enhanced in GDDM R4.0, to allow the use of printer control characters, thus with the use of two GDDM calls (FSLOG – AP126 code 603 and FSLOGC – AP126 code 606), all the standard printing facilities are available to APL, including the ability to print APL characters.

items.title: User Numbers
items.text: Under TSO, there is no way supplied with APL of sharing APL data with other users. In fact APL thinks all users are number 1001. However, an IUP is available which allows data to be shared between MVS regions – MVS Inter Region Access Method (IUP 5796-ATX). This IUP provides general auxiliary processor support for two MVS regions to communicate. It also allows communication with an IMS control region, allowing APL to generate DL/1 calls to IMS databases.

items.title: TSO Information
items.text:
One advantage of VS APL under TSO is that a wide range of additional data about the operating environment is made available to APL through AP100. Extra pseudo-TSO commands have been provided to give the following types of information:

  • Current WSID, and save timestamp
  • Machine resource utilisation (CPU, DASD and other service units)
  • Current USERID, profile prefix
  • List of libraries available
  • List of workspaces in a given library
  • Releases of major pieces of software (MVS/TSO, APL, GDDM, HSM, RACF)
  • Terminal characteristics (Height, Depth)
  • Suppressing terminal output

These facilities are very useful to the APL programmer when interfacing to other systems, or when displaying information to a user on full screen panels.

items.title: Conclusions
items.text: I hope the above points have gone some way to answering the criticisms levelled against TSO by Adrian Smith in the last issue of VECTOR. It is a pity that IBM have not put a little more effort into making TSO friendly to start with. On the other hand, the TSO environment is very general purpose, and by using add-on products (thus cunningly generating more profits for IBM), can usually be made to perform at the desired level. Once implemented, a TSO environment can be very stable indeed.

items.title: Quad-WIN in APL*PLUS/PC Vn.5
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 119

by David Piper

items.title: Abstract
items.text:
One of the problems of using APL*PLUS PC in the past has been the relative difficulty of accessing the screen via some form of “full-screen” mode. Release 5.0 includes two new system functions which enable this form of application to be created much more easily – ⎕WIN and its associated function ⎕WKEY.

Using these functions, an easy to use, full-screen interface can be constructed without the need to resort to packages such as Toolkit 1 or Power Tools. A full screen interface which closely emulates the full-screen interface supplied by IBM in the FSC12x workspaces can also be implemented very easily. This will allow systems implemented on VS APL to be transported to the PC much more easily.

items.title: Introducing ⎕WIN
items.text:
The ⎕WIN system function emulates the facilities provided by the SFOR, SCUR and SREA functions in the FSC12X workspaces supplied by IBM for fullscreen processing in VS APL. That is, it establishes the fields on the screen, positions the cursor in a specific field and then waits for data to be typed and an interrupt made (ENTER or PF-Key).

The only remaining functions to be implemented are those which write and read data to and from fields on the screen – SWRI and \<SGET>. These can be emulated using the ⎕WPUT and ⎕WGET functions implemented in earlier releases of APL*PLUS PC.

items.title: The Format Array.
items.text:
The screen layout is defined in terms of the “format array”, which is passed as the right argument to the ⎕WIN function. The format array is similar to that used in mainframe applications, but some differences are apparent.

COLUMN Description [1 2] Field start position, row and column. The top right of the screen is position 0,0 on the PC, but position 1,1 on the mainframe. [3 4] Field width and depth in rows and columns. Identical to mainframe implementation. [5] Field type – 0=Protected (mf=2), 1=Alphameric (mf=0), 2=Numeric (mf=1). Additional field types can be user defined, to only accept specific characters from the keyboard, e.g. to set up a field which will only accept the Y or N keys. [6] Special feature code: 1=Autoskip when field is full (ASFEND under GDDM). Other features are available, such as automatic numeric validation etc. [7 8] Attributes to be used with/without the cursor. The PC attribute combines colour, intensity and extended attributes in one value. It is therefore more difficult to manipulate than the separate values used on the mainframe. Additionally different attribute values are required for colour or monochrome screens.

Since the attributes on the PC are more difficult to handle than on the mainframe, and it is desirable to be able to convert from a mainframe type format to a PC format, a function \<fCNVT> has been written to perform the conversion. This function takes a mainframe format array as its right argument and returns a PC format array which will emulate the mainframe functionality as closely as possible. The function is capable of handling all the GDDM extended attributes (colour, reverse video etc).

The \<fCNVT> function can also take advantage of column seven of the PC format array. If a left argument is supplied, it is assumed to be an array of attributes to be adopted when the cursor enters the field. The columns must be supplied in the same order as in the mainframe format array (intensity, colour, extended attribute). The ability to change attributes depending on the presence or otherwise of the cursor makes it very easy to implement 1-2-3 or Symphony type menus. The attribute in column 8 (without cursor) displays the field normally, that in column 7 puts it into reverse video when the cursor enters the field.

items.title: Positioning the Cursor
items.text:
The position of the cursor is initialised by the left argument of ⎕WIN. This argument is a numeric vector of up to 4 elements, the first three define the current cursor position in terms of a field number, and the row and column within that field. The field number is the row index of the desired field in the format array, and is therefore ⎕IO dependent.

The fourth element is a time-out factor – if no keys are pressed before the time-out is exceeded, control will be returned to the application. If the time-out is omitted, an infinite value is assumed.

items.title: Detecting an interrupt
items.text:
Once ⎕WIN has been called, control is normally only returned to the user’s application when a key defined for that purpose is pressed. By default, the ESCAPE and CTRL-ENTER keys are defined. The meaning of keys on the keyboard can be changed by using the ⎕WKEY function (described over page).

The result of ⎕WIN includes the following information:

ELEMENT Description [1] Reason for exiting ⎕WIN, normally zero if a valid exit key is used. [2] Numeric value of the key causing the exit. [3] Number of field containing the cursor (in origin-zero). [4 5] Row and column in field of cursor position (origin 0). [6...] Boolean elements indicating if the equivalent field in the right argument was modified or not.

If the special features (such as numeric validation) are specified in column 6 of the format array, then other reason codes may be set in the first element of the return vector.

items.title: Emulating Mainframe Screen Processing
items.text:
One of the major features of screen processing via GDDM is that all I/O to the screen is buffered by GDDM until a request to update the screen is received (ASREAD or FSFRCE). Since, on the PC, no shared variables are involved, I/O must either occur immediately, or must be buffered by being stored in an APL variable. The second approach allows the panel to be placed on the screen using just one call to ⎕WPUT, which is very quick and efficient.

Similarly, by establishing attributes on the physical screen as late as possible, multiple uses of ⎕WIN can be avoided. This is achieved by storing the requested format array in a global variable. Any changes to attributes can be effected simply by changing the relevant element of the global format array.

This process is made even easier if the format array is kept in mainframe format until it is output to the screen. The \<SINT> function listed below gives an example of this. The format array is only processed through the \<fCNVT> function immediately before use by ⎕WIN.

items.title: Reading the Screen
items.text:
When a screen read is requested, two calls to ⎕WIN are required. The first is made to establish attributes for all fields on the screen. This call cannot be used for the actual screen read, since the cursor can be moved to any field on the screen, even to protected fields. To avoid a delay while the attributes are established, a zero time-out is requested. After this, ⎕WPUT is used to write the text of the panel image to the screen.

The second call to ⎕WIN is then made, this time only INPUT fields are passed in the argument. Since only these fields are defined, the cursor cannot be moved to any protected part of the screen. Once control is returned to the application, the updated panel is retrieved using ⎕WGET.

In order to retrieve the data in the input fields, the information is read from the global panel image variable. This is illustrated by the \<SGET> function listed below.

items.title: Using Function Keys
items.text:
⎕WIN cannot detect the keyboard codes associated with the PF keys. In order to allow the PF keys to be detected, an alternative key code must be assigned using ⎕PFKEY. This alternative key code is then detected by ⎕WIN and can be interpreted by the application as a PF key. The best key codes to use appear to be 480-510.

In order to detect these keys, ⎕WKEY must be used in order to change the interpretation of the key. ⎕WKEY allows the interpretation of any key on the keyboard to be changed, either to an alternative character or some other special meaning such as TAB. The \<initialise> function listed below sets up some required global variables and changes the codes associated with the function keys. These new codes are then reinterpreted by ⎕WKEY to mean “return control to the application”. In addition the CAPS-LOCK key is given the same meaning, since CAPS-LOCK is in a similar position to ENTER on the IBM 327X keyboard.

items.title: Conclusions
items.text:
The presence of ⎕WIN in APL*PLUS PC release 5.0 makes the implementation of full-screen processing on the PC very simple. This style of processing can be made as close to the mainframe style as is desired, even to the extent of redefining the keyboard.

The format conversion function, in conjunction with a suitable set of cover functions on the PC, means that systems can be transferred directly from mainframe implementations of APL to the PC with very little conversion work being involved.

The ambivalent implementation of the format conversion function also allows full use to be made of the PC’s extended features, such as changing field characteristics as the cursor enters the field.

    ∇ OF←AA fCNVT FF;AT;BO
[1]   ⍝ Convert Mainframe format to PC format array
[2]   ⍝ FF - Numeric array   MF style format array
[3]   ⍝ AA - Numeric array   Alternate attributes with cursor
[4]   ⍝ OF - Numeric array   Equivalent PC stype format array
[5]   ⍝ Make sure input array has 10 columns
[6]    FF←((1↑⍴FF),10)↑FF

    ∇ FN SINT IN;AT;AV;BO

    ∇

    ∇ DA←SGET FL;CO;CL;RW

[9]   10:RW←(¯1+format[FL[CO];1])+⍳format[FL[CO];3]

[11]  ⍝ Retrieve text
[12]   DA←DA,⎕TCNL,,screen[RW;CL]
