items.title: Using quad-FX with Aux Processors
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 123

by David Piper

items.title: 1. Introduction
items.text:
⎕FX is commonly used in large APL systems for overlaying code in workspaces, fixing local functions containing system specific code etc. ⎕FX is used as a form of “compiler” which allows the conversion of parameter driven systems into hard-coded systems. If any of the parameters have to be changed during the life of the system, the functions can simply be re-fixed using ⎕FX.

⎕FX can also be of use in connection with shared variable processing in an analogous way. In many functions using shared variables, the names of the shared variables are passed as an argument. The function then uses execute to assign or use the shared variables. Typical of this type of implementation are the IBM supplied functions for use in association with AP123.

items.title: 2. Shared Variable Processing
items.text:
The use of execute for processing shared variables arises as a result of the dichotomy inherent between the use of the NAME of the variable and the use of the VARIABLE itself:

  • At share offer/retraction the NAME is used.
  • During processing the VARIABLE is assigned/referenced.

Since the name of the shared variable may change, any function used to cover the use of shared variables must use execute to assign or use the correct variable. This is especially true if more than one set of shared variables is to be used, in which case the names of the shared variables to be used will probably be passed as an argument to the cover function, or as a global variable.

An example of this form of implementation is readily available in the IBM supplied workspace VSAMDATA, which makes use of AP123 to access VSAM clusters. Other examples of the use of execute abound in the IBM supplied workspaces which are involved in shared variable processing.

It is especially desirable to avoid execute in situations such as reading or writing files since the volumes of data input/output (and hence the number of times the executes are processed) is potentially very large. Consider also that up to 3 executes may be involved per file operation – this is certainly true for the VSAM data AP, AP123. To read data:

  • Assignment of the read command to the “control” variable.
  • Use of the “control” variable to check the return code.
  • Use of the “data” variable to retrieve the data.

To write data:

  • Assignment of the data to the “data” variable.
  • Assignment of the write command to the “control” variable.
  • Use of the “control” variable to check the return code.

items.title: 3. Using ⎕FX
items.text:
To avoid the use of execute, a function must be created which contains the references to the control and data shared variables explicitly. The function is created and fixed at the time the shared variables are offered to the auxiliary processor.

The following terminology is used. Each function associated with a single set of shared variables is referred to as a “PATH”. A path is created by “LINKING” to the auxiliary processor and is destroyed by “UNLINKING”. The functions listed at the end of the article, link a new path (VSAMLINK) and unlink an existing path (VSAMUNLINK) with the VSAM auxiliary processor, AP123. The right argument to both functions is the name of the path to be linked or unlinked. The result is a boolean return code, 0 if the action was successful, 1 otherwise.

The pathname is used by the LINK function to customise:

  • The names of the shared variables.
  • The name of the PATH function.

Both sets of names also reflect the auxiliary processor in use, so no name clashes will result if multiple auxiliary processors are used as well as multiple paths per processor. The key function in the LINK process is the VSAMGEN function, the version listed uses features of APL2, but there is no reason why it could not be recoded using VS APL.

The function created by the VSAMGEN function is also listed, essentially it simply assigns values to the control and data shared variables and returns a two item nested vector (APL2 again!). The explicit result consists of the value from the control variable as the first item, with that from the data variable as the second item.

In VS APL, one of the shared variables would have to be referenced as a global variable since nested arrays are not available. As an alternative, a second niladic function could be generated to return the value of the other variable as its explicit result. The pathname used in the example functions to link to the path is “TEST”, the function generated is called VSAMTEST, and is used for all subsequent file I/O operations. At the end of file processing, the path is unlinked by using the VSAMUNLINK function.

One result of using the PATH name to customise the shared variable names is that multiple shares with the same AP can easily be achieved. When using the VSAM AP, this allows multiple VSAM clusters to be open at the same time. Contrast this with the approach taken by the IBM supplied functions which always close a file before allowing another to be opened. Similar techniques, if applied to the QSAM and BDAM auxiliary processors would allow multiple file access using these protocols too.

items.title: 4. Other Benefits
items.text:
The command system implemented using the VSAMGEN function is identical to that for AP123 itself – there is no processing overhead interpreting the commands used. Also, using APL2, the EACH operator can be used to execute many commands without writing looping code. Allowing, for example, many read or write operations to be undertaken without the associated overheads of looping.

User written operators could be used to read or write data from/to a file until a non-zero return code, such as end-of-file, is received (problems with WS FULL may result of course).

The ability to use APL2 operators arises because the same function is used for all file based operations, with only the argument values changing. Arguments can be applied repeatedly without having to reference different functions. In contrast, the approach taken in the VSAMDATA supplied workspace is that of “keywords”, different functions being used to achieve each VSAM operation. When using the keyword approach, there is little or no opportunity to make use of the functional enhancements provided by APL2 operators.

It is worth noting that even in VS APL, the command controlled function can result in more efficient, compact code. For example, it would be relatively simple to rewrite the generated function so that it could either use a vector or array command argument. In the case of an array, each row could be used in turn until the array is exhausted. The only looping code involved in this type of implementation is inside the generated function, rather than in the application code.

A further benefit of the command approach rather than the “keyword” function approach is the reduction in the number of objects (and the volume of code) that has to be copied into the workspace. The only permanent code in the workspace when using the example functions are the LINK, UNLINK and GEN functions. During processing, the path access functions are also created. All these functions are relatively short, so the volume of code involved is small.

The largest function listed is that giving the text associated with the different error codes that may arise. Since an application will typically contain its own error checking and messaging, it may not be necessary to have this function in the workspace at all.

items.title: 5. Extending the concept
items.text:
There is no need to restrict the use of ⎕FX to the avoidance of execute for variable names, function execution is also amenable to the technique.

Mainframe APL provides no in-built mechanism for translating input data from binary, packed or other S/370 formats into APL data formats. A frequent requirement when processing files is the translation of such data, functions are provided in one of the IBM supplied workspaces for this purpose. Before the translation is performed, the record must be separated into its component fields.

A function can easily be generated, which, given a series of field names, lengths and translation requirements will take an input record, extract the fields and translate the data into APL format. The translated data can either be returned as a vector representing the data, or in a series of global variables, one per field. The reverse process can be used for writing records back to the file in S/370 data formats.

The generation of two functions (one for input and one for output) given the layout of the record as input is a relatively trivial problem. The gains in performance by avoiding use of the execute function to perform translation and assignment into the explicit result (or the global variables representing the fields within the record) will be considerable. This is all the more important since it is likely that, as with any file processing, large volumes of data will be processed.

items.title: 6. Conclusions
items.text:
The system function ⎕FX can be used to replace the use of the execute function in many situations. It acts as a form of “compiler” to hard-code the references to variables which would otherwise be referenced through execute.

Some overhead is incurred in the use of ⎕FX as the function being fixed is verified and established in the workspace. It is important therefore that ⎕FX is used in those situations where the gains from the avoidence of execute will outweigh the costs of using ⎕FX.

This technique will be of most use in situations where the execute would be invoked many times. Typical of these are file processing applications where relatively large volumes of file I/O are involved.

Other situations where execute is used, such as the conditional execution of a line of code do not lend themselves to this technique. None the less execute is probably better avoided in these cases.

items.title: Command-driven Interface for BDAM & QSAM
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 118

Doubtful transcription

The listings on pp.129–131 (the generated BDAM and QSAM path functions, and the VSAM functions omitted from the previous issue) are reproduced as images, not transcribed; the prose and short examples are transcribed.

by David Piper

items.title: 1. Introduction
items.text:
The requirements for the successful use of files from within APL can be summarised as being:

Efficient input/output processing A robust, consistent and easy to use interface.

The auxiliary processors associated with the QSAM and BDAM access methods (AP111 and AP210 respectively) are more difficult to use, and generally considered to be less robust than other auxiliary processors associated with file handling in APL (e.g. the VSAM AP, AP123).

Increased difficulty of use arises from the protocols associated with the APs. These are not command driven, but rather depend on the order of assignment/use of the shared variables. The initial values of the shared variables are also crucial, since the file to be accessed is opened at the point of sharing the variables, and closed at retraction, rather than by explicit command after sharing. Also note the data shared variable (prefix REC not DAT) must be shared first.

The APs are considered less robust, since the order of assignment/use of the shared variables is crucial, forming the command interface. Misuse of the variables, in the sense of an incorrect order of assignment/use, can cause the auxiliary processors to abend. If this occurs, the APs may be unavailable for the rest of the TSO session. The QSAM AP is especially prone to this type of failure if only a single (data variable) is shared. In this case, even simple errors, such as attempting to continue processing after end of file, may give rise to an abend in the AP.

items.title: 2. Designing a new interface
items.text:
The criteria behind the design of an interface to cover the use of the APs are threefold:

Efficiency of file I/O. Robustness of the interface. Ease of use for the application developer.

Since the cover functions are intended for use within an application, ease of use in terms of flexibility of command specification etc. is given the lowest priority. Efficiency is given the highest priority so the command interface has as little impact as possible on application performance.

In order to minimise the efficiency impact, each command is made as simple as possible to interpret. Once interpreted, the minimum possible code is used to execute each command. The range of commands is extended to include ‘block’ operations to further minimise overheads. During the execution of blocked commands, the command is interpreted once, then executed in a loop, with no more code than would have to be used if shared variables were used directly by the application code.

Further efficiency is gained by avoiding the use of execute for all operations (except the initial opening of a file). The technique used is to fix an access function, with a given name, in which the references to the shared variables are explicitly coded. For a fuller discussion of this technique, see my article in VECTOR 3.2. Robustness is achieved by containing all file operations within the cover functions. This ensures that all uses of the shared variables are executed in the correct order. It also allows a certain amount of error checking to be performed, such as preventing attempts to write data to a file open in read only mode. Error checking at this point also prevents attempts to process files after an end of file condition is received. Thus the major sources of errors within the auxiliary processors are avoided.

Ease of use is improved by removing the need for initialisation of variables before being shared. The open command performs the correct initialisation and performs all checking necessary to ensure the share was successful. From the applications point of view, the complexity of opening the file is reduced to the simple use of a single command. The same can be said of the close command. The cover function takes care of shared variable retraction and checking of return codes.

Ease of use is further enhanced by the use of the same command structure (as far as possible) across both APs. The command structure has been implemented to resemble as closely as possible that implemented for the VSAM auxiliary processor (AP 123). The similarity of the command structures across all three access methods allows file processing to be used far more easily than when making use of a variety of function driven interfaces.

items.title: 3. Creating/Deleting Access Paths
items.text:
Before any files can be accessed, the path function has to be created (or LINKED). For QSAM files:

RC←∆QSAM_LINK 'name'   ⍝ <name> is used to customise the
                       ⍝ names of the access path function
                       ⍝ and the shared variables)

Commands can then be issued using the path function:

RC←QSAM_name 'command'        ⍝ Opening, Closing or reading

RC←data QSAM_name 'command'   ⍝ Writing data

When file processing is complete, the path function can be erased. The process of UNLINKING issues a close command in case any files have been left open. Paths are deleted using the UNLINK function:

RC←∆QSAM_unlink 'name'

The path function is expunged along with the shared variables.

items.title: 4. Opening and Closing Files
items.text:
As already discussed, opening and closing files is one of the most complex operations under APs 111 and 210. First the variables have to be initialised:

CTLQSAM←'filename (ctl'
RECQSAM←'filename (mode conv'

After this, the variables can be shared – record variable first:

SS←111 ⎕SVO 2 7⍴'RECQSAMCTLQSAM'

Return codes from the open operation must be checked:

RC←CTLQSAM

Using the command interface, the above steps are reduced to a single line of code (assuming the path has already been linked):

RC←QSAM_path 'Om filename conv'

Acceptable values for \<Om> – the access mode – are R(ead), W(rite) or U(pdate). BDAM files can additionally be opened for F(ormat) processing. The return code given by the open operation is fully descriptive of any error that may have occurred. The code can be passed to the relevant error message function to obtain a textual description of the error.

When opened for FORMAT processing, the next command given for the file must be the format command:

RC←data BDAM_path 'F' nnn        ⍝ <nnn> is the number of records

The file is then left open in update mode.

The BDAM file interface ensures that the open/format commands are processed in the correct order without intermediate attempts to read and write to the file.

Closing the file is simply a matter of using the close command. This command retracts the shared variables (thereby closing the file), but leaves the path function intact. This allows further file processing to take place, either in a different access mode, or to another file.

items.title: 5. Reading/Writing Data
items.text:
The only significant differences in syntax between the two file access methods are in the commands associated with reading and writing data. The syntax is bound to be different since BDAM offers direct access to records while QSAM offers only sequential access. BDAM also offers sequential access, the syntax for sequentially processing single records is identical for both access methods.

For efficiency of file access, ‘pseudo-blocked’ access commands are also provided. These read or write a series of records using only one call to the path function. A loop of code within the access function performs the multiple calls to the auxiliary processor. The command is parsed only once, the code loop simply assigning/using the shared variables as required. As soon as a non-zero return code is encountered processing ceases. If a write is being performed, any unwritten records are returned in the data item of the return vector.

To read a single record, the following syntax is used:

(RC DA)←QSAM_path 'R'                    ⍝ QSAM

(RC DA)←BDAM_path 'R'                    ⍝ BDAM sequential
(RC DA)←BDAM_path 'R' record_number      ⍝ BDAM direct

The data is returned as a nested vector, each item of the vector is a record from the file. Since only a single record is read, the vector has only one item.

To perform a ‘blocked’ read:

(RC DA)←QSAM_path 'R' number_of_records  ⍝ QSAM

(RC DA)←BDAM_path 'R' n1 n2 n3 ....      ⍝ BDAM direct

The blocked access terminates as soon as a non-zero return code is encountered. The length of the vector of records (DA) is the same as the number of records read. The return code indicates why the read was abandoned.

To write a single record, the following syntax is used:

(RC DA)←data QSAM_path 'W'               ⍝ QSAM

(RC DA)←data BDAM_path 'W'               ⍝ BDAM sequential
(RC DA)←data BDAM_path 'W' n1            ⍝ BDAM direct

A data vector is always returned, normally this will be an empty nested vector. If a non-zero return code is generated by the write command, the unwritten record is returned.

To perform a ‘blocked’ write:

(RC DA)←records QSAM_path 'W'            ⍝ QSAM

(RC DA)←records BDAM_path 'W' n1 n2 n3...   ⍝ BDAM direct

When performing a ‘blocked’ write using BDAM, records are written until:

Records are exhausted in the data vector. Record numbers are exhausted in the command vector. A non-zero return code is received.

Any over-written records are returned in the data component of the explicit result. The left argument is a nested vector, each item representing a record to be written. If only a single record is to be written, consisting of a simple vector, this need not be enclosed.

The convention of using a nested vector to contain data records is adopted to enable the use of the VAR conversion option. This option allows APL2 variables of any type, rank or level of nesting to be written to file without conversion. To write a series of such arrays, each is enclosed to form an item of a nested vector which is presented as the left argument.

items.title: 6. Conclusions
items.text:
The primary aim of any system of functions covering the use of file access auxiliary processors should be to maintain the highest level of efficiency possible. This is true simply because of the number of times the auxiliary processor is likely to be used, especially if file processing is involved.

The concept of a command driven interface also enables the following advantages to be realised:

Reduction in the number of functions in the workspace. Implementation of a similar syntax across access methods.

Generating a function containing the shared variable names explicitly allows multiple files to be accessed without the need to continually retract/re-offer shared variables, and removes the need to use execute.

(Editor: David supplied more APL2 code than we have room for here. A listing of the functions produced by the BDAM and QSAM ‘LINK’ functions follows.)

Using NameAssociation for Data Translation by David Piper

1. Introduction Whenused in a commercial data processing environment, systems implemented in APL will often be required to addresssignificant volumesofdata from external (i.e. non-APL) files. Since thesefiles are not generated by APL code, they may well contain data in formats notreadily accessible by APL. Prime examplesof such formats include packed decimal and the IBM S/370 floating point format. Oneof the supplied workspaces in both the VS APL and APL2 environments contains functions for translating external data into APL numeric form. Since these functions are coded in APL, makinguse of someof the most complex APL primitive functions (index-of and encode/decode), execution speedstend to be somewhatslow. This poor performanceis of especial concern whenlarge volumesofdata are being translated. 2. NameAssociation (JNA) UNAis a system function provided as part of APL2 (Version | Release 2 andlater). It is designed to allow routines coded in languages other than APL andstored outside the workspaceto be invoked in exactly the same way as APL functions. Thefunctions are invoked by use of an associated processor, one for each language type being used. In the CMS environment, two associated processors are provided; 10 allows use of the REXX language, 11 allows languages compiled into machinecodeto becalled. TSO provides only processor 11, since there is no equivalent to the REXX language. 3. Properties of Associated Objects Oneof the key properties of associated objects is that they obeyall the rules associated with normal APL2 objects: m They appear in{JNL, )NMSetc. @ ONCreturnsthe correct nameclass for the object. = Associated functions and operators can generate APL2 errors. m Theassociation is preserved in a )SAVEd workspace. = Associations can be )COPYed from another workspace. Associationsare dissolved by JERASE or EX. m (ATreturnsthe correct information (even a timestamp can bedefined.) An associated function appears identical to a locked function as far as the application programmeris concerned. 4, Interface Definition Theinterface between APL2 andthe associated objectis definedin a names file. Amongst otherfactors, the namesfile contains descriptionsof:

123

VECTOR Vol.3 No.4

The nameofthe associated function. Theload library where the function can be found. The module nameandentry pointif different from the associated name. Interface type (object, fortran or function). Descriptions of the arguments, including structure and data types if these can be anticipated. @ A description ofthe function and time-stamp. The most complex feature to be defined is the pattern of the arguments. The pattern definition must includedetails of structure thatis the pattern of nesting in the argument. Details of rank, shape and acceptable domain mustalso be included. To facilitate the implementation of assembler coded functions, translation options can also be specified. These will cause an argumentto be translated from APL formatto S/370 on input to the function andtheresult to be re-translated on output. 5. Supplied Functions With APL2several functions coded in assembler are provided. The lack of documentation makes these more difficult to use, several of the functions are, however, extremely useful. Severalofthe functionsallow a vectorto be partitionedin various ways(see also myletter in VECTORVol.3, No.3). These include: CAN- partition on zeroes in a boolean vector. DAN partition on delimiters, removing the delimiters. SAN - partition on delimiters, retaining the delimiters. Other functions are more esoteric such as SVI which allows a systems programmer to investigate which associated processorsare functioning. The functions used for converting data between APL and 8/370 formats and back again are RTA (record-to-array) and ATR (array-to-record). 6. RTA and ATRfunctions These two functionstranslate S/370 data to APL formats and back again respectively. The left argument takes the form of a pattern specification of the data to be translated. The pattern specification is similar to that used to describetheleft and right arguments in the associated functions namefile definition. The RTA and ATRfunctions are capable of translating an entire record, with fields of varying lengths and typesat onecall. The cover functions presented here are more limited, they are designedto replace the IBM functionsin 1 UTILITY. Each function translates any numberofoccurrencesof a given data type into APL format(or vice versa). For example, when read from file, a series of6 byte packedfields will each be represented as 6 APL characters from [JAV. Inthis form, the data cannot be used by APL. Using the PDI (packed decimalinput) function the 6 character representation is converted into valid APLnumerics. Supplying an N by6 array of packed decimal data will result in a numeric vectorof length N. 124

VECTOR Vol.3 No.4

7. Pattern Arguments The key factor in performing the datatranslation is the creation ofthe pattern argument. The pattern argument is of two separate forms, depending on the direction of the translation. When translating from $/370 into APL, the input data is always supplied to the RTA function as a vector, The rank and shapeofthe outputis implied by the rank and shape of the argumentto the cover function. Thefirst part of the pattern argumentdefinesthetranslation option, The optionis in two parts, the data type (e.g. P for packed, I for integer) and the numberofbytes perfield (*P8 will translate 8 byte packed decimal data). The next part specifies the rank (always 1) and length ofthe resulting APL vector. The resulting numeric vectoris reshaped into an array that conforms with the input argument. Whentranslating from APL to S/370, the input data is supplied as an array, theresult is always a charactervector. In orderto be the inverseofthe input coverfunction,this vector is reshaped. The pattern argumentis created slightly differently. The first item is an asterisk (*) stating that the count of items to be translated is unknown. Thenextitem describesthe translation option (as above). Thelast item is anotherasterisk, informingthat the rank ofthe array being translatedis variable. 8. Efficiency

The main aim ofusing the assembler-codedfunctionsis to gain performance and execution speed. The following benchmarks show just how effective the assembler-coded functions are relative to the APL equivalents. The tests are performed by averaging over 1000 conversionsof a specified array. For the BIT conversion functions, 256 bytes of data are converted each time. For the PACKED and INTEGERconversions, integer arrays of 24 rows by 10 columns are converted. Both negative and positive data are included. Floating point conversion uses a 24 by 10 arrayoffloating point numbers, of both negative andpositivesign. Tt

Function Changes The functionslisted below are as identical as possible to those supplied in 1 UTILITY. A few changes have been forced byrestrictions in the ATR and RTAfunctions: = TheIJ and IO functionswill now only accepthalfor full word integers. m The FOfunction is capable of producing single precision as well as double precision floating point output. The integer processing restrictions imposed are not very serious. Nearlyall integerfields are either half- or full-word, Additionally, the performance of the II/IO functionsin ! UTILITYis so poorwith integers greater than 4 bytes, that processing any volumeof data is made impracticable. The FI function in 1 UTILITYis capable of converting full or double precision floating point into APL numerics. The FO function only produces double precision output. Single precision can be produced by dropping thelast four columnsof the output (quote from comments in the function). This technique is obviously inefficient. By default, the FO cover function will produce double precision output. The required precision can be specified in the left argument. 10. Conclusions The requirementto translate data between $/370 and APL formats arises quite frequently in the commercial data processing environment. The useof assembler coded functionsto speed up such translations makes the processingof significant volumesofdata a realistic proposition. The functions given are intended to cover the use of the IBM supplied functions in 1 UTILITY. Tothis end, their syntax and functionality is mirrored as closely as possible. The RTA and ATRfunctionscouldeasily be utilised in a different manner which would further facilitate data conversion work. The documentationofthe supplied assembler coded functionsis very poor. Improvements in this area would makeuse of the supplied functions mucheasier.

items.title: Using quad-NA to Eliminate WS FULL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 107

by David Piper
path: Using quad-NA to Eliminate WS FULL

items.title: Introduction
items.text: Much has already been written about using quad-NA to speed up APL2 function code. A lesser known (indeed undocumented) series of recent enhancements have been implemented which allow workspace size problems to be tackled using quad-NA. These enhancements are unsupported in the current release of APL2 (APL2 V1.R2).
path: Using quad-NA to Eliminate WS FULL

items.title: Using Quad-NA
items.text:
The Quad-NA system function is used to establish linkage with an object outside the APL2 workspace. Typically this object is a function coded in a language other than APL2. The right argument gives the function name with which linkage is to be established. The left argument specifies the name class and attached processor through which the linkage is made. The result is a boolean scalar, 1 if the association is established successfully, 0 otherwise.

      3 11 ⎕NA 'FOO'        ⍝ Associate with function FOO
1                           ⍝ Linkage established

The clue to the newly implemented features lies in the left argument. By changing the specified name class, objects other than functions can be associated with:

      4 11 ⎕NA 'OP1'        ⍝ Associate with operator OP1
1                           ⍝ Linkage established

It must be emphasised at this point that the associated object takes only a minimal amount of workspace. When an association is formed with a function or operator, only about 12 bytes of workspace are used. This memory overhead is used to establish pointers to the correct code outside the workspace.
path: Using quad-NA to Eliminate WS FULL

items.title: Saving Workspace
items.text:
The largest objects in a given workspace are normally the variables to be used during processing. Clearly, opportunities for saving workspace will be maximised by storing variables outside the workspace, then associating with them as required:

      ⎕WA                   ⍝ Current work area
1987103
      FIRST                 ⍝ Reference non-existant variable
VALUE ERROR
      FIRST
      ^
      2 4 ⎕NA 'FIRST'       ⍝ Establish association
1
      ⍴FIRST                ⍝ What is its shape
200 80 100
      ×/⍴FIRST              ⍝ Number of items
1600000
      ⎕WA                   ⍝ Work area with variable
1987091

Note that in the above example, only 12 bytes of work area are used to store an array containing 1.6 million items.

Just as in the examples above with associated function, the associated variable acts exactly as a normal APL2 variable. The only difference is that the variable is stored externally to the workspace. Associated arrays can of course be nested:

      ≡FIRST
5

Existing variables can be placed external to the workspace simply by associating the variable with the associated processor after it has been assigned. Once associated, any assignment to the variable updates the associated version rather than re-creating a copy in the workspace.

      ⎕WA
1987091
      SECOND←(10 8 6⍴480?1000)(15 5⍴'ABCDE')
      ⎕WA
1985056
      2 4 ⎕NA 'SECOND'      ⍝ Externalise the array
1
      ⎕WA
1987079

The space saving that can be achieved using associated variables is obviously tremendous. The enhancement to Quad-NA which implements this facility is referred to as the Fully Integrated Reserved Storage Table (FIRST).
path: Using quad-NA to Eliminate WS FULL

items.title: Saving More Workspace
items.text:
Now that functions, operators and variables can be placed external to the workspace and accessed via name association, the only memory usage within the workspace is that required by the interpreter. In order to minimise memory usage, quad-NA has been further enhanced to allow the storage used by the interpreter to be stored externally also. These areas of storage are then accessed via name association.

      )CLEAR
CLEAR WS
      ⎕WA
2074824
      ¯1 4 ⎕NA 'APL2'
1
      ⎕WA
3187688

Note the use of a ‘dummy’ name and name class on the call to quad-NA. The use of the name APL2 causes the entire interpreter storage to be removed from the workspace. Using other names allows different portions of the interpreter to be removed:

      ¯1 ¯4 ⎕NA 'APL2'      ⍝ Get the interpreter storage back
1
      ⎕WA
2074824
      1 4 ⎕NA '⎕FNS'        ⍝ Only system functions moved
1
      ⎕WA
2215580

Note the use of the negative processor number in the above example. This is used to dissolve the name association, and relocate the interpreter storage back within the workspace.

The enhancement to Quad-NA which allows the interpreter storage to be moved out of the workspace is referred to as Associated Processor Remote Interpreter Linkage (APRIL).
path: Using quad-NA to Eliminate WS FULL

items.title: Using No Workspace At All
items.text:
Once all the defined objects have been removed from the workspace, and the interpreter storage is also relocated, the only remaining use of memory in the workspace is for the associated object definitions (12 bytes per object).

A third enhancement to quad-NA allows even these headers to be moved out of the workspace. Referred to as Full Operation Off-Line (FOOL), this allows your APL systems to run without using any memory at all.
path: Using quad-NA to Eliminate WS FULL

items.title: Conclusions
items.text:
The three enhancements to quad-NA described (FIRST, APRIL and FOOL) allow applications to be written with only very small memory overheads. The ability to store variables outside the workspace reduces the required workspace for a given application.

Memory usage is reduced still further when the interpreter is stored outside the workspace. If the quad-NA headers are stored outside the workspace, memory usage vanishes in a SPOOF of smoke.
path: Using quad-NA to Eliminate WS FULL

items.title: Parallel Computing and APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 113

by David Piper

items.title: Abstract
items.text: Parallel computing is a subject rapidly increasing in importance. Parallel hardware has been available for some time. With the advent of chips such as the Transputer some of the hardware is beginning to demonstrate a level of technical maturity. Development of software has not progressed at the same speed. Useable operating systems for transputer based machines are only now appearing. Programming languages and the development of applications lag further behind. Much of the historical effort has concentrated on the development of parallelizing compilers for existing sequential language code. This paper shows how APL is already a highly developed parallel language and with some functional extensions can be made even more effective as a parallel language.

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
The speed of development of computer hardware is such that the physical limits of design are rapidly being approached. The essential limits are in terms of:

SIZE ………………………… pathways only a few atoms wide SPEED ……………………… close juxtaposition to shorten pathways COMPLEXITY ……………… packing densities and connection patterns

Even with the development of quantum well devices [BATE88], the gains to be made are less than those already made in the development of semi-conductor devices.

Once physical limits have been reached, gains in speed will have to be derived by executing more than one instruction at a time - parallel processing. The performance gains that can be obtained by the use of parallel computing are almost limitless. The problem that remains is making use of the existing parallel hardware; parallel software is still in a relatively primitive state.

items.title: Classification of Parallelism
items.text:
The range of parallel hardware already available is quite extensive. A difficulty arises over the classification of exactly what is parallel and what is not. The definitions of distributed and parallel machines certainly overlap. A range of taxonomies have been defined.

The simplest of these, by Flynn [SHARP87], describes the following classes:

SISD ………… Single instruction, single data (normal sequential processing) SIMD ………… Single instruction, multiple data (vector processors) MISD ………… Multiple instruction, single data (very rare, pipe-lines perhaps) MIMD ………… Multiple instruction, multiple data (full parallel processing)

This classification is good for distinguishing between more traditional machine types (e.g. sequential and vector processors) and the truly parallel processors. It achieves little in terms of classifying the types of parallel machine. Sharp [SHARP87] refines Flynn’s classification scheme by sub-dividing the MIMD class into two. The MISD class can be regarded as a special case of the first of these new classes. Sharp’s full scheme is as follows:

SPS …………… Single processor executing scalar data (SISD) SPA …………… Single processor executing array data (SIMD) MPS …………… Multi-processor executing scalar data (MISD + MIMD) MPA …………… Multi-processor executing array data (MIMD)

items.title: Classification of Software
items.text:
The classification of hardware is a complex subject because there are many potential mechanisms for implementing parallelism. As far as software is concerned, the problem is much simpler. We will want to:

  • Execute a single process on a scalar or array (SPS, SPA)
  • Execute multiple processes on a scalar or array (MPS, MPA)
  • Execute multiple processes on multiple arrays (MPA)

The divide is between function and data, the classification made by Sharp is ideal.

items.title: Parallel Software
items.text:
Much of the research into parallel software has been dedicated to the conversion of sequential software (i.e. existing applications) into parallel software. This is to facilitate the execution of existing libraries of code on faster and more powerful parallel hardware.

The research has fallen into 3 main categories:

  • Conversion of multi-tasking to parallel-tasking
  • Parallelizing compilers
  • New parallel languages or parallel extensions to existing languages

items.title: Multi-tasking to Parallel-tasking
items.text:
Many uni-processor systems have emulated a form of parallel processing by the use of multi-tasking systems software. Even relatively simple single user operating systems have rudimentary multi-tasking facilities (e.g. the MS/DOS PRINT command).

The conversion of such multi-tasking systems to true parallel processing is an obvious, and fairly trivial task. A number of problems with the conversion concept can be identified, in particular there may be a failure to take advantage of all the opportunities for parallel processing. Since multi-tasking is a special feature implemented on uni-processor systems via carefully written systems software, not all the available opportunities for multi-tasking will have been taken advantage of. The cost involved in providing more and more multi-tasking capabilities is too great. The literal conversion from single processor to parallel processing systems will similarly fail to take advantage of all available opportunities for parallelism.

Much of the cost advantage provided by a conversion-only exercise will be lost if a more substantial process of re-writing is undertaken. This may, however, be the only realistic way to gain more significant benefits from parallel processing.

Even if operating system software is fully converted to parallel processing, all of the application software still has to be converted. Existing applications will continue to be non-parallel, many of the potential performance benefits remaining unrealised.

items.title: Parallelizing Compilers
items.text:
Another approach to the introduction of parallelism is the creation of parallelizing compilers. These take sequential source code and attempt to detect, and take advantage of, the opportunities for parallel processing inherent in all such code.

The disadvantages of this approach are similar to those discussed above. In particular a parallelizing compiler can only detect parallelism in the code as it is currently written. There may exist other, explicitly parallel, algorithms which are more efficient. Perhaps knowledge based systems offer opportunities here - an intelligent parallelizing compiler that can recognise sequential algorithms and can substitute more efficient parallel ones.

There is however an additional cost. A great deal of effort may have been put into optimising the sequential algorithm, this will be wasted in the conversion to parallel processing. In addition, the optimised algorithm may be more difficult to translate into parallel code than a naive sequential algorithm.

The technologies discussed in this and the previous sections are essentially linked to migration/conversion exercises. The importance of this issue should not be underestimated; it is, however, a technology with a finite lifetime. Eventually the development of new parallel code will become the dominant issue and a key task in the search for increasing speed of execution.

items.title: Languages with Parallel Constructs
items.text:
By far the best approach to the creation of parallel code is the use of explicitly parallel languages. These come in two major forms:

  • parallel versions of existing languages (e.g. DAP-FORTRAN, PARLOG)
  • new languages with explicit parallel constructs (e.g. OCCAM)

A major criticism can be levelled at both the above approaches - the parallelism still has to be programmed in; it does not arise as a natural consequence of the language syntax and algorithms used. The programmer is responsible for administering the parallelism, deciding which sections can be executed in parallel and which must be performed sequentially. As well as being difficult, this introduces a new potential source of errors into the programming process.

Even new parallel languages such as OCCAM are essentially enriched sequential languages, relying on constructs such as FOR-NEXT loops (though these may be executed in parallel). The code produced by the programmer is essentially sequential with some instructions to permit parallel execution. There is no encouragement to think in terms of parallel processes, and the instructions to permit parallelism may be omitted without penalty (until execution time).

items.title: Functional Languages
items.text:
The functional programming paradigm has been proclaimed as being of great value for parallel processing. Many functional languages have been implemented, but few have achieved much commercial success. Perhaps the major exception is LISP. [MICH89] describes functional languages as having the following properties:

  • a name is only ever associated with one value
  • there is no fixed execution order
  • new values are associated with new names via recursion or function calls
  • functions can be treated as values

Following from the second property, functional languages provide many opportunities for parallel execution without formal language constructs. If there is no fixed execution order, then the constituent parts of a program may be executed in parallel. Since the parallelism is derived from functional independence, functional languages are best suited to the MPS form of parallelism.

items.title: APL as a Parallel Language
items.text:
APL has some significant advantages for the implementation of parallel processing systems:

  • parallelism is inherent in the language.
  • many of the features of functional languages can also be found in APL.

In addition, by adding a single consistent extension to APL, the opportunities for parallelism can be significantly increased.

items.title: SPA Parallelism and APL
items.text:
Single Process, Array data (SPA) parallelism is the form easiest to see in APL, it is apparent in even the simplest APL statements. Conversely, it is frequently the most difficult to implement in other forms of parallel language; this is especially true for functional programming languages. The difficulty arises from the recursive nature of such languages. Parallelizing compilers normally try to pick out this form of parallelism by looking closely at loops or recursion and attempting to “untangle” them in some way.

The difficulties of implementing SPA parallelism are discussed in detail in [SHARP87], chapter 9. On the last page of this chapter, the following appears:

“This chapter has, hopefully, indicated that some problems which initially do not appear suited to array processing may indeed be amenable to such methods. Any APL programmer will need little convincing of that, for many APL one-liners rely on manipulating vectors and matrices as whole objects. It might be argued that rather than adapting strictly sequential languages such as FORTRAN, we ought to have looked at compiling APL for array processes.....”

Consider the following APL statement:

    R←A+B

If A and B are arrays, SPA parallelism is immediately apparent. This simplicity of implementation is the basis of IBM’s VECTOR processor version of APL2. The compilation of such code is discussed in [CHING88], which includes examples of the ease of translation into vector processor code. These points are also discussed in [BROWN88], and other examples are given in [BUCHHOLZ86].

Opportunities for SPA parallelism are increased in APL implementations with nested arrays. The EACH operator applies a function to each of the items in its argument(s). Thus if C is a nested array:

    R←⍴¨C

returns the shape of each item of C; perhaps the EACH operator should be renamed the PARALLEL operator! Using EACH, SPA parallelism can be applied to non-scalar (and thus, in APL2 nomenclature, non-pervasive) functions.

items.title: MPS/MPA Parallelism in APL
items.text:
APL presents natural opportunities for Multi-Process parallelism (on scalar or array data). These are founded on the same basis as the implementation of MPS parallelism in functional languages. Consider the following fragment of function code:

[..] C←A×B
[..] D←⌈/C
[..] E←C>1000

Since the following points are all true:

  • C is not changed after its initial assignment
  • the result of each line is assigned to a different variable
  • the third line makes no use of D

the order of execution of the last two lines of code is immaterial; they may, therefore, be executed in parallel. The same argument can be applied to the parallel execution of defined functions:

[..] C←A CALC1 B
[..] D←A CALC2 B
[..] E←C REPORT D

Assuming CALC1 and CALC2 have no global side effects, then parallel processing is possible for the first two lines. Note this is an additional argument for the avoidance of global variables. Note also that coalescing the lines of code has no effect on the potential for parallelism:

[..] E←(A CALC1 B)REPORT A CALC2 B

Whilst functional languages limit this form of parallelism to MPS (scalar data), APL allows both MPS and MPA parallelism. This results from APL’s ability to operate independently of the rank and shape of its data (subject to the constraints of conformability).

items.title: Extending APL for more Parallelism
items.text:
One frequent proposal for the extension of APL is the implementation of function arrays. This has been discussed elsewhere in VECTOR (see for example [PIPER89] and the references given therein).

The case for function arrays is best illustrated by some simple examples:

    1 2 3 + 4 5 6

can (in versions of APL that support strand notation) also be written:

    (1+4)(2+5)(3+6)

a very similar expression:

    (1+4)(2×5)(3÷6)

has no equivalent compact form. The implementation of function arrays provides this compact form:

    1 2 3(+×÷)4 5 6

the expression:

    (+×÷)

is a function vector.

The applicability of such function arrays to parallel processing should be immediately apparent. User defined functions can also be stranded, so we can re-write the above example as follows:

[..] (C D)←(⊂A)(CALC1 CALC2)(⊂B)
[..] E←C REPORT D

Note that A and B have to be enclosed so that scalar extension is applied.

items.title: Pipe-lining in APL
items.text:
One technique provided by the ability to strand functions is that of pipe-lining. For example, to read a file, format the resulting data and write an output file, code like the following might be written:

[..] EOF←0
[..] START:→EOF/END
[..] (EOF DATA)←READ_INP FILE
[..] RPT←FORMAT DATA
[..] WRITE_RPT REPORT
[..] →START
[..] END:

This may not be executed in parallel since it violates one of the rules listed in section 3.2 - the execution of each line depends on the result of the previous line. If function arrays can be used, however, a more concise formulation can be written:

[..] (DATA RPT)←↓''
[..] EOF←0
[..] START:→EOF/END
[..] (RPT EOF DATA)←(WRITE_RPT FORMAT READ_INP)RPT DATA FILE
[..] →START
[..] END:

The pipe-line construct in the above example permits the re-introduction of parallelism at least to a limited degree. All the functions execute once in parallel then wait for the rest to catch up, before iterating around the loop and commencing again. Note that at the end of file, additional processing is required to allow the FORMAT and WRITE_RPT functions to catch up and process the last couple of records.

items.title: Are Function Arrays Needed?
items.text:
If we look at the above example carefully, we can see that by placing the 3 processing statements inside a subsidiary function we can achieve an identical result without function arrays:

[..] (DATA RPT)←↓''
[..] EOF←0
[..] START:→EOF/END
[..] (RPT EOF DATA)←PROC_REPORT RPT DATA FILE
[..] →START
[..] END:

     ∇RES←PROC_REPORT PARMS;DATA;FILE;RPT
[1]   (RPT DATA FILE)←PARMS
[2]   WRITE_RPT RPT
[3]   RPT←FORMAT DATA
[4]   (EOF DATA)←READ_INP FILE
[5]   RES←(RPT EOF DATA)
     ∇

Despite this, I believe the explicit pipeline using function arrays is much clearer and more easily understood. If (under APL2) we implement an UNTIL operator, we can eliminate the coded loop from our function:

[..] (DATA RPT)←⊂''
[..] EOF←((WRITE_RPT FORMAT READ_INP)UNTIL 2)RPT DATA FILE

Note the right operand indicates which item of the explicit result is to be tested for the end condition. Also the left operand is the entire function vector, an array of functions being regarded as a function in its own right.

items.title: Compiling Parallel APL
items.text:
The idea of compiling APL is now widely accepted. Several commercial products have already reached the market place. A compiler for a parallel APL could easily match the capabilities and performance of compilers for other parallel languages.

For badly written scalar-style APL code, the compiler could make use of all the technique in parallelizing compilers for other languages to optimise the APL code (perhaps this could even be de-compiled to show how the code could have been better written). At the very minimum, a parallel APL compiler could produce performance equivalent to a parallelizing compiler for a sequential language. If the full richness of the parallel constructs is utilised, better performance should be available.

items.title: Conclusions
items.text:
Parallel computing is becoming more and more important as a technology. Hardware products are becoming increasingly commercially available, machines such as the Transputer have achieved a certain degree of acceptance in the market place. IBM’s entry into the commercial world with the 3090 Vector Processor signals another stage in the development of commercial parallel hardware.

Currently the weakness in parallel technology is the lack of effective parallel programming tools. APL represents an excellent parallel programming tool of unparalleled (sic) power. The parallelism is inherent in the APL syntax. Unlike functional programming languages, APL presents opportunities for SPA, MPS and MPA form of parallelism. All these forms are available without any additional language constructs.

The possibilities for parallelism can be further enriched in APL by the addition of arrays of functions. These do not necessarily provide additional opportunities for parallelism, they do, however, make existing opportunities easier to exploit.

items.title: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 118

by D. B. Piper
path: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions

items.title: Abstract
items.text:
Many papers have already been published which discuss arrays of functions in APL. Some of the most significant are listed in the references at the end of this paper. Landaeta (LA86, LA88) and Bernecky (BE84) have made fairly rigorous proposals for APL2 and Sharp APL type interpreters respectively.

The basic concepts behind arrays of functions are discussed first. Landaeta’s proposal (LA86) is re-presented and criticised. Finally, the concept of semantic class is introduced, with an appropriate mechanism for the manipulation of arrays of functions.
path: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
APL supports operations on arrays of data:

      1 2 3 × 4 5 6
4 10 18

Scalar extension allows a constant to be specified as a scalar:

      2 × 4 5 6
8 10 12

An implementation that supports strand notation allows an expression of the sort:

      2 3 4 + 5 6 7                   ..(1)
7 9 11

to be re-written as:

      (2+5)(3+6)(4+7)                 ..(2)

At first glance, the expression

      (2=5)(3-6)(4×7)                 ..(3)

is very similar, but has no “in-stranded” version such as (1) above. An APL supporting arrays of functions would allow such a short form:

      2 3 4 (+ - ×) 5 6 7             ..(4)

The sub-expression (+ - ×) in (4) above is a vector of functions
path: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions

items.title: Operations on Arrays of Functions
items.text:
If a vector of functions can be created in a way analogous to a vector of data, it should be possible to manipulate function arrays in similar ways. For assignment:

      F ← + - ×                       ..(5)

we can then write

      2 3 4 F 5 6 7                   ..(6)

As Brown (BR84) points out, function assignment of this sort is a conforming extension of the syntax of APL2, since it currently produces a SYNTAX ERROR.

Once the concepts of functional arrays and assignment are adopted, it is a short step to manipulating arrays of functions. It is at this point that difficulties begin to arise.

  1. Syntax Class.

    APL embodies the concept of syntax class for each object (primitive or defined) in a workspace. Variables, functions and operators are each given a different class. Name class (as returned by the ⎕NC system function) is a concept similar to that of syntax class. Variables are given syntax class 0, functions class 1, and operators class 2.

    An object of a given syntax class operates on objects only of a lower syntax class. Functions operate on variables, creating new variables. Operators operate on functions (or variables) and return derived functions as a result.

    This restriction on the syntax class of arguments and operands is the basis of the problem. For example, if we wish to alter the shape of a function array, the re-shape function cannot be used since a function array has syntax class 1.

  2. Possible Solutions.

    The concept of a whole new set of operators to manipulate function arrays is impractical (BR84). Presumably it would also be desirable to manipulate arrays of operators, requiring objects of a new syntax class (called Transforms (BK84)). Arrays of transforms then come into question, and so on in an infinite regression.

    Landaeta (LA86, LA88) proposes the concept of an elevator object with a new syntax class. The elevator takes an object of syntax class N and returns a derived object of syntax class N + 1. Landaeta (LA86) uses the symbol $:

    ⍴$

    returns an operator which can be used to manipulate a function array. Repeated use of the elevator can produce an object of arbitrary syntax class, to operate on objects of the correct associated syntax class.

  3. Problems with the elevator.

    A number of problems can be identified with the use of the elevator. Firstly what is the syntax class of the elevator itself? Since it can produce an object of arbitrary syntax class, it can only be assigned an “infinite” syntax class. The problem of an infinite regression of syntax classes still exists.

    The derived object:

    ⍴$                                ..(7)

    is an operator (with syntax class 2), but obeys the syntactic rules of a function. Landaeta argued that since (7) is an ambivalent operator, which does not exist in APL2, a modified syntax was acceptable. This argument seems somewhat contrived and rather violates the idea of keeping APL syntax as simple as possible.
path: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions

items.title: Semantic Class
items.text:
The approach of changing the syntax class of an object gives rise to the problem mentioned above. Note, however, the concern is not with the syntax class of the operation in question, but rather with the syntax class of the arguments. The concept of changing the syntax class of an object without changing its syntactic properties is fundamentally flawed. Since the syntactic properties are not being changed, the syntax class should not be changed. Instead the semantic properties of the operation should be modified.

In order to define the semantic properties of an object, a three-item vector is defined for each object in the workspace. This defines the maximum syntax class of the left and right arguments and explicit result. Each item can take values 0, 1 or 2. The semantic property vector for a variable is empty. By default the semantic property vector for a function is 0 0 0, for an operator it is 1 1 1.

A new operator is defined to allow the semantic property vector to be manipulated. The CONTEXT operator is represented by $ (to maintain consistency with (LA86)). The left operand of CONTEXT is the object whose semantic properties are to be changed. The right operand is the new semantic property vector. The only unusual characteristic of the CONTEXT operator is its default semantic property vector - 2 1 2. The value of 2 for the left operand and explicit result semantic classes allows operators to be manipulated and returned.

  1. Use of CONTEXT.

    To reshape a function array:

    F ← + - ×
G ← 2 2(⍴$ 0 1 1)F                ..(8)

    In (8) above, the CONTEXT operator is used to change the semantic properties of the re-shape function, so that:

    The left argument is a variable. The right argument is a function. The result is a function.

    The array G will be a 2-by-2 function array.

    Catenation of function arrays:

    F ← + -
G ← × ÷
H ← F(,$ 1 1 1)G

    The derived catenate function has semantic class 1 for both arguments and its explicit result. A function vector is passed for both arguments. A new function vector is returned as the explicit result.

  2. Other Functions

          F ← × ÷ ⍴ ∨ ∧
      G ← + ⍴ ∊
      G(∊$ 1 1 0)F
0 1 0

    Membership is being used with both arguments of syntax class 1. The explicit result is of syntax class 0. Note that the symbols in a function vector are not the same as the equivalent symbols in a character vector.

          F ← × ÷ ⍴ ∨ ∧
      G ← '+⍴∊'
      G(∊$ 0 1 0)F
0 0 0

  3. Missing Syntax Classes

    The use of the CONTEXT operator allows objects of mixed syntax class to be created. These have special properties, which will be illustrated below:

    F ← + - ÷
V ← 1 2 3
X ← F(,$ 1 0 0)V

    X is a vector containing objects of both variable and function syntax class. An object of mixed syntax class inherits the highest syntax class of any of its constituents. The object X is therefore a function; it is a niladic function since a right argument is already present (and no function takes a left argument only). These properties can be illustrated:

          X                                ...(9)
¯1 ¯.5 ¯.33333

    Note that X is evaluated as if the expression

          + - ÷ 1 2 3

    had been typed, rather than:

          (+ - ÷) 1 2 3                    ...(10)
1 ¯2 .33333

    Other properties:

          ⍴X                               ⍝ SHAPE OF RESULT OF X
3

      (⍴$ 0 1 0)X                      ⍝ SHAPE OF VECTOR X
6

    Since X is evaluated, a problem arises over displaying the contents of X. In APL2, this can be achieved using the disclose function:

          (⊃$ 0 1 0)X
+ - ÷ 1 2 3

  4. Other mixed syntax-class objects

    The niladic function X is not very useful, however if a single argument is supplied on the left, a named monadic function can be created:

          INCREMENT←1 (,$ 0 1 1) +
      INCREMENT 3
4
      INCREMENT INCREMENT 4 5 6
6 7 8
      ⍴INCREMENT
SYNTAX ERROR
      ⍴INCREMENT
      ^^
      (⍴$ 0 1 0) INCREMENT
2
      (⊃$ 0 1 0) INCREMENT
1+

  5. Properties of mixed syntax-class objects

    From the above examples, (especially (9) and (10)), it is easy to see that a reference to an object containing mixed syntax classes causes an attempt at evaluation. In other words, many variables, functions or operators can be stranded together without any evaluation taking place. As soon as an attempt is made to mix syntax classes via stranding, evaluation is triggered. Objects of mixed syntax class have to be created by the use of catenation or some other function.
path: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions

items.title: User Defined Functions
items.text:
The creation of arrays of functions is not limited to primitive functions. Defined functions may also be used, with beneficial effects on several “traditional” APL problems. For example, in a menu-driven system, one technique for executing a function selected from a menu is to pick the function name from an array and then execute it. The problems associated with the use of execute are discussed elsewhere (PI86,PI88); its use should be avoided.

If function arrays are permitted, execute can be avoided:

      OPTS←OPT_1 OPT_2 OPT_3 OPT_4

      RC←(OPT_NO(⊃$ 0 1 1)OPTS) PARMS

The option number (OPT_NO) is used to pick the correct function from the list. The reference to this function with the argument PARMS causes its evaluation.

  1. ⎕CR and ⎕FX Redefined

    The system functions ⎕CR and ⎕FX are often criticised. ⎕FX is particularly criticised since the function is created as a side effect, it is not the explicit result of the function. ⎕FX could be redefined to use function assignment. The semantic vector of the new function is 0 0 2, that is it takes two data arguments and returns a function:

    MYFN←⎕FX ARRAY

    The right argument contains the code of the function (or defined operator). Note the function is assigned as the explicit result of the system function. The ⎕CR function is defined as the inverse of ⎕FX, its semantic property vector is 0 2 0.

    ARRAY←⎕CR MYFN

    Note the function is passed explicitly as the right argument (rather than simply being named as the right argument). The explicit result is the character representation of the function.

  2. The DEL Editor

    In the same way that ⎕FX was redefined, the DEL editor can be defined as a primitive function with semantic property vector 0 2 2:

    NEWFN← ∇OLDFN

    The facilities provided by DEL are of course implementation dependent. For editing a new function, the jot can be used to represent a null function:

    NEWFN← ∇ ∘

    The left argument of ∇ could be implemented either to specify the execution properties of the defined object (as with ⎕FX in APL2) or to pass an opening command to the editor (as a character vector).
path: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions

items.title: Function Headers
items.text:
Since the function is being named as the explicit result of both ⎕FX and the DEL editor, a question can be raised about the meaning of the function name specified in the function header line. The function assignment capability allows the meaning of names in the header to be rationalised.

Currently, all names in the header of a defined function are local, except for the function name. By explicitly assigning the function to a name, the function name specified in the header can be considered the local function name. This is particularly useful for recursive functions - consider the following definition of a recursive factorial function:

      CODE

R← ∆FACT NUM
⍝ RECURSIVE FACTORIAL FN.
R←1
→(NUM≤1)/0
R←NUM×∆FACT NUM-1

      FACTORIAL←⎕FX CODE
      FACTORIAL 4
24
      ∆FACT 4
VALUE ERROR
      ∆FACT 4
      ^

The benefit of this approach to recursive functions is that the interpreter “knows” it is re-invoking the same function all the time. Because of this knowledge, the local copy of the function re-invoked each time can be a “pre-parsed” version - all the work involving syntactic analysis is performed only once. The impact on performance of recursive code could be considerable.
path: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions

items.title: Conclusions
items.text:
The inclusion of arrays of functions into APL syntax seems at first glance to be a natural extension, relatively simple to implement. The number of papers written on the subject is mute testament to the difficulties that are encountered in practice.

The distinction drawn between syntactic and semantic properties appears to solve many of the problems. Functions remain functions but are semantically transformed to operate on arrays of functions rather than data. Contrast this to the approach of Landaeta where functions are transformed into operators, but retain the syntactic properties of functions.

The three-item semantic property vector allows the semantic properties of the left and right arguments and the explicit result to be specified independently.This independence can be used to rationalise the definitions of ⎕CR and ⎕FX as well as the DEL editor.

The assignment of functions as the explicit result of the editor or ⎕FX clarifies the meaning of the function name in the function header. This development presents the opportunity for a considerable improvement in the performance of recursive functions by removing one of the major performance overheads - the continual re-invocation of the same unit of code (note that some implementations have already by-passed this problem in other ways).

The introduction of arrays of functions to APL is probably the next major enhancement to the language following nested arrays. The implications for the power, flexibility and usability of the language are probably as great as they have been with nested arrays.
path: Semantic Class and Arrays of Functions
