items.title: PostScript Graphics in APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 76

by Adrian Smith (Rowntree Mackintosh Ltd)

items.title: Background
items.text:
The roots of this talk go way back to Vector No.1 Vol.4, which includes my notes on "Getting the Best out of GDDM". One of the points I made then was of the benefits of using IBM’s Presentation Graphics Facility (PGF) rather than the APL Graphpak workspace. PGF ran at least 5 times faster than Graphpak, and had the added virtue of requiring a mere 543 lines of code (of which about half were comments) instead of over 3600. It also led to pretty trivial APL code like:

    ∇ CH∆PIE MAT
[1] ⍝ Form data into multiple pie charts ...
[2] ⍝ one row makes each pie.

[3]   MAT←(¯2↑ 1 1 ,⍴MAT)⍴MAT
[4]   CTLs←796,(⍴MAT),,MAT
[5]   'FAILED TO DRAW PIE CHART' FSM∆ERR CTLs
    ∇

PGF was remarkably good at giving nice defaults for colours and shadings, and its algorithm for picking ‘good’ scales and tick intervals is still the best I have found. This meant that in the vast majority of cases you could simple say "Hi PGF … take that and gizza barchart" without a lot of preliminary setting up. Of course you needed to know that 796 was PGF-speak for "gizza piechart", but that was easy enough to bury in a cover function.

As things moved towards the PC, I kept thinking that someone somewhere must be working on this … all I had to do was sit around until a decent library of C routines came on the market, and I would be able to call these from APL. Occasionally things popped up like "The Turbo Pascal Graphics Toolbox", but invariable these stopped far short of the PGF functionality I was after. Nothing in the APL world went much beyond the basic "draw a polyline" functionality of ⎕Gxx, or GSS*CGI. OK, this is fine for drawing ducks with (as long as you have Dyalog APL!), but leaves all the hard work of designing an effective graphic to the application. "Bother, said Pooh."

items.title: PostScript Basics
items.text:
Your starter for 10 … name a computer language which:

  • has no silly precedence rules
  • has a matrix-inverse primitive
  • allows any array as an array element
  • allows assignment of both functions and variables, with no prior type declarations
  • makes no distinction between integers and reals, and automatically converts between them as required.

Hands up those who said APL!! The more perceptive amongst you might have taken note of the title, and said "PostScript", but I feel I ought to discount that as cheating … although you were quite correct. Obviously, there is no way I can teach you PostScript in half a page - all I want to do here is to leave you with the impression that PostScript is a lot like APL, and that the idea of coding in the "intersection" of the two languages is not as daft as it sounds.

Here is the PostScript to draw a square somewhere near the middle of a sheet of A4 paper (all measurements are in points, or 1/72"):

newpath                     % clear the current path
200 400 moveto              % bottom left corner
300 400 lineto 300 500 lineto 200 500 lineto
closepath                   % back to the start
2 setlinewidth              % use a 2-point line
stroke                      % draw round the path

showpage                    % print it!!

PostScript is entirely stack-based, i.e. all functions are niladic, and pull their input from a stack. If they produce results (none of the above do) the results are pushed on to the stack. You need to think ‘reverse Polish’ to do arithmetic, but otherwise you can get along quite well by regarding the syntax as ‘just like APL’, except that it executes from left to right! All functions are of the form:

    ∇ ARG LINETO DUM
[1]  ⍝ Draw line from current point to ARG
[2]    .... etc
    ∇

The other things you need to know are the syntax for assignment, for function definition, and for representing an array. Assignment is coded like this:

/PPI 72 def         % move the value 72 to the literal PPI
/TXT (Hello!) def   % strings get () round them

PPP←72          ⍝ Move the value 72 to the name PPI
TXT←'Hello!'    ⍝ Strings get '' round them

The def operator takes a literal (the leading ‘/’ flags literals) and a value off the stack, and stuffs the latter into the former. It also allows function assignment:

/M {moveto} def      % for lazy typists
/inch {72 mul} def   % allows us to work in inches

4 inch 6 inch M      % .... etc.

Obviously, functions can call other functions (including themselves), and can refer to defined variables. Everything is global by default, although you can manipulate contexts to give the effect of localisation (see [1] and [2] for details). Arrays are very similar to APL:

/ARRAY [1 2 3 4] def    % 4-element array
[23 34 45 56] 4 3       % 3-element nested array

ARRAY←1 2 3 4           ⍝ 4-element vector
(23 34 45 56) 4 3       ⍝ 3-element nested vector

I think that should be enough to start with … if you really want to know PostScript properly, you should get the Blue Book [1] and the Red Book [2] and a PostScript printer (or some software like GoScript which will put the results on the screen … much cheaper!) and play with it.

items.title: Motivation
items.text:
As Vector moved gradually up-market in its presentation, I began to feel the need of some ‘publication-quality’ graphics for things like benchmark timings. The charts in question were extremely simple, typically just line-graphs or multiple barcharts, but it was important to get the typesetting details right if the result was to look good on the page. It was pretty obvious that PostScript had just what I needed when it came to detailed control over type sizes and text rotation and placement, so I began to play with some basic routines for things like axis-drawing and labelling.

Roughly at the same time, various parts of my user-community began to agitate for the same graphics support on the PC as they had been used to on the mainframe with PGF … clearly I could no longer afford to wait for someone else to implement PGF as an AP (or in STSC’s case ⎕BARCHART, ⎕PIECHART and so on!!). The trigger was provided by a weather station which Richard was given for Christmas … we were accumulating daily records of rainfall and temperature, and soon wanted to produce graphs like this:

As always, when you finally summon the energy to start hacking, things are much easier than you thought they would be. Essentially the exercise splits into two parts:

  1. Write the APL bits for the things PostScript does, but APL lacks (like text handling, scaling and rotation).
  2. Write the PostScript bits for the things APL does (like Polylines, Polybars - ⎕GSHADE, and polymarks).

You can then code in the comfortable region where the languages intersect, with appropriate supporting routines to cover the remainder. As a bonus, it turned out that the HP plotter language HPGL also maps nicely to this region, and it took about half a day to get my functions driving an HP7550! I suspect that the same is true of any vector graphics language (e.g. the new AP207 that comes with APL2/PC); certainly having skimmed the booklet on GSS*CGI that comes with Dyalog APL, I am quite sanguine about implementing all this lot on any APL you can think of!

items.title: Stage-1: The APL End
items.text:
The examples which follow are all from APL*PLUS/PC, using ⎕G-style graphics. I have not attempted complete coverage … if any of this code would be any use to you, APL-385 will oblige for £10 to cover the cost of the disk and postage..

To begin at the beginning … PostScript handles translation, scaling and rotation by holding a ‘Current Transformation Matrix’ in the classical form [3]:

    1     0    0
    0     1    0
   tx    ty    1     ... translation

   sx     0    0
    0    sy    0
    0     0    1     ... x/y scaling

 cosθ  sinθ    0
-sinθ  cosθ    0
    0     0    1     ... rotation counterclockwise by θ

The matrix starts as CTM←3 3⍴4↑1, and successive transformations are applied by matrix multiplications, for example:

    ∇ X ROTATE DUM;D2R
[1]  ⍝ Catenate rotation to current transformation matrix

[2]   D2R←(○2)÷360
[3]   X← 3 3 ↑ 2 2 ⍴ 1 1 ¯1 1 × 2 1 1 2 ○X×D2R ⋄ X[3;3]←1
[4]   CTM←X+.×CTM
    ∇

When it comes to drawing lines, we follow the PostScript philosophy of building a path, and deciding later whether to draw round it (with stroke) or shade it in (with fill). Both these clear the path automatically, but the nervous can use newpath to make sure they start with a clean slate:

    ∇ NEWPATH DUM
[1]  ⍝ Set up an empty path. Cols are [x,y,0/1]
[2]   PATH← 0 3 ⍴0
    ∇

    ∇ A LINETO DUM
[1]  CPT←A ⋄ PATH←PATH⍪(3↑A,1)+.×CTM
    ∇

    ∇ X MOVETO DUM;NP;LEN
[1]     ⍝ Add / update pen move to current path.
[2]      CPT←X
[3]      NP←(3↑X,1)+.×CTM ⋄ LEN←(⍴PATH)[1] ⋄ →LEN↓Add
[4]      →PATH[LEN;3]↑Add
[5]  Rpl:PATH[LEN; 1 2]←2↑NP ⋄ →0
[6]  Add:PATH←PATH⍪3↑2↑NP
    ∇

    ∇ STROKE DUM;SEG;LEN
[1]     ⍝ Draw line segments in PATH, and clear it.
[2]  Loop:LEN←(1↓PATH[;3])⍳0
[3]      SEG←(LEN,2)↑PATH
[4]      GS∆DRAW SEG
[5]      PATH←(LEN,0)↓PATH ⋄ →(1↑⍴PATH)↑Loop
    ∇

GS∆DRAW is a very thin cover on ⎕GLINE. Similar functions will do for the PostScript basics like displaying text:

    ∇ TXT SHOW DUM;XY
[1]  ⍝ Dummy version of () show
[2]   XY←2↑(CPT,1)+.×CTM
[3]   (XY,FONTSCL)GS∆CHAR TXT
[4]   (TXT STRINGWIDTH ⍬)RMOVETO ⍬
    ∇

… but when it comes to working out the space occupied by graphics text, things get nastily device-dependent, not to mention the fact that in APL we are limited to integer multiples of the basic font size:

    ∇ R←TXT STRINGWIDTH DUM;WID;GT
[1]     ⍝ Find width of text string in current font.
[2]     ⍝ Note that this varies for different adaptors!
[3]      WID← 5.16 6.88 6.34 5.42 ⍝ Herc, CGA, EGA, VGA
[4]      GT←4 ⋄ →(0=⎕NC '∆GTYPE')↑Skip ⍝ Assume VGA
[5]      GT←4⌊'HCEV'⍳1↑∆GTYPE
[6]  Skip:R←2↑WID[GT]×FONTSCL×⍴,TXT
    ∇

    ∇ SIZE SCALEFONT DUM
[1]  ⍝ Rough mimic of scalefont
[2]   FONTSCL←1⌈⌊0.5+0.1×SIZE×CTM[1;1]
    ∇

So much for the basics … of course APL is much more efficient when dealing with vectors, so we would really like to work with a polyline:

    ∇ VEC PL DUM;LEN
[1]  ⍝ APL version of polyline, as used by CH∆LINE etc.
[2]  ⍝ Adds line to path ... it will still need stroking!
[3]  ⍝ Last elements give colour, style and thickness

[4]   VEC[¯2+⍴VEC]SETCOLOUR ⍬ ⋄ VEC[¯1+⍴VEC]SETLINESTYLE ⍬
[5]   VEC[⍴VEC]SETLINEWIDTH ⍬ ⋄ VEC←¯3↓VEC
[6]   LEN←⌊0.5×⍴VEC ⋄ VEC←(LEN,2)⍴VEC
[7]   VEC←(VEC,1)+.×CTM
[8]   PATH←PATH⍪VEC[; 1 2],~LEN↑1
    ∇

This is just like lineto, except that it expects a vector of x/y pairs, with some extra bits on the end giving the line attributes. These just get bunged into a rat’s nest of globals (except for the line width, which is a dummy). Now let’s have a look at the PostScript end of all this!

items.title: Stage-2: The PostScript End
items.text:
Another respect in which PostScript is like APL is in its orthogonality. As long as we disregard ⎕functions, APL has almost no redundancy in the primitives; you add new ones to suit your convenience. You might expect to see PostScript functions for right-aligned and vertical text, but (as with APL) you must make your own:

/cshow      % centre text round current point
{ dup stringwidth pop
  neg 2 div 0 rmoveto show
} def

/vshow      % vertical text ... for y-axis titles
{ gsave 90 rotate
  dup stringwidth pop
  neg 0 rmoveto show
  grestore
} def

You might also expect to see a whole string of parameters to specify the writing direction of text … again there is no such nonsense! You simply save the Current Transformation Matrix with gsave, rotate the paper, write your text normally, and restore afterwards with grestore.

Now for something more interesting: the PostScript version of the APL function to tackle Polylines. I shall try to explain this one in detail, because it illustrates a lot of useful concepts. If you are still struggling over the logic of cshow, all should shortly become clear!!

/pL  % Polyline: stack is array of [x,y] pairs; colour style width
  { setlinewidth setlinestyle setcolour
    /xy exch def
    /npts xy length 2 idiv 1 sub def % halve the shape
    xy aload pop                     % disclose it
    moveto                           % pen to 1st point
    npts { lineto } repeat           % loop for each pair
  } def                              % will need stroking!

The top line is mostly a comment, describing what our function expects to find on the stack: this is always good practice when documenting PostScript code. We then peel off the last three elements (in backwards order remember) to set the line attributes. The functions setlinewidth etc. are all primitives.

The next line assigns the remaining element (the array of x/y pairs) to a variable xy (the exch primitive exchanges the top two things on the stack). In order to find out the number of line segments to draw, we need one less than half the shape (remembering the initial moveto):

NPTS←¯1+⌊(⍴XY)÷2      ⍝ /npts xy length 2 idiv 1 sub def

We then disclose (or aload) the array; this dumps the array contents onto the stack, plus the array itself, which we discard with a pop! The stack now holds an even number of x/y pairs, so we pick up the first set with a moveto, and then hoover up the rest by looping npts times. At the end of this, we have the entire polyline defined in the current path, so we can either draw round it with stroke, shade it in with fill, or even make it the outline of a clipping region with clip.

/wedge    % shaded pie slice: stack is x,y,r,α,β,pattern,width
  { setlinewidth setpattern
    /beta exch def /alpha exch def /radius exch def
    /y exch def /x exch def
    x y moveto                    % start at sector root
    x y radius alpha beta arc     % line to edge, and arc
    closepath                     % back to the middle
    gsave currentpatn grestore    % shade it
    [] 0 setdash stroke           % and solid edge
  } def

Here is another example … this time PostScript is quite close to APL in the way we draw arcs, so the code is almost trivial. I’m sure I could get away without all those variables, but my brain starts to hurt as soon as I have to deal with anything not on the top of the stack, so I got lazy and just snaffled the lot at the start! Shading patterns are quite interesting:

/setpattern % set current graphics pattern: stack is int [1..12]
  { /case exch def
    case 0 eq { /currentpatn {} def } if                         % No fill
    case 1 eq { /currentpatn { .98 setgray fill } def } if       % Light grey
    case 2 eq { /currentpatn { .9  setgray fill } def } if       % Medium
    case 3 eq { /currentpatn { .8  setgray fill } def } if       % Darker
    case 4 eq { /currentpatn { .5  setgray fill } def } if       % Half tone

    case 5 eq { /currentpatn   % diagonal shading
                { gsave 1 setgray fill grestore
                  clip newpath 0.2 setlinewidth [] 0 setdash
                  0 6 patscale mul 600 { -60 moveto -240 360 rlineto } for
                  stroke } def  } if

 .... etc

What we are doing is dynamically defining the currentpattern function (analogous to fixing a function with ⎕FX before using it elsewhere) to fill the current path with the selected pattern. Pattern 0 does nothing, patterns 1 to 4 are progressively darker greys, then the fun begins! To get a diagonal shading, we first fill the path with white (using 1 setgray fill), then set it to be the clipping region, and simply shade the whole page! The same strategy works for all the obvious cross-hatchings, which is why I haven’t bored you with the rest of the code.

Markers are dealt with in a very similar way. First we need a polymark routine:

/pM  % Polymark: stack is array of [x,y] pairs; colour marker-type
  { setmarker setcolour
    /xy exch def
    /npts xy length 2 idiv def            % halve the shape
    xy aload pop gsave                    % disclose it
    0.3 setlinewidth                      % set correct weight
    [] 0 setdash  newpath                 % and solid lines
    npts { moveto currentmark } repeat    % loop for each group
    grestore
  } def

Then we need to fix ourselves a currentmark function for repeated use at each x/y pair:

/setmarker  % set current graphics marker : stack is int [1..15]
  { /case exch def

    case 1 eq { /currentmark  % cross
     { -1 -1 rmoveto 2 2 rlineto 0 -2 rmoveto
       -2 2 rlineto stroke } def } if

    case 2 eq { /currentmark  % plus sign
     { -1 0 rmoveto 2 0 rlineto -1 -1 rmoveto
        0 2 rlineto stroke } def } if


 .... and so on

Note that the markers are careful to use relative moves and lines; this is a typical PostScript device to make such functions re-usable. Finally, font selection and size:

/settext  % set text parameters: colour, Size in pts, SSID (0-34)
  { /ssid exch def  /size exch def  setcolour
    ssid  0 eq { /Times-Roman findfont  } if
    ssid  1 eq { /Times-Italic findfont  } if
    ssid  2 eq { /Times-Bold findfont  } if
    ssid  3 eq { /Times-BoldItalic findfont  } if
    ssid  4 eq { /Helvetica findfont  } if
    ssid  5 eq { /Helvetica-Oblique findfont  } if

    ....

    ssid 32 eq { /Palatino-BoldItalic findfont  } if
    ssid 33 eq { /ZapfChancery-MediumItalic findfont  } if
    ssid 34 eq { /ZapfDingbats findfont  } if
    size scalefont setfont
  } def

This has the effect of burying the font names (which you have to get exactly right, including the capitalisation) where I need never see them again.

items.title: Putting it all to Work
items.text:
I would like to end by showing you a selection of examples, where possible with explanations of anything I have so far failed to cover. First, a simple piechart, with spider labels and a heading:

The APL code which generated this undoubted work of art:

    ∇ R←VPIE
[1]  ⍝ VECTOR PIE DEMO
[2]   CHHEAD 'Here be a Piechart'
[3]   CHXLAB 'Fred;Joe;Harry;Albert;Bill'
[4]   CHSET 'CBOX' ⋄ 'HMAR' CHSET 0 1
[5]   CHPIE 12 8 9 18 23
[6]   CHTERM
[7]   R←'PS PG  ⍝ TO SEE IT'
    ∇

… old PGF hands will recognise some of the syntax, and also the mnemonics like ‘CBOX’ to get the chart are boxed! The output from this function is a simple text vector of PostScript code:

newpath gsave  % before we translate the origin
[ 4 4 422 4 422 316 4 316 ] 15 1 1.5 pL
closepath # stroke

40 4 translate

11 18 1 settext # 177 294 M # (Here be a Piechart) cshow

15 10 0 settext
185 150 105 28.3 90 2 0.5 wedge
[233.5 231.1 246.9 253.7] 15 1 .6 pL # stroke
249.9 250.7 M # (Fred) show

185 150 105 -12.9 28.3 6 0.5 wedge
[278.6 162.7 304.7 166.2] 15 1 .6 pL # stroke
307.7 163.2 M # (Joe) show

185 150 105 -59.1 -12.9 1 0.5 wedge
[261.5 94.5 282.7 79] 15 1 .6 pL # stroke
285.7 76 M # (Harry) show

185 150 105 -151.7 -59.1 5 0.5 wedge
[159.9 58.9 152.9 33.6] 15 1 .6 pL # stroke
149.9 30.6 M # (Albert) rshow

185 150 105 -270 -151.7 10 0.5 wedge
[103.9 198.5 81.3 211.9] 15 1 .6 pL # stroke
78.3 208.9 M # (Bill) rshow

grestore
showpage

… note that the ‘#’ characters have nothing to do with PostScript … they get treated as diamonds by my APL code, and are mapped to ⎕TCNL when I write out the file for printing. With a bit more trouble I could get APL to infer these line breaks, and save myself the trouble of putting them in by hand.

…. the bulk of the hard grind having taken place in CH∆PIE:

    ∇ R←CH∆PIE VEC;lab;CT;LAB;TG;TGS;CEN;RAD;ARC;HA;YL;XL;EXP;PEXP
[1]      ⍝ Piechart from given sectors

[2]       TGS←CH⍙XLAB ⋄ TGS←((⍴VEC),¯1↑⍴TGS)⍴TGS
[3]       R←'' ⋄ →(∨/'VALU'⍷CH⍙SET)↓Cum

[4]      ⍝ Add sector values to pie tags ....

[5]       TGS←Lj(Rj TGS),((××/⍴TGS)/((⍴VEC),2)⍴': '),Lj⍕((⍴VEC),1)⍴VEC
[6]  Cum:VEC←+\VEC ⋄ VEC←VEC×360÷¯1↑VEC ⋄ VEC←0,VEC
[7]       PEXP←0⌈0.01×(⍴VEC)↑CH⍙PEXP
[8]       XL←(-/CH⍙AREA[3 1])-+/CH⍙VMAR
[9]       YL←(-/CH⍙AREA[4 2])-+/CH⍙HMAR
[10]      R←(⍕CH⍙LATT),' settext',⎕TCNL,R

[11]     ⍝ Find the centre, and a sensible radius ....

[12]      CEN←0.5×(XL,YL) ⋄ RAD←0.35×XL⌊YL

[13]     ⍝ Build segments and tags as we go round ......

[14] Loop:→lab←1+((¯1+⍴VEC)⍴Loop),End,CT←1
[15]      HA←0.5×+/90-VEC[CT+ 1 0]
[16]      EXP←PEXP[CT]×RAD× 2 1 ○HA×(○1)÷180
[17]      ARC←(CEN+EXP),RAD,90-VEC[CT+ 1 0]
[18]      R←R,(CH∆FMT ARC),' ',(⍕1↑CH⍙PATN),' 0.5 wedge ',⎕TCNL
[19]      TG←(2 2 ⍴ARC[1 2])+ 0.9 1.15 ∘.×ARC[3]× 2 1 ○HA×(○1)÷180
[20]      LAB←Lj TGS[CT;] ⋄ LAB←(+/∨\⌽' '≠LAB)↑LAB ⋄ →(0∊⍴LAB)↑Skip

[21]     ⍝ ========== SPIDER TAGS ===========

[22]      R←R,'[',(CH∆FMT TG),'] ',(⍕CH⍙LATT[1]),' 1 .6 pL # stroke ',⎕TCNL
[23]      →(180<90-HA)↑Lft
[24]   Rt:R←R,(CH∆FMT 3 ¯3 +TG[2;]),' M # (',LAB,') show',2⍴⎕TCNL ⋄ →Skip
[25]  Lft:R←R,(CH∆FMT ¯3 ¯3 +TG[2;]),' M # (',LAB,') rshow',2⍴⎕TCNL
[26] Skip:CH⍙KDEF←CH⍙KDEF⍪5↑2,CH⍙PATN[1] ⋄ CH⍙PATN←1⌽CH⍙PATN
[27]  End:→lab[CT←CT+1]
    ∇

The only utility function I need to describe is CH∆FMT …

    ∇ R←CH∆FMT X
[1]  ⍝ Format data to 1dpl and subst APL negatives.
[2]   X←0.1×⌊0.5+X×10 ⋄ R←⍕,X ⋄ R[(R∊'¯')/⍳⍴R]←'-'
    ∇

Because my printer only resolves to 1/300 of an inch, I reckon I am quite safe rounding distances to 1/10 of a point. I then can just use the APL primitive format (actually it is ideal as it only shows decimal places if there are any, thus saving space), being careful to map the APL high minus to an ordinary dash.

To put it on the screen, I simply run my DIY PostScript interpreter (I don’t think I showed you WEDGE in APL):

    ∇ SPEC WEDGE DUM;XY
[1]  ⍝ Cover PostScript Wedge routine ... x,y,r,from,to,pat,width
[2]   1 GS∆USE SPEC[6] ⋄ SPEC[7]SETLINEWIDTH ⍬ ⋄ SPEC←¯2↓SPEC
[3]   XY←SPEC[1 2] ⋄ SPEC←(2↓SPEC),1
[4]  ⍝ X-scale determines size of pie ... ratio is used as the ellipticity.
[5]   SPEC[1]←SPEC[1]×CTM[1;1]
[6]   SPEC[4]←CTM[2;2]÷CTM[1;1]
[7]   XY←2↑(XY,1)+.×CTM
[8]   15 GS∆WEDGE XY,SPEC
    ∇

    ∇ CLR GS∆WEDGE ARC;D2R;SEED;R;ASP
[1]  ⍝ Pass vector of pie wedge detail ...
[2]  ⍝ ARC: x, y, r, init angle, final angle (in degrees), aspect ratio
[3]  ⍝ The colour was set up by GS∆USE in GS⍙DEF[1].
[4]  ⍝
[5]   ⍎(0=⎕NC 'CLR')/'CLR←15⌊8+GS⍙DEF[1]' ⋄ ⍎(2=GS⍙DEF[6])/'CLR←×CLR'
[6]   R←⎕GMASK ¯1 ⋄ D2R←180÷○1 ⋄ ARC←6↑ARC,1
[7]   ASP←1,ARC[6] ⋄ ARC←ARC÷ 1 1 1 ,D2R,D2R,GS⍙DEF[5]
[8]  ⍝ Find a safe seed point in the middle of the sector!
[9]   SEED←ARC[1 2]+ASP×0.8×ARC[3]× 2 1 ○0.5×+/ARC[4 5]
[10]  ARC[1 3]←GS⍙DEF[5]×ARC[1 3]
[11]  CLR ⎕GCIRCLE 1 1 6 ⍴ARC
[12] ⍝ Fills with GS⍙DEF[1] ... edges with CLR
[13]  GS∆PAINT SEED,CLR
    ∇

… and the result looks a bit like this (what I get on my DeskJet when I hit ⎕GPRINT from APL*PLUS):

I get something rather similar from my HP plotter, only here the functions build an HPGL string instead of a PostScript string, for example:

    ∇ TXT RSHOW DUM;XY
[1]  ⍝ HPGL version of () rshow

[2]   XY←2↑(CPT,1)+.×CTM
[3]   HPGL←HPGL,'PA ',(⍕XY),';'
[4]   HPGL←HPGL,'LO7;LB',TXT,'∊̲',nl
    ∇

… and of course the colours work rather better!!

One final example, just to prove to those guys at MetaPraxis that anything they can do, I can do too….

items.title: Summary
items.text:
I am now reasonably convinced that it will be hard to buy a printer without PostScript in 5 years’ time. I suppose it will have to do Epson and HP emulation as well, but the simplification of having a single standard approach to both text and graphics is overwhelming. Just think how many fewer disks WordPerfect would come on if it only supported one type of printer! Accordingly, it makes sense to target your graphics on PostScript as the primary device, and let the rest take care of themselves. As it happens, it is pretty straightforward to convert the PostScript code to HPGL anyway (I think I have seen some public domain stuff which claims to do the whole job), but there are other benefits:

  • the resulting graphic is amazingly compact. The whole of that MetaPraxis chart takes up a mere 2856 bytes of disk. If you saved it as a monochrome bit image, it would be well over 1Mbyte … multiply by 16 for colour! As well as saving on disk space, this cuts down on network traffic, and gets the print done very much faster. It took GoScript a lot less time to print the high-quality version of my piechart than it took APL to do the screen dump!
  • you can easily pull it back from disk and reshow it on the screen. In fact it is pretty trivial to define functions ABOVE and BESIDE to let you tile the screen with as many charts as you like … obviously a handy thing for slide shows.
    ∇ R←A ABOVE B
[1]  ⍝ Put two charts above and below

[2]   R←'gsave # 1 .5 scale # ',B
[3]   R←R,'# 0 316 translate # ',A,' # grestore '
    ∇

    ∇ R←A BESIDE B
[1]  ⍝ Put two charts side by side

[2]   R←'gsave # .5 1 scale # ',A
[3]   R←R,'# 422 0 translate # ',B,' #  grestore'
    ∇
  • the results really are publication-quality! If you have a half-way decent word-processor, you can link them in to your final copy, and again the print file is far more compact than it would be if you link in bitmap graphics (such as the output from PC-Paintbrush).

Of course, there are one or two snags! PostScript is quite happy with the idea of rotating anything you put on the page, but of course APL fails to rotate the text, and you also come adrift on things like polybar, as this calls ⎕GSHADE, which expects to be given the corners of a rectangle, not a parallelogram!! As a final tour de force, here is my piechart again, this time prefaced with:

130 150 translate
.8 .4 scale
30 rotate

This works beautifully in real PostScript, but I would advise you not to attempt it with my APL version, except possibly for its amusement value at BAA meetings!

items.title: Why I like MS Windows
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 78

items.title: Why I Like Windows
items.text: by Richard Smith (age 7)

items.title: The Mouse
items.text: The mouse is easier to handle than the keyboard, that is, except when dog-hairs get on the ball and the mouse sticks. The only thing about it is, I would like a bigger space to move it in! The mouse’s buttons are also nice - they’re a good size.

items.title: The Icons
items.text: Icons are not only easy to design (if you’ve got an hDC Icon Designer), but they are also easy to ‘do’, because all you have to do is click the hDC icon (a red box with hDC written in it) and select Icon Designer from the menu. When Icon Designer has loaded, a rectangular window will appear. This window will have a: a squared square for ‘doing’ your icons and b: a space which shows all your finished icons. Talking about putting windows down to ‘icons’ is explained in the Windows section. Icons are the little ‘pictures’ in the windows at the start-up.

items.title: Comparing with the Keyboard
items.text: For most things it is either easier or the only possible way to use the mouse. But for some things it is impossible to use the mouse, things like APL or RCS are ‘keyboard only’ functions, and these functions are accessible from Microsoft Windows, or, at least, can be made to be. To pull a menu down, press Alt with the underlined letter in the menu word, then to select an option, press the underlined letter, and you’ve got your option!

items.title: The Windows
items.text: The windows can be worked by the keyboard, for example: in games Alt G gives you the games menu, but this isn’t as easy as doing it with the mouse. When you put a window down to an icon, an icon, usually its own, goes down under Program Manager, with its name label underneath it. By getting hold of window ‘title bars’(the blue/brown stripe at the top of the windows - blue if you are currently using that window, brown otherwise) with the mouse, you can move windows. After moving a window, it will have a blue title bar, until you either click or move a different window.

items.title: Window Menus
items.text: The menus at the top of windows like Write can be used easily, even with the keyboard (as explained in Comparing with the Keyboard). All you have to do with the mouse, though, is click the menu you want and then click the option you want.

items.title: Iconising Uses
items.text: If you are working with anything running under Microsoft Windows and somebody comes and pesters because he/she wants to do something else, you can put whatever you’re using down to an icon (as explained in The Windows). After doing this he/she can get on with whatever they want to, but you haven’t lost your work. After he/she has finished on the computer, you can get on with your work. Putting the start-up windows down to icons saves space.

items.title: Window Buttons
items.text: The buttons at the top of every window can only be ‘pressed’ with the mouse, and I think that there ought to be a way of making use of those buttons with the keyboard. Other than that, the windows are well designed, because they are easy to use with a mouse, as all you have to do is click the left mouse button on the window button you want.

items.title: Why I Like Microsoft Windows?
items.text: by Adrian Smith (Age 38)

items.title: A User’s View
items.text:
A couple of old advertising slogans come immediately to mind: “every home should have one” and “so simple even the cat could use it”. I have no idea what the former was trying to sell me; I believe the latter had something to do with John Cleese and Sony video recorders … anyway …. as Richard rightly points out, Windows software is easier to use than the old text-based stuff. The interesting question is why?

Obviously, for anything involving pointing or drawing, the mouse is an enormous improvement over the keyboard. However in itself this doesn’t explain why Windows software like Powerpoint is an order of magnitude easier to work with than (say) Lotus Freelance. The same difficulty occurs in explaining why Windows Write can be picked up by a 7-year old with absolutely zero instruction, and yet an old warhorse like WordPerfect takes a 3-day course, and you still don’t know how to get a PostScript print to file!

For what it’s worth, I think there are two key reasons why Windows software is a real step forward in both functionality and ease of use:

  • the underlying philosophy. You hear a lot of loose talk these days about empowering the user. I say loose talk advisedly, because of course empowered users are exactly what your average IT department hates. Windows is aimed squarely at individuals; it is another step in freeing users from the strictures imposed by corporate IT, and as such it is both a powerful and a dangerous idea.
  • absolute consistency of use. We have IBM and their CUA guidelines to thank for this one! A lot of developers seem to think that they can claim CUA compatibility simply by strapping on a pull-down menu bar, and using the ‘right’ colour scheme; this is rubbish. Real CUA applications rigorously apply the ‘object-action’ model to dialogues (the converse is neatly illustrated by Lotus-123, where you always pick an action before you select the patch of the spreadsheet to do it to); real CUA applications have a set of menus going ‘File … Edit … View … Options …. Help’, with the Print command under the File menu; real CUA applications already know what printers you have available, and where the output is to go; real CUA applications use your personal choice of colours … and so on.

The main reason why Powerpoint is easier than Freelance is because you can learn it incrementally from Paintbrush; it has a ‘line tool’ and a ‘text tool’ which operate just like the ones you played with before. It also has a ‘text edit’ tool which behaves just like Windows Write, except that it works in a stretchable frame within your artwork. Strangely enough, the spell-checker in Powerpoint is just like the spell-checker in Word, and you can even get them to share dictionaries! If you want to move things around, then you just learned all the necessary skills playing Solitaire and Backgammon, … and so on.

In summary, as a user I like Windows because I am all for giving individuals the freedom to exploit their environment in any way they choose. In the long term, I believe that companies which encourage employees to do this will prosper better than companies which try to control their employees’ every move. By providing an environment where all software looks and operates in the same way, Windows and CUA make it far more practical for users to choose the best package for the job, safe in the knowledge that they won’t be faced with a whole new set of commands and menus.

Oh by the way … you can do things like multitasking and cut-and-paste and background printing. So what! Fast task-switching is all I really use, and I could have had that with Software Carousel for £50 under DOS on my old XT! Windows does the job very prettily (as long as you have an extra £25 to spend on an Icon designer), but I cannot see something selling 3 million copies simply by offering a nice ‘point-and-grunt’ DOS menu and an efficient task switcher, can you?

items.title: A Programmer’s View
items.text:
Cast your mind back to the heyday of motoring, maybe around 1908 when you could have a really fabulous day out in your new machine; OK it frightened the horses, and you soon got used to the joys of retrieving the contents of a ball-race from half a mile of loose gravel … but this was real motorist stuff … no quiche eaters here! But the skills needed to operate the old horse and trap were simple and well-known, and it could beat the fancy new machinery to town and back any day of the week; why on earth should anyone want to change?

I reckon I can operate the old horse and trap technology pretty well … it took me about an hour to write a little C routine to send a bunch of files to a PostScript printer, suitably wrapped up in font selection and pagination. I know how to read and write files, and if I want to display some output, I simply use a file called ‘stdout’ and everything duly appears on the screen. Similarly in APL; we have always had the simple convention that if you leave the result of a statement hanging in mid-air, APL outputs it to the standard output device (usually a screen) after applying some default formatting rules.

Can we continue for ever with the simple life? The motor car opened up vastly wider horizons, and made possible journeys that could never be contemplated in horse-drawn days; once tempted by the promise of a better tomorrow, you will find it hard to stay with the old ways!

Life begins to get a harder once you let your application have full control of the screen. You might need to direct output to specific fields (in GDDM mainframe terms):

'A' FSM∆PUT 6 2⍕DATA
'B' FSM∆PUT DESCR

… and you need to be a bit fussier about getting the shape and type of the data right. On the PC you probably just bung things in windows, and assume that the windows utility will handle details like nice borders, scrolling, and so on:

2 3 WIN∆PUT ⎕NL 3   ⍝ Display function names in scrolling wdw

What you tend to forget is that some muggins has put in an inordinate amount of time and effort in making things this easy! WIN∆PUT is about 40 lines of very solid APL (in APL*PLUS/PC with ⎕WPUT, about 25 lines in Dyalog with ⎕SM) which took a good deal of designing and debugging. On the mainframe, I wouldn’t know a 126 ⎕SVO 'CTLS' if it jumped out and bit me, and yet I once wrote all that low-level stuff to manage the screen through GDDM calls.

My first reaction on opening the manual for the Windows Software Development Kit (the SDK for short) was that it was just like opening the GDDM Application Programmers Guide for the first time. It is written in English, so you feel you ought to be able to understand it, and yet there are so many unfamiliar concepts, and a lot of the words have new, precisely defined, meanings. In short, there is a big learning curve to go up before you can even think about things which were previously almost trivial! Take the obvious example … here is the “hello, world” program in C and in APL:

main()
{ printf("hello, world\n"); }   /* K&R page 6 */

     'hello, world'     ⍝ APL wins even here!

Compare this with Peter Donnelly’s sample to get ‘Press Here’ on the simplest X-widget: a button. Just what happens to you when you ‘realise your widget tree’ (see page 116)? Why might you want your application to activateCallback? Do you really need all that portmanteau of code just to display a simple message? How on earth can ordinary mortals hope to generate useful systems ever again??

Of course the answer is the same as the resolution to the horseless-carriage dilemma (it was predicted that by 1925 half the world’s population would be chauffeurs); we don’t all need to become expert mechanics to drive a modern car. Most of us don’t even know how a modern car works (could you fix the electronic ignition on your 16v fuel-injected Japanese toy?); we just turn on the engine and drive away. It took around 20 years for the car to evolve from a complex engineering marvel to a commodity (Henry Ford had a lot to do with it); the interesting question is how long it will take for windows to get to the same state.

items.title: The Next Two Years
items.text:
Over the next two years, we really are going to see the shape of things to come. The APL developers are already taking the first tentative steps towards integration of MS Windows and X/Motif into the APL development environment (of course MicroAPL and I-APL have already done it for the Mac). I appreciate Peter’s argument that 18 lines of APL is better than 72 lines of C, but I want to write 1 line of APL:

ACTION←XYPOS X∆BUTTON 'Press Here'

… what’s more I don’t want a couple of hundred things with names like disarmCallback listed whenever I do )FNS. For cheap and cheerful output, I want to use the APL default display, and have the user think I just wrote something really fancy in X. If the user grabs my window and pulls it all out of shape, I don’t want my code scattered with ⎕TRAPs just so I can recover. All that stuff should be buried in utilities where the application need never see it.

I think we need two things to happen:

  1. The APL interpreter writers must provide the basic hooks into the underlying window manager in a tolerably clean way. I have a personal preference for auxiliary processors, but if STSC chose to implement another 100 ⎕functions I shouldn’t really mind.
  2. A bunch of APL systems programmers (people who don’t mind coding at the AP level, or who can handle ⎕WIN without flinching) should get together and define a common application-level interface for APL under windows. This should be common across all the different window managers (the Mac, MS Windows, X/Motif etc.) and it should also be common across all the available APLs (APL.68000, APL2/6000, Dyalog APL, APL*PLUS, I-APL etc.).

The first of these is already well underway, and is clearly going to generate the usual variety of different approaches to the same task. The hard part is to motivate someone to begin work on the second; clearly it is in no vendor’s direct interest to write vendor-independent code, and yet in the long term all the vendors will sink or swim together. Just as the car makers reached a rapid consensus on the ‘proper’ positions for the accelerator and brake, so should the APL vendors on the ‘proper’ way to program a push-button. STSC and Sharp did it for component files, so it should be possible for Dyadic, MicroAPL and the rest to do it for windows! The CUA Advanced Interface Guide would be a good place to start.

items.title: Hackers Corner: Proportional Tables in PostScript
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 92

by Adrian Smith

My immediate problem was to output a decent looking table of figures from an APL application to a PostScript printer. Rather than chickening out and just using Courier (and hence falling into the category of someone who thinks WordPerfect is a wordprocessor), I thought it would be more fun to get APL to write a little PostScript program to do the hard work.

Here is the kind of output I was after:

Hello from TEST.TXT … the following lines are tabbed

Name Age Notes Adrian 38 Well known troublemaker Gill 38 Wife of well-known troublemaker Richard 7 Generally a good child Tim 5 Generally a bad child

The end.

The two problems to be solved were the simple one of lining up the columns in a proportional font, and the secondary issue of getting right justification on the numeric data.

The APL code to do this is mostly just a few globals to set up font name, size and pitch, as well as the page layout and tab positions. All the serious processing is done with a few PostScript routines, which go as a prologue on the front of the file:

%!PS-Adobe-2.0
%% Prologue for PostScript print
/inch {72 mul} def
/LM 1.00 inch def /BM 1.00 inch def /TM 1.00 inch def
/PW 11.25 inch def /PH 8.6 inch def

The ‘%’ is simply a comment, and the first line is a useful convention … several printers such as the Qume PS range will switch automatically between Epson, LaserJet and PostScript emulation … they recognise a PostScript file by the ‘%!’ at the beginning. The subsequent lines define a trivial function to convert from inches to points, and a bunch of globals to define the page size and margins.

Next we set up some tabs, measured in inches from the left margin. My simple convention is to make right tabs negative … if you want centred or decimal tabs you will have to devise something better!

/TABS [0 .5 -3 3.2] def /TB 0 def
/PITCH 20 def

Define Top Of Form as the Page Height less the Top Margin, and a null function to Orient the page (not required if we are in portrait mode, but essential for landscape … see below). Then define FormFeed as a function to print the current page, orient it and go to the top …

/TOF    { /VPOS PH TM sub def } def
/ORIENT {} def
/FF     { showpage ORIENT TOF } def

… and NewLine to set the typeball to the next tab, output any pending text, reset the tab bar to the first tab, and drop down Pitch positions. It checks if we have overstepped the bottom margin … if so we need a FormFeed:

/NL     { TAB /VPOS VPOS PITCH sub def  /TB 0 def
          VPOS BM le {FF} if } def

Now for the hard bit! The PostScript ‘get’ primitive is essentially APL’s array indexing, so read the first line of TAB as tb←TABS[TB] (zero origin, of course). The next line reads moveto (LM+inch |tb),VPOS (remember that negative tabs are right aligned, so the sign must be ignored at this stage); then we check that we have not fallen off the end of the tab rack, and if there is another tab to go, we increment the tab counter TB. (length is the PostScript equivalent of ⍴, but because we are in ⎕IO←0, we need to subtract 1.) Finally, we check the sign of the tab and either display the preceeding text directly (using show) or right align it (using our own rshow function)

/TAB    { TABS TB get /tb exch def
          tb abs inch LM add VPOS moveto
          TABS length 1 sub TB gt { /TB TB 1 add def } if
          tb 0 lt {rshow} {show} ifelse } def
/rshow  { dup stringwidth pop neg 0 rmoveto show } def

If the user has requested landscape printing, we can throw in a little function to rotate the paper and shift origin appropriately:

% Landscape mode requested
/ORIENT { PH 0 translate 90 rotate } def
ORIENT TOF

And finally, we select the requested font and display the data. Note that APL needs to make no allowance for pagination … all the hard work is done by the PostScript NL function which will allow for the specified margins and throw pages accordingly.

/Helvetica findfont 18 scalefont setfont
(Hello from TEST.TXT ... the following lines are tabbed) NL
() TAB (Name) TAB (Age) TAB (Notes) NL
() TAB (Adrian) TAB (38) TAB (Well known troublemaker) NL
() TAB (Gill) TAB (38) TAB (Wife of well-known troublemaker) NL
() TAB (Richard) TAB (7) TAB (Generally a good child) NL
() TAB (Tim) TAB (5) TAB (Generally a bad child) NL
() NL
(The end.) NL
FF

Note the final FormFeed to throw out the last page!

Simple lines are just wrapped up in an opening parenthesis and a ‘) NL’; anything between parentheses is treated as a text string, and hence is the argument to the NL function (remember that NL calls TAB to do the output!). Where we would logically insert tab characters in the text, we instead insert the string ‘) TAB (’. This conveniently takes account of the first tab at position zero (i.e. the left margin) by inserting a null string at the first tab … subsequent tabbed sections are output by the TAB function at the appropriate position on the page.

I’m afraid I wrote all this in a boring old first generation APL, and simply hard-coded the PostScript into my reporting function. The correct solution is obviously to write a general-purpose formatter that will take a nested argument (in the example a 3-element array consisting of two text vectors separated by a numeric vector) and the required tab positions, and will automatically generate the PostScript file ready to send to the printer.

It could even use a table of character widths to work out the optimum tab positions for itself (automatically left and right aligning text and numbers); this one is definitely left as an exercise for the reader … I will stick to the trial-and-error approach until I have a real need for something better.

items.title: Hackers’ Corner: Fast Filing with ∆pack
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 125

by Adrian Smith

items.title: Health Warning
items.text: What follows is highly specific to APL*PLUS/PC; it won’t even do you any good under PLUS II, which doesn’t have the IPSA-style package utilities provided.

items.title: Motivation
items.text:
For many years, my APL file system has been built around two almost trivial routines called DUMP and GET. These simple take a named list of APL objects (variables or functions) and sling them on file. The only subtlety is that GET will optionally pull back variables under a different name if you ask it to:

RC←'MYFILE' DUMP '∆CODE,∆DESCR,any∆fun'
RC←GET 'MYFILE'                   ⍝ Simply retrieves the whole file
RC←'MYFILE' GET '∆DESCR'          ⍝ Selective retrieve
RC←'MYFILE' GET 'CHECK←∆CODE'     ⍝ ... with a change of name

This simple approach has the virtue of almost total portability (it even worked under VSPC using sequential text files), but when implemented on APL*PLUS/PC using the obvious strategy of one object per component (co-incidentally the format turns out to be compatible with Statgraphics files, which is quite useful) it is horribly slow for collections of lots of small objects.

      ⍴NL
112 12
      RC←'SCRATCH' DUMP NL   ⍝ 11.2 sec to dump 20480 bytes
      RC←GET 'SCRATCH'       ⍝ 1.3 sec to retrieve whole file

I had toyed with a variety of strategies for improving matters, and the best one I had come up with was to ravel like objects end to end (recording ranks and shapes in a header table) and then write out a maximum of four components. This speeds the writing process up quite a lot, but of course files are read more than they are written, and the slight reduction in reading speed brought about by all that indexing and reshaping was enough to put me off. So … there matters rested until STSC quietly included a bunch of ASMFNS to emulate the Sharp Package concepts.

Essentially, all they do is take any list of objects (in ⎕NL format) and return a magic integer vector with all the objects hidden in it. The inverse process just takes the vector and disperses it into the workspace. Now you may have noticed that the APL*PLUS/PC native file functions are absurdly fast, and that it is quite legal to write out an integer vector at two bytes per element … so without further ado:

    ∇ rC←fI PDUMP vL;⍙⍙pk;p;⎕ELX
[1]       ⍝ Package objects in vL and write as native file
[2]       ⍝ Note blocked write ... a good idea for big objects.
[3]        →(2=⍴⍴vL)↑Mat ⋄ vL←(~p←vL∊',/;: ')/vL←,vL,'/'
[4]        vL←(⍴p)⍴(,p←p∘.≥⍳⌈/0,p←(p≠0)/p←p-1+0,¯1↓p←p/⍳⍴p)\vL
[5]   Mat:⍙⍙pk←∆pack vL
[6]       ⍝ Now create/tie file, clear down and swipe out the data
[7]   Tie:⎕ELX←'fI ⎕NCREATE ¯2 ⋄ →Go'
[8]        fI ⎕NTIE ¯2 ⋄ 0 ⎕NRESIZE ¯2
[9]    Go:⎕ELX←'⎕DM' ⋄ ⍙⍙pk←,⍙⍙pk
[10] Loop:((8000⌊⍴⍙⍙pk)↑⍙⍙pk)⎕NAPPEND ¯2
[11]       →(0≠⍴⍙⍙pk←8000↓⍙⍙pk)↑Loop
[12] Done:⎕NUNTIE ¯2 ⋄ rC←0
    ∇

    ∇ rC←PLOAD fI;⎕ELX;lEN;oFF;iN;⍙⍙pk
[1]       ⍝ RE-LOAD PACKED FILE CONSTITUENT VARIABLES.
[2]       ⍝ Note oddity in shape: vectors are acceptable >32768!!
[3]        rC←6 ⋄ ⎕ELX←'→0'
[4]        ⎕NUNTIE ⎕NNUMS ⋄ fI ⎕NTIE ¯2
[5]        lEN←⌊0.5×⎕NSIZE ¯2 ⋄ oFF←0
[6]        ⍙⍙pk←lEN⍴0
[7]        rC←99 ⋄ ⎕ELX←'⎕ERROR ''UTILITY '',⎕DM'
[8]       ⍝Now drop in file contents in 4000-byte segments ...
[9]  Loop:iN←⎕NREAD ¯2 163 ,(4000⌊lEN-oFF),oFF×2
[10]       ⍙⍙pk[oFF+⍳4000⌊lEN-oFF]←iN
[11]       →(lEN≤4000+oFF)↑Done
[12]       oFF←oFF+4000 ⋄ →Loop
[13] Done:⎕NUNTIE ¯2
[14]      ⍝ Split em out ......
[15]       →(32768≤⍴⍙⍙pk)↑Def ⋄ ⍙⍙pk←(1,lEN)⍴⍙⍙pk
[16]  Def:∆pdef ⍙⍙pk ⋄ rC←0
    ∇

      ⍴NL
112 12                          ⍝ Same data as used above (honest)
      RC←'JUNK.TMP' PDUMP NL    ⍝ 0.45 sec to dump 10342 bytes
      RC←PLOAD 'JUNK.TMP'       ⍝ 0.44 sec to retrieve whole file

Time this yourself … I reckon it beats the socks off component files. Oddly, it also saves rather a lot of disk space.

items.title: Hackers’ Corner: More about VGA Colours
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 132

by Adrian Smith

As Dave Crossley rightly points out, the VGA is grossly under-exploited by the vast majority of PC software. The irritating thing is that the required code is easy to build, and will work under pretty well any APL you care to name. The only snag is having to spend the best part of £30 on Ray Duncan’s book! Accordingly, I thought it might be helpful to compile a little workspace of helpful functions (available from APL-385 free if you send me a disk and enclose return postage, but why not just type them in, and have fun writing a better palette editor?!).

So, with thanks to Dave Selby (for pointing out how easy this is), and Duncan Pearson (for lending me Duncan for the weekend) … here’s all you ever wanted to know about ⎕INT 16 ….

VGA∆RESET               ⍝ Sets everything back to default
VGA∆BLINK 0|1           ⍝ Highlighted | blinking background
VGA∆QPALETTE reg        ⍝ Checks current palette setting(s)
VGA∆QCOLOUR clr         ⍝ Checks current colour value(s)

     ∇ VGA∆RESET;RG;W;C
[1]   ⍝ Reset VGA video to MODE 3 and restore active screen
[2]    W←⎕WGET 3 ⋄ C←⎕CURSOR
[3]   ⍝   AH = 0hex       ... BIOS service 0
[4]   ⍝   AL = 3hex       ... standard VGA text mode
[5]    RG←3 ⎕INT 16
[6]   ⍝ Reset background ...
[7]    RG← 4099 0 ⎕INT 16
[8]   ⍝ Put things back as they were ...
[9]    ⎕WPUT W ⋄ ⎕CURSOR←C
     ∇

     ∇ VGA∆BLINK SW;RG
[1]   ⍝ Flip Background from blinking to intensified.
[2]   ⍝   AH = 10hex      ... BIOS service 10 (EGA/VGA only)
[3]   ⍝   AL =  3hex      ... subservice 3
[4]   ⍝   BL = 0/1        ... 0 = intensify; 1 = blink
[5]    RG←(4099,SW>0)⎕INT 16
     ∇

     ∇ R←VGA∆QPALETTE VEC;AX;RG;lab;CT
[1]      ⍝ Query VGA palette register(s) VEC
[2]      ⍝   AH = 10hex      ... BIOS service 10 (EGA/VGA only)
[3]      ⍝   AL =  7hex      ... subservice 7
[4]      ⍝   BH = 0          ... colour returned here
[5]      ⍝   BL = 0-16       ... palette register to query
[6]       AX←(256×16)+7 ⋄ R←⍳0 ⋄ VEC←,VEC
[7]   Lp:→lab←1+((⍴VEC)⍴Lp),End,CT←1
[8]       RG←(AX,VEC[CT])⎕INT 16
[9]       R←R,⌊RG[2]÷256
[10] End:→lab[CT←CT+1]
     ∇

     ∇ R←VGA∆QCOLOUR VEC;AX;RG;CT;lab
[1]      ⍝ Query VGA colour(s) VEC as RGB values
[2]      ⍝   AH = 10hex      ... BIOS service 10 (EGA/VGA only)
[3]      ⍝   AL = 15hex      ... subservice 15h = 21(dec)
[4]      ⍝   BL = 0-53       ... colour to query
[5]      ⍝ Returns 4-col array of [colour,r,g,b] values
[6]       AX←(256×16)+21 ⋄ VEC←,VEC ⋄ R←⍉(4,⍴VEC)⍴VEC
[7]   Lp:→lab←1+((⍴VEC)⍴Lp),End,CT←1
[8]       RG←(AX,VEC[CT])⎕INT 16
[9]       R[CT; 3 2 4]←3↑, 256 256 ⊤RG[3 4] ⍝ returned as G,R,B
[10] End:→lab[CT←CT+1]
     ∇

For example, to see the current VGA palette, and the standard RGB colours:

      VGA∆RESET ⋄ STD←VGA∆QCOLOUR VGA∆QPALETTE 0,⍳15
      STD
 0  0  0  0              ... 56 21 21 21
 1  0  0 42                  57 21 21 63
 2  0 42  0                  58 21 63 21
 3  0 42 42                  59 21 63 63
 4 42  0  0                  60 63 21 21
 5 42  0 42                  61 63 21 63
20 42 21  0                  62 63 63 21
 7 42 42 42 ...              63 63 63 63

The next group of two functions allows you to change things! Obviously, there is scope here to put together a simple palette editor … mine uses RGB to crank up the colour components and rgb to crank them down. It is also handy to provide + to increase all three colours together, and - to wind them all down.

VGA∆PALETTE pal,clr     ⍝ Set Palette (0..15) to clr (0..63)
VGA∆COLOUR clr,r,g,b    ⍝ Set clr(s) (0..63) to red,green,blue

     ∇ VGA∆PALETTE VEC;RG;BX
[1]   ⍝ Set Vga palette register VEC[1] to VEC[2]
[2]   ⍝   AH = 10hex      ... BIOS service 10 (EGA/VGA only)
[3]   ⍝   AL =  0hex      ... subservice 0
[4]   ⍝   BH = 0-63       ... required colour
[5]   ⍝   BL = 0-16       ... palette register to set
[6]    BX←(256×VEC[2])+VEC[1]
[7]    RG←(4096,BX)⎕INT 16
     ∇

     ∇ VGA∆COLOUR MAT;RG;BX;CX;DX;lab;CT
[1]      ⍝ Set Vga colour register MAT[;1] to MAT[;2 3 4] (RGB)
[2]      ⍝   AH = 10hex      ... BIOS service 16 (EGA/VGA only)
[3]      ⍝   AL = 10hex      ... subservice 16
[4]      ⍝   BX = 0-63       ... colour register
[5]      ⍝   CH = 0-63       ... green intensity
[6]      ⍝   CL = 0-63       ... blue intensity
[7]      ⍝   DH = 0-63       ... red intensity
[8]       MAT←(¯2↑ 1 1 ,⍴MAT)⍴MAT ⋄ MAT←((1↑⍴MAT),4)↑MAT
[9]   Lp:→lab←1+((1↑⍴MAT)⍴Lp),End,CT←1
[10]      BX←MAT[CT;1]
[11]      DX←256×MAT[CT;2]
[12]      CX←(256×MAT[CT;3])+MAT[CT;4]
[13]      RG←(4112,BX,CX,DX)⎕INT 16
[14] End:→lab[CT←CT+1]
     ∇

     ∇ R←SET∆PAL CRGB;W;IN;LD;SD;lab;CT;OFF;POS;CURR;FRM;BLK;LST;BAR;INX;KB;FP
[1]      ⍝ Allow user to fix VGA colour registers for standard palette
[2]      ⍝ RGB is a 16 4 array of [Colour,R,G,B] values (0..63) for each clr
[3]      ⍝ Result is the same array, with adjusted values
[4]      ⍝ <Esc> returns the original array unchanged, in case of disaster!
[5]      ⍝
[6]       KB←1 ⎕POKE 118 ⋄ LST←CURR←1 ⋄ R←CRGB ⋄ VGA∆RESET ⋄ VGA∆COLOUR CRGB
[7]      ⍝ The first bit is all direct screen update with ⎕WPUT ... Yuk!
[8]       LD←'┌┐┘└│─├┤┼◄►' ⋄ FRM← 18 74 ⍴' ' ⋄ BAR←LD[10,(64⍴6),11]
[9]       SD←(1↑⍴FRM)⍴5 ⋄ FRM←LD[6],[1]FRM,[1]LD[6]
[10]      FRM←LD[1,SD,4],FRM,LD[2,SD,3]
[11]      OFF← 3 4 ⋄ FP←(OFF- 1 2),⍴FRM ⋄ W←FP ⎕WGET 4
[12]      FP ⎕WPUT FRM ⋄ FP ⎕WPUT 143
[13]      FP←'Arrows select; rgbRGB+- keys move bars; ! reset; <Enter> exit'
[14]      ((OFF+17,2),1,⍴FP)⎕WPUT FP
[15]      BLK← 3 5 ⍴'█' ⋄ FRM←' ',BLK,' '
[16]      BLK←' '⍪BLK⍪' ' ⋄ BLK←(5 2 ⍴' '),BLK, 5 2 ⍴' '
[17]      SD←(1↑⍴FRM)⍴5 ⋄ FRM←LD[6],[1]FRM,[1]LD[6]
[18]      FRM←LD[1,SD,4],FRM,LD[2,SD,3]
[19]      POS←(16 2 ⍴OFF+ 0 4)+((8⍴1),8⍴5),[1.5]16⍴8×0,⍳7
[20]  Lp1:→lab←1+(16⍴Lp1),End1,CT←1
[21]      FP←POS[CT;], 3 5 ⋄ FP ⎕WPUT CT-1 ⋄ FP ⎕WPUT '█'
[22] End1:→lab[CT←CT+1]
[23]      ((OFF+ 9 3), 1 65)⎕WPUT FP←'Five boxing wizards jump quickly '
[24]      FP←POS-(⍴POS)⍴ 1 2
[25]     ⍝ Frame active colour, and mark it off on each colour indicator ...
[26] Mark:(FP[LST;],⍴BLK)⎕WPUT BLK ⋄ (FP[CURR;],⍴FRM)⎕WPUT FRM
[27]      ((OFF+ 9 3), 1 32)⎕WPUT,⍉ 2 16 ⍴(16×CURR-1)+0,⍳15
[28]      ((OFF+ 9 36), 1 32)⎕WPUT,⍉ 2 16 ⍴(16×0,⍳15)+CURR-1
[29] Rule:((OFF+ 11 1), 1 68)⎕WPUT 'r',BAR,'R'
[30]      ((OFF+ 13 1), 1 68)⎕WPUT 'g',BAR,'G'
[31]      ((OFF+ 15 1), 1 68)⎕WPUT 'b',BAR,'B'
