items.title: Project status
items.text: Updated 12 October 2026, after the Second Pass: every line of every Contents page now has its text, or says where it is.

items.title: What this is
items.text: A development build of the recovered Vector archive: every issue’s contents, every surviving article, and the old article addresses (/art10000000) kept working. The full index and the volume pages list every item on each issue’s printed Contents page, linked to the best text we have.

items.title: Done
items.text:
• Every issue’s Contents page (all but 2:2, of which no copy has been found) transcribed from the scans: the full index and the volume pages list everything printed, about 2,540 items, against the 1,500 in the editors’ index.
  • The text published online: 624 articles converted from it (328 in Volumes 1–21; 296 in Volumes 22–26 and online only), using the restored archive at archive.vector.org.uk where it holds a newer copy. Where several articles share one web page (letters, members’ news), each shows only its own part; where the editors’ index lists an article twice, the second address leads to the first.
  • The First Pass through Volumes 1–9 (1984–1993), from the scanned issues:
    • every article in the editors’ index that survives in a scan transcribed from the page images: 327 of the 367 (three more records — one article indexed twice — were online as text; one, Mandelbrot Sets, is indexed in 7:3 but was held over to 7:4; the other 37 are in 2:2, of which no copy has been found, and 3:4 and 7:4, of which only machine-read text survives). One, XPL, could not be transcribed and awaits a human transcriber. Where an article prints code with its results, the code has been run in Dyalog APL as a check on the transcription, and any misreadings it revealed corrected and noted; other doubts are recorded for review;
    • in Volumes 1–4, the pieces the index omitted from the meetings, general and technical sections also transcribed (150 pieces), and published;
    • everything else on the Contents pages linked to its page in the issue PDF.
  • The First Pass through Volumes 10–21 (1993–2005): from Volume 10 onward most indexed articles were published online and are converted from that text; the indexed articles that were not online (12 in Volume 10, 39 in Volume 11, 60 in Volume 12, 64 in Volume 13, 56 in Volume 14, 34 in Volume 15, 21 in Volume 16, 28 in Volume 17, 36 in Volume 18, 40 in Volume 19, 38 in Volume 20, 24 in Volume 21) have been transcribed from the scans, with the same checks; one article in Volume 12 and one in Volume 21 are left for transcription by hand, and the four in 16:4 survive only as machine-read text.
  • The First Pass through Volumes 22–23 (2005–2008): the 25 indexed articles never published online (2 in 22:1, 1 in 22:2, 2 in 22:4, 3 in 23:3, 15 in 23:4, 2 in the Dyalog at 25 supplement) transcribed: 23:4 and the supplement from the typeset issues’ sources, the rest from the scans. The only scan of 22:2 lacks four pages of APL+SantaFe previewed, and 23:4’s Contents and PDF now follow the printed issue.
  • Every other issue: its articles listed from its Contents page and linked to the issue PDF (with its machine-read text) where we have one; articles with their own scan link to that too.
  • Mathematics in the transcribed articles is typeset in conventional notation (TeX, rendered by MathJax served from this site), following the printed layout, = signs aligned where the print aligns them: 81 articles, each formula re-read from the scan.
  • Subject tags for every article with text, transcribed or converted, from a vocabulary of 20 subjects; see Tags. Articles linked only to the PDF, and section introductions, are not tagged.
  • Index corrections: the editors’ index was compiled by hand; where it disagrees with the printed Contents pages (pages, issue, authors, titles), the Contents pages have been followed. 79 records were corrected; each correction is listed in the build report.
  • The Second Pass (decided 11 October 2026): the pieces the editors’ index left out, transcribed from the scans and each put on its issue’s line in the full index:
    • pieces printed inside a listed section but missing from both the index and the Contents page (letters, reports, columns, errata): 237, found from the First Pass’s notes and by a sweep of Volumes 5–21;
    • every remaining line of the Contents pages: 650 more, among them editorials, the Quick Reference and course diaries, BAA, BCS and sustaining members’ news, the Education Vector and Random Vector introductions, conference programmes and reports, reviews, crosswords and the APL Product Guides. Volumes 22–25 were transcribed from the typeset issues. Lines whose text is already held, or that are only a heading over listed pieces, say so;
    • short pieces printed with no line on any Contents page, mostly section introductions: 47, linked from their sections’ headings or given lines of their own;
    • not transcribed: the indexes to advertisers and the order, subscription and registration forms;
    • contact details: where a person rather than a company is the contact (BAA officers and editors, letter-writers, user-group secretaries, consultants trading on their own), the street address, telephone number and personal e-mail are left out, and a note says so; companies’ and institutions’ addresses are kept.
  • Complete scans of 3:4, 7:4 and 16:4, whose earlier copies were truncated, found on vector.org.uk (2026-11-19): their 31 indexed articles now link to the scan, with its machine-read text.
  • WordPress content (2016–2022): the vector.org.uk database has been catalogued; 11 articles and a page of talks it holds are not in the editors’ index. The talks at the BAA meeting of 20 May 2016 and the 11 articles are online, converted from the posts (some APL characters and two figures that WordPress lost are noted on their pages).
  • Volume 27 (2016–2022): its one issue, 27:1, was never printed; the editor's call for articles, the old site's storage and WordPress's Latest Issue menu all name it. Its 15 pieces (10 from the old site, 5 from WordPress) are listed there in order of publication online. Six other WordPress pieces remain on the home page under In press, never printed.

items.title: Remaining
items.text:
• Review: every transcription is a draft until a reviewer checks it against the scan; see the review checklist.
  • Missing sources: no scan has been found of 2:2 (help find one).
  • 3:4, 7:4 and 16:4: their articles are to be transcribed from the complete scans, and their Contents checked against them.
  • Hand transcription: three pieces the automatic transcription could not complete (XPL in 1:2, an article each in 12:1 and 21:2) and one Second Pass piece (12:2 p.113).

The quality of each article’s text is shown in the full index.

items.title: A Comment on “Announcing The APL Review”
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 10

From: Martin Gfeller, 7 June 1993

I do think a new, refereed APL Journal will be more harmful than beneficial to the APL community, for the following reasons:

  • There are some good APL newsletters such as Quote Quad, Vector and local publications that need material of high quality. Since the APL community is not growing, introducing yet another journal would lower the quantity and quality of material available to the established publications.

  • Quote Quad, being an ACM SIG newsletter, has the largest visibility outside the APL community. To strengthen the outreach of APL into the computer community at-large, we need to strengthen Quote Quad.

  • More reports on applications of APL should be directed to non-APLers, in publications that are not specific to APL. The yearly APL conferences suffice to report APL stories to APLers; but we need to tell more about our applications to application users and to the software community at large.

  • Formal papers about the APL language and system could reach a wider audience by publication in other ACM newsletters and journals, such as SIGPLAN Notices, LOPLAS, or TOPLAS. These communities hardly know that APL is alive and evolving; yet they have a great decision power in education and industry.

  • The quality of APL specific material geared to APL users could as well be enhanced by introducing a reviewing process for APL journals such as Vector; many articles could be edited and condensed to serve the readers better. I know and appreciate that the work of volunteers cannot match the professionalism and resources of major trade publications such as Byte; but this would presumably be the case for a new journal as well.

In publications, as in APL coding, less can be more!

Martin Gfeller Reuters SA Risk Management Software

items.title: BAA-GUI Workshop: November 26th 1993
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 11

items.title: BAA-GUI Workshop: November 26th 1993
items.text:
In order to learn effectively to program for a graphical user interface, with APL or any other language, you need to have a certain level of knowledge and experience, to say nothing of confidence. The November meeting of the BAA will be an all day workshop designed to give you that experience and confidence. You will learn enough about GUI programming to go away and develop an application yourself. You will then be able to work more quickly at solving application problems without getting bogged down in irrelevant technical details.

Part of the ‘hump’ that most users have to get over is the change from controlling the user to being controlled by him. This has significant implications for system and program design. The UK users will be showing what those implications are and explaining how they have adapted to them.

The major interpreters for personal computers will be covered. There will be parallel streams covering APL*Plus II v5/6, Dyalog APL/W and APL.68000 with:

  • Patrick Parkes (the man who wrote the GUI interface for APL*Plus II v5) or an alternative speaker from Manugistics.
  • Peter Donnelly. A director of Dyadic and a designer of Dyalog APL/W.
  • David Eastwood. Managing director of MicroAPL, and an experienced teacher of APL programming techniques.

To show how the interfaces actually are being used and to give some examples from real systems we will have:

  • David Piper from Eagle Star. David is a regular contributor to Vector on system design topics.
  • Adrian Smith from Nestlé. Adrian is the author of ‘APL, A Design Handbook for Commercial Systems’ and has worked hard over the years to better understand the relationship between people and computers.

The workshop will be based on tutorials in which the speaker will present methods to the workshop and then the delegates will try them out on their computers. Each session will be about three hours long, broken at convenient times by coffee or tea breaks. Lunch will be provided and there will be ample opportunity for the delegates to mingle and discuss any aspects of the work with each other and with the speakers.

The venue is not yet fixed but will be within striking distance of central London. There will be a charge of £75 per head to cover the cost of machine hire and catering. In order to plan effectively we need to know the number of people who intend to come, and the streams in which they are interested. Please use the booking form on page 51.

items.title: A Windows GOTCHER for APLIWIN
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 114

From: Anthony Camacho, 15 May 1993

I have been using APLIWIN to provide a customer with a PC version of a system originally written in Sharp APL in 1977. I have been very impressed with APLIWIN even though my stupidity and the lack of a system manual for this specific implementation has caused me some head-banging (for example it took me ages before I found out how to fill a combo box with 20 lines of alternatives).

This letter is being written in WinWord. I have been using WinWord to make notes on the conversion for colleagues and have been delighted to be able to cut functions from the workspace and paste them into WinWord (or Write) and then by selecting the pasted section and changing font to ISIAPL’s TrueType font the correct APL characters are both displayed and printed. Marvellous.

The other evening I had some work to do which required a PostScript font. I set WinWord to use the PostScript printer, did the job (printing to file and using GoScript to emulate the printer) and thought no more about it. I little realised what I had done.

The next time I did a cut and paste from ISIAPL to WinWord the characters were displayed in some default font or other. The ISIAPL font was there in the font list and could be applied to selected text but it appeared not to work: the text obstinately refused to turn into APL.

So of course I tried all the obvious things; I deleted and re-installed the font; I did something which I had intended to do ever since I mistakenly allowed CorelDraw to install hundreds of rarely needed fonts - I deleted about a hundred fonts; I edited WIN.INI to remove the section which specified font substitutions; I rang the Microsoft help line (a mistake - see below); I even bought a book Windows 3.1 Insider (£24.00!) which had a large section on fonts.

The Microsoft help line was worse than useless. An authoritative man told me to do this and that and the other and, like a fool, I did what he said. When we had got as far as to ‘remove’ all fonts and then ‘add’ all fonts I realised that my adviser knew less than I did. The effort of selecting a hundred fonts to delete and waiting for the Windows longwinded deletion process was undone. Then he said he was going to delete and re-install all my drivers and I said that plainly he was unable to see what was wrong and that I might as well re-install windows from scratch as it would take less time than his diagnosis.

The GOTCHER is the shibboleth WYSIWYG [What You See Is What You Get]. Microsoft have programmed WinWord and Write so that if a printer is selected that cannot print TrueType the display will not show TrueType. They could easily have indicated that the TrueType fonts were not available or disabled by removing them from the list of fonts or by some warning or other. But they didn’t; you can select from all the fonts and the substitution is automatic and outside your control and you are not told it is being done to you.

The Insider book (and, to be fair, the Microsoft help line) told me that the printer driver determined what could be displayed. The Microsoft help line did not tell me to check what printer was selected. They didn’t realise the significance of this. They didn’t suggest I tried selecting other printers. All I had to do to recover the ability to cut and paste APL was to select the DeskJet or Epson or any printer that can do TrueType.

Try it! Put something on the screen in an out-of-the-way font. Set up a PostScript printer (you don’t need to have one) or a plotter or daisywheel and select it; the screen miraculously changes its display to the nearest default font. Select a dot matrix printer that can do TrueType and the screen changes back to show the font as you expected.

I have written to Microsoft saying that I think they have made a mistake. If my text will not print as I intend, please warn me but don’t in the name of WYSIWYG convert my intentions to something else. And don’t call it a printer driver if it is really a display and printer driver. Write the message loud and clear WHAT IS SHOWN ON THE SCREEN IS LIMITED TO WHAT YOUR PRINTER CAN PRINT.

Apart from the waste of effort it does make me feel so stupid.

Anthony Camacho

items.title: Errors in “Integrating with Insight”
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 116

From: John R. Clark, June 1993

The article “Integrating with Insight” by Norman Thomson, pages 113 to 116 of Vector Vol.9 No.2 Jan 1993, has some typographical errors and one logical error.

items.title: Logical Error:
items.text: Page 115 line [2] of METHOD should end with ⍳L←Q×⌈L÷Q. For Simpson the number of subdivisions must be even.

items.title: Typographical errors:
items.text:
Page 113. 1/4096 should be 1/4095

Page 115. Line [4] of ROMBERG. EPSL is an undefined variable.

Page 115. Line [3] of ADAPT. EPSn is an undefined variable.

I am not sure what the undefined variables should be. If the L of ESPL is ≤| then ROMBERG works. If the n of ESPn is ≥| then ADAPT works. Perhaps you have a problem with your typesetting software. I believe you need magnitude in both tests.

I receive my copy of Vector through membership in Los Angeles SOCAL SIGAPL and Roy Sykes of Sykes Systems — I do enjoy your publication.

As a past algorithm editor of QuoteQuad I am aware errors do creep into publications.

Keep up the good work

John R Clark

Ed: I created a translate table to convert Norman Thomson’s original text from APL2 ⎕AV into APL*PLUS/PC ⎕AV, which is used for typesetting. Unfortunately I omitted ≤ and ≥ from the translate table, hence the EPSL and EPSn.

items.title: “APL in Business” Conference Prospectus
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 12

items.title: APL in Business18-22 July 1994University College of Swansea
items.text:
The European Business Management School in conjunction with the British APL Association is to host an international conference in Swansea next year. The title ‘APL in Business’ is an umbrella term to signify the inter-related themes of Finance, Operational Research and Statistics which can work together with the aid of modern computing power to enable more effective management. The future for APL lies in an effective synthesis of technical expertise applied by means of APL in co-operation with other software. The conference aims to bring these application areas into contact with the technical developments in operating systems, managing technologies and hardware.

Consequently we would like to take this opportunity to encourage participation from as many of our readers as possible in the following areas:

Finance. Trading systems, actuarial methods, credit scoring.

Operational Research. Rule-based systems, scheduling and rostering, management information and control systems, genetic algorithms.

Statistics. Statistical modelling in general, experimental design and Taguchi methods. Forecasting techniques, Econometrics, Bayesian methods, Reliability analysis.

Technical. Designing fully-functional Windows applications covering the GUI objects, the Windows DLL’s and the Windows Help engine, Working with messages, co-operative processing (using APL as one element in a suite of co-operating applications.

All papers presented at the conference will be published in a conference proceedings. In addition, selected papers will collectively form the first volume of The APL Review, a new international refereed journal to be launched by the British APL Association.

Sessions will take place in the Swansea Conference Centre based on the Taliesin Arts Centre, which houses a 350-seat auditorium, an art gallery, bookshop and bank. All the facilities of the European Business Management School will be available to conference members throughout. The College has its own sports centre including squash, badminton and tennis courts and a heated indoor swimming pool adjacent to the campus, making the college a most attractive conference centre. The organizers are committed to making this a most enjoyable and fruitful conference — all you have to do is to commit yourself to come and participate!

Further details will shortly be available in a ‘Call for Papers’. If you would like to help with the organization of the conference please contact one of us as soon as possible.

Adrian Smith Brook House, Gilling East, YORK YO6 4JJ Tel: 04393-385

Alan Sykes, European Business Management School, Singleton Park, Swansea SA2 8PP Tel: 0792-295296, Fax: 0792-295626.

items.title: Election of Officers
items.text:
The chairman reported that, as one of the two candidates for the only contested post, that of recruitment, had decided instead to stand for the vacant post of activities officer, there was no need for a ballot. He therefore presented the new committee to the meeting.

Peter Donnelly is standing down as activities officer due to the pressure of his work and the chairman expressed the thanks of the BAA for the work he has done on the committee over the past five years. Peter Branson is also unable to continue in the post of recruitment officer. Thanks were extended to him for his valuable service, both as recruitment and as activities officer before that. Jonathan Barman having been the editor of Vector for three years is to become the technical officer. It was noted that during his time as editor Vector had been interesting, timely and professionally produced. Anthony Camacho was moving after three years as secretary to be the new editor of Vector and is replaced as secretary by Duncan Pearson. The new activities officer is Richard Weber, a lecturer at Doncaster College of Further Education, and the new recruitment Officer is Mark Harris of Kestrel Consulting. Other officers continuing in their posts are David Eastwood — Chairman, Nicholas Small — Treasurer, Misha Jovanovic — Publicity and George MacLeod — Projects.

items.title: Chairman’s Report
items.text:
The chairman reported that the year 1992/3 had seen the bid to hold APL94 in York rejected by the board of SIGAPL in favour of a conference in Antwerp. It was thought that this was not due to any demerits of the bid but rather that there had been two major APL conferences in the UK in the last decade.

The BAA had given financial support (£1000) to a project by Ian Clarke on the Apple Mackintosh to write and market an educational software building tool using I-APL as a scripting language. This tool, APLomb, received its UK launch at the meeting which followed the AGM. The organisers of APL93 in Toronto have set up a fund to finance the travel to Toronto of Russian APLers who would otherwise find it impossible to attend. The BAA have contributed £1000 to this fund.

In the coming year the Chairman highlighted the proposed change in the format of meetings with the all-day GUI workshop in November and with support for the business and statistics conference to be held by the European Business Management School at Swansea from the 18th to the 22nd July 1994. The BAA is also launching The APL Review, an academic refereed APL journal about which the chairman hoped he would have some more news at the next annual general meeting.

items.title: APL93 Russian Fund — Further Funding
items.text:
Anthony Camacho read a letter from Robert Bernecky and Benjamin Best of the APL93 organising committee saying that the Russian Fund had grown to nearly US$3,000 by the end of February but that there had been no further contributions by the end of April, and explaining the aims of the fund. Part of the letter is reproduced below. The sum did not include the £1000 from the BAA. He then proposed two alternative means for supporting the fund further, that had been discussed by the committee.

  1. That the letter below be sent to all members of the BAA with payment details to enable them to contribute personally.
  2. That the BAA make a further contribution of £500.

He pointed out that the expenses involved in the first option (postage and exchange costs on individual payments) might exceed £400. The committee had discussed the two options and was in favour of the second. Anthony took a vote to gauge the feelings of those members present at the meeting. The second option was preferred by a large majority.

Part of the letter from Robert Bernecky and Benjamin Best follows.

The APL93 Program Chair has now accepted papers from four Russians for the APL93 Proceedings, three of whom cannot attend APL93 without financial support (the fourth is living and working in the United States). The first priority of the APL93 Russian Fund is to bring these three contributors, plus one of the APL92 organisers, to Toronto. Another group of Russians have written an expert system in APL, which they would like to demonstrate. It would also be nice to bring some of the SovAPL founders as well as APLers from the other former Soviet Republics. We would like to bring 8 to 10 if possible. But this would mean much more money — perhaps US$20,000 — and fairly soon since the getting of Visas can be time-consuming.

The average Russian income is about US$25, but Russia is not just another Third World country. It is a country of many highly educated people and very many skilled scientists. In a country where chess is the national sport and computers must be adapted to a different alphabetic system, APL has a chance to grow and flourish. By helping Russian APLers to be a part of our community, they can acquire the resources to promote the use of APL as part of their new, emerging society.

Some people question why there should be a fund for Russians specifically, rather than for Eastern Europeans, students, APLers from other poor countries, or APLers under economic hardship. This fund was an act of gratitude for the APL92 conference in Russia — and for the groundbreaking efforts to make that conference a reality. The fund is a recognition that the new connections have been made and should not be lost.

The original objectives of the APL93 Russian Fund were modest. In fact there were moments in the Fall of 1992 when one of us (Ben Best) had fears that he would have to top the fund with money from his own pocket to pay for even one Russian to attend APL93 (after having already spent hundreds of dollars on postage). If this fund is successful, however, it can be the precedent for a “World APL Conference Attendance Fund”. It may be that we have colleagues in Eastern Europe, India, China, South America etc. who would submit papers and attend our conferences if they were not subject to such severe economic constraints.

items.title: Kestrel Consulting
items.text:
Our recruiting side is very active; handling both permanent and contract placements. We are always pleased to hear from people with strong technical APL skills, particularly when they are combined with sound business awareness and a grasp of the broader technical context within which APL exists. At the present moment we would be particularly interested to hear from people with up to five years of solid APL2; we are also placing people in areas other than APL, particularly the SAP package.

Consulting activities during the last quarter have included participation in a large-scale audit of APL use at a major British insurance company (more than 2000 workspaces on the mainframe). We have also been evaluating a comprehensive Decision Support System written in APL, and would be happy to discuss requirements with anyone having a particular interest in this sort of software.

The Kestrel Software Library was announced in the last issue and we have been (slowly) collecting software; anyone out there with APL tools and utilities which they would like to see distributed at low cost please contact us. Once again — the idea here is virtually a shareware one with Kestrel acting only as a central library. We are happy to distribute full-fledged commercial software as well of course, on a fully professional basis quite distinct from the Software Library..

items.title: Manugistics Inc
items.text:
Manugistics has had a busy few months since the release of APL*PLUS II/386 Version 5.0 and APL*PLUS PC Version 11.

APL*PLUS II/386 Version 5.1 is now available and is generating a great deal of enthusiasm. Reviews and articles on application building have already started appearing in the US. Our customers are telling us that the improved developer tools and dramatic speedups are just what the doctor ordered.

On the UNIX front, Version 5 development is proceeding apace and we expect to be shipping well before the next issue of Vector reaches you. This release emphasizes code compatibility with APL*PLUS II/386, including the User Command Processor and the APL2-style language model.

Patrick Parks has certainly had a busy time recently. Not satisfied with being the chief developer of Version 5.1, he found time to make two trips to Europe. On the first one he presented a seminar to almost 200 people in Paris on APL*PLUS as a development language, emphasizing GUI and DDE. The next day offered an APLGUI internals class to a smaller, more technical audience. Less than a month later he was back, demonstrating the power of APLGUI to groups in Finland, Germany and the Netherlands. Chris Lee also made a similar presentation in Toronto, Canada in May.

As the APL*PLUS II release work quietens down, more and more of our attention is being devoted to the design and development of “INCA”. We have just finished a week of intensive design meetings which have given the developers plenty to do over the coming months. The most exciting thing about INCA is the frequent realization that programmers won’t have to resort to a lot of the convoluted coding tricks they had to use in a pure APL environment. The incessant chanting by the non-APL community is going to fade away once and for all!

As well as participating in APL93, Manugistics is holding its own User Conference here in Rockville. The conference will be on September 20th and 21st and features presentations, workshops and panels hosted by Manugistics developers and APL programmers as well as a special presentation by Dr Ben Shneiderman, a leading authority on User Design Interface Design. We hope to see some of you there. Immediately following the conference will be a three-day training course on building professional applications with APLGUI and APLDDE.

Something else we’re really excited about — the first APL*PLUS PC SE (Special Edition) book has been published. If you didn’t know, we introduced the SE as a way for authors and educators to provide a fully working version of APL*PLUS PC with their book or course work at no charge. Maurice Delois of Montreal, Canada has published “Introduction to APL*PLUS PC” which is available from EducAPL Inc., 1120 av du Parc, Quebec, Canada G1S 2W7. The price is $30 for 1-5 copies and $20 each for more than 5 (plus shipping). Each copy includes a disk with tutorial materials and a fully working copy of APL*PLUS PC. This has to provide the best available way for newcomers to learn APL. We invite others to take advantage of the SE program. Please contact us if you are interested.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
We are currently finishing off work on an upgrade to APL.68000, which should be complete by the time this issue of Vector appears. The upgrade is mainly devoted to removing those few bugs that have been reported in our Level II product — either in the original 68000-based version or some that were generated by the port to the RISC System/6000. Full details of the upgrade will be issued directly to registered users.

Our applications consultancy work continues to be almost entirely non-APL and, as mentioned in the last issue of Vector, we held a seminar in London at the end of April entitled ‘Developing Windows Applications’. This was held jointly with Maddox Ford Ltd and the principal speakers were Richard Nabavi of MicroAPL and Brian Drury of Maddox Ford.

Richard Nabavi opened the seminar by discussing the convergence of Client-Server computing with Graphical User Interfaces and outlined the various types of GUI development tools that are available — ranging from end-user enquiry applications through to simple tools like Visual BASIC and then on to the professional programming tools such as PowerBuilder. He illustrated his talk with various case studies that MicroAPL and Maddox Ford had been involved with. Brian Drury addressed the issue of managing GUI development projects and the lack of fully thought-out methodologies for GUI development.

The seminar concluded with the presentation of a checklist for the selection of GUI development products.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is delighted to announce excellent progress with the new Motif version of Dyalog APL (ingeniously code-named Dyalog APL/M) which, together with the latest release of Dyalog APL/W for MS-Windows will be the focus of the company’s exhibit at APL93 in Toronto. As many of you know, this “news” is written far ahead of publication date, so it is difficult to say how much of the port will be completed by August. However, by mid-June many of the GUI objects (FORMS, BUTTONS, etc. and even some graphical objects) were working. When complete, Dyalog APL/W workspaces developed under Windows on a PC will run unchanged under Motif on a UNIX workstation, such as the IBM RS/6000. This cross-platform portability will appeal to software developers wishing to market products to a wide cross-section of end-users.

At APL93, Dyadic will for the first time be hosting a number of third-party products developed for Dyalog APL/W. There will be several complete applications on show. The first of these is FREGI, an extremely powerful multi-dimensional planning and control system from Kunzle Planning Systems. The second application is JERRY, a decision-support system similar in concept to ADI, developed by Adviseurs in France. Finally, Dyadic will show an early version of a business graphics application produced by Greymantle Associates which aims to provide very high-quality hard-copy output in addition to the usual attractive screen presentation. All these products take full advantage of the Dyalog APL GUI support and are excellent examples of professional APL applications.

There will also be several add-on products that will appeal to the Dyalog APL developer community. GDDME from Lingo Allegro is a complete emulation of GDDM for Dyalog APL/W including full text and graphics support. It runs as a separate invisible task and is driven from APL by shared variables, just like AP126. This product enables you to port mainframe AP126 applications to Dyalog APL/W with only a few minor changes to the screen driving code. SQAPL is an extremely exciting product developed by Insight Systems in Denmark. It provides the mechanism for Dyalog APL applications to function as both clients and servers using SequeLink Client/Server Middleware from TechGnosis. In practical terms this allows your APL/W application to talk to most SQL databases running on any computer system to which your PC is networked. SQAPL also provided the capability for APL/W workspaces to offload computational and/or data retrieval tasks to Dyalog APL running on a more powerful UNIX server. In short — true client/server computing for APL. Finally, Dyadic will be demonstrating Adrian Smith’s superb presentation graphics package which has already been adopted for a Dyalog APL/W Executive Information System developed in Finland.

If you will not have the opportunity to view these products yourself at APL93, please call Dyadic for details.

Dyadic is also pleased to announce an implementation of Dyalog APL for the DEC Alpha AXP running OSF/1. With a SPECmark92 rating of up to 160 (Intel claims 64.5 for a 66MHz Pentium) the DEC Alpha promises to push the level of performance of an APL workstation even further towards mainframe capability, and perhaps even beyond.

items.title: Soliton Associates Limited
items.text:
Soliton Associates Limited is a newly established software company which has acquired assets related to the APL software business from Reuters Information Services (Canada) Limited. Soliton Associates now owns the right to develop, market, sell and support SHARP APL and the application software products: VIEWPOINT, an end-user reporting facility; MAILBOX, an electronic mail system; and LOGOS, a development environment for APL applications.

SHARP APL was originally developed in the 1970s by I.P. Sharp Associates. It is both a powerful computer language and a high-performance computing environment, supporting high-availability, multi-user, shared-data applications on mainframes and workstations using client-server technology.

Soliton Associates supplies its products and services worldwide and has assumed full responsibility for existing international SHARP APL customers, which include Reuters. President, Clarke Bruce, says “Soliton Associates is focused on continued development of SHARP APL and on the development of new products and new markets that will allow it to become a more broadly based software company.”

Soliton Associates employees represent collectively over 250 years of SHARP APL business and technical experience. Clarke Bruce says “The company is committed to continuing the heritage of quality products and services from Reuters and I.P. Sharp Associates.” The Soliton Associates management team managed the APL business within Reuters, and includes: President, Clarke Bruce; Marketing and Sales, Nancy Lamb; Research and Development, Mike Symes; Software Manufacturing and Support, Margot Tate; and Finance and Accounting, Robert Duncan. The company is headquartered in Toronto, Canada, with offices in Rochester, USA; Coventry, England; and Amsterdam, the Netherlands.

Product announcements from Soliton Associates for the 3rd and 4th quarters 1993 include new releases of SHARP APL for UNIX, MVS-to-UNIX connectivity products and interfaces for the MVS and UNIX environments. SHARP APL Version 21 for MVS is scheduled for general distribution in the 1st quarter 1994.

APL93, the 1993 International Conference on APL, will be held in Toronto on August 15-19, 1993. Soliton Associates is active in the organisation of the conference, with Elena Anzalone as Proceedings Editor, Kirk Iverson as Software Exchange Coordinator, and Larry Moore as Conference Chairman. Don’t miss Soliton Associates’ booth and forum at APL93.

The Soliton Associates head office will relocate in Toronto in July 1993. New telephone numbers were not available at the time of writing. Mainframe development activities were recently relocated from the Reuters Toronto Data Centre to a new site in the Toronto area.

For information about Soliton Associates products and services contact Laurie Howard, Soliton Associates Ltd, Amsterdam, Tel +31 20 570 8733, Fax +31 20 570 8758, or Nancy Lamb, Soliton Associates Incorporated, Rochester, USA, Tel +1 716 256 6466, Fax +1 716 256 6469.

items.text:
Welcome to the APL93 edition of Education Vector. This year’s International Conference on APL is at the University of Toronto, Ontario, Canada, August 15-19, 1993. The British APL Association Journal, Vector (which includes Education Vector), will be available at the Conference, and the Association will be well represented both by speakers and by other delegates. Members of the Association will already have seen in the last edition of Vector the list of Abstracts of Accepted Papers, covering a very large selection of topics, and showing that APL is alive and well throughout the world.

The Guide to Low-Cost APLs in the last edition produced quite a lively response from various readers. If there is sufficient interest, I shall try to compile some of the ideas into a follow-up article. Dick Holt, who wrote the original Guide, now has a new address: HRH Systems, 3802 N.Richmond St, Arlington VA 22207, USA. Also the BBS telephone number, from which APL*PLUS demo and TryAPL2 can be downloaded, is now 703-528-7617 (prefixed by US code). To use this line, set your communications package to 2400 baud, no parity, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit and full duplex.

An addition to the “low cost” list is a new 300-page tutorial “Introduction to APL*PLUS PC” by Maurice Dalois of Quebec. The book costs $30 and is accompanied by a disk with an “educational” version of APL*PLUS called APLSE which appears to be an almost complete APL*PLUS version 10. As I write this, I have just received a copy, which I shall review for the next edition. It is available from EducAPL Inc, 1120 av du Parc, Quebec, Que, Canada G1S 2W7.

In this edition we have another contribution from Ted Emms, taking an APLer’s look at the well-known Chess Queens problem, with a challenge to readers at the end. I have added a note about the game of Cows and Bulls, which I hope may tempt someone to write another solution program — programming the games themselves is a lot easier than programming the solutions!

As always, we are keen to hear from anyone who has new ideas in APL and would like to tell us about their latest projects. We are also looking for new members for the British APL Association.

items.title: Editorial: APL in Business
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Anthony Camacho

Swansea University is host to the conference APL in Business (18-22 July 1994) which is to be sponsored by the European Business Management School with the support of the British APL Association and the British Computer Society.

items.title: What are we Trying to Do?
items.text:
We discussed at length how best to organise and sell a conference. The miracle at St Petersburg; APL 92 and the superlative programme for APL 93 are hard acts to follow. Nevertheless these are our suggestions:

  • Improved value for companies sending staff and for vendors
  • Promote good uses of APL more effectively
  • Make profits to give strength to APL organisations for years ahead.

items.title: Value for Money
items.text:
Too many advertisements for conferences begin with the attractions of the location, with the tours and with the entertainment. Anyone would think that the most important people to attract were the accompanying persons. It is overwhelmingly companies who send people to conferences. A few people will come to every conference they can afford at private expense, but not many. It is companies we have to persuade that they will get value for money by sending their staff. If it looks like a holiday then only generous companies who want to reward their staff may send people — only may.

An APL conference is not a holiday camp and should not look like one. Persuade the employers that APL conferences are harder work than any course and will improve their programmers’ performance better than any course and we will be able to raise the price and have to turn away the late-comers. Conferences must be good value for the vendors too. It is ridiculous to prohibit sales at conferences. Vendors should be encouraged to sell books, disks, programs, workspaces of utilities, interpreters, interfaces between different flavours of APL and the major spreadsheets, databases, word processors and other packages. Why not persuade companies that there will be products on sale that they cannot afford to be without?

items.title: Promoting Good Use of APL
items.text: A conference which promises to teach its delegates how to use APL well starts off on the right foot. A conference which promises to teach techniques which other disciplines can use with advantage will also spread the word about APL. We ought to offer to teach people who use a technique how they can do it easier with APL than any other way. There are many techniques where APL has much to offer. Hard-headed people choose APL and some are willing to say why. The best way to promote something is to show it to the people who would benefit from it. We are surrounded by examples of APL’s advantages and we scarcely use them.

items.title: Making a Profit
items.text:
To make a profit from running a conference we must persuade people to come. The best way is to make it irresistible to the people who spend company training budgets. To stand a credible chance of delivering what we promise the conference program should be planned. Only part of the conference should depend on what papers arrive in the post unasked for. The plenary speakers should be acknowledged experts in their fields with reputations as excellent teachers, commissioned to produce the material required.

The atmosphere should be of work too. More sessions should be spent sitting at a computer per delegate. There should be competitions and workshops. Sessions should be long enough for something to be learned. Many sessions are too short for the presenter to do more that tell the audience what a wonderful product he has to sell. Good planning of the accommodation and conference facilities is the other secret. The conference should break even with a pessimist’s view of the number of delegates and should have as much headroom as possible where every additional delegate adds ninety percent of his fee to the profit and ten percent of it to the costs.

items.title: APL is Still a Success
items.text: The whole thing depends on the continued success of APL. There are more APLers in the world today than ever. APL innovation is far from dead. There are now at least four GUI APLs. You can now write Windows applications in APL as well as, but faster than you can in Visual Basic. You can link APL to other systems and share data, and with Object Linking and Embedding the data can be updated dynamically by APL running in the background. APL still delivers working systems faster; they are still more reliable and they look as good as those produced any other way.

items.title: Review of APL*PLUS II v4.0
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 9

From: James G Wheeler, 1 February 1993

We at Manugistics appreciate the effort lavished by Ray Cannon in preparing his review of the MS Window interface in version 4 of APL*PLUS II for Vector 9.3. The article contains useful technical information and insights on Windows programming. The issues that he raises about the performance and ease of using our first Windows interface are fair, and we have been working very hard for the past fourteen months to address them.

We believe that we succeeded on this front when we completed version 5 in November 1992, and the praise we have been receiving from version 5 users seems to bear this out. As Vector 9.3 arrived in the U.S., we had nearly completed version 5.1, a signifcant improvement on 5.0 with important new features.

In this context, it came as a bit of a disappointment to be reading of shortcomings of version 4 that are long forgotten here. I recognize the difficulties of a quarterly publication in keeping pace with rapidly evolving software. But if there is any way the we can assist Vector in providing more up-to-the-minute information, we will do our best to oblige.

James G Wheeler Manugistics, Inc.

items.title: Manugistics Inc.
items.text:
As many of you will have heard by now, Manugistics Group Inc. made an Initial Public Offering (IPO) on August 13th and is now trading on the NASDAQ as a public company. This achievement is a tribute to all our customers who have helped us grow. By the time you read this, our annual APL*PLUS Users' Conference will be over. Right now, however, we are deep into preparations with only a couple of days left before the welcome reception. This year's conference features presentations and workshops from developers and users with an emphasis on building applications. As soon as this is behind us, we'll be able to turn our attention to the Society of Actuaries conference in New York.

While the marketing folk are busy conferencing, the developers are hard at work. We've just shipped Version 5 of our APL*PLUS II for UNIX product (in four flavours) and now everyone is getting their heads down to work on a true Windows version of APL*PLUS II.

This will be a pure Windows version with no DOS remnants and will run under Windows 3.1 and Windows NT. We're working on a real Windows-hosted session manager and debugger and we'll be putting both the APL*PLUS interpreter and the APLGUI toolkit (re-written in C) in DLLs. This new Windows version is not intended to replace or make obsolete the DOS version of APL*PLUS II — there are still many, many people who are in no hurry to move to Windows. What it will mean is that users will be able to choose whether to stay with DOS, move to Windows, or both. The good news is that the APLGUI applications you are writing now will be compatible with the new facilities — they'll just run a lot faster!

The best thing about APL*PLUS II for Windows is that all the work that is going into it serves a dual purpose. All the new features will also be used for our INCA project. This way, we will ensure that our APL*PLUS users get all the benefit of the new development as soon as possible. And this way, those of you who decide to move to INCA later on will find it easy to do so.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to report that, in terms of product interest, APL93 was its most successful conference yet. The company's stand was busy throughout the show and the attendance at Dyadic's Vendor Forum was greater than at any other in the 10 years since the product was launched. Perhaps though this had something to do with the refreshments that were provided!

The focus of the company's exhibit was the OSF/Motif implementation of Dyalog APL. This is functionally identical to Dyadic's increasingly popular Windows product and offers true portability of APL GUI applications across PC and UNIX-based systems. Dyadic was able to demonstrate several Dyalog APL/W workspaces, including Adrian Smith's PostScript graphics package running unchanged on an IBM RS/6000 under Motif. The Motif product should be available by the end of '93 and will coincide with a new release of Dyalog APL/W.

In addition to the OSF/Motif implementation, Dyadic announced new plans for Dyalog APL. Foremost among these is a commitment to provide compatibility with APL2. This will be implemented by having a new start-up option which will permit users to run Dyalog APL in "native mode" or "APL2-compatible" mode. Features such as "find", which present no conflict with existing Dyalog APL, will be available in both modes. APL2 compatibility will be introduced in stages, with the first of these included in the forthcoming Motif and Windows release at the end of the year.

Secondly, Dyadic announced binary compatibility between Dyalog APL workspaces and component files. This will permit Dyalog APL applications to be run in a heterogeneous network of PCs and UNIX systems and will greatly assist developers who wish to provide applications for both environments. Dyadic also promised to implement )COPY for GUI objects and intends at the same time to permit such objects to be stored on component files. Last, but not least, the company announced plans to provide a fully CUA-compliant APL session and editor. These enhancements will all be included in the planned year-end releases. The company also indicated that it would develop a facility to allow third-party and user-written GUI objects to be accessed from Dyalog APL/W and announced long-term plans to incorporate more object-oriented features into Dyalog APL.

Soliton Associates head-office relocated in July to new office space in the Toronto city centre:

Soliton's mainframe development facility is now operated by a facility management company at a service centre in the Toronto area. Soliton's SHARP APL for MVS customer-base continues to enjoy worldwide network access to Soliton's Electronic Mail System as part of Soliton's 24-hour 365-day Technical Support Service.

Development of SHARP APL for MVS Version 21 is complete, and preparation for general distribution is in progress. The emphasis of Version 21 is on enhanced performance, operability and connectivity.

Version 1.5 of Soliton's MVSLink connectivity product is announced. MVSLink provides SHARP APL for MVS and SHARP APL for UNIX with access to data in the IBM MVS environment. It includes a high-capacity interface to IBM's DB2 relational database product.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
Well, APL93 has come and gone. Many congratulations to the organisers in Toronto for a first class conference. A large contingent from the British APL Association was present, and several members gave papers. One of the spin-offs was an agreement between several of the local APL groups to exchange newsletters and where appropriate to reprint material. This type of cooperation can only be beneficial to the APL community throughout the world, and we look forward to fruitful collaboration in the future. If any other editors of APL newsletters would like to join us, please contact me and we will be pleased to welcome you aboard!

APL94 will be in Belgium in September 1994 — more of that at a later date, but if anyone would like a copy of the first announcement and "call for papers", please drop me a line (or electronic equivalent).

Meanwhile two BAA events are worth noting. There is a GUI workshop in London on 26th November 1993, cost £75, details from the BAA Secretary, Duncan Pearson ([telephone number omitted]). In July 1994 there is an International Workshop "APL in Business" at Swansea University, jointly sponsored by the BAA and the European Business Management School, Swansea, for which most of our readers will have received an Announcement — I will gladly forward details to anyone who wants them. The continued development of GUI's, and the general standardization of interfaces between packages, make APL an invaluable ingredient in any serious business computing venture in the 1990's. These two events are designed to help business people make informed choices — and to realise what they are missing if they reject APL!

In this issue, as promised I have reviewed "Introduction to APL*PLUS/PC" by Maurice Dalois. My note on Cows and Bulls prompted Ted Emms to do a lot of work and produce a creditable effort at solving the 4 by 4 problem. I have included his (substantial!) solution in this edition, and note that he in turn has issued a challenge — can anyone improve on his coding of the tree structure which underlies his solution? Ted was restricted by his use of first-generation APL, but we will be interested in solutions using nested arrays too. Finally, Norman Thomson has written a short article on J, a language which some regard as the logical successor to APL, some regard as a valuable alternative, and others reject as too perplexing to be of any consequence! As usual, I await your views with interest.

If anyone would like to receive the rest of the journal Vector (144 pages!), from which Education Vector is taken, application forms for membership of the BAA are available from Rowena Small, [address omitted]. UK subscription is currently £12 (students £6).

Please note the change in my email address (Edvec front cover) — the old one will work for some time, but the new one is preferable.

items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Anthony Camacho

items.title: Toronto
items.text:
May I thank the APL 93 Committee and their helpers on behalf of the APL community? APL 93 had the best programme of any conference I've attended. That made reporting it hard work. In four and a half days from 8:30 to 17:00 there were three sessions when I was not in one presentation or another; the reports seem to me more earnest than usual. Perhaps I tired myself out. I'm sure the people who ran it did.

Toronto is a very civilised place. Most of it is clean, it has excellent publicly run public transport, it tolerates minorities, there are few street beggars and they are not too threatening, it is safe to walk about at midnight, much of it is even beautiful and it has the most amazing warren of underground walkways and malls which extend about a mile north east from the CN Tower. You can see a lot of Toronto in a heat wave or the cold of winter without suffering from its climate.

The conference, too, was civilised. It ran with the minimum overt control. Many sessions even omitted a chairman. The weather was unusually hot and this made hurrying a bad idea; people often arrived late, especially for the more distant sessions. Luckily the presentation theatres were air conditioned but the room where Donald McIntyre's tutorial was held was not! J is hard enough without sweat tricking down one's face.

The civic reception was run-of the mill as these things go. The location was quite extraordinary. The city hall is a very avant garde building and I was glad of the chance to see inside it. The banquet at Casa Loma offered an excellent range of types of food. The place itself was fascinating to explore and the entertainments varied enough to please everyone. The picnic at Algonquin island was just the sort of relaxed occasion I needed. A pity so few people accepted the implied invitation on the bottom of the instructions how to get there "Yes, you may swim in the lake."

Nominally Jonathan Barman handed over the editor's chair to me after Volume 10 number 1 was printed. The material for volume 10 number 2 was nearly all collected and edited for me. Thank you Jonathan and the working group. Please do go on helping.

There is no charge for entries in the product guide. We are very keen to make it comprehensive and will welcome new entries. Even if you only provide your services in Vancouver or Valparaiso, please send us your entry for the product guide. Vector has a large international readership. What have you got to lose?

items.title: Little-known Feats of APLers:
items.text:
Chris Lincoln, Joint Chairman of APL 89 in New York, has other talents. This July he sailed his windsurfer all round Fire Island in one day. Readers should know that Fire Island, though narrow, is over thirty miles long! Chris reckons that, with tacking, he sailed about eighty miles and the trip took nine hours.

Jim Brown Entertains at the Conference Picnic
