items.title: The APL 93 Russian Fund
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

From: Ben Best, 20 Sept 93

I am happy to say that the APL 93 Russian Fund was a success. The Russian Fund paid transportation, Visa fees, conference registration, living expenses and arranged accommodation for seven Russians. Two additional Russians attending APL 93 received logistical support (and accommodation arrangement, in one case) from the Russian Fund, although they paid other expenses themselves. Andrei Kondrashev (Chairman of APL 92) has been living & working in Chicago and needed no help from the Russian Fund. Thus, there were a total of ten Russian delegates at APL 93.

The APL 93 Russian Fund total revenues were Cdn$10,480.20 and total expenses were Cdn$9,615.37. The APL 93 Russian Fund was closed-out by sending a cheque for US$643.48 to the APL 94 Russian Fund.

Three key elements to the financial success of the Fund were:

  • the fact that Russians could buy round-trip tickets to Montreal for under US$500 (although these prices have been rising rapidly);
  • the willingness of Toronto APLers to open their homes to Russian guests at no financial cost;
  • the generosity of those who contributed to the Fund.

Special thanks go to the two largest contributors:

  • The British APL Association, which contributed about US$2,250.
  • Security APL of Chicago, which contributed US$1,000.

The nine delegates who came to APL 93 from Russia were Alexander Skomorokhov, Dmitri Lukyanov, Pavel Luksha, Oleg Luksha, Alexei Skurikhin, Nikolai Puntikov, Aibarsha Mukanova, Alexei Kononov and Andrei Pakhomov. A brief character sketch of each of these people is the best way to convey the true success of the APL 93 Russian Fund.

Alexander Skomorokhov (Sasha). Dr. Skomorokhov is the president of SovAPL. At APL 93 he presented the paper "Adaptive Learning Networks in APL2". "APL" in Russian is an abbreviation for "Atomic Underwater Submarine". Due to his background in nuclear energy, Dr. Skomorokhov casually bought a book with "APL" in the title at a second-hand bookstore in 1979. It was the textbook by Gilman & Rose. He began looking at the book at midnight one evening, and became so engrossed that he didn't stop reading until 8am next morning. APL was not implemented in Russian until 5 years later (by Andrei Kondrashev).

Dr. Skomorokhov used APL as a formal notation for algorithms, and still uses it for this purpose. He has written many types of software for nuclear power diagnostics in APL, including expert systems, time-series analysis, databases, statistics, etc. He learned of APL2 from Erkki Juvonen, and this discovery was almost as electrifying for him as his initial contact with APL. Teaching APL2 to children in now a favourite hobby of his.

Sasha is very gregarious and he counts many people in the APL community as personal friends. He relished the opportunity at APL 93 to meet these people and make new friends. He appreciated seeing the latest version of APL2 on OS/2. He especially liked the presentation "Undocumented Features of APL" by Tima Laurmaa.

Dmitri Lukyanov. Dmitri is Dr. Skomorokhov's colleague at the nuclear power plant in Obninsk, Russia (near Moscow). Like Sasha, he found Gilman & Rose to be an exciting book, and he enjoyed the problems even without the benefit of a computer. When APL became available on computer he wrote assembler programs to take data from diagnostic sensors and feed that data to APL software. With the advent of a market economy he has taken the initiative to use APL to write a menu system for a restaurant/casino part-time, in addition to his regular work.

At APL 93 Dmitri was particularly interested in learning more about the British ASL (APL Statistics Library). He was very impressed by the Windowing APL systems he saw at the exhibits. And he thought Robert Bernecky's tutorial on Parallel Computing was'great. He hopes the Russian Fund will be unnecessary in a few years.

Pavel Luksha. Pavel is the 16-year-old son of long-time SovAPL member Oleg Luksha. At APL 93 he presented a paper on "Learning Modern Algebra" in which he demonstrated his attempts to solve the Problem of Irreducible Polynomials using APL. At the conference he particularly enjoyed the tutorials by Dr. McIntyre (Introduction to J) and Robert Bernecky (Parallel Computing) as well as the "Undocumented Features of APL" paper.

Oleg Luksha. Oleg is a lecturer at the Obninsk Study and Conference Centre for Nuclear Energy. He has been using APL since 1977 for teaching (to teach algorithms) and for scientific investigation (simulation of the process of dissolution of nuclear fuel). He has been interested in the ASL and was especially glad to meet Alan Sykes. But the high point of APL 93 for him was watching his son present a paper.

Alexei Skurikhin. Alexei presented the APL 93 paper "Identification of Parallelism in Neural Networks by Simulations in the Language J" with his University of Nebraska colleague Alvin Surkan. Alexei has no knowledge-of or interest-in APL. He only has experience in J. His main interest is neural networks, and he uses whatever tools he finds that can further his work. He uses J for prototyping small programs and uses C for large programs where speed of execution is more important. Alexei particularly liked Dr. McIntyre's "Introduction to J" tutorial, Robert Bernecky's "Parallel Computing" tutorial and Chris Lee's "Wicked Problems in APL" tutorial. He also liked the paper "Practical Statistical Computing using J" and he greatly enjoyed all the APL 93 social events.

Nikolai Puntikov. Nikolai was one of the key organizers of APL 92 and has continued to expand his expertise by organizing other, larger conferences in St. Petersburg (unrelated to APL). Nikolai took responsibility for co-ordinating the APL 93 Russian Fund in Russia (helping with visas, plane fares, money distribution and communications). Nikolai's expertise in linguistics was useful when Andrei Kondrashev needed to design a symbol table, keyboard and screen handler for the Russian implementation of APL. Nikolai still works at a language institute, but only uses APL for personal needs. He believes APL is a way of thinking, and he likes people who think in the APL way. He arrived at the final picnic after I left (I'm told he was on a book-buying spree) so I did not get his impressions of the conference.

Aibarsha Mukanova. Aibarsha was the only female in the group — and the only non-Russian. She lives and works in the former Soviet Republic of Kazakhstan, in Alma-Ata. She met Andrei Kondrashev in 1986 when she was doing her PhD thesis in Moscow. Currently she uses APL for differential equations used in modelling turbulent currents in the atmosphere. Studying the movement of particles over the Aral Sea is useful for forecasting dust and salt storms.

She said it was a great pleasure to learn of other scientists' work. She was very interested in Dr. Stephen Jaffe's plenary session on modelling petroleum chemistry. She thought Eric Iverson's tutorial "Windows GUI Programming in ISIAPL" was very good. Eric gave her an APL Windows system for her work, which gives Iverson Software a toehold in Kazakhstan! Moreover, Ray Polivka has induced her to write up her work for Quote Quad.

Alexei Kononov. Alexei received no money from the Russian Fund, but we did help him to find free accommodation — and we helped with logistics. I believe he was sponsored by the Ministry of Atomic Energy. He teaches algorithms by means of APL. He uses APL*PLUS. He won an APL*PLUS II system from Manugistics at APL 92, but he hasn't got the hardware to use it. At APL 93 he took a particular interest in "AGSS: A Graphical Statistical System", APLIWIN, "Wicked Problems in APL" and the (nearly) free run-time system of Manugistics. He thought David Eastwood's presentation on "Structured Functions with Operators" had some good ideas for producing more readable APL code for large systems. Alexei got Ken Iverson to autograph an APL 93 Conference Program.

Andrei Pakhomov. The APL 93 Russian Fund assisted Andrei with the logistics of registration, transportation and accommodation — but these were paid for in full by the company Andrei works for: EXIMA. Andrei had been a PASCAL programmer before meeting Andrei Kondrashev in 1986. Liking APL, he rewrote all his programs in the new language. With Boris Makeev, he developed an APL expert system for economic forecasting.

Then Andrei became more "practical" (he says), and started doing programming with the rapidly-growing new importing company EXIMA. Every aspect of EXIMA business operations is being programmed by Andrei in APL — tailoring the systems to the inflation, taxes and other idiosyncracies of the emerging Russian business environment. Andrei is held in almost god-like esteem by his company, which did about US$25 million worth of business last year (that's a lot of Roubles!). At APL 93 Andrei became convinced that Dyalog APL is the best tool for creating a user-friendly environment for EXIMA's applications.

If the above character sketches are any indication, the APL 93 Russian Fund was not only a financial success, but a success in advancing APL in the rapidly-changing new world of Russia. I believe that contributions to the APL 93 Russian Fund were an investment which will reap many benefits for the APL community in the future.

Contributions to the APL 94 Russian Fund can be sent to: The APL 94 Russian Fund, c/o Madame L. Lemagnen, 174 Boulevard de Charonne, F-75020 Paris, France.

items.title: Workshop — A GUI Standard for APL — Facilitator: David Crossley
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 87

reported by Anthony Camacho and Jonathan Barman

Although billed as a workshop, this was really a panel session with the usual introductory statements followed by audience comment and questions. We had not realised that there were two David Crossleys in the APL world, one who lives in Canada and one who lives in France. The Canadian David Crossley introduced the speakers: James Wheeler, David Liebtag, Peter Donnelly and Eric Iverson. He explained that he had written two systems in APL*PLUS II using quad-WIN and that he doesn't want to learn many windows GUI standards. He supposes the rest of us are equally reluctant and so we need to agree a GUI standard.
path: Workshop — A GUI Standard for APL — Facilitator: David Crossley

items.title: Initial Statements
items.text:
James Wheeler, who has been with STSC/Manugistics for 16 years, told us that Manugistics were committed at least to emulate the behaviour of the current features of their interpreters, so users could write new systems in confidence that they would continue to run in upgrades. He was dissatisfied with the current GUI interface and felt that we are far from reaching a final solution. It would be inappropriate to set a standard until we are sure it will last.

Peter Donnelly, who has been with Dyadic for 14 years and has worked on GUIs for the last three of them, tended to agree that it was too early to standardise. He felt that the GUI interface eventually needed to be part of the language, and to be portable would have to work not only with Windows, Motif and Presentation Manager but with any GUI system. A standard would have to apply to all GUIs. At present competition and the desire to have a competitive edge are strong forces against standardisation. In the process of looking at many GUI toolsets Peter has found that Objects and Events are easy in APL but that Properties are unnatural to it and the Dyadic team had implemented them as quad-functions. The Methods used in Visual BASIC for specifying circle, rectangle and so on are also unnatural in APL. Peter thinks that Visual BASIC has got it wrong. Dyadic found that call-back functions are easy and natural in APL functional structure and so overall APL is a great way to do GUI programming.

David Liebtag had ten years of applications experience before his work with the APL group for the last three or four years; he has recently been working on the OS/2 user interface. He said he admires the Dyadic approach but thinks it is wrong, and so he agrees that it is too early to standardise. Simple GUI interfaces are easy but a full one may be very complex indeed. As in consequence it will be expensive, it is not worth doing unless it is going to last; a two year life would not pay back the investment. In David's opinion the functionality should be in the operating system, not in the language, so IBM's current emphasis was to provide lots of easy-to-use utilities.

Eric Iverson has been an APL implementer for twenty-five years and has been working on the GUI interface for two years. He spoke about the philosophy behind the ISI window driver. The primary design goal was to keep the interface at a high level so that it is easy to use (N.B. NOT like C). A second goal is to make the driver portable to Motif and other windowing systems. So ISI began with the essentials to cover the needs of standard applications omitting the less often needed facilities but allowing the design to be extended when ISI users needed more. Using a windows driver meant that the same mechnism could be used for both J and APLIWIN and so the commands to it are written in a scripting language like PostScript or SQL. This approach preserves the integrity of APL and also makes it possible to sell the driver separately so that it could be driven from any other APL or any other language. ISI intends to improve the windows driver by adding features, but not too many low level controls as ISI does not want to compete with Visual BASIC or Smalltalk. Eric hoped the DLL as an independent product would be put on sale.
path: Workshop — A GUI Standard for APL — Facilitator: David Crossley

items.title: Contributions from the Audience and Panel Responses
items.text:
Ray Polivka confessed he was floundering; he had not been given a clear idea what it is that is involved in standardisation and still wanted to know.

Eke van Batenburg of the University of Leiden wants to be able to port GUI workspaces between PCs, Macs and Ataris. APL porting is easy: GUI porting is hard. He suggested that if we wait too long before standardising we will get another bad split, like that between boxed and nested arrays.

Jim Ryan said that he had been using APL for 25 years and that he would be satisfied if APL communicated with the GUI in a standard way. His preference is for the Dyadic solution to the problem. Willi Hahn later said that he would like to see the equivalent of quad and quote-quad for GUIs (whatever that would be). Steve Hayward asked about the value building GUI interfaces into APL when there are lots of products available to do the same job.

Peter Donnelly replied that Dyalog wished to be able to compete with Visual BASIC, C applications and that using another product to drive the GUI would be giving up the competition.

Adrian Smith said he sat alongside a user of Power Builder and could do the same job in a fifth of the time because he was using APL. He liked the scripting approach — his system writes PostScript in APL — but the problem with scripting is when you want to control the interaction between the user and the system.

Eric Iverson said that ISI had solved this difficulty; a scripting language can handle call-back and so this doesn't have to be a disadvantage of scripting.

Gregg Taylor suggested that he could map most ISI features to Dyalog features and vice versa; he felt these two implementations were not far from as compatible as two implementations of the APL filing system used to be. On the other hand he had found he could not do the same thing with IBM or Manugistics interpreters.

James Wheeler said he was 100% in agreement with John Scholes (of Dyadic) about the conceptual framework of call-back, objects, properties and methods. The differences between Dyalog and APL*PLUS arise from the things that are not intrinsic to the language: he pointed out that features built into quad-functions had not been added to the language, only to the implementation.

Richard Eller of TMT-Team said that using APL with an independent GUI product adds a lot to the complexity.

Asked why, as everyone agreed that APL was good at objects, they could not be added to the language, Peter Donnelly explained that the difficulty is that APL does not have structures: a structure, for example, would be a defined pattern for a nested array. David Liebtag amplified by saying that a structure would be the equivalent of a user-defined type.

A speaker who claimed to come from Harvard (but no-one is listed as such in the list of delegates) suggested that even if we could agree on a specification for the ideal GUI interface, the thing would necessarily be so complex that there would not be enough users to test out all its features and find the bugs in anything like a reasonable time.

Richard Levine thought a good approach would be to emphasise the importance of examples. Try many out in several implementations and compare the elegance and ease of use of each of them. By publishing such comparisons Vector and Quote-quad could serve the community by helping people towards an informed consensus.

Arto Juvonen said he had a Vitaform driver which could drive Dyalog and Manugistics with a scripting language. He had a window looking like an HP45 calculator containing 65 objects which worked in both implementations.

Nikolai Puntikov said that maybe it is too early to standardise the GUI interface but it is most important to be able to do the work using the currently available operating systems and interpreters. To get what he needs he writes DLL code in C and so wants a way to drive this code. It is how APL should control this DLL driver that ought to be standardised. Since an object oriented APL would be a different language, there is no point in trying to incorporate it inside APL.

Zdenek Jizba said that he had been using APL since it was invented and that Iverson's genius was to abstract the concepts necessary to express algorithms of great power. He felt what we needed was a similar genius to abstract the essence of the GUI interface.

Adrian Smith said that no-one has yet had to maintain an APL/GUI system. He foresaw problems and wanted to agree with Nikolai that putting the GUI features into APL, even as quad-functions, compounded the difficulty.

Eric Iverson said that the vendors have provided enough to enable users to write APL GUI systems and that by sticking to the middle of the road users could write fairly portable GUI systems now.

Richard Levine wondered whether the APL Toolkit could be expanded with suitable GUI cover functions.

Keith Sanders wondered whether APLs could be given access to the DLLs in Visual BASIC, but James Wheeler said that Microsoft forbade the use of the necessary hooks.

Eric Iverson hoped that the DDE engine used in APLIWIN and J-WIN would be available in the autumn.
path: Workshop — A GUI Standard for APL — Facilitator: David Crossley

items.title: David Steinbrook and Eugene McDonnell ‘From Trees into Boxes’
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 91

reported by Anthony Camacho

David Steinbrook introduced the presentation by saying it was a report on work in progress. The authors had been given access to the source code for J from the beginning of the project. The original proposal had been to add a tree data type to J, encouraged by Knuth's remark that trees are the most important non-linear structures arising in computer algorithms. The version of J with the new data type was written but there were many overlaps between the operations required to manipulate trees and those provided for boxed arrays.

Eugene McDonnell

On investigation they found that the J boxed data type enabled them to do even more than they had expected. All they needed to implement trees were some specialised verbs, adverbs and conjunctions and so they now have implemented trees as a subset of boxed arrays. This has been done without adding a new data type to the language. The new parts of speech are added as external verbs in the 12!:n range and the C code is very similar to the J model on which it is based.

The main body of the presentation followed the paper fairly closely, going through the representations of a tree, the process of tracing a tree and over fifty facilities for manipulating trees or parts of them. The traditional representation of a tree is of the trunk and its branches; there are no roots (which would make it look double-ended) although the node where they would go is called the root, yet for some reason a tree is usually shown as Ken would put it upside down with the leaves at the bottom. We were told that Ken also says trees are round (3D), although the data type consists entirely of espaliers (2D): how this affects things and how the paper representation falls short was not made clear.

David said that the source code would be made available and looked forward to seeing trees in common use in J.
path: David Steinbrook and Eugene McDonnell ‘From Trees into Boxes’

items.title: Robert Bernecky ‘Array Morphology’
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 92

reported by Anthony Camacho

Robert Bernecky began by saying that the reputation APL has for being slow is deserved when it is used to do lots of operations on small arrays. This is because to execute a line of APL it is necessary to perform a series of initial tasks:

  • Analyse the syntax and put together the actions to be performed
  • Decide the storage needed and allocate it
  • Check the type of each variable and intermediate value for compatibility
  • Check the form of each argument to ensure they conform as necessary

These tasks vary little with the size of the variables; for a line which processes scalars the overhead is almost as much as for a line handling large arrays. When the large array has to be handled by a parallel processor there is extra overhead involved in deciding which bits to send to which processor and this adds to the overhead. According to Bob the average number of elements in an array is only about seven to fifteen. This is far too few for efficiency and the initial tasks require more work than the processing of the variables. It is therefore important to write APL so as to use to the full its ability to process large arrays and this becomes even more important when one wants to use a parallel processor efficiently.

To use a parallel processor in APL one has either to change the language by adding declarations of variable sizes and types or, if one is unwilling to change the language to be able to deduce these. Without changing the language it is possible to add lines of code which force a variable to take a particular type and if, for example they passing a localised variable which is not used the analyser can also omit the processing implied in the line from the final compiled code. The deduction can be done on a preprocessing pass through the code. It is surprising how much can be deduced from perfectly ordinary code; for example in Mike Jenkins' model of domino the Bernecky analyser was able to deduce 100 out of 175 types. Adding just a few declarations raised the total to 174.

The C code produced by the analysis and compilation is often not nice. No-one would want to maintain it. It may then be optimised and after that it may be unrecognisable.

In general the improvements that J makes to the APL syntax reduce the deductions that can be made. For example the APL expression X[1;] enables the analyser to deduce that X has rank 2 but the J equivalent does not give the equivalent information. However declarations by additional code which the analyser can recognise as omittable are equally easy in J and some features of J enhance compilability.

items.title: Norman Thomson ‘Understanding ANOVA the APL Way’
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 93

reported by Sylvia Camacho

Norman is an expert and charming teacher and he began in characteristic style by saying that the consequence of devising the functions he was about to present was that he now feels that he understands ANOVA fully for the first time. The implication was also that the subject is a good deal simpler and more approachable than it has been made by professional teachers of statistics. Indeed this was the theme he was developing when he suddenly broke off to present his last slide in order to ensure that he would not run out of time before presenting his conclusions. This seemed to be an exercise in canny Scottish prescience because two minutes later the lecture was prematurely ended by a false fire alarm.

The paper contains all the functions, of course, beginning with the basic set,

Mean of a vector Vector with mean substitution Sum of squares about the mean Mean polish of array — all axes Fitted values following regression

These are then used to show how to perform:

One-way ANOVA Two-way ANOVA Multi-way ANOVA Analysis of Variance following Regression

The use of the regression function is then developed in a discussion of orthogonal polynomials, regression with two-way data, multi-way ANOVA with regression and maximum decomposition of sums of squares. Finally an illustration is given of the application of the functions to experimental data.

To round it all off Norman provides a Summary of the Principal Functions,

one-way ANOVA two-way ANOVA multi-way (main effects) multi-way (all effects) multi-way interactions 1-way with linear regression 1-way with polynomial regression 2-way with polynomial regression multi-way polynomial regression 2-way total decomposition Balanced incomplete block designs Latin & Youden squares

For maximum impact the following message should be projected as large as possible on the wall at stage back and the lecturer should leave the podium without further comment, allowing the audience to draw its own conclusions.

'These functions have been fully described and their use illustrated in less than ten pages. They are fully sufficient to deal with the computational needs of the many and varied exercises in one of the best known current textbooks "Design and Analysis of Experiments", Douglas C. Montgomery, 3rd edn., John Wiley & Sons, 1991'

Yet we wonder why APL is not popular with the Educational Establishment?

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Alan Mayer

Happy New Year and welcome once again to Education Vector. 1994 sees the tenth anniversary of the first edition of Vector in May 1984, when the British APL Association made the "quantum leap" from a simple newsletter to the professionally produced (and regularly appearing!) journal that is now read throughout the world. Education Vector first appeared two years later, in October 1986, under the editorship of Norman Thomson — who has maintained a close (and valued) interest through the years, and is now contributing articles on J, one of which appears in this edition.

During 1994 the British APL Association plans to introduce another journal, dedicated to papers on original, serious applications of APL, J and other array-orientated languages. The journal was announced last year as "The APL Review", but this title came in for some criticism at APL93, and a more formal title has been adopted: "Journal of Array Processing Languages and Algorithms". All papers will be fully-refereed and edited by an international team of APL experts in a wide variety of fields, such as statistics, econometrics, engineering, actuarial applications, simulation, operational research and so on. People who use APL professionally can learn from each other, even when their fields of study or application are very different. The new journal aims to draw all of these fields together and provide a vehicle for inter-disciplinary communication.

Linked with the launch of the journal is the special International Workshop "APL in Business" at the European Business Management School, Swansea University, in July. Jointly sponsored by the British APL Association and EBMS, under coordinators Adrian Smith (Chairman) and Alan Sykes (Programme Chair), this will use the common medium of APL to draw together the inter-related themes of Finance, Operational Research and Statistics.

In September (11th to 15th), the Annual International Conference, APL94, takes place in Antwerp, and authors are invited to submit papers on APL — the language, its environment, its practice and its applications. The Programme Chairman is Alain Delmotte, [address omitted].

In this edition of Education Vector, I am pleased once again to include a substantial contribution from Walter Spunde, who is no stranger to our readers, and one from Joseph De Kerf, who is the Conference Chairman of APL94.

We are always keen to hear of local initiatives to promote APL. A "first" to my knowledge is an APL Class advertised by Bill McLean (also well-known to our readers) through the University of Glasgow Adult Continuing Education scheme. Well done Bill! Perhaps there are others out there who could promote APL in this way.

The British APL Association is always looking for new members. Application forms are available from Rowena Small, [address omitted]. UK subscription is currently £12 (students £6).

items.title: Note on J for beginners by the Editor
items.text:
Norman Thomson made a mistake in J-ottings 1. It is only too easy to do and as Editor I have to admit that it was my responsibility to spot the error and correct it. I failed and will probably fail again. I find J very difficult.

Unlike Kenneth E Iverson, I feel that what we offer as a correct expression should be correct. Ken is unworried about an error, saying “If it doesn’t work then the reader will have to find out why and the effort will be good for him.” I wonder whether the complete absence of complaints on my desk about the error is because nobody spotted it or because everyone is too kind. The helpful suggestion Ken made in his letter, reproduced here, was that we should commission an article to explain composition.

We have done so. We hope to be able to publish it in April. Experienced APLers too easily think they have the right mindset to understand J. J is a dialect of APL or at least they have a common aim — to enable algorithms to be expressed briefly and without ambiguity but almost everyone has difficulties when they begin to learn J. Even Donald McIntyre admitted to coming close to despair before he could write J expressions which did what he wanted.

There is no single text which we can advocate as the best way to learn J and even the articles in Vector are imperfect as the early ones were written in early versions of J which have been superseded. Some expressions have changed meaning. Even the Dictionary of J has occasional omissions as Gene McDonnell remarks (see At Play with J in this issue of Vector).

A valuable aid to a learner who wants to see how an expression will be evaluated is to enter the expression without arguments. For example when you enter >:@]-[ the system displays its interpretation of this: >:@]-[

┌────────┬─┬─┐
│┌──┬─┬─┐│-│[│
││>:│@│]││ │ │
│└──┴─┴─┘│ │ │
└────────┴─┴─┘

This shows that the effect is ( >: @ ] ) -[ as Norman Thomson says. Another of Norman Thomson’s expressions is: +/%#

┌─────┬─┬─┐
│┌─┬─┐│%│#│
││+│/││ │ │
│└─┴─┘│ │ │
└─────┴─┴─┘

But when you give it an argument its interpretation changes, unless you have inserted parentheses round the expression shown.

Of course if you supply an argument the result is no longer the interpretation of the expression but the result of the expression applied to the argument so you have to use a little cunning to see the effect: you supply an argument in the form of a verb which has a suitable argument as a result +/%#9::

┌─────┬────────┐
│┌─┬─┐│┌─┬─┬──┐│
││+│/│││%│#│9:││
│└─┴─┘│└─┴─┴──┘│
└─────┴────────┘

[Note: the verbs 0: to 9: were added to J in version 6.]

The way to get the result you want is to enter parentheses: (+/%#)9:

┌───────────┬──┐
│┌─────┬─┬─┐│9:│
││┌─┬─┐│%│#││  │
│││+│/││ │ ││  │
││└─┴─┘│ │ ││  │
│└─────┴─┴─┘│  │
└───────────┴──┘

items.title: Letter
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 19

From: Kenneth E. Iverson, Toronto, Ontario, Canada.

I was pleased to see that discussion of J is beginning to appear in the Education Vector. J has a variety of ways of composing functions to produce new functions (using hooks and forks as well as several conjunctions) in addition to the well-known composition of mathematics; I believe that a simple unified introduction to the forms of composition would be helpful to readers of Education Vector. I therefore suggest that you invite submission of such an article.

items.title: Conference Overview
items.text:
The theme of the conference will focus on APL — the language, its environment, its practice, and its applications. A list of application topics covered could be (being not exhaustive):

APL and Education Biology Finance Mathematics Astronomy Economics Binary Algebra Medicine O.R. Numerical Calculus Engineering Decision Support Statistics Process Control Expert Systems Physics Production Control A.I. Chemistry Fuzzy Sets Actuary

APL is a living language, continuously extended and adapted to the evolution of information technology. On the other hand, we must convince the outside world that APL is the most powerful and most productive programming language, by showing its facilities in practice, illustrated by successful applications. We think that applications are important for the outside world. We will attract people to APL if we offer them solutions to their problems: we need running applications to show them.

items.title: Conference Site
items.text: The APL94 International Conference will take place from 11th to 15th September 1994 at the Government House, Antwerp, Belgium. The conference site is in the centre of the city. Hotel reservations available at registration will include the Plaza Hotel and the Waldorf Hotel, both at about ten minutes' walk from the conference site, and the Arcade Hotel. Antwerp is very easy to reach by air, car or by train.

items.title: Papers and Posters
items.text:
Papers will be presented on APL — the language, its environment, its practice, and its applications. There will also be presentations involving related languages, such as Nial and J. The papers will be printed in Proceedings provided to the participants.

Posters give the opportunity to publish later breaking ideas, to announce preliminary results, and to state a claim for first publication. They allow a one-on-one dialogue between presenter and attendees, and permit deeper discussion. There is no deadline for presenting a poster, but if you send a 100 to 120 word abstract and a one or two page summary to the Program Chairman before 31st March 1994, the abstract will be published in the Invitations and Final Program, and the summary will be distributed to all participants of the conference. Posters will be published after the conference in one of the leading APL Journals. We should note that the posters have more importance every year.

items.title: Workshops
items.text: Workshops allow interested parties to discuss specific issues in a small and informal forum. A text, eventually addended by personal notes of potential participants and a bibliography on the subject, will be distributed to the participants of the workshop and will be used as basis for further discussion. At a panel, to be held before the closing session, the conveners will report the discussions made and decisions taken at their workshops. A short post-conference report on each workshop will be published in one of the leading APL Journals.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:

  2. An Introduction to the new language J

The tutorials — except for the lunch — are free of charge for the participants and are open to non-participants to the conference. Other subjects have been suggested. items.title: Insight Systems
items.text:
As a new Sustaining Member, we would like to start off by expressing our thanks to the BAA for providing us with this excellent platform from which to express our continued commitment to APL.

Insight Systems was formed in 1990 from the remains of I.P.Sharp Copenhagen. We suddenly found ourselves with no mainframe to logon to, and spent the first couple of years searching for good development tools on workstations with sufficient algorithmic punch for the type of applications we were used to. Needless to say, we did not find anything until the APL vendors finally got their act together.

The next search was for connectivity tools which would enable us to get at corporate data form the development tools of our choice, whether they be Excel, C++, Smalltalk or APL. To our delight, we discovered that the product which we liked best — SequeLink Client/Server MiddleWare™ — did not have a Danish distributor.

Besides marketing SequeLink to the general Data Processing Public in Denmark, we have created a product called SQAPL. The "SQAPL Client" gives APL applications access to all SequeLink-supported services (which includes practically all major SQL databases) via just about any network protocol. Our "SQAPL Server" product allows APL systems to function as SequeLink Servers. With the SQAPL Server, you can use a Unix APL Server to provide improved performance and security to Windows or OS/2 applications. Client and Server systems need not use the same APL interpreter — you can write a front-end in APL/W or APL*PLUS II under Windows and call APL2/6000 applications if you wish.

To non-APL SequeLink Clients such as Visual Basic, C++ or Excel, the SQAPL Server looks like any other server — with a "non-standard" dialect of SQL. Data is input to APL in the form of "bind variables", and returned in tabular form.

Since we announced SQAPL at APL93, we have distributed SQAPL products to customers using Dyalog APL and APL*PLUS II under Windows, OS/2 and Unix, to connect to Dyalog APL, Ingres, Oracle (6 and 7), RDB, OS/2 DBN, DB2/2 and DB2/370 over TCP/IP, SPX, DecNET, and NetBIOS. SQAPL is also available for APL2/2 and APL2/6000, as soon as these products become generally available.

The development of SQAPL has resulted in some tools for the delivery of APL tools on multiple platforms. We can now generate C-coded tools or utilities capable of handling APL arrays from (or converting between internal forms of) Dyalog APL, APL*PLUS II or APL2 (and we plan to add APL/68000 and Sharp APL), packaged for any of these systems under Windows, OS/2 or Unix. Please give us a call if you have an idea which needs this type of technology.

items.title: Manugistics Inc
items.text:
The phones at Manugistics have been ringing all day long since we announced plans for the new APL*PLUS III for Windows, due for release in Spring 1994. We're very encouraged to hear from so many clients who have expressed excitement and approval of the design plans we announced for APL*PLUS III. Many of you may have had the opportunity to preview the product during James Wheeler's "seven cities in 10 days road show" in Europe this past December where feedback from seminar attendees was overwhelmingly positive.

Here are some highlights of the upcoming release:

  • APL*PLUS III will be built using the Win32 API, Microsoft's official facility for supporting 32-bit applications under Windows. This ensures that the applications you build will also run on Windows NT and the future "Chicago" version of Windows. Win32s will be packaged with the product.
  • APL*PLUS III features a pure Windows-based session manager and full-screen editor that follows Windows style conventions. This consistent graphical user interface means that in addition to having a standard Windows look-and-feel, Windows users will be able to very quickly become productive, probably without even opening the manuals.
  • Free run-time!
  • The APL-based APLGUI workspace in the current version of APL*PLUS II is being replaced with facilities that are written in C and built into the interpreter for APL*PLUS III. This means that the toolkit itself will be smaller, simpler, and fast. Applications written using the APLGUI toolkit in APL*PLUS II will be upwardly compatible with APL*PLUS III/Windows.

Those of you who program in other languages besides APL will be glad to know APL*PLUS III will include control structures similar to those in C for easier code readability and maintenance. Even some hard-core APL purists who have seen how we're implementing control structures admit they will be of value.

Other features in APL*PLUS III include on-line Help, improved DDE and DLL interfaces, and the APL*PLUS Debugger, repackaged with a Windows user interface.

Anyone purchasing APL*PLUS II between now and the time APL*PLUS III is available will receive a coupon for a free migrate to the Windows product when it is released. Beta systems of APL*PLUS III are available through European dealers.

For those of you running DOS applications only, we've also announced that an unbundled version of APL*PLUS II for DOS is now available. This version runs under both DOS and Windows, but will not include the Windows interface and APLGUI toolkit. This represents an opportunity for those of you who do not need a true Windows APL to get the full power of APL*PLUS II at a much lower price (check with your local dealer for pricing).

items.title: MicroAPL Limited
items.text:
MicroAPL is announcing APL Level II for the Apple Macintosh with PowerPC at MacWorld in San Francisco on January 5 1994. I am sure by now that most of you will have read about the new generation of Macintosh computers based on the PowerPC RISC processor which are scheduled for release in the first half of 1994. These computers will, for the first time, bring the power of high-end RISC workstations to the personal computer market.

The new interpreter has been translated to run native on the PowerPC using PortAsm, MicroAPL's 680x0 to RISC assembly-language translation tool. APL Level II is based on and 100% compatible with APL.68000 Level II, which was originally written in 68000 assembler to ensure maximum performance. PortAsm allows us to efficiently translate this code onto the PowerPC architecture while still maintaining a single set of APL interpreter source code. Indeed the compatibility between our Apple Macintosh version and the PowerPC version is so great that even auxiliary processors written in 68000 assembler will work without translation! This is achieved by automatically triggering the 68000 emulator which Apple have designed into the Macintosh for the PowerPC.

As with all our second-generation APLs, APL Level II is designed for maximum compatibility with IBM's mainframe APL2 product. APL Level II workspaces and APL files share the same binary format as those of our APL.68000 products.

Features of APL Level II include:

Close conformance to IBM's APL2 Full Mac user interface Nested and mixed arrays Easy access to Mac toolbox Selective specification APL GUI event handling User-defined operators Multi-tasking N-wise reduction Sophisticated session manager Axis on scalar functions Multiple independent edit windows Overlays (packages) Direct import from other APLs Powerful file system Free runtime licences available

APL for PowerPC will be available simultaneously with the commercial launch of the first PowerPC Macintoshes in early 1994. It comes complete with a collection of support workspaces and complete documentation.

MicroAPL's development staff have also been at work on the RISC System/6000 and the result is the completion of our APL68000/X to C—ISAM interface. Based around the Informix implementation of C—ISAM, this product allows the APL programmer to create multi-key files where the keys themselves may be made up of several sub-parts. Access to files can be by exact key match, generic key match, first record and read forward, or last record and read backwards. It is supplied with a support workspace and full documentation.

As part of our continuing commitment to quality we have been enhancing our in-house APL testing suite. We can now perform over 200,000 automatic tests on new interpreters (or new releases of existing interpreters) to ensure that they are performing correctly. This is achieved by comparing known results with the results from the new interpreter. APL statements and their results are transferred onto the testing environment then the APL statements are executed by the new interpreter and the new results are compared with the originals.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
During the last quarter of '93, details of the "X/Open Common Desktop Environment" (CDE), which was announced earlier in the year, began to emerge. As a result, Dyadic postponed its plans for a December release of Dyalog APL for Motif and a parallel upgrade to Dyalog APL/W for Windows.

CDE is part of a major new initiative which is backed by all the leading Unix vendors to provide a common application programming interface and a standard desktop environment for Unix workstations. CDE is based on OSF/Motif with additional software and tools contributed by members of the consortium. For example, the desktop is developed from Hewlett Packard's VUE and the inter-client communications is based on Sun's ToolTalk. CDE is intended not only to provide standardisation for developers and users alike, but also to deliver all of functionality and ease-of-use features of Microsoft Windows. Indeed, one way of looking at CDE is that it is the Unix answer to Windows.

Although the decision to re-target the Motif version of Dyalog APL for CDE has delayed the product considerably (CDE itself will not be available until mid '94), it will bring major benefits to APL users. In particular, CDE will enable Dyadic to deliver 100% APL/W compatibility in areas where this is impossible to achieve with Motif alone. For example, CDE provides very "Windows-like" printer support and font management facilities that are entirely absent from Motif itself. In addition, CDE's inter-application communication facilities are equivalent to Windows DDE and will permit the full implementation of shared variables in the Unix version of Dyalog APL.

Dyalog APL for CDE will be provided as a free upgrade to existing Dyalog APL/X users who have a current Support and Maintenance Agreement. To allow customers to begin to migrate existing APL/W and APL/X applications to the new product, an interim version for "raw" Motif is available on IBM RS/6000 and Sun SPARC systems. This version lacks certain features such as the PRINTER object and shared variables, and is supplied with the Dyalog APL/W manuals rather than the final CDE documentation. Nevertheless, this version is otherwise complete and will run most APL/W applications (with the restrictions noted above) unchanged. Customers wishing to take advantage of this offer should contact Dyadic or their local Dyalog APL distributor.

Although there will be several months delay before CDE is available from IBM, Sun Microsystems etc. the Dyadic development team will not be idle. Rather than producing a parallel (with Motif) end '93 release of Dyalog APL/W as originally planned, the company intends instead to develop an even richer new version of the product. In addition to the features announced at APL93, this version will include major object-oriented extensions to the APL language and many exciting enhancements to the already extensive GUI support facilities.

In response to the growing number of successful Dyalog APL/W products, Dyadic is planning to produce a third-party software catalogue ("Outer Products"). This will be distributed to existing customers and shipped with each new copy of the software. To obtain an entry in the catalogue, please contact Peter Donnelly at Dyadic.

items.title: Soliton Associates Limited
items.text:
Version 4.02 of SHARP APL for UNIX has been well received by customers, and Soliton's mainframe customer base is showing increasing interest in porting large-scale multi-user SHARP APL applications from IBM MVS mainframes to the UNIX environment. Significant cost savings can be obtained by running such applications under UNIX. Where required, Soliton's NSVP and MVSLink products provide access from UNIX to MVS data and services.

Current development plans for SHARP APL for UNIX include enhanced support for very large SHARP APL applications on SMP (symmetrical multi-processor) UNIX platforms.

An Application Programming Interface (API) for Soliton's Network Shared Variable Processor (NSVP) has recently been announced. The NSVP API supports access from non-SHARP APL software both to SHARP APL and to SHARP APL Auxiliary Processors. The NSVP accessed by the API can be either local or remote, thus the NSVP can be on the same computer as the calling software or on a network-connected computer.

The NSVP API will support the client-server architecture, typically with non-SHARP APL clients accessing SHARP APL or SHARP APL Auxiliary Processor servers. Initially, the NSVP API will be available under UNIX, with support for UNIX-MVS connectivity. This will allow, for example, access from another vendor's APL for UNIX to Soliton's DB2 Auxiliary Processor for MVS. Most of Soliton's major auxiliary processors for MVS can now be installed stand-alone (thus without SHARP APL for MVS) and accessed via NSVP from network-connected UNIX and MVS computers. Support for the NSVP API in additional environments, including Microsoft Windows, is under consideration.

items.title: Dutch APL Users Group
items.text:
The Dutch APL Users group organised an APL day in The Hague in close co-operation with Share Europe. A short summary of the speakers and their main points follows.

  • Theo Zwart of OASIS chaired the day and started with a general introduction.
  • Louis van Geldrop of Pecoma kicked off with an evocative statement about 'The Good, the Bad and the Ugly of APL'. It appeared that the ugly stands for the ugly APL characters, the bad was for the suppliers (insufficient standardisation, APL 2 late) and the good were (of course) the APL programmers.
  • David Eastwood of Micro-APL talked about 'The Advantage of APL in Application Development'. He raised many interesting points in defining the characteristics of 4GLs in general and where to fit in APL. Unfortunately, the tight schedule did not allow for much discussion. David finished with a small APL.68000 demo on the Macintosh.
  • Jim Brown of IBM talked about 'Inside the Human Brain with Parallel Processing'. He showed how you could feed another processor with APL instructions; you can not only transmit data and APL expressions (and get them executed and replied to) but even send APL functions by sending a transfer-file-function. Jim also elaborated about the possibilities of assigning several computations (for example, 128 sections of a brain-slice entomogram) to several processors, or to have a PC session manager for user-interface and a mainframe computer for computation.
  • Peter Donnelly of Dyadic Systems demonstrated his event-driven paradigm for GUI and other objects (graphics in particular). Peter showed the 4 basic GUI quad functions ⎕WCreate ⎕WSet ⎕WGet and ⎕WName, how properties of objects could be set (positional as well as by keyword), deleted and copied (... well, ... next week).
  • Paul Lewi from Janssen Pharmaceutical spoke about 'APL as Tool of Thought; an Instrument of Problem Formulation'. "Not solving, that is less interesting than problem formulation", he said. Paul elaborated upon the virtue of APL's symbols and of simplification. He showed several examples of APL equalities which are obvious in APL's symbols but are not obvious, or may even be impossible in a 3GL. He elaborated about the virtue of being able to simplify (thereby losing details, of course) like Mercator's projection as done in factor analysis. Paul showed several examples of the use of factor analysis. Your acceptance of this tool depends on your being a Platonist (the shadows give you all you can know about reality) or Aristotelian (what you see is all there is to see).
  • Benoit Paquin of Soliton Associates talked about 'Sharp APL for the Nineties'. First he recapped the history of Soliton (I.P. Sharp, Reuters, Soliton; gigantic databases, data, APL). He stressed the strong expertise of Soliton in networking and communication between very different computers. This was also illustrated by means of Soliton's NSVP (Network Shared Variable Processor) where APL on an IBM mainframe under MVS corresponds to APL (SAX actually) on a Unix machine. Benoit invited other vendors to work together more closely and share each others' strengths (a point also raised earlier by van Geldrop).
  • Jim Brown talked about 'Network Programming with Sockets: A Comparison of C and APL2'. Dressed in his socks, Jim said he was wearing a suit and a tie and wanted to talk about sockets (not socks). So he talked about protocols. Jim showed how to communicate by means of the TCP/IP protocol to other machines by AP119. He compared the elaborate way of doing that in C with the comprehensive way of doing the same in APL (mainly due to the need for extensive declarations in C). It seemed wasteful to repeat the character string 'TCPIP' in each command but Jim explained that this was 'a feature', because it would enable them to communicate via other protocols too (if necessary).
  • James Wheeler of Manugistics was unable to come but sent his slides. So in his place Theo Zwart presented them. They mostly stressed that Manugistics is still working to improve the Windows version of APL*PLUS (and they will drop DOS support to some extent). A full Windows version was finally announced, called APL*PLUS III. APL will also have the feature that it can be called from another language, like C, by DLL. Manugistics are also still working at a Windows version for Statgraphics. A positive message was the announcement of a free run-time version in the future.
  • Nancy Wheeler of IBM talked about 'APL2 for OS/2 and APL2 Connections'. Like Benoit she recapped history, but now IBM's view, in particular about the APs. Nancy reported that IBM is working towards more consistency in the use of APs so a user could port his applications between different machines without bothering about differences in AP syntax. Nancy also presented a short wish-list of top-priorities (but apparently still under discussion) including porting to other, non-IBM-machines, Windows NT, Windows? and (after some prompting from the audience) the APL compiler. Finally, she and Jim gave a demonstration of several features of the OS/2 version of APL2: easy printer support, colour font, keyboard handling and the use of name association.
  • Although it had become very late, Bernard Smoor evoked a lively but short discussion about Vendor co-operation.

Leiden, 4 November 1993 Eke van Batenburg

items.title: Obituary: Mike Gregory
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 10

by John Searle

It is my sad duty to inform you of the passing of one of our members, Mike Gregory. Mike died on December 3rd, 1993, following a recurrence of his battle against melanoma, at the age of 42.

Mike was one of those people who could do anything with computers. His CV reveals that he worked on almost all modern operating systems and, apart from his APL skills (in all dialects) he was proficient in languages ranging from C to REXX, SAS and SQL.

Mike's career began at British Oxygen Corporation (BOC) in 1972 and over 10 years moved from programmer in the Gases Division to Technical Manager of Interactive Services at BOC Datasolve. His projects ranged from the development of APLB for ICL mainframe hardware, to MIS systems, to a simulation of the Grand National horserace for the Sun newspaper.

Mike then helped to form IBSL as Technical Director, a company which serviced various clients in the leisure industry, before forming his own company PC Associates in 1985. The variety of his clients was again considerable. After a brief period working for SimCorp, the Danish software house, he returned to his freelance business, specialising in operations research and airline applications.

I met Mike whilst consulting to a well-known favourite British airline, and he helped me understand the complexity of existing APL code (and the maze of freelancing paperwork!) with great patience and humour. What Mike didn't know wasn't worth knowing, and what he did know would fill a database of textbooks. John Scholes from Dyadic Systems told me that in their client contact system, Mike was always listed as "nice bloke".

Mike's passions in life, away from computers, were Jaguar motorcars, motorbikes and good wines. The joys of classic British motoring adorned his conversation, his bookshelves and his driveway. Mike was also very concerned for the environment, and was a keen supporter of wildlife preservation.

Mike is survived by his wife Judith and their children Bill and Claire. Mike did request that if you wish to remember him, please plant a tree in his name.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce Version 7 of Dyalog APL/W. This is a major release packed with many new and exciting features.

One of the most important additions is the ability to use ⎕WC, ⎕WS, ⎕WG etc. to access Visual Basic (.VBX) Controls alongside regular Dyalog APL/W ones with exactly the same syntax. This facility gives the Dyalog APL/W user access to hundreds of commercially available Visual Basic add-ons including various Graph, Grid and Spreadsheet controls; even an OLE client control. In addition, users can add controls of their own design written to the .VBX standard using ordinary Microsoft development tools. Access to Visual Basic Controls is implemented using a general mechanism for defining a new Class of object and will be extended to other standards (e.g. OLE 2.0) and user-defined Widgets under OSF/Motif in the future.

Dyadic believes that with the new VBX interface, coupled with the enhanced DDE and Clipboard support and the facility to access any Windows DLL with ⎕NA, it alone can truly claim to offer an "open" APL for Windows.

A new MDICLIENT object is provided to allow users to develop applications that use the Multiple Document Interface (MDI) style. All of the standard MDI behaviour is supported. In addition, FORM class objects can now be children of other FORMS, and so can be used as general-purpose containers for a wide variety of uses and effects.

Version 7 now provides a variety of EDIT field types that perform built-in validation and formatting of numbers, dates etc.

Other new objects include TOOLBAR, STATUSBAR and STATUSFIELD. The TOOLBAR is normally displayed at the top of a FORM and is used to manage a scrollable set of tool buttons. The STATUSBAR is normally displayed at the bottom of a FORM and contains one or more STATUSFIELDS. These can have pre-defined meanings, such as monitoring the state of the Caps Lock key, in which case they are updated automatically by the interpreter. Alternatively, their contents can be set directly by your application.

All controls can now have associated TIP and HINT properties. A TIP is a (usually) short description which gets displayed as a pop-up message when the mouse pointer dwells over a control, for example over a BUTTON in a TOOLBAR. A HINT is typically a longer help message which gets displayed when an object (e.g. a MENUITEM) is selected. A HINT would normally be displayed in a STATUSFIELD, but you can in fact use any object capable of displaying text.

The TAB_BAR manages a scrollable set of TAB_BTN objects which allow you to provide a notebook-style interface similar to that used by the latest versions of Excel, Paradox, Lotus 1-2-3 and Organiser.

These new objects have all been designed to allow Dyalog APL/W users to build APL applications that provide the bang up-to-date user-interface features of other popular Windows products; and, because all the work is done for you by the interpreter, with the same snappy performance.

All FORMS and Controls now have a 3D property that can be used to achieve a variety of 3D effects. Furthermore, as the value of this property is by default inherited from the parent, setting 3D on the SYSTEM object '.' automatically gives a 3D appearance throughout your entire application.

Version 7 now provides support for Windows Metafiles so that you can incorporate fully scalable graphical pictures into your application. Not only can you import Metafiles, but you can also create them from primitive graphical objects and export them (via file or the ClipBoard) to other Windows applications. A final touch is a facility to disassemble an imported Metafile so that you can edit or rearrange its components within APL.

The APL Session has not escaped our attention and a StatusBar and ToolBar have been added. Furthermore, the components of the Session are directly accessible as named objects whose properties can be set by ⎕WS and read by ⎕WG. New menus, menuitems, tool buttons, status fields etc. can easily be added using ⎕WC, and unwanted items can be removed with ⎕EX. Menuitems and tool buttons can action predefined "system" operations (such as [load] and [edit]) or can execute any APL statement. This allows you to configure the Session exactly as you want and you can dynamically change it (manually or under program control) to suit particular workspaces. For example, your ⎕LX could add special menuitems and/or tool buttons, fully equipped with TIPS and HINTS, to run particular functions in a statistics workspace.

The names of your functions, and variables may be displayed in a separate dialog box and are therefore only a click away for editing, copying to the clipboard, etc. A number of improvements have been made to the Editor and Tracer and fully CUA-compliant select/cut/paste operations have also been implemented.

Finally, Dyadic has introduced Namespaces, a major new enhancement to Dyalog APL. A Namespace provides the means to gather together a collection of objects and acts as a separate "context" in which functions (including callback functions) can be run. This means that local functions and variables can be hidden from the rest of the workspace. The implementation of Namespaces, which encapsulate code and data, is a further step towards Object Oriented technology and is intended to provide major benefits for APL developers. Further information on this exciting new feature will be available by the time you read this announcement. Please call Dyadic for details.

To coincide with Version 7, Dyadic is publishing "Outer Products" a catalogue of third-party tools and add-ons for Dyalog APL. Some "Outer Product" software, such as the RAIN graphics workspace and CAUSEWAY GUI design tool from APL⋄385, are also included in the Version 7 package.

For details concerning price and availability, please contact Dyadic or your local Dyalog APL supplier.

items.title: Insight Systems
items.text:
On the Product Front, we are concentrating our efforts on the design and implementation of a new version of SQAPL which will support Microsoft's Open Database Connectivity (ODBC) specification. The primary design goal is to provide an interface which is completely compatible with our existing product — so that our customers will be able to take advantage of ODBC drivers to access dBase, Btrieve, ACCESS, Paradox (or even Excel and Comma Separated Variable text files) — plus any remote databases for which they have an ODBC Driver — and still be able to use SequeLink without changing the application. SequeLink is still a preferable solution for many Windows environments, and the only solution under Unix and OS/2 or if an APL Server is required.

An ODBC Driver is now available for SequeLink, so SQAPL users will have the option of using SequeLink "direct" or via the ODBC driver. TechGnosis have also announced an ODBC version of their Open Server. Once we have an ODBC SQAPL Client out the door, we will start work on an ODBC version of the SQAPL Server. With an ODBC SQAPL Server, developers will be able to make APL-Coded Databases or Analytical Tools running under Unix available to any development environment which supports ODBC.

We would also like to intentionally leak an official rumour that our ODBC interface will probably be bundled with an upcoming version of Manugistics' APL*PLUS III product. Due to the relatively long lead time for Vector, we have agreed to leak the news despite the fact that the agreement is still under negotiation. By the time you read this, you should be able to contact Morten Kromberg at Insight Systems or Paul Clements at Manugistics to hear whether we succeeded!

On the APL Consulting and Education Front, the Danish market is suddenly full of renewed interest in Graphical APL systems. It seems that many organizations who still use APL on a Mainframe are finally ready to "Downsize" — to the extent that APL courses have become a profitable activity! There was a waiting list for our first "Introduktion til Windows Programmering med Dyalog APL/W", so we will be scheduling several courses during 1994 and will also be "porting" the course to APL*PLUS III.

We would like to take the opportunity to announce that Insight Systems is now an IBM Software Partner, so we now market and support IBM APL2 and APL2-based products (like AGSS) under OS/2 and Unix. We are also authorised RS/6000 resellers, and thus capable of delivering complete "turnkey" systems based on the RS/6000 and any one of APL2/6000, APL*PLUS II/UNX and Dyalog APL/X. We look forward to cooperating with IBM Denmark in providing APL and Client/Server expertise to their APL2 customers!

items.title: Manugistics Inc
items.text:
Manugistics Inc is very pleased to announce the commercial release of APL*PLUS III for Windows. An Advance Release (version 1.0) began shipping on February 25, and the general availability release (version 1.1) will be ready by the time this issue of Vector appears. Please contact Cocking & Drury in the UK, your local APL*PLUS dealer, or Manugistics for specific information.

APL*PLUS III is a 32-bit Windows system that runs on Windows 3.1, Windows for Workgroups, and Windows NT. It is a completely Windows-hosted program, with a graphical development environment that has been designed to be a pleasure to use, whether for personal APL computing or for building Windows applications to be used by others.

APL*PLUS III includes a graphical development environment, event-driven user command processor, a built in graphical debugger, and a visual form editor that allows the programmer to build a graphical user interface by drawing with the mouse. The graphical user interface facilities are supported by fast, built-in system functions, and include regular and 3-dimensional versions of forms, frames, buttons, checkboxes, scrollbars, etc. Graphics support is also built in to the user interface, as is support for Dynamic Data Exchange. System functions provide access to Windows libraries and any other software packaged in a Windows DLL.

The design of APL*PLUS III reflects our views of how APL needs to evolve to become a competitive alternative to other languages in this decade and beyond. The GUI development facility follows a strictly object-oriented structure, using "classes", "events", "methods", and "properties". The APL interpreter is based on the well-proven technology of APL*PLUS II, but the heart of the system has been replaced with an event-driven architecture. Control structures, in the spirit of C or Pascal, provide an alternative to the "spaghetti code" that afflicts too many APL programs.

APL*PLUS III will continue to evolve rapidly both in terms of new tools and in enhancements to the language itself. We welcome the comments and suggestions of Vector readers.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
In the previous issue of Vector, MicroAPL announced APL Level II for the new PowerPC Macintosh computer. APL Level II was one of the first dozen applications to be seen running native on the new PowerPC Macintosh. To coincide with the launch of this important new computer, we have been upgrading our entire family of Macintosh APLs. The details of the upgrade are being finalised as this is written, but we have a fairly clear idea of what the upgrade will include.

The APL programming environment has been enhanced, combining ideas from our APL.68000/X for the RISC System/6000 and features found in Mac System 7 as well as improving our conformance to Apple's System 7 user-interface guidelines. We have added support for Apple Events — multiple workspaces may be launched simultaneously at startup. New Print menu items allow prints of workspace listings as well as contents of the APL window. The new Windows menu identifies multiple APL sessions by workspace name and we have added )IN and )OUT menu items for workspace exchange. The number of simultaneous APL tasks supported has increased as has the number of edit windows and user-defined windows. Improved user-preferences allow control over such items as default workspace sizes, window positions and sizes and default libraries.

APL programmers can now easily access hierarchical menus and popup menus and we have further improved event handling facilities with new event types. Amongst the new support workspaces is the PLOTMAC workspace for high-level business graphics. The interpreters themselves have been upgraded in line with our latest versions for the RISC System/6000 and PowerPC and a number of small bugs in the Level II interpreters have been fixed.

MicroAPL was instrumental in forcing the APL world into issuing free runtime licences and we have now included with our Mac APLs a packager to make stand-alone applications which may be distributed royalty-free.

Pricing details for the upgrades will be announced in April but we can confirm that we will be offering substantial incentives to upgrade to our Level II versions of APL as well as maintaining our policy of realistic pricing across the board.

items.title: Soliton Associates Limited
items.text:
Version 21 of SHARP APL for VMS, shipping in 2nd quarter 1994, offers improved performance and operability, in particular of the SHARP APL File System. For SHARP APL MVS applications requiring 24-hour 7-day availability, Version 21 offers new functionality supporting continuous on-line operation of databases stored in the SHARP APL File System.

Version 4.03 of SHARP APL for UNIX, shipping in 2nd quarter 1994, provides a powerful new Intrinsic Function facility, allowing secure and efficient access from SHARP APL for UNIX to software implemented in other languages.

Version 4.04 of SHARP APL for UNIX, shipping in 3rd quarter 1994, will support Sun's Solaris 2 operating system, allowing major multi-user SHARP APL applications to execute on large Symmetrical Multi-Processor Sun Unix platforms.

NVSP-API, an application programming interface for Soliton's Network Shared Variable Processor technology, will provide access from non-SHARP APL software to local or remote Network Shared Variable Processors, allowing, for example, non-SHARP APL client software to access local or remote SHARP APL server software, including SHARP APL for MVS Auxiliary Processors. Initially, NSVP-API will be available under UNIX and Microsoft Windows, and will support access to Network Shared Variable Processors operating under UNIX and MVS.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Alan Mayer

Welcome to an Education Vector with a difference! The difference is that most of this issue is devoted to a language which is not APL. It will come as no surprise to our readers to learn that the "intruder" is J. Indeed I am delighted to publish the promised article by Donald McIntyre "J: A First Lesson".

I can say without hesitation that everyone who studies this article will find new insights and a new understanding of the language — I certainly did. Of course it helps to have the J interpreter on your computer, and for those looking for a low-cost introductory package we hope soon to have available the interpreter, together with papers by Donald McIntyre, on one disk.

I am also pleased to include in this issue a delightful excursion into the world of Prime Numbers by Ted Emms.

items.title: Preparing for Swansea
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 4

from Adrian Smith (Workshop Co-ordinator)

APL in Business is intended to be a hard-working 3 days! The objective is simple: to prepare you (and your staff) for the future of APL. In a nutshell, this means learning to program your APL alongside Client-Server Architectures, Graphical User Interfaces, and in co-operation with all the wonderful software that populates the Microsoft universe.

The transition from the traditional APL environments (mainframes or stand-alone DOS machines) will not be an easy one, so get started now! Read Morten Kromberg (page 114) on Client-Server — Morten will be sharing a Wednesday afternoon session with Microsoft — and follow up with Gene McDonnell’s lovely tale of Client-Server in action (page 110). Read about a common approach to the Windows GUI (page 64), then spend an afternoon playing with it (choose Dyalog/W or PLUS III) on the Tuesday. Read George MacLeod (page 83) on the tricky details of high-quality graphics, and see the product in action (or maybe even buy it) at the evening street market.

Learn the latest techniques for handling time-series, control charts, actuarial problems, asset management — and then try out your new-found skills in the evenings (the labs will be open as late as you want them to be) with experts on hand to guide you. But remember: this is not a jolly! It has taken me over a year to get comfortable with this new world of Windows programmimg, so start reading now, absorb what you can, and go to Swansea prepared.

items.title: J at Greenock
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 44

reported by Norman Thomson

On the 1st of March, Donald McIntyre gave the latest of his justly acclaimed workshops at the IBM plant education centre in Greenock. The emphasis from the start was on the various forms of function composition about which more appears elsewhere in these pages. Version 7 of J was used, in which caps ([:) used in a fork provides an alternative to @.

Donald has now assembled a vast library of scripts which illustrate the many facets of J. These he selects with considerable flair and enthusiasm to construct individual sessions based on single problems, each of which highlights a generous variety of what most needs to be understood by the beginner. Construction of similarity matrices and of Markov chains are two such examples.

Donald also described the evolution and history of J, and the astounding capacity of the J interpreter to produce interesting results beyond what even its designer and author conceived — a new interpretation perhaps of artificial intelligence.
