items.title: British APL Association: Regulations
items.text:
1. Name

    The Group shall be called The British APL Association.

  2. Affiliation

    The Association is and shall be affiliated to the British Computer Society as a Specialist Group.

  3. Objects

    • a) To promote the use of APL;
    • b) To develop awareness and competence in APL;
    • c) To represent the interests of Association members with other bodies;
    • d) To contribute to the development of the language and definition of international standards.

  4. Constitution

    The British APL Association shall consist of:

    • a) President and Vice Presidents;
    • b) Chairman, Secretary and Treasurer;
    • c) Other elected officers;
    • d) Individual fee paying members;
    • e) Individual fee paying student members;
    • f) Corporate members;
    • g) Sustaining members;

  5. Members in Good Standing

    A member in categories 4(d), 4(e), 4(f) or 4(g) is in good standing with the Association by virtue of having paid all membership fees due to the Association for the current year. Any membership which is not renewed within the first four months after becoming due is deemed to have lapsed.

  6. Appointed Officers

    • a) A President may be appointed at the discretion of the Management Committee.
    • b) A maximum of four Vice Presidents may be appointed in recognition of service to the APL community at the discretion of the Management Committee.
    • c) Appointed Officers may serve for a period of one year with up to two consecutive renewals. Non-contiguous periods of office are permitted with no limit.
    • d) Appointed Officers shall have the right to attend free of admission charge all General Meetings of the Association and all events staged by the Association.

  7. Elected Officers

    • a) The Elected Officers shall be Chairman, Secretary, and Treasurer who must be individual fee paying members in good standing.
    • b) Other officers may be elected to fill posts created by the Management Committee.
    • c) It is the duty of the Elected Officers to attend meetings of the committee.
    • d) Election: The officers shall be elected by postal ballot - to serve from 1 May in the year of election until the following 30 April. Individual members will be sent one ballot paper; corporate and sustaining members will be sent five to be cast by five users of APL where possible.
    • e) Casual Vacancy: A vacancy occurring during the term of office may be filled by an appointment by the Management Committee.
    • f) The occupant of any post who has held it for three consecutive years is not eligible for election to that post in the fourth year.

  8. Management

    • a) The affairs of the Association shall be managed (subject to the control of the AGM) by a Management Committee comprising:
      • i) Appointed Officers
      • ii) Elected Officers
    • b) Co-option: The Management Committee may co-opt members as required, normally to hold office until the following 30 April.
    • c) The General Committee of the Association shall comprise the Management Committee together with members of Sub-Committees and Working Parties which from time to time be set up by the Management Committee.
    • d) Meetings: The Management Committee shall meet at least four times in its year of office and frequently enough to carry out the business of the Association properly.
    • e) Notice: At least fourteen days notice of the place, date and time of meetings shall be given to each member of the relevant committee.
    • f) Quorum: The business of the Association may be transacted by not less than half the members of the Management Committee.
    • g) In the absence of the Chairman, the Management Committee shall elect one of its members to take the chair for the meeting.
    • h) Voting: In determining a question by vote of the majority of members present, each having one vote, the chairman of the meeting shall have a second or casting vote.
    • i) Standing Committees: The Management Committee is empowered to set up Standing Committees to deal with matters that require continuity. A member of the Management Committee shall sit on each Standing Committee.
    • j) Sub-Committees and Working Parties: The Management Committee may set up at any time sub-committees and working parties responsible to the Management Committee which shall appoint a Chairman and provide appropriate terms of reference.

  9. Annual General Meeting

    • a) Each year the Association shall hold an AGM in May.
    • b) Notice: The Secretary shall send, at least 28 days before, notice of the date, time and place of the AGM, together with the Agenda, to all members of the Association. For this purpose a notice printed in the official publication of the Association shall be considered sufficient.
    • c) All members have the right to attend the AGM for which there shall be no attendance charge.
    • d) Agenda: The following items shall be included:
      • i) Minutes of the previous AGM;
      • ii) Minutes of any EGM held since the previous AGM;
      • iii) Chairman’s Report;
      • iv) Management Committee Officers’ Reports;
      • v) Audited Statement of Accounts;
      • vi) Proposals for Alterations to the Regulations;
      • vii) Proposals for Alterations to the Fees;
      • viii) Ratification of Auditors.
    • e) Nominations: A Nominating Committee will draw up a list of Candidates for each elected post; additional candidates may be nominated by a proposer and seconder. All candidates, proposers and seconders must be members in good standing. Closing date for nominations is 1 February.
    • f) Voting: Every question at the AGM shall be decided by a majority of the votes cast. Individual members of the Association each have a single vote. The accredited representative of each corporate and sustaining member have five votes which may be split as desired. If a vote is tied, then there shall be a recount; if this fails to resolve the matter the candidate with the least votes is removed and the vote retaken, this process continuing until there is a decisive vote - or it cannot be continued, in which case the Chairman has a casting vote.

  10. Extraordinary General Meeting

    • a) An Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) shall be convened on a resolution of the Management Committee or within five weeks of receipt of the Secretary of a requisition signed by no less than one quarter of the current membership in good standing stating the business to be transacted at the meeting.
    • b) Regulation 9, except subparagraph (d) and (e) shall apply.
    • c) An EGM shall transact only such business as is specified in the resolutions or requisitions concerning it.

  11. Finance

    • a) The Association shall follow the BCS Financial Guidelines as issued from time to time insofar as they apply to Specialist Groups.
    • b) Bank Account: In accordance with the BCS Financial Guidelines, the Association shall have at least one Account (Account A) at Lloyds Bank, Langham Place Branch, used for normal running expenses. Other accounts at the branch may be used for special events or investment funds.
    • c) The financial year shall start on 1 May.
    • d) The Chairman is responsible to the BCS for submitting draft budgets, recording ongoing expenditure and capital expenditure separately for each year by 30 November in the preceding year.
    • e) The Chairman is responsible for making available to the BCS a receipts and payments statement at the end of every financial year (30 April) in respect of the Association’s normal operations and special events; this statement to be included in the BCS annual accounts subject to audit by the BCS auditors.
    • f) All cheques drawn on the Association’s bank accounts must be signed by any two of Chairman, Secretary, Treasurer and any person selected by the Management Committee for that purpose.
    • g) The accounts of the Association shall be audited each year by an auditor appointed by the Committee.
    • h) All income and property of the Association from whatever source derived shall be applied solely to the promotion of the objects of the Association.
    • i) No member of the Association shall receive payment for his services as a member.
    • j) The Management Committee shall appoint dates in the year to be membership renewal points.
    • k) Membership fees are due initially on joining the Association and subsequently at the latest membership renewal point in the following full year and on that date thereafter for the duration of the membership.

  12. Dissolution

    In the event of the winding up or dissolution of the Association any surplus assets remaining after discharge of liabilities shall automatically vest in the BCS.

  13. The British Computer Society

    • a) The Association shall be governed by the regulations of the BCS as these apply to Specialist Groups of the BCS. Where it is considered that a regulation of the Association is in conflict with a BCS regulation governing Specialist Group activities, the BCS rule shall apply.
    • b) The Chairman of the Association must be a Fellow, Member or Associate Member of the BCS.
    • c) Other Elected Officers of the Association should normally be members of the BCS.
    • d) The Chairman of the Association is ex officio a member of the BCS Specialist Groups Board and is thereby eligible, if nominated and elected, to be one of three representatives of the Specialist Groups Board appointed to the Council of the BCS.
    • e) The Chairman or his representative is expected to attend four Specialist Group Board meetings each year.
    • f) The Association must advise the Vice President (Specialist Groups) of those members of the Management Committee of the Association who are not members of the BCS.
    • g) All members of the Management Committee shall abide by the code of conduct relating to members of the BCS.
    • h) The Association may use the BCS name to enhance the reputation of its own activities but must not bring the BCS into disrepute.
    • i) No member of the Association may speak on behalf of the BCS without proper authority from the BCS.

items.title: Insight Systems
items.text:
Since we introduced our SQAPL Client product a year ago and gave APL developers access to most multi-user SQL databases on the market, the most frequent request for an enhancement to the product has been for it to support local databases or file systems such as Access, dBase or Paradox. We are therefore pleased to announce that version 2.0 of SQAPL supports Microsoft ODBC as an alternative to SequeLink under Microsoft Windows and in the OS/2 Windows box (WINOS2). ODBC drivers are available for almost all PC file formats. Many client/server database vendors also provide ODBC drivers for their own middleware products (such as Oracle’s SQL*NET). If you only need access to a single client/server database, a proprietary middleware solution from the database vendor may be an acceptable solution — but SequeLink remains the best solution in heterogeneous environments, and the only solution if you have client workstations running Unix and OS/2.

We are also pleased to announce that we have entered into redistribution agreements with both Dyadic Systems and Manugistics for the ODBC version of SQAPL 2.0. Contact your regular supplier if you want to use this product with APL*PLUS III/Windows or Dyalog APL/W version 7. Until further notice, we are still handling distribution of SQAPL for SequeLink under Windows, OS/2 and Unix, for APL2, APL*PLUS II and Dyalog APL.

Whether you use SQAPL with SequeLink or with ODBC drivers, the APL function calls are identical across all APL systems and environments in which SQAPL is available. You can easily prototype an application under Windows using a local database, and put it into production running APL under Unix to access DB2 on a mainframe. Unfortunately, although the SQAPL function calls are the same, the “local” ODBC drivers we have tested so far have been quite different when it comes to data types. Data types which have fundamentally the same internal representation can have quite different names from one driver to the next. For example, in testing ten or so drivers for PC files (dBase, Btrieve, CSV, TXT and Excel drivers from Microsoft and Q+E) , we came across VARCHAR data types named VARCHAR, MEMO, NOTE, TEXT and LONGCHAR — usually (but not always) requiring a maximum length declaration in CREATE TABLE statements. You will also find data types with the same name, which have subtly different internal data types.

We are more than a little surprised and disappointed by these differences between ODBC drivers. The differences may not be of great importance to the “personal” APL user — but they will be rather irritating to the software professional who needs to be able to provide portable, scalable solutions. Our strategy to cope with the situation is to provide an Entry Level product for the personal APL user, available immediately at low cost or bundled with an APL interpreter. Within a few months, we will provide Professional Edition with a number of performance and portability features important to the professional software developer. Besides hiding the differences in data type naming and handling, we will try to deal with some of the most irritating differences in transaction processing (are cursors closed after a commit?) — to make it as easy as possible to write portable applications.

In the slightly longer term, we will be transferring our attention to the server side of our product. The two most important goals are to port the SQAPL Server to the mainframe and support IBM APL2 and possibly Sharp APL under MVS. We will develop an ODBC compatible version of the SQAPL Server, so that APL applications can act as ODBC servers for any ODBC-enabled client application (including MS Query, Powerbuilder and other popular prototyping and analysis tools).

Although our customers still see SQL database access as their most pressing need, it is the SQAPL Server which we think is the important product in the longer term. Although we now derive an important part of our income from the sales of APL to SQL interfaces, we make no secret of the fact that we have found very few (APL) applications where SQL had any real functional advantage over APL component files. We have seen customers move multi-dimensional timeseries structures into relational databases and be rewarded with a loss of flexibility, and a hundred- or thousand-fold increase in resource consumption. Ten users of a sales forecasting system which used to consume a small fraction of the machine when using APL component files can consume all of a big mainframe when the data moves to DB2 and they all generate the dynamic SQL statements required to multiply the sales forecast by unit price and currency rate(s), then total it on three dimensions while converting the frequency from monthly to quarterly. The resulting two-dimensional table will most often need a lot of afterburning before it is ready for presentation. Remember that retrieval is the strong side of SQL. After all, the people who designed the language named it a Query language — and anyone who has tried to write non-trivial data entry applications using SQL will agree that it is aptly named.

We believe that the SQAPL Server can provide a more attractive solution. Instead of moving the data to an SQL database, you can turn the sales forecasting system into an ODBC or SequeLink server, which can be used by a frontend coded in APL or called from most other tools on any kind of workstation. You can even put a simple SQL frontend up which allows people to use SQL on virtual tables which are generated by APL. In this way, the APL data and services can become integrated with mainstream applications without sacrificing the advantages of APL. We feel that there are a lot of opportunities open to APL as an application server. We can provide computation engines or specialized database servers which are not only more flexible than relational databases, but also outperform them by one or two orders of magnitude for the types of data that APL is good at handling.

items.title: Manugistics Inc
items.text:
Manugistics Vector Sustaining Member News

A great deal has been happening in Rockville since our last sustaining member news. The most exciting of which has to be the tremendous success we’ve had so far with APL*PLUS III for Windows. We officially began shipping version 1.1 in late April, although we had been selling pre-release versions for nearly two months to customers who couldn’t wait and wanted to take APL*PLUS III for a spin. To be honest, even we were a little surprised at how quickly we reached the 1,000 units shipped mark. Next stop 2,000.

Our development group is busy putting the finishing touches on version 1.2, which we hope to be shipping by the end of August. Version 1.1 has been such a stable system that we have been able to spend the bulk of our time putting more features in 1.2 instead of fixes. Top on the list of new features for 1.2 is support for Visual Basic Custom Controls (version 1). We are also adding the necessary object classes to APL*PLUS III to allow developers to implement MDI style applications and ⎕NA and ⎕WCALL are being modified so both will support 16 bit DLLs directly, so you won’t have to “thunk” any longer.

While building APL*PLUS III, our developers became so enamoured with syntactic colouring, we decided to put it in version 1.2. This really is a nice feature and along with control structures, makes reading APL code much easier. We are also enhancing the product’s graphics capability by adding a “Picture” class, for persistent graphics, and a new “chord” operation to the “Draw” method. Help and prompting tools are also being added to assist the developer in implementing status line and pop-up help messages and a few aesthetic changes to the session manager are liable to sneak in as well including support for the classic APL keyboard.

We see APL*PLUS III evolving into a modular system, with add-on packages being offered by Manugistics as well as other parties. At the time of this writing, an ODBC module, developed by Insight Systems, is about to go into beta test. When commercially released, the product will be available through Manugistics’ regular distribution channels. Please contact Manugistics or your local APL*PLUS re-seller for more information.

Last week we held another successful annual international dealer conference. Re-sellers from various countries came to Rockville for 4 days of speeches, round-table and one-on-one discussions and networking. We want to thank all of our friends for making the trip and participating this year and we hope to see even more next time.

As always, Manugistics welcomes all suggestions, feedback and inquiries from Vector readers. To facilitate this, we have added the following two Internet addresses. In the United States, e-mail us at aplsales@manu.com. Outside the United States, use the address intl@manu.com.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text: In the last issue of Vector, we announced details of an upgrade to our Macintosh versions of APL.68000 Level II. We have now completed work on Version 3 of APL.68000 Level II for the Macintosh and it represents a major enhancement to the leading APL2-compatible interpreter for the Apple Macintosh family.

items.title: ‘Native’ Power Macintosh Support
items.text: With the advent of the new RISC-based Power Macintosh systems, Apple has dramatically improved the potential performance of Macintosh systems, provided applications are re-engineered to run ‘native’ on the new PowerPC processors. For over two years, MicroAPL has been working closely with Apple on tools for converting 68000-family applications to the PowerPC. One of the fruits of this work is that the full power of the Power Macintosh is available to APL applications running under Version 3 of APL.68000 Level II. This provides one of the fastest APL interpreters available for a small computer, particularly for code that makes heavy use of floating point.

items.title: New Object-Based GUI Programming
items.text:
Included in Version 3 is a new system function ⎕WI which provides a simple, consistent and object-based method of controlling user-interface elements such as buttons, list boxes, pop-up menus and pictures. Objects are created using ⎕WI, and their behaviour is defined by setting properties. And to help APL users develop cross-platform applications, the implementation of ⎕WI is largely compatible with Manugistics’ APL*Plus III for Windows, making it straightforward to move applications between the Macintosh and Windows PCs.

The object classes supported by ⎕WI are Window (or Form), Document, Dialog, Static text, (or Label) Button, Radio button (or Option button), Check box, Edit field, List, PopUp menu (or Combo), Icon, Picture, Scroll bar, Line, Rectangle, RoundRect, Arc, Movie and Timer.

items.title: New Callback-Based Event Handling
items.text:
In addition to the GETEVENT function previously available, Version 3 of APL.68000 Level II implements callback-based event handling. A ‘callback’ is an APL function (or other expression) which is run when a given event occurs (for example, if a Button is pressed).

To give you full control of event handling, callbacks are run during the ⎕WE (wait for event) system function, to which you pass a timeout value as the right argument. This allows applications to continue processing events during lengthy calculation or other processing. You also have full control over whether APL’s default event handling takes place, which together with an event triggering feature makes it possible to write APL custom controls.

items.title: Play Quicktime Movies from APL
items.text: Amongst the object classes supported by APL.68000 Level II is the Movie object. This allows an application to take advantage of Apple’s Quicktime movie technology, with the possibility of multi-media applications under APL control.

items.title: Improved Programming Environment
items.text:
Many enhancements have been made to the user interface, further developing APL.68000 Level II’s position as one of the most user-friendly APL programming environments. These include:

  • New Windows’ menu, with multiple sessions identified by workspace name, and improved dialog design.
  • Support for Apple Events — multiple workspaces may be launched simultaneously at start up, and double-clicking on a workspace icon during APL execution opens a new APL task.
  • Improved File Menu with Import and Export options to exchange Transfer format files with other APLs
  • New Print menu items allow print of workspace listing as well as contents of any APL window.
  • Improved editor facilities including new find/replace facility.
  • Closer conformance to Apple’s System 7 user-interface guidelines.
  • Removal of limits on number of edit windows open simultaneously (up to overall limit of 99 open windows).
  • Up to nine APL tasks can run simultaneously!
  • New user preferences dialog for startup configuration.

items.title: 100% Upwards Compatibility
items.text: In implementing the new features in APL.68000 Level II, we have retained 100% upwards compatibility for existing APL applications — even if you have written 680x0-family auxiliary processors and want to run them on a Power Macintosh!

items.title: Royalty-Free Packager Included
items.text: MicroAPL pioneered the concept of royalty-free runtime APL licences, allowing you to distribute your APL applications without paying licence fees. Version 3 of APL.68000 Level II now makes this even easier by including as standard a ‘Packager’ which turns your APL workspace into a standalone Macintosh application.

items.title: Business Graphics Workspace
items.text: The new PlotMac workspace allows you to create simple business graphics with a few easy APL commands, automatically scaling and labelling axes. You can create line and scatter plots; histograms; and pie charts. The graphs can be shown on-screen, printed or exported to other applications.

items.title: Free APL Toolkit
items.text: Finally, we have included a copy of the public domain APL Toolkit produced by the Toronto APL SIG which contains a wide variety of useful APL utility functions that will run under all types of APL interpreter.

items.title: Requirements
items.text: APL.68000 Level II Version 3 runs on all models of Apple Macintosh, including running in native mode on the PowerMac range, and requires Apple System 7.0 or later. APL.68000 Level II Version 3 will automatically use the hardware coprocessor on those 68000-family Macintosh computers which support 68881/2 operations.

items.title: Soliton Associates Limited
items.text:
Viewpoint, Soliton’s APL-based end-user report generator, previously available only for Sharp APL MVS, is now available for Sharp APL UNIX.

DBIUtils, the Viewpoint Application Programming Interface, provides APL access to Viewpoint data, and allows integration of Viewpoint into custom APL applications.

As well as operating upon its own internal databases, Viewpoint/UNIX can operate upon external databases, including DB2. Via NSVP, Soliton’s Network Shared Variable Processor product, Viewpoint/UNIX can access mainframe data, including DB2.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to report the availability of Dyalog APL/W Version 7 that was announced at the end of April. The new release contains a number of improvements and additional features that were not included in the April announcement.

One of the most important additions is the implementation of a built-in Grid object, which has proven extremely popular among audiences that have seen it demonstrated. Originally Dyadic had planned to rely on third-party custom control objects to satisfy the requirement for a spreadsheet-like editor. However, Grid objects designed for Visual Basic turn out to be highly scalar-oriented and not particularly convenient for APL. Dyadic therefore decided to develop its own built-in Grid object which is tailored specifically for the APL language.

The Dyalog APL Grid looks and behaves like a typical spreadsheet. The body of the spreadsheet is (naturally) a matrix, and individual cells can be numbers, character vector or character matrices. This makes it rather more than a simple numeric editor as it will handle the more commonly used nested array structures too. You can specify your own column titles and row titles or you can let the Grid label them with typical spreadsheet defaults. You can also disable the titles to provide a simple scrolling list. The Grid supports ‘in-cell’ editing or lets you use an external edit field. This is done by providing an association between the Grid and an Edit object; indeed it is possible to associate different Edit objects with different cells. Once this association has been done, APL manages the input entirely automatically; and, because the Edit object now supports Numeric, LongNumeric, Currency, Date and Time fields, APL performs most of the routine validation and formatting for you. The Grid also allows colours and fonts to be specified at the individual cell level, so you can readily customise its appearance.

The second major new feature is the provision of an Auxiliary Processor that allows you to access databases that support the Microsoft ODBC standard. Such databases include Microsoft Access, dBase, Paradox, Oracle, Ingres and Sybase. The Auxiliary Processor has been developed for Dyadic by Insight Systems who are specialists in this field. Insight are also the author of SQAPL which provides similar database connectivity using the SequeLink product, and which is already in production use at a number of large Dyalog APL sites. The ODBC interface from Insight Systems is included with Dyalog APL/W Version 7 at no extra charge and is fully supported by Dyadic and the author. When ODBC drivers begin to appear for Unix systems, Dyadic intends to provide the same functionality for the Unix implementations of Dyalog APL.

Another addition is the provision of a DOSFNS DLL together with a set of complementary APL functions. These functions perform many of the standard tasks of ⎕CMD without the overhead of starting a new DOS command processor.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Ian Clark

Readers of Education Vector will join with me in expressing their gratitude to the outgoing editor, Alan Mayer, who has staunchly edited EV since taking over from Alan Sykes in October 1991. It falls to me as the new Education Officer to occupy (I won’t say “fill”) the gap left by the two Alans. Since Alan Mayer has been elected Chairman of the 1994-95 Committee, I know that I don’t have to “fill the gap” in the substantive sense, since I can rely on his continued assistance and encouragement. The same goes for Adrian Smith who would have been content to typeset this edition of EV along with the rest of VECTOR with only infinitesimal input from me.

However, encouraged by both Alan and Adrian to put my mark on this little publication, I’ve decided to introduce my first innovation, a column of jottings on rock-bottom educational matters. Since it’s simply got to have a techie APL title, what better than “Jot-Dot-Floor”?

EV wants to appeal to new readers, even at the risk of telling existing readers what they know perfectly well already. You will begin to see certain elementary facts and well-known sources being quoted time and again, just for the benefit of newcomers. Your editor plans to grasp the IQ-knob firmly and turn it down to just below 99, earning just above zero academic kudos in the process. He plans to spoon-feed the APL novice and those new readers who aren’t sure yet whether they want to become APL novices or not. Deep studies will be welcome, as ever, but always with an eye to publishing just the simple parts, giving a contact address for extended information, or even offering it for publication in the main body of VECTOR. Here in EV you’re firmly in the nursery. Please write and say what you think of this policy as the months go by. This isn’t a new departure, but we get the impression it’s what EV should be doing more and more.

This issue carries The Second Lesson of Donald McIntyre’s introductory J tutorial. Some APLers see the J language as a sort of cuckoo in the nest and may wonder what justifies devoting the major part of an issue of EV to it. For my part I’m delighted to do so. I had wondered in the past whether a J tutorial would not have been better placed in the main body of VECTOR, but I’m convinced that EV is the right place for it. For one thing, it ensures that the two lessons of the tutorial come in a handy, easy-to-distribute form, fit for dissemination to a wide audience. For another, I suspect that career-APLers are going to be the last people to appreciate the advantages of J for educational exposition — and that’s something that will only emerge as more and better educational resources using J get published.

For readers who have only just joined us for this issue, EV forms a bound-in supplement to VECTOR, the official journal of the British APL Association, but EV is sent by itself to a separate mailing list of teachers and educationalists, to whom it primarily addresses itself. The subscription to EV is free. Provided you are a teacher, lecturer or bona-fide educational professional, you don’t have to be a member of anything except EVML — the Education Vector Mailing List! Therefore, if you don’t already receive your own copy of EV, or know of someone who ought to, simply write to me and I’ll put it right.

items.title: EDITORIAL: Back to BASICs?
items.text:
by Robert Bittlestone

This is the first issue of VECTOR: a new journal for a new generation of computer users. Although VECTOR is aimed at those who know and use APL, it’s also very much intended for those who don’t yet but might. So we make no apology for including articles which look at APL from the viewpoint of a non-APLer — including that of the general manager who’d like to know why APL makes sense without necessarily learning it personally.

APL is different from all other computer languages in many ways. These differences are part of what gives the language its strength, but also part of what causes it to be criticised. One of the most interesting points about its users is that there are virtually no cases of reverse conversion. Once you become committed to APL, it seems that you are rarely lured away from it. This kind of loyalty is praiseworthy indeed but also has a dangerous tendency to promote insularity. Events might just be passing APL by.

It’s almost as if there are two kinds of computing. There is the world out there of COBOL and FORTRAN and BASIC and everything else. This world has its bad points — very slow project development and severe design regimentation being two of them. However, it also has its good points, which include a civilised approach to word processing, imaginative use of on-screen colour graphics, the advent of new user-friendly devices such as the “mouse”, the use of a keyboard and character set that is well-nigh universal, and language availability on almost all computers.

Then there is the world of APL. Here we find some bad points too — extremists who confuse complexity with clarity, dreadful legends of undocumented and unsupportable systems, and obscure non-portable techniques required to cope with standard problems such as lower-case output. However, we also find a great many good points, such as elegant structures, powerful and appropriate array handling, flexible and sophisticated intrinsic features and a relational mentality that accelerates design as well as implementation.

I hope I have by now established the notion that VECTOR is not going to be a sycophantic journal. We aim to stimulate by criticism as well as by praise. If we sometimes infuriate, then be sure it is for a purpose. Write us a letter to object: but above all, keep the dialogue going. We have in our hands perhaps the most powerful tool yet devised for harnessing the power of the computer for human needs. So please let’s agree to concentrate on honing its cutting edge, rather than laying out rococo designs for its handle.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is extremely pleased with the way the new version of Dyalog APL was received at APL94. Delegates who attended Dyadic’s Vendor Forum (and most did) heard John Scholes give the first presentation of “Namespaces” outside the UK. The reaction from the audience, most of whom were unaware of this new development, was extremely positive.

Namespaces allow you to organise your functions and variables into logical units and sub-systems, just as the DOS directory structure allows you to organise your files. In Dyalog APL, the active workspace is also known as the root namespace; rather like the root directory in DOS. Objects that you create at this level are held in the root namespace, just like files in your root directory. (If you don’t want to use namespaces, you can define all of your objects in the root namespace, just as before.) However, you can also create a namespace (analogous to a sub-directory) in which you can place other objects and indeed other namespaces. There is no limit to the number of namespaces you can have, nor to the depth they are nested.

Namespaces do not just allow you to organise your workspace better, they also act as different contexts for the execution of code. When a function runs in a namespace, the names of variables and other functions to which it refers are local to that namespace, and do not conflict with objects with the same names in other namespaces or in the outer workspace. This means that, for the first time in APL, you can write a self-contained utility or a complete application that can safely be copied into any other workspace and run without fear of name conflicts. Namespaces also make it extremely easy to implement large application workspaces that contain logically separate sub-systems, without the need to resort to overlay files and similar techniques.

Namespaces provide benefits to all APL developers, but are of particular appeal to those developing GUI applications. This is because GUI objects (Forms, Buttons, Grids and so forth) are also namespaces themselves. This means that you can store all of the callback functions, and any data variables that they require, inside the object to which they apply, rather than having them swill around in the workspace. Namespaces provide a much needed solution for the requirement to pass information between callback functions, and between successive invocations of the same callback, without the use of global variables (i.e. variables that are global to the workspace as a whole). Instead, such variables become static variables, that are local to an object (and thus directly accessible from functions running within that object) but do not pollute the workspace as a whole. Furthermore, as GUI objects are namespaces, you can write a completely self-contained GUI widget that contains all the required APL code and data, together with its GUI components, and save it as a single object that can subsequently be copied into any active workspace and run. The user sees only what the object does; not how it does it, a fundamental tenet of object-oriented programming.

Dyadic intends to use namespaces as the basis of further development towards object-oriented programming, and to provide the advantages (but not the complexities) of this approach for Dyalog APL users in the future.

items.title: Insight Systems
items.text:
So far, the second half of 1994 has left us breathless. After announcing SQAPL for SequeLink at APL93 in Toronto, we slowly sold about a dozen evaluation systems during the next twelve months. A year later, many of these customers are buying 20- to 50-user production systems. The first five beta copies of SQAPL 2.0 with ODBC support went to new customers in Helsinki, London, Melbourne, New York, and Rio de Janeiro. New customers are queuing up, and redistribution agreements are now more or less in place with three major APL vendors. The rumours regarding the death of APL seem to be premature, and the non-APL middleware market seems to be taking off like a rocket too, so we have never been busier.

Dyadic shipped SQAPL/EL with version 7 of Dyalog APL for Windows. The Entry Level version contains all the functionality required to get started with simple ODBC drivers for local databases such as dBase or Access. By the time this is printed, we should have completed the Professional Edition, which contains a number of additional features to increase programmer productivity, and take advantage of performance options in advanced ODBC drivers, especially when using remote databases. We are now concentrating on assisting Manugistics in the packaging of both the /EL and /PE versions of SQAPL for APL*PLUS III, and working with Soliton to provide SQAPL for Sharp APL under Unix. We will also provide a version of /PE for J version 2 from Iverson Software, so you can get started on J using a familiar tool for database access. Upon demand, we will make the tool (SQJ?) available for J under OS/2 and Unix, too. Need a copy of SQK? Please call us!

A second generation of servers, based on SequeLink version 2.5, will provide ODBC access to Unix APL servers (and hopefully also APL2 under MVS) by the end of the year. We are also starting work on a local ODBC driver for APL, which will give direct access to Dyalog APL/W and APL*PLUS III without the use of middleware. This product will also be available before yearend, if all goes well (we need it for a project of our own before that).

The idea of an ODBC driver for a local or remote APL interpreter may seem a bit strange. ODBC is for SQL databases, and the most natural way to call a development tool like APL under Windows would be via DDE or as a DLL? There are dozens of APL applications containing their own databases, which suffer from the fact that their internal databases are inaccessible to mainstream tools. With our ODBC APL drivers, we will provide tools to help you write simple SQL interpreters, so you can let people go into Microsoft Access, connect to APL (which you sold as a high-performance multi-dimensional DBMS) and say:

select high, low, close
  from currdb
  where market='NYC'
   and currency='JPY'
   and date>19940101
   and frequency='WEEKLY'
   and totalling='AVERAGES'

Although the underlying database may be a four-dimensional table with daily rates, we can return a two-dimensional table with massaged data, pretending that we have an SQL table containing weekly averages. This idea can be extended to all kinds of analyses — so APL can contain infinitely large SQL tables. The ultimate virtual database is the one which allows queries like:

select result from apl where expression='2+2'

Once more, a change of Internet address. Our address is now insight@inet.uni-c.dk.

items.title: Manugistics Inc
items.text:
Manugistics released version 1.2 of APL*PLUS III for Windows almost a week ahead of schedule. We feel this version further positions APL*PLUS III as the strategic choice for Windows development. Major enhancements found in this release include support for Visual Basic Custom Controls, calling 16-bit DLLs directly, new object classes for MDI application development and more control structures; including :continue, :leave and :goto.

Currently, there are several beta sites testing the ODBC interface developed by Insight Systems for APL*PLUS III. Reports so far have been very positive and we soon hope to simultaneously release two versions of the product — one designed specifically for the single/ad-hoc user, the other designed for the commercial APL developer who needs to provide an ODBC enabled product with more functionality. For more information on ODBC for APL*PLUS III, please contact Manugistics, Insight Systems or your local APL*PLUS dealer.

The Manugistics troop returned safe and sound from APL94. In keeping with the conference theme of “The Language and its Applications”, a commercial application developed in APL*PLUS III by GEIS called LEX2000 was presented during our vendor forum along with demonstrations of using VBXs and ODBC. Our software drawing winner was Daniel Jonusz of Mobil Oil Corporation in Princeton, NJ and APL*PLUS Sport Radios were won by three other conference attendees.

A very exciting synergy is developing between our mainframe based enterprise-wide planning product and the APL*PLUS Network Sharefile product. Two new sites began using Network Sharefile in the past few weeks with more to come. Network Sharefile allows multiple copies of the APL*PLUS Sharefile system to communicate with one another. A user can be running an application that appears to be using one Sharefile database while a number of Sharefile databases in virtually any location may actually be in use. The benefits of Network Sharefile include better performance and better data security and integrity.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Ian Clark

Welcome to another edition of Education VECTOR. This goes to press just before APL’94, so whatever enlightenment emerges during the symposium will just have to wait for the next issue.

A teacher friend I saw recently congratulated herself on getting through the first week of term. Her face wasn’t grey and the lines on it were fading (I thought) so she must have had a good summer holiday. With the unions all set to continue their boycott of the compulsory testing of the National Curriculum and the Government still striving to re-introduce the eleven-plus in one form or another, with amateur markers to swell the ranks of amateur inspectors, no doubt all riding to work on trains directed by amateur volunteer signalmen, this has got to be the Golden Age of the Amateur Volunteer.

Nowhere is this more evident than the teaching of Mathematics. A recent report on the sorry state of mathematics teaching seems to lay the blame squarely on Primary Schools. Primary teachers might justifiably wonder what it is the country really wants of them. To be the saviours of the next generation? Or to serve as whipping boys for the undesirable side-effects of a society governed by market forces and other gods of darkness? If mathematical skills are to be costed on their current market value by sector, is it any surprise that they’re tending to accumulate in the faster end of the financial sector and desert the junior end (and upwards) of the educational sector?

For years those further up the educational tree have been telling the primary schools that all they require of them are children able to go to the toilet without supervision, tie their own shoelaces and write their own names. Leave the fancy stuff to those better qualified to teach it. Now it emerges that primary teachers have to carry the can back for the state of Mathematics throughout the entire system.

This isn’t the place to discuss the role of specialist teaching in primary schools. Nor the evidence for and against the existence of things called pre-mathematical skills. But I do think that those responsible for the staffing and remuneration of schools should not hide from criticism behind the honest attempts of others to put into effect the results of their own loose thinking. I remember seeing a report, at least six or seven years ago now, about the teaching of Mathematics in both primary and secondary schools in England and Wales. It furnished figures to show that at least 70% of mathematics teachers had no recognisable qualifications in mathematics beyond O-level, and that perhaps 90% were teaching the subject far above the level at which they were technically qualified.

Now never mind the reasons for this state of affairs and why it cannot be otherwise. Never mind asking whether they are doing a good job. Never mind wondering how to compel them to do a better one, by performance related pay, say, or testing their pupils at frequent intervals with nationwide tests. The question we want to ask ourselves is — no, not whether we’re feeling lucky, but whether we would tolerate such a situation in the teaching of French, say, or Spanish.

Now I have a shameful admission to make. I hardly know a word of Spanish (except one or two I learnt from reading Hemingway, which it seems I don’t pronounce correctly anyway). Yet, if Spanish were to be treated as Mathematics is at present, I could be recruited to teach PE, RE or any other ‘E’ for which I might be qualified, then directed to teach Spanish throughout the school. Would any blame attach to me if some official Spaniard came along and castigated my teaching (I think that’s the word)? In a fair and just society, not at all. The blame would lie with the headmaster, or rather with those who made up the rules which forced the headmaster to contemplate such a ludicrous step. And ultimately, in a democracy, that’s all of us. The headmaster might turn round and say he couldn’t get anyone who really knew Spanish for love or money. Market forces, again. But what a slur on our society, and those who lead it.

The government have shown time and again in other spheres that it is possible to manipulate market forces. In fact they’ve spent billions doing so. Let them do so in the sphere of Mathematics teaching, if we all agree it’s so important for the future economic health of the country.

items.title: Chairman’s Impressions: What you Saw was (more or less) what you Got
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 42

by Adrian Smith

After a lapse of a couple of months, it is interesting to reflect on what we set out to do at Swansea, and how close we came to achieving it. Of course the objectives were never totally stable — we were trying to do something quite new — but there were some fixed points in our agenda, and it is reasonable to ask:

  • did we really show you the newest and best work being done under Windows on a PC?
  • did you pick up any leading edge techniques of quantitative management?
  • were you able to spend the afternoons taking apart the morning plenaries in a well-equipped laboratory full of fast PCs?
  • was it a revitalising break from the daily routine?
  • did you get to take away some useful code?

These were all promises that we made on the first page of the invitation: how well do you think we met them? So far, those of you who have written or e-mailed have all been remarkably positive (which makes me feel better), but such samples tend to self-select! I might yet get around to writing to everyone who came, to ask how we could do it better next time, but meanwhile, here are my views on what we did well, what we did badly, and what we left undone.
path: Chairman’s Impressions: What you Saw was (more or less) what you Got

items.title: The Venue, Format and Organisation
items.text:
Swansea was born out of our failed bid to run APL94 at York, and for the much smaller workshop format, I think it was close to ideal. We began by over-estimating the size of the gathering, which caused quite a few headaches as we cut back to match the bookings, but it would have been hard to run such an intensive 3-day workshop with many more people.

The EBMS was a good self-contained base, the only snag being the need to borrow facilities in the nearby computer lab for some of the more heavy-duty afternoon sessions. However most people found their way around, and in the end most of the equipment co-operated, so this somewhat ad hoc approach stood the test — just.

Several people commented favourably on the basic structure of running a morning plenary, with everyone attending all the sessions. This had the great advantage of simplifying administration, as you could always be sure that everyone had got the message about the bus times, or the change of room in the afternoon. I hope the more esoteric statistical stuff didn’t cause the old-time APL hacks too much mental indigestion — I thought Derek Bissell’s talk on Control Charts was brilliant, but then again I learned my statistics by weighing Kit Kat bars! I honestly think that if we had gone for a straight-down-the-line Windows + GUIs agenda, we would have turned everyone off by the end of Day-1. It needed breaking up a bit, and talks like Kath Dowsland’s on Genetic Algorithms were ideal.

I can take no credit at all for the excellence of the organisation! This was all set up by the Alans (Sykes and Mayer) and administered most capably by Haydn Williams and Pam. The coffee was on time, the signposting was pretty good, the overhead projector worked all the time — what more can you ask?!
path: Chairman’s Impressions: What you Saw was (more or less) what you Got

items.title: The Main Topics
items.text:
We took a quick poll around the room at the start of the first day (see Jon Sandles’ notes on page 45), and most people had really come for the experience of Windows programming. We had already warned everyone (Vector 10.4) that this was not a jolly, and I think we went home feeling mentally quite battered by the amount of new stuff we had been exposed to in such a short time.

  • Day-1 was short of ‘talk and chalk’ time for the main topic of programming the GUI APLs, so the afternoon workshop was something of a rabble. I had failed to appreciate the problems of class-control when you take 24 keen APLers, sit them down in pairs in front of a new toy, and try to get them to listen to you. In the end, Duncan and I gave up any attempt at formal teaching and just worked around the various groups as fast as we could. It was OK, but we did much better on Day-3 (see Ray Cannon’s note on the DLL workshop) when we prepared more material in advance.
  • Day-2 was about client-server, timeseries and graphics. I found Morten Kromberg’s lecture on the basics of effective client-server architectures really superb, and I’m sorry I missed the afternoon workshop. The idea of a room full of chunky 486 ‘clients’ all happily running database queries against Morten’s dinky little SparcStation ‘server’ was remarkable enough. What’s more it all worked!
  • Day-3 was initially scheduled for Microsoft, who are anxious to tell the world about OLE2. In the end, we were too small a gathering for them, and instead we had John Scholes on Namespaces in Dyalog-7. I think that for many people this was actually a bonus, and namespaces were a hot topic for the rest of the conference. In the afternoon we had a much better organised workshop on DLLs; we need to remember how we did this one and use it as the pattern when we do this kind of thing again.
  • by Day-4 everyone was pretty shattered, so we had a gentle 2-hour canter through some simple GUI applications, made sure everyone got the most up-to-date software (the workshops turned over quite a few bugs) and unwound gently ready for the trip home.

To summarise, I think that we delivered most of what was promised, but I was too deeply buried in running the thing to get a clear view. Let us know what you think, and the BAA may try to do it all again, better.

items.title: Duncan Pearson’s DDE and DLL Workshop
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 48

notes by Ray Cannon

This very successful workshop was composed of a set of printed exercises, notes and detailed descriptions of several supplied utility functions within the Windows Kernel DLL. It was taught in a room equipped with many 486 PCs completely set up with Excel, Word, Dyalog/W and APL*PLUS/III under Windows.

Although all the main points of Dynamic Data Exchange and Dynamic Link Libraries have been reported within Vector, there can be few readers who have had hands-on experience of them under both major vendors’ APLs on the same machine.

Duncan’s notes were both clear and concise, and highlighted the differences in use between the Dyadic and Manugistics offerings.

By supplying the correctly set up environment (hardware and software), the notes on what to do and the information sheets specifying the syntax details and other data, Duncan created the ideal environment for exploring DDE and DDL. We were not spoon-fed with complete scripts, but were given all the required information, and had to understand the implication of what we were doing to proceed.

The main advantage of a workshop such as this as against trying it at home (relying on, say, an article in Vector) is that we were not distracted by unrelated problems (such as incorrectly set up or incompatible software/hardware). Whenever I have tried playing at home with new features of this sort, I have always found I had a set-up different from the one used by the author of the guiding article, and have been constantly sidetracked finding out why things didn’t work as the article said they should.

All in all I found this workshop one of the highlights of the conference. It alone fully justified my attendance.

Thank you Duncan.

items.title: Reflections of Another
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 59

by Ray Cannon

I saw a lot of reflections of Antwerp, since it rained every day I was there. Luckily I did not go for the sight-seeing, but rather for the APL, or rather, the APLers. I made a few new friends, and met many old ones, but sadly many were missing.

Most of the papers covered the “same old ground” but there were a few papers breaking new ground, in particular Pavel Luksha’s “Probabilistic Studies of I CHING with the Help of APL” and Gérard Langlet’s “The APL Theory of Human Vision”.

As for the Vendors, in the Windows arena Manugistics and Dyadic were battling it out, both giving good accounts of themselves. IBM appeared to be retreating into its OS/2 corner while Iverson Software’s J for Windows seems to be gaining ground. J Locales vs Dyadic Namespaces appears to be the next big fight, or is it between J and Manugistics over control structures?

The closing session was “Acquisition and Processing Data from Normal and Cancer Cells” by the Nobel prize winner Dr Ivar Giaever. As an APL consultant I found this session very interesting. More importantly however, it contained two messages to all APL vendors. If you want to sell APL (or J for that matter) to scientists doing research you must have direct IEEE support and you must have a Plot primitive. (This last point about a plot primitive was also made by Dr Walter Spunde in his paper on the “The Impact of APL on First Year Mathematics”.)

And finally a few key phrases.

“The consequence of the symbols is the symbols of the consequence.”

“Peace in our time, stop the war between APLs.”

Lots of “Little Trojan horses” in our code.

Vendors saying that their Windows Driver was easy to learn is a bit like the Nepalese Tourist Board saying:

“We have lots of very nice mountains, and they are all very easy to climb.”

items.title: APL95: Call for Participation
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

items.title: “APL Does It Today”
items.text:
SIGAPL’s annual international conference for 1995 will take place between June 4 and June 8 in San Antonio, Texas. The technical theme of the conference is meant to emphasize practical use of APL. This breaks down into two sub-themes:

  • APL95 as a showcase for highly-successful use of APL in the real world
  • APL95 as a source of practical education in modern computing techniques using APL.

Of course, our technical program will be open to all forms of APL, J, and related languages, and to all the traditional topics and formats of presentation — but we will be placing special emphasis on material which relates to practical application.

The key to a successful conference is effective publicity, and to make the publicity effective we need to include details of what will happen at APL95. That’s why you’ll see target dates included in all the sections below. Some dates are very firm (paper review, for example, is a serious business that has to adhere to a schedule) — others are more relaxed. But the message about dates is this: We can do more to get a good audience for you if you let us know what you want to do at APL95 in plenty of time.

The conference language is English; there will be no translation facilities at the conference and we request that all technical material be in English. However, we are more than happy to cooperate with prospective presenters who are not English speakers and will work with you on pre-conference translation of presentations.

We invite proposals from all APL practitioners for a presentation in any of the following formats:

items.title: Tutorials and Workshops
items.text:
It’s relatively easy for people to begin using APL; there are several companies who offer introductory courses, and there are textbooks. But, once the initial skills are achieved there are fewer resources for people to advance onto the next rung on the ladder and become contributors of major value to their employers and clients.

The annual APL conference is a great concentrator of APL skills; indeed it’s the one event of the year where nearly all the major players of APL will meet under one roof. At APL95 we want to use them to their best advantage for practical, up-to-date and relevant training — in the form of tutorials and workshops.

One way that you can help us with this is to offer to lead a tutorial or workshop session on the topic of your choice. Some of the things that we have in mind are:

  • Event-driven applications programming
  • Object-oriented programming
  • Large APL applications (high code volume or high data volume)

You will certainly be able to think of others.

Another way you can help us is by telling us the tutorial and workshop topics which would make APL95 irresistible to you as a delegate. If enough people say they would attend a session on a particular subject, we’ll do everything we can to get the best possible presenters. Please let us have your tutorial and workshop proposals by January 1, 1995.

items.title: Reviewed Papers
items.text:
Reviewed papers have long been the backbone of the conference, and we intend this to continue. We invite original technical papers on all aspects of APL. These papers will be subject to double-blind peer review, and those which are selected for presentation will be printed in the APL95 Conference Proceedings, which will be an issue of APL Quote Quad — distributed to the conference delegates, SIGAPL members and libraries world-wide.

In order for us to begin to structure the technical program we would like prospective authors to send title(s) and/or abstract(s) to us as quickly as possible (preferably before November 1, 1994).

Draft papers for review must be received no later than December 1, 1994; you may send a draft paper even though you have not sent a title or abstract earlier than this. Draft papers should not exceed 6,000 words.

items.title: Informal Posters
items.text:
Poster sessions are becoming increasingly important at SIGAPL’s conferences; we will continue to build this aspect of the program at APL95.

Posters are a great way to present your ideas informally and receive feedback from an interested audience. In order to maximize the impact of posters we would like you to submit your proposals in advance of the conference — although you may just turn up at the conference with a poster if you prefer.

The only restrictions on the format of a poster are that it fit onto a metre-square wall area, must be original work, and that it must be a technical presentation (advertisers are expected to book space in APL95’s exhibit area). Posters are not subject to peer review. We invite poster presenters to prepare a one-page summary of the ideas in their poster which may be distributed during their poster session; in addition, we may be able to find room for poster summaries in future editions of Quote Quad.

We are happy to receive advance poster submissions until May 1, 1995.

items.title: Panel Discussions
items.text:
What are the hot topics for APL in 1995? How does APL fit in with the ever-changing outside world? Panels have always been the format we choose to explore these topics, and we see panels as an important part of being at APL95 rather than reading about it later. Some of the things we already know we want to explore in panel sessions are:

  • The reunification of APL
  • Which paradigms of the outside world are passing fads, and which should we absorb into APL?

No doubt you can think of more. We want to hear from you — because a well-prepared panel has far more value than one which is produced late in the day. We’d like your panel proposals by January 1, 1995.

items.title: Software Exchange
items.text:
SIGAPL invites you to send new and useful APL/J software to the APL95 Software Exchange. New GUI software is especially welcome. Software from prior APL conferences is also welcome if it’s been significantly improved.

APL95 conference software will be available in three ways:

  1. The Conference Package: software received by April 5, 1995 will be available for purchase at APL95 in San Antonio.
  2. The APL95 Supplement: software received between April 5 and June 8, 1995 will be mailed at no charge to all who purchase the Conference Package at APL95.
  3. The Conference Package, plus the APL95 Supplement above, will be available by about October 1995 from SIGAPL, the BBS\APL, and the Waterloo archive.

Send software for the APL95 Software Exchange on a 3.5" disk to:

Dick Holt

Software in APL, J, and related languages is invited. English is preferred, but other languages are also welcome. Your material should include an ASCII file that briefly describes what the software does, and what other software/hardware is needed to use it. Please include permission to distribute any copyright software.

items.title: Other
items.text:
What have we forgotten? APL95 is wide open to all of your ideas — whether you are a SIGAPL member or not (and if you’re not we’ll be very happy to tell you how you can become one). If there’s a topic that you’d like to be a part of APL95 that you haven’t seen above — let us know, and we’ll do all we can to fit it in.

If there’s a way you want to present your ideas that doesn’t fit into these categories — let us know that as well.

Above all, APL95 is going to be YOUR conference. The Organizing Committee and the Program Committee are here to turn your ideas into reality — we look forward to your responses!

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Ian Clark

One thing about being an ease-of-use consultant, you get to see a wide range of jobs. Turning my hand to a spot of supply teaching at one of the better girls schools, the headmistress confided in me "We do tend to push the weaker girls towards IT".

So there it is. IT is the Domestic Science of the 90s, fit only for cotton-heads that ought to be barefoot and babbit by the time they're sixteen, and would be if their parents weren't so well-to-do. The sort of girl that's lucky to be leaving school with any sort of qualification. So push-em towards IT. As for the more academically-minded girls, well — who can blame them if they consider anything to do with computers to be beneath their dignity?

I read in a recent issue of CUE Newsletter (Computer-Using Educators, Inc., of Alameda, California): "The dilemma in 1990: we had the technology, we could create powerful, well-designed word-processed documents, charts and graphs, you name it. What power to unleash in a classroom! Unfortunately my students and I shared the same secret — all of these skills only counted in the computer classroom." The writer of the article, entitled "A Goal Without a Plan is a Dream", goes on to recount how things have changed. "The lab had moved from the place where students were learning skills that had little relevance to their real or academic lives to a studio where tools were made available and creatively used."

Assuming that Ms Schandler is not talking through her sweatband, then by comparison we in Great Britain in the Year of Grace 1994 are stuck in a 1980s timewarp. I didn't say 1990 because at that time we were ahead of the Californians in the constructive use of computers in the classroom. But the world moves on — and it seems Britain doesn't. Chris Abbott, writing in Educational Computing and Technology (November 1994), recounts his embarrassment at having to tell erstwhile overseas visitors, who had come to this country to see what had been achieved by the network of LEA centres, that most of them have closed. "The 1993 Education Act suggests that private sector centres will develop overnight, like so many mushrooms, where LEA centres close. No such magical events have taken place." He judges that "there are only two kinds of organisation which now have the funding, the resourcing and the legal right to develop new structures: the universities and the IT industry."

Both of course have their own agenda. Industry will argue, as its running-dogs have been doing in the correspondence column of "Computing", that children must be taught on "industry standard" software and hardware. "Who'd employ somebody trained on an Acorn?" seems to clinch the matter as far as they were concerned. For "Acorn" you might substitute "APL" in the present context.

Of course there were indignant replies pointing out that children being "trained" now won't be looking for jobs for another ten years — and what price now the industry standards of ten years ago? (8-bit computers, 5 inch floppies, 64kb of memory, CIS-COBOL seen as the only way to program a serious commercial application on a PC, if you're silly enough to sidestep the mainframe). Chris Abbott again: "The only definition of industry standard which has long-term credibility is something like 'fitness for purpose at lowest possible cost'".

If people really believed that when purchasing for the classroom, then they would not buy fashionable industry standard systems which "trained", but time-proved, time-proof ones which "taught". Out would go expensive packages which are supposed to exemplify, as closely as the budget will allow, what is out there in the Real World. In would come modelling media in which the mechanisms of a word-processor or a financial package (or genetic engineering or an atomic pile) could be modelled, in terms which the pupil (and even the teacher) could grasp. So it boils down to the choice of a good, cheap durable modelling medium.

Some people build models out of matchsticks. Especially prisoners, who have all the time in the world. Presumably they would use a low level programming language to build a software model. Those of us for whom time (and patience) is in short supply need to model with larger components and subassemblies we could in principle build ourselves — or at least take apart and understand. More like Lego than Lucifers.

Who can manufacture these goodies for us? Universities? When I worked in a university it was academic suicide to be caught making things easy for people with IQ<100. And as for industry — well! Who‡s paying? What are they buying?

I'm not being cynical. Both parties play the game by rules which are handed down to them. It's up to our rulers to make rules which are productive and beneficial, supposing they feel sufficiently motivated to do so. Education of the next generation — isn't that sufficiently motivating? Not if your mentality is straight out of "Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang".

items.title: Nice One, Microsoft!
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 142

from Gérard Langlet via Adrian Smith (Vector Production)

Following the note on fonts in the last Vector, I received a splendid cri de cœur from Gérard, not un-naturally upset about the lack of the oe diphthong from APL2741. He also mentioned a problem in using the Windows clipboard to transfer APL code from Winword back into APL (either Dyalog or PLUS III) for final testing before publication.

Suspecting (as one does) the APL interpreter in one’s life, I set out to investigate. Sure enough, function listings from Winword arrived in Dyalog looking very strange indeed — then I spotted that the execute had come through as a hyphen. If you look carefully at page 106 of Vector 11.2 you will see that execute is opposite en-dash — a vital clue! What the morons of Redmond have (allegedly — they might read this) done is to substitute what they thought you might have meant for what you actually put!

So — for “ you get " and for ” you get ", and yet (oh joy) for ‘ you get `. For • you get o (that’s right, they just knew you meant little letter o when you typed bullet) and so on. Try this from Winword to Write (or Notepad or Works) and you will see what I mean.

The work-around is to save your document in Write format and clipboard from there, or just use a sensible word-processor like MS Works which does not exhibit this ‘helpful’ behaviour. At least we can rule out Winword as a candidate for Vector OnLine.

items.title: Background
items.text:
This was a one-day seminar covering all aspects of GUI programming in APL. It was organised (most professionally) by Dittrich & Partner Consulting of Hanover, and was attended by over 40 delegates from all branches of German commerce and industry. The talks covered:

  • an introduction to Dyalog/W by Peter Donnelly
  • the APL2 product range for OS/2 and AIX by Nancy Wheeler
  • Causeway "Ein sicherer Weg über den Gui" by Adrian Smith
  • An APL2 data bank by Klaus-Peter Friedrich (Rheinischer Sparkassen)
  • APL*PLUS III version 1.2 by Stefan Denker (Dittrich)
  • Migration from mainframe to PLUS III by Dieter Düren (CNL)
  • Using APL*PLUS II for DOS by Christine Biewer (Cosmos Direkt)

Most of the talks were based around a live presentation, and I hope the audience survived my English better than I survived their German! Fortunately the paper by Dieter Düren was accompanied by a comprehensive handout, so we have had time to translate it for you. Thanks to Gill Smith for the translation.

Thanks to Peter Donnelly for arranging the Causeway session, and to Dittrich and Partner for their hospitality.

items.title: Namespaces Special Feature
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 65

Namespaces are the most interesting new thing to happen to APL since nested arrays, and in this Vector we have tried to give you a cross-section of opinions on what they are good for, and where the pitfalls and limitations may lie.

This is still a very young technology, and it is up to you to influence its development. Please follow the advice in Duncan’s Editorial and experiment with these ideas as much as you can (maybe only on paper if you don’t have Dyalog 7 or the latest J release); then let us know what you think and Vector can help form a consensus on what is ‘just right’, what is harder to use than it should be, and what just got left out entirely.

Peter Donnelly works through a simple (but amusing) tutorial which will help you to grasp the basic ideas that objects can have hidden data. I believe that Vector can claim a publishing scoop here — we are the first APL magazine to reveal the co-ordinates of the Dyadic Duck.

Eric Lescasse has contributed a much more technical article which shows you how you can exploit namespaces effectively in building GUI systems.

Finally, Kimmo Kekäläinen offers some suggestions on using the session namespace ⎕SE to manage your utility set, and some warnings about the dangers of going too quickly into this new world. The feature ends with a return visit to Adrian Smith’s ‘Coast-to-Coast’ game to see how much of his APL code namespaces have replaced.
