items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce Dyalog APL/W Version 7.1 for Microsoft Windows. This is a maintenance release that will be distributed to customers free of charge. It does however contain a significant number of enhancements.

As further evidence of Dyadic's commitment to provide greater compatibility with IBM APL2, Dyalog APL/W Version 7.1 includes the following language enhancements: Enclose with Axes, Take and Drop with Axes, Ravel with Axes, and Strand Assignment with parentheses. These enhancements do not conflict with existing Dyalog APL language conventions and are implemented at all migration levels (defined by the system variable ⎕ML). In addition, Version 7 offers an optional APL2-compatible partitioned enclose at migration level 3.

The Dyalog APL/W session now supports drag and drop editing which is implemented in a manner that is consistent with Microsoft Word for Windows. Drag and drop editing provides a fast and convenient method for moving and copying text (both whole lines and partial lines) within an edit window or between edit and session windows.

Namespaces have been extended in several ways. You may now create a GUI object, such as a Form, as a child of a namespace. Indeed, you can insert a namespace at any level in the GUI hierarchy. For example, you could create a namespace as a child of a Form and then create Buttons and other objects as children of the namespace together with any code and data that the objects need to share. Secondly, namespaces and GUI objects may be stored on component files in their ⎕OR form. This feature will greatly simplify the management and re-usability of complex objects and provides the basis for the implementation of class libraries in the future. Further enhancements to namespaces may also be included in Version 7.1.

The popular Grid object now supports the selection of rows, columns and blocks of cells. A selected block can be cut or copied to the clipboard and pasted back into the Grid. This facility also allows the user to transfer data very quickly between the Grid object and other spreadsheets such as Microsoft Excel. You may also drag a block of cells and drop them elsewhere within the Grid. Individual rows and columns may be resized by the user dragging the row and column title dividers. The user may also have the system resize a row or column to fit the contents of that row or column, by double-clicking the mouse over a divider. All of these operations generate new events to which you may attach callback functions and you may also generate these actions under program control. A new mechanism is provided to control the input mode and the behaviour of the cursor keys. All these features have been implemented in a manner that is consistent with Microsoft Excel.

In addition to these changes, the Grid now allows you to associate Combo and Button objects with individual cells. Combos provide a very convenient means for the user to input one of a series of options and Buttons (particularly Check boxes) provide a good way of making and displaying yes/no choices. As Button objects may display bitmaps, icons and metafiles, you can also use them to display pictures in individual Grid cells.

On top of these enhancements, Dyalog APL/W Version 7 users will find that a large number of minor enhancements have been added. Dyadic intends to ship Version 7.1 during January.

items.title: Insight Systems
items.text:
Insight Systems is pleased to announce general availability of the Professional Edition of SQAPL. In addition to being an interface from APL to SQL, the SQAPL product range allows APL to function at both ends of a Client/Server application. SQAPL/PE is available from Insight Systems for Dyalog APL and APL*PLUS II under Windows and Unix, and for IBM APL2 under OS/2 and Unix. It is available from Soliton for Sharp APL under Unix, and from Manugistics for APL*PLUS III under the name APL Link Pro.

Compared to the Entry Level version of SQAPL, which is now also available from Manugistics under the name APL Link, and is bundled with version 7 of Dyalog APL for Windows, the Professional Edition contains the following enhancements:

  • Support for SequeLink drivers as an alternative to ODBC, giving high performance access from Windows, OS/2 and Unix to most popular SQL databases and a number of non-SQL services such as IBM CICS, AS/400 Transaction Programs, or our own SQAPL Server.
  • Automatic detection of performance options supported by good ODBC drivers; most significantly block fetch modes, which can substantially increase performance (in one example with a WatCom ODBC driver, an order of magnitude increase in performance for multi-row fetches).
  • Support for a number of additional APL data types, in particular date/time columns as Julian day numbers, Quad-TS vectors, or base-100 encoded integers, in addition to the ISO Standard character format.
  • The ability to store any APL array in a CHAR or BINARY column, in a format which can be extracted by any other SQAPL/PE client even though data is stored in binary format. This can be used to implement a Component File system, which can be used by all four major APL systems, under Windows, OS/2 and Unix.
  • Support for data sets, so that you can extract a (subset of a) table, make changes to it using APL, and then get SQAPL to generate the required SQL to apply the same changes to the underlying SQL table.
  • Output data can be grouped according to the requirements of your application. For example, you can extract all columns of the same data type in a single cell of output, to conserve space compared to the heterogenous/mixed result returned by the Entry Level product.

For more information, contact us at the address on the back cover, or ask your APL dealer.

We are close to releasing most of the new server products mentioned in our news item in the October Vector. Make sure to get the next issue of Vector to read all about them!

items.title: Coast-to-Coast revisited
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 96

by Adrian Smith

Please refer to Vector 10.1, page 97 for the background to this note. One of the ideas that I introduced was of managing the Dyalog 'data' property using a pair of functions set_data and get_data to store named variables in any GUI object. I commented at the time that I felt this was a "huge step forward in design" and fitted in well with the APL style we already knew. I started with the assumption that I ought to be able to remove all this code, as namespaces were designed to do precisely the job I had coded around.

If you look first at init_icons (page 101) or init_game (page 105) you can see that as long as you know what your object is called, namespaces clean things up nicely:

[8]  'ttmk'⎕WC'BITMAP' ''bmp cm
[9]  ttmk.rtn ttmk.fn ttmk.map←2 'make_term 3' map

[24] BD.ToPlay←'WN'    ⍝ Either player may start!

The fun begins when you have the same callback on many objects, so the object name comes in as an argument. Look at rotate_tile on page 104:

[4] rtn fn←bmp get_data 'rtn' 'fn'   ⍝ Old version

[4] rtn fn←⍎bmp,'.rtn ',bmp,'.fn'    ⍝ New version

This is nasty enough, but putting the data back again gets quite horrible:

[8] bmp set_data ('rtn' rtn)('map' map)  ⍝ Old version

[8] ⍎bmp,'.rtn←rtn ⋄ ',bmp,'.map←map'    ⍝ New version

I know that Dyadic are working on ⎕CS, to let us shift namespace under program control, so I suppose I will soon be able to write:

[8] ⎕CS bmp ⋄ rtn←##.rtn ⋄ map←##.map ⋄ ⎕CS '##'  ⍝ Switch ↑↓

... which is better, but leaves me in danger of forgetting to switch back at the end. I think what I really want is something that looks like:

[8] bmp ⎕CS { rtn←##.rtn ⋄ map←##.map }  ⍝ Execute in namespace

... but I don't hold out much hope of seeing it!

items.title: Namespaces and ⎕SE
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 119

From: [e-mail address omitted], 3rd March 1995

Concerning the Dyalog session-file, I seem to be adopting a minimalist approach! I don’t use any named session.dse; what I need I will load into a namespace under ⎕SE dynamically from a set of little utility workspaces, that are saved and maintained in a quite traditional manner. The functions in them don’t know a thing about been run in a namespace. (Most of them can be used as well under version 6.3.)

My APL loads in at the start a little workspace consisting only of a ⎕lx that moves the most generally used fns & idiomlike stuff (those ROWFINDs) to ⎕SE to be always available. Among those is a two-line function WS2NS by which I’m able to load dynamically whatever tool-ws to a namespace under ⎕SE or #. This gives me the functionality, keeps my application workspace clean and allows me to get rid of the tool whenever space is needed, or if there is no use for it anymore.

There is nothing very brilliant or clever in this, but to me it seems to work perfectly, and brings me the advantages that I consider most relevant in the namespace-concept.

items.title: More on APL 2.5
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 120

From: I Phelphritt (nee Leigh), 1st April 1995

I was thrilled to see your review of IBM’s APL2.5 in April’s Vector 6-4, and felt moved to send you a further couple of examples. One consequence of the direct definition of operators which may not be immediately obvious, is the ease with which you can define the inverse operator for monadic functions:

INV: ωβ

INV produces a derived function which reverses the effect of its operand:

A←→F INV F A

for any array A and any monadic function F. The following examples show the power of this operator.

          ÷4
0.25
          ÷INV 0.25
4
          +\INV 1 3 6
1 2 3

In the case where the inverse is not simple, the system provides a ‘least squares’ solution:

          +/INV 6
6
          ?INV 4
7

and of course, INV may take a system function as its operand, so:

          ⎕EX INV 1
FOO

… re-instates a previously expunged function, and:

2
     ⎕DL INV 2

… produces the same effect as ⎕DL ¯2 in Dyalog APL.

We are only now beginning to appreciate the power of this new implementation, but I’m sure that such examples will soon swell our idiom libraries.

items.title: Causeway Graphical Systems Ltd
items.text:
Adrian Smith and Duncan Pearson have set up Causeway to enable them to work full time on Causeway application development. The company is based in Malton, North Yorkshire, and has two clear aims:

  • to use Causeway (under Dyalog/W or APL*PLUS III as appropriate) to build high-quality decision-support tools with a true Windows 'look and feel'.
  • to offer a professional level of support and training for the Causeway platform to APL sites needing an effective, reliable and future-proof environment for in-house development under Windows.

Over the first two or three years, we shall spend at least 60% of our time developing configuration and decision-support tools for the German software company SAP. The first of these will be included with release 3.0 of their R/3 product later this year. At APL95 we will provide Causeway for APL*PLUS III, and also for Dyalog APL/W version 7.1 (fully exploiting namespaces and other 7.1 features).

The Causeway architecture will remain in the public domain, and the new version of Causeway for Dyalog/W will be bundled free of charge with the interpreter.

items.title: MicroAPL Limited
items.text:
Our last major upgrade to the Macintosh versions of APL.68000 Level II was released last summer when we announced support for the new Power Macintosh computers and also added a significant number of new features to the product.

We are now testing a further upgrade to our Macintosh versions of APL.68000 Level II and customers will shortly be receiving full details of the upgrade. This upgrade combines some features found in our RISC/System 6000 version of APL.68000 together with some additional enhancements to the ⎕WI system function.

We have added the family of native file systems functions that are already available on our APL.68000/X product for the RISC/System 6000. These functions include ⎕NCREATE, ⎕NERASE, ⎕NLOCK, ⎕NNAMES, ⎕NNUMS, ⎕NREAD, ⎕NREPLACE, ⎕NTIE, ⎕NUNTIE, ⎕NWRITE.

Our APL component files on the Mac are now automatically multi-user, with users able to change their user ID via a preference dialog. We have also allowed users to specify the name for the APL component file and HELP file.

The ⎕WI interface has been enhanced in a number of ways - we have added a new read-only property - class (the class of an object). The delete method is tolerated for non-existent objects (for better APL*Plus compatibility and ease of programming). A new Printer object allows control of the printer using ⎕WI. This include 'methods' for printing text, putting up a page dialog and a job dialog, plus properties for font, page size etc. We have added multi-select list boxes and multi-column list boxes. The new 'System' object will allow ⎕WI access information such as screen size.

Finally we have added official support for Auxiliary Processors written in C. This last feature has been available for some time on an 'as required' basis but is now included with the interpreter.

In addition, all bugs reported to us have now been fixed.

items.title: Manugistics Inc
items.text:
One of the comments that Manugistics hears a lot from its customers is "How can we promote the use of APL more?" It seems that while some of us have found the value in this language, many others are still using less powerful tools. In talking with many of the APL special interest groups, we believe that with the support of these groups and a good shareware version of APL we could all spread the word to more people. In order to support this effort, Manugistics plans on making available a shareware version of its APL*PLUS PC product. We intend to begin the distribution of this product through the APL special interest groups. We feel that with the support of a local group of APLers, new APLers can be found and trained.

This shareware version is a fully functional APL*PLUS interpreter with no artificial limitations. It will run under DOS, Windows or OS/2 in the 640K of RAM that DOS provides. There are 6 chapters of basic APL language documentation included online; this documentation was written specifically to address the needs of brand new users.

If you are interested in helping us to make this available to the community, please stop by the Manugistics booth at APL95 in San Antonio, TX or contact us directly at +1-301-984-5468. We hope to see you at APL95!

items.title: Insight Systems
items.text:
By the time this is in print, we expect to be shipping the first copies of version 2.0 of our SQAPL Server for Unix. Version 2.0 will be based on the new SequeLink "Link Engine", which supports ODBC drivers under Microsoft Windows and on the Macintosh. By the middle of 1995, version 2.0 will allow you to turn APL databases or applications implemented using almost any APL interpreter running under Unix, Windows NT or OS/2 into "black boxes", which will appear to other applications as industry-standard ODBC data sources, as if they were Oracle database. Instead of moving APL data into a relational structure, losing flexibility and performance, we can now make data in APL files available to other applications on their terms. We believe that this opens up a lot of new opportunities for APL-based applications, which can be presented as open, "mainstream" products.

For "pure" APL-to-APL distributed applications, we are introducing a new product, which is already being tested by a few customers under the project name "APL Pipes". The APL Pipes product does not use SequeLink for transport, but is based directly upon TCP/IP "sockets". As a result, it is available not only under the server operating systems supported by SequeLink, but also under plain Microsoft Windows. APL Pipes allows a single APL task or workspace under Windows, Windows NT, OS/2 or Unix (if you need VM or MVS support, please call) to support several clients simultaneously. APL Pipes supports transfer of APL objects of any type, rank, shape (and almost any size) between clients and servers which may be based on different APL interpreters. For example, you could use the product to call an APL*PLUS server to read (or write) component files from a Dyalog APL client application (and vice versa). For developers wishing to use C or other compiled languages, we will also supply a library which allows APL servers to be called from such environments, effectively making any APL interpreter available as a C library (or DLL under Windows).

items.title: Sustaining Members' News: Dyadic Systems Limited
items.text:
The latest addition to Dyalog APL/W is a new system function ⎕CS (Change Space), a significant enhancement to the namespace concept. Dyalog APL namespaces allow you to organise your workspace in a similar manner to the way you may organise your disk into different sub-directories. However, this is not all that namespaces do and perhaps more importantly, namespaces provide separate execution contexts in which your APL functions run.

For example, if you make a namespace called MODEL in which you install a function called CALC, when you run MODEL.CALC the function sees only the other functions and variables within the MODEL namespace and avoids potential name conflicts with other workspace objects. This is exactly right if MODEL represents a self-contained sub-system, but what if MODEL represents a particular scenario and you have several other namespaces; PLAN, ACTUALS, FORECAST, and so forth, containing similar, but independent scenarios, that you want to analyse. One thing you do not want to do is to maintain copies of CALC and any sub-functions it calls throughout your namespaces, except where the functions differ. This is where ⎕CS comes in.

⎕CS provides a mechanism for a function to switch its execution context. This means that your CALC function can switch into the PLAN namespace if you want to analyse the PLAN scenario, or into the ACTUALS namespace if you want to use actual data. Functional differences between the way certain calculations are performed can be handled by having different sub-functions within the different namespaces. Functions that apply to all scenarios can be exported to the target namespace (the one that ⎕CS switches into) by specifying their names in its optional left argument.

This technique lets you implement a class of objects (in this case a planning system) as a namespace (MODEL) which contains the base data variables (properties) and functions (methods) that define the behaviour of the class itself. Instances of the class are represented by other namespaces PLAN, ACTUALS, FORECAST, which contain just the differences (different data and perhaps some different calculation routines) between each scenario and the class itself. The main calculation routines exist only in the MODEL namespace. When you execute MODEL.CALC, you supply the name of the instance namespace in which it is to run. CALC then uses ⎕CS to switch into the desired instance namespace, taking with it any class data and sub-functions that it needs.

This technique is not the only way to solve problems of this sort, but it adds yet another powerful tool to your armoury and is a further step towards the goal of object-oriented APL.

items.title: This Nonsense Has Got To Stop!
items.text:
Hands up who never heard that from their old headmaster. A young acquaintance of mine recently described morning assembly as "two hymns and a telling-off", so things haven't changed much since my schooldays.

So it's a novelty to hear the good old message in the mouths of school governors, but this time directed at central government. Now school governors, like local authorities (who are inclined to forget it) are creatures of Parliament, with no constitutionally independent right to exist. It's not as if the UK is a federation of counties — it isn't. Like Rutland, they can be made to disappear and reappear at will. If school governors embark on a campaign of mass disobedience (a distinct likelihood at the time of writing), the government might understandably feel aggrieved at having its hand bitten by the ones it has nurtured as a power independent of the local education authority.

But it's one thing to be a creature of Parliament, and quite another thing to have a school to run. Alarm and despondency is the inevitable result of having inadequate resources (and nobody has actually attempted to defend their adequacy) further squeezed by a national teachers' pay settlement which central government refuses to fund. School governors must be feeling that their localised power is nothing more than the power to take responsibility for a crisis not of their making. They must be wondering whether their sole reason-to-be, indeed the sole reason-to-be of any institution set up in the last twenty years by the Masters of the UK (till God wills) has been — not the better achievement of their nominated goals, but the fragmentation of non-ministerial power for no greater purpose than to sap the power of local authorities, indeed of any public body capable of effectively opposing the ministerial will. Meanwhile the ministry tells all-and-sundry that there's plenty of dead wood to chop in local government administration before one needs to go sacking teachers.

Now let us view this lake of blood from the vantage point of the very people this government has claimed to champion — the little guys of industry. Let us further restrict the discussion to the industry of producing educational materials for schools. Of all the victims of this sorry state-of-affairs, maybe they will be the least lamented, but like the canary down the coalpit their demise may amount to more than one little bundle of feathers. It might point to something unfriendly in the atmosphere. It's no part of this publication to pamphleteer on the wider aspects of social engineering, but to encourage diversity in educational computing, for much the same reasons as we'd all like to encourage biodiversity in the environment. Monocultures mean mega-species mean mega-diseases.

To begin with, the innovation of letting schools manage their own budgets seemed a godsend to suppliers. The bigger they were, the more of a godsend it seemed, since promotion of their goods was henceforth going to rely on marketing muscle rather than on pleasing a small number of discriminating gatekeepers. Hitherto, like the NHS for drugs, there was effectively a single customer — the network of LEA centres which did a good job of buying new computer products for schools, encouraging the exploration of these products by working teachers and publishing catalogues in which the little product got as much space as the heavyweights. Then all of a sudden a vast amount of money was put into the hands of schools governing bodies, money which we are invited to imagine was being squandered on layers of administrators in County Hall, or perhaps on painting buildings that were already the right colour, mending roofs which it would have been cheaper to put a bucket under, or paying senior staff over the odds, most of whose work could be done by a cheaper recruit from today's flexible labour market. New suppliers flocked to the marketplace, big as well as small.

A stroll around the educational shows of the last two years showed a huge investment in promoting basically pedestrian products. Pedagogically pedestrian, but graphically gargantuan — but at the end of the day glitzy graphics are only part of the packaging. We all ought to play more poker, because then we'd understand what is meant by "upping the ante" — making it more expensive for new players to buy into the game. Now, with this throttling squeeze on school budgets we shall see educational products (whether books or software) going the way of cornflakes. More and more attractive packaging and less and less nourishment in the contents, because nourishment comes from a varied diet. Ultimately the innovatory suppliers will die out and a few big players will spend huge sums on competing with each other for a shrinking school budget with a dwindling library of rapidly obsolescent multimedia products. On the home front, Sega and Nintendo will place fantastically powerful hardware in the hands of our youngsters, capable of delivering all the educational principles past ages have had no end of trouble imparting. All to be used for — what? Making the blood and guts fly on even more convincing trajectories? And still mathematics teachers appeal to me for a good straightforward product to teach pupils how to balance brackets and multiply out expressions.

It's not as if the money isn't there. Why do school supplies have to compete with a proper remuneration for the practitioners? Our public utilities have shown how it is possible to keep gas, water and electricity flowing into our homes, yet still be flush with profits and able to pay their top men what they're worth. How about paying teachers what they're worth? Is it beyond the wit of our lords and masters at the same time to keep the educational supplies flowing into our schools? Although we'd feel the pinch sooner, it would do us, the people of Britain, far less harm in the long run to have our gas, water and electricity turned off for a week than to screw down the supply of educational resources to our children. Yet the former could pay for the latter many times over.

This nonsense has got to stop. Otherwise creative British sources of educational materials will dry up and we'll be left with wall-to-wall "Arthur's Teacher Trouble".

items.title: How to Get Hold of J
items.text:
Vector, with its offspring Education Vector, has endeavoured to promote the J language with ample coverage in this and past issues, since we feel it is an important development of APL. However, some educational readers might not be aware that they can get hold of the language free of charge:

J Release 2 is now a fully-fledged product and can be obtained running on a number of platforms (IBM PC Windows and DOS) from I-APL Ltd., 56, The Crescent, Milton, Weston-super-Mare, Avon, BS22 8DU. It costs £55 for this "Personal Edition", plus postage, quite a reasonable price for the professional development system it has become.

However J Version 7 is still available as shareware, and we recommend this to educational newcomers to the language. Disks can be obtained from: I-APL Ltd. for £5. Both PC and Macintosh versions are available. However, for copyright reasons, manuals are no longer available for J Version 7. Instead we recommend the articles in this and back issues of Education Vector to give an introduction to the language. "Programming in J" by K.E. Iverson is still available from I-APL Ltd. for £10.00 plus postage and packing.

items.title: Croeso i Gymru
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

From: John Sullivan, 8 March 1995

I really must complain about the heading on the top of page 50 of Vol.11 No.2.

      Croesoe a Cymru
SYNTAX ERROR
      Croesoe a Cymru
              ^

APL is very pernickety about its syntax. So should APLers be when dealing with other languages. Welsh has some peculiarities which I shall not go into here, but suffice it to say that you cannot have a C on the start of a word following the word a, no matter which version of the word a you are using (it will begin with G or Ch). Assuming that we can mangle our syntax (or make a user-defined function called a) we now get the following:

      Croesoe a Cymru
VALUE ERROR
      Croesoe a Cymru
      ^

because Welsh does not have a symbol called Croesoe in its symbol table (vocabulary).

Enough of this idiocy: you can see what I’m getting at. Let’s just say that I wish to complain that everybody tries to get their English (of whatever variant) correct, they try to get their APL (of whatever variant) correct, they even try to get their Russian correct. But nobody cares about getting their Welsh correct! This kind of thing is typical of the non-Welsh contempt of all things Welsh, and for a journal with delusions of academic excellence it just isn’t good enough.

The correct heading should, of course, be

Croeso i Gymru.

P.S. Maybe Vector ought to contact the Welsh Office in Cardiff and ask about the availability of their Welsh language spell-checker. It won’t find all of your errors, but it should find the ones I am complaining about here. Tel: 01222-488745.

items.title: Insight Systems
items.text:
On April 1st, Insight Systems merged with Adaytum Software Ltd. To quote our Press Release:

Insight Systems ApS, based in Hellebæk, Denmark, announced today a merger with Adaytum Software, one of the UK’s leading providers of Budgeting and Management Reporting software solutions. The merger, which will be in the form of a share exchange, will be effective 1st April 1995.

Adaytum will base its technical development team in Hellebæk, Denmark. Headed by Morten Kromberg, current Technical Director of Insight, Adaytum’s aim will be to attract and build a team of the most talented APL developers available internationally. Their focus over the next two years will be to provide state of the art Client/Server based financial data analysis software solutions. These will complement Adaytum’s flagship product ‘The KPS System’, a multi-dimensional Business Management system, used principally for complex Budgeting, Forecasting and Management Reporting requirements.

The implementation of the merger has kept us quite busy for the last quarter. In addition to the new tasks resulting from the merger, we have seen substantial growth in our consulting business, and as a result we added five people to our headcount during the same period (including three new APL developers). Expanding our offices and the APL95 conference has left us little time for product development, so there is little to announce this time — but now that the situation is stabilizing we will be back in greater strength than ever before.

Our first goal is the completion of the ODBC-compatible version of the SQAPL Server, which will make it possible to “wrap” APL applications in the guise of an SQL database (making APL effectively indistinguishable from for example Oracle, from the point of view of reporting tools). More about this and other new product releases in three months!

items.text:
Fresh back from APL95 in San Antonio, Dyadic has begun work in earnest on the next release of Dyalog APL/W. Although plans have not yet been finalised, the following has been decided and was announced at APL95.

Although the current release of Dyalog APL/W (Version 7.1) runs extremely well under Windows 95 preview, a new version of the product (codename Version 7.95) is being developed specifically for Windows 95 and Windows NT. For the technically minded, the new version will be based on Microsoft WIN32 in place of the equivalent Watcom software which Dyadic has used up to now. This software will provide some benefits in terms of improved memory management under NT, but more importantly, is a qualification requirement for the new Windows 95 logo. Of greater interest to most users is that Version 7.95 will include support for all of the new GUI objects and features provided by Windows 95. These include DragList, ListView, ProgressBar, RichEdit, TrackBar, TreeView and Spinner objects.

The DragList object is a list box that allows the user to re-order its items. The ListView displays items as a set of icons, in a list format or a report format (like File Manager). The ProgressBar is a standard output control that indicates the progress of a time-consuming operation. The RichEdit control is a multi-line text editor that provides extensive word-processing facilities including mixed alignment, fonts and colours. This control will allow Dyalog APL/W applications to exchange complete documents with Microsoft Word and other word-processors. The TrackBar control provides a variety of different sliders for analog user input. The TreeView control may be used to display a hierarchy, such as a function calling tree, a namespace tree, or a directory structure.

The new version of Dyalog APL/W will also support OLE2 and .OCX custom controls.

Dyadic intends to be able to provide an early release of the new product on the day that Windows 95 is released by Microsoft. This will allow Dyalog APL/W users to immediately begin to generate Windows 95 compliant applications and to qualify for the new Windows95 logo themselves.

items.title: Causeway Graphical Systems Ltd
items.text:
I suppose we went to APL95 to get our name known, to get our faces known, and to start convincing some hundreds of sceptical APL developers that we really have hit upon a better way of managing the “concept — prototype — negotiate — build” cycle that characterises effective APL development. To this end, we put our name and Email on the conference pens, we talked at length to the development teams (Dyadic, Soliton, Manugistics, IBM, and Strand), and we threw a party!

Following Dyadic’s example (Manchester, 1986) we ordered more beer than we thought we could possibly need (wrong!) and invited anyone interested to our suite for a Causeway BeerBOF. They left having seen “Distributed Architect” — the tool that SAP are now shipping to selected customers for configuration modelling; they were given a first viewing of the “Rain” business graphics software running under APL*PLUS III, and they had ample opportunity to grill both Adrian and Duncan on the future of Causeway for Dyalog, APL*PLUS, APL2 for OS/2, and J.

The key message that we tried to leave people with is that Causeway pays exponentially increasing dividends as the application gets complex! It takes a very pragmatic APLers’ approach to OOPS, and as a result leaves the way open for rapid evolution while enabling small teams to work concurrently on many components of the same project with a minimum of external co-ordination.

In the longer term, we made a good beginning convincing the major APL vendors to start designing into their interpreters all the right hooks to make Causeway run fast. Dyadic are already well on the way with namespaces, but IBM are developing some really interesting ideas using shared variables, and the latest release of J (from Strand Software) at last has the facilities we need.

We should re-iterate that the Causeway utilities are a by-product — we needed something to help us deliver high-quality decision-support tools that we knew we could support and enhance into the future, regardless of APL platform. The architecture and the Dyalog and Manugistics workspaces will remain in the public domain.

P.S. Registered users have already received workarounds for two interesting new Dyalog bugs which we first noticed in 7.1; try executing ⎕NC'inx⊃vec' having defined inx. The quick fix is to clear everything to the right of the ∧ in Gui_read[21]. Unfortunately the fix for their new configure bug is not so easy, so if you get an ever-growing button in the designer (try it with Snap=1) you will need to register so that we can send you the necessary patch.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
I had a dream last night...

No, no, hang on... this really happened. Or at least it didn’t really happen, but it did, if you see what I mean. I was overtaken in the street by a total stranger, except that I recognised him straight away. It was of course the British Prime Minister, John Major, and he begged a tremendous favour of me. It seemed that the following day he was going to be out of office. He’d picked on me because nobody looks more ordinary than me and he was facing up to the prospect of becoming just an ordinary person himself. A prospect he didn’t relish because he didn’t actually know any ordinary people. He anticipated being dreadfully isolated before he managed to make up socially for all those years in office and he wondered if I might consider taking him down the local pub and introduce him to a few of my friends, just to get him started.

Now some of my best friends are teachers, most of them in fact, or rather ex-teachers (not being able to stand the politically motivated hassle of the last few years). Just as I thought I had a handle on this thing I got a phone call from a BBC reporter I know called Chris. Now Chris has a nose for trouble. He once turned up with an entire camera crew on the off-chance of filming me getting beaten up by angry quarrymen at a protest meeting I was addressing. He was proposing to do the same that evening, since he was covering the story of how John Major managed his first day as an ordinary person. I was going to have to stage a casual introduction, in front of television cameras (and boy! — don’t they take over a place when they arrive) along the lines of:

“Chris, this is — er — John.”

I woke up sweating. Not that the dream was all that nightmarish, but it struck me how much worse it could have been. Just imagine:

“Chris, this is — er — Margaret.”

Lady Thatcher went on record recently (at the time of writing) for castigating the present government for being too lily-livered. Among other things she prescribed wholesale diversion of resources away from the social services to the police.

People like that used to get themselves slung out of the Gestapo for cruelty. There was a time (before the National Health Service, and healthy eating) when it used to be said “Save on food — pay out on the doctor.” To paraphrase it in the present context: “Save on teachers and social workers — pay out on prisons and the police.” Yet Lady Thatcher, if I’m not misrepresenting the darling, seemed to be promoting this as Right and Proper.

One thing I have always admired the Tory Party for is managing to get rid of its leaders just in the nick of time. But I hope it doesn’t get into the habit of putting the skids under its ministers whenever the press say “jump”. Especially when the volatile fraction seem to be treating an apparent desire at the top to correct the excesses of the last 12 years as weakness of leadership.

Cynics will say that there’s no desire to do this at all. Just a general election on the horizon. But I’ve also heard it said, since Harold Wilson’s day, that the British electorate can be bought for the equivalent of two weeks’ salary. This is surely no less true than it ever was. It’s marvellous what you can buy these days. Far more than you ever could under socialism.

So why, if there’s really no problem about getting re-elected, are the government leaning over backwards to give the impression they care about the state of public services, in particular schools? Might they be priming us for something? Might it just be that any fool can see that the taxpayers are going to have to cough up for some good replacements for our wasting educational resources in the not too distant future? After all, like our nuclear power heritage, it would be hard to find a buyer for the schools system in its present state.

items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 56

moderated by Eke van Batenburg & Adrian Smith

items.title: General Information
items.text:
The workshop on portability was held at the APL conference on Wednesday June 7th. There were about 15 attendees, and most of them had experience with portability issues (if not portability problems). This made for an interesting discussion where everybody was very much involved.

The discussions mainly covered the following four topics. Is portability an issue? What can we demand from vendors? What can we do ourselves? Plan of action.

items.title: Is Portability an Issue?
items.text:
As said before, all attendees had some experience with portability problems, but some had more horrible stories to relate to us than others. For example starting with APL on a micro-computer like TRS80, PET or other brands, going to a mainframe and subsequently to another mainframe, and finally to a mini-computer, expecting quite probably to have to migrate to a micro-computer again in the next few years.

Eke van Batenburg

In general, philosophical issues (floating vs grounded arrays) were not a concern, and missing functionality (such as ⎕DAYS in APL.68000 or the APL*PLUS FASTFNS library) was felt to be a nuisance, but one which could be easily covered by global variables or utilities. The real problems were with syntactic incompatibilities (the use of the up-arrow) and subtle variations in behaviour such as the point where integers turn to floats.

Some people were on the move because of the changes in APL support. For example lack of development in STSC’s MacAPL or discontinuing support of APL by Dec which forced, or at least motivated people to switch to another computer. Others had to move because of upsizing (going from 8-bit micro to mini or mainframe) or downsizing (the recent trend to quit the mainframe and go to PCs). One participant had been through 2 enforced migrations (from the MCM micro in 1984 and then from Wicat) when APL vendors went out of business. Another was working on Honeywell APL 66 (one of the first nested APLs) and had only 3 more weeks until the plug was to be pulled on the system!

Another group of people experienced daily portability problems because they have to support an application on different computers. Although the initial start focussed on portability of programs, several participants stressed the importance of porting data, in particular porting data in component files.

items.title: What Can we Demand from Vendors?
items.text:
Of course the easiest solution to portability problems is to demand of vendors that they make their APL identical to that of the others. However, most participants agreed that the variability that gives the problems in porting has a very good side too. APL evolved into the more powerful product that it is today, because vendors introduced new things. On the other hand, it is in every programmer’s interest to have a common set of APL functions that is available on every platform. However, it was recognised that vendors have to make a living and one cannot ask them to make many essential changes if this is not, at least to a certain extent, reflected in more revenue..Nevertheless the participants agreed that some things could be asked of vendors:

Consistency within their own product line. People felt that the products of one vendor on different platforms should not be different. For example differences in Dyalog APL on the Unix platform and Dyalog APL on the PC platform, or differences in Manugistics APL on the Macintosh and Manugistics APL on the PC should be remedied.

Consistency with the ISO standard for Extended APL. Many of the raised topics of portability problems were differences that are unequivocally defined in the standard for Extended APL. Discussions about those topics were cut short because we agreed that it is reasonable to ask vendors to be at least compatible with the APL extended standard. Unfortunately, some of the hardest problems to work around (such as the behaviour of Reshape on empties) are “consistent extensions”; it would be helpful if the standard included some guidance on these.

Some Goodies. Although everybody has a long, long wish list of things that he wants his vendor to include in that particular APL, it seemed that some wishes are more universally shared than others. So, apart from the wishes that were already defined in the APL extended standard, some others that remained and were shared more or less are:

Standardisation of partitioned enclose (=APL2-like) or partition (=APL*PLUS-like). Some people liked the partitioned enclose using cumulative integers to separate, others were afraid that separation of big arrays by integers would result in WS FULL and preferred separation using bits. Which alternative is chosen is of less importance than that there is one standard way only.

Take and drop with axis to avoid having to specify the size of axes that are not changed.

Ravel with axis to make a 1-column or a 1-row matrix and for ravel over several dimensions.

Scalar functions with axis.

⎕Monitor Function to measure CPU time of each function line. It is not only useful to pinpoint hot spots of CPU time devourers, but also to check if a test set covered all lines.

)IN and )OUT for porting. Many vendors like MicroAPL, IBM and Manugistics have already implemented effective IN/OUT commands, others like Dyalog only have an obsolete and buggy alternative.

Negative index. Useful for various constructions (the question was raised if it not implemented because of illogical behaviour with ⎕IO=0?).

Standard position of characters in ⎕AV.

Standard behaviour of “A B C←” and “A B C[...]” (binding to C or to ABC). Some APLs require parenthesis to assign to “A B C”, others do not. Again (as with partitioned enclose) which alternative is chosen is of less importance than that there is one standard way only.

Standard storage (or at least publication of formats) of component files.

Availability of ⎕MONTH for names of months and ⎕DAY for days of the week.

Namespaces

items.title: What Can we Do Ourselves?
items.text:
Of course if you think that you will never have a portability problem your need to protect yourself against future problems is small. Nevertheless the effort to protect yourself is sometimes small.

Be wary of non-portable constructions. Sometimes it is very easy to use an alternative programming construction if you know that some features are not universally supported. For example one can get a single value from a non-nested vector using index, using pick or using squeezed quad. If you know that the latter is not implemented in many APL systems, taking one of the alternatives is no problem at all.

Some participants were rather surprised to learn that some constructions that had easy alternatives were not widely supported, and expressed their intention to change their programming immediately. Apparently it could be useful to publish a list of differences.

Use cover functions. Some actions, especially those regarding input and output, are always different in various APL systems, for example file I/O and graphics, and others will hopefully grow together but are still rather different (like GUI functions). A sensible way to diminish future portability efforts is to hide that machine-specific code in cover functions. In porting, only those cover functions need to be rewritten.

Develop public-domain cover functions. It will be useful if the APL community has some public-domain cover functions. The packages CAUSEWAY for GUI and RAIN for graphics are good examples of this.

Work at the most APL2-like level offered by Manugistics and Dyadic respectively. The bulk of the code in RAIN is now identical in both these environments, having been migrated to ⎕ML 2 in Dyalog and then copied via the Windows clipboard to PLUS III.

items.title: Plan of Action
items.text:
Publish this in QuoteQuad and Vector. Adrian will publish the discussions of this workshop in Vector and Eke will submit a report to QuoteQuad.

Report this to ISO. Eke will report the main topics of the workshop in the ISO meeting.

Develop more public domain software. No action proposed.

Publish a list of deviations. Eke will start a publication of differences between the mainstream vendors and ask Joseph De Kerf to join him if he wants to. Several participants offered to help, so it was proposed to set up preliminary versions on the Internet and ask for help. Eke will do so. The comp.lang.APL forum was suggested as a good repository for this information.

Eke van Batenburg Leiden, 28th June 1995

items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 6

items.title: Who is Organising it
items.text: APL96 will be a sponsored by SigAPL, and managed by C/M Planners, who did such a solid job for us at San Antonio. The Co-chairs are Stuart Yarus and David Eastwood, and the Programme Committee is led jointly by Philip Benkard and Adrian Smith. Gitte Christiansen is working with the vendors, and Anne Faust is working with Lynne Shaw on marketing.

items.title: Where and When will it be?
items.text: The search for a venue is on! At the time of going to press, the favoured site is the British Isles, but Lisbon and Padua have also been earmarked as possibilities. By the time Vector is shipped, we should know the answer to this one, so look out for an insert! The date will be towards the end of July or early in August.

items.title: What Kind of Conference are we Planning?
items.text:
More of what worked well in Texas! Basically fewer streams, more workshops and as much ‘hands-on’ as we can organise/fund. The hot topics look like “Nested Arrays — get it right first time”; an algorithms workshop following up the excellent sessions at San Antonio (Andreas Geyer-Schulz and Ben Best); how to get that “Designed for Windows 95” logo on YOUR software; setting up APL as a server application (TCP/IP for softies) anywhere on your corporate network.

We certainly intend to make the vendors work a lot harder! Rather than shutting them away in an exhibition and making them buy lunch, they can have a decent 3-hour slot to really teach us how to use their stuff!

The idea of evening sessions was floated at the San Antonio banquet, and (on a quick show of hands) many were in favour and almost none against. We will aim for a pattern of mostly plenary mornings, breaking out into parallel workshops alongside contributed papers in the afternoons. Because the workshops are likely to be over-subscribed, we will repeat them in the early evening, and if we have enough good papers, these too may run on after tea.

items.title: Too Much Diversity in APL?
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

From: Joseph De Kerf, 10 April 1995

Maybe the two most important events on the APL front in 1994 were the implementation of control structures in Manugistics’ APL*PLUS and the implementation of namespaces in Dyadic’s Dyalog APL. Personally I wasn’t waiting for control structures: I am feeling myself very comfortable with the goto of APL — the unconditional and conditional branch (→). On the other hand, their implementation neutralizes the objection of some opponents of APL who claim they reject APL because it doesn’t support such control structures. A very important innovation, however, is the introduction of namespaces. Eric Lescasse for instance described it as the first step to Object Oriented APL. As such, it was a very good idea of Vector to devote a special feature section on the concept, containing three papers respectively by Peter Donnelly, Eric Lescasse, and Kimmo Kekäläinen (Vector Vol 11 No 3, pp 65-95). With increasing astonishment however, we read the guest editorial on the concept by Duncan Pearson in the same number of Vector (p 3). He states: “Whatever Manugistics produce I hope that it is different from the Dyalog implementation.” And he goes on to say: “So let us have as many different, independently conceived, approaches to this problem as there are interpreters.” Maybe this is true for experimental implementations, but definitely not for official commercial releases: we are killing APL in that way.

Indeed, APL is a living language, but a strong handicap for its future is the diversity of its implementations. When in 1973 shared variables were introduced, only a few implementations took it over. Other implementations for instance added the possibility to treat component and native files by implementing an appropriate set of system variables and system functions. In 1991, based on a study of about eighty commercial implementations, I published two inventories, containing a list of about eight hundred system variables/functions in use at that time. A lot of them are synonyms, although more or less different in their implementation details, and a lot of them are homonyms providing totally different facilities. And the proliferation still continues. In the meantime, generalized arrays or arrays of arrays were introduced, in some implementations based on the grounded array concept, in most implementations based on the floating array concept. But even those who used the floating array concept did it in different ways. There are about ten implementations which support the so-called Extended APL for the moment, but when a software engineer wants to design portable software, he can only use the defined facilities of the APL Standard ISO 8485. He can’t even use arrays of arrays. All this not only confuses the declared user of APL, but also doesn’t inspire confidence on behalf of the potential newcomer, and is one of the most serious obstacles for the future of APL. So, let us try to ameliorate the situation rather than making things worse. But I am afraid we are preaching in the desert.

Joseph De Kerf

items.title: Minutes of Annual General Meeting, Friday 19 May 1995
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 9

reported by Sylvia Camacho

Friday 19 May 1995 2:00pm, BCS 7 Mansfield Mews W1M 9FJ

Present: Dr Alan Mayer, Nicholas Small, Anthony Camacho, Dr Ian Clark, David Eastwood, Jon Sandles, Duncan Pearson, Sylvia Camacho.

Apologies were received from Jonathan Barman.

George MacLeod arrived after the AGM.

No ordinary members of the Association accepted the invitation to attend the AGM.

Minutes of AGM 27 May 1994 were agreed

The Chairman, Dr Alan Mayer, thanked all members of the Committee for last year’s work. Resignations were accepted with regret from Jonathan Barman and Duncan Pearson, Alan expressing the hope that they would feel able to rejoin the Committee next year when their pressure of work may lessen. (It was learned later from George MacLeod that he also would be unable to serve on the Committee this year.) In his review of the year the Chairman said that he felt the Swansea Conference workshop and the single day workshop had been well received although these experiments had shown where the organisation of such events could be improved. He regretted that other London meetings had had to be cancelled. This arose because no one could be found with sufficient spare time to make the necessary arrangements. He felt that the Association must look for some other way to find volunteers able to do small amounts of work, not necessarily requiring attendance at Committee meetings. In particular he would like to discuss the possibility of exploiting electronic information exchange and conferencing. The Chairman commended the Vector Working Group for the continuing excellence of the journal which is undoubtedly valued by the membership, of which more than half are overseas members.

Anthony Camacho, the editor, said he felt there was no need to make any special report. The Readership Survey had not called for any striking changes. The Vector working group usually finds that there is at least enough material in hand to fill half of the next issue when they meet at the beginning of each Vector quarter.

Dr Ian Clark, editor of Education Vector, pointed out that this, although included within the main journal, has also an independent mailing list which represents a potential growth area for Association membership among non-career programmers. Ian also has the use of a Macintosh based mailing list which he would like to put at the service of the Association.

Jon Sandles, recruitment officer, said that he feels the World Wide Web would be a good recruitment medium and would like to see a sub-group of the Vector working group set up for this purpose.

Nicholas Small, the Treasurer, presented the accounts. He expects these to be audited in time to be published in Vector 12.1. Nicholas Small said that he intends to approach John Sullivan and expects to obtain his agreement to act as Auditor for 1995/96.

The only nominations received for the election of officers were those from within the 1994/95 Committee, of which seven members offered to stand again for the same posts. There thus remain three vacant posts: Technical, Activities and Projects Officers.

Since the AGM Dave Ziemann and Ray Cannon have agreed to advise on, install and maintain the Association’s entry on WWW and they have been co-opted onto the Committee.

items.title: British APL Association News
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 10

from Sylvia Camacho

Members may be interested to know what the BAA is doing about APL 96. As it is to be held in Lancaster one would expect the local APL organisation to be involved. Since the very first international APL conference these conferences have always been controlled by and usually financed by SigAPL, which is a special interest group of the Association for Computing Machinery (usually known as the ACM), the United States equivalent of the British Computer Society.

Below is the text of the reply from our chairman, sent on 22 September to Bob Brown the SigAPL conference co-ordinator.

Thank you for your email requesting commitment from the British APL Association to APL96 at Lancaster.

Several members of the BAA returned from APL95 with the understanding that a budget for the proposed APL96 would be received in early July. The BAA committee met on 7th July, but no budget had materialised and so no decision could be made, as (like ACM) the BCS does not commit funds without a formal budget and proposal.

We did, however, give our backing to the programme proposed by Adrian Smith and resolved to give financial backing to a conference based on that programme as soon as SIGAPL had produced the required budget.

As you may be aware, a year ago the BAA declined an invitation to organise APL96. Those of our members who have the necessary skills are heavily committed elsewhere at this time and so we cannot take the lead in this project.

Financially, we need a budget that breaks even with a relatively small number of delegates, as we believe that a conference in the UK with such a short lead time is unlikely to attract large numbers. If a suitable budget is produced, and Adrian is still willing to organise the programme, we will make BAA funds available as soon as SIGAPL does the same.

Alan Mayer Chairman, British APL Association.

items.title: Insight Systems
items.text:
Insight Systems is proud to present two new Client/Server products, the SQAPL ODBC Server and APL Pipes, which make it possible to integrate application servers written in APL with other development tools, using industry standard interfaces and communications products:

  • The SQAPL ODBC Server allows your APL application or database system to be accessed as an ODBC data source. You can present your APL-based data or the results of analyses as a set of relational tables which can be used as input into other reporting packages. It is also possible to use application generators such as Borland Delphi or Microsoft Access to create front-ends to APL applications via ODBC. The APL application must run under Unix or Windows NT, but becomes accessible from almost any end-user application or development tool on virtually any platform.
  • With APL Pipes, you can write distributed APL applications without the overhead of a relational interface such as ODBC or SequeLink. APL Pipes is a TCP/IP based system which is similar to Shared Variables, except that it supports sharing of data and function calls between APL2, APL*PLUS II or III, Dyalog APL and SHARP APL systems running under Windows, Windows NT, OS/2 and Unix. Before the end of the year we plan to add Microsoft Visual Basic and Borland Delphi to the list of APL Pipes clients. This will mean that developers in these environments will be able to effectively share variables and make function calls to almost any APL application, whether this application is running on the same machine or accessible over the network.

Until the end of the year, Insight Systems will be very busy with the completion of the Windows version of the KPS System for Adaytum KPS Software Ltd. KPS is a multi-dimensional planning system written in APL, and is currently the UK market leader for budgeting software. We are looking forward to developing the Client/Server versions of KPS scheduled to follow the Windows product, which will allow us to practise our Client/Server preaching and enable APL-based solutions to compete head on with mainstream products in a highly competitive market.

items.title: Dyadic Systems LimitedAnnouncing Dyalog APL/W Version 8
What is Version 8?
items.text:
Dyalog APL/W Version 8 is a completely new implementation of Dyalog APL/W that is designed specifically for Windows 95 and for Windows NT Version 3.51. It is fully compatible with the current release of Version 7 (7.1 Release 2), but contains many enhancements to support the Windows 95 user interface and other features.

Version 8 is based on Microsoft WIN32 in place of the equivalent Watcom software used for Version 7. WIN32 provides improved memory management under NT and is a key requirement for the new Windows 95 logo for which the product is intended to qualify.

Version 8 includes support for most of the new GUI objects and features provided by Windows 95 and Windows NT 3.51. These include ListView, ProgressBar, PropertySheet, RichEdit, Spinner, TrackBar and TreeView objects. All new and existing GUI controls have also been enhanced to support the drag-drop feature of Windows 95. This permits the user to drag-drop file icons into a Dyalog APL/W application. It is intended that the new version of Dyalog APL/W will also support OLE2 and .OCX custom controls.

items.title: Availability
items.text: Dyadic expects to be in a position to ship Version 8 by the end of 1995. However, an early release will be available by the end of September that includes much (if not all) of the additional functionality. Customers may obtain this release by enrolling in the Version 8 Preview Program (see below)

items.title: What is the policy for 3.1 and 95?
items.text:
For the forseeable future, it is likely that many customers will continue to use Windows 3.1. Others will migrate immediately to Windows 95. To cater for both requirements, Dyadic intends to maintain two separate versions of Dyalog APL/W for as long as the requirement to do so exists.

Version 7 will continue to be maintained for Windows 3.1 and OS/2 users. Version 7 is also supported under Windows 95, but it is NOT supported under NT. Customers who need to run applications under Windows 3.1 or OS/2, should remain with Version 7. Applications based upon Version 7 will also run under Windows 95, but will not be able to take advantages of the new Windows 95 features.

Version 8 is Dyadic’s product for Windows 95 and NT 3.51 and includes support for many of the special facilities provided by these systems. It is not supported under Windows 3.1. Version 8 is intended to be the state-of-the-art APL for Windows and will be the basis for ongoing developments in the future.

items.title: Prices
items.text: Version 7 and Version 8 will be marketed and supported as separate products. Version 8 is not provided as an upgrade from Version 7. However, there will be a reduced price for customers purchasing both Versions and for customers who already have Version 7 and purchase Version 8 in addition. Please contact Dyadic or your local Dyalog APL distributor for details.

items.title: Version 8 Preview Program
items.text:
The Version 8 preview program is intended to allow customers to begin to develop Windows 95 (and NT 3.51) applications immediately, without having to wait for the final release of the Version 8 product. It also provides a basis for customers to influence development. This program is open only to existing Version 7.1 users and to any customers who purchase Version 7.1 prior to the final Version 8 release until further notice. The Version 8 Preview Program is chargeable but the price includes a copy of the final release which will be supplied as soon as it becomes available. Enrolling in the Preview Program is the cheapest way for existing Version 7.1 users to obtain Version 8. Contact Dyadic or your local Dyalog APL distributor for details.

During the Preview Program, Dyadic will supply a stream of test releases as new functionality is added and as bugs in the existing code are fixed. In addition to bug reports, subscribers may submit suggestions and requests for enhancement to the new Windows 95 and NT features as they are developed. Dyadic does not guarantee to incorporate all of the requests in the final version, but will endeavour to meet popular demands.

items.title: Summary of New GUI Features
items.text:
Version 8 provides 10 new objects, over 30 new properties and over 40 new events. These new features are summarised below.

  • The PropertySheet object is a dialog box that allows the user to view and edit the properties of an item. A Standard PropertySheet contains one or more overlapping child windows represented by PropertyPage objects, each containing controls for setting a group of related properties. Each PropertyPage has a tab that the user can select to bring the page to the foreground of the PropertySheet. The Display Properties dialog (obtained by clicking the right mouse button on the desktop and choosing Properties) is an example of a standard PropertySheet object. A Wizard PropertySheet consists of a sequence of dialog boxes that guide the user through the steps of an operation. In a Wizard PropertySheet, the PropertyPages do not have tabs, and only one page is visible at a time. Also, instead of having Ok and Apply Now buttons, a Wizard PropertySheet has a Back button, a Next or Finish button, and a Cancel button. Windows 95 Setup is an example of an application that uses a Wizard PropertySheet.
  • The ListView object displays items as a set of icons, in a list format or a report format. ‘My Computer’ is an example of an application based upon this object.
  • The TreeView control is a window that displays a hierarchical list of items, such as the headings in a document, the entries in an index, or the files and directories on a disk. Each item consists of a label and an optional bitmapped image, and each item can have a list of subitems associated with it. By clicking an item, the user can expand and collapse the associated list of subitems. ‘Windows 95 Explorer’ is an example of an application based upon this control.
  • The RichEdit control is a multi-line text editor that provides extensive word-processing facilities including variable text and paragraph alignment, fonts and colours. This control allows Dyalog APL/W applications to exchange complete documents with Microsoft Word and other word-processors. Data may be imported and exported using .RTF files or via the clipboard. The object also includes direct printer support.
  • The ProgressBar is a standard output control that indicates the progress of a time-consuming operation.
  • A Trackbar control is a window that contains a slider and optional tick marks. When the user moves the slider, using either the mouse or the direction keys, the trackbar generates events to indicate the change.
  • The UpDown control is a pair of arrow buttons that the user can click to increment or decrement a value, such as a scroll position or a number displayed in a companion control.
  • The Spinner object is a special Dyalog APL object that combines an UpDown with an Edit. The Spinner permits the user to select from a range of numerical values or text strings.
  • The Grid object has been extended to allow Spinner and Trackbar objects to be used to edit cell values.
  • The List object has been extended. It has a new MultiColumn property that allows you to display items in several columns. In addition, the List supports the facility for the user to drag-drop items within it.
  • Most controls support the new AcceptFiles property. If this is enabled, an object will generate a DropFiles event when the user drag-drops one or more file icons onto it from another application, such as ‘My Computer’ and ‘Windows Explorer’.

items.title: Causeway Graphical Systems Ltd
items.text:
Our main item of news is a very simple one: around 3 weeks ago, SAP started cutting our software onto CD to issue with their R/3 3.0a release. From SAP’s point of view, 3.0a is a strategic release and is, to the best of our knowledge, the first truly distributed business management system to hit the world market. Perhaps the most encouraging thing about this is that a major player in the world software market has been willing to rely on APL for a critical configuration tool. This has to be a good thing for the future of our language.

This leads naturally to the second item: Causeway – the Next Generation (working title: CTNG). For the past two weeks, we have had time to relax and work on the future of Causeway rather than hitting the impossible deadlines set by our clients. Since we first released the Causeway utilities in November 1993 (at the British APL Association’s BAA-GUI workshop) we have seen a massive increase in the functionality of the Dyalog interpreter. In particular it can now handle resize and reposition (via the ATTACH property) in the way that we need it, and it has Namespaces. Anyone who has looked through the Gui_xx functions will have noticed that a significant slab of code in Gui_make is no longer necessary, and may have wondered what all the complex use of ⎕OR and ⎕SHADOW is doing in Gui_exec.

Rather than attempting a piecemeal upgrade, we decided to take the bull by the horns and do a top-down rewrite. It was important to preserve the dialogue-box structure, and it is clearly essential that CTNG behaves in exactly the same way as Causeway, to the calling application. However the internal structure of the class table will be very different (and will support managed replication of functions between classes), and the implementation of localisation and event-handling has been built entirely around the namespace model.

The main visible difference is a huge reduction in the lines of APL code needed to support form-level localisation of variables, and local functions on objects. The entire set of Gui_xx functions written so far can be listed on 3 sides of A4, and most of these will never appear outside #.Gui. In particular, all the Causeway ‘modules’ (such as the Rain PostScript interpreter) simply become namespaces, and the code in them can be executed much more simply with statements such as ps.FullScreen replacing ps Gui_do'FullScreen' in application code.

We are on course to have the first release of CTNG included with Dyalog 8; however we also intend to support it under Dyalog 7.1.2 for users who prefer to stay with Windows 3.11 for the moment.

items.title: Floating-Point Precision
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 111

From: Joseph De Kerf, 23 August 1995

In [1], it was shown how the so-called common mean concept may be used to calculate the complete elliptic integrals of the first and second kind. APL user-defined functions were given and illustrated for p = 0.0(0.1)0.9/1.0. Results were displayed with 10 and 15 digits after the decimal point. Calculations were done with VAX APL under VMS (DEC) and for comparison tolerance its default value 1E15.

In a companion note however, the production manager observes he found slightly different results when run in Dyalog/W. So I did my homework again, however with comparison tolerance 1E16 (instead of 1E15). In addition I did the same calculations but with APL user-defined functions based on:

  1. gaussian quadrature (Newton-Cotes formulae) and
  2. series expansion (MacLaurin’s series integrated, Addams-Hippisley series and the series dedicated to A. Caley).

For all of these runs, carefully avoiding the accumulation of errors as far as possible, I found the same results as published in [1]. So, I suppose those results are correct.

On the other hand, I did the same calculations on other APL systems and found, for all of them, some differences similar to or even greater than those observed by the production manager.

I suppose that the origin of the difference lies in the floating-point mantissa precision. For VAX APL under VMS this is more than 16 decimal digits (about 16.86D), such that the 16th decimal digit may be correct. However, for all the other APL systems I checked, floating point representation is based on the ANSI/IEEE Std 754-1985 [2]. This means that for those systems the floating-point mantissa precision is somewhat less than 16 decimal digits (about 15.95D), such that the 16th decimal digit of the intermediate and a fortiori of the end results becomes more or less unreliable.

This is the reason why, in some implementations such as IBM’s APL2/PC and MicroAPL’s APL.68000, the upper limit of the domain of the print precision variable is set to 15. On the other hand, the advantage of the standard is that the largest number representable is about 1.80E308, while in practice, who cares about the accuracy of the 16th decimal digit?

Joseph De Kerf

items.title: References
items.text:
1. Joseph De Kerf; The Complete Elliptic Integrals and APL; Vector, Vol 12, No. 1 July 1995, pp 102-106
  2. ANSI/IEEE Std 754-1985; IEEE Standard for Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic; Published by the IEEE, New York, USA; 12 August 1985

items.title: J Locales
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 141

by Richard Oates

Explicit Definition isolates names with the Local Copula (=.). Locales isolate names with spelling, possibly expressed, usually implied. My trip may have been more worst case than typical. I wrote three verbs.

The name table_bob_, say, is table in locale bob, while table_z_ is table in locale z. The names table_bob_ and table_z_ are locatives. One locale, the base, has no name. One locale, z, is special: its names are known in all locales unless overridden. Locales are usually populated by script. The application is scripted to the base. Secondary verbs script to named locales. If a file called add is:

table=. 1 : 0
by=. ' '&;@,.@[ ,. ]
over=. ({. ; }.)@":@,
tbl=. 1 : '[by] over x./'
 x. tbl
)

... then 0!:0<'\add' scripts the adverb to the base. This scripts the adverb to locale z:

sc_z_=. 0!:0
sc_z_ <'\add'

I script most of my secondaries without change to locale z. If the first sentence of table is removed, and the last two as well, by, over and tbl become global. That is how I script my verb tracking program, and also the DOS editor I described in Vector 11.3. The former is scripted to locale t and the latter to locale e, in each case to keep names isolated by locale after Explicit (:) is removed.

I happened to have cut defined one way in the base and another way in locale z. Locales are populated by definition as well as script. In the next figure 5!:5@< represents the tracking program in locale t. In the figure but not for real, 5!:5@< is also defined in locale z. The verbs trk and zing are distinct. The first box surprised me. I expected trk'cut' to be <;.1. Then I realized locale t knows nothing about the base, just as the base knows nothing about t. After trk_t_ is plugged into z it can be called trk but it still runs in t. On the other hand zing_z_ runs in locale z and zing runs in the base.

cut=. <;.1
cut_z_=. <;.2
zing_z_=. trk_t_=. 5!:5@<
trk_z_=. trk_t_       NB. plug into z
d=. 1 : '(x.''cut'');(x.''cut__'');(x.''cut_z_'')'
(trk d),(zing_z_ d),:(zing d)
┌────┬────┬────┐
│<;.2│<;.1│<;.2│
├────┼────┼────┤
│<;.2│<;.1│<;.2│
├────┼────┼────┤
│<;.1│<;.1│<;.2│
└────┴────┴────┘

After I saw this I added a verb to trk that makes a locative for any name that is not full (cut__ from cut).

My DOS editor in locale e scripts its result to the locale determined by the extension of the file name. I substituted locale for 0!:0 in the definition and added two verbs. For a calendar program in locale c, say, the first verb makes 'sc_c_' from '\j\s\cal.c', and the second verb is almost:

lo=. ('locale=. '"_ ":@, ]) ; (] ":@, '=: 0!:0'"_)
lo'sc_c_'
┌──────────────┬────────────┐
│locale=. sc_c_│sc_c_=: 0!:0│
└──────────────┴────────────┘

For each Format (":) lo really has Do (".). Do is like Execute in APL. I get a nonce error if sc_c_ is not global (=:).

I made no change to applications. I wrote three verbs that construct locatives for two secondaries not in z. All other locatives appear in a profile script. In an application session I never key a locative or see one. Names have grown up in J. Like the best people, they have lost their innocence but kept their simplicity. Locales are a major improvement.

Richard H. Oates [address omitted]
