items.title: APL+Win Release 1.8
items.text:
Release 1.8 of APL+Win is now available to APL Windows developers. This release adds the popular Windows95 controls on all three Windows platforms: NT, Win95 and Windows 3.*. These include a Treeview control for managing hierarchical lists, a Listview control to help organize columnar data, a Selector control to provide Property Sheets and Wizards as well as Statusbar, Spinner, Trackbar, Imagelist, Progressbar, and Owner Drawn Buttons. These controls can enhance your application and give it the new interface clients expect. This release also adds: tooltips, an unlimited number of user-defined data properties, the ability to suppress events from firing when changing properties under program control, and many other useful properties and events.

To enhance your application when run under Win95, we have added the ability to call 16-bit DLLs and long file name support. Long file names may also be used in NT. None of your existing code needs to change, but using these extended file functions you will get better file error messages (in your native language), wildcard searching for filenames, as well as allowing meaningful names. While these extended file functions work under Windows 3.* (so you only need one workspace) the 8.3 character limit still applies. In addition to all of the above, they also allow you to give APL component files any extension you wish.

As if all this wasn't enough, we're also including a set of APL widget workspaces and utilities. These include an AVI movie player, calendar and date controls, and a workspace to demonstrate the new controls and widgets.

items.title: APL+Win Release 2.0: Free to 1996 Purchasers of APL+win 1.8
items.text: Later this year we will be releasing version 2.0 to take further advantage of Windows95 and NT. This newer version will include all of the above as well as adding support for OCX/ActiveX controls. ActiveX is the newest standard for adding custom third-party controls to your application. We will also be including new and enhanced widgets including a RichEdit control and an APL forms browser. To give you the opportunity to get started NOW with Windows95, version 2.0 will be free to all users who purchase version 1.8 this year.

items.title: APL+UNIX: Release 5.2: Improving Compatibility with Other Platforms
items.text: A new release of APL+UNIX is also available. This maintenance release adds control structures (:IF,:WHILE,:FOR, etc.) and numerous small enhancements and corrective services. The addition of control structures makes the UNIX and Windows systems even more compatible, and will enhance your ability to write APL functions which will work on either system.

items.title: Soliton Associates Ltd
items.text:
General distribution of Release 22 of SHARP APL for the IBM MVS mainframe environment is planned for 4th quarter 1996. Release 22 is Year 2000 compliant. The emphasis of Release 22 development was on performance and operability.

The first customer shipments of the SQAPL Client for SHARP APL UNIX were made in 1st quarter 1996. The SQAPL Client provides SHARP APL with access to standard SQL database products on a wide range of server platforms.

Soliton has announced TimeSquare, a time series database manager for the open systems environment. TimeSquare manages the flow of time-based financial market data through a financial organization, from the data feeds provided by commercial data vendors through to the delivery of market data to end-users.

TimeSquare is an ODBC-compliant SQL server based upon the SQAPL Server for SHARP APL. TimeSquare supports both standard SQL and TimeSquare Extended SQL (a set of proprietary SQL extensions allowing sophisticated time series analysis at the TimeSquare Server).

The open systems networking and interfacing capabilities of SQAPL are provided by DataDirect SequeLink Client/Server Middleware from INTERSOLV Inc. Soliton Associates distributes and supports DataDirect SequeLink for use with SHARP APL.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Limited
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce that the long awaited Version 8 for UNIX is now on Beta Test.

With a few restrictions due to differences in the environments, Version 8 for UNIX is fully compatible with Version 8 for Windows 95 and NT and with Version 7.2 for Windows 3.1. This means that you can develop a GUI application under Windows and deliver it to customers running on UNIX platforms. Indeed, as the workspaces are compatible at the binary level, you have only a single set of application code to support and maintain; Dyalog APL takes care of the rest for you. Under UNIX, your application will have a Motif look and feel, but will otherwise behave the same as it does under Windows.

The beta test release of Dyalog APL Version 8 for UNIX is currently available on IBM RISC System/6000. Versions for SUN SPARC (both Solaris and SunOS), DEC Alpha and HP9000 will be available in due course.

The current release of Dyalog APL/W Version 8 supports OLE Controls (OCX's). In OLE terminology, Dyalog APL (and a Dyalog APL application) acts as an OLE Client. In this context, the Server is the .OCX module in which the object (or control) resides. In practical terms, this means that you can use OLE custom controls in your Dyalog APL application.

At APL96, Dyadic will demonstrate the next phase of its OLE strategy, namely the ability for Dyalog APL, and more importantly a Dyalog APL application, to act as an OLE Server. Firstly, this means that you will be able to call Dyalog APL directly from another application such as Visual Basic. For example, you could build the user interface of an application in Visual Basic but perform the calculations using Dyalog APL. Secondly, it means that you will be able to build your own OLE Objects in Dyalog APL. These objects will be based upon Namespace technology and be manipulated by other applications through their properties (variables), events and methods (functions).

items.title: Causeway Graphical Systems Ltd
items.text:
It is hard to believe that three months have elapsed since the last time we sat down to compose our Vector news. During that time we have made solid progress on our two main consultancy projects, as well as bringing our APL product list significantly nearer to completion.

Our major project of 1996 is to extend and integrate the "Organisational Architect" tool fully into the SAP implementation process. Two months ago, we reluctantly made a major design decision — we are moving the implementation from Dyalog APL/W to a mixed platform with Microsoft C++ for the visual components and J for the calculation and logic engine. We will continue to use Dyalog to prototype and design new objects and interfaces.

The reasons for making this move are complex, and partly technical, for example we need to support double-byte characters (Japanese) and a multiplicity of keyboards and fonts, including Unicode. We also felt that we were constantly 'pushing the envelope' of what Dyadic offer in the Gui, and that by moving to C++ we could be sure that we had access to everything that Microsoft offer. Having decided to re-implement the Gui, we then had a choice of only 1 APL interpreter that can run as an in-process OLE2 server, and that interpreter was J! I think it is fair to say that (a) it was the right decision anyway and (b) we would never have moved if the same facility had been available in symbolic APL.

Needless to say, part-1 of the project was to code the core of the Causeway 'change-notify-refresh' logic as a DLL and to ensure that we could continue to benefit from the design principles that have given us such an edge in APL application development. It is interesting to speculate on the possible application of these ideas completely outwith the APL world, particularly given the move to Java which does at least have a partially interpreted approach.

The majority of the product development work has been focussed on getting Rain and NewLeaf up to a common level of functionality and reliability on Dyalog and APL+Win. Rain has already proved to be a major asset in our other consultancy project — migrating VDI-based graphics from APL*PLUS II to APL+Win for a logistics planning package with some very complex charting requirements. Both Rain and NewLeaf are now with APL2000 customers for pre-release testing, and we are confident that we will have shaken out any remaining problems and deficiencies by APL96.

We will continue to ship Causeway as shareware for Dyalog versions 7.2 and 8, and we are targeting the APL2000 user conference as our release date for Causeway for APL+Win as well as the professional version of Rain (including 3D charting) and NewLeaf. Now that we have a solid platform for 95/NT we can begin to move ahead with Causeway/Pro for Dyalog — we see Causeway, Rain and NewLeaf as strongly complementary products and we urgently want all three on both the major APL platforms, sharing common documentation and support.

items.title: LaTeX and Vector
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 121

From: Dietrich Trenkler, June 1996

Vector claims to be the best journal of APL and I dare not contradict. We are proud of its elegance and power but on the other hand I met some unintelligible resistance when I submitted articles written in LaTeX the other day (Vector 12,1 and 12,2).

We are working hard to convince people that APL is also very well suited to the mathematically unsophisticated user, but where is Vector’s support for those who write maths? I hold, in this respect, Vector is unduly conservative, being an attitude we APLers always have to fight against. In the meantime (La)TeX has become an accepted standard in scientific journals and books and Vector resembles a firm fortress withstanding the breakers. I am not willing to believe that this is because the journal is British.

To say it frankly, to my eyes most formulas in Vector look horrible and I shrink back from submitting a paper being forced to use a word processing software (Word) which does not correspond to the standards I am used to and which deprives me of the freedom I enjoy using APL and LaTeX. Bernhard Strohmeier and I struggled hard to force TeX to deliver a format resembling that of Vector’s standard and I felt a little bit let down on the part of Vector especially since articles in LaTeX had earlier been accepted without further ado and other formats have also been accepted. So I want to know what is your attitude concerning the layout of the articles. Is it laisser faire or is it the strict Word dogma? If it is neither some guidelines would be very welcome.

Ed/Production: Obviously we want to get Vector looking as good as possible! It would be helpful to know what Dietrich finds wrong with the Microsoft Equation Editor format; to our eyes there is little to choose between the formulae in his article (Vector 12.2 page 87) and Joseph de Kerf’s which follows it on page 95.

The text of his article was received camera-ready and fitted to page as well as we could. In the first draft, all the font sizes were perfect, but in the copy as printed the body text was too small – the subheads and APL are correct. Unfortunately we did not have time to ask for another run as we were (as usual) running to very tight schedules.

In general we very much prefer to have editable copy, but we have no problems accepting mathematical content as .EPS files for inclusion. APL code can be accepted in most known workspace formats, and again we much prefer to have ‘soft copy’, particularly as most of the material will soon be made available on the BAA Web site for download.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
The last editorial did a demolition job on OFSTED, not undeserved, but maybe unfair on its hard-working inspectors. What was not said (and what should have been said) was that OFSTED is an attempt to replace the irreplaceable — like trying to grow corn on cleared rainforest to provide ground-cover. When the local authorities were rolled back as part of Thatcher's drive to 'roll back socialism' some priceless things got rolled back with them. For instance the network of advisory units on IT. The advice dispensed was free, useful, supplier-independent, unobtainable elsewhere and locally-based. When you destroy a distributed resource you have to put something centralised in its place, even if it's there only to deflect the blame onto broader shoulders for the consequences of what you have done. Hence OFSTED. End of story. Only it isn't, because the editorial in question threw down a gauntlet and vowed to take it up in this issue.

This publication is about APL (which we take to include its new dialect, J). What it is not about is peddling a nostrum for all the ills of the educational world. Have we ever said: "APL is the solution — now what's your problem?" No, but we have explored why this country seems to be such poor soil to nourish the seeds of excellence in Mathematics, Science, Technology and Engineering, and proposed solutions. And we have an idiom for discussing these solutions. It happens to be APL.

But it might have been BASIC. What with the breakneck pace of computer technology, we are all inclined to forget what an achievement the BBC Microcomputer was. For roughly a seven-year span, 1983 to 1989 say, entrants into further education could be relied upon to possess at least one formalism in which computer ideas could be precisely discussed, viz. BBC BASIC. It made the development of effective courseware in technical subjects remarkably easy, in spite of the severe disadvantages from which BASIC suffers as a language. BASIC is too voluminous. Anything beyond the simplest arithmetic needs scores of lines of text to represent, each line by itself superficially clear, but taken as a whole so dilute that the student has difficulty seeing the wood for trees, let alone typing it all in.

Nevertheless, if you're asked for an example of where a nationwide initiative gave a real boost to education, point to the foresight of the BBC to sponsor a standard vehicle for its planned series of educational programmes. Why did it work? Not because of any unique virtue of BASIC. They used the wrong language (but we would say that, wouldn't we?).

Yet the dear old 'Beeb' was a catalyst of innovation, instead of laying a burden of paperwork upon teachers to smother initiative. Well before the National Curriculum (NC) came along, whilst the benefits of the BBC initiative were still making themselves felt, teachers were taking introductory IT courses, in their own time and sometimes at their own expense, because they felt it was empowering. What I mean is that it looked as if it might be good for their work, their careers and good for the pupils too. But there were anxious questions. What exactly was the role of computers in classroom teaching supposed to be? Was the teacher destined to become obsolete?

On my introductory IT course to practising teachers, I once opined that the real place of a computer in the classroom was not as a robot teacher, but as an administrative slave, taking the strain of routine tasks like attendance, drill, assessment, progress tracking and reporting, "leaving you, the teacher, free to do what you're good at."

One student nearly fell off his chair. "To think we've got to come on a computer course to be told that!"

The huge expenditure of time, effort and money that went into the creation of OFSTED, the NC, key stage examinations and published league-tables, not only by the government on coercion, but by every school in the country on compliance, was a total waste, at least prior to Sir Ron Dearing's revision. It remains largely futile because it makes a mockery of the teaching profession in England and Wales. What about other professions? The law of the land requires no doctor to cure me if I'm ill, no lawyer to win my case in court. But if I am a child my teachers are required by law to train me and rate me in a tightly prescribed set of attainment targets, which are supposed to define a sound education. (What is a sound education? Discuss.)

The resources to erect this monstrosity would have been better spent on commissioning and deploying a standard computer system to take the waste of teacher time out of class record keeping. Or, if that's too hard (the Inland Revenue seems to have found it so, with its PC program to do self-assessment) we could have had a national library of software to support all aspects of a recommended, or even a commended curriculum, seamlessly spliced with its delivery vehicle in schools. Much as the French government installed MINITEL and the US Defense Department installed ARPANET in their respective countries. If only we'd gone the whole hog with an empowering infrastructure like MINITEL, and tinkered with a prescriptive straitjacket like the NC, instead of doing it the other way round. Then we wouldn't have needed to take two bites of the cherry and call a moratorium on future changes to stop the project foundering. Just the opposite. The vehicle would have been a living organism, its growing tips practising teachers, instead of the withering of buds and the lopping of sound wood which has been the fruit of the NC and its gendarmerie, OFSTED.

In APL (and J) we have an empowering idiom to formulate such a vehicle. It's time we used it.

items.title: APL Product Guide
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 33

compiled by Gill Smith

VECTOR's exclusive APL Product Guide aims to provide readers with useful information about sources of APL hardware, software and services. We welcome any comments readers may have on its usefulness and any suggestions for improvements.

Pressure on space occasionally prevents us from printing the complete guide, however updates will always be listed. We do depend on the alacrity of vendors to keep us informed about their products. Anyone who is not included in the Guide should contact me to get their free entry — see address below.

We reserve the right to edit material supplied for reasons of space or to ensure a fair market coverage. The listings are not restricted to UK companies and international suppliers are welcome to take advantage of these pages.

For convenience to readers, the product list has been divided into the following groups ('poa' indicates 'price on application'):

  • Complete APL Systems (Hardware & Software)
  • APL Interpreters
  • APL-based Packages
  • APL Consultancy
  • Other Products
  • Overseas Associations
  • Vendor Addresses
  • World Wide Web and FTP Sites

Every effort has been made to avoid errors in these listings but no responsibility can be taken by the working group for mistakes or omissions.

We also welcome information on APL clubs and groups throughout the world.

All contributions and updates to the APL Product Guide should be sent to Gill Smith, at Brook House, Gilling East, York, YO6 4JJ. Tel: 01439-788385, Email: 100331.644@Compuserve.com

items.title: While in J...
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 10

From: Nick Cox, 8 June 1996

The so-called ‘antecedent precipitation index’ is a measure of the wetness of a catchment. Precipitation (rainfall, snow, etc.) makes a place wetter but such water is lost from a site over time by evaporation and drainage.

api[i] = precip[i-1] + k * api[i-1], 0 < k < 1

is one way of trying to capture this balance fairly simply.

The idea is pretty crude engineering hydrology and the API is naturally inferior to any number based on real measurements at a site. In practice, however, daily precipitation measurements for somewhere similar are far more readily available than are comparable soil moisture measurements, especially over long historical periods. I don’t know much folklore on estimating k, but one rough physical guide is that at most places wetness fluctuates about an average, especially on time scales of the order of a year. This allows you to bracket plausible values of k.

That is just context. Like the typical reader of Vector, when reading such simple formulae, I often write down the corresponding simple programs. To me, with a brain warped by too many years of Fortran and Basic, and improved slightly by exposure to various C-like languages, what springs to mind first is something like api1. To any J or APL enthusiast, api1 looks incredibly long-winded for such a mathematically trivial problem. And indeed in the best and worst traditions of APL a program can certainly be produced in one line, as for example api2.

Yet experiments clearly show that api2 is much slower and more demanding of space, as examination of the programs suggests. Can a quicker yet concise J script be produced?

As yet more context, any one who wanted to do this could easily have 1000 daily rainfalls, and in fact I will want to do something similar for more like 40,000 values. (I’ll probably do it with totally different software, but largely for reasons irrelevant to this journal.)

api1 =. 3 : 0
NB. antecedent precipitation index NJC 15 April 1996
NB. k api p
:
k =. x.
p =. y.
api =. 0
i =. 0
while. i < #y. do.
api =. api , (i { p) + k * {: api
i =. i + 1
end.
}. api
)

api2 =. 3 : 0
NB. antecedent precipitation index NJC 15 April 1996
NB. k api p
:
+/"1(* x.&^@i.@-@#)\ y.
)

items.title: Arrays, Arrays, wherefor art thou Arrays?
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 14

From: Richard J. Procter, 24/8/96

Lancaster and APL96 were certainly a highlight on the APL calendar this year for those of us fortunate enough to attend. Indeed, with its many fine pubs and charming old-world appeal, the hamlet of Lancaster itself proved an agreeable selection as conference venue.

Not so well recognized however, by most attendees, is the fact that England is indeed the place where APL and array-oriented languages have been upper most in the minds of some individuals for centuries. In fact, just to prove this, while rummaging around in one of the curio shops in downtown Lancaster, I couldn’t believe my luck when I stumbled upon this extremely obscure snippit of genuine poetry from none other than the immortal bard himself, William Shakespeare.

This work, incredibly written sometime around 423 B.I. (Before Iverson), is indeed a truly remarkable piece for it’s time. Something, I would dare say, that the APL community should proudly point to as its “Magna Carta” of documents, entirely paving the way to the array approach to problem solving in everyday life.

Here’s the text from the dusty manuscript, in its entirety:

To C++, or not to C++: that is the question: Whether ’tis better for the job security to suffer The loops and gotos of outrageous scalar programming, Or to take arrays against a sea of if/else statements, And by boolean compression end them? To )off: to ⎕DL; No more; and by a →0 to say we end The heart-ache and the thousand variable declarations That compiled code is heir to, ’tis a link-edit Devoutly to be abend’d. To )off, to ⎕DL; To ⎕DL: perchance to multi-task: ay, there’s the rub; For in that delay mode what dreams may come When we have shuffled off this if-then-else coil, Must give us interactive systems: there’s the modularity That makes calamity of so long programs; For who would bear the compile and links of time, The compiler’s wrong output, the proud programmer’s frustration, The pangs of despised loops, the rewrite’s delay, The insolence of array-unfriendly management and the rewards That patient merit of the worthy takes and drops, When he himself might his report format With a bare bottom-line? who would ‘for-while’ bear, To grunt and sweat under a weary do-loop, But that the dread of something after installation, The undiscover’d bug from whose general protection failure No programmer returns, puzzles the support person And makes us rather bear those workarounds we have Than kludge others that we know not of? Thus fear of bombing does make cowards of us all; And thus the hue of screen resolution Is dot-matrixed o’er with the pale cast of pixels, And enterprises of great input/output With this regard their proc(main) turns awry, And lose the prompt of abort-retry-fail. Software you now! The fair APL! Nymph, in thy implementation Be all my array solutions remember’d.
path: Arrays, Arrays, wherefor art thou Arrays?

items.title: The Last Great Empty-Array Joke
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 158

by Adrian Smith (Production Manager)

In some ways, Vector assembly just got a great deal easier. With the new release of Dyalog APL come a set of ‘standard’ font layouts and mappings which should result in some consistency across submissions from Dyalog users in different countries. The good news is that virtually all the APL and national language symbols have the same mappings as are used in the APLPLUS font from APL2000; the bad news is that the zilde and squad characters are different! The odd thing is that Manugistics chose to upset the Icelanders — by overwriting the thorn and eth symbols — while Dyalog chose to upset the French by using the left and right guillemot. Given the relative market for their products in these two countries, I find this a little strange!

The obvious solution, adopted by Vector from this edition forward, is to upset both the Icelanders and the French by duplicating zilde and squad in my APL2741 layout, so that I can accept material in either font and the APL characters will print correctly. What is more, when pasted from our Web site into the correct interpreter they will execute correctly. If you paste anything with a zilde into the wrong interpreter, you will get some rather puzzling syntax errors. Squad is not yet a problem.

The moral of the story is: submit APL material to Vector in either APLPLUS or Dyalog International format and I can cope. I know IBM have high hopes for Unicode for their Windows product, but in the short term it would be wonderful if they too adopted one or the other of the accepted mappings for their Windows 95 release. The font (and Duncan’s excellent sans serif screen font to match) are free to anyone who can make use of them.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Limited
items.text:
At APL96, Dyadic announced two major new developments for Dyalog APL. The first of these is a new type of defined function called a Dynamic Function. Dynamic functions are fast, lightweight functions with intriguing possibilities for improving performance and reliability.

The second major new feature is the capability to turn a Dyalog APL namespace into an OLE Server object that can be called from Visual Basic, C++, Excel and so forth. This feature will allow you to package and distribute your APL code in a form that can readily be incorporated into non-APL applications in a totally standard manner.

Articles describing these exciting new features may be found in this issue of Vector.

In addition to the capability to act as an OLE Server, Dyalog APL/W Version 8.1 will also include the ability to act as an OLE Automation client. This facility is also founded upon the direct correspondence between Dyalog APL namespaces and OLE objects and will allow you to drive numerous Windows applications from APL.

Finally, Dyadic is announcing TCP/IP socket support for Version 8.1. Not only will this allow you to access the Internet directly from APL, but it will provide the basis for future client/server operations between Dyalog APL for Windows and Dyalog APL for UNIX platforms.

items.title: Causeway Graphical Systems Ltd
items.text:
The major news for this quarter is the long-awaited release of NewLeaf and RainPro for both the Dyalog APL/W and APL+Win platforms. Adrian and Gill have just been demonstrating the APL+Win versions at the APL2000 user show in Orlando.

RainPro is an extension to the Rain package distributed as shareware with Dyalog APL/W. It includes 3D tower charts, scatter plots and surfaces and has the facility to copy graphs to the clipboard as metafiles. It comes with both the standard help file and a 48-page user guide which has many worked examples.

NewLeaf is a completely new product which breaks fresh ground in providing the capabilities of a desk-top publishing package to the APL programmer. It is a "frame-paragraph-style" based product which takes the difficulty out of producing well laid out reports in proportional fonts. It can print complex tables with ease and supports tree-structured table headings in the same way as the Dyalog APL/W grid control. Indeed it would be the ideal tool to provide the print method for that control.

Each of RainPro and NewLeaf is a set of APL functions that have simple syntax, take array arguments and that you can integrate into your code easily. The Dyalog APL/W and APL+Win versions of NewLeaf and RainPro are functionally identical although the Dyalog versions use namespaces to hide the functions. They are written entirely in APL and so are fully modifiable by the user, something not true of any OCX or VBX solution you might consider.

The second piece of news is that at the end of October we will be joined by Jon Sandles. Many will be familiar with Jon from his role as recruitment and meetings organiser for the BAA and from his work on the Vector Working Group.

Jon has been involved in the development of Causeway from the start and has a deep understanding of its internal structure as well as having written perhaps more Causeway applications than anyone else we know. He also has experience of maintaining a site of Causeway developers and developing his own Causeway classes, that having been part of his job. His experience in this area will be incorporated into the forthcoming CausewayPro for which we have received many requests and on which we are currently working. He will be a major asset to the company and will allow us some much-needed flexibility in scheduling our new developments.

items.title: Insight Systems / Adaytum Software
items.text:
Converting applications to Windows is an unpredictable business. At Insight, we have just completed the process, including rollout of the apparently inevitable bugfix release, for Adaytum Planning, our multi-dimensional business planning product — with only slightly more than a 100% overrun of the project plan. Fortunately, despite the delay, sales of Adaytum Planning have continued to grow rapidly; we now have several customers in Denmark and opened an office in the USA in September. The success allows us to grow our development team to cope with the workload; since August we have recruited an APL Developer, a Quality Assurance Manager, and an Internal Support Manager. We expect to recruit additional APL and C developers during the next six months; if you are an experienced APL or C developer (especially if you are both), and interested in a job in Denmark, drop us a line.

As a result of the delays in our Windows conversion project, even only slightly attentive readers will have noticed that our sustaining news items have remained pretty static; almost all our announced product releases have gradually slipped by between 6 and 12 months. The ideas for and the driving force behind our Client/Server products originate in our own requirements for tools which make it possible to position our APL applications as first class citizens of the emerging world of distributed applications. It is not easy to get ideas while fighting bugs and getting an application to behave itself under Windows.

The good news is that we have now actually started work on new releases of our APL Client/Server products, for internal use in the next release of Adaytum Planning and for general release to APL users. Following discussions with APL vendors and users at APL96, we have decided to start with a revision of the SQAPL Server, with the primary goal of improving performance and making the server available on low-end platforms such as Windows NT, OS/2 and even "stand alone" under Windows 3.x or '95. A revised SQAPL Client, with functionality as described in the April 1996 Vector, will follow later.

So, if any of you intend to downsize to windows and are planning to base connectivity on our products, you may proceed with confidence. By the time you are done with the conversion and have the bugs out, the new SQAPL generation will be waiting for you.

items.title: HMW Trading Systems Ltd.
items.text:
HMW have completed the first two phases of porting their APL*Plus based Trading Room product 4XTRA to Dyalog for Windows Version 7.4. The third and final phase includes converting the remaining code which requires a GUI interface, and then switching to Version 8.

The functionality of the new system is in fact a superset of the existing 4XTRA versions, adding Money Market products such as FRAs and Financial Futures. To reflect the increased capability of the product, the Windows version is now known as iDeal.

The GUI interface uses both Causeway and specialised routines making direct Dyalog calls (dealing systems have some uncommon requirements). The system also has interfaces to databases (using the ODBC links provided by Insight systems) and other generally used Dealing tools, such as Excel.

We have also decided to make several of our own internal products available generally. All are available for APL*Plus and Dyalog, but some features may vary between the versions. They include:

Object Manager — This enables the programmer to build a series of system files, comprising APL functions, global variables, screen designs, etc. and group them into modules (which can be grouped into larger modules). A complete range of search, edit, copy, delete functions are provided, including point and edit, version comparison, etc. Interfaces to Word provide a standardised documentation method.

Configuration Management Suite — based around the system file concept described above, this gives version control of each object (functions, variables and groups) enabling them to be managed through a development, test, release, live cycle. Promotion and rejection mechanisms co-ordinate movement between these levels (which can be redefined) and full client configurations. It is also capable of having multiple development input sources, preventing clashes and documenting the dependency of changes. Interfaces to Word for release documentation in a standard format. Designed to be used with a compression tool, such as PKZIP to give a series of documented modules for upgrades or patches which can be placed on a bulletin board or despatched to the client via modem or diskette.

Multi-Processor Sequence Scheduler. This enables a systems designed to define a series of tasks to be run on any number of PCs and have the activity interlocked and automated as much as possible. Special hardware requirements can be associated with a PC and with a task, ensuring the task gets run with, say, the correct peripherals (e.g. some backup device). The process fully allows for restarts and checkpoints, reprinting of report images, etc. and is very fault tolerant. The task activity is co-ordinated ultimately by file requirements and this is used to drive a task dependency list — a task cannot start until the files it requires have been produced and are available, even though they have been created on a completely different PC. Individual tasks may be assigned different priorities, including "optional", i.e. the failure of the task is not critical and processing may continue. Once started a sequence can cycle indefinitely, initiating or "sleeping" according to parameters, reducing operator intervention to practically nil — one client described it as "the nearest thing to perpetual motion" he had ever seen.

Process Monitor — a central process, running on a single PC capable of monitoring the activity across a network. It can check the status of devices such as printers, monitor errors on user workstations (with the suitable error trapping routines running), broadcast messages (or even code to execute on a user's PC) and provides a graphical monitor of tasks being run via the Scheduler. If any of these tasks fail the APL*Plus version can "take control" of the failed APL session, enabling remote editing of functions and reassignment of variables — in fact about anything you can do directly at the keyboard.

Since we are just in the process of launching these tools as separate products, we haven't decided on a pricing structure yet, but expect the price to be low as development costs have been met largely by sales of the 4XTRA system, which makes extensive use of them.

We are also expanding the general consultancy side of the business, which has languished a bit of late due the development work undertaken on the major products. It is after all where we started 15 years ago! this will be not only APL (and other languages) design and programming, but the project management skills and methodologies that we have developed over the years to implement and maintain our projects.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
Many times over the past few years the New Scientist magazine has deplored the quality of science knowledge in Parliament and Central Government. Perhaps the fashionable 'good schools' beloved of the establishment are mostly incapable of teaching numerate disciplines to any pupils who aren't well-grounded in them already? This tempts one to suggest that any school identified as 'elite' should reserve a sizeable proportion of its places for pupils with existing numerate skills, otherwise the only qualification for rubbing shoulders with the high and mighty of tomorrow will continue to be parental ability to pay.

In Education VECTOR, we have constantly agitated for the provision of good materials in all schools to teach Science and Mathematics. Sufficient computers are simply a question of money, training to use the computers is largely a question of buying the right hardware and software in the first place, and we believe we have the software answer in APL and J. But how does one encourage those magic individuals who can actually teach Mathematics to non-mathematicians? The best we have been able to do is agitate against the massive discouragement that both good and bad teachers have had to endure in recent years.

But there's another factor, equally vital. I remember reading about an American study of the effects of giving high quality education in Mathematics (among other things) to children from deprived backgrounds. It reinforced my suspicions that the intellectual apparatus of a rich child is not necessarily any better than that of a poor child, provided the latter hasn't actually been brain-damaged by deprivation. But it laid down certain essential conditions for a child to benefit. Chief of which was "freedom from inappropriate disapproval". This of course can come from peers, or family, or even the authorities ("This isn't for the likes of you").

That's perhaps the heart of the matter in Great Britain today. Maybe it always has been. We have a culture which is hostile to any sort of 'cultured' ability, Music, Mathematics, Pure Science, whether on the playing fields of Eton or the street corners of Brixton. Whilst this culture pervades, the able pupil learns to hide his or her light under a bushel and the able teacher learns not to cast pearls before swine. Even with a deliberate programme to suppress it, it may take a generation before the practice of Thuggee, both institutionalised and informal, passes away. Only then will 'good' schools flourish, 'good' in our special sense of teaching good Science and good Mathematics to all who want it.

Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 47

J User Conference APL96 at Lancaster

This section of Vector documents all British APL Association meetings, and any other events of interest to the APL world. If you have recently attended any gathering which you feel would be interesting to Vector readers, please let the Editor have a brief note, and we will include it here.

The APL96 pictures are by Ray Cannon and Dieter Lattermann. Also thanks to everyone who helped to document the sessions and workshops.

There are a lot more pictures (including several of the night out at Thurnham Mill) on the COSY web site at www.cosy.com. Bob Armstrong did excellent work with his digital camera, and this collection is well worth a visit.

items.title: Nominations for the British APL Association Committee
items.text:
The next AGM must be held in May 1997 and, seen from this side of Christmas, that seems a long way off. However, there are just two issues of Vector between now and then. Here, therefore, is an appeal for people to serve on the Committee for the year beginning next May.

Please persuade and nominate your friends or colleagues and we shall be happy to publish details of their candidature in the January issue of Vector. The election will be held in April by postal ballot. Anyone who would like to be given a feel for what is expected of the various Committee members should contact someone on the current Committee who would be delighted to receive any expression of interest.

Please send your nominations to the Secretary.
