items.title: APL Press Review
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 27

by David Preedy

Our irregular feature on the press coverage that APL receives is by definition limited to the publications that we, or our various spies around the world, peruse. This issue I feel sure that several articles must have slipped our net.

Our coverage was enhanced by a weighty bundle that fell through my letter-box, coincidentally all covering a certain supplier’s new product announcements. Top of the pile was the extract from the December ’85 issue of Sinclair Gebruiker. I just about struggled through the translation of:

“Micro APL voor de QL”

and discovered that the Dutch for “diskette” is “floppy”, before abandoning the exercise for more productive tasks.

One of the English competitors of Sinclair Gebruiker must be Sinclair/QL World, and their April issue also had a two page introduction to this “more exotic language” now available on the QL. I’m not sure how many of the “floating voters” will have got far beyond the introductory paragraph:

“Though getting a little long in the tooth, having been around since the 1960s, APL . . . has a small but loyal following.”

The rest of the article described some of the features of APL and of the QL implementation, concentrating on some aspects of the keyword facility. Unfortunately it never really explained why you would want to use APL instead of SuperBasic, so it’s unlikely to bring about the mass conversion of all C5 users to APL.

Another of my spies sent me an extract from Minicomputer News, but unfortunately the date was cut off so I can’t identify the exact issue. The context was quite interesting being one of those rare occasions when an application using APL is mentioned without a great song and dance about a strange back-to-front language written in Greek. The application was a foreign exchange pilot system for the Midland Bank Group Treasury. As the Microsystems manager said:

“We had three things going for us. A bunch of ATs; . . . some nine months’ experience of the G/Net IBM PC local area network; . . . in-house expertise in APL, which is ideal for recalculating matrices of numbers.”

Nearer to home, VECTOR itself has being receiving publicity from Datalink. The April 21st issue picked up my own call for a marketing campaign to boost interest in APL (Editorial – VECTOR Vol.2, No.3). I was indeed very impressed by the alacrity of their reporter who was on the phone the day after the issue had been posted. “Is it really as bad as that?” he asked. His article followed up my own comments with those of Romilly Cocking who:

“claimed there was a ‘steady spread of understanding’ which was enough to keep up the impetus behind the language.”

VECTOR obviously gets passed quickly around the Datalink office, because by the following week, its GIGO column was doing its best to spread misunderstanding about APL and revealing major divisions within the ranks of our very own working group!

“Elsewhere in the same issue a press review by Steve Lyus seems to call some of Preedy’s arguments into question in its extremely vigorous defence of all that is APL.”

It seems that the merest hint that APL might make some sacrifice in terms of performance and machine efficiency (albeit to gain significant benefits in terms of development times), is tantamount to a statement that “APL gobbles up machine resources like nobody’s business”! The tragedy is that such attitudes prevent anyone trying to develop a rational debate about the types of application where APL is or is not a suitable language to use.

One of the most enjoyable aspects of doing a press review is looking for the “ones that got away”, those articles that cry out for a mention of APL and yet it never comes. This time the prize goes to Computer Weekly (May 1st) which unveiled “how we arrived at such a prolific number of programming languages”. Despite this prolific number, the table headed “Significant programming languages” includes only 10 – Fortran, Algol, Cobol, Basic, RPG, PL/1, Coral, Pascal, C and Ada.

My thanks to all those who have sent in the cuttings they have noticed. No doubt next issue will report the worldwide coverage of APL86.

items.title: Editorial: The joys of Spring?
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by David Preedy

So Spring is here at last; the birds are in full song; the trees are budding; the sap is rising, and every young buck’s thoughts are directed to APL’86 in Manchester.

That’s all very well for them, but for those of us whose BAA committee regulation beards are starting to grey, there are other more weighty matters that must take precedence. It’s recruitment season, and we have to sit cloistered in darkened rooms, grilling the young aspirants whose very careers may depend on what we think of them.

For those of us who have deserted the big company scene to savour the delights of small business, the process is fairly nail-biting for the interviewers as well. After all the costs of a mistake are proportionately greater for a small team. Anyway, Curricula Vitae arrive by the sack-full and one’s thoughts are divided between the desire to recruit some really able people and the fear of what geniuses these people must be, who have achieved such startling exam results.

However during the process of vetting all these applicants, I was struck by the singular inappropriateness of what they were being taught – particularly those on computer-related courses. Are they being given the breadth of vision to devise inventive ways to use the rapidly-changing technology of today, let alone tomorrow? Far from it! In most cases, they are being fed regurgitated techniques that were probably state-of-the-art when their tutors were being educated, souped up with a couple of lectures on the latest fad – normally expert systems.

Now I’m not pretending that it would be possible to teach only subjects that are likely to be widely applicable in the outside world – there’s nothing to match commercial experience for that. However I would expect some of the students to emerge with an overview of the computing business. They should surely be exposed to the types of problem addressed by computer techniques and to the different sort of technique available. And that general background should at least include some study of the different types of programming language available. I don’t expect, or even want, a generation of graduates fluent in Lisp, Prolog, Cobol and APL. However I would like some of them to have heard of APL – or at least to be able to find out something about it in the library when they get back to college.

Of course my own experience and prejudices predicate that I will be looking for an appreciation of APL, but the issue is more general. If students never get the chance to even hear about one of the languages that has led the way in many application areas – graphics, decision support, information centres, financial planning, to name a few – then how can they hope to develop new and imaginative applications themselves over the next thirty years or so?

So this issue’s editorial ends with a three-fold challenge:

  • to the APL community, to approach your local college and offer to give a brief series of talks to interested students, explaining why you use APL; better still lend them some kit and an interpreter;
  • to the academic community, to ensure that all computing students at least can find out about APL and other minority programming languages – why not for instance subscribe to VECTOR and buy Gilman & Rose?
  • to the students themselves, to choose courses that offer them a broad perspective of the field of computing and whose practical offerings involve more than writing an operating system (in BASIC) and programming someone else’s hidden-line removal algorithm.

items.title: Book reviews
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 39

reviewed by Paul Chapman

items.title: The APL Toolkit, published by CIPS APL SIG, First Edition
items.text:
In the preface, the editor Richard Levine describes the book as the result of efforts by the Canadian Information Processing Society’s APL Special Interest Group (CIPS APL SIG) from 1983 to 1985. It must also be said that he admits that the book is not yet finished, but a second edition will be forthcoming with the last two sections completed, based on feedback from the APL community.

The book is organised in six chapters. The first two provide a general introduction and a guide for the use of the book. A directory of functions grouped under categories follows, and then the functions themselves. Finally come the incomplete chapters, documenting the categories and the functions respectively.

The functions presented range from development tools (name list, function documenting, timing, etc.) through general programming utility functions (looping, timestamp formatting, the ubiquitous BOX, etc.) all the way to application functions (e.g. mortgage amortisation).

The function listings themselves reveal a healthy smattering of comments, and a refreshing avoidance of “one-liners”. All functions are claimed to be standard-conforming and independent of global system variable settings, except, in the latter case, where dependence is natural (e.g. where the global setting of the index origin is used to produce a result containing indexes). Each function should, according to the introduction, contain a standard set of comment lines at the beginning, listing the function category, author, timestamp, version and example. Some of the lines are unfortunately missing from many of the functions, and where they are present the advertised format is not always adhered to.

The functions themselves are listed alphabetically. This seems to be a hangover from the way functions are listed in the active workspace. I cannot see why this is a better way than listing them in different sections according to category, especially in this case where each function belongs to just one category. An alphabetical index is very easy to produce, and presenting functions by category allows the reader to compare the different approaches available to solve his own problem. Much of the detail seems to have been machine-produced, and the on-line version of the utilities workspaces said to contain functions which directly support the idea of categories; so it would seem to have been easy to print the book in sections like this.

My major criticism of the book is the incompleteness of the last section, where the individual functions are documented. Of the 115 functions listed in the book, only 16 appear in this last chapter. Were the functions presented in a machine-readable form, my objection would be less, since one of the oldest (and still one of the strongest) APL maxims around would apply: if in doubt, try it out. However, most of the more interesting functions are more than 50 lines in length, and typing one of these in only to find that it doesn’t quite do what you wanted could be a frustrating exercise.

The one thing that caught my eye in this otherwise straightforward book is a method for defining local functions inside functions, using comment lines whose second character is a single digit defining which local function the line belongs to. Where it is necessary to write monolithic utility functions which can be easily copied from workspace to workspace, this is the clearest way I have seen so far of presenting local functions.

The book is not easy to use, but some of the functions in it may well make it worth obtaining. Many of the functions have been introduced as similar system functions on some APL implementations, but where portability is a concern the book could be very useful.

items.title: FinnAPL Utility Library, published by FinnAPL, First Edition
items.text:
No individual credits are given in this book of APL utility functions. The brief introduction explains that the book comprises the 101 most important functions in the “Special” workspace of the Finnish APL Association, FinnAPL.

The introduction also refers to the “widely accepted standard” of underscoring the last letter of each function name. I don’t know of this standard, but I assume its purpose is to avoid name conflicts between utility functions and application functions. However, if it were to become “widely accepted”, it would defeat its own purpose, since all publishers of utility functions would conform to it, and thereby introduce name conflicts between different sets of utility functions from different publishers. A better approach would be to start each function with the letters “FINN”, or some such, to identify the origin of the function.

Apart from the one page introduction and four pages of contents, the book consists simply of one function per page or two. The functions are grouped alphabetically within categories. The categories themselves appear by name in the contents pages, but are not mentioned thereafter. No full alphabetic function index is provided, which would be a simple and useful addition.

The documentation for each function is consistent and well laid out. Its name and purpose are given, followed by its calling syntax. Then there is a detailed description of each of the arguments and the result, with some additional informal comments. One or two clear examples follow, and finally the function itself is listed. Where a function needs to call other functions listed in the book, their names are listed explicitly.

Many of the functions will be familiar to readers of FinnAPL’s excellent idiom book. Some of the function lines tend towards the obscurity of those one-liners, particularly in their length and their use of embedded assignment. This is quite unnecessary within a function: an extra line or two spent in clarifying the inner workings would be well spent.

No independence from the global environment is claimed, but I suspect from looking at the listings that this is achieved in every case.

This is a most attractive and useful book. Its layout is excellent, and the functions themselves form a consistent set of utilities. Apart from adding an index, all I can suggest by way of improvement is: more please!

items.title: Software Review: AFM
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 41

by Adrian Smith

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
AFM is a file management package which runs as an Auxiliary Processor with either VS APL or APL2. It provides IBM’s APL with component files along the lines of the APL*PLUS shared file system; simple cover functions double for ⎕FTIE, ⎕FREAD and so on.

AFM files can be accessed concurrently by online APL systems and from conventional batch programs (typically written in PL/1 or COBOL). File and record-level locking is provided, with security handled through access matrices in the normal way.

A wide range of ‘housekeeping’ and ‘administrator’ functions are provided, some via an ‘OPFNS’ workspace and some as batch utilities.

The cost of AFM is around $15,000 depending on the particular options chosen. It is marketed by Interprocess Systems Inc in the USA, Cocking and Drury being the UK agents.

items.title: Background to Use at RM
items.text:
AFM was brought in to Rowntrees about a year ago. The motivation for doing this was threefold:

  1. We needed to redesign an antique VSPC (ex CMS) system which made heavy use of direct files. We could have set it all up with keyed VSAM files, but AFM promised a much quicker solution at a very reasonable cost.
  2. We had already anticipated a VSPC to TSO conversion. A pre-emptive move to AFM looked like smoothing the path very considerably.
  3. Experience from RM Canada (under VM/CMS) suggested that we could expect significant CPU savings over our standard file routines.

In addition it was becoming clear that we would soon be faced with implementing APL systems on a variety of PCs, all of which had some variant of the APL*PLUS/PC file system. The idea of a compatible set of file utilities across all environments was obviously very attractive.

At RM the vast majority of APL filing is handled through two utilities called (with startling originality) DUMP and GET. DUMP simply takes a list of APL objects (a delimited vector or in ⎕NL format) and bungs them all on a file. Typically there will be 50 – 80 objects, say 100K of data in all. GET reverses the process; either everything on the file, or selected variables, reappear in your workspace.

Under VSPC by far the best way of doing this turned out to be to format and ravel everything, and then to write it out (via the EBCDIC processor) in 4K chunks. The potential economies from cutting out all those ‘executes’ and ‘reshapes’ are obvious!

items.title: Installation and Housekeeping
items.text:
Getting AFM up and running was simply a matter of following the instructions! However getting it running fast required a fair amount of work from out technical support group; mainly a matter of getting the VSAM files defined right, getting catalogs in the right place and so on. The documentation was felt to be adequate, but could have been indexed better!

The utilities for file dump and restore, and the general overnight housekeeping jobs were well documented, and have caused us no problems. The OPFNS workspace is quite adequate, but can be improved out of all recognition by a bit of attention to the user-interface. Fortunately all the code is unlocked and commented, so simple patches like accepting lower-case responses (our administrator doesn’t have an APL keyboard!) are very easy to do.

There are some minor beartraps, for instance if you mistype the TSO id which you want associated with a particular AFM user, you can run a batch import for that user, but can never again get at the files! You have to wipe them from the system and try again; not serious but avoidable I would have thought.

items.title: Using AFM from an APL Application
items.text:
The first thing I must say is that the User Guide is absolutely first class. It is well organised and is readable as a tutorial as well as being a very adequate reference manual. Experienced APLers have been able to pick up the basics, and to write quite sophisticated systems, with no guidance other than a copy of the manual. I suppose all this proves is that component files are a natural extension of APL, and that it is absurd that they have never been made a native part of the IBM offerings.

My only gripes concern the very peculiar way the AFM cover functions attempt to reproduce APL*PLUS error handling. Functions such as FTIE are result-less, and leave various obscurely named globals lying around for inspection (if you’ve previously set up an equally obscure global to define the range of errors you want to detect . . . otherwise its DOMAIN ERROR time!). I’m afraid I rewrote most of them to return explicit results, again an easy task as the source code is very straightforward. Of course you have problems with things like FREAD; this sends back an empty vector if it fails, and you then have to go looking for that pesky global again. I could almost see a case for nested arrays!

items.title: Performance
items.text:
It proved easy enough to get our DUMP and GET routines to work with AFM, but quite a task to make them as fast as they were before. The simple-minded approach of writing one object per component is hopelessly slow (in elapsed terms) when you have lots of little variables. It also leaves you wondering what to do with the odd whopper; you have to set your maximum record size somewhere, and wherever you set it (16K, 32K, 64K, . . .) sooner or later someone will bust it.

We eventually settled on a compromise of partitioning the file into character, integer and real and ravelling variables of each class together before guillotining at 16K. This still leaves us with the reshape, but does away with the execute on numerics. AFM now gives us about 30% better CPU cost (including time spent by the AP outside APL) and marginally slower elapsed times than we had before. We feel this is acceptable, if not quite up to our initial expectations.

I am more worried about that archaic ex-CMS system I mentioned at the start. Here the files have between 5,000 and 10,000 components, mostly quite small. Typically the application will tie half a dozen of these on signon, reading the odd record off each; this takes a minimum of 6 seconds elapsed, which is barely acceptable. We are too far down the road to start compromising on the design, but with hindsight I wonder if the decision to treat AFM as if it were ‘native’ might have been a mistake.

items.title: Summary
items.text: AFM gives plain old VS APL what it should have had all along; a usable file system. It is well supported with housekeeping utilities and in general the documentation is good. We have yet to find any bugs, and we had good ‘hotline’ support from the States when we confused ourselves during the TSO conversion. Performance is very adequate as long as you minimize interaction with the AP; feed it lots of trivial requests and response times are much less satisfactory. You can design round this, but you shouldn’t really need to! On balance a good product and cheap at the price.

items.title: Benchmarks Updated
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 44

by Adrian Smith

items.title: Introduction
items.text: VECTOR (Vol. 1, No. 4) included some highly unrepresentative benchmarks of various APLs on the IBM PC and the MicroAPL Sage. Several of these were specifically set up to sniff out oddities in the various interpreters, and are probably worse than useless in comparing the speed of the computers themselves. Having had a chance to play with Dyalog APL on the DEC MicroVAX and also on the IBM RT PC (or 6150 as it wishes to be known in this country), I thought readers might be interested in the average performance of the most basic benchmarks across all the tested machines.

items.title: Benchmark Results
items.text:
The times are all relative to the standard PC running APL*PLUS/PC with the co-processor fitted. It was not fitted in the PC/AT. The ‘real’ and ‘integer’ figures are averages of the three tests shown before; the ‘function’ figure represents a simple 1000-looper, which I have found (Dyalog would agree with this) is probably the best test you can perform to get a good all-round picture of application speed.

Computer Integer Real Function IBM PC (8087) 1.0 1.0 1.0 IBM PC/AT 1.8 3.2 3.0 Sage (APL.68000) 2.8 3.8 3.9 DEC MicroVAX 1.9 6.1 2.6 IBM PC/RT (Dyalog APL) 3.0 5.9 5.8

The DEC MicroVAX was the fastest floating-point machine, but was otherwise rather disappointing, being slightly slower than the PC/AT at function execution. I gather from Dyalog that the C-compiler is less than clever at procedure calling, so their APL (being a nice modular beast) is badly penalised.

The IBM PC/RT was (across the board) an impressive machine; marginally slower than the MicroVAX on intensive floating-point, but way ahead of the rest on all-round performance. Running it multi-user had a barely-detectable effect on elapsed times.

items.title: Product Review: PortaAPL for the Macintosh
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 45

reviewed by Normand R. Montour
path: Product Review: PortaAPL for the Macintosh

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
The Apple Macintosh computer has many features which could attract the inveterate APL user: its simplicity, highly interactive concept and a somewhat “futuristic” approach to Data Processing. It was lacking the only element which could make the APLer happy: APL.

The Portable Software Company of Cambridge, Massachussetts, has remedied this situation. The PortaAPL interpreter is a lean, efficient and attractive package both with regard to the Macintosh and to APL. One already sees the horrible spectre of comparison showing its benchmark on the horizon. Being of a lazy nature, I felt that the wheels which were invented by others could turn just as well for me, so I decided to use two benchmarks previously presented in the April 1985 issue of VECTOR by Adrian Smith and David Ziemann. The latter was using what have become known as the “Harris” benchmarks.
path: Product Review: PortaAPL for the Macintosh

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
In the Harris/Ziemann benchmarks, PortaAPL performed extremely well and the vendor uses those benchmarks as a demonstration/marketing tool. I do not include here the findings of Mr. Ziemann, since most readers can refer to their issue of VECTOR.

It is only when I started to execute the benchmarks devised by Adrian Smith for the IBM PC that I found a slight performance problem in the “scan” operator:

I have already reported the problem to the vendor and I do not believe this problem will linger very long. The other benchmarks, however, show that PortaAPL compares quite advantageously to other APL interpreters.
path: Product Review: PortaAPL for the Macintosh

items.title: APL on the Macintosh
items.text:
Once past the benchmarking obsession,we can consider the real beauty of a product such as PortaAPL. The Macintosh offers some excellent user interface tools: the Mouse, pull-down menus, windowing, and a very “solid” user interface. PortaAPL makes intelligent use of all these features plus a few more, including interfacing to other Macintosh products such as MacPaint, MacWrite (through the clipboard) and QuickDraw.

The file system is adequate, vaguely similar to the VAX/APL system (see reference 1), but with the unfortunate restriction of limiting the access method to a sequential file system. All primitives are supported including a few extensions. The PortaAPL interpreter does not offer a Nested Array facility, but this will hopefully reach the mind of the product designers. The most interesting feature of their file system is to access the Macintosh mini-finder from defined functions; this allows the user to select and open files and to choose the disks on which these files reside.

My main reason for buying a Macintosh instead of a more traditional computer of the IBM type was to relieve me of my day-to-day computerized job and to enjoy the plain and simple pleasure of a good and servicable tool to help me with writing music, composing love letters and developing my house floor-plan. I can very well see PortaAPL helping me make a musicological analysis program or getting me involved in the study of cryptography. The Macintosh is a very “visual” machine, and PortaAPL provides all the necessary functions to allow APL to take full advantage of those “visual” features.

The PortaAPL sound generation is very primitive and it does not allow any control of the advanced functions of the built-in Macintosh sound synthesizer. Polyphony is not available, nor is shaping of envelope, timbre and reverb. Other Macintosh applications already use these admirably, so it is regrettable that PortaAPL provides so little access to them.
path: Product Review: PortaAPL for the Macintosh

items.title: Full-screen editor
items.text:
The full-screen editor is substituted for the Del editor. It can edit functions and character arrays. The use of the Mouse and pull-down menus makes it very efficient and one can learn to live without sophisticated functions such as those provided by VM/SP’s Xedit (and its popular interfaces to APL thanks to Norman Brenner – see reference 2). The twelve-fingered APLer may choose the clutch-shift-ctl-alt-esc-key editing style in lieu of the Mouse and menu operations.

The character set is crisp and clean, and no modifications are necessary to either keyboard or circuitry to obtain the proper APL characters for both display and printer (I used an Apple Imagewriter). Character arrays are edited using the ⎕ED system function.
path: Product Review: PortaAPL for the Macintosh

items.title: Usage and Feel
items.text:
The PortaAPL interpreter “feels” very solid and the addition of little details such as “double-clicking” a workspace into the active workspace reveals the Macintosh dimension into the user interface. There is also a communications/terminal emulator mode which I was not able to test, but which seems to provide an adequate means of using host APL resources. The documentation is well written with plenty of examples and illustrations (all of which were drawn on the Macintosh). The supplied workspaces provide some cover functions for the most complex processes and usability functions for control of Mouse, files and external interfaces (Quickdraw, communications, etc.). Most of the other APL features are present, such as Trace and Stop, diamond, and a comprehensive set of System Variables and System Functions adapted either for the Macintosh or for the vendor’s own flavour of APL. Comments are allowed on the right-hand side of the program and blank lines within functions are ignored. User-defined operators are not available.

PortaAPL also provides the ability to )EXPORT and )IMPORT workspaces to and from other systems.
path: Product Review: PortaAPL for the Macintosh

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Although it still contains a few bugs (which most APLers could circumvent anyway), PortaAPL is a very promising package because it opens a whole world of possibilities for the APL authors to spread their ideas in the Macintosh community, and to the Macintosh users to have access to the immense library of applications that were developed in APL during the golden years of Host Programming. I invite my fellow Iversonians to test drive this interpreter and to feed me comments. Perhaps we could even start a PortaAPL special interest group within the British APL Association. Anyone interested can contact me at:

Informaticien, [address omitted]

PortaAPL is available from Portable Software, 60 Aberdeen Ave., Cambridge, Mass. 02138, USA.
path: Product Review: PortaAPL for the Macintosh

items.text:

  2. Editing APL objects using CMS XEDIT, by Norman Brenner, ACM APL84 Conference Proceedings, June 1984.

items.title: PCs, Graphics & APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 51

by Martyn Adams

One of the more enjoyable aspects of my job is to evaluate new pieces of kit and, if they check out O.K., write code for them. Recently I’ve been devoting my attentions to two such pieces of kit – both from IBM – the E.G.A. (Enhanced Graphics Adapter) and the P.G.C. (Professional Graphics Controller – also known as the PGS). Both have been around since last Summer, but the lack of availability will probably have prevented many readers from laying their hands on one.

items.title: IBM Enhanced Graphics Adapter
items.text:
Now we at Metapraxis use APL*PLUS/PC on IBM PC/XTs and ATs and on the whole have been more than satisfied with it. (I have reservations about the choice of some ⎕ functions and which way their arguments go and other niggly things like that but all in all I am pretty impressed.)

It was then with great delight that we received both the E.G.A. system and APL*PLUS release 4.6. (This was before the new release 5 but it supported the E.G.A.) We plugged it all in and hey presto! It worked first time! Now the E.G.A. supports many different modes – most of them the boring emulations of the basic IBM colour graphics card. These, as any discerning PC user will know, are little short of pathetic. The low resolution and poor choice of colours means that the basic colour card has few serious graphics applications. But the E.G.A. is a delight!

Our software package – RESOLVE – is designed to display very good quality colour images, graphs and such, to senior management. Consequently we are a bit fussy about the graphics devices we consider supporting and we had deliberately not used the standard colour card. By purchasing the additional memory expansion for the E.G.A., we were able to use the highest resolution possible on the E.G.A. This is obtained from APL by using mode 6 (APL graphics mode, not the E.G.A. graphics mode) which gives the 16-colour 640 by 350 pixel image. Once you’ve started using this, you’ll never want to hear or speak of the colour graphics card again. Consequently that is the mode with which I am most familiar.

Having sung the praises of the APL interpreter and the E.G.A. I would like now to point out some practical considerations. Back at base, deep in the steamy Metapraxis jungle (our oversized office plants are rumoured to be carnivorous) we run the E.G.A. on a PC/AT. Speed, we thought, would be no problem with the extra horsepower of the AT as against our older XTs.

We used to have a performance problem on the XT with the primitive colour graphics card. It took several seconds just to write a line of text while in graphics mode! The problem seems to lie within ⎕GWRITE which is the function used to write text to the graphics screen. But the E.G.A. on the AT does not improve the speed of the text writing by much – although for most operations it is significantly faster. I think this is simply because there are more pixels to write to on the screen and so the extra speed of the AT is being traded for extra resolution on the card.

Oh well! We do get good graphics even if it is a mite slow. One advantage with the APL is that it takes advantage of the extra resolution and allows you to write 80 columns of text in full colour. The characters are fully programmable from within the APL but it is not a simple process. I have never used STSC’s supplied functions so I cannot say if they supply a character design utility.

With release 4.6 of the APL (I am not sure but I think it is also true of release 5) we were supplied with a little program to define the characters to be used by the E.G.A. card. You see the E.G.A. has a fully programmable character set and STSC thoughtfully supplied a routine to program it. This means that you don’t need the STSC APL character chip if you’ve got the E.G.A., even if you don’t use the graphics options. I don’t know what effect this has on any of the other programs that are lying around which use the PC’s extended character set though. One could expect there to be a few funny characters lying around especially if you use a multilingual word processor. All of those horrid foreign characters are redefined as lovely APL symbols. To top it all the character quality, whether within APL, graphics or not, is very good and note that the E.G.A. still remains programmed even when in DOS.

Well done STSC on that one, but not so well done on the printing side! I have found a bug, or is it a feature? STSC have quite rightly put in a very nice and simple graphics printing function (⎕GPRINT) which takes a snapshot of the displayed image and churns it out to the EPSON FX-100 dot matrix printer. You can decide what character represents what colour as a left argument to the function. This means that you can define black on white or white on black, by judicious selection of the appropriate characters from the STSC modified extended ASCII/APL character set.

I liked that. But the printing is rotated sideways on the printer, so to rotate it back to the correct way the manual recommends ⎕POKE’ing location 234. On simple black and white images this works beautifully – printing a very crisp image which really looks quite impressive. What the manual doesn’t tell you is that your choice of shading patterns goes all funny and if you select anything other than black and white (black is a block character and white is a space character) then your picture will look as if it has put on a set of ghastly striped pyjamas.

This caused me much upset, but at the time of writing the Cocking and Drury Helpline were chasing up the problem with STSC and I am awaiting the answer with anticipation. It does seem a shame that such a nice and simple facility which has been well implemented should have this problem. In fact the other bug I mentioned to C&D was chased up and fixed pretty much straight away. I was very impressed! The bug is simple enough, if you ⎕CR or ⎕VR a function then the interpreter zaps the screen attribute character where the cursor lies. You don’t normally notice it though because it sets the attribute to ‘normal’ display. It only shows up when you have a screen full of other attributes and then suddenly one of them switches off. However, there is a ‘patch’ available from C&D and later releases of APL*PLUS/PC should include that minor correction.

On the graphics side the line drawing, shading and circles all work amazingly well, although one has to be careful with the painting (colour fill). Many a time I have looked with utter dismay as the colour flooded out of the pretty little shape on the screen to obliterate everything else. Make sure your border’s fully enclosed before using the ⎕GPAINT function.

A good alternative option would be to have a graphics function which allows one to specify an arbitrary shape by defining the corners and just say “fill it”. It would make life so much easier. I have often needed to define a shape and fill it without knowing exactly where to start the painting. If you think about it it is not an easy task. What if the shape folds back on itself? What if there is a hole in the shape where the centre of gravity should be? Where do you start painting from? Perhaps STSC would like to consider that as a future development.

The ⎕GINIT function allows you to define the colours you want. All in all you can define up to 16 from a palette of 64. The 64 are not awe-inspiring and some of them look remarkably similar, but if you fancy 8 different shades of blue then you can do that. Actually I found that the choice of 16 colours was about right for nearly all of my applications and for most systems it should be enough. Using the ⎕GINIT function is very easy and you can even define the border colour – a thoughtful touch that.

One of the few nice things about the standard colour card was that after drawing your grotty picture you could ⎕PEEK it off the screen and compress the resultant variable, so that it held only the addresses and values where the screen was non-blank. By ⎕POKE’ing it back to the screen the image took just a second to recreate itself. If that variable was sorted by address or colour value then spectacular results could be acheived when it was written back to the screen again.

Unfortunately life is not so simple on the E.G.A. One can’t simply peek and poke to the screen and get sensible results any more. At least we haven’t found an easy way of doing it yet. Do you know of any way of doing it? It is a shame though, perhaps STSC could come up with a ⎕GPEEK or something which allows a quick read of any supported screen? Please!

Anyway, to compound the problem, the E.G.A. with 128k memory spills over the 64k segment size which was so thoughtfully built into the IBM PC architecture, and a fullish picture would more than likely take up more than 64k. There is no way one can fit a pint into a half-pint bottle. Or is there, STSC?

The Enhanced Colour Display – the special monitor that plugs into the E.G.A. (the older colour ones can’t operate at a fast enough frequency) – has one really dumb feature. On the right of the screen are three knobs; one is the on/off, the middle one is the contrast and the third is the brilliance. Great. Except that when I first got the machine the contrast knob did not appear to work. Oh well, you can’t win them all – I thought.

It turns out however that to activate the contrast knob you have to pull it out. Then it works quite well. As soon as you push it in again, the contrast returns to its factory default setting and you have to pull it out again to return to your desired setting. I think that’s dumb. Why bother with a pull switch at all? And if you’re going to have one, why not document it? Such are the wonders of modern technology I suppose. I wonder if the next screen will have an on/off switch which only works if you pull it out first. . .

To finish up on the E.G.A., I would have to recommend it as a serious graphics card which is more than I can say for the previous IBM offering. If performance is what you want, then you’ll have to have an AT as the XT can be a bit slow. I can guarantee that you will be impressed with the picture quality of the device. I hope that the current rumours about IBM bundling the E.G.A. in with the new ATs as the standard monitor card turn out to be true.

By the way, a flood of E.G.A. compatibles seem to be hitting the market and we’ve successfully run all our software on one of these (Quadram) without having to make a single change.

items.title: IBM Professional Graphics Controller
items.text:
The P.G.C. (Professional Graphics Controller) is a very different animal. IBM started selling them at very high cost because they are very high spec. However earlier this year the prices were slashed by about 50%. Don’t get too excited about this though – we haven’t been able to lay our hands on one in the U.K. since last Autumn, although they have been available to our knowledge in the States and in France.

The P.G.C. has a resolution of 640 by 480 and can display 256 colours from a palette of 4096. Not only that, but it has its own onboard 8088 processor! Unfortunately you can’t speak to it by using the ⎕ Gfunctions in APL*PLUS, you have to send it commands.

I remember the days when my finances ran to an APPLE II. Remember them? I later upgraded it with a keyboard that had its own processor but technology had advanced so fast since I had bought the APPLE that the processor in the keyboard was more powerful than the CPU! It nearly had more memory too! I seriously considered programming the keyboard to be an interpreter for the CPU. Pipelining on the APPLE? No. I’m not that good unfortunately. But I digress. . .

The P.G.C. is one of the products supported by IBM’s version of GKS called VDI. To translate into English that means that Big Blue wrote a packaged offering called Virtual Device Interface which emulates the Graphics Kernel System for its PC range of computers. That should, in theory, permit pictures drawn on one device to be transportable to another. In practice, as I have explained in a previous article (see VECTOR Vol. 2, No. 3), that doesn’t work very well.

Virtual Device? I have visions of a printer zipping about the office on its little wheels, wires dangling, plugging itself into each PC workstation and accepting a line of printed output from each. Providing it doesn’t bump into the virtual graphics screen (a P.G.C. perhaps) also skidding about trying to display at least one frame of a graphics image from each machine – it might work. Until the manager walks in and gets a flying RS232 in the mouth. . .

In the future, despite my previous article in VECTOR on the uselessness of GKS, it may well be worthwhile to write a VDI/APL interface, as VDI currently supports the P.G.C., E.G.A. and that other blotchy thing. For simple drawings it may prove a useful transporting tool but don’t get carried away. Apart from the difficulty of defining pictures using VDI it also has a serious performance overhead. Oh roll on the 80386!

Rumour has it (lots of rumours around these days!) that the P.G.C. VDI driver doesn’t quite work properly and that’s why you can’t lay your hands on a P.G.C. in the U.K. (Ed: It must be something to do with the weather if it works in Silicon Valley and on the Riviera!) Apparently IBM do not think there is much demand for a new graphics screen which uses a different protocol (yes – another graphics protocol) without having the VDI programs.

Anyway we – the amazing APLers – do not need the new proposed Esperanto of the graphics world in order to get the P.G.C. working. Besides which, unlike real Esperanto, VDI can slow down your application by as much as three times – rumour has it of course. I tried to get VDI into the APL workspace but VDI didn’t cooperate and I’d be pleased to know if anyone else has any success in this field.

The P.G.C. is the biggest PC card I’ve come across; it takes two complete expansion slots and there is a little half card stuck between them. It certainly feels like you are getting your money’s worth when you install it. In PC mode the P.G.C. emulates a feeble graphics card, which is not the E.G.A. but that older one, and it will only switch to its high-res mode by a specific command. The graphics commands are sent to it by accessing a memory buffer in the PC memory map and setting pointers. Unlike the E.G.A., the P.G.C. has a command processor on board and so it has to be sent a series of command strings. For this reason APL*PLUS doesn’t yet support the P.G.C. with its ⎕ functions. I have written a function to send the command strings and if anybody wants a copy of my code (unsupported of course), just ask.

Using my function we have been able to draw incredibly pretty pictures with incredible resolution and in incredibly quick times. The P.G.C. does support arbitrary polygon fills and you can dynamically change colour palettes enabling you to emulate rotating planets and flashing arrows and such like. There is a suite of 3-D graphics functions, but be warned – they do not always work properly. You can rotate defined objects through a three-dimensional plane and end up with a really screwy picture. The P.G.C. doesn’t support hidden line/surface removal. Pity that. . .

It will draw in 2D, 3D, convert from one to the other, circles, lines, polygons etc. You can even draw with absolute coordinates or relative coordinates. You can define command lists and run them whenever you want. You call them back in a translated form and you can read pixels from the screen as well as write them. You can program variable sized characters as well and the amazing thing about the P.G.C. is that it could look remarkably like an IBM 3279 graphics terminal if it wants too.

The P.G.C. is a very good device but is not for the casual user unless you really require the resolution or the greater colour selection. Development of programs can have its difficulties. Remember that the P.G.C. is a computer in its own right so that if you lose communications with it and the monitor is displaying the P.G.C. screen – not the PC screen – then tough! You can quite happily display a graphics image and while doing so return to APL with a SYNTAX ERROR and do frightening things, without the P.G.C. batting an eyelid. It still hasn’t been told to return to PC mode and so will quite happily display its graph without you knowing what is happening under the bonnet. Even a soft re-boot won’t help and you may have to switch the PC off and then on again before you can continue. Remember that rebooting the PC will restart the PC but not the P.G.C. IBM have thoughtfully not supplied a reset button on the card.

On the other hand you can draw a graphics image while still in PC mode and then suddenly flash to the graphics image without the user having to watch the graph being built up.

A big let down with the P.G.C. was the proportional spaced lettering which is supposedly able to cope with any character size. I don’t know why I was led to believe that, it certainly isn’t explicitly stated anywhere. With all those CPU cycles to spare you would have thought that the P.G.C. could draw properly proportional characters at any size anywhere on the screen – but it doesn’t. As you increase the character size the spacing within the character string gets bigger until the P.G.C. decides that it can fit a double size character in. Then bang! – the characters are twice as large and closer together.

In conclusion then, I have to say that overall I am impressed with the E.G.A. (especially with the extra memory) and APL*PLUS’s integration of it into their offering, even to the point that they support the extra memory without the manual saying so! STSC could do a little more in the way they handle graphics from APL and I would be only to pleased to make a few constructive suggestions.

VDI does not seem so impressive. The P.G.C. is very good for those who need the extra specification but remember that it didn’t come cheap (and now it doesn’t seem to come at all!). I suspect that there are already a few P.G.C. clones around that support hidden-line removal and one or two little extras which will make them superb for animated graphics.

This section of VECTOR is intended to document the seminars delivered at recent meetings of the Association, particularly for the benefit of those members based away from London who often find it hard to find the time to attend. It also covers other selected events which are likely to be of interest to the wider APL community.

We are dependent on the willingness of speakers to provide us with a written version of their talk, and we would remind them the “a picture’s worth a thousand words”. Copies of slides and transparencies will enhance their articles.

The Activities Officer (see inside back cover) will respond enthusiastically to offers from individuals who wish to contribute seminars and supporting papers.

items.title: Introductory Notes
items.text:
by Adrian Smith

1986 got off to a cracking start with two very well supported meetings at the Royal Overseas League. On 17th Jan we had a batch of papers on APL and OR, and on 21st March a set of talks on APL system design.

Much of the detail from the talks will be available in full as VECTOR articles (Tony Cooper’s is included after these notes – many thanks) so I shall be very brief in giving little more than an outline of the papers.

Many thanks to Nic Cook for taking very thorough notes at the March meeting (and my apologies for not using more of them!).

items.title: A Computing Environment for OR
items.text:
Tony Cooper (British Airways)

Tony is a member of a small group in BA who support OR (and others) on APL*PLUS (mainframe), DEC-10 and so on. His talk covered the themes of:

  • what aspects of computing are helpful to OR.
  • how well does BA measure up?

He concluded with the interesting quote:

“All the really undisciplined people have congregated in the groups that do APL.”

I wonder why . . . see Romilly Cocking’s paper from the March meeting.

items.title: Optimum Pallet Loading
items.text:
Eileen Dyson (Rowntree Mackintosh)

The evolution of a pallet-loading model at Rowntree Mackintosh fell into three phases:

  • 1976 (or thereabouts) saw the design of a ‘best-fit’ algorithm which was implemented in batch PL/1. The output from this was a ‘layout chart’ giving a complete packing schema for a particular pallet size.
  • 1983 saw an APL front-end, which used GDDM graphics to select and display the choice of layouts for any given box size. Using this the product development department could (for example) superimpose two candidate patterns to check interlocking and hence stability.
  • 1985, and the APL package moved down to APL*PLUS/PC for distribution to several factory sites. The graphics lacks the flair of GDDM, but is entirely adequate in day to day use.

Eileen brought along a disk of the model, which attracted an interested gaggle of people when run on a nearby Compaq.
path: Introductory Notes; APL and Operational Research, January 17th 1986 (meeting notes)

items.title: Linear Programming and APL: Pains and Pleasures
items.text:
Phil Chastney

APL effectively grew out of linear algebra; ergo it ought to be ideal for tasks like LP! Unfortunately LP is intrinsically procedural and highly iterative; FORTRAN programs may run for 8 hours . . . what can APL hope to offer?

It is a nice environment in which to use LP, and it does have all the right primitives. In fact the whole basis of LP is two inner products, a division, and an outer product. The problems lie in the implementation of the typical matrix operations when the data is very sparse (1 – 10%). This leaves a niche for APL in relatively small problems, where the answer is wanted interactively, and where the user is willing to pay for the privilege.
path: Introductory Notes; APL and Operational Research, January 17th 1986 (meeting notes)

items.title: Pouring Water on Troubled Oils
items.text:
Dominic Murphy (ex Texaco)

This was a typical Dominic half-hour! Ostensibly it covered the ‘human element’ in the design and implementation of a refinery simulation. As he put it, the motivation went something like this:

UK to USA: We need some more tanks USA to UK: No you don’t UK to USA: Oh yes we do USA to UK: Oh no you don’t . . . we’ve done a simulation!! UK to OR : We need a simulation – and make it snappy!

The whole thing ended up as a vast board game; it cost some phenomenal amount of money to run on IPSA, as everyone collected their printouts and flung them off to the States.

Unfortunately, after all this effort, all they proved was that they really didn’t need the tanks after all. Oh dear, they never spoke to OR again!
path: Introductory Notes; APL and Operational Research, January 17th 1986 (meeting notes)

items.title: Author’s Note
items.text:
by Adrian Smith

As promised, here is part-2 of the VSPC conversion saga. Much of what follows is lifted straight from my Email diary; a potentially fascinating archive for the software archaeologist of 4086!

If there is a moral to be drawn from this tale, it is probably “Panic sooner rather than later”. In general a problem perceived was a problem solved; once we had wound ourselves up to face the fact of TSO the actual conversion rapidly became a well-drilled routine.

The ‘wake’ was scheduled for April 1st at 8.00pm; some of us made it with rather less than 2 hours to spare!!
path: Case Study: VSPC – The Last Rites

items.title: VSPC : The Last Rites
items.text:
IEC161I 056-084,TX02001,IEFPROG,OPTION,,,SYS3.ISPF.OPTIONS.CLUST
IEC161I SYS3.ISPF.OPTIONS.DATA,ICFUCAT3
IEC161I 056-084,TX02001,IEFPROG,OPTION,,,SYS3.ISPF.OPTIONS.CLUST
IEC161I SYS3.ISPF.OPTIONS.INDEX,ICFUCAT3
IEC161I 062-086,TX02001,IEFPROG,OPTION,,,SYS3.ISPF.OPTIONS.CLUST
IEC161I SYS3.ISPF.OPTIONS.DATA,ICFUCAT3

To recap briefly . . . . I left my tale of woe suspended in mid-air towards the end of September 1985. The things that were really bugging me at the time were:

  • the TSO environment, in particular the session manager, and the way workspaces were saved and (?) shared.
  • VSAM record-locking. Could VSAM files be held at the record-level rather than by reserving the whole file?
  • the sheer bulk of data to copy across and check through.
  • the persistent rumours of heavy increases in CPU cost.

In no particular order, this is what we did . . . .
path: Case Study: VSPC – The Last Rites

items.title: VSAM Record Locking
items.text:
The first problem to be tackled was the knotty one of multi-user VSAM files. We depend absolutely on these for all our APL printing; a routine called VTAMPRT scans constantly through a shared VSAM file, pulling off completed prints and dishing them out to the appropriate destinations. Typically up to a dozen users could be spooling prints concurrently to the file, so to try to work with file-level holds would be quite impossible.

Diary: 24/10/85

“Current state of play on VTAMPRT:

As feared the VSAM record locking does not hold up under TSO. We really do need shareoptions 3/4 as otherwise every user locks the whole file while they update. Ergo there are two lines of attack:

  1. Andy writes an assembler routine to book the record for us. This could use shareoptions-4 and then ENQ appropriately. I suspect that we would need a product called CALL/AP (from the same stable as AFM) to do this.

  2. Having booked the frame we then read it back to check that it hasn’t been double-booked. This adds a bit to the VSAM I/O, but is hardly significant as Andy is increasing the record length to 22K. Most prints (168 by 20 = 3360 lines) will fit on one frame anyway.

    The only worry is that each user will simply re-read a buffer, rather than the real record! As soon as Andy has set up a file I suggest we check this. The only way round might be to close/re-open the file . . . yuk!”

Diary: 28/10/85

“More on TSO and VTAMPRT . . .

It appears that with shareoptions-4 we can re-read the control record to check that we really have grabbed it. DJW & I did a quick check of the protocol on Friday, and it behaved as expected (as did shr-3 which simply re-read the buffer and is therefore quite useless). Essentially this is a ‘last-in first-served’ queue; hardly fair but quite effective!

I am now recoding a version of the APL side to fit in with this new protocol, and also to make use of the 22K record length (168 lines of print per record).

To do this efficiently I feel I need to change the way print data is buffered in APL (catenating to the end of a buffer this big could get very slow . . . the cost goes up as the square of the object size). I shall experiment with some alternatives and do a few timings . . . we should be able to cut a fair whack off the CPU cost of printing (as well as chopping the VSAM overhead by about 3/4) if we take a bit of care over the design.”

Diary: 29/10/85

“I think that we are home and dry with TSO/VTAMPRT.

Andy has written a little assembler command which books a frame number and returns the frame number it booked. This is able to queue sensibly on the records, and there is no possibility of a double-booking. It also simplifies the APL routines and seems rather faster. All the APL side now does is generate a random slot number (1 – 99) as the starting point for a sequential search for a free slot.

I don’t think that this is likely to lead to any more searching than the present strategy of trying all 99 slots at random. Apart from this very minor change the new routine is functionally equivalent to the old one. I shall now try some comparative timings of the two systems. I don’t expect to see any significant difference.”

Diary: 4/11/85

“The final timings on the new VTAMPRT for TSO suggest a reduction in CPU (as recorded by APL) to approx 70% of what it was. This is largely due to the 22K blocking, and only really shows up for files of 2000 lines or so. However the new booking arrangement does mean that even for small files (1 line) the new system is ahead (92% of the old).

I think we can safely put this one to bed.”

As you can see, the final solution (found after several blind alleys had been explored) was simple and effective. Because we could ‘book’ a slot on the file with a simple TSO command (the numeric return code suffices to get back the slot number) we could get away with AP100 as the assembler interface. Of course it was much easier for APL to generate the random starting point, so this is passed as a (formatted) number, along with the user number, date and time.

As an aside, I got caught out by the behaviour of ⎕RL when you start with too small a seed. Due to an attack of sloppiness I set the seed to ⎕TS[5 6] encoded to base 100. If you generate ?99 from this the maximum number you get varies from 5 to 48 depending on the number of minutes past the hour! Consequently users were getting dreadful response to print requests just after the hour, because the booking routine always started to search from the very low end of the file. Slots above 49 were never used, which is why the problem soon became painfully obvious!!
path: Case Study: VSPC – The Last Rites

items.title: Workspaces and Files
items.text:
One little note in the TSO-APL manual brought on a bad attack of fear. It pointed out that a system problem in the middle of a )SAVE would not only lose your immediate changes, but would by then have wiped the previous copy! This looked like a sure-fire way to lose a day’s work, and as true believers in Murphy’s Law we felt that we had to do something about it. The obvious line of attack was to use ‘Partitioned Datasets’ (PDSs), rather than simple sequential files, for workspace saving. These preserve the old version during a )SAVE, but have a nasty habit of filling up with old copies and needing compressing just when you don’t want to.

Once again an angel of mercy came to the rescue, in the unlikely guise of PDSMAN. This little wonder will reuse old slots and generally attempt to keep things tidy; it can’t always make full use of the space available, but at least the need for regular compresses is avoided.

Once we had bitten the bullet and patched APL to use our PDS libraries we began to think round our ‘ideal world’ solution to the whole area of project libraries and data sharing. What we needed was some set of conventions which would protect private data, but allow easy read access for crash recovery, and controlled write access for routine maintenance. In general we wanted to get away from our VSPC habit of logging on to other people’s IDs for routine updating.

The structure we settled on gave each TSO user two APL libraries:

APL.GLOBAL.AW002001     ... shared data for user 2001
APL.PRIVATE.AW002001    ... private data

In addition there are any number of ‘Project Libraries’:

APL.SHARED.AW100012     ... updated by anyone in (say) OR

. . . and of course public libraries which are updated only by a select band of initiates:

APL.PUBLIC.AW000020     ... Adrian’s utilities on )LIB 20

From an APL point of view, this works quite nicely once you get accustomed to the distinction between ‘)LIB’ and ‘)LIB 2001’; obviously you need to remember ‘)WSID 2001 MYWS’ if you want the fruits of your labours to be generally available. However it is a bonus over VSPC to have the command ‘)LIB 2012’ return the contents of someone else’s global library; again this saves one from logging on to the owner’s Id to find out what he called things! For the first time, we really don’t need to know each other’s passwords . . . this must be a good thing in the long term.
path: Case Study: VSPC – The Last Rites

items.title: The APL Session
items.text:
I felt that the VSPC Session Manager had been written by someone who used session managers; the TSO equivalent gives quite the opposite impression. It has that unwieldy feel which is so characteristic of ‘design from the outside’; it just doesn’t come comfortably to hand.

The only real bonus is the facility to queue a bunch of lines for re-execution. Particularly during the ‘peak’ of our conversion activity I found I was constantly going through ‘)LOAD this; )COPY that; )WSID the other; )SAVE’ routines; the session manager was very helpful in automating a lot of this.

Now for the gripes . . . the colours you can mitigate (by setting ‘Highlight Off’) or improve (by sneaking on to page 1001 and resetting them) to be quite acceptable. The behaviour on \<CLEAR> still seems inexcusable. To be faced with the rigmarole of \<RESET> \<PA2> and \<ENTER> to recover from a perfectly reasonable assumption (to clear the screen . . . press the key labelled ‘CLEAR’) is absurd. So far I have failed to find any way round this; closing and re-opening the GDDM device with a different ‘clear/PA1 protocol’ leaves you unable to interrupt APL loops. Has anyone else got any bright ideas??

Developing lines of APL ‘at the terminal’ is far less convenient under TSO. VSPC had a very handy \<Last> key which pulled back whatever you just did, for possible modification and re-execution (APL*PLUS/PC has the same thing). Under TSO you have to go and find the damn thing (it might be several screens back) or just give up and re-type it. Oddly enough you often want to repeat a line without changing it at all; to be forced into overtyping (say) blank with blank to get the line back . . . . well what can I say??

In summary the session screen would be improved out of all recognition with two extra facilities:

  • a ‘last command’ facility available via SM command or PFkey.
  • a ‘mark’ key to re-execute a line without the nonsensical modification.

IBM, are you listening?
path: Case Study: VSPC – The Last Rites

items.title: The Conversion
items.text:
TSO does have some nice things, one of the most useful being a sniffer-dog called ‘APL WSID’ which goes poking about in your workspace to find the time and date it was saved. Having discovered this, I did a bit of hacking and came up with the following:

Diary: 26/11/85

“To whom it may concern . . .

I am now in possession of a Trojan Horse routine which will copy into your workspace any utilities which are:

  • already there
  • are on the utility library with a saved date after the date when the workspace itself was saved.

I suggest we adopt this across the board as the latent exec, and will thus be saved all the hassle of recopying changed utilities under TSO”

This simple notion had the enormous benefit that we could ‘preset’ the conversion in existing workspaces. In systems where we needed to move around 20 users ‘simultaneously’ we just wouldn’t have had time to load up all the workspaces, make the changes and resave, in one weekend. All we now needed to do was (at leisure) to patch in AUTOEXEC and let the system cope with the upgrades. Wonderful. What’s more it really did go alright on the night! I think we had between 3 and 5 cases where someone had been ‘naughty’, and had changed a standard function without renaming it. I’m afraid we also had one example of a utility which was not (quite) upward compatible; it suddenly started returning 1-element vectors instead of scalars!! These minor snags apart, everyone carried on as if nothing had happened.

I had been quite right in seeing AFM as a major saving grace; in almost every case we were able to stick to the same user-number (VSPC 32670 became TSO PX32670=AFM 32670), so all those embedded user numbers:

'18750 BUDGET' GET 'VAR1,VAR2,....,etc'

. . . caused us no hassle at all! In general we had completed the AFM conversion several months before the final move to TSO, so it was literally a 5-minute batch run to copy over all the files for a set of target users. Apart from one spectacular cock-up when we accidentally deleted the entire TSO/AFM system, all went astonishingly smoothly.
path: Case Study: VSPC – The Last Rites

items.title: Postscript
items.text:
TSO is undoubtedly a more ‘powerful’ environment than VSPC. The easy access to batch, and the linkage to packages like ‘Focus’, are major improvements. It is also much less ‘protective’; the occasional splurge of red messages is bad enough, however it is quite possible to (say) ‘abend’ the session manager or get hung up somewhere between APL and SPF; in every case your only escape is to ring up and get thrown off the system! With a lot of work, we made TSO bearable; in the long term we may well be better off, but there is a lot of lost ground to make up.

I would like to conclude with two more diary entries, both slightly facetious:

Diary: 19/02/86

“In checking through the vector and image symbol editors I have come across a slight oddity in that my sheep have mysteriously turned green! This turns out to be a minor change in the use of the GSIMG command and is now OK. As far as I can see there is no problem in exporting VSPC-created symbol sets to TSO and building your own library of vector/image symbols.”

Diary: 10/03/86 (Reference VDU menu entry for TSO)

“Most of us tend to see TSOB as short for TSO – B

Most users tend to see it more in terms of T – SOB, which loosely translates as ‘That Son Of a Bitch’. Is this a good idea??”

1986 (May): Concluded
path: Case Study: VSPC – The Last Rites

All such letters should be addressed to the Editor and should indicate whether they are intended for the general or the technical section.
