“These have worn out my body,” the old man exclaimed, “But my brain has been nurtured for years And matrix inversions I’ll do in my head Any night, in the pub, for two beers.”

“What’s the secret old man?” said the boy, “I must know, For I want to be clever – please tell.” “It’s all in the Bible by Gilman and Rose,” Said the man, “and it’s called APL.”

“Tell me more,” said the boy, “of those days long ago.” “Very well,” said the man, “I’ll recall What happened way back in the year eighty-six That greatly affected us all.

“International meetings were held every year For the APL folks of the world: To UMIST in Manchester everyone went Where the welcoming flags were unfurled.

The Cocking and Drury consultants we heard Had suffered an alcohol ban So whenever they wanted a drink, all they’d got Was the lemonade stored in their van.

The conference opened – Ken Iverson spoke About ‘Core APL’ as a tool And for all of those present who didn’t agree He challenged them each to a dual.

There were two competitions the very next night, First a quiz, then a musical game. In a test of his knowledge (from an APL college) A student won prizes and fame.

The musical game had two teams of renown; Neil Mitchison led out the first. The second was captained by Jim Brown2 But in combat it came off the worst.

The Manchester weather is fickle, we know So umbrellas were given ’gainst rain. They could also be used if the weather was hot For keeping the sun off the brain.

Then on Wednesday night, with Bastille day in sight, All the French declared war on the rest. ’Twas their Boules team, with pride a formidable side, That took on and conquered our best.

Now at croquet we found many experts around With their mallets and hoops and skilled roquet. There was rumour that Adrian Smith planned to write A version of APL croquet.

Four teams were established: from STSC, I P Sharp, IBM and SigAPL To challenge each other in Trivial Pursuit And with APL questions to grapple.

At the banquet there were over five hundred guests. The dining room had extra staffing And the speaker we heard at the end of the meal Was the BCS boss, Bob McLaughing.

He poked fun at the Irish, the English and Scots, Raquel Welch and Dick Bowman as well. He described Irish Dartboards (pneumatic of course) And his oratory cast a fine spell.

Apart from the fun and the games I’ve recalled There was much more of interest to find. Both exhibits and papers were excellent stuff With which to encourage the mind.”

“Now I see,” said the youth, “what it is that you did To develop a mind that’s so sharp. So I’ll drink lemonade and I’ll learn how to play Concertina or flute or a harp.”

“And also young lad,” said the bearded old man, “If you want to stay youthful and handsome, Avoid all the women, the beer and the wine And talking to men like John Sansom.”

Then the old man sat back to reflect on the past, On the APL memories he kept. As the boy watched he smiled with a twinkling eye, Put his feet up and quietly slept.

The Old Goat!

[Photographs: two tables of delegates playing a quiz.] The ‘IPSA’ team are deep in thought as David Ziemann tries a tough APL question on them. A tough problem for the ‘STSC’ team.

‘Photographs by permission of Ed Cherlin, Editor APL News’
path: On the Lighter Moments of APL 86; Ode to APL 86

items.title: Papers I Enjoyed at APL86
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 69

by Roy Sykes, Jr.

Dave Ziemann asked me to write a review of APL86 with the above title, so I shall not dwell on other noteworthy or notworthy aspects of the conference. The APL86 committee should be congratulated on organizing and staging a well-run conference and producing an excellent programme and proceedings. In spite of culinary calamities, the hospitality was warm, the ale cool, and the content fulfilling.

Of the fifteen or so sessions and presentations I attended, all had at least some redeeming features. For some, it was merely that the speaker was awake; for others, it was a lively and engaging presentation of cogent and thoughtful ideas. I was fortunate in that my associate, Kyle, also attended most of these sessions with me. Given our propensity to avail ourselves of ale long after the formal sessions had ended, we found we needed spirited presentations just to stay awake. We were complementary: presentation style kept Kyle awake; technical content kept me awake. Unfortunately, we were sometimes fast asleep.

In his opening plenary speech ‘Core APL’ – misbilled as ‘The Split in APL’ – Ken Iverson reiterated his point of view regarding further developments in the language. Never one to be ambivalent, Ken argued forcefully for his ideas of operators and unified syntax and semantics, as contained in ‘A Dictionary of the APL Language’. A relaxed and well-prepared presentation, it nonetheless disappointed many attendees who had come to hear a sage and balanced view of the differences between APL2 and Sharp APL.

Stream 2 on Monday was disappointing, mainly for lack of adequate speaker preparation. Michael Berry’s presentation added nothing to that already contained in the APL86 Conference Proceedings, although his foils were of high quality. Roland Pesch (who also coauthored the Berry paper) gave a somewhat more stimulating talk on the use of ‘nil’ to solve problems associated with empty arrays in Sharp APL. Even in the absence of its implementation, nil rationalizes the treatment of empty frames in Sharp APL somewhat more smoothly than prototypes do in APL2. Nonetheless, IBM’s more complete implementation has yet to be matched by Sharp, and it remains the best working solution.

The content of David Landaeta’s paper ‘a notation for manipulating arrays of operations’, was controversial, particularly regarding his ideas of hyper-operators, which he calls ‘elevators’. Unfortunately, he escalated his talk well beyond its 1.5-hour limit, and, having spent the first half summarizing APL2, had little time to present and clarify his central thesis.

The proponents carried the day in the debate entitled ‘APL enhancements do not help the spread of APL.’ The opponents (Steve Schiavo and John Myrna) failed to adequately address the central issue of the long-term impact of major enhancements, and their smokescreen was blown away by the cogent arguments of the proponents (Richard Nabavi and Valerie Lusmore). It was a sad, if surprising, result that reflected the debating skills of the advocates. The debate had its amusing moments. When the audience was invited to voice its views, one member said “I have a question . . .” to which the chairman replied, “That’s out of order; questions are not allowed.” The attendee, not to be silenced, responded, “Well then, may I reformulate it as a statement?” eliciting a roar from the audience.

Another presentation of merit was Rob Hodgkinson’s report on the notable extensions contained in Sharp APL/HP. Rob gave a provocative and engaging talk on the DEL hyper-operator and its use to construct arrays of APL procedures. His excellent preparation and fluid delivery belied little of his initial nervousness in this, his first conference presentation.

The ever-smooth Jim Brown seemed pervasive at APL86, participating in no less than four sessions dealing with his favourite APL and its applicability to logic programming, multi-user applications, and AI, too. Always well-prepared, Jim’s talks are an optimistic portent of APL’s future direction and usage in state-of-the-art computing.

Another group of talks, given by Clark Wiedmann, Wei-Mee Ching, and others, dealt with the exciting topic of compiling APL. Once considered a remote prospect, at least one compiler (STSC’s) is now commercially available and others are in various stages of development. These papers illustrated dramatic gains in efficiency, in many cases rivaling the performance of traditionally compiled languages such as Fortran.

All in all, APL86 exhibited a bright view of APL’s future. The former insularity of the APL community seems to be giving way to an aggressive pursuit of solutions to the problems holding back APL’s wider acceptance. We hope that Dallas and Sydney will continue this trend.

items.title: General Correspondence
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

The VECTOR working group welcomes correspondence on any topic affecting the APL community. All such letters should be addressed to the Editor and should indicate whether they are intended for the general or technical section. Letters containing APL code will normally appear in the Technical section of VECTOR, and authors are asked to observe the requirements on the inclusion of APL code stated on the inside cover. The Editor reserves the right to edit any letter unless the writer states that the letter is to be published in full or not at all.

items.title: APL popularity
items.text:
From: C E Williams, 24th June 1986

Sir,

VECTOR frequently carries comments bewailing the lack of popularity of APL, and blaming the character set. Has anyone considered the equally plausible reason, the high cost of entry to APL for the home computer user?

MicroAPL alone appear to be taking effective action over this problem, but the QL/APL (at very reasonable cost) has too many hardware drawbacks – the atrocious keyboard, absence of roll-over, non-standard mass storage, and now the sell-out to Amstrad. The next entry point, the Atari, jumps to some £700 and hardware reliability appears to be suspect.

What is required, I believe, is inexpensive software on disc (perhaps bundled with BASIC on Amstrad and BBC machines in place of LOGO ?) for the 8-bit machines which far outnumber the 16-bit machines at the present time, giving the opportunity of much easier access to APL, and hopefully increasing its popularity.

There was such a subset of APL for the TRS80 Model 1, Level 11, called APL80, written by Phelps Gates and published in the USA by RAM software. It was advertised in the UK for £30 about 1980/81. If anyone knows whether this is still available, or where a copy may be obtained, it will be very much appreciated.

Yours faithfully,

C E Williams, [address omitted]

(Editor: As a parent, I have long felt that the combination of APL and LOGO would be a very good base to encourage children to appreciate the concepts behind computers, and would second your call for an inexpensive interpreter. I am sure we all applaud the plans for a public domain interpreter announced at APL86 – see elsewhere in the issue of VECTOR for details – and wish the brave volunteers every success in their venture.)

items.title: Porta-APL benchmark
items.text:
From: Mark Bassett, 25th June 1986

Sir,

In reviewing the APL68000 for the Macintosh, I think I may have found an error in the Porta-APL review (VECTOR, Vol 3, No 1). One of the benchmarks in the first set calculated should involve finding the tenth root of an integer vector. In fact your write calculated the square root, which is considerably easier by a factor of about three!

Yours sincerely,

M S Bassett, Metapraxis Ltd., Hanover House, Coombe Road, Kingston.

items.title: APL Blossom Time, and how to send money to Zeke Hoskin
items.text:
From: Zeke Hoskin, 26th May 1986

Sir,

The original “APL Blossom Time” was written by Mike Montalbano, under the pseudonym of J C L Guest. He brought it to the APL81 conference in San Francisco, and the APL Blossom Choir formed quite spontaneously to sing it at the banquet. (I was not in the damned choir, having come to the damned conference without my damned mandolin!) The lyrics were subsequently published in APL Quote Quad, probably early in 1982. The tune is lifted from a country song named “The Battle of New Orleans”, lyrics by Jimmy Driftwood, popular in around 1961. Driftwood in turn stole it from a fiddle tune named the Nth of January, N being somewhere between 11 and 14. The fiddle tune is probably originally Irish, as is fitting for a song about shooting the bloody British. (In the early-60s, reaction to the song forced somebody to write a pro-British war song called “Sink the Bismarck”, but this is a bit far afield.) I can send you the tune if you really want it.

At APL85 in Seattle, I asked the organisers who was running the APL Blossom Choir and they said, “You are.” Overwhelmed by the honour, I sat down at somebody’s Macintosh to make a set of overhead slides and added a verse and chorus of my own (to go before the original last verse and chorus).

Bob Smith and Bob Bernecky agreed to disagree. They knew they had to build a nest but couldn’t choose a tree. They took a thousand strands of code and wove them round and round, But one was at a NARS-ty height and one was on the ground. They both got arrays and hung them on the networks, And neither had a notion what the other one would do, And one was composed and one was pervasive, And meanwhile Jim Brown was writing APL2.

That is the only verse and chorus sung at APL85 that was not part of the Montalbano epic. I got Jim Brown’s and Bob Bernecky’s permission to publish it in Quote Quad, but was unable to get hold of Bob Smith or Mike Montalbano.

There are two riders: The APL85 version was a thousand “lines” of code, not “strands”. Also Bob Bernecky points out that “neither had a notion what the other one would do” is (of course) inaccurate. The dictates of meter preclude the more correct version:

“The APL Standards committee wished that they (Bob and Bob) wouldn’t do anything until they (the committee) decided what they (Bob and Bob) should do.”

Thank you for the 10 pounds. It was more than twenty Canadian dollars before the bank charged a dollar and a half for converting it. The same thing happens when I try to write a pounds money order to renew my membership in the BAA. Therefore should I happen to win and/or earn anything from VECTOR, please apply the pounds directly to my membership. I’d suggest including that as an option in future contests.

Have a nice APL86 . . . iota rho to Manchester but the C is too wide.

Yours more or less sincerely,

Zeke Hoskin, Control Z Software, [address omitted] Vancouver, B.C., Canada.

(Editor: Your letter probably passed VECTOR Vol 2, No 4, mid-Atlantic, so I expect that know by now that we can accept subscriptions in US dollars, and this may reduce your currency commission charges. As regards prize-money being off-set against next year’s subscription, I’m sure our treasurer will be delighted to receive advance payment whenever you win, but please make sure you repeat your request for this treatment on each competition entry, because the logistics of tracking a different procedure for each individual can become tortuous!)

items.title: A plea for help
items.text:
From: Joe McGrellis, 18th March 1986

Sir,

We are about to start a major development project based wholly on an IBM PC/AT. It will be developed using STSC’s APL*PLUS Application Development and will use as its kernel their STATGRAPHICS package. This letter is a plea for help.

What we need is a standalone device driver for the Hewlett-Packard HP7475A plotter which will allow us more freedom to expand our scope beyond STATGRAPHICS. We have a tentative promise of a new TOOLS workspace that may be available later this year, but our project can’t wait that long.

Being stranded out here in the APL desert, our only contact with the outside world is through VECTOR, but due to the vagaries of the Saudi postal service it can take up to 3 months before an issue of VECTOR is received. Perhaps you could throw my dilemma open to the wider APL community.

It is an excellent magazine, long may it continue, but perhaps a bit earlier to us out here in Saudi Arabia.

Yours sincerely,

Joe McGrellis, c/o Arabian-American Oil Company, P.O. Box 9712, Dhahran 31311, Saudi Arabia. Tel Saudi Arabia (3) 875-6940 (office) [home telephone number omitted]

(Editor: Thanks for your comments, and for your tact in blaming the irregular supply of VECTOR entirely on the Saudi postal service! I hope someone answers your plea.)

items.title: Polygon shading
items.text:
From: Clement Taylor, 12th May 1986

Sir,

For several months I have been searching for a suitable algorithm for shading polygons. I would be most grateful if any of your readers could provide an algorithm expressed as one or more APL functions to shade a simple polygon. I have a Sinclair QL computer with the MicroAPL APL.68000, and I have been playing around with a Tektronix 4661 flat-bed plotter. Using APL it is very easy to draw all sorts of mathematically definable shapes. I have never been able to figure out a workable method of shading the polygons which are being plotted.

On another note, I attended the recent Commodore show in London and I was very pleased to see that MicroAPL are planning an APL implementation for the new Amiga computer. I will be returning to the USA this summer and I am planning to purchase one for myself as soon as I am settled. I understand that in the States you can pick up an Amiga with a quality colour monitor, the plug-in 256k memory expansion and an external disk drive for $1300. An impartial source told me that at that price the Amiga was outselling the Atari by three to one. I also saw a two megabyte memory expansion for around $1000 (£599). The APL.68000 package will be pegged at under $300. To me this could mean real APL on a real personal computer for under $2600, a price about which APL devotees might do some serious thinking.

Yours faithfully,

Clement Taylor, Esher, Surrey.

(Editor: I know that Clement will have returned to the States before this letter is printed. Any readers who can provide a suitable algorithm should send it to myself. To add spice to the challenge, the last such algorithm I saw shaded any polygon, including re-entrant polygons, and drew alternate lines in the opposite directions in order to optimise plotting time. It was written by a sandwich student who knew no APL when he started his year’s industrial placement!

Our technical team have tracked down the following reference on this and closely related topics in the APL literature: Polygon clipping, Quote Quad 15,3 March 1985 (correction in Quote Quad 16,2 December 1985) Parallel shading of polygons, Quote Quad 13,4 & 16,1 September 1985) Hidden Plane Elimination and Surface Shading of Polygons Representing Buildings, Cornell & Julian, APL 81 Proceedings.)

items.title: A reader’s response
items.text:
From: Mr J Sullivan, 16th July 1986

Sir,

I couldn’t disagree more strongly with Mr Devaney’s letter in VECTOR Vol 3, No 1. I will answer his points in order:

(a) Management control: where do you draw the line between the costs of program development and the costs involved in insisting on proper management control? The facts that APL is hard to control and that most managers cannot understand it, are no reason for abandoning it when you calculate the costs of the alternatives. As an example I have just rewritten a badly-working and prone-to-failure PL/1 program in APL. The PL/1 program still didn’t work properly after six months’ solid work and was about 1000 lines long including all subroutines. The APL version works properly after half a day’s solid work (including designing it from scratch) and uses only 80-100 lines of code. This is not an isolated example.

According to Mr Devaney I should not be using APL because my management can’t control it; according to my management I should be using APL because it is very much cheaper and I can clear my applications backlog much more quickly. As for APL being ‘unable to support properly established libraries ...’, has he not heard of IP Sharp’s LOGOS? And if he can’t use LOGOS, can’t he design something similar but simpler, as we have in our environment?

(b) Unintelligibility. To whom? Has Mr Devaney never tried to decipher ‘typical’ FORTRAN code? I know that FORTRAN-77 is better for writing clearer structured code than FORTRAN-66, but not much, and that doesn’t help me try to understand some of the programs we have bought in from ‘reputable suppliers’ that are indecipherable. Rather than carry out maintenance on these programs, I convert them to APL, which makes further maintenance much easier. The point is that you can write unintelligible code in any programming language, so why single out APL?

(c) Lack of portability. ‘The only portability for APL that I know of is typing it all in again!’ (Mr Devaney’s exclamation mark.) I suggest that Mr Devaney does not know much about APL. An APL workspace is interpreter- and/or machine-dependent in much the same way that an executable program (load module) is machine-dependent. You would never dream of transferring a load module from one machine to another; you just transfer the source program and compile and link-edit it again on the new machine. So it is with APL; you put your functions in some kind of transfer file – via IBM’s )OUT command or something similar; (if your APL hasn’t got this command, write a function to simulate it – it’s easy. Then you transfer this file by magnetic tape and do the reverse process. If ⎕AV is incompatible, there is no problem; write a translate function.

(d) Closed, secure systems. Mr Devaney’s last paragraph is incomplete; the user can meddle with ANY program if he/she knows how to. What sort of security against intrusion is he after? Most mainframe manufacturers provide security which will protect anything – data, APL workspaces, etc. – against most prying eyes and fingers, but the most determined intruder will get you in the end. If you want to stop your users meddling with your APL functions, you should:

  • lock all the functions in the production workspaces (keeping the development versions unlocked);
  • error-trap your workspaces so that your users can’t get into ‘raw’ APL.

If you don’t know how to do these you’re not much of an APL programmer and I suggest that you contact one of our Sustaining Members for training!

Yours sincerely,

J Sullivan, Senior Research Officer, Statistics & Market Research, Business Development Division, National Westminster Bank plc., 41 Lothbury, London EC2P 2BP.

(Editor: John’s response is obviously deeply felt; indeed he was so quick off the mark that I think he is the first correspondent whose letter has reached us in time for inclusion in the next copy of VECTOR! I expect replies from other readers to Mr Devaney’s original letter in time for the January issue.)

items.title: APL86 Exhibition Report
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 71

by Martin Malin

APL in Action was the theme of the conference, and the exhibition demonstrated this in a striking way. The first thing that was immediately obvious from the exhibition was that never before has APL been in action on so many different machines in so many different forms. I counted 12 different makes (ie: manufacturers) of equipment with APL running within the exhibition. This excludes different models of machine from the same manufacturer and dial-up links to external mainframes, as well as the lengthy lists of other equipment supported displayed on several stands. APL has clearly joined the Age of the Micro in a big way! Similarly encouraging was the number of APL software products on display for use by both APL and non-APL users.

Another overall impression of the exhibition was the contrast with the conference sessions, in which APL2 and APL interpreter differences were so much to the fore. Even on the IBM stand the only mention of APL2 as such was the video featuring the familiar voice of the ubiquitous Jim Brown. Machines and operating systems supported, speed and power, software packages available and general support or ancilliary functions were emphasised everywhere, but little mention of language features as such was made. Indeed the sense was of a common enthusiasm for APL in general and a determination to see it yet more widely in action, although naturally each supplier was keen to emphasise their own particular contribution and the benefits of their particular products. The dominance of micros in the exhibition was also not reflected in the number of the conference papers relating to micros, though there were some excellent contributions.

The exhibition stands gave a pleasing impression of professionalism and thorough preparation. Those on the First Floor seemed to be better off being on the same floor as all the lecture theatres, and seemed generally better frequented. Most stands, though, were busy during breaks, and had a steady flow of people even during conference proceedings. I would think most of the exhibitors should have been satisfied with the flow of people to their stands.

So what of the stands themselves – what was there to be seen? To avoid offence I will describe them in stand number order.

Stand B1 on the Ground Floor was the bookstall, which was useful but unexciting, having mainly the familiar titles from the APL Book Service. Orders could be given, though, so it provided a useful opportunity to buy or order all those books that you had been meaning to get for ages but had never quite got round to ordering!

Next door Stand B2 was showing the Ampere micro, and seemed to be relatively quiet most of the time. The Ampere is distinguished by being the first (and only??) micro with APL as the standard language, and by having not ROM or tape or floppy disk access to programs and data, but all three! One or two external 3.5in. floppy disk drives are an optional extra and microcassette drive and ROM slots are standard. It also has communications facilities with a built-in autodial speaker phone and 300 baud modem. Like many lap-tops it suffers from a hard-to-read LCD screen, particularly under the direct glare of fluorescent lights as in the exhibition. It is an individual machine, both in looks and configuration and must now face serious competition from some of the more recent PC-compatible lap-tops.

I.P. Sharp Associates had Stand B3-B4, where the theme was the Global Information Centre concept, and the emphasis on the services, facilities and packages which Sharp’s offer. The latest of the software products is Logos, a powerful and interesting product for managing and administering application development and maintenance. A logical extension of the familiar function file (or “paging”) concept, Logos provides a variety of tools for developing code through a full-screen editor, documenting it and storing prior versions after editing, and assembling test or production workspaces from any combination of objects on the Logos files. It keeps track of the occurrences of every object and can disseminate updates, as well as documenting them. It is of value, therefore, to both the programmer and the manager in providing assistance to the former and control for the latter through the discipline and documentation it imposes. Viewpoint is the Sharp Information Centre product and a worthy, and more attractive, competitor for IBM’s Infocenter/1. The sad thing for non-Sharp users is that Sharp APL is a prerequisite for these products, and this plus the cost involved makes it a major strategic decision to make use of them. IPSA, of course, still has its extensive international network and timesharing facility, familiar packages such as Magic and Mabra and a vast range of numeric databases. There is also the Mailbox facility, and Sharp terminals were much in demand for reading the daily mail by the Sharp users present! It is a personal annoyance to me to hear so much talk of the wonders of Electronic Mail, particularly in relation to PC’s, when I was using Mailbox, with telex interface some 10 years ago! Whilst the IPSA private network is a different concept from a national service like Telecom Gold, I do feel that the impression given is that electronic mail is new, and we know differently, don’t we! Altogether the Sharp stand was effective in appearance and interesting in content.

The next 3 stands B5 to B7 were publicity stands for the British APL Association, our worthy hosts, ACM (Association of Computing Machinery), our worthy sponsers, and APL87, our willing hosts next time in Dallas! The call for papers was going out from the APL87 stand, but although without a stand the organisers of APL88 in Sydney were doing their best, with glossy brochures and newsletter registration, to upstage even the Texans – no mean feat!

IBM occupied spacious accommodation on Stand B8-11, with the latest releases of PC APL and Application Prototyping Environment (APE) and Infocenter/1 (IC/1) the main products on display. The new release of PC APL seems to be a big improvement over the original one, and now perhaps compares with APL*PLUS/PC, but it may be too late to recover much of the market which seems to have gone largely to the latter up to now. Infocenter/1 is IBM’s main Information Centre product, and is based around former products ADRS2, ADI and FPS coupled with, under APL2, the interface to SQL. With full-screen front-end encompassing all these facilities as well as graphics, it is an obvious and useful progression for former users of one or more of the previous products. It is also a good front-end for those wishing to make extensive use of the SQL interface. The list of prerequisite software includes APE, whose new release is available exclusively in APL2, the first IBM product in this area not to support VSAPL. APE is an application development tool, providing extensive facilities for screen design, graphics and query building. For relatively simple applications it provides a good range of utilities, though at the cost, as with IC/1, of considerable software cost and processing overhead. Of minority interest, but doubtless exciting to those directly affected, IBM were also showing an implementation of Japanese APL – who says APL symbols are hard to read! Generally a smart, professional but unexciting display overall.

The final stand on the Ground Floor was APL People at B12. The APL People stand had on display, well, what do you expect, PEOPLE! Very friendly and helpful people, and a definite place to stop if your problem was not hardware to use or APL to run on it but fingers to go on the keyboard. As well as APL recruitment and consultancy services, APL People are now agents for Interprocess, who supply the AFM shared file software and other enhancements to VSAPL. They also have several vertical market specialist interests. So there was little to see on this stand, but if your needs were manpower or advice it could have been a valuable stop.

On the busier First Floor the first stand was MicroAPL. Now the full owners of the APL.68000 interpreter MicroAPL are busy porting it to a number of popular 68000 machines, including the Macintosh, Atari ST and Commodore Amiga. With APL already on the QL, it certainly won’t be MicroAPL’s fault if APL does not start to reach a wider ’home’ audience, particularly with their enthusiastic support for the WIMP environment (apologies to the gentleman who was offended by the use of this term which he felt denigrated some excellent tools!). (Ed: Windows, Icons, Mice, Pop-up menus). The problem for them, and APL in general, must be how to create the awareness of and demand for APL in a new market area. The main strength of MicroAPL still lies, however, in the business area. As well as possible sales with the above machines, their main products are the Spectrum and new Aurora machines with APL.68000 under the Mirage operating system. The Aurora is certainly impressive in performance, with the possibility of multiple 68020 32-bit processors and a 68000 chip controlling the disk drives. MicroAPL are also branching out into consultancy and promoting the Integrated APL Strategy concept involving not just their own hardware but a variety of software modules to run with a range of configurations. Though slightly out of the mainstream of IBM mainframe or PC compatible APL implementation, MicroAPL offer an impressively functional and powerful option for many situations.

Next to MicroAPL on stands C4-C6 was Cocking and Drury, placing emphasis on their role as software suppliers rather than their their traditional strength of consultancy. Cocking and Drury now form the sole UK distributors of STSC mainframe products, including APL*PLUS, and the European support for them. They also supply all the STSC PC products, including the new product releases which were announced at the conference. These include release 6 of APL*PLUS/PC, with the object size limitation of 64K finally removed without performance degradation for arrays less than 64K, it was stated. Also announced was release 3 of APL*PLUS/UNX and version 2 of Statgraphics. Statgraphics is an excellent example of the software packages in APL mentioned earlier. With the boost of a highly favourable review in a major PC magazine it has become a highly visible and accepted PC product in a market much wider than just APL specialists. To the average PC user its APL origin is irrelevant, but at the same time it provides an extra dimension for the experienced APL’er. Another interesting new release in the PC Tools range was the Spreadsheet Manager, which provides a simple APL spreadsheet environment, but more importantly can read and write Lotus files for creation or manipulation in APL*PLUS/PC. this provides valuable integration between APL and spreadsheet applications. The stand had an impressive variety of IBM compatible micro hardware, with demonstrations available of all the products being promoted. There was, of course, also details of the consultancy and training services offered by Cocking and Drury available. It was an attractive and busy stand, and well staffed with helpful and knowledgeable people.

Just opposite at C7 was Mercia Software, who also supply STSC micro products as well as a number of mainframe APL products. The mainframe products include Execucalc/Execuplot spreadsheet/graphics package and Infocentre, a competitor of the similarly named IBM product and Sharp’s Viewpoint. All run in either VSAPL or APL*PLUS. The STSC PC products were on display, including Statgraphics and APL*PLUS/PC, plus the EXEC*U*STAT graphics package. The latter has strong similarities with Statgraphics, but with emphasis on the general business rather than highly statistical user. It has a simplified front-end, along with extras such as diary and calculator, but with some of the statistical functions missing. A good product which fills a gap between a very simple business graphics packages and an advanced statistical package like Statgraphics. Most interesting of all on their stand was the low-cost multi-user and networking software Multilink and LANlink. Multilink will allow an AT or compatible to become a multi-user machine supporting 3 users for around the cost of an additional PC, including two terminals, with a theoretical limit of 9 users. The LANlink product has similar software to allow PC’s to be networked without network cards by using RS232 connections via serial ports. Both have the speed limitations one would expect from such low-cost solutions, but if they fit your particular requirements the price/performance could be very attractive. Mercia also provided details of their training and consultancy services from their small but business-like stand. They also provided a valuable service at the end of the week in matching badge numbers for the STSC competition!

Next in line was the Dyadic Systems stand C8-C9 featuring Dyalog APL. Perhaps the most significant comment on Dyalog was the popularity of the kit on this stand for solving the conference competitions! It may not be what it was there for, but it must say something about both the interpreter and the harware on display that it was so heavily used. Dyalog is without doubt the closest to APL2 of other “enhanced” APL’s, which must be added attraction for users into Unix in a big way. As well as a number of APL2 features, Dyalog has some interesting aspects of its own, such as “external variables”. There was also a good deal of technical interest, with Dyalog running on the IBM 6150 (PC/RT) RISC machine in the hospitality suite upstairs. This machine could be the one to bring wider acceptance for both Unix and Dyalog APL, bearing the magic blue letters as it does. On the stand the Sun micro was in use, which both Dyadic and STSC spoke very highly of for sheer performance. There was also the Dyalog APL co-processor, based on the Opus532 Personal Mainframe board which has a 32-bit NS32000 processor. It provides a full Unix V/Dyalog implementation on an expansion board for IBM PC’s and compatibles, with PC- DOS/MS-DOS interface and again opens a potentially fruitful market. For sheer technical interest this good-looking stand was hard to beat, though Dyalog’s fortunes are clearly intimately tied up with those of Unix in general and thus currently, in the UK at least, are linked to something of a specialist market.

Even more specialist was the APL Machine from Analogic on their stand. Featuring enormous power from its array processing architecture, it has considerable attraction for CPU intensive applications. Unfortunately the stand was usually unattended in the latter part of the week, and I was unable to see the machine in action. It is clearly of interest only for specific applications areas, but within those areas must be hard to match for performance.

The centre of the floor was taken up by STSC with stands C11-C20. They were showing all of the products and new releases announced as mentioned above, and had additional booths for their UK and French distributors Cocking and Drury and Uniware. They also had APL*PLUS on the Macintosh, in competition with MicroAPL. APL*PLUS/UNX was running on a Sun micro, as was Dyalog on the Dyadic stand, and the seriousness with which STSC take the competition from Dyalog in the Unix area can be judged by their attempt to tempt users of “other” Unix APLs with a 25% rebate offer for “trade-ins”. MicroAPL also offer APL under Unix, of course, but their emphasis is more on the Mirage or proprietary operating systems. Most encouraging for the spread of APL in general was evidence of STSC’s vigorous activity in the educational area and their software publishing scheme. The stand was smart and spacious, but most of the products have been described elsewhere so there is not a lot to say about it.

Although not part of the the exhibition on the two main floors, mention must also be made of the Merlin spreadsheet package on display from Butel on the second floor. This is a spreadsheet written in APL to be run in VSAPL on a mainframe or on a PC using a run-time version of APL*PLUS/PC. Whilst having a rather different appearance to the traditional spreadsheet packages it is nevertheless a genuine competitor for them in terms of function and ease of use even for a non-APL’er. As with other APL packages the possibility of calling user-defined functions further increases its flexibility in the hands of someone who does know APL. The screen handling is cleverly structured such that it is virtually identical on the PC to the mainframe without seeming to sacrifice too much of the superior screen handling generally available on the micro. The reporting parameters allow much better reports to be created than from most spreadsheets. Like Statgraphics in the graphics area this product is a worthy competitor for established packages in its own right, and for APL’ers has the added attraction of access to APL. The mainframe version also has now or under development links to a number of the most popular database products. It was a shame that this demonstration was hidden away upstairs and not classified as part of the exhibition proper.

So there you have a quick tour of the APL86 exhibition. I hope it brings back (accurate) memories for those who were there and gives those who weren’t an idea of what they missed!.

items.title: Pick of the Week
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 77

by Adrian Smith

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
This little rag-bag of odds and ends is my attempt to convey some of the excitement and sheer fun that we all had at APL-86. I shall draw a decent veil over the exploding Real Ale, the midnight Croquet, and the extraordinary level of design skill applied to the paper aeroplanes at the conference dinner. Suffice it to say that the general intellectual standard at APL86 made your average gathering of academics look like the autumn meeting of the Beano Readers Association.

Many of the papers were tough going; at the end you thought to yourself “I had to work pretty hard, but I think I got some of that”; then you realised that everyone else was thinking much the same! It made me very proud to be a member of such company.

Now for some of the lighter moments – first a selection of my favourite quotes (I’m afraid that many of these are on tape, so the perpetrators would do well to think twice before they commence legal proceedings!):

From the opening plenary:

“I’m grateful they didn’t call it APL” Ken Iverson on APL2.

From ‘APL2 by Example’:

“The trouble with APL2 is that you take 10 minutes writing the code, and then spend the rest of the afternoon telling your colleagues about it”

“CPU time – if you don’t use it now it’s gone for ever” Alan Graham

From the panel on implementations of new APLs:

“We’re building interfaces to IBM acronyms that I really don’t know what they are”

“We’ve got to be able to drive mice, and all those other little critturs that run around.” Bob Bernecky.

“Brackets are the cockroaches of APL; have some respect for them, because they’ll probably outlive mankind.” Adin Falkoff (under extreme provocation).

From the first debate (on the effect of enhancements on the spread of APL):

“The ‘old’ APL is the most fantastic, amazing product the computing world hasn’t seen”

“APL2 was a conspiracy to stop the spread of APL(!)”

“We’re not getting new customers from APL2 – just confusing the old ones” Richard Nabavi.

From the panel on APL thinking:

“Encode is something you use when you give change” Norman Thomson on APL thinking.

“If you disagree with Alan, it’s like standing at the wrong end of a cannon” Norman Thomson on Alan Graham

items.title: Mexican Snacks at Dyalog APL
items.text:
There was almost a surfeit of APL2 at this conference. I don’t know quite why, but APL2 bothers me a lot; the odd thing is that Dyalog APL looks far more attractive, and I can’t for the life of me see why! Having greatly enjoyed Alan Graham’s “APL2 by Example”, I had still come away with no lasting impression other than that of his extreme cleverness and showmanship. What I certainly did not get was a clear vision of where I could really use APL2 to get my job done better.

That basically means using APL to develop and (much more important) maintain and enhance complex screen-based systems over a wide variety of applications. No-one has yet had to maintain a system in APL2; if they are even half as clever as Alan, I think they could be in dead trouble! Which brings me by a round-about way to the point; the only person at the entire conference who significantly helped me along the APL2 road was John Scholes at Dyalog’s unscheduled “Fringe”.

Of course it was marvellous to escape from conference food, if only for an hour or so, but I cannot credit this as the sole explanation. Much more likely is the fact that Dyalog has been developed by a small team (essentially two people) who actually use APL. Contrast this with APL2, which has been brought about through the enforced union of two APL development groups with very different views on the future of the language. John Scholes could talk convincingly about the value of “Compose” because he knew why he wanted it, and because he was the one who wrote it!

He could demonstrate the power of ideas like “Function assignment”:

TOTAL <- +/
TOTAL 1 2 3 4

. . . because he was the one who had wanted it enough to go to the trouble of inventing it! That is the same kind of motivation that Ken Iverson felt when he first sketched out the ideas of APL; I think that is probably why Dyalog APL feels ‘right’, and why I so much enjoyed those early-evening talks.

items.title: The Debates
items.text:
We had two ‘formal’ debates at APL-86; the first acceeded to the view that enhancements to APL do nothing to help the spread of the language, and the second threw out the conjecture that APL is not (yet) a suitable language for Artificial Intelligence. For me, these ranked alongside the panel discussions as events where the rank and file of the APL world could make its views known. There is always a danger at such a prestigious international gathering that the platform will be dominated by the same circuit of ‘names’ year after year, and we ordinary folk will never get the chance to say our bit.

The glory of the debating format is that it positively encourages the outrageous, the controversial, the hyperbolic. You can jump up and say something totally ridiculous, and as long as it ‘scores’ off someone you will very likely get away with it. In the first debate, the floor (and the principals) were to some extent feeling their way; by the end of the second it was beginning to warm up nicely. I hope the committee of APL-87 will take note, and somehow find room for this (very British) tradition in their program. Perhaps a ‘Balloon Debate’ on APL enhancements would be a revealing occassion?

items.title: Postscript
items.text: If you can stand the pace, stay awake, hold your own in the bar, and (at times) work damned hard, APL conferences are a lot of fun. This was my first, I doubt if I will make Dallas, but of course it’s always in Europe in the even years, isn’t it? See you all in ’88.

items.title: APL86 Fun and Games
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 80

by Aelred Tobin

After Monday dinner the hall settled down in anticipation of Dave Ziemann’s games evening.

An APL multiple-choice knockout quiz was first on the agenda – the APL Superquiz. A question was posed, and 4 possible answers given. We had to indicate our choice of answer by standing by one of the appropriately labelled pillars in the hall. Only those with the correct answer being allowed to continue to the next question.

The questions started off ‘straight’ eg. “Is the result of executing the matrix inverse of 2 a RANK ERROR, 0.5, 1 or 2?” (0.5) and “How many characters are therein the shortest possible VS APL expression producing an INDEX ERROR: 2,3,4 or 5?” (5). They soon degenerated to the likes of “Does the ‘E’ in Kenneth E Iverson stand for Eugene, Eustace, Eric or Edward?” (Eugene), and “Was the song APL Blossom Time first performed at APL81, APL82, APL83 or APL85?” (APL81).

It didn’t take long to reduce the assembled to a few inseparable stalwarts following the first person who looked like they actually knew the answer. (I wonder what would have happened if they chose the wrong answer?). A few cunning questions finally broke their resolve however, and the IPSA and Cocking and Drury donated prizes of a Sharp APL PC interpreter and a Pocket APL interpreter were won by Fergal Golding and Jim Brown – two APL86 stewards with little knowledge of APL. So much for the experts!

Dave then added a little spice to the next days debate by calling upon the principal protaganists: Jim Brown(the APL2 one) and Neil Mitchison, to each captain a team for ‘APL Name That Tune’. Each team was supplied with an identical set of APL symbols on pieces of cardboard. A snatch of music was played – something with a reference to APL in the title or artiste’s name, and the first team to hold aloft the appropriate APL symbol gained the points.

It all appeared simple until, when faced with a right arrow symbol for instance, you realise that it could represent TAKE, DROP, ARROW, GOTO, BRANCH, ASSIGN, IS, GETS or FIRST. Not only had the contestants to listen for many key words, but horrible puns were also allowed, eg. Cracklin’ Rose by Neil Diamond (RHO and DIAMOND). Overstrikes were also permitted, so both quad and divide had to be held up for the Fats Domino song!

The choice of music was deliberately catholic eg ‘Bolero’ by Ravel (,), ‘Della and the Dealer’ by Hoyt Axton (DEL, AND and QUESTION MARK) and for a truly international flavour ‘Waltzing Mathilda’ (TILDE) and ‘Wunderbar’ (W).

Neil’s team seemed to always have the edge, though Jim Brown never gave up – at one stage holding up all their cards at once in a sort of APL Name That Tune system crash. Neil’s team never lost the lead, but graciously shared the prize of 3 bottles of champagne (donated by Inner Product Ltd), with the losing team. One-nil to Neil, but who would win the AI debate?

The organised hilarity at an end, ’twas time to repair to the bar.

items.title: Report on the Plenary Panel Session at APL 86
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 81

by Anthony Camacho

“The Differences Between Implementations of Enhanced APLs”

Jim Brown was given the largest round of applause of the whole conference when he said “I want to go on record today as saying that I’m also convinced that Ken [Iverson] is correct in his direction for extending APL”. When the applause died down he continued by asking us not to jump to conclusions: there is more than one correct way to extend APL “and all it means is that different reasonable people that have different objectives in mind can come to different correct conclusions . . .”.

The full transcript of the session took seventeen pages: I will therefore summarise drastically to leave room in Vector for other things. Please forgive me if I leave your question out or misrepresent what you said: I’m sure the editor will be glad to publish your comments.

Jim Brown offered to talk about nested arrays (and the reason why an enclosed scalar was still a scalar), vector notation (and to maintain that there is no function left out between the elements of it), and to explain brackets (which people complain are neither function nor array nor operator).

The fundamental change that APL2 makes is to extend greatly the extent to which the shape of the data can control the work that functions and derived functions will do. There is no need to learn all the rules. Nearly always the simple view of the way things will work is correct; for the occasions when it isn’t it’s probably simpler to insert brackets than to go into the theory of the syntax which explains why. But there is a unified theory, thanks to Phil Benkard, and it is correct. If the brackets are occasinally redundant, who cares?

John Scholes said that Dyadic’s objective was to enhance APL to make it more useful for writing commercial systems by adding error trapping, component files, commercial format, and a wide variety of system functions. Unix was chosen as the operating system because they foresaw its growth in popularity. Dyalog APL has floating arrays like APL2 and is written in C for portability. It has an excellent UNIX interface so programs written in C can be taken into an APL workspace and called just as if they were locked functions. All the features of UNIX are available from within APL. The design of Dyalog APL closely follows STSC’s NARS and John gave credit to Bob Smith “Most of the ideas in there are Bob’s”.

James Wheeler said that the correct origin of NARS is Nested Arrays Research System. From 1979 it was used as a test bed for new language design ideas. In 1982 STSC had chosen the enhancements that had proved most effective in the eyes of the APL community and these are now part of the APL*PLUS/1000 product. STSC also realised that APL needed to be enhanced in other ways to make it easy to use; it needed better editors a user interface with screen control and it needed ways to overcome speed limitations. These are the aims which have guided the people producing implementations on micros and the APL compiler.

James felt that the great debate about axiom systems is over and that the positions taken by the major vendors are now fixed. The set of all possible arrays in APL*PLUS/1000, Dyalog and APL2 is now the same. STSC do not yet have defined operators, selective specification and a few of the less frequently used new primitives. The great range of system functions has made shared variables unnecessary and there are some features that STSC have which APL2 lacks. One he recommended for Jim Brown’s attention is the partitioned enclose which has proved very popular with the users. There are some differences in the way bracket indexing works that ultimately he would need to settle with Jim. In short there are some differences still but STSC is converging with APL2.

Luan Thompson explained that although he has been working in machine code on the Motorola 68000 for some years and with APL for four years, MicroAPL only took control over the 68000 interpreter six months ago and have spent the time since mainly in optimisations for speed. As the interpreter is written in machine code its natural targets among small machines are the QL, Atari, Macintosh and Amiga. On enhancements MicroAPL feel that there is already a dominant vendor in the APL market and that they are not going to try to buck the trend. There are already a few features such as dyadic grade in the interpreter and there are hidden features in it which they believe will be able to handle nested arrays, although these are not at present available to the user. Luan said he believed that the enhancements to user and system interfaces would probably be more important than enhancements to the language. APL competes in a market where BASIC, Pascal, C, and FORTRAN all have multi-window WIMPS (window, ikon, mouse and pop-up menu) interfaces and better editing and error control. MicroAPL will enable programmers to write WIMPS applications which nobody can tell use APL. The main problem is that these features are different on every machine which makes it a lot of work, but MicroAPL think it is worth while to make life easier for the programmer.

Bob Bernecky said that the Sharp philosophy is to make enhancements simple, consistent and general. The more complexity the harder it is to teach and learn and use (and complexity also affects the implementations). Bob too would like to see APL2 and Sharp APL converge and suggested that STSC and IBM might like to consider ‘link’ and ‘rank’ which would help them converge.

Link does the same as strand notation (Bob asserted that strand notation complicates syntax analysis) but because it is a function you can apply an operator to it. With the rank operator you can link say matrices or vectors from two arrays. There’s no obvious way to do that in APL2 because there’s no function for an operator to work on. [Alan Graham interjected that one of his idioms did the trick.]

The benefit of the rank operator is apparent when you look at the bracket axis notation it replaces. In APL2 bracket axis gives rise to many special cases; the definition of ravel takes several pages because of the different ways that things in brackets can affect it. When Ken Iverson and Arthur Whitney proposed the rank operator Sharp realised that brackets had been inconsistent from the beginning; caentate laminate, rotate, reduction all are affected by brackets in different ways and each has to be learned separately. The rank operator replaces the bracket axis notation and applies identically to all functions, even user defined functions. Furthermore if the rank operator is made more efficient it will make every function that uses it more efficient, whereas the brackets would have to be improved one use with one function at a time.

Consistency brings benefits; Sharp had a minor but uninteresting enhancement to take or drop – if the argument shape was a scalar or one element vector and less than the rank of the right argument then the result has a shape of the same rank, defined by the left argument catenated onto the remaining shape of the right argument. So if EH > 2 3 4 5ρ of something then the shape of a 6 ↑ EH is 6 3 4 5. Combined with the rank operator this can be made to yield results of shape 2 6 4 5, 2 3 6 5 and 2 3 4 6 as well. So you start to see some synergy between the enhancements and the ISO APL.

Sharp is trying to put APL back into the mainstream of data processing and this won’t be done by language enhancement but by improving the environment. Sharp are providing a consistent interface which will allow any language to drive APL or an APL function to drive programs written in any language. They are also building special purpose interfaces to all manner of peripheral equipment and a network shared variable processor which enables a user to share a variable with a user in another city or with a PC and it still looks just like a variable in the program.

A lot of Sharp’s work has been to improve large applications with hundreds of users so that the work bring benefit to many people. Now they have signed a co-operation agreement with STSC and hope that this will enable them to do more in the micro field. Bob would like to see ⎕FX < ⎕prime < ⎕CR \<function name> allowing you to edit a function using the operating system’s full screen editing and agreed that the latest things like WIMPS had to be available with microcomputer APLs.

Philip Goacher then called for questions; below is a brief summary of the main discussion.

Alan Graham endorsed the rank operator: when he first heard of it he put it into his workspace as a defined operator and nowadays even has it defined with its own symbol so that he doesn’t have to begin every new workspace with )COPY UTILITIES RANK. He has set his students the exercise of writing all the Iverson operators in APL2 and although there are one or two tricky ones he believes he has correct versions of all of them. Anthony Camacho asked whether he would circulate his code, saying “Send it to Vector and we’ll publish it” and Alan replied “I’ll do that”. He also said that he very much regretted brackets and wished that the fathers of APL had never put them in. Bob interjected that the rank operator made brackets redundant.

This exchange stimulated Adin Falkoff to come to the stage to defend brackets. While he was trying to get enough ink out of a dead pen to put his name on the overhead projector he was asked whether he originated the acronym APL. He confirmed that it was his idea. Adin maintains that there is a good use for bracket-semicolon notation and that is to pass multiple arguments explicitly. He too endorses the rank operator and doesn’t wish to defend every use of brackets. By passing arguments explicitly you avoid having to box things together which have a merely contingent association and also avoid having to unpack them inside the function before using them. You can also leave out an argument between two semicolons with the same meaning as in ambivalent functions. He seriously recommended this extension as consistent with all implementations.

Jon McGrew, speaking personally and not for IBM, thought that we were now stuck with brackets, which people find convenient and easy to learn. Jim Lucas questioned the notion that the divergence in APL was a bad thing; progress is achieved by experimentation and competition and perhaps APL will get superseded by a language which will not have to carry on old mistakes as APL has to.

Neil Mitchison disagreed with Jim Lucas, and felt pessimistic about APL’s chances of wide acceptance if it continued to diverge. He asked what the panel thought should be the role of the ISO in this. Should they create a compromise standard which went over to one side for some things and to the other for others? Jim Brown said that he felt that the Standards Committee were right not to put files into the standard because there wasn’t enough agreement about their form and he would like to see the standards committee sticking to the description of agreed usage. There are wide areas of this; everyone has the same definition of dyadic upgrade and of complex numbers and of replicate. Neil was not satisfied with this and asked what should be done about features where there was no agreement and the versions were incompatible. Jim’s answer in effect was that those features should be left out of the standard.

Anthony Camacho asked about the size of the interpreters, saying that he wanted to run APL on microcomputers small enough to take into school or give to children to use at home and that the size of the interpreter determined how far down the market it could spread. James Wheeler said that the size depended on the machine. The STSC interpreter is written in C and when compiled varies from about 200,000 bytes on a Vax to about 400,000 bytes on the PC; unfortunately larger on the machine where less space can be afforded. He looked forward to cheaper machines with larger memories which would allow enhanced APLs to be run in schools. Luan Thompson said MicroAPL is about 95,000 bytes varying by plus or minus 10,000 bytes according to machine, and that there will be four megabyte memories available before you can blink. Bob Bernecky said that the Sharp PC interpreter was essentially the same as the mainframe version but even with all the bells and whistles it only took 400,000 bytes. He reckoned that each 30 months the capacity of chips was quadrupling and agreed that long term there was no problem about memory size. When prodded by Adin Falkoff he said that the naked interpreter was about 250,000 bytes. John Scholes said that Dyalog APL is also written in C and also varies. Originally (on the Z8000) it was 200,000 bytes with all the frills then available. The decision on enhancements is always to take more space to gain speed and the current version, on say a Stride 68000 based machine, is 400,000 bytes. Jim Brown asked David Selby what the size of the PC APL was and David said 70,000 plus the auxiliary processors. A quite adequate set can be put together and run in a 256K machine. David added that he didn’t agree with the ’memory will be cheap’ argument, saying that we should not expect the user to pour hardware in.

Chris Brady wanted APL to be less greedy of mainframe capacity: his employer seemed likely to cut its APL workforce because of this effect. He also asked when he could see code, variables, the stack and the state of the filing system all on the screen at once. Luan Thompson replied “As soon as I’ve finished the version for the Atari: that is exactly what I’m working on”.

Linda Alvord returned to the problem of getting APL into schools. Her main point was that education authorities and heads of school departments who might consider APL will be put off by the choice of versions since they did not have either an International Standard or any agreed consensus to guide them. If you go to a supplier and say ’I want to buy a standard APL’ nobody has one for sale. Everybody tries to sell you the special advantages of their own version and the consequence is that people decide to wait until the question is settled by another mechanism. She felt that there should be a standard APL which everyone could buy safely and that the enhancements were not of much value in secondary schools. These comments brought a big round of applause. Roy Sykes called out that the ISO Standard version should be available for forty five bucks and that was obviously accepted by general acclamation too.

Comment by reporter:

Philip Benkard called attention to the great applause for Jim Brown’s opening remarks and I would like to do so again.

It shows the strength of feeling in the APL community that regrets the differences between enhanced APLs and wishes to see all APLs converge.

APL used to have the advantage that you could write and test programs on a microcomputer, benefiting from micro editor and response time, and then download the program to a mainframe. Nowadays it would take great self discipline to stick to ISO APL and even that would not work with APL2. And it would take great dedication and unusual opportunity to get to be at home in all versions of APL.

This diversity is not in the APL user or programmers interest. It arises because each vendor wants to offer something better than the others and which, if possible, commits their customer to them.

I believe a powerful alliance of users could and should apply pressure on vendors to converge and perhaps this could be done by persuading the ISO to set a standard for enhanced APL which does exactly what Neil Mitchison suggests above.

Anthony Camacho 2 August 1986

There follows a short collection of interesting quotes heard at APL86. My apologies to those concerned if any distortions have crept in – they are purely unintentional.

“I can’t remember if it’s encode or decode . . . . .” – APL86 speaker, followed by this comment from the audience: “Neither can we . . .”

“There’s only one thing worse than an APL bigot – an APL bigot who works in zero-origin” – Alan Graham, prior to displaying his zero-origin APL2 code.

“I don’t care how much CPU it takes – if you don’t use the CPU time now it’s gone forever” – Alan Graham.

“Scientists have discovered the missing link between Neanderthal man and intelligent man – it’s us” – Jim Brown, in his lecture on APL2 and A.I.

“If this APL thing is so good why isn’t it in my car?” – Roy Sykes’s mother, as quoted by Roy in his closing speech.

items.title: Thoughts on APL design
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 87

by Bob Pullman

There are many facets to the design of an application. As far as APL is concerned there have been many papers and even texts that concern system design. My feeling is that although some of these works are excellent, there has not been enough published on design, and that most of the existing works are hard to find.

I think that the novice applications programmer is particularly hard up in this regard. Even someone who has a couple of years’ experience of APL programming, in university perhaps, is ill-prepared to tackle an applications project. I can recall, for instance, a programmer who asked me plaintively:

“How do I write an application? What do I do to get started?”

Perhaps this fellow was not the self-starter type, but he was certainly bright (he is in fact a lawyer now) and had both a computer science degree and a solid understanding of APL. He had read several texts on APL (Gilman & Rose, Peelle, and others) and was comfortable with NARS (APL2). Just the same he was at a complete loss for what to do.

This predicament, given his background, supports the assertion that APL literature is inadequate, that it is missing critical topics in the general area of applications programming. There is a wealth of papers on particular applications, but these are rarely of much use. Some present algorithms but very, very few reflect the sequence of steps in which the application was actually done.

There is a school of thought which believes that there is no substitute for experience. This school might be called the “experientialists”. The radical wing of this school believes that one should just plunge in, experiment and learn by trial and error. Some believe that this is the way to learn APL to begin with. I would say that it is suitable for a rather small minority, and even for such types it is not necessarily the most expedient approach. One does not learn physics by experiment alone, so why should APL be any different?

On the other hand, experience is the best teacher. There is nothing that can substitute for real-world problems. One only learns by facing new problems. My point is that the learning time could be shortened if the novice had supportive material to study and refer to during the learning phase.

The questions are what sorts of material should be used, and for how long. It’s easier to answer the second. Learning time is infinite, although the percentage of learning time in a project will eventually become quite small. The answer to the first question is more elaborate and I cannot claim in any sense to give it fully. I only hope to open up what has been neglected by the literature so far. The most suitable medium would be an anthology on design, combining several different approaches, even contradictory ones.

If such an anthology were published, it would serve a very useful purpose. It would make APL applications programming more accessible. It might blur the distinction between end-user and applications programmer. It certainly would help to increase the popularity of APL, even perhaps to make APL “the people’s choice”.

Much has been said and done about the problem of making APL more popular. I would guess that there have already been some who have cited education as one of the ways to increase APL’s popularity. More often, however, the focus has been on enhancements to APL, ways of bringing APL to the people. Considering that many APLers fell in love with APL\360, I’m sceptical that enhancements have much essential weight in the matter. My general conclusion is that rather than bringing APL to the people’s level, we need to use the proper educational tools to bring the people to APL. One way to start would be to collect, review and republish the literature on design. To proceed from there one could encourage more people to contribute and to expand the anthology once it has been collected.

I would suggest, as a very first step, that an index of such publications from VECTOR, Quote Quad, APL News, or elsewhere, be developed. VECTOR would seem to be the most appropriate collation point, and the most effective place to disseminate the index.

items.title: Shortened Transcript of Roy Sykes’ Closing Plenary Address at APL 86
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 89

by Anthony Camacho

Transcriber’s note: The full transcript of Roy’s speech was thirteen closely written pages (about six full pages of Vector). This abbreviated version omits the jokes and the politenesses to many contributors to the success of APL 86 and tries to do justice to Roy’s serious theme. Words which are verbatim are in quotations.

After a few introductory jokes Roy asked the serious question why APL is not dominant. “It has been estimated that APL accounts for between two and six percent of programs written in the world today.” He offered the following main reasons why we had not yet persuaded the rest of the world to follow us.

Inertia “Organisations have little reason to discard old yet operational software and are not prepared to retrain entrenched hordes of COBOL programmers. The twelve figure investment in computer software and standards [which] considerably exceeds the investment in computer hardware . . . ” is not on our side.

Cost “The memory required by APL has only recently become . . affordable . . . the speed differential between interpreted APL and compiled scalar languages remains. Furthermore APL implementations are still priced at a premium.”

Insularity APL took longer to gain links to computer peripherals, files and databases than the other languages. This has delayed our integration with the rest of computing. “APL programmers have ignored the garden in favour of a single rose bush.”

“There are hosts of other reasons for the orbit in which we find ourselves with our language. We may think we have charm but the rest of the world thinks we have strangeness. We excel in parallel but collide sequentially. The stable molecules we build from our periodic table are seen by others as unstable gluons. Overall APL and its advocates have a reputation for inhabiting an esoteric world of strange symbols, peculiar terms, dense programs and evangelical fervour.”

After congratulating the organisers (but not on the food – “lunch tickets anyone?”) Roy asked whether APL would ever come to fruition.

“I see the seas parting and the promised land beckoning . . . . Our technology has burst explosively into the mainstream of computing. In less than a decade we have seen the integration of APL with scores of other languages and packages.” APL can now use any equipment, read any file and its speed disadvantage is gradually being eroded. The new data structures, primitives and operators “expand the expressive power of APL explosively yet they retain the fundamental flavour of the language.”

Although Roy voted for the motion that APL enhancements do not help the spread of APL (which was carried) he voted against the proposition that APL was not yet suitable for AI (which was lost). “I wonder if the debate had been based on APL 1 (in Jim Brown’s parlance) would this motion have been defeated? Is VS APL sufficient for the task of AI? I think not.” So he revised his opinion and now believes that enhancements do help the spread of APL and implied they will do so increasingly.

“ . . . the most important technological explosion for APL is the most obvious. The advent of the personal computer and the extraordinary implementations of APL based on it . . . If APL\360 was the first revolution in APL then APL*PLUS/PC is the second.”

The biggest factor in the future of APL is education. “IBM has donated tens of thousands of PCs to universities. Thousands are now running APL . . . Fertile minds are being seeded with APL.”

“It seems to me that we have a more diverse and committed commercial sector devoted to APL than ever before. The UK now has an independent base of APL professionals approaching the size of that in the entire United States at the late 1970s peak of timesharing.”

What can we do now? Roy’s answers were; correct the old misunderstandings about APL; show it to people who should appreciate it; use it to write applications; think big – don’t sell just to programmers which is a small market compared with that of users (the largest used APL system is ADRS); use APL for prototypes (slogan: ‘Get it up fast with APL’). And he gave an example: he had produced an address book and telephone control system in about five days work, superior for his purposes to any of the packages on offer. “The fact is: APL can produce good products. Why don’t we produce them? Why don’t we market them? APL will get us there better and faster and the architecture of future machines favours the parallel structure of our language.”

We need to train APL programmers properly. Too much APL is done by amateurs and users who are not trained and their mistakes bring APL a bad reputation. There are still under a thousand professional APL programmers. Perhaps most of all we need to spread APL downwards in the educational world from universities to schools.

Roy’s closing message was that the great period of enhancements to APL is over. “The APL that we are now using is the one that we will be developing products on now and for the foreseeable future. Let us resolve to exploit APL: to expand its usage and application far beyond its current scope. Our livelihoods depend on it. Our dreams will be satisfied by nothing less. Remember APL is not a programming language. It’s a way of life.”

items.title: Stop Press: The Amstrad PC1512
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 92

The Amstrad PC1512

I have just had a very brief encounter with this machine. It looks and feels rather smart, although the screen resolution (in monochrome white) is only as good as the (standard) IBM colour monitor. However it does make quite sensible use of grey to imitate colour effects.

It ran APL*PLUS/PC with no problems, including screen hardcopy on the Amstrad printer. I am told that you can swop the character ROM, but obviously I was unable to check this! It benchmarks at 2.4 times the speed of a standard PC (i.e. a little below an AT), running the ‘FN 1000’ test in 15 sec.

Further details in next issue.

Adrian Smith

items.title: Technical Editorial: BAA Public Domain Software Library
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 93

by Dave Ziemann and Jonathan Barman

At APL86 the BAA proudly announced their latest project, the Public Domain Software Library. We hope that the library will become the definitive source for public domain software of interest to APL programmers. The BAA have not embarked upon a project of this kind before, and so for the first six months we will be offering a restricted service; only software exchangeable on DOS-format disks will be offered, and we will not undertake the distribution of any paper documentation. Although the software will be free, the disk on to which it will be copied and the postage has to be paid for. Charges are expected to be quite low as it will be possible to purchase the disks in bulk. At this early stage, the software distribution procedure has not yet been finalised, so only the mechanism for donating software will be described. Watch for full details in the next issue of Vector.

The basis of the Software Library is the APL 86 Software Exchange. This produced 16 items, many of which are of a substantial size. A directory of the software available will be a feature of this and future issues of Vector. Although each item in the directory has an abstract which describes briefly what is available, we will publish reviews explaining the purpose and use of selected software in more detail.

Whilst briefly scanning through all the software we kept on coming across things that looked really useful, or had to be saved to be played with later, until we ran out of disk space! Not everything is APL, there are some really good games/play items in machine code, and some useful DOS utilities.

A project of this sort needs plenty of activity to keep it alive, so it is essential that your contributions keep on coming in. Mel Chapman, our treasurer, has kindly agreed to be postbox for any software that you wish to send in before the arrangements are finalised. Details are at the end of the Software Library listing.
