items.title: Recent Meetings (section introduction)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 49

This section of VECTOR is intended to document the seminars delivered at recent meetings of the Association, particularly for the benefit of those members based away from London who often find it hard to find the time to attend. It also covers other selected events which are likely to be of interest to the wider APL community.

We are dependent on the willingness of speakers to provide us with a written version of their talk, and we would remind them that “a picture’s worth a thousand words”. Copies of slides and transparencies will enhance their articles.

The Activities Officer (see inside back cover) will respond enthusiastically to offers from individuals who wish to contribute seminars and supporting papers.

items.title: Introductory Notes; Successful Expert Systems, Royal Station Hotel, York, February 17th 1987
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 50

by Adrian Smith
path: Introductory Notes; Successful Expert Systems, Royal Station Hotel, York, February 17th 1987

items.title: Introductory Notes
items.text:
Three meetings are covered in this section of VECTOR. The first is really nothing to do with APL, but seeing as I was there I thought that I might as well write it up! It was the Yorkshire and Humberside OR Group’s special national event on successful applications of Expert Systems.

The second is a bona-fide BAA meeting, on the subject of Quality Control in APL applications. The talks were by Chris Campen, of the other BAA (the British Airports Authority), and by Linda Kindred of Wellcome. A summary of Chris’s paper is followed by my own notes on Linda’s talk, and Anthony Camacho’s on the panel discussion which followed.

Finally we have some notes on the March meeting on Graphics, together with Dave Preedy’s paper on ‘Graphics in the Boardroom’ (See General Papers). This covered a lot of fascinating ground (Bach Canons in APL on Amigas!) with enough technical hitches to keep all the speakers on their toes!!
path: Introductory Notes; Successful Expert Systems, Royal Station Hotel, York, February 17th 1987

items.title: Successful Expert SystemsRoyal Station Hotel, YorkFebruary 17th 1987
path: Introductory Notes; Successful Expert Systems, Royal Station Hotel, York, February 17th 1987

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
This was a most stimulating and enjoyable day, in spite of the fact that APL wasn’t mentioned once! As you will see, it gives us APLer’s a good deal of hope, in spite of that sad omission. In particular it was a notable feature of the day that the industrialists was singing the praises of ‘shells’ and ‘environments’ whereas the academics were pouring cold water, and sounding some very cogent warnings.

My overall impression was that it is fine to go out and buy Crystal, XI-Plus, or whatever as a way of getting started. Before long you will either hit the limits of what the shell designer thought of, or will end up with 90% of your rules essentially fudging round the constraints imposed. In the long term, what you really need is a plug-in ‘inference engine’ which will fit naturally into your existing software, be it database, spreadsheet, or APL model.

Enough of personal prejudice . . . here is what the speakers actually said!
path: Introductory Notes; Successful Expert Systems, Royal Station Hotel, York, February 17th 1987

items.title: Expert Systems in British Gas
items.text:
Tony Haws

Tony began by summarizing the current position in British Gas. He felt that the key areas to watch were: strategy for implementation; effective knowledge acquisition; interfaces to existing systems; the choice of delivery vehicle. On the first point, he noted that all but one of his 6 examples were drawn from a single enthusiastic expert (3 of these had since joined the ES group). They were now technically and financially successful, but had yet to achieve ‘commercial’ success in the sense of influencing the core of the company operations.

He now described six successful systems in detail:

  • ENRICH. In the entire NW region, there were but 2 experts on noisy central heating systems!! Sometimes it took 6 months for a customer to get attention, and the experts were usually reluctant to be called out to such ’trivial’ matters. The system started off on ICL Advisor at local depots. At least this cut it down to 2-3 visits by the fitter. Now Nth Thames are re-doing it on Crystal on hand-held micros for on-site use.
  • Herbicide Advisor. This time only one expert, who got pregnant! Now a national system for dealing with nasties in the ponds round gasometers.
  • The Stretford Process (coal gasification). All these are sold abroad . . . they often go wrong and the phone calls cost the users lots of money! Now sold with the expert diagnosis as part of the package. (ESP Advisor on IBM compatibles.)
  • CORPS. Corrosion prediction in drill wells and pipes. Does a day’s work in half an hour (See VECTOR 1.3 for a paper on PATTIE . . . . Ed)
  • QUAD. ICL have a 4GL called Querymaster; casual users find it hard to frame queries, so Quad helps them.
  • Physical Risk Analysis. Developed as part of contingency planning to identify the risks to computers (and subsequently to more general installations) from fire, flood, terrorist attack etc. None of the dozen or so experts could co-ordinate or structure their expertise; the ES approach got them together.

In all about 20 similar systems are under way, all of the same general type. Two classes in particular look hopeful:

  • ‘Real’ ES, involving high levels of skill in a small and well bounded domains. ENRICH is the archetype.
  • Simple, but more general, such as the risk analysis system. The savings multiply up rapidly when you apply the same system in many places.

In both types, the design is evolutionary, and will help the expert himself to generate more knowledge.

How to deliver? Software is the key!! Shells are really for beginners, the experts graduate to ‘environments’; typically purpose built Lisp machines costing $15,000 upwards. Of course you can develop on one machine (compilation really hammers the system) and implement on another.

Knowledge acquisition . . . in many of the examples, the expert wrote the system himself (often in his spare time). This is not a long-term option, and apart from very basic Market Research techniques there is little experience here. Some pitfalls to watch for: rare events which the expert forgets; things which ‘everyone knows’; missing links in the logic.

Selling the ideas in the organisation . . . and convincing others to spend the money. Next week they are holding a seminar for 80-odd senior managers with demos of many of the above. With luck it should give an entry into the commercial heart of the business where the real money is.
path: Introductory Notes; Successful Expert Systems, Royal Station Hotel, York, February 17th 1987

items.title: Experience of Expert Systems in ICI
items.text:
Brian Hobson

A total of over 40 systems are in progress or in use, ranging through: technical sales; engineering design; diagnosis; business planning; operator guidance. They are all written using ‘ISI Savoir’ in which ICI have a 50% stake. After some early failures, they have achieved real commercial success from 1984 onwards. Some typical systems were:

  • Wheat Counsellor. This dates back to 1984, and has changed little since. It uses ICI’s private viewdata network to access current data on wheat prices, local weather, soil conditions etc. The farmer is then quizzed about his ‘field’ and is informed of the disease risks and a fungicide is suggested (not always ICI’s!!) Some indication of cost-benefit is also given. It was initially successful, but has rather stagnated as farmers have moved to Amstrads. It is also limited to wheat (some 1200 rules); barley, oats and so on must be included if it is to attain ‘critical mass’.
  • SYSLAG (lagging on pipes). Here the expert spent his last two years before retirement learning the shell and getting the knowledge into the system. Because there is a lot of maths involved, over 50% of the code is actually in Pascal exits, rather than Savoir itself. The inference is all done using Bayesian probabilities; in many cases the maths is dubious (e.g. where the options are highly correlated) but with suitable fudging of prior probabilities it appears to give the right answers! It is used 15 – 20 times per month, took 6 – 9 months to develop (mostly free), and runs in 150K on an IBM PC.
  • Coater Plant Diagnosis. Latex coating on plastic flying by at 60mph! One expert, who fancied Saturday mornings in bed, supported by the plant management, who were aware of the drop in productivity whenever ‘Walter’ wasn’t around. Why not write a handbook? The ES is better for training, forces the operators to explore more options, and keeps a log for the next shift to see. This one took 3 man-months to do, and has definitely increased plant efficiency.
  • Operator guidance. This schedules paint manufacture in a plant which needs running ‘gently’ and with some thought. 30 tons of ‘White with a hint of Black’ could be a problem! Here the knowledge acquisition was a problem, as the various experts shouted at one another across the conference table. At least the ES is consistent! It is attached to ICI’s ‘Auditor’ plant monitoring package to get its data; eventually they hope to feed back directly into the plant control systems.

In summary ‘Small is Beautiful’ in all the really successful cases. Wheat counsellor was an early breakthrough, but has stagnated as it cannot achieve wide enough coverage of a large domain. Of the 42 systems in progress, 5 have paid off, 10 are deemed to be successes, 5 are dead ducks, and the rest must wait and see.
path: Introductory Notes; Successful Expert Systems, Royal Station Hotel, York, February 17th 1987

items.title: Criteria for Successful Expert Systems
items.text:
Bob O’Keefe (University of Kent)

This was a talk with a difference! Bob very briefly outlined a system for screening graduate applicants in a major accountancy firm. Not surprisingly the details were confidential . . . the criteria for screening 2,000 applicants for 200 jobs are not likely to become public knowledge. Instead Bob concentrated on the reasons for success, and gave us his (deliberately controversial) list of the most common reasons for failure.

First the reasons for success:

  • A willing and enthusiastic ‘knowledge Czar’ with a very definite ‘I am right’ attitude. His considerable input of time was worth more than the cost of consultancy, hardware and software put together.
  • Flexible software. ESP Advisor lets you out into Prolog when the going gets tough. The system could not have been done quickly and cost-effectively if they had been ‘locked in’ to a shell. They needed ‘a programming tool, not an imposed paradigm’. Typical symptoms of the latter are systems with 3,000 rules; 2,900 of these are probably getting round the shell!
  • A simple approach to uncertainty. Bayesian inference really is an absolute nightmare! They used simple ‘what’s A worth against B’ comparisons to establish a set of weights; these were then simply combined to give an overall score.
  • Validation. This took more effort (60% of the total time) than knowledge acquisition and building. Random batches of 20 – 30 applicants were run through the system; when these all checked OK, they looked for the real extreme cases and pushed it to the edge of past experience.
  • User interface. It takes a lot of care to get the questions in a sensible order! Users are bothered by some ‘Y/N’, some ‘Enter number (1 – 3)’ and so on; everything was set up as a menu option to avoid this inconsistency.
  • The needs of the user came first. It is quicker and simpler to use the system than to do it by hand. It guides them through the task – maybe this should have been put in a handbook 20 years ago; these days it is easier to put it in an ES.
  • the impact on the organisation were built in. The system gives a better and more consistent recruitment policy, and the reponsibility can be taken lower down the structure.

Some elements which have lead to failure in other systems:

  • the ‘consultative mode’. The system asks all the questions, and does all the reasoning. You sit there and say ‘Y’, or ‘0.35’ and so on. Attempts to use ES in financial planning have been a disaster for this reason … here the use of ‘critique mode’ works much better. The expert has a first go at a plan and the system criticises it. Of course many shells embed ‘consult mode’ in the shell structure!
  • Imposed methods of handling uncertainty. We just don’t know how to do this, and should stop pretending that Bayes and Fuzzy logic are any sort of a solution.
  • Shells. If you have a hammer, you see every problem as a nail. If you have a Backward-chaining Bayesian Inference Engine . . . . . In the US they are moving back to ES environments (e.g. CitiBank have spent $10M on Lisp machines) rather than using shells.
  • Poor validation. ‘It never got implemented, but it’s a useful training tool’. This translates as ‘we couldn’t check its answers’. If you haven’t got documented case studies, or an independent expert, you are in big trouble.

In general, ES are moving fast towards being ‘bottom line’ benefits, rather than just nice toys. Either someone is making better decisions, or lots more people are making good decisions. This is all well and good, but has anyone a clue as to how we should measure the results quantitatively? The DSS people have been trying for years; will the ES fraternity do any better?!
path: Introductory Notes; Successful Expert Systems, Royal Station Hotel, York, February 17th 1987

items.title: Quality Control in Application Development, 20th February 1987 at the Royal Over-Seas League
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 54

by Adrian Smith
path: Quality Control in Application Development, 20th February 1987 at the Royal Over-Seas League

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
This was one of the most interesting and valuable meetings I can remember for a long time. The idea of getting a ‘view from the outside’ was a brave one, and (in my view at least) came off very well indeed.

Chris Campen gave us his view, from the position of Information Systems Policy Manager at the British Airports Authority. Linda Kindred followed up with the perspective of someone whose job it is to maintain (rather than create) systems in a wide range of languages.
path: Quality Control in Application Development, 20th February 1987 at the Royal Over-Seas League

items.title: A Formal Approach to Implementation
items.text:
Chris Campen (British Airports Authority)

Summarised by Anthony Camacho

Chris defined the quality of an information system as fitness for its purpose. To design a fit system large jobs are divided into many small tasks. Quality control includes standards and reviews of work in stages. Each small task must have well defined objectives and targets. There should be regular monitoring. Work must be checked by people controlled by different managers. The users should check that specifications are met when each milestone is passed. Anyone affected by the work or with an interest in it should be allowed to participate.

The planning is thus the key and includes everything; the membership of the teams, the allocation of other resources, the standards, the frequency of various checks and reviews, the fallback and safety procedures to protect the business.

Quality control cannot be imposed because to succeed the whole team has to believe in it. When imposed everyone goes through the motions and the quality control work adds to the load without giving a commensurate benefit.

The big problem is how to change the attitudes of the staff so that they welcome such things as walkthroughs by independent assessors. The right attitude will work with inferior standards whereas no standards can save a project when the staff have the wrong attitude.
path: Quality Control in Application Development, 20th February 1987 at the Royal Over-Seas League

items.title: QC in the Systems Development Cycle
items.text:
Linda Kindred (OR/Appl Support at Wellcome Foundation)

The strategy at Wellcome has been to separate ‘maintenance and firefighting’ out from systems development, and to keep a body of expert programmers and analysts in the ‘applications support’ department. Around 18 people are responsible for some 80 systems, comprising 2,500 programs. Of these 300-400 are APL based.

Linda has the absolute right to refuse to any system which fails her standards of quality control; in the past this has meant bouncing systems at the implementation stage, but the emphasis is now on imposing strict standards of quality throught the development cycle.

Just what is the development cycle? In the beginning there is the Budget. This used to be based on last year’s usage; it is now based on agreed business requirements for the coming year. Priorities are thrashed out with the users as necessary. From then on . . .

  • all work is project based. The project manager is the user. Project management techniques (networking etc) are provided by MS where required.
  • one or two levels of working party are set up, again chaired by the users. MS and Internal Audit would normally sit on these, and they would meet monthly to review the network. Each ‘activity’ would always have an ‘owner’.
  • there would be ‘terms of reference’ to outline the scope, risks and limitations of the project.
  • costs are approved stage by stage. There is no attempt to quantify total project costs at the beginning; the staged approval gives you the chance of killing projects after (say) an outline design phase.
  • no fixed implementation date is set. Instead everyone must sign off the system (including Production Support who could force a re-write on the grounds of resource usage).
  • the Post-implementation review (say 6 months later). What went wrong (and why)? What went well (and why)?

Applications support were traditionally only involved at the final stages. However in recent years there role has broadened (especially on major projects):

  • they are represented on the working parties, with the particular role of checking the interfaces.
  • they provide an inspection service to the analysts, programmers and project leader.
  • they are the ‘custodian’ of the standards. These are all held on line on PROFS, and are used to log the benefits of past experience as well as being a rule-book for development.
  • they have the QA responsibility. Clearly they are committed to this, because it is very much in the interests of the maintenance programmers. Call-outs used to average 2 per week; now 1 per month is typical.
  • if you have quality from the beginning it is free. Systems are no longer bounced at implementation.

So what are their standards, and where do the benefits come from?

  • Applications Support won’t take on any system which ‘ABENDS’ 3 to 5 times per month, or takes a day’s maintenance per month.
  • the split between development and maintenance (at the budgeting stage) makes it quite clear to management just where the costs are coming from. It makes it much easier for the development phase to hit budget!
  • changes and fixes are kept in a system log. In the long term this is used as evidence for re-writes.

The basic long-term aim is to ensure stability in the supported systems, and to free resource for urgent changes rather than basic maintenance.

Questions from the floor . . . .

What is an Abend in an APL system? When the workspace goes down and it takes you half a day to re-create the problem!

What about systems on PCs? This has hidden itself under the carpet, but managers are beginning to realise what they have got themselves into.

Who would be a typical ‘user’ on the working party? Definitely the senior guy, often a divisional manager.

What motivates the project teams to follow the QA standards? They will finish on time, within cost. You always get those who don’t; their annual review reflects it, and they don’t get the plums next time around! (Some have even been known to get ‘special projects’.)

Is there a development team for APL? Lots of it was done in OR; this has been cleaned up and taken over. Some small APL developments have been picked up recently as confidence in APL maintainability has begun to increase.
path: Quality Control in Application Development, 20th February 1987 at the Royal Over-Seas League

items.title: Panel Discussion
items.text:
Dave Parker (in the chair), Les Hollingbery, Adrian Smith, Maurice Jordan, Linda Kindred

DP In the Electricity Council they use Delta to standardize conventional program development, with an in-house front-end. This leads to a common style of code across all applications, and he has followed this with his APL methods. Basically this means standards for function, variable and label names, and a base of common utilities. AS

At the 1985 OR conference, there was an excellent talk from Nissan-UK, where it was emphasised that there are no quality control inspectors in Japan! Quality is built in, not inspected in! At Rowntrees we think we now have a APL community who have been trained from the beginning in ‘the right way’ of doing things; no-one would ever think of using shared variables, or using files other than through cover functions.

Change control: for big systems there is a formal procedure for scheduling changes (e.g. to ensure 2 related changes go in separately). Each workspace has a text variable called RELEASE where programmers leave a log of what was changed and why.

For mainframe APL it doesn’t matter all that much if it stops . . . usually no-one else is hurt, and you can often fix it ‘on the fly’. PCs are a different matter, and delivered systems must be much more robust.

LH Les supports Information Centres at Rank Xerox. APL systems were very much ad hoc, but have now settled down and stabilised. They are looking at LOGOS from IPSA as a way of getting control over development and change. Xerox use a ‘total quality’ approach where everyone is there own inspector. He recommended Myers book for general advice, and a ‘belt and braces’ approach for critical systems (i.e. self checking software). MJ Quality certainly matters on things like the reservation system (a 3-hour down time could lose the MD his job!); in APL they encourage the use of tools and common utilities, but not all systems conform. They suffered from an ‘explosion’ into APL (0 – 30 APLers overnight) and the undisciplined approach this led to. MJ is personally responsible for some 2,500 functions; few of these give him trouble, and he is trying to understand what the differences are. Qn Do you use passwords and locked functions to protect code? AS In the old days )SAVE was our file system. This is still OK for personal systems, but now we try to separate the code (typically on project libraries) from the data (on files on the user’s own ID). We try to avoid knowing other people’s passwords for routine maintenance! DP They do much the same; he owns the workspace and the user owns the data. General Beware the input stack!! At least with APL2 you can turn it off; it is not a safe substitute for a file system. Qn How do APL systems compare on reliability? LK/MJ Historically, APL has caused more trouble LH When an APL program goes down, I have a lot less paperwork! AS You sometimes discover a fault years after the system was implemented (e.g. a missing quote in an error message). However the real problems are caused when the system gives wrong answers, but doesn’t crash! MJ A big APL system went into parallel running after 6 man-years; most of the discrepancies were faults in the original system (unnoticed for years). Lusmore A random-number generator was once left in a sales commission routine for 6 months before anyone spotted it! Qn Does this conflict with the idea of fast development? MJ Things that should have taken a day’s thought and 2 day’s work often took weeks when rushed into! AS Sit on your hands for half an hour! Don’t let the user (whoever he is) rush you into designing at the keyboard! Let the computer find the SYNTAX ERRORS by all means; it is up to you to find the DESIGN ERRORS at your desk. LH There is always the danger that APL will encourage you to tackle things which are beyond you. Qn APL may do things fast, but what kind of documentation should you do? DP Even if you document the functions, it is hard to document the methodology. Where possible get the user to do it for you. AS Most of the ‘user guide’ should be on the screen. Similarly the system documentation should be in the WS; e.g. an active data-dictionary which logs the types and descriptions of variables as well as driving the editing functions. Camacho First write the manual; second write empty (commented) functions; third fill in the code. MJ It is surprisingly easy to read other people’s code. Good APL is really just the specification expressed in a mathematical notation. Cyriax Often it is hard to comment adequately in English; quite often you slip into APL, particularly when describing function arguments. Lusmore Good comments are hard to do; often they look alright until you try to use them! AS APL doesn’t let you do good layout. Compared to Pascal or PL/1 it is a typographic disaster area! You can only comment on separate lines; you can’t indent; you can’t leave blank lines or spaces in the middle of lines. Try reading someone else’s Pascal if all these visual cues are taken out! MJ Perhaps the most valuable documentation is a collection of sample inputs and outputs for functions. Camacho Use meaningful names, not daft standards like ‘L1:’ for labels. AS Often the choice of local names tells me who last changed the function.
path: Quality Control in Application Development, 20th February 1987 at the Royal Over-Seas League

items.title: Announcement
items.text:
Linda closed the meeting by telling us about a group called the QA Forum which meets quarterly to discuss issues related to QC in systems development.

It is an independent body, and costs £300 pa, with a fee of £85 per meeting attended. The members are able to get specific topics on to the agenda, and workshops are held to help with particular problem areas. The collected papers from each meeting are circulated to all members, who are generally people involved in day to day QA work.

items.title: Chairman’s survey of the year
items.text:
Dick Bowman thanked Phil Goacher for making the offer to hold APL 86 in the UK; without that we could not have made the success of it that we did. APL 86 has given us a financial base which greatly increases the scope of what we can do. Some initiatives already begun are listed below.

Vector is now well established in the international APL community and is well and economically run. Its advertisements cover most of its costs. To make it an essential part of every APLer’s life it needs more useful technical contributions.

We have had some difficulties with our regular meetings because the elected Activities Officer was unable to set up a forward plan. He has since resigned and a new activities team is beginning to get that under control.

The initiatives:

Surveys

  1. A survey of members and their views, which will be reported in Vector.
  2. A survey of the awareness and use of APL in higher education: this shows high awareness but that APL will only be used when it is seen to be relevant.

APLication

This is to be a three day special event on APL applications to be held in September 1988 at the University of Kent in Canterbury. It is not APL 88 (Northern Hemisphere).

Awards

The Committee proposes two outstanding achievement awards, which will be:

  1. for recent work in APL, and
  2. for spreading awareness about APL.

These awards will not be made when the Committee does not feel the best candidates are outstanding enough.

Education

A substantial contribution was made to I-APL. A subsidised course for teachers is to be held in July.

Software Library

The catalogue is growing – it made many acquisitions at APL 87 and is now beginning to generate orders. Success depends on members sending good software and telling people about the good software available in the library.

Dick Bowman ended by expressing his personal satisfaction at having been nominated to stand for the board of SIGAPL.

items.title: Secretary’s report.
items.text:
Anthony Camacho reported that the minute book was available for anyone to inspect and included minutes of meetings since the summary in the Turquoise Vector (3.4).

The APL book service is now installed at the University of Warwick bookshop: they take credit card orders by telephone. There will again be a booklist in Vector 4.1.

This AGM had to be postponed: the original date clashed with APL 87. A new Editor could not be elected in time to edit Vector 4.1 so the Secretary had perforce to take that on.

The Secretary had objected to paying the Royal Over-Seas League £40 for the half-day hire of an overhead projector and had found and arranged for the Association to buy the portable machine being used today.
path: Minutes of the AGM of the British APL Association held on 5 June 1987

items.title: Treasurer’s report
items.text:
Mel Chapman circulated a report and accounts. These showed that APL 86 had made about £50,000 profit. This year expenditure on publicity and meetings was well below budget. The £7,000 owed to us is from Vector advertisements and APL 86 delegates. The latter are to be threatened with an international blacklist.

In answer to questions he reported that:

the membership was 432 including 44 corporate and 11 sustaining members. Vector circulation is about 800.

the bank interest for the year is low because the profit for APL 86 was not paid to us until the end of the year. Interest is currently being earned at about £400 per month.

each meeting costs about £220.

Tim Perry asked what financial control there was over the donation to I-APL. Dick Bowman said the committee had approved the Technical Specification and Marketing Plan. Tim was not satisfied, saying that the contribution made in his name had been without his knowledge and against his will. He asked who ran I-APL, what was its status and what had the BAA done to ensure its contribution would not be misused. Dick Bowman emphasised that I-APL was not a BAA project and asked the Chairman of I-APL to answer.

Anthony Camacho explained that the I-APL project was controlled by a committee of five: himself, Ed Cherlin, Norman Thomson, Professor Howard Peelle and David Ziemann. I-APL had been formed into a limited company so that contributors could be sure accounts would be kept and presented at Companies’ House. The Committee were also the directors of the company and had declared that I-APL would never pay a dividend but would devote all funds from donations and sales to the promotion of APL. I-APL (apart from one paid programmer) is entirely a voluntary and non-commercial organisation.

Asked about spin-off from the development of I-APL, Anthony replied that I-APL Ltd had agreed with Paul Chapman that if Paul or the project succeeded in selling the Development Environment as a commercial product, the proceeds would go half to Paul and half to I-APL Ltd.

The Chairman and Secretary then held the election of the 1987-88 committee.

The candidate list was:

Candidate Post Proposer Seconder Anthony Camacho Chairman R. J. Cocking D. Preedy Dick Bowman * " V. Lusmore M. Jordan Graham Parkhouse *Secretary A. J. Camacho P. Donnelly Cathy Dargue Treasurer Peter Cyriax D. Preedy Mel Chapman * " P. S. Goacher V. Lusmore Adrian Smith *Journal A. J. Camacho D. Preedy Norman Thomson *Education M. J. Kingston A. J. Camacho David Ziemann *Technical J. Barman R. J. Cocking Philip Goacher *Activities D. Parker M. Jordan Bernadette Leverton Publicity D. Eastwood A. J. Camacho Jill Moss * " V. Lusmore Cathy Dargue Val Lusmore *Recruitment M. Chapman C. McCree David Eastwood *Projects R. Nabavi A. J. Camacho

* The asterisks mark those elected.

There was a second vote for the post of Chairman as the first vote was a dead heat and the 86-87 chairman declined to make a casting vote. The result was:

Anthony Camacho 6 corporate and 31 individual votes =61 Dick Bowman 9 corporate and 22 individual votes =67

Mel Chapman and Jill Moss won the other two contested elections easily.

The requirement that each candidate submit a brief statement (to be read out by Chairman or Secretary) outlining suitability and intentions should they be elected was not honoured by all candidates. Dick Bowman and Mel Chapman each made a little speech and David Eastwood also spoke briefly in favour of Bernadette Leverton.

The AGM ended at approximately 3.30 pm.

Anthony Camacho, retiring Hon Sec, 7 June 1987

items.title: Purpose
items.text: The purpose of the British APL Association Software Library (BAASL) is to provide useful software to the APL community. In order to achieve a high level of service, we need a good supply of quality software.
path: The British APL Association Software Library: Call for Software; Full Catalogue

items.title: What kind of software?
items.text:
We are looking for anything that could be of interest to the APL programmer, user or manager. It might be a tool for migrating APL workspaces between different interpreters, general APL utilities, APL2 functions for simulating component files, a reverse Polish model of APL or even a DOS adventure game. Each of these examples is an actual disk from the library.

There are no restrictions on the type of software, type of APL or the type of machine on which the software is to be run. As long as it is of interest to APLers, then it is worthy for consideration. The programs do not even have to be written in APL, although we do not want to fill the library with software which is easily available elsewhere The BAASL is primarilly concerned with offering ‘public domain’ software, which should normally include unlocked source code wherever possible. Bona-fide ‘shareware’ software is acceptable, and we are also happy to carry ‘demonstration disks’, which advertise commercially available software, provided that this is made quite clear.

If you are considering creating software for the library, read the software submission form first, so that you know what is expected of you. Please share the fruits of your work with others.
path: The British APL Association Software Library: Call for Software; Full Catalogue

items.title: Transfer medium
items.text: The transfer medium for the BAASL is currently the DOS-format five-and-a-quarter inch floppy diskette. If you can get it onto a floppy disk, then we can make it available to others. If the target machine is not a PC, then appropriate transfer instructions should be included on the disk.
path: The British APL Association Software Library: Call for Software; Full Catalogue

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
The library will not currently handle any medium other than the floppy disk. In particular, we do not undertake to distribute paper documentation of any kind.

All disks must therefore include sufficient user documentation to permit effective use of the software. The donor may include an address where paper documentation can be obtained, possibly at a nominal cost.
path: The British APL Association Software Library: Call for Software; Full Catalogue

items.title: Charges
items.text:
It is not intended that the BAASL make a profit. Our charging policy is designed to cover the cost of materials, postage and handling, although we do make a reduced charge to BAA members in order to encourage membership.

A BAASL software donor must not require payment from the user, although reasonable charges for registration or paper documentation may be advertised on the disk. Disks that demonstrate commercially available products are acceptable, provided that this is made clear.
path: The British APL Association Software Library: Call for Software; Full Catalogue

items.title: Liability
items.text:
A signature is required to declare the donor’s right to allow the BAA to copy the software, and to permit anyone to copy and use it. Software is accepted by the BAA on good faith, and we do not vouch for or make any claims regarding donated software.

The BAA cannot be held responsible or liable for any damage, however caused, by the use or misuse of library software, and shall not be liable in any way in the event that submitted material proves to be the subject of third party copyright.
path: The British APL Association Software Library: Call for Software; Full Catalogue

items.title: Reviewers
items.text:
Unfortunately, we do not have the time to study each submitted disk in detail, although we check that disks do roughly what they claim to, and that they appear to work. We would like to publish reviews of library software in VECTOR, and so we welcome offers from all you keen reviewers out there. In fact we will even send your disks free of charge, if you write a review for VECTOR!

In any event, please write to tell us what you think of a particular BAASL disk, and how you found it useful. If you find glaring holes in the library, let us know what is missing and we will try to plug the gap. Better still, write it yourself.

items.title: APL-Ication
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 19

The Practical State-of-the-Art APL Conference

University of KentCanterbury, England28-30 September 1988

The British APL Association is pleased to announce this three day conference to be held in the beautiful Cathedral City of Canterbury in September 1988.

APL-Ication is designed to be complementary to APL88, being held in Sydney, Australia from 1-5 February and will be an exciting, outward looking conference of interest to all APL practitioners - both newcomers to APL and those with more experience in the use of the language. We extend an invitation to other APL club members, particularly those in Europe, to become involved in APL-Ication by submitting papers, offering presentations and by attending the conference.

items.title: Canterbury
items.text: The City's roots can be traced back to a prehistoric iron age settlement, but the story of Canterbury really starts after the Roman invasion of AD 43. Then known as Durovernum Cantiacorum, it was a trading centre on the main route between London and Europe. After successive occupation by the Vikings and the Danes, the Normans arrived and it was they who began building the Cathedral in 1070. In 1170 Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in the Cathedral. Pilgrims from all over Britain and Europe were soon travelling to Becket's shrine, a typical pilgrimage being recorded in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales. Despite the later attentions of Henry VIII and Cromwell the Cathedral survives to this day as the 'Mother Church of English Christianity', and is famed for its collection of stained glass windows.

items.title: University of Kent
items.text: The conference will be located at the University which overlooks the Cathedral City of Canterbury - a famous City, situated in the heart of the Kent , the county known as the 'Garden of England'. The University campus, opened in 1965, offers outstanding facilities for staging conferences, with on-site accommodation and social amenities. The University can be reached conveniently by road and rail. Canterbury is close to the motorway network affording rapid access to all parts of the UK and Europe via Dover, which is close by. The rail link to London also provides access from all parts of the country and from Heathrow and Gatwick airports.

items.title: APL-Ication
items.text:
The conference has been designed to give a careful balance between the presentations given by invited speakers and contributed papers, with the accent on the practical application of APL in a variety of business disciplines. The conference will also look critically at the world of computing to see what lessons we might learn and how APL can be integrated into non-APL environments.

APL-Ication will have an international flavour, with contributions from overseas, particularly our APL colleagues in Europe. Anyone interested in presenting a paper should follow the instructions for submission given in the following Call for Papers.

Although there will be no formal exhibition, hospitality suites will be available for consultancies and vendors to meet delegates and to display their products, and time will be available in the lecture theatres for presentations of software and hardware for the APL user.

Further details of APL-Ication will be given in the next issue of Vector.

items.title: APL-Ication Conference
items.text: University of KentCanterbury, England28-30 September 1988

items.title: Call for Papers
items.text:
APL-Ication is a three-day conference being organised by the British APL Association, devoted to the topic of the Application of APL in Business. Who uses APL? Why do they use APL? What does the practitioner need to know to apply APL effectively? What changes to APL would make it more useful?

In addition to contributed papers, there will be a number of invited speakers from both within and without the APL world who will present papers and lead tutorial and discussion sessions. These speakers will detail experiences gained in non-APL as well as APL fields, beneficial to the APL professional.

Sessions currently planned include:

APL and Software Engineering.

Case Studies. Why was APL used? What benefits accrued? Will APL be used in similar situations again? What changes to APL would increase its value to such applications?

Teaching APL. What education is relevant to those using APL as a problem solving tool for business? How do we teach it?

APL and the Human Computer Interface.

APL and other systems. The use of APL to augment 'standard' packages and databases. Why in a multi-language system does APL always seem to be the one that bends?

Development and productivity tools for the APL professional.

Other programming languages, particularly functional programming and object oriented languages. What are they, and what are the implications for APL?

APL-Ication will be an exciting, outward looking conference of interest to all APL users at all levels. The event will be highly participative. No talk will exceed half an hour, and all sessions will be concluded by a panel discussion involving the presenters. 'Live' presentations to accompany papers will be encouraged by the provision of a wide range of computing and audio-visual equipment. The University of Kent has excellent facilities for both speakers and delegates.

Papers are welcome from outside the UK, particularly from Europe, as it is our aim to make APL-Ication a truly international event. We would like to share the experiences of using APL gained in the UK with our overseas colleagues and learn how they put APL to effective use in other countries.

It is important that we adhere strictly to a timetable for the submission of papers, leading to publication in the conference proceedings. This timetable has been carefully organised in order that work on your submission to APL-Ication will not interfere with your visit to APL88 next February.

items.title: Submission of Papers
items.text:
Full draft papers, for consideration by a panel of referees, must be submitted by 15 January 1988. Four copies of the paper, which is to be in English and should not exceed 6000 words, must be submitted, together with:

a title, an abstract and a list of keywords for subject identification and classification,

a photograph and a short autobiography, and

a full description of the 'live' presentation and the equipment required.

Notification of the referees' decisions will be sent out on 1 March 1988. Authors of papers must provide final copies of their papers suitable for photo reproduction by 29 April 1988.

All papers accepted and received by the final submission deadline will be published in the Conference Proceedings. Other papers will be considered for publication in Vector.

It is intended that prizes will be awarded for the 'best' papers and presentations given at the conference.

items.title: Membership Projects Scheme
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 23

After APL86, the BAA committee decided to channel some of the proceeds of the conference back to the membership of the Association. In particular, it was decided to establish a 'Membership Projects' award of up to £5,000 in any given year. The awards are for those projects which, in the view of the BAA Committee, will do the most to further the aims of the BAA, viz:

  • Promote the use of APL
  • Help people to use APL well
  • Contribute to the development of APL and international standards
  • Increase the membership of the BAA

The scheme was announced in Vector and the announcement implied that the scheme was only for the year ending June 1987. In fact the BAA Committee has decided to keep the scheme going at least until the next AGM in 1988. We have decided to issue this reminder about the Projects Scheme to prompt further applications for this year's award.

The award is for a total sum of up to £5,000 in any given year for the project or projects which, in the opinion of the BAA Committee, are the most deserving. The choice of project is entirely up to the applicant, but examples might include:

  • Writing/Publishing a new APL book
  • Development of new APL software
  • Development of the APL language itself
  • APL-based research

The award can be used to finance time off work, the purchase or rental of equipment, the preparation of material for publication etc. The awards will be made at the AGM of the BAA and selection will be made by members of a BAA subcommittee and ratified by the full committee. The rules are simple:

  1. Projects must be proposed and carried out by paid-up members of the BAA.
  2. A sum of up to £5,000 is available for the projects deemed most suitable by the BAA committee.
  3. The decision of the BAA committee in choosing suitable projects is final.
  4. Members of the BAA committee are not eligible for this award
  5. A contract governing the terms and methods of payment will be drawn up between the BAA and the recipient of the award.
  6. If the project has some commercial worth, the award will be treated as venture capital funding and the BAA will expect some suitable return on the investment.
  7. The awards will be made to the project or projects which, in the opinion of the BAA Committee, are the most original, best further the aims of the BAA and will not be carried out in the absence of this funding.
  8. Submissions for project awards should be drawn up to include some budget, timescale and objectives.

The progress of the project will be monitored by the BAA committee and in many cases the funding will be released in stages as objectives are met.

Proposals for project awards should be made to the Projects Officer.

items.title: News from Sustaining Members
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 25

Compiled by Cathy Dargue

items.title: Mercia Software Ltd
items.text:
We have now completed two major development projects which extend the capabilities of STATGRAPHICS. A major U.K. oil company commissioned us to develop extensions to the Quality Control routine in STATGRAPHICS in order that the Q.C. methods conform with the new standards that the Ford Motor Company have issued to their suppliers. One of the world's largest chemical companies have for some time used a highly sophisticated CUSUM time series technique. This has now been fully integrated into STATGRAPHICS as a custom modification.

LOGOL, which is our new finished goods control system, has now been installed on a trial basis in two well-known companies. R.G. Brown, the author of the system, will be paying a visit to the U.K. shortly to hold a week's course on Materials Management, and also for discussions with Mercia about future developments to the system.

items.title: APL People Ltd
items.text:
Following the successful completion of a very large financial system for one of the major banks, we now plan to focus more on developing banking and treasury systems for clients, whilst still maintaining our existing consultancy services.

The APL Group's headquarters down in Bath is getting ready for another move - the present offices having become too cramped for all of us following the addition of Chris Cunnane, who has taken over from Jill Moss as Office Manager in Bath. Jill will now be concentrating on the employment agency side of the business, which is still expanding at an encouraging rate.

The new Sheffield office is now up and running, and with two very experienced salesmen working from it, sales of our engineering software packages in the Midlands have really taken off.

The work that APL Tran-Plan is carrying out on the now legendary Canary Wharf development in London's Docklands continues apace. There was one nasty moment when we thought the whole thing had been wound up when the original developer failed to get commitment on the funding of the project. However, literally at the eleventh hour, a new developer was found - who happens to be the biggest single real-estate owner in New York - and now it's all systems go!

items.title: Dyadic
items.text:
Dyadic has announced further details of its new version of Dyalog APL for Intel 80386-based computers.

Dyalog APL/386 is designed to run on a wide range of 80386-based PC AT-compatible personal computers, including those manufactured by Compaq, Wyse, Zenith, Olivetti, ITT and Texas Instruments. It will also run on IBM PC AT-compatible machines which have been 'turbocharged' with a 386 accelerator card.

Dyalog APL/386 is a full implementation of Dyalog APL, but one that is specially configured for personal computers; and it includes support for standard PC keyboards, monitors and printers.

Not only is it a full second-generation APL with nested arrays, but Dyalog APL/386 supports very large objects and workspaces, up to a theoretical limit of 4 gigabytes!

Dyalog APL/386 uses 32-bit native 80386 code, and therefore takes full advantage of the 386 processor. This means that performance of a 386-based PC running Dyalog APL/386 is comparable to far more expensive Motorola 68020-based APL systems. In some cases it is actually faster! Detailed benchmarks are available from Dyadic on request.

Dyalog APL/386 runs under SCO XENIX 386 System V Operating System which is available direct from Dyadic. In addition to supporting Dyalog APL, XENIX 386 provides a full 32-bit multi-user, multitasking environment; and unlike DOS, XENIX 386 releases the full potential of the Intel 80386 processor.

Dyalog APL/386 includes an interface to SCO CGI, a powerful device-independent graphics development system, which is packaged with Xenix. It also includes a workspace containing business graphics functions for producing graphs, histograms, pie-charts, titles and legends. The system supports standard PC displays, dot matrix printers, and other popular graphics devices.

Two important system extensions, SCO Multiview and SCO VP/ix, will soon be available and will be supported by Dyalog APL/386. Multiview is a combined multitasking windowing environment and user-friendly interface to Xenix. SCO VP/ix permits multiple DOS and XENIX applications to be run concurrently from the system console and on attached ASCII terminals. This means that all the benefits of speed, size and functionality of Dyalog APL/386 can be obtained without sacrificing the ability to run DOS applications.

In addition to Dyalog APL/386 and Xenix, Dyadic can also supply a 386 'Turbo' card. Final pricing had not been established at the time of going to press, but can now be obtained from Dyadic on request.

Dyalog APL/386 is the first of a new range of Dyalog APL implementations for personal computers. Other implementations for the IBM Personal System/2 under Xenix, AIX and OS/2 are also planned.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
MicroAPL is heavily committed to making the APL language more popular. As part of this drive, MicroAPL is making DRAMATIC PRICE REDUCTIONS on APL.68000 for the Apple Macintosh, Atari ST, and Commodore Amiga, with effect from 23rd September 1987. The price for all three implementations has been slashed to just £99.95 including VAT. This move, timed to coincide with the PCW Show, where MicroAPL had two stands, has been made in response to market research, which showed that many home computer users who do not know APL might be tempted to try the language if the price was around £100. The price reduction is part of an overall campaign aimed at non-APL users and involving press reviews, advertisements and exhibition appearances in Europe and the USA, and it follows MicroAPL's announcement in May of free run-time licences for APL.68000 on small machines.

Following Atari's launch of the new Mega ST, the price of high-performance APL has dropped dramatically. A full Mega ST system with a massive 4 Megabytes of RAM, 20 Megabytes of hard disc, a high-quality monochrome monitor, and APL.68000, costs well under £2000, and can even run the Mirage multi-user, multi-tasking operating system. This is the ideal APL machine for education, teaching, research, and even commercial use where IBM compatibility is not essential. Workspace size is nearly 4MB, and there are no object-size restrictions!

For its existing corporate APL customers, MicroAPL is pleased to announce an upgrade to APL.68000 for the IBM PC family, running under 68000 and 68020 coprocessors.

The new release includes very much improved full-screen function and variable editing, faster floating-point operations, an interface to the Halo graphics library, and improved STSC emulation. The 68020 version with 4 MB of memory is proving particularly popular for running VSAPL applications which are too big for APL*PLUS/PC.

For Spectrum and Aurora users, MicroAPL now has available a wide range of extra general-purpose software, including the Omnis database software, LISP, Prolog, and specialised vertical applications.

items.title: APL Impetus Ltd
items.text:
Although APL Impetus Ltd was formed only in July this year, when it was decided that 'Impetus' no longer fitted into Boeing's product strategy, the product has been used by customers for 18 months and the concept goes back to 1976 when TABAPL, its mainframe timesharing predecessor, was first marketed.

When the Impetus development was started in 1984, the challenge was to provide all the functionality of the mainframe product in a machine with only 640K memory. The successful result is based on APL*PLUS/PC, enhanced by 30 or so assembler routines for such crucial activities as formatting, scrolling and panning, and displaying without snow on colour and shaded monitors.

Demonstration diskettes are available for consultants and users who would like to know more about this alternative, APL-based, approach to solving those complex modelling problems which are beyond the scope of spreadsheets.

items.title: Cocking and Drury Ltd
items.text:
Quality control is an important part of software product development, and Cocking and Drury are pleased to be heavily involved in the Beta-testing of new releases of APL*PLUS PC and Statgraphics. As STSC's sole UK distributor, Cocking and Drury have agreed new terms for Academic Site Licences, from which their academic customers will soon benefit. The recent upsurge in APL*PLUS PC sales is seen by the company as an encouraging sign for the future of APL.

On the mainframe side, Cocking and Drury is currently developing two major new Auxiliary Processors for use with their APL*PLUS mainframe product; one is an interface to DB/2 and the other is for access to Oracle.

The course business continues to expand; the company's System Design course has been on offer for some years, and although very favourably received it has not enjoyed great popularity until recently. In the last five months Cocking and Drury have given five in-house System Design courses. Overseas courses are becoming more frequent, and the availability of portable lightweight hardware makes courses outside the London area very attractive.

Although Cocking and Drury are happy to work on short projects, most of their consultancy revenue now comes from large projects; in 1978 about 70% of the revenue came from jobs between £2,000 and £5,000 in size, whereas in 1986 over 30% came from projects exceeding the £100,000 mark. In the same year only 3% came from the £2-5,000 range.

Cocking and Drury's recent hirings include Kevin Ryall and Sylvia Kahl, both of whom have a couple of years APL experience; Kevin on mainframes and micros, and Sylvia mainly on PCs. Christian Jensen also joins as a graduate trainee. Christian has moved from Denmark to continue his APL career here in the UK. Harry Casely-Hayford has come to Cocking and Drury for his technical training year, from North Staffordshire Polytechnic.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Adrian Smith

A VECTOR is variously defined as 'a quantity with both length and direction'; 'the course of an aircraft or missile'; 'a carrier of disease or infection'. So far we have managed a fair length (13 issues and still going), and I hope we are beginning to set some kind of course. What we have not yet done is to carry the disease to those not already infected. VECTOR is still circulated largely within the ranks of the BAA, and if anything our print runs are coming down.

I feel that as Editor, I am under pressure to move the journal in two diametrically opposite ways; do we go 'Quote-quad' and try for technical excellence and APL 'whizz-bangs', or do we go 'Education' and 'APLication' to spread the word beyond the inner circle of APL cognoscenti? Are we principally here as a service to the existing membership, or are we a vehicle for converting the masses?

In general the membership survey rated technical articles, software reviews, and application articles as the best items we do. The notes on meetings are seen to be a problem; the most interesting talks are invariably the ones where there is no written paper, or the material diverges so far from it that the paper would be of little relevance to readers.

Here is what we (the working group) intend to do. I cannot pretend that we have all the answers, but at least if we set out our stall in public we can hope for some feedback from our current readership!

items.title: Format and Layout
items.text:
We do not see the need for any major changes here. In particular we propose to ...

  • stay A5, and retain the current cover design.
  • ensure APL code is big enough to read easily!
  • try to find an APL typeface that sits naturally with our normal text face, and standardise on it for all APL code.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
We would like to move towards more regular 'slots' as a way of giving the journal a clearer structure that readers will be able to anticipate and become accustomed to.

  • Product Guide and Public Domain Software Library to continue every issue in its present form. Addresses of overseas associations to be carried every issue, in compressed format.
  • a 'Software Workshop', typically covering a related set of primitives, or programming technique in around 2 pages. Examples could be: quad-FX, encode and decode, PC windows, Laser printers and how to drive them. A technically proficient member of the group would either write these himself, or vet and select from submitted material.
  • part of the above could be a 'Dr Solomon's' column of helpful hints to bemused readers.
  • some regular columnists, selected for their ability to write English rather than APL.
  • regular reviews of both hardware and software. We shall also keep up the Press Review.
  • 'APL Programmers at Work'. A series of interviews, slanted to reveal how we really do the job.
  • other languages ... BASIC, Pascal, C, Macro, HP plotters etc.

There will also be the occasional 'theme' issue, e.g. Education. However we think it would be a mistake to try for a theme every issue ... this would be giving far too many hostages to fortune as regards getting enough of the right copy! We will commission articles well in advance from known experts in the field; a bundle of VECTORs should be bribe enough!

items.title: Summary
items.text: We are aiming for a bit more structure, a guaranteed technical slot of high quality, and a bit more readability. The format and general tone will continue to be much the same as now.

items.title: Addendum
items.text:
On the sore subject of timing! This VECTOR is roughly 4 months late, and has suffered the additional embarrassment of being overtaken by 4.3! Firstly, I would like to apologise to frustrated readers, and to even more frustrated advertisers. In mitigation, I would say that we now have a much improved production method, typically reducing the lead time on material from an absolute minimum of 12 weeks down to as little as a week.

VECTOR 4.3 was begun in anger just before Christmas (Dec 17th I think). Two of us worked on it fairly solidly for one day, and one morning. It rested untouched over the bulk of the holiday, and was finally assembled (along with Dave Weatherby's review and Graham Parkhouse's article which arrived around Dec 29th) for dispatch to the printers on Jan 6th. Copies were available for distribution by January 15th, and a parcel did make it to Sydney in time for APL88.

In other words I believe we now have a Journal that we can sustain without a killing amount of work, or absurdly long-range deadlines on copy. VECTOR 4.4 will be out on time, and VECTOR 5.1 is roughed out. As long as I am running this beast, and as long as I continue to get the support and help of the VECTOR Working Group, it will not be late again.

items.title: Submitting Material to VECTOR
items.text:
I occasionally dare to open 4.1 round about page 123; it is awful!! Please, please ignore what we said there ... if you have something to say then say it. I don't care if it is on scratty bits of paper, or in the most stylish of typesetting. If it is worth saying and is fit to print then we will jolly well print it!

The ideal is plain ASCII text on PC disk (5 inch or 3 inch are fine). Wordstar documents are OK, and if you have MS Word that would be wonderful! APL code is best printed separately ... FX80 quality is actually quite good (but do put a new ribbon in), otherwise daisywheel or laser are fine if you can do it.

If you don't have a PC, but can produce really good copy from a mainframe system (see Norman Thomson's 'Knapsack' in this issue) then inch margins at each side, 2 inches at the top and 1.2 at the bottom would be ideal. Otherwise we will do a bit of 'shrink to fit' on the copier, which degrades the image a bit (and takes time to do), but is infinitely better than the alternative of resetting the whole article. At least you know that the only typos are your own! Use a biggish font (remember that the result will be halved from A4 to A5 at the final printing stage) and generous line spacing. Do a trial run and reduce it down ... then hold the result up against an old copy of VECTOR to see the effect. The closer you can get the happier we will be!

items.title: Outline of Forthcoming Issues
items.text:
VECTOR 4.4 is basically a conference special. Several VECTOR stalwarts made the trip to Sydney, and I have every confidence that they are even now beavering away at their respective keyboards.

VECTOR 5.1 is a special issue on 'interfaces'. We intend to cover the links between APL systems and (for example) Oracle databases on Vax, C programs on the PC, HP plotters, electronic balances, and mainframe databases such as DB2. It is a wide open field - if there is something you know about which fits under this umbrella, then give me a call and book your slot now!

items.title: The Education Vector
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 31

by Norman Thomson

The first APL clear workspace, called CLEANSPACE, came to life in November 1966, and today in APL2, you can still:

)LOAD 1 CLEANSPACE

to which the reply is

SAVED 1966-11-27 23:53:59

21 years later, as APL comes of age, it is appropriate to look back and view it in the context of the education/technology lag whereby today's development becomes after a lapse of time enshrined in tomorrow's curriculum. 21 years ago APL was an off-beat program harboured within the confines of IBM's Yorktown Research Laboratory. Today, as was demonstrated at the Winchester course in July, APL systems twice as versatile can be carried around on a floppy disc and immediately brought to life on a sundry assortment of computers anywhere in the world.

The Winchester course is adequately reported elsewhere in these pages - as a tutor it stimulated recollections of my own first introduction to APL some 16 years ago, when in order to conduct a course with on-line demonstrations, the entire computing service of a major University had to be suspended during the periods when lectures were taking place. APL itself resided on a disc file about the size of a small dustbin, and the University computer required a system IPL to bring even the single terminal to life. The idea of practical sessions was quite absurd.

As the wheels of technology turn, the phases of development will undoubtedly be repeated as the educational part of the cycle comes round. In particular, one recalls the difficulties inherent in APL's special requirements - keyboards, golfballs, EPROMs and so on - and these or similar hurdles will be surmounted anew as I-APL brings the language into the arena of the home and school micro. Already we see some of the first excitement of APL being relived by the teachers and students for whom it has now become affordable, and this will undoubtedly ensure that these hurdles will be overcome, and that APL will become a feature without which a school or college micro is quite unacceptable.

There is nevertheless a danger that the excitement remains within a closed group of enthusiasts, and it is still as vital as ever for members of the Association to be outward-looking and bring others into the fold. Keep in mind the "Please Tell a Teacher" slogan used recently in a VECTOR insert. A mention of APL, however trivial, can be crucially important, since human nature contrives that on first hearing about a new idea, the name is mentally filed but nothing is done. It is the second mention from an independent source that triggers action.

At the last Committee meeting Val Lusmore undertook to compile a list of "mentors" spread around the country who would be willing to act as advice support centres for teachers, and perhaps make visits to introduce APL to schools and colleges. Would members who are prepared to have their names added to this list please contact Val at APL People, 17 Barton Street, Bath BA1 1HQ. Act now, while it is on your mind. You determine your own level of commitment, and you could find such contacts highly satisfying.

A final news item comes from the City University, where a 3-hour Lab session on APL is incorporated into the M.Sc. course on Information Engineering. It is an open-ended activity in which there are no formal lectures, but students explore simple examples with the help of an instruction manual. It is good to hear of still more courses which have an APL content.

items.title: A Report on the Winchester Summer Course on APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 32

by Pauline Hawkes

'APL is the language for mathematicians'. 'If you have to communicate with computers, choose the language you use with care'. 'Why go on using steam engines when the electric motor is to hand?' Remarks like these, and being married to a dedicated APL user, made me want to know more. When I learnt that an APL course for teachers was to be run at King Alfred's College, Winchester, I grasped the opportunity gratefully. The course was sponsored by the British APL Association with the intention of helping to spread the use of the language, which is still almost unknown among teachers, even after 20 years, to large numbers of young people in schools, colleges and at home.

This will be made very much easier with the release of I-APL this year. This is a public domain interpreter which should run on a wide variety of small microcomputers of the kind typically found in schools and in the home, such as the BBC, Atari, Spectrum, etc. The only cost to the user will be the price of a disc and some documentation. You will be able to make as many copies as you like. However, there is still the task of convincing teachers.

Few people in schools and colleges have even heard of APL, and the reaction of most of those who have is 'Oh, yes, it is a very mathematical language.Too many symbols for us, we need something more practical that can be used in business studies or science, etc.'. Well, it is excellent for doing mathematics and this should be encouraged. However, it has a much wider application, and is used particularly for important decision support systems in most of our major companies, where an odd symbol never shows its face. This kind of use should also be brought home to teachers and pupils, but using a rather different approach through practical case studies using supplied software.

Thus it was that I found myself, one of fourteen people from the world of education, in delightful surroundings which I would have loved to explore. However, the intensity of the four-day course, which went on late into the evenings, permitted little respite. It was reminiscent of cramming for finals. Fourteen proved to be a reasonable number in terms of getting to know each other and the level of supervision the course tutors were able to offer. A larger group would certainly have had severe hardware problems. Despite the small number there was an amazing variety of teachers from public and comprehensive schools, a tertiary college, sixth form college, college of higher education, a university and polytechnics. Also there were two people from county education advisory services, one in mathematics and one in computing. Geographically we came from as far afield as Newcastle and Swansea as well as the home counties. Mostly we were mathematicians with only limited computing experience, or computer specialists with limited mathematical training. The few well versed in both disciplines survived the best and astounded the rest by how much could be achieved in such a short space of time with such a powerful tool as APL.

The team of tutors, led by Norman Thomson, consisted of John Durran and Anthony Camacho, supported by his wife Sylvia. The course was primarily aimed at the use of APL in teaching mathematics, although some felt they would have liked more emphasis on uses in teaching other subjects. The presence of guest speakers Paul Barnetson, Matt Taub and Mike Kingston from IBM was very welcome, and it was particularly interesting to hear about applications in business and engineering, such as analysing customer files, costing the construction of a housing development, and the problems of magnetic coatings on tapes and discs. A versatile language indeed! The lecturers were excellent and their enthusiasm infectious. The support they gave each other was admirable: team teaching at its best.

Perhaps some of us were as sceptical as our colleagues when we first arrived. However, after a memorable four days we shall never be quite the same again. At times we felt a bit overwhelmed by the intensity of the course, the power and breadth of a language which can achieve so much so concisely and with such elegance. An important factor for us was to discover that APL has an intellectual attraction, and it is fun. What better recommendation for its use in education? Why struggle with the one-step-at-a-time complexities of BASIC, PASCAL, COBOL etc., which are usually matters of boring, trivial detail, when the power, logic and eloquence of APL is at hand? APL has sparked off a new interest and enthusiasm for computing in those of us who had previously found computing dull.

Lectures and two excellent videos were interspersed with exercise sessions, although the latter proved too short for most of us. We will have more sympathy for our own students in future when they fail to complete their assignments on time. The exercises needed to be more carefully graded. It is difficult to cope with unusual new symbols and concepts while trying to solve fairly hard mathematical problems. We needed a lot of simple problems at first to boost our confidence in assimilating the APL vocabulary and grammar. The overall effect was a little too much detail too fast for most of us to master confidently. It is clear that some of us should have studied more thoroughly the tutorial notes sent to us beforehand; however this had not always been possible. We felt also that it would have been useful to have some discussion about uses in the classroom.

The course achieved its main purpose of giving us a broad feel of APL in a short space of time and encouraging us to go away and learn more. The documentation supplied was excellent and will keep us going for quite some time. In varying degrees we were all converted to APL, and while I doubt if many of us would rush off and immediately start teaching a course ourselves, most of us now feel inclined to encourage the introduction of APL into our own educational environments. One young lady will be able to do so using an old but working IBM 5110, donated by the Decision Analysis Unit at LSE, which she won for her establishment by an eloquent plea on their behalf. The rest of us eagerly look forward to getting our I-APL interpreter. The only real criticism concerned the hardware. The variety of machines and especially the keyboards, some incorrectly labelled with APL symbols, caused quite a bit of difficulty, while one machine per person would have been ideal.

The advent of GCSE makes this an ideal time to introduce APL into schools. The investigative approach encouraged in these new examinations is ideally suited to the use of APL for experimenting with mathematical ideas and for the ease with which statistical data can be explored. One course member, a computer scientist, was a little worried that APL would encourage bad habits, i.e. programming at the keyboard and the 'try it and see' approach. Mathematicians, on the other hand, would see this as one of the attractions! It is quite simply the best way to do mathematics on a computer, and is a potential motivator in the classroom as well as enabling self-taught high achievers to go a long way. The statistics student can explore in detail real data instead of performing routine calculations on artificially simplified data. A big advantage is that APL has a very low threshold, which should enable even quite young children to do something interesting. And yet it also has a very high ceiling which provides a challenge to the highest intellect.

In conclusion, I would like to express the grateful thanks of the participants to the BAA, those behind the development of I-APL, and above all the course lecturers for all the hard work that went into introducing us to APL in a style and at a price we could afford. I hope that similar courses will be run at other locations around the country, perhaps with the formation of local interest groups. If the new 'freeware' interpreter can be made available in significant numbers, and with the right promotion, I expect that, as with the BASIC expansion, the children will soon leave the teachers far behind. We wish the project every success.

Pauline Hawkes

Swansea Tertiary College

VECTOR's exclusive APL Product Guide aims to provide readers with useful information about sources of APL hardware, software and services. We welcome any comments readers may have on its usefulness and any suggestions for improvements.

We do depend on the alacrity of suppliers to keep us informed about their products so that we can update the Guide for each issue of VECTOR. Any suppliers who are not included in the Guide should contact me to get their free entry - see address below.

We reserve the right to edit material supplied for reasons of space or to ensure a fair market coverage.

The listings are not restricted to UK companies and international suppliers are welcome to take advantage of these pages. Where no UK distributor has yet been appointed, the vendor should indicate whether this is imminent or whether approaches for representation by existing companies are welcomed.
