items.title: From Dyadic Systems …
items.text:
From: Peter Donnelly11th April 1988

Thank you for your interesting review of Dyalog APL in VECTOR 4.2. I would like to make one or two comments about the article, which your readers might find informative.

  1. Dyadic chose Unix because it offered portability, speed, multi-user support and unlimited memory. Just the things for an effective APL environment. I agree with you that there is resistance to Unix, but there is always resistance to change, particularly when so many vested interests are involved. Today, virtually all of the major hardware developments in computing (RISC, parallel architecture, vector-processors) are Unix based. In my opinion, DP managers who choose to ignore Unix are paying through the nose for their MIPS!

    Yes, DEC may continue to ‘lock users in’ with VMS, but Hewlett-Packard, NCR and Unisys are firmly committed to Unix, as is IBM. IBM recently claimed that it spends as much time on its Unix product AIX, as on any other of its operating systems, and underlined its long-term Unix strategy with the announcement of the ‘AIX Family Definition’ in parallel with SAA.

  2. You certainly don’t like out editor, do you! Rightly or wrongly, Dyadic decided to emulate the standard Unix editor ‘vi’. This has the advantage that users only have to learn one set of editor commands; not one set for APL and another for the rest of the system. I agree that ‘vi’ can be difficult at first, but like many other powerful tools (e.g. APL?) it more than repays the effort of learning. Lots of our users swear by at.

  3. We too can provide instantaneous screen response. Dyalog APL/386 on an IBM PS/2 Model-80 or a Compaq-386 is every bit as fast as APL*PLUS/PC in terms of screen handling. The particular screens you used in your evaluation are also instantaneous when used in full-screen or graphics mode. They are however comparatively slow at scrolling. I expect that this was your problem.

  4. I have to disagree with you about the error trapping. Having used many different versions of APL I am convinced that Dyalog APL’s error trapping is more powerful and easier to use than any other I have encountered.

    For example ⎕TRAP←9 'E' '→ERR'

    means that if a DOMAIN ERROR occurs in my function, the program will branch to ERR. Surely that’s simple enough!

    If I say ⎕TRAP←0 'C' '→ERR'

    it means that if any error occurs in a function called by this one, the stack will be ‘cut back’ automatically to here before executing the branch.

    Using these two cases in combination, you can quite simply set up very comprehensive error handling, without having to resort to complex lexical analysis of ⎕DM.

    Dyalog APL also has ⎕SIGNAL, which is very similar to ⎕ERROR, but that’s all that’s needed for error-handling. There is no heap of obscure ⎕FNS.

  5. We introduced ⎕NR because a vector of text vectors is so much easier to handle than either a matrix or a line-list. We retained ⎕CR and ⎕VR for compatibility with the ISO standard, and with other APLs.

  6. Really Adrian, there are only 54 system functions, variables and constants in Dyalog APL (including 20 for the component file system) compared with 144 (a gross) in APL*PLUS/PC. I don’t think it is Dyadic who should be accused of taking the ⎕KITCHENSINK approach!

  7. Yes, you’re partly right about modified assignment. Everyone who uses Dyalog APL (including myself) falls over the same thing, i.e. that the ‘pass through’ values of modified assignment is the thing on the right, not the result of the assignment. The problem is that what is theoretically correct is (initially at least) intuitively wrong. Incidentally, we were not the first to implement this feature; Burroughs APL had it too.

  8. You will be please to know that since your evaluation, we have enhanced our graphics APs to take full advantage of nested arrays. Basically, the output functions now accept nested arguments so you can draw more than one object at a time. This means that you can avoid writing loops, so your graphics applications run faster. The most complex of the demo charts you tried is now calculated and displayed in under 3 seconds.

  9. I am glad you liked our interface to Oracle. This seems to be very popular with users. As you noted, you can improve on the standard database management facilities by writing your own tools in APL. Several of our users have already done so, and one customer has even built a fully relational IC1 look-alike.

Finally, a note on performance. The IBM 6150 Model 20 you were using was superseded last year by the model 125. This is 2 - 4 times faster than the old model, and outperforms the Sun 3/140.

Yours sincerely

Peter DonnellyOperations Manager, Dyadic Systems LtdPark House, The High Street,Alton, Hampshire GU34 1EN

items.title: Dyalog APL on the IBM 6151: A Reply
items.text:
From: Allan Prys-Williams8th April 1988

As someone who has been using this system in workstation mode for eighteen months now, perhaps I could be allowed to expand on Adrian Smith’s review in Vector 4.2. Obviously, my view is coloured by my coming to this system from mainframe rather than PC use, but I thought that his review was unfairly critical in some ways, while missing one or two actual problems.
path: Technical Correspondence (Sullivan; Piper; Hayward; Bykerk; Donnelly; Prys-Williams)

items.title: Unix
items.text:
Obviously, any system that gives real flexibility to the user is going to frighten DP managers, but the AIX implementation is already based on a hierarchy of users.

  • The superuser can do anything, but no-one logs in as superuser except for specific purposes. It is too dangerous even for the administrator to use routinely.
  • The system group can do many things that are fairly dangerous, such as altering the status of printers. On my system, I normally work within this group. On a DP-manager-friendly system, most commands would be moved to have this restriction, and only the managers would belong to it.
  • Ordinary users only need a very small set of commands, especially if their profile causes them to wake up in APL. On my system I have a ‘demo’ user configured so that colleagues can try things out without causing any damage.

I have to say that every time I find myself on e.g. a DEC mainframe I can’t wait to get back to UNIX. Only, don’t let yourself get posted as the superuser of any UNIX system that doesn’t have explicit superuser’s manuals. UNIX provides a friendly environment for ordinary users by loading all the awkward bits onto the superuser, which can be terrifying. The IBM6150/1 has good manuals, but the Cadmus I was on before had not.
path: Technical Correspondence (Sullivan; Piper; Hayward; Bykerk; Donnelly; Prys-Williams)

items.title: Editors
items.text: The ‘vi’ editor is pretty horrible, but the really good full-screen editor and file manager provided within AIX – ‘INed’ – is not compatible with APL as it uses the ‘alt’ key to control editing functions. Indeed, if you start this up after running APL from the console, it won’t work at all. In practice, I have found that using the full-screen cut and paste functions in the session manager, combined with the del-editor, is excellent for generating new functions, as you can test code in bits and then capture it into the function. Vi works rather well for documenting things and going through changing names of variables and things like that, so one ends up using both. Many of the session-managing keys work within vi, though the manual omits to say so. At least I have been able to give up using things like ‘///4 A’ and other del-incantations.
path: Technical Correspondence (Sullivan; Piper; Hayward; Bykerk; Donnelly; Prys-Williams)

items.title: The APL
items.text:
External variables are marvellous. Of course, they are only high-class component files (as you find out if the system goes down at the wrong moment) but they have the tremendous virtue of transparency. For database work, I can develop the system using just basic APL and then convert any variables that are going to be changing, into external variables of the same name. These are then sharable; backed up independently; enable me to keep the workspace absolutely fixed; and I don’t need to know where (exactly) everything is. It is also, in emergency, trivial to bring them back into the workspace as standard variables (a single left-arrow does it) when they can be hacked around ad. lib.

The ⎕KITCHENSINK comment is really an attack on the documentation. The different ways of representing a function all do non-trivially different things, but you have to work out the crucial differences for yourself. Personally, I find that the presence of minority-interest goodies makes it much easier to get help from Dyadic over the phone at the practically important level of things like interfacing with Unix files or printers.
path: Technical Correspondence (Sullivan; Piper; Hayward; Bykerk; Donnelly; Prys-Williams)

items.title: Windows
items.text:
In workstation mode, it is practical to have separate full-screen windows open on several different jobs (the operating system for when something goes wrong; the APL under development; the editor for writing it up; a routine data-handling job that has to be done at the same time) and flip between them. This makes it practical to document what you are doing as you do it, instead of as an afterthought. Not only does this save a lot of hassle near deadlines, but you get new insights by trying to explain to an unknown reader what you are up to, and then just flip back to the APL window to try them out. The INed editor allows windows into 3 or 4 files at once with text capture from one to another.

Conversely, it is most desirable to run APL in a window, not the main screen, so that you haven’t disabled the alt-keys when you run your next Unix application. You can even run APL inside the mouse-driven Usability Services shell, though I find point-and-grunt systems dreadfully slow.

Personally, I have only noticed delayed response when the machine is definitely busy elsewhere (multi-tasking plus a virtual system means that you can run monstrous background jobs while thinking what to do next). This is a function of a single chip doing many jobs, and as the 386 machines come in even PC users are going to have to get used to it. Certainly the Prefect full-screen I/O utilities run with exemplary efficiency, with the only delays being caused by heavy data-crunching.
path: Technical Correspondence (Sullivan; Piper; Hayward; Bykerk; Donnelly; Prys-Williams)

items.title: But…
items.text:
There are quite a few I/O problems. While direct communication with the Proprinter is exemplary for sending character arrays, capturing APL session output is hairy. If you split the output to a monitor file (the standard Unix technique) the result doesn’t have carriage returns at the end of lines and tends to print continuously across the page. Personally I use monitored material inside files sent to the ‘mm’ word-processing package, which gives full pagination and scope to comment, as well as eliminating unprintable characters and adding CRs, but this is the sort of elaboration that gets Unix buffs a bad name.

Similarly, the console doesn’t act as an APL terminal at all. If you view a file with APL characters, they aren’t translated. So if you have a monitor file going, all you get is ASCII on the screen and no session-manager. A terminal emulator is supposed to be on the way, but it will be just my luck if it works splendidly with the VT100 emulator, but not with basic paging through a file.
path: Technical Correspondence (Sullivan; Piper; Hayward; Bykerk; Donnelly; Prys-Williams)

items.title: Summing Up
items.text:
My unimproved workstation is vastly better than the University’s new Pyramid mainframe with umpteen MIPS (and no slower, in real life) and I will fight anybody to keep it, but some of its idiosyncrasies seem to demand a dedicated user. However, this also applies to every PC I’ve ever observed.

Allan Prys-WilliamsDepartment of Management Science and StatisticsUniversity of WalesSwansea.

items.title: Hacker’s Corner: a little bit of C
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 102

by Adrian Smith

This little program might help you to see how the other half lives! It will take almost anything, and output a file suitable for Word; to my amazement it even ate Allan Gay's piece, which came as an APL component file! It runs in about 5 sec for a typical article.

/****************************************************************************/
/* tf.c   April 1988   by Adrian Smith                                      */
/* Basic text filter ... passes any input file out to STDOUT having ...     */
/*   - ensured CR/LF pairs (to deal with APL quad-edit vectors)             */
/*   - stripped high bits from WordStar output                              */
/*   - removed white space (including all spaces at the end of paragraphs)  */
/*   - made tabs into visible | characters. Word can always put them back!  */
/****************************************************************************/
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

main(argc,argv)     int argc; char *argv[];

{ FILE *fp;
  int ch, in, cr = 13, lf = 10, tab = 9, bl = 0, np = 0;

  if (argc != 2)  {printf("Please use: tf file[>outfile]\n"); exit(1); }

  fp = fopen(argv[1],"rb");                       /* open for binary read     */
  if (!fp) { printf("Can't open file '%s'\n",argv[1]); exit(1); }

  while ((in = fgetc(fp)) != EOF)                 /* Process whole file       */
    {
      ch = toascii(in);                           /* Strip high bits (WStar)  */
      if (ch == lf);                              /* Forget linefeeds         */
        else if (ch == cr)                        /* CR/LF pair               */
         { if (np)                                /*  ... 2nd in a row        */
             { putchar('\n'); np=0; bl=0; }       /*      gives new para.     */
           else
             { np=1; bl=1; }                      /*  ... get ready for para  */

         }
       else if (ch == ' ') bl = 1;                /* Kill multiple blanks     */
       else
         { if (ch == tab) { ch = '|'; bl=0; }     /* Leave recognisable tabs  */
           if (ch == 96) ch = '\'';               /* Dispose of back quotes   */
           if (bl) putchar(' ');                  /* Output pending blank     */
           if (ch > 32) putchar(ch);              /* Ignore control chars     */
           bl=0; np=0;                            /* Output, and kill flags   */
         }
    }
  putchar('\n');                                  /* Finish off               */
} /*=========================== THE END ===================================*/
path: Hacker’s Corner: a little bit of C

items.title: Duplicate rows idiom
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 103

From: Peter Branson, 19th May 1988

May I thank Bob Bykerk for the first paragraph of his letter in VECTOR 4.4 about removing all duplicated rows in a matrix. Not only is his idiom more elegant than the one in my letter (VECTOR 4.2), but its simplicity makes it easier to remember. Perhaps more important, it is very much more efficient, and runs some 25 times faster under VS APL.

Here is one example of why it is worth publishing not-so-good code - it helps turn up something better!

Of course with hindsight it is obvious, but I always find that the trouble with hindsight is that it never seems to be available at the times when you really need it!

Peter Branson

items.title: General Correspondence
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 11

The VECTOR working group welcomes correspondence on any topic affecting the APL community. All letters should be addressed to the Editor, and should indicate whether they are for the general or technical section. (Letters containing APL code will normally be classed as 'technical'.) The editor reserves the right to edit any letter unless the writer states that it is to be published in full or not at all.

items.title: Re: letters published in VECTOR 4.2
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 11

From: Mark Cranny, 18th May 1988

After they had sat on my desk for several weeks, I finally got round to reading editions 4.2 and 4.3 of VECTOR, and was so amazed at some of the correspondence in 4.2 that I felt the need to stop revising and put pen to paper - or finger to keyboard even.

The first letter was from Dick Bowman claiming that APL goes further than any 4GL in that it is far more flexible. He mentions ADRS, yet doesn’t seem to make the connection between APL and 4GLs. In several issues of VECTOR, there have been full-page adverts for IC/1, which IBM has consistently refused to market as a 4GL, preferring to call it an “integrated multifunction center environment”, yet by the traditional criteria for a 4GL it certainly is one:

non-procedural (menu driven) database query language input validation routines / tables report generator financial planning/analysis facility graphics facility complete application generation facilities interfaces to other systems (OS, DBMS, TP etc.)

For the uninitiated, IC/1 is ADRS II the reporting system, APLDI the APL data interface, ADRS/BG business graphics, FPS II financial planning and APE (application prototyping environment) all thrown together and called IC/1. It emerged from Sweden, was taken over by the Americans when 4GLs first started to become fashionable, and when it didn’t take off was handed back to the Swedes to continue to support and develop (probably after causing quite a lot of damage). IC/1 allows rapid or evolutionary prototyping to take place, with its own inbuilt indexed sequential filing system, or it can act as a front end to other DBMSs such as SQL/DS. The ADRS sections of code provide the reporting and data-validation capabilities, and APE allows screen design for interface creation. The graphics facility is probably the weakest part of the package, and is certainly nowhere near as well developed as the graphics of IBM’s flagship 4GL, Application System (AS). IC/1 is far from being the best 4GL available, but the ideas are there, and (as estate agents are fond of saying) it has potential.

I completely agree with Mr Bowman that current 4GLs only go part of the way to presenting effective application generation, but IC/1-type environments give the best of both worlds: a non-procedural language for fast prototyping, but also the ability to get out of the menus and to get to the actual source code that the package is written in, allowing complete customisation of the application to fit the design requirements. Maybe a future development could be that when an application is completed, all internal documentation and unused functions could be erased to save space, and then the code compiled to create the finished production workspace, only being recompiled after updates and system changes to the original development workspace. Perhaps the “sustaining members” of the BAA are already developing advanced APL tools along these lines?

I first came into contact with APL at university, but it was not until I worked for IBM for an industrial experience year that I really started to use APL and its associated products, such as IC/1. At first I couldn’t understand why IC/1 was not successfully marketed by (probably) the best marketing organisation in the world. However, I think there can be only one conclusion - IBM doesn’t want to market products like IC/1 when it can market the more glamorous AS. As with DB2, IBM tries to get customers interested in AS and then informs them that it needs their biggest and most powerful boxes in order to run it.

There was also a letter from Richard Connor, who claimed that:

“One of APL’s great virtues is that its effective use doesn’t require technical knowledge of computers and software. It is an excellent language for the end-user.”

Of all that I have read about APL, this has to be the biggest load of horse s**t I have come across. Yes, APL is a powerful tool when hidden behind interfaces such as ADI, but Mr Connor seems to be suggesting that end-users get down to the nitty-gritty in raw APL code. I’d love to know what he does for a living, and what experiences he has had of end-user computing! I spent 13 months actually sitting next to the people who were using the systems I had designed, and several that I inherited and had to maintain. It was difficult enough to get users to use IBM’s PROFS office system (based around PF keys), let alone get them to accept a programming language per se.

One particular user had a habit of leaning backwards and hitting me over the back of the head whenever something went wrong or there was something he didn’t understand. If he had been given raw APL to use as an analysis tool I should have had to wear a crash-helmet! There are many computer-illiterate people out there with a very real fear of the keyboard, and if the BAA has been spending its time over the years trying to encourage those people to use APL in its raw form, and not as completed applications, then it is not surprising that APL is still pretty much a dead duck. APLers seem to expect everyone else in the computer world to share their enthusiasm for the aesthetic qualities of the language: in the real world people just want to see results, or to have effective and straightforward end-user tools made available to them.

Barrie Webster’s letter contained an accurate insight into the current position and problems of APL - the language has just not been sold, and has always had the image of being a mathematician’s toy. If 4GLs written in APL were actively marketed, then users could be introduced to the power of APL without realising it, but the facility to go further and to get more involved with the source code would be there if required.

I am constantly surprised when I discover yet another company who use APL - Midland Bank, British Airways, IBM etc - and yet the language still accounts for only a minute proportion of all systems development. It is this business community which needs educating as to the benefits of APL, rather than schoolchildren. Companies have too much investment in COBOL to rewrite their complete applications portfolio in another language, especially one that is also a 60s love-child. However, a move towards prototyping in APL can be encouraged: after all, C started to be more widely used as a result of Unix, so why not use the 4GL environment as a vehicle to get APL more widely accepted?

Commercial organisations are interested in the business advantages to be gained (increased speed of development, flexibility of design, reduced maintenance costs etc.), and at what cost, not how pretty or elegant the code is! Maybe the powers that be in the BAA could “encourage” Computing or Computer Weekly to give a couple of pages over to articles looking into the pros and cons of APL. If APL doesn’t move with the 4GL environment, it will remain with an ever-decreasing band of enthusiasts.

After leaving IBM and returning to college to finish my degree in systems analysis, I joined the BAA in order to keep up with developments in APL. I think that I am addicted to the language, in that I enjoy using it more than any other 3GL I have come across, but I am not a disciple or APL bigot. The BAA have been the Jehovah’s Witnesses of the computer world for too long; when a member of the APL True and Faithful puts their foot in the door of a disbeliever, and starts talking about dyadic iotas and Atomic Vectors, who can blame them for switching off? As a business computing person, I will use any tool necessary to achieve efficient and cost-effective results, and I am not brainwashed to the extent that I see APL as the ultimate systems cure-all. However, I do think that its power has been completely overlooked and underestimated by the business community. The power of APL is there provided it is implemented with good in-house standards for readability and maintainability, prototyping and documenting tools.

The BAA has the image of a group of mathematicians masquerading as computer professionals; developing ever more intricate and useless utilities for other computer scientists. I would suggest that the business-minded members of the BAA form a breakaway party to concentrate on promoting the business advantages of APL, and leave the academics to argue over whatever they want to argue over. However, in light of what has happened to the SDP, maybe that is not such a good idea?!

I would love to see APL become a popular and widely-used language, but to be honest, I don’t think it ever will.

Yours in deepest perspiration (exams only 2 weeks away)

Mark Cranny Dept for Business Systems Analysis City University, London

P.S. E J Sargeants’s letter suggesting an APL-based calculator was a joke, wasn’t it?

items.title: Public Letter to P Chapman
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 14

From: F.H.D. von Batenburg, 3rd May 1988

This month I received my copy of I-APL, and was impressed by what is distributed for just £11. I got a comprehensive language manual by Garry Helzer, describing all the functions clearly with just the right amount of examples to illustrate them. There was also an attractive tutorial by Linda Alvord and Norman Thomson, and a (fortunately) small technical manual.

A small disappointment was the print quality of the language manual, which was in dot-matrix format (granted in a not-too-bad NLQ font, but ugly nevertheless); a pity that this could not be printed on the same laser as the other booklets were.

I consider it a small miracle that Paul Chapman (and his sup-porters) developed such an interpreter in less than a year, and I hope this product will achieve what it set out to do: distributing the gospel of APL. As for myself, I certainly intended to help distributing it to my students, and by starting to write some regular series in Atari and PC magazines.

So I put the floppy in the drive, typed in “IAPL /C” (a character generator for all graphics cards was provided too!!), and in response to the first 5 spaces I typed “[10T]10” and .... a VALUE ERROR was my reward. Then I discovered that the character set is distributed over the various keys in a new way. Although the JOT is still Shift-J (after pressing [INSERT] however), most of the other characters were not in their familiar places. The next 5 minutes showed an heroic struggle to find all the familiar symbols in order to get some simple expressions done.

items.title: Problem
items.text:
This brings forward the point I wish to make. I wholeheartedly support the I-APL project and I hope that it will attract new adepts for APL, but if the character set is not brought into line with the standard keyboard quickly, I think it will seriously hamper the project.

In the discussions about I-APL it was often stated that compatibility with standard APL was of utmost priority. For that reason I read that fractional replicate was removed because it would frustrate any user who might upgrade to a commercial APL. That decision, although painful, was a sensible thing to do.

items.title: Upward Compatibility
items.text:
Now the position of the characters over the keyboard is a similar case. If people are accustomed to the position of the characters in I-APL they will experience an undesirable frustration when they change to commercial APL.

For example I had the intention to start all my APL courses with I-APL. This is a very strong incentive for beginners; it is my experience with other packages that a package which my students are allowed to copy and use at home for study (and to give away to friends) immensely increases the popularity of that program. But after a few weeks I teach file handling and graphics; at that moment I need to switch to a commercial APL.

However, with the character set incompatibility, I don’t dare to burden relative novices with switching to another character set. So unfortunately I had to drop this idea.

items.title: Downward Compatibility
items.text:
You may wonder who will ‘downgrade’ from commercial APL to I-APL? The answer is: “the most important people you have”, experienced APL users and APL professionals who try to promote APL. These people are familiar with the current position of the symbols, and they will not have a one-time mental conversion, but will be frustrated again and again whenever they switch to I-APL for a moment. As experienced APL users devote their time mainly to the professional implementations, they know the standard keyboard layout by heart. As they switch to I-APL only occasionally, they will never be comfortable with the alternative layout of I-APL.

They will always need to fetch the paper with the layout of I-APL; this is very frustrating and it will thwart the quick ‘playing’ in the few minutes left between two big projects. Even when they have the I-APL layout at hand, they have to spend too much time locating the proper symbols.

Even if such a professional doesn’t give up finally, at least his interested visitor will not get a favourable impression of APL if he sees his tutor struggling with ‘a minor detail’ such as the search for a proper symbol. That APL has a lot to offer will probably be lost by this bad impression.

By the way, it will also require that all existing manuals and books have to devote extra sections to the character set location. This is an unjust burden for writers too, and it makes me hesitate to do that for a ‘non-standard’ APL feature.

items.title: Remedy
items.text:
For these reasons I strongly advise a return to standard APL for the position of the symbols. The best thing to do would be to distribute a patch with which to return to the familiar keyboard layout. However, if you don’t want to drop this new layout, at least give the user an option to choose between the new and the standard keyboard.

I feel very positive about this project and I think that Paul Chapman and all the other contributors did a marvellous job. So it’s a shame if such a relatively small thing were to hamper the success of this project. With all respect for the big achievement which I-APL is, please don’t let this small thing of a non-standard character placement endanger the final aim of popularizing APL.

Yours sincerely

F.H.D. van Batenburg Instituut v.Theoretische Biologie Leiden, Holland

items.title: British APL Association News: Report on the Achievements of the 1987/88 Committee
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 19

by Graham Parkhouse

The committee met seven times altogether. Never did we manage all to be present at once. Average attendance at each of the 3 hour sessions was 8 of the 10 strong committee. Everybody attended most of the meetings.

What struck me about the meetings, being a newcomer, was how serious a business it all seemed to be. All members had to circulate written reports before each meeting, and there was an on-going actions list which was reissued after every meeting. I have to report that I think the 168 hours plus travelling time, report writing and minute writing might have been more constructively spent actually doing some of the things that we talked about all year.

What did we achieve? Jill Moss drew up a new BAA brochure which was printed in the autumn, which has been sent out by I-APL Ltd to enquirers, and is freely available. The teachers' course which Norman Thomson organised in Winchester is reported in VECTOR 4.2, and two similar courses are being organised for Winchester and Swansea this summer. A postal ballot was voted in at the Extraordinary General Meeting held on 20th November and the new procedures were put into effect this April. Two delegates have been sponsored to attend the ICME Conference on Mathematical Education at Budapest in July. They are both teachers who said they were prepared to speak out for APL at the conference.

A special committee meeting was convened to discuss further support to the I-APL project. A further £2,000 was given to I-APL Ltd to make BAA's total contribution £8,000. This meeting is reported in more detail in VECTOR 4.4.

The committee made considerable progress towards getting paid administrative help. If current plans meet with approval from the next committee we shall be employing someone to work up to 10 hours per week doing the many jobs that are handled by committee members which would be better done and done better by one person with time available. This might begin on an experimental basis for a year. Watch this space for developments! You may have noticed a sluggishness in the system, such as wrong dates in VECTOR for forthcoming meetings, late notification of meetings, and one very late VECTOR. (Did you realise you got 4.3 before 4.2?) I am partly to blame, but we are sure that the right kind of help will get the system running better.

Preparations for APL-ication (28-30th September) have been handled entirely by the sub-committee set up for the purpose. We hear there are going to be some good speakers.

So what didn't we achieve? A BAA bulletin board was considered but was dismissed as inappropriate to our needs at the moment. A leaflet on APL applications was beginning to be drafted. A conference for senior management was talked about, as was a regional meeting, and these may still be coming. There was discussion of producing an APL bibliography, even of sponsoring a researcher to produce one. This has not been pursued and maybe it has already been done for us; David Eastwood did a nice little bit of research when he called in at the Institution of Electrical Engineers to investigate their on-line information services. He is going to report his findings in VECTOR.

I have tried to give you a realistic picture of what your committee has been up to over the year. If you found yourself reacting to anything I have written, or are left shocked by what I have failed to mention, please ring me or write to VECTOR and let us have your suggestions.

items.title: Chairman's Report
items.text:
This has been another very successful year for the BAA; as you will see from the Treasurer's report membership is significantly up and our financial status is healthier than ever.

Looking at our major activities, we have run the regular series of technical meetings (barring one where adverse weather caused cancellation); our meetings organisers have an exciting forward programme including plans for regular events outside the London area and an upmarket 'APL for Management' event.

By contrast, the Vector group has not had such a strong year, although we would hope that all the production difficulties are now behind them. The committee has given a lot of thought to the content of Vector, particularly to the amount of material of lasting value to non-London members - for whom this is the chief benefit which the BAA has so far provided.

As we continue to grow administration becomes an increasing burden and the committee has decided that it is now appropriate for us to take on someone as (initially part-time) paid help handling many of the tasks we have hitherto relied on volunteer effort for. This we expect to see improving the quality of membership service and freeing the committee for more strategic planning.

Among our other activities has been the first of what could be a regular series introducing APL to teachers, and launching the BAA Software Library.

Something of a disappointment has been the response to our Members Projects Scheme, which we launched last year as one of the ways we wanted to invest the APL86 income in the future of APL. A few projects were proposed, but the only one we wanted to back seemed to go on permanent hold. We have a Projects Officer, whose main mission in life is to give financial backing to worthy projects; we shouldn't let this opportunity go to waste.

More positive progress has been made in the other scheme launched from APL86 - the APL-ication conference to be held at Canterbury in late September is looking like the major APL event of the Northern Hemisphere this year. The Organising Committee (myself, Christine McCree, Mel Chapman, Philip Goacher and Dave Parker) have been at work all year, we are more than happy with the papers received; publicity mailing will begin shortly and we look forward to seeing you all in Canterbury.

In closing I would like to record my appreciation of the work of the whole BAA Committee this year - as I said earlier, we have had a very successful year to a degree which I hope our successors can emulate.
path: Accounts and Minutes of the 1988 AGM

items.title: Treasurer's Report
items.text:
Mel Chapman reported membership figures as currently being 12 sustaining members, 32 corporate members, 7 library members, 445 full members, and 16 freebies. This he said compared to 11,33,7,333 & 16 for last year. An interim statement of accounts was distributed, which showed a total income of £21,542, £12,965 of which was from subscriptions, and an expenditure of £27,726. This included a sum of £20,000 which had been given to underwrite APL-ication, the conference taking place in Canterbury in September, which is expected to be recovered. Net reserves stand at £53,572. Mel reported that £30,000 had been invested on the London money market for one year at just over 9% fixed interest rate, which would mature next February.

In answer to questions from the floor, Mel said that the BAA does not contribute to the British Computer Society, to which the BAA is affiliated as a special interest group. The opposite is true, in that the BAA can take advantage of BCS services to the tune of £500 p.a.

The £20,000 for APL-ication was queried; was it expected to come back? Mel replied it was, with profit.

Income from book sales was noticed to be low this year, at only £100, compared to £738 last year. Last year's figures included book sale income from APL86, it was explained.

In view of the £20,000 earmarked for APL-ication, and the £30,000 locked up in the London money market, was there only £3,572 left for the incoming committee to spend? No, the £20,000 was not included in what had been declared as the assets; the incoming committee had £23,572 to spend plus subs.

There was a query about what the bank charges of £138 were for. They were for getting the facility of being able to receive subscriptions by Access and Visa credit cards. This facility will be especially useful for overseas members. The BAA loses 4% commission on subscriptions paid this way.

The summary of accounts submitted had not yet been audited. An audited version will be published in VECTOR.

items.title: Finding out about APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 26

Bibliographical notes by David Eastwood

One of the perennial enquiries we all get is for APL reference material. There is, of course, a small number of well-known APL reference books that are always mentioned. The BAA Committee produced a 'Top Six' list last year:

APL - An Interactive Approach (Gilman and Rose) Sharp APL Reference Manual (Paul Berry) A source book in APL (Ken Iverson) APL Design Handbook for Commercial Systems (Adrian Smith) APL - the language and its usage (Polivka and Pakin) FinnAPL idiom library

... and these are all stocked by the University of Warwick bookshop who run the APL book service for us. Please note that 'Design Handbook' is now out of print; if you have trouble finding it the residual stock (14 copies!) is obtainable from the author. The University of Warwick also carry a number of other general APL texts.

Whilst the books mentioned above are good for a general grounding in APL and themselves carry further references to APL material, we still receive a number of enquiries along the lines of: '..do you know of anything that covers APL as used in..'. I have made some enquiries about further sources of reference material which may be of interest to the membership.

items.title: IP Sharp
items.text: IP Sharp have a bibliography workspace (1000 BIBLIOG) which is still on the Sharp system and was kept up to date until a couple of years ago.

items.title: INSPEC
items.text:
The Institute of Electrical Engineers run a number of online information services, the largest of which is the INSPEC database which is continuously being updated and covers physics, engineering, computers and control, maths and information technology. I visited the IEE at Savoy Place in London to see what sort of representation APL has in the INSPEC database.

In May 1988 there were in excess of 600 references in abstracts to 'APL' (A Programming Language). This covers virtually all published material that carries some library reference, be it of UK or overseas origin. For example all ACM publications are included.

I think that with so many APL references listed, there must be something which deals with almost any application area.

Access to the INSPEC database is open to all, IEE members or not and current average prices range from £60-70 for non-members (less for members). The library staff will assist in the composition of the enquiry so that you get what you wanted! You can visit, ring or write to:

Technical Information Unit IEE, Savoy Place, London, WC2R 0BL 01 240 1871

items.text:

Compiled by Cathy Dargue

items.title: HMW Computing Limited
items.text:
HMW Computing Limited have relocated to Hamilton House on Victoria Embankment. Here we will be nearer our customers in the City and will be able to bring together the future development of our "4XTRA" Foreign Exchange Dealing and Position Keeping system. In addition to providing demonstration and conference facilities the Hamilton House location will enable us to carry out our maintenance contract commitments more efficiently as we will be much closer to our prestigious clients.

"4XTRA" our front end dealing system for the Banking community is achieving acclaim, and interest has been expressed by Banks, equipment manufacturers/suppliers as well as systems houses. We would be pleased to meet anyone working in the banking and finance fields to discuss how our systems can revolutionise the dealing function.

HMW are also pleased to announce that Phil Last has joined us. He brings his APL2 knowledge to us adding great strength to our growing team of consultants. Our consultancy team is always available for long and short term contract work, and we can supply consultants with experience in other languages in addition to APL, for example C, Oracle and JSP-COBOL. Call Stan Wilkinson for an initial discussion.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
MicroAPL has continued to record healthy levels of sales of our entry-level software - APL.68000 for the Atari ST, Apple Mac and Commodore Amiga. The distribution of these sales worldwide mirrors quite closely the sales of these machines themselves. Thus, for example, APL.68000 for the Commodore Amiga is selling strongly in the USA whereas the the Atari ST version is by far and away the most popular of the three in Germany. The UK sales of the Commodore and Atari versions are roughly equal, but we have noticed some increase in Apple Mac sales recently. We have been particularly encouraged by the take-up on our 'free' run-time version. Software developers are issued with a free run-time version of APL.68000 for use with packages they may develop in APL. The only condition is that APL.68000 receives an acknowledgement in the eventual product. At the moment I am aware of a couple of packages that are being launched in the USA and at least one in Germany with a lot more still in development. Perhaps people can use APL for packaged software!

Users of MicroAPL's own Mirage-based computers, the Spectrum and the Aurora, have been seeing a steady increase in the quantity of non-APL software they can run - they now have a choice of 7 programming languages (as well as APL of course!), wordprocessing, spreadsheet and database packages. The latest addition is a CAD package which is proving highly successful in the scientific area.

MicroAPL's consultancy operations continue to grow. We are currently recruiting extra staff to enable us to meet the demand, and an advertisement appears on page 32 of this issue.

items.title: Cocking and Drury Ltd
items.text:
Steven Weller joins the company as a trainee in late July. Steven is studying for a degreee in Mathematics for Business at Middlesex Polytechnic, and will spend his industrial placement year in both support and consultancy areas. We are again on the lookout for permanent staff with APL skills, to be based in our London office.

There have been several new sales of APL*PLUS Mainframe and Compiler software. The advanced features, efficiency and compatibility with its PC, Unx and Dec Vax counterparts is encouraging its use as the strategic APL for the future.

Testing of the new APL*PLUS System II for the 80386 is going very well; the involvement of selected clients in the Beta-test program is proving particularly beneficial. To remind Vector readers, the new interpreter is a full second-generation system, which takes advantage of the 80386 architecture; 32-bit addressing permits workspace and array sizes that are limited only by installed memory. 15 Megabyte workspaces with nested arrays on your desk are now a reality.

APL*PLUS System II for the 80386 is compatible with both the APL*PLUS PC and APL*PLUS Mainframe systems, further extending the family of APL*PLUS interpreters. The new interpreter is viewed more as a mainframe APL system than a PC system, and will be fully supported under licence with Cocking and Drury acting as the sole UK source. If you require more details about this exciting new development before its launch in September, contact Aelred Tobin, our Micro Products Manager, in our London office.

Statgraphics is proving so popular that we have had to schedule overflow courses to meet the demand. We have also developed a new corporate deal for customers purchasing any of our PC software products.

In order to promote the spread of the APL language Cocking and Drury will include a copy of I-APL/PC, the free international APL interpreter, with each copy of APL*PLUS PC that we send out. In this way APL*PLUS PC programmers will be able to encourage other PC users to try out their favourite language.

items.title: I.P. Sharp Associates Ltd
items.text:
In January 1988 Philips Telecommunication and Data Systems and I.P.Sharp Associates announced the signing of a multi-million dollar agreement for the provision of a Unix implementation of IPSA's decision support tool "Viewpoint". Under the terms of the agreement Philips will market the product, known as "Allround View", worldwide on its Unix-based P9000 computers.

Allround View provides users with a number of features, such as:

  • Access to MVS-based databases such as DB2, Adabas, and IBM OS files.
  • Access to Unix database systems and files.
  • Electronic mail, graphics, ad hoc enquiry facility, and word processing.
  • Integration of multiple P9000's in an Ethernet network.
  • PC integration under Unix.
  • DISOSS support through SNA
  • National language version support.

I.P.Sharp Associates have adopted the 'shareware' concept for Sharp APL/PC; 50 copies of Sharp APL/PC diskettes may be made without paying a royalty or fear of copyright infringement. This does not mean that it is free. Registered copies of the software are available from I.P.Sharp and it is these copies that people are free to reproduce and distribute.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce the appointment of Objectif APL as the new exclusive Dyalog APL distributor for France. Objectif APL has previously specialised in APL training and consultancy, as well as in the development of APL applications. The company is run by Bernard Legrand, a well-known author of APL books, including 'APL et GDDM' reviewed in VECTOR 4.1. In a reciprocal arrangement, Dyadic will market Objectif APL's MERLIN, an APL spreadsheet package which is installed in over 50 VS APL sites in France. Dyadic is nearing completion of its exciting new 'windowing' software for Dyalog APL. This is designed to provide all of the functionality of the APL*PLUS/PC screen software, but will have some important new features such as horizontal and/or vertical scrolling fields. The new windowing features will be on display at APL-ication.

Dyadic has announced new implementations of Dyalog APL for the Hewlett-Packard HP9000-800 series, the Sun-4 and Sun 386i, and the Unisys 5000 models 85 and 95.

Tim Perry's extensive experience in the retail industry has been a major factor in winning several important contracts for the company, thus building on the success we have already had with one of the UK's biggest furniture manufacturers.

items.title: Editorial: Don’t Lose Touch
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Adrian Smith

This VECTOR is all about interfaces. I hate interfaces! At least 90% of the hassle generated during any APL project is at the edges, where the array structure of APL fails horribly to dovetail with the files and records used by everyone else.

The projects I like best are the little hole-and-corner ones, where my file system is called )SAVE and I don't have to bother my head with the niceties of packed-decimal, or the inner secrets of the Lotus worksheet. So ... why a VECTOR about all the things I detest most in this life?

  • it is an unfortunate fact that systems generally have users, and users soon get tired of copying figures off their CICS screens so they can type them in to your APL model. They start saying unreasonable things like "... but it's all on the same computer ...", as if this made life any easier for you.
  • the PC DOS standard has made a huge psychological difference. A PC user assumes that any package he buys will (with a bit of frigging around) read data from any other package. He is much less willing to accept excuses from the mainframe brigade about incompatible formats, or variable length records, or whatever.
  • things are gradually getting better. As mainstream data starts to find its way into databases like DB2 and Oracle, the APLer's life suddenly becomes bearable. At long last, we get data back in tables, organised into rows and columns!

In summary: we can't ignore this problem; it won't go away; and our best excuses don't wash any more. We have to face up to it, and we need all the tools and techniques we can get. In the mainframe world we use things like AP123 to read VSAM data, and where necessary we get new interfaces made to order, for example from APL*PLUS to DB2. At the VAX and PC level, I am more and more convinced that we need to accept C as our programming partner. Unix is written in C, and so is almost any PC package you care to name. If you want to talk to them, you are going to have to talk in C. (You could try shouting in APL, but I don't think it would work.)

This all means broadening our horizons quite dramatically; I hope the papers in our technical section give you the start that you need.

items.title: The Education Vector
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 33

by Norman Thomson

In this, my concluding article in this series, I am happy to record how confident I am that my successor, Dr Alan Sykes of the Department of Management Science and Statistics at the University College of Swansea, will fill the post of Education Officer with distinction. I am sure that he will bring to it an infusion of new ideas, to hasten the day when APL is widely seen in the microcomputer world as the computer language which excels all others in the field of education. The I-APL movement provides a focus for growth and an entry point for all, however limited their means. In the longer view it would be good to see APL, seeded from this base, spread through the entire education world, with I-APL acting as a catalyst to fuel ever greater reactions.

Continuing in valedictory mode, I relate how on sifting through the belongings of an elderly relative, I came on a dusty old book entitled "Tales of Many Tongues". Opening it at random, I came upon:

"Once upon a time a great wizard made a wonderful invention which helped the workmen in his village make their tools with greater speed and precision, and thereby enabled them to trade favourably with their counterparts in neighbouring villages who did not have this advantage. At first the wizard was content that the invention should remain in his own village, but some of the elders persuaded him that not only the the tools, but also the invention itself might be traded more widely. When the word of the great invention spread, people came from all around to marvel at it, and to convey it back to their own villages where they were able to improve their own tool-making skills.

Enthusiasm for the Great Invention grew, so that people from all over the land came to regular joyful gatherings to devote themselves to instruction from the great inventor's disciples. Many wonders and signs were performed, and many lesser inventions were made which sprang from the Great Invention.

As the gatherings grew in size, two types of followers began to emerge; first merchants whose skills were able to transform the Great Invention to profit, and secondly missionaries for whom it became a symbol of salvation from an outmoded culture. In time, the Great Invention spread through all the lands, and merchants and missionaries alike would come together to form local cells of the Great Invention Movement. The teachings of the founder would be written down in books giving guidence to fresh converts, and codes of right conduct to existing believers.

One day the Great Inventor departed from his own village and went to live in a neighbouring one, where he made an even greater invention. Not to be outdone, the disciples who had remained in his old village also made another and greater invention, which they spread through the whole world. Back in the villages, and undeterred by this new division, the missionaries continued to preach, ardent that lack of riches should not deter the enrolment of new believers who continued to increase daily. The merchants sought more books to advance their business, although they were too busy pursuing their trade to find time to write them. The scribes therefore came mainly from amongst the missionaries, and their writings ....... "

At this point, a page had been ripped out of the book - perhaps readers would like to continue the story for themselves ...

items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 4

by Jonathan Martin

The following is my first attempt at collating the suggestions I received at the AGM on 29th April.

  • Tutorial session. Two speakers before tea on fairly technical (specific) topics, then an open session (maybe with an informal panel) on anything anyone wants to ask.
  • APL and the Outside World. Topics such as parallel processing, relational databases, expert systems.
  • APL in Education. Teaching APL to newcomers, further training in advanced techniques, APL in further education. This will probably be an evening meeting, to give teachers more chance to attend.
  • APL - the next 5 years. Representatives from the major suppliers to tell us what they are working on, and what they expect to bring to the market soon.
  • Applications in APL. Four speakers, relating their experiences in implementing a variety of APL systems.

As regards the actual dates, October 21st will be the Tutorial Session, since this follows so closely on the heels of Canterbury. The mapping of the remaining topics to the remaining dates will be published in VECTOR 5.2 (November 88).

items.title: Algorithmics by Harel
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 56

reviewed by Anthony Camacho

This is a very good book. The author's style has a refreshing directness and clarity. The subheadings of the chapters are a good sample and also show you the contents.

Preliminaries

  1. What it's all about
  2. Getting it done
  3. Getting it done by computer

Methods and analysis

  1. Getting it done methodically
  2. Getting it done right
  3. Getting it done cheaply

Limitations and robustness

  1. You can't always get it done cheaply
  2. Sometimes you can't get it done at all
  3. The simplest machines that get it done

Relaxing the rules

  1. Getting it done by co-operating
  2. Getting it done by tossing coins
  3. Are they better at it than us?

More knowledgeable reviewers have written that the book is an excellent survey of computer science (which I never studied) and it is certainly an excellent introduction to the range of computing that I know about and to some unfamiliar bits. I think it could be read with profit by intelligent sixth formers. It does require the reader to think. It encourages him to pause and to try to do things for himself too. Do not expect to get through its 400-odd pages without effort.

The bibliographic notes give, in 55 pages, a first rate survey of the best and seminal books on computer science. With a guide like this there is no excuse to be at a loss for a book on any topic in computer science. Such a guide (but to APL books) is just what we should have in Vector (reprinted say, once a year). If there was such a survey of the APL books in print and a reliable source which stocked them all, yet another small obstacle to the spread of APL in education would be removed.

The sections in the book which most interested me were those on the efficiency of algorithms and the non-computability of some kinds of problems, either because no conceivable machine could be fast enough or large enough or because the problem turns out to be logically undecidable.

Vector readers will be glad to hear that APL has a two page summary in the section on programming languages which, although one could cavil at some things in it, is clearly written by someone who appreciates what APL is like. It is not surprising in a book essentially about programming that APL's strength as a notation is not mentioned. .pa Every subject has its traditions and prejudices. Those of computing are ...... I was going to say what I think they are, but my view is equally prejudiced. How would we find out? An answer is to read a good survey of the subject and look for the occasions where solutions are approved of when no reason is given. This book is full of such value judgements because it is written in a lively style: the author's aim is plainly to explain things as clearly as possible and he doesn't care a bit if this clarity is used against him. In "Algorithmic methods" many of the solutions are described as 'better'. Some authors (should I say all politicians!) try to appear wise by saying things in a way which allows them to escape responsibility for what they dare not say straight.

So here is an illustration of what I found. How do we find the maximum distance across a convex polygon? Find all the distances from vertex to vertex and take the largest? No, he says, it's better to take a vertex, find the two vertices furthest from it, record the distance to the further one and then move one vertex round the polygon and see if one of the next pair of distances is larger and if so record that, until one has tested every vertex. His example allows him to demonstrate the ingenuity called for to reduce computation (which begins to be effective when the number of sides gets large), but he assumes that the solution must be a looping one.

I have said before that I think computer training too often over- emphasises looping so that students' ability to think in parallel is atrophied. I'm sure this is a mistake of the educationists. Parallel solutions (using J. J. Sylvester's 'multiple quantity' as Donald MacIntyre would say) can be just as elegant and can give even more delight than the cleverest recursion.

I do not think it is a fault of this book that parallel thinking appears so little in it. The reason is that it reflects the real world and there is too little parallel thinking there too. As Harel writes at the end of the chapter on Parallelism and concurrency:

"Many of the best parallel algorithms known cannot be implemented because existing parallel computers are inadequate in some way. On the other hand, we still do not know enough about designing concurrent programs and systems to take full advantage of the features those same computers offer. The work continues, however, and many people hope that the next few years will produce developments that will put algorithmic and computerized concurrency on a par with the more manageable notion of sequentiality."

I hope he's wrong about "more manageable", and that it is a computing prejudice; if he isn't yet, I hope he will be made wrong one day.

Algorithmics by Harel Addison Welsey 1987 Price £14.95

items.title: APL-ication: Latest Details
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 6

The Practical State-of-the-Art APL Conference University of Kent Canterbury, England 28-30 September 1988

APL-ication has been planned as an exciting, outward looking conference of interest to all APL practitioners - both newcomers to APL and those with more experience in the use of the language - and it will also provide an insight to the effective use of APL for those wishing to evaluate the use of the language in particular application areas.

APL-ication is designed to give a careful balance between the presentations given by invited speakers and contributed papers, with the accent on the practical application of APL in a variety of business disciplines. Indeed, we believe that the conference will be of interest to those who wish to evaluate the use of APL in specific business areas.

The conference will have an international flavour, with contributions from overseas, particularly our APL colleagues in Europe.

The aim is to make the event highly participative. 'Live' presentations will accompany papers, supported by the provision of a wide range of computing and audio-visual equipment.

Although there will be no formal exhibition, you will be able to meet consultancies and vendors at their hospitality suites and at their presentations of software and hardware in the product forums.

An APL bookstall and a software exchange will be open throughou;t the conference.

The British APL Association invites applications for places at the conference from its members, to whom it offers an advantageious rate. A most important feature of conferences such as APL-ication is the ready made forum for meeting fellow members with whom to exchange ideas and discuss techniques.

We look forward to meeting you there!

items.title: University of Kent
items.text: The conference will be held at the University of Kent which overlooks the Cathedral City of Canterbury. The University campus, opened in 1965, offers outstanding facilities for staging conferences, with on-site accommodation and social amenities. The University can be reached conveniently by road and rail. Canterbury is close to the motorway network affording rapid access to all parts of the UK and Europe via nearby Dover. The rail link to London also provides access from all parts of the country and from Heathrow and Gatwick airports.

items.title: Programme
items.text: We were surprised at the number of interesting papers submitted for this conference, and it has not been an easy task to assemble a three-day programme to amply reflect the diversity of topics offered. The schedule of papers with abstracts is available in our conference brochure - if you have not yet received your copy these may be obtained from the BISL Conference Department at the BCS (for address see Registration Information & Terms).

items.title: Canterbury
items.text: The City's roots can be traced back to a prehistoric iron age settlement, though the story of Canterbury really starts after the Roman invasion of AD 43. After successive occupation by the Vikings and the Danes, the Normans arrived and it was they who began building the Cathedral in 1070. Despite the later attentions of Henry VIII and Cromwell the Cathedral survives to this day as the 'Mother Church of English Christianity', and is famed for its collection of stained glass windows.

items.title: Leeds Castle
items.text:
To ensure that you see something of the local heritage, we are taking delegates to Leeds Castle for the conference banquet.

The castle, not far from Canterbury, was originally a Norman stronghold, later converted into a Royal Palace by Henry VIII. The castle is built on two islands in the middle of a lake within the wooded rolling Kent landscape.

A Royal residence for over 300 years, the Castle was a favourite home for eight of England's medieval Queens. The grounds of the Castle extend for some 500 acres with lakes, streams, gardens and woodland and include an ancient vineyard from which the Castle's own wine is produced. There is a museum at the Castle and the grounds also boast some of the world's most unusual and exotic waterfowl and birds.

items.title: Controlling Real-time Processes in a Brewery (with APL)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 64

notes on a talk by Robert Poate (MicroAPL)

Robert Poate of MicroAPL talked about an application in an area which ordinary APL programs don't normally reach, namely real time control of a continuous flow process. The continuous flow in this case was kegged beer in Romford Brewery, a large plant with a capacity of 1 million kegs per year in a series of highly automated lines. The task which Robert undertook on behalf of MicroAPL was to install a management information system which draws its data from 8 plc's (Programmed Logic Controllers) located at strategic points in the keg-filling operation, and feeds it via RS232 links to a MicroAPL Spectrum running the Mirage-2 operating system.

This allows event handling and multitasking between 9 jobs, one corresponding to each of the plc's and the ninth to a filer job which makes updates to a series of rolling files every 15 minutes. These files contain the material for reports on production and rejects, as well as the current status of each of the filling lanes. About 4 days worth of such files are retained on disk, and the filer job runs a daily compression program which writes a consolidated day file. The total amount of data so stored is about 6 megabytes every 4 days. The shared memory which the Mirage system allows between the communicating jobs works like APL shared variables, and is much faster than a RAM disk.

The effect has been to provide management with a massive amount of information in the form of graphs and tabular reports. Among other things, it has allowed them to monitor cumulative production closely against target patterns. It has also given them the means to discover (for example) which depots have a habit of returning kegs the wrong way up, and a recent inference from the data led to the discovery of a CO2 leak before a substantial loss had occurred.

With factory networks appearing more and more commonly, this sort of application is clearly one of which a lot more instances will be seen, and it is pleasing to know that APL is capable of supporting its share of the action. Robert concluded by making a plea to writers of such systems to make them highly extendable, a quality which APL makes it easier than most languages to instil.

items.title: BAA Technical Meeting25th March 1988 at the Royal Over-Seas League
items.text:
notes by Adrian Smith

This was generally accepted to be one of the best technical meetings we have ever had. There was a good attendance, and some keen questioning, and active discussion in the tea-break. There was however, a rather sad lapse in the organisation, as Romilly Cocking waited in vain for nearly 15 minutes for someone to open the proceedings.

Romilly eventually recalled his session at Loughborough in 1983, when Dick Bowman (who was chairing his session) opened with the words "Here is Romilly Cocking, who clearly feels he needs no introduction - so he isn't going to get one!" To this Romilly wittily added " ... I didn't realise it was a life sentence!!"

This had the undoubted effect of getting the audience thoroughly on the speaker's side, and the rest of the afternoon passed off without a hitch. Maurice Jordan had the benefit of an impromptu introduction from Jonathan Martin, along the lines of "Here is Maurice Jordan, who is my boss. My personal review is due next week ... he's a wonderful boss .... thank you."

by Graham Parkhouse

items.title: Meetings
items.text:
Those present enjoyed an excellent special educational meeting at the Royal Over-Seas League on the evening of September 2nd, when Anthony Camacho, Alan Sykes and Frank Evans gave talks levelled at newcomers to APL. The intention had been to attract teachers and others on the I-APL mailing list, but unfortunately the attendance was very small. Due to administrative fumbling the I-APLers were sent details of APL-ication instead of details of this meeting. This was rectified, but only at the eleventh hour. Only three teachers attended, which was very disappointing. Apologies to the speakers and to those who would otherwise have benefitted from being at an excellent meeting.

A post-mortem at the September committee meeting did not prevent disaster overtaking the October Friday afternoon meeting which had to be cancelled at the last minute because the labels for posting the flyers kept not materialising. Should we consider a scheme of answerphone owner accreditation? The cheery offer to return your call can become so familiar as to breed contempt.

items.title: BAA Administration
items.text:
A solution to our problems may come in the pleasant form of Alison Chatterton, our new paid part-time administrator. Alison has two young children, the youngest at playschool, and it suits her to take on some BAA administration to do at home. She is being equipped with a PC clone and software to be able to set up articles for VECTOR, manage the software library, keep our records up to date, and print off labels. We are not giving her an answerphone!

Valerie Lusmore wants to re-recruit as many experienced APLers as she can, who may have enjoyed corporate membership of the BAA in the past through previous employment. If you know of any such people please give Valerie a ring on [telephone number omitted] in the daytime.

items.title: Outstanding Achievement Award
items.text:
Please may we have nominations for 1989 awards. There are two categories of award, as mentioned at the 1987 AGM, for recent work in APL and for spreading awareness about APL. The award for 1987/88 went to John Scholes for his work in developing Dyalog APL, for which he received a glass apple, which he holds until the next award, and a cheque for £500. This year the prize will again be £500.

Nominations should consist of the name and address of the candidate and two signed and dated statements, one from the proposer and one from the seconder, explaining what the outstanding achievement is and why the candidate merits the award. If, in the adjudicating committee's view, none of the achievements are sufficiently outstanding, no award will be made.

Please send your nominations to the Hon. Secretary of the BAA, Graham Parkhouse, Dept. of Mechanical Engineering, University of Surrey, GUILDFORD, Surrey, GU2 5XH, to arrive by 28th February 1989.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Alan Sykes

Welcome to Education Vector once more. The good news is that Education Vector is to be a regular feature of each issue of Vector. The bad news is that Norman Thomson is no longer Education officer, and as the new incumbent, I must take this opportunity to thank him for all his hard work. I am sure that Norman will continue to play a vital role in the future developments of APL in Britain, and that future pages of Vector will be blessed by his erudite contributions.

The use of I-APL in schools continues to grow. During the summer, two courses were held, one masterminded by Norman in Winchester, and another one in Swansea. As a result, I-APL has been introduced to a number of comprehensive schools and colleges. It is important that Vector recognises this growth of application. Hence the new committee decided that Education Vector would be designed in the form of a supplement that can be mailed directly to the growing numbers of people on the I-APL mailing list in Britain.

The nature of this supplement in the future is largely up to you, the reader. In this first issue I hope newcomers to APL will find the first of a series of articles of benefit in explaining some elementary aspects of APL, and at the same time presenting some useful functions. Also there are reports from John Clift who attended the course at Winchester, and from Bruce Dickson at Mill Hill School. In addition, Anthony Camacho brings us up to date with I-APL news.

I extend an invitation to all readers of Education Vector and Vector to submit articles, letters, and comments for future editions of Education Vector, so that it can truly be a successful forum for the exchange of ideas on the use of APL in all spheres of education.

items.title: A Report on the Second Winchester Summer Course in APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 18

by John Clift

Promoting APL as a suitable language for use in secondary schools seems at first sight an almost impossible task. If the average computing teacher has heard anything at all about APL it is that the language is unreadable and written in a bizarre character set. It goes without saying that the organisers of the APL course for teachers relish the challenge and to add further spice the course is arranged at the end of the summer term when teachers' energies are at their lowest ebb.

A rather apprehensive group of ten teachers assembled at Winchester for the weekend of 8-11 July. We found that we represented a wide range of educational establishments, comprehensives, independent schools and further education colleges. Even one county advisor managed to spare some time from his heavy round of administrative duties. Our experience of computing was equally varied as about half our number were principally teachers of mathematics.

Little time was wasted by our energetic and enthusiastic instructors, Norman Thomson, Anthony Camacho, John Durran and Sylvia Camacho. The computer centre at King Alfred's College was reassuringly equipped with BBC computers, but as these were running the I-APL interpreter we soon found ourselves unlearning familiar concepts: * no longer meant multiply, ÷ was used for division instead of / and arithmetic now had to be done starting from the right.

Adapting to the APL symbols proved less of a problem than might have been expected. We were soon able to solve elementary problems and practise in the "voluntary" evening sessions which only terminated on the arrival of the caretaker at 9 o'clock. The main impression this work left me with was the ease with which APL handles operations on vectors and matrices.

Norman Thomson led the course at a fast pace and, looking back, I am astonished at the number of topics we covered in three days. Guest speaker Michael Kingston helped to place this activity in context by stressing the features of APL which made it attractive in commercial installations.

On the final morning time was found for a discussion on the future of APL in education. No definite conclusions were reached and this may have been because APLers wanted to talk about general principles underlying teaching while the teachers tried to move the discussion to particular applications of APL in the school situation.

I certainly plan to introduce APL into my teaching next year, but I am fortunate in having one class which is not working to any set syllabus, leaving me free to experiment with new ideas. It is much more difficult to see how APL could fit in with GCSE courses or with the developing National Curriculum.

Was the course a success? On the personal level, certainly. The teachers were encouraged to join in the discussion by the informal approach adopted by our tutors, not hesitating to interrupt each other to amplify a point of interest or correct an obscurity. Will significant numbers of schoolchildren have an opportunity to experiment with APL in the foreseeable future? I think this is likely, but without the efforts of I-APL there would be none at all. I am sure all the participants would join me in thanking the organisers and tutors, the British APL Association and those working for I-APL. If we gained nothing else from the course we have seen something of the power of APL and can understand why the APL community feels that the language deserves a wider audience.
