items.title: Books Received for Review
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 53

We have two books which we hoped to be able to review in the next VECTOR. The first of these is called ‘Mathematical Experiments on the Computer’. It is by Ulf Grenander, has been around for several years, and is solid with really useful, well presented APL. I look forward to getting the full review of this one into 6.1 … I only wish the author had mentioned ‘APL’ in the title so that we would have tripped over it sooner!

The second book is called ‘APL: a Problem Oriented Approach’. It is a translation from a German original, and is published by Ellis Horwood. Unfortunately the typesetting of the APL is so impossibly bad that we felt we had to contact the publishers immediately in an attempt to get the book withdrawn before it did the APL community any more damage. I am glad to say that Ellis Horwood have been most co-operative, and are withdrawing the current edition from sale.

*** if you see this book for sale: do not under any circumstances buy it! There will at some point be a corrected version available. We shall then feel able to review it.

items.title: IBM Personal Computing in Schools
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 53

Short Notice by Anthony Camacho

Edited by Paul Barnetson and published by Kogan Page Ltd 1988

This is a collection of 24 articles on using PCs in schools. Many of them are reports on the worthy use made of some 200 PCs installed with joint educational and IBM funding. As a survey of the use of IBM PCs in schools between about 1984 and 1987 it is of general interest. There are two articles that mention APL: “APL in Schools on the IBM PC” by Norman Thomson and “Extra-curricular Activities with an IBM PC” by Paul Barnetson himself. The latter is a much fuller description (but without any of the APL code) of the Charlton Chase system on which there were three pages in Vector 4.1.

Norman Thomson’s article is a 15 page introduction to APL. It is a justification of his assertion that APL is the best way to do mathematics on a computer. He gives functions for: odd numbers, arithmetic progressions, geometric progressions, square and triangular numbers, multiplication and other tables, prime numbers, factorising, perfect numbers, Gregory’s and Euler’s series, sums of reciprocals of Nth powers of integers, average, mean, variance, standard deviation, median frequency distribution and simulation of statistical experiments. It is clear and persuasive - it would be an excellent leaflet to circulate to school maths teachers. I would like to see the BAA reprint it and circulate it.

items.title: Second Generation APLs on the PC
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 54

Introductory notes by Adrian Smith

The Technical Editorial in VECTOR 5.3 made the point that microcomputer hardware is finally catching up with the demands made of it by APL. We can at last have decent workspaces (I get over 3Mbyte of ⎕WA in IBM's APL2/PC on my PS/2 Model-70), and the arithmetic is back to the mainframe standard with proper long integers and real bitty booleans. What's more these beasties go rather fast! Accordingly we have three (going on four) 386-specific APL systems to look at:

  1. STSC's APL*PLUS II system. This is currently at the top end of the scale in terms of both performance and price. Peter Cyriax has taken a technical perspective, and Ajay Askoolum (of the Legal & General Assurance Society Ltd.) has looked at the product from the application side.
  2. SAX from I.P. Sharp Associates. SAX was implemented as a joint development project between I.P. Sharp and STSC. The software is based on the STSC Unix APL, but the language follows SHARP APL, not the STSC product. Please check the note at the end of the review for a statement from IPSA on the availability of this product.
  3. IBM's APL2/PC (32 bit). Dick Bowman is reviewing this for us for VECTOR 6.1. In price performance terms it really is a rather remarkable product. For £348 you get 32-bit arithmetic, workspace up to 15Mbyte (with no restrictions on object size), an APL2 interpreter (with almost nothing that matters left out) and a rather faster system than STSC's APL*PLUS/PC release 8. It requires an 80387 maths co-processor. David Selby gives a brief summary of this APL (or should we say his APL) on page 82.
  4. Dyalog APL for MS DOS. The α-test version of this becomes available at the end of May, and we have every hope of getting a ‘first impressions’ into VECTOR 6.1. Some idea of its features can be gleaned from Peter Donnelly's notes on page 81 of this VECTOR.

I think we are moving into interesting times! We shall soon be looking towards the 80486 (some 5 times the speed of the 386), and towards I-APL on machines like NEXT and the transputer boards. Watch this space!
path: Second Generation APLs on the PC

items.title: APL*PLUS II: STSC’s Second Generation APL System for 80386 Machines
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 55

reviewed by Peter Cyriax

Early last Autumn STSC released APL*PLUS II, a new generation of APL running on ‘386’ type IBM PCs. It offers mainframe power on your desk for a total of four or five thousand pounds; so whether you need to grade up from older PCs, or want to decentralise mainframe based systems, this is something you should know about.

In a nutshell, APL*PLUS II combines the environment of the APL*PLUS/PC with the APL language from the APL*PLUS/1000 mainframe systems. If you have never used either product, that leaves you none the wiser, but at least you have a treat in store.

There are several other versions of APL that will run on 386 machines - Dyalog, Sax and APL2, which I have heard good things about; but this is not a comparative review, it's an attempt to tell you about APL*PLUS II, and relate it to the products it was developed from.

First, what does it run on, and what do you get?

APL*PLUS II runs on an IBM PC or compatible under DOS 3.3 or later; and requires a 386 CPU with at least 2MB of memory. That gives you an APL that seems to run 4 or 5 times faster than APL*PLUS/PC on the same hardware, with a Workspace size of around 800K. For the moment, at least, it's a single user system, though it will run on a network.

If you want a bigger workspace you buy more memory (up to 16MB). There are many flavours of 386 PC - but a good 20Mhz machine with 3 or 4MB of memory is now commonplace, and costs a few thousand pounds. That makes an interesting comparison with a typical mainframe - it will put an APL system on your desk with a 2 to 3MB Workspace, and processing speed somewhat better than the old IBM 3031. The wire from the screen to the CPU is rather shorter on the PC, of course, so the PC is much more responsive - a couple of seconds faster than the mainframe running under light load.

However, most PCs don't have a floating point processor, so engineering, statistics, CAD-CAM or graphics applications can be very slow. If you have a lot of heavy calculations to get through, then a floating point processor should speed them up by as much as ten times, and the WIETEK chip is several times faster again - a real transformation, but still a couple of times slower than a mainframe with otherwise similar performance. You certainly can offload these sorts of applications from the mainframe to a 386 PC, but you have to think about it.

Floating point is not an issue for most people, so what it all comes down to is this:

A modern, single-user APL with mainframe size workspaces running at about one tenth the speed of the fastest CPU that IBM sell.
path: APL*PLUS II: STSC’s Second Generation APL System for 80386 Machines

items.title: APL*PLUS II System
items.text:
The main components of APL*PLUS II are:

  1. APL Nested Array Interpreter
  2. APL Component Shared File System
  3. The Editor, and Access to the rest of the Environment which I will discuss in turn.

As it happens, I still have a Beta test version of APL*PLUS II, not the production version, but so far as I know there isn't a great deal of difference. I have been using the system for development, not trying to crash it; and the main reason I haven't upgraded yet is that I haven't found any bugs. APL*PLUS II seems reliable.
path: APL*PLUS II: STSC’s Second Generation APL System for 80386 Machines

items.title: APL Interpreter
items.text:
APL*PLUS II is a second generation APL supporting Generalized (Mixed and Nested) Arrays with the extra functions and operators needed to handle them. It also has the earlier developments, such as Grade on Characters and on Matrices, plus the extension of Compress to Replicate, of course.

There has been a lot of criticism of Nested Arrays - mainly that they produce incomprehensible, highly inefficient code. This criticism was also made of first generation APL - and with just as much validity. Like any powerful tool, Nested Arrays can be abused; and abused they certainly were, particularly when we were trying to learn how to use them to begin with. My own first attempts are no exception, but even so I find no real difficulty in reading code I wrote five years ago; whereas in some cases traditional APL would have needed a nightmare of globals, making it quite impossible to maintain. The single most important use for Nested Arrays is to pass multiple parameters into Functions, which helps to make them modular and clarifies their interface - hard to argue with.

Neither is efficiency an issue. This is particularly true of APL*PLUS II, which, in common with other modern APLs, was designed from the ground up to support Nested Arrays. The Monitor (⎕MF) facility is quite up to the task of finding out where CPU is going, and it shows that Nested Arrays can lead to simpler and faster code when they represent well how your data is actually organised. I would not be without them.

In language compatibility terms, APL*PLUS II is almost identical to the APL*PLUS/1000 mainframe system, which is a (major) development of VS/APL. The only differences I have found are that Replicate Foreach (/¨) does not work because of the conflict between Replicate (Compress) and Reduction - IVERSON ERROR; and also ⎕SIZE gives the answer you always wanted anyway i.e. how big the object actually is. Dyalog APL is also very similar - it was modeled on STSC's experimental system that preceeded APL*PLUS/1000; and IBM's APL2, though different, shares the same basic definition of Arrays plus many of the extensions. Finally APL*PLUS/PC is a small, non-nested version of APL*PLUS/1000; so altogether APL*PLUS II is generally upward compatible with, or at least similar to most other major APL systems.

The implementation of APL*PLUS II is also impressive, with only one obvious weakness - Index and Replicate are both very slow. Index has always been a problem, because in general it is quite difficult to spot the cases that can be optimised; but Replicate is surprising, though it may have been improved by now. This is a minor quibble for such a new product: overall the Interpreter seems fast - it runs in true 386 chip 32 Bit mode; and like the mainframe product it uses 1 Bit Booleans (faster, and saves a lot of space), 32 Bit Integers (no more floating-point dates and array indices), and 64 Bit Floating-point Numbers. Also, it passes APL values around with internal pointers as much as possible, rather than copying them, so it doesn't waste CPU or use up Workspace.
path: APL*PLUS II: STSC’s Second Generation APL System for 80386 Machines

items.title: APL File System
items.text:
APL*PLUS II supports the Component Shared File System originally developed by Sharp and STSC in the early 70s, and still going strong.

APL*PLUS/1000 and APL*PLUS/PC also have this same Component File System, implemented using the ⎕F… family of System Functions.

An APL Component File is essentially a sequence of Components, each of which is an APL value of whatever shape, rank, depth, type and size you can dream up (or fit into your workspace). It is simple, but it fits APL well, which is why it is so successful.

The mainframe version of the File System is a shared system, which means that different people can use it simultaneously; even updating the same file at the same time in a controlled way. At first sight this feature appears irrelevant on a single user PC system; but it is implemented on both APL*PLUS/PC and APL*PLUS II. This means that both products can be used to share data on a network of PCs, and in due course APL*PLUS II should also work on a multi-user 386 system running under either CDOS or OS/2.

The performance of any File System depends predominantly on disk hardware and buffering, but the APL*PLUS II version is noticeably faster than APL*PLUS/PC. Also it suffers far less from the fragmentation which can occur when Components keep changing their size, particularly if they are large.
path: APL*PLUS II: STSC’s Second Generation APL System for 80386 Machines

items.title: APL PC Environment
items.text:
This I love, and hate. The good news is there is nothing you cannot do, and probably with only one keystroke: the bad news is that, like me, you may find it quite impossible to remember what that keystroke is. To be fair, this problem seems to be endemic to all PC systems, not just PC APL. One of the features that makes APL attractive is the way it fits together to form a coherent whole - it seems a shame to spoil it with a myriad of un-coordinated facilities, however useful each one might be on its own. This is a very personal view, but I do feel that too much use has been made of the freedom that the PC provides. However these facilities are indeed useful, and I must admit that APL*PLUS II is a more productive development environment than either APL*PLUS/PC or any mainframe system.

The principal facilities of the APL PC Environment are:

  1. APL Character Set Support
  2. Session Manager
  3. The Editor
  4. Access to DOS Native Files
  5. Screen Control
  6. Graphics
  7. Communication with other Systems

Support for the APL Character Set is available for almost any screen configuration and a large selection of printers, without any hardware changes, using software defined Character Sets. The old, low resolution mono screens needed a special Character Set ROM, and that is still available, but I cannot see anybody putting a screen like that on a 386 machine. I tested APL*PLUS II on a number of systems before buying one, and they all worked fine. Over the last few years screens and printers have become steadily more flexible, as well as better and cheaper; so Character Set problems should be a thing of the past.

The Session Manager is similar to IBM's Session Manager for VS/APL: it allows you to scroll back over your session log, and to change and re-execute statements; but it also contains other facilities e.g. string search, printer control, cut and paste, change character sets, undo changes and deletions, talk to the mainframe… obtain help on all of these facilities etc., etc.

The Editor is a development of the )EDIT full-screen editor available on earlier versions of APL*PLUS/PC. It is not that different to use, but much more powerful, and has been made available in Release 8 of APL*PLUS/PC as well. You can stack up edit sessions just as you can with mainframe APL XEDIT. The Session Manager itself is integrated into the Edit Stack - the system thinks you are editing the session log - which explains why some of the more ‘advanced’ features are there at all, but it all works cleanly, and it means that you can easily move code between functions or between a function and the session log, or even between workspaces as the edit sessions survives )LOAD - surprising, but very handy. I also like the facility to break lines and glue them back together again. This Editor is also much better suited to text data than XEDIT is - almost as good as a word processor. Overall I like it, though one final facility does seem to be missing - it would be most useful to split the screen and have two sessions available simultaneously, particularly during de-bugging.

Access to DOS native files is via the ⎕NF… (Native Files) family of System Functions. I haven't used them much, but when I tried they did what I expected and ran quite quickly.

Screen Control centres around ⎕WIN and other ⎕W… System Functions. ⎕WIN defines the fields on the screen using a format matrix similar to the one in GDDM's ASMFMT call. This is the same interface that APL*PLUS/PC offers, and I find it somewhat inelegant and a bit slow; though compared with using GDDM via AP126 it is a paragon of simplicity. Unlike GDDM this interface does not provide any graphics capability - that is what the ⎕G… family of System Functions are for. These, again, are the same as the APL*PLUS/PC offering.

However, APL*PLUS II also provides an interface to third-party graphics software (included in the product) that implements the Graphics Standard Interface - GSI - and supports an impressive list of devices. GSI is an ISO and ANSI device independent graphics standard, which means that you can decide what you picture looks like without having to worry what device you will use to produce it; and the definition should work on a wide range of hardware. This has to be the right approach. At the moment you cannot mix Text and Graphics on screen using either GSI or the ⎕G… functions in conjunction with ⎕WIN; but under OS/2 Presentation Manager all screen handling will be in graphics mode - otherwise you cannot scale panels or lay them over each other, so I am sure that STSC will fix that restriction when they produce an OS/2 version.

As far as Communications with other systems are concerned there are really three issues. If you want to drive local devices using the serial or parallel ports - touch screens, for instance, recently reared their heads - ⎕ARBIN is well up to the task. If you want to log on to a mainframe, you need an IRMA board (or something similar) if it's an IBM bi-synch system, otherwise the built in terminal emulation or ⎕ARBIN should do the trick. Finally if you want to call programs in other languages, possibly running in other CPUs on a network, that is a bit harder. This is what IBM's new Systems Applications Architecture - SAA - is all about; and the central APL facility here is ⎕NA, which isn't available, yet. However, all the signs are that STSC intend to provide the necessary features in this area; and my guess is that they will be available before most people actually need them.
path: APL*PLUS II: STSC’s Second Generation APL System for 80386 Machines

items.title: Summary
items.text: I'm glad I bought a copy.
path: APL*PLUS II: STSC’s Second Generation APL System for 80386 Machines

items.title: APL*PLUS II for 80386 PCs
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 61

reviewed by Ajay Askoolum (Legal & General Assurance Society Ltd)

items.title: The Product
items.text:
APL*PLUS II is a second generation APL interpreter for 80386 based PCs (including ATs with an Intel INBOARD/AT), with or without 80387 coprocessor, running DOS 3.3 or later, with RAM size of 2MB or more. The version reviewed is 1.00.07 dated 16th August 1988.

This interpreter, unlike the APL*PLUS/PC interpreters, is protected. Whilst a single copy of the software may be installed on as many PCs as desirable, only one such installation may be used at any time. The interpreter polls a 'dongle' - between the parallel printer port and cable - at random intervals throughout any active session. It cannot be invoked in the absence of this device and if removed during a session, the user is prompted to re-insert it and press ENTER. If ENTER is pressed without the device in place, the session is terminated with the ensuing loss of the workspace.

The software costs £2,000 plus VAT per copy and the run-time system costs £250 plus VAT per copy. An annual maintenance charge equal to 25% of the original purchase price is payable after the first twelve months. The maintenance charge includes all upgrades and (telephone) support provided by the appointed distributors Cocking & Drury (Software) Ltd. Discounts are negotiable on purchases of multiple copies at the same time.

The same package is available from MicroAPL for £1,395 plus VAT - presumably without any maintenance or upgrades.

An APL character generator ROM will be required if the display adapter in use is not EGA or VGA and will be supplied free of charge on request. This ROM is identical to the one which provides APL character generation with the APL*PLUS/PC interpreter. Most 80386 based PCs provide a soft character set facility and will not require this ROM.

APL*PLUS II is a new product from STSC - not intended as a replacement for APL*PLUS/PC - which is closely modelled on IBM's APL2. However, most of the file and ⎕G-style graphics functions in APL*PLUS/PC are available in an enhanced form together with generic information to install and use Graphics Software Systems Computer Graphics Interface (GSS*CGI); this is a device-independent interface to graphics devices for which cover functions are provided in the VDI (Virtual Device Interface) workspace provided as part of the package. The editor, reminiscent of )XEDIT, is a new feature: it allows multiple objects - one of which is automatically the active workspace and which may include native files - to be edited simultaneously. Another new feature is the session manager which is invoked by CTRL / and allows session bound features and parameters to be set via pull-down menus - this is an easier means than keyboard input of the relevant commands to achieve the customisation sought.

APL*PLUS/PC workspaces and files can be migrated into the APL*PLUS II environment and may not require code changes to run - workspaces cannot be loaded directly nor can files be tied as component files. The migration facility is not provided within the interpreter - as in the guise of )MCOPY in APL2. Instead, a number of base functions are supplied with adequate documentation on the syntax and procedure involved in the migration process. The reverse process is not documented - however, there would be little need for this when the APL*PLUS II specific features are used. Instead of the familiar AWS and ASF extensions, WS and SF are used to differentiate workspaces and files. The APL*PLUS/PC subset of this new interpreter is not totally compatible with APL*PLUS/PC - just functionally so, with the aid of the utilities provided.

The packaging, style and feel of this new product shares the same hallmarks as the existing APL*PLUS/PC product: the manuals (three volumes plus a quick reference guide) are precise and the usual range of complementary utility/tutorial workspaces - including printer support, assembler and APL character generation functions - are included on the three 1.2MB diskettes supplied (some GSS device drivers are not included because of lack of space, but are available upon request). Only 5.25 inch diskettes are supplied; however, the software may be supplied upon request and free of charge on 3.5 inch diskettes in lieu.

There are some omissions: there is no SYSHELP.SF file and therefore no help facility on the interpreter itself is available by default. The help facility provided is sparse and barely adequate. The system does not automatically use coprocessor support if available: the invocation must specify whether the version supporting the 80387 chip or the version with software emulation of the chip is used. The WEITEK coprocessor is not supported.

Moreover, the customisation of any APL session comes from the configuration stated in a native file which is CONFIG.APL by default, unlike the APL*PLUS PC method where the desired configuration is achieved by supplying the relevant parameters when invoking the interpreter and an initial workspace to load and an APLLIBS.ASF file.

items.title: Upgrading to APL*PLUS II
items.text:
The interpreter is very powerful and provides a very much more versatile environment than APL*PLUS/PC - the obvious one being the facility for workspace sizes between 1-15MB with APL2 features.

This makes it a rival contender to the mainframe environment for the type of applications developed on the mainframe. However, while there is a definite cost advantage in favour of APL*PLUS II, there will be some loss of flexibility.

APL*PLUS II cannot be seen as a substitute for the APL*PLUS/PC applications currently in use: the cost of the equipment and the interpreter itself is far too prohibitive and does not necessarily offer any obvious critical advantages.

There are alternatives to APL*PLUS II which should also complicate the decision. There is DYALOG APL running under UNIX, with the facility to run up to four terminals and the flexibility to transfer workspaces to and from the mainframe APL2 environment, and with access security which is important in the maintenance of the application run. Also, IBM have announced an APL2 PC interpreter in the same league, at around 20% of the cost of APL*PLUS II with the possibility of free run time systems.

The APL*PLUS II package would be an ideal means for the development of personal productivity applications. These are the development of prototype solutions for use by a small team, probably within the same department - the styling and management of applications are irrelevant but the accuracy and speed of development are vital. In such a situation, the development is undertaken by the people who fully understand the processes involved without recourse to any systems analysis. In other words, APL is simply a well understood personal productivity tool rather than an art form accessible only via third parties.

The effectiveness of APL*PLUS II within this context is limited by at least two factors:

  1. There is no support for full screen applications other than in the standard functions (⎕WIN, ⎕WGET, ⎕WPUT etc.). The available functions are extremely powerful and probably much better than the GDDM equivalent on the mainframe, but are not easy to use effectively. There is no reason why the Society could not write and document standard cover functions so as to simplify the task of developing full screen applications.

  2. There is no provision of help facilities on the system features of APL*PLUS II which are unique to STSC. A system level help facility similar to the one provided with APL*PLUS PC would have been sufficient. Although the same help facility could be invoked from the APL*PLUS II interpreter, this would be deficient in those things which are characteristic of second generation interpreters and may be misleading not only because the two interpreters are not fully compatible but also because certain features are exclusive. Thus training courses would be necessary for those new to the PC environment.

Also, not enough information and utilities are available to assess the effectiveness of APL*PLUS II in a networked environment. The intention would be to share files and workspaces among users - possibly on an alternate basis so that the dongle could be used by say two people - and with the mainframe APL2 environment.

On the other hand, the APL*PLUS II offers an APL2 style interpreter with enhanced file and graphics facilities which are very well documented in the manuals supplied.

I evaluated the package on a COMPAQ 386/20 with 5MB RAM, 80387 coprocessor, BROTHER HL 8 laser printer and colour VGA monitor. The cost of this type of configuration provides a good estimate of the cost of making a transition to APL*PLUS II on a PC from the current APL2 on the mainframe. Also, an assessment of the training needs and the level of support should be made.

The complexity of the task to migrate mainframe applications to APL*PLUS II must not be underestimated. GDDM or auxiliary processor 126 is not available in the APL*PLUS II environment, and file handling is very different on the PC - thus major changes will be required to the mainframe workspaces using GDDM and file facilities before they would run. Even those applications which are workspace based and do not use files may need scrutiny as APL2 and APL*PLUS II are not 100% compatible.

items.title: A Personal Assessment of APL*PLUS II
items.text:
I am familiar with VSAPL under VSPC, VSAPL under TSO, APL2 under TSO and APL*PLUS/PC.

With a good knowledge of APL, APL*PLUS II is a familiar environment from the outset for me, particularly as it retains most of the characteristics of APL*PLUS/PC. A notable difference is the session manager and the new editor. The session manager is very unlike the session manager for APL2 in that it can be relegated to a dormant state. Its obvious advantage being the facility to set session bound parameters within a workspace via a series of pull down menus rather than by keystrokes.

The editor is reminiscent of )XEDIT in VSAPL under TSO. Once within the editor, it responds to the usual ALT/key combinations in the same way as the APL*PLUS/PC editor. The ability to edit and update native files from within a workspace simplifies the procedure a great deal - although when APL*PLUS II writes back an existing native file, called up by the editor but not altered, the new file is larger by a matter of a few hundred bytes. The specification of a workspace name using the DOS path as part of the specification rather than a library number appeared somewhat alien to an APL environment - but the usual convention of library numbers may be selected by modifying the CONFIG.APL file appropriately.

Some irritations with the APL*PLUS PC interpreter still exist - for instance it is still not possible to edit numeric objects in the new editor. Others do not: ⎕TRACE and ⎕STOP survive the editor, there is no need to wrestle with the setting up of virtual workspaces. The usual convention for ambivalent functions is retained. There are some practical enhancements such as )PSAVE which prevents accidental overwriting of a workspace on disk. The )GROUP facility does not exist - in the VSAPL environment this allowed any number of objects which had been grouped to be copied from a saved workspace by simply specifying the group name. It is possible to copy any number of objects from a saved workspace but the individual object names must be known and specified in a character array and the array specified for the )COPY operation.

Given the size of the workspaces, and the fact there is no warning that there may be multiple editor sessions pending when logging off, I would have liked to have a facility within the interpreter which saved the active workspace at random intervals providing something in the guise of the CONTINUE workspaces in APL2. Such a facility would permit most of the work during any session to be partially safeguarded automatically.

The equivalent of ⎕TF in IBM APL2 is absent, as is )MCOPY. Both of these omissions are noted by STSC; a way round the problems created is suggested in the workspace and file migration procedures detailed and the provision of the SLT (Source Level Transfer) workspace which uses the WIC (Workspace Interchange Convention level 1). An )MCOPY facility would be valuable in that developments are very likely to be continued in the APL*PLUS/PC environment and subsequently ported into the (expensive) APL*PLUS II environment.

The migration procedure advocated does work, although it is quite contrived to be contemplated as a matter of routine, as long as the few incompatibilities of the APL*PLUS/PC and APL*PLUS II are remembered. The ⎕CT is different, ⎕KEYW does not exist, system functions are not absorbent, library number convention must be used within the CONFIG.APL file when an application uses library numbers, the help file is defined in the CONFIG.APL file and the few incompatible ⎕POKEs are sorted out.

For the types of applications I have developed, the omission of the ⎕HNAMES system function causes unnecessary problems. It means that it is not possible to change the file to hand when pressing ALT F6 from an APL session. The file accessed is specified in the CONFIG.APL file and cannot be specified in a ⎕LX function as is my current practice. Also, the fact that system functions are no longer absorbent and cause an error condition is very irritating to me - it's a style that I am very fond of and which I use to avoid yet another entry in the Symbol Table - space is at a premium when the maximum workspace size is 440KB. However, this is a minor problem since the APL*PLUS II workspace sizes are appreciably larger and the Symbol Table is dynamic and allows 32767 entries.

The interpreter is fast, the loading and saving of workspaces also appear appreciably faster. My personal preference would be to develop fresh applications from scratch using wherever possible the enhancements of this second generation interpreter. The first objectives would be to develop a workspace of cover functions for full screen applications and another workspace of standard library routines of the type I have developed in APL*PLUS/PC.

items.title: Songs of Innocence & Experience
items.text:
APL*PLUS II offers an unrivalled environment as a personal productivity tool, requiring only a good knowledge of the language for the development of any application without compromise. The power of the language is that it allows its user total control over expression - it allows all its characteristics to be interrogated, offers very good error trapping facilities as well as reporting errors in a constructive way, has operators and primitives which are capable of reducing concepts to a few symbols (think of nested arrays, for instance), offers excellent filing and graphics facilities and allows progress from concept to program code without any intermediate steps with great ease. It has no equal in the absence of automatic code generators.

Unfortunately, the APL environment is marred by its propensity for a variety of programmer abuse, and it requires a run time system - at extra cost - for the distribution of applications. The APL*PLUS II system suffers in a number of respects: the enormity of its workspaces makes a disciplined approach to documentation and maintenance mandatory, the cost of its run time system is high and the cost of putting together an APL*PLUS II work station is very high at between £7,000 to £12,000.

Given that APL*PLUS II is highly unlikely to be considered for application development in a green field situation, I would have liked such utilities as workspace migration from the mainframe and the ability to read data from industry standard applications, such as LOTUS and SMART, bundled with the package. A facility to use APL*PLUS II under Microsoft Windows/386 such that multiple APL*PLUS II sessions were possible might have its uses too - I was unable to use APL*PLUS II under the Windows environment.

The utility workspaces are the ones packaged with APL*PLUS/PC Release 6.0 onwards - that is they are not optimised for the enhanced second generation environment.

Nevertheless, I would have no hesitation in recommending APL*PLUS II as a strategic product for PC applications development.

items.title: SAX
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 67

reviewed by Michael J.A. Berry

I love APL, and at one time I hoped that the qualities which endear it to me would cause it to sweep the world leaving the likes of Fortran and Basic rocking in its wake.

I no longer harbour that hope. My new, more modest, desire is that APL continue to be available as an alternative to those of us who would like to use it. For even this goal to be achieved, two things must happen:

[1] APL must continue to be the best tool available for expressing algorithms in a form which is both readable and executable.

[2] APL must learn to coexist happily with the rest of the software world.

SAX makes significant progress in both of these areas.

items.title: The Language
items.text:
SAX is a partial implementation of the language defined by Dr. Kenneth Iverson in 'A Dictionary of APL' (APL Quote Quad Vol. 18, no. 1, September 1987). Readers who are unfamiliar with the dialect of APL described by Dr. Iverson, may wish to consult it for amplification of the examples in this review. The SAX implementation also includes most, if not all, of the 'bells and whistles' which have accreted to the Sharp mainframe product over the years. ⎕TRAP, ⎕FMT, ⎕PACK and so on are all available.

SAX was implemented as a joint development project between I.P. Sharp associates and STSC. The software is based on the STSC Unix APL, but the language follows SHARP APL, not the STSC product.

For reasons which I will examine in the second part of this review, APL programmers are sometimes forced to use other languages in the course of their work. It is often a painful experience. All those declarations! All those loops! After using SAX for a few months, I now get much the same feeling about the other APL's I have available (STSC's APL*PLUS/PC and SHARP APL/PC). The old familiar APL idioms now seem like clumsy circumlocutions filled with semi-colons and explicit iteration. I return to SAX with a feeling of liberation.

Much of the feeling can be attributed to the differences between any 'advanced' APL and the APL's I have available for comparison which are embellished versions of ISO Standard APL. The most important difference between advanced APL dialects and standard APL is that in the former, operators may take derived and defined functions as arguments. Without that extension, available for several years now in APL2 and its derivatives, other common extensions such as arrays of arrays are robbed of much of their power and appeal.

SAX differs from other advanced APL dialects both in the set of primitive operators provided, and in the centrality of a concept called 'function rank'. The rest of this section examines the consequences of these differences. The information on APL2 comes from 'APL2 Programming: Language Reference' (IBM 1984) and 'APL2 at a Glance' (James Brown, Sandra Pakin, Raymond Polivka. Prentice Hall 1988).

Major steps in the evolution of APL have often come about through the recognition that something already extant in the language as a special case could be described in a general way and then extended. Thus ∧.= became part of APL because Iverson recognized that the inner product used in mathematics was just one member of a useful family of operations. Similarly, reductions and inner products existed in the language long before a theory of operators existed to explain what the / and . were doing there. Once these few special cases were recognized as members of a whole class of operators which produce functional results, the stage was set for adding new ones and extending the old ones to new domains. The resulting proliferation of operators, especially operators for functional composition, has made possible a much more functional style of APL programming. Things formerly accomplished through modification of the control flow through branching may now be accomplished by modifying the way functions are applied. The result is not only more aesthetically pleasing programs, but also programs which preserve the essentially parallel nature of many algorithms rather than obscuring it with branch points.

Function rank is another idea which has always been in the language but has only recently been formalized and generalized. A function's rank is defined by the rank of its arguments at the fundamental level of its definition. All the scalar functions are said to have rank zero. They are defined in terms of scalars, and applied to arrays of higher rank according to rules well known to readers of Vector. In SAX, these rules are extended to cover what are often called the 'mixed' functions. They, too, have default ranks. Monadic ⌽ for example, is of rank one. Its fundamental definition is in terms of vectors. When faced with an argument of rank 2 or higher, ⌽ partitions the array into cells of rank 1 and then applies its fundamental (rank 1) definition to each of them. This is precisely what scalar (rank 0) functions have always done, except that a scalar function partitions its arguments into cells of rank 0 before applying its fundamental definition.

Dyadic functions may have differing left and right ranks. Again, ⌽ makes a good example. It is said to have left rank 0 and right rank 1. In the expression (⍳5)⌽ 5 5⍴⎕AV each scalar cell of the left argument controls the rotation of a vector cell of the right argument. Many functions have infinite rank by default. That is, they apply to the entirety of their array argument without partitioning it into cells. Ravel is such a function, as is enclose.

Once the concept of function rank is recognized, it is natural to want an operator to control it. The ⍤ operator of SAX, with a functional left argument and a data right argument, does just that. The following examples give a feel for its use.

An important consequence of the availability of the rank operator in SAX is that in comparison with other advanced APL's, enclosed arrays are greatly de-emphasized. In examples I have seen from APL2, items are often enclosed solely for the benefit of the each operator. Strand notation also encourages the proliferation of enclosures. In SAX, one tends to use the array structure rather than enclose to define cells on which to operate. This approach is more flexible because each function may partition the data as appropriate to its own algorithm.

The prevalence of enclosed arrays in APL2 may also explain the decision by its designers to make some functions 'pervasive' (operating inside what is nominally a scalar) and others not. Decisions such as this are best left in the hands of the programmer. In SAX, no function is pervasive, but FOO¨> produces a version of foo which pervades one level. FOO¨> is read 'foo dual disclose.' F¨G derives a function which, for each argument cell, applies g, followed by f, followed by the inverse of g. The particular case F¨> is closely related to APL2's F¨ (read 'f each') for pervasive functions. The difference between the two flavours of 'each' in SAX (F⍤0 and F¨> is nicely illustrated using monadic ⍳:

SAX follows dictionary APL in cleaning up many of the messier parts of ISO APL. In SAX, one may dispense with square brackets and semi-colons completely. It is now easy to write functions which work correctly on arguments of unknown rank. The |FROM| function { selects cells from its right argument. The definitions of ↑ and ↓ have been extended so that it is not necessary to know the rank of the right argument in order to construct a meaningful left argument. Indexed assignment is made obsolete by the merge operator } which given a selection function, derives a dyadic function which selects elements from both its arguments to form a new result:

items.title: The SAX Environment
items.text:
The term 'environment' is used in two ways. The first refers to the programming environment and user interface. This includes editors, debuggers, cross-referencers, and the like. The second refers to the operating system environment of linkers, run-time libraries, etc. APL needs to do a better job of fitting into both of these environments. Twenty years ago, when commercial APL systems first became available, The APL work environment was a great leap forward. The interactive interpretive time-shared environment took much of the tedium out of programming. Because there was no existing programming environment as rich as the one which came built into APL\360, there was no reason for APL to run as part of a standard environment.

The world has come a long way in the last two decades. There are now programming environments which offer much more than any APL session manager. Unfortunately, it is not possible to run APL under most of these programming environments because APL interpreters usually come with an inseparable session manager which attempts to do everything the user might want. Even if the built-in full-screen editors and so on were not inferior to general purpose ones such as Emacs, they are different.

Differences are annoying. Before SAX, I could use GNU Emacs to program in C, Fortran, and Lisp, and to read my mail, look at usenet articles, and manage multiple shell windows, but I had to shut it all down to bring up APL. SAX properly separates the language from the environment. I can now run APL like any other UNIX process taking its input form STDIN and writing to STDOUT. This has allowed me to build an APL-Interaction mode for GNU Emacs which is modeled on the Lisp Interaction mode that comes bundled with the (free) GNU software.

I would like to donate this APL mode to the Free Software Foundation to make it part of the GNU software shipped everywhere. Unfortunately, it is not much use without a public domain screen font and printer font. It is time the owners of APL fonts realized that they are more valuable if given away. The first vendor who supplies a free X font for APL will be rewarded by having their ⎕AV become a de facto standard.

Of course, many users may not be inclined to write their own session manager! SAX may also be run under its own session manager which includes the STSC full-screen editor. The 'union' keyboard layout used by the session manager preserves the traditional keyboard locations of ascii characters. This is important in any environment where the same keyboard device is used for more than one purpose.

Another welcome step towards integration with the rest of the computer world is that ASCII≡128↑⎕AV. This means that ordinary files look right when read into APL, and that APL files which avoid the second half of ⎕AV are acceptable to any other program. Now that standard screen tools such as SunView and X support 8-bit (256 character fonts) natively, APL's large character set is no longer a problem.

The documentation came packaged as 3 sets of 3-hole punched paper suitable for inserting in the standard North American ring binder. (Try buying one of these in the UK and see how far you get! Ed.) The three volumes are titled 'Language', 'Environment', and 'System'. Although I usually dislike multi-volume documentation sets, in this case I found that my first guess as to which volume I needed to consult was almost always correct. The Language volume is the one I consulted most often. It is well written and easy to understand. The System volume covers all the ⎕NAMES, system commands, shared variables, etc. The Environment volume covers installation, printing, and how to write your own AP's.

SAX is less successful at integrating with the operating system environment. Communication with Unix is through the traditional APL shared variables. In order to install the shared variable processor, one must recompile the Unix kernel; an operation fraught with peril. Once installed, the shared variable processor did not prove to be very robust. Hiccoughs in the local area network which only slow down other systems, seem to cause shared variable transactions to hang forever. The postscript file printing facility which was packaged with SAX had to be altered in order to run in the SUN OS (Berkeley) Unix system as it contained system 5 commands.

Large systems today are often made up of modules written in several different programming languages. In my own shop, modules written in C, Fortran, and assembler are freely intermixed. Systems written in Lisp, while not as promiscuous as these other languages, may at least call routines written in them. SAX still generally refuses to call or be called. One of the most impressive features of APL2 is the ability to write ∘.FOO where FOO is a Fortran program.

The ultimate goal should be an APL processor which generates .o files which can be linked into an application in the same manner as the output of compilers for other languages. Only when that day comes will I feel that my right to continue using APL in my work is safe.

items.title: Experience
items.text:
I used SAX to build a moderately large application which generates Fortran code from test specification records. I have used this application to generate many hundreds of thousands of lines of Fortran code. Because of the nature of the application, I put great stress on the interface between SAX and Unix. I use both component files (to store the test records which include APL objects), and native files (for the Fortran output). I made a conscious effort to program in a 'new' style, using the rank operator in place of iteration and using functional composition of various kinds to derive just the function which would do what I wanted with a single application, rather than using intermediate results. At times this meant I spent longer writing the programs than I would have had I stuck to the APL vocabulary I have been using for years.

In the end, I was glad I had made the effort to master the new ideas. SAX is a far more powerful language than old-style APL. I would happily recommend this product to anyone. My understanding, however, is that it is not generally available except in quantity due to customer support considerations. My suggestion to IPSA is that they drastically lower the price and make it available with no support.

items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 86

by Jerry M. Brennan and Jennifer E. Daly
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
Score is a general purpose program for the scoring of tests. The program scores data according to a key that is customised by the user, and options exist for keyed, reversed, and weighted scoring of data.

Detailed instructions for the program (a printout of these is included as an Appendix) can be accessed anytime by the user. Two methods of input are allowed:

  1. Interactive input, where the user is queried for up to 512 (including blanks) elements of data.
  2. Batch input, which allows for a virtually unlimited amount of data.

Output includes the scoring key(s), subject identification, input vector, total number of elements entered, and scores for all the factors (i.e. each scoring scale).

Score has three advantages:

  • the program is flexible, with uncomplicated, customised keys that allow scoring of an unlimited number of items and factors.
  • data can be scored in a variety of ways by changing the keys and rescoring.
  • large sets of scoring keys for different tests (e.g. batteries) can be compactly stored and easily retrieved for future use.
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: Score in APL
items.text:
SCORE is a dyadic function with both arguments containing segmented character strings. The right argument KEY contains the scoring key. This argument requires a major segment for each scale and optional minor segments for special scoring features of each scale. The optional left argument DATA contains subject identification and item responses for each subject.

If DATA contains no elements, SCORE reads data interactively and the user is prompted to enter subject identification and item responses. In this mode the major segments of the KEY argument (i.e. each scoring key) as well as each scale in KEY and DATA (or, if interactive, each subject entry) are separated by a carriage return. Thus, for input, each subject's data and each scoring key for that data is entered on a new line. Each minor segment within the scoring key and within the data set is separated by '/'.

Two main functions are used for scoring: SCORE and RECODE. SCORE is the primary function that calls RECODE if recoding of data is done. In addition, two one-line utility functions, sSINDEX and sSSHAPE, are also used. For all functions, the variable DATA contains all subjects' data, and SCORE loops through DATA for each subject. Within SCORE, the variable D contains data for one subject and F is a counter indicating which factor is being calculated. Similarly Nf is the number of factors contained in KEY, S is the subject loop counter, and Ns contains the number of subjects stored in DATA.

[4]   ⍝ DATA is the optional left argument of a character vector
[5]   ⍝ with Subject ID, "/", and the item values. Each on newline.
[6]   ⍝ If DATA does not exist, the program asks for Subj & data.

[13]   →nUM
[14] LOOP:⍞←'----------> Subject ID: ' ⋄ →0×⍳0=⍴⍞ ⋄ ⍞←'Data : '
[15]   →0×⍳0=⍴D←⍞
[16] nUM:→OK×⍳' '∊D ⋄ D←((2×⍴D)⍴ 1 0)\D
[17] oK:D←⍎D ⋄ (⍕⍴D),' numbers entered.' ⋄ F←0
[18] NXTf:→PAU×⍳Nf←F+1 ⋄ V←'/',(1↓(⎕TCNL,KEY)SSINDEX F),'/1/0'
[19]   VALS←D RECODE 1↓V SSINDEX 2
[20]   (1↓V SSINDEX 1),'=',⍕+/(⍎1↓V SSINDEX 3)×VALS+
      (⍎1↓V SSINDEX 4)
[21]   →NXTf
[22] PAU:→LOOP×⍳INT ⋄ →NXTs
      ∇

Lines 1-6 are comments that describe essential features of the program.

The ⎕POKE on line 7 discards the character prompt utilized in the interactive mode.

Line 8 displays the scoring key(s) and determines the number of factors (i.e. the number of major segments) in KEY. The results of this line are then stored in Nf, the loop factor counter.

Line 9 skips to LOOP (i.e. the interactive mode) if DATA does not exist. The program then reads data interactively (lines 14-16).

Line 10 catenates a carriage return to DATA, and calls sSSHAPE to determine the shape (i.e. the number of subjects) in DATA. It stores the result in Ns and initialises the subject counter S.

sSSHAPE, the function used to count the number of arguments in the segmented strings, returns the number of carriage returns present in the string. A carriage return is thus added to KEY (and also to DATA) so that the first element is included in the count.

       R←sSSHAPE SS
       -----------

  [1]   ⍝Returns the shape of a segmented string
  [2]    R←+/SS=1↑SS
       ∇

Similarly sSINDEX returns selected delimited segments from a longer string, the delimiter for the segmented string is the first character (i.e. carriage return).

       R←SS sSINDEX I
       --------------

  [1]   ⍝Function for the indexing of segmented strings
  [2]    R←((+\SS=1↑SS)∊I)/SS
       ∇

Line 11 of SCORE increments the subject counter and exits when all the data has been processed. Otherwise the next subject is selected and the data stored in D.

Line 16 checks if there are blanks in D. If not, spaces are automatically inserted between the single digit integers; this facilitates entry of single digit data.

Line 18 goes to PAU when all of the factors have been calculated. This line also catenates the default multiplier, 1, and the default adder, 0, to the segmented string, and stores the result in V. These default options eliminate the need for user input of values when items are added with equal weight.

Line 19 passes the 'recode' subsegment to the RECODE function. If this subsegment is not empty, the data is recoded:

       R←D RECODE C;T;NR;N;V;M;I
       -------------------------

  [1]  ⍝ Recode data D_from S e.g 1:1=4 3=7$3:1=4 2=9
  [2]  ⍝ IF D→1 2 2 ¯4 then R→4 2 9 ¯4 [2nd value not recoded]

  [3]   →rEC×⍳':'∊C ⋄ R←(×T)×D[|T←⍎C] ⋄ →0
  [4]  rEC:Nr←sSSHAPE C←'$',C ⋄ N←0 ⋄ R←⍬
  [5]  L1:→0×⍳Nr←N+1 ⋄ V←1↓C sSINDEX N
  [6]   V[(V∊':=')/⍳⍴V]←' ' ⋄ I←1↑V←⍎V
  [7]   M←((0.5×¯1+⍴V),2)⍴1↓|V
  [8]   R←R,(×I)×1↑((M[;1]∊D[|I])/M[;2]),100
  [9]   →L1
       ∇

Line 20 of SCORE computes the scale score by multiplying and then adding the possibly recoded values.

Line 21 returns to score the next factor. Finally if the program is being run interactively, line 22 goes to LOOP to query the user for additional data. Otherwise the program returns to nXT for the next subject.

Jerry M Brennan University of Hawaii at Manoa Department of Sociology, Porteus Hall 2424 Maile Way, Honolulu Hawaii 96822
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: Appendix: Screen Hardcopy of Program Notes
items.text:
To PRINT these NOTES, toggle CTRL-PRNTSC on or off.

The APL workspace name is TESTSCOR. Load this workspace with one of the following:

      )LOAD TESTSCOR        [default drive (same as APL system)]
      )LOAD 0 TESTSCOR      [drive (e.g., 0=A 1=B 2=C)]

To SEE the KEYS & DATA in the workspace TESTSCOR, type:

      )VARS
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: SCORING KEY:
items.text:
1. To CREATE the scoring key for the test type )EDIT and some name - probably the name of the test.

For example:

)EDIT SHORTMEMORY   [Up to 77 characters with no blanks.]
  1. ENTER the scoring key for each factor on one line.

For example:

FACTOR NAME/ITEMS ON FACTOR/MULTIPLIER/AMOUNT TO ADD
FACTOR NAME/ITEMS/MULTIPLIER/AMOUNT TO ADD
...etc

WHEN YOU ARE FINISHED CREATING OR MODIFYING THIS KEY, LEAVE THE EDITOR WITH
Ctrl-E.

To SAVE the scoring key for use on another day, save the workspace with:
    )SAVE
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: KEY: EXAMPLE 1: (Note that each factor begins on a new line)
items.text:
ONE/1 2/1 3/¯2
TWO/1 3 4/1/0
THREE/4 ¯5/1/0
FOUR/2:1=10 2=20$5:1=30$¯6:1=5 2=7

This test has three factors labeled ONE, TWO, THREE, and FOUR.

The first factor, ONE, contains Items one and two. The multiplier for Item one is 1 and for Item two the multiplier is 3. Minus 2 is added to all Items. The second factor, TWO, contains three Items and all are multiplied by 1 and have 0 added. The third factor, THREE, contains Items four and five. Item four is added and Item five is subtracted.

Finally, factor FOUR has three Items: Two, five, and six. Items 2 and 5 are added and 6 is subtracted.

If Item 2 has a value of 1, it is scored 10; if it has a value of 2, it is scored 20. All other values of Item two are scored 0.

Similarly, if Item 5 has a value of 1, it is scored 30 otherwise, it is scored 0.

If Item 6 has a value of 1, it is scored 5. A value of 2 on Item 6 is scored seven. Otherwise, this item is scored 0. Note: Since Item 6 has a minus, these values are subtracted.

NOTE: ............':' delimits item numbers from their scoring weights. In the above example, a score of 1 equals 10 for Item 2. '¤' delimits items and their weights from each other. Also, the high minus is used to subtract items. This minus is Alt-2 on the keyboard and may look like a small two on your screen. For all computations, addition is done first, then multiplication and, finally, the sign is changed.
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: KEY: EXAMPLE 2:
items.text:
FACTOR ONE/1 2
FACTOR TWO/3 4 5

EXAMPLE 2 has two factors: The first has two items and the second has three items. By default, nothing will be added to the items and there is no multiplier.
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: KEY: EXAMPLE 3:
items.text:
This last example illustrates a scoring situation in which some items are REVERSED. The scoring for one REVERSED factor might be as follows:

Item 1 is punched 1, 2 ,3 and is to be scored 1, 2, 3.
Item 2 is punched 1, 2, 3 BUT is to be scored 3, 2, 1.

This might be keyed as follows:

FACTOR ONE/1=3$2=2$3=1
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: DATA ENTRY:
items.text:
1. CALL the program with the following command:
SCORE SHORTMEMORY    [The name of the program is always SCORE,
                      you insert the name of your key--in this case
                      SHORTMEMORY.]

The program will query for a "Subject ID". This identification can be any length and any characters--including blanks. After Subject ID is entered, the program queries for the items. Data consisting of all single digit numbers may be entered as a string (i.e., without blanks between each single digit). Data consisting of double (or more) digits must be entered with blanks separating each number. To QUIT data entry, strike RETURN when queried for "Subject ID".

Note: .............. Continue typing at the end of each line. The program will wrap automatically. The limit is 512 characters, including blanks.

  1. Another way to ENTER DATA is to use the editor as you did for the scoring keys. However, this time a variable will be created that contains the data.

For example:

)EDIT SUBS      [Up to 77 characters with no blanks]

Enter the Subjects' ID followed by a "/". Next, enter the data. (See above for information about data entry). Begin each new subject on a new line. For example, the data for two subjects might look like this:

Sally Brown female age 42/12321
Bill Douglas male age unknown/22213

When data entry is complete, quit with CRTL-E and save with )SAVE.
path: SCORE: An APL Program for the Scoring of Tests

items.title: TEST SCORING:
items.text:
1. To RUN the scoring program (using the key and data created in the last two examples):
SUBS SCORE SHORTMEMORY

Many keys and subject data can be saved in this workspace. In fact, you can save over 500 separate variables.

  1. To ERASE a key or a data file, do the following:
)ERASE SHORTMEMORY      [Erase working copy in memory]
)SAVE                   [save the erased copy onto the disk]

items.title: An Ambivalent Operator
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 96

From: David Piper, 24th February 1989

Here is an APL2 operator of use in ambivalent functions. One use of ambivalent functions is to elide the left argument, and thereby force it to take a default value. The methods normally used to achieve this are, for example:

[..]  →(2=⎕NC 'LEFT')/dyadic
[..]   LEFT←default
[..] dyadic:

or perhaps …

[..] ⍎(0=⎕NC 'LEFT')/'LEFT←default'

Neither of these solutions is ideal - the first embodies too much apparent complexity to acheive such a simple effect - code in which errors can be made. The second uses execute, which is bad for all the normal reasons!

The defined operator listed below allows the effect of the second example to be acheived without using execute:

     ∇R←DEFAULT(FUNC ∆MONADIC CLASS) RIGHT
[1] ⍝ OP: default func right if class is not 2
[2]  R←0                                ⍝ ASSUME DYADIC CALL
[3]  →(2=CLASS)/0                       ⍝ EXIT IF CALL WAS DYADIC
[4] R←1(DEFAULT FUNC RIGHT)             ⍝ EXEC WITH DFLT ARGUMENT
     ∇

The operator is used as follows:

     ∇AVE←SIZE AVERAGE NUMS;RUN
[1] ⍝ FN: MOVING OR NORMAL AVERAGE DEPENDING ON ⎕NC 'SIZE'
[2]  →(↑(RUN AVE)←(⍴NUMS)(AVERAGE ∆MONADIC ⎕NC 'SIZE')NUMS)/0
[3]  AVE←(SIZE+/NUMS)÷SIZE
     ∇

I trust the above is of interest, and look forward to any feedback.

Yours sincerely

D.B. Piper

items.title: An IBM Bug to watch for, when moving to APL2
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 96

From: John Warden, 16 May 1989

I would like to draw your attention to a major programming bug in some of the public workspaces distributed by IBM with VSAPL, which only becomes apparent when systems developed using certain of IBM’s utility functions are migrated from VSAPL to APL2.

The problem is in the function OPEN, which is found in all of the utility workspaces for handling AP126. On line 3 of this function is a conditional branch to LO. However, there are two lines labelled LO, lines 6 and 18. In VSAPL, if there are duplicated labels, branching is to the first occurrence, in this case to line 6. This is the correct path through the function so no error occurs. However a problem arises when workspaces which use this function are migrated to APL2. In APL2 the action taken when there are duplicated line labels is to branch to the highest line number. In this case the branch would be to line 18. This line issues an error message and exits the function.

The label LO on line 18 appears to be redundant as there is no apparent reason for a branch to this line. The solution is to check all workspaces migrated to APL2 from VSAPL which contain the IBM utility functions for communicating with AP126 for the existence of the OPEN function and edit it to remove the label on line 18.

Yours faithfully,

John E Warden
path: An IBM Bug to watch for, when moving to APL2

items.title: Setting PF keys and Other Initialization
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 97

From: Nicholas Small, April 1989

I have always found it very convenient for program development to have such frequently used strings as ‘)EDIT’ and ‘)SAVE’ on programmed function keys. With APL*PLUS/PC these strings can be incorporated in the interpreter so that they are there when one starts up APL. Consequently, I was somewhat disappointed when I discovered that it is not possible to have preset PF keys with APL*PLUS II.

We have a number of PC based APL applications, all run via DOS batch files, each of which calls the batch file which runs APL, passing to it the name of the desired workspace. The obvious thing to do to get values on PF keys, without having to edit every workspace, is to use an initializing workspace which, having done its work, loads the application workspace. The difficulty is: how to pass the name of the workspace? The technique I found makes use of the output redirection facility in DOS. My batch file to call APL*PLUS II has the following lines in it:

SET TEMP= %1 %2
IF X%1==X SET TEMP=?
ECHO %TEMP% > C:\TEMP\APLWS.NAM
SET TEMP=
D:\APLII\APLSM J=D:\APLII\XAPL387 Q='8 INIT'

The third line writes the name of the required workspace, or ‘?’ if none was specified, to a temporary file. The last line invokes APL, requesting a quiet load of the initializing workspace. (If you need to have parameters other than the workspace name passed to the APL-calling batch file, then the latter will have to be correspondingly more sophisticated.)

The latent expression in INIT performs the initialization, which clearly need not be restricted to setting up PF keys, and then calls the following function:

     ∇ GETWS;X
[1]   ⍝ Retrieve the name of the ws the user wanted, and load it
[2]   ⍝ If nothing requested, or error, then CLEAR
[3]    ⎕SA←'CLEAR'
[4]    X←¯2↓NCREAD 'C:\TEMP\APLWS.NAM'
[5]    →('?'=1⍴X)/0
[6]    ⍎'⎕LOAD''',X,''''
     ∇

The function NCREAD reads the contents of a native file as a character string (excluding any end-of-file marker); the carriage-return and line-feed, which DOS adds after the workspace name, are dropped. The loading is done via an execute so that, if an error occurs during the ⎕LOAD, the name of the requested workspace will be displayed (rather than just the name of the variable, X).
path: Setting PF keys and Other Initialization

items.title: British APL Association News
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 13

from Graham Parkhouse

We are very proud of Vector and are giving this issue to every delegate at APL89 in New York. While we are a national special interest group, everyone enthusiastic about APL knows that it is a language that bridges cultural barriers, both national and professional. Overseas membership of the British APL Association (BAA) brings with it four airmailed copies of Vector per year for about $45.

Last week I was invited to a meeting of the British Airways APL Association (BAAA?) at Heathrow Airport for the presentation of the BAA's Outstanding Achievement Award. The demonstration of AIMS, the information management system which is the subject of the award, was impressive.

I enjoyed Maurice Jordan's talk which followed the presentation. He covered some of the things he had been up to recently, such as function point analysis and 'assertive comments', comments written in a slightly enhanced APL on characteristics of the data being manipulated. I gathered that these assertive comments could be evaluated for truth at the debugging stage, then were left in as comments, but not evaluated. Maurice said more time was spent debugging the assertive comments than the rest of the code, which might at first sight make them seem self-defeating, but to the contrary were worth every bit of trouble they caused because of the rigorous thought needed to get them right. I am looking forward to hearing more about assertive comments because I suspect Maurice is onto a significant development.

items.title: The British APL Association Special Achievement Award for 1989
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 14

The Special Achievement Award for 1989 has been given to Delia Hickson and Graeme Davison on behalf of their project teams at British Airways. The award was presented at a special meeting of the British Airways APL User Group on 6th June.

The award was given for a suite of APL executive information systems which are in daily use at British Airways. The BAA considers that these APL systems are exceptional in terms of their acceptance by Senior Board Members and for the importance of the information they provide. Within British Airways, these systems have achieved an enormous respect for APL and what it can do.

Delia and Graeme have generously donated the £500 prize to the Dhaka Orphanage Fund; a charity founded by a British Airways stewardess to build a new orphanage with facilities for 750 boys in Bangladesh. The BAA is delighted to see the money go to such a worthy cause.

Following the award presentation by Peter Donnelly, the audience were treated to a demonstration of the applications; AIMS (Airline Information Management System) and a suite of Forecasting programs.
path: The British APL Association Special Achievement Award for 1989

items.title: A Demonstration of AIMS
items.text:
The systems are designed to provide the top brass in British Airways with the sort of information they need to make executive decisions.

First we were shown the various facilities provided. These included charts showing bookings and forecasts broken down in every conceivable manner, actual results, operational statistics (eg the number of delays caused by catering hiccups), competitive information, ... in all a most impressive amount of data presented in a pleasing and informative manner. It was easy to understand how useful it must all be to the Airline's Senior Management.

As evidence of the system's success, Keith Rapley (Senior Manager, Corporate Business Centre) described how they were used during two major crises during 1986, the American bombing of Libya and the Chernobyl disaster. Together these events caused an enormous upheaval in the world travel industry which jeopardised the survival of many of the major international airlines.

At the start of the crisis, bookings fell dramatically and cancellations rose, as tourists (particularly American tourists) decided that it would be safer to stay at home. The AIMS and Forecasting systems, which were normally updated weekly, were now consulted by anxious BA executives on a daily basis. The modifications that were necessary to meet this new demand for information were, naturally, completed in only a few days.

The result was that BA's executives had access to timely, accurate information from a system they had grown to trust which was presented in a (graphical) form they could readily understand. This enabled them to detect a recovery in the confidence of the travelling public long before their competitors. At the same time that other airlines were reducing capacity, BA launched a bold promotional campaign in North America designed to reinforce the recovery in confidence. As a result, BA came out of the crisis more or less unscathed (some other airlines suffered greatly) and was able to continue with its privatisation in February 1987.

A British Airways Director has said that 'Without a doubt, British Airways weathered the storm better than any other airline' and 'without (these systems) we'd have been lost since I'm sure that we'd have reacted like other airlines ... AIMS has been indispensable to running our business and to its privatisation'.

Keith Rapley concluded his talk by emphasising the importance of APL to British Airways and said that 'APL has already played a major role in the airline and will continue to do so for the next decade'. He went on to say 'Some of our junior members of staff occasionally question the use of APL ... I can assure you however that the management is committed to it and recognises APL's strategic importance in the development of present and future information systems for the airline'.
path: The British APL Association Special Achievement Award for 1989

For those of you reading Vector for the very first time, let me introduce myself. My name is Jill Moss and I run a specialist employment agency for the APL Community.
