items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce the launch at APL89 of Dyalog APL for 386 PCs under DOS. The product includes the new Dyalog APL screen manager using ⎕SM (Screen Map) and ⎕SR (Screen Read), which is proving extremely popular with users. The screen manager is the subject of a paper given at the Conference by John Scholes, head of the Dyalog APL development team.

In addition Dyalog APL for DOS contains the first release of a new development environment which Dyadic expects to be equally popular. APL has always offered an interactive environment in which programs can be developed and debugged very rapidly. However, the programmer interface has not kept abreast of modern developments, and even BASIC now provides a more interactive method of programming. The Dyalog APL development environment exploits the workstation environment of a bit-mapped colour screen, mouse and keyboard to provide a more convenient and powerful means of writing applications.

All APLs have you type an expression, then press a special key (usually ENTER or RETURN) to execute it. In Dyalog APL this idea is extended by adding keys that mean EDIT and TRACE (the actual keystrokes mapped to these functions are user-definable). Furthermore the EXECUTE, EDIT and TRACE keys can be mapped to buttons to give you a 'point and click' mouse interface.

If you type FOO and press <TRACE>, the function FOO will appear in a pop-up window on your screen, and your cursor will point to the first executable line which will be highlighted. If you now press <EXECUTE> the line will be executed and the cursor will move on to the next line. If instead you press <TRACE>, the line would be executed with trace on any defined functions and operators referenced on that line. For example, if the statement traced in FOO said Z←AVERAGE Y, a new window containing the function AVERAGE would pop-up overlapping the FOO window. You could then single-step through AVERAGE or trace deeper into your application as you wish. Execution can be restarted at any arbitrary line by simply moving the cursor to that line and pressing <EXECUTE> or <TRACE>.

The function on top of the stack (the APL stack AND the window stack) is always available for editing. Other functions and variables can be edited by pointing at their name and pressing <EDIT>. At any time you can have the SESSION window, the stack in several overlapping windows, and one or more edit windows, active. You can move between windows with a single keystroke or by moving the mouse, and data can be cut from one window and pasted into another.

By default, the debugger will activate automatically when an APL event occurs. The event message (e.g. DOMAIN ERROR) will be displayed as usual, but the stack will appear with the top function in an editable window, and the cursor already placed on the line at which execution halted.

The interactive nature of APL and facilities like ⎕STOP and ⎕TRACE were originally crucial factors in establishing APL as a tool for rapid application development. To some extent, APL has fallen behind other software in this respect. The new Dyalog APL development environment is intended to redress the balance and bring APL once more to the forefront of software development technology.

items.title: I.P.Sharp Associates
items.text:
Version 20 of Sharp APL is due to be released this autumn. The enhancements and new features in this version fall into 3 categories:

  • Language extensions include new primitives for enclosed arrays (raze, permissive disclose) and data searching (in, nubsieve).
  • APL system extensions include task specific names for 'continue' workspaces, access control for file libraries, file (as opposed to component) information, and an alternative character control system for non-APL terminals.
  • Changes to the APL environment include full dumps of workspace libraries with Sharp APL up and running, and transaction recording for improved user statistics. In response to customer requests, a dedicated OPR1 terminal is no longer required to operate Sharp APL.

The APLX interpreter is now available for the Siemens BS2000 environment. This is based on version 19 of Sharp APL and includes Auxiliary processors for BS2000 commands, file and syslist processing, and full screen management. It replaces the first generation APL1 product.

items.title: Cocking and Drury Ltd
items.text:
Release 2 of the APL*PLUS II system for 386 machines is due for international launch this August. The new facilities include the ⎕NA interface to non-APL programs, a numeric full-screen editor, easier migration and a very useful 'point and edit' feature which lets you open an edit session for the name nearest to the cursor, anywhere on the screen.

The ⎕NA facility can be used to call programs written in Microsoft C and Borland Turbo C in real mode, or MetaWare High C in the 32-bit protected mode. APL arrays can be passed into and returned from C programs. The numeric editor is a very welcome facility. Each edit cell is a single number in the numeric matrix. Blocks of numbers can be tagged, moved, imported and exported.

For some time we have had an internal 2-day nested arrays course for mainframe and micro-based APL*PLUS systems. We will develop this into a product if there is sufficient interest from users of these systems.

Readers may be interested to hear that we have successfully migrated two internal Symphony applications into Oracle PC, with interfaces to APL*PLUS PC.

Cocking and Drury are pleased to announce the launch of our new FOCUS consultancy service. We are committed as a company to working with our clients in developing superior business support systems, and this new service gives recognition to the place that FOCUS plays in the portfolio of business support tools at our clients' disposal.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
MicroAPL is continuing to place an increased emphasis on consultancy activities and we still looking for suitably qualified programmers for this area of our business. APL work undertaken in recent months includes Securities analysis, local government contracts and real time management information systems. Non-APL work has included PC network consultancy and installation as well as the provision of systems written in C, Assembly Language and work with some of the modern database software for micros.

Our core business of APL software sales is running at a higher level than in this period last year. Of the various implementations of APL.68000, the Mac version (both for the Mac and Mac II systems) is now the biggest seller having overtaken the Atari version in the last few months. In addition we have supplied various Unix-based versions of APL.68000 for systems such as Wicat and NCR.

Following our release of APL.68000 version 7.20 for the Apple Macintosh version, we have upgraded a number of other APL.68000 implementations to version 7.20. Users of our Mirage-based machines such as the Spectrum and the Aurora will be pleased to hear that version 7.20 is available for their machines - with the most significant feature being the inclusion of the EDIT full screen editor into APL.68000 as a system function (and command). We have also started shipping version 7.20 for the Wicat MCS and Unix versions and will shortly be announcing a release date for the Commodore Amiga. Apple Mac users should note that we have made some minor improvements to version 7 and version 7.30 is now available for the Mac. This is available at no cost for users of version 7. Apply to MicroAPL or its distributors for release details.

MicroAPL will be exhibiting at APL 89 in conjunction with our US distributors, the Spencer Organisation of New Jersey, and we look forward to meeting some of our many US customers in person at the conference. Richard Nabavi will be presenting a paper on his work with Windowing interfaces for APL and David Eastwood will be discussing some of the real time work that our consultancy operations have been involved with.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Alan Sykes

Welcome to Education Vector, the educational supplement to the quarterly journal produced by the British APL Association which is also mailed to all members on the (British) I-APL mailing list. For this edition we also welcome to our readership all attendees at APL '89, the international APL conference in New York in August.

I am glad to report that feedback to Education Vector is increasing and I welcome all contributions, comments and indeed criticisms. I thank those readers who (rightly) criticised some of my coding in past issues and I shall make every attempt to rectify my ways in future! (My use of APL tends to be very much one of getting the job done as soon as possible, and despite definite attempts to improve code presented in these columns, clearly I still haven't achieved the standards of professional APLers.)

In Education Vector (January 1989) I presented the question of how to turn a matrix of marks into grades. The solution I had in mind was duly presented by a number of APLers. This involved indexing the vector 'FEDCBA' according to the number of elements of the vector 70 60 50 40 35 0 that a mark was greater than or equal to. Thus the expression:

'FEDCBA'[⎕IO+¯1++/MARKMATRIX∘.≥70 60 50 40 35 0]

provides the matrix of grades. (The ⎕IO is included to give complete generality to the expression whatever index origin the user is using - see this edition's article by me.)

I did however receive another solution which I had not anticipated and which is really preferable. Thanks to Mike Kingston (of IBM!) who pointed out that if we construct a vector of grades for each possible mark then all we need do is index this vector using MARKMATRIX. The easiest way to do this is to use / to replicate the required values: the vector of 100 grades is given by:

35 5 10 10 10 30/'FEDCBA'

Hence the alternative solution, with virtually no computation, is:

(35 5 10 10 10 30/'FEDCBA')[⎕IO+MARKMATRIX]

In this issue of Education Vector, the theme is 'using APL is fun'. Richard Smith (now aged 5) shows us just how much fun he has had at the APL keyboard. In 'APL ART' I throw open the challenge to readers to use their creative talents to produce pictures using APL characters. Finally in 'Numbers and Bases' we show how APL can be used in an investigative project on numbers and bases. The great beauty of such investigations is that everybody has something to offer - please share your gems of APL fun with us all by submitting comments, notes, or articles for inclusion in future editions. I hope that you enjoy the columns of this edition as much as I have enjoyed compiling them.

Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 25

APLers are often teased concerning their use of strange symbols. Curiously enough, even mathematicians are sometimes guilty of this! Whilst teaching students who use APL in their statistics practical I have sometimes caught them playing with the symbols to see just what shapes can be created from them. All good fun though at the time they had better things to do!

Recently I noticed that my wife Claire (who is both a mathematician and an APLer) was doodling with the APL characters, and I began to wonder just how many works of aplart there are out there. So here is Claire’s contribution to start the ball rolling. The program is called LEAR and it defines global variables OWL CAT and BOAT. So there are no prizes for guessing just what LEAR does. As you can see the results are quite good. (I have to say that!) But of course you, the reader can do better?

items.title: The I-APL News
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 29

by Anthony Camacho

items.title: Problems
items.text:
We are a volunteer organisation and do not expect to be able to match the service standards of the major vendors - but our customers sometimes expect us to! We do not spend money on publicity, relying on what we can get by sending letters and press releases to the magazines. When somebody gets a good letter in a major magazine then I get a flood of letters and spend a few evenings replying to them. When this happens the porter correspondence stops for a few days and APL gets tried by a lot more people.

For example David Piper’s letter (p233 Personal Computer World May 89) produced about two dozen queries and, together with the details I send out, will have induced perhaps a quarter of them to try out I-APL. If you write letters to magazines or could do so please do more of it. The press coverage of APL has been better than ever in the U.K. for the last year or so. Let’s keep it that way.

We caused ourselves considerable extra trouble by issuing the BBC version with two bugs in it. The second bug came to light the day after all the letters about how to cure the first bug had gone out and so I had to do almost the same again. The current versions have no known bugs. Everyone who we know bought a faulty version has been written to and anyone who has a faulty version may get it exchanged for the cost of the postage.

There are two mistakes we know about in the manual:

IAPL/E on the Archimedes does not send the APL font to an EPSON FX printer.

IAPL B is necessary on a BBC B or Master to get APL output (using EPSON graftrax compatible graphic output).

items.title: Progress
items.text:
We are making steady sales and people are still working on ports to other machines. Ed Shaw and Rolf Levenbach are working together on the Apple ][ and Drs Ian Clark and Edwin Ashworth may do a Mac. Emmanuel Roche is working on the Amstrad word processors and Geoff Robinson on the Transputer (on a Bucon board which is a PC add-on).

We are still looking for porters. In particular we would like to find a porter or a group who would collaborate to produce a port for the Commodore CBM64. This is the most important of the machines common in schools that is not progressing as we would like.

We have received camera-ready copy for the second edition of ‘An Encyclopedia of APL’ by Garry Helzer. By the time you read this it will be in the hands of the printer. We have as good as sold out of the first edition of 1000 and as the second edition is laser printed and will be a better-looking product, easier to read, we think it worth doing a larger print run so that we can hold the price. Who, in 1986, would have thought I-APL would last long enough for us to be boasting that we have never had a price increase!

Among the many teachers who have bought a copy of I-APL, most of them BBC or Archimedes users, there are a few that have become enthusiasts for APL overnight as it were. We would very much like to help them. Last year the British APL Association said it was going to ask people who would be willing to help a teacher with APL to register and to make a list publicly available. I-APL is very keen on the idea. If you too are keen, and especially if you would be one of the volunteers, please let someone on the BAA committee know.

At the risk of being boring I repeat my appeal for teachers who use APL to write down anything they feel would be useful in school. If it is short we can put it in the Education Vector; if it is long we can publish it as a pamphlet. Either way other teachers trying APL for the first time may be grateful for the help.

items.title: Editorial: Join the British APL Association
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Peter Donnelly

I am addressing this editorial to the APL89 delegates of APL89, particularly non-UK delegates, who will have received this issue of Vector free of charge. The reason we are giving it away is not entirely altruistic; we want you to join the British APL Association! For overseas members, Vector is the ONLY reason for joining the BAA, so what do you get?

For me, Vector is first of all 'a good read'. It is deliberately NOT a dry technical journal, but tries to be interesting, topical, and occasionally provocative. It contains something for everyone.

First is usually the correspondence columns. Vector's policy is to print any correspondence however contentious, as long as it is at least vaguely related to APL and is not actually libellous. Attacks on the BAA committee are happily printed alongside erudite arguments over the merits of various APL keyboards.

Next there is 'The Education Vector' edited by Dr. Alan Sykes of Swansea University and aimed fairly and squarely at new APL'ers and the growing community of I-APL users. Education vector contains valuable hints for APL novices and often surprises those of us who think we know it all!

Following this you get News from Sustaining Members, a useful update on what the vendors are up to (or at least what they would have you think they are up to) and a comprehensive APL Product Guide. Several overseas organisations already take advantage of free listings in the Product Guide, and we would like to see more. The BAA would also welcome overseas companies as sustaining members - the "News" section gives you an inexpensive and convenient way to keep a significant part of the APL market informed of your products and services.

Then there are the articles. These are split into "general" and "technical". General articles often reach ( and occasionally surpass !) the standard expected of APL conference papers, but they tend to be presented in a less formal and more readable style. The technical section and "Hacker's Corner", is edited by Dave "show me your interpreter and I'll crash it in 5 minutes" Ziemann, and always contains informative snippets for the professional APL user.

Vector is published quarterly. The BAA intends to make it the leading APL journal for the English speaking world. You will find an application form for the BAA at the back of this issue, or you can contact a BAA representative at the conference. Join Today!

items.title: Experience of Using IBM's APL2/PC
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 57

by Anthony Camacho

items.title: Why I Bought It
items.text:
I bought APL2/PC because of its free run time packager, hoping to be able to do some of the work which I was being asked to write in compiled BASIC in my favourite language instead. The end user, I thought, would not be able to tell the difference between one .EXE file and another. Furthermore I would be able to tell him I was doing his job with software supplied by IBM.

Of course there were some vicissitudes; the nature and resolution of these is described below. However I have to say that in general, my best hopes were realised: this product deserves success. I am plainly going to use it a lot.

items.title: The Maths Co-Processor
items.text:
I use an Amstrad portable, which has the advantage that I can take it to the client, and use it to demonstrate things on, even if he hasn't a free machine for me. I can also transfer files on the spot, even if I have not foreseen the need and don't have the file on a disk of the client's format. APL2/PC would not run on it. 1 + 1 gave an answer consisting partly of letters u with grave accents.

I sought advice and was told that some timing characteristics of the processor were not PC compatible: the co-processor emulator will not run properly with this incompatibility. I had to buy a co-processor emulator for my Amstrad. Then it worked and I have had no compatibility problem since. Incidentally I understand that even 1 + 1 uses the maths co-processor and that the strong advice given in the manual to use a co-processor is because almost any program will run as much as four times faster with one.

items.title: Reading in Short Files
items.text:
The jobs on hand each involved reading in several ASCII files of about 20K, and merging selected data from each of them into one or two output files. With BASIC this was difficult because there is insufficient array space to hold the files in memory. In APL2 the workspace available can easily exceed 400K; it depends on which auxiliary processors you load and on how much resident software you hold in memory.

To read the files in there is an auxiliary processor and a FILES workspace containing nice functions to do everything you want without having to read all about the AP. I soon established that READFILEV would read a file into a vector where each element was one line of the file. This form is marvellously convenient for subsequent handling.

A system function 4 ⎕AT <namelist> returns, for each object in the namelist, the number of bytes of memory it occupies and the number of bytes of data. I soon discovered that the nesting overhead on vectors of short vectors was high. 40K of characters (I was reading Financial Times share data) can use up 100K of memory.

items.title: The Shrinking Workspace
items.text:
I encountered the first serious problem one Friday evening when there was no-one to phone for help. I had been trying out various file reading options and I got an unexpected WS FULL. ⎕WA returned 67K. Where had my 400K of workspace gone?

I read the manual. I sometimes have to write manuals and count myself something of a connoisseur. This one is excellent. Every explanation I sought was in there - but not always easy to find. For example it was when reading about the packager that I discovered that APL2's internal tables can be cleared by:

)RESET                   ⍝ Clears the stack (essential for OUT)
)OUT WSNAME              ⍝ Writes WS to .ATF file
)CLEAR                   ⍝ Clear WS
)IN WSNAME               ⍝ Copies WS in from .ATF file
)WSID WSNAME             ⍝ Was CLEAR WS
)SAVE                    ⍝ Cleared tables in saved version

When I did this, I got back my 400K. I now do this routinely, using the .ATF and .APL versions of the workspace to back each other up. On I-APL I alternately save MYWS and MYWSX.

When I tried to repeat the fault I couldn't. It took some time to establish that as I was trying out file reading options, the workspace was mysteriously shrinking. Each time I read one of my small files in, I lost some space ... until eventually something failed with a WS FULL.

Next Monday I rang Dave Selby. Apparently there is at present no garbage collection process to restore to the workspace the space used by shared variables. Once a variable has been shared and retracted, the space it used is lost. In the FILES workspace such processes as READFILEV share the variables, read the file and then retract the sharing, so each time a file is read or written workspace is lost. Dave Selby told me of a simple work-around. Share the variable in the top level function, use it for all file reading and writing operations and only retract it at the end. Setting the control variable to ⍳0 closes the current file. This way the space is only lost once. It was necessary to amend some of the functions in the supplied FILES workspace. After that all was well. How pleasant to discover that they are all unlocked!

items.title: No Errors Found in the Interpreter
items.text:
About the APL interpreter no news is good news. I haven't tried to find a bug and haven't found one by accident. The implementation does not support the diamond for multi-instruction lines, and the standard full screen editor doesn't allow function lines to exceed 80 columns. As I like to write functions which fit easily on a screen, this suits me fine. I haven't discovered how to edit a 200 character line. Maybe it is impossible.

I have not yet used the editors supplied in the EDIT workspace. I believe that they do allow you to edit 160 column lines. Under pressure to get the job done I stayed with the editor I know and have found the del editor perfectly adequate. One thing only I miss - being able to call back the last line with ")<enter>". I have quite often lost a long line I was working on by displaying a variable that was longer than expected. The default session manager does not allow you to scroll back to see items which have left the screen.

items.title: The Packager
items.text:
The packager is a separate program that takes an APL saved workspace, incorporates or omits the co-processor emulator and such auxiliary processors as you specify, and produces a .EXE program. If you forget to set the ⎕LX the .EXE run is very short! Any untrapped error or attempt to return to APL command mode in a packed program immediately returns you to DOS. The packaging process is interactive and fast. On one client's PS/2 model 70 it takes no more time than to enter the details required. Incidentally there is no )XLOAD to load a workspace without executing the ⎕LX, so I got into the habit of pressing CTRL+Break immediately after entering the load command. This prevents the ⎕LX executing and doesn't leave anything on the state indicator. On the PS/2 model 70 I could only rarely do this. The disk is read so fast that nine times out of ten the program would load and begin executing before I could get interrupt pressed. That hard disk is really fast!

I have used the graphics auxiliary processor with success to do experimental map distortions. I have used the printing and DOS auxiliary processors too. DOS has occasionally puzzled me because I've somehow got it into a state where the variable is reported as shared, but commands assigned to it get no reaction. The cure is to reload the workspace. I have promised to seek and provide to Dave Selby a reproducible instance of this - it may be something I am doing wrong. I haven't yet had time to keep my promise. It is not really fair to write about it before he has had a chance to help, but Vector deadlines have to be taken seriously nowadays.

items.title: I Have a Long Way to Go with APL2/PC
items.text:
I have now delivered two jobs using APL2/PC and am delighted with it. As you see I have scarcely scratched the surface of the 27 workspaces or 17 auxiliary processors. I haven't even yet used the AP124 screen manager. I will.

For anyone who wants to deliver working programs to customers fast (where the customer doesn't care how you do it) this is a quite splendid product. For me it was worth its price and the cost of the 8087 just to get away from BASIC on the jobs I've done. I hope to do many more with it.

items.title: Some Additional Remarks ....
items.text:
by Adrian Smith

I too have a copy of this excellent little APL, and I too have liked almost everything about it. Some random thoughts to soak up this spare half page:

  • if anyone would like a Hercules+ Ramfont for APL2/PC I would be delighted to pass mine on. Look out for it on the software library soon.
  • AP124 works rather well. As a pressure test I pulled my GDDM-based editor off the mainframe and took it back to its 1982 status (i.e. to AP124). It runs fine; what's more you can do useful PC-ish things like pop-up help, fancy background colours, and character attributes. I much prefer it to ⎕WIN.
  • this beast deserves a better session manager! I flirted briefly with AP120, but found that it simply hobbles the PC and makes it feel like a mainframe! Like Anthony, I have retreated to using the 'raw' session instead.

Apparently it is shortly going to cost me £330 to upgrade my APL*PLUS/PC from version 5 to version 8. For £348 I could have free runtime, nested arrays, defined operators, and a 3.5Meg workspace. Clearly there is some effort involved in making the transition, but just at the moment I feel like giving it a damn good try!

items.title: Dyalog APL for 386 DOS PC's
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 61

reviewed by Jonathan Martin

items.title: The Reviewer
items.text:
Let me put my cards on the table first. I've been an APLer for over 6 years, most of which was spent using APL*Plus under VM/CMS. However, for the last two years, I have been using Dyalog APL, both on an PC-AT with a go-faster Unix board in it and, for the last twelve months, on an IBM RT-6150 (all to myself!). Consequently, I was a little unsure of "going back" to good old DOS and its single-tasking environment.

My testing was done on a Compaq Deskpro 386 with 4Meg of memory, running at 16MHz. I had hoped to fully test it on an IBM PS/2 model 80, running at 25MHz as well but time caught up with me.

items.title: The Product
items.text: As I'm sure many of you are aware, Dyalog APL has been around for a number of years now but, until the release of this version, it was available solely for the Unix/Xenix world. I'm not sure exactly how many Unix machines it is available on - lets just say Dyadic are experienced at porting it... It is a true second generation APL with all the features you would expect - nested arrays, defined operators, error trapping, file system etc... but a lot more to distinguish it from the other APLs around.

items.title: The Review
items.text:
The hardest part about doing this review is that I am used to using Dyalog - I spend most of my day working with it. Constantly, during this review, my feelings were that I was just using Dyalog APL. Now that may sound stupid. Yes, of course I was using Dyalog, there wouldn't have been much point in the review otherwise. What I mean is that it is just like the other versions of Dyalog I have used.

It was quick - that was something that you notice immediately. Starting up APL and loading a workspace takes three to four seconds. As far as benchmarks go, we have one at British Airways that is a solution to the Eight Queens problem. It is very typical of the work we do - lots of boolean matrices being thrown around, data being expanded to a common form and then compressed down to get the results out - Queens on Dyalog under DOS ran only about 15% slower than it does on my (old) 6150.

A major enhancement to Dyalog that, while not brand new (it has just appeared in the current release of the 6150 version), is certainly worth talking about. It is ⎕SM, the new screen manager. Under this version, they have introduced something called Screen Memory Mapping which, while I do not claim to understand how it does what it does, transforms ⎕SM from being just a superb method of managing and updating the screen to a superb and extremely fast facility. If you have only ever used an AP124/6 type interface and have longed for those flashy PC-style front-ends, then want no more. ⎕SM gives you all that and more and in such an intuitively APL-like way.

Useful things like pop-up windows become trivial and selection bars and "buttons" need only a few minutes coding. You can also do a hundred and one other things with it. Try your hand at Othello, again written using ⎕SM. Simple animation was one thing that was just about possible using the 6150 version. It now becomes much more viable at this speed

Two tests that I wanted to do on this version were to port two very different workspaces down. I must say porting is a bit slow at the moment but given that it is a job that is done once and once only, I can live with it. The first workspace was something I had knocked up quite quickly - a simple database with update/delete/edit facilities. It isn't particularly well written - the sort of thing that everyone writes for themselves and assumes that no-one will ever see. I had two minor problems with it under DOS. Firstly I had written it for 12 PFkeys - this particular set-up only had 10 of the twelve accessible. Moving 'quit' from PF12 to PF10 resolved that. Secondly, the line-drawing characters had been stripped out of the BOXTM function that decorates the help message. Again, only a minor irritation. Apart from that, no problems.

The second workspace was much larger (about 300 functions) and is one that had been moved from APL*Plus under VM to Dyalog about 18 months ago. It is a text editor with facilities for moving text around, inserting and deleting lines, formatting text and drawing graphics characters. The two problems mentioned above obviously occurred here but nothing else. I had effectively moved an application from a Unix machine to a DOS machine with only minor problems. Very impressive indeed.

There were certainly one or two bugs in it - this version is a couple of months away from being released yet - but nothing that appears dramatically difficult to solve. In fact, one of the bugs (excessive use of the cursor keys causing the APL to hang) generally manifests itself whilst playing the version of Othello that they have written for ⎕SM (I was just about to win as well, honest).

items.title: Conclusion
items.text:
This new version looks and feels just like the other versions of Dyalog I have used. I'm sorry to go on about it, but that is the over-riding impression that comes out. Personally, I like the multi-tasking features of running under Unix and the ability to be doing more than one thing at a time. However, there are many people and many companies who do not like Unix for one reason or another or who are bound by company loyalties and budgets to stay with DOS. This version could well be the answer to those people.

If you want to know what is happening to APL, get hold of a copy of this.

items.title: APL90 in Denmark
items.text:
The APL90 conference will take place from 13th to 17th August 1990 at the Marienlyst Hotel in Elsinore (Helsingoer), near Copenhagen.

This seaside hotel offers an excellent environment for APL90, the second APL conference to be arranged in Denmark. We are looking forward to a conference with many valuable papers on the progress of APL and its use in numerous applications areas.

We plan to introduce at this conference the concept of poster sessions, in which the speakers are given a small booth to present a poster with an eyecatching presentation of their work, and with the opportunity to discuss it with by-passers and to hand out written material. We believe that this will allow us to present even more interesting papers at APL90 than we otherwise would have been able to find room for.

We encourage you to submit a paper to the conference. You may choose between submitting a regular paper and submitting a proposal for a poster session. The schedule for submission is as follows:

Please send your abstract before the end of September 1989 to the APL90 address shown at the back of this folder, or to one of the members of the program committee.

Then send a complete draft before the end of November 1989. The submitted papers will be reviewed, and an answer will be sent to all submitters before the end of January 1990.

Both abstracts and complete drafts may be sent by mail, telefax, PC-readable diskette, or by any of the available mailboxes.

For accepted papers we expect to receive a camera-ready copy before the end of April 1990. Detailed instructions on the preparation of the paper will be mailed with the acceptance. We intend to mail the conference proceedings to all participants before the conference.

Plans for the conference include a Software Exchange as well as an exhibition, showing many of the new offerings in APL systems.

A call for participation will be distributed early 1990. Please note that a wide range of accommodation has been reserved already, from four star hotels to family rooms and a youth hostel. Also, a program for the families will be offered during the conference.

items.title: APL90 Program Statement:
items.text:
In line with tradition, APL90 will be a forum for exchange of experience and ideas within the world of APL. 'For the future' is the main theme of the conference, which will illustrate, through the presentations and discussions, why APL not only has been but will remain an excellent tool for Information Management:

Whenever new technologies emerged, APL was there to greet them. Think of SQL/DB2 interfacing and vector processing, to name a few. By its open and dynamic structure, APL is particularly suited for the development and implementation of new ideas and techniques. We encourage papers illustrating how such frontline concepts are delivered through the use of APL. Any bright ideas on Image Processing, Neural Networks ...?

Effective Information Management and Management Information will be increasingly important for the competitive ability of any organization in the future. We invite papers showing how APL can combine the creation and use of corporate-wide information systems with end-user computing by professionals. We especially welcome papers which demonstrate how this can be done in an efficient, structured and well documented way.

We trust that APL90 will provide APL implementors and philosophers alike with the incentive and opportunity to present their current work and to discuss ideas and plans for the future. However, as much program development in other languages now takes place in environments that rival or surpass APL's once unique environment, we hope that users will take this opportunity to put demand on the implementors for modernizing APL's look and feel. We encourage papers that guide the implementors in the right direction, so that our language can remain competitive in the world of windows, CASE, object oriented programming systems and distributed databases.

APL was originally developed for educational purposes and has recently started to find its way back into schools due to its availability on small computers. It is an attractive educational tool because it enables teachers to use data with its natural structure, rather than in a traditional, scalar fashion. We encourage papers which focus on the advantages of this use of APL.

APL implementations continue to evolve, with extensions to the language itself, as well as interfaces to - and from - other environments; recently, encouraging signs have been noted with respect to standardization of 'enhanced' APL dialects. We would very much like to see papers presenting problems in and, hopefully, proposing solutions to these areas.

items.title: Hacker's Corner: Where to Zap APL*PLUS Version-8
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 90

by Adrian Smith

I eventually became bored with the exercise of tracking down the banner in APLx.EXE, so I wrote a function to do it for me ...

     R←STRING NFIND FI;LEN;OFF;IN
[1]      ⍝ Returns position of <STRING> within DOS file (origin-0)
[2]       FI ⎕NTIE ¯2 ⋄ LEN←⎕NSIZE ¯2 ⋄ OFF←0 ⋄ R←⍬
[3]      ⍝ Now check file contents in 4000-byte segments ...
[4]  LOOP:IN←⎕NREAD ¯2 82 ,(4000⌊LEN-OFF),OFF
[5]       R←R,¯1+OFF+(IN ⎕SS STRING)/⍳⍴IN
[6]       →(LEN≤OFF+4000)↑DONE
[7]       OFF←OFF+4000 ⋄ →LOOP
[8]  DONE:⎕NUNTIE ¯2
     ∇

Version-8 is a distinct improvement on its predecessors, as you only need to replace the banner. In earlier releases you had to obliterate the serial number and release information as well! It now has the good sense to detect that the banner has altered, and to suppress the version and serial information. This is probably just as well, as it checks for a valid number before it will load at all!

Here is the much simplified function to install your own signon banner:

     BNRPOS PUTΔBAN BANNER
[1]  ⍝ Patch in <BANNER> to file ⍙EXE at <BNRPOS>.....
[2]   ⍙EXE ⎕NTIE ¯1
[3]   (631↑BANNER,⎕TCNL,630⍴⎕TCNUL)⎕NREPLACE ¯1,BNRPOS
[4]   ⎕NUNTIE ¯1
     ∇

     ⍙EXE←'ZAP6.EXE'                         ⍝ .... set filename
     140932 PUTΔBAN 'HELLO FROM APL6'        ⍝ Replace current banner

Maybe one day they will get the message and restore the B= option.

     BNR←153429          ⍝ Vn8
     BNR←102804          ⍝ Vn8 with SM

items.title: APL89 - Tutorial Sessions
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 101

Reported by Jonathan Martin

Jonathan Martin .... Juggling!

At APL89, I seemed to spend a great deal of my time in the tutorial sessions. This also gave me some ammunition for one of my great hobby horses - that is that APL is very good at doing some things, but there are commercially available packages that do the other things a hundred times better than APL can ever hope to. The only way forward is to enable APL to be the binding, to take up when these packages cannot cope. Here's what I thought of them.

items.title: Nancy Wheeler: APL2 & SQL
items.text:
This was of great interest to me as the Dyalog APL-Oracle link that I use has its origins in this. I also feel that one of the major hindrances that I have come across has been the inability of the rest of the world to access the data that we have had available to our APL systems. At last, here is a standard product that enables everybody to access some common data.

The talk was split up into three sections: SQL, APL2 and SQL & APL2.

The first section on SQL was a basic introduction to Relational Databases, the simple ideas behind them, the simple data constructions and a fairly brief introduction to the SQL language. This was great - about the limit of my knowledge!

Then Nancy talked about the APL2 Auxiliary Processor that they had written at the IBM lab in Santa Teresa. To use an APL-SQL link there is one major prerequisite - you must have a nested array APL. Relational data fits so well into nested arrays that one would appear to have been made for the other. The AP comes with a supplied workspace of about 20 functions which emulate the corresponding SQL features. Fortunately, there were lots of examples of the use of it e.g.:

PREP 'NULL' 'select * from ABC where NAME=''WHEELER'''

OPEN 'NULL'

FETCH 'NULL'   .... which gets all the fields from database ABC into
                    the workspace for which NAME equals Wheeler.

The most important message of the talk, though, was left to the end. "To write a successful application one needs to consider such issues as database design, performance, storage usage, locking, and authority schemes as well as just 'getting the right answers'". How true - a tool as powerful as a relational database mis-used can cause far more damage than, say, a run-of-the-mill third generation language. A relational database used with APL could be the answer to all your problems - or just the start of them.

items.title: Kevin Weaver, Eric Baelen, Rob Lauer, Roy Sykes: Software Tools for Enhancing Performance
items.text:
Reported by John Searle

This session was a "must" for any APL*PLUS/PC application developers. The presenters have combined their resources and considerable experience to give us a free workspace of techniques for speeding up PC applications, achieved mostly by providing cover functions for Assembler or compiled C code. Eric Baelen presented a function for speeding up the wrapping of words in a text vector into a neatly formatted matrix, and functions for improving the robustness of joining text matrices together, and determining whether a sufficient number of files can be accessed for an application. Roy Sykes presented functions for rapidly searching the symbol tables in a library of workspaces for a wanted name, and for speeding up the operation of ⎕WGET and ⎕WPUT. Rob Lauer presented software which implements a complete Windows-like pulldown menu system, with mouse support. All the software was made available on diskette as part of the registration package, and is in the public domain. The benchmarks and documentation were printed in the "Session Tutorials" booklet.

items.title: Harry Bertuccelli: Exchanging Workspaces
items.text:
My feeling on entering this tutorial was that it was going to be one of the more important of the bunch. Porting workspaces from one machine to another is something that all of us will probably get involved in someday with the advent of more and more powerful DOS and Unix machines. Fast going are the days when APL was solely a mainframe language.

But... it disappoints me to have to admit that this was one of the worst presentations I have ever attended at a conference. I lasted getting on for 30 minutes (it was scheduled for 90) before I decided that enough was enough. Most of what I say here is cobbled from the paper in the proceedings - little of note was said during the time I was in the room.

The method itself is fairly simple and standard.

  1. Convert workspace into some text representation
  2. Transfer text file to target machine
  3. Convert text file back into workspace

However, Mr Bertuccelli tries to cloud the issue somewhat by writing out his text file with the last eight characters of his "80-byte 'card image'" with a sequence number. I may be short in the tooth but I can just about remember decks of cards - and yes, sequence numbers were fairly useful for the times you decided to juggle with them. But how often do IBM mainframes randomise the order of text files? Maybe I'm being unfair - the method is based on compatibility with the format of APL2's )OUT & )IN (which is a major plus point as this appears to be becoming the standard form) and maybe this is the reason.

The paper itself is somewhat disappointing also. Reading it, I found, was very hard work, I think because it is pitched at too low a level, preferring to explain the intricacies of "the loop ... beginning at line 5" rather than at the overview level.

Anyway, try reading the paper yourself if you can get hold of it - I'd be interested to hear what other people think about it and to know whether my view is clouded by the fact that I thought so little of the presentation itself.

items.title: Pamela Baron & James Kraemer: Desktop Publishing
items.text:
This was billed as an introductory tutorial on Desktop Publishing (DTP) and was both professionally presented and pitched at the right level. Four major areas were covered: Hardware considerations, Software considerations, DTP Style and a small amount of DTP and APL.

The Hardware and Software considerations were based around the two scenarios:

"I have a computer. What software will give me the best publishing abilities?" (probably the most common problem) and "I want to publish long documents using Ventura Publisher. What hardware do I need?"

The basics for a decent DTP system are adequate memory (2Meg is a good base to start from), a monitor and a mouse. As far as extra memory and faster machines go, the need is regulated by the expectations of the user. I get frustrated using Pagemaker on a 286 machine with 640K memory though find it more than palatable on a 386 with 2Meg.

As to which package to go for, the list is endless with Pagemaker and Ventura being the front-runners in the DOS world. Although I have only ever used Pagemaker, the feeling seems to be that Pagemaker is best suited for small documents (say up to a dozen pages) while Ventura scores on much larger tomes.

Style, and this was rightly stressed in the presentation, is the most important factor in producing any document with a DTP package. Suddenly, going from a standard WP package to a fully blown DTP system, you are faced with what seems like a hundred and one different ways of doing the same thing. Should you use Helvetica for the text and NewCenturySchoolBook for the headings? What about some italicisation for section headings? How about some stresses here and there and should I use bold or underline? Some nice boxes around everything would look nice. Shall I use thin or thick lines?

As ever, simple is best. Use no more than two different fonts, one for headings (sans-serif) and one for the body of the text (serif) but try to break up pages and pages of text with the addition of graphics, pictures or something else appropriate. Standardize on the format throughout the document (fonts, pitch, headers & footers, margin widths etc.) and make sure you stick to it.

The paper provides a wonderful example of what Pamela Baron referred to as the "Ransom Note style". Needless to say, in eight lines of story (written by her young son James) four or five different fonts are employed along with random use of bold, capitals, italics and even underlined italics.

The majority of the talk managed to avoid mentioning APL, but I guess it had to rear its head sometime. Desktop Publishing and APL have, up to now, been very much like oil and water. Despite the numerous fonts available, the chances of getting an APL font were zero. Up to now that is, because the tail of the talk was to have been a demonstration by Ed Cherlin showing Pagemaker, running on a Mac, with a real, live PostScript APL font. Could this be the answer to the APL community's publishing problems. Very much yes and no! After showing off the APL fonts listed amongst all the other available fonts, as soon as Ed selected one of them and tried to use it, the package went haywire, spreading what he had typed in in a rather random fashion across the screen. End of demonstration!

One day (and I don't think it will be too far away now) we will have a true, fully scalable PostScript APL font. I just wish one of the big companies would fund it and have it done properly rather than relying on individuals having to spend their own time cobbling it together themselves. Then we could take another step towards acceptability in the outside world.

items.title: Judson Rosebush: Using APL for Computer Graphics Notation
items.text:
The presentation and the paper in the proceedings were very different for this talk. The presentation mainly consisted of a number of slides and videos of some stunning computer-generated graphics, some that Judson Rosebush had been involved in, some that were just so good he wanted to show us anyway.

However, it is the paper that I will discuss, as there are some very nice algorithms for playing around with graphic shapes. Given an image, there are three main transformations you can perform on it: translation moves it left, right, up or down; scaling makes it bigger or smaller; rotation gives a rotary motion about the origin.

  • Translation is the simplest - if your object is in coordinate form, simply add or subtract constant values to it to move it around.
  • Scaling is almost as simple. Rather than add or subtract, multiply your coordinate representation by the proportions you wish to scale the object along each axis.
  • Rotation, which is probably the most interesting, is, of course, also the most difficult. Simply, it involves a couple of sines and cosines and both a minus and a plus reduction.

A much neater way of doing these translations is through the use of homogeneous coordinates and transformation matrices. A homogeneous coordinate transformation matrix consists of as many rows as there are vertices in the object and columns one greater than the number of axes. The extra column is referred to as the homogeneous coordinate and has the value 1. The transformation is performed using +.× with the data being the left argument and a Transformation Matrix the right. This transformation matrix, in its various forms, copes with translation, scaling and rotation, simply by using different versions of itself.

This method of transformation matrices also enables us to combine transformations, without transforming our data until the very end. For example if you wish to scale and translate your object, it is possible to combine the two TM's into a third and operate that on your data, rather than having an intermediate form. Again +.× provides the link, converting our two initial translation matrices into the new third matrix

TM3 gets TM1+.×TM2 then DATA gets DATA+.×TM3 If you are at all interested in graphics and some simple animation techniques, then this is a good, fairly readable paper with quite a few examples that work. My only trouble was trying to cope with plotting in 3-D.

items.title: The Bonfire of the Variables
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 108

by John Searle

APL 89 was a "steady as she goes" conference. No new or revolutionary products were announced, but it was heartening to see the major vendors pushing ahead on several fronts. Several new releases of existing interpreters are pending.

The conference theme was "APL as a Tool of Thought", borrowed from the title of a series of past conferences run by New York SIGAPL. Many papers illustrated the usage of APL as an effective medium for describing and expanding upon an idea or concept. The practical nature of APL also makes it "a tool for Measuring the Effectiveness of Thought".

The plenary sessions of the conference brought together speakers from various disciplines who have all pushed against and extended the known boundaries of their fields. They were not all APLers, but they have all used the essential ideas of APL in their search for simple yet powerful methods of specification and analysis.

The impact of Mathematica on the computing community will be interesting to monitor. Its author, Stephen Wolfram, acknowledges the parentage of APL in devising its functionality. However, its notation and "flavour" is more closely related to Lisp and Prolog. It uses only the standard symbols found on a keyboard. It is available for 386/DOS machines and the Apple Macintosh, and comes bundled free with the purchase of a NeXT computer. It will probably sell more copies in its first year than APL has ever sold.

The conference program was a good blend of the practical and the theoretical, with something for everyone. Presentations were generally more ambitious than in the past, and the necessary high-tech equipment usually worked well.

The refereeing of papers was questionable. Did the referees know in advance that their names wouldn't appear in the proceedings? Several papers were thinly disguised commercials for vendors, notably "APL in the Workstation Environment" (STSC). A workstation was defined as anything from a PC upwards, and the advertisement went on from there. Other papers did not acknowledge highly relevant work from recent conferences. This is not the author's fault, but that of the referees. SIGAPL is trying to rectify this in part through its Index of APL Articles.

The social side of the conference was, like the weather, hot and cold. The boat ride around New York Harbor was excellent. It was amazing how pretty Manhattan became after it got dark and you could only see the lights, not the architecture. The queue for dinner was a bit long, but the price was right. Thanks to the Danes for providing enough Carlsberg to lubricate the evening (and the next two evenings of private suite hospitality as well). The conference lunch, with musical entertainment by Stanley Jordan, was a real highlight. He uses APL to transform his musical score, using a simple notation. He played a tape of some of his pieces, and they were surprisingly tonal. His next jazz album will apparently acknowledge APL amongst the synthesizer credits.

The conference banquet was a mixture. The food was superb but its distribution was disorganized. I realise that the conference finances did not allow for the provision of any free drinks, but an announcement to that effect would have saved confusion and hoarseness. A.K.Dewdney's talk was entertaining and his Mandelbrot video was riveting. Afterwards, he was bombarded by people hoping to prove that anything Scientific American recreational writers can do, APLers can do better. We already know this, but does the world want to?

Conference handouts and freebies tend to reflect the character of the host city. Previous U.S. conferences have featured coffee mugs, Manchester gave us an umbrella and Sydney a T-shirt. Thus it was entirely appropriate that APL 89 delegates should receive a pocket knife, saw and screwdriver set - a personal defence mechanism suitable for late night subway rides. Readers of Tom Wolfe's famous novel of New York low-life certainly appreciated this data.

Overall, the conference was good value but the Hilton was expensive. It was ironic that the Hilton was put up for sale on the day after the conference. Are APLers improving at running conferences? On this evidence, the answer has to be "no". The American style of big inner-city hotel conventions just seems to be too inflexible, too expensive and too impersonal. The greatest minds in the APL community are not improving at getting their message across to a live audience. The lessons of past conferences are not being learned. Over to you, SIGAPL.

See you in Copenhagen!

items.title: British APL Association News
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 11

from Graham Parkhouse

The first committee meeting of the current year began with our Chairman, Peter Donnelly, suggesting that we scrap a tradition of going over the actions outstanding from previous meetings and introduce more spontaneity. The meetings in May and June were well attended. It was suggested that the AGM should be in June next year, instead of April, to enable the treasurer to be able to present our accounts properly audited. So the next AGM will be on Friday 8th June.

Alison Chatterton

It is time to be thinking about who will be on next year's committee. Adrian Smith is now in his third year as Editor of VECTOR, and according to the constitution therefore his last. Running a voluntary organisation like ours taxes our time and requires a great deal of motivation, and this certainly applies to Adrian and whoever will follow. We are hoping his successor will come from the Journal Working Group. But none of them has volunteered yet, possibly because they know what they would be letting themselves in for! Producing VECTOR is doubly exciting, with the challenge of typesetting APL characters as well as the challenge of presenting APL as a subject. Adrian has achieved much on both fronts: I could have written fonts, because he has been developing an APL font for PostScript to look like the original IBM golf ball font as used in Gilman and Rose. Streamlining the production process has been just one of Adrian's achievements which we need to build upon.

Streamlining the processes of a voluntary organisation is vital for its success. People on a committee should be there for their initiative. As much as possible they should be spared the work which is common to every business. Where it is not feasible to employ the help needed there may be the chance to provide tools to make the work easier. An example of the benefits to be gained from this strategy are becoming apparent in the BAA. Alison Chatterton has been working part time as our administrator for over a year now. The Association provided her with a PC on which she keeps the membership data and the software library.

She has helped Adrian by compiling the news from sustaining members and the APL product guide, looking after advertisements and typing articles. She has taken a substantial amount of work off the Treasurer, who used to maintain the membership data, and is an invaluable support and prompt to the Secretary. You may have already noticed some of the benefits like receiving your July VECTOR in July! While Adrian will willingly bear responsibility for that, Alison helped him achieve it.

That Alison should be a maths graduate and an ex-member of the committee may appear a little over the top, yet that is our good fortune! She first met APL in the OR Department at SE Gas, then worked for Tesco in Cheshunt for nearly three years before going into the family business which allows her, when not looking after Julia (6) and Rachel (4) and her husband, Steve, to work for the BAA. She weathered that initial period when everyone wonders whether their computer is for or against them, and I think she wondered when we were going to give her anything to do. That is now past: she has found her feet and is very busy.

All of this is very gratifying to the Secretary, now in his third year. Who is willing to take over my job in June?

Graham Parkhouse

items.title: Win A Free Trip to APL90 In Denmark!
items.text:
As part of this year's campaign to recruit new members, the British APL Association is running a PRIZE DRAW open to all existing UK members who manage to convince another APLer of the advantages of joining!

All you have to do is to introduce a new member before 1st February 1990 and your name will be entered in the Draw to win a fabulous free trip to next year's International APL Conference!

The Conference will be held from 13th to 17th August 1990 at the Marienlyst Hotel, Helsingor, near Copenhagen, and the lucky winner will travel out at the British APL Association's expense from anywhere in the UK. As well as having the delegate fee paid for by the British APL Association, accommodation and meals at the Marienlyst for the duration of the Conference will also be included.

Helsingor is a picturesque but thriving seaside town on the North coast of Denmark. It has plenty to offer the visitor: a historic port, nearby beaches and scenic countryside, a mediaeval 'Old Town' with cobbled streets, numerous parks, museums and monuments, and a plethora of cafes, restaurants and shops.

The theme of the Conference at Helsingor is 'APL For The Future', and the emphasis will be on the importance of APL as a tool for Information Management in the next decade. As well as presentations designed to illustrate this, there will be plenty of opportunity to meet and exchange experiences and ideas with other APLers from all over the world!

You can enter your name in the Draw each time you persuade someone new to join up! The more new members you sign up, the more chances you have of winning! But they must be genuine NEW members and not lapsed members who are rejoining. Photocopy the form on the opposite page and complete a copy for each new member who joins through you.

Send the completed forms to Alison Chatterton, at the address opposite. Please mark your envelope 'APL90 Draw'.

items.title: Hacker's Corner: Getting Another 128 Colours on your EGA
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 114

by Adrian Smith

Once again, Hackers' Corner takes a delve into the innermost secrets of your PC, but this time it is all decent and honest BIOS-compatible stuff! Sorry John, and all you hackers out there who found that getting at your PSP was less than easy under the PLUS II system: I hope this one will work for you!

Those of you with colour screens will have noticed that several packages allow you the full range of 16 background colours as well as the normal 16 in the foreground. However if you are tempted to try this with say ⎕WPUT 143, all you will get is blinking white on black, rather than white on a nice dark grey. Now one of the packages which does give you the option of bright backgrounds is APL2/PC, so I rang Dave Selby and asked how he did it. In fact it is a standard BIOS call, but only applies to the EGA and VGA monitors, so none of the usual PC reference books mention it.

The little function below will do the trick, or you could just close your eyes and type 4099 ⎕INT 16 if you prefer.

    ∇ BLINK SW;RG
[1]  ⍝ FLIP BACKGROUND FROM BLINKING TO INTENSIFIED
[2]  ⍝   AH = 10H      ... BIOS SERVICE 10
[3]  ⍝   AL =  3H      ... SUBSERVICE 3
[4]  ⍝   BL = 0/1      ... 0 = BRIGHT; 1 = BLINK
[5]   RG←(4099,SW>0)⎕INT 16
    ∇

A couple of small caveats: Ctrl-Esc resets the screen to the default (i.e. blink) state, as does Desqview if you run your APL session in a window. I have incorporated the above code in all my screen routines (specifically WIN∆INIT and FSM∆FMT) so that I don't have any problems restarting after a break.

The improvement in appearance of standard data-entry screens is considerable (I recommend almost any colour on dark grey as a background, bright white on bright blue for fields, black on yellow for warnings, bright white on bright red for critical errors), and you can do a fair impression of OS/2 Presentation Manager with plenty of bright white as background!

Have fun!

items.title: Hackers' Corner: DOS Environment Variables
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 115

From: John Sullivan, 17th July 1989

What is all this hacking around with Program Segment Prefixes? Has anybody tried to do this in APL*PLUS II? No? - Good, because it doesn’t work. However, try the following which does work in both APL*PLUS/PC and APL*PLUS II:

     ∇Z←DOS∆ENV
[1]   ⎕CMD 'SET > SETOUT.TXT'
[2]   'SETOUT.TXT' ⎕NTIE 158
[3]   Z←⎕NREAD 158 82,(¯1+⎕NSIZE 158),0
[4]   ⎕NUNTIE 158
[5]   ⎕CMD 'DEL SETOUT.TXT'
[6]   Z←SSTOMAT ⎕TCNL,Z~⎕TCLF
     ∇

Where SStoMAT is supplied in STSC’s ASMFNS and is the equivalent of your ∆TAB.

items.title: More on Finding the Location of that PSP...
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 115

From: Dave Phillips, 15th September 1989

I was delighted to read that most useful piece of insight regarding how to acquire DOS Environment Variables from an APL*PLUS/PC system. (VECTOR Vol.5 No.4 - Hacker’s Corner). The ability, as you so rightly say, for one’s APL system to get runtime information from the external environment (e.g. the actual name of a data-file to use - almost like tying a DDNAME to a DSNAME in MVS/JCL, only better!) is most appealing.

I would like to point out, however, that the piece of code you supplied will only work for the Standard APL*PLUS/PC System. This is because the location of the Program Segment Prefix address is no longer at the same offset to the function key table in the new Extended System (with Session Manager) that is available in APL*PLUS/PC r8. All is not lost; an alternative method of locating the PSP is provided by DOS itself and is applicable to all flavours/releases of APL*PLUS/PC.

I was recommended to closely examine the IBM DOS Technical Reference, (I have DOS 3.30), wherein is to be found a list of programmed calls that can be made via Int21. A call 62h to this interrupt yields, as a return value, the address of the PSP directly. At least it does for DOS 3.0 and above; for earlier DOS releases, use of the undocumented call 51h produces the desired effect. From there on, your code, or rather M. Philippe Denoyelle’s code, works as is. (Monsieur Denoyelle: merci trez bien!)

I am including a copy of the reworked code below. I hope this may be of some additional benefit. One further point I should make is that this approach is not applicable to the APL*PLUS II System. However, I do have a solution for that environment, care of a private communication from STSC, should you or other VECTOR readers wish to have it.

Dave Phillips Principal Support Consultant Cocking & Drury Ltd.

      ∇ R←DOS∆ENV SEL;AV;DOS;ENV;PSP;V;X;⎕IO;⎕SEG
[1]    ⍝∇DETERMINE DOS ENVT VARIABLES WITH OPTIONAL PREFIX <SEL>
[2]    ⍝∇UNDER APL*PLUS/PC, INCLUDING SESSION MNG IN /PCR8, ET SEQ.
[3]    ⍝∇USAGE: R←DOS∆ENV '' RETURNS ALL DOS VARIABLES
[4]    ⍝∇ R←DOS∆ENV 'C' RETURNS ALL DOS VARS. STARTING 'C'
[5]     ⎕IO←0 ⋄ V←⍬
[6]    ⍝ DETERMINE DOS VERSION USING INT21H CALL 30H
[7]    ⍝ (N.B. CALCULATE 30H←→16⊥3 0 0 0 - I.E. 12288DEC)
[8]     DOS←1↑⌽ 256 256 ⊤''⍴12288 ⎕INT 33
[9]    ⍝ FIND PSP ADDR. USING INT21H CALL 62H (25088) FOR DOS 3.0+
[10]   ⍝ OR CALL 51H (20736) FOR PRE-DOS 3
[11]   ⍝ PSP SEGMENT ADDR. IS SECOND ELEMENT OF RETURN FROM CALL
[12]    PSP←((25088 20736)[DOS<3]⎕INT 33)[⎕IO+1]
[13]   ⍝ OFFSET 2CH (44) IN PSP GIVES SEGMENT ADDR. FOR ENVIRONMENT
[14]    ⎕SEG←PSP ⋄ ENV←256⊥⎕PEEK 45 44
[15]   L1:⎕SEG←ENV ⋄ V←V,⎕PEEK⍳256 ⋄ X← 0 0 ⍷V ⋄ →(∨/X)/L2
[16]    ENV←ENV+16 ⋄ →L1 ⍝ LOOP UNTIL WHOLE TABLE IS READ
[17]   ⍝ TRANSLATE RETRIEVED NUMERIC VALUES INTO TEXT
[18]   L2:AV←⎕AV
[19]   ⍝ AV[64 36 61]←'⍙∆←' ⍝ OPTIONAL TRANSLATE TAILORING
[20]    V←AV[(X⍳1)↑V] ⋄ R←SSTOMAT ⎕TCNUL,V
[21]    SEL←,SEL ⋄ →(⍴SEL)↓0 ⍝ IF <SEL> IS REQUESTED...
[22]    R←(R[;⍳⍴SEL]∧.=SEL)⌿R ⍝ ...TAKE SUBSET
      ∇
