items.title: Ambivalent Operators...
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 117

From: Phil Last, 12th July 1989

With reference to David Piper’s letter in VECTOR 5.4 ... The right operand to David’s operator must be parenthesized to force the value rather than the ⎕NC function itself to become the operand:

  [2] →(↑(RUN AVE)←(⍴NUMS)(AVERAGE ∆MONADIC(⎕NC 'SIZE'))NUMS)/0
                                           ↑          ↑

Once this is done, it works! However both the operator itself and the convoluted expression required to call it are perfectly described by the editorial from the same edition! Nevertheless, if we’re after a tricksy solution, the following avoids all conditional code, be it branch or execute, it tells you what it’s doing, and it works faster:

      ∇
[0]     AVE←SIZE AVERAGE NUMS
[1]    ⍝ MOVING OR NORMAL AVG DEPENDING ON EXISTENCE OF SIZE
[2]     AMBIVALENT 'SIZE'
[3]     AVE←(SIZE+/NUMS)÷↑SIZE,⍴NUMS
      ∇

      ∇
[0]     AMBIVALENT AMBIVALENT
[1]    ⍝ DCL CALLING FN AMBIVALENT WITH NAME OF ITS LEFT ARG.
[2]     AMBIVALENT←⎕FX('R←',AMBIVALENT,' B')('R←B')
      ∇

The function AMBIVALENT, given the name of the left argument to its calling function, attempts to fix a function with that name which returns its only argument. In the example, this would be:

[0]   R←SIZE B
[1]   R←B

This can only be fixed if SIZE does not already exist, in which case the call to plus reduction is genuinely monadic and the right argument to divide defaults to the shape of NUMS.

Phil Last

items.title: APL Standard Update
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 118

by Dave Ziemann (as convenor of BSI APL Standards Panel)

This report primarily covers events that occurred at the ISO meeting held in Princeton University, New Jersey, USA from July 31-August 3rd this year, just before the APL conference in New York city.

The four day meeting of Working Group 3 (WG3) attracted fourteen delegates from Belgium, Canada, France, UK and the USA. Two BSI (British Standards Institute) representatives attended the meeting, Paul Chapman and myself. The meeting was convened by Lee Dickey. Ken Iverson, now retired from I P Sharp Associates was a notable attendee.

The main agenda item was of course the Extended APL Standard, although the status of the original APL Standard, affectionately known as IS8485, was also on the agenda.

items.title: The First APL Standard
items.text:
What news of IS8485 then? Lee Dickey had submitted the document to Sub-Committee 22 (Programming Languages) in Geneva for "International Standards processing" some time ago. Although this at first appears to be a technical term for a bureaucratic black hole, it now seems that we are in imminent danger of having an APL standard. If there are no hold-ups, we can expect publication before the end of this year, apparently.

If you want to get hold of this 275 page document, request document IS8485 from:

Secretariat Central ISO Case Postale 56 CH1211 Geneve 20 Suisse

The standard will be published in English and French, so you should state which you want. A price is not currently available.

Once IS8485 is published as an ISO standard, it can be "endorsed" or "adopted" by the national standards bodies, such as the BSI. "Endorsing" effectively means that the national body establishes a pointer to the international standard, and you have to send to Geneva to get a copy, whereas "adopting" means that it is accepted as a national standard and printed locally.

The original text of IS8485 is currently being transferred from Script into Tex, a project which has been funded by SIGAPL and more recently by I P Sharp Associates. This will bring the document under the control of WG3 once more, and should make work on a new document much easier.

items.title: The Extended APL Standard
items.text:
For some time the ISO group has been struggling with the problem of how to resolve some fundamental differences in the way that certain enhanced facilties should be standardised. In particular, nested arrays (where an array can contain items other than simple scalars) and the reduction operator are subjects upon which effective agreement cannot be found.

At the ISO meeting the BSI submitted a paper which summarised and enumerated the logical possibilities open to WG3, and suggested that WG3 reconsider its direction. The choices open to us are:

  1. Standardise the intersection of the extended facilities in the different dialects
  2. Standardise the union of facilities by a very general approach
  3. Standardise a new dialect of APL which combines desirable facilities from each dialect
  4. Standardise multiple facilities, allowing implementations to select the preferred approach
  5. Pick one approach to standardise (essentially APL2 or Sharp APL)
  6. Develop two distinct extended standards
  7. Postpone work on the Extended APL standard

None of these possibilities is particularly attractive, each resulting in severe technical, political or practical difficulties.

Although possible, compromise solutions involving the combination of facilities, such as in option 3, damage the consistency and synergy of the language, and would result in a standard language which does not actually exist. It has long been the policy of the working group to standardise on the basis of what exists rather than to invent, wherever this is possible. But standardising from what exists in two distinct self-consistent dialects can produce a monster without the consistency or usability of either one.

A standard which includes both APL2's nested and Sharp's boxed arrays, for example, would be a standard for a language which no-one has used, and perhaps one which no-one would want to use. The behaviour of all the associated primitives in one school would have to be carefully defined on arrays of the other school, and vice versa. Even if it were possible, the vendors could not afford to change their systems to conform to such a standard, and the document would then serve little purpose.

items.title: A Way Forward
items.text:
Work on the standard proceeds by discussing and voting on proposals received by WG3. We decided that proposals should be as near "standard-ready" as possible, ie they should be in the same format as pages in IS8485. Before the Princeton meeting many topics had already been rejected by agreement or vote, although several contentious proposals still remained.

After discussion WG3 decided to prepare two publications, a Supplement and a Technical Report. Our main effort, a Supplement to the existing standard, will contain only those proposals upon which agreement has been reached. The Technical Report will describe those topics which have been proposed, but on which consensus has not been reached.

During the course of the meeting twenty-six topics were identified for likely inclusion in the proposed Supplement, and nineteen topics were identified for likely inclusion in the proposed Technical Report. Two topics were dropped from further consideration because proposals in the appropriate format had not been received.

The topics currently marked for inclusion in the Supplement are: replicate, grade extensions, without, underbar/overbar in names, ambi-valent defined functions, ambi-valent primitive functions, transfer form (⎕TF), defined operators, canonical representation of defined operators, locking of defined functions and operators, shared variable extensions to ⎕SVR and ⎕SVQ, )NMS and )OPS system commands, N-wise reduction, comma-bar, nub, left and right, GCD and LCD, commute, complex numbers, formatting complex numbers, heterogenous arrays, fill-items for heterogenous arrays, function rank operator, alpha and omega as names, event handling (⎕EA ⎕EM ⎕ES ⎕ET) and component file cover functions.

The topics marked for inclusion in the Technical Report are: reduction, nested arrays and fills, enclose/disclose/box/open, formatting for nested arrays, pick, partition, depth, link, enlist, strand notation, match, primitive operators applying to non-scalar functions, compose, dual, first, each, national language characters, function rank in standard metalanguage, function assignment.

The two topics droppped from further discussion were ⎕FMT and the "find" function for string searching.

items.title: Future Issues
items.text:
It is unfortunate that the projected Supplement does not include any nested or boxed array extensions, although this is ameliorated to some extent by inclusion of the function rank operator. Many people feel that an extended standard should include nested arrays, whereas others think that the field is still undergoing evolution, and that it is too early to standardise. No doubt this subject will arise again.

Another interesting area is event-handling. Where the model in the standard signals an error, a conforming implementation may replace that error behaviour by some other behaviour - this is the "consistent extension" mechanism by which implementors may add facilities to their conforming systems. Therefore an APL program cannot strictly rely on this error being signalled, and so such a program is deemed non-conforming.

The whole purpose of including the (APL2-style) event handling system functions in the standard is to allow users to trap events and handle them, so currently we have the strange situation that a facility defined in the standard cannot be used by a conforming program! Clearly something will have to change in the next standard.

The meeting also agreed to liaise further with WG2, the ISO committee involved with the standardisation of character sets, and we will be sending them a list of APL characters for inclusion in the new multiple octet character set standard.

Another sad divergence between the APL2-school and the Sharp approach is the reduction operator, and therefore inner product. In APL2-type systems the primary definition of reduction is on vectors, the function being applied between the items of a sub-array of vectors. The Sharp philosophy is to apply the function between the items of a vector of sub-arrays.

In addition, the APL2 definition involves an implicit enclose operation, which means that the result is often nested, whereas the Sharp definition does not involve enclosure, the result being simple. The enclose allows the APL2 definition to preserve the familiar rank-reducing identity, but in the Sharp view that effect was merely due to the domain of the operator being restricted to scalar functions, and is not a general identity. Perhaps for that reason the true Sharpie prefers the name "over" to "reduction". I heard one Sharp advocate offer the opinion that Bob Smith, the inventor of STSC's Nested Arrays Research System, had been "imprisoned by the beauty of the identities he discovered".

Of course, none of these differences manifest themselves in old-fashioned APL, but only become apparent with the requirement to generalise operators to non-scalar functions.

Standards meetings evoke a mixture of feelings; they can be extremely fascinating, sometimes boring, and very often humourous. When faced with a 6-3-3 vote to include the function rank operator, the convenor was not sure that this indicated consensus. So a metavote was agreed, and we each picked a number greater than 50 and not greater than 100, the percentage which we thought fairly represented consensus. We agreed to pick the median number, and the result was 70%. A revote was then called for the function rank operator, and this time it passed 8-3-1.

items.title: The Timeline
items.text:
The next scheduled meeting will take place in August 1990, somewhere in Europe. If sufficient progress on the Supplement has been made by February 1 1990, then an additional meeting will be scheduled for April 1990 in Waterloo, Ontario.

It is hoped that the new document will reach the first Draft Proposal stage by March 1991.

items.title: UK Involvement at Risk
items.text:
Travel to International Standards Organisation meetings for BSI representatives is funded in this country by the Department of Trade and Industry. One representative, nominated the "Principal Expert" is entitled to a fixed amount based on the location of the meeting. For example, for the Princeton meeting the figure was £500, enough to cover a cheap air fare to New York. Accommodation and living expenses are not paid; the expert must rely on a very generous employer or bear the cost directly.

All BSI Technical Committees have now been informed that future claims may not be met, and those that are may have to be at a reduced rate, possibly no more than 50%. Perhaps as many as nine out of ten claims will be rejected.

It therefore looks likely that future UK involvement in ISO APL standards meetings will not be possible. If anybody has any complaints about this they can write to:

Mr Alec Berry Dept. of Trade and Industry Kingsgate House 68-74 Victoria Street LONDON SW1 6SW

with a copy to:

Mr Tony Valvona Business Support Group BSI Standards 2 Park Street LONDON W1A 2BS

items.title: HMW Computing Limited

HMW Computing Limited continue to develop and market "4XTRA" our front end Foreign Exchange Dealing and Position Keeping System. We are exhibiting "4XTRA" at "Computers in The City" on 14-16 November 1989 in the Barbican Centre London. If you would like to visit the exhibition and see our product call Stan Wilkinson on 01-353-4212 for a complimentary ticket.

Our employment agency for the APL community continues to attract permanent positions with a variety of clients throughout the U.K. Currently we have many vacancies for APL technicians from juniors through to consultants with attractive salaries and interesting work content.

To find out what we can offer, please call Val Lusmore on 01-353-4212. If you would prefer to phone out of office hours Val's home number is [omitted].

items.title: APL People Limited
items.text:
Attempts to make APL People into THE premier APL recruitment agency in the world continue! Jill's recent visit to New York for the APL '89 Conference proved most useful - she made contact with a number of companies outside the UK who have vacancies for skilled APL programmers. A subsidiary of a major Publishing company in Washington is prepared to explore the possibility of recruiting a non-US National and all the bureaucracy that involves, so if anyone's interested in working in the States, please get in touch!

On the home front, we currently have a number of exciting new openings in the UK for people with between 1 and 5 years' systems development experience in APL - mostly in London and the South East.

In addition, sales of the software marketed by our sister company, Applied Production Logic, are considerably up on last year, and we are anticipating a lot more interest following the Computers Manufacturing Show in October at which we will be exhibiting.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce the availability of the DOS/386 version of Dyalog APL that was successfully launched at APL89 in New York. American reactions to the new product were extremely positive, although one well-known user was heard to say "it may be better, but it's a foreign APL!". Dyalog is extremely pleased with the reaction to the ⎕SM screen manager, and the new window-based development environment. Several early customers have already reported significant productivity gains.

Coinciding with the launch of the new product is a new corporate image designed to match that of Dyadic's parent company, Hunting plc. The Dyadic and Dyalog APL logos have been revamped, and brown, cream and gold discarded in favour of blue and white.

The new (blue and white) Dyalog APL manual-set comprises two volumes: a user-guide and a reference manual. These are supplemented with spiral-bound booklets for the CGI Graphics, Oracle, and (forthcoming) X-windows interfaces. It is symptomatic of the trend in APL that the amount of documentation concerned with user and other interfaces dominates the Language Reference Manual.

On the Unix front, Dyadic reports a growing demand for Dyalog APL, especially on high-performance workstations like the Sun SPARC range and the widely rumoured new IBM RISC machine.

items.title: I.P.Sharp Associates
items.text:
Our London office has moved to new premises with effect from 4th September. The new address is on the back cover of this VECTOR.

In June, the worldwide launch of AllRound View took place. This product is based on Viewpoint, I. P. Sharp's data management system, and is largely written in Sax - Sharp APL under Unix. AllRound View will be marketed by Philips on its Unix-based P90x0 computers. AllRound View provides end-users with access to corporate data residing on IBM mainframes.

items.title: Cocking and Drury Ltd
items.text:
Cocking and Drury are proud to announce ACT-CALC, an APL*PLUS based package for actuaries, which we have jointly developed with Mercer Fraser Ltd. ACT-CALC is a set of actuarial utility functions available on any system on which APL*PLUS is installed, from PC to Mainframe. The product will help the actuary solve everyday calculations within minutes. The functions are named so that they correspond closely with the symbols of standard international actuarial notation and as a result they feel natural to the actuary. The package provides considerable flexibility, combining various mortality and interest assumptions. It may be used stand-alone, or can be incorporated into other applications.

We have been shipping Release 2 of the APL*PLUS II System for 80386 machines since late August. Customers who bought their APL*PLUS II System from us will by now have received their free upgrade.

The company has been using Oracle in the development of further internal PC based computer systems.

Our 2-day "APL*PLUS Nested Arrays" course has been successfully run within the company, and has been improved as a result. The course is now available to customers in-house or in our London office. This course is aimed at APL*PLUS programmers who want to make appropriate use of their nested array environment. When effectively used, nested array structures and techniques can increase programmer productivity, reduce software development costs and increase the maintainability and robustness of APL applications.

Also on the course front, the availablility of IBM's APL2/PC means that it is now possible to offer our standard "Introduction to APL2" and "APL2 In-depth" courses as public courses in our London office. For further information about any of these courses, please contact Beverley Satterley.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
Richard Nabavi and David Eastwood of MicroAPL attended APL89 to give papers on some of our current work. Richard was discussing the design of MicroAPL's WIMP environment and David gave a presentation on one of MicroAPL's programming projects. We also gave a vendor presentation and exhibited our current products in partnership with our US distributors the Spencer Organisation. Our exhibition stand concentrated on the latest Mac software and previewed the APL.68000 Amiga upgrade. We were also showing one of the latest Unix-based versions of APL.68000.

The visit to New York was a welcome chance to meet some of our North American clients and to see what software they are producing. A number of papers at APL89 dealt with applications based on APL.68000 and we were able to look at some of these applications at the show.

MicroAPL is continuing to expand the availability of APL.68000 for Unix-based systems. The latest new port of APL.68000 is for the Nixdorf Targon family. We have also upgraded our NCR Tower release to 7.30 and other ports are in progress. For details of the range of machines that can run APL.68000, contact MicroAPL.

Version 7.30 for the Commodore Amiga is now under final test and we will be mailing users with upgrade details in the near future. In addition to the work on APL.68000, we are recoding some of the Auxiliary Processors which we wrote for the Mirage environment to run in an Operating System independent fashion. This should widen the range of utility software available for our Unix versions - details will be announced in forthcoming issues of Vector and MicroAPL News.

MicroAPL's consultancy section has signed a number of major new contracts to supply systems on DOS, Mirage and Unix machines. We have also entered into software maintenance agreements with a number of clients to maintain and enhance existing APL systems. As usual, we are still looking for APL programmers for our consultancy activities.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
Editorial - Programming Style Anthony Camacho 18 "APL Programs for the Mathematics Classroom" by Norman Thomson Reviewed by W. W. McLean 20 APL "RISC Programming Style" G. A. Langlet 23 Start Building Your Utilities Peter Branson 25 Minutes of I-APL Board Meeting Sylvia Camacho 29 I-APL Order Form I-APL Ltd. 32

Editor Dr Alan Sykes, Dept of Management Science and Statistics, University College of Swansea, Singleton Park, SWANSEA SA2 8PP

items.title: Guest Editorial
items.text:
by Anthony Camacho

The gap between APL 89 and the British APL Association's conference on the APL Statistics Library is too short. Dr Sykes is overloaded and rather than let the set of Education Vectors become a sparse matrix I offered to have a go at filling the gap. I am asked to make it clear that this is not to be allowed to become a habit. Alan will be back in his editorial chair before you read this. I am starting work on 11 September - after the final copy date - so what you get is what comes to hand.

I-APL Ltd held an open board meeting at APL 89. The minutes are reproduced here. One of the main decisions taken was that, to survive, I-APL must become more commercial. This means that we will begin to pay directors, porters and staff for their services and that we will act as distributors for material which was not produced by I-APL. For example we have begun to distribute Norman Thomson's book "APL Programs for the Mathematics Classroom", published by Springer Verlag. This Education Vector begins with a review of it by William McLean, a physics teacher of Dunoon, who has just begun to try out I-APL. Education Vector ends with a new I-APL order form, simplified by including post and packing charges in the price of each item; there is no price increase.

One of the perennial APL arguments is about style in coding and if there is a theme to this Education Vector it is that. If you read the account of APL 89 you may notice that Adin Falkoff (the man who gave APL its name) is keen on brackets and semicolons and Gerard Langlet would like to persuade everyone to write APL using vectors rather than matrices wherever possible. There is a note from Gerard on the same theme here. Before you reject it out of hand, try it. The effort of trying to adapt to a new style will give you a new insight into APL. In another style we have some advice for beginners from Peter Branson.

Many APLers have strong views about style and there are disagreements that go right back to the roots of the language. If either of these contributions makes your blood boil, please write a rebuttal or a rejoinder. Remember that in the Education Vector we are primarily interested in teaching with APL and the urge for speed which so distorts the style of some commercial programs is less appropriate.

If someone objects that a discussion of style is out of place in Education Vector, saying that new APLers have enough to learn without bothering about it, I answer that the way you say something is indivisibly a part of the thing said, that APL is first a notation and the form of expressions is the essence of notation, and that the decision about what style you adopt should not be left until you have formed habits by default, some of which may be bad.

APL does have the equivalent of spaghetti in BASIC. It is 'semi-globals'. Nobody has a good word to say for them. Globals are bad enough, from the press they get. Just as G. A. Langlet would like to program without parentheses, Eugene McDonnell would like to program without variables. He has produced a beautiful example published by APL press as "The four cubes problem" and the functions are in the I-APL workspace INSANITY. The amount of work this program does is not trivial - it occupies a standard PC for about 28 minutes!

We have received two useful letters in response to my comment in Education Vector 5.4 about transfer of workspaces between BBC, PC clones and Archimedes. They are from John Dallman, who suggests using Kermit and from Malcolm Rigg who uses Beebdos software. Thanks to both.

Kermit is a serial transfer protocol and has been implemented on almost every computer ever heard of that has a serial interface. A simple cable (only three connections, I believe) joins the two machines and you set one machine to listen and the other to shout and the file is transferred rapidly and reliably. Kermit is in the public domain and is distributed by: Kermit Distribution, Department of Computing, Computer Centre, Lancaster University, Lancaster LA1 4YW. Cables may be obtained made up for the machines of your choice from: Fraser Electronics, 42 Elm Grove, Southsea, Portsmouth, Hants or RSD Connections, PO Box 1, Church St, Ware, Herts SG12 9EN

Beebdos is a program which runs on a PC clone and reads or writes disks which can be read by a BBC - DFS or ADFS. Malcolm says the software is widely advertised.

items.title: Start Building your own Utilities
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 25

by Peter Branson

items.title: What are Utilities?
items.text: As you get going with APL, you may find it useful to start building up a library of utility functions. These are functions not tied to any particular APL application, but come in useful all over the place, such as alphabetical sorting, selecting a particular name from a list of names. It may be that your APL has the nucleus of a good set in a supplied workspace. Use them. The odds are that, sooner or later, you will want some of your own. In any case writing utility functions helps extend one’s knowledge of APL, since some care is needed to make them robust.

items.title: A Useful Example
items.text:
Let’s look at an example. When handling character (text) data, there is often a need to join two matrices of characters one above the other - the technical term is catenation on the first axis. The direct APL way of doing this is:-

      (3 3⍴'CATANDDOG') ,[1] 2 3⍴'XYZ'
CAT
AND
DOG
XYZ
XYZ

Here the bracket index join ,[1] tells APL that we want to join the right argument onto the bottom of the left argument. Note that the example above will only work when the two matrices have the same width. If they are not the same you will get a length error (try it and see).

Now, what if the matrices do have different widths, which occurs fairly often? A simple line of APL will no longer suffice, so let’s set up a utility function for this. I will call this VCAT with a header R←A VCAT B. Here A and B may well both be matrices, but it would be useful if the function would work with vectors as well.

For example, we might sometimes want to add just one name to a namelist, in which case B could be a vector. And while we are at it let’s allow for the case where A or B is a singleton; a one-element vector or even a scalar.

How shall we do this generalisation? Well, your first thought might be to do some tests on the shape of A and B and, according to what type of object each is, to branch to different parts of the function to do what is needed. But this is APL, remember, and of course there is a better way, without branches! Here is one way of writing the VCAT function:

    ∇ R←A VCAT B;MAXW;TOP;BOT
[1]  ⍝ VCAT: VERTICAL CATENATION
[2]  ⍝ EXTEND SINGLES AS REQD. FOR MATRIX RESULT - NUM OR CHAR
[3]  ⍝
[4]   A←(¯2↑ 1 1,⍴A)⍴A
[5]   B←(¯2↑ 1 1,⍴B)⍴B
[6]   MAXW←(¯1↑⍴A)⌈¯1↑⍴B
[7]   TOP←((1↑⍴A),MAXW)↑A
[8]   BOT←((1↑⍴B),MAXW)↑B
[9]   R←TOP,[1] BOT
      ∇

Have a look at line 4; this finds the shape of A (the result of shape is always a numeric vector), catenates this onto the vector 1 1 and uses the last two elements of the result to reshape A. If A is a two-dimensional array to start with, it will be unaffected; the reshape will be to its original shape. If it is a vector it will be reshaped to a one-row matrix of the original vector length and if it is a scalar (the shape of a scalar is the empty vector) then it will be reshaped to a one-row, one-column matrix.

The next line does the same for B, and line 6 just gets the larger of the two widths. One of lines 7 and 8 will always be redundant; if either of A and B has fewer columns than the other then a take (↑) with the MAXW number of columns will pad it with blanks if the arguments are characters and with zeros if the arguments are numeric. This capability of take is often called ‘overtake’, a term worth remembering if it helps to fix this in your memory. And as you will have realised VCAT has the added bonus that it works for numeric data as well as characters.

items.title: A Documentation Utility
items.text:
Looking back at VCAT you will see that the first line is a comment showing the function name with a brief description of what it does. Many experienced APLers put comments like this in all their functions, so that by running a suitable documentation utility, a list of names and outline descriptions can be obtained for all the functions in the workspace. This can be useful as the number of functions builds up; it is only too easy to forget what some of them do, and their names (often kept short for typing convenience) may not be mnemonic enough so )FNS won’t do the job.

Let’s see what is needed. We will be obtaining the function as a character matrix from ⎕CR and can pick the appropriate line by indexing. The line lengths will vary but VCAT will allow for this when forming the result.

A suitable function, DOC1, is listed below. I hope the comments obviate further description:

      R←DOC1;NAMES;N;J;CR
      -------------------

[1]       ⍝ LIST FN NAME AND 1ST COMMENT LINE OF ALL FNS IN WS
[2]       ⍝ NAMES IS LIST OF ALL FN NAMES, N IS NO OF NAMES

[3]        N←1↑⍴NAMES←⎕NL 3

[4]       ⍝ R IS INITIAL RESULT - EMPTY CHAR MATRIX

[5]        R← 0 0 ⍴''

[6]       ⍝ SET COUNTER J TO 0

[7]        J←0

[8]       ⍝ NOW TAKE EACH NAME IN ORDER

[9]   LOOP:→(N<J←J+1)/END

[10]      ⍝ CR IS THE FN AS A CHARACTER MATRIX

[11]       CR←⎕CR NAMES[J;]

[12]      ⍝ GO TO NEXT IF HEADER LINE ONLY OR DIRECT DEFINITION

[13]       →(1≥1↑⍴CR)/LOOP

[14]      ⍝ DROP LEADING '⍝ ' AND TRAILING BLANKS FOR NEATNESS

[15]       CR←1↓('⍝'=CR[2;1])/CR[2;]
[16]       CR←(+/∧\' '=CR)⌽CR
[17]       CR←(+/∨\⌽' '≠CR)↑CR

[18]      ⍝ R IS PREVIOUS RESULT PLUS (VCAT) THIS COMMENT LINE

[19]       R←R VCAT NAMES[J;],':',CR
[20]       →LOOP
[21]  END:
      ∇

Can you amend this function so that it will select all the comment lines in any index origin? (Ed: Can you rewrite it without parentheses?)

items.title: Comment or Decomment
items.text:
Experienced APLers often recommend that all functions be extensively commented, either to explain some of the tricky APL or to help describe the overall task. There are times when you may want to remove the comments e.g. if space is short.

You could )SAVE the workspace under a different name and then run DECOMM and )SAVE with the usual name. Don’t fail to keep a commented copy.

      ∇ R←DECOMM FNAME;CR;MASK
[1]   ⍝ DECOMM: DECOMMENT A FUNCTION
[2]    CR←⎕CR FNAME
[3]    MASK←CR[;1]≠'⍝'
[4]    CR←MASK⌿CR
[5]    R←⎕FX CR
       ∇

Here we form CR as before and then do a not-equals comparison of the first column with the lamp symbol. This gives us a boolean vector with ones for the lines we want to keep and zeros for the lines whose first characters are lamp. Then we compress CR to remove the unwanted lines and finally convert CR back to a function with ⎕FX. As it has the same name it will overwrite the previous version.

One disadvantage of DECOMM is that it will remove the first line comment. The simplest modification will keep it: add line:

  [3.5] MASK←MASK∨(⍴MASK)↑0 1

This ensures that line one is always represented by a 1 in MASK.

items.title: Meeting of the Board of I-APL and other Interested Parties on 6th August 1989 at the New York Hilton
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 29

by Sylvia Camacho

Present: Anthony Camacho, Ed Cherlin, Paul Chapman, Dave Ziemann, Norman Thomson, Garry Helzer, Linda Alvord, Sylvia Camacho, Rolf Levenbach, Per Gjerlov, Kim Andreasen, Lee Dickey, Ed Shaw, George Cherlin, Tama Traberman, Curtis Jones.

(1) Last year’s Minutes (2) Commercial decisions (3) Progress to date (4) Plans for Conference (5) AOB
path: Meeting of the Board of I-APL and other Interested Parties on 6th August 1989 at the New York Hilton

items.title: (1) Last Year’s Minutes
items.text: Minutes from last year were taken as read (see Vector Vol.4 No.4).
path: Meeting of the Board of I-APL and other Interested Parties on 6th August 1989 at the New York Hilton

items.title: (2) Commercial Decisions
items.text:
Anthony Camacho suggested the commercial decisions to be taken as:

  1. Whether to stock and distribute Norman Thomson’s “APL for the Mathematics Classroom”.
  2. Whether to print a manual and distribute TryAPL2.
  3. Whether to distribute Sharp APL PC.

In order to do these things I-APL would have to become a profit making (though not profit distributing) organisation which would pay royalties to authors and commercial rates for other work. So far I-APL has not paid anything but expenses to its board members. To make it possible for them to continue the work payment is becoming essential.

Anthony said he would like to hear the opinion of all present on whether I-APL could make this change with a good conscience. Each in turn spoke to this point and there were several differences of emphasis.

Ed Cherlin stated his need to generate cash flow to pay for publicity, admin effort and distribution. Ed favoured extending the products carried with this end in view.

Norman Thomson supported this view and suggested adding paid consultancy.

Paul Chapman suggested other possible products.

Ed Shaw expressed fears that extending the product range would overstretch the organisation (evidence being that he has not yet been invoiced for some stock).

Lee Dickey would support a move to increase the number of distributors.

Dave Ziemann expressed support for increasing the product range providing the effort can be found and that it would not alienate the contributors.

George Cherlin suggested applying for a National Science Foundation grant.

There was general agreement that I-APL must not be seen to favour any commercial vendor or any flavour of enhanced APL.

The proposal that I-APL should move towards being a more commercial enterprise was passed nem con. The proposal to carry other APL products was carried 7 in favour, 2 against and the rest abstaining. The implied advice was that the Chairmen should only do it if there was no danger of diverting effort from important work such as ports to school machines.
path: Meeting of the Board of I-APL and other Interested Parties on 6th August 1989 at the New York Hilton

items.title: (3) Progress to Date
items.text:
Anthony Camacho reported:

  • Well over 1000 copies of I-APL have been sold.
  • The manual has gone into a second edition including BBC and Archimedes machines. [After doing the basic port to these machines without payment, the porter was paid £800 to provide DFILE, graphics, sound and colour interfaces.]
  • Tama Traberman’s ‘APL in Social Studies’ has been printed and added to the product list.
  • Norman and Linda’s Tutorial has been revised and reprinted.
  • Garry has revised An Encyclopedia of APL and the second edition has been printed.
  • The current financial position is that there is about £2000 in the U.K. bank account and £19,000 (at full selling price) of stock.
  • The BAA has paid for production and mailing of the Education section of Vector to the 1400-1500 I-APL mailing list at an approx. cost to them of £600 per quarter. There seems to be no reason why they won’t continue to do this - it is bringing them new members.
  • There are porters working on Apple, Amstrad, Atari, Macintosh, CP/M and Transputer machines but none for Commodore 64.
  • Paul has produced a 32-bit version of I-APL which is currently ported to the Archimedes and gives workspace up to the memory installed. It also runs faster than the version with 16 bit addresses as in that version each address has to be reduced to 16 bits by masking. This 32-bit version can be distributed in the same way as I-APL. As workspaces will not be loadable from the 16-bit into the 32-bit or vice versa, we feel it necessary to provide means to transfer workspaces between the two systems before issuing any 32-bit version.
  • Paul has also produced a compiled and speeded up version for the Archimedes which he would like to earn royalties on and charge a higher price for.
  • The 32-bit IAPL.DEB file will run with an appropriate DEGO on any 32-bit machine. It could therefore be ported to 68000 and 80386 machines and give workspaces up to the size of the memory. It was agreed that such ports could be commissioned and issued.

Rolf Levenbach reported progress on the Apple Port. Most of testport was working and he was part of the way to )SAVE and )LOAD but when he tried the complete interpreter it crashed after displaying the sign-on message. Paul agreed to spend some time with him to see whether he could help. Anthony said that when the interpreter was working, I-APL would pay Rolf to write DFILE and provide appropriate access to colour, graphics and any other Apple ][ facilities.
path: Meeting of the Board of I-APL and other Interested Parties on 6th August 1989 at the New York Hilton

items.text: Ed Cherlin asked for volunteers to man the I-APL Booth, received 6, but in the event this did not happen.

items.text: Per Gjerlov asked that there should be some I-APL papers at APL90 and that some information on the 32-bit version and experience with I-APL in Schools should be included.

items.title: Editorial: We are not Alone!
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Adrian Smith

One of the highlights of the recent APL in Statistics conference was a splendid rendering of "APL is a very funny language" by the Alan Sykes Trio on the second evening. (Full lyrics to be published in Vector 6.3 unless Alan gets to them first!) I suppose we ought to admit that there is something a bit unusual about APL, but perhaps we are not as far from the mainstream as we thought?

I have recently been experimenting with a very well-established programming language, among whose attributes are numbered:

  • general arrays. Arrays may be made up of numbers, text, and other arrays. There is a language primitive to automate the processing of each element of an array.
  • direct definition. There is a language primitive which takes as arguments a function name, and a text array of executable code.
  • no predefined hierarchy of arithmetic functions. Incidentally these convert automatically between integer and floating point as required. The user has no control over (or indeed knowledge of) data types.
  • a workspace in which defined functions and data arrays may be saved, and an execution stack where temporary variables may be kept.

The parallels are really rather remarkable, and I could keep going for some time about the benefits of straightforward recursion and the interpretive environment! However as you probably haven't yet guessed what I'm on about, the language in question is PostScript.

The example to the right takes about eight very simple lines of coding, and serves to demonstrate rather nicely the power of a language whose sole object is the manipulation of graphics and text. Oh, and by the way, it does it all with this very funny concept of matrices ... now who would credit that?!

In the next VECTOR we will have side-by-side reviews of the AFM File System for APL2/PC and the Myriade file manager for APL*PLUS/PC. These products are briefly described on page 44.

items.title: AFM for APL2/PC
items.text:
The AFM Stand at APL89

AFM/PC is a single-user version of the AFM file management system which Interprocess Systems Inc. has provided for IBM mainframe environments since 1978. It supports nearly all of the AFM file commands available on the mainframe, and emulates the mainframe library structure on the PC. Both keyed and component files are supported.

AFM/PC works with DOS 3.1 or later, and with APL2/PC 1.0 (or later) in either 16-bit or 32-bit modes. It is priced at $175 with volume dicounts available. For more details, contact Stella Chamberlain on (404) 992-8400, or write to Interprocess Systems, 9040 Roswell Rd, Suite 690, Atlanta, Georgia 30350-1131

items.title: Myriade File System for APL*PLUS/PC
items.text:
The Myriade File Manager improves upon the functionality of APL*PLUS/PC component files by providing numeric or character keyed access, multi-variable components and efficient space reclamation. Components can be created, read and updated in any order.

Myriade can handle very large files (up to 192Mbyte under DOS) with over 2 million components: there is provision for effective management of the file space, and for crash recovery on startup. Full and incremental backups can be taken.

The latest release of Myriade allows 64K of the system to be loaded into EEMS memory, which practically eliminates the overhead on workspace.

items.title: An APL 89 Roundup
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 60

by Anthony Camacho

Lynne Shaw (programme chair) at the Opening Session

items.title: Thanks for a Great Job
items.text: The volunteers who ran APL 89 deserve our gratitude for the great job they did. Running a conference such as this is an enormous amount of work and every volunteer, when stretched to the limit, then discovers six extra things to do which would make all the difference. I don't think they could have worked much harder than they did. The conference ran smoothly and the hitches were few. Many things were really well organised. At the debriefing we learned of some crises that had to be handled at the last minute: it is amazing how little these showed.

items.title: The Invited Speakers
items.text: The invited speakers were marvellous. Tom Gilb, Stanley Jordan, Arthur Whitney, Stephen Wolfram and A. K. Dewdney each produced something special for us. Dewdney showed a video of part of the Mandelbrot set zooming into ever finer detail! These speakers were thought-provoking, entertaining and well-prepared with excellent material.

items.title: The Boat Trip Round Manhattan
items.text:
The boat trip was an excellent idea well executed; it was on a large boat which could carry the complete conference and all hangers-on with ease, leaving plenty of space to move around, there was ample food and drink and nothing to do but talk to congenial people and watch the skyline and shore of New York as it gradually went dark.

The trip started at 42nd St wharf, went south round the statue of Liberty and up the east river but turned before the first bridge (Brooklyn) and then went north up the main river and turned just below George Washington bridge and returned to 42nd St. There was even one compartment with a Loud Noise in it (allegedly music) for people who preferred not to hear what their companions said! There was real music too - a barber-shop group who sounded great and who seemed to be having great fun. Getting such a large party fed with food and drink without excessive waiting in line was a problem; it was not really solved but as there was two and a half hours to feed oneself in not even the most diehard line avoiders had to go hungry. The occasion was a great success and rounded off the first day of the conference on a high note.

Per Gjerlov (chairman APL90) with some of the Danish Beer the Danes gave us for the boat trip

items.title: More Printed Material Than Ever Before
items.text: The conference proceedings were supplemented by a tutorial volume. There was a separate book containing the Statistics day tutorial. The amount of written material a visitor to APL 89 could take away with him was more, I suspect, than was provided at any other APL conference. Lynne Shaw told me that the amount of work done to raise the standard of the typography and layout was greater than ever before and certainly the results are more uniform than some proceedings have been.

items.title: Panels and Tutorials
items.text: Perhaps I was unlucky with the tutorials I attended. Tutorials and panel sessions are very easy to do badly. I was disappointed by every panel in the conference, even the panel after Arthur Whitney's talk about 'A'. It takes a lot of effort to co-ordinate what various panellists are going to say, and if there is no such planning what too often results is words filling time. Some of the panellists were being recruited as the delegates arrived and the results were what you would expect - inadequately prepared contributions which failed to fit together well.

items.title: Rather a Sad End
items.text: The closing session was a case in point. The session was called 'Thought, Structure and APL' but the three contributions were independent and unlinked. Each of those speakers can hold an audience spellbound for an hour and a half. None of them did himself justice (and these were recruited months beforehand). No doubt each had material prepared for a longer talk. The time allowed was shortened at the last minute and the result was banality or incoherence. Rather a bathetic end, I felt.

items.title: The Self-service Banquet
items.text:
The banquet was self-service and there was not adequate control over when you joined the queues; the consequence was that the queues were too long. It had been intended that there should be a choice of flavours - there was Italian food, Chinese food etc. on offer. This was not announced nor clearly signposted so what you got depended on which queue you happened to join. It turned out that each queue led to a mixture, which in my case tasted good. There was no drink supplied as part of the banquet - we had to pay Hilton prices for a bottle. Many of us felt that the Hilton skimped rather on the banquet. It also skimped on other things. On the first day the coffee arrived with china cups and saucers. By the end of the conference we had grown accustomed to polystyrene beakers.

Fountains near the Hilton

items.title: The Hilton
items.text: Hilton prices were too high: apart from a share in that bottle of wine and two beers, I bought no food or drink at the hotel. Instead we walked round the corner to a delicatessen for breakfast, lunch and dinner. Looking back on this I realise that eating together at other conferences brought the delegates together and gave more opportunities to meet and talk in a relaxed atmosphere - I missed this at the Hilton. We also bought wine; the Chandos Californian champagne from a Lexington Avenue shop at under $10 a bottle was $45 a bottle in the hotel. We carried it back and drank it out of tooth mugs after cooling it with free Hilton ice. I'm sure this way it tasted better.

items.title: The Conference Luncheon
items.text: There was a conference Lunch as well as the banquet. I applaud this innovation. The meal was served - no queuing. The food was good and the after-lunch speakers were first rate. APL is on the whole a very visual notation and it was a pleasant change to be asked to appreciate results through one's ears.

items.title: Will APL 89 help to spread the use of APL?
items.text: What will APL 89 do for the growth of APL? Not many converts to APL will have been made. A few students attended and perhaps the Statistics day will have engaged the enthusiasm of some non-APLers. A conference at a big hotel which targets the company employee and tries to provide sufficient value to justify the cost of sending delegates at company expense, a conference that relies on income from a vendor exhibition and must try to deliver professional users to visit the stands and consider buying the products, such a conference can neither attract the uncommitted nor the poor (which in England includes most teachers) nor is spreading APL likely to be in the forefront of the minds of its delegates. Even the vendors' undoubted aim to sell more APL can only be pursued in such an audience to a limited extent; most delegates already have an APL and for most the cost of a change would be high.

items.title: More Free Interpreters: now we must get them into use
items.text: The only initiative at APL 89 that might have a significant effect on the number of APL users was the launch of TryAPL2 - IBM APL2/PC as freeware (but without many auxiliary processors). To obtain such an effect the APL world will have to make a concerted effort to help and encourage teachers to try using APL with their pupils. This is a much harder task than the production of free APLs (as I have reason to know).

items.title: Pleasant Memories
items.text:
What was memorable about APL 89? Apart from the highlights mentioned above I shall remember with pleasure:

  • Phil Benkard's presentation on three overhead projectors simultaneously with David Landaeta, David Livingstone and Jim Brown as the foil changing machinery,
  • Linda Alvord's Willie-the-snail who wanted to be an architect,
  • Charles Waters' paper from the 'Institute of Geometric Entomology' at Scotch Plains-Fanwood school making observations on flight behaviour in the butterfly,
  • The little torches with colour filters and light-guides which STSC gave away at their reception,

3xOHP Foil Changers! Silhouettes of David Landaeta; David Livingstone; Jim Brown; Phil Benkard (and someone standing in the photographer's way)

  • Last but not least Tangible Math and TryAPL2. Tangible Math is Sharp APL/PC with a workspace that sets error traps to provide help of many kinds and a booklet introducing APL by Ken Iverson. TryAPL2 is IBM's APL2/PC complete but without auxiliary processors. Each of these gives large workspaces and enhancements to APL. Both can be copied and given away. No PC-owning maths teacher should be without these products.

items.title: The Statistics Tutorial Day
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 65

Reported by Chris Brady

The Statistics Tutorial was of a very mixed standard in more ways than one.

The morning sessions were intended to be an elementary guide to statistical techniques but were marred by the hi-tech video projection equipment not locking on to the PC-generated graphics displays. These were prime examples of the need to have a low-tech back-up of slides or foils for when hi-tech things go wrong. Also the early sessions lost momentum (and many people's interest) with the use of too many complicated models (plastic fruit joined by dowel rods to illustrate the concept of stratification in populations - I think!!). Too much time was spent in constructing these during the presentations.

As is usual at conferences the published papers are more informative than were the actual presentations. The first was entitled "Statistics: An Inductive, Conceptual Approach", and the second was "An APL Sampler: A Tool for Illustrating the Central Limit Theorem". This latter paper could be of interest to many end-users of our APL systems.

The afternoon sessions were much better presented and aimed at a higher level of understanding. The papers presented were entitled "Graphical Techniques in Statistical Data Analysis and Inference", "Statistical Analysis of Two-way (and Higher Dimensional) Tables", "Statistical Linear Models Using APL", and "A Statistical Symmetry".

The first was not specific to APL but did illustrate a number of ways of graphing statistical data. The second could be of interest to end-users and developers of our APL systems, especially those in marketing and reservations. It is mainly about the analysis of multi-dimensional contingency tables of frequency data, for which APL is admirably suited. APL expressions for Chi-squared and Fisher's tests are given as well as for more sophisticated tests.

The third paper was about estimating the parameters of a linear model, and hence the 'signal', given a number of observations affected by 'noise' (or random errors). APL may be used very effectively for this since the least-squares regression operator (domino) is powerful and easy to use.

The "Statistical Symmetry" paper was about generating samples from various distributions using random number techniques, which can then be used for simulations and modelling.

items.title: Conference Summary
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 66

by Peter Merritt

The 89 conference in New York was to be my second exposure to large numbers of APLers in a confined space, the first being our own (that is, British) attempt at Manchester in 1986. I had really enjoyed myself there, with its fascinating series of talks and product displays, although equally enlightening was the opportunity to meet and talk with so many other like-minded, slightly crazy people. I'd had to miss Dallas in '87 and Sydney in '88, but a new job with more committed employers provided both the financial and professional impetus needed, so, together with an old colleague (Simon Barker, now of BUPA), I duly sent off my registration and hotel booking form (taking care not to think about the cost of staying at the Hilton...).

My conference began like the bulk of the other attendees with the Monday morning opening plenary session which was to be given by Tom Gilb (for reports on the Saturday talk/welcome and the Sunday statistics tutorial, see elsewhere in this issue). The talk centred on the development of a formal planning/specification language which seeks to express such vague but essential areas as user requirements, test criteria, cost/benefit tradeoffs etc., in a more quantifiable and structured format. Thus, the usual request for "a more efficient warehouse" would be broken down into 'statements' such as "OBJECTIVE: SHELF SPACE UTILISATION 91-95% [Objects less than 10Kg.]". The performance or characteristics of the existing problem (on which design decisions would be made) would again be broken down into smaller statements which would be easy to identify later , such as "PAST: USER LOAD ON STOCK SYSTEM 120 MAX[Average 85]". Or, later on, "TEST: USER LOAD ON STOCK SYSTEM[Development: 10 staff, 2 locations]". The three components of each statement represent the general statement type, the aspect of the problem to which it refers, and (in the square brackets) any refinement or qualifying statement. Comments may be appended to any of the statements at the end of the line. Another good feature was the introduction of a "SOURCE" statement type, in which specific book/chapter/paragraph references are given at the point at which such information may be used to justify a design decision, rather than in the form of footnotes or the almost totally useless list of titles in some forgotten appendix.

The development and use of this planning language has meant that, for Mr Gilb's systems at least, all requirements are stated and fully defined, both in terms of cost and specific benefits etc. Critical information on existing procedures/factors is stated and the source of that information listed with it, and so on. In this way, Mr Gilb has gone beyond normal systems analysis (which has always seemed obsessed with computer program design, at the expense of full problem definition) to such an extent that his specs have been used as the basis of legal contracts for the development of systems. Despite the fact that Mr.Gilb, a Software Engineering specialist currently based in Norway, did not actually touch on APL, to me it was probably one of the most significant talks for business APL system developers that I've ever heard, especially given the increasing interest in quality assurance. Two short paragraphs do not do justice to a two and a half hour presentation, but hopefully readers will go away and read the proceedings or, better still, obtain a copy of his book, "Principles of Software Engineering Management" (Addison-Wesley, 1988).

The afternoon began with a visit to the Workshop on APL Problem Solving. I'd thought that this would be another opportunity for me to pick up some useful techniques etc., but in fact the two presenters were studying us, the audience, and the thought processes which we went through with a given problem. To provide the data for later study, the audience was paired-off, with one partner acting as the solver while the other recorded the thoughts and ideas as they occurred (the solver was supposed to vocalise ideas, the recorder being allowed to probe but not prompt in any way). After an excruciating 20 minutes (which seemed much longer) the roles were reversed. I'm not sure how valuable was the material gathered, but it was an interesting exercise to see the many differences, and similarities, of approach.

The last session before tea was by Diana Cook, High Productivity Systems, which looked at techniques for designing and/or maintaining large systems. By using a detailed analysis of more than 300 bugs encountered in running a large financial system, the various causes were discussed and the advantages of using structured programming methods illustrated. Of particular importance was the adoption of a set of project control guidelines or principles, many of which though 'obvious' are all too often ignored in a number of sites. The use of data dictionaries to control/translate program access was mentioned as this is a useful method of reducing many common maintenance problems, as was the more rigid control of modifications and enhancements (the cause of many of the worst bugs). Finally, the keeping and analysis of an error log was shown to provide useful data on underlying patterns or problem areas not necessarily discernible from installing individual "fixes".

The last two sessions on Monday were quite different, although equally interesting. Firstly Alan Graham, now ex-IBM, put forward his suggestions for a new, simplified version of APL which would also rationalise some of the variations between competing versions/implementations. Being 'simple', of course, means that the ideas in APL0 are too far-reaching to fit into a small article, but many of his suggestions seemed to produce quite a favourable reaction among the audience. Finally, Anthony Camacho gave an illustrated guide to the design of mazes (that's right, Hampton Court and all that). He'd recently been employed to help design and more importantly check-out some new mazes which had been commissioned around the UK. The most important test was to determine approximately how long it would take for someone to get out!

Tuesday is somewhat blurred for me, since I was suffering from extreme giddiness (delayed jet-lag), but I do remember a fascinating talk by young jazz star Stanley Jordan who used programs to help develop harmonics and musical relationships of which he would not otherwise have dreamed. The other session of note for me was given by Nancy Wheeler, covering an introduction to SQL/DS and later on how it can be used with/from APL2. Given APL's simple yet powerful analysis tools, the idea of using products such as SQL to access the vast amounts of existing data out there could give the language a whole new lease of life.

The Wednesday morning sessions APL2 on the PS/2, and APL In The Workstation Environment which followed it were more in the order of product demonstrations, although each was very well done and quite educational. The workstation demo in particular showed just how much power can now sit on a desk, and helped to emphasise the drift in some organisations toward downloading mainframe systems onto one or more such super-micros.

Just prior to lunch, Arthur Whitney (of Morgan-Stanley) told an increasingly interested audience about a streamlined version of the APL interpreter which he had helped to develop in-house. Among the important design principles adopted for this project were portability (I believe it was written in 'C') and simplicity. As an example of the latter, all "idiom recognition" sub-modules were excluded, attention being given to speeding up the basic procedures with assembler routines once the design was finalised. The significant time-savings achieved by this interpreter were illustrated by comparisons with bench marks run elsewhere. Indeed, so interesting were the results that more than one person (myself included) sought more information afterwards, in particular as to whether it would be made more widely available (unfortunately not).

Immediately following lunch, a further plenary session was held at which Stephen Wolfram demonstrated a stunning package called Mathematica. This package utilises the high resolution Macintosh screen to allow "normal" mathematical symbols and constructs to be typed, except that now values can be assigned to abstract formulae. As in many instances values can also be formulae, the more complex examples began to resemble rule-based systems.

The highlight of Wednesday afternoon was a panel presentation by four experienced developers of Practical Development Techniques for Large Systems. What was fascinating to me as a business user/developer was the variety of approach, albeit in some cases dictated by external constraints on time or budget. Panel members who obviously were well in control of their fate extolled the virtues of comprehensive documentation, beautifully structured design, libraries of utilities with their own maintenance programs/procedures, and of course standards - all good stuff, but not always achievable, which is why the last speaker received so many sympathetic nods. This individual explained about rushed projects with compressed deadlines, prototypes which were so successful that they were immediately installed as production systems, no time to develop standards other than the informal exchange of techniques, with the "strongest" becoming naturally the most common as it was generally accepted. What the last speaker did emphasise, however, were APL's speed of development and change, which helps them to keep their users more than satisfied.

Thursday came all too quickly and began with sessions on data typing and user-defined data types in APL2. After the break, Martin Gfeller and Manuel Alfonseca continued with a look at Object-Oriented Programming in APL. I must confess to being an interested novice in this area, and was hoping to pick up some useful insights. In brief conversations with Mr Gfeller during some earlier coffee-breaks, his ideas for OOP and extensions or revisions of APL, were both stimulating and well structured, with potential advantages to those users not necessarily using OOP techniques. The session itself was rather marred, however, in a number of ways. Firstly, the audio-visual equipment was not functioning at all well, at times making the speaker almost inaudible. This, coupled with Mr Gfeller's lack of large-scale presentation skills, unfortunately blurred the very valuable message which he was trying to get across. What did come across was the suggestion (and I hope this is the right interpretation) that data and functions be grouped into general(-ised?) "classes", with rules governing their interaction just as there are in mathematics or interpreter construction. Unfortunately, neither of the two sessions seemed really accessible to the relative novice, with too much of the discussion descending into the realms of pure maths.

While the emphasis on the pure mathematical (not always related to APL) was rather more prevalent than I would have wished - being a simple "business solutions" APL-er - the conference was on the whole a great success for the ACM/SigAPL group which organised it. As with any event such as this, the organisers are somewhat hostage to those who submit material, and so not every session will suit all tastes - and rightly so. Strange indeed will be the taste of someone who finds nothing of interest, or who does not come away better informed than before. I encourage everyone with an interest in the language to attend at least one conference, therefore, so I will close by offering my thanks to SigAPL and wishing good-luck to the Danes for APL90 in Denmark. See you there.

items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

The VECTOR working group welcomes correspondence on any topic affecting the APL community. All letters should be addressed to the Editor, and should indicate whether they are for the general or technical section. (Letters containing APL code will normally be classed as 'technical'.) The editor reserves the right to edit any letter unless the writer states that it is to be published in full or not at all.

items.title: Second Generation APLs - Comment on Items in Vector 5.4
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

From: N.J.Small, 23rd August 1989
path: Second Generation APLs - Comment on Items in Vector 5.4

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
One way of avoiding Heffalump traps is not to behave like a Heffalump - though this may be easier said than done!

The problems described arise from the freedom that strand notation and mixed arrays allow. One defensive action that can be taken is to tighten up one’s programming style, in particular by using unnecessary parentheses to make programs more readable - especially in distinguishing functions and data. Another thing one can do is to learn how to get out of the traps as quickly as possible. A little experience soon teaches one to recognize the type of trap one has fallen into, and that is usually half the way to escaping.

Whilst these new facilities are of great value in creating data structures, I feel that they are not really what one needs to solve the problem of passing multiple parameters to functions. I consider it very inelegant to have to start each function by unpacking parameters (though erasing the original parameter is probably unnecessary with the new data-pointer storage systems). An alternative solution has already been implemented in embryo form in the system function ⎕FMT used by STSC and Sharp; a typical function header would look something like:

  (Z1;Z2;Z3) ← (L1;L2) FN (R1;R2;R3;R4)

(In most cases, left arguments would not be required.)

With data structures one needs to take care if they are to contain more than a small number of elements at the highest level, as there is an overhead of about 30 bytes per element in mixed or nested arrays, plus a performance penalty. For example, if one has a long list of serial numbers and names, these should be stored as a two-element nested vector, rather than as a two column-mixed array.

items.title: Article by Peter Cyriax on APL*PLUS II
items.text:
1. Peter must have a disk cache or some other facility stored in the upper end of extended memory; with all of a 1 Mbyte extended memory available one will get a workspace of 915120 bytes.
  2. As described in the Release Notes, when / and \ are used to the left of another operator there is an ambiguity, because the symbols represent both functions and operators. To indicate interpretation as a function, enclose the symbol in parentheses. For example:
      1 2 3(/)¨'ABC'
A BB CCC

(Without the parentheses one gets NONCE ERROR.)
path: Second Generation APLs - Comment on Items in Vector 5.4

items.title: Articles by Ajay Askoolum on APL*PLUS II
items.text:
1. There is a SYSHELP.SF file, but in my release (1.1) it contains very little. For a help file to be accessible, it must be named as the desired help file in the configuration file; perhaps STSC would like to reinstate the system variable ⎕HNAMES. As F1 is generally recognised as the standard key for help, one could use the keyboard mapping facilities to give this the same value as Alt-F6. Alternatively, one could put one’s home-made help facility on F1 and map Alt-F6 to that.
  2. The function ⎕LIBD is implemented, as in APL*PLUS/PC, so libraries may be defined from within a program, as well as in the file CONFIG.APL.
  3. The session manager editor does not add extra bytes to DOS files.
  4. A numeric editor will be incorporated in release 2 of the interpreter.

Migration from APL*PLUS/PC will, in most cases, be fairly straightforward. Appendix D of the reference manual gives details of the differences between the systems, and suggests three ways of transferring code (none of which will move locked functions):

  • Source Level Transfer (functions implementing the Workspace Interchange Convention of the international APL standard)
  • functions DTFN and LFFN, which use a native file
  • functions WSTOFILE and PCFILETOWS, using an ASF file (this is the quickest and easiest option). The workspace PCFILES contains functions to transfer component files and workspaces in either direction between the two systems (though, obviously, one cannot transfer mixed or nested arrays to the PC version).

File and workspace transfer is very quick and easy; modifying code may take somewhat longer, but can be speeded by making use of the supplied functions WSSHOW, SCAN, and FNREPL to find and edit strings within functions.

Of course, it helps to migrate one’s utility workspaces first, so that functions from them can be copied into application workspaces.

The following are probably the items that will most commonly necessitate code changes:

  • ⎕INKEY - the code for Home has changed, and there are some new codes
  • ⎕KEYW is no longer supported
  • ⎕WGET - type 4 is no longer supported (use type 3 instead)
  • ⎕POKE - a few of the more obscure values do not get translated by the interpreter, and ⎕SEG must be null or 0
  • functions from the ASMFNS workspace should be replaced by their new versions.

In general, the better one’s programming practices and the more modular one’s code, the less work one will have to do. Now may be the time to write those little cover functions that one always intended to do tomorrow!

Yours sincerely,

N.J.Small Assistant Research Manager IT Systems Support Section National Westminster Bank
