items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 94
path: The M61 Problem: a Partial Resolution

items.title: The M61 Problem: a Partial Resolution
items.text:
For readers who own (or are thinking of buying) a PS/2-M61, the keyboard problem highlighted in the last Vector has been partially resolved. Apparently, IBM have changed to a new keyboard controller, which affects the scan codes sent to your application. Of course there is a new keyboard handler to cope with this, so mostly you don’t notice a thing.

However, when APL*PLUS/PC attempts to flash the keyboard lights (e.g. if you hit Caps Lock), or if your code attempts a peek to see if Caps Lock is down, it resets the driver to the old version!! This totally screws the keyboard, as reported in Vector 6.3. The fix is:

      0 ⎕POKE 879   ⍝ Cancel keyboard lights

… this appears to be OK in the APL*PLUS/PC standard system versions 8/9. Obviously, it needs to be the very first line in the very first function in INIO. It worries me slightly that on a couple of occasions I got the problem in a CLEAR WS before I had even touched a key, and on one occasion I got it in DOS having simply done )OFF. This suggests that there may be at least one more trigger in there somewhere, which will sooner or later catch me out!

As far as I can test, the extended system (APL*PLUS/PC or APL*PLUS II) does not show the problem. Watch this space.
path: The M61 Problem: a Partial Resolution

items.title: Yet more VCAT ...
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 95

From: Peter Branson, 6th March 1990

Norman Thomson’s response (Vector Vol.6 No.3) to my Education Vector VCAT example does raise a couple of interesting points (not to mention Adrian’s timing tests!).

Firstly, I don’t know what a ‘modern didactic view’ is, but if we want to use some APL2, why not try a half-and-half approach (⎕IO←1):

R←X VCAT Y
X←(¯2↑1 1,⍴X)⍴X
Y←(¯2↑1 1,⍴Y)⍴Y
R←⊃(⊂[2] X),⊂[2]Y

Fairly obviously, this will handle scalars and vectors also. Norman’s approach means carrying two names for a simple job, and I really don’t like doing that. Working with a plethora of production workspaces, I try to keep to the absolute minimum the number of names that I might need to copy around.

A more serious point was raised in his first paragraph; namely should we introduce beginners (kids and grown-ups alike) to the APL2-type enhancements at an early stage (irrespective of ‘free’ software)? With a requirement in the near future to start training one or more graduates in APL, I have been pondering this question already, and personally I think not. A full grounding in APL1 is essential if the person is going to be maintaining existing code (as most professional programmers are likely to be doing at some time or other) and he or she must be able to recognise the older idioms too. To bring in the enhancements as well is, I think, a bit too much in the early stages.

The final point is raised by Adrian’s timing tests. There are times when good APL1 is needed for efficiency, so a thorough grounding is essential. One small example of this arose when I joined my present company last year. They have a standard utility written using many APL2 features for searching a workspace for occurrences of a character string. Unfortunately, response was poor at the time, and it was rather boring waiting for the result to show. I re-wrote the function with a few APL2 bits, and used a localised function for the individual object searches, leaving only one ‘each’. Result: about 25 times faster, and much less boring!

Peter Branson EDS Ltd.

items.title: Is Function Ambivalence a Good Thing?
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 96

From: David Piper, March 1990

I am amazed by the extent of the feedback generated by my brief letter concerning an ‘ambivalent operator’. The concept was originally simply an exercise for my own intellectual interest and was not (as I hope my response to Claude Henriod in Vector[6;3;93] made clear) a serious attempt at a real solution. Clearly the subject is of interest to many APL users. The suggestion of a potential solution (however great its shortcomings) to the problems of making use of ambivalence begs more serious questions. The most fundamental must be:

"is function ambivalence a good thing?"

To be a ‘good thing’ we presumably mean a facility must provide useful functionality without sacrificing anything (or at most sacrificing less than we gain). What facilities does functional ambivalence provide? - quite simply the ability to elide the left argument of a defined dyadic function. We use this capability to either:

  • supply a default value for the elided argument (as with the subtract vs minus or divide vs reciprocal primitive functions)
  • undertake some different but possibly related action (as with the multiply vs signum or add vs conjugate primitive functions).

What, then, is the cost of using function ambivalence? If used to supply default values for the elided argument, the effects are usually not too serious. Criticism can be made about defining data (i.e. the default value) procedurally rather than as a parameter, but this is rather theoretical. The real weakness can be seen if we examine what happens when the default has to change. The code making use of the default either stops working, or, worse still, continues to work but provides different (presumably invalid) results. Of course, we could always create a brand new function for each different value of default.

When used to implement two separate functions the cost of ambivalence is greater. By implementing two separate functions in a single unit of code we increase the complexity of the code written (back to the start of the discussion; we have to write code to handle the ambivalence). We also reduce the coherence (strength) of the function.

If the two functions are well separated, we may be able to classify the function as having "informational cohesion" (Myers, Reliable Software through Composite Design 1975). This is only slightly inferior to the best case "functional" cohesion and no significant maintenance or quality problems will be introduced. On the other hand, if the functions are not well isolated, the best classification we can assign is "logical" cohesion (Page-Jones, The Practical Guide to Structured Systems Design 1988) with the maintenance and quality problems such a poorly designed function normally introduces.

Note that for both types of use of ambivalence, the coupling between the function and its superior calling functions is increased. It is likely that the level of coupling will be reduced to that of "control" coupling (see Page-Jones). The argument is not only being used to pass data to the sub-function, information is also being passed by the presence or elision of the argument. Since data and control information are passed with the same piece of data, the coupling is more likely to be classed as "hybrid" Page-Jones makes a good job of explaining the problems associated with this type of coupling.

So, then, we are left to consider cases where it may be valid to use function ambivalence. In "open" systems or utilities, ambivalence can be used to enrich the syntax of the language defined for the user. Even here, it should be used with great care, especially if ambivalence is used to set default parameters.

With regard to the contribution from Phil Last (Vector[6;2;117]), I certainly would not countenance the use of ⎕FX to fix functions on the fly. Using this technique, we manage to descend right to the bottom of the quality ladder, to the depths of "pathological" (or content) coupling - one function is being used to modify the contents of another!

The quality impact of using execute as advocated by Claude Henriod and Norman Thomson (Vector[6;3;94 97]) is harder to quantify but still smacks of pathological coupling; my general reaction to it (and all uses of execute) is YUCK!! I guess, on those occasions when I have (or want) to use ambivalence, I shall have to resort to the test and branch syndrome. At least in APL*PLUS I can use the diamond separator to get the test and the branch on a single function line.

Whether the costs in terms of design quality, discussed above, are greater than the benefits derived from the use of function ambivalence is largely a matter of personal judgement. My own opinion is that except for "open" systems cases, the potential costs far outweigh any short term benefits. I hope this provides some helpful (recursive) feedback and clarifies my viewpoint.

D B Piper
path: Is Function Ambivalence a Good Thing?

items.title: Error Trapping or Event Handling?
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 98

From: Richard Nabavi, 14th March 1990

I have been following with interest the recent VECTOR articles on Error Trapping in its different manifestations within APL*PLUS, Dyalog, IPSA, APL.68000 etc. But may I make a plea for greater terminological exactitude in describing what these facilities actually do?

My gripe is a simple one. What I used to think of as Error Trapping is being termed Event Handling. This term is used by Dyalog, by I.P. Sharp, and even by IBM in the APL2 reference material. Now it seems to me that if your APL code is happily tripping along, interpreting and executing statements according to the will of the sentient being who wrote the function, and suddenly it encounters a SYNTAX ERROR, then that is not an event, it is a Bug. The term Event, as used by most of the computing fraternity outside APL, is normally reserved for external events that meet two criteria: (a) they cannot be predicted by following the logic of the code, and (b) they can happen at any time, not just when the system makes a specific operating system call or carries out a particular instruction.

In fact, the only real Event which can normally be trapped in a conventional (non-windowing) APL environment is the user hitting the Attention key; this is indeed a true external event which can happen at any time, and which cannot be predicted by following the logic of the APL code. It is clearly different in nature from a VALUE ERROR or a RANK ERROR. (What about WS FULL, or SYMBOL TABLE FULL? Ed.) However, in modern windowing systems, and on networks or sophisticated multi-user machines, a plethora of other external events can occur, which the APL system might need to know about. Examples of these true Events are:

  • the user has selected a menu item from a pull-down menu
  • the application’s window has been overwritten by another task, and needs to be redrawn
  • the network has sent a message containing an update of the $ to Dmk exchange rate.

Now, as far as I know, these kinds of Events are not really handled by any of the trapping facilities which APL interpreters provide. Even APL.68000 on windowing machines like the Macintosh - which does provide Event Handling through a library workspace - does not yet have these facilities built in to the APL interpreter itself, although the operating system interface is largely built around responding to events. So shouldn’t we use the term Error Trapping to describe what we have got already, so that confusion can be avoided when we finally announce that APL now has Event Handling built in to it?

In fact, when you do start to think about true Event Handling in APL, you begin to realise that it is a difficult subject, and may require fundamental changes in the way APL systems are designed. But that is another matter; in the meantime, let us not use misleading expressions.

Yours sincerely,

Richard Nabavi MicroAPL Ltd.

items.title: APL and MS Word for HP LaserJet
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 99

From: Rex Swain, 28 March 1990

For quite some time, I have wanted to be able to use my word processor to mix APL with other fonts. I recently took the time to solve this problem, and have developed programs that teach Microsoft Word to treat STSC’s APL font for the HP LaserJet as it would any other font.

Now, I can mix APL symbols such as ⎕←⍳⍴ with Helvetica and Times Roman and any other fonts I have, on the same line or in separate paragraphs. (so can I …. Ed!). I format the APL portions with the normal Word commands; Word automatically downloads the APL font when necessary. If you have the STSC APL video characters turned on when you invoke Word, you can toggle between Word’s text and graphics display modes: in text mode you can see the APL characters on the screen; in graphics mode you can see the full PC character set.

Briefly, my programs modify a specified .PRD file, inserting the APL font definition and translate table; create or add to the corresponding .DAT file; and extract the downloadable APL fonts from STSC’s PRINTERS.ASF file. I am willing to distribute these programs on a virtually freeware basis. Anyone who is interested may send me:

  • a diskette (360K, or any density 3.5") and a stamped, self-addressed return mailer; or
  • for $10, or $15 outside the US, (cash only; no checks) I will supply the diskette (specify size), mailer, and postage.

Requirements are:

  • an HP LaserJet printer that accepts downloadable fonts (any model except the original 2686A),
  • Microsoft Word version 5.0, and APL*PLUS/PC version 8 (or higher, I suppose).

Rex Swain

Editor’s Note: this is a rather faster and cheaper way of doing what I do with MS Word and GoScript. We both exploit the availability of APL character drivers (I use the Hercules RAMFONT approach) in similar ways, and we both rely on the excellently open architecture of MS Word.

I would still recommend PostScript as the best long-term solution, but if you already have APL*PLUS/PC and an HP LaserJet, I think Rex’s offer is a most generous and useful one. Many thanks.
path: APL and MS Word for HP LaserJet

items.title: Hackers Corner: Lots More VGA Colours
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 110

by Adrian Smith

I have always been slightly puzzled by those ads in the computer press which talk about the zillions of possible colours you can get out of XYZ Corporation's latest VGA. I always seemed to be stuck with 16 foreground and 16 background (assuming you kill the blink bit) which makes 256 in all.

The first breakthrough was when I noticed that ⎕GINIT can take a left argument specifying up to 16 VGA Palette Registers. Of course there were no clues as to which of the possible 64 colours was which (other than the hint that the normal range was found in the bottom 8 and the top 8 - 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 and 56 57 58 59 60 61 62 63). At the time, I was playing with a Hercules-oriented version of C&D's Starmap workspace, adding a bit of helpful colour. One obvious extension was to put the bright stars into their correct spectral types ... Betelgeuse should be red, and the sun should be orange. Armed with an old star atlas, I experimented with the palette settings, and quickly discovered that colour 38 is a rather excellent orange!

Of course this trick only works for graphics, and APL*PLUS helpfully resets everything when you exit! As a last resort, I read the instructions (in this case a very useful MicroSoft book all about VGA programming) to find the BIOS calls involved. The screen border and palette registers are trivially easy to set, and can be used to good effect to brighten up your screen designs. There are several excellent background colours (e.g. a nice deep green) available, as well as the above mentioned orange. As with all these settings, note that <Ctrl-Esc> resets everything to default in APL*PLUS/PC.

    ∇ VGA∆PALETTE VEC;RG;BX

[1]   ⍝ Set Vga palette register VEC[1] to VEC[2]
[2]   ⍝    AH = 10hex       ... BIOS service 10 (EGA/VGA only)
[3]   ⍝    AL =  0hex       ... subservice 0 (1 sets the border)
[4]   ⍝    BH = 0-63        ... required colour
[5]   ⍝    BL = 0-16        ... palette register to set (0 for bdr)
[6]    BX←(256×VEC[2])+VEC[1]
[7]    RG←(4096,BX)⎕INT 16
    ∇

VGA∆PALETTE 6 38        ⍝ Switch brown to orange
VGA∆BORDER 38           ⍝ Use an orange frame
43 15 55 62 38 52 4     ⍝ OBAFGKM ... star spectral types!

If you want an example of a really good use of this feature, try out a wonderful little program from Quarterdeck called Manifest (comes along with QEMM 5.0). To select an appropriate range of colours for your application, I suggest you set up a simple workspace which splashes colour around the screen, and experiment. Of course different types of monitor may give more or less acceptable results, and users can always wreck the whole thing by fiddling with the contrast button!

Of course 64 colours is more than 16, but we are still some way short of the 64,000 or so that the advertisers claim! The next stage is to fiddle with the Red/Green/Blue balance of any of the 64. Having created a colour which is to your liking, you then map it to one of the 16 palette registers as above.

    ∇ VGA∆COLOUR VEC;RG;BX;CX;DX

[1]   ⍝ Set Vga colour register VEC[1] to VEC[2 3 4] (RGB)
[2]   ⍝    AH = 10hex       ... BIOS service 16 (EGA/VGA only)
[3]   ⍝    AL = 10hex       ... subservice 16
[4]   ⍝    BX = 0-63        ... colour register
[5]   ⍝    CH = 0-63        ... green intensity
[6]   ⍝    CL = 0-63        ... blue intensity
[7]   ⍝    DH = 0-63        ... red intensity
[8]   ⍝ Note that intensities go down by half for -8 from 63
[9]   ⍝ e.g. 63 .... 55 .... 47 .... 39
[10]  ⍝        full... half... qtr ... eighth
[11]   VEC←4↑VEC
[12]   BX←VEC[1]
[13]   DX←256×VEC[2]
[14]   CX←(256×VEC[3])+VEC[4]
[15]   RG←(4112,BX,CX,DX)⎕INT 16
    ∇

      VGA∆COLOUR 38, 48 48 0     ⍝ Set up orange as Red + Green

The intensity of each colour is specified on a scale from 0..63, but the relationship is highly non-linear; a good rule of thumb is that by subtracting 8 you halve the brightness:

63 63 63 ..... bright white 55 55 55 ..... half intensity white 47 0 0 ..... quarter intensity red 42 24 42 ..... Laura Ashley 'Autumn Plum' etc.

When setting you a range of colours, you need to decide whether you belong to the Benetton school (lots of primaries), or the Laura Ashley school (subtle blends). Have fun.
path: Hackers Corner: Lots More VGA Colours

items.title: The Dangers of APL RISC programming ...
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 112

From: Bob Bykerk, 5 Feb 1990

The article by Gerard Langlet on APL Risc programming (Vector 6.2) created the impression that Gerard does not program in the real world. His argument is loosely strung together and not adequately supported by example. Translated, his argument reads something like this:

Here is a function which works on homogeneous data. Here is my way of writing it without GOTOs, locals, or matrices. Therefore, the use of GOTOs, locals and matrices is not good practice. I have written thousands of these functions, so the above must be true.

The example is useful for homogeneous data, and would not require any data structure other than a vector anyway. It merely shows an alternative, shorter solution to the problem, and does not even demonstrate any tangible benefits, e.g. efficiency. Surely he could have used an example derived from one of his thousands of functions which would demonstrate how a problem dealing with heterogeneous data could be more easily solved by stripping out the structure and converting the data to a series of vectors?

I feel that being pedantic about eliminating GOTOs is a useless exercise, especially when structured code can easily be written (to flow from top to bottom, without spaghetti) using them. Sure, trying to reduce the number of GOTOs may reveal a more elegant and efficient solution, but the use of GOTOs for special casing, taking into account particular properties of the data, eliminating redundancies, or selecting only relevant parts of the data often reveal solutions that are many times faster than non-branching solutions. String searching as developed in the Collected Whizzbangs texts is a good example of this.

His idea of not using locals is fundamentally wrong. Not only does it mean that multi-line functions will almost invariably not be restartable, but they also become unreadable, and consequently a nightmare to debug. Local variables are used to store intermediate results. These are most useful for debugging, as one can see the results of all major transformations up to any point in a function, enabling one to retrace one’s steps. That way you don’t burn your bridges.

Vectors are great for data without structure, unless you want the overhead of partitioning or enclosing. Matrices or higher dimensional arrays are ideal for mimicking structure inherent in business operations, and there are many primitives in APL which naturally and optimally manipulate this type of data. These data structures mirror the way that one would view the information, e.g. sales data in 3 dimensions - salesman × month × year would be seen as pages of sales data, one page per year. A complete analysis can be done on this data without breaking it into vectors, so why entertain the idea?

To conclude, I think that the ideas Gerard presented are on the whole quite worthless until he backs them up with substantial examples. These ideas, if presented to beginners in APL could severely warp the process of learning a healthy coding style.

Bob Bykerk
path: The Dangers of APL RISC programming ...

items.title: VCAT in Sharp APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 113

From: E.E. McDonnell, 9 April 1990

I was interested to see Norman Thomson’s note "VCAT: A Response" in Vector 6, 3. He provides a "modern didactic view" of the problem which, as your editor points out, is slower than the "antique, pragmatic" utility which it offers to supplant. It is, of course, not at all uncommon for the initial implementation of a new feature to be slower than the facility it is intended to replace; when the implementors have enough experience (or often enough complaints from customers) they often find ways to make the new facility more competitive in speed.

I can report, however, on an alternative which is also modern, and while I can hazard no guess as to its didactic merits, I do know that it has the merits of being much shorter even than Mr Thomson’s solution, handles the degenerate cases of scalar and vector arguments with no extra fuss, and is faster than the antique it can replace.

The solution is written in Sharp APL. The view of the problem it takes is influence by the design of the monadic format function and by the availability of the table, or matrix-making primitive. A boxed list of the arguments is formed using the link function: l⊃r; this two-element list is made into a two-by-one matrix, using the table function: ⍪l⊃r; and this is formatted using monadic thorn, which has the property that it expands boxed items to match the largest in size: ⍕⍪l⊃r. That’s all there is to it.

Here is the whole function:

[0] z←l vcat r
[1] z←⍕⍪l⊃r

Timings made on the Sharp mainframe system for arguments of varying sizes are as follows:

+-------------------------------------------+
|         |         |      z←l vcat r       |
| ⍴left   | ⍴right  |    eem    |     PB    |
|         |         |    vcat   |    VCAT   |
|---------|---------|-----------|-----------|
|  2   5  |   3 3   |    118    |    115    |
| 12   80 |    23   |    125    |    112    |
| 56  132 |    63   |    137    |    131    |
|100  200 |300  30  |    270    |    320    |
+-------------------------------------------+

Yours faithfully

Eugene McDonnell

items.title: How to Kill More Cats ...
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 115

From: Norman Thomson, 25 May 1990

Peter Branson’s reply (Vector Vol.6 No.4) to my VCAT suggestions rightly takes me to task for using the pompous phrase ‘a modern didactic appraoach’. In simple terms I mean that APL2 allows us to cut through much of the algorithmic obscurity of old-time APL, thereby making APL2 of great value as a specification language. I agree with both Adrian and Peter that my VCAT is horrendously inefficient with screenful-sized matrices, but that I submit is not the point. Consider rather that VCAT is only the tip of an iceberg, in the sense that if you are motivated to have VCAT in your toolkit, you are likely also to want HCAT (horizontal catenation). Then there is the further matter of justification, - do you want primary (left/top) or secondary (right/bottom)? So generalise CAT to take a vector of matrices as right argument R and 1 or 2 as left argument to denote horizontal or vertical:

[0] Z←L CAT R
[1] Z←⊃[L]⊃,/⊂[L]¨R

      A B
WEE  RATHER
ONE  LARGER
     MATRIX


      (1 CAT A B)(2 CAT A B)
WEERATHER  WEE
ONELARGER  ONE
   MATRIX  RATHER
           LARGER
           MATRIX

Justification is then an exercise in using rotate as a dual transformation, and can be embodied in:

[0]  Z←L TAC R
[1]  Z←⌽[L]L CAT⌽[L]¨R

      (1 TAC A B)(2 TAC A B)
   RATHER       WEE
WEELARGER       ONE
ONEMATRIX    RATHER
             LARGER
             MATRIX

Now degeneracy has to be considered. A vector requiring catenation may be regarded either as a row or a column vector, so there is another 1/2 option for the left argument L of the function MAT which which converts its right argument R into a matrix.

[0]  Z←L MAT R
[1]  Z←⊃[L]1/⊂1/R

      (1 MAT 'PIG')(2 MAT 'PIG')
P  PIG
I
G

(1/R) on the right ensures that MAT will also deal with a scalar, but in order to work as a null function for a non-degenerate matrix R it is necessary to add the first line:

[.1]  →(2=⍴⍴R)/0

The eight significant choices, i.e. all combinations of horizontal/vertical, primary/secondary and row/column resolution have now been dealt with in a systematic way, leaving the path open for efficiency if the goal is other than a pure teaching one. I don’t think Peter and I have any fundamental disagreements, and I certainly don’t suggest the abandonment of old practices and idioms where these are of worth at the implementation stage. I do however advocate the use of APL2 at specification and design stages, and invite readers to pondor which the designer for efficiency has by viewing the whole of this particular problem so compactly.

Norman Thomson

Comment: I never though that such an innocuous little function could generate such interest; maybe we should expose some more ‘pragmatic antiques’ to competition from advanced APLs? Ed(ex).

items.title: The INVERSE operator in APL2.5
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 117

From: I. Phelfritt (neé Leigh), May 1990

I was thrilled to see your review of IBM’s new APL2.5 in April’s Vector 6.4, and felt moved to send you a further couple of examples. One consequence of the direct definition of operators which may not be immediately obvious is the ease with which you can define the INVERSE operator for monadic functions:

  INV:⍵β

INV produces a derived function which reverses the effect of its operand. Formally: A ↔ F INV F A for any array A and any monadic function F. The following examples show the power of this operator ...

      ÷4
0.25
      ÷INV 0.25
4
      +\INV 1 3 6
1 2 3

Where the inverse is not unique, the system provides a ‘least squares’ solution:

      +\INV 6
6
      ?INV 4
7

and of course, INV may take a system function as operand, so:

      ⎕EX INV 1
FOO                 ⍝ re-instates a previously expunged function

2
      ⎕DL INV 2     ⍝ has the same effect as ⎕DL ¯2 in dyalog APL

We are only now beginning to appreciate the power of this new implementation, but I’m sure that such examples will soon swell our idiom libraries.

I. Phelfritt c/o Dyadic Systems Ltd.

items.title: The APL*PLUS ‘dead key’ Problem ...
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 118

From: Cedric Heddle, 12 June 1990

I hope that one of your readers may be able to tell me how to solve the ‘dead key’ problem on UK PS/2 keyboards when using STSC APL*PLUS/PC and the Unified keyboard. The key is immediately to the left of ‘Z’, has a key button number of 45, a scan code of 86 and in DOS it produces ‘/’ when unshifted and ‘|’ when shifted. Apparently this key does not exist on American keyboards, whose left-hand shift key is wider than those on the UK keyboard.

STSC say that they believe that the scan code for this key is 86 and that their ⎕POKE 198 197 code should work with this key, although they do not have a UK keyboard with which to test this belief. In my experience, this key remains dead despite poking characters into the 86th row of the keyboard table. I have even poked into every one of the twenty or so empty rows in the 128-row keyboard table without having any effect on this key. Incidentally, the shifted ‘/’ above ‘8’ on the numeric pad, which also produces a ‘/’ seems also to be unchangeable.

An assembler routine executed via )CMD confirms the BIOS scan code of 86. If any of your correspondents has a solution I am sure I shall not be the only grateful reader.

Yours sincerely,

Cedric Heddle, APL Impetus Ltd.

items.title: The Falkoff Keyboard: a Franco-Belgian Response!
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 119

From: Alain Delmotte, Rome 29th of May 90

I read with interest the article of Adrian Smith on the Falkoff keyboard (VECTOR 6.4 p.92). As an inveterate French speaker and typist, I completely agree with the first precept of Falkoff: "If a symbol is shown on a key, then that is where it should go." This makes justice to other languages keyboard layouts.

This is what I did for the SharpAPL/PC and tested also with APL*PLUS. On a French or Belgian keyboard (AZERTY) figures are .uppercase, some specific symbols appear (accented a,e,u and ç) and some common use symbols (@#\^[]) are obtained with Ctrl-Alt-key (key being the key on which these symbols are engraved in front).

I enclose an example of my keyboard on the Toshiba 1000. The left side shows the base and shift normal keys (the engraved normal keytop). The right side shows the Alt and Ctrl combinations (for APL*PLUS Alt-Shift in place of Ctrl).

\ was moved from the <> key to leave room for ≤≥. Mu not existing in ⎕AV was replaced by ¢. There are sometimes problems with the <> key (scan code 43); when redefined it could move to the left of the &1 key or to the left of the W key depending on the keyboard.

It is also possible and very useful to define the numerical keypad in APL*PLUS (Numlock) as it is in SharpAPL: + gives a blank and - a high minus. Smith’s arguments would be:

  NKEY←74 78
  NKEYDEFS←⍉2 6⍴'-¯ +   '

Yours sincerely

Alain DELMOTTE

N.B. I think that Smith’s ⍴AFKEYS should be 51 7 with APL*PLUS unified keyboard, the Shift-Alt being in position [6] with ⎕IO←0.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce Dyalog APL Version 6.0 for Unix systems. This is functionally identical to the DOS/386 implementation and features the same integrated development environment consisting of a window-based Session, Editor, and Tracer. Apart from external system interfaces, Dyalog APL applications are now 100% compatible between DOS/386 and Unix platforms.

In addition to functional improvements the Unix implementation also benefits from the performance optimisation techniques which were introduced in Release 2 of the DOS/386 version. These result in a significant improvement in speed for basic arithmetic primitive functions working on large arrays. Typically this means a speed-up by a factor of 2 in the arithmetic benchmarks published by STSC.

There are in fact two flavours of Version 6.0 for Unix. The first is a multi-user version designed to support APL/ASCII terminals and/or PCs running terminal emulators. In this version, the APL development environment works in a surprisingly effective manner despite the inherent limitations of ASCII terminals.

The second flavour is Dyalog APL/X which is designed to take full advantage of X-windows, the widely accepted basic window manager for Unix workstations. The product is also designed to be consistent with OSF/Motif, which sits on top of X-Windows and provides a standard user interface compatible with Presentation Manager.

In Dyalog APL/X the Session, Editor and Tracer operate in separate X.11 windows which may be moved and resized using the mouse. The User Screen managed by ⎕SM also becomes a separate moveable and resizable window. New trappable event codes have been added to allow such user actions to be handled under program control. For example, if the user resizes the ⎕SM window your APL function can trap a resize event, query the new window dimensions, and reformat the display accordingly. Controls are provided to allow the APL programmer to specify what a user may or may not do.

Dyalog APL/X also includes an Auxiliary Processor which provides a direct interface to X.11 functions. This will initially provide graphics facilities, but is intended to be developed to include access to the Motif "Widget" set, a toolkit of high-level use-interface functions such as dialog boxes, menus, buttons, and so forth. The Auxiliary Processor will allow an APL application to pop-up a new window and display graphical information within it.

Dyalog APL/X will initially be available on IBM Risc System/6000, Hewlett-Packard and Sun workstations. In due course the product will be ported to other popular X.11/Motif platforms. Full details and dates of availability will be announced at APL90.

In response to customers requests Dyadic has developed a software interface that allows Dyalog APL to be called from a C-program. The interface is very simple and requires only a few additional lines of C-code in the calling program. It allows the C-program to invoke Dyalog APL, )LOAD a workspace, and then run any function and capture its result. Data is transferred efficiently between the C and APL tasks in binary form. The interface can be developed to support a network environment.

Dyadic is also proud to announce a change of ownership following a Management Buyout on March 31st 1990. The new directors and shareholders of the company are Pauline Brand, Peter Donnelly and John Scholes who have been with Dyadic for between ten and thirteen years. The company is delighted by its newly won independence, will continue to develop innovative APL products, and looks forward to providing an even more effective service to its current and future customers. By the time this edition of Vector is printed, Dyadic will have moved to new and larger premises. If you miss the mailshot, the new address can be obtained by calling the company's old number 0420-87024.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
MicroAPL is delighted to be able to use the pages of Vector to announce a major new software product - APL.68000 Level II. For the last year or so we have to all intents and purposes given the appearance of being preoccupied with the user interface of our APL.68000 product - notably on the Mac and Amiga versions. This emphasis does indeed reflect our view that the user interface is the most neglected area of APL but we have not been completely ignoring the development of our APL interpreter.

There is a consensus that a 'second generation' definition for APL exists and that this includes, amongst other things, concepts such as nested arrays and heterogeneous objects. The definition of a second generation APL doesn't go much further than that because of the differences in the specifications of those second generation APLs that are on the market.

MicroAPL has made a major contribution to the portability of second generation APL code. APL.68000 Level II is an implementation of APL2 for processors which belong to the 68000 family. As with APL.68000 we have attempted to use as our model the version of APL that we regard as the de-facto standard. That standard is, in our estimation, IBM's APL2. In the same way that the original APL.68000 represents a useful superset of APL.SV, APL.68000 Level II offers a faithful implementation of IBM's APL2 (see below for what we think that is!) together with a number of vital enhancements.

There are actually two main versions of APL2 issued by IBM - APL2/370 and APL2/PC. APL.68000 Level II is midway between these two versions. A full list of the features that we have included is beyond the scope of this article but includes:

Nested Arrays; Mixed Arrays; Selective Specification; Axis Extensions

⊂ ⊃  ∊ (enlist)  ⍷ ↑ (first)  ≡ ~ (without)  ⎕ ¨
⎕AF ⎕AT ⎕CS ⎕EM ⎕EC ⎕ES ⎕EA ⎕ET ⎕FC ⎕PR ⎕TC ⎕TF
)IN )NMS )OUT )RESET )TIME

At the same time APL.68000 Level II incorporates all the features of APL.68000. In fact APL.68000 Level II is upward compatible with APL.68000 and existing workspaces can be )LOADed into the new APL. For those of you who are not familiar with APL.68000's features, this means that we have added ⎕EDIT, ⎕HC (hard copy), component files, ⎕SS, ⎕BOX and many other useful features to the APL2 specification.

The inclusion of the )IN command means that APL code can be transferred to APL.68000 Level II from other APL2 environments with the minimum of fuss. This last point is critical as APL.68000 Level II adds a number of key machines to the family of those computers that run APL2. Users of mainframe or PC-based APL2 systems can now move applications painlessly to the Apple Mac, or any one of a number of Unix computers or even their Atari ST to carry on working in APL2 at home! APL.68000 Level II has been designed by Richard Nabavi and is available for all machines that support APL.68000.

APL.68000 Level II will be officially launched atAPL90 in Copenhagen.

For more details, contact David Eastwood at MicroAPL

items.title: Speculations on Fermat Equations ...
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 121

From: Anne D Wilson, 12 June 1990

Zdenek V Jizba’s article on Fermat type equations led to me to some interesting thoughts on solutions to \(x^2 + y^2 = z^2\) where \(x,y,z\) are integers and cannot be reduced to another equation by division; e.g. \(6^2 + 8^2 = 10^2\) reduces to \(3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2\).

The following discussion uses the concept of modulo algebra and numbers prime to each other. Modulo algebra deals only with the remainders, which can be generated using the APL primitive. If two numbers are prime to each other they have no common factor other than 1. Thus 4 and 9 are pteo, but 12 and 21 have a common factor of 3. The following recursive function returns the highest common factor (HCF) of 2 numbers. Where numbers are pteo the HCF equals 1.

      ∇ R←A HCF B;C
[1]    ⍎'R←B',(0<C←B|A)/' HCF C'
      ∇

It uses a chain of quotients and remainders to find the HCF. The intermediate results for 31 and 12 are:

by calculation                 using the above function
HCF of 31 and 12 is 1, ie they are pteo.
31 = 2 x 12 + 7                           31 HCF 12
12 = 1 x 7 + 5                            12 HCF 7
7 = 1 x 5 + 2                              7 HCF 5
5 = 2 x 2 + 1                              5 HCF 2
2 = 2 x 1                                  2 HCF 1

(1) In the equation \(x^2 + y^2 = z^2\) \(x\) \(y\) \(z\) are pteo. Proof:- If \(x\), \(y\) have a common factor \(k\) \(k^2a^2 + k^2b^2 = k^2(a^2 + b^2)\) and \(k\) is a factor of \(z\); therefore the equation can be reduced by division by \(k\).

(2) In the equation \(x^2 + y^2 = z^2\) \(x\) and \(z\) are odd and \(y\) is even, or \(y\) and \(z\) are odd and \(x\) is even. Proof:- (i) If 2 of the variables are even they have a common factor of 2, and the equation can be reduced by (1). (ii) Odd numbers are either \(4m + 1\) or \(4m + 3\) which when squared give \(4n + 1\) or \(4k + 9 = 4n + 1\) hence the square of any odd number is \(4n + 1\) Even numbers are \(2m\) and the square of an even number is \(4n\).

Considering all possible combinations:

           | x = 4m+1   |   4m+3   |   2n    |
           | x² = 4r+1  |   4r+1   |   4r    |
---------------------------------------------------      Table showing
y = 4n+1   |    4s+2    |   4s+2   |  4s+1   |          derivation of z²
y² = 4r+1  |     X      |    X     |  z odd  |          where x² + y² = z²
---------------------------------------------------
y = 4n+3   |    4s+2    |   4s+2   |  4s+1   |
y² = 4r+1  |     X      |    X     |  z odd  |
---------------------------------------------------
y = 2n     |    4s+1    |   4s+1   |  4s     |
y² = 4r    |    z odd   |   z odd  |  X      |
---------------------------------------------------

As \(x\) \(y\) \(z\) are not all even, and the square of an odd number is \(4s + 1\) the only valid combinations are:

\(x\) even, \(y\) and \(z\) odd or \(y\) even, \(x\) and \(z\) odd

With no loss of generality we can take the case where \(x\) is odd and consider the equation in the form: \(x^2 = z^2 - y^2\)

(3) If \(p\) \(q\) are odd numbers pteo \((p^2 + q^2) \bmod 4 = 2\) Proof:- \(p\) and \(q\) are odd therefore \((p^2 + q^2) \bmod 4 = 1 + 1 = 2\)

(4) If \(p\) \(q\) are odd numbers pteo \((p^2 - q^2) \bmod 8 = 0\) Proof:- \(p\) and \(q\) are odd therefore \(p = 2m + 1\) \(q = 2n + 1 = 2(m - k) + 1\) \(p^2 - q^2 = (p + q)(p - q) = 4(2m - k - 1).k\) Either \(k\) is odd when \((2m - k + 1)\) is even or \(k\) is even when \((2m - k + 1)\) is odd and therefore another factor of 2 can be extracted. Hence \((p^2 - q^2) \bmod 8 = 0\)

(5) If \(a\) \(b\) are odd numbers pteo and \(z = 0.5(a + b)\) \(y = 0.5(a - b)\) then if there exists \(x\) such that \(z^2 - y^2 = x^2\) \(a\) and \(b\) are squares. Proof:- \(z^2 - y^2 = (0.5(a + b))^2 - (0.5(a - b))^2 = ab\) Hence \(ab = x^2\) and \(a\) \(b\) pteo otherwise \(z\) and \(y\) have a common factor; therefore \(a\) and \(b\) are perfect squares.

Indeed any pair of odd numbers \(p\) \(q\) pteo will generate a solution to the equation. Thus it is only necessary to check that the parameters \(p\) \(q\) are pteo to produce triplets of Pythagorean numbers.

\[\begin{alignat*}{1} x &= pq\\ y &= 0.5(p^2 - q^2)\\ z &= 0.5(p^2 + q^2) \end{alignat*}\]

(6) We can deduce some characteristics of these triplets:- (i) \(z \bmod 4 = 1\) i.e. \(z\) has the form \((4m + 1)\) Proof:- \(z = 0.5(p^2 + q^2)\); \(p\) \(q\) are odd therefore \(z \bmod 4 = 0.5(1 + 1) = 1\)

(ii) \(y \bmod 4 = 0\) i.e. \(y\) is a multiple of 4 Proof:- \(y = 0.5(p^2 - q^2) = 0.5(8m) = 4m\) therefore \(y \bmod 4 = 0\)

(iii) \(z - y = q^2\) which is a perfect square.

(iv) \(z - x = 0.5(p^2 + q^2) - pq = 0.5(p - q)^2\) and as \(p\) and \(q\) are both odd it equals \(2 \times\) a perfect square.

Some example generated from \(p\) and \(q\) are ...

   p    q   x=p.q    y=0.5(p² - q²)   z=0.5(p² + q²)
   3    1       3                4                5
  11    5      55               48               73
 101   67    6767             2856             7345
 101   99    9999              200            10001
 998    6    1497           124496           124505
1933  499  964567          1743744          1992745

Although the above discussion depends on the choice of \(x\) as an odd number similiar calculations can be performed when \(x\) is an even number. In this case the parameters \(r\) \(s\) are defined and deduced as:

\[\begin{alignat*}{1} y &= (r^2 - s^2)\\ z &= (r^2 + s^2)\\ x &= 2rs = \sqrt{2r}\,.\,\sqrt{2s} \end{alignat*}\]

However this merely generates the same triplets, but with \(x\) and \(y\) interchanged.

For the triplets generated by Jizba’s function R←K PFERMAT W

where \(K = z - x\) and \(W = y\) or   \(K = z - y\) and \(W = x\)

\(K\) must be either (the square of an odd number) or (\(2 \times\) square) see 6(iii) and 6(iv). This explains why \(K = 3\) and \(K = 4\) do not yield triplets. \(K = 8, 9 , 18, 25\) ..... would yield triplets.

Anne D Wilson Rowntree, York

items.title: APL Standards Update
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 124

items.title: 14th ISO APL Working Group meeting30 April 90 - 4 May 90Waterloo, Ontario, Canada
items.text: report by Dave Ziemann

items.title: Background
items.text:
This is a report of the proceedings of the last ISO meeting for the standardisation of APL, which I attended on behalf of the BSI APL Standards Panel. This was made possible by funding provided by the British APL Association, without which British representation would not have been possible due the withdrawal of funding for ISO meetings by the DTI.

I took to the meeting five sets of BSI comments, and a report on symbol conflicts.

The meeting was relatively small, with eight representatives from Belgium, Canada, UK and the USA. A number of regular attendees, the French group in particular, were not able to come due to funding difficulties.

The main technical work of the meeting involved reviewing newly received documents, and working through the 1st Working Draft of the Extended APL Standard, page by page.

items.title: The New Document
items.text:
The changes to the existing standard are so pervasive that a supplement was not possible, and so a new document was created, based on IS 8485, the existing standard.

The 1st Working Draft was prepared by Eugene McDonnell, the editor, based on the existing standard and twenty-six accepted proposals from the following authors; Eugene McDonnell, Roland Pesch, Everett Allen, Bruce Frost, Greg Jaxon, Joseph de Kerf, Karl Soop, Brent Hawks and Phil Benkard.

The original standard document was produced by Alex Morrow using a version of IBM's Script language. This has now been converted to TeX by Eugene McDonnell with help from a TeX expert, thereby making the document more easily portable.

The topics in the document have not changed substantially since the Princeton meeting; they include, in no particular order: without, GCD and LCM, duplicate/commute operator, table, first-axis join, mixed arrays, use of overbar/underbar in names, replicate, character grade, unique, shared variable extensions, alpha and omega as names, ambivalent defined functions, event handling, transfer form, n-wise reduction, complex arithmetic, left and right, function rank operator, defined operators, )OPS, )NMS, component file cover functions and a revised Workspace Interchange Standard.

items.title: Changes made at Waterloo
items.text:
One significant change is in the area of name-class. Joseph de Kerf had earlier presented a review of name classifications in about forty dialects of APL. We had already agreed to use 4 for defined operators, and now Joseph was suggesting that 5 and 6 be standardised for system variables and system functions. In addition, ¯1 should be returned for arguments to ⎕NC which are not valid names, rather than returning 4 or signalling an unhelpful DOMAIN ERROR.

All three changes were passed, with no votes against.

Although the new document did contain grade-up and grade-down extended for character arrays, they had not been defined for numeric matrices and higher rank numeric arrays. A proposal to plug this hole was accepted.

A number of extensive changes were required in order to fit defined operators into the document. Defined operators follow the APL2 philosophy, which means that they are not "true" operators, but are more accurately described as defined derived functions. Defined operators and the new function rank operator will accept defined function operands in the Extended Standard, even though it is not currently possible to generalise this to the existing primitive operators in the language.

The Annex which describes the Workspace Interchange Standard has been upgraded to WSIS2. Although the Extended Standard itself does not address nested or boxed arrays, WSIS2 describes a convention for dealing with them. The Annex is still termed "Descriptive", which means that a conforming implementation is not required to provide the facility.

items.title: The Technical Report
items.text:
A "Technical Report" is an ISO designation applied to a standard which fails to meet the necessary standardisation criteria. WG3 is using this mechanism to collect all the proposals for which consensus could not be achieved.

The topics to be included in the Technical Report have not changed since the last meeting. They are: reduction, nested arrays and fills, enclose / disclose / box / open, formatting for nested arrays, pick, partition, depth, link, enlist, strand notation, match, generalised primitive operators, compose, dual, first, each, national language characters, function rank in standard metalanguage, function assignment.

The document will contain brief descriptions of why each facility had to be included in the Technical Report, and could not go into the new standard. The Technical Report will be useful for implementors who require guidance, and will provide a strong basis for future standardisation efforts.

items.title: A Warning
items.text:
Standards committees have a habit of changing their minds. A decision made at one meeting can be reversed at the next; this can happen because the meeting composition varies according to the country in which it is held. Also, people do occasionally change their minds.

For this reason none of the information given in this report should be considered final. Anyone who implements an APL on the basis of pre-publication material takes a big risk. Some implementors fell foul of this in the first APL standard, where an early draft required the )RESET system command, which was later changed to the more expressive )SIC (SI Clear).

Editor Alan Sykes

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
Welcome to another edition of Education Vector. And thank you to all readers who took the trouble to reply to my questionnaire. To date, I have had 41 replies. Of these 41, 16 wished to discontinue receiving 'EV', 4 were members of the British APL Association who did not want to receive EV separately, and 19 wished to continue.

Of the 19 who wished to continue, 6 wished to become full members of the British APL Association, and 13 were prepared to pay £2 towards the cost of producing EV.

25 replies assessed the quality of EV as follows: 11 'good', 13 'helpful' and 1 'unhelpful'. Here are some specific comments that were made.

  1. Please keep producing EV as it fills a gap - when you have teenagers interested in the language, it is not always easy to find material to maintain their interest.
  2. Fine from my sideline interest - I don't use APL as a rule but the journal does allow me to view the progress of APL in Education - fine.
  3. It gives some clever ideas, but more straightforward applications (rather than clever ones) would be appreciated.
  4. Haven't got the time. (See the correspondence section for an interesting discussion of this theme.)
  5. Written in a nice friendly style.
  6. Wide variety of subjects required e.g. graphics, data entry forms and validation, discussion on coding/naming standards, how to integrate APL, structured programming, access to non-APL systems (whew! you need VECTOR as well!)
  7. It's nice to see APL written in a way that is understandable by everyone (especially novices) rather than having code that takes 3 days to decipher!
  8. Present form is good and helpful. I would like to suggest a full application related to teaching. Suppose you wanted to teach a subject (e.g. analysis of variance, laws of optics, genetics ...) what are the successive steps to follow from the idea to the package that the students would use in the classroom?

It is too early to say yet what the British APL Association will decide to do with EV in the light of the results of the questionnaire. (Incidentally, if you feel that the results above are unrepresentative and you haven't sent your reply, it is not too late to do so.) However I am confident that it will do all it can to support EV in its endeavours.

Clearly you have given me much food for thought, and I hope that in my last year as editor of Education Vector, some of your many valuable suggestions may be implemented. Please help me to achieve this by sending your contributions for circulation to the many people, at home and abroad who do receive, read, and apparently appreciate reading Education Vector. In this context, please note a slight change in the editorial address.

items.title: Communications
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 19

Looking through my file of correspondence, I realise that there are many letters and notes from people in different countries that I have not acknowledged. So here is some attempt to remedy this.

items.title: From Nottingham, England
items.text: E.J.Sargeant replied to the questionnaire in the last issue, and commented on the problem of retrieving ASCII files into APL using IAPL. I must confess to not having time to investigate this, so may I ask readers who have used IAPL to read an ASCII file please to respond with a note to Education Vector discussing relevant details?

items.title: From Hereford, England
items.text:
Graham Bennett also wrote a reply to the questionnaire. Graham is a Maths and Computing teacher in a comprehensive school. He writes .. ‘I have been getting Education Vector for about two years but still have not bought an interpreter and am not using APL in the classroom. It may help you to know why.

In our school, and in others around, Computer Studies has recently been dropped both at A-level and GCSE because it is not perceived to be a very useful course for most students and it is felt better to devote time and resources on IT for all. This means that no one now studies programming in our school where previously we taught BASIC and Pascal. There is an emphasis on applications instead.

In Maths we are so busy struggling with the National Curriculum that no one has the time to look at how APL might be of use to us. ..... I do not know what you can do to make APL more known and used. The pressure all teachers are under makes it very hard for any but the most enthusiastic and dedicated to devote precious time to an unknown quantity like APL however good it may be.’

items.title: From La Habra, California
items.text: Zdenek Jizba sent a letter to Anthony Camacho describing in part the way IAPL is used in the fifth grade (eleven years of age) to stimulate discovery and exploration. I would like to extend an invitation to Zdenek (and anybody else) to present a typical (or atypical!) exploration in Education Vector:- volunteers please.

items.title: From Dunoon, Scotland
items.text:
Mr Bill McLean may be just such a person to send me an account of using APL in investigative working? Bill tells me of his work in Physics, optical illusions, graphs, and playing Noughts and Crosses. I particularly liked his notes on how to produce Morse Code on a BBC 128 machine using IAPL. The first step is to produce a sound table for a dot, dash, space and longer space.

      TABLE
1 ¯12 101   1
1 ¯12 101   3
1   0   0   1
1   0   0  16

As a result SOUND TABLE[1 3 2 3 2 3;] would produce .-- in sound.

Morse code corresponding to input from the keyboard can be achieved using SOUND TABLE['.- '⍳⍞] if the user presses dot, dash or space.

To translate actual letters, the alphabet is required:

  ALPH←' ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'

together with a 27 by 9 character matrix called CODE whose first row for example contains '. - '.

Then the function MORSE (written here in direct definition) will produce Morse Code corresponding to letters entered at the keyboard:

  MORSE: SOUND TABLE['.- '⍳CODE[ALPH⍳⍞;];]

items.title: From Sendai, Japan
items.text: Makato Kikkawa wrote to Anthony Camacho to report the successful porting of IAPL to NEC machines by Mr Tohru Kawahata. Makato also reports that the translation of ‘An Encyclopedia of APL’ and ‘APL in Social Studies’ is well under way.

items.title: From Kensington, New South Wales
items.text: Jim Douglas wrote to me concerning graph plotting using character graphics after reading an article I wrote in VECTOR on this subject. Jim is in the Department of Statistics at the University of New South Wales so we have lots of interests in common.

items.title: From Amherst, Massachusetts
items.text:
Howard Peelle sent has sent two communications to me from the University of Massachusetts at Amherst where he lectures in the School of Education. First he points out, quite correctly, that the answer to the puzzle on numbers and bases (Education Vector July 1989) given in Education Vector January 1990 was incorrect. There, I stated that the only bases from 10 to 100 that gave rise to two digit numbers being reversed when converted to base 16 were 10 13 16 19 22 25 28 37 46 55 64 73 and 82. These are in fact the bases which give rise to reversals when numbers are compared to base 10 and not base 16. So the correct answer, given by Howard is 10 11 13 16 21 26 31 46 61 76 and 91. Here is his solution:

      ∇ B←L IF C
[1]   B←C/L
      ∇


      ∇ N←SEEK B
[1]   N←B IF ∨/∧⌿((B,[.5]B)⊤N)=⊖((2,⍴B)⍴16)⊤N←⍳99
      ∇

      SEEK 9+⍳91
10 11 13 16 21 26 31 46 61 76 91

(N.B. this one-line solution gave me WS FULL error when I tried it with B←9+⍳91 - so you may have to use it repeatedly to get Howard’s result in toto.)

Howard also supplied a solution to the card collecting problem which he claims to be faster than Claude Henrion’s. It is:

      ∇ R←N CARDS C
[1]   R←1++/∨⌿∧\(⍳C)∘.≠?(N,11×C)⍴C
      ∇

Readers may also be interested in Howard’s ‘awfully inefficient’ recursive function which generates a probability tree in order to approximate the expected number of cards required:

      ∇ R←A CC W
[1]   R←W[1]
[2]   →0 IF (=/A)∨=/W
[3]   R←((÷A)× A CC W+1 0)+(1-÷/A)×(A+1 0)CC W +1 0
      ∇

but of course, the correct expected value for N cards is N×+/÷⍳N.

items.title: From New York
items.text:
Paul Mansour also wrote to me concerning the card-collecting problem. However, his solution makes use of the extra facilities that second-generation APL interpreters have to offer. If X is a vector and M is a matrix, then the inner product using ⌊ and ⍳, i.e. M⌊.⍳X returns a vector of the first occurrence of an element of X in each row of M. Hence it is possible to simulate the card-collecting problem as follows:

      ∇ R←N CARDS C;M
[1]   M←?(N,11×C)⍴C ⋄ R←M⌈.⍳⍳C
      ∇

As you can see, this has been quite a round-the world trip. Please continue to send comments and correspondence particularly including code that you feel other readers might appreciate.

items.title: Editorial: Reliability of APL Systems
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Jonathan Barman

Are APL systems less reliable than systems written in other languages? There was some dismay at the last Vector working group meeting when I indicated that this was the topic of my first editorial, because it looked as if I would be knocking APL. Whilst I think that many APL systems are unreliable, I do not think that this is necessarily caused by APL. A programmer's ability to produce reliable code seems to be much more important than the programming language being used.

APL is a superb language for quick, off the cuff, solutions which are to be used by the writer and no one else. This is the major factor which contributes to the impression that APL systems can be unreliable. However, the impression can be equally true of any language that is superb for quick, off the cuff, solutions - but which language falls into that category? Do you expect quality systems from Lotus 1-2-3? You can get both brilliant and rotten systems written in any language you care to name.

APL is also excellent for writing large quality systems. However, moving from a small quick solution to a quality system is much more time consuming than many people realise. Unless one has had the bitter experience of bugs coming back to haunt one, it is quite difficult to appreciate the care, time and trouble that goes into getting a system right. Time means money, and a quality system is going to be expensive.

Big companies producing major systems keep statistics of the number of errors encountered at the various stages of a product's life cycle: during development, during formal testing, and when the product is in the field. These statistics are compared with some measure of the size and complexity of the code, so that trends and performance can be assessed. I am not aware of any such statistics having been published in the APL world, so I have no hard facts to compare APL with other languages. Perhaps someone will write and tell us what is available?

In the absence of hard facts one is left with perceptions; it is easy to see how APL can get a bad name. For example, supposing there is a key business problem which requires a quick solution: someone creates a solution in APL, and it turns out to be really useful. The system is gradually extended until it is quite large - the users of the system are in the same department as the author, and when something goes wrong it can be fixed immediately. Eventually the author leaves the department and the users are left in the lurch when the system crashes, the DP department is then expected to get them out of the fix.

Exactly the same scenario happens with Lotus, Basic etc., however the problems are not normally quite as bad. The sheer power of APL allows really significant systems to be developed which would be quite difficult to achieve in other languages.

Another charge made against APL is that it is a hackers language. To some extent this is true, but I am not sure that it does or should matter. APL makes it easy to try out ideas. For some reason the trial and error approach is seen as a bad thing, unless you call it prototyping. There are many aspects to this problem; producing code without proper thought leads to stupid errors, time spent at the design stage is usually very worth while but can be overdone. How does one achieve a balance?

Searching for a solution to a problem is a very personal and idiosyncratic thing. Some like to mull over the problem in the bath, others like to bash away at the keyboard to try and generate ideas. Nobody can say which is best! APL allows, and even encourages, the latter approach; the risk is that it is possible to find an APL solution which works with the examples given, but which fails in the general case. Hackers find an apparent solution and barge in and change the system without a second thought. Suffice to say that they tend to produce poor quality systems, but hackers often produce the beginnings of useful systems which would never see the light of day in the traditional DP environment.

Prototyping is very helpful in crystalising user's ideas. It is quite extraordinarily difficult for a user to specify a large system in the complete detail needed by the programmer. Knocking up a sample system which can actually be used is where APL scores. However, there is usually an extreme reluctance to go back and rewrite any code that is working, so a prototype very often ends up as the final system, with only relatively minor changes. Sometimes the APL prototype system becomes to be viewed as the final system and when it creaks at the seams APL gets a bad name. In some ways the special prototyping languages score over APL in that they force a rewrite. At that stage all the proper things can be done, like writing the user manual first, and getting the initial design right.

In conclusion, I think that the reliability of APL systems is no worse than those written in other programming languages, but that sometimes APL gives the impression of being worse because of its power, speed and flexibility.

items.title: APL91: Conference Announcement
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 33

We are glad to bring readers an early and highly provisional draft of the plans for APL 91. Vector will circulate news of the plans as they develop, and will later include the call for papers and details of how you get on to the mailing list.

APL91THE NEXT 25 YEARS

[Provisional Theme]

The International Conference on APL 4 - 8 August 1991Stanford University, California, USA

items.title: Call for Participation
items.text: Sponsored by the Associating for Computing Machinery, Special Interest Group on APL ACM SIGAPL, in cooperation with Stanford University Computer Science Department. Organized by The APL Bay Area Users' Group

items.title: Conference Overview
items.text:
The APL91 conference will take place 4 - 8 August 1991, on the campus of Stanford University, in Palo Alto, California. University accommodation will be available as primary housing with local hotels for those who prefer them. University dining facilities will be available as well, so that subsistence expenses will be quite low. We hope that the low cost, location, and time of year will make it attractive and induce strong international attendance.

The main conference will run from 5 - 8 August, with paper presentations, general sessions, poster sessions, exhibitors, vendor forums, and social events for informal exchange with other attendees. Two tutorial tracks are planned for Sunday, 4 August.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:
The first tutorial will be aimed at APL experts, addressing the use of APL in one or more of these areas:

Artificial Intelligence/Expert Systems:

  • APL has been used in a variety of research and production applications such as medical diagnosis and factory automation.

Object Oriented Programming:

  • Recent papers have shown various ways that APL can be used for object oriented programming style.

Case:

  • APL can be considered a tool for Computer Aided Software Engineering with its proven capabilities and uses in generating code for ADA, assembler, FORTRAN, and C.

The second tutorial is being planned to introduce APL to a new generation of students, through informal sessions. Attendees at this tutorial would receive a package of free APLs to take away and continue learning and using. In addition to the regular conference registrants, students and teachers from local schools and colleges will be invited to participate.

items.title: Papers
items.text: 50 papers will be presented in two or three parallel tracks depending on topic, 45 minutes each.

items.title: Posters
items.text: Posters will have a special session set aside for them and will address short topics. We expect to include work in progress and informal presentations which may later be prepared for publication.

items.title: General Sessions
items.text: Opening and closing sessions will feature prominent speakers in fields of interest to APL users, but not necessarily in APL.

items.title: Vendor Forums
items.text: Vendors will be invited to present products and/or participate on panels.

items.title: Exhibitors
items.text: Exhibitors will display products and services in an exhibit area open during the entire conference and featured during an exhibit reception one evening.

items.title: Discussions
items.text: Rooms will be available for ad hoc scheduling on birds-of-a-feather topics.

items.title: Events (Provisional):
items.text: Welcome Reception: Sunday evening. Exhibit Reception: Monday evening. Exploratorium Evening: Tuesday evening. Bus to San Francisco for a buffet dinner at a science museum where the exhibits are intended to be used. Closing Picnic: Thursday lunch. To be held outdoors on campus.

items.title: Program Statement
items.text:
Important early developments in implementing Kenneth Iverson's mathematical notation as an executable computer language occurred at Stanford in the 60's: the first full working version of APL resulted from collaboration of Stanford graduate students with IBM. APL has now come into wide use in academic, scientific, and commercial endeavours around the world. 1991 will be the 25th anniversary of the availability of an APL system, marked by the date IBM's 1 CLEANSPACE was saved. 1991 will also be the 10th anniversary of the annual international APL conference last held in the San Francisco Bay Area. Now that free APLs make widespread growth of its educational use it seems appropriate that we meet at Stanford to consider the next generation of APL and APL users.

APL development has diverged and converged through many paths over the last 25 years, achieving an ISO standard and enhancement to second generation APLs, and now working on an ISO standard for extended APL. APL has pioneered in many areas, including interactive timesharing; functions acting on whole arrays; dynamic data arrays; array theory; use of vector, array, and multi-processor hardware; cooperative processing; spreadsheet like applications; independence of national languages; free distribution of interpreters; use for AI and expert systems; use by non-programmers and use in education from grade school to university. Computing technology is currently facing several large issues, such as proprietary versus open systems, hardware interchangeability versus new hardware architectures, programming versus CASE, and PCs versus workstations versus mainframes. The recent availability of free APLs for PCs and school computers has made APL freshly available to a wide audience in education. Thus, it seems an appropriate time to consider the role or directions for APL in "The Next 25 Years," the theme for this conference.

APL is subject to an interesting variety of paradoxes:

  • APL is often considered an isolated technology. Yet software developments continue to credit ideas from APL, rightly for example, work on the new standard for vectorized FORTRAN or Mathematica.
  • It has been said that APL cannot be taught; it can only be learned. It is not often taught as such in University. Yet first courses in computer science taught to undergraduates at Yale University with APL had students writing simulators and assemblers by the end of a term. And APL is being used in grade school in parts of Europe to teach mathematics.
  • APL's symbolic basis is widely criticized for requiring special handling. Yet this makes it largely independent of national languages (APL needs no translation). And graphical user interfaces based on icons for mnemonic association are becoming the norm on workstations.
  • Some people think the symbols inhibit portability. Yet the strict syntax of APL easily reveals implementation-specific features, and APL is the only language that can run on PCs, mainframes, and vector-hardware supercomputers without program changes.
  • APL is a powerful tool for non-programmer computer users, such as engineers, statisticians, and actuaries. Yet it still bothers professional programmers to subordinate detail in the expression of algorithms. It has been called too general a tool for production commercial applications. Yet computer science students now graduate thinking that C is appropriate for business applications of all kinds.
  • APL has sometimes been thought to use too many computing resources in return for its conceptual advantages. Yet in other advanced computing technologies such as artificial intelligence, this is expected. And the result of the conceptual advantages is often better algorithms for much larger performance gains.
  • APL permits unstructured programming. Yet its natural programming style is functional and it can utilize structure inherent in the data.
  • APL has proven productivity advantages over other languages, yet it is not uncommon for DP managers to discourage its use. Do we know why?

We hope to receive papers addressing these paradoxes and issues, concentrating on real experiences or work in progress toward new uses. These experiences, together with conference discussions among attendees, general sessions of speakers and panels, and participation of exhibitors, will focus on where and how APL should best be used in the next twenty five years. Is APL a notation, a language, an environment, a system, or a paradigm? Where should vendors and users take it among other technologies? In which areas is APL successful, and in which areas is it not? Now that it can be accessible to schools with limited computing resources, what should the next generation of students be encouraged to think about it?

items.title: Reviews Section
items.text:
introduction by Adrian Smith

Both reviews in this VECTOR are related to the user-interface. Dyalog APL has been greatly enhanced by the inclusion of a ‘modern’ approach to the APL session. This at long last brings APL into line with the vast majority of PC language products (from Quick-C to Turbo Prolog) and will I hope set the tone for all the major PC APL systems in the future.

Powertools has long been an option for those who need to wring the last ounce of power from their PC APL systems. You can now use their CUA routines to develop APL systems that look just like Windows, OS/2, and anything else that supports the CUA/Graphics standards.

Finally, we have a summary of a recent publication ‘APL with a Mathematical Accent’, and (continuing the user interface theme) we have received a review copy of ‘The Computer Display Designers Handbook’ by Eric Wagner. This will be reviewed in Vector 7.2.

items.title: Book Announcement: APL with a Mathematical Accent
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 57

notes by Norman Thomson

APL with a Mathematical Accent Clifford A. Reiter and William R. Jones, Lafayette Collage

Publ. Brooks/Cole Publ Co., Pacific Grove, CA, USA 200 pp paperback UK price approx £35 (Three-five ... no misprint!)

Provided that the reader is happy to stay within the bounds of APL1, this text lives up to all its claims. The format is paper covers with spiral binding, making for convenient use alongside a terminal. The page count of 200 belies the extent of the material contained: the publishers have managed to cram every page with information yet without any general feeling of clutter, and they use a heavy APL font which blends very pleasantly with the main text.

The audience is teachers who want to merge APL instruction with teaching maths, and this is the first text I have come across which addresses this objevtive. The maths reaches quite high levels, e.g. there are functions for eigenvector calculations, Rayleigh Quotionts, Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization, Hamming Codes, and adaptive integration - to mention just a few of the many topics covered.

This need not however deter those of lesser mathemetical accomplishments, to whom the bulk of the material is addressed. there are a generous number of exercises with answers, and the text is fully adequate for learning APL by self-study on the part of any mathematically motivated student. In short this is a book which deserves the notice of any maths teachers who seek to brighten the lives of their students with the gentle light of APL.
