items.title: A Personal View on APL 90
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 80

by Ray Cannon

A week to the day after the end of APL 90, I received my copy of APL Quote Quad, volume 20, number 2, December 1989, in which an invitation to attend APL 90 was included! Luckily, the Danish end of the Conference was better organised, as I received the conference proceedings (APL Quote Quad volume 20 number 4) in July, 2 weeks BEFORE the conference started!

Eric Friis and Stanley Jordan

This was the fourth International Conference on APL I have attended, and the one I have enjoyed the most. The standard of the papers was good, the organization excellent, the food superb, the location wonderful, and probably the best lager in the world!

The main difficulty I have with all such conferences is deciding which of the venues to attend. (APL90 as is customary, had 3 streams.) So, when I talk about the papers I found outstanding, at best I have missed two thirds of the conference. Since the theme of this conference was "For the Future" I decided to try to attend those talks about compilers, parallel computers, and APL linking to other languages with a secondary theme of windows, mice and CUA. I'll bypass the vendors' forums, the time allotted to them was a bit too short, and I felt that the ones I attended were not as good as the BAA's forum held earlier this year.

APL90 was exceptional for another reason. For the first time, delegates from the USSR attended an International APL conference. They gave two papers but I missed the first (it conflicted with one on my pet interest, parallel computers). However I managed to squeeze into the second "The Family of Soviet APL Systems" given by Andrew Kondrashev. This talk was a "sell out", some people were even listening from outside! I for one found it fascinating, for instance, (I hope I noted it down correctly), 37,000 copies of a Russian translation of "APL an Interactive Approach" by Gilman and Rose have been printed in the USSR.

items.title: Reports on the Presentations
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 83

items.title: The People, the Information and the CorporationMads Øvlisen of Novo Nordisk A/S
items.text:
reported by Sylvia Camacho

Mads' talk was professional, well structured and well timed with good slide illustrations. The interest for me was the insight he gave into a Company with a high research and development commitment (25% of employees). This R&D serviced the 44% of employees engaged in production and 21% engaged in marketing the products. The traditional business is a restricted range of pharmaceuticals, particularly insulin. Most R&D is concerned with biotechnology and disease control and other aspects of environmental care. The Company sees its edge over its competitors to be matching its products to the exact requirements of customers. For instance the development of insulin delivery hypodermics convenient for patient use.

There is some tension within Marketing because the direct customers are doctors which means that contact with the actual users, the patients, is mediated by the doctors who do not necessarily have the same priorities. One possible use of Information Technology is therefore to obtain feedback from patients.

Øvlisen made the point that management concern for the interests of the shareholders does not offer the Company a plan of action. This is an obviously true but perhaps not sufficiently realized part of free enterprise ideology. Øvlisen made two other points; that employees usually under-perform and that Companies become conservative because of management anxiety. His remedy for some of these problems is increased dispersion of information among employees and encouragement of their individual differences. This he sees as incompatible with a tight central control of computer systems by DP management.

Øvlisen gave as the major uses of IT within his Company:

  1. Mailbox facilities
  2. Medical Representative System
  3. R&D including molecular modelling
  4. IFCA

The mailbox was prominent among his interests because of the flexible and fast exchange of information that it provided to for a geographically widely dispersed sales force. The Sales Representative System he hopes to base on lap top computers to give management feedback from the grass roots. He made the point that there is no right way to manage R&D. The most that can be done is to match the risks and benefits over a portfolio of research projects and that this has to be directed from the top of the management hierarchy.

Mads' final comment was that the IFCA project which has a concept of adding information to products based on patient needs is a good but costly study by outside consultants and has the difficulty that the technical language used is not familiar to the management. This he said was his own problem and he feels that IT requires too much learning and encourages excessive emphasis on perfection whereas managers need to use less than perfect data. The problem is how to get a dialogue going between IT professionals and management so that if they are offered a better mousetrap they are able to decide whether they need to catch a mouse.

items.title: APL\? (or J) by Roger Hui and Ken Iverson
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

Since this paper was submitted APL\? has been named 'J'. Apparently even Ken Iverson does not know the reason why that particular name was chosen, although he must have assented to the name. Roger Hui chose it and keeps his reasons secret.

Ken Iverson told us that J is a dialect of APL, but it does not offer compatibility with any other dialect. The features it contains have been chosen without regard to any predecessor. This is interesting; it allows us to see what Ken Iverson and his collaborators like and dislike about their previous APLs.

J does away with the special APL symbols; all tokens in J are ASCII symbols or combinations of them. (This caused some dismay among the Scandinavians, who use the ASCII codes for the less used symbols for their special Scandinavian letters.) J preserves some things from APL: it has no reserved word, does not need spaces to punctuate its tokens, the tokens have mnemonic value but are not linked to any natural language, so it is truly international, but its tokens may be one symbol or two, whereas APL tokens are single. J simplifies and is more general than APL. Whereas APL has two 'parts of speech' the function (verb) and the operator (adverb), J has three (verb, adverb and conjunction) and whereas in ISO APL there are limitations which prevent adverbs modifying user-defined verbs, or even the existence of user-defined adverbs, in J there are no such restrictions. User defined conjuctions can join user-defined verbs as modified with user-defined adverbs.

In a brief review of the history of APL development he mentioned that Gene McDonnell had spoken about the 'sociotechnical' origins of APL at the tenth anniversary conference which was also in Copenhagen, and that APL\360 had been able to support 24 users when other time sharing systems had difficulty with three or four or five users. Many great improvements had been made over the years: Sharp had introduced: fast sum-over-booleans, fast indexing, membership, reverse, transpose, general arrays, complex arithmetic, fuzzy residue, dyadic grade, replicate. In 1982 Rationalised APL was circulated as an IPSA internal paper. In 1986 A Dictionary of APL was published and now in 1990 J.

The trends of Dictionary APL are:

  1. Simplification of grammar and syntax
  2. Operators significantly beyond APL\360
  3. A uniform method for associating identifier with object
  4. A strong emphasis on function rank, leading axes, major cells
  5. The removal of dependence on such parameters as index origin
  6. Exclude anything not functionalstrandsbracket semicolon indexingindexed assignmentbracket axis
  7. A preference for functional rather than shape identities

Roger Hui told us something about the implementations of J so far. It is available on the AT&T 3B1, the Macintosh, the PC, the R6000, the MIPS R3000, the NeXt and a Philips machine. The implementations are written in C; the parser is a single page of code and all objects are held in a single C form, which contains the type, the reference count, the number of atoms, the rank, the shape and each atom. Most of the C functions accept arguments in this structure and return such results and, of course, all verbs, adverbs and conjunctions are held in this form as well as the nouns and pronouns.

J is to be freeware and the registration charge which brings a manual is to be $24. Copies of the PC implementation (which is not quite complete) were issued through the software library. The address of Iverson Software Inc. is in the product guide.

items.title: Parallel Computing with APL
items.text:
reported by Ray Cannon

I have an interest in Transputers, so I attended the paper "An APL-Simulator of Non-Von Neumann Computer Architectures" written by A. Geyer-Schulz, Alfred Taudes and J. Mitlohner (who gave the talk). This paper showed how APL could simulate various parallel computer architectures. Unfortunately (for me at least) the paper did not describe transputer array simulation, but the simulation of a theoretical model of a PRAM-machine described by Parberry (Parallel Complexity Theory, New York, John Wiley & Sons, 1987). That apart, I found the paper well presented and most stimulating.

Parallel APLers (in front of the Tycho Brahe Planetarium)Jonathan Martin, Panagiotis Pantziarka, David Toop & Maurice Jordan

The next paper was "Automatic Parallelization of APL-style Programs" written and given by Wai-Mee Ching. (Some of you may remember Ching from Manchester where he gave a paper on an APL/370 compiler.) This paper talked about extending the compiler so that it produces 370 machine code to run applications in parallel mode on IBM 3090 multi-processors.

I talked to Ching about his work afterwards. He has written two compilers, one producing 370 machine code and the other generating C output. Both compilers by the way are written in APL and compile IBM VS APL!

Ching said that "Parallel computing is only interesting if it is transparent to the programmer". Some other gems from his talk I noted down include: "the compiler can find the parallelism in existing programs"; "data is parallel...use nodes not do-loops"; "to efficiently program on a parallel machine, write good sequential APL code".

The next paper in this vein was given by Robert Bernecky, "ACORN, APL to C on Real Numbers". This paper described how the authors wrote an APL to C compiler, in Sharp APL/PC, and had a prototype working within a week! The resulting C code was compared against hand-coded Fortran and benchmarked on a Cray super-computer. The final results show that APL should be able to be compiled to C to run at least as fast as hand-coded Fortran, but there is still a long way to go before we get there.

After giving his paper, Bernecky then chaired a session with an invited speaker Alan Huang, of AT&T-Bell Laboratories on "Massively Parallel Computing". This talk was all about "light computers", "micro-lasers" and "life after electronics". The units Huang is creating are so fast that standard electronic equipment cannot be used to measure their speed, and so small that his laboratory has equalled the world production of lasers, by producing micro-lasers by the thousand on single silicon wafers.

They can now produce "designer crystals" where each atomic layer can be laid down individually. However, Huang said that his physicists only understood HP Basic, his computer scientists Lisp but his machines required A Parallel Language.

items.title: High Quality User Interfaces and fast Data Filing using a PCby Jonny Österman
items.text:
reported by Ray Cannon

Jonny Österman of A-System gave a very good talk on "High Quality User Interfaces and fast Data Filing using a PC". This he backed up with a demonstration, using some of the tools from his APL toolbox (commercially available as "ABOX").

Talking to Jonny on the A-System stand, I discovered that we have both been working on very similar airline charter costing systems for different airlines, he for SAS and myself for BA. These are the only two charter costing systems either of us had come across, and both were written quite independently in APL. Jonny was using a cut down version of his to demonstrate his ABOX utilities, and I was very impressed.

items.title: Compiled Language Interface in APL*PLUS II by James Wheeler
items.text:
reported by Ray Cannon

In his talk, James Wheeler described how, under DOS, (which does NOT have dynamic linking) STSC's APL is able to call non-APL programs. With some background knowledge of 80386 assembler, it all made good sense, and was very revealing.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

The tutorials given by Eugene McDonnell and Philip Benkard were, for me, the highlight of the conference. Both were excellent presentations; both gave new insights into the differences between the main streams of enhanced versions of APL; both contained much too much material for even the best reporter to capture. I hope that the following brief impressions will be superseded by complete accounts prepared with the help of the presenters.

items.title: Tutorial in Dictionary APL by Eugene McDonnell
items.text:
Gene pitched this tutorial to suit people who have some knowledge of Dictionary APL, boxed (and nested) arrays and the ISO standard. It was not a programming lesson but a review of fundamentals, concentrating on identities, symmetries and analogies.

Dick Bowman, John Searle, Jonathan Martin, Maurice Jordan, & Lee Dickey relaxing in the Falkoner Centre

APL was contrasted with FBAPP (FORTRAN BASIC Algol Pascal PL/1) languages: in APL arrays are primitive objects whereas in the others generally a scalar is the primitive object. It is the way a language is parsed that determines its consistency. Gene explained a parsing table, against which expressions were compared from right to left 'until the binding drops' - that is until a match between the rightmost part of the line being parsed and a complete row of the table is found. Finding a match establishes that the part of the line being matched can be executed and the result substituted for the matched phrase before further parsing need be done. Incidentally it was pointed out how valuable it is that in APL it is not necessary to separate tokens by blanks. An analysis of the forms of expressions showed where data, function and operator strands would be.

Gene offered some snappy definitions of syntax and semantics.

Syntax is what goes with what. Syntax is what the user really learns. Syntax is context dependent and of short scope. Semantics is where the action is.

Dictionary BOX (<) was compared with APL2 ENCLOSE (⊂). Everyone knows the difference for shallow scalars, but how many of us can state the differences for other arrays? For example:

      3+<1 5
DOMAIN ERROR
      3+⊂1 5
4 8

So Gene suggested that < is semantics and ⊂ is structure.

items.title: Tutorial in APL2 by J. P. Benkard
items.text:
J. Philip Benkard

Phil Benkard's tutorial was given at a faster pace. By using two overhead projectors a great deal could be shown and compared. Phil produced a fascinating series of insights based on analysis of the simple function to remove duplicates: ((⍵⍳⍵)=⍳⍴⍵)/⍵.

I regret that I was unable both to follow and write down what Phil said and showed us; my notes contain enough pepper to cook a cauldron of soup, but they are too incoherent to offer to Vector. We have asked Phil if we can publish the full tutorial.

items.title: Education Stream: Wednesday Morning
items.text: reported by Anthony Camacho

items.title: APL Trivia by Ed CherlinReading to Write by Ray PolivkaAPLegance by Norman Thomson
items.text:
These three sessions formed the Education Stream. They were a delight to attend. Three expert presenters provided an object lesson in exposition. Your reporter was also the chairman, but his lack of notes is not serious since the presentations did not wander far from the papers in the proceedings.

Ed showed how APL's inner consistency can be revealed in apparently trivial ways. He produced a nice paradox: beginning with a definition of trivial which seemed to leave little scope for anything of importance to creep in, he showed how trivial functions and operators can be valuable both for what they do and for the improved clarity of the code in which they are properly used. Surely what is valuable is important.

Ray suggested that as in natural languages one does not normally write anything until one has progressed quite a long way towards learning to read, APL could be taught by getting the pupil to read code before writing it. He gave some lovely examples, many of which are in the appendix to his paper.

Norman highlighted a common problem of newcomers to APL2 - namely that they find they have enclosed their variables without realising it. His subtitle was 'The Art of Staying within One's Depth'. He gave many useful prescriptions and hints of great value in reaching a more intuitive understanding of APL2 facilities.

This was the education stream, yet there were several questioners who objected to some of the elegant and brief expressions shown on the grounds that they were not the fastest to execute. It was almost as if the only kind of education with APL they could imagine was teaching professional programmers how to earn their living with APL. The APL world ought to want APL to be used in the teaching of other subjects, where its simplicity, consistency and elegance are such a powerful advantage. Surely it is unreasonable to expect any implementation to be most efficient in its use of the machine on the briefest and most elegant expressions. Even if it is not unreasonable surely it is irrelevant. Nowadays machines are very cheap by comparison with the cost of the programmers' time; when the purpose is education the efficiency of the code really can almost be ignored. While so many APLers have their sense of values wrong about this, how are we to persuade the rest of the world?

items.title: Looking Beyond APL2 and NIALInvited Speaker: Trenchard More Jr.
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

This session was a tour de force on Array theory. It started simply by using the hands and feet as examples of hierarchy and nesting. Considerations of consistency and how to handle the degenerative cases of empty arguments according to their shapes and nestedness were dealt with in a breathtaking sequence of slides. Here are two of them. We hope to be able to persuade the author to publish an article about this in Vector.

Two of Trenchard More's slides

items.title: The K. E. Iverson Award for Outstanding Achievement
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

SigAPL announced that the Outstanding Achievement award has been renamed 'The K. E. Iverson Award for Outstanding Achievement' and that the first renamed award goes to Ray Polivka.

Jon McGrew did the presentation and had prepared a splendid testimonial to Ray's work over the years. There were photographs of Ray with his classes, of him teaching, of the books he had written or collaborated in and even of him asleep in an armchair. (Ray later told us that Jon had insisted on Ray's company when he went to buy himself a suit and while he had it fitted Ray, tired after the day's work, went to sleep in an armchair in the shop waiting for him.) Jon's account of Ray's career was fascinating and beautifully illustrated. Ray's work in teaching and writing about APL must be well known to every APLer and the audience obviously was both delighted by the award and felt it to be well deserved.

And the award came as a complete surprise to Ray - he had not suspected anything when he was photographed teaching because it just so happened that no-one else was teaching when the photographer needed some urgent photos of IBM education - neither he nor Jo were even suspicious at the stratagems the organisers used to make sure that they would be present at the session when the award was announced. It was a heart-warming occasion.

items.title: ACM SigAPL report: Lynne Shaw
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

Lynne was pressed for time and the report this year was shorter than, for example, at New York.

Quote-quad: Prof L. J. Dickey has resigned and the new editors of Quote-quad are Adam Kertesz and Jon McGrew. The March issue of Quote-quad and the proceedings will be sent to members soon.

Membership: The membership trend is UP at the latest membership roster as of mid-June.

Charles Schulz with the APL91 Palm Tree

Conferences: APL 91 is to be at Stanford. Charles Schulz made some announcements about it. The aim is to make attendance as easy as possible for people paying their own way or whose employers have little to spend on conferences. There will be cheap university accommodation as well as luxurious hotels for those who want them. It is hoped to encourage far more educators to attend without reducing the conference's value to the professional APL programmer. The APL 91 committee are eager to receive people's suggestions and ideas. They are making great efforts to circulate the call for participation as widely as possible.

APL 92 is not yet allocated. One suggestion is to hold it in Leningrad.

A new award: SigAPL intend to establish a new award for extending awareness of APL. Anyone who wants to suggest a recipient should contact SigAPL for details.

items.title: 1990 Outstanding Achievement Award
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 9

from David Eastwood

items.title: Background
items.text: Each year the British APL Association makes an award for what is, in the committee's estimation, an Outstanding Achievement within the APL community. The terms which govern the award are fairly loose and the Committee are looking for achievements which assist the overall objectives of the BAPLA - be they technical achievements in APL; APL interpreter design; services to the APL community; favourable publicity for APL and so on. The previous Awards have been to John Scholes for his work on the Dyalog APL interpreter and to British Airways for their in-house APL MIS systems.

items.title: The 1990 Award
items.text:
This year, the Awards subcommittee was faced with the widest choice that has been presented to them in the three years since the award was instituted. After much consideration, and a number of visits to some of the contenders, the subcommittee decided unanimously to make the award to Metapraxis for the Resolve package.

Metapraxis, based in Kingston Surrey, was founded in 1984 to supply Executive Information Systems and supporting consultancy services.

In its first 6 years of existence, Metapraxis has been highly successful - with over a hundred major corporate and governmental clients around the world. A subsidiary company was established in the USA in 1988.

A major element of Metapraxis' success has been the Resolve software package. Resolve is one of the leading Executive Information Systems currently commercially available and has been widely acclaimed in numerous review articles in the computer and general press. In 1989 Resolve won a British Design Award.

Resolve is designed for operation on PCs and is written in APL*PLUS/PC.

The Outstanding Achievement Award subcommittee felt that Resolve merited the 1990 award on the following grounds:

  1. Technical excellence of the product.
  2. Public recognition in the shape of the 1989 Design Award.
  3. Demonstration of the use of APL in the commercial packaged software environment.

Most APL programmers and users are well aware of the power of APL, but as a community APLers are rather inward looking. Opportunities to show that, given the right application, APL can hold its own with other programming languages are rarely taken. The Award subcommittee were firstly impressed with the quality of the work that Resolve embodies, but more importantly were pleased to note the Resolve had demonstrably met a real need in the market and had proved its worth against a number of non-APL rivals.

items.title: APL90 Reflections
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 95

by John Searle

The conference was very well organized and APLers are definitely improving in their standard of presentation and use of high-tech audio visual aids. Nearly all of the authors spoke to or about their papers rather than just summarised them, and thus made actual attendance at the conference worthwhile. The organisers are to be congratulated in getting the proceedings out in advance.

items.title: Conference Highlights
items.text: First ever delegates from Moscow and Leningrad. First time the proceedings were distributed to early registrants in advance. Premiere of Iverson's new "J" notation, with free software. Public showing of Dyalog APL/X for HP and RS/6000, and new DOS version 6.1. Public showing of IBM's APL2 for RS/6000 and MicroAPL's APL.68000 level II. Stanley Jordan's APL music and impromptu guitar performance.

items.title: Conference Lowlights
items.text: STSC's reluctance to display any experimental APL version under X windows. Rainstorm timed to coincide with conclusion of fireworks in Tivoli gardens. The price of beer in Copenhagen (although the Swedes come over to drink it).

items.title: Exhibition Wars
items.text: There was healthy competition in the exhibition, and Dyadic systems were clear winners with their readiness to show the pre-release Dyalog APL/X and upcoming new version 6.1 of the DOS product. STSC gave a paper about APL under X but did not show any software. They appear to be hamstrung by the size of their installed user base and are very careful about new features. They have no immediate plans to call APL from C (they say no one has asked for it), but they hope to release a port of APL*PLUS II to Unix by the end of 1990.

items.title: Future of APL
items.text:
As always, there was much discussion about what sort of future, if any, APL has in conventional data processing. I usually leave a conference feeling much more optimistic than at the start, having seen what can be done, and this conference was no exception. Although conference numbers were down to about 300, the depth and variety of APL applications were as broad as ever. APL continues to be a competitive option for programming language choice.

Optimistic points:

  • in Europe, APL continues to be one of the few environments which support different national languages yet provide international compatibility.
  • Jim ("APL2") Brown of IBM has almost convinced the US Dept of Defense that APL2 is the best basis for a common prototyping language for DARPA (the defense advanced research projects agency). If this comes off it will be big.
  • APL is used in the forefront of technical developments in medicine, music and space science, as well as computer processor research and language theory.

Pessimistic points:

  • Reuters have "stabilised" Sharp APL so that there will be no new language developments, and support for the mainframe product could be reduced. There were a lot of ex-Sharp people at the conference looking for work.
  • IBM have not included APL2 in the SAA because there is no AS/400 version. This means that a lot of "true-blue" IBM sites will not consider APL.
  • APL has been around for so long that it has no appeal for managers or users who insist that their systems be leading edge.

items.title: Whither APL Conferences?
items.text:
The family of APL languages has reached quite a mature stage. The conferences now include developments in ISO APL, APL2, A, J, NIAL and even Mathematica. Through the conferences, attendees learn of the latest developments in many related fields, such as OOPS, neural networks, parallel processing, and other buzzwords, mainly because someone can explain them or prototype them very clearly using an APL model or notation. Despite too much navel-gazing, the conferences serve a good purpose. Long may they continue.

The next conference is planned for Stanford University, Palo Alto CA, in August 1991. The one after that may possibly be in Leningrad, June 1992 or 1993, so start saving your roubles for some white nights.

See you in Palo Alto!

items.title: Publicity Officer’s Report
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 10

from Jonathan Martin

APL has not been renowned over the years for attracting a great deal of publicity - and the small amount it does get is seldom good.

Publicity of the BAPLA comes in two forms - publicity of what the committee is doing to its members and publicity to the outside world.

The first is what you as a member (assuming you are one??) see as the fruits of your membership fee. Vector is the most obvious and goes out to all members. The notice of meetings, however, is just as important (for those people who live in Britain) as they have a great bearing on the numbers who turn up on a Friday afternoon in London. If we don’t give people enough notice, they may already have something booked; if we don’t ‘sell’ the meeting well enough, they may decide they can’t afford the time; if we do get these and other things right, the turnout is good and everybody is happy.

The second is much harder though. Publicity to the outside world is mainly through the computer press and here we are not starting from a good base. They have to sell papers and are generally only interested if we have some up-to-the-minute news. Are we CUA-compliant for instance? Do we run under OS/2 or Windows-3? Can we do a bit of co-operative processing here and there? How do we do Object Orientation in APL (APL++?). Generally the answer to all these questions is either we don’t or we can’t.

Consequently we have to rely on more major events like the Outstanding Achievement Award and the sponsoring of the APL Statistics Library, events that aren’t run of the mill and may attract the attention of even the most hardened press hack.

So I don’t think you are going to see APL emblazoned on the front pages of the weekly magazines in the immediate future, but with some effort and a bit of luck you may come across the odd snatch here and there.

items.title: Thoughts on APL 1994
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 11

from David Eastwood (Nov 1990)

The British APL Association is teetering on the verge of putting in a bid to host APL94. I would like to put forward some suggestions regarding such as event and the way in which we plan for it.

There are a number of areas where I feel that previous APL conferences could be improved upon, speaking as someone who is both an APL vendor, APL programmer and (still) an APL enthusiast.

  1. Committee. The decision has already, and quite rightly, been made that the conference committee should exist independently of the BAA Committee as it will have to be in existence for some years. I am however disturbed by the possibility that the Committee will be made up of the usual ‘hard core’ of APL activists, with the choice of members being, at best, made casually in a BAA Committee meeting. I propose that the BAA membership be canvassed for volunteers. We could even elect the committee!

  2. Conference audience. As a precursor to discussing themes and organisation for the conference, I wonder whether we should address the topic of who we would want to attend. I would hazard a guess that the numbers of attendees at APL conferences is gradually declining and that those who do attend are drawn from a pool of long term APLers who are regular attenders at such events.

If we wish to increase the numbers of attendees and to attract new faces we should bear two points in mind. Firstly the cost of the event and secondly the inducement to bring partners and families. Delegates to an APL conference will either be seeking sponsorship by their employer or will be using a portion of the annual leave to attend. In either case the conference should be seen as offering ‘value for money’ - it should offer an attractive mix of informative and educational material as well as a varied support program. Note that I do not count singing appalling songs about APL as a support program.

  1. Conference theme. It goes without saying that a strong theme for the conference should be selected. (I would suggest the controversial one of ‘APL as A Programming Language’ for those of us who couldn’t care less about yet more language extensions.) What I would ask, however, is that the conference actually remembers that it does have a theme and arranges that papers (see below) and the conference itself stick to the theme. The conference theme is there to attract contributions and also to set the overall tone of the event.

  2. Papers. These are the backbone of any conference, and I would hope that some effort be made to improve matters here. There seems to be little evidence that papers are chosen to match a theme, and in line with the comment above, why do we need so many? I think that the desire to have three parallel sessions is excessive. I would also wish to see two classes of paper strictly forbidden:

- Overt attempts to read from sales literature - Papers with no effective content

Both these categories have been in evidence at previous APL conferences. In the second category, I place papers whose sole apparent content was simple minded discussions of topics covered in APL reference manuals.

I have a feeling that program committees set out an empty timetable containing a number of parallel sessions and then attempt to fill them with the submitted papers rather than arranging as many sessions as there are papers worth presenting.

  1. Education Day. At APL86 and APL89 (I missed 88 and 90) the inevitable education day was an embarrassing waste of time. No one other than the usual coterie of enthusiasts turned up. Let’s abandon this part of the conference.

  2. Home users. At the same time I would like to speak on behalf of those neglected home users who buy I-APL, APL.68000 or Pocket APL. Some might spend several times the price of their APL (and indeed of their computer!) to attend, but I suggest that many wouldn’t. Could we make some effort to target some event or events to these users?

  3. Vendor forums. A vendor forum seems to be an excuse to extract yet more money from APL vendors. Invariably the conference organisers make large charges but make no effort to attract an audience. The more astute vendors make their presentations as papers anyway. If this sort of nonsense is to be repeated, make it a free event.

  4. Sponsors. Whilst I believe that Rowntrees have shown interest in sponsoring part of APL94, which is extremely good news, I would sincerely hope that some effort is to be made to canvass other commercial sponsors. I actually believe that a good level of commercial sponsorship will offset the bad impression that is always given by the APL ‘nutters’ who tend to dominate these events.

items.title: Hackers Corner: Check that Disk!
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 125

by Adrian Smith

One of the penalties of running your APL systems across a network is that you never quite know what is happening at the other end of the wire. I could be sitting quite happily in my planning system, having loaded up my data hours ago ... meanwhile someone has pulled a plug on the Vax that I fondly imagine holds my ‘P:’ drive! If I don’t spot the situation until APL reports ‘DRIVE NOT READY ERROR’, I need to do some fancy error recovery to give the user the chance to save things temporarily on the PC hard disk.

A much better way is to ask DOS to check out the disk first, and thus to avoid having to back out of my save routine halfway through:

    ∇ R←CHECK∆DRIVE DRV;⎕ELX
[1]      ⍝ Use INT 33H to verify drive status ...
[2]      ⍝  Returns R[1]←¯1 or 65535 for a dead disk
[3]      ⍝     else R[1]←bytes per allocation unit
[4]      ⍝     (e.g. 512 for floppy, 2048 for typical HD)
[5]      ⍝
[6]      ⍝  Other values of interest are: [2]=disk size
[7]      ⍝                                [3]=bytes used
[8]      ⍝                                [4]=bytes free
[9]      ⍝
[10]      DRV←'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'⍳''⍴DRV
[11]      ⎕ELX←'R←4↑¯1 ⋄ →0'
[12]      R←(4↑ 13824 0 0 ,DRV)⎕INT 33 ⋄ →(R[1]∊ ¯1 65535)↑Err
[13]      R←(×/R[1 3]),(×/R[1 3 4]),(×/R[1 3],-/R[4 2]),×/3↑R ⋄ →0
[14] Err:R←4↑¯1
    ∇

      CHECK∆DRIVE 'C'
2048 42366976 34584576 7782400

      CHECK∆DRIVE 'E'
¯1 0 0 0

The other returned information could be quite useful too ... for example to check that there is sufficient space on a floppy to hold the file you are about to save. Note also the allocation size ... it is quite pointless to set the APL*PLUS/PC file blocking to less than this; you are simply wasting time and saving no space at all. Many network drives allocate in units as high as 16K, so all those tiny little files are really taking 16K bytes at a time off someone’s Vax! Be warned!!

items.title: Workspace search function
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 126

From: Peter Branson, 7th Nov 1990

A couple of final remarks, please, on David Piper’s reply in Vector 7.2.133 to my letter of Vector 6.4.95.

He is partly right about the reason the original workspace search function ran so slowly; it was full of ‘each pepper’, but that was not the only reason. The author of the original had tried to please everybody by looking for all occurrences of the string in everything. By restricting this to functions and operators, and looking for only the first occurrence on each line, a further big saving was made. I find that this suits my needs 99 per cent of the time, and I rarely need to use a fuller version.

My second point takes us back again to the pornography, or otherwise, of dynamic function fixing, and I certainly can’t agree with his use of the word ‘ridiculous’ here. However, I will agree that this technique can only safely be used on very rare occasions, and I contend that mine was one of these. A classic case of the wrong way of doing this occurs in IBM’s ADRS2 code (particularly ADRS2BG) where, in some places, functions are redefined dynamically to ‘fix’ otherwise undetectable bugs!!! (Have you ever tried maintaining that code?)

David’s suggested alternatives are fine in their way, but don’t suit me. I don’t use indirect copy for utilities because I do not want all the utilities cluttering every workspace I am working on; I have spent too much time in the past creating different lists and then forgetting to maintain them.

As regard packaging, I think this is the best way in the long term, especially for central maintenance, and we will probably move this way when (if?) we get some time to clean our act up a bit.

In the meantime I shall continue doing it my way, and I see that I am not the only one. Have a look at Tibor Horvath’s CYCLE function on page 2 of APLBUG Newsletter, June 1990.

items.title: Packaged Workspaces in APL2/370
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 127

From: Nicholas Small, 3rd December 1990

At the recent meeting at which packaged workspaces were discussed, one question (or, rather, a pair of questions) that was given only fleeting consideration was: are there objects that cannot or should not be packaged?

These questions cannot be answered without consideration of how packaging is to be done - if whole applications are packaged into single workspaces then the answer to both questions is, trivially, “no”. If, however, utility functions are to be packaged separately, into a number of workspaces, then the answer is not so obvious.

To ensure that it is possible to package utilities, one must organize one’s packaged workspaces so that no function which requires the use of EXP when invoked from a namescope different from its own is called from its own namescope (when the use of EXP could result in an incorrect reference). The reason for this restriction is that, so far as I am aware, there is no way in APL2 to determine from within a function the name of a calling function and hence whether or not the calling function is in the current name scope (not that this would be desirable, because of the complexity it would introduce); the alternative of using QNS and passing the identity of the calling name scope to the utility is hardly to be countenanced, as this would entail changes to the calling function.

Turning now to the desirability of packaging an object, I feel that any feature that requires more than a simple application of EXP should militate against packaging, because simplicity should be the order of the day. Consider, for example, trying to package the function ISPEXEC, which is supplied by IBM to provide access to ISPF Dialog Manager services (using AP317). Requests are passed as character strings, so calls to ISPEXEC to browse or edit a file are not a problem, but attempts to use VPUT or VGET, to transfer variables to or from the ISPF variable pools are a different matter - AP317 will expect to find variables in the namescope of ISPEXEC and will return values by creating variables there. A packaged ISPEXEC must detect that a VGET or VPUT request has been made and determine appropriate use of EXP, by analysing the request. I think that this is enough to indicate that ISPEXEC provides an example of a function that ought not to be packaged, because of the complexity of the changes that would be necessary.

Another topic of interest is that of utility functions and operators that need extending for use within packaged workspaces, rather than just modification to ensure that they will refer properly to objects in a calling namescope.

A simple example of such a function is the following, which endeavours to ensure that a variable is available, with an optional default value, and provides a result indicating whence the value came.

     ∇ Z←DEFAULT pwFINDVAR NAME
[1]    ⍝ Look for var NAME in current namescope; if not found, look in prev n/s
[2]    ⍝ If still not found, assign value DEFAULT if provided (else undefined).
[3]    ⍝ Z is set according to the source of any value for the variable:
[4]    ⍝ ¯1 - from prev n/s; 0 - undefined; 1 - from current n/s; 2 - default
[5]     →(0≠⎕NC NAME)/0,Z←1
[6]     ⍎(0≠EXP '⎕NC' NAME)/'→0,(Z←¯1),⍴',NAME,'←EXP⊂NAME'
[7]     →(0=⎕NC 'DEFAULT')/Z←0
[8]     ⍎NAME,'←DEFAULT'
[9]     Z←2
     ∇

This function is useful, for example, in a print utility for determining whether or not a printer has been defined.

items.title: PostScript Support for APL under Windows
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 128

From: George MacLeod, 28 November 1990

There has been a lot of interest of late expressed in Vector on the subject of APL fonts and how to mix APL characters with other type faces in a word processing environment. These have ranged from Adrian Smith’s elegant PostScript solution, to Rex Swain’s technique for using the STSC APL*PLUS PC font in Microsoft Word 5. This latter is totally effective and very professionally documented.

We use Word for Windows for Impetus documentation as this gives much of the benefit of a Desk Top Publishing package with a lot less hassle, and is in any case, better suited to large documents. Word for Windows is substantially different to Word 5 in many ways including the fact that it lets Windows look after fonts and printers. This meant that Rex Swain’s code did not help us.

Microsoft pointed us at a company called Fontware Ltd who are experts in these matters and who built an APL font some years ago for one of their customers. This font was built according to the customers specification and is mostly not very good. We were only interested in a subset of 12 APL characters, 10 of these were OK, and we had the other two modified. Fontware then mapped these on to key tops of our choosing.

The characters look very good when printed on a Laserjet. The screen font has, I think, been produced by some automatic process from the printer font, and is horrible. As the screen font is only for our internal usage, its quality is not a problem.

In summary, if anybody needs an APL font in a Windows environment, then Fontware have the rudiments of what is necessary and the knowledge to build something much better. I think all they need is a decent specification and a paying customer.

George MacLeod, Impetus Ltd

Ed: See Vector 7.1, July 1990, pp 96-107 for Adrian Smith’s PostScript solution, and APL Quote Quad Vol 20, No. 3, March 1990, for Rex Swain’s Microsoft Word 5 solution.

items.title: APL People Limited
items.text:
Due to demand from the manufacturing industry, the estimating package, PEFAC (which is written in APL) is now being extended to cover financial estimating as well as time estimating. The company that originally developed the product, H Walton Technical Systems Limited (founded by Herbert Walton - first Chairman of the British APL Association), is being renamed APL Manufacturing Limited.

We have no plans to change the name of APL People however, and it will continue to provide the same high level of service as before, helping clients find suitably qualified people for permanent vacancies and for contract assignments.

Despite the recession, we have placed a record number of people in jobs in 1990, and plan to do even better in ’91! We currently have a good selection of APL consultants registered with us for contract work and are always pleased to visit clients to discuss their APL requirements in detail with them. Companies contemplating recruiting ‘APLers’ or with development work in APL planned for the New Year should contact me, Jill Moss on 0225 462602 to book a free consultation with myself or one of my colleagues.

items.title: Cocking and Drury Ltd
items.text:
Having just completed the introduction of APL*PLUS II Version 3 we are now shipping upgrades to APL*PLUS PC Version 10 - reviewed on page 67 in this issue.

This release marks ten years of APL micro technology and the enhancements are significant. Support for Windows 3 with the ability - on an appropriate machine - to have an APL session running while you work with other software or to have two APL sessions running simultaneously. The inclusion of ⎕NA to call non-APL subroutines written in C or FORTRAN. Support for mice.

January will also see the launch of a new release of the APL*PLUS UNIX product. This release uses X Windows on SUN 4 stations, the DEC RISC platforms and the new IBM RS/6000. Release 4 should also include enhancements to the external processor interface that allow passing of nested arrays between APL and an external processor. There will also be a new APL User Interface specifically written for X Windows that will allow:

  • keyboard handling compatible with APL*PLUS PC and II
  • Full Screen Handling, with colour, compatible with APL*PLUS PC and II
  • Faster APL output and ⎕WPUT.
  • The inclusion of ⎕WIN.

To complete the round of product updates Version 7 of the APL*PLUS System for the Mainframe has now been announced for release now for VM and first quarter 1991 for MVS. And STSC have announced a new product - Network SHAREFILE. This offers users true networking capabilities among remote sites as well as across multiple servers.

You will probably see announcements soon that Cocking & Drury have become UK dealers for Digitalk Inc of Los Angeles - developers of the Smalltalk/V line of object-oriented programming language and development environment.

This does not mean we are turning our backs on the STSC APL*PLUS products - the list of new releases coming out of Rockville means there is plenty of opportunity for further development there. It is quite some time since we have noticed such a strong level of interest in these products, both for the APL*PLUS II System and particularly for the UNIX software. We are hoping to recruit another support consultant in the New Year to assist Dave Phillips with the growing level of APL support.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
As we look back over the last quarter of 1990, we have been pleasantly surprised by the reception given to APL.68000 Level II. Copies of the software have been shipped to most countries in Europe as well as the USA, Japan and Canada. At the time of writing, sales of the Macintosh and Atari versions are running neck and neck with the Amiga lagging considerably. Whilst we expect sales of the Amiga version to catch up as the sales in the USA (our biggest Amiga market) build up, it is interesting to see the continuing strong sales of the Macintosh version.

MicroAPL has begun to plan our upgrade program for next year and we hope to announce details in a forthcoming Vector, but users of our Atari software may care to note that work is in hand on an overhaul of the Atari versions of our software. Both our interpreters (Level I and Level II) make use of the same Supervisor (Operating System interface) on any given port and the work on the Atari ST will, for example, apply equally to the Level I and Level II versions.

Our free runtime policy continues to attract a steady number of licence applications ranging from Real Estate analysis to Music via Restaurant Menu evaluation. Sales of APL.68000 (both versions) into the educational sector continue to be strong, with as much as 30% of our sales going to Universities and Colleges. Readers who use APL in educational establishments should note that we have a highly successful educational site licensing scheme for APL.68000 which offers APL.68000 at very considerable discounts for bona-fide educational establishments.

At a local level, MicroAPL have just released our 1991 Training Program. We continue to specialise in intensive, one day courses either at our London offices or on a client site. We have added a new timetabled course to our schedule - ‘An Introduction to APL2’, which is aimed at users of any of the variants of APL2 (APL2/370, APL2/PC or APL.68000 Level II). Although not a part of the regular training schedule, our APL Programming Techniques course has been run several times in 1990 and seems to meet a gap in the market.

Our consultancy operations continue to cover a wide variety of applications, with a reasonably even spread between PC, Mac and multi-user environments. As we end 1990, for the first time our non-APL consultancy activities are generating as much revenue as our traditional APL work, a fact which reflects the growing quality of packaged software solutions and applications generators.

items.title: Dutch APL User Group
items.text:
The Dutch APL User Group (DAUG for short) is happy to present itself here as a sustaining member of Vector. The DAUG exists now in Holland for about fifteen years. In those years we endeavoured to

  • stimulate the use of APL
  • exchange knowledge and experience about APL between members
  • inform outsiders about APL
  • stimulate standardisation in matters of APL
  • intermediate between users and APL vendors.

The vigour in which we developed activities for each of those topics varied over the years of course. Nevertheless we organised almost every year a one-day mini-congress with several speakers. Here APL users listened to and discussed with the speakers, and the users exchanged ideas among themselves in between the talks.

Currently the DAUG is engaged in the following 2 activities: the organisation of the next mini-congress on 6 April 1991 and the project ASWI which stands for “APL ShareWare Initiative”.

MINI-CONGRESS. The next APL mini-congress is titled “Informal software/experience Exchange” and it will be held on 6 April 1991 in Nieuwegein. It will be organised with various booths in which users as well as official vendors will present some of their products. A booth can be a poster, or a demonstration, or a pile of books, or whatever a person feels comfortable to express his ideas. At the moment we have a minimum of at least the following booths: ASWI, I-APL, RNA-applications in APL68000, Menu-system in APL-2, APL68000, Dyalog APL, STSC, APL68000, APL consultancy, Public domain software. Anybody who is interested in showing his/her application is invited to contact Theo Zwart, [address and telephone number omitted].

ASWI. ASWI stands for APL ShareWare Initiative. This initiative started at the end of 1990 with the aim of developing high-quality software for APL programmers. ASWI aims to attract the attention of professional software developers to use APL and to minimise costs by offering this software on a shareware base.

Two of the most important issues which are almost resolved are: choice of basic hardware/software platform and standardisation. We have chosen IBM’s APL2 for PC’s as the primary platform and we will possibly choose APL.68000 for Mac, Atari and other 68000 micros as the second platform. Our main reasons are the free run-time version, nested arrays, and easy interchange between both platforms by )IN and )OUT. A standard is developed for documentation as well as for programming style. This standard will be submitted for publication in Vector for the next issue.

Various other topics which are still under discussion are: quality assurance, a document library, public relations/communication and many others. Most important of all will be a wish list with priorities of required software. ASWI intends to start with developing functional specifications of those wishes first and subsequently delegate them for implementation to the various interested parties.

And finally, if you are not a member of the DAUG yet, we would like to welcome you. Please write to Postbus 1341, 3430BH Nieuwegein tel.03474-2337. Currently, the board of the DAUG consists of Theo Zwart (president), Bernard Smoor (secretary), Thom Bonnema (treasurer), and Louis van Geldrop, Herman van Loon, Gerrit Teule and Eke van Batenburg.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
Welcome to this edition of Education Vector. As you know from previous discussion in these columns, committee members of the British APL Association have been looking carefully at the current expenditure involved in producing and posting Education Vector. The results of the survey, and letters sent to me indicate that most people appreciate Education Vector in its present form. The committee wish to continue the present distribution lists as far as possible, but are aware of the not insignificant cost of postage, both to readers in this country and particularly abroad.

After much careful thought the decision taken was that in the first place I should take this opportunity to encourage receivers of Education Vector to consider becoming members of the British APL Association for an annual cost of only £10 (£5 student rate). That way you would receive full information concerning the activities of the APL community both at home and abroad in the quarterly issues of VECTOR, which of course includes Education Vector as well as a new section on the progress of the APL Statistics Library project.

Secondly, for those readers abroad who are not able to take up this option, the committee agreed to continue posting Education Vector to anybody that wrote to us asking us so to do. So please send me a postcard or letter as outlined below.

Once again I hope readers will find something of interest in the following pages. I am indebted to those who have sent in comments and contributions; please continue to share your experiences in using APL by writing to the editor.

items.title: 2. A Correction From Bill Smith
items.text:
Bill Smith wrote to tell me that I missed a sentence out of his note on ‘dBase Files and Lotus Files into I-APL’ published in the October edition of Education Vector. (My Apologies.) The corrected paragraph reads as follows.

‘dBaseIII files, output with a COPY TO <filename> TYPE SDF command, yield a series of fixed length records in ASCII format. Lotus spreadsheets, ‘databases’ at least, printed to file result in .PRN files with one record per row in ASCII format. These are only fixed length if the right-most field of each row is of the same size but this is easily managed even if you have to create a dummy column to achieve it. A further problem with Lotus files is that they are preceded by a number of carriage returns/line feed characters which need to be disposed of in the first stages of transfer; actually in the DREAD function.’

items.title: 3. Day-of-Week Algorithm
items.text:
I am grateful to L Llewellyn-Jones of London for sending me a copy of an article by Bhairav Joshi published in COMPUTERWORLD (January 14 1980) who explains the mathematics of calculating the day of the week from the date. The article is easy to follow and also includes an APL program. Unfortunately I am unable to include the article in this column but will supply copies to any interested reader who cares to provide a stamped-addressed envelope. However, here is the supplied function:

[1]    M←12⍴ 7 31 30

[4]    R←1+7|¯1+R+D[2]++/(¯1+1↑D)↑M
[5]    R←(7 9 ⍴'SATURDAY SUNDAY MONDAY TUESDAY WEDNESDAYTHURSDAY
     FRIDAY ')[R;]
     ∇

items.title: Editorial: Solving Problems with APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Jonathan Barman

I was most impressed with the talks given at the September meeting as they showed APL being used as a simple and elegant tool to solve ordinary problems.

Adrian Smith showed how he had developed some functions which mirrored the PostScript language, and which could be used for prototyping and testing PostScript programs. Graham Parkhouse showed how APL enabled him to display engineering ideas in three dimensions with proper perspective and shading. Both had created a ‘tool box’ of APL functions to tackle their respective problems, and I felt that APL had influenced the way they had gone about constructing solutions.

The APL notation seems to exert a strong influence on the way one thinks about problems. In my own case I often find the ordinary mathematical notation in a textbook difficult, and understanding only comes when I have converted it into APL. The power of the APL operators, particularly in the new extended APLs with nested arrays, makes problems easy to state, and having stated them concisely the road to the solution is often easier.

The environment in which APL works is just as important as the notation. The concept of a workspace where data, functions and operators all co-exist, make it easy to test out ideas which may lead to a solution. Having found a algorithm which is a stepping stone towards the final goal, one promptly turns it into a function which can be applied as required.

The APL syntax enabled Adrian and Graham to string functions together in a very natural and obvious way, which made their solutions seem so easy and simple. All languages allow the definition of functions or procedures, but the APL syntax combined with the workspace environment seems to make things much easier than other languages. Recently I have used REXX under VM. REXX is a deservedly popular language and is an interpreter like APL. Being a beginner I naturally looked at the procedures written by experts in order to learn the language. I was quite surprised to find that most of the procedures were self contained and that they did not seem to be built in the normal APL way of using functions as building blocks. REXX has all the facilities needed for creating procedures using the building block approach. I could only conclude that the facilities tended not to be used because passing data between independent REXX procedures was less convenient than passing data between APL functions.

Creating reusable code is vital if programming problems are to be solved quickly. Neither Adrian or Graham created all their functions from scratch - many utilities were copied into their workspaces. The current Object Oriented Programming bandwagon rightly emphasises the importance of writing reusable code, and OOPS languages have excellent facilities for encapsulating functions so that they are truly modular. APL is showing its age in this respect, and Packaged Workspaces have to be used to ensure proper encapsulation. However )COPY has served us well over the last 25 years and will continue to do so.

In my view APL is the ideal problem solving language. The notation, syntax and environment all work together as an integrated whole to give us all a potent and effective tool, both at the computer keyboard and as a way of thinking about problems and solutions.

items.title: Change of Venue for Monthly Meetings
items.text:
From February 1991, we have decided to change the venue of our monthly meetings in London. Meetings will now be held at the Institute of Electrical Engineers, Savoy Place, London.

There are two main reasons for the change. Firstly, the cost of hiring a room at the IEE is considerably less than at Over-Seas House. Secondly (and possibly more importantly), the IEE room comes equipped with a VGA-quality Barco projector, enabling talks with demonstrations at every meeting without the trouble and considerable expense of booking an outside company to provide one.

The committee believe that this move will greatly enhance the quality of our monthly meetings - come along in February and see if we’ve made the right decision.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
The APL Statistics Library project has now been formally running for over a year, with invitational conferences at Gregynog in 1989 (Vector 6.3) and Swansea in 1990 (Vector 7.3). The ASL project, for those readers who have not seen any of the previously published material, is an initiative launched by a number of users of APL for statistical work - largely in higher education. As you will see from Tony O’Hagan’s article later in this newsletter, the purpose behind the project is to underline the usefulness of APL for statistical research and teaching purposes by providing a tested and approved library of statistical routines written in APL.

The British APL Association has been sponsoring the ASL project over this period and has kindly agreed to dedicate a section of Vector to news of the ASL project. It is hoped that we can find a steady series of items which cover the progress of the ASL project and which are also of interest to the general reader. In this issue we begin to look at the history of the ASL project (see also Vector 7.1), review the current status of the project as it runs through the beta test phase for its first volumes and look in a little bit of detail at the concepts that underpin one of the initial ‘Bottom Shelf’ volumes - Basic Graphics.

items.title: The ASL Management Team
items.text:
Perhaps the most important thing for many of you is to know who is running ASL. The management of the project is conducted by the Management Team comprising a Chairman, Deputy Chairman, Manager and two representatives of the British APL Association (BAA). BAA representation is important because it is they who are funding the project, and we are consequently extremely grateful for their support.

Strategic Planning and all major issues are dealt with at full Team meetings, but day to day running is handled by the Manager. Names and addresses are as follows.

Chairman: Tony O’Hagan, Department of Mathematics, University of Nottingham, University Park, Nottingham NG7 2RD.Telephone: 0602-484848 x2800 Deputy Chairman: Alan Sykes, Department of Management Science and Statistics, University College of Swansea, Singleton Park, Swansea SA2 8PP.Telephone: 0792-295296 Manager: Jake Ansell, Business Studies, University of Edinburgh, William Robertson Building, 50 George Square, Edinburgh EH8 9JY.Telephone: 031-667-1011 BAA Representative/ Newsletter Editor: David Eastwood, MicroAPL Ltd., South Bank Technopark, 90 London Road, London SE1 6LN.Telephone: 071-922-8866 BAA Representative: John Searle, [home address and telephone number omitted]

items.title: ASL News and Status - December 1990
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 35

I would like to start by reviewing the way in which the ASL project is organised. It should be stressed that with the exception of the part-time input of our Programmer (see below), all the effort put into ASL is done on a voluntary basis. Whilst it is extremely gratifying to have the willing help and assistance of so many people, they all have other things to do and this does impose different timescales to full-time commercial projects.

items.title: The Programmer
items.text: There are two main ways in which ASL is funded by the BAA. One is by running working conferences or workshops like the one just held in Swansea. The other is by paying for a part-time programmer. She is Tuks Gillespie, who has substantial experience in APL programming and is proving an extremely valuable member of the project. Organising the effective use of Tuks’ time is the responsibility of the Manager, Jake Ansell.

items.title: Working Parties
items.text: The actual specification and planning of ASL software is done by Working Parties,who liaise with the Management Team and the Programmer through Jake Ansell. One key way in which you can support ASL is by serving on Working Parties. So why not write to Tony O’Hagan (address above) and tell him which aspects of statistical software you would be interested in helping to develop? Is there an area of statistical methods in which you have a great interest or expertise? Are you keen to help with the graphics, the numerical algorithms or other utilities that will serve the statistical functions? Or could your experience in developing large non-statistical APL systems be valuable to us in our general operations, or in managing our growing library of functions? WRITE NOW, please.

items.title: Shelves and Volumes
items.text: ASL is a library, which suggested the word “shelf” to cover a collection of functions dealing with a common subject area. Thus, there will be a Regression Shelf. Within a Shelf, there is a smaller unit called a “volume”. A volume is a coherent group of functions that are released together. So shelves grow by the addition of a volume at a time. There is a shelf called the Bottom Shelf, concerned with low-level functions that are likely to be usable both directly and within higher shelves.

items.title: The Official Launch
items.text:
We currently plan to launch ASL by the simultaneous release of three volumes at a special meeting of the BAA on 22 March 1991. The first software to be released will be:

Bottom Shelf Volume 1, Basic Statistics Bottom Shelf Volume 2, Basic Graphics Regression Shelf Volume 1, Generalised Linear Models.

items.title: Within ASL - Basic Statistics
items.text:
The first three volumes of software have been issued for beta test. In this issue of our newsletter, I shall be taking a quick look at what is in one of our first volumes of software - the Basic Statistics volume. Subsequent issues will look at the other shelves.

The Basic Statistics volume owes much to the work of Norman Thomson who made the initial suggestions regarding the scope of the Bottom Shelf at Gregynog in 1989 (and at earlier meetings). Norman’s document (called, not surprisingly, ‘The Bottom Shelf’) contains details of virtually all the statistical routines contained in the Basic Statistics volume, using APL2 as the specification language. The ASL Documentation Working Party is currently aiming to bring Basic Statistics documentation and functions fully into line. As with other ASL documents, copies of Norman’s paper are obtainable from the Management Team.

A review of the contents of the Basic Statistics Volume gives the best idea of its scope, as in most cases the function name alone tells us all we need to know. The workspace contains almost 100 functions, with some duplication covering alternate algorithms (coding for speed, elegance, workspace economy with variants using numerical suffices). Symbol table usage is some 700 symbols.

The contents of the Basic Statistics volume is designed to address the needs of ‘A’ level or first year university students, with groupings suggested as follows:

Univariate Statistics Distribution Functions Elementary multi-variate statistics Estimation and significance testing Non-parametric statistics Times series ANOVA Combinatorics

items.text:
This year’s Outstanding Achievement Award was awarded to Metapraxis of Kingston, Surrey for their world-renowned Management Information system ‘Resolve’. At this months meeting, David Preedy (of Metapraxis) will receive the award, and he will follow with a full demonstration of Resolve.

The remainder of the meeting will be taken up by a talk from Paul Gallagher (British Airways) on a PC-based APL application from British Airways that looks into “long term strategic planning in the modern world”.

items.title: Windows 3: the Implications for APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 61

by Adrian Smith

items.title: Background
items.text: These notes are a brief attempt to explain why I think Windows 3 matters a lot to APL. I will start by outlining some of the things you can do now with Windows and APL*PLUS/PC or APL2/PC; the rest of this note is a look a little further ahead to where I would like to get to in (say) 18 months’ or 2 years’ time. The assumption behind all that follows is that you have at least a 16 MHz 386SX with about 4Mbyte of memory; Windows will also run in ‘standard’ and ‘real’ mode if you insist, but both of these effectively cripple it, and should be disregarded unless you are absolutely desperate!

items.title: What you can do with Windows
items.text:
The most obvious thing is task-switching. I never added up all the time I lost whenever the phone rang: )SAVE and )OFF followed by a quick dive into the mainframe or Word or a spreadsheet, followed by APL and )LOAD to get back to where I was. To leave my APL*PLUS/PC session sitting on the screen, kick out into something else, and recover it exactly as I left it is a huge time saver.

There seems to be no practical limit on the number of DOS applications you can fire off alongside each other; I have often had 6 sessions running and Windows has never fallen below 75% free. Switching is literally instant, you use Alt+Tab to toggle round the sessions, and your screen flicks back the instant you take your thumb off the Alt key. There is only a minimal cost in memory; I lose 17K off my APL workspace as a consequence of running under Windows, and the e=8192 option works fine.

The next thing you might try is setting one or more sessions to run in the background. This is especially handy when that session is doing something slow and wasteful of processor resources, like copying a big file across a slow network. For example to upgrade our MTP system to a remote site requires about 8 minutes over a 2400baud line; I can run this in background at a low priority and get on with something useful in the meantime. Not recommended with things like GoScript which really hammer the CPU! You either slow your printing to a crawl, or make APL so jerky you can’t use the editor ... set the print running in foreground and go for lunch!!

You can get more ambitious, and try cut and paste between sessions! For example I can write a line of code in APL, copy it into the Windows clipboard, and paste it straight into Word. This saves a deal of wondering whether rho is really alt-251 (⍴ ... so it was!) and should speed up Vector production quite a bit. The only snag is that you can only use the clipboard when the application is running windowed, and this switches it to a graphics character set, hence losing all the APL symbols (at least in versions prior to 10). However you can toggle between windowed and full-screen with Alt+Enter, so this is quite bearable in practice.

Amazingly enough, cut and paste works fine in graphics mode too. For example I have an APL function to draw the Rowntree logo (any size, any colour etc.); I copied the logo from APL into Windows Paintbrush, and hence was able to use it to tile my desktop, as well as being able to scribble graffiti all over it with the mouse!

items.title: What you can’t do with Windows
items.text: You can’t run APL2/PC 32bit, APL*PLUS II or Dyalog APL. APL*PLUS II and Dyalog use the same memory management as QEMM, which will only co-operate with Windows if you have QEMM version 5.1. However this still limits you to the Windows ‘standard mode’, in other words applications get swopped out to disk, instead of being stacked away in extended memory. One of the great joys of Windows is the instant switching, so I personally still tend to close Windows down and run Dyalog APL from the DOS prompt.

items.title: Where APL needs to be Right Now
items.text:
Obviously, APL has to co-operate with the Windows memory management, at least to the extent that it will run under Windows as a standard DOS application. Windows is quite happy to allocate extended memory as old-style LIMS/EMS memory, which is why APL*PLUS/PC still gets to use e=8192 to load 64K of the interpreter high. However if you want true, flat, 32-bit addressing, you need to use a new interface called the Dos Protected Mode Interface (DPMI for short) ... see the recent PC edition of Byte (from page 113) for details.

At this point, I go way outside my technical knowledge; all I can say is that it would appear that all the fancy Protected-mode support given by interface software like Phar Lap now comes free with the system, in fact it will probably be in DOS 5.0 even without Windows.

This leaves vendors like Dyalog and STSC in the happy position of being able to wave goodbye to Phar Lap, and hence to the hefty royalties they are paying on every copy of the interpreter they sell. The implications would seem to be:

  • cheaper development systems, and very much cheaper runtime.
  • more straightforward development of APs, ideally in common or garden C, rather than the super-whizzo Meta-ware Hi-C that Dyalog currently demands.
  • you should get as much memory on your system as you can afford! If you want to run 32-bit APL alongside Aldus Pagemaker and MS Word, you are looking at 12 Mbyte minimum.

That will do for starters ... there is one more goody that deserves detailed explanation, and offers APL the chance of a giant step back to the future ....

items.title: Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE)
items.text:
How many of you remember ⎕SVO and ⎕SVC? They actually gave their name to APLSV ... and I don’t mean the perversion of a brilliant design concept into a lousy mechanism for reading and writing files!! I mean genuine user-user shared variables, which are a superb mechanism to manage concurrent processing, and deal with all the problems that arise when you need to organise co-operating tasks.

I last tangled with ⎕SVO under VSPC, when we used it to set up a simple tele-conferencing system between our planners. Essentially, it allowed two or more logged-on users (in York and Edinburgh) to update the same data, and see what each other was doing. With DDE under Windows, you have a defined interface whereby any Windows application can share variables with any other, using the Clipboard to pass messages, and shared memory to exchange data.

In other words, you could imagine a situation where you were running an Excel spreadsheet alongside an APL session, with the values in some range of cells shared with an APL array. As you modify the array in APL, the spreadsheet reflects the changes instantly (possibly on a chart); alternatively when you update the spreadsheet you find that the values in the array automatically stay in step. This sort of thing makes particular sense when one of the partners is a background task, such as an SQL server. Rather than setting up an APL-specific database link through SQL*NET, you just use a standard windows task (probably also used by Excel) via DDE. It all looks so much simpler!

items.title: Where I would like to be in 2 years’ time
items.text:
I want an APL system that is a real pukka Windows application!! That means a lot of work for somebody, but the benefits must surely be enormous for APL in general, and in particular for the first vendor to get there! Here are a few reasons why:

  • if you know one Windows application, you know them all! No more session managers or editors to learn ... just use the Notepad to edit functions and the Clipboard to cut and paste! At last I will be able to throw away all my code for pop-ups and pull-downs and dialog boxes! How much simpler it would be if I let Windows do all this for me.
  • I want to write systems which look for all the world like other Windows applications. No-one need know I wrote them in APL in 1/10th of the time it took some poor hack to write the same thing in C. If anyone asks, I just say that I used this fancy set of C macros, like ⍴ and ∘.= ... it may help.
  • true integration of text and graphics. I want to be able to edit the data in one window, and see the graph change in another. Alternatively, I want to drag the graph around with the mouse, and see the numbers change to match. I want to be able to put a map of Europe on the screen, and see the production plan at Halifax by pointing at it ... and so on.
  • DDE. This should go without saying. I want to share data between background server tasks, APL, and any other Windows applications I happen to be running, like Pagemaker or MS Word.
  • no more hanging on the coat-tails of DOS-extenders like Phar Lap. Assuming Windows really has got the memory management right (and Microsoft aren’t stupid) we should be clear to run up to 15Mbyte and beyond. We may at long last shake the notion of runtime licences out of the system.
  • a whole lot of intangible things, like the far richer visual environment that Windows gives me. Some of the games are quite good too ... I suspect that proficiency at Reversi has taken over from proficiency at Billiards as a sign of a mis-spent youth.

I am sure St Paul felt the same on the road to Damascus ... MicroAPL and their Mac users must be laughing like drains at all this; they have been shouting it from the rooftops for years. I have nothing to say in my defence except that I was blind and now I can see! Please don’t take my mouse away!!
