items.title: APL conference on CIX
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 8

From: Pan Pantziarka, 21st November 1990

The Compulink Information eXchange (CIX) is the premier UK electronic bulletin board enabling a wide range of computer users, from IBM mainframers to the users of the tiniest home micros, to dial-in and exchange data, programs, leave mail and to have chats and discussions in real time. One of the primary attractions of CIX is the large number of conferences available, where people who share a particular interest can “meet” like minded folk, ask and answer questions and swap files.

A new addition to the conference list (which includes such special interests as home-brewing and anarchist politics!) is an APL conference. The conference APL.LANG has the following topics: ‘general’, ‘BAA’, ‘Vector’ and ‘WS’.

This conference could serve as an ideal forum to attract new people to the language, for novices to ask questions and for the British APL Association and Vector to issue announcements, meeting dates and APL news etc.

The ‘WS’ topic is also a good place for public domain and shareware APL interpreters and workspaces to be made available to the public.

To join CIX dial-in on 081-399 5252 (or if your modem supports V32, use 081-390 9787). Once you’ve dialled in, just follow the onscreen instructions to become a subscriber. Alternatively call the CIX voice-line on 081-390 8446 for details on costs etc.

See you all online ….

Pan Pantziarka Compass R&D Ltd

items.title: Projects Report
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 9

from John Searle (November 29, 1990)

I see my role as Projects Officer as a coordinator and facilitator of members’ ideas. If you have an idea for worthwhile expenditure of the Association’s resources (money, expertise, APL skills and/or personpower) please submit it to me. A one-page proposal is quite sufficient, with convincing arguments in sufficient detail to promote further discussion. I undertake to put all proposals to the committee, and if agreed, to try to find someone to implement them. I do not undertake to do them all myself!

Here are some current members’ projects, and their recent status:

  • ASL - APL Statistics Library, which now has its own Management Team, as documented in Vector 7.1, and to be launched at the March 1991 meeting.
  • Membership Records System - would you believe that our membership records are kept in DBASE? An APL solution has been proposed, prompting much debate within the committee as to the suitability of APL for this purpose.
  • Software Library - how can we rescue it from its current state of chaos? (Apologies to those who have suffered through non-supply.) The workload had become too much, but a solution is in sight. Please watch this space for details of a relaunch in the next issue of Vector.
  • ISO Standards work - due to the withdrawal of DTI funding, the BAPLA now subsidises the BSI Principal Expert’s travel and accommodation at ISO/APL technical meetings.
  • Booklist / Book Library proposal - how can we organize and distribute APL literature and reviews to our members as a lending and reference library? (including our international members?). Ideas please.
  • Meeting Venue Change to IEE - an important component of a successful BAPLA meeting is a drink before or afterwards, and if needed, a good meal. I have undertaken to make an extensive review of all of the pubs in the vicinity, and preliminary results reveal that the nearest pub is in fact quite suitable. This is the New Savoy Tavern in Savoy St, and the upstairs bar has been tested and ratified under simulated BAPLA conditions (i.e. a meal at 1pm on a Friday and a drink at 5pm). See you there on February 8th.

items.title: Field Trip to Rowntree Mackintosh
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 93

items.title: The BAA Visit Rowntree Mackintosh
items.text:
reported by Sylvia Camacho and Jonathan Martin

The decision to hold some meetings away from London was amply justified by the success of this visit to York. About 20 chose to arrive mid-morning to take a tour of the factory and found themselves kitted out in white overalls, caps and hairnets before being allowed into the world of Kit Kat, Smarties, Polo mints and Black Magic. Attendance at the afternoon meeting also exceeded expectation and the speakers were very well received.

items.title: Why we use APL by Tom McGuffog (Purchasing, Logistics and IT director)
items.text:
The theme running through this talk was that computers and the software which runs on them are too valuable to be monopolised by Data Processing departments. Rowntree has backed this judgement by moving its Operational Research facility away from IT management into an area now called Logistics. They argue that Rowntrees are looking for people interested in the problems they need solving and not those whose primary interest is in computers.

They look upon computer facilities as a way of adding value to bright people and use APL to help them articulate and prototype their problems and solutions. Experience shows that people who can make computers sing are often not good at messy business problems, and they also find that IT departments have inappropriate career structures.

items.title: Supply Chain Management
items.text:
Mr McGuffog continued by describing how Rowntrees use computers in supply chain management. He pointed out that whereas the goods flow from the suppliers through warehouses and on to the customer, the data flow is naturally in the reverse direction from the (probably EPOS) checkout, through goods packaged in ‘outers’ by pallet loads, to the orders (often on Electronic Data Exchange), to the invoices and delivery instructions and so through to contract and production plan.

As the parties involved in these activities become more automated, the control demanded becomes more stringent. Tesco, for instance, will not only specify a day for delivering but a precise time to fit with their own warehouse throughput schedule.

The hardware Rowntrees use is becoming increasingly distributed, nationally and internationally. Mainframes are seen as file servers to mini computers (VAX) which service networked (Ethernet) micro computers (mostly IBM PCs). Data is held on a relational database (Oracle) from which it is pulled down and uploaded using SQL. This allows a fast and flexible access to data on 30-40 Brands presented in about 1000 varieties of pack. The packs change continually so that there may be 3000 in the course of a year.

items.title: Chocolate Monitoring demonstrated by Adrian Smith
items.text:
Adrian was able to bring the factory into the lecture room by plugging into the live, real time chocolate making system enquiry and scheduling packages which monitors production for 6-8 ingredients and displays the activity of the various machines in 1/4 hour schedule slots.

The data is brought down to the PCs via SQL from a Vax ORACLE database. This delegates all problems of data integrating to the ORACLE software. It is a matter of horses-for-courses, ORACLE to handle large amounts of data but APL to manipulate it as arrays. Postscript is used for the graphics because it has a defined public standard. It is very important not to get locked into any particular vendor.

items.title: Medium Term Planning by Vicki Wright
Interactive Planning Board by Andy Gibson
items.text:
There has been a system from 1983 onwards. The object of medium term planning is to reduce stock-holding and improve service to customers and thereby increase value added to the raw materials. The system provides an interface between otherwise incompatible systems. In the spirit of the time the mainframe is gradually giving way to PC based systems.

Products are organised hierarchically, and frequent packaging changes impose many restraints on planning. The system provides an immediate response to any data edited. Colour is used extensively and standards for its use have been devised.

Data is taken weekly from the mainframe via a local VAX. The planners maintain their preferred product tree structure. They find that Export production tends to require bottom up planning, but the home market is better suited top-down. The front end is a short term schedule into which actual data is linked as it becomes available.

An unconsidered but intriguing trifle of information emerged from this talk - some Smartie tubes are abbreviated to ‘Tooth’ which is short for ‘toothpaste tube’, but they aren’t tubes, they’re cardboard boxes - quite square; they’re for Irish Smarties! (Andy said “That’s not a joke. Its true.”)

It was also pointed out that for the first time an APL system had made the front page of the Company Newpaper! (captioned “Daddy - I want your job”).

items.title: APL Training at Rowntrees by Richard Taylor (OR Manager)
items.text:
The first contact Rowntrees had with APL was via time-sharing in 1976. The second system they set up (1979) after bringing it in house is still running. They used VM CMS and then VSPC and AP124, going in 1983 to GDDM & PGF graphics and occasionally to APL*PLUS/PC & APL 68000 on a SAGE IV. By 1986 they had over 150 mainframe users and by 1987 were beginning a serious move to PC systems integrated with the company Ethernet and Dec’s PCSA. By 1989 they could develop major systems on 386 machines as a consequence of the facility to copy the code and data easily (and quickly) over the network.

Rowntrees have a recruitment policy biased towards numerate graduates. They offer 8 weeks structured training, after which graduates are eased into existing systems via routine maintenance and simple changes. Where possible, graduates are given little ‘stand-alone’ projects as soon as possible, so that they can grow in confidence (and so that their inevitable mistakes cannot cause too much damage!).

Staff turnover averages 16% with an average service of 4 years. About one third of the recruits tend to stay in the Company, with a good spread about the different functions (e.g. the current head of I.T. is ex-OR, and there is ex-OR representation in Marketing, Production, and Product Development).

items.title: Don’t Even Think About It!
items.text:
a (sore) footnote by Jonathan Martin

Quite possibly those words don’t mean anything to you. They are taken from the back page of the notice for the meeting at Rowntree’s concerning methods of getting to York, in this case by air. But, hang on a minute, I work for an airline - flying is the most obvious (and most convenient for me) way of travelling north. So that’s what I did.

I set off from home early Friday morning and arrived at Heathrow Terminal 1 in plenty of time, only to find that (because of bad weather up north) the plane was late arriving and would consequently be about an hour late departing. This was not good news - I had worked out my timetable (fly to Leeds, pick up a hire car and drive up to York) so that I didn’t have a great degree of leeway. However, there was nothing I could do about it.

Eventually we boarded the plane to the wonderful smells of a British Midland cooked breakfast wafting around. Just before we pushed back, the Captain came on and announced that we had a problem - there weren’t enough breakfasts to go around! How could he possibly resolve this situation? - send all the breakfasts back and make us do without!

Thirty minutes later and we began our descent into Leeds. The captain immediately warned us that the weather at Leeds had deteriorated and that we may not be able to land. Sure enough, after two attempts and not even a whiff of a view of the airport, we diverted to Teesside airport (near Darlington).

Things were now getting desperate as it was 11:30 and I was due in York at 10:30. So, off the plane, skip the coaches back to Leeds and straight to the Hertz desk to beg for a car. Fortunately I was one of the first there and they had some spares. So into the car and off into the wilderness of North Yorkshire, not altogether knowing where I was going except that I wanted to go South. Ninety minutes later I finally arrived at Rowntrees, just in time to catch the end of lunch. A very interesting but thankfully (with respect to the morning) uneventful meeting followed.

Back to the journey - the meeting finished at about 5:15 and my plane back from Leeds was at 7:05 - plenty of time. For a change, I made it quite easily, even managing to call in at my sister-in-law’s for a cup of tea before going to the airport.

At the airport, all was still gloom and doom (in that order) - the fog had well and truly settled in and they had cancelled the evening flight to London. Instead they were going to bus everyone down to Heathrow on coaches! Now the M1 to London on a Friday night in the fog is not my idea of a good time - so back to my sister-in-law’s I went and spent a very comfortable evening with a glass of gin and tonic...

First plane Saturday morning was 7.05! I woke just about in time and glanced out of the window - no prizes for guessing the state of the weather. So the options open were either to sit in Leeds and wait for it to clear (anyone who knows where Leeds/Bradford airport is will know that this could take a long time) or to drive over to Manchester and get on the shuttle. Manchester it was, over the M62, over the pennines.

Now if Leeds/Bradford is not the best place to put an airport, then the top of the Pennines is not necessarily the best place to put a motorway - needless to say, the fog was as bad (if not worse) on the M62 as it had been at the airport. So I crawled my way, in visibility down to about 20-30 feet in places, over to Manchester, where surprisingly there was bright sunshine (a rare occurrence!) and some flying aircraft. Thankfully, from then on normal service was resumed and I arrived home somewhat later and a touch more crumpled that I had expected.

Hindsight is a wonderful thing.

from Charles Schulz (December 1990)

items.title: Summary
items.text: Plans for the APL91 conference, to be held at Stanford University 4-8 August 1991, are well under way. We are meeting regularly to build this conference into a major event, conferring with our planning firm, APL user group contacts, vendors, and media contacts. Interest so far has been very encouraging: we have received over 250 interest cards to date, from more than 25 countries, and these continue to come in daily as distributions are reaching APL users worldwide. We have received nearly 60 papers, and are expecting over 90 on a wide range of topics and from a wide range of locations. 10 draft papers have been submitted from the USSR.

items.title: Call for Participation
items.text: Nearly 20,000 copies of the “Call for Participation”, which included an interest card, were circulated at APL90 in Copenhagen, mailed directly to ACM SIGAPL members and SIGAPL local chapter members, and continue to be distributed by several user groups and vendors’ mailings. Contact the conference office if you need copies.

items.title: Papers
items.text: About 100 “Information for Authors” instructions have been mailed to prospective authors indicated on the interest cards, and many of the papers have already been received. The official deadline for paper submission has passed, if you have special circumstances, please contact the conference office.

items.title: Program Committee
items.text: We are fortunate to have assembled an international and qualified program committee who will travel to California in February 1991 make final paper selections.

items.title: Speakers
items.text: We are exploring several possibilities for keynote speakers. We may also have room in the program for invited speakers on particular topics or applications. If you have particular ideas or nominations, please forward them immediately to the conference office.

items.title: Exhibits
items.text: We have had an amazingly strong exhibitor response, with over 35 vendor request for booth information! What new products are they working on?

items.title: Publicity Help Requested
items.text: Help spread the news about APL and APL91. Please send us media addresses and contacts from your industry or field, where APL91 announcements would be noticed.

items.title: APL: A Productive Language?
items.text:
We hope to publish a bibliography of APL productivity references for the conference. APL is frequently cited for productivity advantages over other languages, now more clearly illustrated with function point analysis measures. However for most users considering using APL, actual references are harder to come by than general impressions.

We encourage you to send your specific and favourite references of APL productivity, describing comparative results with other methods, solutions not possible without APL, and for good measure, cases where APL turned out not to be appropriate. References can be from published papers or articles, public remarks, or results of company internal studies, with permission. Send your references to the conference office today!

items.title: Dyadic Systems Limited
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce an implementation of Dyalog APL for Windows 3.0. The new product is called Dyalog APL/W and is based on Dyalog APL/X for the X Window System. Dyalog APL/W is written specifically for Windows 3.0 and makes full use of the Windows environment. It is a true Windows 3.0 product and cannot be run under DOS alone.

Like Dyalog APL/X, this new implementation will provide the APL developer with the facility to concurrently edit/view functions and variables in separate windows on the screen. The product also features the unique Dyalog APL debugger which lets you step through an application watching the functions pop up and down in windows as they run. Dyalog APL/W will include a means to invoke Windows menus, dialog boxes, scroll bars and so forth in end-user applications. It will also provide DDE support.

In addition to a Windows 3.0 environment, Dyalog APL/W requires a 386 or 486 processor with (ideally) 4Mb+ of memory. On a 386-based system, a 387 coprocessor is strongly recommended. The product runs as a protected mode application in Windows 386 enhanced mode. This means that it can support very large workspaces and even utilise Windows demand paging if required.

Early trials (and this announcement was written in May) indicate that performance will be every bit as good as Dyalog APL for DOS/386.

A detailed specification for Dyalog APL/W will be available at APL91, or can be obtained by post from Dyadic or any Dyalog APL distributor.

As an Authorised IBM RS/6000 VAR, Dyadic is pleased to report significant price reductions, and improvements in performance and specification across the range. The new Model 320H now comes as standard with 16Mb RAM, 400Mb disk and offers 38 MIPS and 11.7 Mflops performance. Based on this model, a single-user workstation with a 16" colour 1280x1024 display, X-Windows, Motif, and Dyalog APL costs around £16,500. A 10-user Dyalog APL system, using ASCII terminals or PCs, can be put together for under £25,000.

items.title: Cocking & Drury Ltd
items.text:
First of all we’d like to apologise to you all for our non-appearance in the last issue. We had anticipated a lot of the news in the issue before, but we should have tried a bit harder to dream something up! We have a lot more to tell you this time around though.

Many of you will have received our publication ‘Upgrade’ around mid-June. This publication, which used to be a regular feature in Cocking & Drury activities, lapsed some years ago and we were pleased to be able to re-instate it. The 8 page issue contained news of developments at C&D, developments with APL*PLUS, a user-story from London Life, a technical article by Allan Gay on migrating from APL*PLUS PC to the II System for the 386 and more.

Anyone who didn’t get a copy but would like one - give us a call.

At the time of writing (early June) we are deep in the throes of preparing for our presence at Software Tools ’91. We shall be showing APL*PLUS PC, II System for the 386 and II System for UNIX. (We shall also be showing the full range of Smalltalk/V products - but that’s another story for someone else’s newsletter!)

The launch of the new APL*PLUS II for UNIX for the IBM, SUN and DEC RISC machines has gone really well. James Wheeler - Vice President of STSC in charge of development - did a presentation in our training room to many of our leading customers the day before his presentation to the BAA.

That - and our marketing work and several mentions in the computer press - has led to a steady stream of enquiries and all our demonstration copies are currently out on loan which bodes well for future sales.

James also gave us an insight into future developments for APL*PLUS. DOS-based machines remain dominant, in their view, with the 32-bit architecture becoming standard but with an increasing interest in extending DOS with Windows - and in UNIX workstations.

STSC strategies will be to concentrate R&D on 32-bit software, exploiting Windows in DOS and X Windows in UNIX. There will be considerable improvements in interfaces to non-APL software - Database managers, graphics, SQL-based client-server databases over networks etc. But more importantly the future of APL*PLUS will include the ability to call APL from other programmes.

STSC have clearly committed themselves to developing APL*PLUS to interface with the various GUI’s and to achieving the highest level of compatibility between them. The result will inevitably be to achieve even more sales for APL*PLUS in the future.

We at Cocking & Drury are delighted to be involved with these developments. We are currently celebrating the most successful year for software sales ever - having set ourselves the target of £500,000 from APL*PLUS products in 1991 we are happy to report that 21 weeks into the year we are ahead of target by over 10% and are now wondering if we can make it £600,000 for the year! We’ll let you know.

Our course programme is busy - in the weeks surrounding the writing of this news we shall have given 3 courses in Ireland and one on the Isle-of-Man. Our course tutors are becoming well-travelled.

On the consultancy front we can report that we recently started work for a first-time client, not new to APL but new to us, and that hasn’t been a common occurrence in recent months. There are several similar contracts currently under negotiation, as well as new contracts with existing customers, and we have job offers out to two consultants with more to follow. More news on that next time.

items.title: MicroAPL
items.text:
In Vector 7.1, exactly one year ago, MicroAPL announced the launch of our second generation APL - APL.68000 Level II. In this issue of Vector, we hope to do even better. We have two major product announcements to include, one of which signals an entirely new area of operation for MicroAPL.

First of all we have completed work on the first significant upgrade to APL.68000 Level II. Version 2 of APL.68000 Level II removes most of the remaining differences between APL.68000 and IBM’s APL2/370. APL.68000 Level II has always been much closer in its specification to APL2/370 than any other APL, even IBM’s own APL2/PC, and we have now further narrowed the gap. At the same time we have managed to include some dramatic optimisations in certain key areas of the interpreter.

The main features in Version 2 of APL.68000 Level II include format-by-example; axis on scalar functions; extensions to selective assignment; N-wise reduction; partition with axis. At the level of system commands and system functions we have now implemented the name sorting and string range rules for system commands and we have implemented )SIS.

The optimisations we have implemented focus on simple cases of some of the most widely used functions. For example, scalar integer arithmetic (e.g. +-⌈⌊) has been substantially improved. Catenation operations with simple vectors have been enhanced as have indexing operations with integer indices. The effect of these improvements can lead to marked speed-ups - STSC’s benchmark 4 (Mixed functions) is some 2.75 times faster! The final optimisation of note is with respect to pick selective specification where, in some cases, speed-ups of two orders of magnitude have been achieved.

Version 2 of APL.68000 Level II is, however, just the warm-up act to our main product launch of 1991. At APL91 in early August, MicroAPL will be launching the first of a whole new series of implementations of APL.68000. Since early this year we have been working on porting the source code for APL.68000 onto a wide variety of RISC systems (Reduced Instruction Set Computers) and our first release is for the IBM RISC System/6000 family of computers.

The RISC System/6000 is making dramatic inroads into the workstation and supermicro market and here at MicroAPL we felt it to be an appropriate first machine to support. APL.68000 running on the RISC System/6000 will bring with it a number of powerful benefits for APL users. On the one hand we have based our product specification on IBM’s APL2 specification (ensuring compliance with large system APLs). On the other hand we have included a number of features in our APL.68000 which are of major importance to the user. There are a whole host of APL language features to complement and enhance the APL2 specification. APL.68000 on the RISC System/6000 will offer a fully thought out and fully developed windowing interface for APL programmers to use. The five years that we have spent developing windowing interfaces on machines like the Mac and the Amiga have allowed us to get the interface right without the burden of all sorts of inappropriate hang-overs from previous implementations.

So what will APL.68000 for the RISC System/6000 include? Firstly it will support either dumb terminal connection or X-terminal connection. The windowing interface will use OSF/Motif and will include all the sorts of features that our Mac users are used to. We are also including on-line documentation in the shape of the entire APL.68000 manual. As usual we will not be subscribing to the theory that binary compatibility is impossible. Any APL.68000 file or workspace from any other version of APL.68000 will be directly usable on the RISC System/6000.

APL.68000 for the RISC System/6000 will be launched at APL91.

On a closing note, our many Atari ST users will be pleased to know that we have completed and are now shipping the upgrade to APL.68000 on the ST. All registered users will have been contacted by post.

items.title: Report of the Dutch APL Users Group
items.text:
In Vector 7.3 the Dutch APL Users Group reported the start of the APL ShareWare Initiative (ASWI). The recent activities of ASWI were as follows:

  1. The first activity of ASWI was to decide about the hardware platform and for which APL system the software should be developed. The result of the first discussion was as follows:

    Hardware Software primary target PC's APL2/PC secondary target Atari Mac APL.68000 II

  2. The next activity was to establish a set of standards about coding and documentation. The result of this has been submitted for publication in Vector.

  3. The third activity will be to compile a priority list of useful programs and subsequently their specifications.

On Saturday April 6th the Dutch APL Users Group organised a fair at the OASIS premises in Nieuwegein.

A number of microcomputers and workstations were installed with all available APL interpreters such as APL.68000 level I and II, IBM’s APL2/PC, Dyalog APL/386, Dyalog APL/X, APL*Plus/PC and APL*Plus II. Various people showed their products and their applications (in alphabetical order):

  • Eke van Batenburg showed a simulation for biological research in order to answer the biological question whether left-coiled snails can invade a population of right-coiled snails. Furthermore he demonstrated 2 games which were developed for his son in 1 day using APL.68000.
  • In Tom Bonnema’s booth one could get various public domain APL systems, such as I-APL, TryAPL2, Sharp APL/PC and J.
  • M.Bouwma demonstrated a very useful database package for STSC APL. This package used inverted files and contained a number of functions to create on-screen dialogues in an easy way. A substantial amount of programming was invested to ensure the integrity of the database.
  • Louis van Geldrop showed a menu system developed for APL2/PC using the new AP124 processor. He also showed 2 packages already developed for ASWI: a component file system, an object library system and a system of relational data functions for arrays.
  • Oasis hosted the whole event. The smooth organisation was mainly due to the efforts of the people of Oasis. They received the visitors in a nice and productive atmosphere. Furthermore, Oasis showed various APL interpreters.
  • Jean-Jaque Riethoven showed STAR, a package to analyse the folding of RNA strings, using APL.68000.
  • Bernard Smoor organised an extensive display of APL literature.
  • Fred Visser was present with I-APL together with English and Dutch documentation.

The fair was attended by about 60 persons among whom nine copies of STSC’s Pocket APL were raffled by Oasis Decision Support Systems B.V. The greater part of the visitors were well-known with APL, but also some new faces were discovered.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Alan Sykes

Welcome once again to Education Vector. This editorial will be my last as editor of Education Vector. It seems incredible that I have been doing the job for three years now. Tempus Fugit! It is with some regrets that I relinquish my job - on the one hand I have very much enjoyed the challenge of writing articles designed to encourage the use of APL; on the other hand, it does take time, an all too precious commodity. In any case, fresh ideas and enthusiasm generated by change is generally a good thing.

So I take this opportunity to thank all my readers who have expressed appreciation of Education Vector, including those that have sent their contributions. (See for example the Letters section this issue.) In addition I must thank Adrian Smith for his dedication in type-setting so superbly all that I have submitted, not to mention exercising his prerogative, both as type-setter and extraordinarily-capable-APL programmer, to include apposite ‘extras’ from time to time! Thanks too to all members of the British APL Association for allowing a very amateur APL programmer to benefit from close contact with the APL professionals.

What of the future for Education Vector? First of all its editorship is in the very capable hands of my friend and colleague Alan Mayer (so only half the name has changed in the new editorial address!) Secondly, I am sure the British APL Association will continue to send out copies of Education Vector to those on the mailing list. If you are a reader abroad, wish to continue receiving it, and have not yet written to me, please do so as soon as possible, so that in the near future the Association can up-date its lists accordingly.

If, however you wish to keep up to date with a somewhat wider spectrum of APL activities, may I recommend that you become a member of the Association and receive those ‘glossy’ quarterly copies of VECTOR (see Letters). (A lot of the content of VECTOR is technical, and perhaps writers of articles for VECTOR ought to be a little more careful to avoid the danger of being unnecessarily exclusive by using too much unexplained jargon. Nevertheless, it does represent remarkable value for money - there is no other APL journal to beat it. In addition the recent introduction of Random Vector, which reports on the APL Statistics Library Project, should be of interest to many readers of Education Vector.)

But back to Education Vector. To fill sixteen pages of interesting APL once a quarter is not an easy task. But it is worthwhile, as many of the letters I have received attest. Please find that extra bit of time to write up your latest APL activities for inclusion in these columns. APL professionals too have their role to play - not by using its columns just to demonstrate how clever they are, but by providing helpful hints on programming methods and idioms, tools for readers to make use of, and in short, encouragement for those of us who are still in the early stages of learning a language that has so much to offer, both in terms of intellectual enjoyment and practical usefulness.

items.title: Letters
items.text:
Since the plea in a previous column for readers (particularly those overseas) to write in to say they wish to continue receiving Education Vector a number of letters came my way which could be regarded as ‘fan’ mail. Their expressions of interest in these columns have helped to make my time as Editor very rewarding.

From: Julian Vincent, University of Reading

I have been meaning to write this letter some time - I was a member of the British APL Association for 3 years, receiving its very glossy publication Vector, and finding little in it of interest, since I am neither a totally committed APLer nor am I terrifically computer-literate . I hack around in BASIC sufficiently to be able to write routines for analysing data and controlling one or two bits of lab. machinery. However I feel that as a supervisor of research students, and also because I am curious about most things, I should acquire some knowledge of various aspects of science and its analysis. Hence my tangential interest in APL. However, your column was the only bit of Vector which I found to be consistently interesting, amusing and (even!) useful. When I realised that it would be sent to me even if I was not on the mailing list for Vector, I’m afraid I let the Vector find its own way home.

So this letter is by way of fan mail, perhaps to the extent that your little pamphlet is to me the most important bit of APL education I can pick up. Please keep sending it. If you need a subscription in the future, don’t be afraid to ask for it!

items.title: Letter from Manfred Storn
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 19

From: Manfred Storn, Euskirchen-Kirchheim, Germany.

I am a teacher in a secondary school (Hauptschule) in Germany and have been taking computer lessons since 1982.

I first met APL 3 years ago, by accident, while looking for a programming language - something like COMAL on an Atari ST. I tried C and Modula 2, saw MicroAPL and bought it. Usually I get I-APL or TRY-APL for my pupils to effect the first interest for APL which can be handled more or less by intuition and interactive work. Why write pages of code if there is APL available?

We can get a pretty good German translation of Garry Helzer’s manual at a low price, so that everybody can afford it. But I have a lot of difficulties writing complete programs which can be handled by anyone. In most of the literature there are lots of tricky or highly mathematical functions. But what I need are simple menu-structured useful programs.

At the moment the Education Vector seems the only script which can be used in secondary schools without any further adaptation. The programming code is short enough to put it into the computer without getting square eyes!

As a member of the APL-Club in Germany I get the APL-journal, but it isn’t meant to be used for introducing APL to pupils. So I have to translate some parts of the Education Vector.

Just a little information about my school: it has 260 pupils in the age range 10-17. Most still use computer C-64 (even at school); there are very few pc’s, but a lot of Amigas (for games!) and some Atari STs. Languages preferred are PL-COMAL and German LOGO for the beginner. At the moment there is a trend to let the programs remain as black boxes.

items.title: 1 Archimedes 32-bit version - I-APL/32
items.text: Paul Chapman has finished it! (He says I can’t write a paragraph without exclamation marks and brackets). Although the precision and accuracy of the arithmetic is the same as the previous version, this version gives access to all the available memory so the maximum workspace size is within a quarter megabyte of the memory installed. The disk and notes on differences will be supplied to people who have bought the previous version for £2 plus the packing charge from the enquiry address only. It includes a version of DFILE.IWS which will read or write any size of file; previous versions of I-APL only give access to the first 32K. It also includes mechanisms to convert I-APL workspaces into I-APL/32 workspaces and vice versa. All the other facilities of I-APL are available in the 32-bit version. We do not plan any other 32-bit versions of I-APL.

items.title: 2 ISI Product Changes
items.text:
ISIAPL01, ISIAPL02 and ISIAPL03 have been superseded by new products. Instead of upgrades to Sharp APL/PC these are each complete products. None of them is shareware. They each include the Sharp APL/PC system documentation, but if you already have this then you may buy disks only without documentation which is much cheaper. The advantage of the new product range is that the purchaser no longer has to carry out any upgrade process. The new product runs straight out of the wrapping. A minor disadvantage is a slight increase in cost as now what you get is three disks in the set instead of a single disk.

~~Sharp APL/PC is the same~~ mainframe version 17 with 370 emulator as before. The interpreter is shareware and is available on two disks from any owner of a copy. Its enormous range of features and facilities make it impractical for anyone but an expert to get the best out of it without the system manual.

APLI/PC is version 20 of mainframe Sharp APL. It supports APL characters on CGA, EGA and VGA. It runs on 8088, 8086 and 80286 machines and the largest workspace possible, with no shared variable processors and the minimum use of DOS memory, is 280K. There is a simplified session manager and editor and there is a simplified asynchronous comms workspace. The FSCR screen workspace is fast. There is an AP124 screen manager. There is a character mapping option which uses only the standard IBM PC character set. This can be used when there are no APL characters available or to avoid CGA graphics which makes FSCR and the editor unuseable.

APLI386/PC is version 20 for 80386 or 80486 machines only. It runs in real mode and requires an XMS driver. It gives all the APLI/PC facilities and runs about 40% faster than Sharp APL/PC. There is a SHELL facility which can run DOS commands and programs in the 640K DOS memory when the interpreter and workspace are in extended memory. Most of the other options of APLI/PC are available.

Both enhancements give colour, and, if you have VGA, function key flip between 25 and 50 row screens. Both drop some Sharp features for the sake of speed (such as the date and time stamp on file components and numeric arguments to ⎕arbin and ⎕arbout). Both require extra care with the DOS Shared variable processor.

Anthony Camacho 8 July 1991

items.title: Editorial: Windows and APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Jonathan Barman

Windows are wonderful! Most of you must be getting pretty fed up with those sentiments which seem to be getting ever more strident since Windows 3 has sold by the million.

Actually I think that windows are pretty hot stuff. My conversion came about after using OS/2 for about a year. As far as I am concerned the two key ingredients are the consistency of the user interface, and the ability to have several tasks running simultaneously.

The stated advantages of multiple tasks always seemed to me to be rather thin. Constantly switching from one task to another appeared to be a very disorganised way of working. However, having used multiple windows and multiple tasks I have now changed my tune. My basic ‘window set’ is APL in one window, the favourite text editor in another, a mainframe session in a third, and an appointments reminder running in the background. Hopping about between windows in order to use the best facilities in each seems to speed things up substantially. APL can be used as a super calculator and the results can then be pasted across into the word processor. Of course, if substantial quantities of data need to be transferred then you need functions and files, which comes down to much the same thing as running separate sessions.

The thing that really switches me on is the consistency of the user interface. Window hopping demands consistency. Constantly switching between mainframe and PC applications, where the user interfaces are so very different, is quite difficult to learn and is a bore. Most of the OS/2 applications that I have seen so far are very good, but unfortunately I have come across some which don’t stick to the rules.

Applications written in APL need to stick to the rules, as does the APL interpreter itself. Getting the APL interpreter to work with windows is a one time job, and one can only buy a version that has this feature. However, writing an APL application that is properly integrated with windows means that the APL programmer must be able to access all the windowing facilities. There should be no differences in the user interface just because the application has been written in APL. All the little features should be present, the dialogue boxes, standard editing of text, changing fonts, menu bars, buttons, etc. etc.

An APL application simply running in a window is not the same as one which is fully integrated into the environment. If I change the printer driver will the APL application know about it? The APL programmer may have taken great care to create buttons which look and feel like the real thing, but what happens if I change the button colour?

APL interpreters are now able to interface with windows. MicroAPL have had APL integrated into the Macintosh environment for some years. IBM, STSC and Dyalog have all recently announced interfaces with X Windows. We should expect a Windows 3 interface to be announced ‘real soon now’. In this issue there are several articles explaining how the interfaces work and how you can use them.

Windows programs seem amazingly complex, with several hundred function calls and as many global variables to set or access. A very low level interface is obviously desirable so that you can poke and tweak exactly what is needed, but APL’s interpretive overhead may make it too slow for some of the very low level activities - leave that for C programmers. APL needs a high level interface as well as a low level one.

I have a nasty feeling that every APL supplier will produce radically different high level interfaces. The big problem is that this is a chicken and egg situation. Until a high level interface is available it will be quite difficult to create serious, window-integrated, applications. It will be quite easy to provide APL cover functions to hide the awful window complexities, but I suspect that they may be too slow for live applications. There may be a small band of dedicated enthusiasts, but there probably won’t be a large enough group of people with strong views to influence the suppliers before something is actually produced. The APL ‘hacker’ will not be interested unless there is an interface available which is really easy to use.

This is the first issue of Vector with substantial articles about windows. Hopefully we will be able to have a constant supply of articles to keep you informed about progress on this important topic.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
The official launch of the first three volumes of ASL took place at a British APL Association meeting in London in March 1991. Jake Ansell presented Volume 1 (Basic Statistics), Tony O’Hagan demonstrated the facilities of Volume 2 (Basic Graphics) and Alan Sykes discussed the facilities and recent amendments to Volume 3 (Regression and Generalised Linear Models). This issue of Random Vector contains articles on Volumes 1 and 3.

The article by Jake Ansell and Alan Sykes, in particular, illustrates some of the reasons for starting the ASL project in the first place. In much the same way that collections of APL idioms and toolkit functions are a useful resource for general APL programming, it was felt that the use of APL for Statistical purposes could be encouraged by the provision of a range of tried and tested APL routines. As ASL enters the phase of public availability, I would like to recall some of the guidelines for ASL laid down in 1989 (Vector 6.3 - ‘ASL after Gregynog’ Tony O’Hagan):

  • ASL should consist of APL functions primarily to perform statistical calculations, with basic facilities for displaying the results, but without attempting to develop a sophisticated user interface.
  • ASL should be independent of commercial interests, and the ASL functions should be made freely available for only a nominal charge.
  • ASL should be documented in book form, giving detailed information on the functions including full code.
  • The even wider audience of users of statistics packages will need a user-friendly front-end and more eye-catching graphics. There should be a real commercial interest for companies to provide such a package. Commercial exploitations of ASL for this and other markets should be licensed so as to provide income to continue the development of ASL. The financial management should be handled through the BAA.

Now that the documentation for the first release of ASL is nearing completion, we will be able to set the prices for the various elements of ASL. As stated above, and in our other publications, it is intended that educational and personal users of ASL will only have to pay for the duplication and distribution costs of the software and documentation. Commercial users - either corporate or software houses wishing to include ASL routines in their packages - will have to enter into a licensing agreement with the BAA. As soon as we have finalised duplication details and costs we will publicise the details. In the meantime - contact the ASL committee.

Tony O’Hagan announced, at the launch of the first three volumes of ASL, that he will be standing down as Chairman of the ASL Management Committee at the next ASL Conference due to the pressure of his real work. I would like to take this public opportunity to thank Tony for all the work he has put into the ASL project over the last few years. He has contributed to the project at all levels - submitting code, testing other submissions, chairing Management Committee meetings in a relaxed and effective manner and also making a number of presentations on ASL.

As I mentioned in the last Random Vector, the next ASL conference is set to take place at Gregynog between 30 Sept and 2 Oct 1991. The only costs for delegates will be their travel expenses and we are keen to hear from interested parties who would like an invitation to attend. This will be an important staging post in the ASL project as we hope to start considering the next volumes to add to the library. We shall also be seeking nominations for a new Chairman at the conference and also for an influx of new blood onto the various ASL committees - another good reason to attend(?).

As usual, I include the contact details of the current ASL Management Committee who are:

items.title: IBM Announces APL2 for the RISC System/6000
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 59

APL2 is IBM’s strategic interactive programming language; APL2/6000 brings this powerful and productive environment to the IBM RISC System/6000 family of processors. It is a full nested array implementation under AIX, compatible with mainframe APL2 and APL2 on the PC.

The APL2/6000 session manager has the same “look and feel” as the PC and host APL products, with the added benefit of a new AP to give you a programmable interface to X-Windows, including mouse support.

items.title: The Art of Amazement
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 60

Review of article in the Guardian, 13 December 1991

APL featured in the Computer section of the Guardian last December with an article about mazes. Adrian Fisher, of Minotaur Designs, has been experimenting with maze designs and has come up with a new variant: colour mazes. Colour mazes require the walker to change colour at every junction, making it more difficult to plot a route. The traditional maze increases difficulty by restricting the view of the overall plan with high hedges. A colour maze may allow an overall view and still be sufficiently difficult to make it fun.

An example of a three-coloured maze would be one with a traffic light sequence of colours: red, yellow and green. Say you start on red. At the first junction only the yellow can be followed according to the rules. This leads to the next junction where a choice of two green routes is offered, plus a yellow path which cannot be taken. If there was no red line to this junction then this would be a dead end if you entered it on one of the green lines.

It is simple to ensure that every node has all the possible colours entering it, but it is very difficult to determine if there are any ‘black holes’ from which there is no escape, particularly if the ‘black hole’ involved a lengthy sequence of moves.

Anthony Camacho developed a maze testing program, using Sharp APL on a PC, which checks out proposed mazes prior to it being laid out for real. Anthony presented a paper about his work at the APL 89 conference. Reading the Conference Proceedings after having read the Guardian article is quite interesting as one can recognise the origin of some of the wording! Obviously the Proceedings go into much more detail than would be possible in the Guardian, but it was surprising how much one could glean from the article.

Adrian Fisher has written a book on mazes, The Art of the Maze, published by Weidenfeld & Nicolson at £18. The Guardian article did not exactly review the book, but it certainly gave the impression that it would be a well worth while purchase for anyone interested in mazes.

items.title: SovAPL 5th Anniversary Conference “APL Methodology and Application” 23-25 April 1991, Leningrad, USSR
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 61

notes by Thomas M Olsen

About 70 people attended the conference, 52 from the USSR. Most of the Soviets were for Obninsk nuclear reactor centre (near Moscow), where almost all computer work is done in APL! One woman, Aya Aibarsha, came from Almà Atà, in Kazakhstan. More were expected but, perhaps because of the recent 300% increase in USSR prices, did not arrive. Those who did were greatly appreciated. I enjoyed the young engineers, who were shy at first, but eager to speak English, with questions about Three-Mile Island. One was on his way to Chernobyl.

The conference site, with accommodation, was the Central Institute for Increasing Qualifications of Leningrad Branches (of technology etc.). Each guest room was quite comfortable, with shower-tub, window to courtyard, Soviet made colour TV and a small thermoelectric refrigerator.

In the Soviet papers I saw user-friendly menus of panels and the Cyrillic alphabet used freely. STSC APL*PLUS PC is common among Soviet APL users, but APL2/PC is gaining popularity. The Soviet APL/85 interpreter (APL90 Conf. Proc.) works only on Soviet machines.

The paper I found most interesting was A. Kononov’s, on The View of a Potential (APL) User. He saw four user categories, relating these to operating environments and specific software products. The author was asked to send a copy to ACM which may undertake to offer it in English.

There were minor technical problems at the presentations, such as no lapel microphones, or the translator getting ahead of the speaker (we spoke a paragraph at a time, waiting for this to be translated), or the moderator losing control during the Question and Answer session.

items.title: SovAPL ’91 Conference Notes by Alain Delmotte
items.text:
I was been invited to attend the annual conference of the Union of Soviet APL Users which took place on 23rd to 25th April 1991. This was my first visit to an Eastern European country. Apart from being the sixth seminar of SovAPL and the celebration of the fifth anniversary of the Association, this conference was also a kind of rehearsal for the APL92 conference. The first conference took place 62 months ago, but this was not the real start of APL in the USSR. In ’74 already there was a microcomputer with a one line display and two cassette recorders which was working in APL; but that is another story.

With the exception of some minor problems in timing and temperature in one of the conference rooms, the organisation was very good, and I must even say that the foreign visitors were almost spoiled by the kindness of our Soviet hosts. The majority of the participants were from the USSR, from as far as Almà Atà; there were some fifteen foreign guests from the USA, Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Italy and Belgium. Our Soviet friends regretted the absence of K. Iverson who unfortunately could not come.

The conference was opened by A. Kondrashev, the President of the SovAPL, with the theme: “APL Methodology and Application”. There were presentations by some of the foreign visitors and by Soviet APL users.

Perspectives of International APL Cooperation. E. Juvonen (Finland). Erkki saw this conference as the realisation of old dreams (he said that he wouldn’t even have dreamt of that as too fantastic) and was looking forward to increased cooperation. He was happy to announce APL92 in Leningrad, 6-10 July, with the theme: “APL: The Language in Common” This major event owes a lot to Erkki. Lynne Shaw (USA) gave to A. Kondrashev the Charter making SovAPL the first chapter of SigAPL/ACM in the USSR.

Academician V.P. Ivannicov supported the creation of SovAPL. He is the editor of the magazine of the Academy of Sciences “Programming”. He finds it important to see the creation of other specialised societies which could eventually be united in a Federation of Programmers’ Societies (he is himself interested in LISP).

LMFBR Diagnostics System: on the way from APL to APL2. D. Lukyanov & A. Skomorokhov (USSR). The authors work at Obninsk at the Nuclear Research Institute. APL is extensively used in the domain of monitoring radioactivity for the security of the nuclear reactors. The authors have developed several APL functions libraries accessible from menus. APL is used because the problems require frequent adjustments. The system had to be divided into sub-systems as the computer did not have enough power.

Is APL2 better than APL? J. Brown (USA). This subject is well known and doesn’t need more development.

The Soviet Union is ready for APL2. A. Skomorokhov (USSR). What is interesting here is that it is TRYAPL2 which is professionally used (waiting for the full package!). Alexander also explained his present activity in spreading TRYAPL2 in the nuclear industry, other industries, institutes, schools,.... He organises courses and seminars for schools. A lot of enthusiasm.

Practical experience with APL in the USA. T. Olsen (USA). Thomas presented his personal experience with APL (APL2) and extended the view to the other systems available (including J and Mathematica). He also gave some information on APL Journals and Publications as well as a brief view on the evolution and comparison of notation. Thomas spoke some Russian as did Erkki.

The Use of APL in the Teaching at the Technical University of Denmark. P. Gjerlof (Denmark). Per related his experience of teaching APL and problem solving for the intensive courses at the Technical University. The subjects offered to the students are life problems: wave action on sea structures, satellites, whale song recording and analysis,... The students who use APL go further and faster than those using FORTRAN (even if they have to learn APL, FORTRAN is a prerequisite for the courses). Per enjoys his teaching and finds that “There is no better means to learn and understand something than teaching it.”

R. Kornemark (Sweden) presented APL2/6000 on IBM AIX.

C. Holter (Sweden) presented APE. He had to explain the acronym WYSIWYG, especially to the interpreter. I forgot to say that all presentations were translated into either English or Russian; the interpreter standing next to the speaker.

Can APL*PLUS/PC speak Russian? A. Kondrashev & N. Puntikov (USSR). It is of utmost importance to have the APL systems speaking in both Latin and Cyrillic alphabets: keyboard access, screen displays, printers,... and it should be possible to mix the two. The authors went through different solutions but none fulfilled all the needs. They eventually designed a new character table to have the 66 Cyrillic characters along the Latin and APL ones. It still remains a problem when importing external Russian files, but this is solved by external modules.

APL-KRON Portable Russian speaking system for the IBM PC. V. Dubonikov (USSR). APL-KRON is an extended (APL2) PC-portable APL. It has been developed by the Soviet-British Joint Company “Ural/TEKNESIS”. Apart from the APL2 type of extensions, APL-KRON includes new functions for Relational DataBase management and for windows handling (including graphics). There is a language function which allows you to switch from English to Russian and back. Future plans include compatibility with FoxBase files, crossed tables, mouse support, generalised arrays. APL-KRON is a commercial product ($349) and has a runtime version.

APL as a Profession. N. Gritsenko, E. Korovina, A. Miroshnikov (USSR). The authors presented their views on the requirements of the present day APL programmer. If before, the productivity of the programmer increased by regular small steps from beginner to expert, now there is a plateau and a large step before reaching expertise. This is due to the necessity to include non-APL techniques like X-windows, networking,.... Furthermore the work can no longer be done by one person but requires a teamwork and information exchange. The authors are part of a new company, Infostroy, created in December 1990 in Leningrad by a State Building Company. Their work is primarily but not only oriented to the building industry. They also support the users of legal APL*PLUS/PC.

Non Linear Models Identification with non-Traditional Statistical Methods. V. Kupriyanof, O. Luksha, O. Obraztsov (USSR). A fully integrated system was presented to identify non-linear models. The system is interactive and provides graphical representations of the match of the identification to the observed values. The process is iterative and allows one to choose between different techniques (random search, simplex, Marquardt, bootstrap). It was first written in FORTRAN but then migrated to APL*PLUS, as the first version was bulky and required a preliminary knowledge of the model. The authors plan to move to APL2 as this would allow them to call FORTRAN routines (they have only APL*PLUS/PC v.7).

There were other presentations in parallel sessions.

The cultural activities allowed us to visit some beautiful museums and castles, including the Ermitage; but we could only have a short apercu as these would have required some months or years to appreciate fully. We had a welcome dinner, a get-together, a banquet, a wonderful ballet evening (Nutcracker), a circus evening (myself in Moscow, but the others in Leningrad).

SovAPL has created an Award for outstanding achievement in the development of APL in the USSR. The first award was granted to E. Juvonen for his action in opening the Soviet APL community to the world. A new publication was distributed during the conference. It is in Russian and is called APL Language World. Our Soviet guests, and I would prefer to say our Soviet friends, have fully understood the value of extra-session contacts and work. The participants in the “night seminars” will not forget the hard work undertaken on those occasions.

In general I was only disappointed by the excessive marketing aspect of some presentations (IBM). Also there were no representatives from other companies especially STSC. At present the APL interpreters in the USSR are either very good locally developed interpreters (on mini and now micro-computers) or APL*PLUS/PC. Why nobody from STSC? It is very difficult to understand. If the figures of Personal Computer World (Jan 90, p.104) are correct, I cannot understand that a market of 28 million micro-computers by the year 2000 is not worth moving for.

Altogether I very much enjoyed the conference and the other activities. I would then suggest: TRYAPL92. It will be a full package of APL work, cultural activities and above all hearty friendship.

items.title: “APL Under Windows”
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

From: Adrian Smith, 5th June 1991

I think someone should take STSC (and in the UK their agents Cocking and Drury) severely to task for making potentially misleading statements in a series of press releases about APL*PLUS/PC release 10. In particular, my attention was brought to this by a banner headline in “PC Shopper” magazine:

APL Under Windows

… reading on I quickly discovered that this referred simply to APL*PLUS/PC, and in my view anyone who bought the product and subsequently found that the documentation quite explicitly stated “This will run under Windows as a non-Windows application” would be justifiably annoyed. You know and I know that APL*PLUS release 9 runs quite happily under Windows, but this surely does not excuse such a blatant attempt to con the public into making yet another unnecessary upgrade.

Adrian Smith

From: Dick Bowman, 5 May 1991

The final sentence on page 37 of Vector Vol.7 No.4 contains a couple of inaccuracies which I would like to correct.

Having been part of the ACM SIGAPL Executive Board for almost 4 years now, I can say most emphatically that we consider ourselves to be an international group rather than an American one. We welcome participation from all nations and direct our activities so that the benefits of SIGAPL membership are as widely accessible as they possibly can be.

On the subject of ASL/STATGRAPHICS ‘competition’ - I can say that when the Board informally considered the possibility of contributing to ASL funding, although this was one of the factors which influenced our decision, it was not the only one.

items.title: Treasurer’s Remarks on the Annual Accounts.
items.text:
The Association’s overall bank balance has increased over the last two years. As the assets summary shows, this is largely the result of a substantial decrease in the level of outstanding debts, chiefly advertising revenue. Payments for advertising may now be considered to be up to date, so this will not be a factor in future. However, advertising revenue will continue to fall because the number of advertisements placed in Vector has halved over the last two years. This may be due in part to failure to meet publication schedules - advertisers please note that Vector now regularly appears on time!

High interest rates have contributed significantly to income recently, but can be expected to be less important in the present financial year.

Administration costs were higher in 1990/91 only because of exceptional costs incurred in sorting out the accounts for 1989/90, and may be expected to fall.

Following the change of venue from the Royal Overseas League to the IEE, there has been a considerable reduction in the cost of meetings and there will be a further reduction in the annual cost of meetings this year.

As has been explained elsewhere, the increase in subscription rates approved at the extraordinary general meeting in March was proposed by the committee so that running costs would be met by subscriptions and advertising revenue, leaving our reserves to be available to spend on projects that will promote the use of APL or otherwise benefit the APL community. The committee would welcome suggestions for suitable projects.

items.title: Stirling numbers by recursion
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 95

From: Norman Thomson, 20 May 1991

David Appleton in his article on generating Stirling Numbers of the second kind (Vol.7 No.4) concludes that it may be appropriate to use the recurrence relation:

\[\begin{equation*} \sigma^{n}_{t} = n\,\sigma^{n}_{t-1} + \sigma^{n-1}_{t-1} \end{equation*}\]

I agree, but surely the appropriate development is a recursive function, e.g. ST0 below which generates the nth row of the table:

[0]   Z←ST0 N;T
[1]   →0 IF N=Z←1
[2]   Z←(¯1⌽T)+(⍳N)×T←(ST0 N-1),0

If the entire table is required, use

[0]   Z←ST1 N;T;U
[1]   →0 IF N=↑Z←1 1⍴1
[2]   Z←U,[1](¯1⌽T)+(⍳N)×T←,(¯,N)↑U←(ST1 N-1),0

which contains redundant zeros in its upper triangle but could trivially be transformed to David’s compressed table where Stirling rows are read as diagonals.

Norman Thomson IBM UK Laboratories Ltd

items.title: X-Windows interfaces from APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 11

From: Richard Nabavi, 6th September 1991

Dear Sir,

I am sure that lots of Vector readers will have found Vector 8.1, the “Windows Special”, particularly interesting. But I fear that they may also have been unnecessarily disheartened by it. Eager to consider bringing their APL applications into the new world of X-Windows and the Motif windowing interface, they will have turned to the articles by Jensen & Beaty, and by Peter Donnelly - and they will have been horrified.

Take IBM’s X-Windows interface, AP144. A 103-line function just to do a simple “Hello World” program? The window doesn’t even appear until line 51! Is this really the kind of developer-friendly high-level software tool which is going to make life easier for us?

Maybe graphics is a bit hard. Let’s turn to Peter Donnelly’s article. After all, user dialog boxes are a pretty standard feature for windowing systems. His last example seems to address a fairly straightforward requirement - a selection list with four “radiobuttons” and two exit buttons. That shouldn’t be too difficult. But look at the code! What is all this stuff about “XmATTACH_POSITION” and “XtManageChildren”? Things are even worse here than in the “Hello World” example - you get to line 72 before you “realize the widget tree” (which I think means show the dialog box).

The problem - as always with this sort of thing - is that in both cases, the work is being done at the wrong level. It is important not to fall into the trap of providing an APL interface which comprises a one-to-one correspondence between low-level language calls - in this case the C interfaces to X-Windows and Motif - and APL functions. Whilst this may very occasionally be necessary, for 99% of cases it gives you the worst of all worlds - code which is as long-winded as C, without the advantages of C’s high speed as a compiled language and the documentation and type-checking advantages of including standard interface files.

The APL programmer does not want to know about “XtInitialize” or “XLookupString” - and he most certainly does not want to be bothered with mapping X-windows data types to and from APLs. He will not be very impressed by the fact that giving a wrong argument to a function can crash APL, as will certainly be the case if C pointers are directly manipulated from APL. He will be concerned at the CPU usage of an APL function which takes 100 lines to do a simple part of a screen display. And he will be very worried about how difficult it will be to port these massive functions to other windowing systems.

Fear not - it does not have to be done this way. The X-Windows example can be done in about nine easily-readable lines of APL. Peter’s Multiple Widget Example can be done in about eight, depending on exactly what functionality is desired (bringing up the dialog box takes three lines). It can be done using an APL system which provides sensible defaults for everything which is not explicitly specified, and which can be used without specialist X knowledge. And what is more, it can be done in such a way that the code will be portable from (say) Motif to Open Look without change. And it can be written using an APL system which itself conforms to the style guidelines of Motif, with the proper scroll bars and menus and dialog boxes built in, all controllable using the standard Motif resource mechanism.

You will not be surprised to hear that I am referring to MicroAPL’s way of doing things, as refined into APL.68000/X for Unix machines such as the IBM RS/6000. But you might be surprised - as I was - that no less than five years after we first launched our Macintosh version of APL.68000, others are still at the level of transliterating C subroutine names into APL functions, providing clever solutions to the wrong problem. The problem is not “How can we call the X-Windows C interface from APL?”, but “How can we avoid having to call the X-Windows C interface from APL?”.

Richard Nabavi MicroAPL Ltd

items.title: News from Sustaining Members
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 13

Compiled by Alison Chatterton

items.title: Cocking & Drury
items.text:
Cocking & Drury is delighted to welcome Dave Ziemann back to the fold following his round-the-world (or halfway-and-back- again) travels.

We have had a busier summer than expected. STSC have been advertising APL*PLUS heavily in US magazines like Byte and Dr Dobbs Journal. This has led to a large number of leads from their UK readers.

We are also about to ship upgrades to existing APL*PLUS II customers to Version 3.5. This allows users to exploit the multi-tasking Windows environment and is the first step in a process which will lead to a full GUI version of APL*PLUS II, running under the true 32-bit Windows NT environment, together with a Windows toolkit and DDE support. This migration path will maintain compatibility with existing versions of APL at the same time as taking advantage of the Windows environment.

Version 4 - the next step in that development - is already in Beta-test and is expected for release early in 1992.

We also had a busy time at the Software Tools '91 exhibition in June. We met a lot of people - new faces as well as old - and collected a large number of leads both for APL*PLUS and for Smalltalk.

STSC have announced new pricing structures for Run-Time for APL*PLUS PC and II. The price of PC Run-Time falls by over 60% (!) and Developer Kits for both - giving unlimited distribution rights for APL*PLUS Run-Time applications - become more readily available and more affordable. We have also been able to reduce our pricing on most APL*PLUS PC and II System products by up to 34%; details in the next Product Guide.

There is also a limited special offer on APL*PLUS Mainframe add-on software with 50% off the APL*PLUS Compiler and 25% off most other add-ons. Bargain basement time!

Both consultancy and course business are recovering slowly from the effects of the recession with prospects for the final quarter already better than the previous six months.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
At APL91 in August, MicroAPL announced what is probably our most important new product for some years - APL.68000/X for the IBM RISC System/6000. APL.68000/X is the first version of APL.68000 for IBM hardware and the first implementation of our APL windowing interface to run under X-Windows, using OSF/Motif. This marks the culmination of two years' development work on our range of APL interpreters to upgrade them to include second generation features and to allow them to run on computers which use RISC technology.

APL.68000 now conforms closely to the APL2 language specification for second generation APLs. This means that a serious APL user can now standardise on one dialect of APL in the confident expectation of being able to run the same APL code on virtually any hardware platform - a consideration of key importance bearing in mind the current, entirely reasonable, drives towards software standardisation and the 'downsizing' of applications.

Our latest issue of a MicroAPL News, issued to coincide with APL91, discusses how we have managed to port APL.68000 onto RISC systems such as the RISC System/6000 and retain the advantages of Assembly Language source code. We still have one master set of source code for APL.68000, with all the advantages this brings in terms of source code control. As far as the user is concerned, it also means that APL workspaces written using any version of APL.68000 can be immediately loaded and run by any later version of APL.68000.

APL.68000/X is now completing its beta test program and we shall shortly start shipping the first release. We have also announced proposals to cover run-time variants. We shall be supplying developers with a 'packager' which takes an APL workspace and 'packages' it with an interpreter to make a single executable file. Having bought the packager, developers will be free to distribute as many packaged copies of their application as they wish without further licence fees being payable to MicroAPL. We believe that this is the first time such as scheme has been applied to a Unix-based APL. We are confident that, like our free runtime policy on smaller machines such as the Apple Macintosh, this approach will encourage professional software developers to use APL for developing general applications.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Limited
items.text:
Those members of Dyadic who took part in the exhibition at APL91 reported a busy stand and a high level of interest from attendees.

Pride of place on Dyadic's stand was given to a PC running an early version of Dyalog APL/W for Windows 3.0. Although the planned release date for this new product is not until January 1992, visitors to the stand were able to gain a very good idea of what it will look like and how it will operate. In particular, the Dyalog APL session, editor and tracer were shown fully operational, popping up and down using genuine windows, and looking just like the X Windows implementation of the product. Being the first APL to be fully integrated with the Windows GUI, Dyalog APL/W generated some excitement and early orders.

Dyadic was also showing Dyalog APL Version 6.1 under DOS and the same version under X Windows on an IBM RISC System/6000 and a Sun SPARCstation 2. The new version includes the facility to display the value of a variable in a window. This lets you browse large arrays in a convenient fashion, and you can watch values change as you execute code. Coupled with the Tracer, this new facility is a great aid to debugging.

On the IBM RS/6000, Dyadic was demonstrating an Auxiliary Processor interface to OSF/Motif. This experimental AP lets you drive all of the Motif widget set and produce end-user applications, written in Dyalog APL, that conform fully to the OSF/Motif Style Guide. Dyadic originally developed this AP to investigate strategies for integrating the Dyalog APL Screen Manager (⎕SM/⎕SR) with Motif and other GUIs such as Windows 3.0 and Presentation Manager. Although integration with ⎕SM is Dyadic's intended direction, the AP can be made available as a stand-alone product if required. Anyone interested in obtaining a copy should contact Dyadic.

Dyadic has announced an implementation of Dyalog APL for the Hewlett-Packard HP9000 Series 700 range. The HP9000-720 delivers 57 MIPS and 17 MFlops, while the 730 is even faster at 76 MIPS and 22 MFlops. In APL benchmarks, the "entry-level" 720 runs 3 times faster than a 25MHz 486 on general operations, and up to 10 times faster on floating-point calculations.

items.title: APL People Limited
items.text:
We continue to work towards 1992 and the advent of the Single European Market by cultivating our contacts overseas - we have just helped a major financial institution in Switzerland to recruit an APL specialist from the UK for a year's contract. So come on, all you employers out there looking for skilled APLers in France, Germany, Switzerland, Sweden, Spain and elsewhere - give me a ring! I've got lots of really good people eager to widen their horizons by working abroad (some already have foreign language skills). The recession in the UK means that many people are prepared to accept very modest rates or salaries at the moment.

However, I'm sure that most of you reading this will be pleased to read that we have detected signs that the economy is starting to pick up at long last. Several companies have been recruiting at graduate trainee level, although at the time of writing, I still have one or two graduates with APL experience yet to be placed, and would be keen to hear from any companies who might be interested.

On the software side. our sister company, APL Manufacturing, looks set to secure a contract to supply £70,000 of software to a manufacturer of Formula 1 Grand Prix racing cars - so we're all hoping to swap our boring old company Fords for something a bit faster!! Going from one extreme to another, PEFAC, the estimating system written in APL, has been sold to a company employing just 8 people! The last time this happened, using PEFAC enabled the company concerned to expand its workforce to 50 within the year! The software has also been sold recently to a furniture manufacturer, employing disabled people, which has resulted in a number of enquiries from similar factories elsewhere.
