items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Alan Mayer

Welcome to Education Vector. The more observant reader (who bothers to look at the front page) may have noticed a change of four letters in the name and address of the editor. The bad news is that the change occurs in the surname: after three hard but successful years of entertaining and educating us, Alan Sykes has made his first big mistake and handed the job over to me. The good news is that I work in the office next door to Alan, and he has assured me that he will continue to take a lively interest in the affairs of Education Vector.

I know that I write on behalf of many of you when I thank Alan for what the journal has become under his leadership - I know, because I have inherited a whole file full of letters expressing your appreciation. Perhaps the aspect I appreciate most is that we have all been encouraged to take part by contributing our thoughts, our objections, our prejudices, our APL functions - so that others may benefit from our experience (and our mistakes!).

So how can we build on the foundation that has been laid? May I emphasise the word we - everything written in these pages is open to every reader to criticize (constructively if possible!). Personally, I identify two major objectives: to encourage beginners in APL, and to promote the use of APL in Education. I believe that considerable progress is being made on both of these fronts, and I know of several individuals who are using Education Vector for these purposes. Perhaps there is also a third objective: to create new "beginners". In other words, I want articles, letters, suggestions please - not for myself, but for the thousands of people out there who need APL, but don't know it yet.

Among those thousands, I suggest that a major target should be secondary school teachers. I have been told that many of them are too busy with the National Curriculum to spend time on "side-lines" like APL. Part of their problem seems to lie in the area of coordinating and manipulating marks from tests. Perhaps we should tell them about a computer language that makes that sort of task much easier?

I know that there is much more to the National Curriculum than coordinating marks - but don't let that stop you from telling me! How? Well, like your latest notebook computer, I respond to several modes of data entry: post, telephone, fax, email (I even talk to people sometimes!). The relevant addresses and numbers are on the title page. This edition contains contributions from several readers, for which we are all grateful. Why not add your name to the contributors' list for the next edition?

items.title: Letters
items.text:
From: Robert L. Briechle, Cleveland, Ohio.

IF-THEN-ELSE (Education Vector, April 1991, p.27)

A slight modification to allow the simpler construct, IF-THEN without the ELSE to operate if that was desired:

      ∇ R←A ELSE B
[1] ⍝---FL1: IF <APL chrstr> THEN <APL chrstr>
                             ELSE <APL chrstr> construct
[2]  M←(⍴A←,A)⌈⍴B←,B ⋄ R←(2,M)⍴(M↑A),M↑B
      ∇

      ∇ IF S
[1] ⍝---FL1: IF <APL chrstr> THEN <APL chrstr>
                             ELSE <APL chrstr> construct
[2] ⍎S
      ∇

      ∇R←C THEN A
[1] ⍝---FL1: IF <APL chrstr> THEN <APL chrstr>
                             ELSE <APL chrstr> construct
[2] ⍎(~¯1+⍴⍴A)/'→0,0⍴R←(⍎C)/A' ⋄ R←A[1+~⍎C;]
     ∇

I write APL code entirely without interaction with any humans, relying heavily on VECTOR, SIGAPL and the like for guidance. If you can recommend a good screen data input facility, I’d sure like to hear about it. I have written four or five for specialized use myself and have looked at several packages and bought one of them. I do not wish to have my workspaces prostituted with all kinds of objects about which I know little and which are named to conventions different from my own. I want a single object, perhaps written in C, which can be invoked on a setup basis (giving it a map of the screen together with a table of fields and attributes) and then called to manage screen input, allowing functions of my own to be executed (optionally) upon leaving any field. I want the data to be automatically sent from the screen to be scrollable or pageable up and down as I need that. And I want function-key-callable dialog boxes and information messages to pop up as needed. I know there are products which meet some or all of these requirements. If you know of any which you can recommend, I’d appreciate it.

(Editor’s comment: Any suggestions will be forwarded. If they are of general interest, they will be published.)

items.title: Let's Integrate - Using APL (Education Vector, July 1991, p.22)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 20

From: Tony O’Hagan, University of Nottingham.

Let’s Integrate - Using APL (Education Vector, July 1991, p.22).

I would just like to make a technical point about Simpson’s rule. Applied to 3 points it is unarguably a good thing. It integrates a quadratic exactly, and so on. You can easily justify the weight 4 in the middle because of smoothness of the function. Whichever way it curves, the area under a piecewise linear interpolant (trapezium rule) underestimates or overestimates the integral according as the middle point is high or low. So we want more weight than the value 2 given by the trapezium rule.

What is not sensible is applying the rule repeatedly on 2m+1 points with weights 1, 4, 2, 4,…, 4, 1. I know this is often found in textbooks, but think about it. That will integrate exactly a function that is piecewise quadratic. That is, a quadratic on intervals 1 and 2, then a different quadratic on 3 and 4, and so on. Why is this sensible? Why not a function that is quadratic on intervals 2 and 3, 4 and 5, etc.? That makes just as much sense. Why not use that, with a bit of trapezium rule on the first and last intervals? Then you get weights 1.5, 2.5, 4, 2, 4,…, 4, 2.5, 1.5. If this is just as good as the other, why not average the two sets of weights, giving 1.25, 3.25, 3, 3,…, 3, 3.25, 1.25. Now you have almost exactly got back to the trapezium rule with weights proportional to 1, 2, 2,…, 2, 1.

There is no good heuristic argument for weighting the even points 4 and the odd points 2. Repeated use of Simpson’s rule looks odd, and it really does not make sense. I always use the trapezium rule for a lot of equally spaced points in one dimension. (In high dimensions, when the sheer number of function evaluations is a problem, then we need other rules, but I still do not use Simpson’s in practice.)

items.title: More String Manipulations (Education Vector, July 1990)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 21

From Peter Branson, Uxbridge, Middlesex.

More String Manipulations (Education Vector, July 1990)

In this article, Alan Sykes gives a little function named DAYOFWEEK which, given the month and year, finds the weekday number (starting with Monday). Alan attributes DAYOFWEEK to Jerry Turner and professes to not even trying to understand it. As they say: “Me too, neither!”. Instead, I give below an alternative called WEEKDAY, which I believe is rather easier to understand:

      ∇WD←WEEKDAY;CONST;YRMO;DAYS
[1] ⍝ Get day of the week     Peter B  Util  Apr 91
[2] CONST←0 8 25 5 1 9 5 13 21 17 25 21
[3] YRMO←(⎕TS[1]-1900)+CONST[⎕TS[2]]
[4] WD←7|⎕TS[3]+(7|YRMO)+⌊((28|YRMO)+3)÷4
[5] ⍝
[6] ⍝ To return name of day, instead of no, add next 2 lines
[7] ⍝ DAYS←7 4⍴'SUN MON TUE WED THU FRI SAT '
[8] ⍝ WD←DAYS[WD;]
      ∇

Note the different calling syntax since it doesn’t need any arguments at all. Also there are a suggested couple of fairly obvious extra lines which can be de-commented to give the name of the day, instead of the number, if preferred. Note also that I am a bit more conventional, so Sunday is Day 1 here.

On the same sort of theme, another sometimes-useful utility function, using a similar technique, is JULDAY which gives the Julian Day number:

      ∇JD←JULDAY
[1] ⍝ Get Julian day number  Peter B  Util  Nov 90
[2] JD←0 31,(28+0=4|⎕TS[1]),31 30 31 30 31 31 30 31 30
[3] JD←⎕TS[3]++/⎕TS[2]↑JD
      ∇

items.title: Guest Editorial: Wanted: Programmer Support
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

Guest Editorial by Gregg W Taylor

Extended APLs are no longer new products. By now, there should be evidence of a fair amount of proficiency in the use of nested arrays, user-defined operators, and the various new functions that manipulate nested arrays. Yet, I am compelled to say that the level of proficiency in these areas is disappointingly low.

I have not collected hard evidence in the form of surveys or extended research; this conclusion is based on observations I have made at several corporations, several user groups, and chats with other APLers. As a disclaimer, I will say that there is a good amount of code that is being written using extended features - by a few good programmers. But the majority (!) of people that use APL to program are still using a small subset of the capabilities available to them. WHY?

I think there are four basic reasons:

  • the cost and effort of conversion
  • the prices of the newer systems tend to be higher
  • extended systems seem more complicated
  • a lack of good examples

I will briefly cover these in the order listed.

Moving out of flat APL into the broader realm of ragged arrays and the each operator is really not that difficult. Migration tools are provided, and by and large, flat APL is a proper subset of nested systems. But on a practical basis, there are those nagging differences. IBM no longer supports the 124 processor; strand notation and ambivalent functions allow code that once failed to now successfully execute; and if you have never tested for complex numbers, you may be inclined to start. In short, it is a simple application that migrates trivially; the more sophisticated, the more considerations.

And I know of large corporations that are intimidated by the prospect of migrating hundreds, or even thousands, of workspaces out of a system that is working fine. This situation is worsened by purists (like myself) who have to improve the systems in the process by rewriting existing methodologies. All of this is for the better, mind you; but it is all at a cost.

The newer systems, mainly on the PC, tend to carry higher price tags. IBM has reduced the price of their mainframe product to approximately the VSAPL price, and their APL2PC product is still $500, but compare STSC's two PC offerings. I am not suggesting that there should not be a price differential between flat APL and an extended system, but I do think the pricing should be accessible to the fellow who can afford an 80386 machine. When you can buy C compilers and assemblers for under $200 (and even under $100 in some cases), it's no wonder that even $500 seems high. Is APL priced more for corporations than individuals?

But I can't blame the vendors for the programmer inertia which prevents (flatland) APLers from learning to use the extended systems. I remember my own misgivings about learning a new way to do APL - all the timings that had to be done, all the new idioms to be discovered, the pitfalls to be avoided. It is easier to just keep on doing things the same old way. For me, this is the most frustrating thing to witness - complacent programmers, no longer interested in growing in their professions.

Some have said that the new flavours of APL are simply too complicated. I even remember listening to one APLer saying that, since a printer could only print pages, why work in dimensions higher than two? More sophisticated data structures are intended to more closely model more complicated physical realities. Flat APL provided a method of organising data dimensionally; extended APLs provide a broader range of data structures, hence a close match with real data in more situations. Once the data structure is decided upon, the other new features are needed to manipulate that data.

The process of abstraction and generalisation leads to richer structure and function. To paraphrase Einstein: keep things as simple as possible, but no simpler. Some solutions are not adequate when over-simplified. Extended APLs provide more capabilities when dealing with non-trivial problems.

If the new APLs are more complicated, I think this is a result of the lack of understanding about them. Once you get acquainted with and use the new features, it becomes a lot more difficult to solve a problem using flat APL. Overcoming the reluctance to learn new tricks and the fear of not catching on quickly are the two real problems facing APL programmers, not the language itself.

But the learning process could be made a lot simpler if there were more samples of good coding techniques in the extended APLs. Not all of us will do the timings, discover the nifty algorithms, and warn of the nasty pitfalls. Yet publications like this one are much too rare, and there are only a few books on techniques in extended APLs. The New York APL users' group has undertaken, with the support of the SIGAPL, the compilation of a book of APL phrases that deal only with extensions in the various dialects. This promises to be quite good - hopefully combining good coding style with interesting idioms, all the while illuminating the differences in the several flavours of APL available today.

Really getting the newer APLs into proper use is not that difficult a task. But it will require the efforts of corporations, vendors, programmers, and (a few) writers. It's hard, and often expensive, to keep up with new technology. Hardware has typically outstripped software in these areas, but I dare say that extended APLs are in the software vanguard, waiting for more of us to catch up.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
The copy for this issue of the ASL Newsletter is being compiled as preparations for the third ASL Statistics Conference near completion and I shall be discussing the topics that we hope to cover at the conference. A number of us who are involved in the ASL project have just returned from APL91 at Stanford University and, in common with other articles in this issue of Vector, we shall report on the ASL presentation at APL91.

We take the opportunity to reprint David Appleton's article on Stirling Numbers which was savaged by the printers in an earlier issue of Vector and finally Tony O'Hagan steps down as ASL Chairman with some parting thoughts.

As usual, I include the contact details of the current ASL Management Committee who are (unless voted out at Gregynog!):

items.title: ASL at APL91
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 35

Members of the ASL project were invited to give a tutorial presentation at APL91. Alan Hawkes, Alan Sykes and Alan Mayer from Swansea and Jake Ansell from Edinburgh gave a 90-minute team presentation on the ASL project. The audiovisual team at Stanford obviously deeply resented being asked to do anything as demeaning as audiovisuals and managed to live down to their customary low standards, but despite this the large audience of early birds who attended evidently enjoyed the presentation and were able to see most of the material being presented.

Alan Hawkes gave an introductory overview which covered the original aims of ASL and the way in which the ASL project has taken shape over the last few years. He outlined why it was originally felt that another set of APL functions for Statistical work might be beneficial to the APL community - and mentioned some of the standard works in this area (see the references I reproduce at the end of this review). Alan felt that the relative lack of success of earlier works in this area might be due to the common preference exhibited by APLers to write their own code rather than using code written by someone else. The ASL project hopes to overcome this ‘acceptance’ hurdle by the production of a definitive range of APL functions and, perhaps most importantly, functions which are supported by a large group of APL statisticians. This will lead ultimately to a comprehensive range of APL Statistics functions for all types of analysis. In a sense ASL could be thought of as a statistical equivalent of the Fortran NAG library.

At that stage it was realised that the concept should go beyond these bounds. It was necessary to create not just another set of APL software for Statistics but a wholly new concept. A unified structure and philosophy was required. It was subsequently perceived that the ASL project was attempting to create, paraphrasing APL itself, a statistical language.

There was an important realisation of the need to define the market of future users of ASL which arose out of the discussions held at the first ASL Workshop. It was fairly easy to list those who might use or be encouraged to use ASL: APL Statisticians, those teaching Statistics, Statistical Research workers, users of Statistics, etc. The real question was which group had priority? For the sound reason of knowing the group it was felt that ASL should attempt initially to satisfy APL Statisticians. Next would be college teachers of Statistics with the aim of exposing undergraduate students to ASL and hence APL. In Britain this could well be all students except those in the Arts Faculties. Once exposed, it was hoped that they would remember APL and wish to apply it in the future over a diverse range of careers. A potential consequence is the further acceptance of APL within colleges and hence its spread into other areas. This established in our minds the key aim of ASL, which is to increase the use of APL, not just within Statistics but as widely as possible. The production of a suite of good APL Statistics functions then becomes almost a by-product of the main objective.

Alan Hawkes cited a number of references to APL in statistics and I reproduce some here:

Anscombe, F.J. [1981], ‘Computing in Statistical Science through APL’, Springer-Verlag, New York.

Douglas, J. ‘Stat APL’.

Grenander, U. [1982], ‘Mathematical Experiments on the computer’, Academic Press, New York.

Hawkes, A.G. [1990], ‘Markov Processes in APL’, APL Quote Quad, Vol 20, No 4, 175-185.

Smillie, K.W. [1969], ‘Statpack 2: An APL Statistical Package’, 2nd Edition, Dept of Computing, University of Alberta Publication.

Jake Ansell then outlined the design philosophy that has evolved over the course of the ASL project and the way in which the software production cycle has been managed, paying a particular tribute to Maurice Jordan’s work in the automatic testing of APL code. For more details on these two topics, see Jake’s article in Vector 8.1 ‘Bottom Shelf: Basic Statistics) and Maurice’s paper published at APL91 (APL91 proceedings, ‘CATS - Computer Aided Testing of Software’).

The main part of the tutorial was based around live demonstrations of the three ASL Volumes now available - Basic Statistics, Generalised Linear Regression and Basic Graphics. The first two, Basic Statistics and Generalised Linear Regression are available to run under APL*PLUS, Dyalog APL, APL.68000 and APL2/PC. Basic Graphics is currently written for Dyalog APL with ports to other interpreters under way.

Alan Sykes ran the tutorial on Regression and Basic Graphics and Jake Ansell gave the tutorial on Basic Statistics. Alan Mayer managed admirably in typing the examples as fast as the presenters introduced them.

Of the three sessions, I have chosen to include the Basic Statistics tutorial here. The Basic Statistics volume of ASL has so far had least coverage in Random Vector and this tutorial should serve as a good introduction to the scope of the functions included in the volume.

items.title: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 49

by Tony O’Hagan

As I step down from the ASL Management Team, I thought it might be useful to take stock of what has and has not been achieved so far with the project. This may help to set priorities and realistic objectives for the future.

What have we got? By the time of the third ASL conference, we should have formally released the first three volumes. Although they are late in coming, their actual release is a landmark in ASL. We must ultimately leave it to others to judge how good they are, but I believe they already form a very useful set of tools for any statistician. Volume 1 gives us a valuable collection of basic calculations. Even I sometimes want significance points of standard distributions, or want to calculate a correlation matrix, and having those functions so conveniently to hand is great.

Volume 2 gives me a really good toolkit for building graphs. They are much quicker and easier to use than the basic low-level graphics functions supplied with most commercial interpreters, but much more flexible than the high-level suites of ‘presentation graphics’ functions that are often also provided. Of course, you cannot use Volume 2 yet if it is not yet implemented for your graphics system, but that is a good reason to call loudly for an implementation or port to your system (or do it yourself!).

Volume 3 gives me a very powerful system for linear and generalised linear models. Many statisticians will need nothing more.

I think that we can be proud of what has been achieved so far, so if I now go on to dwell on what has not been done it is not meant as a criticism. The fact is, one can always do more and better. It is easy to focus on the ‘more’, which in ASL terms means starting on new volumes, but it is useful to think a little about the ‘better’ - how we can improve on what we have done.
path: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?

items.title: Programming Standards
items.text:
We set out with high ideals. ASL was to set the standard for statistical work in APL. Functions would be well designed, well programmed and well documented. I think we have achieved the first of these, because in my opinion the functions are well designed. We have not achieved the other two.

I know it is difficult to say what constitutes good APL code, but I am pretty sure that very little of what we have done would satisfy the best professional programmers. I know this to be a fact for Volume 2 because I wrote most of the final version! It was my first attempt at using second generation APL features in a serious application, and I am sure that I must have used them badly in many places. Alan Sykes would not claim to write consistently good APL either. Like me, he has learnt a lot through ASL, but Volume 3 grew out of a much older workspace, and probably looks patched and messy to any professional programmer. We talked about publishing our code, as part of ‘setting the standard’: with the current versions that would be unwise! It is debatable whether we should really try for good code, or settle for code that works. What should we do with future volumes?
path: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
We also hoped to produce good documentation. A standard was set for internal documentation by comments. It was never written down and enforced, and I am afraid that under pressure to produce Volume 2 even this fell by the wayside. Did Volumes 1 and 3 manage to get this part right?

Documentation also means user manuals and technical manuals. This is something else that slipped through lack of time and manpower, but if ASL is to succeed it is vitally important. I believe that we must set as a high priority the production of high quality documentation of Volumes 1 to 3, in a consistent ASL-standard format, and that this must be maintained for future volumes. It is no good having good software if nobody can understand how to use it.

We also planned a book to introduce non-APLers to doing statistical analysis with ASL. This is a very big nettle that I believe must also be grasped. We know what we want to do; we even have a major publisher interested. But who will write it? And will it be done soon enough to be of any use?
path: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?

items.title: The Library
items.text:
ASL was expected to grow so big that good management tools would be needed for any user to draw into the workspace precisely the functions needed for the job. A Working Party was going to develop these, but did not deliver. As it happens there was no real urgency because ASL is not yet that big, but that is not a satisfactory view. We designed the functions carefully and we should design the library and its management carefully from the outset. Otherwise we will end up with volumes that need major revision to fit whatever format is ultimately chosen.

We talked endlessly about naming conventions and even appointed a ‘custodian of names’, but he was never given any names to take custody of! Who knows whether we have made any blunders? I know that in Volume 2 there is an odd hang-over from earlier conventions in the use of ASL as a prefix to names of global variables, but not as a prefix to function names. There was simply not enough time to resolve this.
path: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?

items.title: Implementing WAGS
items.text: If Volume 2 is to be of any real value, a high priority must be its implementation on as wide a variety of systems as possible. We have a Dyalog PC version that works on screen and outputs to some printers, but is not tested on other printers because we did not have them available. We have an APL*PLUS PC version that works on screen with the (obsolete) ⎕G graphics but is not reliable for output on a printer. That is all. We do not need to do the development work ourselves if vendors are willing to take on implementations for their own systems. But we should take the lead in positively encouraging them to do so. Then what do we do about the ones that we know will not yield to that persuasion?
path: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?

items.title: Future Manpower
items.text:
I have spent some time on saying just how Volumes 1 to 3 fail to deliver at the level of our early high hopes. In thinking about the future of ASL, we should ask why. The reason is that wonders were achieved with the available resources, but the available resources were inadequate. Each one of the three volumes was developed by one or two dedicated people in their spare time. The work they put in dwarfs the input of any other person in ASL. Again, I am not really criticising. Whereas it was clear that without their efforts there would be no software, the effort of other people was always more marginal. Our working party on Standards and Implementation did relatively little not because of a lack of goodwill, but because the software could be produced (and was produced) largely without them.

So there are two manpower issues to face. How do we get new people to develop whole new volumes (particularly if they can guess how much work the first three entailed)? And how to we get goodwill to turn into a comparable amount of time and effort from those whose involvement is more peripheral? A lot of what I have said about the shortcomings of the current offerings revolves around the failure to bring forward this second kind of manpower - and make no mistake, this is just as important as getting in people to write new volumes.

We also need to decide whether we can make better use of a specialist programmer than we did do. Perhaps we were unlucky in the ways things worked out this time, but I have my doubts whether such a programmer can ever play a big part in the original development of a volume. There may be a compensating case, however, for a specialist programmer to come along afterwards to add any internal documentation, ensure adherence to standards (when we have them) and improve coding.
path: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?

items.title: Not doing everything that the last minute
items.text:
One thing is clear, software always ends up with a frantic rush to deliver by some date. No matter how many times the delivery date is postponed (which is usually somewhere near infinity) there is always a last minute rush. In fact, the more postponements it has had the more bouts of frantic effort the poor finished product will carry the scars of!

Therefore we cannot expect the refinements of good documentation, thorough testing and good coding to be put in at the end. Either they are built in all the way through or they will not be there at the first release. I have a suggestion - we should try hard to build in these refinements all the way through but, when we inevitably fail, we should plan for an early second release in which they are all there.

So, give Release 1 of Volumes 1 to 3 a few months to find the main bugs, then go full ahead to give Release 2 all the good things that I have said they lack at the present. Now is the time to recruit an experienced programmer to work on that. Now is the time to get the Standards and Documentation teams up to speed.
path: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?

items.title: Some final words
items.text: I am sorry I could not be at Gregynog this time. I hope to be involved with ASL in the future, through a continuing interest in Volume 3, as a user of ASL and perhaps as a contributor to new volumes. I would like to see ASL go from strength to strength, still trying to set ‘the standard’. Although lofty ideals must always be compromised in practice, let us not lose those ideals. They are what drives us forward.
path: ASL - where have we got to and where do we go from here?

items.title: Gregynog 91
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 49

By the time you read this, the third ASL Conference will have just taken place at the University of Wales Conference Centre at Gregynog. We are expecting the usual 30 plus delegates of whom about half will be from the academic community. Our university delegates will include representatives from Swansea, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Newcastle and Monterey. The conference is primarily devoted to consolidating and advancing the ASL project.

Presentations are being given on testing ASL functions and also on proposals for ASL utilities. As the project gets larger and the software is released under more APL interpreters, this aspect of testing and management becomes more important. On the statistical front we have presentations which propose future volumes for the ASL:

Time Series Smoothing and Density Estimation Contingency Tables Non-Linear Regression

and we shall be seeking to reach some collective consensus about the form and content of these shelves. We also will be seeking to review our experiences in working on the first three volumes of ASL, so that we can make life a little bit easier for the next volumes. items.title: APL 91 Report: Conference Round Up
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 56

reported by Anthony Camacho

APL 91 was a social, financial and technical success. About 400 people attended, well over the break-even figure and all visible signs were that everything went to plan.

A Typical Stanford Arcade

We stayed in the student accommodation. We would not have paid $110 a day for our non-air conditioned room with communal washing and lavatories if we had known w e could get a good clean air conditioned motel room for $41 a day. The $69 a day difference would have paid to hire a car and eat grandly, leaving plenty over. The food, though not worth anywhere near $69 a day, was excellent. I didn't hear a single complaint about it.

There was no formal banquet; I don't know whether it was replaced by the Exploratorium Evening or by the final barbecue picnic. The food and drink at both were excellent.

Sessions began early at 0830 and I felt we were worked really rather hard, but the quality of the papers I attended was as high as any conference I've been to.

The Conference Proceedings, edited by Jan Engel, were if anything of a higher standard than ever before. I am sorry that the Danish precedent could not be followed. I would have benefited greatly from a chance to read proceedings before the conference. I found I simply did not have time to look at papers before attending presentations and that too many presenters assumed that I had. Every evening was occupied, some by more than one event. Sunday evening there was a welcome reception, Monday an Exhibitors' reception and a Russian evening, Tuesday the Exploratorium, Wednesday a visit to Fry's and on Thursday, for some hours after the final session there was the final picnic.

The Software Exchange

The panels I attended were better than most previous conferences. Each speaker seemed to have something prepared which was a reasonable length for the time allotted. The worst over-run was the 25 year panel - Ken only began to speak after it should have ended - but Roy Sykes was right to let it run.

The plenary speakers were Phil Smith of IBM on IBM's Personal Scientific Laboratory, Therese Myers of and on Quarterdeck Office Systems, Dr William Scherlis of DARPA and Ted Nelson of the Xanadu hypermedia project. Phil Smith did a neat demonstration and William Scherlis gave an excellent summary of DARPA's work on the computer side. Therese Myers, whose excellent products I use, seemed to me to do a straight plug for her company. Ted Nelson went on too long and had too few visual aids.

Tresidder Union was a good place to hold the exhibition. It was equipped with cafes and a bar. There was plenty of space to sit and talk or rest. The notice board, the enquiry desk and the software library were well arranged.

There was also a museum of historical APL exhibits - first editions, the first logon to a cleanspace and an interesting collection of APL ephemera - tags, stickers, labels, posters and so on. The museum exhibits were collected and displayed by George Mendonsa, who would be glad to hear of other items which could be given or lent to the museum for next time it is displayed.

People talking - at the Exploratorium

The Exploratorium describes itself as 'a playful museum where you make discoveries for yourself'. It has over 650 experiments which the visitor can take part in, arranged in 13 large subject areas. A good many APLers are overgrown kids and this suited us perfectly. The experiments are designed with flair: you are sat on a freely rotatable stool before you try to turn a bicycle wheel gyroscope through 90 degrees; there are trays of soap bubble mixture and frames to dip into them; there are wind (with condensed water vapour) and water (with sand) vortices; lots of things to hit or listen to; dozens of computer keyboards controlling things and even frogs' legs and octopus nerves set up to respond to controllable electrical stimuli. Among all this were tables of several varieties of ethnic food and more tables giving out as much beer or wine as you wanted to drink. I never got to the beer, and it was good beer, because the wine was so good. It was the right recipe for an excellent evening. I had a wonderful time. Congratulations to all concerned.

The conference debriefing is really confidential, but I'm sure I don't reveal too many secrets by saying that when the Meeting Planning Associates staff left (before we went on to discuss the future) they were given a spontaneous ovation.

reported by Jonathan Barman

One of the best things about any conference is meeting people, and this conference was no exception. The social events were informal and relaxed, and it seemed easier than usual to mix and talk APL and other gossip.

Hiring the whole of the Exploratorium for the evening normally reserved for a formal banquet was a brilliant idea. The Exploratorium caters for children with enquiring minds which exactly fits the APLers attending the conference. There was so much to do and see that if I had tried to cover all the items there would have been no time to eat or chat.

There was an evening outing to a computer supermarket called Fry's. I experienced culture shock due to the sheer quantity and range of goods for sale. The store was laid out in much the same was as a conventional supermarket. There must have been over 100 different computers on display, and there was a complete aisle of shelves filled with different sorts of fax machines, and another with telephones, then another with memory chips, and it seemed to go on and on.

Charles Schulz, Therese Myers, Tibor Horvath

The administration of the conference was excellent. The only area where there was a minor slip was for the tutorials. As the tutorials started at 8:30am on the Sunday, before registration, everyone who booked should have been notified when and where they started. There was a bit of milling about, but everything was soon sorted out.

reported by John Searle

APL91 was a very successful conference, with over 400 delegates, which I understand was the break-even point for financial success. Stanford University is a charming campus and a very lively place at all hours. I think that the Stanford Bookstore is the best technical bookshop I have ever been in.

The campus accommodation was adequate and clean, even though I did tend to bounce off my bed whenever I lay on it. Or perhaps that was the fault of the late night glasnost sessions. (For "glasnost" read "vodka".)

reported by Ray Cannon

As Ted Nelson said in the closing address "Stanford University is a city". Many a time while at Stanford, I thought back to my university days at Salford (part of Greater Manchester), and compared the two. Stanford won hands down (with the possible exception of cricket at Old Trafford). May I congratulate the organisers on their choice of site, the generally good weather (remember the Manchester 86 umbrellas?), the Welcome Reception (even if it was a bit windy), the visit to the Exploratorium (enjoyed by kids of all ages from 7 to 70, and I swear I saw the base of one of the Golden Gate towers through the fog on the way there), and the Closing Picnic (I was lucky, and found a table in the shade). So once again well done and thank you.

Once again, there were (as in previous conferences) 3 streams for the presentation of papers, so any one delegate could only hope to attend at best one third of the talks. At APL90 the proceedings were available well before the conference, and one had time to read the papers and choose which to attend. Unfortunately, this was not the case at Stanford, but the extract that appeared in the final program provided a good guide to deciding which to attend.

items.title: Sunday 4 August
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 61

items.title: Introductory Tutorial: An Introduction to APL by Ray Polivka
items.text:
reported by Anthony and Sylvia Camacho

One of the most notable features of APL is the low threshold that newcomers need to cross to do useful work and the high ceiling they discover as they challenge APL with more complex problems. For a teacher this poses its own challenge: whether to reassure by demonstrating the low threshold or impress with a brief glimpse of the high ceiling. Ray refused all compromise and chose to give his audience a glimpse of the imposing height of a full nested array implementation. This required that he went beyond the ISO standard and be frank in his partiality for APL2. What resulted was a tour de force by a practised teacher, and notable for the ability of Speaker and Chairman to finish all sessions to specification and on time.

Anthony Camacho and Ray Polivka

Ray Polivka's Tutorial was billed as an introduction to APL and was clearly not intended to impart skills to the participants. It was in two parts: a description and illustrations. The description covered Array Orientation, the Rich Set of Primitives, Syntax & Grammar, Programming, Operators and Control Constructs. Ray gave those aspects of APL which so often alienate newcomers, a hard sell. He described APL as a conceptually parallel, highly symbolic array-oriented language which had been 10 years in gestation. He showed Donald McIntyre's list of mathematical symbols and the dates each was first used. Perhaps it is not so odd that logical AND (∧) was only first used in 1933; it is amazing that PLUS (+) was not used before 1489.

After this short toe-dipping ession Ray pushed his audience into the deep end. He started with heterogeneous arrays, concepts of dimension, vectors of vectors, nesting and definitions of 'depth'. For the programmers he made the point that APL is self-describing and that the data carries with it a description of its own data type, shape/rank and structure. Complex numbers were mentioned in passing as an example of a vector.

In what amounted to a digression, the relation of APL (as a computer language) to its environment was given a slightly breathless overview covering system commands, libraries, workspaces and the nested array display function.

Now was the time to 'taste the beef' with a review of APL2 language pure and not simple. With a reminder that 'APL manipulates whole arrays as well as items within them', Ray gave his gloss on the job of a programming language, saying it must do simple things simply, such as data transformation, array construction, array enquiry, data selection, data rearrangement, and data replacement.

With this as a framework the primitives were then presented, including such APL2 extensions as string search and enlist. Passing from primitives to definitions was then made a little more challenging by moving from defined functions to defined operators. 'There is no difficulty', said Ray, 'functions use variable data, operators have variable functions'.

Within two minutes of the appointed time the pupils were dismissed to afternoon coffee break with the promise of a final session to look at the solutions they had found to the problems they had been set to keep them from idleness over lunch.

This hard day's work was advertised as 'free'. Those attending might, if they wished, buy, for $25, a package of papers and software demonstrating various aspects and implementations of APL.

This contained Ray's slides, leaflets from vendors, and three free APL interpreters: TryAPL2 (manual and disk), I-APL (manual, tutorial and disk) and APLISW (the shareware version of Sharp APL/PC now being produced by Iverson Software Inc). This last does not need a manual as it includes extensive help files on disk and some of the start-up options are no longer the problem they were with Sharp's version.

They certainly had their money's worth!

items.title: Introductory Tutorial: An Introduction to APL by Ray Polivka
items.text:
reported by Lee Ann Estep

During the APL91 conference I enrolled in the Introduction to APL Tutorial. My expectation of a beginning APL class was that it would begin at the beginning and proceed at some reasonable rate toward, perhaps, the beginning of the middle. What I needed was the elementary school version of beginning APL, but found myself in the graduate school version.

Several minutes actually were spent on the beginning but by the lunch break we had covered the beginning, middle, and the far end of APL. The majority of the material went so far over my head it never even ruffled my hair. No enquiry was made as to the level of ability or expectations of the students. We were treated to a pre-packaged script delivered at lightning speed. Questions were not encouraged.

There was no sign of a computer, either for the students, which I did not expect, or for the instructor, which I certainly did expect.

At the beginning of the session I knew nothing about APL. I still do!

items.title: Advanced Tutorial: Computer-Aided Software Engineering (CASE) by Larry Zeidner
items.text:
reported by Jonathan Barman

I found the initial sessions of the CASE Tutorial rather difficult to understand. I am still not sure just what CASE is supposed to be, apart from the initials standing for Computer Aided Software Engineering. It looks as though most of the APL tools and utilities that people usually create for themselves could be described as CASE. The demonstration of the new editor in IBM's APL2/PC seemed to be irrelevant to CASE, though the editor itself looks useful.

Larry Zeidner and his Multiprocessor

The afternoon session turned out to be very interesting. Dr Zeidner gave a scintillating presentation of his CASE tool, which enables the APL programmer to create a system which will run numerically intensive computations on several machines at once. The particular application for which the CASE tool had been used was in the calculation of the complex path a numerically controlled machine tool has to traverse when machining an arbitrary shape. The Conference Proceedings contain a paper by Dr Zeidner which describes the details of the system.

After the official tutorial was over many of us went to a demonstration of the software. It was fun to see a partly machined golf club head, which Dr Hazodny brought along, and then see the system calculate the path that a machine tool would have to traverse to make some of the initial cuts. The number of calculations involved is enormous, so farming out the job to several machines at once is essential if the job is to be finished in a reasonable time. Even with multiple processors the full golf club head machining calculations take all night to complete.

I feel sure that this CASE tool will be applied in many other disciplines.

The Welcome Reception4 Smiths and Ray Cannon in the BackgroundEd Cherlin and The Cat in the Hat in the Foreground

items.title: Monday 5 August
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 65

items.title: Invited Speaker: Phil Smith. Reflections on Magic, Dreams, and Programming
items.text:
reported by Jonathan Barman

Phil Smith came onto the platform with electronic sensors attached to his forehead. These were hooked up to a PC display so we could see his brain waves in action during the presentation. The first 10 minutes were pre-recorded, with both voice and PC display. I could not make out if he was controlling the recording by changing thought patterns, or if he was just well rehearsed. Later on he gave a demonstration of choosing an item from a menu by thought control, but again I could not make out if it was real. I feel sure it was not a hoax.

I thoroughly enjoyed the display of capturing data from simple devices, and then using APL to display the results. One of the devices was based on the infra red measuring instrument used for focusing a Polaroid camera, and could measure distances very fast and accurately. The PC captured the stream of distance measurements, and then APL functions were used to display the data. Phil walked towards the device and then displayed the speed and acceleration of every footstep. He put it on the floor and flexed a bouncy spring over it and then showed the resulting damped sine wave. Another device was a freely rotating arm with an accurate measure of the angle traversed. Demonstrating that the frequency of a pendulum depends on length and not on amplitude could be carried out in minutes. When I was at school the same thing took days of preparation and computation, and at the time seemed quite tedious. There must be some very lucky students who benefit from Phil's work.

items.title: MicroAPL Vendor Forum
items.text:
reported by Adrian Smith

This was probably the most interesting vendor session, as MicroAPL had taken a good deal of trouble to keep their product under wraps until the conference. It was however slightly marred by the fact that the conference Barco stoutly refused to accept the signal from the RS/6000.

David Eastwood and Richard Nabavi

MicroAPL's strategy is similar to IBM's in that they have one source code copy in a relatively low level language (68000 Assembler / Series-1 assembler) which can be transliterated into other assemblers, as long as these have a broadly similar structure. With the SPARC and RISC instruction sets, the mapping is typically 1->2 or 3, but the structural fit is quite good, so the end product runs quite fast. The other respect in which MicroAPL resemble IBM is in their total commitment to the APL2 standard. This leaves the user in the fortunate position of being able to choose a totally compatible APL on any of the PC, Mac, Unix or mainframe platforms; whatever your views on APL2, this has to be good news.

The user-interface is fully Motif/CUA compliant, with all the standard cut&paste actions, an easy printer interface and the complete APL manual available as on-line help. The interface to Motif was designed from the outset to be easy not to use! The problem with managing 1034 C-calls from your APL application is that you have to turn yourself into a C programmer to do it. MicroAPL have tried to make a reasonable subset of the facilities available to APL with a simple set of functions (e.g. ALERT to put up a warning box) which are designed for APLers, not C-folk. The Motif resource mechanisms are used to fill in the details, e.g. if you want a dark blue button you set that up in Motif, and APL will automatically use it.

The next steps are towards SPARC (MIPS and HP machines), more optimisations, a clean implementation of ⎕NA and an OpenLook version. MicroAPL intend to offer a free runtime policy with a packager available 'at a modest price'. They are beta-testing through September, and are aiming to launch on September 26th.

items.title: Panel: Modes of Thinking and Their Implications for APL
items.text:
reported by Jonathan Barman

Hal Macklin has a special interest in the way the brain processes APL. Research with people who have suffered brain damaged has shown that Japanese Kanji characters take a different route through the brain compared with normal script. Mathematical symbols seem to bypass language areas of the brain, and so does music.

Devon McCormick stressed the difference between parallel and serial modes of thought. APL needs parallel thinking which seems to be more complex, but APL enables one to cope with complexity. Someone coding a string search routine serially usually fails to notice the overlapping match problem, but coding in APL in parallel highlights this problem.

Phil Smith has had personal experience of the way APL changed his way of thinking, and has analysed the nature of this change.

Stan Kelly-Bootle felt that APL was not the only area where special thought processes must occur. He was impressed by the fact that the topologist who finally solved the problem of turning a sphere inside out happened to be blind.

Hal Macklin wondered why APL provoked such strong reactions from people. Could it be that an extraordinary number of the APL creators and enthusiasts are left handed?

Stan Kelly-Bootle thought that APL is not dying, but is just a minority cult.

items.title: Psycho-Biographical Analysis with APL, by A V Kondrashev & A A Kronik
items.text:
reported by Sylvia Camacho

The subject matter of this application of APL is intriguing: the investigation of differences in subjective assessment of life experiences and expectations of longevity between populations assumed psychologically balanced and those requiring therapy. We were told that the prototype for this model was produced in one day and then developed in spare time. The model allows data to be captured, transferred to a database, subjected to statistical analysis and the output to be presented graphically.

One finding of the research is that expectation of a long life is a good indicator of psychological well-being. A recent analysis of differences between groups of men and women in their attitude to perestroika showed, on this assumption, that soviet men are considerably more optimistic than soviet women.

items.title: Supply-Chain Management at Rowntree: Critical Success Factors for APL, by Adrian Smith
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

The presentation was a first-rate guide on how to survive with APL, disguised as a workmanlike summary of the advantages and disadvantages of APL in the Rowntree-Mackintosh environment.

I extracted the following precepts: don't use any vendors' special features; they tie you to the vendor and make your APL non-portable. Don't use any vendor-supplied workspaces. Only use code you fully understand and can maintain. Write cover functions for machine-dependent features such as graphics to simplify porting. Prefer PC work to mainframe; the PC user interface is far better. Don't use enhancements. Nested arrays and defined operators greatly increase the amount staff have to learn before they become effective. Buy faster PCs to make such simple code fast enough for your needs.

Adrian Smith

Collect a well designed and tested, centrally maintained set of utilities. This will improve robustness, reduce training time for new staff, reinforce coding standards by example, and greatly reduce development time on new systems (in Rowntree 85% to 90% of a system is utilities). Bear in mind that the scope of packages will grow. APL's advantage is as a notation for expressing hard sums effectively; use APL in circumstances where this advantage is decisive and don't fight the battles you might lose.

reported by Ray Cannon

Adrian Smith's talk on Supply-Chain Management was the most amusing, and all done without mirrors or any other visual aid.

items.title: Invited Speaker: Therese Myers. Simplifying the View of a Complicated Technology
items.text:
reported by John Searle

Therese Myers is President of Quarterdeck Office Systems of Santa Monica, California, the software company responsible for DesqView, which is a "multi-tasking" organiser for DOS machines. Her talk was an aggressive marketing pitch for her company and its forthcoming DesqView/X product, which will allow PCs to simulate X-terminals in a Token Ring or Ethernet network. This will enable existing investment in DOS machines to be carried forward into a Unix workstation environment.

The basic theme of her talk was that Quarterdeck is better than Microsoft, and whatever we do they copy about two years later. Now that Microsoft is the top of the heap, I suppose they are the prime target for criticism, but I felt there was too much emphasis on the put-down in her talk.

In technical terms, Quarterdeck have ported X11 Release 4 to DOS, and the user interface will be able to look like either Motif or OpenLook. Networking will be available through TCP/IP, Decnet or PC/NFZ.

The only reference to APL in the talk was that an APL Application Programming Interface is available "if there is an interest in it". (For "interest", read "profit".) It has been written by one of her APL-enthusiast colleagues. Unfortunately, her view of the limited APL market will probably prevent it from emerging.

items.title: The Exhibition Area
items.text:
notes by Adrian Smith

Suddenly, all APLs are starting to look the same! Even Digital were there, running under DECWindows, to merge with the crowd of RS/6000s. STSC were oddly placed in the exact centre of the room, and seemed to be ignored by the majority of delegates who followed a natural path around the four walls, and thus found themselves back at the exit without ever visiting the little island in the middle!

Getting the IBM Stand Ready

Dyadic were actually showing their APL under Windows-3, but I was advised in no uncertain terms that it was more than my life was worth to even think about touching the mouse. They were right ... even under the careful guidance of John Scholes it still crashed with glorious unpredictability at the worst possible moments. IBM and MicroAPL were there too, but I couldn't get their stuff to break ... how boring!

items.title: APL - The Language in Common: APL 92 Program Statement
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

The APL Community has been gathering in international conferences since 1973. We have believed these conferences are the showplace of worldwide APL activities. Quite recently we have however become aware that we have been missing a major area of APL development and APL applications because the Soviet Union APL community has not been represented in our international meetings.

This long time ignorance and negligence was caused by political and language barriers and by missing contact between western and Soviet Union APL people. In the broadest sense we could say that we did not have a common language, we did not know how to communicate.

APL 90 in Copenhagen was a big door-opening event where the western and eastern APL communities met. It was found that the Soviet Union is one of the APL countries. The USSR Academy of Sciences, the Ministry of the Nuclear Industry, and other state and public organisations sponsor APL development in the Soviet Union.
path: APL - The Language in Common: APL 92 Program Statement

items.title: The first GLOBAL Conference on APL
items.text:
APL 91 in Leningrad is meant to be the first truly global APL conference where western and eastern APL communities, hitherto virtually unknown to each other, will meet and create fruitful new contacts. We would like to build a world of mutual understanding, but we remember the story about builders of the Tower of Babel, who failed due to the lack of a common language. We want to show in practice how APL is the Language in Common for people with different cultural and language backgrounds. To overcome still existing language barriers all conference presentations and speeches will be translated from English to Russian and vice versa and there will be bilingual helpers around to facilitate personal communication. The proceedings will be published in English.

The data processing field in the Soviet Union is in a strong expansive phase. The Soviet APL community is well prepared for the expanding market. The western APL community can help Soviet APL people to fight for a better position in this dynamic environment. The technology and the experience from the West combined with the "new blood" from the East can give a strong impulse to the success of APL world wide.

The APL 92 Program Committee expects a broad spectrum of papers dealing with various aspects of the language, APL implementations, supporting software, and applications. We also want to focus on APL in the mixed environment where multiple national languages, multiple currencies, and different standards are used. The integration of the world economies requires new solutions, and APL can show its strength there. We would also like to get papers concerning teaching technology and the role of APL in it.
path: APL - The Language in Common: APL 92 Program Statement

items.title: Conference Overview
items.text:
The APL 92 Conference will take place 6 - 10 July 1991 in Leningrad, northwestern Soviet Union. The Conference site is the Architecture and Building Training Centre of the State Committee of the Nuclear Energy Usage. Its own hotel can accommodate 270 participants at a reasonable cost and city international hotels will be available for those who wish to live near the attractions. The Centre is situated about 3 miles from the city centre near a metro station with fast service all around the city. In addition, a convenient taxi and special bus shuttle services will be provided at a fixed price. Two restaurants in the Centre will be in the service of the participants for lunches and dinners. A coffee shop for refreshments will be open all day.

Leningrad is the second largest city in the USSR. It was founded in 1703 by Peter the Great as the new capital of the Russian Empire. Leningrad is situated on the delta islands of the river Neva. There are more than one hundred rivers and canals with more than 300 bridges across them. Some of the bridges are drawbridges which are raised every night. Leningrad has a vast number of historical and architectural monuments, churches, palaces and museums, minutely preserved, all open to the public. The famous Leningrad "white nights" in the high summer make it possible to enjoy its beauty twice around the clock.

Activities: The main conference will run from 6 - 10 July, including: submitted papers presented in parallel tracks; sessions of posters addressing short or informal topics; opening and closing sessions featuring prominent speakers in fields of interest to APL users; vendor exhibits and vendor forum. Rooms will be available for special sessions organised by user groups, committees etc.

Tutorials: On Sunday, 5 July, tutorials will be given in two parallel tracks, one to give an introduction to APL language, the second on general computer science topics. Both are intended to focal students and other interested individuals, given mainly in Russian. The tutorial sessions are open to anybody even without registration.

Social events and cultural programme: A variety of social events will provide opportunities to meet other attendees informally. Leningrad is rich in cultural events like concerts, ballet and circus performances, theatres etc. The conference office will help with reservations. Special tours for accompanying persons will be offered during the conference and side trips will be organised after the conference. One of the planned post conference tours is an International Conference on Computers in Education on board a comfortable ship. It will cruise along the northern rivers of Russia and visit the centres of the Russian wooden architecture, the islands Kigi and Valaam. The participants of APL 92 are exempt from the registration of this second conference.

items.title: Travel and Communications
items.text:
Leningrad was chosen as conference site partly because it is near Finland and its capital Helsinki, served by all major international airlines. Leningrad is 40 minutes from Helsinki by airplane, six hours by train or by bus. In order to ensure reliable and speedy mail and telecommunications services, a conference sub-office is operating in Helsinki.

Official carrier of the APL 92 Conference is Finnair. Finnair is an expert in travelling to Soviet Union from the United States, Europe and Japan, and will provide a traveller kit with telephone numbers, schedules and other useful information to make your planning and travelling easy and economic.

Paul Chapman & Lee Dickey booking for APL92 with Olga Kondrashev

items.title: Tuesday 6 August
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 70

items.title: Mastering J, by Donald McIntyre
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

APL, which nearly got called Iverson's Better Math, encounters resistance because it requires people to learn new symbols. Now, ironically, J is encountering resistance among APLers because it does not use the symbols they know. Donald admitted he himself suffered distress making the change.

Donald McIntyre with Peter McDonnall's Drawing

It is, in any case, the ideas that matter and Donald McIntyre has no doubt that the ideas in J are an improvement on APL. J is the best as well as the latest version of Iverson's notation.

Donald is still Mastering J and feels that his difficulties may be encountered by other non-theoreticians. He needed more examples than are given in the terse Dictionary of J and he sets out to provide some in this paper.

Through the good offices of Vin Grannell this session was videorecorded. With luck, if the recording was successful, Donald's presentation may reach a wider audience.

One of Donald's specialities is illuminating asides. I learned that we owe the rank operator to Arthur Whitney and that a conjunction in J, is like a dyadic operator in APL. I assumed that a conjunction and two verbs produce a verb. Then one of his examples produced a verb from a conjunction and nouns! I didn't note the phrase; I hope it is on the tape.

items.title: Tacit Definition, by Roger Hui, Kenneth Iverson and Eugene McDonnell
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

I felt it fitting that Gene McDonnell presented this paper because, in The Four Cube Problem (APL Press 1981) he presented to the world the best example I've seen of how to write programs without variables. It convinced me that there was something superior about direct definition.

Within the direct definition, however, one did refer to arguments as ⍺ and ⍵. Gene pointed out that there is no ambiguity about the meaning of the expression +/ even though there is no argument. Further expressions may be added which specify what to do with the result returned by +/. In J, such collections of expressions can be assigned to a name. Some of the features of J make this extremely terse and elegant style of programming much easier to use than it was in APL; such things as fork, hook, with, atop and commute.

Explicit definition in J uses x. and y. where APL used ⍺ and ⍵. In J one can define average explicitly, thus: average=. (+/y.)%#y. or, using tacit definition, thus: average=. +/%#, which uses a fork (q.v.).

The later versions of J contain a primitive (:11) which converts an expression from explicit to tacit form. This is an extension of the parser. A tacit definition does not need to be parsed but can be executed at once so tacit definitions are, in effect, compiled and are executed significantly faster. Gene said that the parse tree also indicates what can be done in parallel and what has to be done serially. This augurs well for a J implementation on parallel processors.

A questioner recalled that Al Rose, in 1966 or '67, proposed the high minus as a suffix should be the symbol for commute with the mnemonic 'the dashing commuter operator'.

items.title: Nuclear Power Plant Diagnostics in APL, by Alexander Skomorokhov
items.text:
reported by Sylvia Camacho

This paper, in the proceedings, is a sober professional piece of work. The paper as presented was a pleasure to attend and a triumph over the odds. Alexander began by thanking his audience for attending despite the rival attraction of a paper by Iverson. He followed this by a cartoon show that produced appreciative laughs for every overhead he showed. This made his apology for his English pronunciation 'you should consider it as noise on the line' quite superfluous. Mention of a model of a nuclear power plant was accompanied by a picture of Madonna and Child followed by a reference to Chernobyl and Three Mile Island and a picture of the Old Man with the Scythe.

The timescale for the application is interesting. Their first introduction to APL was via Gilman and Rose in 1979 and they realised their own interpreter in 1985. The incentive to use APL to try for early warning of incipient problems within nuclear reactors was explained by a cartoon of a Greenpeace Protest.

The first version of the system was in 1989 and, as a result of a meeting with Per Gjerlov, Erkki Juvonen and Jim Brown, this was converted to APL2 with a consequent reduction of two thirds of the code. In the way of Management world-wide this was met by a question from the boss 'Why do we have to pay more for less code?'

The final 'thank you for listening' was displayed on the screen including a seven replicate of 'very' much and a good round of applause for a good Show Man.

Questions revealed an interesting concern among the audience that APL should be used in such security-critical circumstances. The response was that APL is currently an investigative tool and prototyper and would probably be converted into other languages for use in production.

items.title: Invited Speaker: William L Scherlis, DARPA Software Activities and Opportunities for APL
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

Dr William Scherlis of the Defence Advanced Projects Research Agency (DARPA) told us that the agency's mission was to develop advanced technologies for the Department of Defence: it has 160 staff and a budget of a billion dollars a year.

There are two kinds of activity, military-specific (with a known military aim), and multiple-use which covers computer systems and scientific research.

On the computer systems side there are four main efforts:

  1. High performance computer systems - teraflops is the goal.
  2. Advanced software technology - the grand challenges here are:
    • major problems such as the numerical simulation of thunderclouds;
    • the component-based approach to managing large software systems (a million lines of code);
    • automatic conversion from serial to parallel.
  3. The national research and education network - the aim is gigabit speed networks. Arpanet is part of this effort.
  4. Basic research and human resources.

Software has to cater for a long life cycle of twenty years or more, much higher reliability than for commercial work and must be organised so that requirements that change during development can still be satisfied.

The component-based approach to managing the development of large systems must allow each component to be developed by an appropriate method; not all necessarily in the same language or even the same computing environment.

Dr Scherlis ended his survey by listing the opportunities he saw for APL.

  • as one of the systems for development
  • as a fast prototyper with a wide spectrum
  • as a rich source of ideas for array-specific designs

and he wondered whether it was possible to scale up the interactive experimental APL approach so that large systems could be developed faster.

DARPA is a technology investor - not a policy-making organisation. Its prototyping project is unlikely to lead to any language being specified as the prototyping language for defence.

reported by Jonathan Barman

It was interesting to hear that APL can fit into the mega software projects that DARPA initiates. The main requirement is that APL should be able to interface smoothly with other languages and systems, for example, an interface between APL and Oracle.

The primary opportunity for APL is in the rapid prototyping of systems. Some concern was expressed from the audience that one of the software projects is to identify a common prototyping language for DOD. Apparently there won't be an 'official' language.

items.title: Plenary Session. APL Standards Report
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

Professor L J Dickey brought us up to date on the latest meeting of the Standards Committee. About ten people attended, from USA, Canada, France and Belgium. IBM, DEC and STSC were represented: others were users or consultants. The meeting agreed to add enlist, pick, depth, match and each (on floating nested array systems) and are moving in the direction of adopting strand notation. They may even make 1 2 3[2] an error to allow them to adopt strands. [Your reporter expected a chorus of boos at this point: there was not one.] Anything added will be as addenda to the standard. The group hopes to speed its work by greater use of electronic mail.

ISO group 11 is interested in language-independent data types and arithmetic.

There are two groups standardising character sets. Unicode is supported by about a dozen of the major players and aims at a single character encoding. ISO 10646 is a competing effort. The APL standards group is trying to persuade both groups to include all the APL characters. If they succeed it will simplify moving functions between platforms.

items.title: The User Command Processor, by Jim Weigang
items.text:
reported by Ray Cannon

Jim Weigang's paper on STSC's user command processor was, to me, the least interesting talk that I went to, but that may be because over the last year, I have implemented and now support over 150 commands using the User Command Processor.

The paper was a blatant advertisement for a useful but badly implemented product. Fortunately it is possible to improve the implementation, and Dave Ziemann and Peter Cyriax have done exactly this.

items.title: Pure Functions in APL and J, by Edward Cherlin
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

Ed Cherlin made a few concessions to people who did not know something about combinatorial logic, but not enough for me; all my logic was learned before the seminal book Combinatory Logic was published. Concealed among the logic was the proposition that all expressions in J can be written without explicit reference to variable names. In some sense, if this is true it makes J functionally complete.

Ed proceeded to prove this proposition to his satisfaction, but I did not follow the proof.

The advantage offered for functional completeness did not seem very great. If all expressions can be written as abstracts (i.e. without variables) then this simplifies the construction of expressions under program control and the application of operators (adverbs) to expressions. I had the feeling that I had missed something: in my bones I feel that the elegance of abstracts (the same things, I am sure, as tacit definitions) must bring other extra advantages. But my bones are not exactly a reliable oracle.

items.title: Gerunds and Representations, by Bob Bernecky and Roger Hui
items.text:
reported by Anthony Camacho

Someone (Arthur Whitney?), at APL 89, when asked to give the three most desirable improvements to APL answered (1) speed, (2) speed and (3) speed. Bob Bernecky and Roger Hui are interested in compiling for speed. "The real reason for disliking GOTO is that it makes compiling difficult." Bob wants to be able to compile for parallel processors. Most languages are Single Instruction, Single Data (SISD). APL is Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD). Bob wants to find ways to compile APL so that it becomes Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data (MIMD).

His slide on motivation read:

  • No syntax change
  • Generalised adverbs
  • Improved reliability
  • Easier compilation
  • Partial support for MIMD
  • Parallel control structures: CASE, IF ....., DO.....
  • Makes verbs first class objects (I think this means that verbs can be the subjects and results of computations)

A gerund is a form derived from a verb which can be used as a noun: for example the word programming in the sentence programming is an art. This paper is a proposal that an operation done to a verb in J should convert it to an atom. This atomic form can be handled like a noun. Another operation could convert the noun back to verb and as a result various interesting control structures can be created.

The verbal nouns thus formed can be put into arrays and some of the benefits that various people have suggested might arise from arrays of functions can be obtained. A design goal is to make compilation possible without limiting the expressive power of J.

items.title: APL Technology of Computer Simulation, by A Boozin and I Popselov
items.text:
reported by Sylvia Camacho

Both authors of this paper are academic mathematicians and their use of APL is just where one might expect it to be: in modelling linear differential equations and stochastic Markovian processes.

Questions put showed that they first used APL 15 years ago on terminals to what was described as 'a big old computer'. Currently they use APL*PLUS/PC. They have set up an environment in which they can split the screen and display data graphically with some zoom facilities. This environment can be used in conjunction with raw APL while exploring the results of a model, or can be used in conjunction with data derived from APL or some other source.

In fact it is often used by Pascal programmers. Most recently they have been setting up economic models to try to come to terms with the consequences of decentralisation and privatisation. They use both Roman and Cyrillic alphabets.
