items.title: APL91 Final Report
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 8

by Charles Schultz

We were glad that so many of you could travel to APL91 in this year of uncertain international events and economic problems. We were gratified to hear many compliments and to see the (mostly) positive reviews in the previous Vector. Of course there were some problems. A couple of years ago, when some of us were first thinking of hosting APL91, I thought "Hmm, I've been to a lot of these conferences, I know what I've liked and not liked - sure, we could do this." I can now report that I, for one, have learned my lesson.

items.title: Attendance
items.text: The final full registration was about 370, representing 22 countries. We had an additional 75 spouse and child registrations. About 40 attended the CASE Sunday tutorial, and 30 attended the Sunday introduction to APL tutorial.

items.title: Outreach Publicity
items.text:
We undertook several efforts to reach outside the APL community. We sent press releases, calendar notices, and other materials to 700 magazines and newspapers. In California, we sent materials to 200 scientific centers, such as university and corporate research institutes. We sent introductory tutorial fliers to 350 high schools in the Bay Area and 250 college computer science departments.

We solicited vendor interest among producers of word processors to handle APL features and gain access to an international community, of terminal emulators to handle APL communications, and of hardware that runs APL. We even invited a list of Silicon Valley celebrities to the closing picnic. Steve Jobs did give his personal regrets by telephone; John Sculley had his secretary do it for him.

items.title: Author Kit and Font Table
items.text:
We were ambitious about contributing to momentum on author tools, since we view the APL publishing problem as one of the reasons it is so difficult to promote APL. We requested author tool proposals from several individuals. The few tool proposals we received were interesting, but not in an "install and go" form that we could pass on. All had dependencies on computer system, word processing software, and APL system. The only tool we were able to publish was an IBM BookMaster style file for the paper format (BookMaster contains standard APL features).

We requested information from all authors on the word processing systems they were using (very few provided this). We solicited WordPerfect and Microsoft as the leading word processing vendors to take a vendor booth and to consider providing an APL font to capture an international market of APL programmers. We included references to some PostScript font work that has been done. Jan Engel, the proceedings editor, is now corresponding with a contact at WordPerfect. IBM is now working on a PostScript APL font for OS/2 Communications Manager.

The Font Table at the conference was conceived as a result of all the troubles we had with publishing APL for the proceedings. We hope this effort will continue in and outside future conferences towards some distinct and "pluggable" solutions.

items.title: APL91 Museum (George L. Mendonsa)
items.text:
The APL Museum at the APL91 conference was set up ad hoc toward the end of the conference preparation period, as other more pressing items fell into place. George Mendonsa, with the assistance of Jan Engel, put the Museum together. (Because of its informal nature and set-up a more appropriate term might have been "Scrapbook" instead of "Museum".)

The museum was initiated to take advantage of the historic nature of the conference, a desire to begin to identify APL material of potential interest, and to find out the nature of the interest in such an endeavour. Calls for contributions to the museum were made to likely sources in part suggested by the APL91 committee. These people in turn suggested other sources. Contributors were asked to provide materials in one of 2 categories:

  1. Items of Historical interest in the evolution of the APL milieu.
  2. Related items of APL interest which were not necessarily historical.

We had about 25 to 30 contributors who included APL92, Linda Alvord, Ev Alan, Paul Berry, Larry Breed, Jim Brown, Carl Cheney, Ed Cherlin, Jan Engel, Adin Falkoff, Garth Foster, Vern Griffith, Interprocess, Curtis Jones, Ken Iverson, Gene McDonnell, Don Mattern, George Mendonsa, Don Peter, Marilyn Pritchard, Lynn Shaw, Bob Stephan, STSC, Rex Swain, and Joey Tuttle. The Museum was coordinated by George Mendonsa. Larry Breed had an extensive collection of items and was available at the Museum for much of the time. Lew Robinson, Jan Engel, Bob Stephan, Carl Cheney also acted as Docents at various times.

Items on display included buttons, books, papers, documents, and items from previous APL conferences such as The APL jig-saw puzzle, APL Tool-kit, Apple Blossom Time record, 1130 keyboard, Proceedings, T-shirts, etc. Larry provided the listing of the very first logon to APL. This was duplicated and handed out at the conference. Linda Alvord had sent The APL Genealogy project report (begun at APL88) which was displayed and added to at the conference by over 100 individuals. Don Mattern demonstrated his Ampere WS-1 APL laptop. Don Peter set up an on going demo of the IBM 5110. We also had a book as a memorial to Alan Perlis, Mike Montalbano, and Bill Bergquist which included some of their works. Interprocess had a collection of 40 APL buttons.

The Museum was well attended with over one half of the conference attendees stopping by. As indicated there does seem to be a interest such a facility at conferences.

Let us be very clear: this was a one time experimental event. The museum ceased to exist at the end of the conference. All items with a few exceptions were picked up by the contributors when the Museum closed. There was an attempt at the conference to determine who was interested in creating some such repository. Although a few expressed interest, no formal funded organization is in place. If you are interested in such a function, perhaps you could volunteer to your national APL organization.

It may be difficult to have an actual museum, but an on-going Ad Hoc portable museum (or scrap-book) could be put together for future conferences (as was demonstrated by this one). But even more important would be a repository. This would be a listing of items of interest that people had that: 1. they would like to contribute to a museum or 2. they would retain themselves but would like other people to know about.

Further, a repository could be created for each country and perhaps maintained and exchanged through the national APL organizations. Also, the genealogy project could continue as an ongoing activity in each Museum.

items.title: J Questionnaire
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 90

by Jonathan Barman

In mid November I sent out a questionnaire to everyone who had had a copy of J to find out what their reactions were to the language. Articles for Vector have to be ready by 30 November, so this left very little time for replies. It was gratifying that 15 people were able to respond by that date.

Several of the respondents have got J but have no knowledge of APL, and their views are particularly interesting as their thinking has not been coloured by APL.

Q: Was J easy to install?

The majority found J so easy to install that they must have wondered why I asked the question. Chas Yates was the only one to have problems. He found that the tutorial files were written for J version 3.0 whereas he had been sent version 2.9. The 'spelling' is different between the two versions, so he had to fiddle about changing such things as : to :: and [ to }:. He also had to replace the line ending characters. I think Chas was unlucky in this respect, as my version 2.9 of J for the IBM PC had the correct tutorial files. Chas also had to change the J.PRG file to J.TOS to stop the Desktop (Presentation Manager) fouling up the system.

Q: When you first fired up J did you find any difficulty with the editor? Was it obvious how to exit from J?

The majority had no difficulty with the editor or in exiting from J. Donald McIntyre pointed out that the session manager has changed greatly and that the present version in 3.5x4 is great. The APL users found no difficulty with )off to exit. Now that exit has changed to 0!:55 in version 3.5 it is suggested in STATUS.DOC that you assign off =. 0!:55 in your PROFILE.JS.

The Atari users did not get an editor at all. Characters can be typed on the command line and there is a destructive backspace, but nothing else. Not surprisingly, the Atari users were pretty rude about the 'editor'. Chas Yates hoped that the Atari was not going to be fobbed off as merely a games machine. It provides a cheap solution for those who cannot afford a PC or a Mac.

Q: Is J easy to learn? Does a knowledge of APL help the learning process?

Most found J difficult to learn, and felt that knowledge of APL was essential given the current state of the documentation. Simon Barker summed it up with the comment that learning J without the aid of a wide range of material means playing with the interpreter and relying on APL skills to aid experimentation. Donald McIntyre said that J is not easy to learn from the Dictionary, and, like APL, is best learned from a teacher.

Those who had little knowledge of APL had a slightly different view. Chas Yates felt that J was no harder than Forth, and Mark Whippey said that it was easy enough to get started. R Gillan said J was enjoyable to learn and useful in some areas of mathematics, especially induction and recursion formulae.

Q: Do you like the Dictionary of J as a definition of the language?

The Dictionary was generally liked. Simon Barker felt that it was a succinct and clear description of the language and useful as a basic reference text.

Q: Could you learn J from the Dictionary of J? Was the tutorial in Appendix B useful?

Donald McIntyre pointed out that it is not intended that you should learn J from the Dictionary. Since the Dictionary was all that Konrad Hinsen had, it had to be sufficient. Another commented that he felt that he was worrying away like a dog with a rag when someone could explain it better. Others felt it would be possible to learn J from the Dictionary, but it would take a lot of effort.

Several respondents with early versions of J did not have Appendix B of the Dictionary, but those who did have it found it useful.

Q: Which features of J are difficult to understand?

All of them, says Donald McIntyre, if you do not have the information! Simon Barker had difficulty using conjunctions and adverbs to derive verbs because they require a very clear understanding of how these constructions work in J. He also felt that J 'spelling' is more difficult than APL because of the use of modifiers to produce related symbols. Chris Brunsdon and Malcolm Rigg found function definition difficult, and the Suite variable an awkward method of program control.

Q: Would you have found it easier to learn J if there were more extensive examples and exercises?

A resounding YES to this one.

Q: Did you enjoy learning J?

Another resounding YES.

Q: Which features of J are not very useful and could be dropped from the language?

Most dared not comment, mainly because they had limited experience with J. Chris Brunsdon suggested that either APL-like programs with line numbers should be introduced, or insist entirely on tacit definition and operators for everything.

Q: What additional features should be included in the language?

Dave Ziemann suggested a better front end. Donald McIntyre and Chris Brunsdon would love graphics support. The remainder felt that they did not know enough about J to comment.

Q: Does J give you new insights into programming techniques? Can you see improvements that should be carried over into APL?

Most felt that they had benefited from studying J. Simon Barker likes the way that scan has been redefined to apply a verb monadically to increasing subsets of data. Chris Brunsdon likes the ability to assign verbs, adverbs and conjunctions to names, and could see this feature being incorporated in a new version of APL. Donald McIntyre says J is APL!

Q: What should J be used for?

The majority felt that J was best for teaching, education, intellectual stimulation, mathematicians and APL-type problems. Donald McIntyre uses it for everything now. Chris Brunsdon finds it useful for geographical data since he can handle arrays of complex numbers, but finds the inability to link J to graphics functions frustrating.

The only contrary note was from E Sargeant who thinks J will quickly become shelfware.

Q: What sort of problems would be easier to solve in J than any other language?

Dave Ziemann summed it up by saying that J is best for data transformations and array processing.

Q: Would you be able to use J commercially?

The majority of replies were a definite NO. Chris Brunsdon thought that there might be a possibility if the 640K barrier was broken, and Konrad Hinsen felt that an up-to-date user interface would be essential.

Q: Why did you get a copy of J?

The main reason seemed to be due to an interest in new languages, particularly one developed by Ken Iverson. Chas Yates and Konrad Hinsen wanted the power of APL without the hassle of special characters.

Q: Do you like J?

Everyone said YES. Chris Brunsdon thinks that J is an excellent idea, both as a 'tool of thought' and for rapid solutions of certain problems in practice. His complaints are just minor irritations.

One question that I did not ask was about the character set, and it was interesting to note that two users specifically got J because of APL character set problems. Simon Barker had ambivalent feelings about the subject. He likes being able to write and print J scripts in ASCII, but feels that J has lost something valuable without APL's symbology. APL was primarily a powerful notation that was then implemented as a programming language, but J is primarily a programming language that can be used as a (reasonable) notation. Because of this he finds J much harder to read than APL, J text is littered with the period and colon modifiers necessary to provide its rich symbol set and subsequently sacrifices some of the clarity and conciseness of APL.

Many thanks to the users who took the time and trouble to reply to the questionnaire. It is marvellous to be able to share their experiences in the language at this early stage of its development.

items.title: Note to Members on the Data Protection Act
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 10

The British APL Association keeps its membership records on a computer and relies on conditional exemption from the Act:

"(ii) data held by unincorporated members' clubs and relating only to club members."

[Guideline to the Data Protection Act 1984 page 24]

In order to qualify for such exemption the British APL Association is required to have asked each "Data Subject" whether they object to our use of the data we hold about them and they must not have objected.

The British APL Association is also required to monitor the situation to ensure that the conditions of the exemption continue to be met.

If you object to our holding your membership details on our computer, please write to us to let us know. We shall then remove your details from our computer. The consequence of this would be that you would be omitted from all future mailings.

Compiled by Gill Smith

items.title: Cocking & Drury Ltd and Cocking & Drury (Software) Ltd
items.text:
By the time you receive Vector we shall have shipped Version 4 of the APL*PLUS II System for the 386/486. This is the only APL product which allows you to build both Windows and DOS applications from one package.

The programmer interface to the Microsoft Windows libraries enables the building of true GUI interfaces for APL applications that run in Windows. You can:

  • use standard Windows components to build interfaces
  • set up APL applications so users access them through icons
  • develop applications that create multiple Windows
  • use the Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) facility to share data between APL and other applications
  • call third-party software through the use of a Dynamic Link Library (DLL)

In addition to this powerful new feature the new release of APL*PLUS II also includes the first evolutionary step towards compatibility with APL2; an interface to the Borland Paradox Database Manager, s Screen Interface Toolkit to aid the building of text-based application interfaces, enhancements to ⎕NA which mean other programs can now call APL functions, effectively as sub-routines, and many new utilities and tools.

The price of APL*PLUS II remains unchanged. All customers on maintenance will have received their free upgrades — others can upgrade for £310 (from Version 3) or £395 (from Version 1 or 2). We are also now shipping STATGRAPHICS Plus from STSC — this uses APL*PLUS II as its calculating engine to give significant performance improvements over regular STATGRAPHICS and, because it uses all installed RAM, virtually eliminates restrictions on data-set sizes.

Our 8-page magazine 'UPGRADE' was sent out to 7,500 people early in February with news of developments with APL*PLUS and STATGRAPHICS — and Smalltalk/V. If you didn't get a copy give us a call — it's free.

We're going to be busy attending trade shows this year. The Windows Show which happened in February will be followed by Software Development '92; The Euro Object-Oriented Show and Business Computing (and if we have any energy left maybe Computers in the City too!). Most of the activity on our stand at these shows focuses on Smalltalk/V (monthly sales of which increased twelve-fold in 1991!) but we shall be showing the new APL*PLUS II as well.

On the consulting front 1992 began with a bang! Three significant new APL jobs began in the first five weeks and two more are in the offing. All of a sudden our resources are thinly stretched — and the imminent beginning of two Smalltalk jobs makes recruitment look very likely for the near future; though we are looking more for Smalltalk people than APL'ers.

The European PANAPL group of STSC dealers continues to be active — a three-day meeting in Paris at the end of February is set to look at further development of the APL*PLUS II system for GUIs and the development of more programmers' tools.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
We start again with news of IBM's APL software range. At the time of writing, APL2/PC Version 1.02 is being prepared for release in the UK on April 14th, and is already shipping in the USA. This new version of APL2/PC contains a number of important features which relate both to the language specification of the product and also to the development aids supplied with the product. TryAPL2, the free packaged version of APL2/PC, has been updated to use APL2/PC Version 1.02 and is available from MicroAPL on request. Both the 16 and 32 bit interpreters will run under OS/2 and Windows3 and 32-bit workspaces may be packaged to produce run-time modules (and hence free runtime licences).

At the language level new features include N-wise reduction; partition and partition with axis; index (⌷) and index-with-axis; axis on scalar functions; selective specification (with minor exceptions); complex arithmetic in the 32-bit interpreter (with minor restrictions); the diamond (⋄) statement separator; system commands may be entered in combinations of upper and lower case letters; the system commands )SIC is implemented

The environment has been enhanced by the addition of new features and APs. The Session Manager (AP120) has been enhanced with new features including a pop-up help panel and a disc-based session log. Editor 3 has been added offering function, operator and text matrix editing; DOS file editing; sorting of local name lists; flagging of errors in header, and mismatched quotes, brackets and parentheses; flagging of duplicate labels; on-line help; hot key between editor and session manager. In addition Editor 3 offers a range of debug facilities such as automatic display of a failing line; break point setting; single step facility; stepping over called functions and operators.

AP124 has been enhanced to allow pop-up windows and other new features. Network support (AP172) has been extended to allow communication between PCs running APL2/PC with AP172. In addition facilities allow exchange of data between APL2/PC and other common programming languages. The new Universal Graphics AP (AP207) gives a simple but powerful interface to all standard IBM graphics adaptors (CGA, MCGA, EGA, VGA)

A range of new workspaces has been added to increase APL2/370 compatibility. In addition a workspace is added to read or write .WKS or .WK1 files. Printer support is extended to a wider range of IBM printers and the HP LaserJet. Facilities are supplied to provide an APL2/PC version of APE Version 2.

The development team here at MicroAPL have been busy too. Whilst APL.68000/X has been under beta test at a number of RISC System/6000 sites, we have refined the shared variable interface to allow ⎕SVO to dynamically bind auxiliary processors. This is a slight variant on our previous mechanism for auxiliary processors and brings us more into line with mainframe conventions. The first auxiliary processor to benefit from this treatment is AP124. We have developed a widget-based implementation of AP124 which will automatically run AP124 code in its own window. We were pleasantly surprised at how good some of our old AP124 systems look. Despite putting most of our efforts into the windowing version of APL.68000/X, we have not neglected dumb terminal users. Most of our Mirage and Unix dumb-terminal facilities have now been implemented on the RISC System/6000, including most of the major auxiliary processors we have developed over the years.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Limited
items.text:
At the end of January, Dyadic distributed Test copies of Dyalog APL/W for Microsoft Windows 3. This new product is a true 32-bit Windows application, and contains many exciting and powerful features.

Foremost of these is support for the Windows GUI that is implemented at the interpreter level. It is not just a set of cover functions to drive C or Assembler subroutines. By implementing this support within the interpreter, Dyadic has managed to achieve a result that is fully integrated with the Dyalog APL language and development environment. A second key feature is that the GUI support has been designed to support other systems including PM, Motif and Open Look. This means that Dyalog APL workspaces will be portable between Windows, OS/2 and Unix. You won't have to write different code to handle the different GUIs.

The system is based on three concepts: objects, properties, and events. Objects (often called "widgets") are user-interface components such as Forms, Buttons and Scrollbars. Each object has associated with it a set of properties. For example, the properties of a Form include its size, position, caption (title), border (yes or no) and so forth. Objects generate events. For example, Pushbuttons and Menuitems generate a SELECT event when the user clicks them or presses the appropriate key. To process a particular event in a particular object, you associate an APL function with it. This is termed a "callback" function, and will be invoked automatically by the interpreter whenever the event occurs. Callback functions can create new objects or change the properties of existing ones, so that a highly dynamic and responsive user-interface can be easily provided. Developing Dyalog APL applications is thus a matter of establishing a set of objects, assigning values to their properties, and attaching callback functions to various events. The need for complex control code to steer the user through an application is removed. Finally, a neat but important feature is the ability to TRACE callback functions like any others. When you TRACE your system, the callback functions pop up in windows on the screen as they are fired. You can then step through them line by line, open windows to watch your variables change, and so forth. This greatly simplifies and accelerates the task of testing and debugging a GUI application.

A second major feature of Dyalog APL/W is its interface to Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE). Again, this has been designed with other environments in mind and is not limited to Windows. The interface is based on Shared Variables which have been implemented in accordance with the APL standard. To share an APL variable X with a block of cells in an Excel spreadsheet, you simply type the expression: 'DDE:EXCEL¦SHEET1' ⎕SVO 'X R1C1:R20C30'. X now contains the Excel data, and assigning new values to X will poke them back into the spreadsheet. The DDE interface is a general one, and allows data to be passed freely between Dyalog APL/W and any other application that supports DDE. Shared variables will also be implemented in other versions of Dyalog APL using the communications protocols that are appropriate for those environments.

items.title: APL People Limited
items.text:
At the time of writing (early February) things are still pretty quiet on the recruitment front, although I have noticed a marked increase in activity compared to the three months before Christmas. I currently have several vacancies for people with APL2 experience to work in Paris, and am also looking for someone with sound APL coding skills for a position in London. Anyone who's interested, please call me on 0225 462602.

Fortunately, sales of our engineering software have been quite buoyant, with large orders from a company called Breknell Willis, who specialise in making switching gear for light railways, and from British Nuclear Fuels, plus a lot of interest from British Steel! Let's hope it continues!

items.title: HMW Trading Systems Limited
items.text:
The most advanced foreign exchange dealing system in the world - now the most affordable. With over five years of evolutionary development to its credit, 4XTRA from HMW is now being launched as the leading edge technology capable of maximising profits and maintaining a competitive edge.

Developed as a front end deal capture and management system, 4XTRA provides the functionality required to monitor real time multi-currency positions, enter deals and calculate profit opportunities. With NPV profit and loss accounting as standard, the dealer is able to cover his positions accurately whilst providing his management with a real time picture of the overall risk.

4XTRA's comprehensive position keeping and deal entry screens enhanced to meet the demands of forward, spot and corporate trading together with facilities such as automatically generated spot cover deals, overnight tom-next switching and value added reporting give the trader the tools he needs to deal effectively.

And 4XTRA won't burn a hole in the IT budget. Cost is based on the number of users, and because the system is PC-based, you can forget about mainframe investment and maintenance costs - a simple PC network is all that's required. However, low cost doesn't mean low performance. Already installed in one of the world's busiest dealing rooms, 4XTRA easily manages over 4000 deals a day and can accommodate peak rates of over 60 deals a minute.

The next release of 4XTRA will use Dyalog APL-W, which will allow the system to run on other platforms (UNIX as well as DOS). A Windows version of Dyalog APL is being released later this year, with a full OS-2 version following on.

If you would like to hear more about how 4XTRA can help your FX business expand, please contact: Rob Thurston, Business Development Manager, HMW Trading Systems Limited, 1 Temple Avenue, London EC4Y 0HA. Tel: 071-353-4212; fax 071-353-3325.

items.title: Hackers’ Corner: Reshaping your Mouse
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 112

by Adrian Smith

There are times when a simple reverse-video block is not the kind of mouse pointer you need. To save you the (not inconsiderable) effort of decoding the appropriate page of Ray Duncan's book, here is a simple extension to MSΔINIT which does the trick:

    ∇ CH MSΔINIT CU;RC

[1]    ⍝ Initialize mouse ... sets global ⍙mouse←1 if OK ... else 0
[2]    ⍝ CU is the cursor type ... 0=mouse cursor; 1=hardware cursor
[3]    ⍝ (CH) is the character and colour to be used for the mouse block.

[4]     RC←0 ⎕INT 51 ⋄ ⍙mouse←0≠1↑RC ⋄ →⍙mouse↓0
[5]     →CU↑Hw ⋄ →(⎕NC 'CH')↓0

[6]    ⍝ Use left arg as mouse character, possibly with colour ...

[7]     ⍎(0≠1↑0⍴CH)/'CH←¯1+⎕AV⍳CH'

[8]    ⍝ Colour defaults to bright white ...

[9]     CH←2↑CH,15

[10]   ⍝ CX is set to 'F000' Hex to retain background only;
[11]   ⍝ DX is the encoded character and foreground ...

[12]    RC←(10 0 ,¯4096,CH[1]+256×CH[2])⎕INT 51 ⋄ →0
[13] Hw:RC← 10 1 ⎕INT 51
    ∇

This defaults to the normal mouse block, unless you provide a left argument. This may specify the mouse character (as a character scalar or ⎕AV index), and optionally a colour. APL*PLUS II users should note that the ¯4096 is really Hex(F000), but that in APL*PLUS/PC you trip over the 2-byte integer line, and have to pretend that you mean Hex(-F + FFF).

'⌹' MSΔINIT 0     ⍝ Mouse pointer is a white Domino ...
4 14 MSΔINIT 0    ⍝ ... or a yellow diamond!
MSΔSHOW           ⍝ Let's see it!

That's it folks. Next issue, the .EPS format exposed, or how to get your fancy PostScript graphs into MS Word, Aldus PageMaker and so on. Watch this space.

items.text:
It seems that another three months have passed since I wrote the last editorial for Education Vector. Looking back, I note my comment about the possible demise of the USSR - by the time anyone read it, of course, the event itself was ancient history (does anyone apart from the editor read editorials?). Perhaps I should confine my comments to things less transient than mere empires - such as the continued growth of the world-wide APL community.

On the subject of the last edition, I must apologise to Neil Sheldon for two typographical errors in our reproduction of his letter about Simpson's Rule. The quantities h3 and h4 should have referred to the third and fourth powers of h respectively.

I am keen to keep in close touch with developments at schools where APL is being used, and in this context I particularly welcome the contribution to this edition by Bill McLean of Dunoon Grammar School. If you are a teacher or pupil at a school using APL, or for that matter if you are considering using APL in future, please write and tell me about it. Our readers will also, I know, be pleased to see a contribution from Alan Sykes, my predecessor as editor.

Readers of Education Vector may not all be aware that it is reprinted from Vector, the official journal of the British APL Association. The sixteen-page reprint is delivered free of charge to anyone who is interested in APL. So if you are reading someone else's copy, or know of someone who would like to receive a copy, just drop me a line/phone/fax/email - I will be glad to add names to our distribution list.

The full journal, Vector, is distributed to members of the Association. If you are interested in joining, please write to Rowena Small, [address omitted]. Currently the UK private subscription is £12 per annum, for which you get four copies of Vector (144 pages per edition) and notice of meetings etc. Members and non-members are welcome to attend the meetings, most of which take place in the IEE Building (next to the Savoy Hotel) in London. Our programme for the coming months includes: (i) "A Tutorial in J" by Donald McIntyre on 27th March, (ii) a talk on the ISO APL language standards and talks by Adrian Smith and Maurice Jordan on 1st May, (iii) the Annual General Meeting, with news from SigAPL and their idiom collection (by Dick Bowman) and a video of the APL91 panel discussion "25 Years of APL" on 12th June.

items.title: Email Contact
items.text:
We have received several email messages from readers in recent months, and it has been suggested that this could be a useful medium to encourage communication between APLers. We are compiling a list of email addresses, with a view to distributing news items, suggestions and APL tips to those who are interested.

If you have an email address, contact me (MAYER@UK.AC.SWAN.MS) and tell me what you think we should be doing for you.

items.title: More on MULTIPLY
items.text:
My program MULTIPLY in the last edition seems to have interested a few people, but as yet I have received no contributions in that line. In response to the suggestion that I could generalise the program to test things other than multiplication, I offer the following:

[0]    FUN TEST VALS;RV;ANS;I;TARGET;T
[1]    RV←¯1+VALS[2]+?(2×VALS[1])⍴1+-/VALS[3 2]
[2]    ANS←⍳0
[3]    I←1
[4]    T←0 60 60⊥¯1↓¯4↑⎕TS
[5]   LOOP:TARGET←(VALS[1],2)⍴RV
[6]    ⍎'TARGET←TARGET[;1]',FUN,'TARGET[;2]'
[7]    'What is ',(⍕RV[I]),FUN,(⍕RV[I+1]),'?'
[8]    ANS←ANS,1↑⎕
[9]    →((2×VALS[1])≥I←I+2)/LOOP
[10]   'You scored ',(⍕+/ANS=TARGET),' out of ',⍕VALS[1]
[11]   'in ',(⍕(0 60 60⊥¯1↓¯4↑⎕TS)-T),' seconds'

The left argument of TEST is a function, such as +, -, ÷, ×, etc. and the right argument is a 3-component vector: the number of questions, followed by the minimum and maximum values to be used. For example:

'+' TEST 10 5 15

will give you 10 sums (additions) of numbers chosen from the range 5-15. This is all pretty unsophisticated stuff - if you've got something better, please share it with us!

items.title: Review of I-APL for the Macintosh
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 23

by Bill McLean (Teacher, Dunoon Grammar School, Argyll)

John: (Our Doubting Thomas)...It’s slow like the Master...

Muiry: (with the spec’s)........................and my P.C.

John: and uses 32k WS size. The WS’s are too high-fallutin’ for me and I’ve a better collection of idioms already!

Jason: (Our American with the economist Galbraith American/Canadian accent) But John! If these limitations are irksome, the APL people intend you to use a “proper” APL like our APL 68000 (or one for my PC, butted in Muiry)...Besides, the notation is concise and allows lots of functions. See our Battlegame on the BBC.

Muiry: It’s dearer but cheap by comparison; I like the photocopied manual. And it does support Direct Definitions!

John: Yes. I’m glad of that. I’d like to know more about the Editor window. I’m quite happy with the Del editor; I can still re-input lines there. I’m fast with that.

Teacher: Line numbers are omitted. Cut and paste are possible. Get back via “finish editing”. Direct definitions are seen in the usual way...type and return.

Muiry: Do we have the equivalent of the VDU commands to build a graphics package? I saw Struan trying something with the clipboard.

Teacher: The graphics package has circles, rectangles (empty or pattern-filled), USA map or world map. With the machine code calls at the end of the book, we can use direct definitions to position rectangles, sense mouse co-ordinates. Just imagine what we can do with that! (Long pause).

John: It has a VOICE demo! How to do it looks difficult to me!

Muiry: The Session Log allows me to double-click previous items to re-input them. And we can move the cursor up and down with the arrow keys.

Teacher: Too much use of the session log seems to crash it. Better to clear rubbish now and again.

Struan: (in best bed-side manner) The Clear Window looks useful there. No bother printing on the Laser Printer. Very Macintoshy with menus, dialogues, Load, Save, Save As. No Undo as I saw somewhere.

Teacher: (QXPress?) “Save workspace?” on Quit....type a colon or something...it thinks you’ve changed the WS. The H.P. DeskWriter is OK so it’s likely OK with an Imagewriter.

John: Except how to print a graphics window. That looks difficult to me! 73 chars per line and a warning.

Teacher: The BBC WS’s are compatible (except graphics) and can be transferred to the Mac and laundered (given an icon) with the Exchange program down in the Maths dept. where they have a Mac and BBC side by side.

Muiry: I like the Nails, Rounds etc. for finding symbols.

Jason: But Muiry! Have you not learned your mnemonics yet! And you with a PC too. And did you see the customisable menu: Control. That should be a convenience for newcomers.

Struan: A real give-away! Like it better than Comal, but some will say “horses for courses”, that a Mac application would be better in some other language.

Jason: Well, I’m amazed at how powerful it is. We can do things with it that would be difficult for a £300 database!

Struan: Yes, the Text window is like a wordprocessor; no word wrapping, needs CR, but both upper and lower case with Ctrl K or switch back to APL style with Ctrl K.

Muiry: I’m not worried about System 7! but will it wear?

John: Ah! But what about WINDOWS!

Jason: Nothing that the author couldn’t fix! If someone paid him for about 3 man-months of work! Really, our Basic friends just don’t know what they are missing. Imagine a future priest like me doing APL on the side!

items.title: Guest Editorial: Now is the Time for APL
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 3

by Peter Donnelly

Is APL dying? On the contrary, APL is alive and kicking and there is every reason to believe that its golden age has yet to come. "Rubbish", I hear you say, "you vendors are paid to sound optimistic; you wouldn't believe the opposition I get when I try to promote APL in my organisation. What possible justification can you have for such a claim?" Well, here is why I think I am right.

In many ways, the position of APL in recent years has been rather like that of Unix. Its adherents know it to be an extremely powerful, productive, and rewarding environment for developing applications. If only they could persuade others to take it seriously! Its critics, on the other hand, see it as arcane, obscure, unfriendly, unnecessarily complex, heavy on machine resources, and, in extreme cases, downright subversive.

Ever since I have been involved in Unix, pundits have been forecasting that NEXT year its growth would suddenly start to increase exponentially. Then, when it has only achieved a modest increase, they point to the year after, and then the year after that. This has often been called Unix's "moving hockey-stick" syndrome. Yet in the last two years the forecasts have come true, and even the most conservative of organisations, the banks, building societies and insurance companies, are moving enthusiastically into Unix. Why has Unix now succeeded after years in the doldrums? The answer I think is twofold. Firstly, thanks to the Reduced Instruction Set Computer (RISC), machines have become VERY much more powerful and dramatically less expensive. Secondly, users are demanding more and more sophisticated man-machine interfaces, which are easy to use, yet difficult to program using conventional software technology.

Let's consider the first of these reasons. Back in the mid '80s when my company first launched Dyalog APL, Unix systems were only marginally faster than personal computers. Indeed I can remember trying to explain to one sceptical customer why APL on a £200,000 1-MIP Vax 780 was no faster than on his £5,000 1-MIP PC. It as hardly surprising therefore, that Unix failed to supplant mainframe computing and was an ineffective competitor for MS-DOS, which is simpler and less power-hungry. Moreover, for many years the growth in performance of the 32-bit Motorola processors, upon which most Unix systems were built, has been matched, and occasionally bettered, by faster and faster Intel chips. The situation has recently changed dramatically, and RISC-based workstations from Sun Microsystems, Digital, IBM and Hewlett Packard have now outstripped PC technology in the race for ever-increasing performance. The differential in terms of floating-point operations, upon which most APL applications depend, is especially wide.

The impact of this technology in the financial trading arena is an interesting pointer. Once upon a time, dealing systems were entirely mainframe-based. Such applications needed the speed and communications capabilities that only mainframes could provide. Then PCs took over as people realised that a PC on each of 100 desks gave the same performance, and a great deal more convenience, than a single mainframe computer serving 100 terminals. In latter years, Unix workstations have begun to creep in to supplement the PCs. More recently, as markets have become more and more sophisticated, traders have become increasingly reliant on advanced software to guide them; power-hungry software that gobbles memory and cpu like never before. Today in leading institutions, especially on Wall Street, the Unix workstation has ousted both the mainframe and the PC as the computing tool for day-to-day applications.

So is there a parallel for APL? I think there is. Now that machines are becoming so fast, the argument that APL is interpreted (and therefore slow) is increasingly irrelevant. Indeed, APL is one of only a handful of development tools that are capable of using today's power effectively. Does it matter that a compiled C program, that took months to write, executes in 0.1 seconds versus 1 second for the APL equivalent developed in a few days? I think not. Two years ago when we were talking about 1 second versus 10 seconds, it patently did.

The second reason for the recent success of Unix is the modern requirement for a Graphical User Interface (GUI). The GUI, pioneered by Xerox and enthusiastically championed by Apple Computer, is now an accepted part of computing technology. Although a GUI is (or should be) easy to use it is NOT easy to program. Microsoft Windows is taken for granted as a handy, friendly tool for end-user computing, yet it is notorious as one of the most difficult computer programming environments yet conceived by man. Unix GUIs are based upon the X Window System. With thousands of man-years of development behind them, they are substantially better engineered, offer genuine multi-tasking and are much easier on the applications developer. But their concepts have been developed by deep-thinking, earnest computer scientists, and are not easy to grasp. It is not surprising therefore that all the major GUIs have spawned a host of application development aids which make it relatively easy for the programmer to build an attractive user-interface. However, most of these tools fall down when you come to define the logic for your application — they just don't have the linguistic flexibility for the job. This is where APL will score. APL is, or should be, as efficient at driving a GUI as any other programming language. The fact that it is interpreted is an advantage, not a disadvantage, in this field. APL vendors are all busily working on developing means of driving GUIs, and the healthy competition amongst them will ensure a good result.

I first took to APL because it enabled me to excel at my job, yet still play golf three times a week. I was able to produce cost-effective, successful, interactive applications at a time that my non-golfing colleagues were still punching card-decks. When computing moved away from mainframes onto PCs APL still held its own, thanks to the foresight shown by STSC in realising the potential of these small machines. But APL in both environments has been held back by cost/performance considerations. Only now that MIPS and MFLOPS have become both plentiful and cheap can APL really thrive. The competition from other software products is daunting, but if the APL vendors meet the challenge, the prospects for a golden age of APL have never been better.

by David Eastwood

As a slight change from our normal articles restricted to considerations of the ASL software, this issue of Random Vector features two articles by Dietrich Trenkler who is involved in statistics education at the Economics department at the University of Osnabrück in Germany. He uses APL in a course which complements and gives a deeper treatment to material covered in a one year introductory course in Statistics. His article 'Simulating Sampling Distributions' hints at the lively nature of the course and students. Dietrich also holds regular courses in APL for students who will be using APL when working towards their diplomas.

As far as the ASL software is concerned, this issue of Vector should be accompanied by an order form for the first two volumes of ASL to be ready for distribution. We cover the presentation made by Alan Sykes at a recent BAA meeting regarding availability and distribution of ASL software. If you want to order ASL software, you can also contact Alan Sykes at the address below.

The error was compounded by the fact that BATS is actually correctly listed in Vector's product guide! items.title: BATS
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 36

by David Eastwood

In the last issue of Vector, the program BATS - Bayesian Analysis of Time Series - was wrongly attributed. BATS is produced by and copyrighted to Andy Pole, Mike West and Jeff Harrison (see the entry in the Product Guide).

For those readers who are unfamiliar with BATS, I thought it might be useful to include a little detail on the software and the authors.

Andy Pole is visiting professor at, and Mike West is Director of, the Institute of Statistics and Decision Sciences at Duke University in North Carolina, USA; Jeff Harrison is professor of statistics at Warwick University.

BATS is an interactive system for modelling, analysing, and forecasting univariate time series using dynamic linear models. A wide range of dynamic models may be selected, including components for polynomial trend; seasonal patterns; exogenous variable regression; and variance laws. The analysis features include reference or user-defined initialisations, forecast monitoring, subjective intervention, step ahead forecasting, and smoothing. Non-stationarity, missing data, and outlying observations are routinely handled by the Bayesian paradigm. BATS is graphically oriented. Tabulated results may be written to text files.

BATS was originally developed in APL*PLUS/PC but has now been redeveloped in C (with the same ‘look and feel’) to improve performance. Both versions are available from the authors but support and future development will be restricted to the C versions.

items.title: Invited Speakers
items.text:
Igor Pospelov - Russia on the Way from Plan to Market: The Experience of Modelling. Professor Pospelov is a well-known Russian mathematician who specialises in economic modelling. He works in the laboratory for mathematical modelling of economic systems in the Computing Center of the Russian Academy of Sciences. Prof. Pospelov has over ten years' experience using APL. His presentation deals with the modelling of different transformations of the economy, along with a discussion and interpretation of the results.

Howard Peelle - Education and the Future of APL. Dr. Peelle is an accomplished APL teacher, author, and educator. As Associate Editor of APL Quote Quad, he continues to make a contribution to this area. His presentation will cover a number of questions of great concern to every APL enthusiast. Potentially, the educational system can provide a well-head for new members of the APL community. Dr. Peelle is working together with a team to prepare other activities on the theme of APL and Education for APL92.

Per Gjerlov - The Song of the Whale. Since APL90 (Per was Program Chair) our closing Plenary speaker has been travelling the Atlantic Ocean with an oceanographic team, recording and analysing audio data from groups of whales. Per will explain some of his work in detail, and show us some marvellous images (of whales and data!) to bring APL92 to a rousing close.

The final program will include additional invited speakers on APL and its development and future in Russia.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:
On the day before APL92 officially opens, a Tutorial day will be held in classrooms at the Education Center.

An introduction to APL - by Ray Polivka, noted author and teacher of APL, and winner of the ACM/SIGAPL Iverson award. This tutorial is oriented towards those with little or no exposure to APL.

An APL tutorial for Russian Children - is being organized in conjunction with the "APL in Education" theme.

Russian for APLers - Proposed tutorial, to run on Sunday and during APL92. Those attending this tutorial will gain some understanding of simple Russian sufficient to ask and understand simple questions, small phrases, and words useful for polite greetings and common dialogue.

Please note: Scheduling for this tutorial is based on the interest level expressed by those registering. A check-box on the registration form can be used to show your interest, and a tutorial session may then be organized.

items.title: Call for Posters
items.text:
Poster sessions, and poster submissions, are traditional for conferences in many technical disciplines. Posters are relatively new to APL conferences, having been introduced first at APL89. The name "Poster" comes from the practice of submitting material in the form of a poster (or sign), which is displayed at the conference.

Posters are used to show novel ideas and reports of work in progress. A separate session will be devoted to poster presentation. Authors of posters can discuss the poster, and distribute related materials as conference participants circulate to discuss them.

If you would like to show a poster, please send a title and abstract by 1 June to the APL92 conference office. We can include it in the final program, and ensure that space will be available for your poster presentation.

items.title: Vendor Exhibition
items.text:
An area of the Center has been set aside for use by vendors for showing products and services of interest to the APL community. We also encourage exhibitions from any organization needing exposure to well-placed computing professionals within and beyond the Commonwealth of Independent States.

Vendor forums are offered for those who wish to present commercial products in detail. Some forums will not conflict with the APL92 technical program, and provide attendees with a good chance to meet APL vendors. If you attend APL92, we expect that vendor forums will provide another interesting facet of the conference. If you are a vendor, please contact one of the APL92 offices, as some exhibit facilities and vendor forum times are still available.

items.title: Accepted Papers - APL92
items.text:
Warren Julian, Australia - Writing Macintosh Applications in APL. Features of a student enrolment and record system for use on Macintosh computers are described, emphasising the development of the interfaces between the user and the APL file environment.

Ruby Lim, Australia - Cannibals and Missionaries. The old game of Cannibals and Missionaries is presented. The solution (sometimes surprising!) is derived, and is implemented using APL.68000.

Moishe Sniedovich and Suzanne Findlay, Australia - Jogging With APL Along the Shortest Path. The classical shortest path problem is examined and the modelling issues are illustrated by formulating APL code for a number of generalizations, including multi-objective problems.

Walter G. Spunde, Australia - Challenging the Mathematics Curriculum. Packages accompanying mathematical texts often try to make computing power serve as a simple non-disruptive adjunct to the current syllabus. The author asserts that instead it should serve to accomplish that which previously could not be done, rather than merely to expedite drudgery.

Andreas Geyer-Schultz and Thomas Kolarik, Austria - Distributed Computing with APL. APL is suggested as a prototyping and debugging tool for distributed applications in the growing UNIX market segment. Several programming constructs are implemented via shared variables in the distributed environment.

Jacob Mitlohner, Austria - Porting APL Programs via Readable ASCII Transliteration. A translation scheme for writing APL code to a plain text file is introduced, and a transfer system is developed which reads and writes objects to and from files.

Robert Bernecky and Gert Osterberg, Canada - Compiler Tools in APL. Compiler development tools in APL, including finite state machines and parsers, are shown to be of significant value in a number of common applications. Examples include a financial trading system and a UNIX tab expander.

Edward Y.H. Lin, Canada - Multiple Choice Programming: An APL Approach. This paper introduces a set of APL code for the optimisation of multiple choice programming using the special-ordered-set branch-and-bound procedure incorporating the partitioning strategy of the weighted mean method.

Norman Thomson, England - APL2 Specification of Statistical Algorithms. APL2 has striking affinities with the apparatus needed to specify statistical algorithms. Some rules and conventions for the basis of such a standard are proposed, and the appropriateness of APL2 is illustrated.

Gustav Tollet and Peter Harrison, Finland - A Bezier Curve Builder. A Bezier curve provides a cubic approximation to a curve between two points. Two additional points specify a tangent and a relative weight at each end point. The paper describes techniques used to smooth a broken line approximation. Applications (Font generation, Graphics) are covered and emphasised.

Jean-Jacques Girardot, France - The CTalk Programming Language: A Strategic Evolution of APL. CTalk, a new programming language quite different from APL, is presented. An attempt to combine the best features of APL and languages such as LISP and C, it looks "modern" according to the criteria of the mainstream of computer science.

Gerard A. Langlet, France - Towards the Ultimate APL-TOE. Can the laws of nature be reconstructed independently from research in theoretical physics (on elementary particles and matter in general)? Can the same process be applied to algorithms using APL?

W. Hahn, Germany - Auxiliary Processor AP87. An auxiliary processor, supporting extended precision (IEEE 754 standard) arithmetic for APL/PC is described. This tool provides a number of techniques for dealing with extended precision numbers in APL.

Cristoph Pospiech, Germany - An APL2 Tool Box for Investigating Schwarz Methods. An APL tool box is described which allows one to interactively investigate and compare algorithms for solving elliptic partial differential equations by Schwarz methods.

Tien Chi Chen, Hong Kong - Globally Convergent Polynomial Iterative Zero Finding Using APL. The paper describes a global iteration theory for polynomial zero-finding. A new formula, based on the target function and its first two derivatives, is demonstrated to have better convergence properties than two classical schemes.

Renato Capra, Italy - 3D Layout Manipulation Functions with a Glance to Optimization Problems. APL syntax provides a very simple and expressive way to generate and manipulate 3D parametric objects. The paper describes a user-friendly interactive graphic system for 3D layout manipulation.

F.H.D. van Batenburg, Netherlands - Sorting and Optimizing Star - A Case Study of Suffering and Surfacing. After a brief description of an application in micro-biology, the paper reports on the migration of the system between workstation platforms.

Valery Kalinin and Boris A. Makeev, Russia - APL as a Tool for Scientific Forecasting. An expert system for forecasting development within fields of science is discussed. APL*PLUS/PC is chosen as the implementation language and the rationale for the choice is presented.

Alexander Skomorokov, Russia - Do Russian Children Like APL2? Describes experiences teaching children about computer science using APL2. Both goals and methods are included, along with proposed extensions to use APL to teach many other subjects.

Alexey N. Skurihin, Russia - Neural Networks in J. The attempt to implement Artificial Neural Systems is described. The language J is used to facilitate a straightforward implementation.

Manuel Alfonseca, Spain - Object-Oriented Graphics in APL2. The paper describes a general and extensive graphic system in two or three dimensions, built in APL2 by means of the object-oriented programming paradigm. The system fully demonstrates the appropriateness of the language to develop real-life applications.

Martin Gfeller, Switzerland - Walks into the APL Design Space. APL is evolving. The choices for future work constitutes a "design space" for future development. This paper assists the reader in exploring the APL design space on one's own. References to books and articles about problems and solutions are given.

J. Philip Benkard, USA - Introduction to Nested Arrays and Operators. Continuing exploration of the implications of nested data structures, comparing and contrasting the importance of the rank operator.

James Brown and Erik Kane, USA - APL2 Implementation of Cross System Shared Variables. The requirement for inter-machine communication is discussed. It is met with APL2's cross-system shared variables. In particular, the mapping of APL2's cooperative peer-to-peer communication model onto a client server data transport mechanism is described.

Evan Jennings, USA - An Object-Oriented APL2 Expert. An expert system which can answer questions posed in English about APL2 is described. The programs are written in APL2 using object-oriented programming techniques. The knowledge is hierarchical and frame based.

Curtis A. Jones, USA - Left to Its Own Devices, APL Plots on the Bus. A PC with APL can be used as a device on the IEEE-488 General Purpose Interface Bus. An APL workspace which emulates an x-y plotter illustrates some uses.

Peter A.W. Lewis, USA - A Full-Screen, Scrollable, APL2 Spreadsheet Input/Output Editor. A spreadsheet editor based on IBM's APL2 language for 386 machines is used for entering, analysing, editing, and outputting data. APL functions can be applied to blocks of data, drawing on the full computational and notational power of APL.

John Mizel, USA - Using SCCS to Manage APL Development Projects. A Change Control System for managing large-scale APL projects is described. Certain APL-specific problems are discussed.

Richard Neidinger, USA - Differential Equations Are Recurrence Relationships in APL. A differential equation can be seen as a recurrence relation, which can be used to produce the Taylor coefficients. The paper describes an addition to an automatic differentiation workspace, which produces a useful tool from this idea.

Steve Promisel, USA - A Multi-National Sales Planning System in APL. An APL-based logistics planning system is described, with emphasis on the discussion of requirements arising from the need for the system to operate across international borders. Topics include managing multiple currencies, languages, product orientation, and time-phased planning.

Alvin J. Surkan, USA - WSDM: Weighted Sparse Distributed Memory Prototype Expressed in APL. A functional style application of APL notation succinctly describes the architecture and principles of operation of one kind of Connection Machine. APL programs can provide precise descriptions of operational machines. Two adaptive variants of the sparse distributed memory machine are modelled in APL and presented in the paper.

Robert G. Willhoft, USA - Matrix Operations Over Integral Domains Using Nested APL. The paper deals with the use of APL to solve matrix theory problems with elements that use members of an integral domain.

Robert G. Willhoft, USA - Petri Net Evaluation Using APL2. A Petri net is a graphical and modelling tool useful in the analysis of a variety of problems; the paper introduces a method of representing Petri nets in APL2.

Scott Williams, USA - EZHONE: A Perfect Application for APL2 Name Association. A widespread application on a modified VSPC has been migrated to APL2. Migration chains are described, with emphasis on how the name association facility can replace disparate older facilities.

items.title: Workshops and Panel Sessions
items.text:
A series of workshops is planned for APL92. These events will be at minimum two hours' duration, but more normally a complete half day is planned. Attendance at the sessions will be limited. Please indicate your interests on the registration form. We will endeavour to honour workshop preferences if you register. The sessions described below are in an advanced stage of planning, but circumstances beyond our control may prevent one or more from taking place. If these sessions are critical to your attendance plans, please contact the APL92 office before making your travel plans. We will try to confirm the exact status of workshops for you. Indeed it is likely that additional workshops will be set up between now and July. We welcome your enquiries. You are invited to contribute a short (one page or less) written statement for distribution to other participants at workshop sessions you have checked on the registration form. Please send any materials you wish to be distributed to: Dick Bowman, [address omitted], England, by 1 June, 1992. The preferred format is as an ASCII file on an MS-DOS compatible diskette.

Applied Statistics Library Workshop: to be presented by Alan Sykes. The Applied Statistics Library is a project which has been underway for several years, building a library of statistical software written in APL and intended to allow the professional statistician to bypass the limitations of commercial packages. The workshop will explore ASL, and its use in a number of case studies.

Using J: presenter to be announced. J represents a further development of some notational aspects of APL (although everybody has their own personal view on this). The purpose of the workshop is to explore the implications of using J to tackle real-life problems, and to identify the benefits and difficulties that this new notation brings.

APL and Education: presenter Howard Peelle. The dual concepts of introducing APL in education and educating people about APL have been constant themes of APL conferences for many years. This workshop brings together many people who have been active in these areas, and aims to take a proactive stance in defining a future and effective strategy for APL.

Modern User Interfaces: presenter(s) John Scholes/Richard Nabavi. There have been many advances in user interfaces in recent years; APL has arguably either ignored these advances or been left behind by them. What are the considerations behind applying a modern user interface to applications? What tools does APL offer? How do we build modern user interfaces into modern APL applications?

Out of the tool box: conducted by Robert G. Brown, with others. APL software developers require more tools than are provided with many interpreters. This workshop will survey some of the commonly needed tools, attempt to define a required set of tools for all APL users, and techniques that can be adapted to their use. Software related to this workshop will be available via the Software Exchange.

The Future of APL: moderator Lynne Shaw. This plenary panel discussion brings together a number of well-known and experienced APL personalities from several countries. This panel will confront issues relevant to the future use of APL, and possible roles for APL in the software development cycle. Current obstacles (and possible solutions) to further development of APL will be addressed.

If APL is so great, why isn't everybody using it? Conducted by Cory Skutt. The history of computing is rich in languages that have been bypassed. About 10 years ago, LISP was about to become one such language, until the LISP community took some steps to avert the demise of LISP. There are lessons to be learned from this experience, and they can be used by the APL community to help secure a future for APL in an increasingly competitive computing environment. Cory will also be a participant in The Future of APL, but will develop his ideas in more depth for potential APL activists.

items.title: Registration
items.text:
You are encouraged to complete and return the registration form with your payments as soon as possible. The deadline for early registration is 8 May. A participant will be considered registered only when all fees are paid. Payments including accommodation must be made in advance to APL92, by credit card, international money order in US dollars or by cheque on a United States bank in US dollars. The Registration Fee covers:

For Participants (members and non-members): attendance at all sessions, the conference proceedings, coffee breaks and refreshments; lunches Monday, 6 July, through Friday, 10 July, and all social events (with dinners) Sunday, 5 July, through Thursday, 9 July.

For Students: attendance at all sessions, the conference proceedings, coffee break refreshments; five lunches Monday to Friday, and all evening social events except the closing banquet on Thursday (additional tickets for the closing banquet are available for US $35.00).

For Accompanying Adults: sightseeing package and all evening social events (including dinners). The sightseeing package consists of four sightseeing tours selected from those offered Sunday through Friday. Each tour includes lunch in a city restaurant.

For Accompanying Children: all the features for accompanying adults except the Exhibitors' Reception on Monday and the Closing Banquet on Thursday. (Additional tickets for closing banquet are available for US $35.00. Child care will be available during these two events.)

A participant who includes an ACM/SIGAPL membership form and dues payment with the APL92 registration form is entitled to register for the conference at the discounted member rate.

Please return the APL92 registration form as soon as possible. An official invitation from the Russian Academy of Sciences will be extended to all registrants. This invitation, necessary to obtain a Russian (business) visa, will be sent when the registration form is received. Residents of Finland should send the registration forms to Erkki Juvonen.

Fees:

Before 8 May After 8 May ACM/SIGAPL Member $400 $500 FinnAPL Member $400 $500 Non-Member $475 $575 Accompanying Adult $275 $275 Accompanying Child $120 $120 ACM/SIGAPL Student $120 $120 Single Day $125 $125

items.title: Report on St Petersburg Visit
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 57

by Anthony Camacho

I attended the meeting of the APL 92 program committee in St Petersburg from 9 to 12 January 1992 as a representative of the British APL Association. I had to be bullied to go as at that time of year the hours of daylight are few and the temperature is low; I don't like the dark and cold. The conference itself will be in July when you can read your watch by natural light at midnight and the weather is warm.

items.title: First Impressions
items.text: Nikolai Puntikov met me and drove me to the centre in his car. The airport is the far side of St Petersburg from the centre. Even though it was dark it was plain that St Petersburg is a very beautiful city, with hundreds of eighteenth century buildings and intersected by about seventy canals and rivers; there are about three hundred bridges.

items.title: The Leningrad Education Centre
items.text:
The Director told us they are in process of reorganising; for 20 years they have worked in industrial training. They don't intend to change direction, but to undertake much more international work, especially in management and marketing. They already have many links with foreign partners and hold many events in conjunction with institutes and companies abroad (there was a flag in his office left by a group from Dallas). There are lots of problems to solve if they are to keep going in this unstable time. They have to earn money independently; there has been no state subsidy for the last two years.

At present the centre is still a State Institute called the Leningrad Education Centre but they may change the name to reflect both St Petersburg and the fact that there is no longer a USSR for them to be a State Institute of. Perhaps it will become an independent international management school; they are seeking partnership with a European Bank. Obviously they are jumping at the chance to cater for an international conference at least partly paid for in hard currency.

The Director expects that by the summer a satellite telephone link to the world network will be working (a firm from Denver is currently installing it). The Centre contains its own medical facilities and staff. The building is 7 minutes from the nearest metro and 15 minutes by car from the centre of St Petersburg.

The Leningrad Education Centre is three buildings on six floors. It contains:

Rooms for about 300 people,

A restaurant and bar,

One large hall which will seat over 300 in raked seats and which has room for even more seats if needed.

Two smaller halls with TV projectors which will each seat 60 or more, also with raked seating.

One specially large room which will seat 100 or more

About fifteen rooms which could seat 20 to 30 each

A room of 60 square metres which could be the software exchange

A library and the usual associated facilities.

Each room used for presentations will have two OHPs, one with an LCD screen for projecting a computer screen for the audience to read.

items.title: The Accommodation for Delegates
items.text:
I had a single room with bed, desk, wardrobe, table, desk lamp, silent fridge (absorption) and a television aerial (some rooms had sets - I guess the one from mine was being repaired). There was a private bathroom with shower, WC, washbasin, heated towel rail and a bowl with a washboard for washing clothes. These are the very same rooms that will be used for the conference. The accommodation was much better than at Stanford or Manchester.

A view of my room

items.title: Food for the Conference
items.text:
The food for the conference will be much better than the news would lead one to believe. The real problem is the volatility of the currency. Farms are having to trade by barter to ensure that they don't lose too much when the value of the rouble changes rapidly so it is hard to buy for roubles — i.e. you queue. You can buy anything with foreign (hard) currency. Since the conference expects to entertain many visitors from abroad the organisers have signed contracts for the food with a Russo-Finnish company to be paid for in Finnmarks. This is a contract which is very attractive to the supplying company and provides them with some stability in the Russian world of unstable prices. This company can thus buy any food they want in Russia and anything they can't get there, they can import from Finland. It is about four hours by road from Helsinki.

The room for the Software Exchange

items.title: As Tourists, Delegates may be Rich
items.text:
While I was there the shortage of hard currency was so severe that five U S dollars would buy food for a family of four for a week. This makes the price of souvenirs — indeed more or less everything — very cheap indeed for visitors from any country which uses hard currency. There were touts who were offering bottles of Russian Champagne (very good it is) to tourists on buses at $2 a bottle. It seemed cheap but not when one found out what it could be bought for elsewhere. One can hope that the currency problems are reduced by the time the conference happens; if they aren't life as a tourist will be comparatively luxurious and incredibly cheap.

A view of the 60-seat lecture theatre

items.title: Conclusion
items.text: APL 92 will be well fed, comfortably accommodated and in a beautiful city. Visitors from abroad are likely to find that the exchange rate is still very favourable. My impression is that the Russian organisers are making a great effort to ensure that the occasion will be a memorable one. I haven't seen the program yet, but of course I have a good idea of some of the papers. Sylvia and I are going. I hope we see you there.

items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 61

Compiled by Gill Smith

VECTOR's exclusive APL Product Guide aims to provide readers with useful information about sources of APL hardware, software and services. We welcome any comments readers may have on its usefulness and any suggestions for improvements.

We do depend on the alacrity of suppliers to keep us informed about their products so that we can update the Guide for each issue of VECTOR. Any suppliers who are not included in the Guide should contact me to get their free entry - see address below.

We reserve the right to edit material supplied for reasons of space or to ensure a fair market coverage.

The listings are not restricted to UK companies and international suppliers are welcome to take advantage of these pages. Where no UK distributor has yet been appointed, the vendor should indicate whether this is imminent or whether approaches for representation by existing companies are welcomed.

For convenience to readers, the product list has been divided into the following groups:

  • Complete APL Systems (Hardware & Software)
  • APL Timesharing Services
  • APL Interpreters
  • APL Visual Display Units
  • APL character set printers
  • APL-based packages
  • APL Consultancy
  • APL Training Courses
  • Other services
  • Vendor addresses

Every effort has been made to avoid errors in these listings but no responsibility can be taken by the working group for mistakes or omissions.

All contributions and updates to the APL Product Guide should be sent to Gill Smith, at the address on the inside back cover.
