items.title: Comments on “ASWI Programming Standards”
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

From: Ray Cannon, 1 February 1992

I would like to raise some objections to some of the standards as put forward in the paper “ASWI Programming Standards” by FHD v.Batenburg et al in Vector 8.2.

The main reasons for standards are human readability and maintainability; as the authors state “Good APL functions are readable”. They may, as in this case, also need to define a common subset of APL that all the target machines can work with.

First, the naming of “sub-functions”. Adding a System ID (SID) as a prefix to all sub-function, not only makes it far harder to maintain the workspace but, in extreme cases, may cause difficulties with the symbol table. Trying to find the name of a function from the results of )FNS or ⎕NL 3 is much harder if most of the functions start with the same letters. If the SID has to be included in the name, at least put it last, not first.

Next, “imported sub-functions”. This naming convention for these utility functions seems silly to me. What SID is applicable for the utility function IOTA? Is it SIM_IOTA because it came from the SIMulation of whaling population growth first? Sorry, I’ve missed a point here, it would not be called SIM_IOTA but something like SIM_CNSPIOTA because it occurred as a sub-function to “splitting” which is a sub-function to “continuous”. Surely, a true utility’s name should be independent of its origin. If the origin of a function is important, then comment it, don’t clutter up the name space.

The standard specifies the use of the underbar character in sub-function names, and lower case alphanumerics in global variable names. These are invalid characters in important mainframe APLs, for example, VSAPL and APL*PLUS Mainframe. Also APL2 Version 1 does not support lower-case letters. The standard should have given alternative characters to be used in these APLs.

Local variable names are often short, but it seems unnecessary to force local variable names to 4 characters or less as this could make the code less readable. Often a variable may have a “natural name”. Shortening such a natural name to 4 characters may make it so cryptic that the code becomes unreadable.

In the section defining “Good APL functions:”

Point 5:

“work for missing left arguments” implies ambivalent functions. Again this is an extension to the ISO standard and may not work on all implementations.

and Point 6:

“receive data in the right argument and control in the left” is a gross over simplification. Are scalar dyadic function not “Good APL functions” because they receive data in both arguments?

I am sorry to be so negative about this, but standards like these cannot be imposed. If standards are to be implemented by programmers, they have to be useful to the author, reasonable and work. For shareware, they must work on any APL ISO conforming implementation, and should work on most of the others.

Following good standards will aid readability. Try rewriting some of the functions from Education Vector following these standards and then asking it’s audience if it helps or hinders.

Ray Cannon

items.title: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 72

reviewed by Adrian Smith
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: General Comments
items.text:
This is clearly the most important collection of APL material for at least the past 10 years. It ranks alongside "A Source Book of APL" as an important milestone in the evolving history of the language, and I feel that anyone with a library of APL books should take steps to add this one to his or her collection.

Because of the importance of this work (and the relative difficulty and expense for non-IBM employees in getting hold of it), the British APL Association is hoping to agree a bulk shipment arrangement with the publisher, so that copies will be available to members at significantly less than the nominal $20 subscription rate. Details will be advised to members as soon as possible.

The presentation is excellent, with good typesetting of both APL and J, and diagrams up to Scientific American standard. There are remarkably few typos (I have just failed to re-find the only one I noticed on first reading), and the balance of material is about right. I was particularly pleased to see that the text is not totally limited to APL2 (NARS, Sharp APL and J all get coverage), and that several of the APL2 papers refer to implementations on small machines. A brief precis of each paper follows.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: The Preface
items.text: How gratifying to see an explicit reference to the British APL Association, and specifically the ASL project, in the introduction to Norman Thomson's paper. If this helps to get the ASL concept known outside the APL world, it can only do us good.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: The IBM family of APL systems
items.text:
by A.D. Falkoff

A nice easy read, with a lovely diagram illustrating the genealogy of IBM's APL interpreters. Plenty of surprises, and some fascinating new insights on the influence APL has had on the designers of small machines. Recommended for all readers.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: APL2: Getting started
items.text:
by J.A. Brown & H.P. Crowder

A gentle introduction to second-generation APL, with some nice examples from graph-plotting to the manipulation of sparse arrays. Recommended for all except APL2 buffs!
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Extending the domain of APL
items.text:
by M.T. Wheatley

This is more or less a formalized version of Mike's talk to the British APL Association at Canterbury in 1988. As I said in Vector 5.2 (Nov 88) "A lot of really good hard 'inside information' on the early development of APL, and the way it fitted into its environment. The rationale behind ⎕NA and the shared variable processors." Recommended for mainly ⎕SVO and ⎕NA freaks.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Storage management in IBM APL systems
items.text:
by R. Trimble

This is quite a tough technical paper, but the excellent diagrams help a lot! It could have a major influence on interpreter design in the approaching world of multi-gigabyte workspaces. Recommended for interpreter writers, and those of the rest of us who like to know how these things really work.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Putting a new face on APL2
items.text:
by J.R. Jensen & K.A. Beaty

More or less a rerun of their APL91 paper, but again the high quality diagrams and colour images help to make the point. Definitely a skim-read for most of us; recommended for X-windows hacks.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: The APL IL Interpreter Generator
items.text:
by M. Alfonseca, D. Selby & R. Wilks

I first came across this one at Copenhagen (at a G.U.I.D.E. meeting) in 1979! (see 'Design Handbook' Chapter 13 for my thoughts on using APL to run your central heating system.) It is quite hard going, but worth the effort for anyone who wants to know where IBM APL2/PC and APL2/6000 are coming from. Recommended for all techies and most of the rest of us.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Parallel expression in the APL2 language
items.text:
by R.G. Willhoft

If APL is to exploit the parallel architectures of the future, it must build on the high degree of parallelism already implicit in the language. This paper explores the boundaries of present APL2 implementations, and makes a number of important recommendations for future language design. I suspect it may generate quite a vigorous debate! A skim-read for most of us ... recommended for language designers and anyone interested in the far future of APL.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: The foundations of suitability of APL2 for music
items.text:
by Stanley Jordan & Erik S. Friis

This is a much easier read than the preceding papers! It shows how APL2 nested arrays can be used at a high level to model underlying musical structures (not just the actual notes). Recommended (not just for musicians).
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Verification of the IBM RISC System/6000 by a dynamic biased pseudo-random test program generator
items.text:
by A. Aharon et al

This paper provides the general reader with an excellent introduction to the basic methodology of automated system testing, and then shows how (and why) VS APL and APL2 were used to build the test suite for the RS/6000 architecture. I felt it was most valuable as a primer in automatic verification techniques, rather than for its APL content. Recommended for anyone interested in systems methodologies.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: APL2 as a specification language for statistics
items.text:
by N.D. Thomson

Norman briefly introduces the ASL project, and goes on to show how APL2 can be used to specify a collection of basic statistical algorithms. Recommended.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Advanced applications of APL: logic programming, neural networks, and hypertext
items.text:
by M. Alfonseca

The title says it all! The sections on Neural Nets and a Hypertext on-line dictionary are probably those of most general interest. Recommended for appropriate specialists.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Language as an intellectual tool: from hieroglyphics to APL
items.text:
by D.B. McIntyre

If you ever wanted to know how the ancient Egyptians managed to do division (with Hieroglyphs), you should read this paper! It is a fascinating ramble through the long and confused history of mathematical notation, and I would say it has something for everyone. The APL examples are shown in the classic ∇ form, in direct definition and also in J; I found it most refreshing that an IBM publication was able to include so much material from non-IBM versions of APL!

There are over two pages of closely-spaced references which should form a superb starting point for any reader who wants to take the subject further. Highly recommended, but don't try to take it all in at one sitting.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: A personal view of APL
items.text:
by K.E Iverson

This paper needs to be read in conjunction with several earlier works (e.g. "The Design of APL" and "The Evolution of APL") to which it refers. It is actually a thinly disguised polemic on where APL went wrong, and why J is better! It discusses in detail such issues as the banning of niladic functions from J, and the ruthless elimination of the [I;J] notation on favour of an indexing function. APLers should be prepared to take several deep breaths, and count to 100 slowly. Recommended for J freaks and APLers of an equable temperament.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Summary
items.text: Whether or not you agree with everything in it, if you are serious about your APL you should find a way of obtaining this collection of important and influential papers.
path: IBM Systems Journal: APL 25th Anniversary Edition

items.title: Byte ‘Classic Languages’ Article on APL
items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 76

items.title: Byte Magazine, December 1991, pp141 - 146
items.text:
reviewed by Adrian Smith

Whenever I see 'APL Feature' billed on the cover of a computing magazine, I get that unpleasant sinking feeling! I was half-expecting Byte to run an article on APL in its 'Classic Languages' series, and I knew that Byte was one of the few computing journals to take APL seriously, so I opened my December 1991 issue at page 141 with a mixture of anticipation and dread.

Fortunately, I need not have worried; STSC had helped them over the obvious technical hurdle by providing a reasonable typeface, and Doris Appleby did a really good job of providing the average Byte reader with a broad-brush introduction to the notation.

Her article covers the early history of APL, and reviews the current commercial applications areas. It stresses the power of APL as a prototyping tool, and mentions its recreational value for "people who get a kick out of thinking". Modern implementations (e.g. APL.68000, APL2/6000, APL*PLUS and J) get good coverage, as does the 'A' development at Morgan Stanley. I-APL gets an honourable mention, as does APL92 at St Petersburg (the international appeal of APL is noted).

The Byte "Action Summary" concludes ...

If you want to do complex mathematical operations in just a few keystrokes, the APL language is well suited to your needs, but it will require a modified keyboard. Nonetheless, APL is used by specialists throughout the world.

You can't say fairer than that ... well done Byte.

items.title: APL Goes Fuzzy
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 77

previewed by Oleg Pöhl

Just as the principles of statistical quality control were invented in the West (by Edward Deming and Dr Walter Shewhart in the 1940s) and exploited in the East, so might be the obscure ideas of Fuzzy Logic. The core concepts go back to Poland in the 1920s, with the work of Jan Lukasiewicz, and the theory was developed by Prof. Lotfi Zadeh of the University of California (See Robert Bittlestone's review in Vector [1]). He coined the term "Fuzzy Logic" in his paper in the academic journal "Information and Control" in 1965.

Since that time, fuzzy systems have occasionally turned up in real process control applications, for example running a cement kiln in Copenhagen in 1980, but limitations in available hardware have prevented mass acceptance of the technology. For example, IBM Research developed APL/360 (so called because it reduced the power of the System/360) in late 1976, but unfortunately it reduced it so much:

      ⍳12
1.2 1.9 3.03 3.98 5 5.92 7.12 8.0002 9.21 9.976 11 12.07

... that an expression like the above took over 3½ hours to execute on a 370/148. Even IBM realised that this was over-doing it, and APL/360 never made it to the marketplace.

items.title: Understanding Fuzzy Systems
items.text:
The best way to approach the ideas of fuzzy logic is to find a really fuzzy system, and watch it working for a while. A typical example was explored in Vector by Smith [2], where APL was used to derive the uncertainty function for an automatic checkweigher. This device is supposed to accept all boxes over a certain weight, and reject all boxes that fall below. A perfect device could be drawn as a step-function, with the probability of acceptance jumping from 0% to 100% as the set weight was passed.

Of course in the real world the machine is subject to random influences (vibrations, small variations in the spacing and orientation of the packs etc.) which 'blur out' this sharp edge. You can demonstrate this effect by making up a set of test packs at known weights which straddle the set point, passing them repeatedly over the checkweigher in a random sequence, and recording the pass/fail rate at each weight. What you find looks a bit like this:

The fitted curve was generated using the Logistic function:

PACKS←219+⍳13   ⍝ Set of test packs at 1gm intervals
UNC←1.31        ⍝ Uncertainty parameter
SET←224.48      ⍝ Best fit to 50% rejection rate

FITREJ←100×÷1+*(PACKWT-SET)÷UNC

If you extend the plot to 3 dimensions, the importance of the uncertainty parameter becomes clear:

items.title: A Natural Extension to APL
items.text:
If we discount those first-generation APLs which implemented fuzz accidentally, we find that some kind of nested array structure is essential for an efficient representation of fuzzy data. For some time, IBM Japan have been working on a series of extensions to APL2/PC which exploit the power of the Togai InfraLogic Fuzzy expansion card. Instead of generating simple vectors, functions such as ⍳ produce nested objects, where each element is a 'fuzzed' set of numbers, obeying the logistic probabilities:

      ⎕FUZZ←5 0.5     ⍝ each point generates 5 numbers, with U=0.5
      NOS←⍳5
      ⍴NOS
5                     ⍝ Shape is not fuzzy!
      ⍴¨NOS
5 5 5 5 5
      2⊃NOS
1.91 1.96 2 2.04 2.09

Things get interesting when you start doing arithmetic with these fuzzy objects ... the system responds by adding levels of nesting, and effectively producing the 'outer product' of the fuzziness:

      XX←NOS×2      ⍝ note that '2' is also fuzzy
      ⍴XX
5
      ⍴¨XX
5 5 5 5 5
      ⍴2⊃XX
5 5 5 5 5

... to stop things getting totally out of hand, the implementors have added a second system variable ⎕FUZZDEPTH which results in the aggregation of the blurring when the arrays get to this depth. By default, ⎕FUZZDEPTH←5 which is more than adequate for the majority of applications. The APL/360 example at the top of this preview effectively had ⎕FUZZDEPTH←0, but used a different (randomised) strategy for generating the uncertainty.

items.title: Applications
items.text:
Already, fuzzy technology is on sale in the UK in the shape of Panasonic's new NV-S1 camcorder; this effectively eliminates 'jitter' by storing images and using earlier images to smooth incoming data.

In the APL world, there are obvious uses in the areas of Sales Forecasting, Dealing-room systems, and so on, in fact anywhere where the system must take decisions based on uncertain information.

In a typical forecasting system, there will be an inherent uncertainty associated with each product group (fleet cars are a more reliable market than luxury limousines), and also an extra uncertainty which increases with time. It is also possible that some markets might have more volatile sales patterns than others. If you add to this the effects of currency fluctuations, you soon realise that ⎕FUZZDEPTH←5 is likely to be about right, and that it is essential that the system handles these rapidly ramifying structures for you. In fact, the implementors are experimenting with a further extension to ⎕FUZZ to allow a 2-column matrix to represent increasing uncertainty with time:

      ⎕FUZZ←(4+⍳12), [1.5] 0.5×(⍳12)*.5
      NOS←⍳5
      ⍴NOS
5                     ⍝ Still 5 elements
      ⍴¨NOS
5 6 7 8 9             ⍝ but more detail underneath

Note that many functions and system variables (including of course ⎕FUZZ itself) implicitly localise ⎕FUZZLEVEL←0!

items.title: Correspondence
items.text:
From: R.H. Oates, February 26, 1992

I saw your request for comments on J typefaces in the January Vector. The quote character on page 72 is too light. I was reading Vector on the bus and thought both f f expressions had open quotes until I looked over at the APL side. And the bulk of $ makes that character too dark. It almost looks bold. How is your @? You want to establish an even blackness throughout the font, and to do that you have to compensate for the relative bulk of the characters. You can't just make them all two pixels wide, or whatever. It's not easy.

I find Programming in J and Tangible Math easier to read than the Dictionary and Arithmetic because they use bold characters for J (at least in the 1991 editions) consistently throughout. If you go with bold, then the problem becomes generating a bold Dot and Quote, say, that will be blacker than the normal At and Dollar Sign. It gets harder. My own fonts, which I got for APL2, are not very good, even within a font and particularly in the contrast between bold and normal fonts.

The J dictionary does not use bold consistently, just at the heading of each entry, and that is a mistake. Ken is following English dictionary format too closely. When people complain about the dictionary what they usually mention is its terseness. I like the terseness and think the typography is the real problem.

There is more white space (to accommodate figures) within the entries of the J dictionary than in an English dictionary. The contrast between bold and normal in the J dictionary is less than an English dictionary. Entries in the J dictionary divide into sub-entries in small caps, while entries in an English dictionary are homogeneous. Entries in the J dictionary begin either with a single J word or with a phrase like m : n. J words average 1.65 characters in length and phrase words average 1.1 characters in length, while English words average maybe 5 or 6 characters.

All of these things conspire to keep the J dictionary page from breaking down into distinct entries like a page in an English dictionary does. The J page is just one big blob. It would be much improved if a blank line were left in front of each entry and if the bold typefont were used consistently throughout for J words. When I get a new J dictionary the first thing I do is rule it off in black ink. I know that sounds stupid, but I do and it makes a big difference.

Typography is an art, of course, not a science, a profession, actually. But I wish you well and look forward to experimenting with your font.

R.H. Oates, [address omitted]

Typesetter's note: your comments are much appreciated, and I hope I have fixed the obvious infelicities in the design. See Roger Hui's article (page 91) for the revised '$"@%& in action! At the moment, this is implemented as a PostScript type-3 font, using stroked characters (except for simple fills like dot). I am in the process of converting my APL2741 face to an Adobe type-1, which demands filled characters throughout. Fortunately, the font currently exists as numbers in an APL workspace, so much of the geometry is automatic, but I am not clever enough to convert complex shapes like ⍺ totally mechanically!

The obvious advantage of a type-1 is that all Windows software will display it (at any sensible size) and will also render it on paper on most reasonable printers (like HP Deskjets) very well. All you need to do is buy Adobe Type Manager, or wait for Windows 3.1 and TrueType. I will try to have both fonts available by APL92.

items.title: Comments on J Questionnaire
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 83

From: Roger Hui and Ken Iverson, 4 February 1992

We were pleased by the interesting articles appearing in the J Section of the January VECTOR, and by the report on the questionnaire. We offer the following comments:

  1. “The Atari user did not get an editor at all. Characters can be typed on the command line, and there is a destructive backspace, but nothing else.” Terminal input/output are implemented in such a way as to avoid interference with underlying facilities. A line editor would have been available if the system had one; that line editing is not more “user friendly” on the Atari is a deficiency of the underlying system.

  2. “... the Suite variable an awkward method of program control”. Since the effect of $.=. label is equivalent to branch to label, it is hard to see what the difficulty is. Perhaps readers are looking for something like if then else, do while, or case statements, matters that are better handled by gerunds combined with agenda (@.) and power(^:) as illustrated in part by the following examples from An Introduction to J:

       +:'-:'*:'%: @. (4&|@<.)"0 i. 10
0 0.5 4 1.73205 8 2.5 36 2.64575 16 4.5
   1:'(]*$:@<:) @. * "0 i. 6
1 1 2 6 24 120

  3. “... or insist on tacit definition and operators for everything.”. Whereas we encourage tacit programming, we do not agree that proscription (even of obscenities) belongs in language design. In particular, beginners in tacit programming find it useful to make an explicit definition in the form m : d, and then enter m : 11 and d : 11 to see the equivalent tacit forms.

  4. “... would love graphics support.”. The current availability of the documented J Source (in C) will make it possible for others to port J to further systems, and to provide links to graphics and other resources appropriate to the particular system.

  5. “... if the 640K barrier was broken” This barrier was imposed by the limitations, both technical and legal, of the C compilers previously available. J for the 386 is now compiled using WATCOM C386, and the barrier no longer exists.

  6. Although McIntyre’s use of names such as lesser_of is valid, we would advise instead the use of names such as lesserOf and LesserOf. The reason is that a name with an underscore will be treated as a locative; for example, abc_def refers to the name def in the locale (or file) abc. Locatives are referred to and assigned in the normal manner.

From: Ken Iverson, January 12, 1992

I would like to comment on two papers in the October issue of Vector.

I believe that the point of the limits observed by Parkhouse might be clarified by the observation that if repeated application of a function g converges to a limit y, then y is the solution of the equation y = g y. In J, experimentation with this can be expressed using the power conjunction (dyadic operator) ^:, and the corresponding adverb (monadic operator) lim=. ^:_ for the limiting case of infinite power.

Thus:

   i=. 0 1 2 3 4 5
   cos^: i 1

   lim=. ^:_

0.739085

   g lim 1
1.47099

1.47099 1.47099 1.47099 1.47099

In his Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers (McGraw-Hill, 1962), R. W. Hamming introduces Stirling numbers in order to relate the coefficients c of a polynomial (expressed in J as +/c*x ^ i.#c) and the coefficients cf of a factorial polynomial.

If k is zero, the product over x plus k times iota n is equivalent to x to the power n; if k is negative one, it is Hamming’s factorial function. Moreover, if c is the vector of coefficients of an ordinary polynomial and cf the coefficients of an equivalent factorial polynomial, then cf is given by the matrix product of S2 and c, where S2 is the matrix of Stirling numbers of the second kind. In J, the fit conjunction !. produces a “variant” function; in particular, the function ^!._1 is Hamming’s factorial.

Although Hamming says “There is no simple formula for the Stirling numbers ...”, the relations outlined above lead to an expression of the form b times the inverse of a, where a is a Vandermonde matrix, and b is the corresponding “Vandermonde matrix” for the factorial polynomial. In J, the matter may be expressed as follows:

   fvm=. ^!._1/ i.@#

   x vm c

The matrices S1 and S2 are Stirling numbers of the first and second kinds. Since Abramowitz and Stegun (and consequently Appleton) do not include the leading row and column, Appleton’s result is given by }.}."S1. This formulation does not provide transformation of the constant term which, of course, remains the same in the two types of polynomial. Finally, functions to generate the Stirling numbers (as function of the order) are defined by:

items.title: Minutes of the AGM of the British APL Association at the IEE on 7 June 1991
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 9

The retiring Chairman, Peter Donnelly, opened the meeting at 2pm by thanking all the members of the Committee who had worked with him during his three years as Chairman. In particular:

the Secretaries, Graham Parkhouse and Anthony Camacho;

the Treasurer, Nicholas Small;

the Education Officer, Alan Sykes, who not only edited Education Vector but also took a leading role on the ASL project and in promoting APL in education;

the Editor, Jonathan Barman, in whose first year Vector had not only maintained its standard but also come out on time. Peter has no hesitation in saying Vector is now the best APL magazine in the world;

the Activities Officer, Peter Branson, who has improved the quality of our meetings and now, with the move to the IEE, made better presentation affordable, as the Barco large screen display is always available.

Peter also called attention to the great efforts put into the APL Statistics Library. He believes the Library will fill a great need and the Association should support it and wish it great success.

Peter then summarised the state of APL in Britain:

It is under pressure in many large companies.

Software is now often bought as a fashion item.

British APL developments are as good and numerous as those in the rest of the world (he mentioned APL2/PC, Dyalog and MicroAPL II among others).

Insurance companies and Actuaries are large users but few attend our meetings.

Many excellent packages have been written in APL and this is one of its best uses (he mentioned Metapraxis, Saladin, HMW and Devon Systems) Open systems such as ADI seem old-fashioned.

Finally, Peter commended the new committee (the list was circulated with the notice of the meeting) to the Association, and in particular, the new Chairman, David Eastwood.

The Treasurer, Nicholas Small, circulated accounts for the year and the two previous years for comparison. The accounts had been done on a cash basis. He pointed out that running expenditure for 1990-1991 exceeded regular income (subscriptions and Vector advertisements), which was the reason for the subscription increase. Next year running expenditure will approximately balance the income. Project and special or extraordinary expenditure will be paid for from reserves and interest on reserves.

In answer to a questioner who asked about the variation in Vector advertising income, Nicholas explained that there was a reduction in income from 1989-90 to 1990-91 as fewer advertisements had been placed, but that the main reason for variation was late invoicing and late payment for 1988-89 advertisements which had reduced that year's income and inflated the 1989-90 receipts.

There were no other questions and the AGM was closed at 2.15pm.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
This issue of Vector coincides with the annual international APL conference, which this year is being held in St Petersburg, and our regular readership will be increased to include delegates to APL92 who are being given copies of Vector. Alan Sykes, the ASL Deputy Chairman, will be one of the delegates from the UK and will be giving a presentation about ASL at the conference. Alan will be basing his presentation on areas of application for the ASL software, in Education, Research and Commerce and will be discussing some of the future plans for ASL. We will seek to print his presentation in a future issue but in the meantime I hope that it proves an interesting introduction to the ASL software for delegates at APL92 and in particular our Russian colleagues.

We have, at long last, begun distributing copies of ASL software and by the time this issue of Vector appears we will have added the Basic Statistics shelf to our release set. Order forms are available from the BAA or from members of the ASL Management Committee. It has been interesting to note that a substantial proportion of our initial ‘orders’ for ASL software has been from overseas APLers and we hope to encourage our overseas colleagues to contribute to ASL both in terms of additions to those shelves we have released and also by contributing to new shelves for ASL. Of necessity the initial ASL offerings have come from a relatively small nucleus of UK-based statisticians. Our conference last autumn included contributions from a number of new faces, and I shall be publishing some of their work in Random Vector, starting with Peter Hingley’s article in this issue. At that conference, ideas for a number of new shelves for ASL were discussed (see Vector 8.3, January 1992), and as the first phase of the ASL project is completed we are keen to turn some of these suggestions for new shelves into tangible offerings.

At the time of writing this copy, the ASL Management Committee has not settled on a venue for the next ASL conference, which means that we will probably miss the traditional autumn slot we have booked for our conferences in years gone by. We would be interested in canvassing views from readers as to whether we should alter the format of the ASL conference from a three-day residential conference to a one-day conference (say in London), thereby possibly allowing a wider attendance.

As a final point I would like to record our thanks to John Searle for the work he has put into the ASL project over the last few years. John is being posted overseas by his employer and has had to stand down from both the BAA Committee and the ASL team. Pending the results of the current BAA Committee elections, we would envisage the incoming Projects Officer of the BAA joining the ASL Management Committee.

As usual, I give contact addresses for the ASL Management Committee:

Chairman: Jake Ansell, Business Studies, University of Edinburgh Deputy Chairman: Alan Sykes, European Business Management School, University of Wales, Swansea BAA Representative: David Eastwood, MicroAPL Ltd

items.title: Stirling Numbers
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 129

From: David Appleton, 10 March 1992

I am delighted that Norman Thomson and Ken Iverson were interested enough to comment on my article on Stirling numbers. As a result, I have learned enough J to understand and execute the wonderfully concise and interesting expression in the latter’s letter, thanks to my colleague Chris Brunsdon. Unfortunately, I ran out of workspace on my micro long before I could execute it with a sufficiently high parameter value (60) to compare the results with those of the programs I presented.

It might help anyone interested in this correspondence if I gave an APL version of the method (index origin is zero as in J).

K←⍳N
D←K∘.-K
S←D≥0
F←⍉(⍴D)⍴!K
A←K∘.*K
B←(F×S)÷!D×S
S1←B⌹A
S2←A⌹B

The relationship between the two kinds of Stirling number is certainly made very clear, though as a practical method of calculation it is not as useful as Norman’s recursive function.

Perhaps I should come clean! I wrote the original article because the expression ⍎1↓(7×P)⍴'×+\(⍳N)' amused me, and I thought it might amuse others. I am sure that J can produce the same sort of expression without using character vectors, but I am afraid I cannot yet construct it. However, I also had a real problem involving Stirling numbers, or, as it turned out, the ratios of Stirling numbers, and I needed a good algorithm. Recursion seems to fit the bill best, and my eventual function to calculate \(t\sigma^{n}_{t-1}/\sigma^{n}_{t}\) was (with index origin back to 1):

    ∇Z←STIRRAT T;U
[1] →(T=1)/0,Z←1
[2] Z←(T×(¯1⌽U)÷T-1+(⍳T-1)×U←¯1⌽U←STIRRAT T-1),0
    ∇

If this looks very like Norman’s function, that is because I modelled the final version on it!

items.title: British APL Association NewsSecretary’s Report for 1991-92
items.text:
by Anthony Camacho, Honorary Secretary, 19 May 1992

This is the Secretary’s selection of the interesting items that were dealt with in your committee this year. Intentionally omitted are such things as arranging meetings (they are reported fully elsewhere), settling budgets and reviewing expenditure, booking rooms, maintaining contact with the British Computer Society (your Chairman and Treasurer both attend meetings) and a good deal of regular work such as answering queries, protecting our copyrights and other administration. Also omitted apart from a mention are initiatives which have scarcely begun such as the schools educational initiative or the publicity initiatives arising from a meeting held by the publicity officer.

There were Committee meetings on 7 June 91, 20 September 91, 22 November 91, 14 February 92 and 1 May 92. There will be another on the morning of 12 June 92.

items.title: 1. APL Conferences
items.text:
We sponsored a Russian to attend APL 91. We did some preliminary investigation, visited York University, discussed arrangements and contacted conference organisers and are planning to hold APL 94 at York. A nucleus of a committee has been formed under Adrian Smith as conference Chairman and Peter Donnelly who will organise the exhibition.

A proposal has been sent to SigAPL inviting them to collaborate by not asking for financial sponsorship, which will not be necessary if we obtain approval for our plans from the BCS as our funds with them will be adequate. We have helped with publicity for APL 92 and we hope our reports on APL conferences encourage the world to attend.

At APL 91 Vin Grannell paid for video recordings to be made of several sessions. When we heard he had done this we contributed half his costs in return for copies of the tapes and some have already been shown at our meetings.

items.title: 2. Administration
items.text:
The Association acquired access to email by paying for the Secretary to join CIX (the email address is acamacho@cix.compulink.co.uk). Many items for Vector have been solicited and received by this route.

The Administrative Assistant, Alison Chatterton, who has served us so well for some years, resigned and her place was taken by two people: Rowena Small who does the membership records and Gill Smith who does the Vector work. The Royal Mail freepost licence was transferred to Rowena’s address.

The steps necessary to demonstrate that we comply with the Data Protection Act were taken and appropriate messages printed in Vector and on our membership forms.

The Association’s policy on payment of expenses was discussed, clarified and recorded in writing. The Association’s policy on membership records was changed. We now wish to hold a name and address for each APLer who is a member by virtue of working for a sustaining or corporate member. It is intended that the collection of the extra records will begin with the membership renewals for the year 1992/3.

items.title: 3. Sponsorships
items.text:
As well as sponsoring a Russian APLer at Stanford the Association has agreed to pay for the printing of the Russian edition of the I-APL Manual. We support the Regional Enterprise Grant Scheme proposal of Dr Ian Clark to write enhancements to the I-APL/Mac interpreter, and are considering a contribution towards sponsoring it.

The Association has continued to sponsor the APL Statistics Library with a conference at Gregynog, a presentation at APL 91 and the launch of the first part of the library at one of our meetings.

The outstanding achievement award is to be given to Paul Chapman in recognition of his achievement in writing the portable interpreter for I-APL. The presentation may be made at the AGM on 12 June 1992.

items.title: 4. Publications
items.text:
Vector is now fairly well established as the leading APL journal; it appears regularly and contains an excellent mix of articles from all over the world. For some time now it has been 144 pages or more instead of the 128 pages promised. It is the major expense and main activity of the Association as well as the main benefit to members. The committee has actively supported the Vector working group and done its best to ease their task. APLers (members or not) who feel they might write for it are encouraged to try their hand and to contact the Editor or one of the working group.

The Committee is currently considering suggestions that we might launch a Beginners’ Vector as part of Dr Mayer’s schools initiative. Also proposed is a fully refereed journal of high academic standard that might be called The Transactions of the APL Association. The title is provisional as if launched it will attract papers from the whole world as there is no other wholly refereed publisher of APL papers. Perhaps the title could reflect this.

items.title: BAA Publicity Ideas
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 17

by Misha Jovanovic

If any of you have ever looked at the inside back cover of VECTOR you might have wondered who the Publicity Officer is and what he does. Well, last year when I joined the Committee in this very role, the same thoughts went through my mind. The way I see it, the Publicity Officer is someone who promotes APL by whatever means possible, to keep existing BAA members happy and to raise the profile of APL. As a result, I have put together a list of possible ideas for publicising APL and the BAA.

items.title: Improving Attendance at Meetings
items.text:
There should be some incentive to come to meetings. There could be an APL brain teaser competition in VECTOR with the various solutions discussed and a prize given out at the next meeting. This type of activity would increase audience participation at meetings. The J workshop was a great success where everyone had a go at J on the machines provided.

Ideas for interesting topics to be presented at meetings are desperately needed. In order to attract people other than the few committed members, and those who have only vaguely heard about APL, it might be a good idea to host meetings with other language specialists, for example Mathematica or Smalltalk. Work would be needed to find out how to contact the potential participants.

The meetings are usually in London, but we need to analyse the membership list and work out other locations. Many people cannot make it to London, so we should go to them. I believe that we have had this type of meeting in the past, and that they have been well attended. The members of the committee that took part in the Publicity Meeting all agreed that this is a good idea and that we should approach people who live and work elsewhere to help us organise such an event.

Rather than going to the pub after the meeting, maybe we could hold a social occasion, such as wine tasting at or near the IEE. This way, members could bring their partners and friends along, or even bring a colleague along to the meeting as well!

Meetings should be more widely advertised so that we attract those who have only just heard about APL.

The corporate membership is being split into individuals, who will then get all news of meetings, etc. A lot of people working in companies probably do not know that they are members!

Some years ago we used to sell APL books at meetings, and this could be started up again.

items.title: Education
items.text:
Do an APL presentation at a teachers’ conference or similar. Find out which conferences would be most appropriate and get suitable APL experts to attend to try and spread the word. Education Vector could be used to show what we have done already.

Make sure that schools and colleges are kept informed of BAA activities, and have a permanent invitation to attend meetings.

items.title: Outreach
items.text:
APL diary, general stationery, calendar with meeting agendas.

Communicate with APL groups all over the world and find out what they are doing. Co-ordinate with them to host joint events either in the UK, overseas, or produce joint articles through a medium such as VECTOR.

Past copies of VECTOR could be used as publicity material to send to people who might be interested in APL.

We could hold a 1 day event which is both social, has vendors and speakers. David Eastwood went to one such event in Copenhagen which was very successful. Having this on the weekend would mean that APLers from Europe could attend, people could bring their families. There could be a family event or Cricket match.

items.title: HMW Trading Systems Limited
items.text:
The most advanced foreign exchange dealing system in the world - now the most affordable. With over five years of evolutionary development to its credit, 4XTRA from HMW is now being launched as the leading edge technology capable of maximising profits and maintaining a competitive edge.

Developed as a front end deal capture and management system, 4XTRA provides the functionality required to monitor real time multi-currency positions, enter deals and calculate profit opportunities. With NPV profit and loss accounting as standard, the dealer is able to cover his positions accurately whilst providing his management with a real time picture of the overall risk.

4XTRA’s comprehensive position keeping and deal entry screens enhanced to meet the demands of forward, spot and corporate trading together with facilities such as automatically generated spot cover deals, overnight tom-next switching and value added reporting give the trader the tools he needs to deal effectively.

And 4XTRA won’t burn a hole in the IT budget. Cost is based on the number of users, and because the system is PC-based, you can forget about mainframe investment and maintenance costs - a simple PC network is all that’s required. However, low cost doesn’t mean low performance. Already installed in one of the world’s busiest dealing rooms, 4XTRA easily manages over 4000 deals a day and can accommodate peak rates of over 60 deals a minute.

The next release of 4XTRA will use Dyalog APL-W, which will allow the system to run on other platforms (UNIX as well as DOS). A Windows version of Dyalog APL is being released later this year, with a full OS-2 version following on.

If you would like to hear more about how 4XTRA can help your FX business expand, please contact: Rob Thurston, Business Development Manager, HMW Trading Systems Limited, 1 Temple Avenue, London EC4Y 0HA. Tel: 071-353-4212; fax 071-353-3325.

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
In the last couple of issues of Vector we have concentrated on our new relationship with IBM UK, focussing on recent product announcements for APL2 both on mainframe and PC systems. David Eastwood is progressively making contact with IBM’s mainframe APL users and indeed if any readers have questions relating to IBM’s product range they should contact David at our offices.

In this issue of Vector, we shall be reviewing some of the work our developers have been doing on our own APL product range — the APL.68000 family of products.

We have recently issued a minor upgrade for our Macintosh users to support the new Quadra range of Macintoshes. These are the latest 68040-based systems and are the fastest models in the Mac range. In common with other versions of APL.68000 we have had to make minor changes to the interpreter to support the data and instruction cacheing facilities on the Quadra. This upgrade is available at no charge for owners of APL.68000 Level I Version 7 or APL.68000 Level II Version 2.

Users of APL.68000/X — our version of APL.68000 for the RISC System/6000 — might be interested to note that we have implemented our ‘MicroPLOT’ business plotting language under APL.68000/X. MicroPLOT has been available for many years both under APL*PLUS/PC and for our multi-user versions of APL.68000. MicroPLOT is designed to simplify the production of routine business graphics and to present a device-independent syntax for APL programmers. We have versions of MicroPLOT available for HP plotters, Tektronix terminals and PostScript devices. Using MicroPLOT on the RISC System/6000 allows APL programmers to produce two dimensional business graphics without having to delve too deeply into the XLib facilities supplied on this system. The code is supplied in an unlocked form to permit customisation.

Our experiences with graphics on the RISC System/6000 coupled with numerous user enquiries have led us to recognise that there is a considerable demand for this sort of software on other windows-based platforms and we are in the midst of producing a Macintosh version of MicroPLOT.

APL.68000/X has been designed to make writing new applications which have a Graphical User Interface (windows, menu bars, dialogs, etc) as simple as possible. At the same time, because the IBM RS/6000 is so fast, APL.68000/X is being used to ‘down-size’ existing mainframe APL applications. Many of these older applications communicate with the user through AP124, an auxiliary processor performing screen layout and forms entry on IBM 3270 terminals.

MicroAPL have recently developed a windows-based AP124 for APL.68000/X. In APL-programming terms, the new processor is an exact replacement for AP124, so all the screen layout arrays and expressions like CTL←3 to update the screen will work unmodified. However, the new AP124 is a true widget-based implementation using the Motif/X-Windows user interface.

An AP124 screen under APL.68000/X appears in its own window. It is implemented as a special case of a generalised Motif dialog, in which all the elements are either labels or text entry fields. Under Motif text entry fields will have a border, and our AP124 processor takes this into account when laying out the dialog. As well as using the normal AP124 keystrokes, the user can move around the dialog with the mouse and use it to select and edit text. Also, being a true Motif implementation, the dialog is customisable through the Motif resource mechanism, so you can change the colours and fonts used very easily. The result is that unmodified AP124-oriented programs take on a whole new lease of life and look like true windows applications.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
by Alan Mayer

Welcome to the “APL92” edition of Education Vector. The British APL Association Journal Vector (of which Education Vector forms a small part) will be available at the APL 92 Conference at St. Petersburg in July. We wish our hosts well, in what may be regarded as the most truly international gathering the world APL community has ever experienced.

If you are not one of the lucky ones who will be attending APL92, you may like to know that you can get your own copy of Vector by becoming a member of the British APL Association. Write to Rowena Small, [address omitted] — the subscription is £12 per annum, for which you get four editions of Vector (144 pages each) and notice of meetings of the Association. Also, if you know of anyone who would like a (free) subscription to Education Vector, please send me his or her name and address.

My thanks to those who have responded to my request for functions. I have included a selection in this edition: some games from W.W. McLean, and some mathematical functions from C.E. Williams. Also thanks to Alain Delmotte, of the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the UN in Rome, for his programs to list the contents of I-APL workspaces. Together, the contributions make a good mixture of entertainment, application and utility — but if we are missing out something, write and tell me about it (preferably enclosing a contribution!).

I am currently assembling APL material suitable for use in schools. Later in the year I will be offering an APL interpreter and sample educational material, free of charge to any school that would like to try introducing it into their curriculum. Schools that have already tried APL have found it useful in a variety of areas, and I want to give as many young people as possible the opportunity of experiencing the power and flexibility of the language.

I look to readers of Education Vector (members and non-members alike) for help in this work. First, if you are involved in education and have used APL, tell me about your experiences, and if you have developed programs you are willing to share, let me see them. Second, bring this initiative to the attention of teachers who may like to take part — if they drop me a line, I will make sure they receive the material. Third, let me know what sort of material you think should be developed for this purpose. Fourth, if you are willing to spare some time and share your own expertise, this may be invaluable to schools in your area — sometimes the availability of a person with some experience of the language can save a great deal of time, particularly when the system is first introduced. If you are interested in helping in this way, please let me know.

A meeting will be arranged later in the year for anyone interested in discussing these ideas. Birmingham has been suggested as a possible venue, but I am open to suggestions of alternatives.

items.title: Two Mathematical Functions
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 30

by C.E. Williams

C.E. Williams writes: a couple of functions which may be of use to someone. The function CHAR4, to find the characteristic equation of a 4×4 matrix, uses Bocher’s formulas which is a good illustration of APL’s ease of programming. It is easy to adapt for any order of matrix.

[0]     RES←CHAR4 A;B;C;D;A1;A2;A3;A4;S1;S2;S3;S4
[1]     S1←+/1 1⍉A        ⍝ Sums major diagonal
[2]     B←A+.×A           ⍝ Matrix multiplication
[3]     S2←+/1 1⍉B        ⍝ Repeat
[4]     C←B+.×A
[5]     S3←+/1 1⍉C
[6]     D←C+.×A
[7]     S4←+/1 1⍉D
[8]     A1←-S1
[9]     A2←(S2+A1×S1)÷¯2
[10]    A3←(S3+(A2×S1)+(A1×S2))÷¯3
[11]    A4←(S4+(A3×S1)+(A2×S2)+(A1×S3))÷¯4
[12]    RES←1,A1,A2,A3,A4

To test the function:

      A←4 4⍴1 ¯4 ¯1 ¯4 2 0 5 ¯4 ¯1 1 ¯2 3 ¯1 4 ¯1 6
      A
 1 ¯4 ¯1 ¯4
 2  0  5 ¯4
¯1  1 ¯2  3
¯1  4 ¯1  6
      CHAR4 A
1 ¯5 9 ¯7 2

i.e. the solution for this matrix is x⁴ - 5x³ + 9x² - 7x + 2 = 0.

items.title: Romberg’s Integration
items.text:
The second function is a version of Romberg’s method for numerical integration. It is slower than Simpson’s Rule. I hope someone will improve it — it is a start anyway!

[0]     ROMB X;A;B;C;J;M;L;S;T;I;I2;I3;A1;B1;W;N;K;⎕IO
[1]    ⍝Romberg integration, function in ∆FN
[2]    ⍝X is vector of lower, upper limits and N
[3]     ⎕IO←0 ⋄ A←X[0] ⋄ B←X[1] ⋄ N←X[2]
[4]     A1←∆FN A
[5]     B1←∆FN B
[6]     I←20⍴0
[7]     C←B-A ⋄ L←1 ⋄ M←K←0
[8]     J←(A1+B1)÷2
[9]     I[0]←C×J
[10]   L1:L←2×L ⋄ M←M+1 ⋄ W←1
[11]   L3:J←J+∆FN A+W×C÷L
[12]    →((L-1)≥W←W+2)/L3
[13]   I2←J×C÷L ⋄ S←0 ⋄ T←4
[14]   L2:⎕←I3←((I2×T)-I[S])÷T-1
[15]    →(N=K←K+1)/PRINT
[16]    I[S]←I2 ⋄ I2←I3 ⋄ S←S+1 ⋄ T←T×4
[17]    →(S<M)/L2
[18]    I[S]←I2
[19]    →L1
[20]   PRINT:'Integral is ',⍕I3

Running the function, to integrate the square root of x² + 3x - 4, with N=10, (the exact value is 1.577186) gives:

      ROMB 1 2 10
 1.513789887
 1.554609508
 1.557330816
 1.569181806
 1.570153293
 1.570356824
 1.574352706
 1.574697433
 1.574769562
 1.574786867
Integral is 1.574786867

Repeating the process with N=50 and N=100, gives 1.577181348 and 1.577185956 respectively (but be warned - it takes a long time!)

VECTOR’s exclusive APL Product Guide aims to provide readers with useful information about sources of APL hardware, software and services. We welcome any comments readers may have on its usefulness and any suggestions for improvements.

We do depend on the alacrity of suppliers to keep us informed about their products so that we can update the Guide for each issue of VECTOR. Any suppliers who are not included in the Guide should contact me to get their free entry — see address below.

We reserve the right to edit material supplied for reasons of space or to ensure a fair market coverage. The listings are not restricted to UK companies and international suppliers are welcome to take advantage of these pages.

Fully Updated for Vector 9.1 Replies are awaited from entries marked with sidebars: these may be removed from Vol 9.2

For convenience to readers, the product list has been divided into the following groups (‘poa’ indicates ‘price on application’):

  • Complete APL Systems (Hardware & Software)
  • APL Interpreters
  • APL Visual Display Units and Printers
  • APL-based Packages
  • APL Consultancy
  • Other Products
  • Vendor Addresses

Every effort has been made to avoid errors in these listings but no responsibility can be taken by the working group for mistakes or omissions.

items.title: Six Months in the Life of VECTOR
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 50

by John Searle
path: Six Months in the Life of VECTOR

items.title: Conception
items.text:
Firstly, a bit of APL. Let us consider the creation of the issue Volume X number Y (X.Y), and refer to the next issue as (X.Y)+1. However, since VECTOR is a quarterly journal, the previous issue may be more exactly specified as:

      ∇ R←A PLUS B
[1]    R←0.1×10⊥ 0 1 + 0 4 ⊤B+4⊥ 0 ¯1 + 0 10 ⊤10×A
      ∇

      8.3 PLUS 2
9.1

An issue of VECTOR has a gestation period of about six months. The working group meeting discusses the next issue (X.Y+1) in some detail and a draft contents page is created. This gives the Editor enough time to identify the holes so that we can all help to fill the gaps. If all goes well, we can then get down to planning the issue after, X.Y+2.

Material for an issue of VECTOR comes from a variety of sources, and much of it now has its own momentum, meaning that the Editor does not have to write it. The Editor will decide if this to be a thematic issue, and request articles relevant to the theme well in advance. Other articles are either requested or arrive through the post with a wonderful irregularity.

One of the main aims of recent VECTORs has been a drive to have regular features appearing either in every issue or in every annual issue. VECTOR X.1 is now always produced in time for the annual APL conference, and is given away free to each delegate. Advertisers: this is a very good issue to aim for! The following issue X.2 always has a comprehensive report of the conference, with summaries of the main papers and lots of photographs. The January issue X.3 is generally a thematic issue with invited papers. The April issue X.4 can be relied upon for the abstracts of the forthcoming conference, and may contain an article that wanders from the truth in the best of April 1st traditions.
path: Six Months in the Life of VECTOR

items.title: The Meeting
items.text:
VECTOR requires a quarterly Working Group gathering; a meeting of minds and travelling bodies prepared to risk the motorways and railways of Britain in order to bring you the latest in the world of APL. It is an amalgam of creative thinking, a free orange juice at BAPLA’s expense, another opportunity for a hotbed of crazy ideas for the next April 1st issue piece. Verily, a travelling show from Yorkshire to Berkshire, from York to London to East Garston (where’s that??) to St. Albans and back again.

The best thing about the meeting is getting a copy of the pending issue hot from the printer’s press. If you are very lucky, Adrian will let you take it home afterwards. Fingers quickly flick through this pristine copy for the vital signs - does my latest contribution appear? Does it have any (more than the usual number) of misprints.

The tangible output from the meeting will be a fleshed out Contents Page and Anthony’s minutes, with hopefully my name in bold Action font not too often repeated.
path: Six Months in the Life of VECTOR

items.title: Afterbirth
items.text:
Who are you? Who actually reads VECTOR? We know who we send it to, but who eventually reads it? As the BAPLA does not keep the names of APLers in corporate memberships, we do not really know the full story, although steps are being taken to change this. My reading of the BAPLA membership numbers suggests there is an increasing number of you, but feedback to the Editor is very low. Please write! A brief note of con-, in- or de-structive criticism would be very valuable to the working group.

Another question for you - how do you store your VECTORs? (Assuming you keep them!) In chronological order or in rainbow colour order?

The working group is very proud of your journal. It is all done for love, a lack of money, and a feeling of doing something professionally worthwhile. However, the group constantly needs fresh blood. Your interests could range from the technical, statistical, commercial or sociological, to the not to be forgotten right of just having a say in the industry that employs you.

And finally, the last and most important question: what colour should the cover of the next issue be?
path: Six Months in the Life of VECTOR

items.title: The Hungarian Naming Convention
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 9

From: Ray Cannon, March 1992

The Hungarian naming convention has been well documented elsewhere, but is basically a naming convention in which the object class or type is used as a prefix in its name. Thus lots of objects of the same class will all start with the same prefix. This can, depending on implementation, have one very big disadvantage in large APL systems: it can slow them down.

The reason for this is the way symbol tables are often designed to work. They use some hashing algorithm to convert the object’s symbol into an address to start searching from. However, if lots of symbols produce the same address, as might happen if they all start with the same prefix, the number of symbol entries needing to be searched is much higher than if all the symbols produced very different addresses.

As an example of this type of behaviour, I have seen a system running extremely slowly due to the fact that every file in the file system started with the same letter. Renaming all the files with different letters speeded up the whole process.

So the idea I would like to put forward, is to use a class postfix rather than a class prefix. That way the names would not all start the same and the hashing algorithms would produce different addresses, hence shorter searches. This naming convention could then be called Reverse Hungarian Notation.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
Welcome to Education Vector. I note, with some surprise, that I am embarking upon my second year as Editor. My first year has been one in which much has occurred in the world at large, and many plans have been laid. I am grateful to so many readers who have contributed their work, their views and their ideas. My receipt of “email” in particular has increased considerably since I took over the editorship of this journal!

I am particularly pleased with the response to my request for material for use in education. Several people have responded with ideas and offers of help. My own inability to devote enough time to the task has tended to make progress slower than it should be, but I shall endeavour to clear the back-log and make some of the material available as soon as possible. I am still very keen to hear from any schools that would be interested in trying out APL.

In the last issue, Bill McLean contributed a game called MAGIC and issued a challenge to readers: “Any offers of an algorithm (in APL of course) to solve MAGIC problems?”. Dave Ziemann has taken up that challenge, and a good deal of this issue of Education Vector is devoted to his solution. Dave’s approach to programming by direct definition is instructive, and his article demonstrates very well how this form of APL can be used to “mimic” the thought processes involved in problem-solving. His approach is fundamentally second generation, and he uses APL*PLUS II.

I have added a note of my own on direct definition, including a workspace to provide direct definition facilities, which I hope will help those who do not have this mode of input implemented in their APL, or who have not come across this method before.

Alain Delmotte has asked me to include a small correction to his paper on “Workspace Listing in IAPL”. On page 38 of the last issue, the functions ΔΔHEADINGS and ΔΔLIST were “glued” together. I think the line-numbering makes it clear where function ΔΔHEADINGS ends and ΔΔLIST begins. Those few lines should read:

[8]   ΔΔPRINT ''
     ∇

     ∇ ⍺ ΔΔLIST ⍵
[1]  ⍝ Successively lists the variables and functions

items.title: New Email Discussion List
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 15

For those who have not come across them before, an Email Discussion list is a forum in which anyone with an EMAIL address can take part. You “sign on” by sending an Email in a specified format to the “list server” address, after which you will automatically receive any correspondence sent to the list. If you wish, you can contribute items yourself. You can, at any time, “sign off” as easily as you signed on.

A list called APL-L has existed for some time, and includes discussion on all sorts of aspects of APL. I am grateful to Alain Delmotte for drawing my attention to a new list, which was created following a workshop at APL92. It is called APLEDU-L, and is specifically concerned with teaching APL.

To subscribe to either list, send a message to:

LISTSERV@UNB.CA (on INTERNET)             ... or
LISTSERV@UNBVM1 (from BITNET/EARN)

The message should have no name or subject, and the first and only line should read:

SUBSCRIBE APL-L your-name                 ... or
SUBSCRIBE APLEDU-L your-name

information about the list and instructions for signing off will be received automatically.

by David Eastwood

In this issue of The Random Vector, we have a mixture of articles, reviewing the current state of the ASL and introducing some ideas for future developments. Jake Ansell, the ASL Chairman, gives a brief review of the current status of the project and also introduces a proposal for another volume for the ASL based on some work he and a colleague are carrying out at the moment.

Now that two volumes of the ASL are on general release, we are beginning to get some useful feedback on the software. I am pleased to include a review of ASLGREG, the Linear Regression volume, which has been submitted by Jon Sandles of Nestlé-Rowntree. Alan Sykes has submitted a number of minor corrections to the ASLGREG software and has also responded to some comments made in the review of ASLGREG.

If you would like to order copies of the ASL software, order forms are available from both the ASL Management Committee and from the BAA Administration (Rowena Small).

As usual, I give contact addresses for the ASL Management Committee:

items.title: ASL - The Future
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 31

by Jake Ansell

The experience gained over the production of ASL software shows that ‘voluntary’ software development is a slow process. This is not only true of ASL for it occurs with other software. For example users of GLIM are still awaiting the imminent arrival of GLIM 4.

The problems that arise are manyfold. The initial burst of software follows the interest of the author. Hence often a volunteer will provide the interesting element where thought is necessary. The difficulty arises of getting the other functions, which are more basic, written. These are often supposedly trivial functions which are required to provide either general utility or a minor support function.

ASL was originally fortunate that both Alan Sykes and Tony O’Hagan had the desire and commitment to complete their tasks. Hence we have the two volumes: ASLGREG and ASLGRAPH. Unfortunately the Basic Statistics Volume of the Bottom Shelf has existed in embryonic form for too long. Hopefully by the time this edition of Vector is published it too will be available.

It is time to stress though that the ASL project continues and that there will be future releases of software. In this edition of Vector an article appears detailing a suggested volume of the Reliability shelf. There are other shelves in the process of production.

Beyond this there are a number of possible shelves to be constructed/developed. However, these shelves will only be added if individuals are willing to come forward to assist. In the past there has been considerable effort given on a voluntary basis and many need to be thanked. But the project will require further assistance.

At the present time ASL has developed an in-house coding standard. It also has had a team of willing software testers who have helped considerably the production of the current ASL software. If there are statisticians or others with code which they think would be appropriate for ASL then they should contact either Alan Sykes or myself at addresses given above.

THE SUCCESS OF THE PROJECT IS IN YOUR HANDS.

items.title: Comments on the ASLGREG Review
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 34

by Alan Sykes

I am grateful to Jon Sandles for his careful review of ASLGREG. I think it is fair to say that his views on the software have been echoed by other people who have used it, which is very heartening to those of us who have been involved in its production! It has now been available for some 10 months, and in that time only five bugs have materialised. They are easily put right and the corrections are listed below.

Jon raises a number of important points that deserve some response. On the question of prediction, I do have a beta-test version of a function PREDICT which allows the user to obtain predicted values corresponding to given values of predictor variables. (This is not a simple function to write in view of the generality of model specification!) Further work might perhaps incorporate confidence intervals. Such a function would be useful in producing graphical output e.g. plotting fitted values. (On this subject Norman Thomson has sent me some first thoughts on graphical tools for ASLGREG, but I have not had time to do further work in this direction as yet.)

I agree that there may well be problems of formatting and welcome specific examples to aid in correcting this. (Note however that the user does have the option of outputting straight unformatted numbers to the screen.)

Finally, on the question of dealing with missing values, it is not quite true to say that there are no provisions. Suppose that all your regression data was contained in a matrix M with missing values indicated by 9999. Then APL comes to the rescue to create the zero-one vector

      WT←∧/M≠9999

and this can be declared as a priorweight vector so that the regression analysis is performed only on the data points for which all information is available. However, I agree that no further missing data facilities such as those in GENSTAT are available.

items.title: Corrections to Known Bugs in ASLGREG (September 1992)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 35

by Alan Sykes

Since its release, five software defects have been discovered in ASLGREG. These may be easily rectified by following the instructions below. (Not necessarily all the defects will be pertinent to your copy, and copies dated September 1992 will incorporate all the changes.)

1. YVAR

The function YVAR contained a local variable 'S'. All references to it (including the header) should be replaced by the variable name 'ΔS' so that a statement such as

YVAR 'S'

will work as required.

2. ORTHOG

The function ORTHOG in its original form is a complete mystery to me! Somehow it got corrupted: fortunately it is short so here is the correct version.

      ∇A←ORTHOG A;M;K;T;TT
[1]    M←(⍴A)[2]
[2]    K←1
[3]   lp:A[;K]←T←T÷(T+.×T←A[;K])*.5
[4]    A[;K↓⍳M]←TT-T∘.×T+.×TT←A[;K↓⍳M]
[5]    →(M≥K←K+1)/lp
      ∇

3. MODEL

In line 8 of MODEL, the links variable was originally indexed on id and not il, amend the line to read as below.

      ∇R←MODEL
[8]    ⍎(0≠⎕NC 'il')/'R←R,''Link Function  '',links[il;],'' ⋄'''

4. MUHAT

The function MUHAT did not refer to the offset variable. Amend it as below noting the crucial space within the quotes before the word 'offset'

      ∇ΔR←MUHAT
[1]    ⍎(0=⎕NC 'dis')/'START'
[2]    ⍎(inhib)/'ΔR←emess[15;]⋄→0'
[3]    ΔR←⍎'ΔMU',(⍕il),' offset+desmat+.×parest'
      ∇

5. The CHECK function

The CHECK function contains a superfluous line in the section pertaining to checking whether a variable is a vector or matrix of positive integers. In APL*PLUS, APL*PLUS II, Dyalog APL, and APL.68000 this consists of deleting line 29 of ΔCHECK, whereas in APL2 it consists of deleting line 62 of ΔCHECKΔ. The amended section, with the line deleted is shown below:

[26] ⍝CHECK VARIABLES ARE POSITIVE INTEGER VARIABLES
[27] four:TΔ←⍎¯1↓,((DΔ,6)⍴'(0=∧/,'),NAMESΔ,((DΔ,2)⍴'=⌊'),NAMESΔ,(DΔ,2)⍴'),'
[28]  TΔ←TΔ∨⍎¯1↓,((DΔ,7)⍴'(1=∨/0≥'),NAMESΔ,(DΔ,2)⍴'),'
[29]  →(1≠IΔ←∨/TΔ)/lp1
[30]  RΔ←RΔ,IΔ/linefd,emess[5;],,TΔ⌿NAMESΔ,' '
[31]  →lp1

items.title: BAA overseas subscription (letter)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

From: David Crossley, July 1992

I am appalled to find that my BAA subscription for private membership costs £20 as I now live in France, as opposed to the UK subscription rate of £12. Why is this? Postal rates to EEC countries are the same as within the UK. So does the BAA have a policy to soak members living outside the UK? I look forward to a change in policy and a refund of £8.

ED: Sorry David, but the postage rates are not the same on packets, only on letters under 20gm (a 220gm Vector costs £0.88 airmail printed paper, as against £0.49 second class postage within the UK). However EC countries are considerably cheaper than the rest of the world, so perhaps the committee should take note.

items.title: Six Months in the Life of Vector (letter)
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 7

From: John Searle, 26 July 1992

Thank you for improving upon my submitted function in the article Six Months in the Life of Vector. It was much more interesting than my original. Unfortunately, if you type it into IBM’s APL2/PC in TryAPL2 it reveals a bug in their interpreter! Using the published example, the expression to the right of the 0 4 ⊥ should be integer 36, giving a result of 9 0. However, APL2 calculates an expression very close to 36, but gives a result of 8 4, and hence the function returns 8 5, not 9 1.

The IBM stand at APL92 was not impressed, but the Mangled-Logic APL*PLUS and Dyalogdic interpreters gave the “correct” results.

ED: Thanks John, I should have written ⌊10×A rather than relying on APL*PLUS to demote the result of the multiplication to integer. Not sure that this is a bug in any interpreter, as Encode is not ⎕CT dependent and one should not depend on an interpreter demoting floating point numbers to integer. These little things are set to trap the unwary!
