items.title: Cocking & Drury
items.text:
Cocking & Drury are delighted to welcome Manugistics as Sustaining Members of the British APL Association. Now news of the latest developments in the world of APL*PLUS will come directly from the horse’s mouth — and won’t depend on our rather vague attempts to meet the Editor’s generous and often, but vainly, extended deadlines!

We at Cocking & Drury continue to be busy assisting with migrations from APL mainframe (mostly APL2) to APL*PLUS II for the 386/486. In one classic encounter a consultant managed to out-run the mainframe with one migrated workspace.

In the course of such work we have developed several tools to ease the work involved in migrating mainframe APL2 to APL*PLUS II for the 386/486. Anyone considering a similar move should call to enquire about features and prices. On October 9th Chris Burke, a UK qualified actuary working with Manugistics’ Canadian dealer Strand Software, will be giving a talk on the use of APL in actuarial work. The event is free and attendees will be given copies of the Strand APL utility library which contains several standard actuarial utilities.

Later in October, Chris Lee of Manugistics will be presenting a preview session on Version 5 of APL*PLUS II for the 386/486. This event is also free. For more details and for reservations on either of these, call Beverley Satterley on 071-436 9481.

items.title: APL People Limited
items.text:
Things are still pretty slow on the recruitment front, although we have noticed a slight increase in demand for contract staff. July and August are traditionally quiet months, so we hope that the Autumn will see an increase in the number of vacancies. Companies which are recruiting are taking their time in selecting the right candidate and there is a tendency for interview procedures to become more rigorous.

On the manufacturing side, APL People’s sister company, APL Manufacturing, has at long last received an order from British Steel (it’s only taken them two and a half years from their initial inquiry!). Orders are imminent from British Dental Floss and British Nuclear Fuels among others. Plans are afoot to re-locate from our present offices in Hounslow to something a bit more prestigious, to take advantage of the excellent value for money of commercial property at the moment.

items.title: Reuters APL Software Division
items.text:
SHARP APL UNIX Version 4 is announced for delivery in the 4th quarter 1992. Supported hardware platforms include the IBM RS/6000 and Sun SPARCstation. This new SHARP APL UNIX version provides extensive facilities for UNIX-UNIX and UNIX-MVS communication. The SHARP APL Network Shared Variable Processor (NSVP) supports LU 6.2 based shared variable communication in between SHARP APL UNIX and SHARP APL MVS, and TCP/IP based shared variable communication for LAN-connected SHARP APL UNIX systems.

The SHARP APL Network Shared Variable Processor can be used for communication between SHARP APL applications and remote SHARP APL auxiliary processors. New stand-alone versions of SHARP APL MVS auxiliary processors are announced for use with SHARP APL UNIX Version 4. These stand-alone auxiliary processors can be installed on an MVS system without SHARP APL MVS, and accessed via NSVP from SHARP APL UNIX. Auxiliary processors available or planned in stand-alone versions include SSQL (for access to DB2), TSIO (for access to MVS QSAM data sets) and FCAP (for calling MVS software written in other languages than APL).

Using NSVP and stand-alone MVS auxiliary processors, SHARP APL UNIX can extract data from non-APL mainframe databases and transfer it to UNIX for processing. The Function Call Auxiliary Processor (FCAP) can be used from SHARP APL UNIX to access any MVS application with a well-defined Application Programming Interface.

Current SHARP APL MVS development activity is centred on performance improvement and connectivity. During 1992, a Performance Upgrade for SHARP APL MVS Version 20 increased performance significantly at large SHARP APL MVS sites, the largest of which support in excess of 1000 simultaneous users of SHARP APL applications.

Within Reuters, a major new SHARP APL MVS service, with world-wide network access, has been established in Frankfurt to support global risk management and trading applications.

For information about Reuters SHARP APL products, please contact Laurie Howard, Reuter Nederland BV, Amsterdam, Tel. +31 20 570 8733, fax +31 20 570 8758; or Larry Moore, Reuter Information Services (Canada) Limited, Toronto, Tel. 416 364 5361, fax 416 364 2910.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
As usual, Dyadic took a stand at the annual APL conference which was held this year in St Petersburg. Getting PCs in and out of Russia proved to be an “interesting” experience that our intrepid representatives will probably not wish to repeat. Nevertheless, everything was operational when the conference opened and the company was delighted by the enthusiastic response to the new version of Dyalog APL for Windows. This product actually began shipping during the conference and the reactions of early users has been equally gratifying. The DDE interface (which allows APL to talk to other Windows applications) has proved to be a two-edged sword, as we now get support calls from users wanting help with Excel!

Back at base, there was no respite for the developers and work on the next release started immediately. This will include full colour support, object-oriented graphics, Dynamic Link Library (DLL) interface and a host of other improvements. This release will be supplied free of charge to existing customers, and is scheduled for November/December shipment. An interim “maintenance release” was distributed free of charge during September. Any customer who failed to receive this update is urged to return his/her registration card immediately.

Although the production of Dyalog APL/W has been top priority for several months, work has continued on the Unix version of the product. There are two new implementations available, one for SCO Unix (replacing the Xenix version), and one for Digital’s RISC DECstations under Ultrix.

Dyadic takes this opportunity to remind VECTOR readers that it is a fully authorised IBM Business Associate (IBM-speak for Dealer) for the RISC System/6000. This now represents a wide range of computers from desktop workstations to large multi-user machines. In Dyadic’s opinion, the RS/6000 represents the “best-buy” in the Unix market and is undoubtedly a superb machine for running Dyalog APL. Companies who are still running APL applications on their mainframe would do well to examine the possibilities of “downsizing” onto RS/6000. Not only will you save money, but your applications may actually run faster!. Contact Pauline Brand at Dyadic for further details.

items.title: Manugistics
items.text:
Manugistics, Inc. is very pleased to join the other Sustaining Members of the British APL Association in supporting its many valuable contributions to APL. Among these we particularly value the publication of Vector, which many of us regard as the best, and certainly the most punctually published, journal of APL.

A great deal of activity has been occurring in our company in recent months, not least of which is our name change from STSC to Manugistics. Our new name reflects our application products for manufacturing, logistics and statistics, all of which have found gratifying commercial success. The name change is only that — we remain exactly the same employee-owned company as before, with the same people, the same products, and the same plans for the future.

There likewise need be no concern that our name change signals a change in our commitment to the APL*PLUS product line. Our APL business is growing and solidly profitable. Our last fiscal year produced record high sales throughout the company, and 75% of those revenues came from APL and APL-based application products. We have increased the size of our APL development department, and are looking forward to announcing major innovations in APL on these pages in the months to come.

February 1992 saw the appearance of version 4 of our flagship product, APL*PLUS II for the 386/486, and sales have far surpassed all prior releases in Europe and North America. As our warehouse staff struggled to fill the flood of orders, the development team scarcely paused for breath before setting to work on version 5, which we plan to ship before the end of 1992.

Version 5 will include major improvements to the Microsoft Windows interface introduced with version 4. Most notable of these is the introduction of APLGUI, a high-level object-oriented toolkit that makes Windows programming easy. In keeping with our philosophy of Open APL, APLGUI does not block access from the rest of the Windows software world. One can use a resource editor such as Borland’s or Microsoft’s to design APL dialog boxes, or build them entirely within APL. APLGUI is built as a layer on top of the APL-Windows interface, so applications that need to can directly access any of the 600+ Windows system calls as well as other vendors’ products that are packaged as Dynamic Link Libraries. Those who have no desire to plumb the depths of Windows programming will be able to develop complete applications using only the easy high-level utilities.

Version 5 also will include utilities that simplify the use of Dynamic Data Exchange from APL and a rewrite of the APL-Windows communication facility that lets the DOS-hosted APL*PLUS II interpreter respond to Windows as briskly as if it were itself a Windows program.

Also coming in version 5 is a true debugger that is woven into the fabric of the interpreter itself. The APL*PLUS II debugger permits visual tracing of program code line by line, statement, or individual primitive. Breakpoints can be set on individual statements, and watchpoints can be set on variables with optional APL test expressions. The full capabilities are too numerous to mention, so we recommend that UK readers ring Cocking & Drury (071-436-9481) for details, plus a list of the other delights coming in the new release.

On other fronts, version 11 of APL*PLUS/PC is coming soon, featuring the Screen Interface Toolkit and a facility for converting workspaces into .EXE files, with no runtime interpreter or royalties involved. The UNIX version of APL*PLUS II is now available on Hewlett-Packard’s breathtakingly-fast 700 and 800 series workstations and minicomputers. Details on any APL*PLUS product are available from Cocking & Drury. Outside the UK, please contact our International Sales department (Tel: +1-301-984-5412; Fax: +1-301-984-5094).

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
We usually feature news on our various APL interpreter products in Vector; as a change we will be discussing some of the consultancy work we are doing at the moment. We provide consultancy services in three broad areas, strategic management consultancy, applications consultancy for windows-based projects and APL applications consultancy. Overall, our consultancy services account for over half our revenue.

As a company, MicroAPL has now built up some 8 years experience in programming graphical user environments starting with our early work on the Apple Macintosh and coming right up to date with X-Windows and Windows 3. At present the computer industry is experiencing a period of exceptional change with new alliances emerging and difficult choices to be faced over the choice of future hardware and software. Over the last few months we have conducted a number of studies advising clients on their strategic options for IT, focussing particularly on the choice of development tools for new software projects. We have also undertaken an extensive review of the ever growing number of packaged Executive Information Systems.

On the applications consultancy front our non-APL work is becoming progressively more important and we have undertaken work recently using a range of development tools starting with Visual Basic for prototyping and for some simple applications and then moving on to products such as Gupta’s SQLWindows or PowerBuilder from Admiral Software, both driving a variety of database servers.

Our APL consultancy work divides between support services for a number of well-established APL systems and a variety of new APL applications. As one would expect the sort of application being written in APL varies widely — we have recently completed work on communications software for the Apple Macintosh; an interpreter to convert Hewlett Packard HPGL instructions into PostScript; and software to format and forward data for an electronic parts ordering system.

I have not included our systems programmers in this analysis since they are primarily involved in development of our software products such as APL.68000. In recent months work here has been focussed on MicroAPL’s ‘Portable Assembler’ product which is now being sold to developers who are moving applications onto the new range of RISC-based Macintoshes which are under development.

items.title: APL92 — BEKTOP at St Petersburg
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 88

notes by Ray Cannon

Pizza Express Staff worked 20-hour days

The slogan of Pizza Express (the Finnish firm who provided most of the catering for the conference) is “We deliver in Leningrad”. Well, they almost did not.

As is now usual, Vector was to be given out to the delegates. The problem was, how to get it hot off the press from the printer’s in the UK to the conference site. The solution was to send it to Helsinki by air mail, and then overland (via a Pizza Express lorry) to St Petersburg. Sounds fine in theory but … the Vectors (or BEKTOPs) were put on the P.E. lorry bound for St Pete’s but did not arrive in time to be included in the delegates’ handouts on Sunday. They still had not arrived on Monday. By the end of Tuesday, I was giving up hope of ever seeing them. Finally on Wednesday, someone found them (in Pizza Express’s deep freeze storage?) and they were delivered to the Conference. All’s well that ends well.

IBM had hoped to provide all the delegates with a copy of the IBM Systems Journal which featured APL. Unfortunately, they appeared to have used a more conventional mode of transport. They never arrived.

I am sure there’s a moral in there somewhere.

items.title: Evening Seminars
items.text:
Summer evenings in St Petersburg are long, and the bar at the conference centre stayed open till about 1:30am. The normal beverage consumed was a Finnish canned beer called “Lapin Kulta”. This was quickly renamed Rabbit Beer. There was also available “APL 92 Vodka” which has the slogan “Cool before discussion” printed on it.

By the time the bar closed, it would be starting to get light again (not that it really got that dark) and it would be time for “Evening Seminar”. This ritual meeting of minds normally occurred in Sasha(Alexander Skomorokov)’s room. Often the participants would be adding the final touches to their paper (to be given the next day at the conference). These meetings lasted till about 3 or 4 am.

I used to wonder why most Russians walk round looking so glum; now I know, it’s just a permanent hangover.

items.title: Modern User Interfaces
items.text:
James Wheeler and John Scholes

James Wheeler (Manugistics STSC APL) and John Scholes (Dyadic Dyalog APL) hosted an excellent workshop on APL and Windows. Both vendors were offering a new version of their own product running under MS Windows. Surprisingly, at the workshop there appeared to be no rivalry, also neither product was shown or promoted. (This was reserved for the vendor forums.)

The workshop explained the different approach needed to program systems to run under Windows, and how the vendors had implemented the Windows interface. The whole talk was rounded off with an excellent slide of “A piano designed by Bill Gates”.

Manugistics APL under Windows. This product seems to provide a complete interface to MS Windows, by providing low-level access to every Windows procedure, thus allowing full Windows capabilities at the cost of a lot (in APL terms) of coding. As someone who has written Windows programs in C++, this APL Windows environment makes Windows programming a lot simpler and easier to debug.

DYALOG APL for Windows. Dyadic’s Windows product is quite different. It is designed as an interface which is GUI-implementation independent. It provides a high-level control and a simple Windows interface. Although (at present) it does not provide access to all types of Windows resources (e.g. icons and bitmaps), it is VERY easy to use. (It took me about 20 minutes to produce a window containing “Bill Gates’ Piano”. Prior to that I had only had a 5 to 10 minute introduction to Dyalog for Windows.)

APL & WINDOWS. Dyadic and Manugistics products are very different and satisfy very different requirements. In the future they will both come closer together. In the meantime, some enterprising independent APLer should be able to write a set of high-level windows drivers for them, so that the same APL code can run under both vendors’ products.

items.title: APL92 and the KGB
items.text:
At APL92 we were very lucky to have as one of the invited speakers a former Colonel in the KGB, Alexander Kalinin. He was correctly introduced as “perhaps the most unusual speaker at our Conference”.

Although his talk was interesting in its own right, as Andrei Kondrashev pointed out, it was more important to the Russian audience merely because it was now possible for such a talk to take place at all.

Alexander Kalinin worked in a special department that was responsible for information security and cryptography. Needless to say, he gave away no “trade secrets”.

items.title: CTalk, an Acceptable Alternative to APL?
items.text:
Jean-Jacques Girardot’s paper “The CTalk Programming Language: A Strategic Evolution of APL” presented a theme that has been bandied about APL conferences for many years now; that of producing a new language with all the strengths of APL but packaged to look more like C, Algol, PL/1, Pascal etc.

However, what made this admirable paper different, not only was the new language CTalk proposed, it had already been implemented, and was available (in several machine formats) at the software exchange. Well done.

(Unfortunately for me, when I got home and tried to decompact my copy of CTalk, I found that I have got the wrong version of the utility PKUNZIP to extract the files. Has anyone else out there got a copy of CTalk (for IBM PC) I could have?)

items.title: The Ultimate Question.
items.text:
G.A.Langlet “Towards the Ultimate APL-TOE” (TOE=Theory of Everything)

As is well known to fans of The Hitch Hikers Guide to the Galaxy, the Answer to Life, the Universe and Everything, is 42. However, if you attended APL92, you might be forgiven for believing it to be “Difference Scan”. In his excellent paper (and in many of the question and answer sessions following other papers) Gérard postulates that the NotEqual Scan is the ultimate (and possibly only required) algorithm. If you enjoyed reading Douglas Hofstadter’s book “Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid” read Gérard’s paper.

items.title: Water Joke
items.text:
Question. What’s the difference between tap water at the Conference centre and its coffee?

Answer. The coffee is hot sweet black water, the tap water is cold bitter black water (and there’s no milk in either of them).

St Petersburg is built on islands, hundreds of islands so water (and bridges) played a large part in the conference visits.

First the cruise to Kronstadt by high speed hydrofoils, to visit Menshikov’s Palace at the Russian Naval base. I took several photos of Russian military hovercraft, and naval vessels. It was a very strange feeling openly walking around a former USSR naval base with a camera in my hand! On the trip back (by bus convoy) we had a police escort complete with flashing blue light. Heaven knows how many red traffic lights we passed.

Then the fireworks over the lake outside the Chinese Palace at Lomonosov, after an evening of Russian Music, Food, Culture, Dancing and Mosquitoes. (Followed by an exciting bus ride, with escort back home.)

The Chinese Palace at Lomonosov

Not forgetting the pond and fountain in the Hotel Petersburg before the Closing Banquet; the entertainment at the banquet reminded me of Las Vegas. Again the evening was ended by a high-speed dash though the streets of St Petersburg.

Poetry at the Chinese Palace

However my lasting memories of St Petersburg will not be the conference, the architecture, the bridges, the food, or the trips, but the stalls which surround the Metro stations like small shanty towns, selling almost anything from books to beer, and toothpaste to Vodka, but never windscreen wiper blades.

items.title: An Offer you Cannot Refuse?
items.text:
The British APL Association has funds available to give as grants to members of the Association to fund or partly fund projects that fit in with the BAA constitution.

The constitution says that the objects of the Association are:

  1. To promote the use of APL.
  2. To develop awareness and competence in APL.
  3. To represent the interests of Association members with other bodies.
  4. To contribute to the development of the language and definition of international standards.

items.title: Recent Projects
items.text:
The major recent project, which is still on-going, is the APL Statistical Library where the BAA funding included paying a programmer and paying the costs of the annual conferences.

A recent small project was the printing of the I-APL manual in Cyrillic.

Another project currently under way is being carried out by Dr Ian Clark which involves the porting of I-APL to System 7 operating system on the Macintosh. This will form the heart of Ian’s development of a tool to assist in the production of educational monographs which will be accompanied by I-APL workspaces which will demonstrate the principles being taught. Ian’s I-APL TrueType font is freely available via I-APL Ltd (see Product Guide); a small sample is illustrated overleaf. Most of the funding for this project has come from other sources but that funding was contingent on some funding by the BAA as a mark of its approval.

APLomb: an I-APL TrueType Font, by Ian A Clark

Here is a sample from page 20 of Education Vector set at 13/15 point:

      Z←HERO FIGHTS ORC
[1] DRAW: BAR HERO[1],ORC[1]
[2]  →STOP IF 0 = HERO[1] × ORC[1]
[3]  SCORE ← RESULT HERO[2], ORC[2]
[4]  →(WIN, DRAW, LOSE) IF SCORE = 1 0 ¯1
[5] WIN: ORC[1] ← ORC[1] - 1
[6]  →DRAW
[7] LOSE: HERO[1] ← HERO[1] - 1
[8]  →DRAW ⍝ Run as e.g. 12 3 FIGHTS 15 4

items.title: How Do I Get Some Money?
items.text: Contact George MacLeod, the BAA Projects Officer, at the address at the back of Vector and tell him what you have in mind. If it seems like the project is within the rules then a description of the project needs to be produced. The Projects Officer can assist with this. Once this is done the Projects Officer presents the description to the BAA Committee at its next meeting and usually approval is forthcoming.

items.title: Where’s the Catch?
items.text: There really is not a catch. A condition of the grant will be a description of the project for Vector and if it is appropriate a presentation at one of the BAA meetings. Sometimes it is possible to put part of the project in the public domain for the wider use of the APL community. Part of Ian Clark’s project was the production of a TrueType I-APL font which is now freely available for people who need an I-APL font for producing documents under Windows 3.1 and elsewhere.

items.title: Will this help me to my First Million?
items.text: It might, but the grants are not really intended to fund commercial ventures. However, it is possible that the BAA may act as lender of last resort, if the project is believed to be worth while, but other sources of funds are not available. Also the funds available are not enormous. A grant or a loan would be measured in hundreds or thousands of pounds, rather than tens of thousands.

items.title: APL2 Packages: a Cautionary Tale
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 100

From: Nicholas Small, 12 Dec 1992

The following cautionary tale, relating to the use of packaged workspaces in APL2, may cause readers some amusement.

On 3rd November I made some modifications to a workspace and saved it. A few days later one of my users came to me to complain that the date appearing on the printout produced by the program was incorrect, although the data were up to date. The date being printed was 3rd November.

A quick examination revealed that the date was put in the output from an object named TODAY — but this object was not a variable set by the program, rather, it was a function, and a packaged function at that. Examination of the listing for this function revealed all: function TODAY looks to see if a variable Today exists and if it does then the value of Today is returned; otherwise Today is set to the current date and that is the value returned. (I guess that it was written like that to facilitate the production of a report with a given date.) When I saved the modified workspace, the value of Today was saved with it. What I should have done next (see my article in Vector 7.2) was to )CLEAR, )COPY the workspace, reset the latent expression, name the workspace, then )SAVE again. Simple enough, I suppose, but easy to forget when one’s attention is distracted.

Nicholas Small

items.title: Manugistics Inc
items.text:
A lot of feverish activity has been happening at Manugistics over the past few months, mostly involved with preparing our latest version of APL*PLUS II. What started out as a small project grew rapidly into a major release as we saw the potential in our Windows support.

We started shipping Release 5 of APL*PLUS II early in December. The new release features an easy-to-use GUI Toolkit that makes building Windows applications an enjoyable task. The interface is much faster than Release 4 and your applications will run quickly and smoothly. New DDE tools include powerful sample functions to exchange data and instructions with EXCEL, Lotus 1-2-3 and Visual Basic. Functions to access the Common Windows Dialogs (like Open File Name and Choose Colour) are included.

Perhaps the most generally useful new feature is the fully integrated Debugger which is by far the most advanced APL debugging tool ever offered. It lets you step through your code primitive by primitive, literally watching your data change as it passes through the functions. The new Watchpoint feature lets you have the Debugger stop whenever a particular variable is referenced or modified, in a specific function, every so many iterations, and/or when a particular condition is met. Breakpoints can be set on lines and on statements within lines and execution can be recommenced from any stop point, even between two primitives.

For the DOS environment we have incorporated Rick Butterworth’s Graflib tools which make it easy to convert your data into line and bar charts, complete with titles, legends, gridlines, etc.

Among the other features you will find our new Install Program which will get you up and running on Version 5 in no time.

Now that Version 5 is out the door, we are turning our product hats to a new version of APL*PLUS/PC. Version 11, due out early next year, will include the Screen Interface Toolkit introduced in APL*PLUS II Version 4 and a Free Runtime .EXE Builder that will let you distribute your APL*PLUS/PC applications at NO COST.

In addition to the PC release, we will be working hard on Version 5 of the UNIX product. Watch this space for more information.

One of our major goals for 1993 is to bring APL to a much wider audience. Chris Lee has just finished touring Europe and the U.S. presenting to any current APLers. Next year the emphasis will be on taking the message to the (slightly larger) group of non-APLers out there. To start with, we will be presenting APL*PLUS at the Software Developer’s Conference in San Francisco in February. This will be attended by programmers who are currently using C, Pascal et al. We think that they deserve to see what array-oriented thinking can do to their productivity. We are also presenting a tutorial at the Application Developer’s SIG (SIGAPP) at the ACM’s annual conference in Indianapolis, Indiana. These two events will just be the start of a major campaign to broaden the market for APL.

Lastly we have just published our first Catalogue of Third Party Software. We are sending this out with all new software orders so you will get one when you get your next upgrade. If you have software you would like to see in the next catalogue, please contact us for more information.

Happy New Year!

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
Users of our APL.68000/X product for the IBM RISC System/6000 should all have received notice of the latest upgrade by now (to version 1.2). This upgrade has been triggered by the recent release of AIX 3.2 which has been a significant upgrade to AIX and appears to have fixed a number of bugs, some of which had been showing through into APL.68000/X. The ‘look and feel’ of Motif programs has also been improved. Our new version of APL.68000/X also includes an improved interface to routines written in ‘C’, BDF-format fonts for X-terminals and a number of minor bug fixes. The somewhat thorough nature of the AIX upgrade means that older versions of APL.68000/X must be upgraded to version 1.2 if you are upgrading AIX. As is our usual practice for most of our routine upgrades, we are not charging for this upgrade.

In what is planned as the first of a series of free seminars, we recently held a half-day seminar on ‘Trends in Workstation Technology’. This included an overview of the workstation market given by Richard Nabavi which looked at the various leading hardware platforms as well as the new generation of operating systems. We contrasted the various GUIs in use and assessed the significance of the RISC System/6000 in the workstation market. Readers of Vector who would like copies of the notes for this seminar should contact David Eastwood at MicroAPL.

We shall be starting 1993 with one or more seminars devoted to the new breed of GUI development tools that are now available and offering practical advice based on recent Windows projects we have undertaken. Again, contact David Eastwood for details.

items.title: Cocking & Drury Ltd
items.text:
By the time you read this we will have shipped upgrades to APL*PLUS II Version 5. This new version includes the APL Graphical User Interface Toolkit — a collection of object-oriented tools that make it easy to design and build Windows applications. There is also a complete interface to the core Windows system libraries, so you can reach beyond the APLGUI tools and use any of the hundreds of Windows library routines. The Windows interface is profoundly faster than in Version 4 thanks to a new virtual device driver. DDE utilities enable easy linking of APL*PLUS II with other Windows applications.

The DOS user is not forgotten however — the same package still allows the creation of DOS programs, and OS/2 users will now find APL*PLUS II running happily in an OS/2 DOS session. Other enhancements include the APL*PLUS II Debugger — a visual code debugger woven into the fabric of the interpreter. The GSS*CGI interface has been revised and is now supplemented by a new )PLOT command which provides high-quality line and bar charts in any workspace. And those of us who struggled somewhat with Version 4’s installation will be delighted to hear that an automatic installation routine is included which allows for the selection of components.

Manugistics are rightly pleased with the outcome of the effort they have put into this new version and we are co-operating with them in a special offer for existing users of APL*PLUS/PC, who may purchase copies of APL*PLUS II Version 5 at the discounted price of £700 plus VAT.

Anyone who missed the talk by Chris Burke of Strand Software, Canada, on the use of APL in actuarial work can obtain a free copy of the utility disk by calling us on 071-436-9481. Cocking & Drury now have available a range of tools to assist in the migration of APL2 mainframe workspaces to APL*PLUS II 386/486 — we have seen a number of companies reaching the decision to ‘down-size’ their APL use to networked PCs for greater flexibility (and considerable CPU savings!) and we have developed these tools in response to that need.

Levels of APL consultancy work and of APL training have remained fairly constant over the last 12 months. Our consultants are kept busy in other fields of endeavour and we have recently expanded into a new area of training which is proving to be very popular.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
Dyadic is pleased to announce the availability of Dyalog APL/W Version 6.3 for Microsoft Windows. This release contains a host of new features of which the following are a selection:

  • A new system function, ⎕NA, is included. This provides access to Windows Dynamic Link Library (DLL) routines. Using ⎕NA, you can call any DLL subroutine (16 and 32-bit) using familiar APL function syntax.
  • Full control over foreground and background colours in GUI objects.

  • Five new “graphical” objects, namely:

    POLY (lines, polygons, filled areas) MARKER (for marking a series of points) RECT (rectangles) ELLIPSE (ellipses, circles, arcs, pie-charts) TEXT (arbitrary graphical text)

    All the graphical objects allow you to draw several things at once (and with a single name). By default, APL handles repaint for you and automatically resizes your graphics when the user resizes a FORM. Graphical objects can even be dragged and dropped! A new GRAPHS workspace containing high-level “business graphics” functions is also provided.

  • New BITMAP, CURSOR and ICON objects which you can import from standard files or create from APL matrices.

  • Ability to associate bitmaps with BUTTONs and MENUITEMs, so that you can provide customised “toolbars” for your users. You can specify individual bitmaps for when a BUTTON is “out”, “in” and “inactive”, so that the appearance of the BUTTON changes instantly when it is pressed.
  • A new FILEBOX object which provides a standard Windows 3.1 File Selection dialog box.
  • Direct support for the printer via a new PRINTER object which provides for the output of device-independent text and graphics.
  • Clipboard support via a new CLIPBOARD object. This allows you to move data to and from the Windows Clipboard under program control. The CLIPBOARD object has a CHANGED event so that your application can react immediately when (for example) the user copies data to the Clipboard from Excel or from any other Windows application.
  • A new AUTOCONF property to simplify control over resize. An object can now optionally enable/disable automatic resize independently on both itself and on its children.
  • The coordinate system has been extended to provide user-definable coordinates and origin.
  • Improvements to the handling of CHANGED, GOT_FOCUS and LOST_FOCUS events to simplify validation etc.
  • A new general DATA property allows you to associate any APL array with an object. This reduces the need to use global variables to communicate between callback functions.
  • ⎕NQ has been extended to allow you to send a message to an object instantly, bypassing the normal queue. If there is one, the appropriate callback function is invoked at once. This extension permits an even more “object-oriented” approach to programming.

Version 6.3 completes the definition of the Dyalog APL GUI support, and will be the basis for the forthcoming OSF/Motif, OS/2 and Windows NT implementations. These versions of Dyalog APL will be 100% compatible with one another and with Dyalog APL/W for MS-Windows. This will permit true portability of APL applications between different GUIs and different hardware platforms.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
Happy New Year, and welcome once again to Education Vector. In this edition we have two substantial contributions from authors who have considerable experience in teaching with APL. I am grateful to them both for sharing their experiences with us.

Walter Spunde has been teaching I—APL programming to school children (I am informed that a “Grade 9er” approximately equates to Form Five in a British school), by developing computer fantasy games. His direct definition approach encourages good structure and allows initially very simple games to be developed into ever more complex strategies.

Howard Peelle uses APL to teach Mathematics, and his publications on APL will be well known to many of you. In this initial article, he describes the environment and equipment required, the design of introductory workshops and the constructivist teaching methods on which they are based. The actual teaching materials, of which he has a large variety, will be of interest to many readers, and a selection will be published in future editions of Education Vector.

I often have enquiries, especially from members of educational establishments, about low-cost APL interpreters. There are several to choose from, and each has advantages and disadvantages. I intend to publish a detailed comparison in the next edition, and will be pleased to hear from anyone who has experience (good or bad) that they would like to share with us. For now I offer the following list of products and sources:

  • I—APL (free). Enquiries: [address omitted].
  • TryAPL2 (free — specify disk size). IBM APL Development, M46/D12-278B Santa Teresa Lab, Box 49023, San Jose, CA 95161-9023 USA.

items.title: Note to Members on the Data Protection Act
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 9

from Nicholas Small

The information in Vector 8.4, and on recent Membership Application forms is incorrect — for which I must take the blame, as I was in full possession of the facts, but failed to match them up.

The British APL Association is not an unincorporated members club, because it is part of the British Computer Society (BCS). Hence the exemption referred to in the earlier note does not apply. On the other hand, the BCS has to register under the Data Protection Act, because of its various activities, and this registration extends to cover the activities of the British APL Association, for which purpose it is more than adequate.

This means in particular that, subject to the conditions laid down in the Act, we are permitted to process on a computer personal data relating to our members with or without their express consent.

items.title: BAA Chairman’s report - Activities
items.text:
It is with some regret that I must report Peter Donnelly’s resignation as Activities Officer of the BAA. Peter has served on the committee of the BAA for a number of years, notably as my predecessor as Chairman. As the current Chairman I can fully appreciate the time and effort Peter devoted to the BAA Committee and I would like to record our thanks for his many valuable contributions. Peter unfortunately feels unable to continue as Activities Officer due to pressure of work and has stepped down from the position with effect from February 1993. Pending the election of a new activities officer, I will be holding the fort myself.

In addition to finding a new Activities Officer, I am keen to enlarge the activities working group which supports our Activities Officer. I shall take this opportunity to describe the work that lies behind the activities programme of the BAA in order to stimulate the flow of willing volunteers.

Experience has shown that in many respects the most difficult part of the Activities Officer’s job is to come up with ideas for meetings — both for topics and speakers. The danger of having one person do all the work is that we are thereby limited in the range of topics covered. The prime role of the activities working group is to generate helpful suggestions about meetings and, if appropriate, to approach potential speakers. The current activities working group (comprising myself, Misha Jovanovic, Duncan Pearson and Anthony Camacho) have each arranged one meeting this year by agreeing a theme and finding the two or three speakers required.

At the time of writing, we have arranged the remainder of the 1993 programme and are now considering the 1994 programme. You should note that the committee of the BAA has no hard and fast views about the preferred format for meetings and we are prepared to consider any views on revisions to the number, location and duration of meetings. You will note, for example, that our November meeting will be a full day meeting rather than the usual afternoon meeting.

Once a programme of events has been established, the Activities Officer assumes responsibility for briefing the speaker on what is expected and ensuring that the speaker remembers the engagement. We also need to ensure that the correct audiovisual equipment is available on the day. The Activities Officer has to liaise with the Secretary over room bookings and the Publicity Officer to ensure that members are told about meetings.

If any members would like to help out with the pre-planning of meetings, I would be delighted to hear from them — the actual commitment in terms of time is not high, and is often not much more than an informal get-together after a regular BAA meeting and a few phone calls.

items.title: The 1993/4 BAA Committee
items.text:
The elections for next year’s committee will take place in time for the AGM on 11 June 1993. As in previous years, a number of current committee members have indicated that they are willing to continue in office. We are always keen to have as many nominations as possible for committee membership and this year we already have the prospect of at least one contested place.

I can confirm, therefore, that we will be having a postal ballot this year, so please send in lots more nominations!

The election timetable is:

10 May final date for nominations 17 May ballot papers posted 07 June voting closes 11 June results announced at the AGM

At the time of writing the following individuals have indicated their desire to stand for the Committee:

Chairman David Eastwood (*) Secretary Duncan Pearson Treasurer Nicholas Small (*) Journal Editor Anthony Camacho Activities — Education Alan Mayer (*) Technical Jonathan Barman Projects George Macleod (*) Publicity Misha Jovanovic (*) Recruitment Richard Weber AND Mark Harris

(*) — Holds this position in 1992/3

We would positively welcome further nominations, which must be proposed and seconded by current, paid-up members of the BAA. Candidates will be asked to provide me with a short statement for circulation with the voting papers.

We currently have two candidates for the post of Recruitment Officer: Richard Weber who teaches at Doncaster College of Further Education and currently helps on the Vector Working Group. Mark Harris runs Kestrel Consulting in partnership with Dick Bowman.

You will note that we are still looking for a nomination for activities officer and if anyone is contemplating standing for that (or any) post, they are welcome to contact me to discuss the work in more detail.

items.title: Announcing “The APL Review”
items.text:
A new and unique Journal for the International APL Community will be launched by the British APL Association in 1994. The APL Review will be fully refereed to the high standards required by the academic and research world, and edited by an international team of APL experts in a wide variety of fields.

Why a refereed journal? For many years now APL (and more recently J) has been employed by researchers who require more flexibility in their computing than is offered by other languages. For the result of their work to be added effectively to the accepted body of scientific knowledge two things are needed: (i) it must be “audited” (refereed) by their peers and (ii) it must be disseminated as widely as possible among those who may wish to use or add to the work. People who use APL professionally are well aware that they can learn a great deal from each other, even when their fields of study or application are very different. While an accountant is unlikely to read a software engineering journal, APLers in both disciplines will read an APL journal.

Why not Vector? A good question — Vector itself is one of the most widely read APL journals. But part of its appeal lies in its informal treatment of its subject matter. The more formal language and presentation of scientific “papers” sits awkwardly with the lighter tone of Vector, although many of the articles included in Vector over the years could have been presented as papers, and researchers have difficulty gaining credibility with peer review bodies when their articles are published in a journal alongside matter of a lighter nature. Vector will continue in its rôle, serving the whole of the APL community at all levels.

What about the annual International Conference proceedings? The APL Quote Quad volumes containing the papers presented at the annual conferences certainly play a vital rôle in disseminating the work of those who participate in the conferences, and we hope that they will continue to do so. Not everyone who works with APL can attend the conferences, however, and not all work can be presented in a paper of suitable length to be included in the proceedings. More extensive topics often have to be presented as tutorial sessions, and for academics in particular this does not satisfy the need to have their work fully refereed and published. It is right that we should bring our work to the conference and share our experiences in this invaluable way, but for many areas of study a short paper for the purposes of conference presentation does not do justice to the work.

What sort of subjects will be covered? Virtually any original, serious application of APL or J. We will be looking for statistics, econometrics, engineering, actuarial applications, simulation, operational research and so on — all the areas where the language can be used to promote research and insight. At the same time, it will provide a vehicle for discussion of theoretical aspects of the languages themselves.

Who will read The APL Review? Everyone interested in APL. The wide subject coverage should ensure that there is something for everyone. Although by its nature it is a “serious” journal, this does not mean that the subject matter should necessarily be dry or purely technical. Journals are about communication, and The APL Review will publish papers that communicate at a level that is accessible to a large readership.

items.title: Kestrel Consulting
items.text:
Kestrel Consulting combines the recruiting and entrepreneurial skills of Mark Harris (known to many British APL Association members from Kestrel Executive Selections) with the technical experience of Dick Bowman (former chairman of the British APL Association and presently a member of the ACM SIGAPL Executive Board).

Kestrel’s objectives are two-fold.

The recruitment side of the company will continue to concentrate on specialist recruitment and placement of both permanent and contract staff, not only in APL but also in other focussed markets. Our aim is for our recruitment and placement services to operate globally. At the present time we have a very high demand for APL contract staff for the USA, and an equal if not greater demand for contractors with SAP experience. We intend to provide the very highest possible levels of service both to the individuals and to the employers.

On the technical side we view the introduction of GUI systems as an excellent opportunity for APL to re-establish itself as the high-productivity solution of preference. Our technical consultants have worked on hardware from the IBM PC right through to the largest mainframes, with operating systems from MSDOS to MVS/TSO, with software from Multimate to DB2, and on applications from accounting to zymurgy.

One of the means by which we aim to increase the amount of effective use of APL is widespread adoption of standardised tools and utilities; an initial step along this path is the Kestrel Software Library which is currently collecting software. If you have any software related to APL which you’d like to see widely distributed please contact us. Our emphasis is on wide distribution of low cost software; we are collecting now and plan to begin distribution in mid-1993.

Whether your needs are temporary hiring of maintenance programmers, custom development using an entire project team, consultancy and training, or any aspect of APL-related computing, Kestrel Consulting is only a telephone call, fax or email message away.

items.title: Manugistics Inc
items.text:
Here at Manugistics we’ve just come back from the U.S. Software Developers Conference, held every year just outside San Francisco. Bill Gates and Philippe Kahn were there, showing off their latest labour-saving devices for Windows programmers. We were there too, introducing a lot of ‘C++’ and Visual Basic fans to the concept of Array Programming. Now that APL*PLUS works in Windows and talks to databases and other applications, we’re turning a lot of heads — some “I haven’t used APL for twenty years” folk, and quite a few “What is this APL stuff anyway?” types. It seems that even with all the promises (“Now you can build applications without writing a line of code!”), nobody else has a good solution to ad hoc problem-solving or complex data analysis. We are greatly encouraged by this state of affairs and will be pushing hard this year to open new doors and new minds to the power of APL.

Back in Rockville, we have just experienced a surge in sales as our year drew to a close at the end of February. APL*PLUS II Version 5.0 was so successful that we ran out of our (anticipated) six months of stock less than three months after we started shipping. The release of APL*PLUS/PC Version 11 was also responsible for a big boost as customers rushed to get their hands on the Runtime Binder so they can start sharing and selling their applications.

As you may be aware, the only way we could get APL*PLUS II Version 5.0 out to the public was to lock the developers in a closet. The trouble with developing for Windows is that every neat new thing you add makes you realize there are three other things that would make it really, really neat. When you stay up all night to sneak those three in, there are, you guessed it, nine more the next afternoon when you get up. Well, as we expected, the developers broke out of the closet fairly quickly and have been working hard to get Version 5.1 ready. The development work is now nearly done and we are having a great time building 3-D forms with icons and bitmaps and graphic buttons and drawing pictures and using the vastly improved Wed form design tool and... ...and you’ll have to wait for the rest. Actually, by the time you read this, we should be almost ready to start shipping!

In and around the work on Version 5.1, the team is working hard on preparing the next release of APL*PLUS II for UNIX. Version 5 will include the APL2 features we have put into the 386 product and the ]User Command Processor as well as a lot of improvements and speed-ups. Release is planned for the summer.

With 5.1 finished, our Windows team can concentrate its design and development efforts on our “third generation” APL*PLUS system, code-named INCA. This project is generating a great deal of discussion, white-board wizardry, project journal writing and feature prototyping, but is still a way away from “Now Appearing on a Hard Disk Near You.” As many of you will have heard or read, it will include Object-Oriented Extensions, Control Structures and an Alternative to Funny Characters. Stay tuned to this space for more details.

As you can see, we’re doing everything we can to keep APL alive and growing well into the next century. Help us (and yourselves) by introducing (or re-introducing) your friends and colleagues to the new generation of APL!

items.title: MicroAPL Ltd
items.text:
On the APL front, much of our development work is aimed at the summer. We have, however, now completed the Macintosh version of our MicroPLOT business graphics software — PLOTMAC. Our MicroPLOT software is designed to facilitate the quick and easy production of business graphics. In common with all our GUI APLs, APL.68000 for the Macintosh includes an interface to the native graphics facilities but up to now the user will have had to write his or her own scaling routines to produce sensible, labelled, graphs.

The Quickdraw colour graphics available on the Macintosh offers the typical primitive graphics routines that one expects as standard — line drawing; shape drawing; pattern selection; fill routines; graphics text and so on. The MicroPLOT routines allow an APL programmer to set up a labelled graph via cover functions for the Mac Quickdraw routines. The PLOTMAC code is compatible with our MicroPLOT software for other systems such as the RISC System/6000 or for plotting devices such as Hewlett Packard plotters.

Registered Mac users will have received separate notification about the PLOTMAC software, but further details are available from MicroAPL.

Much of our consultancy work in recent months has been involved with producing Windows applications and we have scheduled another free seminar for the end of April 1993 entitled ‘Developing Windows Applications’. This seminar is being jointly hosted by MicroAPL and Maddox Ford and will cover many of the practical problems encountered in designing and developing commercial Windows software.

In preparation for this seminar, we issued a GUI development questionnaire to our UK contacts. As you would imagine, the common factor that underlies our database is an interest in APL linked with a higher than usual number of non-PC owners (Mac, Atari, Amiga etc). Analysis of the results threw up some interesting statistics which we will be discussing in more detail at the seminar, but as a preview, it is worth noting a few of the findings. Bear in mind that multiple answers are quite possible, so numbers don’t add up to 100%

We asked people about their choice of GUI environment and came up with figures that seem to match the standard industry figures:

Windows 76% Unix 21% OS/2 10% Mac 6%

The most favoured database was Oracle with 21% followed by Informix (8%) and Sybase (6%). The most popular database server was Novell (32%), followed by Unix (28%) then OS/2 (15%).

We asked about GUI development tools in two categories — ‘low level’ (such as C) or ‘high level’ (such as SQL Windows). For low level tools, C++ led with 26%, followed by C with 19% (APL clocked up 6%). The most favoured ‘high level tool was Visual Basic (19%). There was an even spread of names for other high level tools and APL re-appeared here as a possible high-level tool. Only one version of APL was mentioned.

items.title: Dyadic Systems Ltd
items.text:
All registered Dyalog APL/W users should by now have received their (free) upgrades to Version 6.3. The reception to 6.3 during the Beta Test was extremely positive and judging from the efforts of some users commercial APL-based products — that are indistinguishable in terms of look and feel from other Windows applications — should soon begin to appear.

The new ⎕NA facility to call Windows DLL routines is proving to be exceptionally popular, not least because it is entirely dynamic and very fast. With ⎕NA, users have themselves been able to generate powerful and efficient interfaces to various other products including Oracle and Microsoft SQL Server. Insight Systems in Denmark is even using ⎕NA to provide a facility that will connect Dyalog APL/W users to practically any commercial database running on almost any host system — directly from a Windows workstation. Contact Morten Kromberg on +45-4210-7022 for details.

The device-independent graphics in Version 6.3 has also been well-received, as has the fact that you can at last produce APL listings on practically any printer with no effort at all. For this, Dyadic is grateful to Adrian Smith for allowing the distribution of his excellent TrueType APL font with Dyalog APL. The new version of WSDOC, which is included with 6.3, has a Windows front-end, and makes the production of attractive looking APL listings a very simple matter indeed.

To illustrate the powerful new bitmap-handling capabilities, Dyalog APL/W includes a version of the “Arachnid” card game (a form of Patience) which is coded entirely in APL. This game requires a certain amount of skill, and none of the beta-testers discovered the APL coding error that crashed the workspace when the game was successfully completed! On a reasonably fast PC, the APL workspace is practically identical in look and feel to a standard Windows card game, and it amply demonstrates that Dyalog APL/W can compete effectively with other GUI development tools. The new version of the WDESIGN workspace takes full advantage of the graphical facilities built in to the interpreter. New objects are created by clicking on a “Visual Basic look-alike” toolbar (in place of the buttons used in version 1), and the workspace now includes interactive facilities to design icons, cursors, bitmaps, and your own custom “toolbars”. WDESIGN supports all the new object types provided in Version 6.3, so you can also use graphics to add 3-D effects to your dialog boxes.

On the Unix front, Dyadic has produced new releases of Dyalog APL for the IBM RS/6000 (AIX 3.2) and for Sun Workstations (Solaris 2.1). The RS/6000 version is up to 10% faster than previous releases. Work on a Motif implementation, based on Dyalog APL/W, has begun in earnest.

Dyadic is pleased to announce the recruitment of Graeme Robertson, ex IPSA, who joins the team as an APL consultant. The company is also delighted to report its most successful year of trading since it was established in 1979.

items.title: Editorial
items.text:
Hello, and welcome to your “Spring” copy of Education Vector. This is written with a certain amount of sarcasm, as I gaze out over a wind-swept and rain-soaked Swansea. But I trust that by the time you read it Spring will indeed have come and the sun will be shining (you see, I am an eternal optimist at heart).

Last time, I promised you a detailed comparison of the low-cost (and in some cases free) APL interpreters. The article by Dick Holt in this edition, which has been circulated in various forms via various media, is an attempt at a “beginner’s guide”. It originates from the APLSIG of the Capital PC User Group, who invite everyone to circulate/republish it as widely as possible. As always, I shall be pleased to send copies of this edition and future editions of Education Vector to anyone who sends me their address.

While I am grateful for the work that has been done to make this comparison between interpreters, I feel that there is more that could be done, perhaps with contributions from our own readers. The report as it stands is largely aimed at business applications, which do not always share the requirements of educational establishments. For example, I-APL may be slower and offer less memory than its rivals, but the fact that it is available for a wide variety of machines, many of which are currently being used in our schools, makes it an attractive option for educational purposes.

For many, of course, the low-cost interpreters provide an easy path into the use of APL, whether for business, educational or other purposes. It is clearly part of our job to encourage this growth in the applications of APL. I should point out, however, that I have yet to find a low-cost interpreter that is a serious rival to those produced for professional purposes. For my own work I use Dyalog and APL*PLUS, and I have colleagues using APL.68000 and APL2 — none of us is about to give up the professional environment for a low-cost option. That having been said — I will be pleased to hear from anyone with contributions to make to the discussion, especially those who have used one or more of the packages in the educational environment.

The promised follow-up to Howard Peelle’s article on Workshop Design is a Sample Topic on “Triangular Numbers”. I find the method of presentation very instructive, and I hope it helps and encourages others to produce material of similar high standard.

Finally, all you APLers out there — drop me a line to tell me about your latest APL project. I am always looking for material that may be of interest to our readers. And if you are not already members, why not think about joining the British APL Association? If you do not have an application form, write to Rowena Small, [address omitted]. UK subscription is currently £12 (students £6).

We do depend on the alacrity of suppliers to keep us informed about their products so that we can update the Guide for each issue of VECTOR. Any suppliers who are not included in the Guide should contact me to get their free entry — see address below.

items.text: Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 8

items.title: Welcome: Conference Chair
items.text:
In the Spring of 1973, a conference called APL5 was held in Toronto at the Inn on the Park. The banquet was held at the Ontario Science Centre, and the guest speaker was Dr. Kenneth Iverson, the inventor of APL. Twenty years later, Toronto will again host an international APL conference. This time it will be held in the Medical Sciences Building of the University of Toronto, which is near the centre of the city.

I am delighted that Professor Leroy J. Dickey has volunteered to be the Program Chairman for the conference; he has provided a rich and varied formal program. Further, Bob Bernecky has volunteered to take responsibility for all the other program events which do not involve the formal delivery of papers. These include tutorials, workshops, panels, poster sessions, birds-of-a-feather sessions and an APL Art Gallery, all to round out and enrich the program. There will also be an exhibitor’s area which we expect will be well supported by vendors.

Toronto in August is a delightful place to be. It is a safe, walk-about city, with literally hundreds of activities within a short walk of the conference site, including sightseeing, shopping, dining and theater. Delegates are encouraged to bring their families, and a variety of activities will be available for accompanying persons. Toronto is easy to reach, having an international airport with direct flights from many European, American and Canadian cities. It is also within a day’s drive of Boston, New York, Washington, Pittsburgh, Cincinnati and Chicago.

I look forward to greeting you at the APL93 Conference in Toronto.

Larry Moore, Conference Chair

items.title: Program Chair
items.text:
Hello. I am pleased to report to you that the papers for this year’s conference are among the best that I have seen for any APL meeting in the last ten years. I find the range of topics particularly exciting, as I am sure you will too, when you browse through the attached list. I am impressed at the wide variety of applications to which APL has been put both in research and in production, in science, industry, business and academia. Not only are the applications of APL being developed, but the foundations of APL are being explored as well. There are new areas of research, and new linguistic features. Are these things just a flash in the pan, or are they elements that will join the mainstream of computing and be taken for granted in years to come? We leave that question for time to resolve, but we invite you to be a part of the fomentation and excitement now.

Come, attend the invited talks, attend the contributed papers, participate in a tutorial, participate in a workshop, bring a poster, bring some shareware, participate in a Birds of a Feather session, and have a good time. A friend of mine says that the best part of a conference is the people that one meets in the halls, outside of sessions. For me too, a high point of APL meetings, is the people that I meet.

Come to APL93, and let us meet and share ideas about APL.

Leroy J Dickey, Program Chair

items.title: Tutorials Chair
items.text:
Welcome to Toronto! APL93 represents a dramatic improvement over previous conferences — we have encouraged a varied and plentiful selection of tutorials, fully integrated with the remainder of the technical program, to enhance your educational opportunities while in Toronto. We have rethought a number of other conference activities, including posters sessions, the APL art gallery, the APL software exchange, Birds-of-a-Feather sessions, with an eye toward enriching your experience here, by changing their focus to be of greater benefit to attendees and to perform outreach to the community beyond that of the APL community.

Do you feel that tutorials at APL conferences are somehow peripheral to the main program? Have you ever been frustrated by short presentations of research papers, in which time constraints prevent The Really Interesting Questions from being answered. Do you want to have the time to actually learn how some of these new gadgets work?

APL93 has turned that whole idea on its head, by making tutorials a well-integrated part of the conference, open to all attendees. Yes, there is the ever-present hazard of coming away from APL93 knowing more than you did when you arrived, but I know you’ll get accustomed to it and enjoy it!

The tutorial program for APL93 offers a wider selection of topics than any previous APL conference, and registration for two half-day tutorials is included with your pre-registration fee. We are making attendance at tutorials possible at very low cost, because we want to make education an integral part of the conference program.

Robert Bernecky, Tutorials Chair

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:
Many tutorials this year will be hands-on, with each attendee sitting at her or his own PC or SUN workstation, provided by the University of Toronto Department of Computer Science. Subjects (and speakers) will be:

  • Teaching Calculus — Kenneth E. Iverson
  • An Introduction to J — Donald McIntyre
  • Image Processing in APL — Manuela Schäfer, Dinu Scheppelmann
  • APL for Actuaries — Richard L. Vaughan
  • 3D-Visualization of Medical Images in APL — Pitt Meinzer
  • AGSS: A Graphical Statistical System — Peter A.W. Lewis
  • An Introduction to Parallel Computing — Robert Bernecky
  • Mathematica for APLers — Richard J. Gaylord
  • An Introduction to APL — Ben Best
  • Windows GUI Programming in APL — Eric Iverson
  • Wicked Problems and APL — Chris Lee

Please be advised that registration at specific tutorials will be opened to non-registrants on a space-available basis on the day of the tutorial. I believe that such outreach is an important activity, particularly when APL has a vital role to play in the emerging area of massively parallel computing.

Therefore, to avoid disappointment because of Standing Room Only crowds, please be sure to register for your tutorials at the time of pre-registration. Otherwise, you may be left out, due to lack of space. In particular, hands-on tutorial space is limited by machine availability. Pre-registration will let us find appropriate venues for the tutorials so that you won’t be left out or sitting on the stairs.

The registration form allows you to specify alternate choices for each tutorial timeslot, in case the tutorial you prefer is fully booked. Also, you’ll save money, because early pre-registration offers you two free tutorials, whereas you only get one if you register late.

Most of the tutorials will be offered on Sunday, August 15th and again during the conference, for the convenience of conference delegates. I am very grateful to those presenters who have volunteered to take on this extra workload!

Robert Bernecky, Chair of Tutorials

items.title: The Triumph of Symbols over Words
items.text:
Professor Donald McIntyre

Professor Donald McIntyre illustrates highlights in 5,000 years of evolving notation. Ideas, once expressed in rhetorical form, are increasingly represented by symbols. Early forms of symbolism were often subsequently modified or replaced. The new symbolism of Iverson and Hui’s J language provides a reason for reflecting on this history

Donald McIntyre is a retired Professor of Geology who has been using computers and teaching computer programming for over 30 years. He has been an invited speaker at many APL Conferences, and was a Distinguished Lecturer for ACM from 1985-1990. He has given workshops on J in London and in many cities in the United States and Canada. He contributed one of two papers on J included in the IBM System Journal’s special issue marking the 25th Anniversary of APL. His 70th birthday will coincide with his Sunday presentation of this tutorial.

items.title: Modelling Petroleum Chemistry in the Era of Clean Fuels
items.text:
Dr. Stephen B. Jaffe

Today’s environmental issues require the Oil Industry to make a product of specific chemical composition and specific physical properties. To meet these new targets, petroleum refiners and planners must turn to mathematical models for guidance. The challenge for these models is to follow the chemistry of thousands of molecular species through hundreds of thousands of chemical reactions. A new approach called Structure Oriented Lumping (SOL) has been developed which represents petroleum molecules as collections of structural increments. Models using SOL are capable of predicting far more detail than ever before.

APL plays a crucial role in every aspect of Structure Oriented Lumping. Experimental data is organized, reduced, and analyzed with APL. Reaction networks are generated using a rule-based approach for specifying the appropriate chemistry with APL. Finally, FORTRAN code is automatically generated by APL to integrate the pertinent differential equations. This novel solution of a major problem is a direct consequence of our long-time familiarity and use of APL.

Stephen B. Jaffe has been an active APLer for more than twenty years. He has authored many papers on APL, served on the ACM SIGAPL Board, has organized APL conferences, and taught APL. Dr. Jaffe is a Senior Research Consultant at Mobil Research and Development in Paulsboro, New Jersey.

items.title: APL — New Release
items.text:
Transcribed from the printed issue; not yet reviewed. Read it in the PDF of the issue, page 80

reviewed by Jon Sandles

This new release of APL comes in a plain white sleeve and although there is no documentation available, I do not believe it will ever be commercially available. Believe it or not I first heard of this on the television. Well how does it shape up against its competitors? … all the standard features are there. A full heady riff is developed slowly and steadily with a nod and a wink to past masters of this genre. The pulsating beat never lets up and by the end you are left drained of all emotion. Of all APL releases this well could be the first to break the top 40. Criticisms of the 12" disk format (I could not find any commercially available 12" drives for PC’s) will abound, and the black vinyl format is rumoured to be obsolete. That aside Manugistics, Dyalog, MicroAPL et al could learn a lot by the fulsome groove. I also wonder — where did they get that silly name.

The influences are worn proudly, from Joy Division to the KLF with snatches of old — Floyd, Genesis and even Tangerine Dream. Will these people get better? — I hope so because few records these days sound as fresh as this. (Note: as usual with APL products the release date of this record has been put back — it is on the Beyond label and the track is called ‘the calling’.)
